# Toyota 4Runner (1984–present)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/

The 4Runner started life in 1983 as a Hilux pickup with a removable fibreglass top, sold in the US from the 1984½ model year. It has been body-on-frame ever since, through six generations, which in this segment makes it something close to a living fossil — and that is exactly why people buy it. The pickup DNA faded generation by generation: a steel body in 1989, an all-new Prado-shared chassis with coils all round for 1996, Prado 120 underpinnings and an optional V8 for 2003, then the J150 platform it shared with the Lexus GX and FJ Cruiser for a marathon 2010–2024 run. The sixth generation, revealed in April 2024, moved to the TNGA-F frame shared with the Tacoma and swapped the long-serving V6 for turbo and hybrid fours. For hands-on owners the appeal is simple: Toyota durability, a huge shared aftermarket with Tacoma and Prado cousins, and forums with a DIY write-up for nearly every bolt. The third generation is the cult favourite, but every generation has its own following — and its own list of things to check before you hand over cash.

Verdict: Toyota's mid-size body-on-frame survivor — forty years of refusing to become a crossover while everything around it did.

## Toyota 4Runner 1st Gen (1984–1989)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/1st-gen/
Codes: N60

Verdict: A Hilux pickup with a removable fibreglass hat, a four-cylinder that refuses to die and — for 1984–85 only — a solid front axle. Slow, rusty, uncomfortable and utterly charming, which is exactly why the prices went up.

The first 4Runner was less designed than improvised: take Toyota's redesigned 1984 Hilux 4x4 pickup, give the bed a fibreglass lid and a back seat (sometimes), and ship it to America. It went on sale in the US in May 1984 as a 1984½ model — two doors, a four-cylinder, a five-speed and, for its first two seasons, a solid front axle on leaf springs. Four decades on it is the 4Runner people call 'pure', and the one Hagerty says can't be ignored now that clean examples keep getting more expensive.

### A PICKUP WITH A HAT
Toyota had already seen the idea work. Between 1981 and 1983 Winnebago and Toyota turned short-bed Hilux 4x4s into the Trekker — a fibreglass-lined bed, an extra seat and a fibreglass top — and Curbside Classic counts only around 1,500 of them. The factory version arrived as the Hilux Surf in Japan in October 1983 and as the 4Runner in North America a few months later, just as the FJ40 Land Cruiser left the US market and the small-SUV class filled up with the S-10 Blazer, Bronco II and Jeep Cherokee.
Hagerty describes the details that make owners grin: a rear roof held on by 14 bolts, a standard rear roll bar, and a power rear window that drops into the tailgate. SR5s added an altimeter and inclinometer on the dash, a rear seat, strobe-stripe graphics and chrome wheels; the base DX often came without a rear seat at all, and Toyota never fitted rear shoulder belts.

### ENGINES, AND THE AXLE ARGUMENT
The 1984½ trucks used the carburetted 2.4-litre 22R making 96 hp, paired only with a five-speed. Fuel injection arrived for 1985 as the 22R-E — Wikipedia lists 116 hp — and 1986 brought the 135 hp 22R-TE turbo, mostly sold with the automatic in SR5s and far rarer than the plain 22R-E. For 1988 the 3.0-litre 3VZ-E V6 joined the range, rated at 145–150 hp depending on the source. Hagerty's verdict on the whole run: 0–60 times improved 'from months to weeks to about 12 seconds'.
The bigger change came underneath. For 1986 the solid front axle was replaced by independent front suspension with a three-inch-wider track, which made the truck calmer on the road and, by most accounts, a little less heroic off it. That split defines the generation today: 1984–85 trucks are the solid-axle purist's choice, while 1986–89 trucks ride better and share their front end with the second generation. Both keep a leaf-sprung rear axle that Wikipedia notes was never upgraded for the extra weight of the seats and top — so sagging is normal.

### WHY IT MATTERS NOW
In its own time the N60 was a slow starter: US sales were 6,498 in 1984 and dipped below 4,000 in 1987, before jumping to 20,880 in 1988 and 36,927 in calendar 1989 (a figure that includes the first 2nd gens). Today the story has flipped. Hagerty reported average values of $8,400 in #3 condition, $13,700 in #2 and $21,100 in #1, with Bring a Trailer sales of a 100,000-mile 1984 SR5 at $19,250, and found that millennials and Gen-Xers made up a far larger share of 4Runner insurance quotes than of the market overall.
The Autopian's David Tracy goes further, naming the 1985 — fuel-injected, solid-axled, convertible-topped and under 3,500 lb — his perfect 4Runner. The catch is survival. Open tops let water in, floors and quarter panels are not reproduced, and Hagerty notes that original seats and upholstery are close to unobtainable. Mechanically, though, the 22R-family engines are among the easiest Toyota ever built, and LC Engineering still runs a whole 1984–1989 4Runner catalogue.

### THE AFTERMATH
For 1990 Toyota replaced it with a four-door, fixed-roof second generation that kept the independent front end and swapped the rear leafs for coils. The removable top never returned, and by the third generation the pickup-with-a-lid idea had vanished entirely. The first gen became something else: the cheap, simple base for solid-axle swaps, V8 conversions and camper builds — Expedition Portal's classifieds once listed a 1985 SR5 on Old Man Emu springs with a FlipPac pop-up roof for $8,000. Nobody is building them that way from new any more, which is rather the point.

### Data plate

- Years: 1984½–1989 (US model years)
- Body: Two-door, removable fibreglass top
- Engines: 22R / 22R-E / 22R-TE 2.4 I4 · 3VZ-E 3.0 V6
- Output (1987 Sr5): 116 hp @ 4,800 · 140 lb-ft @ 2,800
- Transmission: 5-spd manual / 4-spd auto
- Front: Solid axle 1984–85 · IFS 1986–89
- Rear: Leaf-sprung live axle
- Ground Clearance: 7.7 in at diff (1987 SR5)
- Cargo: 81 cu ft (1987 SR5)
- Price New: $14,548 (1987 SR5)
- Us Sales Peak: 36,927 (calendar 1989, incl. early 2nd gens)

### Engineering
Mechanically the N60 is a Toyota Hilux 4x4 pickup, nearly part-for-part. That means a ladder frame, a leaf-sprung live rear axle, a part-time transfer case and an engine bay designed for the simple 22R family. The interesting choices are the 1984–85 solid front axle with manual locking hubs, the switch to torsion-bar independent front suspension for 1986, and a removable fibreglass rear roof.
- Chassis: Hilux 4x4 ladder frame (Nearly mechanically identical to the 1984-on Hilux pickup.)
- Front: Solid axle → IFS (Leaf-sprung solid axle with manual hubs 1984–85; torsion-bar IFS with a 3 in wider track from 1986.)
- Rear: Leaf-sprung live axle (Hotchkiss drive; springs weren't uprated for the seats and top, so they sag.)
- Engine: 22R-E 2.4 I4 (Carburetted 22R in 1984; EFI from 1985; turbo 22R-TE from 1986; 3VZ-E V6 from 1988.)
- 4Wd: Part-time, two-speed (Manual locking hubs; automatic hubs added to SR5s for 1988.)
- Body: Two-door, removable top (Fibreglass rear roof held by 14 bolts, standard roll bar, power tailgate glass.)

### Versions
- 1984½ · N60 · solid axle · 22R 2.4 I4 (carb) · 96 hp · Five-speed manual only. DX or SR5.
- 1985 · N60 · solid axle · 22R-E 2.4 I4 (EFI) · 116 hp · Fuel injection arrives; the last solid-axle year.
- 1986–1989 · N60 · IFS · 22R-E 2.4 I4 · 116 hp / 140 lb-ft · IFS with 3 in wider track; two-segment grille from 1986.
- 1986–1987 · N60 · IFS · 22R-TE 2.4 turbo I4 · 135 hp · Mostly automatic SR5s; much rarer than the 22R-E.
- 1988–1989 · N60 · IFS · 3VZ-E 3.0 V6 · 145–150 hp · Optional V6; auto hubs on SR5s. Sales take off.

### Year-by-year
- 1984½: US sales start May 1984: two doors, removable fibreglass top, carbureted 22R, five-speed, solid front axle; base DX has no rear seat
- 1985: Fuel-injected 22R-E (116 hp) arrives; rear seat available on all trims. Last year of the solid front axle, which Hagerty says purists still seek out; an Expedition Portal member rates carbureted trucks less desirable [buy]
- 1986: Hi-Trac independent front suspension replaces the solid axle, track 3 in wider; 22R-TE turbo (135 hp) added
- 1987: No changes
- 1988: 3.0 3VZ-E V6 (145 hp) replaces the turbo on SR5; SR5 gets automatic locking hubs
- 1988–89 (V6): 3.0 3VZ-E V6 trucks: a Hagerty expert says most enthusiasts avoid the six and choose the four, and the 3VZ-E's head-gasket history starts here [avoid]
- 1989: Minor cosmetic and option changes before the 1990 replacement

### Capability
- Curb weight: 3,520–3,760 lb (1,597–1,706 kg)
- Fuel economy: EPA 17 mpg city (22R-TE) (14.5 mpg observed in period testing)

### Wheels and tires
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 31x10.50R15 (Toyota-4Runner.org owners run 31s with no lift and no regear; 33x12.50s rub the front valance, wheel-well corners and rear pinch weld)
- Biggest tire, ≈1.5–2 in lift: 33x12.50R15 (IH8MUD: 'about an inch and a half' of lift plus hammering the pinch weld/valance; a narrower 33x10.50 rubs less. Owners call stock gearing 'a dog' on 33s)

### Buying checks
- Rust, everywhere: Forum owners point to the frame ahead of the rear spring perches, the rear quarters and wheel wells, the left rear near the exhaust exit, and, on sunroof-equipped trucks, A-pillars that owners say rotted from blocked drains. Hagerty warns that floors and quarter panels aren't reproduced, so a rusty body is a fabrication job, not a parts order.
- Know which axle you're buying: 1984–85 trucks have the solid front axle; 1986–89 have IFS. Solid-axle trucks carry a price premium and some sellers stretch the truth, so look underneath: leaf springs and manual hubs up front mean solid axle; torsion bars and CV axles mean IFS.
- 22R-E timing chain guides: The plastic timing-chain guides are a known breakage item — LC Engineering makes metal-backed replacements specifically for it. A cold-start rattle from the front of the engine, or no record of the job, means budget for chain, guides and tensioner.
- V6 head gaskets: The 1988–89 3VZ-E shares the V6's head-gasket reputation. Toyota's October 1996 policy adjustment (1988–94 V6 trucks) is long expired and the later V06 campaign only covered 1/90–10/94 builds, so check for coolant loss, overheating history and white exhaust, and ask for paperwork on any head work.
- Sagging rear and tired suspension: Rear leafs sag on nearly all of them. Feathered front tyres can mean worn front-end parts or a bad alignment; on IFS trucks check idler arm and tie-rod play.
- Top, glass and seals: Removable tops and ageing seals leak; a tarp over the roof in the ad is a clue. Check the power tailgate window works — IH8MUD members flag it as a weak point on both early generations.
- Interior parts: Carpets can be found, but Hagerty says reproduction seats and upholstery generally can't, and owners say good seats are especially scarce. An intact original interior is worth paying for.
- Rear seats and belts: Many 1984–86 base trucks came without a rear seat, and Toyota never fitted rear shoulder belts. If you plan to carry kids, factor that in.

### Common repairs
#### 22R-E timing chain, guides and tensioner
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Most of a weekend for a first-timer · cost Metal-backed guides ≈ $64 (LC Engineering), plus chain, tensioner and gaskets
Symptoms: Rattle or slap from the timing cover at start-up, broken guide pieces in the oil pan, or simply no record that it's ever been done.
Fix: Drain coolant, remove the fan, radiator and accessories, then the timing cover. Fit the new guides positioned toward the outside of the block without tightening, install the crank gear, then the cam gear and chain with the bright link on top. Tighten the straight guide to 9 ft-lb, install the tensioner (also 9 ft-lb), position the curved guide toward the outside so the tensioner is mostly retracted, torque everything and refit the cam gear (per LC Engineering's instructions). Reassemble with a new cover gasket set.
Tools: Metric sockets · torque wrench · gasket scraper · LCE metal-backed guides (single row, 1985–95) · timing chain · tensioner · timing cover gasket set

#### 3VZ-E head gaskets (1988–89 V6)
Difficulty 5 / 5 · time Several days; heads usually go to a machine shop · cost MLS head gasket set ≈ $116 (LC Engineering), plus machining and a timing belt kit
Symptoms: Coolant loss with no visible leak, white exhaust after warm-up, overheating, misfires — 4Runners.com members say cylinder 6 is the usual victim.
Fix: This is an engine-out-of-the-car level job in all but name: drain fluids, strip the intake and exhaust crossover, remove the timing belt and cams, pull both heads and have them checked flat. Fit MLS gaskets (they need a very smooth deck finish), new head bolts or studs, and do the timing belt, water pump and thermostat while it's apart. Many owners add an exhaust crossover delete to reduce heat at the back of the engine.
Tools: Full metric socket set · torque wrench · cam/crank pulley tools · LCE MLS head gasket set · 3VZ OE head bolt set (88–95) · 3VZ timing belt kit (1988–92)

#### Rear leaf spring replacement
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Rear sitting low or level with the front, bottoming out over bumps, cracked or flattened leaves.
Fix: Support the frame on stands and take the weight off the axle with a jack. Remove the shocks' lower mounts, the U-bolts and spring plate, then the shackle and front hanger bolts. Swap in new springs (LC Engineering sells 1984–89 4Runner sets at +2, +3 and +4 in) with new bushings, refit the U-bolts and torque everything with the truck back on its wheels so the bushings aren't preloaded.
Tools: Floor jack · stands · breaker bar · penetrating oil · new U-bolts · LCE 1984–89 4Runner rear leaf spring set

#### IFS idler arm and steering slop (1986–89)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Parts plus labor; a Total Chaos 'Caddy' idler arm costs more than a stock one
Symptoms: Wander on the highway, play at the wheel, a clunk over bumps, especially on bigger tyres.
Fix: With the front supported, check for play at the idler arm, tie-rod ends and pitman arm. To replace the idler arm, separate the centre link from it with a puller, unbolt it from the frame and fit the new one, then re-torque and get an alignment. IH8MUD members recommend a stronger idler arm or brace on any IFS truck that sees off-road use.
Tools: Pitman/tie-rod puller · torque wrench · Total Chaos Caddy idler arm 95130 (1986–95 4Runner) or OEM-type arm

#### Solid-axle front end refresh (1984–85)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A weekend · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Grease or gear oil weeping from the knuckles, wheel bearing play, clicking from worn birfields on tight turns in 4WD.
Fix: Pull the hubs, spindles and birfield axles, clean and inspect the joints, then replace wheel bearings and seals and rebuild the knuckles (trunnion bearings and wiper seals). Repack with fresh grease and set bearing preload on reassembly. Trail-Gear's Classic front lift kit for 1979–85 solid-axle trucks bundles a knuckle rebuild kit and wheel bearing kits for exactly this reason.
Tools: Hub socket · slide hammer · snap-ring pliers · knuckle rebuild kit · wheel bearing kits · Longfield or RCV axle upgrades if you're running bigger tyres

#### Sunroof drain and leak control
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time A quick job · cost Next to nothing — until it rots an A-pillar
Symptoms: On sunroof-equipped trucks: wet headliner or carpets, rust bubbling at the base of the A-pillars, a musty cab.
Fix: Owners report blocked sunroof drains rusting out A-pillars on trucks fitted with a sunroof. Clear the drain tubes with trimmer line or low-pressure air, check the outlets aren't crushed, and replace hardened top and window seals. Treat any surface rust in the pillars before it goes through.
Tools: Trimmer line · low-pressure air · rust converter · new seals

#### Swap failing auto hubs for manual hubs
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon, including a bearing repack · cost Aisin manual hubs ≈ $249 a set (1986–95 IFS) or ≈ $415 a pair (1979–85 solid axle), plus a ≈ $28 conversion kit (LC Engineering)
Symptoms: Front hubs that won't lock, slip under load or let go in reverse. 4Runners.com notes the auto hubs fitted to some 1984–89 4Runners are less reliable than manual hubs and will sometimes unlock in reverse.
Fix: Confirm you have auto hubs (no dial to turn on the hub cap). Remove the auto hub assemblies and the auto-hub hardware on the spindle. Fit LC Engineering's conversion kit: the locking nuts and plates that hold the hub and rotor on the spindle once the auto-hub parts are gone. Repack the wheel bearings and set the preload to the factory manual while it's apart, then fit the manual hubs on new gaskets. Solid-axle (1984–85) and IFS (1986–89) hubs have different spline counts, so order the right ones.
Tools: Sockets · spindle-nut socket · snap-ring pliers · torque wrench · wheel-bearing grease and new seals

#### Power tailgate window that sticks or drops
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Parts plus labor; one Toyota-4Runner.org member recommends a used motor
Symptoms: The roll-down rear glass works only some of the time, stalls part-way or suddenly drops into the tailgate. IH8MUD members flag the electric rear window as a weak point on both early generations; Toyota-4Runner.org owners trace it to tired motors, regulator gears and drag in the channels.
Fix: Pull the tailgate's inner access panels. Run the glass up and down and check it stays in its tracks, then push and twist the regulator to see whether its gears stay meshed. If the regulator is sound, test the motor directly on a battery, then check the relay. Clean the channels and put silicone spray on the glass edges and rubber seals; one owner says a dealer clean-and-lube cured his. Toyota-4Runner.org members describe the motors as easily overwhelmed by drag, and one says 1st and 2nd gen motors are the same apart from the connector plug. If the glass has dropped and broken before, check the regulator was actually fixed, not just the glass.
Tools: Trim-panel tools · screwdrivers · 12 V jumper leads · multimeter · silicone spray

### Baseline service
Assume nothing on a 35-plus-year-old truck: baseline every fluid, filter and wear item the day you buy it, then keep records. Factory capacities and fluid grades for the N60 aren't reliably published online. Figures marked AMSOIL come from AMSOIL's application guide for the 1987 22R-E, and plug data from Denso's catalogue; check those and anything still marked below against the owner's or factory service manual, and know which hubs and axle you have before ordering parts.
- Engine oil & filter: 22R-E: 10W-30, 10W-40 or 10W-50 above −23 °C (15W-40 to 20W-50 above −12 °C) · ≈4.5 US qt with filter (AMSOIL, 1987 22R-E) · 3VZ-E V6 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase, then per the manual (Watch for a 22R-E burning oil at high mileage; leaks often come from the valve cover gasket.)
- Air filter: Panel filter · At purchase; more often on dusty trails (Check the airbox seals and intake boot for cracks while it's open.)
- Fuel filter (EFI trucks): EFI in-line filter · At purchase if no record (On the 22R-E it sits below the intake manifold. 4Runners.com owners pull the driver's front wheel for access, mind the flow arrow, and fit new crush washers.)
- Spark plugs, wires, cap & rotor: 22R-E: Denso W16EXR-U, gap 0.8 mm (0.031 in) (Denso catalogue, 22R-E 4Runner from 08/87) · earlier trucks and 3VZ-E V6 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (Old ignition parts cause most rough-running complaints on distributor-ignition 22R-Es and 3VZ-Es.)
- Timing chain & guides (22R-E): Single-row chain; metal-backed guides recommended · Inspect at purchase; replace if noisy or undocumented (Plastic guides are a known breakage item; broken pieces end up in the oil pan.)
- Timing belt & water pump (3VZ-E V6, 1988–89): Belt, tensioner, idlers, water pump · A 4Runners.com member recalls 4 years / 96,000 km (≈60,000 mi) as typical (Do it immediately if there are no records; owners recommend an Aisin-quality kit.)
- Coolant: Toyota-type long-life coolant · 22R-E ≈9 US qt (AMSOIL, 1987 22R-E) · V6 capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Drain and refill at purchase (4Runners.com owners: use a coolant that meets the manual's spec ('Asian formula for Toyota'); Toyota pink is pre-diluted red. Never let either engine overheat — especially the V6.)
- Manual / automatic transmission fluid: Manual: GL-4 or GL-5 gear oil, 75W-90 or 80W-90 (AMSOIL, 1987 22R-E) · capacity and automatic fluid [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (drain and refill) (Automatic trucks: check for burnt-smelling fluid before you buy.)
- Transfer case & differentials: Transfer case (manual-gearbox trucks): GL-4 or GL-5 gear oil, ≈3.4 pt (AMSOIL, 1987 22R-E) · differential grades and capacities [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (Break the fill plug loose before the drain plug. 1984–85 solid-axle trucks also have closed knuckles that need fresh grease or oil.)
- Front wheel bearings & hubs: Clean, inspect, repack, set preload · At purchase (1984–89 trucks came with manual or automatic hubs; 4Runners.com owners say the auto hubs are less reliable and often get swapped for manual ones.)
- Brake fluid: Type [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush at purchase (No ABS on these trucks — fresh fluid and healthy rubber lines matter all the more.)
- Steering & front-end wear (IFS trucks): Idler arm, tie-rods, pitman arm · Inspect at purchase (Idler-arm slop is the classic cause of wander on 1986–95 IFS Toyotas.)
- Rear spring bushings & U-bolts: Leaf-spring bushings · Inspect at purchase (Sagging rear leafs are near-universal; replace bushings when you replace springs.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: Owners' consensus is 31x10.50R15 — Toyota-4Runner.org members say 31s fit with no lift and you can get away without regearing. 33x12.50s on a stock truck rub the front valance, wheel-well corners and rear pinch weld; IH8MUD owners estimate about 1.5 in of lift (plus some trimming) for 33s, and say the 22R-E will want lower gears.

Q: Which years have the solid front axle?
A: 1984 and 1985. Toyota switched to independent front suspension with a three-inch-wider track for 1986, so 1986–89 trucks are IFS. Solid-axle trucks are the off-roader's favourite; IFS trucks ride better on the road.

Q: 22R-E or V6?
A: Most enthusiasts prefer the 22R-E four-cylinder — Hagerty says so, and Expedition Portal members advise skipping the V6. The 3.0 V6 (1988–89) has more power but carries the 3VZ-E's head-gasket reputation and is harder to work on; the 22R-E is slow but famously simple.

Q: Can I take the roof off?
A: Yes. The rear fibreglass top is held on by 14 bolts, and a rear roll bar was standard. Owners note the open-top experience mostly benefits rear passengers — and that ageing tops are a common leak point.

Q: Was there a diesel 4Runner?
A: Not in the US. Diesel engines were offered in Hilux pickups, but Wikipedia records that no diesel 4Runners were imported to the US.

Q: What about the turbo?
A: The 22R-TE turbo four arrived for 1986 with 135 hp, mostly paired with the four-speed automatic in SR5s. It's much rarer than the 22R-E, and LC Engineering still sells dedicated 22R-TE short blocks and turbo parts.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: Not much. Wikipedia records an EPA city rating of 17 mpg for the 22R-TE turbo truck and 14.5 mpg in period testing; Trail4Runner quotes 19 city / 23 highway for a stock four-cylinder, which looks optimistic. Expect less with bigger tyres, a lift or a tired engine.

Q: Is a 1988–89 V6 covered by Toyota's head gasket campaign?
A: Not any more. An October 1996 Special Policy Adjustment extended head-gasket coverage for 1988–1994 V6 trucks; the later V06 campaign covered 1/90–10/94 production and expired on 24 September 2018. Today a blown 3VZ-E head gasket is on you.

Q: What's a first gen worth?
A: Hagerty's write-up on rising 1984–89 values gave averages of $8,400 (#3 Good), $13,700 (#2 Excellent) and $21,100 (#1 Concours), and cited Bring a Trailer sales of $19,250 for a 100,000-mile 1984 SR5 and $17,500 for a 168,000-mile 1986 SR5. Expedition Portal members reckoned a maintained 22R-E truck under about 170,000 miles could still be found for under $5,000.

Q: Should I solid-axle swap an IFS truck?
A: IH8MUD members are split. Some say the 1986–95 Toyota IFS is 'pretty stout' unless you rock-crawl hard; others who broke IFS shafts say to 'spend the money on a SAS and never look back'. Kits for 1979–85-style solid axles, long-travel IFS and stronger axles are all still sold.

Q: Can I still get parts?
A: Mechanical parts, yes — the 22R family is shared with Toyota pickups and LC Engineering runs a dedicated 1984–1989 4Runner catalogue. Body panels, floors and interior trim are the hard part; Hagerty notes reproduction seats and floors generally don't exist.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: For a trail truck, a 1985: it's the last year of the solid front axle that Hagerty says purists still seek out, and it gets the fuel-injected 22R-E — an Expedition Portal member rates carbureted trucks less desirable. For a daily driver, several of the same forum's members point to a 1986–89 IFS truck with the 22R-E and a manual. Skip the 1988–89 V6: Hagerty's expert says most enthusiasts avoid it in favour of the four. Rust decides more than the model year does.

## Toyota 4Runner 2nd Gen (1990–1995)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/2nd-gen/
Codes: N120, N130

Verdict: The middle child: four doors, a steel roof and coil springs out back, but still a Hilux where it counts. Overshadowed by the cult 3rd gen, haunted by the V6's head gaskets — and quietly one of the cheapest ways into an old-school Toyota.

For 1990 the 4Runner grew up a little. The removable fibreglass top went, a one-piece steel body with rear doors arrived, and the rear leaf springs were swapped for coils on a four-link axle. Underneath, though, it was still a Hilux pickup — the same independent front end, the same 22R-E four and 3.0-litre V6. Car and Driver records that the four-door quickly became the volume seller, and US sales passed 74,000 in calendar 1994. Today it's the generation people skip on the way to the 3rd gen, which is exactly why it's worth a look.

### DOORS, A ROOF, AND COILS
The second generation was released in 1989 for the 1990 model year, built at Toyota's Tahara plant in Japan. Wikipedia notes that most were four-doors; a two-door was built only from 1989 to May 1993, with US sales ending in August 1992 and Canada carrying on through 1993. The first gen's leaf-sprung rear gave way to a four-link solid axle with a Panhard rod and coil springs — better riding, though Wikipedia notes it was also prone to sagging. The torsion-bar independent front suspension carried over from 1986.
Two engines were offered in the US. The 2.4-litre 22R-E four made 116 hp and 139 lb-ft; the 3.0-litre 3VZ-E V6 made 150 hp and 180 lb-ft. Gearboxes were a five-speed manual or the four-speed A340H automatic. One detail matters to anyone building one: Wikipedia records that the gear-driven transfer case was phased out on V6 models in favour of a chain-driven unit, while the four-cylinders kept the gear drive. Car and Driver's test V6 took 15.7 seconds to reach 60 mph.

### UPDATES, SAFETY AND A V6 WITH A REPUTATION
The 1992 model year facelift, introduced in 1991, brought one-piece front bumpers, modular headlamps in place of sealed beams, and a new interior pattern. Rear-wheel ABS was standard on the SR5 V6 from 1990 with four-wheel ABS optional, and side-impact beams were added for 1994 and 1995 after criticism of the early doors. Crash performance was still of its era: Wikipedia lists a one-to-two-star frontal rating for the driver.
Then there's the 3VZ-E. Toyota extended head-gasket warranty coverage on 1988–1994 V6 trucks in October 1996 and later ran Special Service Campaign V06, replacing head gaskets on 1/90–10/94 production 'regardless of leakage or not'. That campaign expired in September 2018. Forum theory blames the exhaust crossover pipe cooking the back of the engine — cylinder 6 is the usual casualty — and owners still swear by cooling-system maintenance and crossover deletes to keep them alive.

### THE MIDDLE CHILD
Toyota replaced it for 1996 with the third generation, built on the Land Cruiser Prado chassis with coils all round and an optional rear locker — and the N120/N130 slid into obscurity. 4Runners.com members complain that trim and body parts are now harder to find than for both the 3rd gen and, oddly, the 1st gen. Mechanically it's another story: the front end, 22R-E and much of the drivetrain are shared with Toyota's 1986–95 pickups, so suspension, armour and engine parts are still plentiful.
That makes the 2nd gen the bargain of the old-4Runner world, if you can find a straight one. ToyTec, Old Man Emu, Total Chaos and Coastal Offroad all still make parts for it, and Japan's Hilux Surf twin offered diesels that America never got — the roughly 130 hp 1KZ-TE turbodiesel among them — which the US 25-year import rule now makes fair game. Just budget for rust repair and a head-gasket job, and you'll have the most underrated 4Runner on the trail.

### Data plate
- Chassis: N120 / N130 (Hilux-based)
- Years: 1990–1995 (US model years)
- Body: Four-door; two-door to 1992 (US)
- Engines: 22R-E 2.4 I4 / 3VZ-E 3.0 V6
- Output (V6): 150 hp · 180 lb-ft
- Output (I4): 116 hp · 139 lb-ft
- Transmission: 5-spd manual / 4-spd A340H auto
- Front: Torsion-bar IFS
- Rear: Four-link solid axle, coils, Panhard rod
- 0–60 Mph: 15.7 s (V6, Car and Driver)
- Epa City: 15 mpg (V6 auto)
- Us Sales Peak: 75,962 (calendar 1995, incl. early 3rd gens)

### Engineering
The N120/N130 is a halfway house between pickup and SUV. The frame, independent front suspension and engines come straight from Toyota's 1986–95 pickups, but the steel four-door body and coil-sprung four-link rear axle were new. Rear-wheel ABS and a chain-driven transfer case on V6 models show where Toyota was heading; the open differentials (a limited-slip was only offered in Japan and Europe) show where it wasn't yet.
- Chassis: Hilux-based ladder frame (Still mechanically a Toyota pickup underneath; four-door steel body (two-door to 1992 in the US).)
- Front: Torsion-bar IFS (Carried over from the 1986–89 trucks; shared with 1986–95 Toyota pickups.)
- Rear: Four-link solid axle on coils (Panhard rod located; replaced the 1st gen's leaf springs. Also prone to sagging.)
- Engine: 3VZ-E 3.0 V6 (150 hp / 180 lb-ft, timing belt; 22R-E 2.4 four (116 hp / 139 lb-ft) also offered.)
- Transfer Case: Chain (V6) / gear (I4) (Gear-driven case phased out on V6 models; four-cylinders kept it.)
- Brakes: Rear-wheel ABS (Standard on SR5 V6 from 1990; four-wheel ABS optional.)

### Versions
- 1990–1995 · N120/N130 · 4-door · 22R-E 2.4 I4 · 116 hp / 139 lb-ft · Five-speed manual or A340H auto; gear-driven transfer case.
- 1990–1995 · N120/N130 · 4-door · 3VZ-E 3.0 V6 · 150 hp / 180 lb-ft · Chain-driven transfer case; head gaskets covered by the (now expired) V06 campaign for 1/90–10/94 builds.
- 1990–1992 (US) · N120/N130 · 2-door · 22R-E / 3VZ-E · As above · US sales ended Aug 1992; Canada to 1993. Priced higher due to the chicken tax.
- 1992–1995 · Facelift · 22R-E / 3VZ-E · As above · One-piece bumpers, modular headlamps; side-impact beams added for 1994–95.
- N130 era · Japan · Hilux Surf · 1KZ-TE 3.0 turbodiesel I4 · ≈130 hp · Japan-market; 2L-TE and 3L diesels also offered. Importable under the US 25-year rule.

### Year-by-year
- 1990: All-new steel body on the Hilux frame; coil-sprung four-link rear axle; 22R-E or 3VZ-E; rear-wheel ABS standard on SR5 V6
- 1990–94: V6 trucks built 1/90–10/94: Toyota said its 3VZ-E head-gasket failures were primarily limited to this production window (campaign V06, expired 2018). Ask for proof of the gasket job [avoid]
- 1992: Facelift: one-piece front bumper, modular headlamps, new interior trim; US two-door sales end August 1992
- 1993: Two-door production ends May 1993; Japan's Hilux Surf gains the 1KZ-TE 3.0 turbo-diesel (August)
- 1994: Side-impact door beams added for the US
- 1995: Final year; keeps door beams. V6 trucks built after October 1994 fall outside the V06 campaign window. Replaced by the Prado-based 1996 4Runner

### Capability
- Towing: 3,500 lb (1,590 kg)
- Curb weight: 3,760 lb (1,705 kg)
- Fuel economy: EPA 15 mpg city (V6 automatic) (14.3 mpg observed in period testing)

### Wheels and tires
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 31x10.50R15 (IH8MUD and Toyota-4Runner.org agree 31s fit with no lift or regear)
- Biggest tire, Stock (squeeze) lift: 33x10.50R15 (Possible with pounding/trimming; expect rubbing at the valance and rear pinch weld)
- Biggest tire, ≈1.5–2 in lift: 33x10.50R15 / 33x12.50R15 ('About an inch and a half' of lift is the usual recommendation for 33s; narrower 10.50s rub less than 12.50s)

### Buying checks
- Head-gasket history (V6): Ask for paperwork. Forum owners report that trucks repaired under the V06 campaign got a label on the left front door hinge post near the check strap. Otherwise look for coolant loss, overheating, white exhaust after warm-up or a misfire on cylinder 6.
- Timing belt on the 3VZ-E: The V6 is belt-driven. A 4Runners.com member recalls four years or 96,000 km as the typical interval; owners recommend an Aisin kit with the water pump. No records means do it now.
- Frame and body rust: Check frame rails and crossmembers, the tailgate bottom, rear bumper and wheel arches. A rust-free body and frame is rare outside dry states, and replacement panels are hard to find.
- Sagging rear coils: The four-link rear was new, but Wikipedia notes it sags too. A nose-high stance usually means tired springs; Old Man Emu sells 2 in replacement coils in two rates for these trucks.
- Power rear window and tailgate: The roll-down rear glass and tailgate lock are known trouble spots — IH8MUD members say the electric rear window 'can be problematic' on both early generations. Make sure it goes up and down.
- Four-cylinder or V6?: The 22R-E is slower but simpler and has no head-gasket campaign behind it; the 3VZ-E has more torque but more to go wrong. A four with a gear-driven transfer case is the stronger base for big gearing changes.
- Front-end wear: On the IFS, check idler arm, tie-rod ends and CV boots, and look for a wandering steering feel on the test drive.
- Trim and interior parts: Mechanical parts are easy; interior and exterior trim isn't. 4Runners.com members report even dealers struggle to supply 2nd gen trim, so a complete truck is worth more than a cheap one missing bits.

### Common repairs
#### 3VZ-E head gaskets
Difficulty 5 / 5 · time Several days; heads usually go to a machine shop · cost MLS head gasket set ≈ $116 (LC Engineering), plus machining and a timing belt kit
Symptoms: Coolant disappearing with no external leak, white exhaust, overheating, cylinder 6 misfire. 4Runners.com members call blown gaskets almost inevitable on an un-repaired 3VZ-E.
Fix: Drain coolant and oil, remove the intake plenum, exhaust crossover and timing belt, then the cams and both heads. Have the heads checked for flatness and resurfaced if needed — MLS gaskets want a very smooth deck finish. Refit with new gaskets and head bolts or studs, and replace the timing belt, water pump and thermostat at the same time. Use OEM or reputable Aisin/Denso parts, as owners advise.
Tools: Full metric socket set · torque wrench · cam pulley holder · LCE MLS head gasket set or MLS head gasket & stud kit (3VZ) · 3VZ timing belt kit

#### 3VZ-E timing belt and water pump
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A full day for most · cost Timing belt kit plus water pump; parts plus labor
Symptoms: Unknown history, a cracked or glazed belt, a weeping water pump. A snapped belt leaves you stranded.
Fix: Drain coolant, remove the fan, shroud and drive belts, then the crank pulley and timing covers. Set the engine to TDC and mark the belt and pulleys. Replace the belt, tensioner (and spring), idler and water pump, confirm the timing marks after two full turns of the crank, then reassemble and bleed the cooling system. Forum members suggest Aisin parts over bargain kits.
Tools: Crank pulley holder and puller · torque wrench · paint marker · LCE timing belt kit (3VZ 1988–92 or 93–95) · water pump · thermostat

#### Exhaust crossover delete (V6)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time An afternoon, plus exhaust shop time · cost Kit plus exhaust fabrication
Symptoms: Not a failure so much as prevention: the crossover pipe that runs behind the engine puts heat into the back of the heads, which 4Runners.com members link to cylinder 6 head-gasket failures.
Fix: Remove the factory crossover pipe and blank off or re-route the rear manifold so both banks exit separately or join further back. Yota1's 1988–95 3VZ crossover delete kit supplies the manifold-side parts, but the kit doesn't include the pipe — additional exhaust work is required.
Tools: Penetrating oil · stud extractors · new gaskets and nuts · Yota1 3VZ 3.0 exhaust crossover delete kit

#### Rear coil spring replacement
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost OME 2 in coils ≈ $240 per pair (LC Engineering)
Symptoms: Rear sitting low, bottoming out loaded, a nose-high stance.
Fix: Support the frame on stands, remove the rear wheels and support the axle with a jack. Disconnect the shocks at the lower mounts and make sure brake lines and ABS wiring have slack, then lower the axle until the coils come free. Swap in new springs (OME sells 2 in coils rated for 180 lb or, HD, 330 lb of constant load), raise the axle, refit the shocks and torque with the truck on its wheels.
Tools: Floor jack · stands · breaker bar · OME 2 in rear coils (1990–95 4Runner) · OME 10 mm coil spacer if needed

#### 22R-E timing chain and guides
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Most of a weekend for a first-timer · cost Metal-backed guides ≈ $64 (LC Engineering), plus chain, tensioner and gaskets
Symptoms: A rattle from the front of the engine on start-up, or broken guide pieces in the oil pan.
Fix: Remove the timing cover, fit new guides positioned toward the outside of the block, install the crank and cam gears with the chain's bright link on top, tighten the straight guide and tensioner bolts to 9 ft-lb, set the curved guide so the tensioner is mostly retracted, then torque and reassemble with a new gasket set (per LC Engineering's instructions).
Tools: Metric sockets · torque wrench · LCE metal-backed guides (1985–95) · chain · tensioner · timing cover gasket set

#### Idler arm and front-end slop
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Wandering on the highway, play in the steering, clunks over bumps — worse on bigger tyres.
Fix: With the front supported, check the idler arm, tie-rod ends and pitman arm for play. Separate the centre link from the idler arm with a puller, unbolt the arm from the frame and fit a new one, then torque and align. Off-roaders often upgrade to a heavier-duty arm or brace.
Tools: Tie-rod puller · torque wrench · Total Chaos Caddy idler arm 95130 (1986–95 4Runner) or OEM-type arm

#### Power tailgate window that sticks or drops
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Parts plus labor; one Toyota-4Runner.org member recommends a used motor
Symptoms: The roll-down rear glass works only some of the time, stalls part-way or suddenly drops into the tailgate. IH8MUD members flag the electric rear window as a weak point on both early generations; on 2nd gens Toyota-4Runner.org owners blame weak motors, slipping regulator gears and dirty channels.
Fix: Pull the tailgate's inner access panels. Run the glass up and down and check it stays in its tracks, then push and twist the regulator to see whether its gears stay meshed. If the regulator is sound, test the motor directly on a battery, then check the relay. Clean the channels and put silicone spray on the glass edges and rubber seals; one owner says a dealer clean-and-lube cured his. Toyota-4Runner.org members describe the motors as easily overwhelmed by drag, and one says 1st and 2nd gen motors are the same apart from the connector plug. If the glass has dropped and broken before, check the regulator was actually fixed, not just the glass.
Tools: Trim-panel tools · screwdrivers · 12 V jumper leads · multimeter · silicone spray

#### 4WD won't engage: the ADD vacuum system
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An hour or two to diagnose · cost Parts plus labor; vacuum hose is cheap, Aisin manual hubs ≈ $249 a set (LC Engineering) if you convert
Symptoms: The lever goes into 4H with no noise and no front drive. On ADD trucks the hubs are locked all the time and the front axle is only connected when a vacuum-operated collar in the driver's-side axle tube moves (4Runners.com).
Fix: Confirm you have ADD: plastic hub caps instead of locking-hub dials (IH8MUD). Drop the front skid plate and check the two vacuum lines at the actuator on the front differential, which can get knocked loose. Then trace them to the electrically switched vacuum valves on the inner fender and check the valves and their wiring. Plugging or swapping the lines to force the actuator tells you whether the diff side works. If you'd rather lose the system, 4Runners.com members lock it out or delete it with a pre-1990 driver's-side axle tube and fit manual hubs. LC Engineering notes that ADD trucks don't need its auto-hub conversion kit for that swap.
Tools: Hand vacuum pump with gauge · test light or multimeter · sockets for the skid plate

### Baseline service
Most surviving 2nd gens have 30 years of deferred maintenance, so baseline everything. On a V6, treat cooling-system health as life-or-death for the head gaskets. Factory capacities for the N120/N130 aren't reliably published online. Figures marked AMSOIL come from AMSOIL's application guide for the 1992 3VZ-E, and plug data from Denso's catalogue; check those and anything still marked below against the owner's or factory service manual.
- Engine oil & filter: 3VZ-E: 10W-30 above −18 °C, 5W-30 below 10 °C · ≈4.8 US qt with filter (AMSOIL, 1992 3VZ-E) · 22R-E [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase, then per the manual (Milky oil or a sweet smell on the dipstick on a 3VZ-E means head gaskets — walk away or budget for it.)
- Air filter: Panel filter · At purchase (Check the intake boot between airflow meter and throttle body for cracks — a common source of unmetered air.)
- Fuel filter: EFI in-line filter · At purchase if no record (On 22R-E trucks it's below the intake manifold; owners pull the driver's front wheel and watch the flow direction.)
- Spark plugs, wires, cap & rotor: 22R-E: Denso W16EXR-U · 3VZ-E: Denso K16R-U · gap 0.8 mm (0.031 in) for both (Denso catalogue) · At purchase (Wire sets differ by year on both engines — match the terminal style on your cap.)
- Timing belt, tensioner & water pump (3VZ-E): Belt kit + water pump + thermostat · A 4Runners.com member recalls 4 years / 96,000 km (≈60,000 mi) as typical (No records = do it now. Owners favour Aisin parts over bargain kits.)
- Timing chain & guides (22R-E): Metal-backed guides recommended · Inspect at purchase (Listen for slap from the timing cover at cold start.)
- Coolant & cooling system: Toyota-type long-life coolant · 3VZ-E 4WD ≈9.5 US qt (AMSOIL, 1992 3VZ-E) · 22R-E capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Drain/refill or flush at purchase, then keep it fresh (4Runners.com's 3VZ-E advice: never let it overheat, refresh coolant regularly, and keep up with the belt and water pump. Pressure-test the system if coolant level drops.)
- Automatic transmission fluid (A340H): Fluid type and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Drain and refill at purchase (Prefer repeated drain-and-fills over a pressure flush on a high-mileage unknown.)
- Transfer case: Manual-gearbox trucks: GL-4 or GL-5 gear oil, ≈2.3 pt (with ADD) / 3.4 pt (without); A340H automatics take ATF, ≈1.7 pt (AMSOIL, 1992 3VZ-E) · viscosity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (V6 trucks have a chain-driven case; four-cylinders kept the gear-driven unit — confirm which you have before ordering parts.)
- Front & rear differentials, ADD: Front (ADD): GL-5 hypoid, SAE 90 above −18 °C, 80W-90 or 80W below, ≈4 pt (AMSOIL, 1992 3VZ-E) · rear [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (1990-on 4Runners use Toyota's vacuum-operated ADD (automatic differential disconnect) with locked hubs; per 4Runners.com, check that 4WD actually engages and the vacuum lines are intact.)
- Front wheel bearings & seals: Clean, repack, set preload · At purchase (Any hum or play on the test drive means do it now.)
- Brake fluid: Type [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush at purchase (SR5 V6s have rear-wheel ABS; bleed per the factory procedure.)
- Steering & front end: Idler arm, tie-rods, CV boots · Inspect at purchase (Idler-arm wear is the usual cause of highway wander.)
- Rear coil springs & shocks: Coils + shocks · Inspect at purchase (Most have sagged; Old Man Emu 2 in coils come in 180 lb and 330 lb (HD) constant-load rates.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: 31s — IH8MUD members call 31s the right size for a stock 2nd gen, and Toyota-4Runner.org owners agree 31x10.50R15 fits without a lift or regear. A narrow 33x10.50R15 can be squeezed in with some pounding and trimming, but expect rubbing at the valance and pinch weld; about 1.5 in of lift is the usual recommendation for 33s.

Q: Was my V6 covered by Toyota's head-gasket campaign?
A: Special Service Campaign V06 covered 3VZ-E trucks, 4Runners and T100s built from 1/90 to 10/94, replacing head gaskets regardless of whether they leaked. Forum owners report completed trucks got a label on the left front door hinge post. The campaign expired on 24 September 2018, so any repair now is at your cost.

Q: 22R-E or 3VZ-E?
A: The V6 makes 150 hp and 180 lb-ft against the four's 116 hp and 139 lb-ft, which matters in a heavier four-door. The 22R-E is simpler, more durable and outside the head-gasket saga. Owners generally say a maintained 3VZ-E is fine — but it must never overheat.

Q: Were there two-door 2nd gens?
A: Yes, built from 1989 to May 1993. US sales ended in August 1992 and Canada continued through 1993. They cost more than the four-door because of the US chicken tax, so they're rare.

Q: How often does the timing belt need doing?
A: A 4Runners.com member recalls four years or 96,000 km (about 60,000 miles) as the typical interval for the 3VZ-E. Do the water pump at the same time and use a quality kit.

Q: What fuel economy does it get?
A: Not much. Wikipedia lists an EPA city rating of 15 mpg for the V6 with the four-speed automatic, with observed testing at 14.28 mpg. Bigger tyres and a lift make it worse.

Q: Does it have ABS or a locker?
A: Rear-wheel ABS was standard on the SR5 V6 from 1990 and four-wheel ABS was optional. There was no factory locker in the US — differentials were open, with a limited-slip only offered in Japan and Europe. Aftermarket lockers are the usual fix.

Q: What lift options are there?
A: The common recipe is a 2 in lift: ToyTec sells a kit with rear coils for 1990–95 4Runners, Old Man Emu sells 2 in rear coils in standard and HD rates, and ball-joint spacers or torsion-bar adjustment lift the front. Total Chaos makes long-travel IFS kits for 1986–95 trucks if you want more.

Q: Should I do a solid-axle swap?
A: Only if you need it. IH8MUD members describe the 1986–95 Toyota IFS as 'pretty stout' unless you rock-crawl hard; those who break IFS shafts tend to go solid axle. Long-travel IFS and SAS conversions can cost similar money.

Q: Can I get a diesel one?
A: Not from a US dealer — US trucks were 22R-E or 3VZ-E only. Japan's Hilux Surf offered the 2L-TE, 3L and 1KZ-TE diesels, and every 2nd gen is now old enough for the US 25-year import exemption.

Q: How safe is it?
A: By modern standards, not very. Wikipedia lists a one-to-two-star frontal crash rating for the driver; side-impact door beams were only added for the 1994 and 1995 model years.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: No year is a consensus pick, so buy the truck, not the date. Toyota's own V06 campaign paperwork says the 3VZ-E head-gasket failures were primarily limited to trucks built from January 1990 to October 1994, so a V6 built after that — or one with receipts for the gasket job — is the safer bet, and the 22R-E four sidesteps the issue entirely. Autotrader names no best year either, noting only that 1994 added side-impact door beams.

## Toyota 4Runner 3rd Gen (1996–2002)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/3rd-gen/
Codes: N180, 5VZ-FE, 3RZ-FE

Verdict: The 4Runner that finally stopped being a pickup with a roof and became a proper SUV — without going soft. Small, simple, stupidly durable, and now priced like everyone figured that out at once.

For its first twelve years the 4Runner was, essentially, a Hilux pickup wearing a hat. The third generation, launched in late 1995 as a 1996 model, was the moment Toyota stopped bolting a lid onto a truck bed and built the thing as an SUV from the frame up. It got coil springs at all four corners, rack-and-pinion steering, a chassis shared with the Land Cruiser Prado (J90) and, for the first time on a 4Runner, an optional electric rear locker. Nearly three decades later it is the generation trail people lower their voices about — and the one sellers have noticed.

### THE BREAK FROM THE HILUX
The first 4Runner arrived in 1983 as a Hilux with a removable fibreglass top; the second generation swapped that for a one-piece steel body but still rode on the pickup's bones. The N180 cut the cord. Wikipedia records an all-new body and chassis shared with the J90 Prado, a wheelbase 2.3 inches longer than before, coils all round, rack-and-pinion steering and dual airbags. MotorWeek's 1996 test noted towing jumping from 3,500 to 5,000 lb, and the 3.4-litre V6 rising to 183 hp and 217 lb-ft from the old 3.0's 150 hp.
It was not expensive, either. MotorWeek priced a two-wheel-drive four-cylinder base model at $19,908 and the 4WD SR5 V6 most people actually wanted at $25,568. Under the hood sat two engines borrowed from the brand-new Tacoma: the 150 hp 2.7-litre 3RZ-FE four and the 5VZ-FE V6. Gearboxes were a five-speed manual or four-speed automatic, and two-wheel drive was standard — so plenty of the 3rd gens for sale are not the trail trucks they look like. Check the badge, then check underneath.

### FACELIFT, MULTI-MODE AND THE LOST LOCKER
The 1999 refresh brought a new nose with revised bumper and headlights, a reorganised centre stack and — the bit that matters — an optional Multi-Mode transfer case that could run full-time 4WD on slippery roads. Wikipedia records the rest: a 'fat lip' bumper that lengthened the front crush zone, multi-parabola headlamps, a new instrument panel with a digital odometer, and colour-keyed bumpers, flares and running boards on the Limited and the Highlander, a trim later renamed Sport Edition. The rear E-locker stayed on the options list.
Then came 2001. The final two years made VSC stability control standard, fitted the Multi-Mode transfer case (with its lockable centre differential) to every 4WD truck and added brake-based traction control — but, as Wikipedia and HotCars both record, they lost the optional rear E-locker that had been available from 1996 to 2000. The manual had already gone for 2000 and the four-cylinder followed for 2001, leaving a V6-automatic-only line-up. For a lot of buyers that makes the 1999–2000 Limited or SR5 with a locker the sweet spot, while purists still argue for the simpler pre-facelift trucks.

### WHY THE TRAIL CROWD WORSHIPS IT
The electric rear locker was the headline. Wikipedia notes Toyota had offered an electric rear locker on the US Land Cruiser since 1993 — the 80 Series was the big brother in showrooms at the time — and the 3rd gen was the first 4Runner to get one. Combine that with a compact footprint, decent ground clearance and a 105.3-inch wheelbase, and you have a truck that fits trails a full-size SUV has to winch around.
Then there is the 5VZ-FE. It is not fast — MotorWeek clocked 9.5 seconds to 60 — but it is the sort of engine owners talk about in hundreds of thousands of miles. 8020 Automotive calls it non-interference, so a snapped timing belt usually means a tow rather than a rebuild, and SlashGear notes the 3rd gen consistently ranked among the SUVs most likely to pass 250,000 miles. Because it shares so much with the first-generation Tacoma, the aftermarket for suspension, armour and parts is enormous.

### THE AFTERMATH
Production ended in August 2002 and the fourth generation reached US showrooms that October as a 2003 model, built on the bigger Prado 120 platform that also underpins the Lexus GX 470. It brought a V8 and more comfort, and a lot more mass. The N180, meanwhile, slid into the used market and became the default answer to 'what cheap 4x4 should I build?' — right up until it stopped being cheap. Its shared DNA with the first-generation Tacoma kept parts plentiful long after the dealer stopped caring.
Today the clean ones are collector items in all but name: Yahoo Autos reports unmodified examples under 100,000 miles mostly trading in the mid-to-upper $20,000s. The rest are rolling restoration projects held together by forum knowledge — lower ball joints, rear axle seals, frame rust and timing belts are the usual list. None of it is exotic, all of it is documented, and that, more than any spec sheet, is why the 3rd gen refuses to die.

### Data plate
- Chassis: N180 (Prado J90-based)
- Years: 1996–2002 (US model years)
- Engine: 5VZ-FE 3.4 V6 / 3RZ-FE 2.7 I4
- Output (V6): 183 hp @ 4,800 · 217 lb-ft @ 3,600
- Transmission: 5-spd manual (to 1999) / 4-spd auto
- 4Wd: Part-time; Multi-Mode from 1999
- Locker: Rear electric, optional 1996–2000
- Wheelbase: 105.3 in
- Length: 183.3 in (2002 SR5)
- Curb Weight: 3,616–3,902 lb (Wikipedia; Auto Channel lists 4,245 lb for a 2002 SR5 4x4)
- Towing: 5,000 lb
- Fuel Tank: 18.5 gal

### Engineering
Underneath, the N180 is old-school Toyota done properly: a ladder frame shared with the J90 Prado, double-wishbone independent front suspension, a solid coil-sprung rear axle, and Tacoma-derived engines tuned for longevity rather than lap times. The clever bits are in the drivetrain — an optional electric rear locker in the early years, and the Multi-Mode transfer case that arrived with the 1999 facelift.
- Chassis: Ladder frame (Shared with the Land Cruiser Prado J90; 105.3 in wheelbase.)
- Front: Double-wishbone IFS (Coil springs and rack-and-pinion steering, both new to the 4Runner.)
- Rear: Solid axle on coils (Coil springs all round gave a better ride than you'd expect from a body-on-frame truck.)
- Engine: 5VZ-FE 3.4 V6 (183 hp / 217 lb-ft, DOHC 24-valve, timing belt; a 2.7 3RZ-FE four was also offered.)
- 4Wd: Part-time → Multi-Mode (Part-time case at launch (lever, with a pushbutton for H4 on Limiteds); Multi-Mode with lockable centre diff optional from 1999 and standard on 4WD for 2001–02.)
- Locker: Electric rear (opt.) (Factory option on 4WD trucks 1996–2000; dropped for 2001–02 in favour of VSC/TRAC.)

### Versions
- 1996–2000 · N180 · 2WD/4WD · 3RZ-FE 2.7 I4 · 150 hp / 177 lb-ft · Base engine; five-speed manual (dropped for 2000) or four-speed auto. Four-cylinder gone after 2000 in North America.
- 1996–1998 · N180 · pre-facelift · 5VZ-FE 3.4 V6 · 183 hp / 217 lb-ft · Lever part-time 4WD; rear E-locker optional on 4WD.
- 1999–2000 · N180 · facelift · 5VZ-FE 3.4 V6 · 183 hp / 217 lb-ft · New nose and dash; Multi-Mode t-case optional; E-locker still offered. Highlander ('99) and Sport Edition ('00) trims.
- 2001–2002 · N180 · late · 5VZ-FE 3.4 V6 · 183 hp / 217 lb-ft · Auto only; VSC and traction control standard, Multi-Mode standard on 4WD. No rear locker.
- N180 era · Japan · Hilux Surf KZN185 · 1KZ-TE 3.0 turbodiesel I4 · ≈130 hp · Japan-market only; intercooled version (≈140 hp) from July 1996. Importable to the US under the 25-year rule.

### Year-by-year
- 1996: All-new Prado-based chassis: coils all round, rack-and-pinion, dual airbags, 3RZ-FE four or 5VZ-FE V6, optional rear e-locker
- 1997: Minor updates, colour-keyed cargo cover
- 1998: New switch panels and four-spoke steering wheel with redesigned airbag
- 1999: Facelift ('fat lip' bumper, multi-parabola headlights), new dash; optional Multi-Mode transfer case. IH8MUD regulars rate 1999–2000 the best years, a '99 with the E-locker above all [buy]
- 2000: Manual gearbox dropped (last manual 4Runner); rear e-locker still optional. The other half of the forum-favourite 1999–2000 pair [buy]
- 2001: Four-cylinder dropped; VSC and Multi-Mode standard on 4WD; rear e-locker replaced by traction control
- 2002: Chrome liftgate trim; final year

### Capability
- Towing: 5,000 lb (2,270 kg) (V6)
- Fuel tank: 18.5 gal (70 L)
- Ground clearance: 8.5 in (216 mm)
- Curb weight: 3,616–3,902 lb (1,640–1,770 kg)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 225/75R15 (base), 265/70R16
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Offset: +15 mm (stock 7 in wheels)
- Center Bore: 106.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M12x1.5
- Lug Torque: 83 lb-ft (110 N·m) per Toyota's 1999–2002 owner's manuals
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 265/75R16 (Toyota-4Runner.org consensus (about 31.6 in); wide aggressive treads or spacers can rub at full compression)
- Biggest tire, ≈2 in lift: 285/75R16 (One owner reports no rub on 16x8 wheels with 4.5 in backspacing and about 2 in of front lift (not yet wheeled))
- Biggest tire, 3 in lift: 285/75R16 (Common 33-in setup; expect to fold the pinch weld and trim the fender liner, and keep backspacing around 4–4.5 in. Spacers make it worse)

### Buying checks
- Frame rust, properly: Crawl under it. Forum members flag the crossmember-to-frame welds, the rear lower control arm mounts, the triangular trailing-arm brackets, the area behind the axle where the spare hangs, and the rocker ends. Probe with a screwdriver: a hole or two is fixable, a frame thin from end to end is not.
- Lower ball joints: The stock LBJ is the 3rd gen's famous weak link — if it lets go the control arm drops and the wheel folds under. 2001–02 trucks were covered by Toyota safety recall 50J (NHTSA 05V-225), which replaced the lower ball joints; on any year, ask what was fitted. AdventureTaco's advice is OEM Toyota only.
- Timing belt records: The V6 wants a belt at roughly 90,000-mile intervals, ideally with the water pump and thermostat. It's a non-interference engine, so a failure is usually a tow, not a rebuild — but no paperwork means budget for the job.
- Rear axle seals and brakes: Blown rear axle seals are a known 3rd gen habit; gear oil then soaks the drum brake shoes and washes out the wheel bearing. Look for wet backing plates and listen for a bearing growl on the test drive.
- Locker and 4WD function: If it's a 1996–2000 4WD with the E-locker, make sure it actually engages (it's meant for 4Lo and low speed). On Multi-Mode trucks, cycle every mode. 2001–02 trucks have no factory rear locker regardless of what the ad says.
- Steering slop: Wandering or a clunk over bumps often points to worn steering rack bushings (common around 100k miles) or tie-rod ends. Both are cheap to fix but useful bargaining chips.
- Recalls and readiness: 1996–98 trucks are covered by NHTSA recall 02V-021 (Toyota campaign 20A), under which dealers replaced rear suspension parts; ask whether it was done. And plug in a scanner — IH8MUD members warn about sellers clearing codes to hide a dead catalytic converter, so check all readiness monitors are complete.
- Who lifted it?: A tidy lift with known parts is a bonus; a mystery spacer lift with no alignment records is a project. Forum veterans' advice is blunt: skip a lifted truck unless the lift was done properly.

### Common repairs
#### Lower ball joint replacement
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 30–60 min per side · cost Dealer did the 2001–02 campaign in about 3 hours; otherwise parts plus labor
Symptoms: Stiff steering, poor self-centering, front-end clunks or squeaks, a torn boot. Toyota's 50J letter warns a worn joint can separate from the knuckle.
Fix: Support the truck on stands and pull the wheel. Remove the four 14 mm bolts holding the LBJ to the knuckle, pull the cotter pin and loosen the 24 mm castle nut, then pop the stud from the lower control arm with a pitman-arm puller (repeat for the 19 mm tie-rod castle nut on a 4Runner). Swing the hub aside, fit the correct left/right joint, torque the knuckle bolts with blue Loctite (37 ft-lb black washer bolts or 59 ft-lb green flanged bolts), castle nuts to 103 ft-lb (LCA) and 67 ft-lb (tie rod), then new cotter pins.
Tools: 14/19/24 mm sockets · OTC 6295 front end service set · torque wrench · blue Loctite 242 · new cotter pins · OEM 4Runner LBJs L 43340-39465 / R 43330-39585

#### Timing belt and water pump (5VZ-FE)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ 8–14 hours (AdventureTaco's first attempt took about 14) · cost Parts ≈ $200–400 with water pump, labor ≈ $200–300 (8020 Automotive)
Symptoms: Due at around 90,000 miles or with unknown history; a cracked belt, misfires or rough running. It's non-interference, so failure usually strands you rather than wrecking the engine.
Fix: Drain coolant, remove the fan, radiator and drive belts, then the upper timing cover. Hold the crank pulley and break the bolt, pull the pulley, remove the lower cover and set #1 to TDC. Remove tensioner, belt and idlers; replace cam and crank seals, water pump and thermostat (AdventureTaco fits the thermostat jiggle valve at 6 o'clock). Fit idlers and belt, then the hydraulic tensioner, rotate two full turns to confirm marks, torque the crank bolt to 217 ft-lb, refill and bleed.
Tools: Harmonic damper holder · OTC 4518 puller · cam pulley holder · seal puller · Toyota belt 13568-69095 · tensioner 13540-62021 · Aisin water pump 16100-69398-83 · new crank bolt 90119-16006

#### Rear axle seals and bearings
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ a full day for most (press work) · cost ≈ $250 per side at a shop (IH8MUD owner estimate), more if the brakes are oil-soaked
Symptoms: Gear oil on the backing plate or inside the drum, oil-soaked shoes that won't stop the truck, a growling rear wheel bearing.
Fix: Lift and support the rear, pull wheels and drums, disconnect the e-brake cable, brake line and ABS sensor, and drain the diff. Remove the four backing-plate nuts and pull the axle. Press off the retainers and tone ring, press the old bearing out and the new one in with its dust seal, fit a new snap ring and retainers. Drive in a new inner seal square with a matched driver, reinstall the axle (backing-plate nuts 48 ft-lb), refill with 80W-90 and bleed the brakes. Do both sides.
Tools: 20-ton press · axle bearing puller/installer · seal driver · slide hammer · inner seal 90310-50006 · bearing 90363-40020-77 ('96–'00) or 90363-40068 ('01–'02) · O-rings 90301-88077

#### Steering rack bushings
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 3–4 hours · cost Parts plus labor; urethane kits are inexpensive
Symptoms: Vague steering, wander and clunks; rack visibly shifting in its mounts. AdventureTaco treats about 1/16 in of play as normal and 1/4 in or more as time for new bushings.
Fix: Support the front, remove wheels and the front sway bar, and separate the outer tie-rod ends from the knuckles. Unbolt the passenger bracket, centre bolt, driver bolt and power-steering line bracket, then wiggle the rack free (support it on a jack). Press out old bushings with a C-clamp and receiver cups, clean the seats, grease and press in urethane bushings with the matching sleeve. Reinstall: passenger bracket and centre bolt 123 ft-lb, driver nut 141 ft-lb, tie-rod castle nuts 67 ft-lb. Get an alignment.
Tools: 12–22 mm sockets · OTC 6295 puller · OTC 7249 ball-joint press kit · torque wrench · Energy Suspension 8.10103 kit (4Runner, per AdventureTaco) or Total Chaos urethane rack bushing kit

#### Valve cover gaskets (5VZ-FE)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 3–5 hours (intake plenum access) · cost Gaskets under $40; shop labor ≈ $250–500 (8020 Automotive)
Symptoms: Oil seeping down the heads, a burning-oil smell after a drive, slowly falling oil level.
Fix: Heat cycles harden and crack the gaskets, so leaks only get worse. Access is the work: clear the intake plumbing to reach the covers, unbolt them, clean the sealing surfaces thoroughly, fit new gaskets and grommets, and torque the covers down evenly.
Tools: Metric sockets and extensions · torque wrench · gasket scraper · RTV · new valve cover gaskets

#### Spare-tire crossmember and frame rust repair
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ a weekend · cost Parts plus labor; welding required
Symptoms: Flaking scale where crossmembers meet the frame, holes behind the rear axle, a spare carrier that won't release or sags.
Fix: Salt and debris pack in between body and frame and rot the rear crossmember from the inside — often discovered when the spare won't come down. Cut out the rotten section and weld in a replacement such as the Rust Buster 11-gauge crossmember (replaces Toyota 51209-35171), then treat surrounding metal with rust converter and a yearly oil- or grease-based inhibitor.
Tools: Welder · angle grinder · Rust Buster crossmember · rust paint · inhibitor spray

#### 4WD won't engage: ADD vacuum system and actuators
Difficulty 2 / 5 (diagnosis, hoses, VSV) · 3 / 5 (actuator rebuild) · time An hour or two to diagnose · an actuator rebuild needs a day for the glue to cure · cost Parts plus labor; vacuum hose is cheap
Symptoms: Lever or button in 4WD but only the rear wheels drive, and the 4WD light stays off. On a part-time truck, a slow tight turn on pavement should make 4WD bind within about thirty feet. No bind means no front drive (Toyota-4Runner.org).
Fix: On 1996–2000 trucks the front axle is engaged by vacuum. With the engine running and 4WD off, check for vacuum at the twin VSVs on the driver's-side fender wall. No vacuum: check the check valve to the intake manifold, the hoses and the reservoir. If one hose has vacuum, engage 4WD and see whether it moves to the other. If it moves but the axle doesn't engage, suspect the diff actuator or its line. If it doesn't move, mark and swap the two hoses: if the truck now goes into 4WD the diff is fine, and a test light shows whether the transfer-case switch signal changes sides. Signal but no change in vacuum means a bad VSV. Check the fuse and the ADD relay too; one 1998 SR5 owner found it behind the passenger kick panel. 2001–02 trucks use an electric front actuator, so the vacuum tests don't apply. On push-button trucks the transfer-case actuator motor can quit when its magnets come loose. One owner rebuilt his (1996 Limited, A340F, actuator 36410-35040) by re-gluing the magnets and fitting a new O-ring.
Tools: Hand vacuum pump with gauge · test light · marker · 12 mm and 10 mm sockets · dielectric grease

#### Rear hatch window drops or won't rise
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Parts plus labor; owners hunt used relays and switches to save money
Symptoms: The back glass drops into the hatch and won't come up, often in wet weather, or lowers itself unasked.
Fix: Start with the fuse and the rear-door power-window relay. One 1997 SR5 owner on Toyota-4Runner.org found the relay shell melted and burned wires at the window limit switch, with the damage spread into neighbouring harness wires to the rear door ECU. Pull the hatch trim, repair the harness, then feed the motor 12 V directly, using the wiring diagram to pick the right leads. That tells you whether the motor or the controls are at fault. If the window drops by itself, another owner cured it by removing the short harness section between the hatch key lock and the hatch harness; after that the window works only from the dash switch. The thread gives the limit switch as Toyota 84290-35020.
Tools: Trim-panel tools · multimeter · fused 12 V jumper leads · soldering iron or crimper · heat-shrink

### Baseline service
Assume nothing on a 20-plus-year-old 4Runner: unless there are receipts, do the timing belt, every fluid and the cheap 5VZ-FE wear items in one go. The 5VZ-FE is non-interference, but with a 90,000-mile belt interval most trucks are on their third or fourth belt, or overdue on their second. Capacities below come from Toyota's own 1999–2002 owner's manuals, cross-checked against Toyota-Club.net's compilation.
- Engine oil & filter: API SJ/SL 'Energy-Conserving' or ILSAC multigrade · SAE 5W-30 preferred · 5.2 L (5.5 US qt) with filter (Toyota owner's manual) · Then every 5,000 mi or per the owner's manual (Spin-on filter on the 5VZ-FE. Check for valve-cover seepage while you're there (see repairs).)
- Engine air filter: Panel filter in the airbox · Inspect at every oil change; replace when dirty (Dusty-trail trucks clog these fast.)
- Cabin air filter (add-on): None from the factory · Optional add-on (AdventureTaco notes the 3rd gen 4Runner never had a cabin filter; their kit fits in the blower-motor housing under the glovebox (three T25/8 mm screws).)
- Spark plugs: Denso K16TR11 (Toyota 90919-01192) or NGK BKR5EKB-11 · gap 1.1 mm (0.043 in) (Toyota 2001–02 owner's manuals; Toyota-Club plug table) · Replace now if history unknown (Six plugs; Toyota-Club lists the same plug for the 5VZ-FE in the 1999–2003 Tundra and the Hilux Surf.)
- Timing belt, water pump & thermostat: Belt 13568-69095 · Aisin pump · 82 °C thermostat 90916-03075 · Every ≈90,000 mi (or now, if undocumented) (Do the pump, idlers, hydraulic tensioner, cam/crank seals and thermostat with the belt — AdventureTaco's OEM kit list. See the repair card above for the procedure.)
- Coolant: Toyota red Long Life Coolant (00272-1LLAC concentrate, mixed with distilled water) · 8.0 L (9.0 L with rear heater) · Drain and refill now; renew with every timing belt (AdventureTaco refilled with two gallons of red concentrate plus distilled water after the belt job. Don't mix in green conventional coolant.)
- Drive belts: A/C 99364-20870 · alternator 90080-91090 · power steering 90080-91126 · Replace with the timing belt (All three come off for the timing job anyway; part numbers from AdventureTaco's OEM kit.)
- Automatic / manual transmission: Automatic: ATF Dexron II/III · ≈2.0 L per drain and refill (4WD). Manual: 75W-90 GL-4/5 · 2.2 L · Drain and refill now, then per the owner's manual (A drain and refill replaces only part of the automatic's fluid, so on a truck with unknown history repeat it two or three times over a few hundred miles rather than one high-pressure flush.)
- Transfer case: 75W-90 GL-4/5 · 1.0 L (lever control) / 1.2 L (lever + button control) · Change now, then with the diffs (Crack the fill plug before you drain.)
- Front & rear differentials + rear breather: Hypoid GL-5 · front 1.15 L: owner's manual gives SAE 75W-90 for A.D.D. trucks, Toyota-Club lists 80W-90 · rear 2.45 L (no locker) / 2.75 L (with locker): SAE 90 above −18 °C, SAE 80W or 80W-90 below (owner's manual) · Change now; after any deep water crossing (The rear axle's breather sits on the housing and can suck in water when a hot diff is submerged. AdventureTaco's fix: a union plus hose run up to a breather plug behind the fuel door.)
- Power steering fluid: ATF Dexron II/III · Check; turkey-baster refresh if dark (Same fluid as the automatic transmission.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 or DOT 4 · Flush now if history unknown, then per the owner's manual (Rear drums: inspect for gear oil on the shoes (see rear axle seals).)
- Fuel filter: Toyota 23300-62030 (4Runner-specific bracket; Tacoma's differs) · With the timing belt (≈90,000 mi); every 30,000 mi in very dusty country (Frame-mounted; 14 mm flare-nut wrench plus a 19 mm to hold the filter. AdventureTaco skips the FSM's fuel-pump-disconnect step and catches the spill.)
- PCV valve & grommet: Valve 12204-62010 · grommet 90480-18001 · hose 12261-62041 (optional) · Replace now (cheap, 30 minutes) (Old grommets harden and crumble into the engine on removal — pick out every piece.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: The Toyota-4Runner.org consensus is 265/75R16 (roughly a 31.6-inch tire) on stock suspension. Some owners see rubbing at full compression off-road with wide, aggressive tread or wheel spacers; if you want zero drama, 265/70R16 or 265/70R17 are the conservative picks. Anything bigger is lift territory.

Q: Does my 4Runner have the factory rear locker?
A: Only if it's a 1996–2000 4WD truck that was ordered with it — it was an option on Base, SR5 and Limited 4WD models, never standard, and it wasn't common. For 2001–02 the rear E-locker was dropped in favour of VSC, traction control and a centre diff lock.

Q: How should I use the E-locker?
A: The owner's manual guidance quoted on the forums is to engage it only in 4Lo and keep speed below about 5 mph. It locks both rear wheels together, so it'll fight you in turns on high-traction surfaces — use it for the obstacle, then switch it off.

Q: When does the timing belt need doing — and is the 3.4 an interference engine?
A: Plan on about every 90,000 miles, and do the water pump, thermostat and seals while you're in there. The 5VZ-FE is non-interference, so a broken belt shouldn't destroy valves, but it will leave you stranded.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: Up to 5,000 lb when properly equipped — a big jump from the 3,500 lb of the previous generation. Owners on Expedition Portal report fuel economy dropping to roughly 11–13 mpg when towing.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: EPA ratings were around 17 city / 19 highway for the 1996 V6 and 16/19 for a 2002 SR5 4x4; owners typically report 16–18 mpg. The 18.5-gallon tank and a notoriously inaccurate fuel gauge mean range is modest, so carry a jerry can on long trips.

Q: What are the fluid capacities?
A: From Toyota's 1999–2002 owner's manuals: 5VZ-FE oil 5.2 L with filter (5W-30 preferred); coolant 8.0 L (9.0 L with rear heater); automatic drain-and-refill up to 2.0 L (4WD) of Dexron III/II; transfer case 1.0–1.2 L of GL-4/5 75W-90; front diff 1.15 L, where the manual gives 75W-90 for A.D.D. trucks and Toyota-Club gives 80W-90; rear diff 2.45 L (2.75 L with diff lock) of GL-5 SAE 90, or 80W-90 below −18 °C.

Q: Which years should I buy or avoid?
A: IH8MUD's 3rd-gen regulars come closest to a consensus: 1999–2000 for a driver, ideally a Limited, and a '99 with the E-locker is the one most often called best (members say its springs sit about an inch longer than the '98 and 2000). 1996–98 trucks are cheaper and make good trail rigs. 2001–02 lose the locker for VSC and traction control, and one member flags occasional automatic planetary-gear problems. Rust and the lower ball joints matter more than any model year.

Q: Is the four-cylinder worth considering?
A: Most owners steer you toward the 3.4 V6: 183 hp and 217 lb-ft versus 150 hp and 177 lb-ft for the 2.7 four, for similar running costs. The four is a durable engine, but it'll struggle with big tires and a loaded roof rack.

Q: What lift options are there?
A: The classic is an Old Man Emu kit of about 2–3 in, with ICON, Total Chaos and others offering springs, coilovers and control arms. As a lift grows, aftermarket upper control arms help restore alignment range; Total Chaos makes both UCAs and a bolt-on lower ball joint conversion for this truck.

Q: How long will a 3rd gen last?
A: With maintenance, a long time. SlashGear notes it consistently ranked among the SUVs most likely to pass 250,000 miles, and 8020 Automotive puts a well-maintained 5VZ-FE at 300,000–400,000 miles. Frame rust and neglected ball joints usually kill these trucks before the engine does.
