## Toyota 4Runner 4th Gen (2003–2009)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/4th-gen/
Codes: N210, 1GR-FE, 2UZ-FE

Verdict: The 4Runner in a suit: Prado 120 bones, a third row, cushy X-REAS dampers and — for the only time in its life — a V8. Softer than the trail purists like, but a 4.7 V8 with a lockable Torsen centre diff still hits harder than anything wearing the badge since.

Car and Driver called the fourth generation the largest, heaviest, most luxurious and most powerful 4Runner yet, and that is the whole story in one sentence. Built on the Land Cruiser Prado 120 platform and launched in October 2002 as a 2003 model, it brought a 4.0-litre V6, the first and only V8 4Runner, a third-row seat and trick suspension options. It kept the things that matter, too: a ladder frame, a solid rear axle and a lockable centre differential. Two decades on, it's the generation that quietly does everything well — and costs less than the cult ones on either side.

### PRADO UNDERNEATH
Production ran from August 2002 to August 2009, with the Japanese Hilux Surf twin built until September 2009. Wikipedia describes the recipe: double-wishbone independent front suspension, a solid rear axle 'retained for strength and durability', and the Prado 120's chassis — the same underpinnings as the Lexus GX 470. Launch trims were SR5, Sport Edition and Limited; the SR5 and Sport wore grey cladding, the Limited body colour, and Sport models got a non-functional hood scoop.
The 4.0-litre 1GR-FE V6 made 245 hp and 282 lb-ft; the optional 4.7-litre 2UZ-FE V8 — the same engine family as the Land Cruiser 100's — launched at 235 hp and 320 lb-ft and gained VVT-i for 2005, rising to roughly 270 hp and 315 lb-ft (Wikipedia says 268 hp, Car and Driver quoted 270). Car and Driver clocked a 2005 V8 at 7.2 seconds to 60. Everything was automatic: a four-speed on early V6s, with a five-speed standard on the V6 from the 2005 model year.

### THE CLEVER BITS
Four-wheel drive came in two flavours. V6 trucks used Toyota's part-time Multi-Mode system; V8s ran full-time 4WD; both used a lockable Torsen centre differential, with Hill-start Assist and Downhill Assist Control standard on 4WD models. Towing was rated at 5,000 lb for the V6 and up to 7,300 lb for a rear-drive V8 (7,000 lb with 4WD). The 3rd gen's optional rear E-locker, however, did not return until the very end.
Then there was X-REAS — standard on the Sport Edition and optional on SR5 and Limited — which links diagonally opposite dampers through hydraulic lines and a centre valve to cut body roll. Some Limiteds paired it with rear height-control air suspension. Both work well when new and become expensive with age, which is why replacing them with conventional shocks or coil springs is now a common 4th gen job.

### YEAR BY YEAR
Toyota kept fiddling. Late 2003 brought standard tyre-pressure monitoring and an optional third-row seat on SR5 and Limited for 2004 — making this, as the Autopian notes, the first 4Runner with a third row. 2005 brought the five-speed V6 and the VVT-i V8; the 2006 refresh added new bumpers, grille, projector headlamps and LED tail lamps; 2007 had the oddball Urban Runner package; and 2008 made curtain and front-side airbags standard. The IIHS rated it Good in frontal offset and side tests but Poor for rear-impact protection.
Sales tell the arc. US buyers took 109,308 in 2003 and a peak of 114,212 in 2004, before demand slid to 47,878 in 2008 and 19,675 in calendar 2009. The fifth generation replaced it for 2010 — on the J150 platform, with a V6 only. No 4Runner has had a V8 since, and the current 6th gen runs four-cylinders. That, more than anything, is why a well-kept V8 4th gen has a following.

### Data plate
- Chassis: N210 (Prado 120-based)
- Years: 2003–2009 (US model years)
- Production: Aug 2002 – Aug 2009
- Engines: 1GR-FE 4.0 V6 / 2UZ-FE 4.7 V8
- Output (V6): 245 hp · 282 lb-ft
- Output (V8, 2005+): ≈270 hp · 315 lb-ft
- Transmission: 4-spd auto (early V6) / 5-spd auto
- 4Wd: V6 Multi-Mode · V8 full-time · lockable Torsen centre
- Towing: 5,000 lb (V6) · 7,000 lb (V8 4WD)
- Epa: 17/20 mpg V6 · 15/19 mpg V8
- Seating: 5, or 7 with optional third row (2004 MY on)
- Us Sales Peak: 114,212 (2004)

### Engineering
The N210 is a Prado 120 in 4Runner clothing: a ladder frame, double-wishbone front suspension, a four-link solid rear axle on coils, and either Toyota's timing-chain 1GR-FE V6 or the timing-belt 2UZ-FE V8. The engineering story is in the drivetrain — full-time 4WD on the V8, Multi-Mode on the V6, a lockable Torsen centre diff on both — and in optional electronics and hydraulics (X-REAS, rear air suspension, DAC) that were sophisticated in 2003 and are maintenance items now.
- Chassis: Ladder frame (Prado 120) (Shared with the Land Cruiser Prado 120 and Lexus GX 470.)
- Front: Double-wishbone IFS (Strut-type front shock assemblies with top mounts; X-REAS-linked on equipped trucks.)
- Rear: Solid axle on coils (Retained for strength; some Limiteds got rear height-control air springs.)
- Engines: 1GR-FE 4.0 V6 / 2UZ-FE 4.7 V8 (V6 245 hp (timing chain); V8 235 hp, ≈270 hp with VVT-i from 2005 (timing belt).)
- 4Wd: Torsen centre, lockable (Full-time on V8; Multi-Mode part-time on V6. HAC and DAC standard on 4WD.)
- Damping: X-REAS (opt.) (Diagonally cross-linked hydraulic dampers; standard on Sport Edition, optional on SR5 and Limited.)

- 2005–2009 · N210 · V6 · 1GR-FE 4.0 V6 · 245 hp / 282 lb-ft · Five-speed automatic standard. 2006 refresh: projector headlamps, LED tails.
- 2005–2009 · N210 · V8 · 2UZ-FE 4.7 V8 (VVT-i) · ≈270 hp / 315 lb-ft · Tows up to 7,300 lb (RWD) / 7,000 lb (4WD).

- 2002–2009 · Japan · Hilux Surf · 1KD-FTV 3.0 turbodiesel I4 et al. · — · Japan-only diesels (1KD-FTV to 2005) and 2.7 fours; Surf built until Sept 2009.

### Year-by-year
- 2003: Prado 120-based launch: 4.0 1GR-FE V6 (245 hp) or first-ever 4.7 2UZ-FE V8 (235 hp); X-REAS optional; HAC and DAC on 4WD
- 2003–05: V6 head gaskets: Autotrader says failures on 2003–05 V6s are reported more than average, and Expedition Portal owners put most of them in 2003–04. Wikipedia dates the revised gasket to late in the 2006 model year [avoid]
- 2004: TPMS standard; optional third-row seat (first seven-seat 4Runner)
- 2005: V8 gains VVT-i (≈270 hp / 315 lb-ft); five-speed auto standard on the V6
- 2006: Mid-cycle refresh: new bumpers and grille, projector headlamps, LED tail lamps. HotCars picks the 2006-on V8 trucks as the better buys, and late-2006 V6s get the revised head gasket [buy]
- 2008: Curtain and front side airbags standard; VSC-off switch; Urban Runner package on Sport V6 4x4
- 2009: Trail Edition: factory rear e-locker, A-TRAC switch and Bilstein dampers

### Capability
- Towing: 5,000 lb (V6) · 7,300 lb (V8 2WD) · 7,000 lb (V8 4WD)
- Fuel tank: 23 gal (87 L)
- Fuel economy: EPA 17 city / 20 hwy (V6) · 15 / 19 (V8)
- Curb weight: 4,280 lb (1,941 kg)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 265/70R16, 265/65R17, 265/60R18 (2006+ Limited)
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Offset: +30 mm (16/17 in), +25 mm (18 in)
- Center Bore: 106.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M12x1.5
- Lug Torque: 81 lb-ft (110 N·m) per Limitless Tire [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 265/70R17 (Largest with no modification per the LexusGXOR wiki (same chassis); 255/75R17 needs the front fender-liner bolt moved)
- Biggest tire, ≈2 in lift: 285/70R17 (Reported on a 2 in OME lift with 17x9 −6 wheels; 275/70R17 fits without rubbing. At stock height 285s need a body-mount chop)
- Biggest tire, ≈3 in lift: 285/70R17 (Expect fender-liner trimming and a body-mount chop; can still rub under heavy compression or at full lock)

### Buying checks
- Frame rust: Not as notorious as contemporary Tacomas, but salt-belt trucks rot. Inspect the rails, crossmembers and rear suspension link mounts with a hammer and a light — and note the 4Runner wasn't part of Toyota's Tacoma/Tundra/Sequoia frame programmes.
- V8 air-injection pump and manifolds: CarComplaints owners report the V8's secondary air injection system failing around 100,000–150,000 miles, triggering a check-engine light and limp mode, with $2,000–4,000 repair bills. Cold-start ticking can be a leaking exhaust manifold, which on the V8 is integrated with the catalytic converters.
- V8 timing belt records: The 2UZ-FE has a timing belt (the V6 has a chain). Toyota's maintenance guide lists replacement at 90,000 miles or 108 months (as summarised by Cherish Your Car); LC Engineering suggests inspecting from about 60,000 and doing the water pump at the same time. No records means budget for it.
- V6 coolant loss: 2003–05 V6s are the ones Autotrader says report head-gasket failures more than average, and forum owners point to 2003–04 in particular; a cylinder 6 misfire (P0306) plus coolant loss is the red flag. Check the overflow level, watch a cold start, and consider a combustion-gas test.
- X-REAS and rear air springs: X-REAS shocks leak and rust with age and TacomaWorld members note they're replaced in pairs at real cost. On Limiteds with rear height control, check the rear doesn't sag overnight. Either can be converted to conventional parts.
- Brake actuator: Listen with the engine running: a TacomaWorld member found the ABS accumulator pump cycling every 30 seconds with pedal vibration on one test truck — a sign the actuator is on its way out.
- Steering, CVs and bushings: Turn to full lock and look for a wet inner rack boot (fluid seeping into it damages the inner joint), torn CV boots past 100,000 miles, and clunky front sway-bar bushings.
- Dash and interior: Cracked dashboards were common enough that Toyota's ZE6 warranty enhancement covered 2003–2005 4Runners, but that coverage has long since lapsed. Check that the third-row seat, power rear window and interior lights all work.

### Common repairs
#### Replace X-REAS with conventional shocks
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A day · cost Bilstein 5100 four-shock set with front mounts ≈ $650 (ShockWarehouse)
Symptoms: Leaking or rusty X-REAS shocks, a floaty or wallowy ride, a quote for four OEM units that's more than the truck feels worth.
Fix: Lift the truck so all four shocks are fully extended, then disconnect the X-REAS lines at the junctions about a foot from each shock — Toyota-4Runner.org members note there are built-in valves, but the system is pressurised, so follow the factory manual or expect a spray of hydraulic fluid. Drain the system and tie off the hose ends, then remove the old front strut assemblies and rear shocks and fit conventional units with new front mounts. Leaving the brackets and tubing in place does no harm.
Tools: Spring compressor (fronts) · metric sockets · drain pan · Bilstein 5100 front 24-324359 · rear 33-313146 · KYB SM5640 front mounts

#### Rear air suspension to coil conversion (Limited)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Conversion kit plus coil springs
Symptoms: Rear sagging after sitting, a compressor running constantly, a height-control warning on the dash.
Fix: Support the frame and axle, deflate and disconnect the air springs, remove them from their seats, and install a bolt-in coil conversion — Metal Tech 4x4 sells CNC-machined kits for 2003–2009 4Runners and GX 470s with rear airbags — then fit coil springs of the right rate for your load and disable the height-control system per the kit instructions.
Tools: Floor jack · stands · metric sockets · Metal Tech 4x4 rear coil conversion kit · coil springs

#### Differential and transfer case fluid service
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time A short afternoon · cost Gear oil ≈ $5–15 a quart plus crush washers
Symptoms: Unknown service history, whining diffs, a 4WD system that's never been exercised.
Fix: Always break the fill plug loose first. Rear diff and transfer case use 24 mm plugs; the front diff needs a 10 mm hex after removing the 12 mm-bolted skid plates. Drain each, fit new washers, and refill until it drips from the fill hole. Toyota-Club's owner's-manual data calls for GL-5 75W-90 in the front diff and transfer case but GL-5 80W-90 in the rear (some owners run 75W-90 throughout); 4Runners.com quotes roughly 1.5 qt front, 1.5 qt transfer case and 3.2 qt rear. Cycle 4Hi and 4Lo afterwards.
Tools: 24 mm socket · 10 mm hex · 12 mm socket · fluid pump · GL-5 75W-90 and 80W-90 · washers 90430-18008 (t-case), 12157-10010 and 90430-24003 (diffs)

#### Front wheel bearing / hub assembly
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Hub assembly plus labor
Symptoms: A hum or growl that changes with speed, play in the front wheel, an ABS light.
Fix: Pull the wheel, unbolt the ABS and brake-line bracket, remove the caliper (two 17 mm bolts — support it, don't hang it) and the rotor. Pop off the dust cap, remove cotter pin and nut cap, and break the axle nut with a 35 mm socket. Remove the four 17 mm hub bolts (open-end wrench only), tap the axle free with a soft drift, and pry the hub off evenly. Replace the knuckle dust seal while you're there, then reassemble to factory torque specs.
Tools: 35 mm socket · 17 mm sockets and wrench · breaker bar or impact · soft drift · new hub assembly · knuckle dust seal

#### Radiator replacement and external trans cooler (V6)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Aftermarket radiator ≈ $134 and trans cooler ≈ $39 (2014 prices quoted on 4Runners.com)
Symptoms: Coolant weeping from the bottom of the radiator — the driver's-side bottom is a common failure point on 4th gen V6s — or an old original radiator you don't trust with transmission cooling.
Fix: Remove the top trim and (optionally) the front bumper for access. Drain the radiator, unbolt the overflow tank, disconnect the transmission cooler lines on the driver's side (keep them upright), unbolt the fan shroud and the four radiator mounts, and lift it out. Mount an external cooler on the condenser, route the transmission lines through it, fit the new radiator, refill and bleed, then check transmission fluid level.
Tools: Metric wrenches to 17 mm · hose-clamp pliers · drain pans · radiator · Hayden-type transmission cooler and hose

#### 2UZ-FE timing belt and water pump (V8)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A full day for most · cost LC Engineering 2UZ belt kit ≈ $145, plus water pump
Symptoms: Due by mileage or age, no records, a weeping water pump. A failed belt can do severe engine damage, per LC Engineering.
Fix: Drain coolant, remove the fan, shroud and drive belts, then the crank pulley and timing covers. Set the engine to TDC and mark the belt and pulleys. Replace the belt, tensioner pulley, idler pulley and hydraulic belt adjuster, and the water pump — which is driven by the belt — then rotate the crank two full turns to confirm the marks before reassembly.
Tools: Crank pulley holder and puller · torque wrench · LCE 2UZ-FE timing belt kit · hydraulic timing belt adjuster · Aisin water pump

#### VSC / TRAC light zero-point calibration
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time Minutes · cost Free
Symptoms: VSC, TRAC or TRAC OFF lights that stay on after a battery change, alignment, sensor work or a fluid service — with no actual fault.
Fix: Park on a level surface with the wheels straight, and perform Toyota's yaw/deceleration sensor zero-point calibration by jumping the diagnostic connector terminals with a paper clip as shown in widely shared guides (4Runners.com members link a YouTube walkthrough). If the light persists, scan for real codes before chasing anything else.
Tools: Paper clip · level ground · OBD-II scanner if it doesn't clear

### Baseline service
The 4th gen is young enough that Toyota's owner's-manual data is published — Toyota-Club's US-market tables are used below — but old enough that most examples are on their second or third owner with patchy records. Baseline every fluid, find out whether the truck has X-REAS or rear air springs, and on a V8 assume the timing belt is due until proven otherwise.
- Engine oil & filter: API SL / ILSAC · 1GR-FE 5.2 L, 2UZ-FE 6.2 L with filter · At purchase, then per the manual (Viscosity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]. Capacities from Toyota-Club's owner's-manual data.)
- Engine air filter: Panel filter · At purchase; more often on dusty trails (Shared with Tacoma/FJ/Tundra 1GR applications in the aftermarket.)
- Cabin air filter: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (Cheap, often forgotten.)
- Spark plugs: Type and interval [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Per the manual (Forum advice on plug intervals conflicts — go by the manual. On the V8, owners suggest doing plugs alongside the timing belt.)
- Coolant: Toyota-type long-life coolant · 1GR-FE 9.8 L, 2UZ-FE 12.3 L · Drain and refill at purchase (Capacities per Toyota-Club; use a Toyota-spec ('Asian formula') coolant. 4th gen V6 radiators commonly leak at the driver's-side bottom.)
- Automatic transmission fluid: 4-speed: Toyota ATF T-IV, 2.0 L drain/refill · 5-speed: Toyota ATF WS, ≈3.0 L drain/refill · Drain and refill at purchase; repeat to refresh more of the fluid (2005-on trucks use the 5-speed with WS fluid (the 2005 owner's manual says 'up to 3.0 L'). There's no dipstick on later trucks — level is checked at a set fluid temperature, so owners use a scan tool to read ATF temp.)
- Transfer case: GL-5 75W-90 · 1.4 L · At purchase (24 mm drain/fill plugs; break the fill plug loose first. Fill until it drips from the fill hole.)
- Front differential: GL-5 75W-90 · 1.5 L (V6) / 1.4 L (V8) · At purchase (10 mm hex plugs behind the 12 mm-bolted skid plates; new washer 90430-24003 on the drain.)
- Rear differential: GL-5 80W-90 · 3.05 L · At purchase (Toyota-Club lists 80W-90 for the rear (some owners run 75W-90 throughout). 2009 Trail Editions have the factory rear E-locker — cycle it in 4Lo after the service.)
- Power steering fluid: ATF Dexron II/III · Drain/refill reservoir at purchase (While you're there, check the inner rack boots for fluid — a TacomaWorld-flagged 4th gen weak point.)
- Brake fluid: Type [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush at purchase; a 4Runners.com member says Toyota's interval was 4 years in 2008 (Listen for the ABS accumulator pump cycling constantly — a sign the brake actuator is failing.)
- Timing belt & water pump (2UZ-FE V8 only): Belt, tensioner pulley, idler, hydraulic adjuster, water pump · 90,000 mi or 108 months (Toyota schedule, per Cherish Your Car); LC Engineering suggests inspecting from ≈60,000 mi (The 1GR-FE V6 uses a timing chain and needs no belt service.)
- X-REAS / rear height-control air springs: Inspect for leaks and sag · At purchase (Leaking X-REAS shocks are replaced in pairs; many owners convert to conventional shocks and coils instead.)
- CV boots, sway-bar bushings & front hubs: Inspect · At purchase (TacomaWorld members flag leaking CV boots past ≈100,000 mi and clunking front sway-bar bushings; replace the knuckle dust seal if you do a hub.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: 265/70R17 (about 31.6 in) is the size the GX 470 community — same chassis and fitment — says fits with no modification, and owners on both platforms report no rubbing on factory wheels. 255/75R17 may need a front fender-liner bolt repositioned. 285/70R17 (about 33 in) needs a body-mount chop and fender-liner work even with a small lift.

Q: V6 or V8?
A: The V8 is the reason many buy a 4th gen: about 270 hp and 315 lb-ft from 2005, full-time 4WD and up to 7,000 lb of 4WD towing. The V6 has a timing chain instead of a belt, part-time Multi-Mode 4WD and better EPA numbers (17/20 vs 15/19). The V8's air-injection pump and exhaust manifolds are its known expensive faults.

Q: Does it have a locker?
A: All 4WD trucks have a lockable Torsen centre differential. A factory rear locker only came on the 2009 Trail Edition, along with an A-TRAC switch and Bilstein dampers.

Q: What is X-REAS, and should I keep it?
A: It links diagonally opposite shocks through hydraulic lines and a centre valve to reduce body roll. It was standard on the Sport Edition and optional on SR5 and Limited. It works, but the shocks are costly and replaced in pairs, so many owners swap to conventional shocks such as Bilstein 5100s when they wear out.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: 5,000 lb with the V6; 7,300 lb with a rear-drive V8 and 7,000 lb with a 4WD V8.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: Wikipedia lists EPA estimates of 17 city / 20 highway for the V6 and 15/19 for the V8. A 4Runners.com owner reported 17–18 mpg combined and 18–19 on the highway from a stock 2003 V8 4WD over 12 years, less when towing.

Q: What fluids do the diffs and transfer case take?
A: GL-5 hypoid gear oil: 75W-90 in the front diff and transfer case and 80W-90 in the rear, per Toyota-Club's owner's-manual data (front 1.5 L V6 / 1.4 L V8, transfer case 1.4 L, rear 3.05 L). A 4Runners.com write-up gives roughly 1.5 qt, 1.5 qt and 3.2 qt; fill each until it drips from the fill hole.

Q: Why are my VSC and TRAC lights on?
A: Often nothing is broken: after a battery disconnect, alignment or sensor work the system can need a zero-point calibration, done on level ground with a paper clip across the diagnostic connector. If the lights stay on, scan for codes.

Q: Is there a dash-cracking recall?
A: Not a safety recall. Toyota's ZE6 warranty enhancement covered cracked or sticky dashboards on 2003–2005 4Runners, but coverage was time-limited and has expired. A dash cover is the usual fix now.

Q: Which years should I look for?
A: A 2006–09 V8 is the safest pick. HotCars rates the 2006-on V8 facelift trucks the better buys, Jalopnik says the 2UZ-FE V8 has a reputation for being indestructible (with VVT-i and 270 hp from 2005), and Wikipedia says the V6's revised head gasket arrived late in the 2006 model year. The ones to be careful with are 2003–05 V6s: Autotrader says their head-gasket failures are reported more than average, and Expedition Portal owners put most in 2003–04. Whatever the year, a V8 needs its timing belt at 90,000 miles.

Q: Does it have a third row?
A: It can. A third-row seat became optional on SR5 and Limited from late 2003 (the 2004 model year), making the 4th gen the first 4Runner offered with seven seats.

## Toyota 4Runner 5th Gen (2010–2024)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/5th-gen/
Codes: N280, 1GR-FE

Verdict: Fifteen model years with the same V6, the same five-speed and roughly the same dashboard — and it sold better at the end than at the start. The most successful act of automotive stubbornness of the century.

Toyota started building the fifth-generation 4Runner at Tahara, Japan, in August 2009, unveiled it at the State Fair of Texas on 24 September, and then essentially forgot to replace it. Production ran until August 2024. In between, the world got turbo fours, ten-speed gearboxes and touchscreens the size of tea trays; the 4Runner kept its 4.0-litre V6, its five-speed automatic and its roll-down rear window. Car and Driver called it "basically made of bronze and granite." Buyers called it a bargain at any price: US sales climbed from 46,531 in 2010 to a peak of 144,696 in 2021.

### A PRADO IN A COWBOY HAT
Underneath, the N280 shares its platform with the J150 Land Cruiser Prado, the Lexus GX 460 and the FJ Cruiser, and like them it is a proper ladder-frame truck with independent front suspension and a live rear axle. It was built only in left-hand drive and never sold in Japan. The 4th gen's 4.7 V8 did not survive the transition; instead, every truck that mattered got the 1GR-FE V6, now with Dual VVT-i. A 2.7-litre four-cylinder lingered on 2WD models for 2010 only.
Launch trims were SR5, Trail and Limited. SR5 and Trail 4x4s got a part-time system with a two-speed transfer case; the Limited went full-time. All had A-TRAC brake-based traction control, but the Trail was the one that mattered: Crawl Control, an electric rear locker and the optional Kinetic Dynamic Suspension System (KDSS), kit that had previously been reserved for Toyota's posher off-roaders. Nobody was going to mistake it for a sports car — but nobody buying one wanted that.

### THE LONG PLATEAU
The 2014 facelift brought the pointier face with projector headlamps, LED tail-lamps, a revised dash with the Optitron cluster, better brake lines and Trailer Sway Control — and, notably, no driveline changes. For 2015 Toyota added the TRD Pro, with TRD-tuned Bilstein remote-reservoir shocks (later TRD Pros, including Car and Driver's 2022 test truck, ran Fox dampers), TRD front springs and a front skid plate. For 2017 the Trail became the TRD Off-Road, mechanically the same truck with more badges. The Nightshade package arrived for 2019.
For 2020 every 4Runner finally got Toyota Safety Sense-P, plus a new head unit with Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. 2022 added push-button start, LED headlights and a TRD Sport trim that borrowed the Limited's X-REAS suspension and 20-inch wheels. 2023 brought a 40th Anniversary Special Edition limited to 4,040 units, and 2024 a TRD Pro-only paint called Terra. Car and Driver noted the truck hadn't had a major facelift in a decade; sales suggest nobody minded.

### WHY THE TRAIL CROWD KEPT BUYING IT
It certainly wasn't the numbers. Car and Driver's 2022 TRD Pro needed 7.7 seconds to reach 60 mph, averaged 15 mpg overall and wallowed on pavement with "a huge amount of body roll and brake dive." What it had instead was a powertrain with no surprises: the 1GR-FE runs a timing chain with no scheduled replacement, the five-speed is old enough that every failure mode is documented, and the chassis is shared with enough Toyotas that the aftermarket is vast.
That aftermarket became the point. Trail4R alone has catalogued everything from transmission services to KDSS geometry correction, and suppliers sell lifts, control arms, sliders, bumpers, lockers and long-travel kits by the pallet. The KDSS debate became a 5th gen rite of passage: brilliant for a stock truck's flex and road manners, a headache once you lift it past about three inches. Owners argued about it for fifteen years, which is roughly how long Toyota left the truck alone.

### THE AFTERMATH
The 6th gen arrived for 2025 on the TNGA-F frame shared with the Tacoma and Land Cruiser 250, swapping the V6 for a 2.4-litre turbo four and an optional hybrid. Even so, the old truck racked up 92,156 US sales in its final calendar year, according to Car and Driver. Its towing rating was 5,000 lb; the new one manages 6,000.
Used, the 5th gen is now the default 'buy once, build forever' SUV. TrueCar notes that 2010–2013 trucks under 150,000 miles can often be had for under $20,000, while Drivingline observed TRD Pros "regularly selling for well above MSRP." The usual inspections are frame rust, KDSS leaks, front axle seals and torn CV boots on lifted trucks. None of it is exotic, which is precisely why these trucks keep getting bought, lifted and driven into places a crossover would never come back from.

### Data plate
- Chassis: N280 (J150 Prado platform)
- Years: 2010–2024 (built Aug 2009 – Aug 2024)
- Built: Tahara, Japan · LHD only
- Engine: 1GR-FE 4.0 V6 (2.7 I4 2WD, 2010)
- Output: 270 hp @ 5,600 · 278 lb-ft @ 4,400
- Transmission: 5-spd auto (4-spd with the I4)
- 4Wd: Part-time 2-speed / full-time (Limited)
- Locker: Rear electric · Trail / TRD Off-Road
- Wheelbase: 109.8 in
- Length: 189.9–191.3 in
- Curb Weight: 4,400–4,805 lb
- Towing: 5,000 lb

### Engineering
The N280 is the J150 Prado recipe adapted for America: a ladder frame, double-wishbone front suspension, a coil-sprung live rear axle on links, and the 1GR-FE V6 bolted to a five-speed automatic. The interesting parts are electronic and hydraulic — A-TRAC on every truck, a rear locker and Crawl Control on the off-road trims, and KDSS, which hydraulically links the front and rear anti-roll bars so they can let go when the axle needs to droop.
- Chassis: Ladder frame (J150 Prado / GX 460 / FJ Cruiser platform; 109.8 in wheelbase.)
- Suspension: IFS + live rear axle (Control arms up front; coil-sprung four-link rear with a panhard rod.)
- Engine: 1GR-FE 4.0 V6 (270 hp @ 5,600 / 278 lb-ft @ 4,400; Dual VVT-i; timing chain. 2.7 I4 on 2010 2WD only.)
- 4Wd: Part-time or full-time (Two-speed part-time on SR5 / Trail / TRD trims; full-time on the Limited. A-TRAC on all.)
- Locker: Electric rear (Trail (2010–16) and TRD Off-Road (2017–24), with Crawl Control and Multi-Terrain Select.)
- Kdss: Hydraulic anti-roll bars (Optional on Trail / TRD Off-Road. Wikipedia describes it as fully mechanical: interconnected cylinders free the bars when a wheel drops.)

- 2014–2019 · N280 · facelift · 1GR-FE 4.0 V6 · 270 hp / 278 lb-ft · New face and dash; Trail renamed TRD Off-Road for 2017; Nightshade for 2019.
- 2015–2024 · N280 · TRD Pro · 1GR-FE 4.0 V6 · 270 hp / 278 lb-ft · TRD-tuned remote-reservoir shocks (Bilstein at launch, Fox on later trucks), front springs and skid plate; a new exclusive colour each year.
- 2020–2024 · N280 · late · 1GR-FE 4.0 V6 · 270 hp / 278 lb-ft · TSS-P standard, CarPlay/Android Auto; TRD Sport added for 2022; 40th Anniversary (4,040 units) for 2023.

### Year-by-year
- 2010: J150 Prado-platform launch: 4.0 1GR-FE V6 (270 hp), Trail Edition with KDSS, rear locker and Crawl Control; 2.7 four on 2WD only, 2010 only
- 2014: Facelift: projector headlamps, LED tail lamps, Optitron cluster, upgraded brake lines, Trailer Sway Control
- 2015: TRD Pro added: TRD-tuned Bilstein remote-reservoir shocks (Fox on later trucks), TRD front springs, front skid plate
- 2017: Trail and Trail Premium renamed TRD Off-Road and TRD Off-Road Premium; same hardware
- 2019: Nightshade package on the Limited
- 2020: Toyota Safety Sense-P standard; Entune 3.0 with Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. Autotrader says buy a late fifth gen, preferably 2020–2024 [buy]
- 2022: Push-button start and LED lighting standard; TRD Sport trim with X-REAS; TRD Pro gets Multi-Terrain Monitor
- 2023: 40th Anniversary Special Edition (4,040 units); heated wheel on upper trims
- 2024: Final year; TRD Pro in exclusive Terra paint

- Fuel economy: EPA 16 city / 19 hwy / 17 combined (C&D observed 15 mpg overall, 17 mpg at 75 mph (2022 TRD Pro))
- Curb weight: 4,400–4,805 lb (1,996–2,180 kg)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 265/70R17, 245/60R20 (Limited)
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Offset: +15 mm
- Center Bore: 106.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M12x1.5
- Lug Torque: 76–83 lb-ft (103–112 N·m) per Limitless Tire [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 275/70R17 or 255/75R17 (≈32 in) (Trail4R: true 32s shouldn't rub; 285/70R17 is 'questionable' and may need a body-mount chop)
- Biggest tire, ≈2 in (leveling) lift: 285/70R17 (Needs the fender liner pushed back; Trail4R says 33s on a 2 in level will need a body-mount chop)
- Biggest tire, 3 in+ lift: 285/70R17 (Expect mild liner rubbing and probably a BMC. 285/75R17 (33.8 in) means trimming, chopping and removing mud flaps)

### Buying checks
- Frame and underbody corrosion: Salt-belt and coastal trucks need a proper crawl underneath: frame rails, crossmembers, suspension mounts and the KDSS hard lines along the frame. Surface scale can be cleaned and treated (Trail4R's corrosion guide walks through it); flaking, holed metal is a different conversation.
- KDSS health: On Trail and TRD Off-Road trucks, look for wet KDSS cylinders, weeping lines or a truck that leans. Owners on Expedition Portal describe leaking cylinders as difficult and expensive to fix. If it's lifted, ask how the KDSS was handled — Trail4R notes most lifts aren't designed around it.
- Open recalls: Run the VIN at NHTSA. The big ones are the Takata passenger airbag inflator recalls covering 2010–2016 4Runners (19V-005, 19V-741 and earlier campaigns) and the Denso low-pressure fuel pump recalls for 2014–2015 (20V-012) and 2018–2019 trucks (20V-682).
- Lift quality and CV boots: A lifted IFS truck runs steeper axle angles. Check for torn CV boots and grease slung around the wheel well, aftermarket upper control arms on bigger lifts, and an alignment record. Trail4R's writer tore CV boots repeatedly from excessive droop until fitting limit straps.
- Front axle seals: Gear oil where the CV axle enters the front differential means a leaking axle seal. It's a DIY job, but budget for it and check the diff level.
- Driveline fluid history: Ask for transmission (Toyota ATF WS only), differential and transfer case service records. Toyota's severe-service schedule changes diff oil every 15,000 miles when towing or loaded; many owners just do everything at about 30,000.
- Rear window and liftgate: Run the power rear glass all the way down and up. A window that bounces back as if obstructed often just needs re-initialising or its tracks cleaned (see repairs), but a dead motor or regulator is a bigger job.
- Pick your year: Autotrader says the fifth gen has no major issues and recommends a late truck, preferably 2020–24 (TSS-P standard and CarPlay). 2014+ gets the facelift, better brake lines and Trailer Sway Control. SlashGear flags 2013–2016 for higher complaint and recall counts. The 2.7 four was 2WD-only and 2010-only.

### Common repairs
#### Automatic transmission drain and fill
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Trail4R's author budgeted about 6 hours including parts runs · cost ≈ $174 in fluid and parts (Trail4R, Hawaii prices)
Symptoms: Due on mileage or unknown history; dark or burnt-smelling fluid. There is no dipstick — the level is set at temperature through a check plug.
Fix: With the truck level, remove the 24 mm refill plug first, then the 14 mm drain plug (about 5 qt comes out). Drop the pan (20 × 10 mm bolts), replace the filter and O-ring, clean the magnets and fit a new pan gasket; pan bolts 62 in-lb, filter bolts 7 ft-lb. Refill (Trail4R used 5.5 qt), then jumper OBD-II pins 4 and 13 to enter maintenance mode, cycle the shifter until the 'D' light stays solid, and check level through the 5 mm Allen check plug at 104–113 °F (solid D = in range, blinking = too hot). Let it drip to a dribble, refit the plug at 15 ft-lb.
Tools: 10/12/14 mm and 24 mm sockets · 5 mm Allen · fluid pump · jumper wire · torque wrenches · Toyota ATF WS 00289-ATFWS · filter 35330-60050 · filter O-ring 90301-31014 · pan gasket 35168-60010 · plug gaskets (Trail4R and readers cite 35178-30010 for drain/check)

#### Front and rear differential + transfer case fluids
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time A morning · cost Fluids and crush washers; Toyota transfer fluid runs $60–90 per litre (Trail4R)
Symptoms: Due at 15,000 miles under severe service (towing, roof loads) per Toyota, or at whatever interval you set — Trail4R's author does all driveline fluids every 30,000.
Fix: Warm the drivetrain with a 5–10 mile drive. Always crack the fill plug before the drain. Front diff: 10 mm hex plugs, about 1.6 qt (part-time) or 1.5 qt (full-time) of 75W-85 GL-5; drain 48 ft-lb, fill 29 ft-lb. Rear diff: 24 mm plugs, 36 ft-lb; Trail4R quotes about 2.9 qt with locker / 2.8 qt without, but Toyota-Club's owner's-manual table lists 2.70 L without and 2.65 L with the locker [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] — fill to the bottom of the fill hole either way. Transfer case: 24 mm plugs, 27 ft-lb, about 1.1 qt (part-time) or 1.5 qt (full-time) of Toyota Transfer Gear Oil LF 75W (Red Line MT-LV is the commonly cited alternative). Clean the magnetic drain plugs and use new crush washers.
Tools: 10 mm hex bit · 24 mm socket · fluid pump · torque wrench · Toyota LT 75W-85 GL-5 · Toyota LF 75W transfer oil · washers: transfer case 90430-A0003, front drain 90430-24003, front fill 12157-10010

#### Front axle (differential-side) seal
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Half a day · cost Parts plus a refill of gear oil
Symptoms: Gear oil weeping where the CV axle enters the front differential; a puddle under the front of the truck.
Fix: Drain the front diff, support the truck and pull the wheel. Unplug and move the ABS sensor, separate the tie-rod end, remove the axle dust cap, retainer and 35 mm axle nut (4WD engaged and parking brake on to hold it). Remove the two lower control arm bolts, tap the axle out of the hub and pop the inner joint from the diff. Note the old seal's depth, pull it, clean the bore, oil the new seal and drive it in to the same depth (Trail4R used a 2 in PVC coupler). Reassemble: LCA bolts 118 ft-lb, axle nut 174 ft-lb, tie-rod castle nut 67 ft-lb, lugs to spec (Trail4R lists 85 ft-lb; a reader quoting the repair manual gives 76 ft-lb for alloy and 83 ft-lb for steel wheels) [CONFIRM IN MANUAL], then refill.
Tools: 19/21/35 mm sockets · breaker bar · seal puller · ball-joint separator · CV axle removal tool · seals: left 90311-47027; right 90311-47026 (2014+) or 90311-47013 (2010–13)

#### CV boot replacement (inner and outer)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A day; Trail4R's first axle removal alone took 2 hours · cost OEM boot kit plus grease; a shop if the axle won't release
Symptoms: Grease flung around the wheel well, a split boot, clicking on turns once dirt gets in. Lifted trucks with excessive droop tear boots on the lower control arm.
Fix: Jack only the side you're working on (keeps diff oil in), pull the wheel, unbolt the brake-line bracket (10 mm) and ABS sensor (12 mm), free the tie-rod end (19 mm castle nut) and remove the 35 mm axle nut. Unbolt the LCA (2 × 19 mm), swing the hub away and release the axle from the diff by tapping the inner cup while rotating it until the internal clip lines up. Mark the tripod and rollers, remove the C-clip, swap both boots with the kit's yellow (inner) and black (outer) grease, crimp the clamps with proper pliers — over-tightening tore Trail4R's on the trail — and refit with red Loctite on the LCA bolts and anti-seize on the hub splines.
Tools: OEM CV boot kit 04427-60131 · optional dust cover 41336-35020 and axle nut 90178-28002 · 19/35 mm sockets · impact or breaker bar · CV clamp pliers · retaining-ring pliers · torque wrench (50–250 ft-lb)

#### Aftermarket upper control arms
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time An afternoon with a helper · cost Arms plus a professional alignment
Symptoms: After a lift: out-of-spec caster/camber, upper ball joint at its angle limit, or you're installing coilovers anyway.
Fix: Grease the new arms' bushings and zerks first. Pull the wheel well splash shields, unbolt the ABS sensor brackets (10 mm) and brake-line bracket (12 mm), remove the cotter pin and 19 mm upper ball-joint nut, then the 19 mm pivot bolt (it's long; the inner fender may need bending). Fit the new arm with the correct spacers, pivot bolt front to back. Total Chaos's instructions, as followed by Trail4R: pivot bolt about 100 ft-lb, ball-joint 'king' nut about 82 ft-lb. Recheck after 100 miles and get it aligned before highway speeds.
Tools: 10/12/14/19 mm sockets · torque wrench to 100 ft-lb · grease gun · jack stands · e.g. Total Chaos 2010–2024 4Runner UCAs

#### Brake pads and rotors
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 4–6 hours front and rear with two people (Trail4R) · cost Parts plus your Saturday
Symptoms: Steering-wheel shake under braking (warped rotors — Trail4R blamed cold water crossings), noise, thin pads.
Fix: Front: unbolt the brake-line bracket (12 mm) and the caliper bolts, hang the caliper, push the pistons back, swap pads, pins and anti-rattle spring, knock off and replace the rotor. Rear: remove the caliper bracket bolts, release the parking brake before pulling the rotor (it has a drum-in-hat parking brake), fit new rotor, bracket and pads. Pump the pedal before driving. Trail4R lists 17 mm front caliper bolts but a reader reports 19 mm at 91 lb-ft — confirm against the FSM.
Tools: 12/17/19 mm sockets · piston compressor or clamp · mallet · brake grease · torque wrench · e.g. Powerstop kit (fits 2013+ per Trail4R)

#### Rear hatch window won't close (re-initialise and clean)
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 15 minutes · cost Free, unless the motor or regulator is actually dead
Symptoms: The rear glass bounces back down as if it found an obstruction, or stays down. Common after a battery disconnect or an obstruction event.
Fix: Initialise it: hold the switch down until the glass is fully open, then hold it up until it closes and keep holding about a second longer (Toyota TSB T-SB-0279-09 covers back-door window initialisation for early trucks). If it still balks, blow out the tracks with compressed air and wipe inside them with rubber cleaner on a doubled rag over a screwdriver. Check the hatch switch isn't physically stuck.
Tools: Compressed air · rubber cleaner · rags · flat screwdriver

#### Propeller shaft greasing
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost A tube of grease
Symptoms: Due every 5,000 miles on dirt or dusty roads, or when towing/heavily loaded, per Toyota's schedule as quoted by Trail4R. Dry joints may pop when greased.
Fix: 4x4 trucks have two shafts with six zerks total (two spider joints and a slip yoke on each). Clean each fitting, pump NLGI No. 2 lithium grease into the spider joints until fresh grease shows at all four caps, then wipe the excess. Go easy on the slip yokes — Trail4R uses about four pumps rear and two front, since over-packing stops the shaft extending properly. The front shaft is tight against the exhaust; rotate it by hand for access.
Tools: Grease gun (a locking coupler helps) · NLGI No. 2 lithium chassis grease · shop towels · wheel chocks

### Baseline service
The 1GR-FE and A750 drivetrain are durable but rarely serviced past oil changes: Toyota calls most driveline fluids 'inspect' unless you tow, carry roof loads or drive dusty roads — which describes most 4Runners. Baseline everything, including the transmission, then put the propshafts on a grease schedule.
- Engine oil & filter: 0W-20 full synthetic · ≈6.6 US qt with filter (Trail4R; Toyota-Club lists 6.2 L) · Toyota: 10,000 mi; Trail4R's authors run 5,000 mi (Cartridge filter in a plastic housing behind the front skid: drain the housing with the plastic tool in the filter box, fresh O-rings, 64 mm cap wrench, and line the metal tab back up. Don't over-tighten; use genuine housings.)
- Engine air filter: Panel filter · Check at every oil change (Replace when moderate dirt is visible (Trail4R).)
- Cabin air filter: Behind the glovebox · At least yearly (First suspect for a musty interior smell.)
- Spark plugs: Iridium long-life · part number and interval [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Replace if past the scheduled interval or undocumented (Pull and read the old plugs — they tell you how the engine has been running.)
- Coolant: Toyota Super Long Life Coolant (pink, pre-mixed) · 10.5 L (Toyota-Club) · Drain and refill if over 100,000 mi or undocumented; interval [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Pre-mixed — don't dilute.)
- Automatic transmission (5-speed A750): Toyota ATF WS · 10.7 L total; a drain and fill swaps ≈5 qt · Drain and fill now if undocumented (No dipstick: the level is set through the 5 mm Allen check plug at 104–113 °F in maintenance mode (see the repair card). A filter-and-pan job is a good baseline on a truck with no records.)
- Transfer case: Toyota Transfer Gear Oil LF 75W · ≈1.1 US qt (part-time) / 1.5 qt (full-time) · Toyota: 30,000 mi on dirty or dusty roads; Trail4R does all driveline fluids every 30,000 (24 mm plugs, 27 ft-lb. Don't swap with diff oil; Red Line MT-LV is the aftermarket alternative cited.)
- Front & rear differentials: Toyota Differential Gear Oil LT 75W-85 GL-5 · front ≈1.6 qt (part-time) / 1.5 qt (full-time) · rear ≈2.65–2.75 L / 2.8–2.9 qt (Trail4R and Toyota-Club disagree on which version holds more) [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Toyota: 15,000 mi when heavily loaded or with roof gear (Fill plug first. Front uses 10 mm hex plugs (48/29 ft-lb); rear 24 mm (36 ft-lb).)
- Power steering fluid: ATF Dexron II/III (Toyota-Club) · Check level and colour (Hydraulic rack on the 5th gen.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 · Toyota: every 2 years or 60,000 mi (per Trail4R) (Rear bleeds use the ABS pump with the ignition on and the pedal weighted — don't run it more than 100 seconds at a time. Bleeders 8 ft-lb.)
- Propshaft grease points: NLGI No. 2 lithium grease · six zerks on 4x4 trucks · Every 5,000 mi on dirt/dusty roads or when towing (Toyota schedule via Trail4R) (Spider joints until fresh grease shows at all four caps; only a few pumps on the slip yokes.)
- Serpentine belt: Toyota 90916-A2015 · Toyota: inspect at 63,000 mi, then every 18,000 mi (Spin the idler and tensioner pulleys by hand while the belt is off. The 1GR-FE uses a timing chain with no service interval.)
- PCV valve: Threads into the driver-side rear of the engine · 19 mm deep socket · Threebond 1324 · 20 ft-lb · No Toyota interval; Trail4R's author replaced his at 60,000 mi (If the ball inside doesn't rattle, it's stuck.)
- Battery: Group 34 fits (Trail4R used an Odyssey) · Load-test now (Switch any accessory that doesn't need constant power to avoid parasitic drain.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: Trail4R's short answer is 32 inches. Stock is 265/70R17 (31.6 in). A 275/70R17 or 255/75R17 (about 32.1 in) shouldn't rub; a 285/70R17 (32.7 in) is 'questionable' and may need a body-mount chop; 255/80R17 (33 in) and anything bigger needs a lift and trimming. Tire brand and wheel offset change the outcome.

Q: Which trims have the rear locker?
A: The Trail (2010–2016) and its renamed successor, the TRD Off-Road (2017–2024), which pair the electric rear locker with Crawl Control and Multi-Terrain Select. SR5 and Limited owners who want one retrofit an aftermarket unit — Trail4R documents an Eaton E-Locker install in an SR5.

Q: Do I want KDSS?
A: If you'll stay stock or near-stock, yes: owners praise the reduced body roll and slightly better articulation. If you plan a big lift or long travel, it's a complication — Trail4R puts the practical lift limit at about 3 inches and lists bracket, sway-bar and panhard fixes for lifted KDSS trucks. Leaking KDSS cylinders are an expensive repair.

Q: Part-time or full-time 4WD?
A: SR5, Trail and TRD Off-Road 4x4s use a part-time two-speed transfer case with no centre differential, so 4H locks the front and rear driveshafts together. The Limited used full-time 4WD. All trucks have A-TRAC.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: 5,000 lb, per Car and Driver. The 6th gen raised that to 6,000.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: EPA-rated 16 city / 19 highway (17 combined) in later years. Car and Driver's 2022 TRD Pro averaged 15 mpg overall and 17 mpg on its 75-mph highway test, good for about 390 miles of highway range.

Q: Does the 4.0 V6 have a timing belt?
A: No — the 1GR-FE uses a timing chain with no scheduled replacement interval, meant to last the life of the engine. The serpentine belt is the wear item: Toyota calls for inspection at 63,000 miles and every 18,000 thereafter.

Q: What are the fluid capacities?
A: Per Toyota-Club's N280 data: engine oil with filter 6.2 L (Trail4R refills with about 6.6 qt of 0W-20); ATF WS 10.7 L total; front diff 1.55 L (part-time) / 1.40 L (full-time); rear diff 2.70 L without locker / 2.65 L with; transfer case 1.00 L (part-time) / 1.40 L (full-time); coolant 10.5 L. Diff oil is Toyota LT 75W-85 GL-5.

Q: Which years should I buy or avoid?
A: There's no bad engine year, so buy on condition. Autotrader says the fifth generation has no major issues of concern and recommends a late truck, preferably 2020–2024, which get TSS-P safety tech and CarPlay; it's 'OK' with 2013–2015 and notes owner reports of brake, electrical, rust and paint gripes on 2010–2012. SlashGear singles out 2013–2016 for higher complaint and recall counts. Whatever the year, confirm the Takata airbag (2010–2016) and fuel pump (2014–2015 and 2018–2019) recalls are closed.

Q: What lift options are there?
A: Trail4R's shortlist runs from Old Man Emu (2.5–3 in) and Bilstein 6112/5160 to Eibach, Falcon, OME BP-51, Dobinsons MRR, ICON, Fox and King. Beyond about 2.5–3 in, plan on aftermarket upper control arms and, on KDSS trucks, sway-bar and panhard corrections.

Q: Why does my truck lean to the driver's side?
A: Toyota puts heavy items — battery, driveshafts, transfer case, fuel tank — on the driver's side, leaving that side typically ¼ to ¾ in lower. Trail4R fixed it with a thicker top spacer on the driver's-side coilover than on the passenger side.

## Toyota 4Runner 6th Gen (2025–present)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/4runner/6th-gen/
Codes: N500, i-FORCE, i-FORCE MAX

Verdict: Toyota finally replaced the V6, the five-speed and the 2009 dashboard — and somehow kept the roll-down rear window and the attitude. Quicker, smarter and far nicer to live with; whether a turbo four and a hybrid will rack up 300,000 miles like the old truck is the one test it hasn't sat yet.

After fifteen model years of the 5th gen, Toyota revealed its replacement on 9 April 2024 and started building it at Tahara, Japan, that December — later than planned, because parts shared with other models were in short supply. The N500 rides on the TNGA-F (GA-F) ladder frame that also underpins the Tacoma, the Land Cruiser 250 and the Lexus GX 550. It swaps the old 4.0 V6 for a 2.4-litre turbo four, offers a hybrid for the first time, and still lowers its rear glass into the tailgate at the touch of a button.

### THE TACOMA WITH A ROOF
Car and Driver put it bluntly: the new 4Runner is "essentially an SUV version of the Tacoma," sharing its mechanicals, cabin switchgear and much of its styling. The wheelbase grows 2.4 inches to 112.2, matching the Land Cruiser and GX 550, and most of that stretch went in ahead of the front doors to free up space around the body mounts. That is why TRD Off-Road, TRD Pro and Trailhunter trucks can leave the factory on 33-inch tires — something 5th gen owners did with a grinder.
There are nine trims: SR5, TRD Sport, TRD Sport Premium, TRD Off-Road, TRD Off-Road Premium, Limited, Platinum, TRD Pro and Trailhunter. KDSS, the hydraulically linked anti-roll bars of the old truck, is gone. In its place the TRD Pro and Trailhunter get an electronically disconnecting front anti-roll bar, optional on the TRD Off-Road. Those three trims also get an electronic rear locker; the rest make do with a limited-slip rear differential.

### FOUR CYLINDERS, EIGHT GEARS, ONE BATTERY
Every 6th gen uses the T24A-FTS 2.4-litre turbo four and an eight-speed automatic. In i-FORCE form it makes 278 hp and 317 lb-ft, with peak torque at 1,700 rpm against the old V6's 4,400. The i-FORCE MAX hybrid sandwiches a 48-hp motor between engine and gearbox for 326 hp and 465 lb-ft; it is standard on the TRD Pro, Trailhunter and Platinum and optional on the TRD Off-Road and Limited. Towing rises from 5,000 lb to 6,000 lb with either.
Car and Driver's numbers are good rather than transformative: 7.5 seconds to 60 mph for a gas 4WD truck and 6.7 for a hybrid Trailhunter, against 7.7 for the last V6 TRD Pro it tested. EPA ratings climb to 21–22 mpg combined for the gas truck and 23 for the hybrid, though C/D's heavy Trailhunter managed only 17 mpg observed. The same test noted transmission temperatures 'flirting with the red zone' after repeated acceleration runs — an observation 6th gen forum owners have echoed on long off-road climbs.

### TRD PRO VERSUS TRAILHUNTER
The two flagships split the off-road mission. The TRD Pro runs manually adjustable 2.5-inch Fox internal-bypass dampers (C/D's reveal identified them as QS3s), forged-aluminium upper control arms, a TRD intake and a cat-back exhaust — tuned, like the Tacoma's, for fast desert running. The Trailhunter is the overlander: ARB Old Man Emu 2.5-inch dampers with rear remote reservoirs, an ARB-designed roof rack, steel skid plates, an onboard compressor in production form, and 10.1 inches of ground clearance against at least 8.1 on lesser trims.
Both wear 33-inch Toyo Open Country A/T III tires in 265/70R18 and list at $68,350 in Car and Driver's 2025 pricing, against $42,220 for a base SR5. That puts the top trims uncomfortably close to the Land Cruiser 250 and GX 550; C/D's own pick was the $50,640 TRD Off-Road 4WD. Toyota sold 98,805 4Runners in the US in 2025, so the formula clearly still works, and for 2026 Car and Driver reports no major changes.

### Data plate
- Chassis: N500 · TNGA-F (GA-F)
- Years: 2025–present (production from Dec 2024)
- Built: Tahara, Japan · LHD only
- Engine: T24A-FTS 2.4 turbo I4
- Output (I-Force): 278 hp · 317 lb-ft
- Output (I-Force Max): 326 hp · 465 lb-ft
- Transmission: 8-spd automatic
- 4Wd: Part-time w/ low range or full-time w/ locking centre diff
- Wheelbase: 112.2 in
- Length: 194.9 in
- Curb Weight: 4,456–5,454 lb
- Towing: 6,000 lb

### Engineering
Mechanically the N500 is a TNGA-F truck: a new ladder frame shared with the Tacoma, Land Cruiser 250 and GX 550, double-wishbone front suspension and a multilink live rear axle, with geometry reworked from the old J150-era layout. The drivetrain menu spans rear-drive, part-time 4WD with low range, and full-time 4WD with a locking centre differential, while the off-road trims trade KDSS for an electronic front anti-roll-bar disconnect.
- Chassis: TNGA-F ladder frame (Shared with Tacoma, Land Cruiser 250 and GX 550; 112.2 in wheelbase, stretched at the front for tire clearance.)
- Suspension: IFS + multilink live axle (Control arms up front; TRD Pro adds forged-aluminium UCAs and Fox dampers, Trailhunter gets OME.)
- Engine: T24A-FTS 2.4 turbo I4 (i-FORCE: 278 hp / 317 lb-ft, peak torque at 1,700 rpm. Eight-speed automatic on every truck.)
- Hybrid: i-FORCE MAX (48-hp motor in the transmission; 326 hp / 465 lb-ft. Battery (≈0.9 kWh, per Car and Driver's estimate) under the cargo floor rules out the third row.)
- 4Wd: Part-time or full-time (Part-time with low range on most 4WD trucks; full-time with locking centre diff on Platinum and hybrid Limited.)
- Locker & Bar: Rear e-locker + front disconnect (Locker on TRD Off-Road, TRD Pro, Trailhunter (others: limited-slip). Disconnecting front bar std on Pro/Trailhunter, optional on TRD Off-Road.)

### Versions

- 2025– · N500 · TRD Off-Road (Premium) · i-FORCE or i-FORCE MAX · 278 / 326 hp · 33-in tires, Bilstein shocks, rear locker; front bar disconnect optional. C/D's pick at $50,640.
- 2025– · N500 · Limited / Platinum · i-FORCE or MAX (Platinum: MAX) · 278 / 326 hp · Adaptive dampers and extra drive modes; full-time 4WD on Platinum and hybrid Limited.
- 2025– · N500 · TRD Pro · i-FORCE MAX hybrid · 326 hp / 465 lb-ft · Fox 2.5 internal-bypass dampers, forged UCAs, front bar disconnect, rear locker, 265/70R18.
- 2025– · N500 · Trailhunter · i-FORCE MAX hybrid · 323 hp (C/D) · OME 2.5 dampers, ARB rack, high intake, steel skids, 10.1 in clearance.
- 2026 · N500 · Unchanged · — · Car and Driver reports no major updates for 2026.

- 2025: Launch: 2.4 turbo i-Force (278 hp) or i-Force Max hybrid (326 hp), eight-speed auto, nine trims including new Trailhunter and Platinum; towing up to 6,000 lb
- 2026: No major changes reported by Car and Driver

- Towing: 6,000 lb (2,720 kg) (gas and hybrid)
- Fuel tank: 19 gal (72 L)
- Ground clearance: 8.1–10.1 in (206–257 mm) (trim-dependent; Trailhunter 10.1 in (Car and Driver))
- Approach / departure: 32° / 24°
- Fuel economy: EPA 20 city / 24 hwy / 21 combined (Limited 4WD) · hybrid 23 / 24 / 23 (C&D observed 18 mpg (Limited 4WD) and 17 mpg (hybrid))
- Curb weight: 4,456–5,454 lb (2,021–2,474 kg)

- Center Bore: 95.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M14x1.5
- Lug Torque: 97 lb-ft (131 N·m) per 4Runner6G owners' torque list [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 285/70R17 (≈33 in) (4Runner6G SR5 owners report no rubbing at stock height; some say the stock 17x7 wheel is too narrow for it)

### Buying checks
- Hybrid or not?: The hybrid is mandatory on TRD Pro, Trailhunter and Platinum and a $2,800 option elsewhere (C/D). It brings torque and 23 mpg combined but also weight, a higher cargo floor and no third row. C/D's first drive would skip it; its Tacoma tests found the non-hybrid quicker.
- Know which trims have what: Only the TRD Off-Road, TRD Pro and Trailhunter have the electronic rear locker; the front anti-roll-bar disconnect is standard on Pro and Trailhunter and optional on the TRD Off-Road. Check the window sticker rather than the badge.
- Transmission temperatures: Car and Driver saw transmission temps near the red zone during repeated acceleration runs, and forum owners report warnings on long off-road climbs. On a test drive with grades, watch the transmission temperature display; owners suggest 4Lo or holding lower gears in S mode.
- Brake squeal TSB: Front brakes that squeal in reverse are covered by Toyota TSB T-SB-0046-25, since superseded by T-SB-0006-26, which replaces pads, shims and fitting kit under the 36-month/36,000-mile warranty. Ask whether it has been done.
- Steering clunk: Some early owners on 4Runner6G.com report a clunk felt through the wheel and brake pedal that Toyota fixed under warranty with a new steering shaft assembly. Drive over broken pavement and feel for it.
- Water where it shouldn't be: Owners have found water collecting inside the liftgate, cured by removing plugs from its weep holes, and threads report water dripping from the rear doors and mildew in window mouldings. Open the liftgate after rain or a wash.
- Recalls and campaigns: Run the VIN at NHTSA: 2025 trucks are in an instrument-panel software recall (25V-595), several 2026 trucks in load-capacity label recalls (26V-571, 26V-282), and owners have received a front air-dam hardware campaign letter.
- Range: Forum owners complain of roughly 280 miles between fill-ups in mixed use. If you tow or roam far from fuel, plan for a jerry can — an aftermarket long-range tank wasn't confirmed for the 4Runner in that thread.

### Common repairs
#### Front brake squeal fix (TSB pad and shim kit)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Dealer flat-rate ≈ 0.9 hours (TSB op BR2503) · cost Free under the 36-month/36,000-mile warranty; owners estimate ≈ $20 in shims and grease DIY
Symptoms: Squeal from the front brakes, typically when reversing and often worse cold. TSB T-SB-0046-25 applies to 2025 4Runner and 4Runner Hybrid (and 2024–25 Land Cruiser).
Fix: Follow the bulletin's repair procedure (now T-SB-0006-26): remove the front pads, spread the caliper pistons with the wide piston-spreader tool, and fit the revised pad kit with the new anti-squeal shims and anti-rattle springs, greased with the supplied caliper grease. Owners on 4Runner6G.com believe the original shims were the culprit. Pump the pedal before driving and bed the pads in.
Tools: Disc brake piston spreader (Toyota SST 09719-77020 / 09719-77050) · caliper grease · torque wrench · pad kit 04465-34040 · shim kit 04945-0C060 · fitting kit 04947-0C030

#### Front and rear differential fluid
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time A morning · cost ≈ $220 DIY with aftermarket fluids to ≈ $500 all-OEM; dealer about $800 including transfer case (forum estimate)
Symptoms: Due every 15,000 miles under severe use (towing, roof loads, heavy loading) per the maintenance chart; otherwise inspect. Many owners do an early break-in change.
Fix: Remove the skid plates (12 mm, eight bolts). Always loosen the fill plug before the drain. Front: 10 mm hex plugs; refill with 75W-85 GL-5 to about 1.4 qt (part-time 4WD) or 1.3 qt (full-time); drain 48 ft-lb, fill 29 ft-lb. Rear: 24 mm plugs, about 5.9 qt (6.9 qt on Trailhunter), both 36 ft-lb. Crush washers go smooth side toward the housing.
Tools: 10 mm hex bit · 24 mm socket · 12 mm socket · fluid pump · 6-qt drain pan · Toyota LT 75W-85 GL-5 (00279-DGOLT-01) · washers 12157-10010 (front fill, both rear) and 90430-24017 (front drain)

#### Transfer case fluid
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost Toyota LF fluid ≈ $46–66 per litre (forum prices)
Symptoms: Due at the transfer-case interval in the maintenance chart for dusty roads or towing; first change is a common break-in item.
Fix: Crack the fill plug, then drain. Refill with Toyota Transfer Gear Oil LF to 0–5 mm below the bottom lip of the fill hole — about 1.2 qt (part-time) or 1.5 qt (full-time) — wait five minutes and recheck. Plugs 27 ft-lb with new washers. Don't swap diff oil and transfer fluid; Red Line MT-LV 70W/75W is the aftermarket alternative cited for part-time gas trucks.
Tools: 24 mm socket (per Tacoma/LC250 data; confirm on your truck) · fluid pump · torque wrench · Toyota LF 00279-DGOLF · washers 90430-A0003 ×2

#### Engine oil and filter (2.4 turbo)
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost Oil and a filter
Symptoms: Every 10,000 miles or 12 months normally; every 5,000 miles or 6 months when mostly on dirt or dusty roads, per the maintenance chart.
Fix: Remove the access panel, drain the oil and change the filter. Owners cite a 5.9-qt capacity. A member confirmed 30 ft-lb for the drain plug from dealer repair documentation; filters are typically spun on hand-tight plus about three-quarters of a turn. Reset the maintenance reminder.
Tools: Drain pan · filter wrench · torque wrench · new drain-plug washer · Toyota-spec synthetic oil

#### Cabin and hybrid-battery filters
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 20 minutes · cost Filters only
Symptoms: Weak HVAC airflow; on i-FORCE MAX trucks used on dusty roads, clogged hybrid battery intake filters that can let the pack run hot.
Fix: Cabin: lower the glovebox by pushing in its sides, pull the filter cartridge, fit the new filter with the airflow arrows pointing down (Toyota says check every 15,000 miles). Hybrid: the two intake filters sit behind the second-row seats, one per side — pry the lower outer corner of each cover with a trim tool, pull the cover off, swap the filter and clip it back with the top tabs first.
Tools: Trim tool · cabin filter 87139-0C010 (or carbon 87139-30110) · hybrid battery filters G92DH-34010 / G92DJ-34010

#### Propeller shaft greasing
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost A tube of grease
Symptoms: Part of dusty-road and towing maintenance. Owners count five zerks on a 4WD truck.
Fix: Grease both spider joints on each shaft and the front slip yoke (a couple of short pumps only; over-packing a slip yoke is bad). The rear slip yoke is booted with no zerk, so servicing it means dropping the shaft. Wipe off excess grease.
Tools: Grease gun · lithium-base chassis grease · creeper

#### Water in the liftgate (weep-hole plugs)
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 10 minutes · cost Free
Symptoms: Water sloshing inside the liftgate or dripping from the inner panel with the gate open, after rain or a wash.
Fix: Under the liftgate, find the small rubber plugs in the drain holes and pull them so water can escape — a 4Runner6G.com owner had water gush out. Leave the large centre plug in place; another owner points out it's an access hole, not a drain.
Tools: Trim tool or small screwdriver

### Baseline service
A 6th gen is new enough that 'baseline' mostly means confirming the dealer did what the warranty schedule asks and catching up the severe-service items Toyota lists for dusty roads, towing and roof loads. Check that the front-brake squeal TSB (now T-SB-0006-26) and any campaigns are closed out, then do the driveline fluids if the truck has seen dirt.
- Engine oil & filter: SAE 0W-20 (5W-20 only as a stopgap) · ILSAC GF-6A · ≈5.9 US qt per owners (Toyota-Club lists 5.6 L) · 10,000 mi / 12 months; 5,000 mi / 6 months on dirt or dusty roads (Filter 90915-YZZN1: hand-tight plus ¾ turn after gasket contact. One Trailhunter owner's VIN lookup flagged that filter as a possible misfit — check by VIN on hybrids.)
- Engine air filter: 17801-YZZ11 (standard). TRD Pro / Trailhunter use a reusable conical filter (Toyota PTR03-35241-AA) · Inspect every 5,000 mi on dusty roads (The Pro/Trailhunter filter is meant to be cleaned, not binned.)
- Cabin air filter: 87139-0C010 (standard) or 87139-30110 (carbon) · Check every 15,000 mi (Behind the glovebox; airflow arrows point down.)
- Hybrid battery intake filters (i-FORCE MAX): G92DH-34010 and G92DJ-34010 · Inspect at every oil change if you drive dusty roads or carry a dog (Behind the second-row seats, one per side. Owners report clogged filters; driving dirt roads with the rear window down makes it worse.)
- Spark plugs: Toyota 90919-01303 is listed for the T24A-FTS (in the NX350) — confirm 4Runner fitment by VIN · Per the maintenance chart [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Required service under the emission-control warranty, so keep receipts.)
- Engine (and intercooler / inverter) coolant: Toyota Super Long Life Coolant · gas ≈12.0 L; hybrid 11.4 L engine + 2.3 L inverter (PCU) · First at 100,000 mi / 120 months, then every 50,000 mi / 60 months (Inspect level and freeze point of both loops on hybrids.)
- Automatic transmission (8-speed): Toyota ATF WS · 11.5 L (gas) / 12.5 L (hybrid) total · Inspect per chart; replace under severe service (towing, long idling) (Owners report overheating on long low-speed climbs off-road — worth a fluid check on any truck that's been worked hard.)
- Transfer case: Toyota Transfer Gear Oil LF 75W · 1.1 L (part-time) / 1.4 L (full-time) · Replace on the severe-service schedule (dusty roads, towing) (Fill to 0–5 mm below the fill hole, wait five minutes, recheck. Plugs 27 ft-lb.)
- Front & rear differentials: Toyota Differential Gear Oil LT 75W-85 GL-5 · front 1.3 L (part-time) / 1.2 L (full-time) · rear 5.6 L (6.5 L Trailhunter) · Every 15,000 mi when towing, using a roof carrier or heavily loaded (Many owners do an early break-in change. The rear holds far more than a Tacoma's — buy about 8 qt for both diffs.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 / DOT 4 (SAE J1703/J1704) · Inspect level/condition per chart (Confirm the squeal TSB pads were fitted if the truck squeals in reverse.)
- Propshaft grease & bolt torque: NLGI No. 2 grease · five zerks on 4WD (rear slip yoke is booted) · Grease on the dusty-road schedule; the chart also calls for propeller-shaft bolt re-torque (Short pumps on the front slip yoke only.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: TRD Off-Road, TRD Pro and Trailhunter trucks already run 33-inch tires (265/70R18) from the factory. SR5 owners on 4Runner6G.com report 285/70R17 (about 33 in) on stock height without rubbing, though they argue about whether the stock 17×7 wheel is too narrow for that tire; one owner saw the tread balloon and moved to 8.5-in-wide wheels.

Q: Should I get the hybrid?
A: It's the only choice on the TRD Pro, Trailhunter and Platinum. Elsewhere, Car and Driver says the extra cost isn't worth it: the gas truck is lighter, keeps the optional third row and is rated 21–22 mpg combined against the hybrid's 23. The hybrid's real gain is torque — 465 lb-ft against 317.

Q: Which trims have a locker and the sway-bar disconnect?
A: The electronic rear locker comes on the TRD Off-Road, TRD Pro and Trailhunter; other trims get a limited-slip rear differential. The disconnecting front anti-roll bar is standard on the TRD Pro and Trailhunter and optional on the TRD Off-Road.

Q: Does it still have KDSS?
A: No. Car and Driver confirms KDSS is gone, replaced by the electronic front bar disconnect, and Wikipedia notes that from 2025 KDSS is exclusive to Lexus.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: 6,000 lb, hybrid or not — 1,000 lb more than the 5th gen.

Q: What fuel economy and range should I expect?
A: EPA: up to 20 city / 26 highway / 22 combined for the gas truck (21 combined in 4WD), 23 combined for the hybrid. Car and Driver's 4WD Limited returned 21 mpg on its 75-mph highway test; its Trailhunter averaged 17 mpg. Owners complain about range, with one reporting about 280 miles between fill-ups.

Q: Is the transmission overheating issue real?
A: Car and Driver saw the eight-speed's temperatures approach the red zone after repeated acceleration runs, and some owners report warnings on long, slow off-road climbs. Owners' advice: use 4Lo at low speeds or hold a lower gear in S mode, and report it to Toyota if it happens.

Q: What are the oil change and fluid intervals?
A: Oil and filter every 10,000 miles or 12 months, or 5,000 miles / 6 months if mostly on dirt or dusty roads; differential oil at 15,000-mile intervals under severe use. Owners cite 5.9 qt of engine oil, about 1.4 qt front and 5.9 qt rear diff oil (6.9 qt on the Trailhunter), and 1.2–1.5 qt in the transfer case.

Q: Can I get a third row?
A: Only on the SR5 and non-hybrid Limited, and Car and Driver describes the rearmost seats as little more than floor-mounted jump seats. The hybrid's battery lives under the cargo floor, so no hybrid gets a third row.

Q: What lift options are there yet?
A: The aftermarket moved quickly: leveling and lift kits from ReadyLift and TORQ, Total Chaos kits with King shocks, Dirt King coilovers, plus upper control arms from Total Chaos, Peak and Westcott. Forum members are still waiting for news of an OEM TRD lift.

Q: Did it keep the roll-down rear window?
A: Yes. Wikipedia notes the engineers kept it by evaluating every component of the mechanism and trimming weight where they could.
