# Chevrolet K5 Blazer & Suburban (1969–1991)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/chevrolet/

Chevrolet came late to the off-road wagon fight. Ford had the Bronco and International had the Scout, so for 1969 Chevrolet shortened its K10 half-ton pickup from a 115-inch to a 104-inch wheelbase and called the result the K5 Blazer. It was bigger than both rivals, with a removable top, an optional passenger seat and the same engines and parts as the pickup. By 1970 it was outselling them. That year GMC also started selling it as the GMC Jimmy. The first trucks, the 1969–72 K5 Blazer, had a full-length lift-off top. For 1973 GM moved to the 'Rounded Line' platform that enthusiasts call the square body. The 1973–91 K5 Blazer got a half-cab body in 1976, small-block V8s, a 6.2-liter diesel from 1982 and a military version, the M1009. Its rear roof still came off right up to 1991. The 1973–91 Suburban was built on the same chassis as a truck-based station wagon with four doors and up to nine seats. Chevrolet and GMC both sold it under the Suburban name. For 1992 the whole family moved to the GMT400 platform. The Jimmy became the GMC Yukon, and the full-size Blazer later became the Tahoe.

Verdict: General Motors took a half-ton pickup, cut a bit off the back and made the roof optional, and the Bronco and Scout never quite recovered. Then it did the opposite with the Suburban, giving it nine seats and four doors. Neither one is subtle, and both are easy to keep running.

## Chevrolet K5 Blazer (1st generation) (1969–1972)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/chevrolet/k5-blazer-1st/
Codes: K5, GMC Jimmy, KE/KS-1550

Verdict: Chevrolet showed up late to the Bronco-and-Scout party, so it brought a bigger truck: a half-ton pickup with the back cut off and the roof made optional. Four model years, one full-length lift-off top and a parts bin shared with every Chevy pickup made it the one rivals had to answer.

By 1969 Ford had the Bronco, International had the Scout and Jeep had the CJ-5, and General Motors had nothing in the small, go-anywhere class. Chevrolet's answer was not small at all. The K5 Blazer took the half-ton K10 4x4 pickup, cut the wheelbase from 115 to 104 inches, and gave it a removable top. Wikipedia credits that pickup basis with three advantages over the rivals: more cargo room, a better on-road ride from the wider track and longer wheelbase, and lower cost, because most of the parts were already on a production line.

### A PICKUP WITH THE BACK CUT OFF
MotorTrend's history of the K5 puts it bluntly: Ford had the Bronco, Jeep had the CJ, even a tractor company had the Scout, and GM had nothing. Basing the Blazer on the short-box K10 let Chevrolet reach the market quickly and with more capability than the competition. The base truck was spartan to the point of comedy. MotorTrend notes that early base Blazers came without a roof or a passenger seat, so the driver had the only seat in the house.
Underneath it was all 1969 Chevy truck: a ladder frame, tapered leaf springs at both ends, a Dana 44 front axle and a GM 12-bolt rear. Chevrolet's 1969 spec sheet lists 8 inches of ground clearance, a 35-degree approach angle, a 25-degree departure angle, a 23.5-gallon tank and a 5,000 lb maximum GVW. Engines matched the pickups: the 250 six as standard, a 307 V8, and the 350 V8, which came only with the four-speed SM465 or the Turbo Hydra-Matic 350.

### THE TOP COMES OFF
The first-generation Blazer is the only K5 whose whole roof comes off. MotorTrend describes a completely removable hardtop that left only the windshield sticking up. Chevrolet's 1971 brochure describes the auxiliary top as reinforced fiberglass with textured paint in black or white, with side rear windows and a lift tailgate, and says it 'bolts on' and 'lifts off quickly.' A canvas soft top on steel framing was a dealer-installed accessory. Chevrolet claimed it went up or down in under two minutes.
The 1973–75 Blazers on the new square-body chassis kept a fully removable top. From 1976 a fixed steel roof covered the front seats and only the rear section came off. If you want to drive with nothing above you but sky and the windshield header, the 1969–72 trucks are where the K5 story begins. They're also the shortest K5s, at 177.5 to 180 inches against 184.8 for the 1973 truck, which helps on tight trails.

### THE 1971–72 TRUCKS
The changes came fast. For 1970 Chevrolet added a two-wheel-drive Blazer with coil-spring independent front suspension, and GMC got its own version, the Jimmy. For 1971, power front disc brakes became standard across GM's light trucks, replacing four-wheel drums. The 1971 truck also got an egg-crate grille and grew to 180 inches long. That year's brochure pushed the CST package: bucket seats, a console, chrome bumpers, extra insulation and deep-twist carpet.
For 1972 the 292 six disappeared from the option list, and the 350 was rated at 175 net horsepower. Then sales took off. CK5's model-year figures show production going from 4,935 in 1969 to 44,266 in 1972, matching MotorTrend's claim that sales grew roughly tenfold over the first generation. In April 1970 Car and Driver wrote, and Chevrolet happily quoted in its 1971 brochure, that someone had finally discarded the idea that four-wheel-drive vehicles could only be operated by ex-tank commanders and veteran truck drivers.

### WHY IT MATTERS
Wikipedia says the Blazer had overtaken its rivals by 1970. Dodge answered with the Ramcharger and Jeep with the SJ Cherokee for 1974, and in 1978 Ford moved the Bronco onto a shortened F-100 platform specifically to fight the K5. The truck-based SUV recipe that the later K5, the Tahoe and nearly every full-size SUV since have followed starts with these four model years.
Today the early Blazer and Jimmy are serious collector trucks. Recent Bring a Trailer results for original-spec examples run from the mid-$20,000s to $100,000, with resto-mods higher still. Parts are easy because so much is shared with 1967–72 Chevy and GMC pickups, and reproduction sheet metal and seals are plentiful. Rust and tired frames are where the money goes, so buy the best body you can afford and fix the drivetrain later.

### Data plate
- Model Years: 1969–1972 (GMC Jimmy from 1970)
- Basis: Shortened 1969–72 K10 half-ton 4x4
- Wheelbase: 104 in (2,642 mm)
- Length: 177.5 in (1969) · 180 in (1971)
- Width: 79 in
- Engines: 250 I6 · 292 I6 (1970–71) · 307 V8 · 350 V8
- Transmissions: 3-spd manual · SM465 4-spd · TH350 3-spd auto
- Transfer Case: Dana 20 (manual only) or NP205
- Axles: Dana 44 front · GM 12-bolt semi-floating rear
- Brakes: Drums (1969–70) · power front discs (1971–72)
- Ground Clearance: 8 in · 35° approach / 25° departure (1969)
- Fuel Tank: 23.5 gal (1969 spec) · 21 gal (1971 spec)
- Max Gvw: 5,000 lb
- Wheel Bolt Pattern: 6 x 5.5 in

### Engineering
The first K5 is a 1969–72 K10 half-ton 4x4 shortened to a 104-inch wheelbase. It has a ladder frame, tapered leaf springs at all four corners, a Dana 44 front axle and a GM 12-bolt semi-floating rear. The engine drives through a three- or four-speed manual or a TH350 automatic to a two-speed transfer case, which is either a Dana 20 or a New Process 205. The open body takes a full-length fiberglass hardtop or a canvas soft top.
- Chassis: Shortened K10 ladder frame, 104 in wheelbase (Cut down from the 115 in half-ton pickup. 177.5 in long in 1969, 180 in from 1971.)
- Front Axle: Dana 44, leaf springs (Open-knuckle Dana 44 with manual locking hubs (BaT 1969 listing). 3.73 gears standard, 3.07 optional with the 350.)
- Rear Axle: GM 12-bolt, semi-floating (8.875 in ring gear per CK5's spec sheet. Positraction was optional.)
- Transfer Case: Dana 20 or NP205, part-time (The Dana 20 (2.03:1 low) came only with manuals. The gear-driven NP205 (1.96:1 low) came with the automatic and was optional with manuals.)
- Engines: 250 I6 · 307 V8 · 350 V8 (1971 ratings: 110, 135 and 170 net hp. The 292 six is listed for 1970–71. The 350 was rated at 175 net hp for 1972.)
- Roof: Full lift-off top (Textured fiberglass hardtop in black or white, or a dealer canvas top. The only K5 generation with no fixed roof.)

### Versions
- 1969 · K5 Blazer (4x4 only) · 250 I6 · 307 V8 · 350 V8 · 110 / 135 / 170 net hp · Launch year. Four-wheel drums, top and passenger seat optional. 4,935 built.
- 1970 · K5 Blazer · GMC Jimmy (new) · + 292 I6 · 292: 125 net hp · Two-wheel-drive Blazer and the GMC Jimmy arrive. New grille with six groups of 'dashes'. 11,527 built.
- 1971 · K5 Blazer / Jimmy · 250 I6 · 292 I6 · 307 V8 · 350 V8 · 145 / — / 200 / 250 gross hp · Power front disc brakes standard. Egg-crate grille, 180 in length. 17,220 built.
- 1972 · K5 Blazer / Jimmy · 250 I6 · 307 V8 · 350 V8 · 350: 175 net hp · 292 dropped. Grille surround no longer black. 44,266 built.
- 1970–1972 · GMC Jimmy KE/KS-1550 · Same as Chevrolet · — · GMC grille and badging. 4,600–5,000 lb GVW on the 4x4s (1971 brochure).

### Year-by-year
- 1969: K5 Blazer launches as a 4x4 only. 250 six, 307 and 350 V8s; four-wheel drum brakes; hardtop, soft top and passenger seat all optional. Aluminum grille center embossed CHEVROLET, bowtie on the hood. 4,935 built
- 1970: Two-wheel-drive Blazer with coil-spring IFS (fewer than 1,000 built that year per CK5). GMC Jimmy introduced. 292 six optional. New grille with six groups of 'dashes'
- 1971: Power front disc brakes standard across GM light trucks. Egg-crate grille, length grows to 180 in
- 1972: 292 six dropped; 350 rated at 175 net hp. Grille surround no longer black. Production jumps to 44,266
- 1973: Replaced by the square-body K5 on the new Rounded Line chassis, which kept a fully removable top until 1975

### Capability
- Wheelbase: 104 in (2,642 mm)
- Ground clearance: 8 in (203 mm) (1969 spec sheet)
- Approach / departure: 35° / 25° (1969 spec sheet)
- Fuel tank: 23.5 gal (89 L) (1969 spec sheet; the 1971 sheet lists 21 gal)
- Max GVW: 5,000 lb (2,268 kg)
- Front axle capacity: 3,300 lb (1969 and 1971 spec sheets)
- Turning circle: 36.66 ft (11.2 m) curb to curb (1971 brochure, 4x4)
- Curb weight: 3,875 lb (1,758 kg) (Wikipedia, citing Popular Science (May 1969))

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 7.35-15 (1969 standard), E78-15B (1971 standard, 4x4), Options to 10.00-16.5 (1969–71 spec sheets)
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 33x12.50R15 (On 15x8 wheels with healthy springs. Owners say 32x11.50 is the limit on sagging springs, and 33x14.50s rubbed the springs on one truck. Expect contact off-road at full stuff.)
- Biggest tire, 4 in lift: 35 in (One CK5 owner ran 35s on a 4 in lift on the highway, but warns that 4 in isn't enough off-road once the axle articulates.)
- Biggest tire, 5 in lift: 33 in (A 5 in Tuff Country lift runs 33s with no rubbing. The owner thought 35s would fit but would need gears deeper than the stock 3.73s.)

### Buying checks
- Rust first, drivetrain second: Velocity Restorations lists the floorboards, wheel wells, inner fenders and door bottoms as the usual rust spots. The Drive adds the top of the windshield frame. Fresh paint can hide all of it, so bring a magnet and look underneath.
- Inspect the frame at the steering box: Offroad Design says straight-axle GM trucks are notorious for frame cracks where the steering box mounts, especially with lifts, big tires and off-road use. Look for cracks and old weld repairs on the driver's-side rail ahead of the front axle.
- Is the top there, and does it fit?: Many first-gen trucks have lost their hardtop or soft top. The Drive notes that the fiberglass top's textured finish is hard to match in repairs. Check the top's mounting edge, the liftgate and the seals, because a leaky or missing top is expensive to sort out.
- Work out what has been swapped: Recent BaT results include LS, Vortec, 383, 454 and 6.2 L swaps alongside original trucks. Velocity advises caution unless swap work is documented and done by a qualified builder. Decide whether you're paying for originality or for the build.
- Read the SPID decal: Factory equipment and paint are listed on the Service Parts Identification decal inside the glovebox, per a 1969 BaT listing. Use it to check a claimed CST, Positraction or V8 truck.
- Expect a loose chassis: The Drive warns that the chassis is flexible and the steering has play, and that a big power upgrade can make the handling worse. Budget for steering-box, tie-rod and bushing work, and drive it before you agree a price.
- Check which transfer case and hubs it has: Manual trucks may have the Dana 20 or the NP205. Automatic trucks have the NP205. Offroad Design notes the NP205's tag sits above the front output and that the case is one piece of cast iron. Make sure the hubs lock and unlock.
- Mind the brakes on 1969–70 trucks: Front discs became standard for 1971. Earlier trucks have four-wheel drums unless they've been converted, so ask what has been changed and how well it was done.

### Common repairs
#### Brace the steering box mount before the frame cracks
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost Parts plus a drill and basic hand tools
Symptoms: Steering that wanders or clunks, the steering box moving on the frame when someone saws at the wheel, or visible cracks around the box mounting bolts on a lifted or big-tire truck.
Fix: Clean and inspect the frame rail around the box mounting area first, since a crack needs welding before a brace. Offroad Design's bolt-in brace for 1967–72 GM 4WD trucks triangulates the box mount to the crossmember and frame. It bolts on, but you have to drill one hole. Follow ORD's instructions, which note that some frames need washers to space the brace out. Re-torque everything after the first few drives.
Tools: Drill and bits · socket set · torque wrench · wire brush · ORD instructions PDF

#### Reseal the hardtop, liftgate and doors
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend · cost Seals plus adhesive
Symptoms: Water on the floors after rain or a car wash, wind noise at speed, or rust starting under old seals.
Fix: Remove the old rubber and scrape the channels back to clean metal and fiberglass. Treat any surface rust you find. Fit new hardtop quarter-glass seals, door-opening weatherstrip and the liftgate seal with weatherstrip adhesive, working a short section at a time. Refit the top and check the fit at the bedsides before you tighten the bolts fully. Water-test with a hose.
Tools: Plastic scrapers · adhesive remover · weatherstrip adhesive · masking tape · garden hose

#### Cut out and replace rotten floors, rockers and wheelhouses
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ Several weekends · cost Panels are cheap; welding time isn't
Symptoms: Soft or perforated floor pans, bubbling rockers and door bottoms, or rotten rear inner wheelhouses. These are the areas Velocity Restorations and The Drive flag.
Fix: Strip the interior and get the truck on stands with the doors shut, so the body doesn't move. Cut out one area at a time and leave sound metal to weld to. Trial-fit the reproduction panel, then plug- or butt-weld it in short stitches to avoid warping. Seam-seal and prime, and cavity-wax the rockers once they're closed up. For anything structural, measure the door gaps before and after.
Tools: MIG welder · cut-off wheel · spot-weld drill · clamps · seam sealer · weld-through primer

#### Repack front wheel bearings and replace spindle seals
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Bearing kits plus grease
Symptoms: Play at the top and bottom of the tire, a growl that changes as you turn, or grease and water inside the hub after deep water.
Fix: Lift and support the front, then remove the wheel, the brake and the locking hub. Remove the spindle nuts and slide the hub off. Clean everything, inspect the races, and replace the bearings, races and hub seal as a set if anything is pitted. Pack the new bearings with grease, refit, set the preload per the shop manual and fit a new spindle seal while you're in there.
Tools: Spindle-nut socket · bearing race driver · grease packer · torque wrench · shop manual

#### Replace worn locking hubs
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost A pair of hubs
Symptoms: Hubs that won't engage, pop out in four-wheel drive, or let the front driveshaft spin in two-wheel drive.
Fix: With the truck on stands, remove the hub cover bolts and pull the old hub body and inner drive gear. Clean the hub and spindle area, check the bearings while it's apart, and install the new hub with the gasket and hardware supplied. Test both positions by hand, then on a slippery surface. Offroad Design sells Yukon Hardcore hubs for 1978-and-older GM Dana 44s (19-spline). Confirm the spline count on yours first.
Tools: Hex or socket bits · snap-ring pliers · grease · torque wrench

#### Rebush the leaf springs and shackles
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day · cost Bushing kit plus new hardware
Symptoms: Clunks over bumps, vague steering, a truck that leans or sits low on one side, or cracked rubber at the spring eyes and shackles.
Fix: Support the frame and take the weight off one spring at a time. Remove the shackle and eye bolts, burn or press out the old bushings and fit the new ones. Offroad Design's leaf-spring bushing page lists which bushing fits each spring position. If the truck leans, ORD's advice is to measure the free arch of the springs on the floor and swap them side to side before blaming the spring rate. Torque the bolts with the truck at ride height.
Tools: Floor jack and stands · press or bushing tool · torch for old rubber · penetrating oil · torque wrench

#### Service the brakes (drums to 1970, front discs from 1971)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Parts plus brake fluid
Symptoms: A pull to one side, a low or spongy pedal, or seeping wheel cylinders. Also any truck that has sat for years.
Fix: Inspect every hose and steel line, since old trucks rust their lines from the outside. On 1969–70 trucks rebuild or replace the wheel cylinders, fit new shoes and adjust the drums. On 1971–72 trucks fit new pads and inspect the calipers and rotors. Bleed with fresh fluid from the wheel farthest from the master cylinder inward. Stainless front hoses are worth fitting on a lifted truck.
Tools: Line wrenches · drum adjuster tool · bleeder kit · fresh brake fluid

### Baseline service
Assume a 50-year-old truck's fluids are any age and its rubber is original until proven otherwise. Baseline everything, then deal with the frame, steering and brakes before you trust it on a trail. Factory capacities for 1969–72 weren't available from sources we could verify, so check the Chevrolet shop manual for those.
- Engine oil & filter: Grade and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now, then every 3,000–5,000 mi [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Check which engine you actually have: many trucks now run a later small-block or an LS.)
- Ignition: points or HEI, cap, rotor, plugs, wires: Points gap and timing [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now, then at every tune-up (Points ignition was original. Many owners convert to a GM HEI distributor, as on BaT's 1972 Highlander truck.)
- Coolant, hoses, radiator & thermostat: Coolant type and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush now, then every 2 years (The 1969–72 option lists included heavy-duty cooling with air conditioning or an automatic. Upgraded aluminum radiators are common on restored trucks.)
- Brake fluid, hoses & hardware: DOT 3 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush now, then every 2 years (1969–70 trucks have four-wheel drums and 1971–72 trucks power front discs. Replace any rusty steel line rather than patching it.)
- Transmission fluid: SM465 / 3-speed manual or TH350 automatic [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now (On a TH350, drop the pan and change the filter, then check for metal in the pan.)
- Transfer case oil: NP205: 80W-90 gear oil per CK5 members, filled to just below the fill hole · Dana 20 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now (Identify the case first. The 205 is a one-piece iron case with a three-bolt idler cover on the back (Offroad Design).)
- Front (Dana 44) & rear (12-bolt) differential oil: Gear oil grade [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · friction modifier if Positraction · Now, and after any deep water (Check the axle tag and the SPID decal for the ratio (3.73 standard, 3.07 optional on V8 trucks) and for Positraction.)
- Front wheel bearings & spindle seals: Repack with wheel-bearing grease · Now, then after water crossings (Inspect the hubs while you're in there.)
- Driveshaft U-joints & slip yokes: Grease the serviceable joints · Every oil change (Any lift changes the driveshaft angles. Offroad Design has a tech page on driveshaft angles.)
- Spring & shackle bushings: Inspect for cracking and play · Now (Original rubber is usually finished. Greasable bolts help on a truck that sees water and mud.)
- Steering box mount & linkage: Inspect the frame for cracks · check for play · Now (Straight-axle GM trucks are known for frame cracks at the box mount (Offroad Design).)
- Fuel filter, pump & tank: Inline filter · inspect the tank and sender · Filter now, then yearly (Trucks that have sat often need a new tank and sender, as several recent BaT sellers report.)
- Top & door seals: Inspect and water-test · Now (Leaks rot floors. Reseal before you put down new carpet.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: On a 67-72 Chevy Trucks thread about a stock 1972 Blazer, several owners run 33x12.50s on 15x8 wheels. Others call 32x11.50 the limit if the springs have sagged. One owner found 33x14.50s rubbed the springs, so width matters as much as height. On CK5, a member calls 33s about 2 inches bigger than stock 31s, fine for a while on the road but likely to hit off-road.

Q: What's the difference between a K5 Blazer and a GMC Jimmy?
A: Badging and trim. GMC started selling the Jimmy for 1970, and MotorTrend calls the two essentially identical apart from a few styling tweaks. GMC's 1971 brochure lists 4x4 Jimmys as KE-1550 and KS-1550, with the same 250, 307 and 350 engines as the Chevrolet.

Q: Does the whole roof really come off?
A: Yes. On 1969–72 trucks the hardtop is a full-length fiberglass shell that bolts on and lifts off, leaving just the windshield. A canvas soft top was a dealer accessory. From 1976 the K5 had a fixed roof over the front seats and only the rear section came off.

Q: Which engines did it come with?
A: The 250 six was standard, with the 307 and 350 V8s optional. A 292 six is listed for 1970–71. Chevrolet's 1971 brochure rates the 250, 307 and 350 at 110, 135 and 170 net horsepower (145, 200 and 250 gross). CK5 lists 175 hp for the 1972 350.

Q: Which transfer case do I have?
A: The Dana 20 came only with manual transmissions. The NP205 was fitted with the automatic and offered with manuals too. Offroad Design says the 205 is one piece of cast iron, with a small three-bolt idler cover on the back and an ID tag above the front output.

Q: When did it get disc brakes?
A: For 1971, when power front disc brakes became standard across GM's light trucks. 1969–70 trucks have drums at all four corners unless they've been converted.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: There's no buyer consensus on a best year. In a CK5 thread on which K5 to buy, the owners who pick a first-generation truck do it for the looks and the full-length removable top, and one calls 1971–72 the best looking. The mechanical difference worth knowing is the brakes: 1971 and later trucks have power front discs, while 1969–70 trucks have drums all round unless they've been converted. After that, rust, the top and the quality of past work decide it.

Q: Were there two-wheel-drive Blazers?
A: Yes. Wikipedia says the 2WD version was added for 1970, and CK5 says fewer than 1,000 were built that year. It used coil-spring independent front suspension and coil springs with trailing arms at the rear, so check for a front driveshaft before you assume a truck is a 4x4.

Q: How many were built?
A: CK5's spec sheet gives 4,935 for 1969, 11,527 for 1970, 17,220 for 1971 and 44,266 for 1972. Wikipedia lists the same numbers but flags them as uncited.

Q: What axle gears did it have, and should I regear for bigger tires?
A: The 1971 spec sheet lists 3.73 gears as standard on the 4x4, with 3.07 optional on V8 trucks. Owners on CK5 warn that 33s feel big with 3.08s. Offroad Design generally recommends gearing a lifted truck deeper to keep the engine in its useful rev range.

Q: What's the wheel bolt pattern?
A: Six lugs on 5.5 inches, shared with 1967–87 half-ton GM 4x4s. That makes period wheels and later GM 6-lug wheels easy to find, but check backspacing before buying.

Q: What does one cost now?
A: On Bring a Trailer, original-spec first-gen Blazers and Jimmys sold for about $24,000–100,000 between March 2025 and October 2026, with a median a little under $50,000. Resto-mods with modern engines have reached $146,000–170,000.

## Chevrolet K5 Blazer (1973–1991) (1973–1991)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/chevrolet/k5-blazer/
Codes: K5, K10 / V10 Blazer, GMC Jimmy, M1009 CUCV

Verdict: It's a half-ton pickup with the back seat where the bed should be and a roof you can unbolt. It has a small-block V8 you can fix with a wrench, axles that half the junkyard will fit, and a frame that cracks at the steering box. Owners love it anyway, and it's one of the easiest classic 4x4s to keep on the trail.

For 1973 General Motors redesigned its whole light-truck line. GM called it the 'Rounded Line', but everyone else calls it the square body, and the K5 Blazer came along with it. The formula stayed the same: take a four-wheel-drive half-ton pickup, shorten it, and make the roof removable. The new Blazer was 7 inches longer than the first generation on a wheelbase 2.5 inches longer. It stayed in production for 19 model years, through two facelifts, a diesel and an Army contract. GMC sold the same truck as the Jimmy, and the long-wheelbase Suburban as the GMC Suburban.

### A PICKUP WITH THE ROOF OPTIONAL
The K5 was built as an answer to the International Scout and the Ford Bronco. Because it shared its platform with the C/K pickups, it was bigger, roomier and more stable on the road than either. It also cost less to build, and buyers could add pickup options such as automatic transmissions, air conditioning and radios. By 1970 it was outselling its rivals. Rivals soon copied the idea. Jeep shortened its Gladiator into the Cherokee for 1974, and Ford moved the Bronco onto the F-100 platform for 1978.
From 1973 to 1975 the Blazer was a fully open truck behind the windshield, with a choice of a removable hardtop or a convertible top. In 1976 GM made it a half-cab: a fixed steel roof over the front seats, which improved rollover protection and shared more parts with the pickups, and a removable fiberglass top over the back. That rear top still came off in 1991. The tailgate had a glass window that wound down inside it, either by hand crank or by an electric motor. The motor is a known weak point, so many of these windows no longer work.

### SMALL BLOCKS, ONE DIESEL AND FOUR TRANSFER CASES
The 250 straight-six was the base engine until 1982. Most buyers chose a small-block V8: a 307, 305 or 350, or from 1975 a 400. In 1973 Popular Science tested a 175 hp 350 automatic with full-time 4WD. It took 22.5 seconds to reach 60 mph, and the testers recorded 9.6 mpg at a steady 45 mph. For 1982 GM added a 6.2-liter diesel V8 developed with Detroit Diesel. It made 130 hp and 240 lb-ft at launch and fit the same mounts as the gas V8. In 1987 throttle-body injection arrived, and after that the TBI 350 was the standard engine.
Transfer cases tell you the truck's age. From 1973 to 1980 you got either the gear-driven, part-time NP205 or the chain-driven, full-time NP203 with a lockable center differential. GM dropped full-time 4WD after 1979. For 1981 the aluminum NP208 arrived, a part-time case you could shift into 4WD at up to 25 mph, along with automatic locking hubs. From 1989 the NP241 replaced it. Up front, early trucks had a Dana 44, and GM switched to its own corporate 10-bolt from 1977. The rear axle was a 12-bolt, then a 10-bolt. A full-floating 14-bolt from a three-quarter-ton truck is the swap owners usually make.

### SILVERADO, CHEYENNE AND THE ARMY
Trim levels followed the pickups. Custom Deluxe was the base model. Cheyenne added carpet, a headliner and extra insulation, and from 1975 Silverado was the top trim. Cheyenne trucks are usually 1970s models, because the name was dropped after 1981 and came back as a lower trim on the 1989–91 R/V trucks. Silverado ran to the end. GMC's Jimmy used Sierra names. In 1976 and 1977 a camper conversion was also offered: about 1,800 Blazer Chalet and Jimmy Casa Grande trucks with a pop-up camper body built by Chinook.
Then the Army bought some. Between 1983 and 1987 GM built the M1009, a K5 rated at three-quarter-ton capacity, as part of its Commercial Utility Cargo Vehicle program. It used the 6.2 diesel, a TH400 automatic and an NP208 transfer case. GM built about 70,000 CUCVs of all types, and many have since gone through government surplus sales. Some were replaced by the Humvees they had been bought to supplement. Ex-military M1009s now come up for sale regularly, and one sold on Bring a Trailer for $20,500 in 2026.

### HOW IT ENDED
When the smaller S-10 Blazer appeared in 1983, GM officially renamed the big one the 'Full-Size Blazer' and the GMC version the 'K-Jimmy'. For 1987 the old trucks were renamed the R/V series, because the new GMT400 pickups took over the C/K name, and the Jimmy became the V-Jimmy. The Blazer, Suburban and crew cabs stayed on the old chassis. In 1988 the K5 badges disappeared. The 1989 trucks got a flatter grille in the style of the GMT400, plus the NP241 and 30-spline 10-bolt axle shafts. Rear anti-lock brakes and double-sided galvanized panels arrived for 1990.
1991 was the last year. The 1992 replacement moved to the GMT400 platform with a fixed roof, the Jimmy became the GMC Yukon, and in 1995 the full-size Blazer was renamed Tahoe. The square-body K5 is now an affordable classic that's very easy to modify. On Bring a Trailer, stock trucks often sell for less than $30,000, while LS-swapped restomods have reached six figures.

### Data plate
- Built: 1973–1991 model years · Flint Truck Assembly, Michigan (1990–91)
- Badges: Chevrolet K5 / Full-Size / V10 Blazer · GMC Jimmy, K-Jimmy, V-Jimmy
- Chassis: Ladder frame, leaf springs, live axles front & rear
- Wheelbase: ≈106.5 in (2.5 in longer than 1969–72)
- Body: Full-open (1973–75) · half-cab with removable rear top (1976–91)
- Engines: 250 I6 · 305 / 307 / 350 / 400 V8 · 6.2 diesel V8
- Transmissions: SM465 4-speed · TH350 · TH400 · 700R4 / 4L60
- Transfer Case: NP205 · NP203 (to 1979) · NP208 (1981–88) · NP241 (1989–91)
- Front Axle: Dana 44 → GM 10-bolt (from 1977)
- Rear Axle: GM 12-bolt → GM 10-bolt
- Trims: Custom Deluxe · Cheyenne · Silverado (GMC: Sierra range)
- Military: M1009 CUCV, 1983–87 · 6.2 diesel, 24/12 V

### Engineering
Mechanically, the square-body K5 is a shortened K10 pickup. It has a ladder frame, leaf springs and live axles at both ends, a transfer case bolted straight to the transmission, and the driveline mounted high to clear obstacles. Most parts are shared with GM's light trucks, which is why they're still easy to find. The details changed a lot over 19 years, so identify the axles and transfer case before you buy parts.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, ≈106.5-in wheelbase (2.5 in longer than the 1969–72 truck; prone to cracking at the steering box)
- Suspension: Leaf springs, live axles (Front and rear; M1009s got an extra spring leaf)
- Front Axle: Dana 44 → GM 10-bolt (10-bolt phased in from 1977; 30-spline shafts from about 1989)
- Rear Axle: GM 12-bolt → 10-bolt (Some 12-bolts into the early '80s; the 14-bolt is a popular swap)
- Transfer Case: NP205 / NP203 → NP208 → NP241 (NP208 from 1981; NP241 from 1989)
- Engines: 250 I6 · 305/307/350/400 V8 · 6.2 diesel (TBI fuel injection from 1987; 350 standard after that)

### Versions
- 1973–1975 · K5 Blazer / Jimmy, full-open body · 250 I6 · 307 / 350 V8 · 400 V8 from 1975 · 350: 175 hp (1973 test) · Removable hardtop or convertible top over the whole body. NP205 or full-time NP203; Dana 44 front.
- 1976–1980 · Half-cab · 250 I6 · 305 / 350 / 400 V8 · — · Steel roof over the front seats, removable rear top. GM 10-bolt front phased in from 1977. NP203 dropped after 1979.
- 1981–1986 · 1981 facelift · 250 I6 (early years) · 305 / 350 V8 · 6.2 diesel from 1982 · 6.2: 130 hp / 240 lb-ft at launch · Lighter body and new front end. NP208 with shift-on-the-fly and automatic hubs. 700R4 four-speed automatic available from 1982.
- 1983–1987 · M1009 CUCV · 6.2 diesel (non-emissions) · 155 hp / 240 lb-ft · TH400, NP208, 10-bolt axles, 3.08 gears, Eaton automatic rear locker, 24/12-volt electrics.
- 1987–1988 · R/V series (V10 Blazer, V-Jimmy) · 305 TBI (1987) · 350 TBI · 6.2 diesel · — · Throttle-body injection on all gas engines. K5 badges dropped for 1988.
- 1989–1991 · Final facelift · 350 TBI (L05) · 6.2 diesel · — · GMT400-style grille, NP241, 30-spline 10-bolts, serpentine belt. Rear ABS and galvanized panels from 1990.

### Year-by-year
- 1973: 'Rounded Line' square body launches. The truck is 7 in longer overall on a 2.5-in longer wheelbase. The body is fully open behind the windshield, with a removable hardtop or convertible top. NP205 part-time or NP203 full-time 4WD; Dana 44 front, 12-bolt rear. Tilt wheel optional
- 1975: 400 V8 joins the K-series engine list. Chevrolet adds the Scottsdale and Silverado trims, and Silverado becomes the top trim. Catalytic converters on trucks under 6,000 lb GVWR
- 1976: Half-cab body with a fixed steel roof over the front seats and a removable rear top, through 1991. Blazer Chalet / Jimmy Casa Grande camper (1976–77, about 1,800 built)
- 1977: GM corporate 10-bolt front axle phased in alongside the Dana 44. Power windows and locks offered for the first time
- 1980: Full-time 4WD (NP203) dropped from K-series. NP205s get a slip-yoke rear output
- 1981: Facelift with available stacked square headlamps and reduced weight. NP208 shift-on-the-fly transfer case and automatic locking hubs
- 1982: 6.2 L diesel V8 (130 hp / 240 lb-ft at launch). 700R4 four-speed overdrive automatic available
- 1983: S-10 Blazer arrives, so the big truck becomes the 'Full-Size Blazer' and the 'K-Jimmy'. M1009 CUCV production begins (1983–87). The 250 six, standard through 1982, is no longer the base engine
- 1987: Throttle-body injection on all gas engines, and the 350 becomes the standard engine. The trucks become the R/V series (V10 Blazer, V-Jimmy) as GMT400 pickups take the C/K name. In CK5 threads on which year to buy, most owners point to these 1987–91 TBI trucks for drivability and fuel economy [buy]
- 1988: K5 emblems dropped; fender-mounted mast antenna replaces the windshield antenna; trip odometer
- 1989: GMT400-style grille; NP241 transfer case; 30-spline 10-bolt axle shafts; serpentine belt on the 5.7. Cheyenne returns as the base Chevrolet trim. CK5 owners rate 1989–91 as the best of the TBI trucks for the NP241, the 30-spline shafts and the updated 700R4 [buy]
- 1990: Rear-wheel anti-lock brakes, electronic speedometer, double-sided galvanized exterior panels, rear three-point belts
- 1991: Final year. 700R4 renamed 4L60; CS130 alternator. Replaced for 1992 by the GMT400 Blazer and GMC Yukon

### Capability
- Wheelbase: ≈106.5 in (2,705 mm) (2.5 in longer than the 104-in 1969–72 truck (Wikipedia))
- Payload (M1009): 1,200 lb (544 kg) (Army rating)
- Towing (M1009): 3,000 lb (1,361 kg) (Army towed-load rating; Wikipedia says six-cylinder Blazers weren't recommended for towing)
- 0–60 mph: 22.5 s (Popular Science, 1973, 175 hp 350, automatic, full-time 4WD)
- Fuel economy: 9.6 mpg at 45 mph (350 V8) · 13.7 mpg at 45 mph (250 I6) (Popular Science steady-speed tests, 1973 and 1974)
- Top speed (M1009): 55 mph (89 km/h) (Governed, CUCV series)

### Wheels and tires
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5") on half-ton K5s; 8-lug on one-ton axle swaps
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 32 in (33 in with minor trimming) (Hogback Fabrication on CK5: a stock K5 fits 32s without trimming and 33s with minor trimming. Other owners report 33s touching the inner fender at full lock and full bump. On 16-in wheels, 285/75R16 is reported not to rub. For 33x12.50s, one member suggests 15x8 wheels at about 3.5 in backspacing.)
- Biggest tire, 3 in lift: 33x12.50R15 (Offroad Design's 1988 Suburban (same chassis) ran 33x12.50R15s on 15x8 steel wheels with 3 in of lift at the front and 4 in at the rear, plus a dropped pitman arm and 4.5-in bump stops.)
- Biggest tire, 4 in lift: 33 in (35 in with trimming) (CK5 members: 33s clear without rubbing on a 4-in lift, while 35s rub and need some trimming. Plenty of owners run 35s on 4 in with modest trimming.)

### Buying checks
- Frame cracks at the steering box: This is the classic K5 fault. On CK5 and GMSquareBody, owners say the frame cracks around and behind the steering-box bolts, often on the inside of the rail. You may not see the cracks with the box bolted on. Unbolt it if you can, or have someone rock the steering wheel while you watch for the frame moving. A properly welded reinforcement plate is fine; a bolt-on brace over an old crack isn't a fix.
- Rust in the usual places: CK5 members list the rockers, the front floor and the front seat-belt anchors, the rear wheel arches, the tail pan, the bottoms of the doors and tailgate, the cab mounts and the rear floor supports by the tailgate hinges. Pull up the carpet and smell for mildew. If the paint is bubbling from outside, the rust underneath is usually already serious.
- Tailgate window and top seal: Try the rear window. It winds down inside the tailgate by crank or motor, the motor and its drive cable are known to fail, and a safety switch stops the glass going up if the tailgate isn't latched. Ask whether the top has been removed. Owners disagree on whether that always causes leaks, but the seal between the top and the body is the usual leak point.
- Is it really a 350?: One CK5 member warns about 305s being sold as 350s, engines described as 'rebuilt' that never were, and a TH350 in a truck that should have a 700R4. Look for clean grease between the engine and transmission, which suggests nothing has been apart. Check the freeze plugs for weeping.
- Identify the axles and transfer case: On the front axle, a 10-bolt cover is nearly round with no flat sides, while the Dana 44 has the familiar Dana shape. Mismatched gear ratios front and rear, or a missing front driveshaft, mean someone has swapped parts. NP205 and NP203 cases carry ID tags above the front output. On 1989–91 NP241s, a leaking slip-yoke rear output is common.
- Hubs and 4WD engagement: 1981 and later trucks came with automatic locking hubs, which seize with age. One King of the Hammers K5 owner bought a truck with a 'blown transmission' that turned out to be a transfer case stuck in neutral and seized automatic hubs. Engage 4WD on the test drive, and budget for manual hubs.
- Previous owners' work: Look for hacked-in wiring, stereos and lights, cheap lift blocks and poor welding. One CK5 member says to pay extra for a properly done one-ton axle swap (8-lug axles) rather than a cheaply lifted 6-lug truck. Another suggests 1987–91 trucks for fuel injection, with 1989–91 the favorites.
- M1009 specifics: Check whether the 24/12-volt system is original or has been converted. If the resistor pack has been bypassed for 12-volt glow plugs, the starter, the alternator and the NATO slave receptacle in the grille also need dealing with. Expect 3.08 gears, 10.00-15 tires and a governed 55 mph top speed as delivered.

### Common repairs
#### Repair and brace a cracked steering-box frame rail
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend (more if the rail needs welding) · cost Parts plus welding labor
Symptoms: Wandering steering, a box that visibly moves on the frame when someone turns the wheel, or hairline cracks running from the steering-box bolt holes. Big tires and hard wheeling make it worse.
Fix: Unbolt the steering box, swing it aside and clean or blast the rail inside and out, because cracks often show only on the inside. GMSquareBody members drill a stop hole at the end of each crack, gouge it out, weld it, grind it flat, and only then add reinforcement. Offroad Design's weld-on repair kit wraps the outside and bottom of the rail. A bolt-in brace ties the box to the opposite rail and is good insurance on an uncracked frame. Some members also replace loose front-crossmember rivets with grade 8 7/16-inch bolts.
Tools: Welder and grinder · drill and bits · socket set · torque wrench · magnaflux or dye penetrant for hidden cracks

#### Swap a worn or leaking steering box
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 3–4 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Play at the wheel, wandering on the highway, fluid weeping from the box's seals, or a box that has been loosened by a cracking frame.
Fix: Inspect the frame first, because a new box on a cracked rail will soon loosen. Disconnect the steering shaft coupler and the pressure and return lines, pull the pitman arm with a puller, and unbolt the box. Fit the new box with new hardware and a new or rebuilt coupler. Refill and bleed the power steering by turning lock to lock with the front end raised. Lifted trucks often get a dropped pitman arm at the same time to correct drag-link angle.
Tools: Pitman arm puller · flare-nut wrenches · torque wrench · drain pan

#### Convert seized automatic hubs to manual locking hubs
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost Parts only for DIY
Symptoms: The truck won't pull with the front wheels in 4WD, grinding from the hubs, or front wheels that drive at one corner only. Automatic locking hubs arrived with the NP208 for 1981 and are now old.
Fix: Raise and support the front, remove the wheel, then remove the automatic hub assembly, its retaining ring and the drag sleeve parts. Check the wheel bearings and the spindle nut adjustment, and repack or replace the bearings if they're dry or rough. Fit the internal-style manual hub kit to suit your axle (10-bolt or Dana 44, spline count). Then check that 2WD and 4WD both engage.
Tools: Snap-ring pliers · spindle nut socket · bearing grease · torque wrench

#### Reseal an NP208 or NP241 and fix a leaking slip yoke
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A day (case out of the truck) · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: ATF dripping from the rear output, a driveline clunk, or a slip yoke pulling out as the suspension droops on a lifted truck. A worn chain can also skip or slap.
Fix: Both cases are aluminum, chain-driven and filled with ATF. Drain the case, drop both driveshafts and unbolt the case from the transmission adapter. Split the halves, check the chain for stretch and the bearings for wear, and replace all seals and gaskets. On a lifted NP241, a slip-yoke eliminator gives you a fixed rear yoke and a shorter shaft. Offroad Design's kit uses a common 32-spline yoke shortened by 1/4 inch. Refill with ATF.
Tools: Transmission jack · snap-ring pliers · seal drivers · RTV · torque wrench

#### Rebuild the front axle ends (ball joints, U-joints, bearings)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Death-grip steering, clunks over bumps, uneven tire wear, a front end that won't hold alignment, or clicking from the axle U-joints in tight turns in 4WD.
Fix: Identify the axle first. A Dana 44 and a GM 10-bolt look alike, but CK5 members warn that the inner parts and shafts don't interchange. Strip the hubs, calipers and spindles, pull the axle shafts, press out the old U-joints and ball joints, then press in new ones. Replace the spindle bearings and seals, repack the wheel bearings and set the preload. Finish with new hub seals and a front-end alignment.
Tools: Ball joint press · U-joint press or vise · spindle nut socket · slide hammer · torque wrench

#### Renew leaf spring bushings and shackles
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Clunks, wandering and axle wrap. Sagging rear springs are also common, and cracked rubber bushings often squeak.
Fix: Support the frame and take the weight off one spring at a time. Unbolt the shackle and main-eye bolts, press out the old bushings, and fit new ones that match your springs, since stock and aftermarket lift springs use different bushings. Fit greasable heavy-duty front shackles while you're there. Torque everything with the truck on the ground at ride height. Offroad Design publishes a chart of which bushing fits each stock or aftermarket spring.
Tools: Jack stands · bushing press or vise · penetrating oil · torque wrench

#### 6.2 diesel glow plugs and controller
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost Parts only for DIY
Symptoms: Hard cold starts, long cranking, white smoke until warm, or a wait light that misbehaves. On an M1009, a bad resistor pack or a mixed 12/24-volt conversion can cook new plugs.
Fix: Test each glow plug's resistance and check that power reaches each one during the glow cycle. Replace failed plugs (or all eight) and the controller or relay if it isn't cycling. On M1009s, confirm whether the truck still has the 24-volt starting system and the firewall resistor pack before you buy plugs. The plugs are 12-volt even on CUCVs, and the resistor pack drops 24 volts to 12.
Tools: Multimeter · deep sockets and extensions · anti-seize

### Baseline service
Assume nothing has been done. These trucks are 35 to 50 years old, and most have had several owners and swaps. Before you buy fluids, identify the engine, transmission, transfer case and axles, since they changed every few years. Pull the steering box and look at the frame while you're under there. Capacities vary by drivetrain, so check them in the factory manual.
- Engine oil & filter: Grade and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase, then per manual (Look for leaks at the rear main seal and the oil pan.)
- Air filter: Element to suit engine · At purchase; inspect at every oil change (The diesels are especially sensitive to dust ingestion, so check the airbox seals.)
- Fuel filter: Gas (TBI from 1987) or diesel element · At purchase (Old fuel and rusty tanks are common on trucks that have been sitting.)
- Spark plugs, cap, rotor & wires (gas): Plug type and gap [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (Most trucks have had an ignition swap at some point, so check what's fitted before ordering.)
- Glow plugs & controller (6.2 diesel): 12-volt plugs, including on 24-volt M1009s (resistor pack on the firewall) · Test at purchase (On an M1009, find out whether the 24-volt starting system is still original before buying parts.)
- Coolant, thermostat, hoses & belts: Coolant type and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush at purchase (Check for a leaking heater core while you're at it. One CK5 member lists it as a common annoyance. Trucks through 1988 use V-belts; the 5.7 switched to a single serpentine belt for 1989.)
- Automatic transmission (TH350 / TH400 / 700R4 / 4L60): ATF type and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Pan drop, new filter and refill at purchase (Know which one you have. The 700R4 became available in 1982 and was renamed 4L60 for 1991, and M1009s use the TH400.)
- Transfer case: NP208 and NP241: automatic transmission fluid (ATF) · NP205 / NP203: lubricant [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Change at purchase (The chain-driven NP208 and NP241 take ATF, not gear oil. Check the NP241's slip-yoke seal for leaks.)
- Front & rear differentials: Gear oil grade and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Change at purchase (The M1009's rear has an Eaton automatic differential lock. Check the gear ratio on both axles, since mismatched swaps are common.)
- Front wheel bearings & locking hubs: Repack with wheel-bearing grease; set preload per manual · At purchase (1981 and later trucks have automatic hubs, which often seize. Plenty of owners switch to manual hubs.)
- Steering box, power steering fluid & frame check: Power steering fluid [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (With the box off or the frame cleaned, look for cracks at the steering-box bolts. It's the K5's best-known weak spot.)
- Brake fluid, hoses & rotors: Brake fluid type [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush at purchase (On 1988–91 trucks, check whether recall 93V119 (corroded composite front rotors) was done. Rear ABS arrived for 1990.)
- Driveshafts & U-joints: Grease greasable joints · At purchase, then at every oil change (Lifted trucks wear driveshaft joints quickly because of the steep angles.)
- Battery & charging: Single 12 V on civilian trucks; two 12 V batteries and alternators in series on M1009s · Test at purchase (On an M1009, test both batteries and both alternators.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: About 32 inches. Hogback Fabrication says on CK5 that a stock K5 fits 32s without trimming and 33s with minor trimming. Other owners report 33s rubbing the inner fender at full lock and full bump, but fine on the road. On 16-inch wheels, 285/75R16s are commonly said not to rub. Wheel width and backspacing matter: one member suggests 15x8 wheels at about 3.5 inches of backspacing as the easy fit for 33x12.50s.

Q: Which years should I look for?
A: It depends on what you want. The 1973–75 trucks have the fully open body, which MotorTrend calls the K5's sweet spot for that reason, and 1976–80 trucks are the classic half-cab with the NP205 or NP203 and simpler mechanicals. For a truck to drive, CK5 owners mostly point to the 1987–91 trucks for throttle-body injection, and many name 1989–91 as the best of those for the NP241 transfer case, 30-spline axle shafts and the updated 700R4. Others prefer 1990–91 for the electronic speedometer. Whatever the year, check the frame at the steering box.

Q: Does mine have a Dana 44 or a 10-bolt front axle?
A: Look at the cover. Torque King describes the GM 10-bolt cover as an oval about 11 by 10-1/4 inches with no flat sides, unlike the Dana 44's. 1973–76 half-tons used the Dana 44, 1977–78 trucks could have either, and from 1979 Blazers used the 10-bolt through 1991, according to one GMSquareBody member's list (another CK5 member says GMC used up its last Dana 44s through 1982). Thirty-spline 10-bolt shafts came in around 1989.

Q: Which transfer case do I have?
A: Up to 1980 you'll find the gear-driven NP205, a one-piece iron case with a small three-bolt idler cover on the back, or the full-time NP203, a long four-section case with a separate range box on the front. From 1981 the aluminum, chain-driven NP208 took over, and the NP241 replaced it from 1989. The 208 and 241 both take ATF.

Q: Is the 6.2 diesel any good?
A: It's slow but simple. At launch it made 130 hp and 240 lb-ft, with a mechanical injection pump and indirect injection, and it fits the same mounts as the gas V8. Known problems include cracked main-bearing webs, and crank failures linked to worn harmonic balancers. Inspect the balancer and find out the engine's history before you buy.

Q: What's different about an M1009?
A: It's a 1983–87 Army K5 with the 6.2 diesel, a TH400 and an NP208, 10-bolt axles with 3.08 gears and an Eaton automatic rear locker, heavier springs and 10.00-15 tires. It has a 24/12-volt electrical system and is rated for 1,200 lb of payload and 3,000 lb towed. GM built about 70,000 CUCVs of all types.

Q: How does the removable top work?
A: On 1973–75 trucks the whole roof behind the windshield came off, with a hardtop or a convertible top. From 1976 the front roof is steel and fixed, and only the fiberglass rear top unbolts. That stayed true through 1991. Offroad Design still sells a soft top for 1969–91 K5s and Jimmys.

Q: How good is the fuel economy?
A: Bad with a gas V8. Popular Science's 1973 test of a 350 automatic with full-time 4WD recorded 9.6 mpg at a steady 45 mph. A 1974 250 six with an automatic managed 13.7 mpg at the same speed. Offroad Design got 11–12 mpg on a road trip in its lifted 1988 TBI Suburban, which has the same drivetrain.

Q: What gears do I need for bigger tires?
A: More than you'd think. Offroad Design put 4.56 one-ton axles under its 1988 Suburban, with a TBI 350, a 700R4 and 35-inch tires, and found it had enough rpm but still not enough power. On CK5, one member recommends at least 4.56 for 38s and 5.13s for 35-inch-and-up tires on one-ton axles. M1009s left the factory with tall 3.08s.

Q: Can I put one-ton axles under it?
A: Yes. A Dana 60 front and 14-bolt rear from a K30 is the classic upgrade. CK5 members note that the K30's rear spring pads sit about 2 inches narrower than the Blazer's, and the perches and shock tabs need moving. Driveshaft lengths change too. The bigger brakes may also need a larger master cylinder.

Q: What is it worth?
A: Prices vary a lot. Bring a Trailer's 15 most recent K5 sales (August–October 2026) ran from $4,600 for a 1986 project to $130,000 for an LSA-powered 1973, with a median of $29,500. Stock trucks mostly sold for $15,000–38,500, and a 1984 M1009 sold for $20,500. Hagerty noted in 2019 that the Blazer's median #2-condition value had risen 164% since 2009.

Q: Can it tow?
A: The Army rated the M1009 for a 3,000 lb towed load. Wikipedia says the six-cylinder Blazer wasn't recommended for towing. For a civilian truck, go by the GVWR, axle ratio and hitch it actually has, and check the factory trailering guide for your year.

## Chevrolet/GMC Suburban (1973–1991 square body) (1973–1991)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/chevrolet/suburban-square/
Codes: K10, K20, V1500, V2500

Verdict: A three-quarter-ton pickup wearing a station wagon body, with seats for nine and room for a camp kitchen behind them. It's thirsty and it rusts like any 40-year-old GM truck, but nothing else this old tows the trailer, carries the family and still gets you down the trail.

For 1973 GM rebuilt its whole truck line, and the Suburban came out the other side as something new: a full-size wagon with four passenger doors. Chevrolet's 1973 brochure called it a 'Superwagon' and, counting the standard double rear doors, a 'six-door wagon.' Underneath it was still all truck, with a pickup frame, leaf springs and, on the K-series, a solid front axle and a two-speed transfer case. Its short-wheelbase sibling was the K5 Blazer. That mix of wagon body and truck hardware ran for 19 model years, and it's why these Suburbans still tow trailers, haul families and turn up at trailheads.

### FROM CARRYALL TO 'SIX-DOOR WAGON'
The 1967–72 Suburban had an odd door count: one door on the driver's side and two on the passenger side. The 1973 truck switched to four side doors, more than a decade after the Jeep Wagoneer and International Travelall, according to Wikipedia. From the front doors back it shared its body with the new crew-cab pickup. Double panel-type rear doors were standard, and Chevrolet quoted an opening 40 inches high and 59.6 inches wide. A tailgate with a wind-down window was optional, cranked by hand or by an electric motor.
Chevrolet sold it in two series: the half-ton 10 and the three-quarter-ton 20, with C for two-wheel drive and K for 4x4. GMC used 15 and 25. The 1973 brochure lists GVWs of 5,400 to 8,200 lb, up to 144 cubic feet of load space and seating for nine with the second and third seats fitted. It also claims that a properly equipped Series 20 could move up to 14,000 lb of trailer, truck, passengers and luggage combined.

### WHAT'S UNDER A 4x4 SUBURBAN
The engine you most often find in a K-series Suburban is the 350 small-block, rated at 175 net horsepower in four-barrel form at launch. The 400 V8 was a K-series-only option from 1975 to 1980, and the 6.2-liter Detroit Diesel V8 arrived for 1982. The 454 big-block is the exception. Hagerty and Chevrolet's own 1982 and 1987 spec sheets list it only in two-wheel-drive Suburbans, so a 454 4x4 'Burb is a swap.
Four-wheel-drive hardware changed several times. Early trucks used the gear-driven NP205 part-time case or, with a V8 and automatic, the NP203 full-time case, which had a lockable center differential. Full-time 4WD was dropped for 1980. For 1981 the aluminum, chain-drive NP208 arrived with automatic locking hubs that let you shift into 4WD at up to 25 mph. Its low range is 2.61:1, against 1.96:1 for the 205. Behind it sat a TH350 or TH400 automatic, an SM465 four-speed manual, or, from 1981, the 700R4 overdrive automatic.

### NINETEEN YEARS OF RUNNING CHANGES
Hagerty's quick spotter's guide: 1973–80 trucks have round headlamps, a styled hood and vertical side markers; 1981–88 trucks have rectangular lamps, a flat hood and horizontal markers; and 1989 brought four small rectangular headlamps. For 1987, gasoline engines switched to throttle-body fuel injection and, because the new GMT400 pickups had taken the C/K name, the Suburban became the R (2WD) or V (4x4). Badging moved to 1500 and 2500.
The 1989 facelift gave it a flush, mostly black grille and a new steering wheel. For 1990 came power mirrors and optional rear-wheel ABS, and Wikipedia says the electronically controlled 4L80-E replaced the 700R4 for 1991. That was the last year: for 1992 the Suburban moved to the GMT400 platform, after 19 model years on the square body, and the K5 Blazer moved over with it. Late V1500s are the most refined of the breed, with fuel injection and an overdrive automatic, but they share the same frame, axles and rust problems as the early trucks.

### WHY OVERLANDERS AND TOWERS STILL BUY THEM
Its appeal today is what Chevrolet sold it on in 1973: space and pulling power. Chevrolet's 1982 spec sheet lists gross combination ratings of 11,000 lb for a gas K10 and 12,000 lb for a K20. Behind the second row there's room for a fridge, a drawer system and a sleeping platform. When Offroad Design needed a family camping and four-wheeling truck, it bought a fuel-injected 1988 Suburban, gave it a modest lift and 33s, and drove it on Moab's Hell's Revenge, Kane Creek and Steel Bender trails without a winch or strap.
Plenty of dealers saw the same appeal when these trucks were new. Bring a Trailer has sold a 1990 GMC V1500 that Trail Wagons of Yakima, Washington, converted when new with its Chinook Trail Boss package, and a 1990 V1500 modified when new by Truk-Mate of Minnesota. The price for that ability is fuel and rust. Hagerty warns about rockers, floors and wheel wells, and says lifted trucks on big tires need frame bracing at the steering box or the frame will likely crack.

- 4X4 Series: K10 / K20 (GMC K15 / K25) → V10 / V20, V1500 / V2500 (1987–91)
- Wheelbase: 129.5 in (3,289 mm)
- Length / Width: 219.1 in / 79.6 in
- Doors: 4 side doors + double rear doors or tailgate
- Seating: Up to 9
- 4X4 Engines: 250 I6 · 307 · 350 · 400 V8 · 6.2 diesel V8 (1982–91)
- Transmissions: 3- and 4-spd manuals · TH350 · TH400 · 700R4 (1981+) · 4L80-E (1991)
- Transfer Case: NP205 · NP203 full-time (1973–79) · NP208 (1981+)
- Gvw: 5,400–8,200 lb (1973)
- Stock Tires: P215/75R15 (K10) · LT235/85R16 (K20), 1982
- Towing (Gcwr): 11,000 lb K10 · 12,000 lb K20 (1982, gas)

### Engineering
The square-body Suburban uses GM's 1973–91 Rounded Line truck frame on a 129.5-inch wheelbase. K/V-series 4x4s have a live front axle on leaf springs, a GM Dana 44 or corporate 10-bolt depending on year and series, and a semi-floating rear axle, also on leaves. Chevrolet's spec sheets reserve the full-floating rear axle for the two-wheel-drive 454 trucks. The body has four side doors, with double rear doors as standard and a tailgate with a wind-down window as an option.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, 129.5 in wheelbase (219.1 in long and 79.6 in wide, per Wikipedia. Heights are 73.8 in (V10) and 76.1 in (V20).)
- Front Axle: Live axle on leaf springs (Rated at 3,600 lb (10 series) and 3,800 lb (20 series) in the 1982 and 1987 spec sheets. ORD's 1988 V1500 had a 10-bolt.)
- Rear Axle: Semi-floating, leaf springs (Rated at 4,000 lb on the 10 series and 6,000 lb on the 20. Chevrolet's 1982 spec sheet lists a full-floater only with the 454 (2WD).)
- Transfer Case: NP205 · NP203 · NP208 (NP205 part-time and NP203 full-time (1973–79). From 1981, the NP208 with auto-locking hubs; manual hubs were still offered.)
- Engines (4X4): 250 I6 · 307 / 350 / 400 V8 · 6.2 diesel (1987+ TBI 350: 210 hp (10 series). 6.2 diesel: 130 hp (LH6) or 148 hp (LL4). No factory 454 in the 4x4s.)
- Body: 4 side doors + rear doors (Double panel doors were standard; a tailgate with a manual or power window was optional. Up to nine seats and 144 cu ft of cargo space (1973).)

### Versions
- 1973–1974 · K10 / K20 (GMC K15 / K25) · 250 I6 · 307 V8 (1973) · 350 V8 · 350: 175 hp / 275 lb-ft (4-bbl) · New four-door body. NP205 part-time or NP203 full-time. Custom Deluxe and Cheyenne Super trims.
- 1975–1980 · K10 / K20 · 350 V8 · 400 V8 (K only) · 400: 185 hp / 300 lb-ft · Scottsdale and Silverado trims from 1975. Estate woodgrain package to 1979. Full-time 4WD dropped for 1980.
- 1981–1986 · K10 / K20 · 350 V8 · 6.2 diesel V8 (from 1982) · 6.2: 130–148 hp · Facelift with rectangular lamps. NP208 with auto-locking hubs. 700R4 four-speed automatic available.
- 1987–1988 · V10 / V20 (V1500 / V2500) · 5.7 L TBI V8 · 6.2 diesel · TBI 350: 210 hp / 300 lb-ft (10 series) · R/V naming. Throttle-body fuel injection on all gasoline engines.
- 1989–1991 · V1500 / V2500 · 5.7 L TBI V8 · 6.2 diesel · As above · Flush black grille and new steering wheel (1989). Rear ABS option (1990). 4L80-E for 1991, per Wikipedia.
- 1973–1991 · C/R 2WD (for comparison) · 454 V8 option · 230 hp · The big block was only a factory option on 2WD Suburbans.

### Year-by-year
- 1973: Rounded Line Suburban launches with four side doors, standard double rear doors and an optional tailgate with a wind-down window. K10/K20 4x4s use the NP205 or the full-time NP203. 307 V8 offered this year only
- 1975: 400 V8 added for K-series trucks. Trims become Custom Deluxe, Scottsdale and Silverado (GMC: Sierra Classic replaces Super Custom)
- 1978: Front bucket seats offered
- 1979: Quick-release third-row seat. Last year for the Estate woodgrain package
- 1980: Full-time 4WD dropped; K-series go part-time. Last year of the 400 V8
- 1981: Major facelift. NP208 transfer case with automatic locking hubs and shift-on-the-fly up to 25 mph. 700R4 overdrive automatic available
- 1982: 6.2 L Detroit Diesel V8 option. Three-quarter-ton trucks switch from 16.5 to 16 in wheels
- 1987: Throttle-body fuel injection on all gasoline engines. C/K renamed R/V (R = 2WD, V = 4x4). Owners on GMSquareBody and CK5 point to the TBI trucks for better mileage, more power and reliability than the carbureted ones [buy]
- 1989: Largest facelift since 1973: flush, mostly black grille and a new steering wheel
- 1990: Power mirrors; rear-wheel ABS optional
- 1991: Final year. Wikipedia says the 4L80-E replaced the 700R4; check the transmission on any given truck

- GVW: 5,400–8,200 lb (1973) · 6,100–6,800 lb K10, 8,600 lb K20 (1982)
- Payload: Up to 3,325 lb (1973 brochure)
- Cargo space: Up to 144 cu ft (1973 brochure)
- Seating: Up to 9
- Wheelbase: 129.5 in (3,289 mm)
- Length: 219.1 in (5,565 mm)
- Height: 73.8 in (V10) · 76.1 in (V20)
- Rear door opening: 40 in high × 59.6 in wide (1973 brochure, panel doors)
- Curb weight: 5,837 lb (2,648 kg) (Wikipedia infobox figure; varies by series and equipment)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: P215/75R15 (K10/V10, 1982 and 1987), LT235/85R16 (K20/V20, 1982 and 1987)
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5") on half-ton 4x4s
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 31x10.50R15 (Owners report no rubbing on half-tons, even aired down. 33x10.50s fit on factory rims. 33x12.50s fit a stock three-quarter-ton, but a half-ton will almost certainly need trimming (GMSquarebody).)
- Biggest tire, 3 in F / 4 in R lift: 33x12.50R15 (Offroad Design's '88 Suburban ran these on 15x8 steel wheels with a 3 in front and 4 in rear lift, including Moab's slickrock trails.)
- Biggest tire, 6 in lift: 35x12.50 (BaT's Chinook Trail Boss V1500 runs 35x12.50 BFGoodrich tires on a 6 in Rough Country lift with ORD shackles. Plan on gears, steering bracing and brakes.)

### Buying checks
- Rust: rockers, floors and wheel wells: Hagerty names these as the main problem areas, especially on early trucks. Also check the bottoms of all four doors and the rear doors or tailgate, and look under the carpet. Mill Supply and Auto Metal Direct sell the panels, but a structurally rotten 'Burb is a big job.
- Frame at the steering box: Hagerty says lifted 4x4s on bigger tires need frame bracing at the steering box or cracking is likely. Offroad Design calls frame cracks there notorious on straight-axle GM trucks. Look for cracks, fresh welds or a brace that's already been fitted.
- Is it really a 4x4, and which case?: Look for a front driveshaft and a V or K in the model badging. BaT has sold a C2500 with a 4x4 swap. Then identify the case: the NP203 (full-time, 1973–79) is long and in four sections, the NP205 is one piece of iron, and the NP208 is aluminum.
- Hubs on 1981-and-later trucks: From 1981 GM fitted automatic locking hubs with the NP208, and manual hubs were optional. Make sure the front engages in 4WD and frees up in 2WD. Many owners have already swapped to manual hubs.
- Check rear HVAC and the dash: Hagerty notes that the Suburban-only rear heater and air-conditioning parts can be hard to fix, and that dash pads often crack down the center. Run both front and rear air and heat before you buy.
- Rear window and tailgate: Wikipedia notes that the wind-down rear glass is heavy, that hand-crank gears and electric motors wear, and that a drive cable links the motor to the regulator. A safety switch stops the glass rising if the tailgate isn't latched, so check that the tailgate is latched before you blame the motor.
- Check modifications carefully: Hagerty's advice is to inspect any modifications carefully. Lifts, engine swaps and wiring jobs vary widely in quality. A stock, rust-free V1500 often makes a better starting point than someone else's half-finished build.
- 6.2 diesel trucks: Wikipedia lists crankshaft failures related to age-worn harmonic balancers, plus main-bearing web cracks, as known 6.2/6.5 problems. Ask about the balancer and listen for knocks. A diesel is slow, but it gives you range.

### Common repairs
#### Brace or repair the frame at the steering box
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day (bolt-in) · longer if welding · cost Brace kit; add welding if the frame is already cracked
Symptoms: Steering that wanders or clunks, the box moving on the rail, or cracks around the box bolts. It's most likely on lifted trucks with big tires.
Fix: Clean the driver's-side frame rail and inspect it closely. If it's cracked, stop-drill the crack and weld in a repair plate first. Offroad Design sells a weld-on frame repair kit for 1973–91 GM trucks. Then fit a bolt-in steering-box frame brace, which ties the box mount across to stiffen the rail. Re-torque the box and brace bolts after the first few hundred miles.
Tools: Wire wheel · drill · socket set · torque wrench · MIG welder for crack repair

#### Replace rotten rockers and floor supports
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ Several weekends · cost Panels are affordable; labor is the cost
Symptoms: Rust bubbling along the rockers below the doors, soft floors under the carpet, and doors that sag or won't line up.
Fix: Support the body properly and work one side at a time, leaving the doors in place so you keep the gaps. Cut out the outer rocker, inspect and replace the inner rocker and floor supports, then fit the new outer panel. Plug-weld it at the original spot-weld locations, seam-seal it and cavity-wax inside. Mill Supply sells OEM-style inner and outer rocker kits and floor supports for these trucks.
Tools: MIG welder · spot-weld drill · cut-off wheel · clamps · seam sealer · cavity wax

#### Convert automatic locking hubs to manual hubs
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost A pair of hubs
Symptoms: On 1981-and-later trucks, a front axle that won't engage in 4WD, grinding as the hubs try to lock, or hubs that stay locked in 2WD.
Fix: With the front on stands, remove the auto hub cover and the internal parts, including the drag sleeve and spring assembly. Inspect the bearings and spindle while you're in there. Install the manual hub body and dial per the manufacturer's instructions, using the correct spindle-nut hardware. Offroad Design sells Warn internal-style hubs that fit all half-ton GM axles and 1977-and-later three-quarter-ton axles, and Yukon Hardcore hubs for 1979-and-later 8.5-inch fronts and Dana 44s. Check that the hubs turn freely in FREE and lock in LOCK.
Tools: Snap-ring pliers · spindle-nut socket · torque wrench · grease

#### Repack front wheel bearings and replace spindle seals
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Bearing and seal kits
Symptoms: Play at the top and bottom of the tire, a growl that changes on turns, or water in the hubs after crossings.
Fix: Remove the wheel, caliper, hub and spindle nuts and slide the hub off. Clean and inspect the bearings and races, and replace them as a set if they're pitted. Pack the new bearings, fit a new hub seal and spindle seal, and reassemble, setting the bearing preload to the shop-manual spec. Reuse nothing that looks tired.
Tools: Spindle-nut socket · race driver · grease packer · torque wrench · shop manual

#### Fix a power tailgate window that won't move
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2–4 hours · cost Motor, cable or regulator, plus switch if needed
Symptoms: The rear glass won't go up or down from the key switch or the dash switch, the motor runs but the glass doesn't move, or the motor gets hot and stops.
Fix: First make sure the tailgate is fully latched. Wikipedia notes that a safety switch stops the glass rising if it isn't. Check for power at the motor from both the key switch and the dash switch. If the motor spins but the glass doesn't move, the cable between the motor and the regulator (similar to a speedometer cable) has probably failed. If the motor doesn't run, or overheats, replace it. Remove the inner tailgate panel, support the heavy glass, and replace the cable, motor or regulator. Lubricate the tracks before you refit the panel.
Tools: Trim tools · test light or multimeter · socket set · white lithium grease · a helper to hold the glass

#### Rebush the leaf springs and cure the sag
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day · cost Bushing kit; springs if they're flat
Symptoms: Clunks, wandering, and a 'Burb that sits low at the rear or leans to one side.
Fix: Replace the spring-eye and shackle bushings with the truck supported on the frame, one corner at a time. Offroad Design's leaf-spring bushing chart lists the right bushing for each position. If the springs have lost their arch, replace them. ORD describes the Suburban as 'typically saggy' and built its own '88 with 3 inches at the front and 4 at the rear so it would sit level. On a lean, ORD suggests swapping the springs side to side before assuming one is bad.
Tools: Floor jack and stands · press or bushing tool · penetrating oil · torque wrench

#### Replace a cracked dash pad
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost A reproduction dash pad
Symptoms: A dash pad split down the center or cracked by the sun. Hagerty says this is common.
Fix: Disconnect the battery. Remove the instrument-cluster bezel and any trim that overlaps the pad, then the screws along the windshield edge and at the lower edge. Lift the pad out carefully, fit the new one, and refit the bezel and trim. A dash cover or windshield shade will keep the new one from cracking.
Tools: Screwdrivers · nut drivers · trim tools

### Baseline service
These trucks are 35 to 50 years old, so assume every fluid, hose and bushing is overdue. Identify what you actually have (transfer case, engine, half- or three-quarter-ton), because the service differs. We couldn't verify factory capacities, so confirm them in the GM shop manual.
- Engine oil & filter: Grade and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · the 6.2 diesel takes a diesel-rated oil and more of it · Now, then every 3,000–5,000 mi [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Check for leaks at the rear main seal and oil pan.)
- Ignition (gas) or glow plugs (6.2 diesel): Plugs, cap, rotor and wires · or glow plugs and controller · Now (Hard cold starts on a diesel usually mean glow plugs or the controller.)
- Coolant, hoses, radiator & fan clutch: Coolant type and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush now, then every 2 years (Towing and big tires load the cooling system. On a 6.2, check the harmonic balancer while the front of the engine is accessible (Wikipedia lists balancer-related crank failures).)
- Automatic transmission fluid & filter: TH350 / TH400 / 700R4 / 4L80-E [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Pan drop and filter now (Recall 93V016 added a longer transmission vent hose to 1988–91 trucks after heat pushed fluid out of the vent. Check yours has it.)
- Transfer case fluid: NP208: Dexron ATF · NP205: 80W-90 gear oil · NP203: CK5 members use 10W-30 motor oil (debated) · Now (Identify the case first. The 203 is long, in four sections and full-time; the 205 is one piece of iron; the 208 is aluminum (ORD, Wikipedia).)
- Front & rear differential oil: Gear oil grade [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now, and after deep water (Many trucks have the G80 automatic locking rear differential, which locks itself below about 20 mph when a wheel slips (Wikipedia). Don't mistake its clunk for a failure.)
- Front wheel bearings, spindle seals & hubs: Repack with wheel-bearing grease · Now (On 1981-and-later trucks, check that the automatic hubs engage and release.)
- Brake fluid, lines, rotors & hoses: DOT 3 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush now, then every 2 years (Recall 93V119 replaced front rotors on 1988–91 Chevrolets, because road salt could separate the steel hat from the cast outer section. Inspect the rotors on salt-belt trucks.)
- Steering box mount, box & linkage: Inspect the frame · check box and linkage for play · Now (Lifted trucks on big tires need the box mount braced (Hagerty, ORD).)
- Spring & shackle bushings, shocks: Inspect for cracking and sag · Now (Measure ride height at all four corners; Suburbans commonly sag at the rear.)
- Driveshaft U-joints & slip yokes: Grease the serviceable joints · Every oil change (The long rear shaft and any lift change the driveshaft angles. ORD has a tech page on driveshaft angles.)
- Fuel filter, pump & tank: Inline filter (TBI) or carburetor filter · Now, then yearly (Recall 06E043 covers certain FRAM G3727 replacement filters with 2005–06 date codes sold for 1987–91 trucks. Check what's fitted.)
- Front & rear heat and A/C: Function check · refrigerant type depends on year and any conversion · Now (Hagerty warns that the Suburban-only rear HVAC parts can be hard to fix.)
- Tailgate glass, rear doors & seals: Operate the glass · water-test the seals · Now (The power glass won't rise unless the tailgate is latched (Wikipedia).)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: On a half-ton, 31x10.50R15s are the safe choice: GMSquarebody owners of a 1987 Suburban 4x4 and a 1987 short-box report no rubbing at all. 33x10.50s on factory rims also work. A moderator ran 33x12.50s on a stock three-quarter-ton Suburban with no rubbing, but says a half-ton will almost certainly need trimming. On CK5, owners of the related half-ton K5 Blazer call 32s safe and say 33s rub at full lock.

Q: How many doors does it have?
A: Four side doors, plus double rear panel doors as standard or an optional tailgate with a wind-down window. Chevrolet called it a 'six-door wagon' in 1973. The three-door layout (one door on the driver's side, two on the passenger side) belongs to the 1967–72 Suburban.

Q: Was there a factory 454 4x4 Suburban?
A: No. Chevrolet's 1982 and 1987 spec sheets list the 7.4-liter 454 only for the two-wheel-drive C20/R20, and Hagerty agrees it was 2WD only. The 4x4s got the 350 (plus the 400 from 1975 to 1980) or the 6.2 diesel. A 454 K-series Suburban has had an engine swap.

Q: What's the 6.2 diesel like?
A: It's a naturally aspirated, indirect-injection 379 cu in V8 offered in Suburbans from 1982 to 1991. The 1987 spec sheet rates it at 130 hp and 240 lb-ft in 10-series trucks and 148 hp and 246 lb-ft in 20-series trucks. Wikipedia says it was built for fuel economy, and lists main-bearing web cracks and balancer-related crank failures as known problems. It's the same engine family as the Hummer H1's.

Q: What's the difference between the NP203, NP205 and NP208?
A: The NP203 (1973–79 option) is full-time, with a center differential you lock for off-road use. The NP205 is a gear-driven, part-time cast-iron case with a 1.96:1 low range. The NP208 (from 1981) is aluminum and chain-driven, has a 2.61:1 low range, and with automatic hubs can shift into 4WD at up to 25 mph.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: Chevrolet's 1982 spec sheet gives gross combination ratings of 11,000 lb for a gas K10 and 12,000 lb for a K20 with the trailering package. The 1973 brochure says a properly equipped Series 20 could move up to 14,000 lb combined. A trailer's weight counts toward that total, along with the truck, its passengers and cargo.

Q: Half-ton or three-quarter-ton?
A: In 1982 a K10 rode on P215/75R15 tires with 6,100–6,800 lb GVW, while a K20 had LT235/85R16s and 8,600 lb. The 20 series has heavier front and rear axle ratings (3,800 and 6,000 lb against 3,600 and 4,000). Half-tons ride better and use the common 6-on-5.5-inch wheel pattern.

Q: Which years have fuel injection?
A: 1987 to 1991. For 1987 all the gasoline engines switched to throttle-body injection, and the 5.7-liter V8 was rated at 210 hp and 300 lb-ft in 10-series trucks. The diesel already had mechanical injection.

Q: What does R/V mean?
A: For 1987, the new GMT400 pickups took the C/K name, so the old-body trucks became R (2WD) and V (4x4) to avoid confusion. A V1500 is a half-ton 4x4 and a V2500 a three-quarter-ton.

Q: Which years should I look for?
A: It depends on what you want. 1973–80 trucks have round headlamps and the NP203 or NP205, and Hagerty notes that the earlier trucks tend to have more rust. 1981–86 trucks have the NP208, overdrive and the 6.2 diesel option, which is slow and has known crank and balancer problems. For a truck to use, owners tend to recommend the 1987–91 trucks: one GMSquareBody member says TBI brings 'better mileage and more power stock than the carbed version', and on CK5 one owner says to stick with 1989–91 for their transmission and transfer-case setups. There's no harder consensus than that, so buy the straightest one.

Q: What's one worth?
A: Hagerty says a usable example can be had for under $10,000 and an excellent one for $25,000–30,000. On Bring a Trailer, mostly original 4x4 Suburbans sold for about $7,900–37,250 between 2024 and 2026, with a median near $16,000. An exceptional 1973 Cheyenne Super Estate 4x4 reached $70,000.
