# Ford Bronco (1966–present)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/bronco/

Ford announced the Bronco in August 1965 as a 1966 model, its first SUV and its answer to the Jeep CJ-5 and the International Scout. The idea came from product manager Donald Frey, who had also conceived the Mustang. The early Bronco rode on its own short frame with coil springs up front and four-wheel drive as standard, and Ford offered it as a roadster, a half-cab pickup and a wagon before building the last one for 1977. For 1978 the Bronco became the full-size Bronco, a short-wheelbase F-Series with a lift-off fiberglass rear top that outsold the Chevrolet K5 Blazer and Dodge Ramcharger. It stayed on F-Series underpinnings through five generations, switching to Twin Traction Beam front suspension in 1980, until the last one left Michigan Truck in Wayne on June 12, 1996, and the four-door Expedition took its place. Along the way Ford used the name on the smaller, Ranger-based Bronco II (1984–1990), which is a different truck altogether. After a 25-year gap the sixth-generation Bronco arrived for 2021, built in Wayne again and aimed squarely at the Wrangler: body-on-frame, two or four doors, removable doors and roof, and locking front and rear differentials. Its styling borrows from the first truck, and the designers scanned their design chief's 1976 Bronco for reference. The Bronco Sport crossover and a China-only Bronco New Energy share the name but not the hardware.

Verdict: Ford's first SUV started as a 92-inch tin box with flat glass and a Dana 20, grew into an F-Series with a lift-off roof, vanished for 25 years and came back to fight the Jeep again. The first one is still the one everybody wants.

## Ford Bronco (1966–1977) (1966–1977)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/bronco/early-bronco/
Codes: U13, U14, U15

Verdict: A 92-inch tin box with flat glass, a column shifter and a coil-sprung front axle that the Jeep didn't have. It rusts, it wanders if the caster is off, and a good one costs what a new truck does. Nobody who owns one cares.

In August 1965 Ford announced a truck that owed almost nothing to its pickups. The Bronco got its own box-section frame, a 92-inch wheelbase, flat glass all round and door skins that were the same left and right until the hardware went on. It came only with four-wheel drive and was aimed straight at the Jeep CJ-5 and the International Scout. Twelve model years and roughly 225,600 trucks later, it had lost the sales war. Fifty years after that, it is the Bronco collectors want most.

### THE MUSTANG MAN'S OTHER IDEA
The Bronco began with Ford product manager Donald Frey, who had also conceived the Mustang. Paul Axelrad engineered it, clay models were built in mid-1963, and Lee Iacocca approved it for production in February 1964. Its targets were the CJ-5, the Scout and Toyota's Land Cruiser. The wheelbase sat between the Jeep's 83 inches and the Scout's 100. Up front, instead of the Twin I-Beam of Ford's bigger trucks, the Bronco used a solid axle on coil springs, located by radius arms and a track bar. Ford quoted a 34-foot turning circle.
Launch power was the Falcon's 170-cubic-inch six, rated at 105 hp and toughened with solid lifters, a six-quart oil pan, an oil-bath air cleaner and a carburetor float that coped with steep angles. A 289 V8 followed in March 1966. Every truck had a column-shifted three-speed and a Dana 20 two-speed transfer case. You could have a wagon, a half-cab pickup or an open roadster, and the dealer could add a snowplow, a winch, a power take-off or a posthole digger.

### GROWING UP, SLOWLY
The Bronco changed in small steps. A Sport package arrived for 1967, along with a dual master cylinder. The roadster, which never sold, was dropped after 1968. The 302 replaced the 289 for 1969, and electric wipers took over from vacuum ones that year. In 1970 the Sport became its own model. Midway through 1971 the Dana 30 front axle gave way to a stronger Dana 44, and 1972 brought the plush Ranger trim and the end of the half-cab.
For 1973 Ford finally offered a C4 three-speed automatic and power steering, and the 200-cubic-inch six replaced the 170. The transfer-case lever changed from a T-handle to a J-shaped pattern. Sales peaked at 25,824 in 1974. The last big update came for 1976, with power front disc brakes, a front anti-roll bar and a new Y-type steering linkage that owners still argue about. The 1977 trucks got a heavier-duty 9-inch rear housing and fuel doors in place of exposed caps.

### BAJA, AND THE RACE TRUCKS
In 1965 race-car builder Bill Stroppe put together a team of Broncos for long-distance off-road racing, partnering with Holman-Moody. The Stroppe/Holman/Moody trucks ran the Mint 400, the Baja 500 and the Mexican 1000, the race that became the Baja 1000, and in 1969 SHM entered six Broncos in the Baja 1000. The most famous Stroppe-shop Bronco of all, Parnelli Jones's Big Oly, won the Baja 1000 in 1971 and 1972.
Ford cashed in. From 1971 dealers sold a Baja Bronco package designed by Bill Stroppe, with an automatic, quick-ratio power steering, fender flares over Gates Commando tires, a roll bar, reinforced bumpers and red, white, blue and black paint. It cost $5,566 when a regular V8 Bronco was $3,665, and only 650 were sold over the next four years. Genuine ones now sell for serious money: Bring a Trailer results from 2025–26 run from $72,500 to $178,315.

### HOW IT ENDED, AND WHY IT NEVER DID
By the early 1970s buyers wanted more room and more comfort, and the Chevrolet Blazer and the Scout II had both. Ford planned a bigger F-100-based Bronco for 1974, but the fuel crisis pushed it back to 1978. When the full-size Bronco arrived it was a foot longer in wheelbase and up to 1,600 pounds heavier. The little Bronco was done.
The afterlife has been something else. Hagerty says values nearly doubled between 2016 and 2019, and the restomod business took off. On Bring a Trailer, 306 complete early Broncos sold between August 2025 and October 2026. The middle half of the Coyote-swapped and shop-built restomods went for about $122,000–166,500, and the top sale reached $325,000. Ford noticed: its designers scanned the design chief's 1976 Bronco while shaping the 2021 Bronco. Hagerty did record a 12 percent drop in the second quarter of 2026, but a driver still costs $50,000 or more.

### Data plate
- Built: Michigan Truck Plant, Wayne, Michigan · 1965–1977
- Production: ≈ 225,600 (Autotrader Classics)
- Bodies: U13 roadster (to 1968) · U14 half-cab (to 1972) · U15 wagon
- Chassis: Box-section ladder frame, unique to the Bronco
- Wheelbase: 92 in · length 151.5 in
- Engines: 170 & 200 I6 · 289 & 302 V8
- Transmissions: 3-speed manual (column shift) · C4 3-speed auto from 1973
- Transfer Case: Dana 20 · 2.46:1 low (T-handle) / 2.34:1 (J-shift)
- Front Axle: Dana 30 to mid-1971 · Dana 44 after; coil springs, radius arms
- Rear Axle: Ford 9-inch on leaf springs
- Brakes: Drums · power front discs 1976–77
- Turning Circle: 34 ft curb to curb (Ford, 1965)

### Engineering
The early Bronco is a body-on-frame 4x4 built on a box-section ladder frame of its own, shared with no other Ford. A solid front axle rides on coil springs, located by two forged radius arms and a track bar, while the Ford 9-inch rear axle sits on leaf springs. Every Bronco had four-wheel drive through a gear-driven Dana 20 transfer case, with locking hubs at the front. The factory data plate on the glovebox door records the body series, engine, transmission and axle codes.
- Chassis: Box-section ladder frame (92-in wheelbase, 151.5 in long; frame unique to the Bronco)
- Front Suspension: Coils, radius arms, track bar (Caster is set by the C-bushings; Ford quoted a 34-ft turning circle)
- Axles: Dana 30 → Dana 44 · Ford 9-inch (Dana 44 front from mid-1971; king pins on the Dana 30, ball joints on the Dana 44)
- Transfer Case: Dana 20, gear-driven (2.46:1 low with T-handle (1966–72); 2.34:1 with J-shift (1973–77))
- Engines: 170 / 200 I6 · 289 / 302 V8 (289 from March 1966; 302 from 1969; 200 six from 1973)
- Brakes: Drums → power front discs (1976) (Dual master cylinder from 1967; disc conversion kits for 1966–75)

### Versions
- 1966–1968 · U13 roadster · U14 half-cab · U15 wagon · 170 I6 · 289 V8 (from March 1966) · 170: 105 hp · 289: 200 hp · Column-shift three-speed only. Sport package from 1967. The roadster was dropped after 1968.
- 1969–1972 · U14 half-cab · U15 wagon · 170 I6 · 302 V8 · — · 302 replaces the 289; electric wipers from mid-1969. Sport a separate model from 1970. Dana 44 front from mid-1971. Half-cab ends in 1972; Ranger trim arrives.
- 1971 on (≈ 4 years) · Baja Bronco (Stroppe) · 302 V8, automatic · — · Quick-ratio power steering, flares, Gates Commando tires, roll bar, tricolor paint. $5,566 new; 650 sold.
- 1973–1975 · U15 wagon · 200 I6 · 302 V8 · 302 (1975): 125 hp net · C4 automatic and power steering optional from 1973; J-shift Dana 20 with 2.34:1 low.
- 1976–1977 · U15 wagon · 200 I6 · 302 V8 · — · Power front disc brakes, front anti-roll bar and Y-type steering linkage. 1977: heavy-duty 9-inch housing, fuel doors, plastic tanks.

### Year-by-year
- 1966: Launched in August 1965 as a roadster (U13), half-cab (U14) and wagon (U15) with the 105 hp 170 six, column-shift three-speed and Dana 20. The 289 V8 arrives in March 1966. 23,776 sold
- 1967: Sport package, dual master cylinder with split brakes, self-adjusting brakes, optional 11.5-gal auxiliary tank
- 1968: Locking front hubs, revised bumpers and side-marker reflectors. Last year of the roadster
- 1969: 302 V8 replaces the 289; electric wipers replace vacuum ones midyear; steering stabilizer standard
- 1970: Evaporative emissions controls and smaller fuel tanks. The Sport becomes a separate model
- 1971: Dana 44 front axle replaces the Dana 30 midyear. Baja Bronco package introduced
- 1972: Ranger trim arrives; last year of the half-cab; fuel tanks reduced again
- 1973: C4 automatic and power steering optional; 200 six replaces the 170; J-shift Dana 20 with a 2.34:1 low range from midyear
- 1974: California-specific emissions equipment; best sales year at 25,824
- 1975: Catalytic converter and unleaded fuel. CJ Pony Parts lists the 302 at 125 hp net
- 1976: Power front disc brakes, larger rear drums, front anti-roll bar, quicker steering box (about four turns lock to lock) and a Y-type steering linkage that Autotrader Classics says was poorly received
- 1977: Heavy-duty 9-inch rear housing, fuel doors instead of exposed caps, 14.4-gal plastic main tank and 8-gal auxiliary. Last year before the full-size Bronco

### Capability
- Wheelbase: 92 in (2,337 mm)
- Length: 151.5 in (3,848 mm)
- Turning circle: 34 ft (10.4 m) curb to curb (Ford launch release, 1965)
- Fuel tank: 14.4 gal main + 8 gal auxiliary (1977) (Capacities varied by year; an 11.5-gal auxiliary tank was optional from 1967)
- Transfer-case low range: 2.46:1 (1966–72) · 2.34:1 (1973–77)
- Engine output: 170 I6: 105 hp · 289 V8: 200 hp · 302 V8 (1975): 125 hp net
- Pickup box (half-cab): 32.8 cu ft (Ford launch release)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: G78-15 and similar bias-ply sizes on 15-in steel wheels (factory), H78-15 largest factory option (1970 owner's manual, as quoted on ClassicBroncos)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x139.7 (5x5.5")
- Offset: Backspacing 3.75–4.25 in for uncut fenders (Performance Plus Tire)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 30x9.50R15 (The safe choice on uncut fenders; 31x10.50R15 may lightly rub at full stuff or full lock, and 235/75R15 bolts on)
- Biggest tire, 2–3 in lift: 31x10.50R15 (up to 32 in) (Uncut fenders, with 3.75–4.25 in of wheel backspacing)
- Biggest tire, 2–4 in, cut fenders lift: 33x12.50R15 (Rear fenders cut for flares; backspacing 3.25–3.75 in. Check caster and C-bushings after lifting)
- Biggest tire, Bigger lift plus body work lift: 35x12.50R15 (Bigger suspension or body lift and trimming)

### Buying checks
- Rust, everywhere, even in dry states: Autotrader Classics calls rust the biggest concern and warns that surface rust can hide serious rot. Check the rocker panels and the floor pans they join, the cargo floor (especially where it meets the half-cab wall), the door posts around the hinges, the firewall and inner fenders, the tailgate and the frame rails. Velocity Restorations notes that structural rust can cost more than it's worth to fix.
- Cut or uncut rear fenders: Many early Broncos had their rear fenders cut to fit flares and bigger tires. Uncut trucks are rarer and worth more, and flared trucks sell for less. Look closely at the quarter panels for filler or patched-in arches.
- Frame at the steering box: Wild Horses points out that the frame takes a lot of load where the steering box bolts on, and that area can weaken or crack. With the engine running, have someone turn the wheel and watch the box. If it moves on the frame, check for cracks before you buy.
- Does it drive straight?: A wandering early Bronco usually has the wrong caster, according to Wild Horses, especially after a lift with the wrong C-bushings. Lean of 2 inches or more is common after a suspension change. Neither is expensive to fix, but both tell you how carefully the truck was built.
- VIN and data plate: The VIN is stamped on the frame rail, just ahead of the firewall under the engine, and the full data plate is inside the glovebox door. Check that they match the title. The first three characters give the series (U13, U14 or U15) and the fourth the engine code; a mismatch is common after decades of swaps, which matters most on a claimed original.
- Baja, Sport and Ranger claims: Only 650 Baja Broncos were sold, and they now bring far more than a standard truck, so clones exist. Ask for documentation of any special edition. The data plate and VIN won't prove a Baja by themselves, so lean on build records and a marque specialist.
- Who built it?: Most early Broncos for sale are modified, and many are full restomods. Velocity Restorations suggests asking what was done and by whom, whether there is documentation, whether the frame has been repaired or replaced, and how it drives at highway speed. A cheap build can cost more over time than a good one.
- Hard-to-find parts: Mechanical parts are easy because the trucks use common Ford engines and Dana axles. Autotrader notes that thin steel grilles dent easily and are often cut for plows or PTO gear, and good tailgates are also scarce. Price those in if they're bad.

### Common repairs
#### Floor pan, rocker and door-post rust repair
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ Several weekends, depending on how far it goes · cost Parts plus welding labor; full floor and platform sets cost several hundred dollars
Symptoms: Holes or soft spots in the floor, bubbling along the rockers, sagging doors that won't latch cleanly, rust around the door-post hinges and water on the floor after rain.
Fix: Strip the interior and probe every seam with a pick. Brace the door openings before cutting anything structural, then cut back to clean metal. Reproduction floor pans come with the grooves and body-mount recesses, and the floor channel support rails underneath are sold separately; replace them if they've gone. Fit inner and outer rockers and front door posts as needed, check door gaps before final welding, then seam-seal and coat the new metal. If the firewall, inner fenders or frame rails are also rotten, Autotrader and Velocity both warn that the bill can outrun the truck's value.
Tools: MIG welder · cut-off wheel and spot-weld drill · door-opening braces and clamps · seam sealer and weld-through primer

#### Front disc brake conversion (1966–75)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day · cost Kits $675 (Bronco Graveyard, with proportioning valve and bracket) to $849.99 (Wild Horses)
Symptoms: Fading, pulling or long stops from the original four-wheel drums, especially on bigger tires. 1976–77 trucks already have factory power front discs.
Fix: Jack up the front and remove the wheels, locking hubs, drums and the drum-brake spindles. Wild Horses' kit fits 1966–early 1971 Dana 30 and 1971–75 Dana 44 axles with six-bolt drum knuckles, and includes disc spindles, caliper brackets, calipers and pads, hub-and-rotor assemblies and new wheel bearings. Bolt on the new spindles and brackets, pack and fit the bearings in the new hubs, and set the bearing preload. Fit new caliper hoses and a proportioning valve for disc-front, drum-rear brakes, then bleed the system. Wild Horses recommends aftermarket locking hubs such as Warn or Mile Marker, and buyers suggest doing the outer axle seals and U-joints and adding a brake booster at the same time.
Tools: Spindle-nut socket · bearing packer and seal driver · flare-nut wrenches · brake bleeder

#### Fix wandering and lean: caster, C-bushings and track-bar bushings
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day to a day · cost Parts about $100–150 (C-bushing kit plus track-bar bushings)
Symptoms: The truck darts and wanders on the highway, needs constant correction, shimmies after bumps, or sits visibly lower on one side at the front.
Fix: Wild Horses says about 90 percent of wandering early Broncos have incorrect caster, and its spec is +4 to +9 degrees. Lifting the truck moves caster negative, which is why offset C-bushings exist; 7 degrees is the standard. Support the frame on stands (not the axle), unbolt the radius-arm caps and fit the new C-bushings the right way up, following the 'front bottom' and 'rear bottom' markings. A bushing installed upside down changes caster and can make the truck lean. If it still leans, Brian Cooke's fix is to check that both radius arms touch a level floor at the same time and reseat the C-bushings by retightening the cap bolts in a different order. For shimmy and death wobble, Wild Horses names worn upper track-bar bushings as the number one culprit.
Tools: Jack stands under the frame · floor jack · socket set and torque wrench · angle finder for caster

#### Front-end rebuild: ball joints (or king pins), wheel bearings and spindle seals
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day for both sides · cost Ball joints $38.99 per side (Wild Horses); bearing and seal kits extra
Symptoms: Loose or sloppy steering, wander and uneven tire wear. With the front jacked up, the wheel rocks when you grip it at the top and bottom.
Fix: Dana 44 axles (mid-1971 on) use upper and lower ball joints; earlier Dana 30s use king pins with tapered bearings instead. On a Dana 44, remove the hub, bearings and spindle and slide out the axle shaft. Owners on ClassicBroncos remove the castle nut, unscrew the upper ball joint's adjusting bushing with a spanner tool, then separate the knuckle with a pickle fork, alternating taps top and bottom. Press out the old joints and press in the new ones, keeping the upper grease fitting accessible. While it's apart, replace the spindle bearing and seal and the axle-stub slinger and seal, fit new hub seals with the inner bearings, and consider new axle U-joints. Pack the wheel bearings and set the preload.
Tools: Ball-joint press (rentable) · Dana 44 ball-joint spanner · pickle fork · brass drift · spindle-nut socket

#### Steering box mount, play adjustment and power-steering conversion
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day for a conversion; more if the frame needs welding · cost Bronco Graveyard's complete Delphi conversion is $1,199
Symptoms: Steering play, a box that shifts on the frame when the wheel is turned, cracks in the frame around the box, or heavy manual steering (manual was standard through 1972).
Fix: Check the box is tight to the frame first: a loose box moves and makes the steering feel vague. Inspect the frame rail around the mounting bolts and, as Wild Horses suggests, weld in extra support if it's cracked or thin. Never turn the play-adjusting screw on top of the box more than one turn in, or the sector shaft jams against the piston. To add power steering, you need double-groove crank and water-pump pulleys, a pump bracket and a pump. On trucks with vacuum wipers fed from the fuel pump, the pump can't go in its normal place, so convert to electric wipers first. Bronco Graveyard's Delphi kit has a 3.75-turn box that bolts on with the three stock bolts (a fourth hole can be drilled), plus the pump, hoses, pulleys and a collapsible lower shaft for a 3/4-inch 36-spline aftermarket column.
Tools: Pitman-arm puller · socket set and torque wrench · welder and grinder (if the frame is cracked) · drill

#### Dana 20 transfer case leaks and rebuild
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend · cost Master bearing and seal kits $109–125 (Bronco Graveyard)
Symptoms: Oil weeping from the case or the joint with the transmission's intermediate housing, gear whine, jumping out of range, or a stiff shift.
Fix: Work out which case you have before ordering. Wild Horses notes that 1966–72 cases use a T-handle with a 2.46:1 low range and 1973–77 cases a J-shift with 2.34:1, and the front output, bearings, shift rails and detents differ. Drain the case, disconnect both driveshafts, the speedometer cable and the shift linkage, and unbolt the case from the intermediate housing. Replace the bearings, seals and gaskets; a deluxe kit adds a new cluster shaft, thrust washers and shims. Fit a new intermediate seal and gasket, reinstall, and fill to the plug. ClassicBroncos regulars say Ford specified 50-weight motor oil for the Dana 20, and some warn that GL-5 additives can harm its brass and bronze parts.
Tools: Drain pan · snap-ring pliers · bearing puller and press · seal drivers · torque wrench

#### Vacuum wipers to electric (1966–69)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Parts plus your time
Symptoms: Wipers that slow down or stop when you accelerate uphill, the classic vacuum-wiper failure, or a vacuum-wiper fuel pump blocking a power-steering pump.
Fix: Ford switched from vacuum to electric wipers in mid-1969, and on the early trucks the vacuum supply runs through the fuel pump. Remove the vacuum motor and its lines, fit the electric motor and bracket on the windshield frame, connect the motor arm to the existing linkage and run the wiper harness to a switch. An electric-wiper cover finishes the job. Replace the fuel pump with a non-vacuum V8 pump while you're there, which also frees up the spot a power-steering pump needs.
Tools: Screwdrivers and sockets · drill · wire strippers and crimpers · test light

### Baseline service
Assume nothing has been done, and assume plenty has been changed: most early Broncos have been modified, so check what engine, axles and transfer case you actually have before buying parts. The data plate on the glovebox door gives the factory engine, transmission and axle codes.
- Engine oil & filter: 302 V8 capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · the 1966 170 six has a 6-quart oil pan (Ford press release) · At purchase, then per manual (Swapped engines are common. Check what's actually in the truck before ordering a filter.)
- Air filter: Paper element on most trucks · early sixes had an oil-bath air cleaner · Inspect at every oil change (An oil-bath cleaner needs its reservoir cleaned and refilled with oil, not a new element.)
- Spark plugs, cap, rotor & wires: Plug type and gap [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (Points-type ignition is still common on unmodified trucks. Set dwell and timing afterward.)
- Coolant, thermostat, hoses & water pump: Coolant type and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush at purchase, then every 2 years (The stock Bronco V8 water pump has its inlet on the passenger side, which matters for pump and bracket fitment.)
- Belts: Fan and alternator belt; extra belt with power steering · At purchase (Carry a spare on the trail.)
- Manual transmission (three-speed): Gear oil; ClassicBroncos owners use 75W-90 · grade and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Change at purchase (Many trucks now have floor shifters or swapped four- and five-speeds. Identify the gearbox first.)
- Automatic transmission (C4, 1973–77): ATF · type and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Pan drop and new filter at purchase (Check the cable shift linkage for wear while you're under there.)
- Dana 20 transfer case: Factory spec was 50-weight motor oil (ClassicBroncos) · fill to the plug · Change at purchase (Some owners avoid GL-5 gear oil because of its effect on brass and bronze parts. Look for leaks at the intermediate housing.)
- Front & rear differentials (Dana 30/44, Ford 9-inch): Hypoid gear oil around 90 weight (75W-90/80W-90) · friction modifier for limited-slip · capacities [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Change at purchase and after deep water (Factory ratios were 3.50, 4.11 and 4.57, some with limited-slip; the axle code on the data plate tells you which.)
- Front wheel bearings, hub seals & locking hubs: Repack with wheel-bearing grease; new seals · At purchase (Replace the hub seals whenever the inner bearing comes out. Check the locking-hub O-rings too.)
- C-bushings, radius-arm & track-bar bushings: Caster +4° to +9° (Wild Horses) · Inspect at purchase (Worn upper track-bar bushings are the top cause of shimmy. Make sure the C-bushings are the right way up.)
- Brake fluid, hoses & lines: Fluid type [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush at purchase, then every 2 years (Replace old rubber hoses and rusty rear axle lines.)
- Fuel pump, filter & sending unit: Mechanical pump; in-tank sending-unit filter · At purchase (On vacuum-wiper trucks the wiper vacuum comes through the fuel pump. Replace cracked rubber fuel hose.)
- Factory shop manual: Ford truck shop manuals on CD (1966 and 1977 editions listed) · Once (Worth having for torque specs, capacities and adjustment procedures.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: On an uncut truck at stock height, Performance Plus Tire calls 30x9.50R15 the safe choice and says 31x10.50R15 may lightly rub at full stuff or full lock. ClassicBroncos owners agree: 235/75R15 bolts on, and a few squeeze 33x9.50s on with fender trimming and some rubbing. For 31–32-inch tires on uncut fenders, plan on a 2–3-inch lift and 3.75–4.25 inches of wheel backspacing; 33x12.50s generally mean cut fenders.

Q: Does mine have a Dana 30 or a Dana 44 front axle?
A: Ford switched from the Dana 30 to the stronger Dana 44 partway through the 1971 model year. A quick tell is the knuckle: Wild Horses notes the Dana 30 uses king pins, while the Dana 44 uses ball joints. Every first-generation Bronco has a Ford 9-inch rear axle.

Q: Which engine should I look for?
A: Most buyers want a V8. The 289 arrived in March 1966 and was replaced by the 302 for 1969, which ran to 1977; CJ Pony Parts lists the 1975 302 at 125 hp net. The sixes are the 170 (105 hp at launch) and, from 1973, the 200. Plenty of trucks now have swapped engines, from 351 Windsors to modern Coyote V8s.

Q: How do I read the VIN?
A: An early Bronco VIN is 11 characters, such as U15GLxxxxxx. U13 is the roadster, U14 the half-cab pickup and U15 the wagon. The fourth character is the engine (F for the 170 six, N for the 289, G for the 302) and the fifth the plant (L for Michigan Truck). The VIN is stamped on the frame rail ahead of the firewall, and the data plate is inside the glovebox door.

Q: Why does my Bronco wander?
A: Wild Horses says about 90 percent of wandering early Broncos have incorrect caster. The spec is +4 to +9 degrees, and lifting the truck moves it negative. Offset C-bushings (7 degrees is standard) bring it back, and taller lifts may need drop brackets or long radius arms. For shimmy and death wobble, check the upper track-bar bushings first.

Q: Does it have front disc brakes?
A: Only 1976–77 Broncos came with power front disc brakes from the factory. Earlier trucks have drums all round, and conversion kits for 1966–75 Dana 30 and Dana 44 axles are widely available. Wild Horses' kit uses new spindles, brackets, calipers and hub-and-rotor assemblies.

Q: Did it come with power steering?
A: Manual steering was standard through 1972, and power steering was optional from 1973. According to Wild Horses, 1973–75 power boxes take about six turns lock to lock and 1976–77 boxes about four. Many owners convert to a modern Delphi box; Bronco Graveyard's kit has 3.75 turns lock to lock.

Q: What oil goes in the Dana 20?
A: ClassicBroncos regulars say Ford specified 50-weight motor oil for the Bronco's Dana 20, filled until it runs out of the fill plug. Some owners use synthetic manual-transmission fluid or 75W-90 gear oil instead, and some warn that GL-5 additives can harm the case's brass and bronze parts.

Q: What's a Baja Bronco?
A: A package designed by Bill Stroppe and sold through Ford dealers from 1971, with an automatic, quick-ratio power steering, fender flares over Gates Commando tires, a roll bar, reinforced bumpers and red, white, blue and black paint. It cost $5,566 against $3,665 for a standard V8 Bronco, and only 650 were sold in four years. Insist on documentation.

Q: Are uncut fenders worth paying for?
A: Yes, if originality matters to you. Many trucks had their rear fenders cut for flares and bigger tires, so uncut ones are rarer and bring more money, and flared trucks sell for less. If you plan to run 33s or bigger anyway, a well-done cut truck can save you money.

Q: What are they worth?
A: A lot, and it depends on who built it. Of 306 complete early Broncos sold on Bring a Trailer between August 2025 and October 2026, the middle half of stock and mildly modified trucks sold for about $41,500–70,000, with a median near $55,500. Projects mostly went for $9,600–37,000, and Coyote-swapped and shop-built restomods for about $122,000–166,500, topping out at $325,000. Hagerty recorded a 12 percent drop in the second quarter of 2026, but says a driver still costs $50,000 or more.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: There's no consensus year, and Velocity Restorations says condition matters more than year. It calls 1969–72 'the sweet spot' for the 302 V8 with a vintage feel, and 1973–77 the most refined, with power steering, the automatic and, from 1976, front disc brakes. Autotrader Classics notes the stronger Dana 44 front axle from mid-1971 and that the 1976 steering linkage was poorly received, while CJ Pony Parts calls 1974–75 among the most desirable and most available years. Originality and uncut fenders move the price more than the model year does.

## Ford Full-size Bronco (1978–1996)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/bronco/full-size/
Codes: 1978–79, 1980–86, 1987–91, 1992–96

Verdict: Ford took an F-Series four-by-four, cut a foot out of it and bolted on a roof you could lift off, and in doing so built the Bronco most people still picture. Simple pushrod engines, parts in every junkyard and a Twin Traction Beam front end that rewards anyone who owns an alignment gauge.

For 1978 Ford stopped pretending the Bronco was a small truck. The early Bronco had been a 92-inch-wheelbase box that fought the CJ-5 and the Scout; the new one was a shortened F-100 four-by-four aimed at the Chevrolet K5 Blazer, the Dodge Ramcharger and Jeep's two-door SJ Cherokee, cousin of the Grand Wagoneer. Wikipedia's figures show what that meant: 12 inches more wheelbase, about 28 inches more length, 11 inches more width and between 1,100 and 1,600 pounds more weight, depending on the powertrain. In an era of downsizing, Ford went the other way on purpose, and it worked.

### 1978–79: PROJECT SHORTHORN
Development ran under the name Project Shorthorn and the truck was meant to launch for 1974. The 1973 fuel crisis pushed it back four years, so by the time the second-generation Bronco went on sale, its 1980 replacement was already nearly finished. Ford built it on the 1973–79 F-100 chassis with a 104-inch wheelbase, a coil-sprung Dana 44 front axle and a leaf-sprung Ford 9-inch rear. It was the last Bronco with a solid front axle until the nameplate went away. Part-time 4WD with a gear-driven New Process 205 was standard; a full-time, chain-driven NP203 was optional.
There was no six. The 351M V8 was standard and the 400 was optional, both two-barrel engines with about 156–158 hp; the 400 made 277 lb-ft against the 351M's 262. Doors, forward roof and dash came straight from the F-100, and Dick Nesbitt's lift-off fiberglass top covered only the area behind the B-pillars, with the seals designed to beat the leaks of the Blazer's top. The rear glass wound down into the tailgate. Demand was strong enough that buyers waited months, and Ford built 77,917 in 1978 and 104,038 in 1979, outselling the Blazer and the Ramcharger for the first time.

### 1980–86: TWIN TRACTION BEAM
The 1980 Bronco moved to the new seventh-generation F-150 but kept the 104-inch wheelbase. To chase fuel economy, Ford gave the 1980–81 trucks a lighter frame with holes stamped in it, saving 375 lb, then went back to a stronger frame for 1982. The big change was up front: a Dana 44 Twin Traction Beam, Ford's patented independent front drive axle. Each side pivots on its own beam, there is a U-joint in the middle, and the differential sits offset to the driver's side. Wikipedia sums up the reputation: unloved by some slow-speed crawlers, praised by high-speed desert racers.
Engines got smaller first. The 4.9-liter 300 inline-six became standard (manual only), the 302 V8 came back, the 400 was dropped and the 351M gave way to the 351 Windsor in 1982. A 210-hp high-output 351 arrived for 1984, and in 1985 the 302 gained multiport fuel injection and 190 hp. The blue oval replaced F-O-R-D lettering on the hood for 1982, and the Eddie Bauer package, with color-keyed two-tone paint, arrived for 1985. The rear axle went from the 9-inch to the 8.8 by the end of 1986.

### 1987–96: FUEL INJECTION, AIRBAGS AND A BOLTED-ON ROOF
The 1987 facelift brought the eighth-generation F-150 nose, composite headlights, a new dash and standard rear-wheel ABS. Fuel injection reached the 300 six for 1987 and the 351 for 1988, the year a Mazda-built M5OD five-speed manual and standard transfer-case skid plates also arrived. The C6 automatic gave way to the overdrive AOD and E4OD around 1990. For 1991, the Bronco's 25th year, the Silver Anniversary Edition brought exclusive Currant Red paint and the first leather seats in a Bronco.
The 1992 truck got a rounder ninth-generation nose. Four-wheel ABS followed for 1993, a driver's airbag for 1994, and the 300 six left the line-up, making every later Bronco a V8. Three-point rear belts and a center brake light now mounted in the hardtop, so Ford stopped describing top removal in the owner's manual and fastened the top with #40 security Torx bolts. The last Bronco left Wayne, Michigan, on June 12, 1996, and the four-door Expedition replaced it. Ford says the white 1993 Bronco on the 405 freeway in June 1994 had nothing to do with that decision, because sales were already falling.

### THE RESTOMOD ERA
Thirty years on, the full-size Bronco has become the affordable way into Bronco ownership and also a favorite donor for restomods. Bring a Trailer's 1978–79 page alone listed 263 auctions by October 2026. Prices run from a $14,000 1979 Ranger XLT to a Coyote-swapped 1979 Ranger XLT at $81,500. In August 2026 a 1979 Custom with a 7.3-liter Godzilla V8, a 10-speed automatic and Super Duty axles sold for $191,000. The 1987–96 trucks are the bargain: most ordinary XLTs and Eddie Bauers on BaT sell for between $7,500 and $32,500. They are simple and plentiful, and since 2021 they have shared the name with the sixth-generation Bronco, but they are still at their best covered in mud.

### Data plate
- Model Years: 1978–1996 (second to fifth generations)
- Assembly: Michigan Truck Plant, Wayne, Michigan; also Broadmeadows (Australia, 3rd gen) and Valencia (Venezuela, 4th–5th gen)
- Body: 3-door wagon with lift-off rear hardtop
- Wheelbase: 104 in (1978–86) · 104.7 in (1987–96)
- Length: 180.3 in (1978–79) to 183.6 in (1992–96)
- Width: 79.1–79.3 in
- Curb Weight: 4,663–4,718 lb (1978–79) · 4,343–4,374 lb (1980–86)
- Front Axle: Dana 44 solid (1978–79) · Dana 44 TTB (1980–96)
- Rear Axle: Ford 9-inch · Ford 8.8
- Engines: 4.9 300 I6 · 5.0 302 V8 · 5.8 351M/351W V8 · 6.6 400 V8
- Wheels: 5 x 139.7 mm (5 x 5.5 in) bolt pattern
- Built: ≈ 902,500 (sum of Wikipedia's annual figures)
- Replaced By: Ford Expedition (1997)

### Engineering
Every full-size Bronco is a short-wheelbase F-Series. From the B-pillars forward it shares the pickup's cab, doors and dash, and behind them sits a three-door wagon body with a removable fiberglass top and a tailgate whose glass winds down into it. The chassis is a conventional ladder frame. The front axle changed from a solid Dana 44 to a Twin Traction Beam Dana 44 in 1980, and that change splits owners more than any other.
- Chassis: Ladder frame · 104 in (1978–86) / 104.7 in (1987–96) wheelbase (1978–79 on the F-100, 1980 on the new F-150. The 1980–81 frame was lightened with stamped holes; 1982 went back to a stronger frame.)
- Front Axle: Dana 44 solid, coil springs (1978–79) · Dana 44 TTB (1980–96) (TTB is independent: two beams, a center U-joint, a slip yoke on the long side and the differential offset to the driver's side.)
- Rear Axle: Ford 9-inch, leaf springs → Ford 8.8 (Wikipedia says Ford moved its half-ton trucks to the 8.8 by the end of 1986.)
- Transfer Case: NP205 / NP203 (1978–79) · NP208 or BW1345 (from 1980) · BW1356 (later trucks) (Push-button electric shift was optional from 1987.)
- Engines: 351M, 400 (1978–79) · 300 I6, 302, 351M, 351W (1980–96) (302 fuel-injected from 1985, 300 from 1987, 351 from 1988. The six was dropped after 1993.)
- Roof: Lift-off fiberglass rear top (From 1994 the top carries the rear seat-belt anchors and the third brake light, and is held on with #40 security Torx bolts.)

### Versions
- 1978–1979 · 2nd gen · F-100 (1973–79 F-Series) · 351M V8 · 400 V8 · 156–158 hp · 262 / 277 lb-ft · Solid coil-sprung Dana 44 front, 9-inch rear. T-18 or NP435 4-speed, or C6 automatic. NP205 part-time or NP203 full-time.
- 1980–1986 · 3rd gen · F-150 (1980–86 F-Series) · 300 I6 · 302 V8 · 351M · 351W · 302 EFI 190 hp (1985) · 351 HO 210 hp (1984) · TTB Dana 44 front. 351W replaces 351M from 1982. Eddie Bauer package from 1985.
- 1987–1991 · 4th gen · eighth-generation F-150 styling · 300 I6 · 302 V8 · 351W · — · EFI on the 300 (1987) and 351 (1988). Rear ABS, M5OD 5-speed from 1988, E4OD from 1990. Silver Anniversary Edition for 1991.
- 1992–1996 · 5th gen · ninth-generation F-150 styling · 300 I6 (to 1993) · 302 V8 · 351W · — · 4-wheel ABS 1993, driver airbag 1994, OBD-II 1996. The hardtop is bolted on with security Torx from 1994.

### Year-by-year
- 1978: Second generation launches on the F-100 chassis: 104 in wheelbase, solid coil-sprung Dana 44 front, 9-inch rear, 351M standard and 400 optional, lift-off half hardtop. 77,917 built.
- 1979: Rectangular headlights standard on all trucks; catalytic converters added; 104,038 built, the best year of the full-size run.
- 1980: Third generation on the new F-150: Dana 44 Twin Traction Beam front, 300 six standard (manual only), 302 returns, 400 dropped. 1980–81 frames are lightened with stamped holes.
- 1982: Stronger frame returns; 351 Windsor replaces the 351M; blue oval replaces F-O-R-D on the hood.
- 1985: 302 gets multiport fuel injection (190 hp); Eddie Bauer package arrives. (A 210-hp 351 HO came for 1984.)
- 1987: Fourth generation: new nose and dash, composite headlights, standard rear ABS, optional push-button 4WD, fuel-injected 300 six.
- 1988: Fuel-injected 351; Mazda M5OD five-speed manual; transfer-case skid plate standard.
- 1990: Overdrive automatics replace the C6: AOD (1990) and E4OD (1990 on).
- 1991: Silver Anniversary Edition (Currant Red, gray leather) and Nite package; V8 and automatic only.
- 1992: Fifth generation: rounder ninth-generation F-Series nose, revised dash, optional leather and power mirrors.
- 1993: Four-wheel ABS replaces rear-only ABS.
- 1994: Driver's airbag; 300 six dropped; rear three-point belts and third brake light mount in the hardtop, which is now held on with security Torx bolts.
- 1996: OBD-II engines; the first Ford with turn signals in the mirrors. The last Bronco is built on June 12, 1996.

### Capability
- Wheelbase: 104 in (2,642 mm) 1978–86 · 104.7 in (2,659 mm) 1987–96
- Length: 180.3 in (1978–79) to 183.6 in (1992–96)
- Curb weight: 4,663–4,718 lb (1978–79) · 4,343–4,374 lb (1980–86) (Wikipedia infobox figures)
- Seating: Up to 6 (Three-across front bench and a folding, removable rear seat from 1978)

### Wheels and tires
- Bolt Pattern: 5x139.7 (5x5.5") on all 1978–96 trucks
- Lug Thread: 1/2"-20 UNF (listed for 1992–96)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 33 in (e.g. 33x12.50R15) (Bronco Zone owners run 33x12.50R15 on 15x10 wheels on stock-height 1980–96 trucks. Some needed the bumper ends trimmed or shimmed, and there can be slight radius-arm rub depending on the wheel. 31x10.50 clears with no contact.)
- Biggest tire, 3 in body lift lift: 35 in (The bare minimum for 35s according to one Bronco Zone owner, who warns of a lot of tire-to-body contact off-road.)
- Biggest tire, 4–6 in suspension lift: 35 in (4 in of suspension lift is the better option for 35s, and 6 in is called optimal. Plan for TTB camber bushings and lower gears.)
- Biggest tire, ≈ 6 in (8 in preferred) lift: 38 in (Needs serious fender trimming and strains the stock running gear.)

### Buying checks
- Rust in Ford's favorite places: Bronco Zone's long-time checklist names the inner rear fender lips, the bottoms of the B-pillars and the bottom of the tailgate, where spot-welded seams trap moisture. Also check the radiator core support where it bolts to the frame (mostly the passenger side), the floor around the rear seat-belt mounts, rain gutters, body mounts and the frame itself.
- Run the tailgate glass both ways: Lower and raise the rear window from the key and from the dash switch, then open and close the tailgate. Check the tailgate drains and the outer glass seal. A window that works from only one control points to the circuit, not the motor. On many trucks the driver's window switch must be in the center position before the tailgate key switch will work.
- Read the tires before the TTB: Uneven inner or outer tread wear means camber trouble. Look at the radius-arm bushings, which perish (one Bronco Zone owner replaced his at 80,000 miles), and check the ball joints and tie-rod ends. If the truck is lifted, ask whether adjustable camber bushings were fitted, because Bronco Graveyard says even 1–2-inch lift springs normally need them.
- E4OD fluid and the O/D light: On 1990–96 automatics, the fluid should be red, not brown or burnt-smelling, and read full at operating temperature. A flashing overdrive light (TCIL) while driving means the transmission has stored a fault code. Owners recommend fluid and filter service every 30,000 miles, and sooner for towing.
- Try 4-High and 4-Low: On push-button trucks, the shift motor and its connector are known trouble spots, often from a broken travel stop or a fouled connector. Ford recalled some 1993 trucks (93V-089) whose transfer cases had the wrong shift motor and could slip out of 4-High.
- Compression, cooling and leaks: Owners call a bad compression or vacuum test a deal-breaker. The plastic side seams of the radiator leak, most visibly after the engine cools overnight. Check the rear main and timing-cover seals, look for a cracked exhaust manifold or Y-pipe, and check for water in the oil.
- Decide whether you need a removable top: 1978–93 tops were designed to come off. From 1994 the top carries the rear three-point belts and the center brake light and is held with security Torx bolts. You can still remove it, but Wikipedia notes that driving without it can earn a ticket in some places.
- Open recalls: Old trucks still show up with open campaigns. The 1994–96 speed-control deactivation switch (05V-388) and its 1993 equivalents (07V-336 and 08V-051) can overheat and burn, and 1988–91 trucks had an ignition-switch short-circuit recall (96V-071). Check the VIN on NHTSA's site.

### Common repairs
#### Fix a tailgate window that won't move
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–3 hours · cost About $20 for a pair of regulator rollers (Wild Horses lists them at $9.99 each); a motor gear kit or a regulator costs more
Symptoms: The rear glass won't go up or down, moves from the key but not the dash switch (or the other way round), or grinds and stalls part-way.
Fix: First find out whether the motor or the circuit is at fault. Remove the tailgate access panel, find the motor connector near the bottom center of the opening, and power the motor directly from a battery with jumper leads; reversing the leads reverses it. If it runs, trace the circuit: the safety limit switch (in the latch handle on a 1980 truck), a corroded ground or broken wire, or the driver's window switch, which must be centered for the tailgate key switch to work. If the motor hums but the glass doesn't move, replace the nylon regulator gear with a gear kit. If the glass binds or cocks, replace both regulator-arm rollers that run in the lift channels under the glass, and lube the tracks with white lithium grease.
Tools: Trim tools · screwdrivers · 12 V jumper leads · test light or meter · white lithium grease.

#### Correct TTB camber with adjustable bushings
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours plus an alignment · cost Parts plus an alignment
Symptoms: Tires wearing on the inner or outer edge, especially after new springs or a lift, and an alignment shop saying it's 'out of adjustment'.
Fix: On a TTB Dana 44, camber is set by an offset bushing (sleeve) around the upper ball-joint stud. Bronco Graveyard describes the swap: remove the wheel, the cotter pin and the upper ball-joint nut, break the stud's taper free of the sleeve, pull the old sleeve with a sleeve puller and fit the new adjustable one. Adjustable sleeves cover 0.75 to 2.75 degrees, and any correction you don't need for camber can be turned into caster. Set both sides, torque the nuts, fit new cotter pins and have it aligned.
Tools: Jack and stands · camber/caster sleeve puller · hammer or pickle fork · torque wrench · camber gauge (optional).

#### Replace radius-arm bushings
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2–4 hours · cost Parts plus an alignment
Symptoms: A clunk over bumps or on braking, wandering steering and caster that won't hold. The rubber at the rear of each radius arm, where it passes through the frame bracket, is cracked or squashed out.
Fix: Support the frame on stands with the axle on a jack so the arms are unloaded. Remove the nut at the rear end of each radius arm, slide off the washers and old bushings, and pry the arm down out of the bracket just far enough to fit the new bushings and washers. Bronco Graveyard's 1980–87 kit swaps the rubber for polyurethane and replaces the loose washers; adjustable bushings are available if you need to correct caster after a lift. Torque at ride height and get an alignment.
Tools: Jack and stands · large sockets and breaker bar · pry bar · torque wrench.

#### Rebuild the TTB knuckle: spindle bearings, axle U-joints, ball joints
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ 4–6 hours per side · cost Parts plus your weekend
Symptoms: Clunk or play at the front wheel, grease flung around the hub, a clicking U-joint when turning in 4WD, or a ball joint that moves when you lever the wheel top to bottom.
Fix: With the hub and rotor off, unbolt the spindle and pull it to get at the outer axle shaft. Replace the spindle needle bearing and seals with a Spicer kit (1980–92 and 1994–96 kits differ), and replace the axle-shaft U-joints while the shafts are out; confirm the joint size for your shafts before ordering. If the ball joints are loose, press them out with a C-frame press and adapters, fit new Spicer joints, and reset the upper adjuster sleeve. Repack the wheel bearings, reassemble and set the bearing preload.
Tools: Hub/spindle-nut socket · slide hammer or seal puller · ball-joint C-press and adapters · U-joint press or vise · torque wrench.

#### Replace the TFI ignition module (1985–91 EFI)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 30–60 minutes · cost Parts plus a little patience
Symptoms: Hard hot starts, intermittent stalling that clears once the engine cools, misfires or erratic running on a fuel-injected V8.
Fix: The Thick Film Ignition module bolts to the side of the distributor, close to the thermostat housing, where Bronco Graveyard says engine heat eventually kills it. Disconnect the battery, unplug the module, remove its two screws (a long T20 driver or Ford's module tool helps), and slide it off its terminals. Coat the mounting face of the new module with dielectric grease, which acts as a heat sink, and fit it. Bronco Graveyard recommends genuine Motorcraft modules and notes that many owners carry a spare on the trail.
Tools: T20 Torx or Ford ignition-module tool · offset distributor clamp wrench (if the distributor has to come out) · dielectric grease.

#### Fix a push-button transfer case that won't shift
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: The 4WD lights blink or the case won't go into (or out of) 4-High or 4-Low on an electric-shift truck.
Fix: Bronco Zone owners point first at the shift motor and its connector: clean and reseat the connector and check for a broken travel stop. If the motor still doesn't respond, unbolt it from the BW1356, note the shift-shaft position and fit a new motor, replacing the shift seal while it's off. Match the new motor's position to the shift shaft before bolting it on. On a 1993 truck, check that recall 93V-089 (wrong shift motor) was done.
Tools: Sockets · electrical contact cleaner · multimeter · new shift seal.

#### Service the E4OD (1990–96)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2 hours · cost Parts plus fluid
Symptoms: Late or harsh shifts, a flashing overdrive light, or dark, burnt-smelling fluid.
Fix: Drop the pan, change the filter, clean the pan and magnet, and refill with Mercon V, which the factory manual quoted on Bronco Zone specifies for the E4OD. A pan drop only replaces about 8.5 of the roughly 16 quarts, so repeat the job, or add a drain plug or a deeper pan, to replace more of the old fluid. If you find particles or white (water-contaminated) fluid, get it diagnosed before you refill it. Read any stored codes if the O/D light flashes.
Tools: Drain pan · sockets · gasket scraper · funnel · torque wrench.

#### Cut out and patch the rust
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A weekend per area · cost Patch panels plus welding
Symptoms: Bubbling paint along the rear wheel-arch lips, holes at the bottom of the B-pillars or tailgate, a soft floor near the rear seat-belt anchors, a rotted radiator core support.
Fix: Bronco Zone owners blame Ford's spot-welded seams, which trap water, so the rust usually runs further than it looks. Strip back to clean steel, cut the panel out beyond the rot, and butt-weld in a patch or a full panel. Seam-seal, prime and paint, and treat the inside with cavity wax. On the tailgate, clear the drains and fit new internal hardware while it's apart.
Tools: Cut-off wheel · MIG welder · flap discs · panel clamps · seam sealer · cavity wax.

### Baseline service
These are thirty-year-old trucks with simple pushrod engines, so assume nothing has been done and baseline every fluid. Treat the front axle as a service item too. The TTB's spindle bearings, U-joints, ball joints and radius-arm bushings decide how the truck drives, and on most Broncos for sale they're original.
- Engine oil & filter: SAE 5W-30 preferred in all climates (Ford ESE-M2C153-E); 10W-30 acceptable in hot weather · 6 qt with filter (1992 5.8) · Then every 5,000 mi, or every 3,000 mi on Ford's severe-duty schedule (1996 workshop manual) (Drain-plug torque 15–25 ft-lb (AMSOIL lookup). Owners of tired, high-mileage engines often move to thicker oils.)
- Engine air filter: Panel element [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Check every oil change; Ford's 1996 schedule replaces it every 30,000 mi or 30 months, sooner in dust (Check the airbox seal and the intake tube after any trail trip.)
- Ignition: plugs, cap, rotor, wires, TFI: 1996 workshop manual: 5.8 Motorcraft ASF-32C, gap 0.042–0.046 in · 5.0 ASF-42P, gap 0.052–0.056 in · 4.9 BSF-44C, gap 0.042–0.046 in. Check the VECI decal on earlier trucks · Baseline once; Ford's 1996 schedule replaces plugs at 60,000 mi (On 1985–91 EFI trucks, inspect the distributor-mounted TFI module and fit any replacement with dielectric grease as a heat sink.)
- Coolant & hoses: Ethylene glycol, 50/50 premix · 14.8–15.9 qt (1992 5.8, by transmission and A/C) · Flush at purchase, then every 30,000 mi or 36 months (Ford 1996 schedule; first change from new at 50,000 mi/48 months) (Check the plastic side seams of the radiator, which tend to leak after the engine cools overnight.)
- Automatic transmission (E4OD): Mercon V · 16.2 qt total, ≈ 8.5 qt on a pan drop (4WD E4OD) · Fluid and filter every 30,000 mi (owners' recommendation); sooner if towing (A single pan drop replaces only about half the fluid. C6 (13.5 qt total) and AOD (12.3 qt) trucks: use the fluid stamped on the dipstick.)
- Manual transmission (M5OD-R2): Motorcraft MERCON ATF · 3.8 qt (7.6 pints) for the Mazda R2 five-speed (1996 workshop manual); AMSOIL lists 6.8–7.6 pints · Drain and refill at purchase; Ford changes it every 60,000 mi (Owners recommend resealing the rubber plugs in the M5OD shift cover, which shrink and leak. Check the slave cylinder for leaks.)
- Transfer case: BW1356: Mercon V (factory manual), ≈ 4 pints · BW1345: ≈ 6.3 pints · Drain and refill at purchase (AMSOIL notes Ford has since updated the spec to Mercon LV. On push-button cases, clean the shift-motor connector while you're under there.)
- Front differential (Dana 44, solid or TTB): Ford 4x4 Gear Oil F1TZ-19580-A (WSL-M2C191-A) · 3.6 pints for the Dana 44 IFS (1996 workshop manual, F-150/Bronco). The manual's table doesn't state a viscosity, so match the Ford spec · Change at purchase and after deep water (Check the axle vent tube, and look for gear oil weeping from the slip-yoke seal on the long side of a TTB.)
- Rear differential (8.8 / 9-inch): SAE 80W-90 (Ford XY-80W90-QL, WSP-M2C197-A) · ≈ 5.5 pints (8.8 Traction-Lok) plus 4 oz Ford friction modifier (F3TZ-19B546-MA) · Change at purchase (Fill to 1/4–9/16 inch below the filler hole (factory manual via Bronco Zone). Seal the 8.8 cover with silicone (D6AZ-19562-AA or equivalent).)
- Front wheel bearings, spindle bearings & hubs: Ford High Temperature 4x4 Front Axle and Wheel Bearing Grease E8TZ-19590-A (ESA-M1C198-A), which the 1996 manual also specifies for the spindle needle bearings and axle U-joints · Repack at purchase (On a TTB truck, do the spindle needle bearings and seals and the axle U-joints while the hub is apart.)
- Steering & front-suspension wear parts: Radius-arm bushings · ball joints · tie-rod ends · Inspect at purchase (Have a helper rock the steering wheel while you watch each joint. Perished radius-arm bushings are common.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 (Ford C6AZ-19542-AA/BA, ESA-M6C25-A) · Flush at purchase. Ford's 1996 schedule sets no fluid-change interval, only hose and line inspections every 15,000 mi (On manual trucks the hydraulic clutch shares the same fluid type.)
- Power steering: Ford Premium Power Steering Fluid E4AZ-19582-C or E6AZ-19582-AA (ESW-M2C33-F), per the 1996 workshop manual. Some owners use Mercon V instead · Check level and hoses at purchase (A leaking box can be resealed rather than replaced; seal kits are available.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: A 33-inch tire. On Bronco Zone, one moderator ran 33x12.50R15s on 15x10 wheels on a stock-height 1986 with no rubbing; another owner said 33s fit without a lift but snugly, sometimes needing the bumper ends trimmed or shimmed, with slight radius-arm rub depending on the wheel. For 35s, a 3-inch body lift is the bare minimum, a 4-inch suspension lift is better and 6 inches is ideal. 38s need about 6 inches plus serious fender trimming. Check your axle ratio before going bigger.

Q: Which years should I look at?
A: It depends what you want, because there's no consensus best year: Bronco Zone owners argue engines (the 351 'feels like a truck motor', the 302 is smoother) and OBD-I versus OBD-II rather than model years. The 1978–79 trucks are the only ones with a solid front axle and 400 V8s, and they bring the most money. The 302 got fuel injection in 1985, the 351 and the five-speed manual came in 1988, and four-wheel ABS and a driver's airbag followed in 1993 and 1994. From 1994 the top is effectively fixed, and the 1996 trucks have OBD-II diagnostics.

Q: Can I take the hardtop off?
A: Yes on 1978–93 trucks, which were built for it. From 1994 the top carries the rear three-point belts and the third brake light, so Ford removed the instructions from the owner's manual and fastened the top with #40 security Torx bolts. It still comes off, but driving without it can mean inoperable rear belts and a missing brake light, and in some states a ticket.

Q: Is Twin Traction Beam bad off-road?
A: It's divisive. TTB was Ford's attempt to combine solid-axle simplicity with independent-suspension ride, and Wikipedia notes that slow-speed crawlers tend to dislike it while high-speed racers praise it. The practical issue is that camber changes with ride height, so lifted trucks need adjustable camber bushings: Bronco Graveyard says they're normally needed even with 1–2-inch lift springs.

Q: What oil and fluids does it take?
A: The 1996 shop manual, quoted on Bronco Zone, prefers 5W-30 in all climates. AMSOIL's capacity lookup for a 1992 5.8 lists 6 quarts with the filter. The E4OD and BW1356 transfer case take Mercon V; AMSOIL lists 16.2 quarts total (about 8.5 on a pan drop) for a 4WD E4OD, and 4 pints for the 1356. The 8.8 rear takes 80W-90 (Ford XY-80W90-QL), about 5.5 pints, plus 4 oz of Ford friction modifier in a Traction-Lok. Coolant is a 50/50 ethylene-glycol mix. The 1996 workshop manual adds Mercon ATF for the Mazda five-speed (3.8 quarts), Ford 4x4 gear oil for the Dana 44 front (3.6 pints) and Ford Premium Power Steering Fluid for the pump.

Q: 9-inch or 8.8 rear axle?
A: The 1978–79 Bronco and early third-generation trucks have the leaf-sprung Ford 9-inch. Ford moved its half-ton trucks to the 8.8 by the end of 1986, so most later Broncos have the 8.8. If it matters to you, confirm which axle a given truck has from its axle tag or with the seller.

Q: Can I get one with a manual gearbox?
A: Yes, through 1996. The 1978–79 trucks offered Borg-Warner T-18 or New Process 435 four-speeds, and the 300 six was manual-only in the early 1980s. A Mazda-built M5OD five-speed arrived for 1988. The 1991 Silver Anniversary and Nite editions, and the Eddie Bauer, came only with a V8 and an automatic.

Q: How many were built?
A: Wikipedia's year-by-year figures add up to about 902,500: 181,955 in 1978–79, 322,429 in 1980–86, 235,451 in 1987–91 and 162,703 in 1992–96. Treat the total as approximate, because the table repeats identical figures for 1983–84 and for 1987–88.

Q: Did the O.J. Simpson chase kill the Bronco?
A: No, according to Ford. Al Cowlings's white 1993 Bronco XLT made the June 17, 1994 chase famous, but Ford said sales were already declining. The Expedition replaced the Bronco for 1997, and the last one was built on June 12, 1996.

Q: What are they worth?
A: On Bring a Trailer in 2025–26, ordinary 1987–96 trucks mostly sold for $7,500 to $32,500, and the best Eddie Bauers and celebrity-owned trucks went higher (a 1995 Eddie Bauer sold for $67,500). 1980–86 trucks ran from a $7,750 project to $50,000. The 1978–79 trucks are the most expensive: stock examples sold for about $14,000 to $49,000, and big-engine restomods sold for $80,000 to $191,000.

## Ford Bronco II (1984–1990)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/bronco/bronco-ii/
Codes: 1984–88, 1989–90

Verdict: Ford put a roof on the new Ranger, cut the wheelbase to 94 inches and sold more than 760,000 of the result. It is light, narrow, simple and genuinely good on a tight trail, and it carries the heaviest safety file of any small 4x4 of its era. Buy one with your eyes open and drive it like what it is.

In March 1983 Ford introduced a second Bronco that had almost nothing to do with the first two. The Bronco II was the new Ranger compact pickup with a short enclosed wagon body where the bed would be, built alongside it at Louisville Assembly from January 1983 and sold as a 1984 model. It was roughly the size of the early Bronco, nearly a foot shorter than Chevrolet's new S-10 Blazer, and it arrived the same year as the Jeep Cherokee XJ and the first 4Runner. MotorTrend liked it so much it decided XLT stood for "Xcellent Little Truck". Then the rollover numbers came in.

### 1984–85: A RANGER WITH A ROOF
Under the skin it was all Ranger: a ladder frame cut to a 94-inch wheelbase, Ford's Twin Traction Beam front suspension with a Dana 28 differential, coil springs and radius arms, and a leaf-sprung Ford 7.5-inch axle at the back. Wikipedia notes that nearly the whole driver's compartment came straight from the pickup. Every early truck was four-wheel drive, with a Borg-Warner 1350 transfer case, and power came from the German-built 2.8-liter Cologne V6: carbureted, 115 hp and 150 lb-ft. A Toyo Kogyo four-speed or a C5 three-speed automatic sent it rearward.
Ford sold it as a lifestyle object from the start. Its own marketing called it a vehicle for "men, single people, or young couples", the sort of John Wayne truck that made buyers feel they could conquer anything. The 1984 range already included an Eddie Bauer edition, which The Ranger Station calls the first Ford to wear the outdoor brand: two-tone paint over Light Desert Tan, a tan interior with pine-tree stitching, and Eddie Bauer luggage shipped to the buyer's house. For 1985 the four-speed became a five-speed, the A4LD four-speed automatic replaced the C5 from November 1984 builds, and power windows and locks finally arrived.

### 1986–90: FUEL INJECTION, 2WD AND A NEW FACE
For 1986 the 2.8 gave way to a fuel-injected 2.9-liter Cologne V6 with 140 hp and 170 lb-ft, and the push-button Touch-Drive electric transfer case appeared late in the year. A Mitsubishi 2.3-liter turbodiesel was listed as well; The Ranger Station says it was offered for 1986 only, Wikipedia says 1986 and 1987, and everyone agrees almost nobody bought it. Rear-wheel drive arrived too, though NHTSA's sales figures show the first 2WD trucks counted in the 1987 model year. Rear-wheel ABS became standard for 1987, and the XL Sport, with a brush guard, fog lamps and a tubular rear bumper, followed for 1988.
The 1989 facelift matched the restyled Ranger: new hood, fenders and front bumper, a new dashboard with the Touch-Drive buttons moved into it, and 3.6 more inches of overall length on the same wheelbase. The front-door vent windows disappeared, the 2.9 got stronger "89TM" cylinder heads, and Eddie Bauer trucks switched to Light Sandalwood lower paint. The last trucks brought the BW1354 transfer case on electric-shift models and, after November 1989, a Dana 35 front axle in place of the Dana 28. Production ended in early 1990. The Bronco II had been built for barely seven model years, while the full-size Bronco carried on until 1996.

### THE ROLLOVER RECORD
The trouble started before production. Automobile Magazine reports that Ford engineers calculated a stability index (a figure based on track width and center-of-gravity height) significantly lower than the S-10 Blazer's and slightly lower than the Jeep CJ-7's, that some test maneuvers were dropped for the drivers' safety, and that proposals to widen the track or lower the truck were mostly vetoed because they would have delayed the launch. In the summer of 1982 Ford's Office of General Counsel collected more than 100 documents on the truck's handling, 53 of which later turned out to be missing.
In March 1989 NHTSA opened an engineering analysis of 1984–89 Bronco IIs after its study of the Suzuki Samurai. That study counted 43 fatal single-vehicle Bronco II rollovers, or 19 per 100,000 vehicles, against 6 for the Samurai, 6 for the S-10 Blazer and Jimmy, and 2.5 for the Cherokee. Two months later Consumer Reports, published by Consumers Union, told readers to avoid the truck after it failed the magazine's emergency-handling tests. NHTSA closed its investigation on October 31, 1990, without a recall. Using its preferred measure, first-event single-vehicle rollovers per single-vehicle crash, the agency found the Bronco II similar to other small SUVs.
The argument never went away. NHTSA turned down a 1997 petition to reopen the case in May 1999. It repeated that the truck's rollover rate did not stand out, but added that its crashworthiness in rollovers was "a cause for concern", with a much higher share of occupants killed in first-event rollovers than in most peer vehicles. By 1997 about 260 people had died in Bronco II rollovers. Ford had paid $113 million to settle injury and death suits, and it offered a class settlement covering about 658,000 owners: new warning labels and manuals, $100 toward worn suspension parts and up to $200 for certain modifications. Ford has always maintained that driving and modifications, not design, caused the rollovers.

### THE EXPLORER, AND THE TRUCKS THAT SURVIVED
Ford replaced the Bronco II with the Ranger-based Explorer, introduced in March 1990 as a 1991 model with a 160-hp 4.0 V6 and the four doors the Bronco II never had. Even the two-door Explorer Sport was about a foot longer. According to PBS Frontline, Ford engineers ran an Explorer prototype through the same test the Bronco II had failed and saw it lift its wheels too. Thirty-odd years on, the surviving Bronco IIs are cheap, light and narrow, and owners build them around Explorer parts: Dana 35 front axles, 8.8 rear axles and 4.0 engines. Driven sensibly, kept low and treated as the narrow-track short-wheelbase truck it is, a Bronco II will go places a modern SUV won't fit.

### Data plate

### Engineering
The Bronco II is a first-generation Ranger under a short wagon body: a ladder frame with a 94-inch wheelbase and a 56.9-inch track, Twin Traction Beam independent front suspension on coil springs and radius arms, and leaf springs over a solid Ford 7.5-inch rear axle. Almost everything mechanical is shared with the 1983–92 Ranger and much of it with the 1991–94 Explorer, which is why the parts supply is good and the swap culture is strong.
- Chassis: Ladder frame · 94 in wheelbase · 56.9 in track (Shortened Ranger frame. Length grew from 158.3 in to 161.9 in with the 1989 facelift.)
- Front Suspension: Twin Traction Beam, coil springs, radius arms (Two pivoting beams with a U-joint in the middle give independent travel. Camber changes as the suspension moves, so lifts need geometry correction.)
- Front Axle: Dana 28 TTB (1984–89) · Dana 35 TTB (built after Nov 1989) (Dana 28: 23-spline shafts, 6.625 in ring gear, rated for about 31 in tires. Dana 35: 27-spline, 7.56 in ring gear. In 1989 the ball joints moved from the beam to the knuckle.)
- Rear Axle: Ford 7.5 in, 28-spline, overslung leaf springs (Bronco II shafts are about 1-5/8 in wider than Ranger shafts on the passenger side. Ratios 3.45, 3.73 or 4.10; limited slip optional.)
- Transfer Case: BW1350 (to 1990) · BW1354 (1990 electric shift) · BW1359 dummy (2WD) (Part-time, chain-drive, aluminum, 2.48:1 low range. Touch-Drive push buttons from late 1986, in the overhead console until 1988 and in the dash from 1989.)
- Engines: 2.8 Cologne V6 (1984–85) · 2.9 Cologne V6 EFI (1986–90) · 2.3 Mitsubishi turbodiesel (1986) (2.8: 115 hp, carbureted, gear-driven cam. 2.9: 140 hp, chain-driven cam; bank-fire injection in 1986–87, sequential from 1988.)

### Versions
- 1984 · Launch · 4WD only · 2.8 Cologne V6 (carbureted) · 115 hp · 150 lb-ft · TK4 four-speed or C5 three-speed automatic. BW1350 manual-shift transfer case, Dana 28 TTB, 7.5 rear. Standard, XLS, XLT and Eddie Bauer trims.
- 1985 · 4WD only · 2.8 Cologne V6 · 115 hp · 150 lb-ft · Five-speed manuals (TK5, FM145). A4LD four-speed automatic from November 1984 builds. Power window and lock group. Last XLS.
- 1986 · 4WD (first 2WD per Ford production records) · 2.9 Cologne V6 EFI · 2.3 Mitsubishi turbodiesel I4 · 140 hp · 170 lb-ft (2.9) · Fuel injection, 58 mm throttle body and EGR on 1986–87 2.9s. Touch-Drive electric shift arrives late in the year. The diesel sold poorly.
- 1987–1988 · 2WD and 4WD · 2.9 Cologne V6 EFI · 140 hp · 170 lb-ft · Rear ABS standard from 1987. 1988: sequential injection, FM146 and Mazda M5OD five-speeds, dual-solenoid A4LD from mid-year, XL Sport trim.
- 1989–1990 · Facelift · 2WD and 4WD · 2.9 Cologne V6 EFI · 140 hp · 170 lb-ft · New nose and dash, 161.9 in long, no vent windows, improved 89TM heads. XLT Plus package. 1990: BW1354 on electric-shift trucks, Dana 35 TTB after November 1989.

### Year-by-year
- 1983: Production begins at Louisville in January and the Bronco II is introduced in March as a 1984 model. Four-wheel drive only, carbureted 2.8 Cologne V6 (115 hp), TK4 four-speed or C5 automatic, Dana 28 TTB, 7.5 rear.
- 1985: Five-speed manuals (TK5, FM145); the A4LD four-speed automatic replaces the C5 from November 1984 builds; power window and lock group; side glass changes from glued to bolted-in late in the year. Last year of the XLS.
- 1986: Fuel-injected 2.9 Cologne V6 (140 hp); Mitsubishi 2.3 turbodiesel offered; Touch-Drive electric-shift transfer case late in the year. The Ranger Station says 1986–88 2.9 heads are known to crack, and rates 1985–87 A4LD automatics the least reliable. [avoid]
- 1987: Rear-wheel ABS standard; 2WD sales begin in earnest (22,286 sold per NHTSA). Still crack-prone 2.9 heads and the early A4LD, which The Ranger Station's builder's guide says to stay away from. [avoid]
- 1988: Sequential fuel injection; FM146 and Mazda M5OD five-speeds; dual-solenoid A4LD from mid-year; XL Sport arrives. Last year of the front-door vent windows and the early body.
- 1989: Facelift to match the Ranger: new hood, fenders, bumper and dashboard, 161.9 in long. Redesigned 89TM 2.9 heads largely eliminate the cracking, and The Ranger Station rates 1989-on A4LDs noticeably better than 1985–87. Ball joints move from the TTB beam to the knuckle. XLT Plus package. [buy]
- 1990: Final year, with the 89TM heads. BW1354 on electric-shift trucks; Dana 35 TTB on 4x4s built from November 1989; some 2WD trucks get a true 2WD transmission. Production ends in early 1990 and the Explorer replaces it for 1991. [buy]

- Wheelbase: 94.0 in (2,388 mm)
- Length: 158.3 in (1984–88) · 161.9 in (1989–90)
- Width: 68.0 in (1,727 mm)
- Height: 68.2 in (1984–88) · 69.9 in (1989–90) (Wikipedia infobox figures)
