### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 205/75R15 (≈ 27.1 in tall), the factory size per The Ranger Station
- Bolt Pattern: 5x114.3 (5x4.5")
- Center Bore: 70.5 mm
- Lug Thread: 1/2"-20 UNF
- Offset: Listed fitments 6Jx15 and 7Jx15, ET12
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 31x10.50R15 (Shown on The Ranger Station with no lift and trimmed fenders. Its rule of thumb pairs 31s with about 1.5 in of lift plus trimming. The Dana 28 front axle is rated for about 31 in tires.)
- Biggest tire, 1.5 in lift: 32x11.50R15 (Fits with the bottom rear corner of the front fender trimmed.)
- Biggest tire, 4 in lift: 31–32 in (33 in with cut-out flares or a 3 in body lift) (The Ranger Station's chart: 31s fit, 32s need trimming, and 33s need cut-out flares or a 3 in body lift.)
- Biggest tire, 6 in lift: 33 in (35 in with a 2–3 in body lift and cut-out flares) (35s also show up on 3–5.5 in lifts with body lifts and cut-out flares, and on solid-axle swaps. At this size, plan for a Dana 35 or a solid axle, an 8.8 rear and regearing.)

### Buying checks
- Look for a cracked 2.9 head before anything else: The Ranger Station says early North American 2.9 heads lost material around the valve guides and rocker pedestals, and some cracked after a single overheat. Symptoms are white exhaust smoke when warm, clean spark plugs, low compression on a cylinder, and milky residue on the oil cap or dipstick (check it warm, since condensation looks similar). Rectangular rocker pedestals and an 89TM casting mean the improved heads have been fitted.
- Listen to the valve train: On the 2.9, oil reaches the lifters, rocker shaft and rockers through the two center cam bearings, so slight bearing wear can starve the top end. Loud clatter, especially after a long highway run, warrants an oil-pressure check. The Ranger Station's figures are about 20 psi at warm idle and 55 psi at 2,000 rpm. Coolant in the oil from a cracked head quickly wipes out those bearings.
- Hunt for water leaks and cowl rust: The cowl drains on 1984–88 trucks clog with leaves and rust through, putting water on the front carpet and in the glove box. The 1989–90 trucks got a mesh cowl. Every year leaks at the A-pillar and roof seam, the rear drip rail, the side-glass seals and behind the top of the hatch. A passenger floor that is always wet, rain or not, is usually the heater core.
- Judge the A4LD, especially on 1985–87 trucks: The Ranger Station rates 1985–87 A4LDs as the weakest, with reliability improving after the dual-solenoid change in mid-1988. Heat is the main killer. Look for dark or burnt fluid, slow or missing overdrive, and hard or erratic shifts, which can mean a ruptured vacuum modulator. Fluid in the modulator's vacuum line confirms it, and so does white exhaust smoke from ATF being drawn into the engine.
- Read the door sticker and the front axle: The certification label on the driver's door post carries axle and transmission codes, so you can confirm the ratio, a limited-slip rear and the original gearbox. Dana 28 axles have 12 cover bolts and date codes starting with E; the Dana 35 has a 10-bolt cover and F codes. Only 1990 trucks built after November 1989 left the factory with a Dana 35.
- Check the TTB and the hubs: Uneven tire wear points to tired beam pivot bushings, ball joints or radius-arm bushings, or a lift without camber correction. The Ranger Station advises checking the beam pivot bushings whenever the front end is apart. The factory automatic locking hubs become unreliable with age, and owners usually replace them with manual hubs.
- Is it really a 4x4?: A 2WD Bronco II often has what looks like a transfer case, the BW1359 pass-through, so look for a front driveshaft, a front differential and a shifter or Touch-Drive buttons. Also look for 2WD-to-4WD conversions, which are common. Check the quality of the swapped axle, the driveshafts and the transfer-case linkage.
- Run the recalls and question the modifications: NHTSA lists campaigns for locking-hub cams (1984), seat-belt anchors (1984), fuel lines and an EEC harness short (1986), handling-warning stickers on the sun visor (1987) and missing front wheel-bearing keys (1989). Ford blamed many rollovers on unsafe modifications. Treat a tall lift on a narrow 94-inch truck with suspicion and ask how it was engineered.

### Common repairs
#### Replace cracked 2.9 cylinder heads
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 days · cost Parts plus machine-shop inspection
Symptoms: White smoke when warm, clean spark plugs, low compression on one or more cylinders, coolant loss with no external leak, or milky "snot" on a warm dipstick or oil cap.
Fix: Stop driving it: The Ranger Station warns that coolant in the oil destroys the crank bearings and turns a head job into a rebuild. Drain the oil and coolant, pull the intake and both heads, and have them magnafluxed to confirm the crack. Fit the improved 1989-on heads (89TM castings with rectangular rocker pedestals) or aftermarket heads from World Products. Torque the head bolts in three steps: 22 lb-ft, then 51–55 lb-ft, then a further 90 degrees. Tighten the intake manifold to 15–18 lb-ft in five steps and retorque it after warm-up. Old valve covers with turned-down flanges tend to leak on the newer heads, so use later covers with turned-up flanges. Change the oil again after the first run.
Tools: Torque wrench and angle gauge · gasket scraper · compression tester · machine-shop magnaflux.

#### Replace 2.8 valve stem seals without pulling the heads
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 4–6 hours · cost Under the price of a set of seals plus an air adapter
Symptoms: Blue smoke on start-up or overrun, and oil consumption on a high-mileage 2.8. The Ranger Station says the original rubber valve seals deteriorate and leak oil into the cylinders.
Fix: Remove a valve cover, then the spark plug and wire for the cylinder you're working on. Loosen the rocker-shaft stand bolts two turns at a time from the ends toward the middle, lift off the shaft and oil baffle, and remove both pushrods. Screw an air adapter into the 14 mm plug hole and pressurize the cylinder to hold the valves shut; if they won't hold, the seats are damaged and the head has to come off. Compress the spring, remove the keepers, retainer and spring, replace the seal and reassemble. Repeat on each cylinder, then reset the valve lash (0.014 in intake, 0.016 in exhaust).
Tools: Air compressor · spark-plug-hole air adapter · valve spring compressor · feeler gauges · torque wrench.

#### Reseal leaking valve covers
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost Parts only
Symptoms: Oil weeping down the heads onto the exhaust manifolds, a burning-oil smell after a drive, an oily engine bay.
Fix: The Ranger Station calls Cologne valve-cover leaks messy but not dangerous, apart from rare fires when a lot of oil reaches the exhaust. Remove the intake plumbing or wiring that's in the way, unbolt the covers, clean both sealing surfaces completely and fit Fel-Pro rubber or Fel-Pro Blue gaskets. If the engine has the improved 1989-on heads, use the later covers with turned-up flanges, because old-style covers leak on the flatter surface. Tighten the bolts evenly and only lightly.
Tools: Sockets and extensions · gasket scraper · brake cleaner.

#### Replace or relocate the TFI ignition module
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 30 minutes (replace) · 2–3 hours (relocate) · cost Parts plus a donor heat sink
Symptoms: The engine dies or won't restart when hot, then runs again after it cools down, without leaving a trace of the fault.
Fix: The Thick Film Ignition module is mounted on the distributor, one of the hottest places under the hood. Disconnect the battery and remove the two screws with a thin-wall 7/32 in (5.5 mm) socket or a T20, depending on the screw. Slide the module down before pulling it away from the distributor, or it won't come off. For a permanent fix, The Ranger Station shows how to mount the module remotely on a finned heat sink from a 1989–95 Mercury Cougar or an Aerostar, trimming fins to clear the Ranger's connectors. Don't paint the heat sink. On the 2.8, owners also convert to Duraspark, GM HEI or aftermarket ignition.
Tools: Thin-wall 7/32 in (5.5 mm) socket or ignition-module wrench · T20 driver · basic hand tools.

#### Service the A4LD, replace the modulator and add a cooler
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost Parts plus fluid
Symptoms: Dark or burnt-smelling fluid, slipping, no overdrive, hard or erratic shifts, a missing 1–2 shift or third gear, or white exhaust smoke from ATF being drawn through a ruptured modulator.
Fix: Drop the pan, change the filter, clean the pan and refill with Mercon-type ATF (The Ranger Station recommends Mercon V as the modern replacement; total capacity is about 9.5 quarts). Pull the vacuum hose from the modulator: fluid in the hose means the diaphragm has failed, and you can confirm it with a vacuum gauge before fitting a new one. Heat is the main enemy of the A4LD, so fit an auxiliary cooler in the return line to supplement the radiator cooler. On 1988-on dual-solenoid units, test the 3-pin connector if overdrive or lock-up is missing.
Tools: Drain pan · sockets · gasket scraper · hand vacuum pump or gauge · funnel.

#### Refresh the TTB front end and set camber
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 4–6 hours plus an alignment · cost Parts plus an alignment
Symptoms: Tires wearing on the inside or outside edge, clunks over bumps, wandering, or play when you rock the wheel top to bottom.
Fix: Support the frame and unload the front axle. Inspect the beam pivot bushings where each beam meets its frame bracket, the radius-arm bushings, the ball joints and the tie-rod ends, and replace whatever is worn. Camber on a TTB is set with an offset cam bushing around the upper ball joint, and the right bushing brings worn or lifted beams back into spec. On 1984–88 axles the ball joints are in the beam; from 1989 they moved to the knuckle. If the truck is lifted, check that it has drop brackets for the beam pivots and radius arms and a dropped pitman arm. The Ranger Station warns against kits that lower the passenger beam pivot with a bolt-on drop plate, because the differential can strike it. Finish with a proper alignment.
Tools: Jack and stands · ball-joint press · pickle fork · large sockets · torque wrench.

#### Find and seal water leaks
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–8 hours depending on the leak · cost Seam sealer plus any parts
Symptoms: A wet front floor, water in the glove box, drips from the headliner just behind the windshield, a wet cargo carpet, fogged windows and a musty smell.
Fix: First rule out the heater core: a passenger floor that stays wet without rain is usually coolant, and the core sits behind an easy-to-remove panel under the dash. On 1984–88 trucks, clear the cowl drains and seal the cowl-to-firewall seam. Small holes can be sealed through the access covers, but rusted cowls mean drilling out spot welds. For the A-pillar and roof seam, the rear drip rail and the area above the hatch, dig out the cracked factory seam sealer and apply new sealer (silicone is only a temporary fix). Leaking side glass has to come out: remove the trim, unbolt the glass, cut the old seal with piano wire with a helper and reseal it with tar ribbon. Don't force it, because the glass breaks easily and is expensive.
Tools: Trim tools · seam sealer · tar ribbon · piano wire · drill (for cowl repairs).

#### Fix a liftgate that won't release
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 30 minutes · cost One washer
Symptoms: You turn the handle, feel resistance and a click, and the tension lets go without the gate opening, or it only opens if you push on the handle while turning it.
Fix: This is the Bronco II Corral fix for a worn release catch. Remove the inner trim panel (screws around the edge, then slide it forward and pop the push-pins). Remove the two 9 mm nuts and the retaining plate and pull the handle out. Take out the 7/32 in screw on the end of the handle, lift off the latch arm, put a 9/16 in washer under it as a shim and refit the arm the right way round (the nub faces away from the word "Gate"). Test the gate before refitting the panel. If you're stuck in the meantime, you can open the gate from inside by pulling one of the latch rods toward the center.
Tools: Phillips screwdriver · 1/4 in ratchet · 9 mm and 7/32 in sockets · push-pin pliers.

### Baseline service
Most Bronco IIs for sale are 35-plus years old and have passed through several cheap owners, so baseline everything. On a 2.9, the cooling system is a priority, because The Ranger Station says one overheat can crack an early head, and it calls synthetic oil and good cooling maintenance essential. On a 4x4, service the transfer case with ATF, not gear oil, and inspect the TTB front end.
- Engine oil & filter: 2.9: 5.0 qt with filter (4.0 qt without) · 2.8: 5 qt with filter · grade [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Change at purchase, then per the owner's manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Check oil pressure if the valve train is noisy: The Ranger Station quotes about 20 psi at warm idle and 55 psi at 2,000 rpm for the 2.9. Look for milky residue under the filler cap.)
- Coolant, thermostat & hoses: 7.2 qt (with A/C) / 7.8 qt (without A/C) per The Ranger Station · coolant type [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush at purchase; fit a new thermostat and hoses if their age is unknown (The single most important item on a 2.9. Pressure-test the system and check the radiator, fan clutch and water pump.)
- Spark plugs, wires, cap & rotor: Motorcraft AWSF-42C gapped 0.044 in · timing 10° BTDC · firing order 1-4-2-5-3-6 · Replace at purchase (These specs are listed for both the 2.8 and the 2.9. On the 2.8, check that the distributor hold-down and rotor screws are tight, because loose ones change the timing.)
- TFI ignition module: Distributor-mounted thick-film module · Inspect at purchase; carry a spare (Heat makes it fail intermittently on a hot engine. Relocating it to a heat sink is a well-documented fix.)
- Air & fuel filters: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Replace at purchase; check the air filter after dusty trails (The 2.9 is fuel-injected (30–40 psi fuel pressure per The Ranger Station), so relieve the pressure before opening the lines. Recall 87V-139 added retainer clips to spring-lock fuel couplings on 1986–87 trucks.)
- Automatic transmission (A4LD): Mercon ATF (Mercon V as the modern replacement) · ≈ 9.5 qt total · Pan drop and filter at purchase (A pan drop replaces only part of the fluid. Check the vacuum modulator line for ATF and add an auxiliary cooler. 1985–87 units are the most fragile.)
- Manual transmission: TK4, TK5 and M5OD: Mercon ATF · FM145 and FM146: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Drain and refill at purchase (Identify the gearbox from the TRANS code on the door-post label. On an M5OD, replace the three rubber top-cover plugs with steel cup plugs (Dorman 555-108 or Dana 219-3052), because leaks there can run it low.)
- Transfer case (BW1350 / BW1354): ≈ 2 qt ATF: Dexron III/Mercon, Mercon V or Mercon LV per the factory manual, NOT gear oil · Drain and refill at purchase (The 2WD BW1359 pass-through case is a special case: some contain ATF and some are dry. On Touch-Drive trucks, test every mode from the buttons.)
- Front differential (Dana 28 / Dana 35 TTB): Hypoid gear oil SAE 80W or 90W · The Ranger Station lists 2 qt (Dana 28) / 3 qt (Dana 35) [CONFIRM AT FILL PLUG] · Change at purchase and after deep water (Check the slip-yoke seal on the long side and the axle vent.)
- Rear differential (Ford 7.5): Hypoid gear oil SAE 75W-80 or 80W-90 · ≈ 5 pints · add 2 oz friction modifier for a limited slip · Change at purchase (The axle code on the door-post label tells you the ratio and whether it's a limited slip.)
- Front hubs & wheel bearings: Wheel-bearing grease [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Repack at purchase (Check that the bearing-adjusting nut retaining keys are present (recall 89V-109 covered trucks that left the factory without them). Replace failing automatic hubs with manual hubs.)
- TTB bushings, ball joints & steering: Beam pivot bushings · radius-arm bushings · ball joints · tie-rod ends · Inspect at purchase (Uneven tire wear is the tell. Fix camber with offset bushings, not by ignoring it.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush at purchase (Front discs and rear drums, with rear-wheel ABS from 1987. On manual trucks the hydraulic clutch is worth bleeding at the same time.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: Stock was 205/75R15, about 27 inches tall. The Ranger Station shows a stock-height Bronco II on 31x10.50R15s with trimmed fenders, and its rule of thumb is that 31s need about 1.5 inches of lift plus fender trimming. 32x11.50R15s have fitted on a 1.5-inch lift with the bottom rear corner of the front fender trimmed. Remember that the Dana 28 front axle is rated for about 31-inch tires.

Q: 2.8 or 2.9: which engine should I want?
A: The carbureted 2.8 (1984–85) is simple, with gear-driven cam timing, but it makes 115 hp, burns oil through worn valve seals, and its aging feedback carburetor tends to misbehave. The injected 2.9 (1986–90) makes 140 hp and 170 lb-ft. Its early heads crack and its top end is sensitive to cam-bearing wear, but 1989-on 89TM heads largely cured the cracking. A well-maintained 2.9 with the later heads is the pick.

Q: Was there really a diesel?
A: Yes. Ford offered a Mitsubishi 2.3-liter turbodiesel four-cylinder. The Ranger Station's specification table lists it for 1986 only, while Wikipedia and a Hemmings history say 1986–87. Everyone agrees it was slow and sold poorly, so factory diesel Bronco IIs are rare today.

Q: Is the Bronco II really more likely to roll over?
A: NHTSA twice declined to call it defective, in 1990 and 1999, because its rollover rate per single-vehicle crash was similar to its peers. The same 1999 review called its crashworthiness in rollovers "a cause for concern": a much larger share of occupants died in first-event rollovers than in most comparable SUVs. IIHS figures cited by Automobile put the 1986–90 rear-drive truck at 3.78 rollover deaths per 10,000 vehicles and the 4x4 at 1.74. It's a narrow, short truck, so drive it accordingly and be careful about adding height.

Q: Dana 28 or Dana 35: what do I have and does it matter?
A: Almost every Bronco II has the Dana 28 TTB: 23-spline shafts, a 6.625-inch ring gear and little aftermarket support for gears or lockers now. Only 1990 trucks built from November 1989 got the Dana 35, with 27-spline shafts and a 7.56-inch ring gear. Count the cover bolts (12 on a Dana 28, 10 on a Dana 35) or read the date code. Serious builders swap in a Dana 35 from an Explorer.

Q: Can a 2WD Bronco II be converted to 4WD?
A: Yes. It's a common, well-documented job because most 2WD trucks already have the 4WD-style transmission and a BW1359 pass-through case in the transfer-case position. You need a front TTB axle, a working transfer case and shifter, a front driveshaft and the matching parts. Late 1990 2WD trucks with a true 2WD transmission and a flange adapter need more work.

Q: Which transmission is best?
A: Manuals are the safe bet: Ford fitted TK4 (1984), TK5 and FM145 (1985–87), and FM146 or Mazda M5OD five-speeds (1988–90). The M5OD runs on Mercon ATF and tends to leak from rubber plugs in its top cover, which owners replace with steel cup plugs (Dorman 555-108). The Ranger Station rates the 1985–87 A4LD automatic as the weakest and says it improved from mid-1988. Whatever you have, add an auxiliary cooler to an A4LD.

Q: What fluids does it take?
A: According to The Ranger Station's specification pages, the 2.9 takes 5.0 quarts of oil with the filter and the 2.8 takes 5. The BW1350 and BW1354 transfer cases take about 2 quarts of ATF (Dexron III/Mercon, Mercon V or Mercon LV, never gear oil). The A4LD takes Mercon (Mercon V is the modern replacement), about 9.5 quarts. The 7.5 rear takes 75W-80 or 80W-90 hypoid oil, about 5 pints, with 2 oz of friction modifier for a limited slip. Check grades in the owner's manual.

Q: What engine swaps do people do?
A: The most common is the 4.0 V6 from an Explorer or later Ranger, which shares Cologne family roots with the 2.9, and The Ranger Station has wiring guides for 4.0 swaps into both early and late dashes. The 5.0 V8 is the bigger project. Bring a Trailer has sold several swapped trucks, including 4.0-powered 1988 and 1989 Bronco IIs and a 302-powered 1989.

Q: How is it related to the Ranger and the Explorer?
A: It is a first-generation Ranger underneath, built on the same Louisville line with the same TTB front end, 7.5 rear and Cologne V6s, and nearly the same driver's compartment. The Explorer replaced it for 1991, still Ranger-based but bigger, with four doors available and a 4.0 V6. Its Dana 35, 8.8 rear axle and 4.0 are now the standard Bronco II upgrades.

Q: What are they worth?
A: Not much yet, which is part of the appeal. On Bring a Trailer in 2025–26, most stock XLTs and Eddie Bauers sold for $6,450 to $15,750. A 9,000-mile 1989 Eddie Bauer reached $28,550 in April 2025, and a 1989 Eddie Bauer five-speed was bid to $12,000 in August 2026 without selling.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: 1989–1990. The Ranger Station says the 2.9's cylinder heads were redesigned for 1989 (look for '89TM' castings and rectangular rocker pedestals), largely ending the cracking that plagues 1986–88 engines, and that 1989-on A4LD automatics are noticeably better than the 1985–87 units its builder's guide says to stay away from. A late-1990 4x4 may also have the stronger Dana 35 front axle. If you do buy a 1986–88, check the oil for coolant, or for proof the heads have been swapped.

## Ford Bronco (sixth generation) (2021–present)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/bronco/sixth-gen/
Codes: U725, 2-DOOR, 4-DOOR, RAPTOR

Verdict: Ford spent 25 years working out how to beat the Wrangler and mostly managed it: a boxy, doors-off, body-on-frame 4x4 whose independent front suspension rides well, plus a factory 35-inch package that ends most tire arguments. Early trucks had their teething troubles in the roof and on the recall list, so buy one with the VIN check done.

Twenty-five years after the last full-size Bronco, the name came back because of a factory. In Ford's 2016 contract talks with the UAW, Michigan Assembly in Wayne was set to lose the Focus and C-Max. Instead it was retooled for a new North American Ranger and, since one truck wouldn't fill the plant, a new Bronco. Ford confirmed it at the 2017 Detroit show, showed it on July 13, 2020 after pandemic delays, and built the first customer trucks on June 14, 2021, in the same plant as the previous five generations. Its target was obvious: the Wrangler JL and JL Unlimited, in both two- and four-door form.

### HOW IT'S BUILT
Underneath is Ford's T6 body-on-frame platform, shared with the Ranger. Unlike the Jeep, the front suspension is independent, with twin A-arms. The rear has a solid axle on five links and coilovers, and Ford claimed 17 percent more front wheel travel and 10 percent more rear travel than the Wrangler. Styling borrows from the 1966–77 first Bronco; the design chief's own 1976 truck was digitally scanned for reference. The doors are frameless and come off with one bolt per hinge. The mirrors stay behind on the cowl, and the doors can ride in protective bags in the cargo area.
Two engines launched it. The 2.3 EcoBoost four makes 300 hp and 325 lb-ft and the 2.7 twin-turbo V6 330 hp and 415 lb-ft, both on premium fuel and both well above Ford's original estimates. The four is offered with a Getrag seven-speed manual, which is really a six-speed plus a crawler gear marked 'C', or Ford's 10-speed automatic. The V6 is automatic-only. Two transfer cases were offered: a part-time unit with a 2.72:1 low range, and an advanced one with a full-time 4A mode and a 3.06:1 low range. Ford quoted a 95:1 crawl ratio for the manual with the crawler gear.

### SASQUATCH, HOSS AND THE RAPTOR
The Sasquatch package is the headline option: 315/70R17 tires (35 inches) on +30 mm-offset wheels, 4.7 axle gears, a mild lift, and the Bilstein dampers and sway-bar disconnect of the off-road trims. On 35s, MotorTrend measured 11.6 inches of ground clearance and approach, departure and breakover angles of 43.2, 37.2 and 29.0 degrees for the two-door. Ford calls its suspension packages HOSS. Badlands trucks get position-sensitive Bilstein dampers and a hydraulic front anti-roll-bar disconnect that reconnects itself at speed. The Wildtrak's HOSS 3.0 uses Fox dampers. For 2025, Badlands buyers could add full HOSS 3.0, with Fox 2.5-inch internal-bypass shocks, the Raptor's severe-duty steering rack and stronger tie rods.
Then there's the Raptor, added for 2022 as a four-door only. It has a 3.0-liter twin-turbo V6 with 418 hp and 440 lb-ft, Fox suspension, 37-inch tires, 13.1 inches of ground clearance, F-150 Raptor brakes and a body widened to 85.7 inches. It gets 'FORD' across the grille instead of 'BRONCO' and is rated to tow 4,500 lb, 1,000 lb more than the standard Bronco. The cost is fuel: the EPA rates a 2023 Raptor at 15 mpg combined.

### TWO DOORS OR FOUR
The two-door rides on a 100.4-inch wheelbase and is 174.8 inches long. MotorTrend noted it is 6.9 inches longer than a two-door Wrangler on a 3.6-inch-longer wheelbase, and much roomier inside. The four-door stretches to 116.1 inches between the axles and about 190 inches overall. That costs breakover angle (26.3 degrees against 29.0 on 35s), and the four-door weighs up to about 400 lb more, but it has the bigger fuel tank (21.1 gallons against 17.4) and, at launch, the soft-top option, and the Raptor was built only as a four-door. Both come with removable roofs; the standard hardtop is molded in black or white, and a painted top arrived later.

### TEETHING TROUBLES
Demand was huge: Ford sold 117,057 in the US in 2022 and 146,007 in 2025. Early trucks had problems. In August 2021, Ford began replacing molded-in-color hardtops whose finish crazed and delaminated, and a 2026 recall covers 2021–22 roof panels that can separate on the road. Some 2021–22 2.7 V6s can break intake valves. Bilstein rear shocks on 2021–24 trucks can corrode until the reservoir detaches. A service bulletin covers seven-speed manuals that grind. By September 2026, Jalopnik counted about 20 recalls since launch. Buy a sixth-gen Bronco on its VIN history.

### Data plate
- Code: U725 · Ford T6 platform
- Assembly: Michigan Assembly, Wayne, Michigan · Jiangling Ford, Nanchang (China, from 2024)
- Production: From June 14, 2021
- Body: 2-door or 4-door, removable roof and frameless doors
- Wheelbase: 100.4 in (2-door) · 116.1 in (4-door)
- Length: 174.8 in (2-door) · 189.4–190.5 in (4-door)
- Curb Weight: 4,294–4,699 lb (2-door) · 4,466–5,109 lb (4-door)
- Engines: 2.3 EcoBoost I4 · 2.7 EcoBoost V6 · 3.0 EcoBoost V6 (Raptor)
- Transmissions: 7-speed manual (6 + crawler) · 10-speed automatic
- Ground Clearance: Up to 11.6 in (35s) · 13.1 in (Raptor)
- Towing: 3,500 lb · 4,500 lb (Raptor)
- Fuel Tank: 17.4 gal (2-door) · 21.1 gal (4-door)
- Wheels: 6 x 139.7 mm bolt pattern · up to 315/70R17 (Sasquatch) or 37 in (Raptor)

### Engineering
The Bronco is a body-on-frame Ranger derivative with a removable roof and doors. It has independent front suspension, a coil-sprung solid rear axle and Dana axles, with electronic lockers optional front and rear. Off-road settings are chosen with a dial and the G.O.A.T. ('Goes Over Any Type of Terrain') drive modes, not a second lever.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, Ford T6 (U725) · 100.4 / 116.1 in wheelbase (Shared with the Ranger; built at Michigan Assembly, Wayne, Michigan, and for China by Jiangling Ford in Nanchang from 2024.)
- Front Suspension: Independent, twin A-arms, coilovers (Badlands and Sasquatch add a hydraulic front sway-bar disconnect that reconnects above about 20 mph.)
- Rear Axle: Dana solid axle, five-link, coilovers (MotorTrend describes trailing links and a Panhard rod; electronic locker available.)
- Transfer Case: Part-time, 2.72:1 low · Advanced with 4A, 3.06:1 low (Electric shift on both; Ford quoted a 95:1 crawl ratio with the manual's crawler gear.)
- Engines: 2.3 EcoBoost I4 · 2.7 EcoBoost V6 · 3.0 EcoBoost V6 (Raptor) (300 hp / 325 lb-ft · 330 hp / 415 lb-ft on premium · 418 hp / 440 lb-ft)
- Transmissions: Getrag 7MTI550 manual (2.3 only) · 10R60 10-speed automatic (The manual is a six-speed with a dog-leg crawler gear; about 15% of early orders chose it.)

### Versions
- 2021– · 2-door / 4-door · 2.3 L EcoBoost I4 · 300 hp / 325 lb-ft (premium) · 275 / 315 on regular · 7-speed manual or 10-speed auto. EPA 21 mpg combined (2021, either gearbox).
- 2021– · 2-door / 4-door · 2.7 L EcoBoost twin-turbo V6 · 330 hp / 415 lb-ft (premium) · 315 / 410 on regular · Auto only. 2021–22 trucks covered by the intake-valve recall 24V-635.
- 2021– · Sasquatch package (any engine) · 2.3 or 2.7 · As above · 35s on +30 mm wheels, 4.7 gears, Bilstein dampers, sway-bar disconnect. EPA 17–18 mpg combined.
- 2021 · First Edition · 2.3 or 2.7 · As above · Badlands mechanicals, Wildtrak exterior, Outer Banks interior; 35s standard.
- 2022– · Bronco Raptor (4-door only) · 3.0 L EcoBoost twin-turbo V6 · 418 hp / 440 lb-ft · 37s, Fox suspension, 85.7 in wide, 4,500 lb towing. EPA 15 mpg combined (2023).
- 2025–2026 · Stroppe Edition · — · — · Baja-Bronco tribute: a two-door for 2025 ($77,665), then a four-door for 2026 ($69,995).

### Year-by-year
- 2021: Production starts June 14, 2021 at Michigan Assembly. 2.3 (manual or auto) and 2.7 (auto) EcoBoost; Base, Big Bend, Black Diamond, Outer Banks, Badlands, Wildtrak and First Edition; Sasquatch package. CarGurus says to steer clear of 2021–22: the year with the most recalls, including 2.7 intake valves (24V-635), molded-in-color roof panels and airbags. [avoid]
- 2022: Bronco Raptor (four-door, 3.0 twin-turbo V6, 37s) and the four-door-only Everglades edition arrive. Still inside the 2.7 valve recall, and 2021–22 molded-in-color roof panels are recalled in 2026; CarGurus says to avoid it. [avoid]
- 2023: Heritage Edition and Heritage Limited Edition arrive, both with a painted top instead of the molded-in-color one. CarGurus' pick of the generation, with fewer complaints than 2021–22, provided the recalls are done. [buy]
- 2024: Badlands and Sasquatch trucks get the Wildtrak's HOSS 3.0 steering gear. Chinese-market Broncos go on sale (2.3, four-door). Last year of the Wildtrak trim.
- 2025: Full HOSS 3.0 (Fox 2.5 internal-bypass shocks, Raptor steering rack, stronger tie rods) optional on Badlands. Painted hardtops in Oxford White, Shadow Black or body color. Two-door Stroppe Edition ($77,665). Front control-arm fastener recalls on early builds.
- 2026: The Stroppe Edition moves to the four-door, at $69,995.

### Capability
- Towing: 3,500 lb (1,588 kg) (4,500 lb (2,041 kg) for the Bronco Raptor)
- Ground clearance: 8.4–11.6 in (213–295 mm) (Base tires to 35s; 13.1 in (333 mm) for the Raptor)
- Approach / departure / breakover: 43.2° / 37.2° / 29.0° (2-door) · 43.2° / 37.0° / 26.3° (4-door) (On 35-inch tires; 35.5° / 29.8° / 21.1° (2-door) on base tires)
- Crawl ratio: Up to 95:1 (7-speed manual crawler gear with the advanced transfer case (Ford figure))
- Fuel tank: 17.4 gal (2-door) · 21.1 gal (4-door)
- Fuel economy: EPA 20 city / 22 hwy / 21 combined (2021 2.3; 2.7 is 18/20/19; Sasquatch 17–18 combined; 2023 Raptor 15/16/15)
- Curb weight: 4,294–4,699 lb (2-door) · 4,466–5,109 lb (4-door)
- Wheelbase: 100.4 in (2,550 mm) 2-door · 116.1 in (2,949 mm) 4-door

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 255/70R16 (Base, steel wheels), 255/75R17 · 265/70R17 · 255/70R18 · 285/70R18 (trim and wheel options), LT285/70R17 (Badlands), 315/70R17, 35 in (Sasquatch package, First Edition), 37 in (Bronco Raptor)
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Offset: +55 mm (factory wheels) · +30 mm (Sasquatch)
- Center Bore: 93.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M12x1.5 (tire-retailer listing)
- Lug Torque: 100 lb-ft (135 Nm), M12x1.5; retighten within 100 mi after any wheel removal (2021 owner's manual)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 285/75R17 (≈ 33.8 in) (Runs on factory wheels and suspension with no rubbing reported.)
- Biggest tire, 1.25–1.5 in level lift: 35x10.50R17 or 35x11.50R17 (Narrow 35s fit factory 17-inch wheels once the front crash bars are removed.)
- Biggest tire, 1.5–2 in lift: 35x12.50R17 (Full-width 35s need about +30 mm offset wheels and high-clearance flares. Recalibrate the speedometer (about 7% slow) and consider 4.46 or 4.7 gears.)
- Biggest tire, Factory lift: 315/70R17 (Sasquatch) · 37 in (Raptor) (The factory options for big tires.)

### Buying checks
- Run the VIN before anything else: There are many open-recall possibilities. The big ones are the 2.7 intake valves (24V-635), the rear shock reservoirs (25V-025), 2021–22 molded-in-color roof panels (26V-299, remedy expected November 2026), engine-bay wiring (26V-468), fender flares (26V-403) and, on 2024–25 trucks, loose front control-arm and ball-joint fasteners (24V-770, 25V-260, 25V-308, 25V-310). Get a printout from NHTSA's VIN lookup.
- Look hard at the hardtop: Molded-in-color tops were standard on 2021–23 trucks and most 2024s. Crazing or delamination means the top needs replacing: Ford's August 2021 program fitted 'MIC 2.0' tops, and some owners are on their third or fourth. Painted tops arrived for 2025. Check the headliner and seals for leaks and make sure every panel latches.
- 2.7 V6: ask about the engine test: Recall 24V-635 covers 2021–22 2.7 and 3.0 Nano EcoBoost engines whose intake valves can break. Dealers run an engine cycle test and replace the engine if needed. Bronco Nation names V6s built from May 1 to October 31, 2021 as the bad batch. Get proof the test was done.
- Rear shocks on Badlands and Sasquatch: Bilstein rear shocks on trucks built from September 23, 2020 to July 23, 2024 can corrode until the external reservoir detaches (25V-025). Look at the reservoirs and their mounts and confirm the replacement was done.
- Drive the manual through every gear: On 2021–23 seven-speed trucks, a scraping noise in neutral, first or second is the subject of a Ford service bulletin. Check for clean engagement of the crawler gear and reverse.
- Steering and tie rods on modified trucks: Owners have reported tie rods failing during hard off-road use, usually on lifted trucks with bigger tires. Inspect the inner and outer tie rods for bends. The 2023 Wildtrak and 2022 Raptor had a steering-gear recall (23V-155) for internal damage that could lock the wheel.
- Was it flat-towed?: 2021–22 trucks had a neutral-tow problem: Ford issued a temporary fix in May 2022 and an over-the-air update by March 2023. Bronco Nation warns that flat-tow damage to the transmission can be hard to get covered under warranty, so ask how the truck traveled behind a motorhome.
- Is it a real Sasquatch?: Factory Sasquatch trucks have 315/70R17 tires on 17x8.5, +30 mm wheels and 4.7 gears. A truck that only has aftermarket 35s may still have the original gearing and +55 mm wheels. Check the window sticker or the build data.

### Common repairs
#### Rear shock reservoir corrosion (Bilstein, HOSS 2.0)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours to replace a pair · cost Free under recall 25V-025 on eligible trucks
Symptoms: Rusty or swollen reservoir bodies on the rear shocks, a reservoir hanging by its hose, oil on the shock body, or a bouncy rear end.
Fix: Check the VIN first: Ford's remedy for 2021–24 Badlands and Sasquatch trucks built from September 23, 2020 to July 23, 2024 is free rear shock replacement (Ford campaign 25S01; owner letters went out in August 2025). On an out-of-scope or modified truck, support the axle on a jack, unbolt the upper and lower shock mounts and the reservoir clamp, fit the new shocks, and torque at ride height. Rinse road salt off the reservoirs in winter.
Tools: Jack and stands · sockets · torque wrench.

#### Hardtop crazing, delamination and leaks
Difficulty 1 / 5 (inspection) · dealer replacement · time ≈ 30 minutes to inspect and reseat · cost Covered by Ford's program and recall on eligible tops; Bronco Nation cites out-of-warranty figures of $2,000 to $5,000+
Symptoms: Spider-web crazing or bubbling in the outer skin of a molded-in-color top, water dripping at panel joints, or a roof panel that won't latch flush.
Fix: Look over every panel in daylight for crazing and delamination. Affected 2021-on tops were replaced with MIC 2.0 tops under Ford's August 2021 customer-satisfaction program, and recall 26V-299 (2021–22) covers roof panels whose outer skin can separate on the road; owners were notified in May 2026, and the remedy is expected in November 2026. For leaks, remove each panel, clean the seals and sealing faces, check that no seal is pinched or folded, and refit, latching the panels in the order the owner's manual shows.
Tools: Mild soap and water · seal conditioner · the factory panel bags for storage.

#### Upgrade or replace tie rods
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours plus an alignment · cost Parts plus an alignment
Symptoms: A bent tie rod after a hard hit on the trail, toe out of spec, the steering wheel off-center, or a tie rod that has failed outright on a lifted truck with big tires.
Fix: Ford's own answer was stronger hardware. The 2024 Badlands and Sasquatch got the Wildtrak's HOSS 3.0 steering gear, and the 2025 HOSS 3.0 option added upgraded inner and outer tie rods with the Raptor's severe-duty rack. To replace a tie rod, mark or count the turns on the old outer end, separate it from the knuckle, unscrew the inner rod from the rack under the boot, fit the new parts to the same length and torque them, then get an alignment.
Tools: Tie-rod separator · inner tie-rod tool · torque wrench · tape measure.

#### Fit 35s to a non-Sasquatch Bronco
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A weekend with a level kit · cost Wheels, tires and a level kit; regearing extra
Symptoms: You want 35s, but your truck has +55 mm wheels and stock height.
Fix: Performance Plus Tire's guide splits it by tire width. A 285/75R17 (about 33.8 in) fits stock wheels and suspension without rubbing. Narrow 35s (35x10.50R17 or 35x11.50R17) fit factory 17-inch wheels once the front crash bars come off, usually with a small 1.25–1.5-inch level. Full-width 35x12.50R17s need about +30 mm wheels, high-clearance flares and roughly 1.5–2 inches of lift. Afterwards, recalibrate the speedometer (35s read about 7% slow) and get an alignment. Regearing is optional: the Sasquatch uses 4.7s, and the guide says 4.46s work fine for many owners.
Tools: Jack and stands · spring compressor or pre-assembled coilovers · torque wrench · speedometer calibration tool.

#### Check the front suspension fasteners (2024–25)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost Free under recall where it applies
Symptoms: A clunk from the front end, or nothing at all: a missing or loose upper ball-joint nut or lower control-arm bolt may give no warning before the arm separates.
Fix: Four campaigns cover this (24V-770, 25V-260, 25V-310 and 25V-308). For 25V-260 and 25V-308, Ford told owners not to drive the truck until it was repaired. The remedy is to inspect and, if needed, tighten or replace the fasteners, ball joint and knuckle. On any lifted or modified truck, check the torque on the upper ball-joint nuts and the lower control-arm pivot bolts after installation and again after the first trail run.
Tools: Torque wrench · sockets · jack and stands.

#### Re-secure loose fender flares
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 30 minutes · cost Free under recall 26V-403 on 2022–26 trucks
Symptoms: A flare that flaps, gaps or rattles at speed, or missing clips along its edge.
Fix: Recall 26V-403 covers 2022–26 Broncos whose fender flares may not be properly secured and can come off; dealers inspect and repair or replace them. Between visits, check every flare fastener after washing or trail use, especially on trucks whose owners have removed the flares for bigger tires and refitted them.
Tools: Trim tools · Torx and socket set.

#### Protect the engine-bay wiring
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost Free under recall 26V-468
Symptoms: Chafed or melted insulation on the harness in the engine bay, intermittent electrical faults, or a burning smell.
Fix: Recall 26V-468 covers 2021–26 Broncos and Bronco Raptors whose engine-compartment harness can be damaged and short-circuit; dealers add protective sheathing. Ford phased the campaign: 2026 Raptors first, then 2021–25 Raptors, then all other Broncos from about September 2026. Until it's done, look along the harness for chafe points and keep added wiring for lights and accessories well clear of it.
Tools: Flashlight · split loom and zip ties for your own accessory wiring.

### Baseline service
A used sixth-gen is new enough that recalls matter more than wear, so start with NHTSA's VIN lookup. Then baseline the fluids owners skip, the axles and transfer case, and check the 2.7's oil level against the dipstick, because Ford's published capacities have been inconsistent.
- Engine oil & filter: SAE 5W-30 synthetic blend (WSS-M2C961-A1); 0W-30 (WSS-M2C963-A1) for extreme cold · 2.3: 6.2 qt with filter · 2.7: 7 qt listed (≈ 6 qt drain-and-fill per a later Ford bulletin, as reported by owners) · Then per the oil-life monitor: Ford expects 7,500–10,000 mi in normal use, 5,000–7,500 with towing, mountains or off-road, 3,000–5,000 at maximum load; off-road operation schedule says every 5,000 mi or six months. Never more than 1 year or 10,000 mi (2021 owner's manual) (Filters: Motorcraft FL-910-S (2.3) and FL-2062-A (2.7). On the 2.7, fill to the dipstick rather than to a number.)
- Engine air filter: Motorcraft FA-2022 · Ford: replace every 30,000 mi; on dusty or off-road use, inspect frequently and replace as required (2021 owner's manual) (Desert and trail dust load it fast.)
- Cabin air filter: Motorcraft FP-93 · Ford: every 20,000 mi (2021 owner's manual) (Doors-off driving fills it quickly.)
- Spark plugs: Motorcraft SP-594 (2.3 and 2.7) · Ford: every 100,000 mi; every 60,000 mi if you tow or idle for long periods (2021 owner's manual) (Turbo engines are hard on plugs; replace on schedule.)
- Coolant: Motorcraft Yellow prediluted (WSS-M97B57-A2) · 2.3 auto 10.5 qt · 2.3 manual 9.6 qt · 2.7 12.4 qt · Ford: first change at 10 years or 200,000 mi, then every 5 years or 100,000 mi (2021 owner's manual) (Don't mix with other coolant types.)
- 10-speed automatic (10R60): Motorcraft Mercon ULV (WSS-M2C949-A) · ≈ 13.1 qt dry fill · filter FT-202 · Ford: change fluid and filter every 100,000 mi; the 2021 manual's towing and off-road schedules don't shorten it, so an earlier change is owner's choice (Drain-and-fill replaces only part of the fluid. Check for the 23V-070 (loose bolt) and 25V-164 (valve body) recalls on affected years.)
- 7-speed manual: ≈ 2.4 qt dry fill · Motorcraft Dual Clutch Transmission Fluid XT-11-QDC (WSS-M2C200-D2), per the 2021 owner's manual · Change at purchase on a hard-used truck (Yes, the manual really specifies Ford's dual-clutch fluid for this Getrag manual; Ford schedules a change every 100,000 mi. Grinding in neutral, first or second on 2021–23 trucks is covered by a service bulletin.)
- Transfer case: Motorcraft Mercon LV (WSS-M2C938-A) · 1.3 qt (part-time) · 1.6 qt (advanced 4A) · Change at purchase; Ford: every 150,000 mi, or sooner if leaking or submerged (If the truck has had transmission or transfer-case work, check that recall 26V-236 (misaligned joint after a previous repair) doesn't apply.)
- Front axle: Motorcraft SAE 80W-90 (WSP-M2C197-A) · 26.2 fl oz with electronic locker · 29.2 fl oz without locker or disconnect · 30.4 fl oz without locker, with front-axle disconnect · Ford: every 150,000 mi, or sooner if leaking or submerged. Change at purchase and after deep water crossings (The front axle takes conventional 80W-90; the rear takes synthetic 75W-85. Don't mix them up.)
- Rear axle: Motorcraft SAE 75W-85 synthetic hypoid (WSS-M2C942-A) · 63.6 fl oz with electronic locker · 65.3 fl oz without · Ford: every 150,000 mi, or sooner if leaking or submerged. Change at purchase; more often if towing or on 35s (Check the axle vent after water crossings.)
- Brake & clutch fluid: Motorcraft DOT 4 LV (WSS-M6C65-A2) · Flush at purchase, then every 3 years (2021 owner's manual) (The manual's clutch shares the brake reservoir fluid.)
- Rear shocks & front-end fasteners: Inspect reservoirs (25V-025) · torque-check UCA ball-joint nuts and LCA bolts (2024–25 recalls) · At purchase and after every hard trail day (On lifted trucks, check the alignment and tie rods at the same time.)
- Battery: Motorcraft BAGM-48H6-760 / BAGM-94RH7-800 (per build) · Test at purchase (Bronco Nation lists bad batteries among the electrical complaints.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: On stock wheels and suspension, a 285/75R17 (about 33.8 in) with no rubbing reported. Narrow 35s (35x10.50R17 or 35x11.50R17) fit factory 17s once the front crash bars are removed, usually with a small level of 1.25–1.5 in. Full-width 35x12.50R17s need about +30 mm wheels, high-clearance flares and roughly 1.5–2 in of lift. The factory way to get 35s is the Sasquatch package (315/70R17); the Raptor runs 37s.

Q: 2.3 or 2.7?
A: The 2.3 four (300 hp, 325 lb-ft) is the only engine with the manual and the more economical one: the EPA rates a 2021 at 21 mpg combined, against 19 for the 2.7. The 2.7 V6 (330 hp, 415 lb-ft) is automatic-only, and 2021–22 versions are covered by the intake-valve recall. Both ratings are on premium fuel; on regular, Ford quotes 275 and 315 hp.

Q: Is the seven-speed manual really a seven-speed?
A: Not quite. It's a Getrag six-speed with an extra crawler gear marked 'C', down and left of reverse in a dog-leg. It's for rock crawling and steep ramps, and with the advanced transfer case Ford quoted a 95:1 crawl ratio. About 15% of early buyers chose it.

Q: Is the Sasquatch package worth it?
A: If you off-road, yes. You get 35-inch tires, 4.7 gears, position-sensitive Bilstein dampers, the sway-bar disconnect, ground clearance up to 11.6 in and much better angles. The EPA cost is real: a 2021 2.3 automatic Sasquatch is rated 18 mpg combined against 21 for the standard truck. Adding the same parts later costs more than the package.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: 3,500 lb for the standard Bronco, the same as a Wrangler. The Bronco Raptor is rated at 4,500 lb.

Q: Two-door or four-door?
A: The two-door (100.4 in wheelbase) is shorter, lighter and has the better breakover angle (29.0° against 26.3° on 35s). The four-door (116.1 in) has the rear doors, more cargo room, a 21.1-gallon tank instead of 17.4, offered the soft top at launch, and is the only body offered as a Raptor.

Q: How do the doors and roof come off?
A: Lower the window, slip on the door bag, unplug the connector and remove one bolt from each hinge. The doors are frameless and the mirrors stay on the cowl. The two roof panels over the front seats release with quarter-turn latches and stow on board in bags. On four-doors a third panel over the rear seat also comes off but doesn't stow on board, and the remaining rear section is small enough to handle easily.

Q: Which years should I buy or avoid?
A: Avoid 2021–22 unless the paperwork is perfect: CarGurus says to steer clear of both, and they carry the 2.7 intake-valve recall (24V-635) and the 2026 molded-in-color roof-panel recall. CarGurus calls 2023 the best year, with no investigations and fewer complaints, as long as its recalls are fixed. Later trucks get MIC 2.0 or painted tops, the HOSS 3.0 steering gear on 2024 Badlands and Sasquatch, and a full HOSS 3.0 option for 2025, but 2024–25 trucks have their own front-suspension fastener recalls, so check any year's VIN. Jalopnik, citing Bronco Nation, notes relatively little discussion of failures on the 2.3 four.

Q: What oil does it take, and how much?
A: SAE 5W-30 synthetic blend meeting WSS-M2C961-A1. The 2.3 takes 6.2 qt with the filter (Motorcraft FL-910-S). The 2.7 is listed at 7 qt (FL-2062-A), but owners on Bob Is The Oil Guy report a later Ford bulletin giving 6 qt for a drain and fill, so fill to the dipstick. The 10-speed takes Mercon ULV and the transfer case Mercon LV.

Q: Is it reliable?
A: So far Consumer Reports calls it average, according to Jalopnik, which counted about 20 recalls by September 2026. Most problems were in the 2021–22 trucks: hardtops, 2.7 valves, rear shocks, manual-transmission noise. Bronco Nation's view is that tie-rod failures are rarer than the internet suggests and usually involve lifts, big tires or hard driving.

Q: What's different about the Bronco Raptor?
A: It has a 3.0 twin-turbo V6 (418 hp), Fox suspension, 37-inch tires, a body 85.7 in wide, 13.1 in of ground clearance, F-150 Raptor brakes, a reinforced bumper and frame, and 'FORD' on the grille. It's four-door only, tows 4,500 lb and the EPA rates a 2023 at 15 mpg combined.

# Mercedes-Benz G-Class (1979–present)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/

The Geländewagen began as a military truck, commissioned in the early 1970s after the Shah of Iran — then one of Mercedes-Benz’s largest shareholders — pre-ordered some 20,000 of them. Mercedes engineered it; Steyr-Daimler-Puch built it in Graz, Austria, and production began in 1979. The utilitarian W460 and later W461 served armies, border police and farmers. In 1990 the civilian W463 moved upmarket with full-time four-wheel drive and three locking differentials — and slowly turned into a luxury icon without ever losing its ladder frame. For off-roaders, the sweet spot is the solid-axle W463 era, from the Europa International imports of the 1990s through the G 500 and G 550. The second-generation truck of 2018 is better on the road, with independent front suspension, and still carries three lockers.

Verdict: A military box that became the world’s most expensive school-run accessory. Still devastating off-road — which most owners will never find out.

## Mercedes-Benz G-Class W460 (1979–1991)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/w460/
Codes: W460, 230 GE, 280 GE, 300 GD

Verdict: The original Geländewagen: built for a Shah, bought by armies, blessed by a Pope and slower up a motorway on-ramp than most tractors. It is the purest G there is, and it will happily outlive you if you keep the rust and the hydraulics in check.

Every G-Class that has ever crushed a trail or a valet stand descends from this one. The W460 is a ladder frame, two coil-sprung rigid axles, a lever for the front axle and a choice of engines that ranged from leisurely to geological. Mercedes engineered it, Steyr-Daimler-Puch hand-built it in Graz, and for twelve years it was sold mainly to people who needed it: border guards, soldiers, farmers and the occasional explorer. Nothing about it was designed to impress the neighbours, which is exactly why off-roaders still want one.

### A SHAH, A WOODEN MOCK-UP AND GRAZ
Development began in 1972 under a cooperation agreement between Daimler-Benz and Steyr-Daimler-Puch, pushed along by the Shah of Iran — then a major Mercedes shareholder — who pre-ordered some 20,000 military vehicles. Design studies were built in wood in 1973, and prototypes were tested everywhere from the Arctic Circle to the Sahara. The Shah lost his throne in 1979, the year production began, and the order never happened.
The W460 was launched at a press event on the off-road proving ground in Toulon, France, and went on sale in September 1979 with three engines and five body variants on two wheelbases: 2,400 mm and 2,850 mm. In Austria, Switzerland, Yugoslavia and the COMECON countries it was badged Puch G, and in France Peugeot built a licensed military version, the P4, with its own engine and gearbox. The French Army ordered 15,000, later cut to 13,500.

### BORDER GUARDS, A POPE AND THE DAKAR
Customers arrived quickly. In 1980 Germany's Federal Border Guard and riot police took delivery of short-wheelbase 230 Gs and long-wheelbase 280 GEs, and Mercedes built a Popemobile on a 230 G cabriolet for Pope John Paul II's first visit to Germany. The Argentine Army started using the military model in 1981, and in 1982 Mercedes won the Swiss Army tender.
Then it went racing. In 1983 Jacky Ickx and Claude Brasseur won the car category of the Paris–Dakar Rally in a 280 GE, which ended any argument about whether this was a real off-roader. Porsche even built a G with a 928 V8 as a support vehicle for its 959 rally programme in the mid-1980s.

### SLOWLY GETTING CIVILISED
The W460 picked up comforts gradually. In 1981 came an automatic gearbox, air conditioning, an auxiliary fuel tank, headlamp grilles and a cable winch. Fuel injection arrived with the 230 GE in 1982, along with better seats, wider tyres and fender flares. From 1985 front and rear differential locks, central locking and a tachometer were standard on every W460, and by 1986 more than 50,000 G Models had been built.
The engines barely changed. The 300 GD's five-cylinder OM617 diesel was the most popular, the 280 GE's straight-six was the most powerful, and although Mercedes put turbodiesels in its saloons, it never fitted one to a W460. Mercedes didn't sell the truck in America either. Grey-market importers federalised a few in the 1980s until the 1988 Imported Vehicle Safety Compliance Act made that much harder and more expensive.

### HOW IT ENDED — AND DIDN'T
At the 1989 Frankfurt show Mercedes revealed the G for the next era: permanent four-wheel drive, a wood-trimmed cabin and optional ABS. That truck became the W463, and it took the G-Class upmarket. The W460 ended production in 1991, but its job didn't. Its body and chassis carried on as the W461, a working G for armies and agencies built with W463 running gear.
That makes the W460 the last G built purely as a tool. Today it is a classic with a strong following, and Classic & Sports Car notes that a pre-1990 soft-top in show condition can make £75,000 or more. Rust-free W460s are rare, because most spent their lives in wet European winters.

### Data plate
- Chassis: W460
- Years: 1979–1991
- Built By: Steyr-Daimler-Puch, Graz
- Wheelbase: 2,400 / 2,850 mm
- Drive: Part-time 4WD, low range
- Transfer Case: VG 080
- Lockers: Front & rear (std from 1985)
- Engines: 2.0–2.8 L petrol, 2.4–3.0 L diesel
- Original Tire: 205 R16
- Also Sold As: Puch G · Peugeot P4 (licence)
- Succeeded By: W461 (work) · W463 (civilian)

### Engineering
The W460 is about as simple as a serious 4×4 can be. A separate steel ladder frame carries the body, and coil springs hang a rigid axle at each corner, located by radius arms and a Panhard rod. Drive goes to the rear wheels until you engage the front axle through the VG 080 transfer case, which also has low range. The front and rear locks are mechanical-hydraulic: a dash control drives a dedicated master cylinder, and slave cylinders on each axle shift the locks.
- Chassis: Ladder frame (Separate steel frame with coil-sprung rigid axles, handmade in Graz from 1979.)
- Drivetrain: Part-time 4WD (Front axle engaged by lever through the VG 080 transfer case, with high and low range. Permanent 4WD only arrived with the W463.)
- Lockers: Front & rear (Standard on every W460 from 1985. Hydraulic actuation from their own master cylinder. Engagement can take a few wheel turns.)
- Wheelbases: 2,400 / 2,850 mm (SWB and LWB; cabrio, pickup, wagon and panel-van bodies.)
- Steering: LS2 steering box (The same box family serves the W460, W461 and W463, so seals and bearings are still available.)
- Engines: 2.0–2.8 petrol, 2.4–3.0 diesel (From 72 PS (240 GD) to 156 PS (280 GE). No factory turbodiesel.)

### Versions
- 1979–1982 · 230 G · M115 2.3 L I4 (carburettor) · 90 PS · Early petrol; four-speed manual
- 1982–1990 · 230 GE · 2.3 L I4, fuel-injected · ≈125 PS · Fuel injection arrived in 1982. Auto Bild rates it a top pick
- 1979–1990 · 280 GE · M110 2.8 L I6 (K-Jetronic) · ≈150–156 PS · The most powerful W460; Dakar winner in 1983
- 1979–1987 · 240 GD · OM616 2.4 L I4 diesel · 72 PS · 0–100 km/h in 32 seconds, according to Mercedes
- 1979–1991 · 300 GD · OM617 3.0 L I5 diesel · 88 PS · The most popular W460, and the engine in Otto
- 1987–1991 · 250 GD · OM602 2.5 L I5 diesel · 84 PS · Later diesel with hydraulic valve lifters
- 1986–1991 · 200 GE (Italy) · M102 2.0 L I4 · 118 PS · A tax special for Italy and other markets

### Year-by-year
- 1979: W460 goes on sale in September with petrol and diesel engines and short- and long-wheelbase bodies, hand-built in Graz
- 1980: Deliveries to the German riot police and Federal Border Guard; a 230 G Cabriolet becomes the Popemobile
- 1981: Automatic gearbox, air conditioning, auxiliary fuel tank, headlamp guards and winch added to the options list
- 1982: Fuel-injected 230 GE replaces the carburetted 230 G; Swiss Army tender won
- 1983: Jacky Ickx and Claude Brasseur win the Paris–Dakar car category in a 280 GE
- 1985: Front and rear differential locks, central locking and a tachometer become standard
- 1986: More than 50,000 G models built; Italy-market 200 GE added
- 1990: The civilian W463 takes over; the military and commercial line continues as the W461
- 1991: W460 production ends

### Capability
- Top speed: 79 mph (127 km/h) 300 GD; 103 mph (165 km/h) 280 GE (factory figures via Wikipedia)
- 0–100 km/h: 27 s (300 GD); 14 s (280 GE); 32 s (240 GD)
- Power / torque: 88 PS / 172 N·m (300 GD); 156 PS / 226 N·m (280 GE)
- Fuel economy: 11.7–18.8 L/100 km (12.5–20 mpg US) 300 GD; 14.0–22.4 L/100 km (10.5–16.8 mpg US) 280 GE (Mercedes cycle figures)
- Wheelbase: 112.2 in (2,850 mm) long wheelbase

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 205 R16 or 215/80R16 on 16x5.5 steel wheels, depending on model
- Bolt Pattern: 5x130
- Offset: ET63 or ET38 on the factory 16x5.5 fitments
- Center Bore: 84.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M14x1.5
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 235/85R16 (≈32 in) (An Expedition Portal owner runs 235/85R16s on standard steel wheels on a short-wheelbase G. Many owners stay near 215/85R16 because the naturally aspirated diesels struggle with bigger tires. For 33s, plan on lift springs.)

### Buying checks
- Rust first, everything else second: Classic & Sports Car says rust starts in the rear body corners. Check the inner wings, the bottom of the rear door and the shock top mounts visible in the wheel arch. Auto Bild adds the sills, the area under the windscreen, the spring mounts and the fuel tank. Most W460s lived in salty European winters, so a rot-free one costs more for good reason.
- Work the front-axle lever and the lockers: Engage 4WD and low range, then lock the rear and front diffs on a loose surface and listen for clean engagement. On a W460 the locks are hydraulic and can take a few wheel turns to bite. A lock that never engages usually points to a tired master cylinder, slave cylinders or flex lines.
- Overheating history: Classic & Sports Car warns that overheating and cylinder-head warping are common, and that an old radiator is probably clogged. Check the coolant for oil, look for weeps, and budget for a new radiator if the original is still fitted.
- Steering box and springs: Look for oil leaking from the bottom of the steering box, broken coil springs, leaking dampers and signs of hard off-road abuse. Excess play at the wheel usually means box, tie-rod or drag-link wear.
- Water where it shouldn't be: Classic & Sports Car flags leaks from the wiper spindles, sunroof and heater plenum, and the rear-door hinge seals perish with age. Lift the mats and look for stains and soft metal under them.
- Originality and paperwork: Hagerty, quoting Club G-Wagen co-founder Mike Serpe, says buyers pay up to 30% more for an all-original G and that any grey-market truck needs an expert inspection. Mercedes-Benz Classic sells factory data cards for most cars built from 1986, so a late W460's original spec can be checked; ask the seller for it.
- Know what you're buying into: A 300 GD makes 88 PS and tops out around 127 km/h (79 mph). An IH8MUD owner says even his truck, swapped to a mildly built OM617 turbodiesel, ran out of steam at about 70 mph. If you need it to keep up on the interstate, buy a different G.

### Common repairs
#### Front axle rebuild (bearings, kingpins, swivel seals, CVs)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A full weekend (estimate) · cost Kit $610 plus bronze bushing (Expedition Imports)
Symptoms: Oil or grease weeping from the steering ball (the big swivel housing behind the hub), play at the wheel, clicking on full lock, torn CV boots.
Fix: Do the whole corner at once, as specialists recommend, because bearings, kingpins and CVs wear together. Lift and support the axle and pull the wheel and brake caliper. Remove the hub nut and lock with the W460 hub-nut socket, then pull the hub and wheel bearings. Remove the kingpin caps and bearings, lift off the knuckle, and withdraw the axle shaft and CV. Replace the wheel bearings and seals, kingpin bearings and seals, steering-ball gasket and wipe seals, inner axle seal and bronze bushing, then repack and reassemble. Ask the supplier for written instructions, which Expedition Imports provides on request.
Tools: W460 front axle service kit (W460AXLEKIT) · bronze inner bushing 463 337 00 49 (sold separately) · kingpin bearing 000 981 59 05 ×4, seal 460 997 00 40, cap 460 332 00 33 · steering-ball wipe seal 460 331 01 80 · W460 hub-nut socket 460 589 02 07 00 · 1979–81 trucks use different inner axle seals

#### Diff locks won't engage (hydraulic system)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Half a day (estimate) · cost Rebuild kits ≈$142 each (Expedition Imports)
Symptoms: The dash control moves but the lock indicator never lights, locks engage then drop out, or fluid is low or weeping at an axle.
Fix: Check the reservoir and look for fluid at the slave cylinders on each axle and at the flex lines. On a W460 the rear locker line and front brake hose are a matched pair of flex lines, so replace aged ones together. Bleed the system, then test on loose ground. If it still won't hold, rebuild the dash master cylinder and the slave cylinders, and check the indicator switch and its rubber boot on the axle.
Tools: Locker master cylinder rebuild kit 000 353 24 55 (all W460) · late-style slave cylinder kit 460 350 07 84 (later W460s, by axle number) · front brake / rear locker flex line 460 420 50 48 · indicator switch 000 545 50 11 · brake bleeding kit

#### Steering box leak
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Half a day (estimate) · cost Seal $12.50; bearing set $111 (Expedition Imports)
Symptoms: Power-steering fluid on the frame rail under the box, low reservoir, groaning on lock, or play in the steering.
Fix: Classic & Sports Car lists steering box leaks as a standard W460 check. A likely culprit is the inexpensive sector-shaft seal at the bottom of the LS2 box. Disconnect the drag link, remove the pitman arm and replace the seal. Bad play or notchiness calls for the three-bearing set, which means removing and opening the box. While you're under there, check the steering damper and tie-rod ends.
Tools: Sector-shaft seal 016 997 13 47 (Corteco) · steering box bearing set · pitman-arm puller · W460 steering damper 000 463 60 32 if worn

#### Cooling system refresh
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 4 hours (estimate) · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Temperature creeping up on climbs or in traffic, weeping radiator end tanks, coolant smelling of oil. These engines warp heads when they overheat.
Fix: Replace the radiator before it fails. An old one is likely clogged, and overheated iron-block, alloy-head engines warp their heads. Fit a new thermostat and hoses, check the fan and its shroud, and pressure-test the system. Aluminium W460 radiators are made in manual-gearbox and automatic versions; the automatic version has the transmission cooler.
Tools: Radiator 001 501 07 01 (aluminium versions for manual or automatic) · thermostat 110 200 05 15 · engine-specific hoses and fan shroud · 300 GD late water pump 616 200 07 20 if weeping · pressure tester

#### Transfer case output seals
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 3 hours (estimate) · cost ≈$45 per outer seal (Expedition Imports)
Symptoms: Oil dripping from the transfer case flanges or slung around the propshaft ends, and a low transfer case oil level.
Fix: The VG 080 transfer case has three output flanges, each with an inner and an outer seal. Unbolt the propshaft, hold the flange and remove the nut, pull the flange, then replace both seals. Inspect the flange's sealing surface for a groove. Refill, and change the transfer case and axle oils while you're at it, because Classic & Sports Car recommends asking for their service history.
Tools: Outer seal 020 997 57 47 and inner seal 020 997 56 47 64 (one each per flange) · flange holding tool · front transfer-case flange nut 460 282 03 72 · seal driver

#### Sagging doors and rear-door leaks
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time 1–2 hours per door (estimate) · cost Hinge pin $8.50; rear hinge seal $22 (Expedition Imports)
Symptoms: Doors that drop when opened and have to be slammed, wind noise, or water and rust around the rear door hinges.
Fix: Support the door, drive out the worn hinge pins and fit new ones. Swap the rear-door hinge seals while the hinges are accessible, using the original recessed seals rather than the stick-on type. Clean and treat any rust you find under them.
Tools: Hinge pin 460 723 00 52 (front and rear doors) · rear single-door hinge seal 460 743 01 78 64 · barn-door hinge seal 460 743 00 78 · drift and hammer · rust converter and seam sealer

#### Springs and shocks
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours per corner (estimate) · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: A thump over bumps (a broken coil), a truck sitting low or leaning, a wallowing or bouncy ride, oily shock bodies. Classic & Sports Car lists broken coil springs and leaking dampers among the things to look for.
Fix: Support the chassis on stands, take the axle's weight on a jack, then remove the shock and the sway-bar link. Lower the axle carefully until you can lift the spring out, without stretching the brake hoses and locker lines. Fit springs in matched pairs using the correct Mercedes colour code for your wheelbase and load. Then refit the shocks and torque everything at ride height.
Tools: Koni Raid shocks (W460/461/463) or OE dampers · colour-coded W460 springs for your wheelbase (e.g. front LWB 460 321 06 04, rear LWB 460 324 07 04; confirm fitment) · jack and stands · spring compressor if required

#### Water leaks (wiper spindles, windscreen, sunroof, heater plenum)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time 1–2 hours for the wiper spindles. Most of a day for a windscreen reseal (estimate). · cost Wiper shaft washer kit $38.10; windscreen gasket $173.80 (Expedition Imports)
Symptoms: Wet carpets, damp footwells, a musty smell, rust under the mats. Classic & Sports Car flags leaks from the wiper spindles, sunroof and heater plenum.
Fix: Water-test with a hose and a helper inside to find the source. At the wiper spindles, replace the washers, nuts, seals and caps as a set. Clear the sunroof drains and check the plenum drains. A leak at the windscreen perimeter means taking the glass out to fit a new gasket. Inspect the frame for rust while it's out, because Handsome Motors lists the windshield gasket perimeter as a classic G rust spot. Dry the floor and replace missing body drain plugs.
Tools: Hose · trim tools · wiper shaft washer kit 000 824 35 72 · windscreen gasket 463 671 02 20 · body drain plug 460 997 11 81 · rust converter and seam sealer

### Baseline service
Assume nothing was done. Classic & Sports Car tells buyers to ask about oil changes for the engine, gearbox, transfer box and diffs, and most W460s are now 35 to 45 years old. Change every fluid, fix the cooling system and get the locker hydraulics working before the first trail trip. Factory capacities vary by engine and gearbox, so check the manual for your truck's numbers.
- Engine oil & filter: Oil grade per manual for your engine [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase, then per manual (Filters differ by engine: 300 GD/240 GD, 280 GE, 230 GE and 230 G (M115) each have their own part.)
- Air filter: OE-type element · At purchase; more often in dust (Two element types: 230 G/240 GD/300 GD and 280 GE/230 GE.)
- Fuel filter(s): OE-type; diesels also have a pre-filter · At purchase (Old fuel and rusty tanks block filters. Auto Bild lists the fuel tank as a rust spot.)
- Spark plugs / ignition (petrol): Engine-specific plug [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (Classic & Sports Car says poor running is often caused by vacuum leaks, so check the hoses while you're there.)
- Coolant, radiator & thermostat: Mercedes-approved coolant [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase; coolant every few years (Classic & Sports Car warns of overheating and head warping, and says an old radiator is probably clogged. Pressure-test the system and replace a tired radiator.)
- Gearbox oil (manual) or ATF & filter (automatic): Per manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (Automatics take a filter and O-ring. Check manual boxes for noise and clonks (Classic & Sports Car).)
- Transfer case (VG 080) oil: Per manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (Look for leaks at the three output flanges while it drains.)
- Front & rear differential oil: Hypoid gear oil per manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase; after deep water crossings (Fit new drain/fill plugs and cover gaskets if they're weeping.)
- Locker hydraulics: Fluid per manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (Bleed the system and test both locks. Locker lines are paired with the brake hoses on a W460, so replace aged flex lines together.)
- Brake fluid & hoses: DOT 4 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase, then every 2 years (Check calipers, rotors and the rear drums on early trucks.)
- Steering box & power steering: Fluid type marked on cap [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (Classic & Sports Car lists steering box leaks as a standard check. Replace the pump filter.)
- Front axle: kingpins, swivel seals, wheel bearings: Inspect and grease · At purchase (A weeping steering ball or bearing play means doing the whole corner.)
- V-belts: Engine-specific sizes · At purchase (Older engines use several V-belts rather than one serpentine belt; match the sizes to your engine.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: About a 32-inch 235/85R16 on the stock steel wheels. An Expedition Portal owner of a short-wheelbase diesel G runs 235/85R16s on standard steel wheels and reports they work well on and off road. The original fitment was a skinny 205 R16, and another owner whose truck came on 215/85R16s is sticking with that size. For 33s and up, plan on lift springs.

Q: Is the W460 full-time four-wheel drive?
A: No. It's part-time: you engage the front axle by lever through the transfer case, with high and low range. Permanent 4WD arrived with the 1989–90 W463. Don't drive a W460 in 4WD on dry pavement.

Q: Do all W460s have locking differentials?
A: Not all of them. Mercedes made front and rear locks standard on every W460 from 1985, so earlier trucks may not have them. Look for the locker control on the dash and the slave cylinders on the axles. A W460 never had the W463's third (centre) lock.

Q: Which engine should I buy?
A: The 300 GD was the most popular W460 and the 280 GE the most powerful. Auto Bild names the 230 GE and the 300 GD, with their long-lived manual gearboxes, as the ones to have. The OM617 five-cylinder in the 300 GD has a reputation for reaching huge mileages, but it's slow and was never turbocharged in a W460.

Q: How fast will it cruise?
A: Not very. Factory figures for a 300 GD are 88 PS, 0–100 km/h in about 27 seconds and a 127 km/h (79 mph) top speed. An IH8MUD owner says his truck, re-engined with a mildly built OM617 turbodiesel, ran out of steam at about 70 mph. A 280 GE is good for about 165 km/h.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: Mercedes' cycle figures for the 300 GD run from 11.7 to 18.8 L/100 km, roughly 12.5–20 mpg US. The 280 GE is thirstier, at 14.0–22.4 L/100 km (about 10.5–17 mpg). Big tires, a roof rack and a lift make both worse.

Q: Was the W460 sold in the US?
A: Not by Mercedes. Grey-market specialists federalised some in the 1980s until the 1988 Imported Vehicle Safety Compliance Act made it much harder. Official US sales didn't begin until the 2002 model year, and before that Europa International imported later W463s.

Q: W460, W461 or W463 — what's the difference?
A: The W460 (1979–1991) is the original, with part-time 4WD and two lockers. The W461 kept the W460's body and chassis but used W463 running gear, and was built for armies, authorities and NGOs. The W463 is the civilian luxury G from 1990, with permanent 4WD, three lockers, ABS and wood trim.

Q: Are parts hard to find?
A: In the US they're scarce and expensive, according to IH8MUD owners. In Europe, Auto Bild says Mercedes dealers still stock most parts at high prices and used parts are plentiful. Specialists such as Expedition Imports stock W460 axle, locker, steering and cooling parts, and some components are shared with Mercedes cars and vans.

Q: What is a W460 worth?
A: Classic & Sports Car's 2023 guide put a pre-1990 hardtop at £5,000 as a project, £14,000 average and £27,000+ for a show truck. Soft-tops run £12,000 / £30,000 / £75,000+. For a US example, a rusty, re-engined 1986 300 GD project sold for $13,000 on PCARMARKET in January 2022.

Q: Can I use the diff locks on pavement?
A: No. A locked diff stops the wheels turning at different speeds, so on grippy surfaces the driveline binds and the tires scrub. Lock on dirt, sand, snow or rock at low speed, and unlock before you're back on tarmac.
