## Mercedes-Benz G-Class W461 (1992–2022)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/w461/
Codes: W461, G 290 GD, G 300 CDI Professional

Verdict: The G that never went to finishing school: W460 body, W463 running gear, rubber floors and a 24-volt habit. Armies bought it by the thousand, and the few civilians who could get one bought the best tool Mercedes ever made.

When the G-Class split in two at the end of the 1980s, the W463 got the leather, the wood and the attention. The W461 got the work. It kept the W460's body and chassis, gained the W463's drivetrain, and spent three decades carrying soldiers, medics, foresters and border police where roads give out. It's the G-Class with the luxury removed and the useful parts kept: barn doors, panel vans, cab-chassis trucks, three locking diffs and, on military trucks, a 24-volt electrical system.

### TWO Gs FROM ONE
Mercedes showed the luxurious W463 in 1989, and W460 production ended in 1991. For buyers who needed a tool rather than a status symbol, the W460 became the W461 in 1990, initially as the 230 GE and 290 GD, and the series was formally introduced in 1992. Wikipedia sums up the formula as the W460's chassis and body with the W463's powertrain, built specifically for militaries, public authorities and NGOs.
The split shows in the details. The W463 got no panel vans and no barn doors; those stayed exclusive to the W461. The W461 kept the narrow body, the plain dash and, on government trucks, 24-volt electrics. Some military trucks carried the 461 designation even earlier: the Argentine Army began using a 'model 461' in 1981.

### THE WOLF AND ITS PACK
Mercedes' own timeline lists the Bundeswehr receiving 12,500 'Wolf' G-Wagens under 1992; Wikipedia, which dates deliveries from 1993, puts the total at more than 12,000. Expedition Motor Company, which restores them, describes the 250 GD Wolf as an ex-military W461. By its definition a true Wolf is a two-door convertible with a fold-down windscreen and frameless windows, and it left the factory with a diesel engine.
Other armies joined the pack. Canada ordered 1,159 G-Wagons from late 2003 as its Light Utility Vehicle Wheeled, replacing the VW Iltis, with turreted, non-turreted and military-police versions. The US Marine Corps bought 157 Interim Fast Attack Vehicles based on a modified 290. Norway, Greece and Finland ran Gs from 240 GDs to armoured 270 CDIs. Australia replaced its army Land Rovers with W461s, and a 2010 Australian tender produced a 6×6 version of the 461 range.

### DIESELS THAT GOT SERIOUS
The engines started out painfully slow. The 1992 290 GD made 95 PS from a naturally aspirated 2.9-litre five-cylinder and took more than 25 seconds to reach 100 km/h. In 1998 the 290 GD Turbodiesel replaced it, with direct injection, about 120 hp, a driver's airbag and an automatic gearbox only. Common rail arrived with the G 270 CDI in 2001. For 2007 the G 280 CDI brought the 3.0-litre V6 diesel, detuned to 135 kW and 400 Nm so it could cope with poor-quality fuel.

### CIVILIANS ALLOWED, BRIEFLY
For the G-Class's 30th birthday in 2009, Mercedes sold the W461 to civilians as the G 280 CDI EDITION.30 PUR. It was a long-wheelbase wagon with four hard-wearing seats, rubber floors, drain holes in the footwells, a walk-on bonnet, flexible wheel-arch flares, headlamp grilles and barn doors. It sold well enough to spawn the G 280 CDI Professional in 2009 and the G 300 CDI Professional in 2010, offered as a wagon, panel van, cabriolet and cab-chassis.
Australia, where the army had adopted the W461, got the cab-chassis in 2016 and the wagon in 2017. Civilian production ended in 2019. Military trucks continued until 2022, when the W464 replaced them; Mercedes announced it on 1 October 2021. The W461 is the bridge between the W460 and today's working Gs, and the closest thing to a new W460 anyone could buy in the 2010s.

### Data plate
- Chassis: W461
- Years: 1992–2022 (civilian to 2019)
- Built In: Graz, Austria
- Body: W460-based, narrow
- Drive: Full-time 4WD, dual range
- Lockers: Centre, rear, front
- Electrics: 24 V (military)
- Crawl Ratio: 41.0:1 (G 300 CDI)
- Tires: 265/75R16 (G 300 CDI Pro)
- Clearance: 245 mm (cab-chassis)
- Approach / Dep.: 38° / 35°
- Succeeded By: W464 (2022)

### Engineering
Under the plain body the W461 is a W460 chassis carrying W463 running gear. That means a separate ladder frame, coil-sprung solid axles front and rear, and permanent four-wheel drive through a two-speed transfer case with three individually selectable locking differentials. In late G 300 CDI Professional form, the result is a 41:1 crawl ratio and a cab-chassis that can carry more than two tonnes.
- Chassis: Ladder frame (The W460's chassis and narrow body, kept for military, agency and NGO buyers.)
- Drivetrain: Full-time 4WD, dual range (50:50 torque split on the G 300 CDI Professional. The centre diff can be unlocked even in low range.)
- Lockers: Centre, rear, front (Three locks, each individually activated and selectable on the move.)
- Crawl Ratio: 41.0:1 (G 300 CDI Professional cab-chassis, per 4X4 Australia.)
- Engine (Late): OM642 3.0 V6 diesel (135 kW / 400 Nm, detuned from Mercedes' passenger-car V6 to tolerate poor fuel. The bonnet bulge clears an emissions air pump.)
- Electrics: 24-volt (military) (Military W461s run 24 V. The Australian civilian Professional wagon carries two 12-volt batteries.)

### Versions
- 1990–1991 · 250 GD 'Wolf' · OM602 2.5 L I5 diesel · 92 PS · Bundeswehr spec. Wikipedia lists it under the W461
- 1992–2001 · 230 GE / G 230 · M102 2.3 L I4 · 125 PS · Petrol working G
- 1992–1997 · 290 GD · OM602 2.9 L I5 diesel · 95 PS · Naturally aspirated; 0–100 km/h in 25–27 s
- 1998–2001 · 290 GD Turbodiesel · OM602 2.9 L I5 turbodiesel · 120 PS · Direct injection; automatic only
- 2001–2006 · G 270 CDI · OM612 2.7 L I5 turbodiesel · 156 PS · Common rail. Canada's LUVW used a 2.7 five-cylinder
- 2007–2014 · G 280 CDI · OM642 3.0 L V6 turbodiesel · 184 PS · Military 'Worker', plus the 2009 EDITION.30 PUR and Professional
- 2010–2019 (civilian) · G 300 CDI Professional · OM642 3.0 L V6 turbodiesel · 135 kW / 400 Nm · Wagon, van, cabrio and cab-chassis; military trucks built to 2022

### Year-by-year
- 1990: W460 becomes W461 (230 GE and 290 GD); 250 GD 'Wolf' built for the Bundeswehr
- 1992: Series 461 formally introduced; Mercedes' timeline records 12,500 'Wolf' trucks for the Bundeswehr
- 1998: 290 GD Turbodiesel with direct injection and a driver's airbag replaces the prechamber diesel; automatic only, 120 hp
- 2001: G 270 CDI brings a common-rail five-cylinder
- 2006: Bundeswehr renews its fleet with long-wheelbase G 270 CDI and G 300 'Greenliner' trucks
- 2007: G 280 CDI with the OM642 3.0 V6 turbodiesel
- 2009: Civilian sales return: G 280 CDI EDITION.30 PUR and G 280 CDI Professional
- 2010: G 300 CDI Professional launches; a 6×6 variant is added for an Australian tender
- 2016: G 300 CDI Professional cab-chassis launches in Australia at A$119,900; the wagon follows in 2017
- 2019: Civilian production ends
- 2022: Military production ends; the W464, announced on 1 October 2021, takes over

### Capability
- Towing: 2,210 kg (4,872 lb) (G 300 CDI Professional cab-chassis, 4X4 Australia)
- Payload: about 2,080 kg (4,586 lb) (cab-chassis, 4,490 kg GVM; 6,700 kg GCM)
- Fuel tank: 96–97 L (25.4–25.6 US gal) (WhichCar (wagon) / 4X4 Australia (cab-chassis))
- Ground clearance: 245 mm (9.6 in) (cab-chassis)
- Approach / departure / breakover: 38° / 35° / 22° (cab-chassis)
- Crawl ratio: 41.0:1
- Curb weight: 2,410 kg (5,313 lb) (cab-chassis)
- Engine: 135 kW / 400 N·m (OM642 3.0 V6 turbodiesel, G 300 CDI Professional)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 215/80R16 or 255/75R15 (1993 230 GE / 290 GD listings), 265/75R16 (G 300 CDI Professional)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x130
- Center Bore: 84.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M14x1.5
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 235/85R16 (≈32 in) (An Expedition Portal owner runs 235/85R16s on standard steel wheels on a narrow-body G, which is a sensible no-lift ceiling. Beyond that you need lift springs, and bigger tires can trigger ABS/ESP warnings on later trucks.)

### Buying checks
- Know which W461 you're looking at: Ex-military trucks such as the Bundeswehr Wolf, the civilian EDITION.30 PUR and the G 280/300 CDI Professional are all W461s, but they differ in electrics, equipment and paperwork. Check the VIN and the Mercedes data card rather than the seller's description.
- 24-volt systems: Military W461s run 24 V, and parts follow suit. Expedition Imports sells separate 12 V and 24 V heater blower motors, for example. Make sure accessories, lights and chargers match the system, and that no previous owner has half-converted it.
- Rust in the usual G places: These are steel bodies on a steel frame, and ex-fleet trucks often lived outdoors. Handsome Motors' G checklist covers the windscreen gasket, door hinges, rear spring perch mounts, the metal under the tail-lights and rear door, and the body seams; Autocar adds the inner wheel arches.
- Cardan shaft recall (late diesels): Autocar reports that Mercedes recalled G 280 CDI and G 300 CDI models built between 4 April 2016 and 13 September 2021: the cardan shaft can strike the clamping body, causing power loss and transmission failure. Confirm the recall work has been done.
- Lockers and low range: Engage low range, then each lock in turn on loose ground. If a lock won't engage, specialists say to flush the hydraulic system first before chasing parts.
- Springs and shocks: Autocar notes that G-Class coil springs crack, especially in cold weather, and a loud thump over bumps is the clue. Ex-fleet trucks may have had hard lives, so check the dampers and the bushings on the radius arms and Panhard rods.
- Set your expectations on pace: A naturally aspirated 290 GD makes 95 PS and needs 25–27 seconds to reach 100 km/h. The 1998–2001 turbodiesel, the CDIs and the G 300 CDI are far happier at highway speed.

### Common repairs
#### Cardan shaft recall check
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time Minutes to check · cost Recall work is done by Mercedes
Symptoms: On affected G 280 CDI and G 300 CDI trucks built from 4 April 2016 to 13 September 2021: power loss or drivetrain failure caused by the cardan shaft striking the clamping body.
Fix: Give the VIN to a Mercedes-Benz dealer and ask whether the cardan-shaft recall is open. If it is, book it in before using the truck hard. Keep the paperwork, because buyers will ask.
Tools: VIN · dealer recall lookup

#### Front axle service (bearings, kingpins, swivel seals)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A full weekend (estimate) · cost Kits from ≈$610 (Expedition Imports)
Symptoms: Weeping from the steering-ball swivel housings, wheel-bearing play, clicking CV joints, torn boots.
Fix: Strip each corner to the knuckle: hub, wheel bearings, kingpin bearings, steering-ball gasket and wipe seals, inner axle seal, CV joint and boot. Expedition Imports sells complete front axle kits for the W460 and for 2001-and-older and 2002-and-newer W463s. Kingpin parts differ for 2002-on trucks, which need a different lower bearing. Match the kit to your axle number and build year before ordering.
Tools: Front axle service kit for your axle · kingpin bearing kit (to 2001) or the 2002-on kit · steering-ball wipe seal 460 331 01 80 (fits all G-Wagens; one per side) · hub-nut socket

#### Locker won't engage
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time 2–4 hours (estimate) · cost Hoses ≈$28; slave kits ≈$143 (Expedition Imports)
Symptoms: Lock indicator stays dark, a lock drops out under load, or one lock works and another doesn't.
Fix: Handsome Motors, which has owned more than 200 Gs, says to have the hydraulic system flushed before anything else. Check the flex lines; on many W461s the rear locker line is paired with the front brake hose, so replace both. Bleed the system and retest. If a lock still won't move, rebuild the slave cylinder on that axle and check the indicator switch and its boot.
Tools: Front brake / rear locker flex line 460 420 50 48 (all W460 and many W461) · slave cylinder rebuild kit 460 350 07 84 · indicator switch boot 601 546 03 35 · brake bleeding kit

#### Springs and shocks
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours per corner (estimate) · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: A thump over bumps (a cracked coil), sagging ride height, a wallowing or bouncy ride, oily shock bodies. Corrugated roads kill shocks: see the Canning Stock Route sidebar.
Fix: Support the chassis on stands, take the axle's weight on a jack, remove the shock and sway-bar link, and lower the axle carefully until the spring can be lifted out, without overextending the brake hoses and locker lines. Fit springs in matched pairs using the correct Mercedes colour code for your wheelbase and load, then refit the shocks and torque everything at ride height.
Tools: Koni Raid shocks (W460/461/463) or OE dampers · colour-coded W460-pattern springs (e.g. front LWB 460 321 06 04, rear LWB 460 324 07 04; confirm fitment for your truck) · jack and stands · spring compressor if required

#### Steering box reseal
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Half a day (estimate) · cost Seal $12.50 (Expedition Imports)
Symptoms: Fluid weeping from the bottom of the steering box, low power-steering fluid, vague steering.
Fix: The W461 uses the same LS2 steering box family as the W460 and W463. Replace the sector-shaft seal at the bottom of the box: disconnect the drag link and pull the pitman arm. Heavy play calls for the bearing set and a box rebuild.
Tools: Sector-shaft seal 016 997 13 47 · steering box bearing set · pitman-arm puller

#### No heat or fan (24-volt blower)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time 1–2 hours (estimate) · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: The blower is dead or works on only some speeds, or a fuse blows repeatedly.
Fix: Check the fuse, switch and resistor before buying a motor. When replacing the motor, order the right voltage, because Expedition Imports lists separate 12 V and 24 V blower motors for these trucks.
Tools: 24 V blower motor 000 830 35 08 (12 V version 000 830 13 08) · multimeter · trim tools

#### Sagging doors and hinge rust
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time 1–2 hours per door (estimate) · cost Hinge pin $8.50; rear hinge seal $22.20; door seal $113.30 (Expedition Imports)
Symptoms: Doors that drop when opened and need a slam to latch, wind noise, and bubbling paint or rust around the hinges. Handsome Motors lists every door hinge as a G rust zone.
Fix: The W461 uses the W460 body, so W460 door parts apply. Support the door, drive out the worn hinge pins and fit new ones. Swap the rear-door hinge seals while the hinges are accessible, using the original recessed seals rather than stick-on replacements. Treat any rust under them. Replace hardened door seals if water or wind gets past them.
Tools: Hinge pin 460 723 00 52 · rear single-door hinge seal or barn-door hinge seal 460 743 00 78 · door seal 460 727 08 30 · drift and hammer · rust converter and seam sealer

#### Windscreen gasket, wiper spindle and floor leaks
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Most of a day for a windscreen reseal (estimate) · cost Windscreen gasket $173.80; wiper shaft washer kit $38.10; floor drain kit $47.20 (Expedition Imports)
Symptoms: Wet footwells, rust bubbling around the windscreen frame, water tracking down the A-pillars. Handsome Motors names the windshield gasket perimeter as a classic G rust zone.
Fix: Water-test with a hose and a helper. Reseal the wiper spindles with a new washer kit. If the leak is at the windscreen, the glass has to come out to fit a new gasket. Treat the frame properly while it's exposed, because rust there only spreads. Expedition Imports sells the floor drain kit that's common on 461 trucks and can be retrofitted to a 460, so make sure the floor drains are clear and fitted.
Tools: Windscreen gasket 463 671 02 20 · wiper shaft washer kit 000 824 35 72 · floor drain kit · glass-removal cord and trim tools · rust converter and primer

### Baseline service
Ex-fleet and ex-military W461s are often maintained by the book but stored for years, so refresh every fluid and rubber part. Military trucks run 24 V, and glow plugs, bulbs and blower motors must match the system. Specs vary by engine, from the 290 GD to the OM642 CDIs, so confirm capacities and fluid approvals for your VIN.
- Engine oil & filter: Oil approval per manual for your engine [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase, then per manual (290 GD and 300 GD-era trucks share filters with their W460/W463 relatives. CDIs use cartridge filters.)
- Glow plugs (diesel): 24 V plugs on 24 V trucks · At purchase if starting is slow (Fitting 12 V parts to a 24 V truck, or the reverse, kills them quickly.)
- Air filter: OE element; check the dirty-filter warning · At purchase; often in dust (The Australian G 300 CDI Professional has a dirty-air-filter warning (WhichCar).)
- Fuel filter & water separator: OE-type · At purchase (Military trucks may have sat with old diesel. Drain the water separator.)
- Coolant: Mercedes-approved coolant [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (Pressure-test the system and check the radiator and hoses.)
- Automatic transmission fluid & filter: Per manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (The 1998–2001 290 GD Turbodiesel and later trucks are automatic-only.)
- Transfer case: Per manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (Full-time dual-range case. Check that the centre lock engages and releases.)
- Front & rear differentials: Hypoid gear oil per manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase; after water crossings (Three lockers: test each one after the change.)
- Locker hydraulics: Flush and bleed · At purchase (Handsome Motors advises flushing the hydraulic system first when a lock won't actuate.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 4 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase, then every 2 years
- Front axle: kingpins, swivels, bearings: Inspect and grease · At purchase (Kits differ by axle and year, so check the axle number.)
- Batteries & charging: 24 V system (military) or 12 V · At purchase (Load-test both batteries and replace them as a pair. Check the 24 V alternator output on military trucks.)
- Cardan shaft recall (2016–21 G 280/300 CDI): Dealer recall check · At purchase (Recall for trucks built 4 April 2016 to 13 September 2021 (Autocar).)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: The G 300 CDI Professional comes on 265/75R16s, about 31.6 inches. On narrow-body Gs, an Expedition Portal owner runs 235/85R16s (about 32 inches) on the standard steel wheels, which is a sensible no-lift ceiling. Beyond that you're into lift springs: GwagenParts' ROGUE spring listing talks about 33- and 35-inch tires, and warns that bigger tires can trigger ABS and ESP warnings.

Q: What's the difference between a W461 and a W463?
A: The W461 uses the W460's narrow body and chassis with W463 running gear, plain trim, and barn doors and panel-van bodies you can't get on a W463. Military trucks also have 24-volt electrics. The W463 is the luxury civilian G with wood, leather and more electronics.

Q: Is the 250 GD 'Wolf' a W460 or a W461?
A: Expedition Motor Company, which restores them, calls the 250 GD Wolf an ex-military W461, and Wikipedia lists the 1990–91 Wolf in the W461 table. The line between late military W460s and early W461s is blurry, so check the VIN and data card on the truck in front of you.

Q: Could civilians buy a new W461?
A: Yes, in limited form. Mercedes sold the G 280 CDI EDITION.30 PUR in 2009, followed by the G 280 CDI Professional (2009) and the G 300 CDI Professional (2010–2019). In Australia the G 300 CDI Professional cab-chassis launched in 2016 at A$119,900, and the wagon followed in 2017 at A$109,900.

Q: How much can it carry and tow?
A: 4X4 Australia's figures for the G 300 CDI Professional cab-chassis: 2,410 kg kerb weight, 4,490 kg GVM, about 2,080 kg payload and 2,210 kg towing capacity, with a 6,700 kg GCM.

Q: Is it full-time four-wheel drive?
A: Yes. The G 300 CDI Professional has permanent all-wheel drive with a 50:50 split, a two-speed transfer case and three locking diffs selectable on the move. Unusually, you can unlock the centre diff even in low range.

Q: Does it really run on 24 volts?
A: Military W461s do. Wikipedia lists the 24-volt system as one of the W461's defining features, and parts suppliers stock 24 V components such as blower motors. The Australian civilian Professional wagon is described as carrying two 12-volt batteries. Check what your truck actually has before wiring in accessories.

Q: Which engine should I look for?
A: For highway use, the 1998–2001 290 GD Turbodiesel or later: the G 270 CDI (156 PS, 400 Nm) and the OM642 V6 in the G 280/300 CDI (184 PS, 400 Nm). The naturally aspirated 290 GD (95 PS) and the 250 GD Wolf are charming and simple but very slow.

Q: How big is the fuel tank?
A: 96–97 litres on the G 300 CDI Professional, depending on whether you read WhichCar or 4X4 Australia.

Q: Why does the late W461 have a bonnet bulge?
A: It clears an air pump that's part of the emissions equipment, according to 4X4 Australia. The W460 doesn't have one.

Q: Is the W461 still built?
A: No. Civilian production ended in 2019, and military production continued until 2022, when the W464 took over. Mercedes announced the W464 on 1 October 2021.

## Mercedes-Benz G-Class W463 (1990–2018)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/w463/
Codes: W463

Verdict: Twenty-eight years and engines from four to twelve cylinders, all on the same ladder frame and two solid axles. It became a rapper's accessory and stayed a real off-roader the whole time. Buy one for the three lockers and keep a budget for the vacuum lines.

The W463 is the G-Class most people picture: square, upright, faintly absurd, and still built on a ladder frame with a solid axle at each end. Between 1990 and 2018 it went from a farmer's tool with a wood dash to a twin-turbo V12 AMG with more than 600 PS, a 6×6 cousin and a Maybach landaulet. Mercedes fitted it with more engine types than any other model it has built, and it never lost the three locking differentials that make it so good off-road.

### FRANKFURT, 1989: THE G GETS A LIVING ROOM
For the G's tenth birthday, Mercedes showed a new version at the 1989 Frankfurt show, and production started the following April. It had a new chassis number, W463, and a new mission. Permanent four-wheel drive replaced the W460's part-time system, the diff locks became electrically switched from the middle of the dash, ABS was available, and for the first time the cabin got wood and leather. Autocar's 1991 test said permanent 4WD and ABS made it 'a much more convincing tool on the road.'
The working trucks went elsewhere. The W463 dropped the panel vans and barn doors, and they carried on in the utilitarian W461 for armies and agencies. Early W463s used carryover engines, with petrol 230 GEs and 300 GEs and diesel 250 GDs and 300 GDs. In 1994 the line was renamed the G-Class, the manual gearbox disappeared, and ventilated front discs and a driver's airbag became standard.

### V8s, AMERICANS AND AMG
Mercedes started testing what the G could carry. The 1993 500 GE squeezed in a V8 for a run of 446 trucks. In 1996 an electronically controlled five-speed automatic arrived, and the 1997 update brought V6 engines and dual airbags. The G 500 made the V8 a regular-production option in 1998, and in 1999 the G 55 AMG became the most powerful G yet.
America came next, by a back door. Mercedes didn't sell the G in the US, so Europa International of New Mexico started certifying and selling them in 1993. Those Europa trucks proved the demand, Mercedes bought the distribution rights, and the G launched officially in the US with the 2002 model year. That facelift brought ESP, Brake Assist and the four-wheel electronic traction system, 4ETS.

### LUXURY, LOCKERS AND A LOT OF CYLINDERS
From there the W463 kept adding power. The G 55 AMG got a supercharger in 2004, the 5.5-litre M273 V8 created the US G 550 for 2009, and in 2012 came the twin-turbo G 63 and the V12 G 65. Mercedes sold just over 100 G 63 6×6s, and the portal-axled G 500 4×4² followed in 2015. Ninety-nine Maybach G 650 Landaulets closed out the run. By the end there were 22 paint colours and engines from four to twelve cylinders, naturally aspirated, supercharged, turbo and twin-turbo.
Underneath, almost nothing changed. The frame, the solid axles and the three lockers were the same on a 2018 G 550 as on a 1990 230 GE. Hagerty quotes 36°/31° approach and departure angles, 80% grades and 30° side slopes for the G. Handsome Motors, a dealer who has owned more than 200 Gs, estimates that each truck still took roughly 100 hours of hand labour in Graz.

### HOW IT ENDED
In late 2017 Mercedes announced the end of the first-generation W463. Its replacement, revealed at Detroit in January 2018, kept the shape, the ladder frame and three lockers. It also brought independent front suspension, rack-and-pinion steering and the first formal crash test of any G. The second generation is the better road car by a wide margin.
For the trail crowd, though, 2018 marks the last year a new G came with a solid front axle. That's why clean W463s, from the 1990s diesels to the last G 550s, are now bought as off-roaders as much as status symbols.

### Data plate
- Chassis: W463
- Years: 1990–2018
- Built In: Graz, Austria
- Bodies: SWB 3-door, cabrio, LWB 5-door
- Drive: Full-time 4WD
- Low Range: 2.16:1
- Lockers: Centre, rear, front
- Axles: Solid, coil-sprung
- Approach / Dep.: 36° / 31° (Hagerty); 34° / 29° (2015 G 550)
- Engines: I4 to V12, petrol & diesel
- Us Sales: Europa 1993–2001; MB from MY2002
- Succeeded By: Second-gen G (2018)

### Engineering
Mercedes never changed the W463's hard parts. A separate ladder frame carries the body, coil springs suspend a rigid axle at each end, and the recirculating-ball steering box comes from the same family as the W460's. Drive goes to all four wheels all the time through a two-speed transfer case. The three locks are where the complexity lives: an electronic controller enforces the order (centre, then rear, then front), vacuum engages the centre lock and switches the valves, and hydraulic slave cylinders on the axles slide dog sleeves into the front and rear diffs. An auxiliary vacuum pump backs up the engine's own vacuum.
- Chassis: Ladder frame (Body-on-frame for the whole 1990–2018 run, still hand-assembled in Graz.)
- Axles: Solid, front & rear (Coil-sprung and link-located. Independent front suspension arrived with the 2018 redesign.)
- Drivetrain: Full-time 4WD (Two-speed transfer case; low range is 2.16:1.)
- Lockers: Centre → rear → front (Electric switches, vacuum control, hydraulic actuation. Each engages after the truck has moved a little.)
- Steering: Recirculating ball (Replaced by electric rack-and-pinion only on the 2018 second generation.)
- Electronics: ABS → ESP + 4ETS (ABS from 1990; ESP, Brake Assist and 4ETS traction control with the 2001–02 update.)

### Versions
- 1990–1994 · 230 GE · 300 GE · 250 GD · 300 GD · M102 / M103 petrol · OM602 / OM603 diesel · 94–170 PS · Carryover engines. Manual gearbox dropped in 1994
- 1992–2001 · 350 GD Turbo · G 320 · G 300 Turbodiesel · OM603 3.5 TD · M104 3.2 I6 · OM606 3.0 TD · 136–211 PS · The six-cylinder era. Hagerty says the 1996–99 diesel G was the last built to be field-serviceable
- 1997–2006 · G 320 · G 400 CDI · G 270 CDI · M112 3.2 V6 · OM628 4.0 V8 TD · OM612 2.7 I5 TD · 156–250 PS · V-engines arrive; common-rail diesels from 2001
- 1998–2008 · G 500 · M113 5.0 V8 · 296 PS · First regular-production V8 G; US from MY2002
- 2006–2018 · G 320 CDI · G 350 CDI / BlueTEC · G 350 d · OM642 3.0 V6 TD · 211–245 PS · Autocar's 'best all-rounder' (G 320 CDI)
- 2008–2018 · G 500 / G 550 · M273 5.5 V8, then M176 4.0 V8 TT (2016–18) · 388 → 422 PS · Seven-speed automatic. The M176 replaced the M273 in 2016
- 2012–2018 · G 63 AMG · G 65 AMG · M157 5.5 V8 TT · M279 6.0 V12 TT · 544–630 PS · The fast ones. Expensive brakes and cooling-system work

### Year-by-year
- 1990: W463 launches: permanent 4WD, three electrically selected locking diffs and ABS, with carryover 230 GE, 300 GE, 250 GD and 300 GD engines
- 1992: Cruise control, walnut trim and stainless spare-wheel cover added; the 100,000th G is built in Graz
- 1993: 500 GE V8 limited edition (446 built); Europa International begins US certification and sales
- 1994: Renamed G-Class; 200/230/300 GE dropped and the manual gearbox ends
- 1996: Electronically controlled five-speed automatic, passenger airbag and headlamp washers
- 1998: G 500 brings the M113 V8 into regular production
- 2001–02: ESP, Brake Assist and 4ETS traction control arrive; Mercedes-Benz USA starts official sales for MY2002
- 2002–04: Early US trucks have the electrical gremlins: Handsome Motors lists seat motors and controls, window regulators and motors, door-lock actuators and transfer-case actuators. Expedition Portal owners say the same about 2002–03 [avoid]
- 2005–08: The G 500 sweet spot. Handsome Motors says the early electrical faults were mostly gone by 2005–06; the US switch to the seven-speed came for MY2007 [buy]
- 2007: Seven-speed automatic in the US G 500, plus HID headlamps, reversing camera and TPMS
- 2009: G 550 with the 5.5-litre M273 V8 replaces the US G 500; no factory towing hardware for 2009–2010
- 2012: G 63 AMG (M157 biturbo V8) and G 65 AMG V12 arrive
- 2016: M176 4.0-litre twin-turbo V8 replaces the M273 in the G 500/G 550. Handsome Motors calls 2016–18 trucks a reliable option but rates 2002–15 trucks higher for outright reliability
- 2018: Second-generation G-Class launched in Detroit in January, ending the original body

### Capability
- Towing: 7,000 lb (3,175 kg) (braked; 1,653 lb (750 kg) unbraked — 2015 G 550/G 63 manual)
- Fuel tank: 25.4 US gal (96 L) (about 3.7 gal (14 L) reserve; 2013–2015 US manuals)
- Ground clearance: 8.1 in (205 mm) G 550; 7.7 in (196 mm) G 63 AMG (2015 US manual)
- Approach / departure: 34° / 29° (G 550); 27° / 27° (G 63 AMG) (2015 US manual)
- Wading depth: 24 in (60 cm) (loaded and ready to drive; less in flowing water — 2015 US manual)
- Roof load: Not rated (The 2013 and 2015 US manuals say the roof is not suited for transporting loads)
- Low range: 2.16:1
- Turning circle: 44.6 ft (13.6 m) (listed as turning radius, 2015 US manual)
- GVWR: 7,055 lb (3,200 kg) (2015 G 550/G 63)
- Wheelbase: 112.2 in (2,850 mm) (long-wheelbase five-door)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 265/70R16 on 7.5Jx16 ET63 (OE on the 2001–2006 G 270 CDI; also the 500 GE's factory size), P265/60R18 (2002–2008 US G 500), 265/60R18 on 7.5Jx18 ET43 (2015 US G 550), 275/50R20 on 9.5Jx20 ET50 (2015 US G 63 AMG)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x130
- Offset: ET63 on most pre-2009 factory sizes; ET43 (G 550) and ET50 (G 63) on 2015 US trucks
- Center Bore: 84.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M14x1.5 (lug bolts)
- Lug Torque: 96 lb-ft (130 N·m) — 2013–2015 US operator's manuals
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 275/70R18 (≈33 in) (Fits unlifted G 500/G 550s on factory 18s per Expedition Portal owners; 285/65R18 rubs slightly at full left lock. One G 500 owner reports 315/75R16s with no lift, but 35s on stock springs usually rub somewhere.)
- Biggest tire, 2–2.5 in lift: 33x11.00–33x12.50 (JWO 2-in and Eurowise 60 mm springs are sold as 33-in setups; wheel offset +30 or lower (or a ~30 mm spacer) and longer shocks.)
- Biggest tire, 3 in lift: 35 in (GwagenParts' ~75 mm front kit (2002–2018 G 500/G 55/G 550/G 63/G 65) claims room for 35s; spacers may be needed, caster bushings included.)
- Biggest tire, 4 in lift: 35x11.00–35x12.50 (JWO 4-in springs: offset +20 or lower (typically 50 mm spacers on stock wheels) and caster-correction bushings; adjustable panhard bars recommended.)

### Buying checks
- Rust, rust, rust: Handsome Motors lists the places to check: the roof around the sunroof, the metal under the tail-lights and rear door, every door hinge, the rear spring perches, the windscreen gasket, the mirror bases, the 'dog-leg' cavities inside the doors and every body seam. Autocar adds the inner wheel arches and the area around the rear bumper.
- Test all three lockers: Engage centre, rear and front in order on loose ground and watch the indicators. Lockers that 'were never used' often don't work. Handsome Motors says to have the hydraulics flushed before chasing parts; vacuum leaks are the next suspect.
- Drive it at 55–70 mph: Judder or shaking can mean a failing propshaft (Autocar budgets £1,500 or more). Harsh 2–3 shifts, flares or speed-sensor codes on the five-speed 722.6 point to old fluid or a failing conductor plate.
- Early-2000s electrics: Handsome Motors says 2002–04 trucks suffer seat-motor, window-regulator and door-lock-actuator gremlins, along with transfer case motor and actuator faults, and that these improved each year until 2005–06. Test every switch.
- A sagging headliner means water: Handsome Motors notes that 2002 US trucks have a hard fibreboard headliner while 2003-on trucks got a fabric one that is probably sagging by now. Autocar warns a sagging headliner can also mean water is getting in, so check the sunroof drains, the rear-door hinge seals and the fuse box area for damp.
- Listen for a thump: Coil springs crack, especially in cold weather, and a loud thump over bumps is the sign. Autocar puts the fix at about £120 per corner.
- Engine-specific weak spots: M113 (G 500, early G 55): harmonic balancer and viscous fan. M273 (G 550, 2009–15): starters every 50–60k miles, cam magnets and intake swirl flaps. M176 (2016–18): a failed crankcase-vent oil separator can cause rear-main and valve-cover leaks, with $3–5k in labour for the rear main seal (Handsome Motors). M157 G 63: inspect the cooling system and water pump.
- Is it really an AMG?: Autocar warns about standard Gs converted to look like AMGs. Check the VIN and the factory data card, not the badges.

### Common repairs
#### Lockers won't engage: find the vacuum leak
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time 2–4 hours · cost Often a few dollars in fittings; vacuum reservoir ≈$74 (Expedition Imports)
Symptoms: One or more lock lights never come on, the centre lock drops out (and takes the rear with it), or locks release when engine revs fall.
Fix: Follow the MBWorld owner who fixed his 2005 G 500. Pull the vacuum hose at the transfer case and test for vacuum there. Then work back toward the source: intake manifold, the vacuum reservoir in the front-left wheel well, then the switchover valve block on the firewall, teeing a gauge into each segment. His leak was a split plastic connector inside a rubber Y-piece under the brake booster. Replace brittle hoses and weak check valves as you go, then flush and bleed the hydraulic side.
Tools: Hand vacuum pump with gauge · tee fittings · vacuum line and connectors · diff-lock vacuum reservoir 102 070 00 68 if cracked · brake bleeder for the hydraulic slaves

#### Centre diff lock vacuum diaphragm
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours (estimate) · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Vacuum reaches the transfer case but the centre lock still won't engage, or a hand pump on the actuator won't hold vacuum.
Fix: With the truck safely supported, test the centre-lock actuator on the transfer case with a hand vacuum pump. If it leaks down, replace the diaphragm unit, reconnect the lines and confirm the centre lock engages and the light comes on before testing rear and front. G-luxe Travel films the job on a W463 G 500.
Tools: Hand vacuum pump · replacement centre-lock vacuum diaphragm for your transfer case · basic metric sockets · video: G-luxe Travel

#### Transfer case actuator motor
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2 hours (estimate) · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Low range won't select or deselect, a warning on the dash, or the shift sits half-done. Handsome Motors flags transfer case motors and actuators as a weak spot on 2002–04 trucks.
Fix: Confirm the fault with a diagnostic scan, then unbolt the actuator motor from the transfer case, fit the new unit, then clear the codes and test the range shift with a scan tool. Service the transfer case fluid at the same time, because specialists note owners tend to put it off.
Tools: Mercedes-capable scan tool · replacement actuator motor · transfer case fluid to spec · video: G-luxe Travel 'W463 Transfer Case Fix'

#### Propshafts: grease, flex discs, judder
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time 1–3 hours · cost Grease is cheap; Autocar budgets £1,500+ for a replacement shaft
Symptoms: Vibration or judder at speed, clunks on take-up, cracked rubber flex discs, notchy U-joints.
Fix: Grease the propshaft joints and slip yokes at every service; G-luxe Travel has a quick W463 guide. Inspect the flex discs (guibos) and the centre support bearing. Replace flex discs in pairs if either looks marginal, and recheck the bolt torque after a few hundred miles. A shaft that still judders after that needs rebuilding or replacing.
Tools: Grease gun with needle adapter · new flex discs and bolts · torque wrench · centre-drive-shaft bolt N000000006359 / nut N910113010003 as needed

#### Cracked coil springs (front and rear)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time 1–2 hours per axle (estimate) · cost ≈ £120 per corner (Autocar)
Symptoms: A loud thump over bumps, a corner sitting low, a visibly broken coil, often after a cold snap.
Fix: Support the chassis on stands and take the axle on a jack. Disconnect the shock and sway-bar link on that side, then lower the axle slowly until the spring comes free, watching the brake hoses, ABS wires and locker lines. Fit the new spring with its isolator, raise the axle, and refit the shock and link. Replace springs in axle pairs. G-luxe Travel has front and rear DIY videos on a G 500.
Tools: Floor jack and stands · spring compressor if needed · matched springs · new shocks if tired · videos: G-luxe Travel

#### 722.6 transmission service and conductor plate
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2 hours (service) · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Harsh 2–3 shifts, flares, limp mode, speed-sensor codes such as P0715, ATF wicking up the harness.
Fix: If the service history is unknown, service it now: drop the pan, replace the filter and pan gasket, replace the electrical connector sleeve (the usual oil-wicking point), refill with MB 236.14 ATF and set the level hot. If speed-sensor codes persist, a failing conductor plate is a common cause. For the later seven-speed (2007-on), Handsome Motors advises fluid changes every 40–50k miles.
Tools: ATF to MB 236.14 · filter and pan gasket · connector sleeve · dipstick tool and thermometer or scan tool for level setting

#### Viscous fan clutch (M113 G 500)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours (estimate) · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Temperature climbs in traffic or on slow trails, or the fan freewheels easily with a hot engine (or roars all the time).
Fix: With the engine cold, check the fan for wobble and how it resists turning. Hold the pulley and undo the fan clutch from its hub, fit the new clutch and refit the shroud. G-luxe Travel's 'How I won the battle with my viscous fan' covers the G 500 job.
Tools: Fan-clutch holding tool and wrench · replacement viscous coupling · video: G-luxe Travel

#### Front axle service (bearings, kingpins, swivel seals)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A full weekend (estimate) · cost $630 (≤2001) or $680 (2002+) kits (Expedition Imports)
Symptoms: Grease or oil weeping from the steering-ball swivels, torn CV boots, wheel-bearing play.
Fix: Strip each front corner: hub, wheel bearings, kingpin bearings, steering-ball gasket and wipe seals, inner axle seal and bushing, CV and boot. Expedition Imports sells separate kits for 2001-and-older and 2002-and-newer W463s, and 2002-on trucks use a different lower kingpin bearing.
Tools: W463 front axle service kit for your year · kingpin bearing kit (to 2001) or the 2002-on kit · steering-ball wipe seal 460 331 01 80 · axle shaft bushing 463 337 00 49 · W463 hub-nut socket

### Baseline service
Baseline everything, because a W463 that 'never needed anything' usually has locker vacuum leaks, old ATF and a sagging headliner. The specs below are the published ones for the common 1999–2008 M113/722.6 trucks (Toolsource). Diesels, AMGs and 2007-on seven-speed trucks differ, so confirm capacities and approvals in WIS or the owner's manual for your VIN.
- Engine oil & filter: MB 229.5 synthetic, commonly 0W-40 or 5W-40 (M113) · capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase, then per FSS; Handsome Motors runs 3–5k miles on the M176 (Cartridge filter in a top-mounted housing. Use a 74 mm, 14-flute cap wrench.)
- Air filters: OE-quality (Mann/Mahle/Hengst) · At purchase; more often in dust (M113 trucks use a pair of filters.)
- Cabin filter: OE-quality · At purchase
- Spark plugs / glow plugs: M113: 16 plugs (two per cylinder), correct heat range and gap · At purchase if history unknown (Oil in the plug wells means valve-cover gaskets. Inspect the coil boots. Diesels: test the glow plugs.)
- Coolant & thermostat: MB 325.0 / 325.5 approved, 50/50 with distilled water · capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (Pressure-test the system and replace the thermostat proactively. Check the water pump weep hole, radiator end tanks and fan clutch.)
- Automatic transmission (722.6 five-speed): ATF to MB 236.14, new filter, pan gasket and connector sleeve; set the level hot · capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase, then about every 40–60k miles (Drain-and-fill with filter is the norm. For the 2007-on seven-speed, Handsome Motors suggests every 40–50k miles.)
- Transfer case: ATF to MB 236.14 (verify on the spec plate or in WIS) · At purchase (Specialists say owners tend to defer transfer case fluid and actuator work.)
- Front & rear differentials: GL-5 gear oil, viscosity suited to climate · At purchase; after deep water (Change the fluids before chasing locker faults, as the MBWorld owner did.)
- Locker vacuum system & hydraulics: Replace brittle hoses and weak check valves; flush the hydraulics · At purchase (Test each lock in order. Vacuum leaks are the usual cause of a lock that won't engage.)
- Power steering fluid: Type marked on the cap (ATF or CHF-type, by VIN) · At purchase (Replace the reservoir filter.)
- Brake fluid & hoses: DOT 4 or DOT 4 LV · Every 2 years (Replace aged rubber brake hoses.)
- Belt, idlers & tensioner: Replace if cracked or glazed · At purchase if unknown
- Propshafts & flex discs: Grease the joints; inspect flex discs and the centre bearing · At purchase and every service (Replace flex discs in pairs and recheck torque after a few hundred miles. G-luxe Travel has a W463 greasing guide.)
- Fuel filter: Replace if age/mileage unknown · At purchase

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: About 33 inches. Expedition Portal owners report a 275/70R18 on an unlifted G 500 and a 285/65R18 with only a slight rub at full left lock. One owner says he has run 315/75R16s on his G 500 for nearly a decade with no lift and no rubbing, but that's an outlier. Wheel offset matters: one owner's rubbing went away when he swapped ET63 wheels for ET43 G 550 wheels, while another says ET63 wheels tuck the rear tires better on 35s. JWO designed its 4-inch springs specifically to clear tires bigger than 33 inches.

Q: Which W463 engine is the most reliable?
A: Handsome Motors ranks it G 500 → G 55 → G 550 → G 63 for mechanical reliability, and calls the 2002–2015 V8s the safest bets. In Europe, Autocar names the G 320 CDI diesel V6 the best all-rounder. Avoid neglected G 63s unless you've budgeted for big brakes and cooling-system work.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: In the US, a 2005–08 G 500. Handsome Motors says the 2002–04 trucks suffer electrical gremlins (seat motors, window regulators, door-lock actuators, transfer-case actuators) that were mostly gone by 2005–06, and Expedition Portal owners tell the same story about 2002–03. CarGurus adds that the very last 1999–2000 Europa G 500s are considered very reliable, and that 2009-on trucks have fewer problems than the early US ones. The 2016–18 twin-turbo trucks are a reliable option, Handsome Motors says, but not the most reliable. In Europe, Autocar's pick is the G 320 CDI.

Q: What's the low-range ratio?
A: 2.16:1 through the two-speed transfer case.

Q: How do the three lockers work, and in what order?
A: You press the dash buttons and a controller engages them in sequence: centre first, then rear, then front. Each one locks after the truck has rolled a short distance. Vacuum operates the centre lock and the valves; hydraulics move the front and rear locks. Unlock everything before you're back on pavement.

Q: Was the W463 sold in the US before 2002?
A: Yes, but not by Mercedes. Europa International of New Mexico federalised and sold them from 1993, and became the exclusive US importer of the G 500 with small-volume-manufacturer status. Those trucks have US VINs. Mercedes took over with the 2002 model year.

Q: When did the manual gearbox disappear?
A: In 1994, when the 200, 230 and 300 GE were dropped. From 1996 the automatic was an electronically controlled five-speed. The seven-speed came in for 2007 on the US G 500.

Q: Which years have ESP and traction control?
A: ESP, Brake Assist and the four-wheel electronic traction system (4ETS) arrived with the 2001–02 update that coincided with the official US launch. Earlier W463s have ABS but rely on the lockers alone for traction.

Q: How often should I service the automatic?
A: Toolsource cites a 40–60k-mile interval for the five-speed 722.6, using MB 236.14 ATF. Handsome Motors suggests every 40–50k miles for the seven-speed. If the history is unknown, do it now.

Q: Are the 2016–2018 G 550s with the twin-turbo V8 a good buy?
A: Handsome Motors says yes. The M176 is a lower-stressed relative of AMG's M177, and by those years the early electrical gremlins were gone. Watch for a failed crankcase-vent oil separator causing rear-main-seal and valve-cover leaks. The same dealer personally recommends 3–5k-mile oil changes. For outright reliability, though, he still rates the 2002–2015 trucks higher.

Q: What does 'W463A' mean?
A: It's an enthusiast label for the 2018-on second-generation G, which kept the W463 chassis code. Mercedes doesn't use the term itself.

Q: How do I spot a fake AMG?
A: Check the VIN and the factory data card. Bumpers, flares, wheels and badges are easy to bolt on, and Autocar specifically warns about Gs converted to look like AMGs.

Q: Can I use the diff locks on pavement?
A: No. Locked diffs stop the wheels turning at different speeds, so on grippy surfaces the driveline binds and the tires scrub. Use them on dirt, sand, snow or rock at low speed.

## Mercedes-Benz 500 GE V8 (1993–1994)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/500ge/
Codes: W463, M117 5.0 V8

Verdict: The first V8 G exists because Mercedes had a pile of old engines and nowhere better to put them. Only 446 were built, nearly all in purple-ish blue, and it is the one G that ships without a front locker.

The 500 GE is the G-Class that answered a question nobody had asked yet: what if the army truck had a V8? Shown at the Geneva Motor Show in March 1993, it was the first eight-cylinder G, sold only as a long-wheelbase five-door. It came in one standard colour and with every comfort option fitted, and the price was roughly double a G 320's. Mercedes planned 500. It built 446, and the reason has nothing to do with marketing.

### A PILE OF ENGINES AND A SMALL ENGINE BAY
By 1993 the old two-valve M117 V8 was on its way out. Mercedes' newer four-valve M119 had replaced it in the saloons, but the M119 was too big for the G's engine bay. That left a limited supply of M117s, so the 500 GE's production run was set by the number of engines on hand. Mercedes' own anniversary history says the run stopped at 446, built over about two years. Wikipedia describes it as a leftover batch of 446 engines.
The engine is the 4,973 cc M117, rated by Mercedes at 177 kW (240 PS) and 375 Nm. That was enough for 0–100 km/h in 11.4 seconds and a 180 km/h top speed, which felt quick for a long-wheelbase brick in 1993. An automatic gearbox was standard; a surviving owner-documented example has the four-speed automatic. Wikipedia says the body and chassis were adapted for the V8 at AMG in Affalterbach, then still an independent tuner; Mercedes' own anniversary story doesn't mention AMG.

### WHAT DM 178,250 BOUGHT YOU
At launch the 500 GE cost DM 178,250. A six-cylinder G 320 cost DM 88,500, and even a 500 SE S-Class was DM 129,030. Standard equipment included air conditioning, cruise control, an electric sliding sunroof, heated seats and a leather steering wheel. The cabin was black leather with medium-grey contrast panels and walnut veneer on the console, handbrake and both selector levers. Outside, the Amethyst Blue Metallic paint ran onto the bumpers, wheel-arch flares and mirror housings, so not a single black plastic panel showed.
Off-roaders should note the compromises. Mercedes deleted the front differential lock, leaving the centre and rear locks. The suspension was softened for comfort, and fording depth is slightly less than a standard G's. The tyres were Bridgestone 265/70 R16 H on alloy wheels, which Mercedes says were the only off-road tyres then approved to 210 km/h. In other words, this is a G meant for the Autobahn that can still handle a dirt road.

### AMG, PUCH AND A SAUDI PRINCE
The standard 500 GE was the tame version. Later in 1993 AMG offered the 500 GE 6.0, with the M117 enlarged to 5,959 cc and 220 kW (about 300 PS), according to Mercedes. It was a one-off customer order on top of an already expensive truck, and RM Sotheby's believes only around 13 were officially converted. The option code to look for is ZB6. Not every special 500 GE is a 6.0, though: one car built for Saudi Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz has the 5.0 but was specified with a wider track, larger front wings and Avantgarde green paint. It sold at RM Sotheby's for $148,500.
Then there are the Puchs. In Austria and Switzerland the G was sold under the Puch name, and RM Sotheby's describes a Puch-badged 500 GE as the first of only three. Steyr-Daimler-Puch used it for homologation, testing and press drives. As for what replaced it, the V8 dropped out of the range until the G 500 arrived with the M113 in 1998. The G 55 AMG followed in 1999 and turned the 500 GE's limited-run idea into a regular model.

### OWNING ONE NOW
Mercedes never sold the 500 GE in the US, and it was never part of the Europa International programme. American examples arrived later through private importers. One car on the German Cars For Sale Blog went through Wallace test labs in 2005, after a costly and slow process, and has been registered in California ever since. Thirty years on, a well-kept 500 GE in Germany can qualify for historic H plates. Prices run from the twenties for a high-mileage import, as the blog judged one, to six figures for documented AMG and special-order cars at auction.

### Data plate
- Chassis: W463, long wheelbase
- Years: 1993–1994
- Built: 446
- Engine: M117 5.0 L V8, 2-valve
- Output: 240 PS · 375 Nm
- Gearbox: Automatic (4-speed)
- Drive: Permanent 4WD, low range
- Lockers: Centre & rear
- Tyres: 265/70 R16 H
- 0–100 Km/H: 11.4 s
- Price New: DM 178,250
- Built In: Graz, Austria

### Engineering
Under the paint and walnut, the 500 GE is a standard early W463: a separate ladder frame, coil-sprung solid axles at both ends, and permanent four-wheel drive through a two-speed transfer case. The changes are in the details. It has a big two-valve V8 where a six-cylinder normally sat, comfort-tuned springing, speed-rated road tyres, and one fewer locking differential than any other W463.
- Chassis: Ladder frame (Separate steel frame, long wheelbase only (2,850 mm).)
- Axles: Solid, front & rear (Coil-sprung; tuned softer than other Gs for comfort.)
- Drivetrain: Permanent 4WD (Unchanged W463 system with low range, apart from the deleted front lock.)
- Lockers: Centre & rear only (Mercedes deleted the front differential lock on this model.)
- Engine: M117 5.0 L V8 (Two valves per cylinder, 4,973 cc, 240 PS, 375 Nm. The M119 didn't fit.)
- Tyres: 265/70 R16 H (Bridgestone, on alloys. The only off-road tyre then approved to 210 km/h.)

### Versions
- 1990–1994 · W463 300 GE · M103 3.0 L I6 · 170 PS · The petrol W463 the 500 GE sat above
- 1993–1994 · W463 500 GE · M117 5.0 L V8 · 240 PS · 375 Nm · 446 built; LWB only; Amethyst Blue; no front lock
- 1993 · W463 AMG 500 GE 6.0 · M117 6.0 L V8 (5,959 cc) · ≈300 PS · Individual AMG customer order; RM Sotheby's believes about 13 were converted
- 1993–1994 · Puch 500 GE · M117 5.0 L V8 · 240 PS · Puch-badged for Austria/Switzerland; RM Sotheby's says three exist
- 1998–2008 · W463 G 500 · M113 5.0 L V8 · 296 PS · 456 Nm · The V8 returns as a regular-production model
- 1999 on · W463 G 55 AMG · M113 5.4/5.5 L V8 · 354 PS at launch · AMG's V8 G becomes a series model

### Year-by-year
- 1990: W463 launches with permanent 4WD and three locking diffs, setting the base the 500 GE is built on
- 1993: 500 GE V8 launches at DM 178,250 with the 240 PS M117 V8, developed with AMG; planned run of 500
- 1993: AMG offers the 500 GE 6.0 (5,959 cc) as an individual customer upgrade; RM Sotheby's believes about 13 were officially converted
- 1993: Puch-badged 500 GEs built for the Austrian market; RM Sotheby's says three exist
- 1994: Production ends at 446 units, limited by M117 supply because the newer M119 wouldn't fit the G's engine bay
- 1998: The V8 returns in regular production as the G 500, with the M113 and all three locking diffs
- 2018–19: The first 500 GEs pass 25 years old and become legal to import to the US
- 2023: 30th anniversary; well-kept examples now qualify for Germany's H (historic) plate after appraisal

### Capability
- Power / torque: 240 PS (177 kW) / 375 N·m (M117 4,973 cc V8)
- 0–100 km/h: 11.4 s
- Top speed: 112 mph (180 km/h)
- Wheelbase: 112.2 in (2,850 mm) (long wheelbase only)
- Wading depth: Slightly less than other Gs (Mercedes doesn't publish the figure in its 30th-anniversary story)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 265/70R16 H (Bridgestone, factory) on 16-in alloys
- Bolt Pattern: 5x130
- Center Bore: 84.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M14x1.5
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: ≈32 in overall diameter (There's no 500 GE-specific consensus. On unlifted W463s, Expedition Portal owners say up to about 32 in clears without rubbing; 33s fit on 18-in wheels with a slight rub at full lock. Most owners keep these trucks on period-correct 16s.)

### Buying checks
- Prove it's a real 500 GE: Check the VIN and the factory data card. Genuine trucks are W463 long-wheelbase V8s in Amethyst Blue Metallic with black/grey leather. Commenters on one US listing questioned whether an M117 was correct, so make sure the engine is original rather than a transplant.
- AMG 6.0 claims need paperwork: RM Sotheby's points out that pre-merger AMG conversions are hard to verify and lookalikes exist. Look for option code ZB6 ("500 GE (AMG)") on the data card and factory documents before paying a 6.0 premium.
- Don't panic about the front locker: There isn't one. The 500 GE was built with centre and rear locks only. Test that both engage and show on the dash.
- Import and title paperwork: None were sold new in the US. American trucks came in privately: one documented example was cleared through Wallace test labs in 2005 at considerable cost. Make sure the title, import and compliance documents match the VIN.
- Fuel delivery: Owner records on surviving trucks show fuel pumps, the fuel accumulator and filters being replaced. Ask when that was done, and expect to do it on a truck that has sat.
- Front axle oil: Gear oil on the inside of the front wheels or on the brakes means axle seals. Even a low-mileage collector truck sold by RM Sotheby's needed a front-axle oil leak fixed during recommissioning.
- Binding in tight turns: A truck that binds or hops in tight U-turns on pavement may simply have a lock engaged. If it's unlocked and still binds, suspect the CV joints or transfer case, as one seller did, and price the repair.
- Rust in the usual places: Tailgate lower edge, door bottoms, sills, rear frame tubes and strut mounts. A rust-free original body matters more on a 446-unit truck than on any other G.

### Common repairs
#### Front axle seal leak
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A day · cost $600–1,500 (W463 typical)
Symptoms: Gear oil on the inner front wheels, a gear-oil smell, oil on the caliper or rotor, braking that pulls to one side.
Fix: Replace both front axle seals, not just the leaking one, and check the shafts for scoring. If oil has reached the brakes, fit new pads and resurface or replace the rotors.
Tools: Axle seals (both sides) · seal driver · gear oil · brake pads and rotors if contaminated

#### Front axle repack (knuckle & wheel bearings)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time 1–2 days · cost $1,500–2,000 (owner estimate, 2002)
Symptoms: Grease weeping from the steering knuckles, torn CV boots, play or noise from the front wheel bearings, or simply no record of the service.
Fix: Strip the front hubs and knuckles, replace the CV boots and wheel bearings, and repack with fresh grease. Europa recommended doing it every 40,000 miles; one owner found it necessary by about 75,000. Bearing clearances are critical, so if you don't own a dial indicator and the factory procedure, use a G-experienced shop.
Tools: Factory service procedure · hub nut socket · dial indicator · CV boots · wheel bearings · grease · seals

#### Fuel pumps & accumulator
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Half a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Weak or noisy pumps, hard starting, or a truck that's been stored for years.
Fix: Replace the fuel pumps, the fuel accumulator and the filter together, then check the lines and tank for old-fuel varnish. Both documented 500 GEs cited here had this work done as part of their recommissioning.
Tools: Line wrenches · fuel-safe catch pan · new pumps, accumulator and filter · new sealing washers

#### Diff locks won't engage
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Diagnosis-dependent
Symptoms: The centre or rear lock won't engage, or engages and drops out. On W463s the fault is usually in the vacuum supply, not the differential.
Fix: Check for vacuum where the lines meet the actuators, then work back through the reservoir, hoses and switchover valves, teeing in a gauge on each section. Owners regularly find split connectors or perished rubber fittings. Remember the 500 GE has no front lock, so there's nothing to fix there.
Tools: Hand vacuum pump with gauge · vacuum tees and line · replacement connectors

#### Steering damper & front-end wander
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost $300–800 (W463 typical)
Symptoms: Wander at highway speed, shake around 55–70 mph, vague on-centre feel, clunks over bumps.
Fix: Replace the steering damper, check the drag link and tie-rod ends for play, then align. The 500 GE was sold on high-speed tyres, so it deserves a tight front end.
Tools: Steering damper · basic sockets and wrenches · tie-rod or drag-link ends if worn

#### Sunroof drains & water ingress
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 30 minutes · cost Cheap if caught early
Symptoms: Damp headliner, wet carpets, odd electrical faults. Every 500 GE had an electric sunroof as standard.
Fix: Clear all the sunroof drains, then check the carpets, fuse box and climate components for water damage. Leaving it is what makes it expensive.
Tools: Trimmer line or drain wire · low-pressure air · towels

#### Rust on the frame and body
Difficulty 2–5 / 5 · time Ongoing · cost $400–8,000 (W463 typical)
Symptoms: Bubbling at the tailgate's lower edge, door bottoms and sills; scale on the rear frame tubes and strut mounts.
Fix: Catch it early: blast and treat, or weld in repair panels. Cavity-wax the doors and underbody and keep drain holes clear. On a car this rare, use original-spec panels and keep the paint code (DB3338) correct.
Tools: Wire wheel or blaster · rust converter and primer · cavity wax · welder for panel repair

### Baseline service
Treat a 500 GE as a recommissioning, not an oil change: most surviving examples have low miles and long storage, so rubber, fuel and fluids are old even when the odometer isn't. Parts for the M117 V8 and the 1993-era W463 chassis are model-specific — order by VIN and engine number, and keep the old parts for originality.
- Engine oil & filter: MB sheet 229-approved oil · capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now, then yearly (M117 5.0 V8. Change it before any long drive on a stored car, and check for leaks once warm.)
- Air filter: M117 element [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now (Check the airbox for nests on a stored truck.)
- Spark plugs & ignition: 8 plugs (one per cylinder) [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now if no record (Inspect the leads, cap and rotor if fitted.)
- Coolant & hoses: MB 325.0-approved coolant, 50/50 with distilled water · capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now (Replace any hard or swollen hoses; a stored car's hoses age faster than its odometer suggests.)
- Automatic transmission (4-speed): ATF to the MB 236.x sheet for this gearbox [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now (Drain-and-fill with a new filter and pan gasket; check the shift quality cold and hot afterwards.)
- Transfer case: GL-4 gear oil on period W463 cases · ≈3 qt (1997 G 320 owner) [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now, then every 60,000 mi (MB interval quoted by owners) (Fill plug on the front right, drain underneath (14 mm hex). Don't fill it with GL-5 diff oil.)
- Front & rear differentials: GL-5 hypoid gear oil (MB 235.0, 85W-90) · front ≈1.4 L, rear ≈1.8 L (W463 owner data) [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now (The 500 GE has centre and rear locks only — test both on loose ground afterwards.)
- Front knuckles, swivels & wheel bearings: Repack knuckles and bearings; grease the swivel balls · If no record; Europa's interval was 40,000 mi (Bearing clearance is set with a dial indicator — use the factory procedure or a G specialist. Owners report much lighter steering after re-greasing the swivels.)
- Power steering fluid: MB power-steering fluid · Now
- Brake fluid & lock hydraulics: DOT 4 Plus (MB sheet 331.0) · Now, then every 2 years (Stored cars collect moisture in the fluid; flush and bleed every circuit.)
- Fuel pumps, accumulator & filter: Pumps, accumulator and filter replaced together · Now on any stored truck (Both documented 500 GEs cited on this page had this done during recommissioning. Check the tank and lines for varnish.)
- Vacuum system & lock test: Vacuum reservoir, hoses and switchover valves · Now (Smoke-test or tee in a gauge; replace perished rubber with vacuum-rated hose, not fuel line.)

### FAQ
Q: How many 500 GEs were built?
A: 446, against a planned 500. The run was limited by the supply of M117 V8s, since the newer M119 wouldn't fit the G-Class engine bay.

Q: Does the 500 GE have three locking differentials?
A: No, only the centre and rear locks. Mercedes deleted the front lock and also gave the 500 GE softer suspension and a slightly lower fording depth than other Gs.

Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: The factory tire is 265/70R16, about 30.6 inches. On unlifted W463s, Expedition Portal owners run 33-inch tires (275/70R18 and 285/65R18 on 18-inch wheels), with a slight rub at full left lock on the 285s. One owner says up to about 32 inches should clear with no rubbing. On the 500 GE's 16-inch wheels, aim for a similar overall diameter (around 32 inches) and test full lock. Many owners keep these trucks on period-correct 16s.

Q: How fast is it?
A: Mercedes quotes 0–100 km/h in 11.4 seconds and a 180 km/h (112 mph) top speed, from 240 PS and 375 Nm.

Q: What gearbox does it have?
A: An automatic was standard and no manual was offered. A documented US-imported example has the four-speed automatic.

Q: Is the 500 GE an AMG?
A: Partly. Wikipedia says AMG modified the body and chassis, and RM Sotheby's says the V8 was developed with AMG, but the standard car wears Mercedes badges. The true AMG version is the 500 GE 6.0, a 5,959 cc, roughly 300 PS customer-order upgrade (option code ZB6). RM Sotheby's believes about 13 were officially converted.

Q: What did it cost new?
A: DM 178,250 in 1993, about twice the DM 88,500 price of a G 320 and well above a 500 SE S-Class at DM 129,030.

Q: Was it sold in the US?
A: Not new. It isn't part of the Europa International story either. US cars were imported privately later; one went through Wallace test labs in 2005 and is California-registered. Now that it's more than 25 years old, US import is much simpler.

Q: What are they worth?
A: Prices vary a lot. German Cars For Sale Blog once put a high-mileage California import at $20,000–35,000. RM Sotheby's has sold a Saudi-delivered special-order car for $148,500 and an AMG 6.0 for $218,500, while a Puch-badged car estimated at €60,000–90,000 went unsold.

Q: How is it different from the later G 500?
A: The 1998-on G 500 uses the newer three-valve M113 V8 (296 PS), was a regular-production model, and has all three locking differentials. The 500 GE has the older two-valve M117, a front-lock delete, one colour scheme and a 446-unit production run.
