## Mercedes-Benz Europa International Gs (1990s–2001)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/europa/
Codes: 300 GE, G 320, G 500

Verdict: A small company in Santa Fe spent years and a lot of money proving to Washington that the G was legal, and ended up building the US market that Mercedes then bought from it. The trucks are simpler, plainer and often the better G to own.

Before 2002 you couldn't walk into a Mercedes dealer in America and buy a G-Class. You could buy one from Europa International in Santa Fe, New Mexico. Europa took the civilian W463, crash-tested and certified it at its own expense, and sold 300 GEs, G 320s and eventually V8 G 500s, federalized and certified for US sale. They were 50-state legal, not gray-market. In practice these are the first American G-Wagens.

### AMERICA SAYS NO
The G was never planned for the US. In the 1980s gray-market specialists brought W460s in anyway, but the Imported Vehicle Safety Compliance Act of 1988 largely ended that trade. Hagerty notes that gray-market buyers had always paid through the nose for the privilege. Anyone who wanted a G legally needed someone to do the certification properly.
A Motor Trend feature quoted by German Cars For Sale Blog credits Santa Fe's Dave Holland with the idea. His company, Europa, decided to certify the truck to federal emissions and safety standards, crash tests included. Dealer Ferraris Online's account says the programme took five years, finished in October 1993 and cost $500,000. Wikipedia says Europa started selling Gs that year.

### FROM CONVERTER TO MANUFACTURER
The early trucks were European Gs modified to US specification. Hagerty says Europa later persuaded Mercedes to build them to DOT standards at the factory. Then came the bigger step. Ferraris Online says that after almost two years and more than $1 million, Europa gained US Small Volume Manufacturer status, making the trucks legal in all 50 states. Wikipedia ties that status to the arrival of the V8 G 500 in 1998 (Ferraris Online dates it to 1999) and says it made Europa the exclusive US importer and distributor.
The line-up followed Europe's. It started with the 3.0-litre inline-six 300 GE, then the 3.2-litre inline-six G 320. In 1998 the G 320 switched to a V6, so both engines exist for that year. The 5.0-litre V8 G 500 joined at the top, and Europa also certified a handful of short-wheelbase Cabriolets. Volumes were small and margins were large. Hagerty reports that some trucks sold for as much as $135,000.

### WHAT A EUROPA G IS LIKE
From outside, a 2000 Europa G 500 looks almost the same as a 2002 Mercedes-Benz USA truck. Jalopnik points to the black-painted bumpers, where later trucks have body-colour ones. Inside it's plainer: the steering wheel and instrument cluster come from the pre-facelift W210 E-Class, there are no radio buttons on the wheel, and the 722.6 five-speed automatic has no tip-shift gate. The dash-top screen on some trucks is Mercedes' optional navigation.
Under the skin it's still a full W463. Overland Journal's Scott Brady bought a 1996 Europa truck for the Expeditions West fleet. It had ABS, airbags and three dash buttons for the centre, rear and front locks, and Brady praised the early Europa Gs for their simple systems, durable six-cylinder engines and late-1990s build quality. German Cars For Sale Blog likes them for the same reason: fewer US-specific electronics to go wrong.

### THE HANDOVER
Europa's success was what ended its import business. Mercedes-Benz bought the US distribution rights and launched the G officially for the 2002 model year, with the G 500 and G 55 AMG. Europa moved into service, parts and accessories, and kept importing a few models America never got officially, such as the three-door Cabriolet. Jalopnik reports that Europa is still in business, selling parts, service and modifications to the G community. The importer itself is a footnote now, but its trucks are not: a Europa G is the sweet spot for anyone who wants a 1990s G with proper US paperwork.

### Data plate
- Importer: Europa International, Santa Fe NM
- Us Years: 1993–2001
- Chassis: W463
- Models: 300 GE · G 320 · G 500
- Engines: 3.0 I6 · 3.2 I6 · 3.2 V6 · 5.0 V8
- Drive: Permanent 4WD, low range
- Lockers: Centre, rear, front
- Status: US VIN, 50-state legal
- Certified: October 1993
- Price New: Up to $135,000
- Succeeded By: MBUSA G 500 (MY2002)

### Engineering
Mechanically, Europa trucks are civilian W463s from the 1990s: a ladder frame, coil-sprung solid axles front and rear, permanent four-wheel drive with a two-speed transfer case, and three differential locks on the dash. The differences are in the engines and the amount of electronics. They also predate the COMAND system of Mercedes-Benz USA's 2002 trucks, though late Europa G 500s already have the electronic ignition (EIS) and smart key.
- Chassis: Ladder frame (Separate steel frame; LWB five-door, plus a few SWB Cabriolets.)
- Axles: Solid, front & rear (Coil-sprung and link-located, as on every W463 until 2018.)
- Drivetrain: Permanent 4WD (Two-speed transfer case with low range.)
- Lockers: Centre, rear, front (Three dash buttons, confirmed on a 1996 Europa truck.)
- Engines: I6, V6, V8 (M103 3.0 I6 (300 GE), M104 3.2 I6 and M112 3.2 V6 (G 320), M113 5.0 V8 (G 500).)
- Gearbox: 4- or 5-speed auto (Four-speed automatic on the I6 G 320; 722.6 five-speed on the G 500.)

### Versions
- 1993–1994 · W463 300 GE · M103 3.0 L I6 · 170 PS · 190 Nm · Europa started selling in 1993 after finishing certification
- 1994–1998 · W463 G 320 · M104 3.2 L I6 · 211 PS · 300 Nm · Four-speed automatic; head-gasket seep is the known weakness
- 1998–2001 · W463 G 320 · M112 3.2 L V6 · 218 PS · 300 Nm · 1998 was the changeover year, so both engines exist
- 1998–2001 · W463 G 500 · M113 5.0 L V8 · 296 PS · 456 Nm · 722.6 five-speed; arrived with Europa's Small Volume Manufacturer status
- 1990s · W463 SWB Cabriolet · I6 or V8 · — · Fewer than ten certified as US models, per Ferraris Online
- 2002 on · MBUSA G 500 / G 55 AMG · M113 V8 · 292 hp / 349 hp · Mercedes takes over US distribution

### Year-by-year
- 1993: Europa International finishes US certification (October 1993) and starts selling the 300 GE
- 1994: G 320 with the 3.2-litre M104 inline-six replaces the 300 GE; manual gearbox dropped from the W463; driver's airbag added
- 1994–1998: M104 G 320s are the ones with the known head-gasket seep; German Cars For Sale Blog calls the head gasket the G 320's only drawback against the 300 GE and G 500 [avoid]
- 1997: Dual front airbags; six-cylinder petrol engines move from inline to V-form
- 1998: G 500 V8 arrives once Europa gains Small Volume Manufacturer status; G 320 changes over from M104 inline-six to M112 V6 during the year
- 1999: 20th-anniversary G 500 Classic special edition (500 built worldwide); Neiman Marcus Christmas Book G 500 at $160,000, six sold
- 1999–2000: Late Europa G 500s. CarGurus says the very last 1999–2000 G 500s are considered very reliable, and Expedition Portal owners prefer their manual transfer-case lever and sturdier window regulators to the 2002-on trucks' [buy]
- 2001: Final Europa model year
- 2002: Mercedes-Benz USA takes over with the G 500 and G 55 AMG (MY2002)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 265/70R16 (16-inch wheels), 265/60R18 (18-inch wheels)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x130
- Center Bore: 84.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M14x1.5 bolts
- Lug Torque: 96 lb-ft (130 N·m)
- Offset: ET35–63 compatible range (2001 G 500)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 275/70R18 (≈33 in) (Expedition Portal owners report no rub on sensible offsets; 285/65R18 rubs slightly at full left lock, and ET63 aftermarket wheels rubbed. Re-code the tire size afterwards)
- Biggest tire, 2.5 in (60 mm) lift: 33 in (Eurowise's recommended maximum for its 60 mm W463 kit, which it lists for the G 500, G 55, G 550 and G 63, so confirm parts fit a 1990s Europa G. Eurowise notes only light wheel-well trimming with its King shock option)
- Biggest tire, 4 in (100 mm) lift: 35 in (Eurowise's recommendation for 100 mm of lift; its 100 mm kit is listed for 2002-on trucks, so confirm parts fit a 1990s Europa G. Above 4 in, extended brake lines are required)

### Buying checks
- US VIN and Europa paperwork: A real Europa truck has a US VIN and federal compliance, not a foreign VIN cleared later by an independent lab. Match the VIN, the compliance label and any Europa invoices.
- Which G 320 engine?: 1998 was the changeover year, so a G 320 can have the M104 inline-six or the M112 V6. Check the engine code, since the two have different weak points.
- M104 head gasket: Look under the right rear of the inline-six for oil seeping from the head gasket. Owners say a proper repair, about $2,000 at a dealer in 2002, usually lasts.
- Front axle service history: Ask when the front knuckles and bearings were last repacked. Europa recommended every 40,000 miles; owners say it's definitely due by 75,000.
- Test all three lockers: Engage centre, rear and front on loose ground and watch the indicators. Lockers that 'were never used' often don't work.
- Ignition and key system: German Cars For Sale Blog warns that the electronic ignition (EIS) and smart key fitted to late Europa trucks (around 2000, possibly a year or two earlier) can strand you without warning and are expensive to replace. Make sure every key starts the truck.
- Rust from snowy states: Scott Brady's 1996 Europa truck had two corrosion spots from its time in the Northeast. Check the tailgate's lower edge, door bottoms, sills and rear frame tubes.
- Originality pays: Hagerty says enthusiasts will pay up to 30 per cent more for an all-original G. Keep the factory parts if you modify one.

### Common repairs
#### Front axle repack (knuckles & wheel bearings)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time 1–2 days · cost $1,500–2,000 (owner estimate, 2002)
Symptoms: Grease weeping from the swivels, torn CV boots, wheel-bearing noise or play, or no record of the job.
Fix: Strip the front hubs and knuckles, replace the CV boots and wheel bearings, and repack. Europa's own interval was 40,000 miles. Bearing clearances are critical, and one owner found local Mercedes dealers didn't know the job, so use a G-experienced technician if you lack the factory procedure and a dial indicator.
Tools: Factory procedure · hub nut socket · dial indicator · CV boots · wheel bearings · grease · seals

#### M104 head-gasket seep (I6 G 320)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time 2–3 days · cost ≈ $2,000 at a dealer (2002)
Symptoms: Oil seeping at the right rear of the cylinder head, visible from underneath; oil smell after a run.
Fix: Replace the head gasket and resurface the head if needed, with new head bolts and seals. Owners report the leak doesn't return after a proper repair. The same PeachParts owner still recommended a G 500 for long-term ownership.
Tools: Head gasket set · head bolts · torque wrench and angle gauge · access to a machine shop

#### Harmonic balancer (V6 & V8)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2.5 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: On the M112 V6 and M113 V8, vibration at idle, a wobbling crank pulley, cracked or bulging rubber, or belt chirp that changes with revs. If the outer ring separates you lose the belt drive.
Fix: Remove the belt, lock the crank, and replace the balancer with a new centre bolt and front crank seal. Use a new balancer, not a used one.
Tools: Crank counter-hold tool · 27 mm socket · breaker bar or high-torque impact · balancer · centre bolt · crank seal

#### Front axle seal leak
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A day · cost $600–1,500 (W463 typical)
Symptoms: Gear oil on the inner front wheels or calipers, brakes pulling to one side.
Fix: Replace both front axle seals and check the shafts. Replace the pads and resurface the rotors if oil has reached them. It makes sense to do this with the axle repack.
Tools: Axle seals · seal driver · gear oil · pads/rotors if contaminated

#### Diff locks won't engage
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Diagnosis-dependent
Symptoms: One or all locks won't engage, or drop out. It's usually the actuation, not the differentials. On a 2005 G 500 an MBWorld owner found the centre lock vacuum-operated and the front and rear locks hydraulic, and a 1997 G 320 owner notes the locker circuit uses brake fluid; confirm your truck's system in the factory manual.
Fix: Check vacuum at the centre-lock hose on the transfer case, then trace back through the reservoir, hoses and switchover valves with a tee-in gauge. Split connectors and perished rubber fittings are common. For the axle locks, check the hydraulic lines and fluid. Change the diff and transfer-case fluids while you're in there.
Tools: Hand vacuum pump with gauge · vacuum tees and line · connectors · brake-bleeding kit · gear oil

#### Steering damper & front-end wander
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost $300–800 (W463 typical)
Symptoms: Wander and shake at 55–70 mph, vague on-centre feel, front-end clunks.
Fix: Replace the steering damper, check the drag link and tie-rod ends, then align. Some Europa trucks, like Jalopnik's 2000 G 500, already have an aftermarket stabiliser; check that it isn't worn out.
Tools: Steering damper · sockets and wrenches · tie-rod/drag-link ends if worn

#### Rust on the frame and body
Difficulty 2–5 / 5 · time Ongoing · cost $400–8,000 (W463 typical)
Symptoms: Bubbling at the tailgate's lower edge, door bottoms and sills; scale on the rear frame tubes and strut mounts.
Fix: Blast and treat early, or weld in repair panels. Cavity-wax the doors and underbody and rinse off salt after winter. On a 25-year-old truck from a snowy state, inspect before you buy, not after.
Tools: Wire wheel or blaster · rust converter and primer · cavity wax · welder

### Baseline service
Start by confirming exactly what you bought: a Europa truck can have the M103, M104 or M112 six or the M113 V8, a 4- or 5-speed automatic, and drivetrain fluids that changed through the 1990s. Then reset everything — these are trucks more than 25 years old, and service records rarely made the trip.
- Engine oil & filter: MB 229.5 synthetic on M112/M113 · G 500 (M113) ≈8.0 L (8.5 qt) with filter · M103/M104 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now, then yearly (M112/M113 use a top-mounted cartridge filter (74 mm, 14-flute cap wrench). The listed filter fits the 1998-on V6 and V8 only.)
- Air filter: M112/M113: paired elements · M103/M104 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now
- Spark plugs & wires: M112/M113: twin-plug heads (12 or 16 plugs), Bosch FR8DPP33 · M103/M104: 6 plugs [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now if no record (Oil in the plug wells points to valve-cover or (on the M104) head-gasket leaks.)
- Coolant & thermostat: MB 325.0-approved coolant, 50/50 with distilled water · Now (On an M104 G 320, watch for oil–coolant cross-contamination and the right-rear head seep.)
- Automatic transmission: G 500: 722.6 5-speed, MB 236.14 ATF, ≈9 qt total · 4-speed (I6): ATF per its MB 236.x sheet [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now, then every 40,000–60,000 mi (On the 722.6, replace the 13-pin connector sleeve and set the level hot with the dipstick tool.)
- Transfer case: GL-4 gear oil · ≈3 qt (1997 G 320) — later cases may differ; check the tag [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now, then every 60,000 mi (MB interval quoted by owners) (Owners find these filled with diff oil by mistake. Fill on the front right, drain underneath, 14 mm hex.)
- Front & rear differentials: GL-5 hypoid gear oil (a 1997 G 320 owner used Red Line 75W-90) · front ≈1.4 L, rear ≈1.8 L (owner and AMSOIL figures) [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now (Loosen the fill plug before draining; drain plug to ≈60 Nm (owner figure). Test each lock afterwards.)
- Front knuckles, swivels & wheel bearings: Repack knuckles and bearings; grease the swivels; CV boots · Europa's interval: every 40,000 mi (One owner found local dealers didn't know the job — use a G specialist or the factory procedure with a dial indicator.)
- Power steering fluid: MB power-steering fluid · Now
- Brake fluid & lock hydraulics: DOT 4 Plus (MB sheet 331.0) · Now, then every 2 years (The 1997 G 320 owner notes the locker circuit uses brake fluid — bleed it with the brakes.)
- Drive belt, hoses & harmonic balancer check: Poly-V belt and tensioner; crank pulley · Replace belt now if age unknown (On the M112/M113, a wobbling or cracked balancer is a replace-now item.)
- Fuel filter: M112/M113: 002 477 30 01 · others [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now if no record
- Vacuum system & lock test: Reservoir, hoses, switchover valves · Now (Tee in a gauge on each section; replace split connectors and perished rubber with vacuum-rated hose.)

### FAQ
Q: Is a Europa G a gray-market truck?
A: No. Europa certified the trucks to US emissions and safety standards, including crash testing, sold them with US VINs, and gained Small Volume Manufacturer status, making them 50-state legal. Gray-market Gs were private imports cleared one at a time.

Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: About 33 inches. An Expedition Portal owner runs 275/70R18 on an unlifted 2000 G 500 and only rubbed on aftermarket ET63 wheels. Another runs 285/65R18 with a slight rub at full left lock. Another owner says up to about 32 inches should clear with no rubbing. Have the tire size re-coded with Mercedes diagnostics so the speedometer and ESP stay accurate.

Q: Which Europa G should I buy?
A: A late G 500. Forum regulars usually prefer the G 500 for its much greater power at similar mileage, and CarGurus says the very last 1999–2000 G 500s are considered very reliable. Expedition Portal owners who've lived with both like the Europa truck's manual transfer-case lever more than the 2002-on electric shifter, and say its window regulators are sturdier. The catch, one notes, is that non-MBUSA trucks are harder to get parts and repairs for. German Cars For Sale Blog says the head gasket is the inline-six G 320's only real drawback against the 300 GE and G 500. One Expedition Portal owner says his V6 G 320 gets several more mpg than a 2002 G 500, though the gap narrows when towing large trailers.

Q: Do Europa trucks have all three lockers?
A: Yes. Scott Brady's 1996 Europa truck had dash buttons for the centre, rear and front locks, plus ABS and airbags.

Q: How is a Europa G 500 different from a 2002 Mercedes-Benz USA G 500?
A: It looks nearly the same outside, apart from black-painted bumpers. Inside it has a pre-facelift W210 E-Class steering wheel and cluster, no wheel-mounted radio controls, older climate control, and a 722.6 automatic without the tip-shift gate. German Cars For Sale Blog also warns about electrical problems on 2002–2005 Mercedes-Benz USA trucks.

Q: How much did they cost new?
A: Hagerty says some sold for up to $135,000. The 1999 Neiman Marcus Christmas-catalogue G 500 was $160,000, and six were sold.

Q: What are they worth now?
A: Usually about the same as 2002-on trucks. Recent asks include a 202,750-mile 2000 G 500 at $32,000 (Jalopnik) and a well-documented 1998 G 320 at $47,500 (German Cars For Sale Blog), which the blog called high but understandable. Clean Europa G 320s come up only every few years and tend to sell quickly.

Q: How many did Europa import?
A: We couldn't find a reliable total. The rarest variant is better documented: fewer than ten short-wheelbase Cabriolets were certified as US models, according to Ferraris Online.

Q: How often should the front axle be serviced?
A: Europa recommended repacking the front axle (knuckles, wheel bearings, CV boots) every 40,000 miles. One owner thought that was early but agreed it's needed by about 75,000. Expect to pay around $1,500–2,000 at a specialist (2002 figures).

Q: Are they good overland trucks?
A: Yes, by most accounts. Scott Brady put a 1996 Europa G into the Expeditions West fleet, and its previous owner had driven it from the Northeast to Labrador and Newfoundland with a fridge, compressor and winch. Brady expected it to last another 10–15 years without major problems.

## Mercedes-Benz G 500 (1998–2008)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/g500/
Codes: W463, M113 5.0 V8

Verdict: A Cold War military design with leather, a V8 and three locking differentials. Lock all three at least once, if only to justify owning it.

The G 500 is what happens when a military truck is asked to wear a suit and refuses to take its boots off. It was the first V8 G-Class built in regular production, the first one most Americans could buy from a Mercedes dealer, and — underneath the wood and leather — the same ladder-framed, triple-locked machine that armies bought by the thousand.

### A SHAH, AN ARMY AND A FACTORY IN GRAZ
The name goes back to Daimler-Benz’s six-wheeled G1 of 1926 — a Geländewagen, or cross-country vehicle — but the modern truck began in the early 1970s, when the Shah of Iran, then one of Mercedes-Benz’s largest shareholders, pre-ordered some 20,000 military vehicles. Mercedes engineered it; Austria’s Steyr-Daimler-Puch would build it in Graz. Design studies were carved in wood from 1973, and production began in 1979 — the same year the Shah fled Iran and his order evaporated.
It found other customers fast: border police, the Argentinian army and, in 1980, Pope John Paul II, who got one with a clear viewing platform. In 1983 a 280 GE driven by Jacky Ickx won the Paris–Dakar Rally, which settled any argument about whether it was a real off-roader.

### THE W463 GOES UPMARKET
In 1990 the civilian G was reworked as the W463: a nicer cabin, full-time four-wheel drive and three fully locking differentials, while the utilitarian W460 and later W461 carried on separately. America still couldn’t buy one officially. New Mexico importer Europa International converted European trucks to US spec — later persuading Mercedes to build them to DOT standards — and some sold for as much as $135,000.
The G 500 arrived in 1998 as the first regular-production V8 G — the hand-picked, limited-run 500 GE of 1993 had come first — with the 5.0-litre M113, good for 292 hp. When Mercedes finally launched the G officially in the US for the 2002 model year, the G 500 and G 55 AMG were the two trucks in the showroom. The G 500 ran in America through 2008; for 2009 the same truck returned as the G 550 with a 5.5-litre V8. The seven-speed automatic had already replaced the old five-speed in US G 500s during 2007.

### Data plate
- Chassis: W463
- Us Years: 2002–2008
- Engine: M113 5.0 L V8
- Output: 292 hp · 456 Nm
- Drive: Full-time 4WD, low range
- Lockers: Centre, rear, front
- Build: Body-on-frame
- Axles: Solid, front & rear
- Approach / Dep.: 36° / 31°
- Built In: Graz, Austria
- Succeeded By: G 550 (US, 2009)

### Engineering
Strip the G 500 down and you find a 1970s off-roader that was never diluted. The body sits on a separate ladder frame. Both axles are solid, located by links and sprung on coils, so a twisted trail keeps the tires planted. Power goes through a two-speed transfer case to all four wheels all the time, and the three differential locks — centre, rear, front — let you turn it into something closer to a tractor when traction runs out.
- Chassis: Ladder frame (Separate steel frame under the body — the reason Gs survive decades of abuse.)
- Axles: Solid, front & rear (Coil-sprung and link-located. Independent front suspension only arrived with the 2018 redesign.)
- Drivetrain: Full-time 4WD (Two-speed transfer case with low range.)
- Lockers: Centre, rear, front (Three 100% locks, engaged from the dash.)
- Engine: M113 5.0 L V8 (292 hp, 456 Nm. Shared with the era’s E-, S- and ML-Class — parts are plentiful.)
- Geometry: 36° / 31° (Approach and departure angles quoted by Hagerty for the G; Mercedes' 2015 G 550 manual lists 34° / 29°. Track: 56 inches.)

### Versions
- 1998–2008 · W463 · M113 5.0 L V8 · 292 hp · First regular-production V8 G. Pre-2002 US trucks came via Europa International; Mercedes sold it officially from MY2002; US trucks switched from the five-speed 722.6 to the seven-speed 722.9 for MY2007 (June 2006 production); 2008 was the last US G 500
- 2008–2015 · W463 · M273 5.5 L V8 · 382 hp · Badged G 550 in the US from MY2009; 7-speed automatic
- 2015–2018 · W463 (late) · M176 4.0 L twin-turbo V8 · 416 hp · Final years of the original body
- 2015–2018 · G 500 4×4² · M176 4.0 L twin-turbo V8 · 416 hp · Portal axles, raised chassis — the wild one
- 2018–2024 · Second generation (“W463A”) · M176 4.0 L twin-turbo V8 · 416 hp · Independent front suspension; G 550 in the US. “W463A” is a fan label, not Mercedes’ own
- 2024– · Second generation, updated · 3.0 L turbo inline-six, mild hybrid · 443 hp (US G 550) · The V8 leaves the non-AMG G-Class

### Year-by-year
- 1998: G 500 launches with the 5.0-litre M113 V8 — the first regular-production V8 G
- 1998–2001: Not sold by Mercedes in the US; Europa International federalised G 500s and sold them with US VINs
- 1999: G 500 Classic special edition marks the G's 20th anniversary — 500 built
- 2001–02: Update brings ESP, Brake Assist and the 4ETS traction system; Mercedes-Benz USA starts official sales for the 2002 model year
- 2002–04: Early US trucks have the electrical gremlins: Handsome Motors lists seat motors and controls, window regulators and motors, door-lock actuators and transfer-case actuators. Expedition Portal owners say the same about 2002–03 [avoid]
- 2005: Grand Edition: 500 G 500 and G 55 AMG trucks for the US
- 2005–08: The sweet spot. Handsome Motors says the early electrical faults got better every year and were mostly gone by 2005–06. 2005–06 trucks keep the simpler five-speed 722.6; 2007–08 trucks get the seven-speed 7G-TRONIC, HID lamps and a reversing camera [buy]
- 2006–07: June 2006 production: the seven-speed 7G-TRONIC (722.9) replaces the five-speed 722.6 (ADAC). In North America that is the 2007 model year, which also brings HID headlamps, a reversing camera and tire-pressure monitoring
- 2008: Three-bar grille; last US model year for the G 500 name
- 2009: Replaced in the US by the G 550 with the 5.5-litre M273 V8

### Capability
- Towing: 7,000 lb (3,175 kg) (braked; KBB lists 7,000 lb for the 2002 G 500)
- Payload: 1,411 lb (640 kg) (2002 G 500, KBB)
- Fuel tank: 25.4 US gal (96 L) (KBB, 2002 G 500)
- Ground clearance: 8.3 in (211 mm) (minimum, KBB, 2002 G 500)
- Fuel economy: 11 city / 13 hwy / 12 combined mpg (2002 G 500, KBB; premium fuel)
- Curb weight: 5,423 lb (2,460 kg) (2002 G 500, KBB)
- Turning circle: 43.5 ft (13.3 m) (turning diameter, KBB)
- Wheelbase: 112.2 in (2,850 mm)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: P265/60R18 on 18-in alloys (2002–2008 US G 500)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x130
- Offset: ET63 on the 18x7.5 fitment (later 2015 G 550 factory 18s are ET43)
- Center Bore: 84.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M14x1.5 (lug bolts)
- Lug Torque: 96 lb-ft (130 N·m) — figure from the 2013–2015 US G-Class operator's manuals
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 275/70R18 (≈33 in) (Fits an unlifted G 500 on factory 18s per Expedition Portal owners; a 285/65R18 rubs slightly at full left lock, and an ET63 aftermarket wheel rubbed where ET43 G 550 wheels didn't. Re-code the tire size so the speedo and ESP agree.)
- Biggest tire, 2–2.5 in lift: 33x11.00–33x12.50 (or metric equivalent) (JWO 2-in and Eurowise 60 mm springs are sold as 33-in setups; JWO says keep wheel offset at +30 or lower (about a 30 mm spacer on most stock wheels) and fit longer shocks.)
- Biggest tire, 3 in lift: 35 in (GwagenParts' ~75 mm front kit claims room for 35s; spacers may be needed to stop rubbing, and the kit includes caster-correction bushings.)
- Biggest tire, 4 in lift: 35x11.00–35x12.50 (JWO 4-in springs: offset no higher than +20 (typically a 50 mm spacer on stock wheels), caster-correction bushings required; adjustable panhard bars and a steering stabilizer recommended. Distronic likely won't work at this height.)

### Buying checks
- Test all three locking differentials: Engage each lock on a loose surface and watch the indicators. Lockers that ‘were never used’ by the last owner often don’t work — budget for the vacuum diagnosis below.
- Is it really an AMG?: Plenty of standard Gs have been dressed as AMGs. Check the VIN and data card against the badges before paying an AMG premium.
- Work every window, lock and seat: Especially on 2002–04 trucks. Handsome Motors lists seat motors and controls, window regulators and motors, and door-lock actuators as the early trucks' electrical gremlins, along with the transfer-case actuator. Try every switch, every door from inside and out, and shift the transfer case.
- Listen at idle: Vibration or a chirp that changes with revs on an M113 points at the harmonic balancer — a known failure on early-2000s Mercedes V8s.
- Look for oil on top of the engine: Wetness at the front of the V points at the oil filter housing seals; oil on the coil packs and exhaust manifolds points at valve cover gaskets or breather hoses. Neither is serious if fixed early, and both are reasonable DIY jobs (see repairs).
- Look behind the front wheels: Gear oil on the inside of the wheels or the brake calipers means leaking front axle seals — and possibly contaminated brakes.
- Drive it at 55–70 mph: Wander or steering shake at highway speed usually means a tired steering damper and worn linkage.
- Rust where nobody cleans: Check the tailgate’s lower edge, door bottoms, sills, rear frame tubes, inner wheel arches and around the rear bumper.
- A sagging headliner means water: Usually blocked sunroof drains. Water can reach the fuse box and climate actuators, so check those too.

### Common repairs
#### Harmonic balancer (M113)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2.5 hours · cost $250–450 labor
Symptoms: Vibration at idle, a visibly wobbling crank pulley, rattle or chirp that changes with RPM, cracked or bulging rubber, belt squeal. Don’t keep driving it: if the outer ring lets go you lose power steering, charging and the water pump.
Fix: Remove the belt and fan as needed, hold the crank pulley with a counter-hold tool, and break the 27 mm centre bolt loose. Fit the new balancer with a new front crank seal while you're there; a new centre bolt (112 031 00 71, M16 × 1.5) is cheap insurance. MercedesMedic's M112/M113 guide gives the bolt torque as 200 Nm plus a further quarter turn (90°) — confirm against WIS for your engine.
Tools: Crank pulley counter-hold tool (e.g. CTA 7270) · 27 mm socket · long breaker bar or high-torque impact · centre bolt 112 031 00 71 · front crank seal · balancer (match the part number by VIN)

#### Oil filter housing gasket leak (M113)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost Parts cheap; most of the bill is labor
Symptoms: Oil collecting at the top front of the engine in the V, running down the front of the block onto the belt, pulleys or harmonic balancer; a burning-oil smell once it reaches hot parts. Owners often get misdiagnosed first — on one M113 the first shop blamed the power steering pump.
Fix: Confirm the source by degreasing the engine and checking again after a drive. Remove whatever sits over the housing (air intake ducting and covers), unbolt the housing, clean both mating faces completely and fit new seals. Use genuine Mercedes or Elring seals, torque to the factory figures, then degrease again so any remaining leak is easy to spot.
Tools: Metric sockets and Torx/E-Torx bits · torque wrench · gasket scraper (plastic) and brake cleaner · new oil filter housing seals (genuine or Elring) · fresh oil and filter while you’re in there

#### Valve cover gaskets & breather hoses (M113)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A weekend morning · cost ≈ $200 parts vs ≈ $2,000 shop quotes (owner report)
Symptoms: Oil on the coil packs, plug leads and the top of the exhaust manifolds; a burning smell after a drive; in bad cases oil reaching the plugs and causing misfires. Breather hoses on the same engine family crack and leak too, so leaks around the covers aren’t always the gaskets.
Fix: Remove the intake ducting, then the coil packs and plug leads (label them — the M113 runs two plugs per cylinder), then the cover bolts. Lift the covers, clean every trace of old gasket and sealant, and fit new gaskets plus the bolt grommets. Replace the crankcase breather hoses at the same time; where sealant is specified, owners report a continuous bead with no gaps and spotless surfaces is what stops repeat leaks. Torque the cover bolts evenly to the factory figure — overtightening distorts the covers.
Tools: Sockets and Torx bits · torque wrench (low range) · plastic scraper and brake cleaner · valve cover gaskets and bolt grommets (genuine or Elring — owners report aftermarket gaskets leaking) · breather hoses · Mercedes-approved sealant where called for

#### Diff locks won’t engage
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Diagnosis-dependent
Symptoms: One or all locks refuse to engage, or engage then drop out; sometimes paired with central-locking oddities. The fault is usually the vacuum system, not the differentials.
Fix: Confirm vacuum at the transfer-case hose. Then work from the pump and reservoir (front-left wheel well) through the manifold and the switchover valve block on the firewall, teeing in a gauge at each segment. One owner’s 2005 G 500 fault was a split plastic connector inside a rubber Y fitting under the brake booster. Change transfer-case and diff fluids and bleed the hydraulic locker lines while you’re in there.
Tools: Hand vacuum pump with gauge · assorted vacuum tees and line · replacement connectors · diff and transfer-case fluid · bleeding kit

#### Front axle seal leak
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A day · cost $600–1,500
Symptoms: Gear oil on the inner front wheels, a gear-oil smell, oil on the caliper or rotor, brakes pulling to one side.
Fix: Replace both front axle seals, not just the leaking side, and inspect the shafts for scoring. If oil has reached the brakes, replace the pads and resurface or replace the rotors.
Tools: Axle seals (both sides) · seal driver · gear oil · brake pads and rotors if contaminated

#### Steering damper & front-end wander
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost $300–800
Symptoms: Highway wander, wheel shake around 55–70 mph, vague on-centre feel, clunks over bumps.
Fix: Swap the steering damper (OE Stabilus or an equivalent quality unit). Check the drag link and tie-rod ends for play while you’re under there, then get an alignment.
Tools: Steering damper · basic sockets and wrenches · tie-rod or drag-link ends if worn

#### Cracked coil springs
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Half a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: A loud thump over bumps, uneven ride height, especially after cold weather.
Fix: Replace springs in axle pairs. If you’re lifting the truck anyway, this is the moment to fit a lift spring kit (2-inch kits are common for the W463) with matched shocks.
Tools: Springs (pairs) · jack and stands · spring compressor if required by your setup · new shocks recommended

#### Sunroof drains & water ingress
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 30 minutes · cost Cheap if caught early
Symptoms: Damp or sagging headliner, wet carpets, electrical gremlins from a wet fuse box or climate actuators.
Fix: Clear all four sunroof drains, then check the headliner, fuse box and blend-door actuators for water damage. Leaving it is what makes it expensive.
Tools: Trimmer line or drain-cleaning wire · low-pressure air · towels and patience

#### Propshaft judder
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Half a day · cost Autocar: £1,500+ for a shaft
Symptoms: Shake or judder under way, often worse under load.
Fix: Inspect the joints and couplings for play before condemning the shaft. A worn shaft is a remove-and-replace job; mark the orientation so it goes back phased correctly.
Tools: Sockets and wrenches · paint marker · replacement shaft or joints

#### Rust on the frame and body
Difficulty 2–5 / 5 · time Ongoing · cost $400–8,000
Symptoms: Bubbling at the tailgate’s lower edge, door bottoms and sills; scale on the rear frame tubes and strut mounts.
Fix: Catch it early: blast and treat, or weld in repair panels before it spreads. Cavity-wax the doors and underbody, rinse off road salt after winter, and keep drain holes clear. Severe frame rust can often be fixed in sections rather than with a whole new frame.
Tools: Wire wheel or blaster · rust converter and primer · cavity wax · welder for panel repair

### Baseline service
Assume nothing was done and reset every fluid and filter in the first month: on a 15–25-year-old G 500 the expensive failures (722.6 shifts, diff locks, front axle seals) usually trace back to old fluid, perished vacuum lines or a skipped knuckle service. Read the tags on the transfer case and axles before buying fluid — W463 drivetrains changed through the years.
- Engine oil & filter: MB 229.5 · 0W-40 or 5W-40 full synthetic · ≈8.0 L (8.5 qt) with filter · Then yearly or at the service indicator (Cartridge filter in a housing on top of the engine — use a 74 mm, 14-flute cap wrench. While it's open, look for weeping at the filter-housing gaskets.)
- Air filters: Paired elements, one per bank · Now, then with every second oil change or sooner on dirt roads (Check the airbox for leaves and rodent nests on a truck that sat.)
- Cabin filter: Mahle/OE 463 830 00 18 · Now, then yearly (A clogged filter on a G is often wet too — check for sunroof-drain water while you're in there.)
- Spark plugs, wires & coils: 16 plugs (M113 runs two per cylinder) · Bosch FR8DPP33 · Now if no record; then per the maintenance booklet [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Oil in the plug wells means valve-cover gaskets — fix those first, then fit plugs, wires and any oil-soaked coil boots.)
- Coolant & thermostat: MB 325.0-approved coolant (blue) mixed 50/50 with distilled water · ≈12.7 US qt (≈12 L) per AMSOIL [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now if history is unknown (Bleed carefully; replace the thermostat and any soft or swollen hoses while the system is drained.)
- Automatic transmission (722.6): MB 236.14 ATF · ≈9 qt total fill per AMSOIL (a pan drain replaces only part of it) · Service now if history is unknown; then every 40,000–60,000 mi (common technician practice) (Drop the pan, fit a new filter and gasket, and replace the 13-pin connector sleeve — ATF wicking through it ruins harnesses. Set the level hot, on level ground, with the 722.6 dipstick tool. US trucks built from 2007 have the seven-speed 722.9 instead — check the tag and use the fluid and procedure for that gearbox.)
- Transfer case: Check the tag: many W463 cases take MB 236.14 ATF; earlier cases ran GL-4 gear oil [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now, then every 60,000 mi (MB interval quoted by owners) (Fill plug on the front right, drain plug underneath with a small magnet; both are 14 mm hex. Inspect the propshaft flex discs (in pairs) and the centre support bearing while you're under it.)
- Front & rear differentials: GL-5 hypoid gear oil (MB 235.0, 85W-90; synthetic 75W-90 is common) · front ≈1.4 L (3 pt), rear ≈1.8 L (3.8 pt) per AMSOIL [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now, then with the transfer case (Crack the upper fill plug before you pull the drain (14 mm hex; owners torque the drain to 60 Nm). Afterwards test each lock one at a time on loose ground — the dash lamp should go from flashing to solid.)
- Front knuckles, wheel bearings & CV boots: Repack knuckles and wheel bearings; replace torn boots · If there's no record; Europa's own interval was every 40,000 mi (Bearing preload is set with a dial indicator — use the factory procedure or a G-experienced shop. Replace the front axle seals at the same time.)
- Power steering fluid: MB power-steering fluid · ≈1 L system · Now (suction-and-refill if you can't flush) (Check the box and hoses for weeps while you're there; the steering damper is a 1-hour job if the front end wanders.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 4 Plus (MB sheet 331.0) · Now, then every 2 years (Owners bleed the hydraulic diff-lock lines with the same fluid when they do the brakes [CONFIRM IN MANUAL].)
- Drive belt & tensioner: Single poly-V belt with automatic tensioner · Replace now if age unknown (Spin the idlers and watch the crank pulley for wobble — a separating harmonic balancer takes the belt with it.)
- Fuel filter: Inline filter 002 477 30 01 · Now if no record [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Depressurise the system first and catch the fuel; fit new clamps.)
- Battery: Group 49 AGM · Test now; replace if over 4–5 years old (Weak voltage on these trucks shows up as random electrical faults and lock-switch oddities before it shows up as slow cranking.)

### FAQ
Q: What’s the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: A 275/70R18 — roughly a 33-inch tire — on the factory 18-inch wheels. Owners on Expedition Portal report it fits an unlifted G 500; one saw rubbing only on aftermarket ET63-offset wheels. A 285/65R18 can rub slightly at full left lock. Re-code the tire size with a Mercedes diagnostic tool so the speedometer and ESP stay accurate.

Q: What size are the factory tires?
A: P265/60R18 on 18-inch wheels for 2002–2008 US G 500s — about 30.5 inches tall, which is why there’s room to go up.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: 7,000 lb with a braked trailer, across 2002–2008 G 500s. Unbraked limits are far lower — check your owner’s manual and local law.

Q: What kind of fuel economy should I expect?
A: EPA figures for a 2003: 11 mpg city, 13 highway, 12 combined, on premium fuel. Bigger tires, a roof rack and a lift make it worse.

Q: Does it have low range?
A: Yes. The two-speed transfer case gives you low range for crawling, alongside full-time four-wheel drive.

Q: Can I use the diff locks on pavement?
A: No. Locked differentials stop the wheels turning at different speeds, so on grippy surfaces the driveline binds and tires scrub. Use them on dirt, sand, snow or rock at low speed, and unlock before you’re back on tarmac.

Q: What’s the difference between a G 500 and a G 550?
A: Mostly the engine and the badge. In the US the 2002–2008 G 500 has the 5.0-litre M113 V8; from 2009 the same W463 truck became the G 550 with the 5.5-litre M273 V8. The seven-speed automatic isn't a G 550 exclusive: US G 500s switched from the five-speed 722.6 to the seven-speed 722.9 for the 2007 model year (production from June 2006). See the next question for how to tell which one you have.

Q: How can I tell whether my G 500 has the five-speed or the seven-speed automatic?
A: Go by the build date, then confirm on the truck. Mercedes switched the G 500 from the five-speed 722.6 to the seven-speed 7G-TRONIC (722.9) in June 2006 production: Germany's ADAC catalogue ends the five-speed G 500 at 06/06 and starts the 7G-TRONIC version the same month. In North America that lined up with the 2007 model year. The EPA lists the 2006 G 500 as a five-speed and the 2007 and 2008 as seven-speeds, and Mercedes-Benz Canada's 2007 release says the G 500 "now gets" 7G-TRONIC. To check yours: (1) the 10th character of the VIN is the model year, so 6 means a 2006 five-speed and 7 or 8 means a 2007–08 seven-speed; (2) the certification label on the driver's door jamb or B-pillar gives the month of manufacture, and anything built from June 2006 should be a seven-speed; (3) confirm on the truck: the 722.6 has a transmission dipstick tube with a locking cap, while the 722.9 has no dipstick and is checked at the fill and overflow plug on the pan. The type number on the gearbox's own ID plate, or a Mercedes-Benz Classic data card, settles it for good. Double-check trucks built right around the change, and European Grand Edition trucks, which ADAC lists through August 2006. The G 55 AMG kept the five-speed.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: 2005–08. The 2002–04 trucks are the ones with the electrical gremlins. Handsome Motors, a G specialist dealer, lists seat motors and controls, window regulators and motors, door-lock actuators and transfer-case actuators, and says the faults got better every year until they were mostly gone by 2005–06. Expedition Portal owners say the same about 2002–03. One owner notes that Mercedes changed some electronics partway through 2003. CarGurus is harsher: it says 2002–05 trucks draw the most complaints, mostly electrical, and that the 2009-on G 550 is better still. Within 2005–08 you're really choosing a gearbox. 2005–06 trucks have the five-speed 722.6 with a dipstick, which one Expedition Portal regular prefers because it's easier to service. 2007–08 trucks have the seven-speed 7G-TRONIC, plus HID lamps and a reversing camera (see the question above for how to tell them apart). Some owners would rather have a pre-2002 Europa G 500 with its manual transfer-case lever and fewer electronics, but parts and paperwork are harder. Whatever the year, test every window, lock and seat before you hand over money.

Q: Will it fit in my garage?
A: Kelley Blue Book lists a 2002 G 500 at 185.6 in (about 15.5 ft) long on a 112-inch wheelbase. Mercedes' 2015 G 550 manual gives a height of 76.8 in (1,951 mm), so plan on about 6 ft 5 in before you add a roof rack or a lift — and note that the same manual says the factory roof isn't rated for loads.

Q: Is the G 500 reliable?
A: The frame, axles and V8 are tough; the age-related jobs are predictable — harmonic balancer, vacuum lines for the lockers, axle seals, steering damper, sunroof drains. A truck with records of these is a far safer buy than a low-mileage one that’s never been touched. On 2002–04 trucks, add the electrical gremlins to the list: windows, door locks, seat motors and the transfer-case actuator.

Q: How do I know if a G 500 is a real AMG?
A: Check the VIN and the data card. Many standard Gs wear AMG bumpers, wheels and badges, so the badges alone tell you nothing.

## Mercedes-Benz G 55 AMG (1999–2012)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/g55-amg/
Codes: W463, AMG 5.4 V8

Verdict: AMG gave a 1970s military truck up to 507 PS (500 hp) and changed almost nothing else. It's fast in a straight line, still has three lockers, and drinks fuel at a rate that makes a G 500 look economical.

The G 55 AMG is the G that made speed part of the G-Wagen's reputation. AMG took the ladder-framed, solid-axle W463, fitted its own 5.4-litre V8 and later a supercharger, and sold it through the regular showroom from 1999 into 2012. It still has full-time four-wheel drive, low range and three locking differentials. It also has 700 Nm of torque and a top speed limited to 210 km/h, which is about as fast as anyone should drive something with this shape.

### AMG'S SECOND TRY
AMG had tuned a G before. In 1993, 13 of the 446 500 GEs got AMG's 6.0-litre upgrade kit. The G 55 was different because anyone could order one. Introduced in 1999, it was the most powerful G yet: 354 PS (349 hp) and 525 Nm from AMG's naturally aspirated M113 V8, with 0–100 km/h in 7.4 seconds. That made it about four seconds quicker than the 500 GE to 100 km/h.
When Mercedes-Benz USA took over G distribution from Europa International for the 2002 model year, the G 55 AMG launched alongside the G 500 as the only other G-Class in American showrooms. Hagerty credits the AMG with pushing US G sales higher in the following years.

### THE KOMPRESSOR YEARS
In 2004 (the 2005 model year in the US) AMG added a supercharger. The M113K, the same supercharged 5.4 used in the era's CL 55 and SL 55, made 476 PS (469 hp) and 700 Nm, cutting 0–100 km/h to about 5.6 seconds. From 2006 it was rated at 500 PS. For 2009 a new engine control unit raised it to 507 PS (500 hp), with torque unchanged.
The 2009 update also brought a three-bar grille, Kompressor lettering, polished 19-inch AMG wheels on 275/55 R19 tyres, an anthracite Alcantara headliner, designo leather, COMAND APS and a stronger ESP with hill-start assist. All G 55s used the five-speed 722.6 automatic. Some enthusiasts prefer that well-proven gearbox to the seven-speed fitted to later Gs.

### HOW IT ENDED
The G 55's last US model year was 2011. For 2012 the US G-Class range was just the G 550. In 2012 AMG replaced the supercharged 5.4 with a 5.5-litre biturbo V8 and renamed the truck G 63 AMG, arriving in the US for 2013. That made the G 55 the last AMG G with a supercharger and the five-speed automatic.
Values have settled well above ordinary G 500s. autoevolution's study of 2019–2022 auctions found average Kompressor prices around $60,000 in 2021–22, with low-mileage 2011 trucks reaching $72,500 and $94,000. High-mileage 2005 and 2007 trucks sold for $27,000–40,000. For an off-roader, those cheaper, well-serviced trucks are the interesting ones. You don't need perfect paint to use the lockers.

### Data plate
- Chassis: W463
- Years: 1999–2012 (US MY2002–2011)
- Engine: M113 5.4 L V8 / M113K supercharged
- Output: 354 PS → 507 PS
- Torque: 525 Nm → 700 Nm
- Gearbox: 722.6 5-speed automatic
- Drive: Full-time 4WD, low range
- Lockers: Centre, rear, front
- Axles: Solid, front & rear
- 0–100 Km/H: 7.4 s → 5.5 s
- Top Speed: 210 km/h (limited)
- Succeeded By: G 63 AMG (2012)

### Engineering
Beneath the side pipes, the G 55 is still a W463. The body sits on a separate ladder frame. Both axles are solid and coil-sprung. A two-speed transfer case drives all four wheels all the time, and there are three lockers on the dash. AMG changed the engine, the brakes, the wheels and arches, and the cabin. The driveline layout that wins off-road stayed the same.
- Chassis: Ladder frame (Long-wheelbase five-door for the US; AMG wide fenders and stainless running boards.)
- Axles: Solid, front & rear (Coil-sprung and link-located; independent front suspension didn't arrive until 2018.)
- Lockers: Centre, rear, front (Three 100% locks plus low range, as on every W463.)
- Engine (1999–2004): M113 5.4 L V8 (Naturally aspirated, 354 PS / 525 Nm. US 2002–2004.)
- Engine (2004–12): M113K 5.4 L V8 (Supercharged and intercooled, 476→507 PS, 700 Nm. US 2005–2011.)
- Gearbox: 722.6 5-speed auto (Used for the G 55's whole production run.)

### Versions
- 1999–2004 · W463 G 55 AMG · M113 E55 5.4 L V8 · 354 PS · 525 Nm · Naturally aspirated; US MY2002–2004
- 2004–2006 · W463 G 55 AMG Kompressor · M113K 5.4 L SC V8 · 476 PS · 700 Nm · Supercharged; US from MY2005; 0–100 km/h ≈ 5.6 s
- 2006–2008 · W463 G 55 AMG Kompressor · M113K 5.4 L SC V8 · 500 PS · 700 Nm · Power bump; OE tires 285/55R18 in the US
- 2008–2012 · W463 G 55 AMG Kompressor · M113K 5.4 L SC V8 · 507 PS · 700 Nm · New ECU, three-bar grille, 19-inch wheels, COMAND APS; last US MY2011
- 2012–2018 · W463 G 63 AMG · 5.5 L biturbo V8 · 544 PS · Replacement; US from MY2013

### Year-by-year
- 1999: G 55 AMG debuts in Europe with the naturally aspirated 5.4-litre M113, 354 hp
- 2002: US launch (MY2002) alongside the G 500 as Mercedes-Benz USA takes over from Europa; 349 hp, 722.6 five-speed
- 2002–04: Early US trucks share the G 500's electrical gremlins (seat motors, window regulators, door-lock actuators). Handsome Motors says they were mostly gone by 2005–06; CarGurus counts early G 55s among the least reliable US Gs [avoid]
- 2005: Supercharged M113K Kompressor (US MY2005), 469 hp; 500-unit G 500 / G 55 Grand Edition built for the US
- 2007: Power up to 500 PS (MY2007 in the US); HID headlamps, reversing camera and TPMS arrive for the range. G 55 keeps the 722.6 five-speed
- 2009: 507 PS; three-fin grille, KOMPRESSOR lettering, titanium-grey wheels and 275/55R19 tires
- 2011: Last US model year for the G 55
- 2012: Replaced by the biturbo G 63 AMG (MY2013 in the US)

### Capability
- Towing: 7,000 lb (3,175 kg) (braked; spec data for a 2005 G 55)
- Fuel tank: 25.1 US gal (95 L) (2011 G 55)
- Fuel economy: EPA 12 city / 14 hwy (2003); 11 city / 13 hwy (2005 and 2011 Kompressor)
- Curb weight: 5,540 lb (2,513 kg) (2005 G 55 spec data)
- 0–100 km/h: 7.4 s (naturally aspirated) → 5.6 s (Kompressor)
- Top speed: 210 km/h (130 mph), limited

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 285/55R18 (US trucks through 2008), 275/55R19 on 9.5-inch AMG wheels (2009 update)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x130
- Center Bore: 84.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M14x1.5 bolts
- Lug Torque: 96 lb-ft (130 N·m)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 275/70R18 (≈33 in) (Expedition Portal owners of unlifted W463s report no rub on sensible offsets; 285/65R18 rubs slightly at full left lock. Check that 18s clear the AMG brakes and re-code the tire size)
- Biggest tire, 2.5 in (60 mm) lift: 33 in (Eurowise's recommended maximum for its 60 mm W463 kit; Eurowise says a G 55 needs only light wheel-well trimming with its King shock option)
- Biggest tire, 4 in (100 mm) lift: 35 in (Eurowise's recommendation for 100 mm of lift; its kit lists 2011–2012 G 55 fitment. Above 4 in, extended brake lines are required)

### Buying checks
- Is it really an AMG?: Plenty of G 500s and G 550s have been dressed as AMGs. Check the VIN and the data card, not the badges.
- Naturally aspirated or supercharged?: US 2002–2004 trucks are naturally aspirated; 2005–2011 are Kompressors. Make sure the model year, VIN and engine all match the price.
- Heat soak and the intercooler pump: On a Kompressor, ask when the intercooler pump was replaced. A truck that pulls hard when cold and goes flat when hot is the classic symptom.
- Listen at idle: Vibration or an RPM-dependent chirp on the M113 points to the harmonic balancer. Don't drive far on a failing one.
- Mounts and suspension: Commenters on German Cars For Sale Blog advise checking engine and transmission mounts and suspension wear. With 700 Nm going through them, mounts wear out faster.
- Test all three lockers: Engage the centre, rear and front locks on loose ground. Lockers that 'were never used' by the last owner often don't work.
- Rust, even on the fancy one: Owners warn G 55s rust like any G, especially near the coast. Check the tailgate's lower edge, door bottoms, sills and rear frame tubes.
- Gear oil behind the front wheels: Oil on the inner wheels or the large AMG calipers means front axle seals, and possibly contaminated brakes.

### Common repairs
#### Intercooler pump (Kompressor)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time 1–2 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Power drops after heat soak, especially in traffic or at crawling speed; intake temperatures climb.
Fix: Replace the electric intercooler circulation pump with the updated Bosch unit, then bleed the low-temperature circuit. Victory Road Performance recommends replacing it as routine maintenance because the original pump failed often. GwagenParts sells a higher-flow bolt-in pump for 2006–2010 G 55s.
Tools: Updated Bosch intercooler pump or upgrade pump · coolant · hose clamps · bleeding funnel

#### Harmonic balancer (M113)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2.5 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Vibration at idle, a wobbling crank pulley, cracked or bulging rubber, chirp or rattle that changes with RPM. If the outer ring lets go you lose the belt drive.
Fix: Remove the belt, lock the crank with a counter-hold tool, and replace the balancer with a new torque-to-yield centre bolt and a new front crank seal.
Tools: Crank counter-hold tool · 27 mm socket · breaker bar or high-torque impact · new balancer, centre bolt and crank seal

#### Engine & transmission mounts
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Half a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Clunk on take-off or shifts, extra vibration in the cabin, engine movement when you blip the throttle.
Fix: Replace the fluid-filled engine mounts (VRP notes they leak and collapse, and wear quickly in high-power cars) and the transmission mount together. Support the engine from below and lift each side in turn.
Tools: Engine support or jack with wood block · sockets and extensions · new engine and transmission mounts

#### Spark plugs, wires & coils
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time 2–3 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Misfire codes, rough idle, hesitation under boost. Many owners don't know when the plugs were last done.
Fix: Replace all 16 plugs (the M113 has twin plugs per cylinder) and inspect the wires and coil packs. VRP suggests heavier-insulated wires if the originals are tired. Fix any misfire before adding power.
Tools: Spark plug socket and extensions · dielectric grease · plugs · wires · coils if needed

#### 722.6 service & 13-pin connector
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time 2–3 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Harsh or delayed shifts, limp mode, or ATF wicking into the wiring at the gearbox connector.
Fix: Drop the pan, replace the filter and fluid, and check the 13-pin connector (203-540-02-53) for leaks. VRP says to check the conductor plate too in many cases. Use the correct Mercedes-spec ATF and fill by temperature.
Tools: ATF · filter and pan gasket · 13-pin connector (203-540-02-53) · dipstick tool

#### Diff locks won't engage
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Diagnosis-dependent
Symptoms: One or all locks refuse to engage or drop out. On mid-2000s W463s the centre lock is vacuum-operated and the axle locks hydraulic, so one vacuum leak can disable the whole sequence.
Fix: Confirm vacuum at the transfer-case hose, then work back through the pump, reservoir and switchover valve block with a tee-in gauge. One 2005 owner's fault was a split plastic connector inside a rubber Y-fitting under the brake booster. Bleed the hydraulic lines and change the fluids while you're there.
Tools: Hand vacuum pump with gauge · vacuum tees and line · connectors · diff and transfer-case fluid · bleeding kit

#### Front axle seal leak
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A day · cost $600–1,500
Symptoms: Gear oil on the inner front wheels, a gear-oil smell, oil on the caliper or rotor, brakes pulling.
Fix: Replace both front axle seals and inspect the shafts. Replace contaminated pads and resurface or replace the rotors. Oil on brakes this big is not something to leave.
Tools: Axle seals (both sides) · seal driver · gear oil · pads and rotors if contaminated

#### Steering damper & front-end wander
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost $300–800
Symptoms: Wander and wheel shake at 55–70 mph, vague on-centre feel, front-end clunks. On a 500 hp truck you'll notice it quickly.
Fix: Swap the steering damper (OEM or an upgrade such as a Bilstein B6), check the drag link and tie-rod ends, then align.
Tools: Steering damper · sockets and wrenches · tie-rod/drag-link ends if worn

### Baseline service
Baseline everything the week you buy it. The G 55 adds an AMG engine, and from 2005 a supercharger with its own low-temperature intercooler circuit, to a W463 chassis that still needs knuckle, axle and diff-lock care. Note which engine you have: 2003–04 US trucks are naturally aspirated, 2005-on are Kompressor (M113K), and several parts differ.
- Engine oil & filter: MB 229.5 · 0W-40 or 5W-40 full synthetic · ≈8.5 L (9 qt) with filter on 2005+ Kompressor; ≈8.0 L (8.5 qt) on 2003–04 · Then yearly or at the service indicator (Same top-mounted cartridge filter as the M113 G 500. If an oil cooler is drained you'll need extra oil.)
- Air filters: Kompressor: 113 094 00 04 elements · 2003–04: 273 094 04 04 set · Now, then every second oil change (A dirty filter costs a supercharged engine more than an NA one — don't stretch it.)
- Cabin filter: Mahle/OE 463 830 00 18 · Now, then yearly
- Spark plugs, wires & coils: 16 plugs (twin-plug heads) · Kompressor: NGK ILFR6A / Bosch FR6MPP332 · 2003–04: Bosch FR8DPP33 · Now if no record [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Fix any misfire before adding boost; check coil boots for oil from the valve covers.)
- Intercooler circuit & pump (2005+): Separate low-temp coolant circuit · MB 325.0 coolant · Replace the pump as routine if it's original; bleed the circuit afterwards (Heat-soak power loss in traffic is the pump. An upgraded higher-flow pump is a bolt-in.)
- Engine coolant & thermostat: MB 325.0 coolant, 50/50 with distilled water · ≈12.7 L · Now if history is unknown (Bleed thoroughly; inspect the hoses near the supercharger for heat damage.)
- Automatic transmission (722.6): MB 236.14 ATF · ≈9 qt total fill (pan drain replaces only part) · Now if no record; then every 40,000–60,000 mi (common technician practice) (New filter and pan gasket, and replace the 13-pin connector sleeve. Fill by temperature with the dipstick tool; check the conductor plate if shifts are erratic.)
- Transfer case: Check the tag: many W463 cases take MB 236.14 ATF; earlier cases ran GL-4 gear oil [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now, then every 60,000 mi (MB interval quoted by owners) (Drain and fill plugs are 14 mm hex. Inspect the flex discs and centre bearing — 500 hp is hard on them.)
- Front & rear differentials: GL-5 hypoid gear oil (synthetic 75W-90 commonly used) · front ≈1.4 L, rear ≈1.8 L (AMSOIL 2006 G 500 data) [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now, then with the transfer case (Loosen the fill plug before draining. On mid-2000s trucks the centre lock is vacuum and the axle locks hydraulic — test each lock separately afterwards.)
- Front knuckles, wheel bearings & seals: Repack knuckles; check bearings and axle seals · If no record (Europa's interval was 40,000 mi) (Oil on the front brakes means axle seals — on brakes this size, fix it immediately.)
- Power steering fluid: MB power-steering fluid or Dexron III ATF · 1 L · Now
- Brake fluid: DOT 4 Plus (MB sheet 331.0) · Now, then every 2 years (Bleed the hydraulic axle-lock lines too [CONFIRM IN MANUAL].)
- Fuel filter: 2005–10: 002 477 27 01 · 2003–04: 002 477 30 01 · Now if no record [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
- Engine & transmission mounts: Fluid-filled engine mounts + transmission mount · Inspect now; replace as a set if collapsed or leaking (High-output trucks wear them quickly; a clunk on take-off is the tell.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: About 33 inches on 18-inch wheels. Owners of unlifted W463s on Expedition Portal run 275/70R18 with no rubbing on sensible offsets, and 285/65R18 with a slight rub at full left lock. Fitment data lists 285/55R18 for 2004 and 2008 US G 55s, so 18s clear those brakes. One owner warns 18s won't clear G 63 brakes, so test-fit before buying 18s for a 19-inch 2009–2011 truck. Re-code the tire size so the speedometer and ESP stay accurate.

Q: What size are the factory tires?
A: 285/55R18 on US trucks through 2008 (Goodyear and TireSize.com fitment data). The 2009 update moved to 275/55R19 on 9.5-inch-wide AMG wheels.

Q: Which years are supercharged?
A: In the US, 2002–2004 G 55s are naturally aspirated (349 hp) and 2005–2011 are Kompressors (469 hp, later 493 and 500 hp). In Europe the supercharger arrived in 2004.

Q: Does it have low range and lockers?
A: Yes. It's a full W463 with permanent four-wheel drive, a two-speed transfer case and centre, rear and front locking differentials. AMG didn't take any of that out.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: 7,000 lb with a braked trailer, according to the spec data on a 2005 example. Check your owner's manual and trailer brakes.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: EPA figures are 12 mpg city, 14 highway and 13 combined for the 2003 naturally aspirated truck, and 11 city, 13 highway and 12 combined for Kompressors such as the 2005 and 2011. Bigger tires and a rack will make it worse.

Q: G 55 or G 550?
A: An MBWorld owner who drove both found the gap smaller than expected: the G 550's 382 hp feels quick, but the G 55 has power in reserve at any speed, feels tighter and is much louder. For trail use they're mechanically the same truck; the G 55 adds supercharger cooling to maintain.

Q: When did the G 55 end?
A: The last US model year was 2011. The 2012 US range was only the G 550, and the 5.5-litre biturbo G 63 AMG replaced the G 55 in 2012 (the 2013 model year in the US).

Q: Is the G 55 reliable?
A: The frame, axles and V8 are strong. Common jobs are predictable: the intercooler pump on Kompressors, the harmonic balancer, mounts, front axle seals, the steering damper and locker vacuum lines. One owner commenting on German Cars For Sale Blog calls the windshield a consumable. Buy on service records, not low mileage. On 2002–04 trucks, also test every window, lock and seat. Handsome Motors says those early electrical gremlins were mostly gone by 2005–06.

Q: What are they worth?
A: autoevolution's 2019–2022 auction study found Kompressor averages around $60,000 in 2021–22, with high-mileage 2005–2007 trucks at $27,000–40,000 and low-mileage 2011s up to $94,000. Deep Black and Fire Opal Red cars sold best.

## Mercedes-Benz G 550 (2009–2018 (US))
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/g550/
Codes: W463, M273 5.5 V8, M176 4.0 TT V8

Verdict: The last G-Class sold new in America with a solid front axle. Underneath the chrome running boards it’s the same triple-locked tractor as ever — just with a bigger V8, a seven-speed and, from 2016, a pair of turbochargers.

The G 550 is the old G-Class at the height of its contradictions. By 2009 the boxy W463 cost north of a hundred grand, wore a navigation screen and was more likely to be photographed outside a gym than in a riverbed. Yet nothing that mattered had been diluted: a separate ladder frame, solid axles at both ends, permanent four-wheel drive with low range and three fully locking differentials. For the US the name changed and the engine grew; the truck itself carried on until 2018, when an all-new G with independent front suspension finally replaced it.

### A NEW NAME, A BIGGER V8
For 2009 the US-market G 500 became the G 550, swapping the 5.0-litre M113 for the 5.5-litre M273 V8: 382 hp and 391 lb-ft. Mercedes had begun phasing the 722.9 seven-speed automatic into the US G 500 during 2007, so the G 550 arrived with seven ratios from the start. The 2008 update had also brought a new grille with three thicker horizontal fins and a COMAND APS system with its own off-road menu.
A later update lifted the dashboard and centre console from the ML-Class and added LED daytime running lamps, new mirrors, DISTRONIC cruise and blind-spot monitoring. Along the way came special editions — the 2011 Edition Select, a Japan-only G 550 Night Edition of 100 trucks, and a 30th-anniversary G 500/G 550 with designo leather — none of which changed the hardware underneath.

### TWIN TURBOS AND A LONG GOODBYE
For 2016 the naturally aspirated V8 gave way to the 4.0-litre twin-turbo M176, with its turbochargers tucked between the cylinder banks: 416 hp and 450 lb-ft. Mercedes-Benz USA quoted 0–60 mph in 5.8 seconds and an electronically limited 130 mph — for a 5,724-lb brick with the drag coefficient of a filing cabinet. The 2016 G 550 started at $119,900.
The off-road numbers barely moved over the decade: 9.3 inches of ground clearance, 23.6 inches of wading depth, 30° approach and departure angles and a 24° breakover, per Mercedes-Benz USA. The same twin-turbo engine went into the outrageous portal-axle G 550 4×4² for 2017. Then, at Detroit in January 2018, Mercedes revealed the second-generation G — and the solid front axle was gone.

### WHY OFF-ROADERS STILL WANT ONE
A solid front axle is a simple, strong, articulating thing, and it makes the G 550 the most modern G you can lift and tire the old-fashioned way. One Expedition Portal member put BFGoodrich KO2s in 275/70R18 on his stock-height 2014 G 550, with no rubbing even when flexing the axles in opposite directions, then added a Gobi roof rack — which knocked his fuel economy from about 12–13 mpg to 10–11.
The same owner later dropped the truck into a sinkhole in a creek. Recovery took about five hours, three tow services and, finally, a family member’s tractor; he noted the doors hadn’t leaked a drop. That’s the G 550 in a sentence: tougher than its reputation, and nowhere near as clever as a lifted 80 Series at avoiding trouble in the first place. Its contemporaries — the Land Cruiser 200, LX 570 and Range Rover L322 — were all softer, newer designs with independent fronts.

### Data plate
- Chassis: W463
- Us Years: 2009–2018
- Engine: M273 5.5 V8 (to 2015) · M176 4.0 TT V8 (2016–)
- Output: 382 hp → 416 hp
- Transmission: 7-speed automatic
- Drive: Permanent 4WD, 50:50, low range
- Lockers: Centre, rear, front
- Axles: Solid, front & rear
- Clearance: 9.3 in
- Wading: 23.6 in
- Towing: 7,000 lb
- Built In: Graz, Austria

### Engineering
The G 550 is the end of the line for the original engineering recipe. The body bolts to a separate steel ladder frame; both axles are rigid, located by links and sprung on coils; steering is a hydraulically assisted recirculating-ball box. Power flows through a two-speed transfer case to all four wheels all the time, split 50:50, and three 100% differential locks — centre, rear, front — are engaged from switches on the dash.
- Chassis: Ladder frame (Separate steel frame under the body, as on every G since 1979.)
- Axles: Solid, front & rear (Link-located, coil-sprung. The last US G built this way.)
- Drivetrain: Permanent 4WD, 50:50 (Two-speed transfer case with a low range for crawling.)
- Lockers: Centre, rear, front (Three 100% locks — the G’s party trick since the W463 arrived in 1990.)
- Engine: 5.5 V8 → 4.0 TT V8 (M273, 382 hp (2009–2015); M176 twin-turbo, 416 hp (2016–2018).)
- Geometry: 30° / 30° / 24° (Approach, departure, breakover (MY2016 Mercedes-Benz USA figures). 9.3 in clearance, 23.6 in wading.)

### Versions
- 2007–2008 · W463 G 500 (US) · M113 5.0 L V8 · 292 hp · The 722.9 seven-speed automatic arrives on the 2007 US G 500
- 2009–2015 · W463 G 550 · M273 5.5 L V8 · 382 hp · 391 lb-ft · G 500 renamed for the US; 7-speed automatic
- 2016–2018 · W463 G 550 · M176 4.0 L twin-turbo V8 · 416 hp · 450 lb-ft · 7G-TRONIC PLUS; 0–60 mph 5.8 s; $119,900 base for 2016
- 2017 · G 550 4×4² (US) · M176 4.0 L twin-turbo V8 · 416 hp · 450 lb-ft · Portal axles, 17.2 in clearance, $225,000
- 2019–2024 · Second-generation G 550 · M176 4.0 L twin-turbo V8 · 416 hp · 450 lb-ft · Independent front suspension, 9-speed automatic

### Year-by-year
- 2007: US G 500 starts switching from the 722.6 five-speed to the 722.9 seven-speed; HID headlamps, reversing camera and TPMS arrive
- 2009: G 550 replaces the G 500 in the US with the 5.5-litre M273 V8 (382 hp) and seven-speed automatic
- 2013: Biggest interior update in years: ML-Class-derived dashboard with COMAND moved up, LED daytime lamps, new mirrors, DISTRONIC and blind-spot assist (2012 update, MY2013 in the US)
- 2016: 4.0-litre M176 twin-turbo V8 (416 hp, 450 lb-ft) replaces the M273; 7G-TRONIC PLUS; $119,900 base
- 2017: G 550 4×4² joins the US range
- 2018: Final model year of the original W463; the redesigned G arrives for MY2019
