- Biggest tire, 2.5 in (60 mm) lift: 33 in (Eurowise's recommended maximum; with its King shock option Eurowise says 2013–2018 G 550s need only minor wheel-well trimming)
- Biggest tire, 4 in (100 mm) lift: 35 in (Eurowise's recommendation for its 100 mm kit (listed for 2009–2015 G 550). Above 4 in, extended brake lines are required; expect the speedometer to read 5–8 mph off until re-coded and DISTRONIC to be affected)

### Buying checks
- Decide on the engine first: 2009–2015 trucks have the naturally aspirated 5.5-litre M273; 2016–2018 trucks have the 4.0-litre twin-turbo M176. Same chassis, same lockers, different maintenance profile — and the 2016-on trucks command more money.
- Test all three lockers: Engage centre, rear and front in order on a loose surface and watch the dash indicators. A truck whose lockers ‘were never used’ often has a vacuum or actuation fault waiting.
- Watch the temperature gauge (M273): A slow-to-warm or erratic coolant temperature, or codes P0597–P0599, points at the map-controlled thermostat — the most common M273 failure.
- Scan for swirl-flap codes (M273): P2004, P2005 or P2006 mean the intake-manifold flap mechanism has failed. Don’t ignore it: broken flap pieces can be ingested by the engine.
- Look behind the front wheels: Gear oil on the inner wheels, calipers or rotors means leaking front axle seals — and possibly contaminated brakes.
- Drive it at 55–70 mph: Wander, wheel shake or a vague on-centre feel usually means a worn steering damper and tired linkage — common on the solid-axle G.
- Rust where nobody cleans: Tailgate lower edge, door bottoms, sills, rear frame tubes, strut mounts, inner wheel arches and around the rear bumper. Salt-belt trucks deserve a lift and a flashlight.
- Check the headliner and the badges: Autocar warns that a sagging headliner can mean water has got in, so check the sunroof drains and seals. And plenty of G 550s wear AMG bumpers and badges — check the VIN before paying a G 63 premium.

### Common repairs
#### Thermostat (M273)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Engine slow to warm up or running cool, erratic temperature gauge, poor heater output, codes P0597, P0598 or P0599. Note that 80–95 °C can be normal on a working map-controlled thermostat.
Fix: Drain enough coolant to drop the level below the housing, unplug the thermostat’s electrical connector, release the hoses and unbolt the housing. If the history is unknown, replace the radiator hose at the same time — old hoses often seal poorly at the O-ring on the new part. Refill with Mercedes-approved coolant and bleed the system. FCP Euro suggests treating it as a roughly 60,000-mile wear item.
Tools: Map-controlled thermostat · radiator hose · MB-approved coolant (genuine or Pentofrost NF) · Torx sockets · hose-clamp pliers · multimeter (heater element should read about 15.2 Ω ± 1.5 Ω)

#### Intake manifold swirl flaps (M273)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Most of a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Check-engine light with P2004, P2005 or P2006; sometimes a lumpy idle or flat spot. The operating lever on the flap shaft breaks.
Fix: Repair kits for the lever exist, but FCP Euro recommends replacing the complete manifold assembly because the flaps can also fail internally and send pieces into the cylinders. Remove the engine cover and air intake, disconnect the throttle body and sensors, unbolt the manifold, fit the new one with new gaskets, and clear the codes.
Tools: Intake manifold assembly (e.g. Pierburg) · manifold gaskets · Torx and hex sockets · torque wrench · scan tool

#### Crankcase breather & oil-cooler seals (M273)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–3 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Oil residue around the breather cover’s screws; in bad cases a burning-oil smell in the cabin as oil drips onto the exhaust manifold. A grimy belt tensioner hints at oil-cooler seal seepage.
Fix: Replace the plastic breather cover/O-ring assembly — the rubber O-ring is what hardens and leaks. If the oil cooler is weeping, replace its seals at the same time and degrease the area so you can confirm the fix.
Tools: Breather cover assembly · oil-cooler seal kit · Torx/external-Torx bits (early vs later engines differ) · brake cleaner

#### Oil in the cam-magnet connectors
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost Cheap if caught early
Symptoms: Oil inside the camshaft-adjuster magnet connectors; on neglected engines oil wicks up the harness toward the engine control unit.
Fix: Unplug each connector and inspect for oil. Replace leaking cam magnets and fit Mercedes’ sacrificial adapter pigtails so any future seepage stops short of the main harness. Clean contaminated connectors with electrical cleaner.
Tools: Camshaft-adjuster magnets · factory sacrificial pigtails · electrical contact cleaner · Torx bits

#### Diff locks won’t engage
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Diagnosis-dependent
Symptoms: One or all locks refuse to engage or drop out, indicator lights flash or stay off. The fault is usually actuation, not the differential. On a 2005 G 500 an MBWorld owner found the centre lock vacuum-operated and the front and rear locks hydraulic, so check both circuits. Mercedes' 2013 US and 2016 Canadian booklets confirm the G 550's lock mechanism runs on brake fluid from its own reservoir; whether your year's centre lock is vacuum-operated [CONFIRM IN MANUAL for your year].
Fix: Follow the same path MBWorld owners use on earlier W463s: confirm vacuum at the transfer case, then work back through the reservoir, lines and switchover valves with a gauge teed into each segment until you find the split line or connector. Exercise the locks regularly once fixed — disuse is their enemy.
Tools: Hand vacuum pump with gauge · vacuum tees and line · replacement connectors

#### Front axle seal leak
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A day · cost $600–1,500
Symptoms: Gear oil on the inner front wheels, a gear-oil smell, oil on a caliper or rotor, brakes pulling to one side.
Fix: Replace both front axle seals even if only one is leaking, and check the shafts for scoring. If oil reached the brakes, replace the pads and resurface or replace the rotors — contaminated pads are a safety issue.
Tools: Genuine axle seals (both sides) · seal driver · gear oil · brake pads and rotors if contaminated

#### Steering damper & highway wander
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost $300–800
Symptoms: Highway wander, wheel shake at 55–70 mph, vague on-centre feel, clunks over bumps.
Fix: Swap the steering damper for an OEM or upgraded unit (Bilstein B6 is a common choice), check the drag link and tie-rod ends for play, then get a front-end alignment.
Tools: Steering damper · sockets and wrenches · tie-rod or drag-link ends if worn

#### Cracked coil springs
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Half a day · cost Autocar: about £120 per corner
Symptoms: A loud thump over bumps, uneven ride height — often discovered after cold weather.
Fix: Replace springs in axle pairs. If a lift is on the cards, do it now with a matched spring-and-shock kit rather than buying stock springs twice.
Tools: Springs (pairs) · jack and stands · spring compressor if your setup needs one · new shocks recommended

### Baseline service
A G 550 that’s changed hands has usually been serviced for the showroom, not the trail — assume nothing below the engine has been touched and baseline every fluid. Split the list by engine first: 2009–2015 trucks have the 5.5-litre M273, 2016–2018 trucks the 4.0 twin-turbo M176, and many parts differ.
- Engine oil & filter: MB 229.5 (e.g. 5W-40) · 9.0 L (2.4 US gal) with filter. That's the same for the M273 (2013 and 2014 operator's manuals) and the M176 (2016 and 2018 manuals; the 2016 manual also accepts MB 229.3) · Now, then per the service indicator. Mercedes' 2013 US booklet sets it at every 10,000 mi or 1 year (Both engines use a cartridge filter in a housing on top of the engine — replace the cap O-ring and drain-plug washer every time. FCP Euro also sells a 229.52 kit for the M176, but the operator's manuals list 229.5.)
- Air filters: M273: two filter elements in the air box · Now if undated. Mercedes: every 40,000 mi or 4 years for the M273 (2013 US booklet); every 40,000 km or 2 years for the M176 (Canadian 2016 booklet); sooner in dust (FCP Euro notes the M273 air box holds two filters — replace both together. Dusty trail use shortens the interval.)
- Cabin air filter: W463 cabin filter · Now, then yearly (Cheap, and an old one makes the climate control work harder.)
- Spark plugs & coils: M273 and M176 spark plugs (Mercedes-spec) · Now if no record. Mercedes: every 60,000 mi or 6 years for the M273 (2013 US booklet); every 100,000 km or 5 years for the M176 (Canadian 2016 booklet) (FCP Euro suggests doing M273 plugs alongside the oxygen sensors (≈100,000 mi). Check misfire counters before buying coils.)
- Coolant & thermostat: M273: Genuine Mercedes or Pentofrost NF · 2015-on: MB 325.6 listed by FCP Euro · 50/50 with distilled water · Coolant now if undated; M273 thermostat at 60,000 mi (FCP Euro recommends replacing the M273’s map-controlled thermostat at 60,000 miles — it’s the engine’s most common failure.)
- Automatic transmission (7G-TRONIC 722.9): MB 236.14 for gearboxes built before June 2010 · MB 236.15 (blue) from 21 June 2010 on · Now if no record. Mercedes: oil and filter every 40,000 mi or 4 years on the M273 G 550 (2013 US booklet); every 120,000 km on the 2016 (Canadian booklet) (No dipstick: drain the pan, fit a new filter and gasket, then set the level at temperature with a scan tool. A drain-and-fill only swaps part of the fluid — a second change soon after improves the ratio. Check the build date before buying fluid.)
- Transfer case: Gear oil, not ATF, if your truck has the VG 150 E case: Mercedes' WIS fluid table, as reproduced for a 2011 G 55 (W463), lists SAE 80, 80W or 80W-85 for it (SAE 90 or 85W-90 in hot climates) · capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now if no record. Mercedes: every 50,000 mi or 5 years (2013 US booklet); every 120,000 km (Canadian 2016 booklet) (Two-speed, 50:50 case with the centre lock. Check for weeps at the input and output seals while you’re underneath.)
- Front & rear differentials: Hypoid gear oil. FCP Euro lists 75W-90 GL-5 for 2009–2014 G 550s, and the WIS table (approval sheet 235.0) allows 75W-90, 80W-90, 85W-90 or 90 for hypoid axles · capacities [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now if no record. Mercedes: every 50,000 mi or 5 years (2013 US booklet); every 80,000 km or 4 years (Canadian 2016 booklet) (Both axles carry 100% lockers. Look for gear oil on the inner front wheels and brakes — the front axle seals are a known leak point.)
- Diff locks & vacuum lines: Inspection — engage centre, rear, front in order · Now, then monthly exercise (Disuse is what kills lockers, and Mercedes' service booklets have you engage them at every service. The locking mechanism has its own reservoir filled with brake fluid, which is changed with the brakes (2013 US and 2016 Canadian booklets). If one won't engage, check the fluid level and look for a split vacuum line or connector before suspecting the differential.)
- Power steering fluid: MB 236.3 power steering fluid (recirculating-ball box) · Now if dark or no record. Mercedes' 2013 US booklet only checks the level at service and gives no replacement interval (Never mix with ATF. A turkey-baster swap of the reservoir, repeated a few times, refreshes most of it.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 4 Plus (MB 331.0) · also fills the diff-lock mechanism · Now, then every 2 years / 20,000 mi (2013 US booklet). The Canadian 2016 booklet says every year (Brake fluid absorbs water. A heavy truck that tows or descends trails needs a fresh, high-boiling-point fluid.)
- Drive belt, tensioner & idlers: M273: belt + tensioner + idlers · M176: belt · M273 tensioner & idlers every 60,000 mi (FCP Euro recommends replacing M273 belt tensioners and idler pulleys every 60,000 miles; check for oil on the belt from the oil-cooler seals.)
- M273 oil-leak inspection: Breather cover, oil-cooler seals, cam-magnet connectors · At purchase (Unplug each cam-magnet connector and look for oil — caught early it’s a cheap fix; left alone, oil wicks toward the engine control unit.)
- Steering damper & battery: Steering damper · group 49 AGM battery · At purchase (A tired damper causes highway wander and shake. Load-test the battery.)

### FAQ
Q: What’s the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: About 33 inches — a 275/70R18 on 18-inch wheels. A 2014 G 550 owner on Expedition Portal ran BFGoodrich KO2s in that size at stock height with no rubbing at full flex, and a G 500 owner rubbed only on aftermarket ET63-offset wheels (ET43 was fine). A 285/65R18 can rub slightly at full left lock; a 265/65R18 (about 31.6 in) fits with room to spare. Later trucks came on 19s–21s, and owners warn 18s don’t clear every caliper — check before buying wheels, and have the tire size re-coded.

Q: What size are the factory tires?
A: A 2012 G 550 came on 265/60R18; optional sizes listed for that year run 275/55R19, 275/50R20 and 295/40R21. An Expedition Portal owner measured his 2017 G 550’s stock tires at about 30.5 inches tall.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: 7,000 lb with a braked trailer for a 2012 G 550. Check your own truck’s manual and hitch rating.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: Bad. EPA figures for 2012 are 12 mpg city, 15 highway, 13 combined on premium — and every G 550 from 2010 to 2018 is rated 13 combined, twin-turbo or not. A roof rack cost one owner a couple more mpg.

Q: How big is the fuel tank?
A: 25.4 gallons, on both the 2012 G 550 and the 2017 4×4² spec sheets.

Q: Should I buy a 5.5-litre or a 4.0 twin-turbo?
A: The 2016–2018 M176 twin-turbo has 416 hp and 450 lb-ft versus 382 hp and 391 lb-ft for the 2009–2015 M273, but EPA economy is identical. The M273’s faults are well documented and DIY-friendly; the twin-turbo is quicker and newer. Service history matters more than the engine choice.

Q: Does the M273 balance-shaft/idler-gear problem affect the G 550?
A: It’s associated with early-production 2004–2008 M272 and M273 engines, which largely predates the 2009 G 550. If you see codes such as P0059, P0060, P0064, P0272, P0275 or P0276, or Mercedes codes 1200/1208, have it checked anyway.

Q: Can I use the diff locks on pavement?
A: No. Locked differentials stop the wheels turning at different speeds, so on grippy surfaces the driveline binds and tires scrub. Lock on dirt, sand, snow or rock at low speed, and unlock before you’re back on tarmac.

Q: How much ground clearance and wading depth does it have?
A: 9.3 inches of ground clearance and 23.6 inches of wading depth, with 30° approach and departure angles and a 24° breakover, per Mercedes-Benz USA for the 2016 G 550.

Q: Will it fit in my garage?
A: A 2016 G 550 is 76.9 inches tall, 80.9 inches wide and about 187.6 inches long, on a 112.2-inch wheelbase. Add a roof rack and measure again.

Q: Is the G 550 reliable?
A: The frame, axles and drivetrain are tough; the age-related jobs are predictable — thermostat and swirl flaps on the 5.5, axle seals, steering damper, locker actuation, rust and sunroof drains. A truck with receipts for those beats a low-mileage one that’s never been touched.

## Mercedes-Benz G 63 AMG (2012–2018 (US 2013–2018))
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/g63-amg/
Codes: W463, M157 5.5 biturbo V8, 7G-TRONIC

Verdict: The last G 63 built on the old W463 body: a 5.5-litre biturbo V8, three lockers and solid axles. It's the quickest way to make a 1979 truck feel modern. Hard-used examples are cheaper than you'd expect, and an M157 that has missed its maintenance costs more than you'd expect.

The G 63 AMG replaced the supercharged G 55 AMG in 2012 and reached American showrooms that August as a 2013 model. It ran until the 2018 model year, the last before the redesigned second-generation G. It uses AMG's 5.5-litre biturbo V8 and a seven-speed automatic, and it was the first AMG G with neither a supercharger nor a five-speed. The W463 underneath is unchanged: ladder frame, solid axles on coils, a two-speed transfer case and three locking differentials. AMG gave the truck a much bigger engine and left the off-road hardware alone.

### TURBOS REPLACE THE SUPERCHARGER
Mercedes revealed the G 63 and the V12 G 65 in April 2012, ahead of the Beijing show. The M157 V8 displaces 5,461 cc and makes 544 PS with 760 Nm (560 lb-ft) from 2,000 rpm. Mercedes quoted 0–60 mph in 5.3 seconds and a 130 mph limiter, and claimed 13 per cent lower fuel consumption on the European cycle than the G 55. The engine drives an AMG SPEEDSHIFT PLUS 7G-TRONIC with three modes, automatic throttle blips on downshifts and ECO start/stop.
The rest of the update came from the 2012 G-Class refresh. The dashboard and centre console came from the ML, and the truck gained a colour TFT instrument cluster, a tablet-style COMAND screen, DISTRONIC PLUS, Blind Spot Assist and LED daytime running lights. AMG added a twin-blade grille, a bumper with three large intakes, six-piston front calipers from the ML 63 on 14.8-inch discs, and 20-inch wheels on 275/50 R20 tyres. AutoGuide priced a 2013 US truck at $134,300, about $20,000 more than a G 550.

### WHY OFF-ROADERS SHOULD CARE
In the bodywork that matters off-road, a G 63 is the same truck as a G 550. Kelley Blue Book listed a 36-degree approach angle and a 7,716 lb tow rating. MotorTrend gave 27 degrees of departure, 21 degrees of breakover, about 8 inches of ground clearance and 24 inches of wading depth. It still has a low-range transfer case and centre, rear and front locks controlled by dashboard buttons. The off-road weak points are AMG's own choices: low-profile 20s, a side exhaust that exits ahead of the rear wheels, and huge front brakes that limit which wheels will fit.
Buyers liked it. MotorTrend reported in late 2013 that the G 63 had become the best-selling AMG product in the US. That's why so many are on the used market. Most owners drove them on pavement, so the lockers on a typical used truck have rarely been used.

### 2016 UPDATE AND THE END
For the 2016 model year the truck was renamed Mercedes-AMG G 63. Output rose by 27 PS to 571 PS (563 hp), with torque unchanged at 760 Nm and 0–100 km/h in 5.4 seconds. All G-Class models got new shock absorbers, revised ASR and ABS calibration, new bumpers and new instrument dials. AMG also offered an Edition 463 package with 21-inch wheels and a stainless underguard, and a colour package with bright paints such as alien green and sunset beam. The G 550 switched to the 4.0-litre twin-turbo M176 at the same time, and the 4×4² followed in 2015 on a shortened chassis from the G 63 AMG 6×6, AMG's six-wheeler derived from the Australian Army's W461-family truck.
The 2018 model year was the last for this body in the US. Its successor kept the G 63 name but moved to the twin-turbo 4.0-litre M177 and independent front suspension. That makes the 2013–2018 truck the last AMG G with a solid front axle. On Bring a Trailer it has also become the cheapest way into a biturbo AMG G: from 2025 to October 2026, the median sale was about $65,500.

### Data plate
- Chassis: W463
- Years: 2012–2018 (US MY2013–2018)
- Engine: M157 5.5 L biturbo V8
- Output: 544 PS → 571 PS (2016)
- Torque: 760 Nm (560 lb-ft)
- Gearbox: 7G-TRONIC 7-speed automatic
- Drive: Full-time 4WD, low range
- Lockers: Centre, rear, front
- Axles: Solid, front & rear
- 0–60 Mph: 5.3 s (2013)
- Top Speed: 130 mph (limited)
- Epa: 12 city / 14 hwy / 13 comb.

### Engineering
Under the AMG trim, the G 63 is still a W463. The body sits on a separate ladder frame, both axles are solid and coil-sprung, a two-speed transfer case drives all four wheels permanently, and three dashboard switches lock the centre, rear and front differentials. AMG changed the engine, gearbox, brakes, exhaust, wheels and damper settings.
- Chassis: Ladder frame (Long-wheelbase five-door body; AMG flares, running boards and side-exit exhaust.)
- Axles: Solid, front & rear (Coil springs on link-located beam axles. This is the last AMG G before the 2019 switch to independent front suspension.)
- Lockers: Centre, rear, front (Three 100% locks and low range, as on every W463.)
- Engine: M157 5.5 L biturbo V8 (5,461 cc, direct injection; 544 PS / 760 Nm, 571 PS from 2016.)
- Gearbox: 7G-TRONIC (722.9) (AMG SPEEDSHIFT PLUS calibration, three modes, ECO start/stop.)
- Brakes: 6-piston front (ML 63 calipers on 14.8 × 1.42 in front discs; they rule out most 18-inch wheels.)

### Versions
- 1999–2012 · W463 G 55 AMG · M113 / M113K 5.4 V8 · 354 → 507 PS · Predecessor; five-speed 722.6, supercharged from 2004
- 2012–2015 · W463 G 63 AMG · M157 5.5 L biturbo V8 · 544 PS · 760 Nm · US MY2013–2015; 2012 interior update, 7G-TRONIC
- 2012–2018 · W463 G 65 AMG · M279 6.0 L biturbo V12 · 612 → 630 PS · 1,000 Nm · V12 sibling, same chassis
- 2013–2015 · W463 G 63 AMG 6×6 · M157 5.5 L biturbo V8 · 544 PS · 760 Nm · Three portal axles, five lockers; about 100 built
- 2015–2018 · W463 Mercedes-AMG G 63 · M157 5.5 L biturbo V8 · 571 PS (563 hp) · 760 Nm · US MY2016–2018; new dampers, revised ASR/ABS
- 2018– · Second-generation G 63 · M177 4.0 L biturbo V8 · 577 hp · 627 lb-ft · Successor; independent front suspension

### Year-by-year
- 2012: G 63 AMG and G 65 AMG revealed in April with the 2012 interior update; M157 5.5 biturbo V8 (544 PS, 760 Nm) and 7G-TRONIC replace the G 55's supercharged V8 and five-speed
- 2013: US launch (MY2013, on sale August 2012) at $134,300; EPA 12/14 mpg
- 2013: G 63 AMG 6×6 goes into limited production at Magna Steyr in Graz
- 2015: Last pre-facelift model year; the cheapest way into a W463 G 63 today
- 2016: Renamed Mercedes-AMG G 63; 571 PS (563 hp), new shock absorbers, revised ASR/ABS and instruments; Edition 463 and colour packages
- 2016: Recalls 17V178 (door cable) and 17V713 (ESP with DISTRONIC PLUS) cover 2016 trucks; 17V250 (steering coupling) covers 2013–2016
- 2018: Last model year of this body; EPA highway rating rises to 15 mpg
- 2019: Replaced by the second-generation G 63 with the M177 4.0 V8 and independent front suspension

### Capability
- Towing: 7,716 lb (3,500 kg) (KBB, 2013 G 63)
- Approach / departure / breakover: 36° / 27° / 21° (KBB and MotorTrend)
- Ground clearance: ≈8 in (≈210 mm) (MotorTrend)
- Wading depth: 24 in (600 mm) (MotorTrend; Mercedes quotes 600 mm for the production G)
- Fuel economy: EPA 12 city / 14 hwy / 13 comb (2013–2017); 12 / 15 / 13 (2018) (premium fuel)
- Curb weight: ≈5,876 lb (2,665 kg) (MotorTrend test truck; KBB says 'well over 5,600 pounds')
- 0–60 mph: 5.3 s (2013, Mercedes) (0–100 km/h 5.4 s from 2016)
- Top speed: 130 mph (210 km/h), limited

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 275/50R20 on 9.5 × 20 AMG wheels (2013–2018 US), 21-inch wheels with the Edition 463 package
- Bolt Pattern: 5x130
- Center Bore: 84.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M14x1.5 bolts
- Lug Torque: 96 lb-ft (130 N·m)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 275/55R20 (≈32 in) (Run by Expedition Portal G 63 owners; one Expedition Portal member says 18-inch wheels will not clear the G 63's front brakes, so test-fit smaller wheels first. Recode the tyre size)
- Biggest tire, 2.5 in (60 mm) lift: 33 in (Eurowise's recommended maximum for its 60 mm W463 kit; light wheel-well trimming possible)
- Biggest tire, 4 in (100 mm) lift: 35 in (Eurowise's recommendation for 100 mm of lift on a W463; above 4 in, extended brake lines are required)

### Buying checks
- Is it really a G 63?: Many G 550s have been fitted with AMG bumpers, grilles and badges. US G 63 VINs from Bring a Trailer listings begin WDCYC7DF (2013–2016) and WDCYC7DH (2018). A same-era G 550 reads WDCYC3HF. Check the VIN and data card, not the bodywork.
- Recall paperwork: Make sure NHTSA 17V250 (steering coupling, 2013–2016) has been done. On 2016–17 trucks, also check 17V713 (ESP with DISTRONIC PLUS). Run the VIN through NHTSA's recall lookup before you hand over money.
- Oil consumption and misfires: Ask how much oil it uses between services and scan for stored codes. The M157 can suffer cylinder scoring at higher mileage. Misfires are often plugs, coils or oil-soaked cam-magnet connectors, but persistent misfires or consumption justify a borescope before purchase.
- Coolant around the turbos: Look for coolant crust or a sweet smell around the turbos and the lines that feed them, and check both coolant reservoirs. MBWorld owners report cracked turbo coolant lines, and a pressure test is cheap.
- Oil at the cam magnets: Unplug a camshaft-adjuster magnet connector. If there's oil inside, it is wicking into the harness, and the magnets need replacing with sacrificial pigtails fitted.
- Seals under the truck: Check for gear oil on the inside of the front wheels and on the big AMG calipers (front axle seals), at the transfer-case outputs and at the pinion seals. An MBWorld member says pinion seal leaks are 'very common around 60k–80k'.
- Test all three lockers: Engage centre, rear and front in order on loose ground and watch the indicators. A truck that has only ever been driven on pavement can have lockers that don't engage.
- Rust and drains: Check the tailgate's lower edge, door bottoms, sills, rear frame tubes and spring mounts. A G 63 rusts like any other G, and 20-inch wheels don't stop road salt.

### Common repairs
#### Spark plugs & ignition coils (M157)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time 2–3 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Misfire codes (P0300-series), rough idle, hesitation under boost. Often the plugs' age is simply unknown.
Fix: Remove the engine covers and intake trim, pull each coil, and replace all eight plugs with Mercedes-spec plugs torqued to the service manual figure. Euro Premium Parts' M157 guide recommends inspecting or replacing the coils at the same time, at about 40,000–50,000 miles. Before replacing a coil, check its connector and boot for oil.
Tools: Thin-wall spark plug socket · extensions and swivel · torque wrench · dielectric grease

#### Camshaft-adjuster magnets leaking oil
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time 1–2 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Oil inside the four camshaft-adjuster magnet connectors at the front of the heads. Possible cam-timing codes. On neglected engines, oil wicks along the harness toward the engine computer.
Fix: Replace all four magnets. Fit sacrificial wiring pigtails so any future leak stops at a cheap connector. Clean the harness plugs with electronic cleaner and check the far end of the harness for oil. FCP Euro's kit is built for this job on the M157, M278 and related engines.
Tools: Torx bits · electrical contact cleaner · rags · magnets and pigtails

#### Turbo coolant lines & water pump
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A day or more · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Coolant loss with no obvious puddle, coolant crust or a sweet smell near the turbos, low-coolant warning, overheating. An MBWorld owner of a 2014 G 63 found a cracked coolant line at the driver-side turbo.
Fix: Pressure-test the system to find the leak. Replace the turbo coolant feed and return lines as a set, and on a high-mileage engine do the water pump and thermostat housing at the same time. FCP Euro calls the lines 'a common failure item that can lead to coolant loss and engine overheating.' Access is tight. MBWorld owners disagree on whether it's a sensible DIY, so plan to remove intake parts.
Tools: Cooling-system pressure tester · hose-clamp pliers · flare and line wrenches · MB 325.6 coolant · vacuum fill tool helpful

#### 7G-TRONIC fluid & filter service
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time 2–3 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Harsh or delayed shifts, flare between gears, or just no service record. FCP Euro notes that the 722.9's most common failures are electronic.
Fix: Drain the pan and the torque converter, replace the filter and pan gasket, refill with MB 236.15 ATF and set the level at the specified fluid temperature with a scan tool. AMSOIL lists the 722.9 total fill as 9.5 qt, and a drain-and-fill replaces only part of it. If shifts are erratic, have a scan tool read the gearbox fault codes before replacing parts.
Tools: Scan tool for ATF temperature · fluid pump · torque wrench · new filter, gasket and plugs

#### Front axle seal leak
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A day · cost $600–1,500
Symptoms: Gear oil on the inner front wheels or the six-piston calipers, a gear-oil smell, brakes pulling.
Fix: Replace both front axle seals and inspect the shafts for scoring. Replace contaminated pads and resurface or replace the rotors. au7o lists this leak for G 63s and rates it critical because the oil ends up on the brakes.
Tools: Seal puller and driver · hub tools · GL-5 gear oil · brake parts if oil-soaked

#### Pinion & transfer-case seal leaks
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Half a day per seal · cost $500–1,200 (transfer-case output seal, au7o)
Symptoms: Oil drips at the front of either differential or at the transfer-case outputs; oil spray on the driveshafts.
Fix: First make sure the axle breather tube isn't kinked or blocked, because pressure pushes oil past seals. Pinion seals need care: an MBWorld member notes the pinion bearing preload is set by a crush sleeve, so mark and measure before removing the nut. For transfer-case output seals, refill with Mercedes-approved fluid and check the flanges for wear.
Tools: Flange holding tool · seal puller · inch-pound torque wrench · fluids

#### Steering damper & front-end wander
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost $300–800
Symptoms: Wander, wheel shake at 55–70 mph, vague on-centre feel. au7o reports this as the most common W463 complaint.
Fix: Replace the damper with an OEM or upgraded unit. Check the drag link and tie-rod ends for play and align afterwards. Ask whether recall 17V250 (steering coupling) has been done.
Tools: Sockets and wrenches · tie-rod end puller · alignment afterwards

#### Frame & body rust treatment
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A weekend · cost $400–8,000 (au7o, depending on depth)
Symptoms: Bubbling at the tailgate lower edge, door bottoms and sills; scale on the rear frame tubes and spring mounts.
Fix: Remove loose scale, treat with a converter, then apply cavity wax inside the frame and doors and an underbody coating. Keep the drain holes clear. Cut out and weld anything perforated.
Tools: Wire wheels · rust converter · cavity-wax wand · underbody coating

### Baseline service
Baseline everything the week you buy it. On top of the usual W463 knuckle, axle and diff-lock care, the G 63 has a twin-turbo direct-injection V8 with two coolant circuits and a seven-speed whose fluid is easy to neglect. Assume nothing was done unless there's a receipt.
- Engine oil & filter: 0W-40 or 5W-40 full synthetic to MB 229.5 · 9 qt with filter (AMSOIL) · Then every 10,000 mi or yearly (Euro Premium Parts' M157 guidance) (Shorter intervals protect the cam adjusters and turbos. Check the level again after the refill, as AMSOIL advises.)
- Air filters: 278 094 00 04 elements · Now, then about every 20,000 mi; sooner on dusty trails (Twin turbos draw a lot of air, and a clogged filter shows up as lost boost.)
- Cabin filter: W463 cabin filter · Now, then yearly
- Spark plugs & coils: 8 plugs (Mercedes 004 159 81 03) · coils checked or replaced together · Now if no record; about every 40,000–50,000 mi (Check coil boots and the cam-magnet plugs for oil while you're there.)
- Engine coolant (high-temperature circuit): MB 325.6-approved coolant, 50/50 · ≈14.6 qt (AMSOIL) · Now if history is unknown; then about every 4 years (Pressure-test and inspect the turbo coolant lines and the plastic expansion tank.)
- Charge-air cooling (low-temperature circuit): Separate circuit · ≈3.1 qt (AMSOIL) · Check the level now; bleed after any work (Low-speed heat soak on the trail is when this circuit works hardest. FCP Euro lists a Pierburg auxiliary water pump for 2013–16 G 63s.)
- Automatic transmission (7G-TRONIC 722.9): MB 236.15 ATF · 9.5 qt total fill (AMSOIL) · Now if no record; Euro Premium Parts suggests every 40,000 mi (Drain the pan and converter, fit a new filter, and set the level at temperature with a scan tool.)
- Transfer case: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]: AMSOIL lists no recommendation · Now, if no record (Look for leaks at the output seals (a common G 63 job, according to au7o).)
- Front & rear differentials: Hypoid gear oil, GL-5 · front ≈3 pt, rear ≈3.8 pt (AMSOIL) · Now, then with the transfer case (Loosen the fill plug before draining, check the breathers, and test each locker afterwards.)
- Front knuckles, wheel bearings & seals: Inspect bearings and axle seals; repack · If no record (Oil on brakes this large needs fixing right away.)
- Power steering fluid: MB 236.3 power-steering fluid · Now (Recirculating-ball box; check the damper and tie-rod ends at the same time.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 4 Plus (MB sheet 331.0, per AMSOIL) · Now, then every 2 years (The six-piston front calipers hold a lot of fluid, so flush until it runs clean.)
- Battery: Group 49 AGM · Test now (Start/stop, COMAND and the locker electronics all react badly to low voltage.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: About 32 inches, on 20-inch wheels. An Expedition Portal owner runs 275/55R20 (about 32 in) on an unlifted G 63, and another 2017 G 63 owner was told by his dealer the size 'will work fine'. Most unlifted W463s fit 33-inch 275/70R18s, but one Expedition Portal member says 18-inch wheels 'will not fit on the G63' over its big front calipers, so try a wheel on the hub before you buy a set. Recode the tyre size so the speedometer and ESP stay accurate.

Q: What size are the factory tires?
A: 275/50R20, according to TireSize.com's fitment data for the 2015, 2016 and 2018 G 63. The launch press material lists 9.5 × 20 AMG wheels. The Edition 463 package offered 21-inch wheels.

Q: Does it have low range and lockers?
A: Yes. It is a full W463 with permanent four-wheel drive, a low-range transfer case and centre, rear and front locking differentials.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: 7,716 lb, according to Kelley Blue Book's 2013 G 63 guide. Check your own truck's manual and hitch.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: EPA: 12 mpg city, 14 highway, 13 combined on premium for every model year from 2013 to 2017, with 2018 rated 15 highway. Bigger tyres and a roof rack lower it.

Q: What oil does it take, and how much?
A: AMSOIL lists 9 qt with the filter, in 0W-40 or 5W-40 full synthetic meeting Mercedes approval. Euro Premium Parts cites MB 229.5/229.51 and recommends changing it every 10,000 miles or yearly. FCP Euro's G 63 oil kit comes with 9 litres.

Q: Is the M157 reliable?
A: It's strong when maintained, but neglect gets expensive. The well-documented jobs are spark plugs and coils, oil-leaking cam magnets, turbo coolant lines, and turbo oil feed lines on older engines. Cylinder scoring is the serious risk at higher mileage. Buy on service history and a borescope inspection, not on mileage alone.

Q: G 63 or G 550?
A: Off-road they are the same truck: same frame, axles, transfer case and lockers. The G 63 adds roughly 150 hp, bigger brakes that rule out 18-inch wheels, and a more complicated twin-turbo engine. If you'll mostly drive trails, a G 550 is cheaper to buy and fit with tyres. If you'll mostly drive pavement, the G 63's engine is the reason to buy it.

Q: Which years are best?
A: There's no consensus best year, so buy on condition. 2016–2018 trucks have 563 hp, new dampers and recalibrated ESP and ABS, and they sell for roughly $15,000 more on Bring a Trailer. 2013–2015 trucks are the bargain. Handsome Motors says the M157 in the G 63 got timing-chain and head-bolt updates, and wants the cooling system and water pump inspected on any of them. Whichever year you buy, make sure the steering-coupling recall (17V250, 2013–2016) is done.

Q: Can I use the diff locks on pavement?
A: No. Locked differentials stop the wheels turning at different speeds, so on grippy surfaces the driveline binds and the tyres scrub. Lock them on loose ground at low speed and unlock before you're back on tarmac.

Q: What replaced it?
A: The second-generation G 63 for the 2019 model year. It has a 4.0-litre twin-turbo M177 with 577 hp, a 40:60 torque split and independent front suspension, and it still has three lockers.

## Mercedes-Benz G 63 AMG 6×6 (2013–2015)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/g63-6x6/
Codes: W463, 6×6 portal axles, 5 locking diffs

Verdict: An Australian Army six-wheeler fitted with an AMG biturbo V8 and a quilted-leather cabin. It has portal axles, five lockers and tyre pressures you set from the roof console. It's absurd, it really works off-road, and about 100 were built.

The G 63 AMG 6×6 is a three-axle, four-door G-Class pickup that Mercedes built in small numbers at Magna Steyr in Graz from 2013 to 2015. It takes the G 63 AMG's 5.5-litre biturbo V8 and seven-speed automatic, adds portal axles at all six corners, five locking differentials and an onboard compressor that inflates the 37-inch tyres from inside the cab, and gives it a designo leather interior. Mercedes called it 'the most spectacular cross-country vehicle of its time'. It began as a show car, but the response was strong enough that Mercedes sold slightly more than 100.

### AN ARMY TRUCK WITH AN AMG ENGINE
The 6×6 was developed from a military truck. In 2007 Mercedes-Benz became the preferred tenderer for Australia's Land 121 Overlander project to replace the army's Land Rover Perenties. Australia eventually bought 2,268 G-Wagens in ten variants, from the working W461 range, including a six-wheeler. The Australian army was the first military customer for the 6×6, which Wikipedia describes as the first six-wheeled military vehicle Mercedes had built since 1941. Autocar reported that the military 6×6 used a 3.0-litre V6 diesel of up to 220 bhp and the older five-speed automatic.
MotorTrend reported that most of the civilian truck's cab, its three-axle frame and its retuned transfer case came from the Australian military G. The engine, the seven-speed and the diamond-quilted leather came from the G 63, the biturbo successor to the G 55 AMG. The new parts were 18-inch two-piece beadlock wheels, 37-inch tyres, Öhlins gas bypass shocks, stiffer springs, heavier bump stops and, most expensively, the geared portal hubs. Australian magazine 4×4 Australia credits those hubs to the German company LeTech, which designed and builds them.

### FIVE LOCKERS, ONE COMPRESSOR
The transfer case has a 0.87:1 high range and a 2.16:1 low range. Torque is normally split 30:40:30 between the front, middle and rear axles, and an extra shaft drives the rearmost axle. Three dashboard switches lock five differentials in stages. The first locks the transfer case and the through-drive, the second adds both rear axles, and the third adds the front. MotorTrend gave the locked split as 31/42/27 and found, unlike on a normal G, that the locks would engage in high range. Mercedes quotes 460 mm (18.1 in) of ground clearance and a metre of wading depth. A Mercedes display board for the truck gives approach and departure angles of 50° and 45°.
The tyre system is what sets it apart. A compressor feeds four 20-litre tanks hidden in the rear arches. Switches in the overhead console set pressures separately for the front axle and the two rear axles, and Mercedes quotes 0.5 bar for sand to 1.8 bar for the road in under 20 seconds. The beadlocks let the tyres run very soft without coming off the rims. The truck weighs about 3,850 kg, and it carries two fuel tanks totalling 159 litres.

### SOLD OUT, THEN COLLECTED
Autocar quoted £370,000 in the UK, making it the second most expensive Mercedes road car of the time after the SLS Electric Drive. MotorTrend calculated a little under $625,000 at 2013 exchange rates and noted that it was not sold in the United States. Mercedes declared it sold out in February 2015, and the last customer truck left Graz that May. A few right-hand-drive trucks were converted for buyers in South Africa, and Brabus built its own B63S-700 6×6 version. The 6×6 also appeared in Jurassic World.
It also led to later trucks. The G 500 4×4² put a long-wheelbase G body on a shortened 6×6 chassis with portal axles, and the Maybach G 650 Landaulet used the 4×4²'s running gear. In the US, the 6×6s on Bring a Trailer are legal only through NHTSA's Show or Display exemption, which limits them to 2,500 miles a year. Sale prices since 2020 have run from $500,000 to $1.17 million. That makes this the most expensive G-Wagen on the site to use off-road, and the one most likely to get through whatever you point it at.

### Data plate
- Chassis: W463, three axles
- Years: 2013–2015
- Built: About 100, Magna Steyr, Graz
- Engine: M157 5.5 L biturbo V8
- Output: 400 kW (544 PS) · 760 Nm
- Gearbox: 7G-TRONIC 7-speed automatic
- Drive: 6×6, 30:40:30, low range
- Lockers: Five, in three stages
- Axles: Portal, rigid ×3
- Clearance: 460 mm (18.1 in)
- Wading: 1,000 mm (39.4 in)
- Weight: ≈3,850 kg (8,488 lb)

### Engineering
The 6×6 is built from G-Class and military G parts and assembled on the same Graz line as every other G. It has a ladder frame and three rigid portal axles. Each axle is located independently so it can articulate on its own. Five differential locks and a tyre-pressure system do the rest. The engine and gearbox are the same as in the G 63.
- Chassis: Three-axle ladder frame (From the Australian military G; 5,875 mm long, 3,120 mm to the middle axle (Autocar).)
- Axles: Portal, rigid ×3 (Hub reduction gears give 460 mm of ground clearance and 1 m of wading depth.)
- Lockers: Five, in three stages (Transfer case and through-drive, then both rear axles, then the front.)
- Drivetrain: 30:40:30, low range (0.87:1 high and 2.16:1 low; extra shaft to the third axle.)
- Tyres: 37 in on 18 in beadlocks (Compressor and 4 × 20 L tanks; 0.5 to 1.8 bar in under 20 s.)
- Engine: M157 5.5 L biturbo V8 (400 kW (544 PS), 760 Nm; 7G-TRONIC automatic.)

- 2017 · Mercedes-Maybach G 650 Landaulet · V12 · — · Used the 4×4²'s portal axles and raised suspension

- 2013: G 63 AMG 6×6 shown and driven by press in Dubai; limited production begins at Magna Steyr, Graz

### Capability
- Ground clearance: 460 mm (18.1 in) (Mercedes)
- Wading depth: 1,000 mm (39.4 in) (Mercedes)
- Approach / departure: 50° / 45° (Mercedes display board and MotorTrend; Autocar quoted 52° / 54°)
- Breakover: 22° (Autocar)
- Fuel tank: 96 L + 63 L auxiliary (159 L / 42 US gal) (New Atlas; MotorTrend says 38.6 gal total)
- Curb weight: ≈3,850 kg (8,488 lb) (Mercedes; other sources quote 3,775–4,083 kg)
- Fuel economy: 15.6 L/100 km (≈15 mpg US) (European cycle, per Wikipedia)
- Top speed: 160 km/h (100 mph), limited
- Length / width / height: 5,875 / 2,110 / 2,210 mm (Autocar)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 37-inch tyres on 18-inch two-piece beadlock wheels (37×12.50R18 seen on Bring a Trailer trucks)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 37×12.50R18 (Factory size; portal axles already provide 460 mm of clearance)
- Biggest tire, KW coilovers (aftermarket) lift: 38×13.50R18 (One Bring a Trailer truck runs 38×13.50R18 Toyo Open Country M/Ts on LeTech-developed KW coilovers)

### Buying checks
- Factory truck or conversion?: Aftermarket 6×6 conversions of ordinary G 550s, G 63s and G 65s exist and have sold on Bring a Trailer. Factory trucks sold there carry chassis numbers such as WDB4632721X…, plus overhead tyre-pressure controls and a VDO auxiliary fuel gauge. Ask for Mercedes build paperwork.
- US paperwork: In the US, check the NHTSA Show or Display exemption letter, the EPA conversion label and whether NHTSA has approved the transfer. A clean title alone doesn't make it legal to drive.
- Tyre inflation system: Run the pressures down and back up. Mercedes quotes under 20 seconds from 0.5 to 1.8 bar. Slow inflation or a pressure drop overnight points to rotary seals or lines; one Bring a Trailer truck had its CTIS seals and lines replaced.
- Portal hubs and seals: Look for gear oil at each of the six hubs and the pinion seals. Ask when the hubs, differentials and transfer case were last serviced. Bring a Trailer service records mention a replaced centre-axle planetary gear and pinion seal on one truck.
- All five lockers: Engage all three stages and confirm every indicator. The locks are supposed to engage quickly, even in high range, and slow or partial engagement needs investigating.
- The G 63 engine underneath: It's an M157, so check the same things as on a G 63: oil consumption, coolant at the turbo lines, oil in the cam-magnet connectors and plug or coil misfires.
- Modifications and tunes: Brabus, Weistec and other tuners have modified these trucks. Find out exactly what has changed, including engine, exhaust, suspension and tyre size, and whether the original parts come with the truck.
- Tyre age: 37-inch beadlock tyres in the right size are a special order. Read the date codes; a low-mileage truck can easily have tyres ten years old.

### Common repairs
#### Tyre-inflation (CTIS) leaks
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Specialist job · cost Specialist quote
Symptoms: Slow inflation, one axle losing pressure overnight, the compressor running a long time, hissing at a hub.
Fix: Soapy-water test the tanks, lines and fittings, then the rotary seals at each hub. Replace the seals and lines that fail, re-test at road and sand pressures, and check the gauges against a handheld one. One Bring a Trailer truck had its CTIS seals and lines replaced by the US LeTech distributor.
Tools: Spray bottle and soap solution · calibrated tyre gauge · line wrenches

#### Portal hub & differential oil service
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Half a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: No record of hub service, weeping at a hub, metal on a drain plug magnet.
Fix: Drain and refill the six portal hubs, three axle differentials and the transfer case with the specified oils, cleaning every magnetic plug. Investigate any weeping hub before it reaches the brakes.
Tools: Hex and Torx sockets · fluid pump · drain pans · new crush washers

#### Differential locks slow or not engaging
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time An afternoon to diagnose · cost Diagnosis-dependent
Symptoms: A locker indicator that flashes or stays dark, or a lock that engages slowly or drops out.
Fix: Check each stage separately and read fault codes with a scan tool. Then inspect the actuators, wiring and connectors at each axle, where mud and water collect. One Bring a Trailer truck's records list a diff-lock system service by a G specialist.
Tools: Mercedes-capable scan tool · multimeter · contact cleaner

#### Turbo coolant lines (M157)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A day or more · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Coolant loss, coolant crust near the turbos, low-coolant warning.
Fix: Pressure-test the system and replace the turbo feed and return lines as a set. FCP Euro calls them 'a common failure item' on the M157. The job is the same as on a G 63, but with more height to work at.
Tools: Pressure tester · line wrenches · MB 325.6 coolant

#### Plugs, coils & cam magnets (M157)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time 3–4 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Misfires, rough idle, oil in the cam-adjuster magnet connectors.
Fix: Replace all eight plugs and check the coils, as on a G 63. If you find oil in the cam-magnet connectors, fit new magnets with sacrificial pigtails and clean the harness.
Tools: Spark plug socket and extensions · torque wrench · contact cleaner

#### 7G-TRONIC fluid & filter
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time 2–3 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Harsh or delayed shifts, or no record of the job.
Fix: Drain the pan and the converter, replace the filter and gasket, refill with MB 236.15 ATF and set the level at temperature with a scan tool.
Tools: Scan tool · fluid pump · torque wrench

#### Steering damper & front-end play
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Wander, shimmy on the big tyres, clunks over bumps.
Fix: Check the drag link, tie-rod ends and damper. One Bring a Trailer truck was fitted with an upgraded damper and new drag links and toe links. Align after any change, and re-torque the beadlock ring bolts while the wheels are off.
Tools: Tie-rod end puller · torque wrench · alignment afterwards

#### Beadlock wheel & tyre service
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Tyres plus labor
Symptoms: Slow leaks at the bead ring, old tyres, mismatched sizes after a replacement.
Fix: Deflate, remove the ring bolts in sequence, inspect the inner bead and O-ring, then refit with the bolts torqued evenly. Owners have fitted both 37×12.50R18 and 38×13.50R18 tyres. Recode the size and recalibrate the tyre-pressure gauges.
Tools: Torque wrench · bead breaker · thread locker as specified

### Baseline service
Treat a 6×6 as a G 63 engine and gearbox on top of a fleet of differentials: three axles, six portal hubs, a transfer case with a through-drive, plus a compressor and air system. Mercedes and specialist service records matter more here than on any other G. Where a capacity isn't published, have a G specialist confirm it rather than guessing.
- Engine oil & filter: 0W-40 or 5W-40 full synthetic to MB 229.5 · ≈9 qt with filter on the G 63's M157 (AMSOIL; confirm for 6×6) · Then every 10,000 mi or yearly (Same M157 as the G 63, so short intervals protect the turbos and cam adjusters.)
- Air filters: M157 elements (as G 63) · Now, then sooner than usual after desert use (Sand is the 6×6's natural habitat. Check the airbox for dust trails.)
- Spark plugs & coils: 8 plugs (Mercedes 004 159 81 03) · Now if no record
- Engine & charge-air coolant: MB 325.6-approved coolant · two circuits · Now if history is unknown (Pressure-test and inspect the turbo coolant lines.)
- Automatic transmission (722.9): MB 236.15 ATF · Now if no record (Set the level at temperature with a scan tool.)
- Transfer case & through-drive: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now (6×6-specific. Ask a G specialist for the fluid and capacity.)
- Three axle differentials: Hypoid gear oil · capacities [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now (Clean every magnetic plug and check all three breathers.)
- Six portal hubs: Hub reduction gear oil [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now, then with the differentials (Check each hub for weeping and metal on the plug.)
- Tyre-inflation system: Compressor, 4 × 20 L tanks, rotary seals and lines · Leak-test now, then before every trip (Drain water from the tanks if they have drains, and check the gauges against a handheld one.)
- Diff-lock actuation: Five locks in three stages · Test now (Engage each stage on loose ground; scan for codes.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 4 Plus (MB sheet 331.0) · Now, then every 2 years (Six calipers make for a long bleed.)
- Beadlocks & tyres: 37 in on 18 in two-piece beadlocks · Check tyre date codes and ring-bolt torque now (Old tyres on a low-mileage truck are the norm, not the exception.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: It comes with 37-inch tyres on 18-inch beadlocks, and Bring a Trailer trucks show 37×12.50R18 tyres. One owner went up to 38×13.50R18 Toyo Open Country M/Ts, along with KW coilovers. There's no known need for anything bigger.

Q: How many were built?
A: Slightly more than 100 between 2013 and 2015, according to Wikipedia citing GT Spirit. Mercedes declared it sold out in February 2015 and delivered the last customer truck in May 2015.

Q: Is it street legal in the US?
A: Only with restrictions. Mercedes never sold it there. Trucks in the US were federalized by G&K Automotive Conversion and run under NHTSA's Show or Display exemption, capped at 2,500 miles a year, with NHTSA approval needed for each sale.

Q: How many locking differentials does it have?
A: Five, worked by three switches: first the transfer case and through-drive, then both rear axles, then the front. Locked, MotorTrend calculated a 31/42/27 torque split.

Q: How fast does the tyre inflation work?
A: From 0.5 bar (sand) to 1.8 bar (road) in under 20 seconds, according to Mercedes. A compressor fills four 20-litre tanks in the rear arches, and front and rear axles are set separately from the overhead console.

Q: How much ground clearance and wading depth?
A: 460 mm (18.1 in) of ground clearance and 1,000 mm (39.4 in) of wading depth, according to Mercedes. A Mercedes display board for the truck lists 50° approach and 45° departure.

Q: How heavy is it, and what does it drink?
A: About 3,850 kg (8,488 lb), according to Mercedes. Wikipedia lists 15.6 L/100 km (about 15 mpg US) on the European cycle. Two tanks hold 96 + 63 litres (159 L in total), and the auxiliary tank is switched on from the overhead console.

Q: Is it the same as the Australian Army 6×6?
A: No. It's derived from it. The cab, three-axle frame and transfer case come from the military G. The army truck used a 3.0-litre V6 diesel and a five-speed automatic, while the civilian truck has the AMG V8, the seven-speed, portal axles, beadlocks and tyre inflation.

Q: What did it cost new?
A: £370,000 in the UK, according to Autocar. MotorTrend calculated a little under $625,000 at 2013 exchange rates.

Q: What are they worth now?
A: Bring a Trailer sales since 2020 run from $500,000 (a 56k-mile 2014 in May 2026) to $1.17 million (an 8k-mile Brabus B63S-700 in 2022). Several have failed to sell at bids of $800,000–831,000.

Q: How is it different from the 4×4²?
A: The G 500 4×4² is the four-wheel follow-up. It puts a long-wheelbase G body on a shortened 6×6 chassis with portal axles and uses a 4.0-litre V8, but it has four wheels and three lockers rather than six and five.

## Mercedes-Benz G 500 4×4² (2015–2018)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/g-class/4x4-squared/
Codes: W463, Portal axles

Verdict: A G-Class on stilts: portal axles, two springs per corner and 22-inch wheels. Utterly unsubtle — but the 17 inches of ground clearance are entirely real.

The 4×4² — say it “four-by-four squared” — is what happened when Mercedes took the running gear of its six-wheeled G 63 AMG 6×6, removed an entire axle and bolted the result under an ordinary long-wheelbase G. The result stands 88 inches tall, clears 17.2 inches of rock and wades through 39.4 inches of water. Mercedes-Benz USA called it the most capable G-Class ever, and charged $225,000 to prove it.

### FROM SIX WHEELS TO FOUR
It started as a show car. At the Geneva Motor Show in March 2015 Mercedes displayed the G 500 4×4² with no commitment to build it, saying production would depend on the reaction. The reaction was enthusiastic, and Mercedes put it into production in 2015. Underneath it is the body of the five-door long-wheelbase W463 on a shortened version of the 6×6’s chassis.
The trick is the portal axle. A gear drop at each hub puts the wheel centre below the axle tube, so the diffs and axle housings ride far higher than on a normal G — 450 mm (17.7 in) of ground clearance in European spec, against 9.3 inches for a standard G 550. The track grew too, by 299 mm, filled out with detachable carbon-fibre wheel-arch flares and 325/55R22 tires. For the 2017 model year the truck came to America as the G 550 4×4², at $225,000 plus destination.

### TWO SPRINGS PER CORNER
Each wheel gets two spring struts in parallel — one with fixed damping, one adjustable — and Mercedes claimed the switch between Comfort and Sport took 15 milliseconds. Two stabilizer bars help keep it upright, and the drivetrain is pure G: permanent four-wheel drive split 50:50, a low-range transfer case and three 100% differential locks. Power came from the 4.0-litre twin-turbo M176 V8, rated 416 hp and 450 lb-ft in the US, driving through a seven-speed automatic.
Mercedes first showed the idea as a concept nicknamed “Extreme-G”. According to Car and Driver's prototype drive, cited by Wikipedia, the G-Class had sold more than 14,000 units in 2014, and that demand freed up budget for low-volume spin-offs like this one. KW developed the dual-strut suspension, and the truck could reach 60 mph in under six seconds. On paper it beat the Hummer H1 in almost every off-road measurement. The exception was side slope: it was limited to a 28.4° bank angle against the Humvee's 30°.
Mercedes-Benz USA’s numbers are absurd in the best way: 51.6° approach, 43.8° departure, a breakover of 44.6° at maximum load in the spec sheet (47.4° in the launch release), 69-inch-plus track widths, a 46.9-foot turning circle and a 6,694-lb curb weight. It returned 11 mpg city, highway and combined, according to the same sheet. Expedition Portal, not given to gushing about concept trucks, said Mercedes had knocked it “straight out of the park.”

### THE END, AND WHAT CAME NEXT
With the second-generation G due in 2018, Mercedes announced it would stop taking 4×4² orders at the end of October; in Germany it had cost €231,693. Its portal axles and raised suspension lived on in the Mercedes-Maybach G 650 Landaulet, and in 2022 the idea returned as the G 63 4×4² — now with independent front suspension, 585 hp and a $350,050 sticker, and 379 lb lighter than the old truck.
Today the original is a collector’s off-roader that people actually use. Bring a Trailer regularly lists them — one 2017 G 550 4×4² with 39k miles came on Pirelli Scorpion ATRs, with plugs, a coil and transmission service in its records — and shops now build lookalikes: Houston’s Banyan Motors converted a 2000 G 500 with a LeTech dual-suspension setup, portal axles and beadlocks. Rivals? Nothing from the factory, though the new Defender and Grenadier owners will happily argue.

### Data plate
- Chassis: W463 (4×4²)
- Years: 2015–2017 (US: 2017 MY)
- Engine: M176 4.0 L twin-turbo V8
- Output: 416 hp · 450 lb-ft (US)
- Transmission: 7G-TRONIC PLUS 7-speed
- Axles: Portal, rigid front & rear
- Suspension: Dual springs, adjustable dampers
- Clearance: 17.24 in
- Wading: 39.4 in
- Approach / Dep.: 51.6° / 43.8°
- Curb Weight: 6,694 lb
- Us Msrp: $225,000

### Engineering
The 4×4² keeps the G-Class fundamentals — ladder frame, rigid axles front and rear, full-time four-wheel drive and three lockers — and changes the geometry around them. Portal hubs lift the axle housings; a wider track and dual-spring suspension keep the tall truck stable. Mercedes-Benz USA noted that the portal design let it leave suspension geometry, steering links and driveshafts essentially unchanged from other G-Class models while reducing driveshaft load.
- Chassis: Ladder frame (Shortened version of the G 63 AMG 6×6’s chassis under a long-wheelbase W463 body.)
- Axles: Portal, rigid (Longitudinal and transverse links front and rear; hub reduction gears drop the wheel centre below the axle.)
- Suspension: Dual springs, adjustable dampers (Two struts per wheel; Comfort/Sport switching claimed at 15 ms. Two stabilizer bars.)
- Drivetrain: Permanent 4WD, 50:50 (Low-range transfer case; 7G-TRONIC PLUS seven-speed automatic.)
- Lockers: Centre, rear, front (Three 100% locks, engaged on the move.)
- Geometry: 51.6° / 43.8° (Approach and departure. 17.24 in clearance at max load, 39.4 in fording (MBUSA).)

- 2015–2017 · G 500 4×4² (Europe) · M176 4.0 L twin-turbo V8 · 310 kW (422 PS) · €231,693 in Germany; orders closed ahead of the 2018 second-generation G

### Year-by-year
- 2013: G 63 AMG 6×6 introduced. Its portal-axle running gear is the basis for the 4×4²; just over 100 sold, last delivery May 2015
- 2015: G 500 4×4² goes into production after a positive reaction to the concept car; four-litre twin-turbo V8, KW dual-spring suspension
- 2017: Sold in the US for MY2017 as the G 550 4×4² at $225,000 plus $925 destination; deliveries from early 2017
- 2017: Mercedes-Maybach G 650 Landaulet inherits the portal axles; 99 built
- Oct 2017: Ordering closes ahead of the second-generation G; some US trucks are titled as 2018 models
- 2022: Mercedes-AMG G 63 4×4² revives the idea on the new G, with portal axles and independent front suspension
- 2022–2023: Rear differential housing recalls (22V937, 23V851) on the new G 63 4×4²; check the VIN

### Capability

- Approach / departure / breakover: 51.6° / 43.8° / 44.6° (breakover at maximum load; launch release quoted 47.4°)
- Wading depth: 39.4 in (1,000 mm)
- Max tilt angle: 28.4°
- Fuel tank: 25.4 US gal (96 L)
- Fuel economy: EPA 11 city / 11 hwy / 11 comb
- Curb weight: 6,694 lb (3,036 kg)
- Turning circle: 46.9 ft (14.3 m)
- Height / width: 88.0 in / 86.2 in with mirrors

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 325/55R22 on 9.5x22 wheels (≈36 in)
- Biggest tire, Stock (portal axles) lift: 37x12.5R18 mud-terrain (Mercedes said 37x12.5x18 mud-terrains would be available for production trucks, and concept photos showed 37-inch tires on beadlocks. Mercedes-Benz USA says larger tires don't need a speedometer recalibration. Check caliper clearance before going to 18-inch wheels)

### Buying checks
- Make sure it’s a real one: Shops build 4×4² lookalikes from ordinary Gs — some, like Banyan Motors’ portal-axle G 500, are serious builds, but they aren’t factory trucks. Confirm the VIN, window sticker and data card.
- Price the tires before the truck: Factory fitment is 325/55R22 on 9.5×22 wheels — big, heavy and not cheap. Check tread depth and date codes, and whether the spare matches.
- Test the adjustable dampers: Switch between Comfort and Sport on the drive. You should feel the difference immediately; a fault light or no change means a damper or control problem.
- Test all three lockers: Engage centre, rear and front on a loose surface and watch the indicators. Trucks that never left pavement often have lazy lockers.
- Inspect the carbon flares and roof: The detachable carbon-fibre arch extensions and roof-mounted lights live high and wide — look for cracks, chips and scratches (one BaT example noted roof scratches).
- Ask for the service file: Spark plugs, ignition coils, transmission fluid and filter, brake fluid — the BaT example’s history shows the kind of records to expect. Ask specifically about portal-hub and axle oil changes.
- Measure your garage: It’s 88 inches tall and 86.2 inches wide with mirrors. Parking structures and automatic car washes are now hostile territory.
- Rust where nobody cleans: It’s still a W463: check the tailgate lower edge, door bottoms, sills, rear frame tubes and strut mounts.

### Common repairs
#### Spark plugs & ignition coils (M176)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Misfire codes, rough idle, hesitation under load. Plugs are a scheduled item; coils fail individually.
Fix: Remove the engine covers, unplug and pull each coil, and replace the plugs with the correct Mercedes-spec part, torqued to spec. Swap any coil that misfire data points to — or move coils between cylinders to confirm before buying.
Tools: Mercedes-spec spark plugs · ignition coil(s) as needed · thin-wall spark-plug socket and extensions · torque wrench · scan tool

#### Seven-speed fluid & filter service
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Harsh or slurred shifts, or simply no record of a service. The 7G-TRONIC has no dipstick, so fluid level is set by temperature.
Fix: Drain the pan, replace the filter and pan gasket, refill with the Mercedes-approved fluid, then set the level at the specified temperature using a scan tool to read transmission temperature.
Tools: Filter and gasket kit · MB-approved ATF · fill adapter/pump · scan tool for fluid temperature · torque wrench

#### Diff locks won’t engage
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Diagnosis-dependent
Symptoms: A lock refuses to engage or drops out; indicator lights flash. On W463s the cause is usually actuation — vacuum or wiring — rather than the differential.
Fix: Work the system from the actuator back: confirm vacuum or signal at each lock, then trace lines and connectors toward the source with a gauge or meter. Fix the leak, then exercise the locks regularly.
Tools: Hand vacuum pump with gauge · multimeter · vacuum tees and line · replacement connectors

#### Steering damper & wander
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost $300–800
Symptoms: Wander, wheel shake at highway speed, vague on-centre feel, clunks — amplified by tall tires and a rigid front axle.
Fix: Replace the steering damper with an OEM or upgraded unit, check drag link and tie-rod ends for play, then align. The 4×4² keeps the G’s steering linkage, so the usual W463 diagnosis applies.
Tools: Steering damper · sockets and wrenches · tie-rod or drag-link ends if worn

#### Sunroof drains & water ingress
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 30 minutes · cost Cheap if caught early
Symptoms: Damp or sagging headliner, wet carpets, electrical gremlins.
Fix: Clear all four sunroof drains, then check the headliner, fuse box and climate actuators for water damage.
Tools: Trimmer line or drain-cleaning wire · low-pressure air · towels

#### Frame & body rust treatment
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A weekend · cost $400–8,000 (severity-dependent)
Symptoms: Bubbling at the tailgate lower edge, door bottoms and sills; scale on the rear frame tubes and strut mounts.
Fix: Wire-brush or blast back to sound metal, treat and paint, or cut in repair panels where needed. Inject cavity wax into doors and frame rails, keep drain paths clear and wash off road salt after winter.
Tools: Wire wheels or blaster · rust converter and primer · cavity wax with extension wand · welder for panel repairs

#### Brake booster vacuum hose recall (17V-817)
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time Minutes to check. Dealer visit for the fix. · cost Free under recall
Symptoms: A hard brake pedal that needs more effort than usual to stop the truck. The booster's vacuum hose can collapse.
Fix: NHTSA recall 17V-817 covers 432 model-year 2017 G 550 and G 550 4×4² trucks. The brake-booster vacuum hose may collapse and raise braking effort, and dealers replace the hose as needed for free. Run the VIN at nhtsa.gov/recalls before you buy, and ask for the paperwork if it's been done. On a 6,694-lb truck, this is not one to put off.
Tools: VIN · Mercedes-Benz dealer

#### Oil leaks from the crankcase vent oil separators (M176)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time Separators: a few hours. Rear main seal: transmission out (shop job). · cost Rear main seal: about $5 in parts but $3,000–5,000 in labor (Handsome Motors)
Symptoms: Oil seeping from the valve covers or from where the engine meets the transmission, a burning-oil smell, and oil consumption between changes.
Fix: Handsome Motors, which has owned more than 200 Gs, says the 2016–2018 G 550's M176 suffers rear main seal and valve cover gasket leaks triggered by a failed crankcase-vent oil separator. The 4×4² uses the same engine. Fix the cause first by replacing the left and right oil separators, which FCP Euro lists for the G 550 4×4², and then deal with any valve cover leaks. A rear main seal leak means removing the transmission. Handsome Motors also suggests 3,000–5,000-mile oil changes on these engines.
Tools: Socket set · torque wrench · trim tools for the engine covers · new seals and gaskets

### Baseline service
The 4×4² shares its engine, gearbox and lockers with the 2016–2018 G 550, so the drivetrain basics are the same — but the portal axles add hub reduction gears that a regular G doesn’t have, and many shops have never serviced one. Baseline everything, and confirm portal-axle specs with a Mercedes dealer.
- Engine oil & filter: M176 4.0 twin-turbo · MB 229.5 · 2.4 US gal (9.0 L) with filter (2018 G-Class manual, G 550) · Now, then when the ASSYST service interval display calls for it (owner's manual) (The 2018 manual, which also covers the 4×4², lists MB 229.5 for all models. FCP Euro lists its 9-litre 229.52 kit and the Mann filter kit for the G 550 4×4². Check that whatever oil you use carries an approval your manual allows.)
- Air filters: M176 air filter set · Now if undated (Dusty trail use loads the filters quickly.)
- Cabin air filter: W463 cabin filter · Now, then yearly
- Spark plugs & coils: M176 spark plugs (Mercedes-spec) · Now if no record [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Pulling the coils means removing the engine covers; read the misfire counters first.)
- Coolant: MB 325.6 (FCP Euro lists Genuine Mercedes for the 2015-on G 550) · approx. 14.9 US qt (14.1 L) (2018 manual, G 550) · Now if undated (Check hoses and the expansion-tank cap while you’re there.)
- Automatic transmission (7G-TRONIC PLUS 722.9): MB 236.15 (blue) · Now if no record [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (No dipstick: new filter and pan gasket, then set the level at temperature with a scan tool.)
- Transfer case: Fluid type and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now if no record (Same two-speed case and centre lock as the G 550.)
- Front & rear differentials: Gear oil type and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now if no record (The portal axles come from the G 63 AMG 6×6 — don’t assume standard G 550 capacities.)
- Portal hub reduction gears: Oil type and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now if no record (Each wheel has its own gear set. The 2018 G-Class manual tells owners of the 4×4² to change the axle differential and portal transmission oil after a 2,000-mile (3,000 km) break-in period, so ask for proof it was done. Check every hub for weeps and compare the oil from each corner. A dealer that has done one before is worth finding.)
- Diff locks: Inspection — engage centre, rear, front in order · Now, then monthly exercise (Disuse kills lockers. If one won’t engage, trace vacuum or wiring before suspecting the differential.)
- Power steering fluid: Type [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] — MB 236.3 on earlier hydraulic W463s · Now if dark or no record (Never mix power steering fluid with ATF.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 4 Plus (Genuine Mercedes) · MB approval 331.0 (owner's manual) · Now, then every 2 years [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (At 6,694 lb on 22-inch wheels, the brakes work hard — start with fresh fluid.)
- Drive belt: M176 accessory belt · Inspect now; replace if cracked or undated
- Tires, dampers & battery: 325/55R22 tires · dual springs with adjustable dampers · group 49 AGM battery · At purchase (Check the tire date codes — replacements are big and expensive. Look for leaking dampers at all eight units. Load-test the battery: these trucks often sit for long periods.)

### FAQ
Q: What’s the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: It doesn't need one — the portal axles are the lift. Stock tires are 325/55R22, about 36 inches tall. When Mercedes showed the truck, it said 37×12.5×18 mud-terrains would be available for production trucks, and its concept photos showed 37-inch mud-terrains on beadlocks. Mercedes-Benz USA says larger off-road tires can be fitted without recalibrating the speedometer, because it reads from the axles. Check caliper clearance before going to 18-inch wheels.

Q: Was the 4×4² sold in the US?
A: Yes, for the 2017 model year, as the G 550 4×4². Mercedes-Benz USA listed it at $225,000 plus a $925 destination charge, with deliveries from early 2017.

Q: How much ground clearance and wading depth?
A: 17.24 inches at maximum load and 39.4 inches of fording depth in US spec — up 7.9 and 15.8 inches respectively over a 2016 G 550. European figures are 450 mm and 1,000 mm.

Q: What are its approach and departure angles?
A: 51.6° approach and 43.8° departure. Mercedes quoted breakover as 47.4° in its launch release and 44.6° at maximum load in the spec sheet.

Q: Is it just a G 63 6×6 with an axle missing?
A: Partly. It uses a shortened version of the 6×6’s chassis and portal running gear, but with the five-door long-wheelbase body, the G 500/G 550’s 4.0-litre twin-turbo V8 and a seven-speed automatic.

Q: What fuel economy does it get?
A: Mercedes-Benz USA’s spec sheet lists 11 mpg city, 11 highway and 11 combined. The fuel tank holds 25.4 gallons.

Q: Will it fit in my garage?
A: Maybe not. It’s 88.0 inches tall, 86.2 inches wide including mirrors and 177.1 inches long, with a 46.9-foot turning circle.

Q: How heavy is it?
A: 6,694 lb curb weight — almost a thousand pounds more than a regular G 550.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: Mercedes-Benz USA’s 2017 spec sheet listed towing as “TBA,” so check the owner’s manual and hitch rating for your specific truck rather than assuming the regular G 550’s figure.

Q: Can I use the diff locks on pavement?
A: No. Locked diffs bind the driveline on grippy surfaces. Lock up on loose ground at low speed and unlock before tarmac.

Q: How is it different from the newer G 63 4×4²?
A: The 2022-on G 63 4×4² is built on the second-generation G with independent front suspension, makes 585 hp and costs $350,050. It has less clearance (13.8 in) and wading depth (35.8 in) than the original, and weighs 379 lb less.
