# AM General Hummer H1 (1992–2006)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/hummer/

In 1983 AM General won the Army contract for the M998 High Mobility Multipurpose Wheeled Vehicle, the HMMWV, and it had already trademarked the nickname its prototypes went by: Hummer. After the Gulf War made the truck famous, and with Arnold Schwarzenegger lobbying for a road-legal version, AM General began selling a civilian Hummer in 1992. It was built in Mishawaka, Indiana, alongside the military trucks. The Hummer H1 kept the hardware that matters off-road: geared portal hubs, inboard disc brakes, a central tire inflation system and 16 inches of ground clearance. GM diesels powered most of them, from the 6.2 to the 6.5 turbo, plus a 5.7 gas V8 for two years and the Duramax in the final 2006 Alpha. AM General built 11,818 of them, ending in June 2006. GM bought the Hummer brand in 1999. It renamed the original truck the H1 and added its own H2 and H3, both built on GM truck platforms, before closing the brand in 2010. GM revived the name in 2020 for the electric GMC Hummer EV. Only the H1 is a HMMWV underneath, and it's the only one this site covers.

Verdict: An Army truck with carpets, built on the same line as the real thing and twice as wide as common sense. It goes almost anywhere, seats four, and asks for an idler arm in return.

## AM General Hummer H1 (1992–2006)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/hummer/h1/
Codes: HMMWV-based, 6.2 / 6.5 / 6.5 TD, 5.7 V8, Alpha 6.6 Duramax

Verdict: A military truck with a stereo, built on the same line as the Army's and engineered to follow tanks. It's slow and wide, and it eats front ends, but geared hubs, inboard brakes and CTIS let it go places nothing else this size can.

The Hummer H1 is what happened when a defense contractor took a call from a movie star. Underneath, it's the Army's M998 HMMWV with gloss paint, carpet and a stereo. The frame, axles and brakes are shared with the military trucks, and so are the hood, tailgate and quarter panels. AM General built both versions on the same Mishawaka, Indiana, line from 1992 to 2006, 11,818 civilian trucks in all. It is 86.5 inches wide, seats four either side of a driveline tunnel the size of a footlocker, and can climb a 22-inch step. Nothing else on this site was built to that brief.

### FROM JEEP'S DEFENSE ARM TO THE HUMVEE
AM General began as the General Products Division of Kaiser Jeep, the old Studebaker defense plant in South Bend. American Motors made it a subsidiary in 1971. In 1979 the Army published draft specifications for one truck to replace the M151 jeep, the M561 Gama Goat and the commercial-based CUCV pickups. It had to have a diesel, 16 inches of ground clearance and enough ability to climb a 60 percent grade. AM General developed its entry as a private venture and finished its first prototype in August 1980.
In July 1981 the Army ordered 11 prototypes each from AM General, Chrysler and Teledyne. They were tested at Aberdeen Proving Ground and Yuma. On March 22, 1983, AM General won the production contract for 55,000 HMMWVs. That same year LTV bought AM General: Renault had taken a large stake in AMC, and federal rules barred defense contractors owned by foreign governments, which included partly state-owned Renault. AM General had nicknamed its prototypes 'Hummer' and had the foresight to trademark it. Humvees were in service by 1985.

### ARNOLD'S TRUCK
AM General had considered a civilian model since the late 1980s. Gulf War photographs and Arnold Schwarzenegger, who saw an Army convoy while filming Kindergarten Cop in Oregon, made the case. The civilian Hummer went on sale in 1992, and Schwarzenegger bought the first two. At first there were no dealers. You ordered from the factory and could collect the truck in Indiana. Flash Off-Road's year-by-year guide lists the 1992 truck with a mechanical 150-hp 6.2-liter GM diesel, a three-speed 3L80 automatic and a 65-mph top speed. It built 316 that year.
Then came constant change. Because of how the military contracts were written, AM General slipped fixes into production as soon as they were ready, not just at model-year changes. In 1994 the trucks got the 6.5 diesel and a four-speed 4L80-E. For 1995 a 5.7-liter gas V8 was offered to buyers who were wary of diesel, and it was dropped during 1996. In 1996 the 6.5 turbo diesel and a second fuel tank arrived, and by 1997 the turbo made 195 hp and 430 lb-ft.

### HOW IT CLEARS 16 INCHES
The H1's clearance doesn't come from a lift. Each wheel has a geared hub, a portal reduction box with a 1.92:1 ratio in the 1999 brochure. It sits the axle shaft above the wheel center, so the halfshafts and differentials ride high in a channel down the middle of the truck. The disc brakes are inboard, next to the differentials, rather than in the wheels. Suspension is independent double A-arms with coil springs at every corner, and the track is 71.6 inches, wide enough to follow tank tracks. Mercedes used the same portal-axle trick decades later on the G 500 4×4².
Wading depth is 30 inches with a diesel, thanks to a high air intake and a radiator mounted high and sloped over the engine. The central tire inflation system lets the driver air the tires down or up from the cab, front and rear pairs together, and runflat inserts were optional. Torsen I differentials handled traction through 1998. In 1999 ABS arrived, along with Torsen II units and electronic TorqTrac4 traction control, and Eaton electric lockers followed from 2003.

### GM, THE ALPHA AND THE END
In December 1999 General Motors bought the Hummer brand name and took over marketing. AM General kept building the truck, now called the H1, and also built GM's own H2 under contract. GM's smaller H3 came from a GM plant in Shreveport, Louisiana. In 2001 AM General began building the 6.5 diesels itself, having taken over GM's engine plant, and the 2004 'Optimizer' 6.5 made 205 hp. That set up the last and best H1: the Alpha, shown in Anaheim on October 27, 2004.
The Alpha used GM's 6.6-liter Duramax LLY, rated at 300 hp and 520 lb-ft, with an Allison five-speed automatic. To make room, AM General lifted the body 2 inches and redesigned the cooling. It also fitted helical-cut gears in the hubs, a stronger steering box and 51 gallons of fuel. There was no 2005 model year. Only 729 Alphas were built, at about $128,000 to $140,000 each. In May 2006 GM announced the end, with sales slow and new diesel emissions rules due for 2007, and production stopped in June. The Hummer brand itself closed in 2010. The name returned in 2020 on the electric GMC Hummer EV.

- Wheelbase / Width: 130 in / 86.5 in
- Ground Clearance: 16 in
- Engines: GM 6.2 & 6.5 diesel · 6.5 TD · 5.7 V8 gas · 6.6 Duramax LLY (2006)
- Transmissions: 3L80 3-spd · 4L80-E 4-spd · Allison 1000 5-spd (2006)
- Transfer Case: New Venture NVG 242, full-time
- Axle Ratio: 2.73:1 to 1997 · 2.56:1 from 1998
- Geared Hubs: 1.92:1 portal reduction
- Fording: 30 in diesel · 24 in gas

### Engineering
The H1 is the HMMWV's driveline under a civilian body. A steel ladder frame carries independent double-A-arm suspension at all four corners. The engine sits well back, and the transmission, transfer case and both differentials run down a central tunnel. Halfshafts from the differentials drive geared hubs at the wheels, which drop the wheel center below the axle line. That's where the 16 inches of clearance comes from, along with the inboard brakes mounted at the differentials.
- Chassis: Steel box-section ladder frame (Five crossmembers; 130-in wheelbase, 86.5-in width (1999 brochure))
- Suspension: Independent double A-arms, coils (16-in ground clearance; 71.6-in track)
- Geared Hubs: Portal reduction at each wheel (1.92:1 (1999). Spur gears, cross-cut for noise from 1999; helical on the Alpha)
- Brakes: Four-wheel inboard discs (10.5-in rotors at the differentials; ABS from 1999; 12-in rotors on the Alpha)
- Driveline: Full-time 4WD, NVG 242 transfer case (Torsen I to 1998, Torsen II with TorqTrac4 from 1999; Eaton E-lockers from 2003)
- Tires: Central tire inflation (CTIS) (Inflate or deflate front and rear pairs from the cab; runflat inserts optional)

### Versions
- 1992–1993 · H1 · 6.2 diesel · GM 6.2 V8 diesel (mechanical injection) · 150 hp · 3L80 three-speed automatic, 25-gal tank, batteries under the passenger seat. No overdrive; 316 built for 1992.
- 1994–1998 · H1 · 6.5 diesel · GM 6.5 V8 diesel, naturally aspirated · 170 hp / 290 lb-ft · Electronic controls and the 4L80-E four-speed from 1994. The non-turbo diesel was dropped for 1999.
- 1995–1996 · H1 · gas · GM 5.7 L05 V8, throttle-body injection · 190 hp / 300 lb-ft · 23-gal tank and 24-in fording depth. Dropped during 1996.
- 1996–2003 · H1 · 6.5 turbo diesel · GM (from 2001 AM General) 6.5 V8 turbo diesel · 190 hp / 385 lb-ft (1996); 195 hp / 430 lb-ft (1997 on) · Second fuel tank from 1996. Blocks from 1996 to early 1999 are at risk of a crack at the No. 8 cylinder.
- 2004 · H1 · Optimizer · 6.5 V8 turbo diesel with Caterpillar-built ECM · 205 hp / 440 lb-ft · Changed to meet emissions rules. New interior; optional front and rear Eaton lockers. There was no 2005 model year.

### Year-by-year
- 1992: Civilian Hummer launches: mechanical 6.2 diesel (150 hp), 3L80 three-speed, 25-gal tank, batteries under the passenger seat, non-adjustable seats. Sold factory-direct at first. 316 built
- 1994: Electronic 6.5 diesel (170 hp, 290 lb-ft) and 4L80-E four-speed; batteries move under the hood; new HVAC, adjustable seats, catalytic converter
- 1995: 5.7 gas V8 option (23-gal tank, 24-in fording); extended-cab pickup and full-door open top added; wagon gets barn doors. From VIN 163985, stronger steering arms, center link and ball joints
- 1996: 6.5 turbo diesel arrives (190 hp, 385 lb-ft) with a second fuel tank on every truck; new CTIS with solenoid valves; body raised 3/4 in; gas engine dropped mid-year. Start of the No. 8-cylinder crack risk period
- 1997: Turbo diesel to 195 hp and 430 lb-ft with oil-cooled pistons; sound insulation; Detroit Locker optional. From VIN 176477 ('97.5') a much better redesigned HVAC system
- 1998: Flash Off-Road says many consider it the quintessential pre-Alpha H1: 2.56 axles, cam camber adjustment, quieter hubs, and the last Torsen I year before ABS. But '97–'98 turbo diesels are the most common No. 8 crack years, so test the block [buy]
- 1999: ABS, TorqTrac4 traction control and Torsen II differentials; naturally aspirated diesel dropped. AM General starts fitting improved 6.5 blocks from May. GM buys the Hummer brand in December
- 2000: Slant-back body offered (39 built, per Flash Off-Road); 16.5-in and 17-in aluminum wheel options; redesigned cabin. Later 2000 trucks (after VIN 137ZA9037YE188469) not at risk of the No. 8 crack
- 2001: First AM General-built 6.5 engines ('F' in the fourth VIN digit); redesigned gauges and heated mirrors
- 2002: Higher torque-bias differentials; H1 badging; 10th Anniversary edition of 65 orange wagons; two- and four-door hardtops dropped except for fleets
- 2003: Optional Eaton electric rear locker; factory leather and heated seats
- 2004: 'Optimizer' 6.5 turbo diesel with Caterpillar-built ECM (205 hp, 440 lb-ft); all-new interior; optional front and rear Eaton lockers. Flash Off-Road calls it the best stock truck yet. No 2005 model year follows [buy]
- 2006: H1 Alpha: 6.6 Duramax (300 hp, 520 lb-ft), Allison five-speed, 2-in body lift, helical-gear hubs, 12-in brakes, 51 gal of fuel. 729 built; production ends June 2006 [buy]

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 37x12.50R16.5 LT load range D Goodyear Wrangler MT radial on 16.5-in wheels (1999 brochure), 37x12.5R17 on 17-in aluminum wheels (offered from 2000; 16.5-in aluminum wheels discontinued by 2002)
- Bolt Pattern: 8x165.1 (8x6.5")
- Offset: 7-in backset on all factory wheels; a GT/Cepek 17x9 is +50 mm
- Center Bore: About 4-3/4 in on the hub-centric factory one-piece steel wheel
- Lug Thread: 9/16-18 (7/8-in hex nut; a 22 mm socket fits)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 38x15.5 (Flash Off-Road calls this the largest tire for stock wheels without a lift. Watch for contact with the suspension in tight turns. Load ratings on 38s are lower than on most 37s.)
- Biggest tire, 1 in (body) lift: 40 in (MT/R) (Flash Off-Road saw a 40-in MTR on a turbo diesel with a 1-in body lift, but notes the 40s were load range C against E for the 37s.)
- Biggest tire, 2 in (body) lift: 39.5 in (Owners quoted by Flash Off-Road ran 39.5s with a 2-in body lift and no rubbing. Flash estimates 42s need about 3 in and slight trimming.)
- Biggest tire, 4 in (2 in suspension + 2 in body) lift: Up to 42 in (Predator Inc's recommendation for its combined 4-in kit.)

### Buying checks
- Cold-start the turbo diesel and check the coolant: 1996 to early-1999 6.5 turbo diesels can crack at the No. 8 cylinder. Flash Off-Road's test: with the engine stone cold, open the radiator cap, run the engine for about a minute, shut it off and open the cap again. Pressure in the coolant, foaming at the bleeder once it's warm, or milky sludge in the CDR valve point to a cracked block or head gasket. A 'Z' in the fourth VIN digit is a GM-built turbo engine; an 'F' is the later AM General engine.
- Front-end play: Flash Off-Road calls the front end the H1's biggest weakness: idler arms, pitman arms and steering gears wear out. With the engine running, if the steering wheel moves an inch or two before the front wheels do, suspect the pitman arm. If the steering turns more easily one way than the other, suspect the steering box. Uneven tire wear points to worn front-end parts or a bad alignment.
- Geared-hub and halfshaft leaks: A fan of oil sprayed on the inside of a tire means a leaking hub seal. So does a CTIS that won't hold air, through the spindle seal. Look for torn halfshaft boots, and wet spots where the shafts meet the differentials and hubs. Wet calipers can be differential oil, because the brakes sit right next to the differentials.
- Make the CTIS work: Run the pump on the fronts, the rears and all four, and watch the cab gauge. Owners do abandon CTIS when the pump dies, and Flash Off-Road says a new pump can cost well over $1,000. Retrofitting CTIS, the four-speed transmission or the second fuel tank to a truck that lacks them is hard and rarely worth it, so buy the features you want.
- Transfer case fluid and the 'vampire': Pull the transfer case fill plug. If fluid pours out, the cooler loop inside the case may be leaking transmission fluid into it, the 'vampire' that AM General addressed with customer-satisfaction campaign R0101 in 2001. Brown, burnt fluid is a sign of long stretches at 80 mph. Flash Off-Road recommends keeping it under about 65 mph (2,400 rpm).
- Heater and A/C: pre- or post-1997.5: The HVAC system used from 1994 leaked heater cores and was replaced from VIN 176477 (the '97.5'). Flash Off-Road says the old parts are discontinued and the upgrade runs $3,000 to $4,000. Upgraded systems use a vacuum-controlled heater valve and lack separate recirculate and A/C buttons on the control head.
- Correct wheels and tires: Every H1 wheel uses an 8x6.5-in bolt pattern with a 7-in backset. Flash Off-Road says only AM General and GT/Cepek wheels have the right offset and load rating. Wrong wheels stress the front end, need custom CTIS lines and throw dirt up the sides. Tires for 16.5-in wheels are scarce, so check the spare.
- Body, rockers and underside: The body is aluminum but the doors and wagon top are steel. Expect some corrosion where the two meet and around the marker lights, and lift the wheel-well carpet on wagons to check the inner seams. Look for bent rockers and undercarriage protection pushed up against the exhaust, which comes from off-road use.

### Common repairs
#### Replace geared-hub output and spindle seals
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 1.5–2 hours per hub (Flash Off-Road) · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Oil sprayed on the inside of a tire, oil dripping off the lower ball joint, or a CTIS pair that loses pressure overnight. Pull the hub's breather line and put it under water: bubbles mean CTIS air is leaking past the spindle seal into the hub.
Fix: Jack under the lower A-arm and chock the truck. Disconnect the CTIS line on the opposite wheel so it doesn't deflate. Drain the hub with a 5/16-in hex. Remove the CTIS line and the four 3/4-in steering-arm cover bolts, then the snap ring, and tap out the small spindle seal. Remove the clamp-nut lock screw and the clamp nut, and lay out the nut, keyed washer and bearing in order. Pull the spindle, drive out the output seal, clean the bore and the spindle's sealing surface, and drive the new seal flat. Reassemble following the AM General manual's clamp-nut sequence with red Loctite 272 inside its 10-minute window (lock screw 90 lb-in). Clear the hub vent line, then refill with GL-5 80W-90 or 75W-90 to just under the fill plug, about half a quart.
Tools: 5/16-in hex · 5/8 and 13/16-in wrenches · 3/4-in socket · 5/32-in hex socket · clamp-nut socket (Flash Off-Road made one from a NAPA 2467 Dana 44 spindle socket) · snap-ring pliers · inch-lb and ft-lb torque wrenches · Loctite 272 and 518 · output seal 5579060, spindle seal 6005193 (Flash Off-Road)

#### Replace the idler and pitman arms
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Steering wheel off-center or loose, with an inch or more of free play before the wheels move. Front tires that splay apart over obstacles. A shimmy at around 35 mph that fades by 40. The shop manual's limits are 5/16 in of vertical play at the center link for the idler, 1/8 in for the pitman, and 1/32 in at either ball stud.
Fix: Unbolt the idler arm from the frame and separate it from the center link with a puller or pickle fork. Flash Off-Road had to cut away the rubber seal first. With the idler off, the center link drops and the pitman arm comes off the steering box shaft. Pack grease around the box output shaft. Fit the new pitman on the splines and the center link together, torque the big nut to 180 lb-ft and the 15/16-in ball-stud nut to 80 lb-ft, and line up the cotter pin. Bolt the new idler to the frame at 60 lb-ft and its ball stud at 80 lb-ft, then grease both. 1993–94 trucks with the 7/8-in center link need spacers; the 1-in link started at VIN 163985.
Tools: Pitman puller · 1-5/16-in socket and breaker bar · 18 mm, 11/16 and 5/8-in sockets · torque wrench to 180 lb-ft · jack stands · cotter pins · AM General idler 5745558 and pitman 6011300 (Flash Off-Road, 2005)

#### Relocate the 6.5 TD's pump-mounted driver (PMD/FSD)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ An afternoon · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: A turbo diesel that stalls when hot and restarts once it cools, then gets harder to restart as the fault worsens. Codes P0251 and P0370 point at the injection pump's optical sensor and the PMD. A fuel shutoff solenoid problem is different: it sputters before stalling.
Fix: First rule out fuel: change the filter, check the lift pump and look for a kinked return hose. The Stanadyne DS4831 pump on 1996–2004 turbo diesels carries its electronic driver (PMD, also called FSD) on the pump itself, in the engine's heat. Fit a new PMD on a remote heat sink outside the engine bay, with thermal paste and the extension harness. If codes persist, have a Stanadyne shop check the pump; Flash Off-Road says to fit a DS4831-5288 or -5521, not the early -5067.
Tools: Torx and socket set · thermal compound · scan tool to read and clear codes · Stanadyne fuel additive

#### Replace the fuel shutoff solenoid
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 30 minutes · cost Parts only (about $70 rebuilt in 2012, per Flash Off-Road)
Symptoms: Occasional hard starts, sputtering and stalling while driving, and an engine that won't restart straight away. This differs from a PMD fault, which usually stalls without sputtering.
Fix: Disconnect the connector and unscrew the solenoid from the top of the injection pump (1/2-in hex). Don't lose the coil spring in the bore, and keep dirt out of the pump. Install the new solenoid, torque it to 200 lb-in per Stanadyne, and reconnect it.
Tools: 1/2-in wrench · inch-lb torque wrench · clean rags

#### Find and fix a CTIS leak
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ An afternoon to several days of testing · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: One axle's tires drop pressure overnight, or CTIS won't inflate or deflate at all. The fronts and rears are paired, so a leak can be in either tire, either hub seal, the lines, the manifold solenoids, the over-pressure valve or the pump.
Fix: Spray soapy water on the tires, rims, lines and fittings. Inflate to normal, pull both quick-disconnects at the wheels and leave it overnight. If the cab gauge drops, the leak is in the lines, manifold or pump; if not, reconnect one wheel at a time to find the leaking tire or hub. Bubble-test each hub vent for a bad spindle seal. Check the braided hose swivel at the hub with the wheels turned both ways. Clean sand out of the manifold solenoid valves. If the pump won't run, jump it from the battery, then check the 5-amp (1G) and 40-amp fuses and the relay, per Gil Herman's checklist on Flash Off-Road.
Tools: Spray bottle · 7/8-in and 1-3/16-in deep sockets (the latter sold as a GM oil-sender socket) · 9/16-in wrench · multimeter · jumper lead

#### Rebuild or replace a halfshaft
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day per shaft · cost Boot kits under $10 locally in Flash Off-Road's report; a shop charged $25 a boot or $50 a joint
Symptoms: Torn boots throwing grease, clicking on turns, or a worn seal surface where the shaft enters the hub input seal.
Fix: The halfshaft bolts to the inboard brake rotor at one end and splines into the geared hub at the other. On the right rear you must remove the parking brake cable to get it out. Each CV joint has a star, cage and six balls, and the cage is usually what fails. Flash Off-Road says the 1994-on joints share Rockford parts with the 1993–98 Mercury Villager and Ford Explorer. Fit new boots and clips, and a Speedi-Sleeve (99199) if the seal surface is grooved. Reinstall the six M10 class 10.9 bolts with new Nord-Lock washer pairs and red Loctite at 57 lb-ft. Overtightening can warp the rotor.
Tools: 3/8-in drive short socket and extension · retaining-ring pliers · CV boot crimper · torque wrench · Nord-Lock washers · Loctite 272

#### Replace inboard brake pads (and rotors)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Pads under 1/8 in, chatter from new pads, a pulsing pedal from warped rotors, or fluid on the caliper from a piston seal.
Fix: The front and rear pads are the same; the front calipers are Jeep parts and the rears carry the parking brake. Fronts retract with pliers, while the rear pistons must be turned to retract. Flash Off-Road shows how to do it without the $350 Kent-Moore tool. Chamfer the edges of new pads to stop chatter. Rotors have a minimum thickness of 0.815 in cast into them. Replacing or turning them means removing the halfshaft bolts, so have new Nord-Lock washers ready.
Tools: Channel-lock pliers · piston tool for the rears · 3/8-in flare-nut wrench (1/2-in for the caliper fitting) · brake fluid (DOT 5 silicone to 1998, DOT 3 from 1999) · AM General pad 5745162C (Flash Off-Road)

#### Test and replace glow plugs
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost Plugs about $10–12 each in Flash Off-Road's report
Symptoms: Hard cold starts that get worse as temperatures drop, or black smoke and a stall right after starting. Flash Off-Road's 1996 turbo diesel wouldn't start below 50°F when its plugs failed.
Fix: With the ignition on, the voltmeter should dip as the plugs draw current. Measure about 50–55 amps per bank and 13–14 amps per plug while they cycle (6.5 non-turbo procedure; military 24-volt trucks are different). Replace failed plugs; Flash Off-Road recommends the self-limiting AC 60G. Check the controller and alternator voltage too, because both can burn out plugs. They aren't a routine service item.
Tools: Multimeter with a DC amp clamp or in-line ammeter · deep sockets · anti-seize

### Baseline service
Assume the last owner skipped things. H1s changed constantly in production, so decode the VIN first: the fourth digit is the engine and the fifth the transmission. AM General's HUMMER Recommended Maintenance Schedule (#0574480) runs on a 3,000-mile cycle with inspection groups A, B and C, and a truck that's over 24,000 miles and behind on service should start at the 12,000-mile service.
- Engine oil & filter: Diesel-rated oil (Flash Off-Road uses Shell Rotella T) · 6.5 TD ≈ 7.5 qt, 6.5 NA ≈ 8 qt with filter · Every 3,000 mi on the factory schedule (Flash Off-Road uses a Delco PF-1218 filter. Diesel oil turns black almost at once, which is normal.)
- Chassis grease: NLGI-LB chassis grease · 26–27 fittings · Every oil change (Don't forget the two steering-column fittings behind the kick panel and the one in the steering shaft U-joint under the hood. Go easy on the front driveshaft slip joint or you'll pop the cap.)
- Fuel filter (diesel): Replace element; drain water from the filter bowl · Element every 6,000 mi on the factory schedule; drain as needed (Water reaching the injectors destroys them. Carry a spare filter off-road.)
- Air filter: Factory-type paper element · Clean or replace every 6,000 mi (Flash Off-Road advises against K&N filters on H1s. The geared hubs and transfer case vent into the air cleaner, so keep the housing sealed.)
- Coolant & thermostats: Coolant type [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · ≈25 L (26 US qt) system on the 6.5 diesels (Liqui Moly lookup) · two 195°F thermostats, GM 12559336 · Flush every 12,000 mi on the factory schedule (Flash Off-Road weighs nitrite-protected diesel coolants such as Fleet Charge against regular antifreeze; its author went back to regular antifreeze, citing the 6.5's thick, unsleeved cylinder walls. It also reports a batch of bad thermostats in the supply chain around 2000. On a turbo diesel, run the No. 8 cylinder pressure check at the same time.)
- Automatic transmission: Dexron III per Flash Off-Road · Allison 1000 fluid on the Alpha [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Service every 12,000 mi on the factory schedule (There are three different filter and pickup designs depending on the year and pan depth, so match the filter. Flash Off-Road flushes every 35,000 mi or so and changes the filter after 50,000.)
- Transfer case (NVG 242): Dexron III; Flash Off-Road recommends synthetic Dexron · Service every 12,000 mi on the factory schedule (If it's overfull or pours out when you open the fill plug, the cooler loop is leaking ('the vampire', AM General campaign R0101).)
- Differentials: GL-5 gear oil · trucks with Eaton E-lockers need AM General synthetic 75W-90 with friction modifier · ≈1.9 L (2.0 US qt) per differential on the 6.5 diesels (Liqui Moly lookup) · Check level and condition at every Group A inspection (Tags on the covers give the ratio and Torsen type. 1998 and later trucks use 2.56:1, earlier ones 2.73:1.)
- Geared hubs: GL-5 80W-90 or 75W-90 · about 1/2 qt per hub · Check at every Group A inspection; change after deep water (Milky oil means water got in through a seal or a cracked vent line. Drain and fill plugs need only 8–13 lb-ft.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 5 silicone on 1992–1998 trucks; DOT 3 on 1999-on trucks with ABS (Flash Off-Road) · Flush at purchase, then per the manual (Never mix the two: silicone DOT 5 and glycol DOT 3 don't blend, and Flash Off-Road says two colors in the reservoir mean someone has. The 1999–2000 trucks had a recall for chafing master-cylinder-to-ABS lines. Check the brake lines for corrosion.)
- Steering & front end: Idler arm, pitman arm, tie rods, ball joints · Inspect every 3,000 mi; alignment check every 12,000 (Flash Off-Road says aligning a pre-'97.5 truck means shimming the upper A-arms and can take 6–8 hours; eccentric washers made camber adjustable from 1998.)
- Halfshaft bolts & boots: 57 lb-ft with Nord-Lock washer pairs · Inspect bolts every 3,000 mi and boots every 6,000 mi (The factory figure was originally 48 lb-ft; Flash Off-Road gives 57 lb-ft as the current recommendation.)
- CTIS function: Inflate and deflate test, front, rear and both · Every Group A inspection (Flash Off-Road suggests 30–37 psi cold on the road, depending on the tire.)
- Serpentine belt & batteries: Inspect the belt; check battery voltage and condition · Belt every 6,000 mi; batteries checked at 24,000 mi (Batteries moved under the hood in 1994; 1992–93 trucks keep them under the passenger seat.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: The factory tire was a 37x12.50R16.5, and later trucks used 37-inch tires on 17-inch wheels. Flash Off-Road says a 38x15.5 is the largest you can run on stock wheels without lifting the truck, though you need to watch for rubbing on the suspension at full lock. Taller tires need a body lift: Flash Off-Road reports owners running 39.5s with a 2-inch body lift and no rubbing.

Q: Which year should I buy?
A: Flash Off-Road says many owners consider the 1998 the quintessential pre-Alpha truck. It has the 1997.5 HVAC, better sound insulation, the 2.56 axles and the last of the Torsen I differentials, before ABS and TorqTrac4 arrived in 1999. Its turbo diesel sits right in the No. 8 crack window, though (see the next question), so test the block or look for a replacement engine. Flash Off-Road calls the 2004, with its new interior, Optimizer engine and optional Eaton lockers, the best stock truck yet, and says 2004 is a big step up from 2001 for noise and comfort. The 2006 Alpha is 'an order of magnitude better' on and off road. Autotrader calls it the ultimate H1, and Hagerty found Alphas worth over 40% more than a comparable 2004. The 1992–93 6.2 trucks are simple and a favorite of hard-core off-roaders, but slow.

Q: Should I worry about the 'No. 8 cylinder' crack?
A: On turbo diesels from 1996 to early 1999, yes. One large Hummer dealer told Flash Off-Road that most cracks appear on '96 through early-'99 trucks, with '97s and '98s most common. GM changed the block casting from casting number C-159 (March 15, 1999); AM General started using the new blocks at E-019 (May 1, 1999). An 'F' in the fourth VIN digit means an AM General-built engine, which isn't at risk. Many at-risk engines were replaced under warranty.

Q: Diesel, turbo diesel or gas?
A: The turbo diesel. Flash Off-Road owned all three. His 1995 gas truck could barely hold 40 mph over Loveland Pass, while his 1996 turbo diesel held 55 and returned about 11.5 mpg in town and 15 on the road. The gas and non-turbo diesel trucks run out of power at altitude. The gas truck also fords only 24 inches, versus 30 for the diesel, because the diesel's starter is waterproof and it has no ignition to drown.

Q: What does CTIS do, and do I need it?
A: The central tire inflation system lets you inflate or deflate the tires from the cab, front and rear pairs together, through seals in the geared hubs. Airing down gives more grip in sand and rock. It was optional on some years (it's on the 1999 options list). Flash Off-Road says retrofitting it is hard and rarely economical, so buy a truck that has it if you want it.

Q: Torsen, TorqTrac4 or lockers?
A: Through 1998, H1s use Torsen I differentials, which owners can coax into locking with brake-throttle modulation. When ABS became mandatory in 1999, AM General moved to Torsen II with electronic TorqTrac4 traction control, which Flash Off-Road says is good in snow and loose dirt but weaker for rock crawling. The 2002 trucks got a higher torque-bias ratio. From 2003 a rear Eaton electric locker was offered, and front and rear lockers came with the 2004 and 2006 Off-Road Adventure package.

Q: How fast can I cruise?
A: Flash Off-Road says not to run it past about 2,400 rpm, which is around 65 mph, if you want it to last. Faster driving burns the transfer case oil and strains a truck designed for unimproved roads. Below 65 he saw 13 to 15 mpg from a turbo diesel. A 1999 turbo diesel took 18 seconds to reach 60 mph according to the brochure; the Alpha took 13.5 according to Edmunds.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: The 1999 brochure gives a maximum towed load of 7,710 lb for a turbo-diesel wagon and 8,050 lb for an open top. Edmunds says a properly equipped 2006 Alpha open top can tow 9,300 lb.

Q: Can I run aftermarket or H2 wheels?
A: H1 wheels use an 8x6.5-inch bolt pattern with a 7-inch backset. Flash Off-Road says only AM General and GT/Cepek wheels have the correct offset and load rating for a truck that weighs 7,000 to 8,000 lb. Owners on Hummer4x4Offroad report that H2 wheels fit with modification, and Moab tour operators have run them. Non-factory wheels also need custom CTIS lines.

Q: How deep can it wade?
A: 30 inches for a diesel, according to the 1999 brochure and Wikipedia, and 24 inches for the 1995–96 gas trucks. The geared hubs and transfer case vent to the air cleaner, so check that the vent lines and intake seals are intact before deep water.

Q: Is the Alpha just a re-engined H1?
A: No. AM General told Flash Off-Road that the control arms were the only parts under the truck carried over from 2004. The Alpha has the 12,100-lb GVW upgrade's bigger brakes, halfshafts and springs, a new Sheppard steering box, helical-gear hubs, a longer front driveshaft and reshaped 51-gallon fuel tanks. The downside is that most of those parts are unique to one model year.

# International Scout (1961–1980 · revival announced)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/scout/

International Harvester had been building trucks since 1907, but in the late 1950s it set out to build a rival for the Jeep CJ. Chief designer Ted Ornas later recalled his brief from the engineering manager: 'design something to replace the horse.' The result, the Scout 80, went on sale in late 1960 as a 1961 model and was built in Fort Wayne, Indiana. The original Scout 80 and 800 grew from a fold-down-windshield utility into something you could take on holiday, adding six-cylinder and V8 engines along the way. In 1971 the Scout II took over, and in its decade it added the long-wheelbase Traveler and Terra, Dana 44 axles at both ends, a Nissan diesel and the stripped-out SSII that went desert racing. Production ended on October 21, 1980, after 532,674 Scouts. For off-roaders the Scout II is the one to have: a ladder frame, leaf springs, solid axles and an IH V8, with a parts and club scene that never went away. Volkswagen Group now owns the name, and its Scout Motors revealed a new Traveler SUV and Terra pickup in October 2024.

Verdict: A tractor company's answer to the Jeep that accidentally invented the American SUV. Rusts like it's paid to, and owners forgive it every single time.

## International Scout 80 / 800 (1961–1971)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/scout/scout-80-800/
Codes: Scout 80, 800, 800A, 800B

Verdict: A tractor company was told to build something to replace the horse, and ten years later it was selling V8 wagons with bucket seats. Same 100-inch wheelbase, same honest steel box, and more rust than any seller will admit to.

International Harvester had built farm machinery and trucks for half a century when, in the late 1950s, it decided to build a rival to the Jeep CJ, then in its CJ-5 era. Chief designer Ted Ornas later said the brief from the engineering manager was to "design something to replace the horse." The result, the Scout 80, went on sale in late 1960 as a 1961 model and was built in Fort Wayne, Indiana. Autotrader Classics puts first-year sales at about 28,000. Not bad for a tractor company's first go at a small 4x4.

### A HORSE REPLACEMENT FROM FORT WAYNE
According to Silodrome, the early proposals looked a lot like the Jeep and the Series Land Rover. Ornas's curvier sketches, drawn for a plastic body, won management over. Plastic turned out to be too expensive, so the Scout was built in steel. Ornas recalled that a full-size clay model was started in late July 1959 and approved that November. For an engine, IH took its 304 cubic-inch V8 and used one bank of it: a 152 cubic-inch slant-four, rated at 93 horsepower.
The first Scout was basic. It had a fold-down windshield, vacuum wipers mounted on top of the glass, and, until early 1962, side windows that slid out rather than wound down. It sat on a 100-inch wheelbase with Dana 27 axles front and rear, both offset to the passenger side, and a Dana 18 transfer case behind a three-speed. You could buy it as a pickup, an open roadster or a TravelTop wagon, in two- or four-wheel drive. Sports Car Market says the four-wheel-drive TravelTop was the one buyers wanted most.

### THE 80 GROWS UP
IH marked its 100,000th Scout with the Red Carpet edition, about 3,000 trucks in white with red interiors. The Scout 800 arrived in 1965 with a fixed windshield, wipers moved to the bottom of the glass, an aluminum grille, bucket seats, better gauges and a better heater. It was the start of the Scout's slow move from work truck toward family wagon. Japan's FJ40 was a contemporary rival.
The engines grew too. A turbocharged 152 made 111 horsepower. The 196 cubic-inch four, half of IH's 392 V8, arrived in 1966 with the same 111 horsepower and better fuel economy. An AMC-built 232 inline-six followed, and in 1967 the Scout got its first V8, IH's own 266. The 1966 Sportop had a raked fiberglass roof and a nicer interior, and the rare factory Campermobile came with fold-out bunks. Both were early signs of the lifestyle SUV, years before anyone called it that.

### 800A AND 800B: THE LAST OF THE ORIGINALS
The 800A arrived in November 1968 with a three-piece grille and black headlight bezels. The other half of the 304 V8 was now in the options list, and running gear was heavier. Wikipedia lists a Dana 44 rear axle and a quieter Dana 20 transfer case for the 800A, while Autotrader Classics dates both changes to 1967, so check the truck rather than the paperwork. The 800A also brought the Aristocrat, the dressiest of the original-body Scouts, in blue and silver with a chrome roof rack.
The 800B, built from August 1970 to March 1971, was almost identical except for chrome headlight bezels. It came with a Comanche package, with its own paint and decals, and a SnoStar snowplow package offered only with the six. Production of the Scout II began in April 1971. Hagerty sums up the original run well: the Scout beat Ford's Bronco to market as a more practical alternative to the Jeep CJ, and it was among the early SUV pioneers.

### OWNING ONE NOW
Hagerty credits early Scouts with a reputation for durable drivetrains, which it puts down to IH's tractor-building background. The same sources agree that the bodies are the problem. Silodrome warns that trucks driven on salted roads can end up "looking like a colander", and the catalogues of IH Parts America and Super Scout Specialists, full of replacement floors, rockers and patch panels, tell the same story. The good news is that the parts exist. Autotrader Classics notes that large panels such as fenders are not reproduced, but small steel is.
Prices have moved a long way. Sports Car Market recalled that its author bought a 1967 Scout 800 V8 TravelTop for $800 in 2003. In late 2024, Autotrader Classics advised budgeting at least $40,000 for a good one and warned that anything under $15,000 is a major project. Volkswagen Group now owns the Scout name, and its Scout Motors revival is building a factory in South Carolina. Its website's coordinates, 41°03'N 85°04'W, point straight back to Fort Wayne.

### Data plate
- Models: Scout 80, 800, 800A, 800B
- Years: Late 1960 (1961 MY) – March 1971
- Built: Fort Wayne, Indiana
- Designer: Ted Ornas
- Chassis: Ladder frame, leaf springs all round
- Wheelbase: 100 in
- Engines: 152 I4 (93 hp), 152 turbo and 196 I4 (111 hp), 232 I6, 266 V8, 304 V8
- Transmission: Warner T-90A three-speed (Scout 80); four-speeds on many later 800s
- Transfer Case: Dana 18, later Dana 20
- Axles: Dana 27 front and rear; Dana 44 rear on later trucks
- Gearing: 3.31, 3.73 or 4.27 common
- Brakes: Four-wheel hydraulic drums

### Engineering
The Scout is a steel body on a ladder frame with a 100-inch wheelbase, leaf springs at all four corners and drum brakes all round. Four-wheel-drive trucks use Dana axles, closed-knuckle at the front, with a two-lever Dana transfer case and hubs that stick out past the hub caps. Power steering and power brakes were options, and Silodrome says a truck with both is the better buy. The engines all came from one family: the fours are halves of IH's V8s.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, 100-in wheelbase (The same basic body was used from 1961 to 1971.)
- Suspension: Leaf springs front and rear (Forward-shackle front springs. CPT says its reverse-shackle conversion "significantly" improves ride quality.)
- Axles: Dana 27 front and rear; later Dana 44 rear (Closed-knuckle front axle, both axles offset to the passenger side. Power-Lok limited-slip was optional.)
- Transfer Case: Dana 18, then Dana 20 (Twin-stick shifter on the 80 and 800. The Dana 20 is quieter.)
- Engines: 152 and 196 slant-fours, 232 six, 266 and 304 V8s (The 152 is half a 304 V8, and the 196 is half a 392.)
- Brakes: Four-wheel hydraulic drums (Power brakes were optional. Front disc conversions are a common upgrade.)

### Versions
- 1961–1965 · Scout 80 · 152 cu in (2.5 L) slant-four · 93 hp / 137 lb-ft · Fold-down windshield, vacuum wipers on top of the glass, Dana 27s, Dana 18, three-speed. Red Carpet edition in 1964.
- 1965–1968 · Scout 800 · 152 four; 152 turbo · 93 hp; 111 hp (turbo) · Fixed windshield, bucket seats, better heater. Turbo dropped in early 1968.
- 1966–1968 · Scout 800 · 196 four; 232 AMC six; 266 V8 (from 1967) · 111 hp (196); others not confirmed · Sportop fiberglass roof from 1966. Four-wheel drive standard by 1968.
- Nov 1968–1970 · Scout 800A · 196 four; 232 six (early 1969); 266 and 304 V8s · Not confirmed · Three-piece grille, black headlight bezels, Dana 44 rear, Dana 20 transfer case. Aristocrat and SR-2 packages.
- Aug 1970–Mar 1971 · Scout 800B · 196 four; 232 six; 304 V8 · Not confirmed · Chrome headlight bezels. Comanche and six-cylinder-only SnoStar packages.

### Year-by-year
- 1961: Scout 80 debuts in late 1960 as a 1961 model: 152 cu in four-cylinder, Dana 27 axles with offset diffs and a Dana 18 transfer case, fold-down windshield, vacuum wipers at the top of the glass. Removable sliding side windows on 1961 to very early 1962 trucks
- 1965: Turbocharged 152-T (111 hp vs 93 hp) offered until early 1968. Late-1965 trucks built from leftover 80 parts are titled as 800s; there are thought to be about 3,000 of these '1965½' Scouts
- 1966: Scout 800: bucket seats, new dash, better heating, fixed windshield with wipers at the bottom, aluminium grille. Sportop arrives early in the year, and the 196 four (from August) and 232 six become options
- 1967: IH's 266 cu in V8 is offered from March. The V8 package brought a heavier-duty Dana 30 front axle
- 1968: Four-wheel drive becomes standard on the 800, and the 152-T is dropped early in the year. Rear axle shafts change from two-piece to one-piece around 1968–69
- 1969: Scout 800A (from November 1968): centred Dana 44 rear axle, quieter Dana 20 transfer case and a 304 V8 option. The 232 six lasted only into early 1969. Aristocrat and SR-2 packages followed
- 1970–1971: Scout 800B (August 1970 to March 1971): an 800A with chrome headlight bezels. Comanche package; Sno-Star plow package from late 1970, six-cylinder only. Replaced by the Scout II

### Buying checks
- Rust is the whole story: Autotrader Classics says to check the rockers, the windshield and side-window frames, and the lower corners of the removable top. Silodrome adds the spring mounts, the insides of the fenders and the welds, and warns that rust starts on the inside and works out, so bubbling paint is a bad sign. The fact that IH Parts America sells front and rear floors, inner and outer rockers, and fuel-tank compartment panels tells you where else to look.
- Count the big panels: Small steel parts are widely reproduced, but Autotrader Classics notes that no one makes large panels such as fenders. A truck that needs fenders is a much bigger job than one that only needs floors.
- Is it really a 4x4?: Scouts were sold in two-wheel drive too. Autotrader's quick test: if the hub sticks out through the hub cap, it's a four-wheel-drive truck. Then look for the twin transfer-case levers.
- Confirm the year and the engine: Binder Planet hosts Jim Allen's list of starting and ending serial numbers for the 80, 800, 800A and 800B, compiled from IHC records, so you can date the truck and confirm which model it is. On an IH V8, Super Scout Specialists says the displacement is stamped on a domino-sized flat spot on the right side of the block, toward the front and just below the head. Engine swaps are common.
- Listen to the driveline: Autotrader Classics advises checking the axles and transfer case for wear. A transfer case that pops out of gear needs to come out for a rebuild, according to an IH Parts America moderator. On the front axle, look for worn knuckle wipers and sloppy kingpins.
- Power options matter: Silodrome says Scouts with both power steering and power brakes are the better buy, because without them steering and braking take real effort. Autotrader Classics calls the four-wheel drums archaic and says a four-cylinder probably won't reach 75 mph.
- Ask what's been changed: Suspension and other modifications are common, so ask the seller for details. That includes lifts, shackle swaps, disc conversions and engine transplants. A good conversion can be a plus. An undocumented one is a list of questions.

### Common repairs
#### Floor pan and rocker replacement
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time Multi-weekend welding job · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Soft or holed floors under the mats, rockers bubbling at the bottom of the doors, and daylight around the fuel-tank compartment. Silodrome warns that rust usually starts inside and works out.
Fix: Strip the interior and measure everything before cutting. Cut out the rotten metal and fit replacement front floor halves (sold by side), the rear floor, and inner and outer rockers as needed, with the front floor X-brace if it's gone. Weld the panels in, seam-seal and paint. If the body is lifted or off, replace the body-mount bushings while you're there.
Tools: MIG welder · cutoff wheel and spot-weld drill · clamps and self-tapping screws for fitting · seam sealer and weld-through primer.

#### Swap the vacuum wipers for an electric kit (800 series)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Kit plus a few hours
Symptoms: The original vacuum wipers on an 800 are dead, sluggish or simply not worth rebuilding.
Fix: IH Parts America's bolt-in kit mounts below the windshield where the vacuum motors were. One two-speed, self-parking 12-volt motor drives both arms through a linkage, and the kit is designed to clear the original gauges, radio, speaker and glove box. Remove the vacuum motors and linkage, fit the brackets and bushings, mount the motor, run power through the new switch, and fit the arms and blades. The optional deluxe switch adds intermittent and washer functions. The Scout 80's top-mounted wipers are a different design, so check fitment before ordering.
Tools: Basic hand tools · drill · wiring crimpers · test light.

#### Front knuckle seals and kingpin bearings (closed-knuckle Dana)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A weekend for both sides · cost $19.95 per IHPA seal kit (two per axle); kingpin bearings extra
Symptoms: Grease weeping from the knuckle balls, torn wipers, and play in the knuckle when you rock the wheel top to bottom. One IHPA forum owner described his 1968 800 this way: "the wipers for the knuckles are shot and the king pin bearings are worn out."
Fix: With the axle supported, pull the wheel, hub, spindle and axle shaft. Inspect the axle U-joint while it's out. Remove the knuckle seal retainer and the kingpin caps, then replace the kingpin bearings and races and set preload with shims. Fit the new seals and wipers, reassemble, and repack the wheel bearings. The IHPA seal kit fits the small eight-bolt knuckles, not the large 12-bolt ones, and you need two kits per axle. We couldn't source the kingpin preload figure, so use the IH shop manual.
Tools: Floor jack and stands · hub/bearing nut socket · seal driver · torque wrench · inch-pound scale for preload · wheel-bearing grease.

#### Transfer case pops out of gear: Dana 20 rebuild
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A weekend · cost Overhaul kit plus labor, or buy a rebuilt case
Symptoms: The transfer case jumps out of 2-High or won't fully engage 4-High. On a 1967 800, an IHPA forum member found the shift-cover opening was too small for the levers to travel fully, so check that before you strip the case.
Fix: Drain the oil first. Support the engine and transmission with a second jack or blocks, and disconnect both prop shafts at the output flanges. The case weighs about 70 lb. An IHPA moderator recommends a full rebuild with a master overhaul kit rather than band-aid fixes. The service manual lists bent forks, a bad spring or bearings as possible causes. Refill with SAE 90 GL-1 mineral oil, or straight 50-weight motor oil as a substitute, and not 80W-90 GL-5. Early Scout 80s and 800s use the Dana 18, so order the right kit.
Tools: Transmission jack or a second floor jack · puller · snap-ring pliers · seal drivers · gasket scraper.

#### Front disc brake conversion
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A weekend · cost Kit plus a day of labor
Symptoms: Four-wheel drums that fade, pull or simply don't stop a V8 Scout on modern roads.
Fix: The CPT kit sold by IH Parts America for 1966–71 800s with Dana 27 or 30 front axles includes new hubs, 11 3/4-inch vented rotors, caliper brackets, calipers, pads, stainless hoses, a disc/drum master cylinder, a proportioning valve and a pushrod. It reuses your wheel bearings, and the knuckles must be ground for caliper clearance. It replaces the dual-circuit master cylinder found on 1967 and later 800s. Single-circuit trucks and Scout 80s need extra hard lines. Some stock 15- and 16-inch drum-brake wheels won't clear the calipers. Bleed the whole system afterwards.
Tools: Die grinder · flare-nut wrenches · bearing packer · brake bleeder · tube flaring tool for 80s and single-circuit trucks.

#### Springs, shackles and bushings (fix the sag and the ride)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A weekend · cost Kit plus labor
Symptoms: A tired stance, clunks from worn spring eyes and shackles, and the choppy ride of forward-shackle front springs.
Fix: Replace the springs, shackles, bushings, U-bolts and shocks as a set. IH Parts America says its CPT system for 1961–71 Scouts nets 1 to 3 inches of lift, about 2 inches on most trucks. It includes heavy-duty springs, 4-inch shackles, 1/2-inch U-bolts, 2-degree caster shims, Bilstein shocks and an extended rear brake hose. You may need to notch around the front driveshaft and transmission crossmember and enlarge the U-bolt plate holes. For a better ride, CPT's reverse-shackle kit moves the front shackle. It needs welding and drilling through the frame, and a longer-travel front driveshaft is recommended.
Tools: Jacks and stands · penetrating oil and heat for seized bolts · torque wrench · drill (and welder for a reverse-shackle kit).

#### Points to electronic ignition
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost Module or distributor plus an hour
Symptoms: Hard starting, a misfire that comes and goes, and points that keep closing up. Silodrome lists electronic ignition among the sensible upgrades.
Fix: First identify your distributor, because Super Scout Specialists sells different Pertronix Ignitor modules for the Holley and Delco distributors used on the fours. Pull the cap and rotor, remove the points and condenser, fit the Ignitor to the breaker plate, and wire it to the coil as the instructions show. Set the timing with a light. A complete HFI distributor is the alternative if the shaft or bushings are worn.
Tools: Timing light · screwdrivers · test light.

### Baseline service
Treat any early Scout as a 50-plus-year-old machine whose fluids could be any age. Baseline everything, then inspect the front knuckles, brakes and steering before trusting it on the trail. Factory capacities for the 80 and 800 weren't available in sources we could verify, so check the IH shop manual or owner's manual for those. The one firm rule from IH specialists: keep GL-5 gear oil out of the transfer case.
- Engine oil & filter: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] for grade and capacity · Change now, then regularly [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Super Scout Specialists lists a canister-type oil filter for the IH four-cylinder and V8 in these Scouts. Check what your engine has before ordering.)
- Ignition: points, cap, rotor, plugs: Points or Pertronix · gap and timing [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now, then at each tune-up (Points-type distributors on the fours are Holley or Delco. Identify yours before buying an electronic conversion.)
- Fuel filter, pump & sender: Inline filter · pump and sender condition · Filter now, then yearly (Old tanks shed rust and varnish. If the gauge is wrong, the sender is cheap. Check the tank selector valve too, if the truck has one.)
- Coolant, hoses & radiator: Coolant type and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush now, then every 2 years (Original radiators are often tired. Aluminum replacements are made separately for 4-cylinder and V8 trucks.)
- Manual transmission: Oil type and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Drain and refill now (Silodrome says the Scout 80 used a Warner T-90A three-speed; many later 800s have four-speeds. Identify the gearbox before choosing oil. Check the mount while you're under there.)
- Transfer case (Dana 18 / Dana 20): SAE 90 GL-1 mineral oil, or straight 50-weight motor oil · about 2.5–3 qt (IHPA moderator's estimate) · Drain and refill now (Fill to the bottom of the filler hole with the truck level. An IHPA moderator says: "You should not use 80-90wt GL-5 gear oil in the t-case.")
- Front & rear differentials: 80W-90 gear oil; add limited-slip additive for Power-Lok/Trac-Lok · capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Drain and refill now (One IHPA forum owner found Mobil 1 gear oil made his Power-Lok clutches chatter, while Red Line and Royal Purple did not.)
- Front knuckles & kingpins: Inspect seals, wipers and kingpin play · Now, then every season off-road (These are closed knuckles. Torn wipers let water and grit into the kingpin bearings.)
- Wheel bearings: Clean, inspect and repack with wheel-bearing grease · Now, then yearly or after deep water (Do the front bearings with the knuckle service, and fit new inner seals.)
- Brake fluid, hoses & wheel cylinders: Fluid type [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush now, then every 2 years (Rubber hoses this old should be replaced, not inspected. Note whether the truck has a single- or dual-circuit master cylinder, because dual-circuit arrived on 1967 and later 800s.)
- Steering linkage & grease points: Chassis grease · inspect drag link, tie rods, steering bell joint and U-joints · Grease now, then at each oil change (Check every joint in the linkage before blaming the steering box. If it is the box, IH Parts America sells rebuilt Ross boxes for the 80 and 800.)
- Charging & starting: Inspect the battery, cables, voltage regulator and starter solenoid · Now (IH Parts America lists an external voltage regulator for 1962–71 Scouts. Clean every ground while you're checking it.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: We couldn't find a forum consensus for a bone-stock 80 or 800. The best data point comes from IH Parts America, which says "a 31" tire should fit fine" with its CPT spring system. That system adds 1 to 3 inches, about 2 on most trucks, and IHPA's own 800B runs 31x10.50 Duratracs on Scout II rally wheels. IHPA also notes that the front tires can hit the rear of the front wheel well, which its reverse-shackle kit addresses by moving the axle forward. So on stock springs, stay close to stock size. With fresh lift springs, 31s are the realistic ceiling.

Q: What's the difference between the 80, 800, 800A and 800B?
A: The 80 (1961–65) has the fold-down windshield, top-mounted vacuum wipers and the 152 four. The 800 (1965–68) got a fixed windshield, bucket seats, better heating and gauges, plus the 196 four, 232 six and 266 V8. The 800A (late 1968–70) added the 304 V8, a three-piece grille and black headlight bezels. The 800B (August 1970 to March 1971) is the same truck with chrome bezels.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: There's no agreed best year: rust decides, and an early Scout with a rotten frame is the expensive mistake. If you're choosing, the 800A (from late 1968) brought the Dana 20 transfer case and a Dana 44 rear axle, and the V8s are the ones for highway speed. Cars Counsel rates every 80 and 800 'good with inspection' because of parts scarcity and age.

Q: Which engine should I look for?
A: The 152 four makes 93 hp, and Autotrader Classics warns that a four-cylinder probably won't hit 75 mph. The 196 four makes 111 hp, the same as the 152 turbo, with better economy. For trail use and highway speed most people want the 266 or 304 V8, but they sit in a heavier nose. Check the block stamping to confirm what's actually fitted.

Q: Is the four-cylinder really half a V8?
A: Yes. The 152 is one bank of IH's 304 V8, and the 196 is half of the 392 V8. That's why the engines share so many parts, and why the fours lean over in the engine bay.

Q: What oil goes in the transfer case?
A: IH specialists on the IH Parts America forum recommend SAE 90 GL-1 mineral oil, or straight 50-weight motor oil as a substitute, filled to the bottom of the filler hole with the truck level. One moderator estimated the capacity at about 2.5 to 3 quarts. Don't use 80W-90 GL-5.

Q: What gear oil for a Power-Lok or Trac-Lok rear axle?
A: Use 80W-90 with a limited-slip additive, according to IHPA forum regulars. One owner found Mobil 1 gear oil made his Power-Lok chatter, while Red Line and Royal Purple worked.

Q: Were all Scouts four-wheel drive?
A: No. The Scout was sold in two- and four-wheel drive from the start, and Wikipedia says four-wheel drive became standard by 1968. To check a truck, see whether the hub protrudes through the hub cap.

Q: How do I date my Scout and confirm the model?
A: Use the serial number. Binder Planet hosts a list of starting and ending serial numbers and VINs for the 80, 800, 800A and 800B, plus the special models. Jim Allen, author of the International Scout Encyclopedia, compiled it from IHC records and microfiche. The data plate is on the driver's side of the cowl.

Q: What is an early Scout worth?
A: In late 2024 Autotrader Classics advised budgeting at least $40,000 for a good example. It said a semi-decent one starts around $25,000 and anything under $15,000 is a major project. Restored trucks have sold for far more, including $33,000 for a Scout 80 at Barrett-Jackson in 2014 and a $114,900 asking price for a frame-off 800A.

Q: Can I still get parts?
A: Yes, and more than for many trucks this age. IH Parts America and Super Scout Specialists list floors, rockers, patch panels, brakes, axle seals, transfer-case kits and wiring. Silodrome notes that engine and transmission parts are widely available. The gap is large panels: Autotrader Classics says no one reproduces fenders.

Q: Can an early Scout be made into a usable daily or trail truck?
A: Yes, if you upgrade the right things together. Common jobs are a front disc conversion, a power-brake booster, a power-steering conversion (CPT makes one for 800A and 800B with the IH V8), new springs and shackles, and electronic ignition. Silodrome's advice is that any power upgrade should come with better brakes, a stronger transmission and better suspension.
