## International Scout II (1971–1980)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/scout/scout-ii/
Codes: Scout II, Traveler, Terra, SSII

Verdict: Built by a tractor company, designed to beat the Jeep, and rustier than a shipwreck. The Scout II is also a properly tough ladder-frame 4x4 with a 345 V8, Dana 44s and a parts and club scene that makes keeping one alive easier than it should be.

In April 1971 International Harvester replaced the Scout 800B with a truck it had been sitting on for years. A version nearly identical to the production Scout II was shown to IH management in December 1967. It kept the formula: a short ladder frame, leaf springs, solid axles and a removable top. What changed was everything you touched. It was longer, lower, roomier and much more civilized. Over the next decade it became the Scout most people picture, and the one most still on the trail.

### REPLACING THE HORSE, TAKE TWO
The first Scout existed because IH engineering manager Mr. Reese told Ted Ornas to 'design something to replace the horse.' By 1964 IH was already planning its replacement, and the concept was approved for production in mid-1965. The Jeep CJ was still the target, but the market had moved. Ford's Bronco and Chevrolet's Blazer had shown that buyers wanted a 4x4 they could live with every day.
So the Scout II launched with a 196-cubic-inch four, a 232 AMC straight-six and IH's own 304 V8, then added the 258 six and the 345 V8. You could order the steel Traveltop, the half-cab Roadster top or a soft top. Early trucks had a Dana 30 front axle and drum brakes. Late in 1974 power front disc brakes became standard, and after 1974 every Scout II got Dana 44 axles at both ends.

### LONGER, THEN DIESEL
In 1975 IH raised the Scout's gross weight rating to 6,200 pounds and badged it XLC, for Extra Load Capacity. That put it out of reach of stricter light-duty emissions rules, and Scouts didn't get catalytic converters until 1979. In 1976 the 118-inch Traveler and Terra arrived, 18 inches longer between the door and the rear wheel arch and topped in fiberglass. The Traveler replaced the truck-based Travelall, which ended in 1975, and it became a popular RV tow vehicle.
1976 also brought a 3.3-liter Nissan SD33 straight-six diesel. Jim Allen, author of the International Scout Encyclopedia, credits IH with the first domestically built diesel SUV. In late 1979 the turbocharged SD33T replaced it. Super Scout Specialists' figures give 10,182 diesel Scouts in all, more than half of them 1980 turbos.

### BAJA, AND THE SUPER SCOUT
Privateer Jimmy Jones won his class in the 1972 Baja 1000 in a '72 Scout II. Five years later IH was sponsoring four desert racing teams and selling the SSII, a stripped-down Scout with soft doors, a plastic grille and a roll bar, aimed squarely at the CJ-7. It ranged from the barebones four-cylinder Rancher Special, on which even the passenger seat was a cost option, to the dressier Sport and Baja Cruiser.
In the 1977 Baja 1000, an SSII driven by Jerry Boone finished first among production 4x4s, almost two hours ahead of the next car, a CJ-7. Boone later said his team had a month to prepare a stock truck and only got IH sponsorship after the race. About 4,000 SSIIs were built between 1977 and 1979, and today they're the most valuable Scout IIs.

### HOW IT ENDED
IH experimented with Scout-based minivans, station wagons, dune buggies, Hurst-built special editions and even a small motorhome, and it built a Scout III SSV concept prototype in 1979. The 1979–80 International Harvester strike and a lack of money ended all of it. The 1980 trucks got a one-piece plastic grille, the turbo diesel and, for one year only, a Dana 300 transfer case. Only 13,106 were built. The last Scout came off the Fort Wayne line on October 21, 1980.
Hagerty counts about 260,000 Scout IIs. Rust has taken many of them, and the survivors are now real money. Gen X buyers make up more than 46 percent of Scout buyers. Volkswagen Group now owns the name, and Scout Motors is reviving the Traveler and Terra badges for new electric and range-extended trucks.

### Data plate
- Built: Fort Wayne, Indiana · April 1971 – Oct 21, 1980
- Production: ≈ 260,000 (Hagerty)
- Chassis: Ladder frame, leaf springs front & rear
- Wheelbase: 100 in · 118 in (Traveler, Terra)
- Bodies: Traveltop, Roadster half-cab, soft top · Traveler, Terra · SSII
- Engines: IH 196 I4, 304 & 345 V8 · AMC 232/258 I6 · Nissan SD33/SD33T
- Transmissions: Borg-Warner 3- & 4-speed manuals · 3-speed auto incl. Chrysler A727
- Transfer Case: Dana 20 · Dana 300 (1980 only)
- Axles: Dana 30 / 44 to 1974 · Dana 44 / 44 after
- Ratios: 2.72 to 4.54 · Trac-Lok optional
- Brakes: Power front discs standard from late 1974
- Gvwr: 6,200 lb from 1975–76 (XLC)

### Engineering
The Scout II is a body-on-frame 4x4 with live axles on leaf springs at both ends. Most were four-wheel drive, with a manually shifted transfer case (2WD high, 4WD high and 4WD low) and free-wheeling front hubs. Engines were IH's own fours and V8s, AMC sixes and Nissan diesels, behind Borg-Warner manuals or a three-speed automatic. Factory line tickets record each truck's exact axles, ratios and options.
- Chassis: Ladder frame (100-in wheelbase; 118 in for the 1976–80 Traveler and Terra)
- Suspension: Leaf springs, live axles (Front and rear; the frame can crack at the steering box and spring hangers)
- Axles: Dana 30 / 44 → Dana 44 / 44 (Dana 44 at both ends after 1974; Trac-Lok limited-slip optional)
- Transfer Case: Dana 20 · Dana 300 (1980) (Gear-driven, manually shifted; the Dana 300 was a one-year fit)
- Engines: IH 304 & 345 V8 · 196 I4 (Plus AMC 232/258 sixes and Nissan SD33/SD33T diesels)
- Brakes: Power front discs from late 1974 (Drums all round before that; rear drums throughout)

### Versions
- 1971–1975 · Scout II · 196 I4 · 232 then 258 I6 (AMC) · 304 / 345 V8 · — · Launched with the 196, 232 and 304; the 258 six and 345 V8 came later. Dana 30 front and Dana 44 rear; power front discs standard from late 1974.
- 1976–1980 · Traveler / Terra · As Scout II, plus diesel · — · 118-in wheelbase, fiberglass full top (Traveler) or half-cab (Terra).
- 1976–1979 · Scout II diesel · Nissan SD33 3.3 I6 diesel · 95 PS (Nissan rating) · Naturally aspirated; 4,222 built from 1976 to 1979 per Super Scout Specialists.
- 1977–1979 · SSII · 196 I4 · 304 / 345 V8 · 345: 163 bhp / 292 lb-ft (1978 test) · Soft top and doors, plastic grille, roll bar. Rancher Special, Brush Buster, Sport and Baja Cruiser.
- 1980 · Scout II / Traveler / Terra · SD33T turbo-diesel · 304 / 345 V8 · 196 I4 · SD33T: 110 PS (Nissan rating) · One-piece plastic grille, Dana 300 transfer case, T-19 manual with the turbo-diesel. 13,106 built.

### Year-by-year
- 1971: Scout II replaces the 800B in April. 100-in wheelbase, Dana 30 front and Dana 44 rear; launched with the 196 four, AMC 232 six and IH 304 V8, with the 258 six and 345 V8 added soon after (Hagerty). Some early trucks have 'Scout 810' glovebox badges. Three-bar grille with chrome headlight rings for 1971–72
- 1973: New grille with 14 vertical bars. From September 30, 1972 the serial numbers switch to the CGD prefix
- 1974: Power front disc brakes become standard late in the year (a rare option earlier in 1974)
- 1975: Dana 44 front and rear become standard on all Scout IIs. GVWR raised to 6,200 lb (XLC, 'Extra Load Capacity') to sidestep stricter light-duty emissions rules
- 1976: 118-in-wheelbase Traveler and Terra arrive. Nissan SD33 diesel option. Automatic shifter moves to the floor. Spirit of 76 and Patriot editions
- 1977: Super Scout II (SSII) introduced in February: soft top, soft doors, roll bar and plastic grille, in Rancher Special, Brush Buster, Sport and Baja Cruiser versions. Built until 1979. New grille for 1977–79
- 1979: Catalytic converters arrive on Scouts
- 1980: Final year: one-piece ABS plastic grille, turbocharged SD33T diesel, and the Dana 300 transfer case (2.62:1 low range), fitted only in 1980. The last Scout was built on October 21, 1980

### Capability
- GVWR: 6,200 lb (2,812 kg) (XLC rating from 1975–76 (Super Scout Specialists dates it to 1975; Wikipedia to 1976))
- Fuel tank: 19 US gal (72 L) (1972–80 rear tank, per replacement-tank listings)
- Curb weight: about 3,800 lb (1,724 kg) (1979 Scout II Traveltop V8 automatic, per Hagerty)
- Wheelbase: 100 in (2,540 mm); 118 in (2,997 mm) Traveler and Terra

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 10-15LT on 15x7 chrome rally wheels (1976 Spirit of 76 line-ticket codes)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x139.7 (5x5.5")
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 30–31 in (31s marginal) (One 1977 owner reports 31s rubbing on stock springs. IH Parts America recommends a reverse-shackle kit and a 2.5-in spring lift to run 31s without rubbing.)
- Biggest tire, 2.5 in lift: 32x11.50R15 (One owner on a Rough Country 2.5-in spring lift with 10-in rims says they never hit on the street but definitely hit the back of the rear wheel wells off-road. 33s need more lift (body or spring) and longer bump stops.)
- Biggest tire, Spring-over lift: 33x12.50R15 (Even with a spring-over, a 1-in body lift and minor trimming, 33x12.50s can still touch at full articulation. Stiffer springs or lower bump stops help.)

### Buying checks
- Structural rust first: Scouts were never fully galvanized. Corsetti Cruisers says to start with the rear spring mounts, the body mounts and the area under the doors. Structural rust around the rear crossmember or along the inner rockers can mean a full rebuild. Surface rust is manageable.
- Look under bedliners and fresh paint: In one Scout II rebuild reported on the 4WD Mechanix forum, a previous owner's bedliner reportedly hid so much floor rust that the repair ran past budget. Front fenders, door sills and the tailgate area hold moisture and can hide filler.
- Frame cracks at the steering box: The frame is prone to fatigue cracks where the steering box bolts on, behind the front spring hangers and at the body mounts. Pull the box (three bolts) or at least inspect the welds, especially on a truck with big tires.
- Panel gaps aren't always crash damage: Scouts were hand-assembled with wide, uneven gaps even when new. Very uneven panels, doors that won't close properly or messy welds can still point to a bent frame or a poor repair.
- VIN tags, title and line ticket: Check for a clean title and matching VIN tags on the chassis and body. The line ticket (the factory build sheet) lists the engine, transmission, axles, gear ratio, paint and options. On 1971–76 trucks it's under the hood on the cowl; on 1977–80 trucks it's inside the glove box door. Replacements can be ordered.
- Which front axle?: Dana 44 axles became standard on all Scout IIs after 1974. Compare the covers: if the front cover is smaller and rounder than the rear, it's a Dana 30. The line ticket also shows the axle, the ratio and whether there's a Trac-Lok rear.
- Engine swaps and wiring: Many Scouts now have LS or other swaps. Check the wiring, cooling and driveline geometry; Corsetti warns that amateur conversions cause endless electrical and mechanical trouble. Look under the dash and around the firewall for brittle, patched factory wiring.
- Diesels and small parts: The SD33 diesels are rare and interesting. IH Parts America still lists filters, water pumps and seals for them. Dash pads, gauge clusters and original seat frames are hard to find for any Scout II, so price those in.

### Common repairs
#### Floor, rocker and rear crossmember rust repair
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ Several weekends, depending on how far it goes · cost Panels from about $89 (outer rocker) to $1,429.95 (complete aftermarket rear floor), plus welding
Symptoms: Bubbling under the doors, soft or holed floors, a sagging door opening, water on the carpets, and rust at the rear spring mounts and rear crossmember.
Fix: Strip the interior and probe everything with a pick or screwdriver. Support the door openings before cutting out any rocker or floor structure, then cut back to clean metal. Anything Scout advises leaving a 1–2 inch lip of the old floor for a new pan to rest on. Weld in the floor pans, rocker panels, door-post braces and, if needed, the rear floor sill crossmember. Seam-seal and coat the new metal. If the inner rockers and rear crossmember are badly gone, Corsetti Cruisers says a frame-off restoration is often the better long-term answer.
Tools: MIG welder · cut-off wheel · spot-weld drill · clamps and door-opening bracing · seam sealer and weld-through primer

#### Reinforce a cracking steering-box frame mount
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day, more if cracks need welding · cost Plate $16.95; Straight Steer brace about $164.95–199
Symptoms: Wandering steering, a box that moves when someone turns the wheel with the engine running, or visible cracks in the frame rail around the three steering-box bolts. Big tires and front lockers make it worse.
Fix: Remove the steering box (three bolts) and clean the frame. Drill the ends of any cracks, weld them, and grind the face smooth so a reinforcement plate sits flat against it. Fit a 3/16- or 1/4-inch plate (the CPT plate bolts straight on and can also be welded), and reinstall the box with new grade 8 bolts. While you're there, check behind the front spring hangers and the body mounts for cracks too. A Straight Steer-type brace ties the box to the opposite rail and is suggested for 33-inch or larger tires.
Tools: Socket set · drill and bits · welder and grinder (if cracked) · torque wrench

#### Rear main seal on an IH V8
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend (the transmission has to come out) · cost Seal $69.95 plus spacer; full V8 gasket set about $162
Symptoms: Oil dripping from the bellhousing area and a wet oil pan rear lip. The engine-to-transmission joint is the giveaway, since valve-cover and pan-gasket leaks run down from higher up.
Fix: On Binder Planet, owners point out that the IH V8 uses a one-piece rear main seal, so the transmission has to come out to replace it properly. Remove the transmission (and clutch on manuals) and the flywheel or flexplate, then the old seal, and fit the new seal and spacer. Owners recommend a licensed reprint of the factory manual for the procedure. If you're chasing low oil pressure as well, check that oil reaches the rockers before replacing bearings: the SV V8's cam bearings feed the top end, and 5–10 psi at hot idle isn't unusual on these engines.
Tools: Transmission jack · flywheel holder · seal driver · factory service manual

#### Points or tired electronic ignition → Pertronix
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost Module about $144.95–196; coil extra
Symptoms: Hard starting, misfires, burnt points, or a failing stock electronic module that's hard to find.
Fix: Work out what you have first. Anything Scout sells three versions for V8 Scout IIs: 1971–75 points distributors, the 1975–77 'gold box' electronic system and the 1978–80 Prestolite electronic distributor. The first two install under the distributor cap. The 1978–80 Prestolite version needs the distributor removed, and Anything Scout says it must be used with a points-style coil, not the stock coil. Set the timing afterward. One Binder Planet owner's module and Flame-Thrower coil caught fire when a mechanic left the key on with the engine off for half an hour, so don't leave the ignition on.
Tools: Timing light · distributor wrench · test light

#### Front ball joints (Dana 30 / Dana 44)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day for both sides · cost About $157 per side (Spicer pair) or $49.95 per joint (Moog greaseable)
Symptoms: Wandering, clunks over bumps, uneven tire wear, and play at the top and bottom of the tire with the front end jacked up.
Fix: Scout II Dana 30 and Dana 44 open-knuckle axles use the same ball joints: two upper and two lower per axle. They press into the knuckles, and the lowers have snap rings. Remove the wheel, caliper, locking hub, wheel bearings and spindle, then slide out the axle shaft. Unbolt the tie rod, separate the knuckle from the axle C, and press out the old joints with a ball-joint tool. Press in the new joints, reassemble, set the camber sleeve, and get the alignment checked. On the IH Parts America forum, one owner advises to buy good joints rather than doing the job twice.
Tools: Ball-joint press (Dana 30/44 adapter) · spindle-nut socket · pickle fork · torque wrench

#### Front disc brakes, wheel bearings and seals
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day · cost About $350 for a complete front disc kit; wheel bearing kit $74.95
Symptoms: Pulling, a soft pedal, grinding, or play in the wheel. Even when new, the brakes were the weak point: Motor Sport's 1978 test said they tended to pull and twitch.
Fix: Jack and support the front, remove the wheels, calipers and locking hubs, and take off the hub and rotor. Clean out the old grease, replace the inner seal, and repack or replace the bearings. Fit new rotors, pads and calipers, adjust the bearing preload with the spindle nuts, and bleed the brakes. Anything Scout's front kit covers 1974–80 Scout IIs with a Dana 44, and it notes that excessive lateral wheel movement means you need new bearings and seals. Do the rear drums at the same time.
Tools: Wheel-bearing (spindle nut) socket · bearing packer · seal driver · brake bleeder

#### Tired leaf springs and shackle bushings
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend · cost Bushing kit $33.95; stock-height spring set $819.95; reverse-shackle kit $349.95
Symptoms: A truck that sits low or leans, clunks from the shackles, tires rubbing on 31s, and a harsh ride.
Fix: Support the frame, jack each axle in turn and unbolt the U-bolts, shackles and spring eyes. Swap worn bushings or whole springs, check the spring hangers for cracks, and torque everything with the truck's weight on the wheels. For 31-inch tires without rubbing, IH Parts America's owner recommends its CPT reverse-shackle kit with a 2.5-inch spring lift. Anything Scout says the Rough Country 2.5-inch kit fits up to a 32-inch tire safely.
Tools: Floor jack and stands · breaker bar · penetrating oil · bushing press or vise

### Baseline service
Assume nothing has been done. Scout IIs are simple and almost everything is still available, but they're also 45-plus years old. Start by finding your line ticket, which tells you exactly which engine, axles, ratio and transmission you have. The IH V8s are flat-tappet engines, so choose oil with enough zinc.
- Engine oil & filter: 7 qt with filter on Scout II 4x4s (IH Parts America tech moderator) · high-zinc (ZDDP) oil, e.g. 15W-40 or 20W-50 for a worn engine · Then every 3,000–5,000 mi [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (It reads one quart over on the dipstick. On Binder Planet, owners warn that modern low-zinc oils aren't right for the IH flat-tappet cam.)
- Air filter: IH 196/266/304/345/392 element; separate elements for SD33 and SD33T diesels · Inspect at every oil change (The 1980 turbo-diesel uses its own filter.)
- Spark plugs, cap and rotor: Champion RJ12YC or NGK 3332 (IH Parts America fitment) · gap [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase, then per manual (Caps differ by distributor: Holley, Delco or Prestolite. Check yours before ordering.)
- Coolant, thermostat & water-pump tube O-rings: Capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (AMSOIL's lookup lists about 20 qt for the 1980 5.0 L V8) · coolant type [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush at purchase, then every 2 years (The IH V8 water pump feeds through a separate tube sealed with O-rings. Replace them whenever the pump comes off; a complete IH V8 gasket set includes four.)
- Automatic transmission (Chrysler A727): ATF · capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (AMSOIL's lookup lists a 5 qt initial fill) · fluid type [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Drain, new filter and refill at purchase (Moses Ludel of 4WD Mechanix credits the A727's lack of overdrive with helping it survive. Do a pan drop and filter change, not a pressure flush.)
- Manual transmission (T-19 / T-18 / T-15 etc.): AMSOIL's Scout II listing gives engine-oil grades (10W-40 class) for the manual gearboxes · [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Change at purchase (Factory boxes vary by year and engine. The line ticket tells you which one you have.)
- Transfer case (Dana 20; Dana 300 in 1980): Capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (AMSOIL's lookup lists 3.4 pints for the two-speed case) · lubricant grade [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]. IH specialists on the IHPA forum recommend SAE 90 GL-1 or straight 50-weight motor oil in Dana 20s, not GL-5. · Change at purchase; check for leaks at the output seals (The 1980 Dana 300 was a one-year fit. Gasket, seal and overhaul kits are still made for the Dana 20.)
- Front & rear differentials (Dana 30 / Dana 44): GL-5 gear oil · grade and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (AMSOIL's lookup lists 4.2 pt front, 3 pt rear) · add friction modifier for Trac-Lok · Change at purchase and after deep water (The line ticket or the axle tag shows the ratio (2.72 to 4.54) and whether there's a Trac-Lok.)
- Front wheel bearings, seals & locking hubs: Repack with wheel-bearing grease · new inner seals · At purchase, then per manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Pull the locking hubs and check them while you're in there. Rebuilt or replacement Warn hubs are available.)
- Steering: power steering fluid, rag joint & box bolts: Power steering fluid type [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (AMSOIL's lookup lists an ATF-type fluid) · Check at purchase (Check the rag joint for play and the steering-box frame mount for cracks. New grade 8 box bolts are cheap.)
- Brake fluid & hoses: DOT 3 · Flush at purchase, then every 2 years (Replace old rubber brake hoses. If the pedal is poor, check the master cylinder and booster too.)
- Fuel filter & rubber fuel lines: Inline 5/16-in filter on V8s; spin-on filter on SD33 diesels · At purchase (Replace cracked rubber fuel hose. In-tank sender filters are also available.)
- Driveshaft U-joints & grease points: Chassis grease · At purchase and every oil change (Greaseable ball joints (Moog) add zerks up front.)
- Line ticket & factory manual: Build sheet for your VIN; licensed IH service manual reprints · Once (The line ticket settles every 'which part do I need' question. Factory service manuals are split 1971–75, 1976–77 and 1978–80.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: There's no clean stock answer, because 31s are already marginal. One owner of a 1977 Scout II said his 31s rubbed. IH Parts America's owner recommends a reverse-shackle kit and a 2.5-inch spring lift to run 31s without rubbing, and at least a 1-inch body lift plus a steering upgrade for 33s. Anything Scout rates the Rough Country 2.5-inch kit for up to a 32-inch tire. Plan on stock-sized tires (around 30 inches) if you won't lift it.

Q: Which engine should I look for?
A: The 345 V8 is the one most people want. Moses Ludel of 4WD Mechanix calls it 'one of the strongest and most durable gasoline V-8s ever built,' and Motor Sport's 1978 test of a 345 automatic gave 163 bhp and 292 lb-ft. The 304 is the same family. The 196 four is slow but simple, and the AMC sixes and Nissan diesels are rarer.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: There's no consensus year, and rust matters more than any of them. After 1974 every Scout II has Dana 44s at both ends and power front discs. Moses Ludel of 4WD Mechanix calls 1979 'a good model year' and says the only advantage of a 1980 is the one-year Dana 300 transfer case with its lower low range. Hagerty says the 1977–79 Super Scout II is the most valuable.

Q: Does mine have a Dana 30 or Dana 44 front axle?
A: Until 1974 the Dana 30 was standard at the front, with a Dana 44 as a special order in 1974. After 1974 every Scout II had Dana 44s at both ends. If the front cover is smaller and rounder than the rear one, it's a Dana 30. The line ticket confirms the axle and ratio.

Q: How do I tell what year it is?
A: Look at the grille. 1971–72 trucks have three horizontal bars; 1973 has 14 vertical bars; 1974–75 adds a vertical-bar overlay, with square chrome-and-black headlight rings on 1975. 1976 has a one-year 15-bar grille in three sections, 1977–79 has two big horizontal bars, and 1980 has a one-piece plastic grille with square headlights.

Q: What's a line ticket and where do I find it?
A: It's the factory build sheet for your VIN, showing the engine, transmission, axles, gear ratio, paint and options. On 1971–76 Scout IIs it's under the hood on the cowl; on 1977–80 trucks it's inside the glove box door. If yours is missing, you can order a replacement.

Q: What oil should I run?
A: About 7 quarts with a filter, according to an IH Parts America tech moderator. The IH V8 has a flat-tappet cam, and Binder Planet members recommend a high-zinc oil such as a 15W-40 diesel oil (or 20W-50 in a worn engine) rather than a modern low-zinc synthetic.

Q: How good is the fuel economy?
A: Not good with a V8. Motor Sport got 10 mpg on a fast motorway run in a 345 automatic and expected about 14 in gentler use. Super Scout Specialists claims 20 mpg in the city and up to 30 on the highway for the Nissan diesels.

Q: Is the diesel worth hunting for?
A: If you want something rare, yes. Super Scout Specialists counts 10,182 diesel Scouts: 4,222 naturally aspirated SD33s from 1976 to 1979, then 571 SD33T turbos in 1979 and 5,389 in 1980. Filters, water pumps and seals are still listed, but it's a slow, specialist engine, so check that the seller has records.

Q: Traveltop, Traveler, Terra or SSII: what's the difference?
A: The Scout II is the 100-inch-wheelbase truck with a steel Traveltop, half-cab Roadster top or soft top. The 1976–80 Traveler and Terra are 18 inches longer, with a fiberglass full top and hatch (Traveler) or a half-cab pickup (Terra). The 1977–79 SSII is the stripped soft-top off-roader with a plastic grille and roll bar.

Q: Does it have lockers, and how does the 4WD work?
A: There were no factory lockers. Trac-Lok limited-slip differentials were optional. The transfer case is manually shifted, with 2WD high, 4WD high and 4WD low, and the front hubs are free-wheeling. For 33-inch tires, Jim Weed's Off-Road.com build list recommends a front locker, a Detroit or ARB at the rear, and 4.10 gears.

Q: What are they worth?
A: Hagerty gives a median condition #2 value of $42,200 for 1972–80 Scout IIs. SSIIs are the most valuable at $64,750, while some configurations sit below $30,000. Values have levelled off or dipped slightly since 2022.

Q: How many were built?
A: Hagerty puts Scout II production at about 260,000. Super Scout Specialists' yearly figures run from 31,866 (1975) to 44,434 (1979), with only 13,106 in 1980. About 4,000 SSIIs were built from 1977 to 1979.

## International Scout Motors Traveler & Terra (Announced 2022 · revealed 2024)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/scout/scout-motors/
Codes: Traveler, Terra

Verdict: A boxy, body-on-frame 4x4 with a solid rear axle and lockers at both ends is exactly the kind of truck this site exists for. The catch is that it doesn't exist yet: as of October 2026, Scout is welding validation bodies in South Carolina and says customer deliveries start in 2028.

The Scout name went quiet when the last Scout II left Fort Wayne on October 21, 1980. Volkswagen Group came to own it in 2021, when its truck arm Traton completed the purchase of Navistar, International Harvester's successor. On May 11, 2022, Volkswagen approved a new, independent US company to design, build and sell off-road vehicles under the Scout name. Scout Motors Inc. was founded on May 24, 2022, and former Volkswagen Group of America boss Scott Keogh became its CEO on September 1, 2022. Everything on this page is as officially announced by Scout Motors, with dates. None of it has been driven by a customer.

### A FACTORY IN SOUTH CAROLINA
On March 3, 2023, Scout announced a $2 billion factory in Blythewood, South Carolina, designed to build up to 200,000 vehicles a year and to employ more than 4,000 people. Scout says its vehicles will be engineered in Detroit and built in South Carolina; its product, design and engineering teams work at an Innovation Center in Novi, Michigan. On November 12, 2025, Scout announced that its headquarters would move to Charlotte, North Carolina.
Scout plans to sell directly rather than through franchised dealers. Its website says retail stores will debut in 16 metro areas, expanding to about 100 locations in the US and Canada by 2032. That plan has drawn lawsuits: Volkswagen and Audi dealers in Florida sued in February 2025, and the California New Car Dealers Association sued Scout and Volkswagen Group of America in federal court. On March 30, 2026, a federal judge let the California association's main claims proceed.

### THE REVEAL
On October 24, 2024, at an event outside Nashville, Scout revealed two concepts: the Traveler SUV and the Terra pickup. The specification read like an off-roader's wish list. Scout announced a body-on-frame platform with a solid rear axle, four-wheel drive with an electric drive unit on each axle, front and rear mechanical locking differentials and a front sway-bar disconnect. It also projected an 800-volt architecture, up to 35-inch tires, more than 10,000 lb of towing for the Terra and more than 7,000 lb for the Traveler, and nearly 2,000 lb of payload.
Scout offered two powertrains. The battery-electric versions are projected to reach up to 350 miles of range. The "Harvester" extended-range versions add a gasoline generator and are projected to reach 500 miles or more. Scout said entry prices would start under $60,000, or as low as $50,000 for the Traveler and $51,500 for the Terra with incentives available at the time. Reservations opened that evening for $100, fully refundable. In January 2025 Keogh said there were more than 50,000 reservations, about 70% for the Traveler, and that more than half of buyers had picked the Harvester. At the November 2025 Los Angeles Auto Show, Scout showed refreshed concepts, with the Terra on 37-inch tires.

### THE WAIT
At the reveal Scout targeted the start of production for 2027, and its model pages still say "initial production targeted for 2027, subject to change." In March 2026 Keogh told a Detroit audience, "When do I see the cars in the hands of a physical customer? I see that sometime in 2028," and said reservations had reached about 160,000, roughly three-quarters of them for the Traveler. On April 13, 2026, a Scout spokesperson said, "We expect customers will begin taking delivery of new Scout vehicles in 2028."
In July 2026 Scout welded its first validation Traveler body at Blythewood. Keogh said the milestone gets the company "one step closer to delivering Scout vehicles in 2028." For now, the original Scout 80 and the Scout II remain the only Scouts you can actually drive.

- Price (Expected): Entry models under $60,000
- Reservations: $100 refundable; about 160,000 by March 2026 (Keogh)
- Deliveries: 2028 (Scout)

### Engineering
These are concept-stage specifications as announced by Scout Motors or reported at launch, up to October 2026. Scout says dimensions and specifications are estimates and subject to change, and nothing has been EPA-rated or delivered.
- Chassis: Body-on-frame (A new platform for both the Traveler and the Terra.)
- Axles & 4Wd: Solid rear axle; drive unit on each axle (Four-wheel drive. The front suspension design hasn't been detailed.)
- Lockers: Front and rear mechanical locking differentials (Announced for both models.)
- Powertrains: BEV or Harvester EREV (Projected range: up to 350 miles (BEV), 500 miles or more (EREV).)
- Electrical: 800-volt architecture · NACS charge port (Terra offers a 240-volt outlet, plus 120-volt and USB-C outlets.)
- Capability (Claimed): Terra 10,000+ lb tow · Traveler 7,000+ lb (Nearly 2,000 lb payload, as projected by Scout at the October 2024 launch.)

### Versions
- Revealed Oct 24, 2024 · Traveler SUV (concept) · BEV or Harvester EREV · Not announced · Seats up to six, Cabana retractable roof, front trunk, swing-out spare carrier.
- Revealed Oct 24, 2024 · Terra pickup (concept) · BEV or Harvester EREV · Not announced · 5.5-ft bed, front bench (seats up to six), retractable rear window, 240-V outlet.
- Nov 2025 · Refreshed concepts, LA Auto Show · BEV or EREV · Not announced · Traveler on 35-in tires; Terra on 37-in tires and 18-in wheels.
- 2028 (Scout's delivery target) · Traveler and Terra · BEV or Harvester EREV · Not announced · Scout says customers will begin taking delivery in 2028 (April 13, 2026); it hasn't said which model comes first.

### Year-by-year
- 2021: Volkswagen Group gains the Scout name when its truck arm Traton completes the purchase of Navistar, International Harvester's successor
- 2022: May 11: Volkswagen approves an independent US company to build electric off-roaders under the Scout name. Sept 1: Scott Keogh leaves Volkswagen of America to become Scout's CEO
- 2023: March 3: Scout announces a $2 billion plant in Blythewood, South Carolina, able to build 200,000 vehicles a year
- 2024: Oct 24: Traveler SUV and Terra pickup revealed near Nashville as production-intent concepts, battery-electric or with the 'Harvester' gas range extender. Reservations open; initial production targeted for 2027

- 2026: Sept 2: Scout says validation vehicles are being built in Blythewood in 2026, continuing into 2027, and that customer deliveries are expected to begin in 2028

### Capability
- Towing: over 7,000 lb (3,175 kg) Traveler; over 10,000 lb (4,536 kg) Terra (projected, Scout Motors, Oct 24, 2024)
- Payload: nearly 2,000 lb (907 kg), both models (projected, Oct 2024)
- Ground clearance: over 1 ft (305 mm) (projected, Oct 2024)
- Wading depth: nearly 3 ft (914 mm) (projected, Oct 2024)
- Range: up to 350 mi (563 km) battery-electric; more than 500 mi (805 km) with the Harvester range extender (anticipated, Oct 2024; repeated Nov 2025)
- Acceleration: 0–60 mph in as little as 3.5 s; nearly 1,000 lb-ft torque (battery-electric, anticipated, Oct 2024)
- Off-road hardware: Body-on-frame, solid rear axle, front and rear mechanical lockers, front sway-bar disconnect; electric drive unit on each axle (announced Oct 2024; Nov 2025 release calls the lockers 'available')
- Charging: 800 V architecture, NACS port, up to 350 kW DC, bidirectional (announced Oct 2024)
- Bed: 5.5 ft with two 120 V outlets and one 240 V outlet (Terra) (announced Oct 2024)

### Wheels and tires
- Biggest tire, Stock (announced) lift: up to 35-inch (Scout says the platform is 'intended to offer up to 35-inch tires' (Oct 24, 2024). Show concepts have run 35s on 22-in and 18-in beadlock wheels (Traveler) and 37s on 18-in wheels (Terra, LA Auto Show, Nov 2025); those are concepts, not production specs.)

### FAQ
Q: When can I actually buy one?
A: Scout says it expects customers to begin taking delivery in 2028 (spokesperson statement, April 13, 2026; Keogh said the same in March 2026), though its model pages still say initial production is targeted for 2027, subject to change. Scout hasn't said which model or powertrain comes first.

Q: How much will it cost?
A: Scout says entry-model pricing is "expected to start under $60,000" for both the Traveler and the Terra (scoutmotors.com, checked October 2026). At the October 2024 launch, coverage quoted as low as $50,000 for the Traveler and $51,500 for the Terra with incentives available at the time. Scout says final pricing will be confirmed closer to production.

Q: EREV or BEV: what's the difference?
A: The battery-electric version is projected at up to 350 miles of range. The Harvester extended-range version adds a gasoline generator and is projected at 500 miles or more. In January 2025 Keogh said more than half of reservation holders had chosen the Harvester.

Q: Is it a real off-roader?
A: On paper, yes. At the October 2024 reveal Scout announced body-on-frame construction, a solid rear axle, four-wheel drive, front and rear mechanical locking differentials and a front sway-bar disconnect, and projected more than 12 inches of ground clearance and up to 3 feet of water fording. Those are projections until production specifications are published.

Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: Unknown, because production specifications haven't been published. The concepts were shown on 35-inch tires (Traveler) and 37-inch tires on 18-inch wheels (Terra, November 2025 LA Auto Show).

Q: Where will it be built?
A: At Scout's $2 billion Production Center in Blythewood, South Carolina, announced March 3, 2023. It's planned for up to 200,000 vehicles a year and more than 4,000 jobs. Scout welded the first validation Traveler body there in July 2026.

Q: How do reservations work?
A: Reservations cost $100, are fully refundable and are non-binding. They opened on October 24, 2024. Keogh said there were more than 50,000 by January 2025, and about 160,000 by March 2026, roughly three-quarters of them for the Traveler.

Q: Will I buy it from a dealer?
A: No. Scout plans to sell directly, and says retail stores will open in 16 metro areas and grow to about 100 locations in the US and Canada by 2032. Dealers have sued over the direct-sales plan: Volkswagen and Audi dealers in Florida in February 2025, and the California New Car Dealers Association in federal court, where a judge let the main claims proceed on March 30, 2026.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: At the October 2024 reveal Scout projected more than 10,000 lb for the Terra, more than 7,000 lb for the Traveler, and nearly 2,000 lb of payload for both. Scout says capacities vary by model and trim, and nothing is final until production specifications are published.

Q: Is it related to the original Scout?
A: In name and styling only. Volkswagen Group acquired the Scout trademarks in 2021 through Navistar, and the new trucks borrow the original Scout's shape. Scout Motors now owns the Scout, Traveler, Terra and Travelall trademarks, and IH Parts America notes that it uses them under license for parts for the original trucks.

# Isuzu Trooper (1981–2002)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/trooper/

Isuzu built the Trooper from September 1981 to September 2002, across two generations. It started life as a wagon on the company's pickup chassis and grew into a full-size, V6-powered family 4x4. Japan knew it as the Bighorn, and the rest of the world met it under other names: Holden Jackaroo and Monterey in Australia, Opel and Vauxhall Monterey in Europe, Honda Horizon in Japan, Acura SLX in the US, plus Chevrolet Trooper and Subaru Bighorn. SsangYong even built it under licence with its own bodywork, as the Korando Family. The first generation (1981–1991) is the boxiest: a narrow, upright wagon with independent torsion-bar front suspension, leaf springs at the back and four-cylinder engines, sold in the US from 1984 as the Trooper II. The second generation (1991–2002) added Isuzu's aluminium 3.2- and 3.5-liter V6s, coil springs at the back and, from 1998, Torque On Demand. It won its class in the 1994 Paris–Dakar and won the Australian Safari again and again as the Holden Jackaroo. In America the second generation is also remembered for a fight. Consumer Reports rated the 1995–96 Trooper and Acura SLX 'Not Acceptable' for rollover risk in 1996. NHTSA declined to open a defect investigation, Isuzu sued, and in 2000 a jury found some of the magazine's statements false but awarded no damages. Today both generations are cheap, capable boxes. Buy a first-generation truck for its simplicity and check it for rust; buy a second-generation one for space and towing, and check the oil.

Verdict: Isuzu drew a box, sold it under about a dozen badges on four continents, then spent four years in court defending its honour. The first one is a tall, honest tool; the second is a roomy V6 cruiser with a solid rear axle and a thirst for oil.

## Isuzu Trooper (first generation) (1981–1991)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/trooper/trooper-1/
Codes: UBS, Trooper II, Bighorn, Jackaroo

Verdict: A pickup truck wearing a shoebox, and that's a compliment. The first Trooper is narrow, tall, slow and gloriously honest, with more cargo room than it has any right to. Buy the rust-free one, not the shiny one.

In September 1981 Isuzu announced a compact four-wheel-drive wagon called the Rodeo Bighorn. Underneath it was the company's own pickup, sold in America as the Isuzu P'UP and Chevy LUV. Car and Driver reckoned that almost everything under the squarish steel skin, from the chassis to the driveline, was identical or very similar to the four-wheel-drive pickup. On top sat a body drawn with a set square: flat glass, flat sides and a roof you could land a helicopter on. It would be sold under more names than almost any SUV in history, and every one of them was a box.

### THE TROOPER II ARRIVES
America got it for 1984 as the Trooper II, a two-door imported as a truck. Isuzu chose to pay the 25 percent duty on light trucks rather than squeeze it into Japan's car import quotas, which is why the rear seat was a $300 option. The 'II' marked that truck version; a passenger-car 'Trooper I' was promised and never came. Car and Driver's May 1984 test car had the 1.95-liter four with 82 hp, a four-speed manual and a 13.2-gallon tank. The magazine called the power modest and the ride about as plush as a 4x4 got, and estimated the base price at well under $9,000.
Isuzu's own 1985 brochure shows how quickly the truck grew. That year brought a four-door body, a 2.3-liter gas four, a 2.2-liter turbo-diesel (not sold in California), a five-speed, auto-locking front hubs, three skid plates and a 21.9-gallon tank. The brochure also boasted that the Trooper II had been named 4-Wheel & Off-Road magazine's 1985 '4x4 of the Year', ahead of rivals including the Jeep Cherokee and Toyota 4Runner.

### GROWING UP, 1987–1991
For 1987 the Trooper II got flush rectangular headlights, a bold new grille, a wider track and bigger P235/75R15 tires, and the four-door could now be had as a plusher LS. The brochure quoted 96 hp and 123 lb-ft from the 2.3-liter four, and the same brochure shows a Trooper II racing in the Baja 1000's Class 14 in November 1986. For 1988 the 2.6-liter 4ZE1 with fuel injection and 120 hp arrived, and for 1989 Isuzu added an optional 2.8-liter General Motors V6, the pushrod engine from the Chevrolet S-10, until its own V6 was ready.
Late trucks could also be had with a four-speed automatic: Wikipedia says four-cylinder trucks used an Aisin A340H and V6 trucks a GM 4L30E. The basic hardware never changed much. An independent front end on torsion bars, a live rear axle on leaf springs, part-time four-wheel drive and a two-speed transfer case made it more capable than its skinny tires and narrow track suggested. In 1989 only, Isuzu sent America the short-wheelbase, two-door Trooper RS (see the sidebar).

### ONE BOX, MANY BADGES
Outside the US the truck was everywhere, under different names. Australians and New Zealanders bought it as the Holden Jackaroo, named after the word for a young man working on a sheep or cattle station. Indonesia and South America knew it as the Chevrolet Trooper, Venezuela built it locally as the Caribe 442, and in Japan it was the Isuzu Bighorn. From November 1988 Subaru sold a Bighorn of its own, only with Irmscher trim and the 2.8-liter turbo-diesel. Isuzu also offered a limited run of 100 Bighorn Irmscher R models, with Recaro seats and graphics but no extra power.
The strangest relative came from Korea. In November 1988 SsangYong began licensed production of the Trooper under its own bodywork as the Korando Family, first with the Trooper's 2.2-liter diesel and later with Peugeot and Mercedes-Benz diesels. Rival boxes of the era included the first Mitsubishi Pajero and Toyota's 4Runner, while Curbside Classic's owner story compares the Trooper's shape to the Range Rover at less than half the price.

### HOW IT ENDED
Isuzu replaced it with a bigger, more luxurious second-generation Trooper in December 1991. The old shape went out on a high in Australia, where a short-wheelbase Holden Jackaroo won the Marathon class of the 1989 Australian Safari in Peter Lockhart's hands, and it lived on for years in Korea as the Korando Family.
Today the first Trooper is a cult truck with modest prices: Bring a Trailer sales from 2024 to 2026 run from $3,500 for a 2.6-powered 1986 project to $14,250 for a 1986 two-door LS five-speed, with a Japanese Bighorn Irmscher at $25,000. Owners love the space and the visibility. They also warn about rusted rear-door hinges, cracked cylinder heads and failed head gaskets on the fours, and wheel studs that strip at the first impact gun. Parts support has thinned, so many owners rely on the Planet Isuzoo community for help.

### Data plate
- Chassis: UBS (UBS13 / 16 / 17 / 52 / 55 by engine)
- Production: September 1981 – 1991 (Japan)
- Us Model Years: 1984–1991 (Trooper II)
- Body: Two-door (three-door) and four-door (five-door) wagon; short and long wheelbase
- Engines (Us): 1.95 L, 2.3 L, 2.6 L I4; 2.2 L diesel / turbo-diesel; 2.8 L GM V6
- Transmission: 4-spd manual (1984); 5-spd manual; 4-spd automatic (late)
- Drive: Part-time 4WD, two-speed transfer case
- Wheelbase: 104.3 in (2,650 mm); RS / SWB about 90 in (2,300 mm)
- Width: 65 in (1,650 mm)
- Ground Clearance: 8.3 in (at rear differential)
- Curb Weight: 3,366–3,421 lb (1987 gas)
- Fuel Tank: 21.9 gal (1985 on)
- Wheel Bolt Pattern: 6 x 139.7 mm

### Engineering
The first Trooper is a pickup-derived ladder frame with an independent, torsion-bar front end and a leaf-sprung live rear axle. Four-wheel drive is part-time, through a two-speed transfer case and either auto-locking or manual front hubs. Engines started as small Isuzu fours and finished with a GM V6, and the wheels bolt on with six studs on a 139.7 mm circle.
- Chassis: Ladder frame from the Isuzu P'UP / Faster 4x4 pickup (Wheelbase 2,650 mm (104.3 in) for the long three-door and five-door; 2,300 mm for the short-wheelbase body.)
- Front Suspension: Independent double wishbone on torsion bars (Isuzu's 1987 brochure quotes a front stabilizer bar over an inch thick.)
- Rear Suspension: Live axle on two-stage semi-elliptic leaf springs (Front disc and rear drum brakes on 1987 US trucks.)
- 4Wd System: Part-time, two-speed transfer case (Selected with a separate lever. Isuzu auto-locking hubs or Aisin manual hubs; with the hubs engaged you can shift between 2WD and 4WD high without stopping.)
- Engines (Us): 1.95 L, 2.3 L and 2.6 L fours; 2.8 L GM V6 (1989–91) (Plus a 2.2 L diesel and turbo-diesel in the mid-1980s. Overseas: 2.8 L 4JB1 diesels.)
- Protection: Three skid plates (Isuzu's brochures list plates for the radiator, the transfer case and the fuel tank.)

### Versions
- 1984 (US) · Trooper II 2-door · G200Z 1.95 L SOHC I4 / C223 2.2 L diesel I4 · 82 hp / 101 lb-ft; diesel 62 hp / 96 lb-ft · Four-speed manual, 13.2 gal tank. Imported as a truck; the rear seat was a $300 option.
- 1985–1987 (US) · Trooper II 2-door and 4-door · 4ZD1 2.3 L SOHC I4 / C223T 2.2 L turbo-diesel · 96 hp / 123 lb-ft; turbo-diesel 80 hp / 125 lb-ft (1987 brochure) · Five-speed, auto hubs, 21.9 gal tank. Turbo-diesel not sold in California. Facelift with rectangular lamps for 1987.
- 1988–1991 (US) · Trooper II / Trooper · 4ZE1 2.6 L SOHC I4, fuel-injected · 120 hp · Five-speed manual or Aisin A340H four-speed automatic.
- 1989–1991 (US) · Trooper · GM LL2 2.8 L OHV V6 · 122 hp / 204 N·m · Borrowed from the Chevrolet S-10; automatic trucks used the GM 4L30E.
- 1989 (US) · Trooper RS (short wheelbase) · 4ZE1 2.6 L I4 · 120 hp · About 90 in wheelbase, 4.77:1 gears, 15 x 7 in 'snowflake' alloys. One year only.
- Late 1980s (export) · UBS55 Bighorn / Jackaroo / Trooper · 4JB1 2.8 L diesel and 4JB1-T turbo-diesel · 95 PS (turbo), up to 115 PS intercooled · Never sold new in the US.

### Year-by-year
- 1981: September: Isuzu announces the Rodeo Bighorn in Japan, a compact 4WD wagon on its pickup chassis
- 1984: US launch as the Trooper II two-door: 1.95 L gas four (82 hp) or 2.2 L diesel, four-speed manual, rear seat optional
- 1985: Four-door body, 2.3 L gas four, 2.2 L turbo-diesel (not in California), five-speed, auto-locking hubs and a 21.9 gal tank
- 1987: Facelift with flush rectangular headlights and a new grille, wider track, P235/75R15 tires and a four-door LS
- 1988: Fuel-injected 2.6 L 4ZE1 with 120 hp arrives
- 1989: Optional 2.8 L GM V6; one-year-only short-wheelbase Trooper RS two-door
- 1990–1991: Recalls for the oil-cooler hose (90V166) and automatic transmission overfill (90V167); NHTSA's owner complaints include under-hood fires and stripped wheel studs
- 1991: December: replaced by the second-generation Trooper

### Capability

- Fuel tank: 21.9 US gal (83 L) (From 1985; 13.2 gal on the 1984 two-door)
- Ground clearance: 8.3 in (211 mm) (Minimum, at the rear differential (Isuzu brochures))
- Fuel economy: EPA 21 city / 27 hwy (1984 1.95); 17 / 20 (1987 2.3 five-speed) (Car and Driver averaged 21 mpg in 1984)
- Curb weight: 3,366 lb (2-door) / 3,421 lb (4-door) (1987 gas trucks)
- Turning circle: 38.8 ft (11.8 m) curb to curb (1987)
- Cargo volume: 79.0 cu ft without the rear seat (45.5 cu ft with the seat up)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: P235/75R15 on 6.0 x 15 (Deluxe) or 6.5 x 15 (LS) wheels, 1987 US, 15 x 7 alloy 'snowflake' wheels on the 1989 Trooper RS

- Offset: +3 mm (stock 15 x 6.5, per ThreePiece.us)
- Center Bore: 100 mm
- Lug Thread: M12x1.5

### Buying checks
- Rust first, everything else second: Check the rear cargo doors, their hinges and pins, the floors and the sills. Isuzu recalled 1984–87 trucks (92V093) because salt-belt corrosion in the rear-door hinges could let the doors close in a false latch, and a Curbside Classic reader summed up the rest: once the rear doors started to rust, it was game over.
- Look at every wheel stud: Stripped or snapped wheel studs and galled lug nuts are among the most common owner complaints logged with NHTSA for 1988–91 Troopers, and Curbside Classic's owner broke them too. Make sure all 24 studs are present and the nuts thread on by hand.
- Ask about the head and head gasket: NHTSA's complaint files for 1988 and 1989 Troopers include several cracked cylinder heads and repeated head-gasket failures, and a Curbside Classic reader lost his truck to 'the head gasket issue'. Look for a history of overheating, coolant in the oil and a radiator that hasn't been neglected.
- Check that the recall work was done: 1990–91 trucks were recalled for an oil-cooler hose that could touch the exhaust manifold and melt (90V166), and for automatic transmissions that could spill overfilled fluid onto the exhaust (90V167). On 1987–88 trucks (89V001), a heater bolt could rub through a fuel pipe. NHTSA's 1990–91 complaint files also include several under-hood fires.
- Engage the hubs and the low range: Put it in 4WD high and low on loose ground. Auto-locking hubs should lock and unlock reliably, and the transfer case should shift without a fight. Many owners swap tired auto hubs for manual ones.
- Know which engine you're getting: Early 1.95s and 2.3s are slow. The injected 2.6-liter four (1988–91) and the 2.8-liter GM V6 (1989–91) are the stronger engines, but NHTSA's 1988–89 complaint files include cracked heads, so the history matters more than the badge. US turbo-diesels from the mid-1980s are rare and were never sold in California.
- Drive the automatic hard: A Curbside Classic reader's automatic failed at about 175,000 miles, and NHTSA's 1990–91 complaint files include several slipping, leaking or failed transmissions. A five-speed is the simpler buy.
- Ask for the timing-belt receipt: The Isuzu four-cylinder petrol engines use a timing belt (the 2.3 switched from a chain to a Kevlar belt), so a truck with no record needs one before it goes anywhere remote.

### Common repairs
#### Replace stripped or broken wheel studs
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Lug nuts that won't thread on, studs that snap when a tire shop uses an impact gun, or a wheel that loosens. Owners have reported all three to NHTSA.
Fix: Support the truck safely and pull the wheel. On the front, remove the caliper and rotor to reach the back of the hub; on the rear, pull the drum. Drive out the damaged stud, clean the hub, then draw the new stud in with a stack of washers and a lug nut, or press it in, until the head seats fully. Fit new lug nuts with any damaged studs, start every nut by hand and torque them to the factory spec in a star pattern. Tell your tire shop to do the same.
Tools: Hammer and punch or a stud press · washers · torque wrench · factory torque spec [CONFIRM IN MANUAL].

#### Timing belt on the 2.3 and 2.6 fours
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: None until it fails. A truck without a belt receipt is due.
Fix: Disconnect the battery, drain the coolant and remove the fan, drive belts and crankshaft pulley, then the timing covers. Set the engine to top dead center and line up the cam and crank timing marks before you loosen anything. Fit the new belt and tensioner, check the marks again after turning the engine over twice by hand, and replace the cam and crank seals if they're weeping. Many owners do the water pump at the same time.
Tools: Socket set · crank-pulley holding tool · torque wrench · factory service manual.

#### Cooling-system refresh to protect the head
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time A morning · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Creeping temperature, steam, coolant loss or a sweet smell. NHTSA complaint files describe cracked heads and blown head gaskets on 1988–89 trucks.
Fix: With the engine cold, drain the radiator and replace the thermostat, the radiator hoses and the cap. Inspect the radiator for blocked or weeping cores and replace it if in doubt. Refill slowly with the heater on and bleed out air pockets: one 1988 owner blamed air pockets in the head for coolant reaching the cylinders. If the oil looks milky or the cooling system pressurizes quickly, pressure-test it and do a compression or leak-down test before deciding on head work.
Tools: Drain pan · pliers · cooling-system pressure tester · funnel · the coolant type specified for your engine [CONFIRM IN MANUAL].

#### Service or replace the front locking hubs
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time A couple of hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Hubs that won't lock in 4WD, grind or clunk when they engage, or won't release.
Fix: Jack up one front wheel at a time. Remove the hub cover bolts and pull the hub body, then clean out old grease and water, check the internals for wear and broken parts and regrease lightly. While it's open, check the wheel-bearing preload and the axle shaft splines. If an auto hub is worn out, many owners fit a pair of manual hubs. Test 4WD high and low on loose ground afterwards.
Tools: Hex keys or sockets · snap-ring pliers · grease · factory manual for bearing preload.

#### Front CV boots and axles
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Half a day per side · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Grease flung around the inside of the wheel, or a click on full lock under power.
Fix: Support the truck, pull the wheel and the hub, disconnect the lower ball joint or knuckle as the manual describes, and slide the axle out of the differential. Either rebuild the joint with a new boot, clamps and grease, or fit a complete replacement axle. Check the differential output seal while the axle is out.
Tools: Socket set · ball-joint separator · boot-clamp pliers · new axle nut.

#### Free up and protect the rear-door hinges
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Rear doors that sag, bind or don't latch properly. Isuzu's 1992 recall (92V093) covered 1984–87 trucks for exactly this in salt-belt states.
Fix: Support each door before you work on it. Soak the hinge pins with penetrating oil, work them free, clean the knuckles and grease them. Treat rust around the hinge mounts and the bottom of the door shells. Then adjust the latch strikers so each door closes positively, with no false latch.
Tools: Penetrating oil · brass drift · grease · rust converter and paint · screwdrivers for striker adjustment.

#### Automatic transmission service (and the 90V167 recall check)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An hour or two · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Late or harsh shifts, a fluid smell or smoke from the exhaust manifold. On 1990–91 automatics, overfilled fluid could escape onto the exhaust (recall 90V167).
Fix: Drop the pan, replace the filter and gasket, and refill with the specified fluid. Check the level exactly as the manual describes and do not overfill. Confirm with an Isuzu or Chevrolet dealer, or the NHTSA VIN lookup, that the recall work was done.
Tools: Drain pan · socket set · torque wrench · funnel · Dexron-III-type ATF (Liqui Moly lookup; it lists ≈4.5 L for the 1990–92 2.6 automatic).

### Baseline service
Treat any first-generation Trooper as unserviced until receipts prove otherwise. These trucks are 35 to 40 years old, so the cheap fluids and rubber parts are what keep the engine and drivetrain alive. Isuzu's factory specs aren't widely published online. The fluid types and capacities below come from Liqui Moly's lookup, which uses European-market Isuzu data, so confirm viscosities and US figures in the owner's or service manual for your engine.
- Engine oil & filter: ≈4.7 L (5.0 US qt) with filter on the 1988–90 2.6; ≈5.4 L (5.7 US qt) with filter on the 1990–92 2.6 (Liqui Moly lookup, European data) · grade [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Then at the owner's-manual interval (Watch for leaks at the oil-cooler hoses on 1990–91 trucks; recall 90V166 rerouted a hose that could touch the exhaust manifold.)
- Air filter & fuel filter: Replace both · Then inspect at every oil change (Old fuel filters and tired pumps cause many hard-start complaints on old trucks.)
- Ignition: Plugs, wires, distributor cap and rotor (2.6) · Then per the manual (The 1988–91 2.6-liter uses a distributor, so the cap and rotor are part of a tune-up.)
- Timing belt (four-cylinder petrol): Belt, tensioner, cam and crank seals · Now, if there's no record; then per the manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (The 2.3 and 2.6 Isuzu fours use a belt.)
- Coolant, hoses and thermostat: Coolant type per the manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · ≈9.8 L (10.4 US qt) system on the 2.3 and 2.6 (Liqui Moly lookup) · Flush now (Owners report cracked heads and head gaskets on these engines, so a healthy cooling system is cheap insurance.)
- Manual transmission oil: Engine oil, not gear oil (Liqui Moly's lookup lists multigrade engine oils) · ≈2.95 L (3.1 US qt) in the 2.6 five-speed; on the 2.3 it lists 4.6 L for gearbox and transfer case together · viscosity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Drain and refill now (Check the clutch hydraulics while you're under there.)
- Automatic transmission fluid & filter: Dexron-III-type ATF (Liqui Moly lists its ATF III) · ≈4.5 L (4.8 US qt) for the 1990–92 2.6 automatic (Liqui Moly lookup) · Pan drop and filter now (Don't overfill. That's what recall 90V167 was about on 1990–91 trucks.)
- Transfer case: Engine oil, as in the gearbox (Liqui Moly lookup) · ≈1.45 L (1.5 US qt) on the 2.6 · viscosity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Drain and refill now (Shift through 2H, 4H and 4L afterwards to check the linkage.)
- Front & rear differentials: GL-5 hypoid gear oil; LSD-rated oil in a limited-slip rear · 2.6: ≈1.5 L (1.6 US qt) front, ≈1.8 L (1.9 US qt) rear; 2.3: ≈1.0 L front, ≈1.5 L rear (Liqui Moly lookup) · viscosity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Drain and refill now (Check the pinion seals for leaks.)
- Front hubs & wheel bearings: Clean, inspect, repack · Now, then as needed (Water in auto hubs is a common cause of hubs that won't engage.)
- Brake fluid & hoses: Flush; inspect the rubber hoses · Every two years (Front discs and rear drums; check the rear wheel cylinders for leaks.)
- U-joints & driveshafts: Grease the fittings; check for play · At every oil change (One 1990 owner reported a driveshaft falling while driving; check for play in the joints and loose bolts.)
- Wheel studs & lug nuts: Inspect every stud and nut · Every tire rotation (Hand-start every nut and torque to spec; never let a shop hammer them on with an impact gun.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: The factory size from 1987 was P235/75R15, about 29 inches, on 6.0- or 6.5-inch-wide 15-inch wheels. We couldn't verify a first-generation forum consensus for the largest no-lift size, so check the tire-fitment chart and build threads on Planet Isuzoo before you buy, and check the rear-door-mounted spare carrier too. Wheels are 6 x 139.7 mm with a 100 mm center bore and M12 x 1.5 studs.

Q: Why is it called the Trooper II?
A: American Isuzu's product-development manager told Car and Driver in 1984 that 'II' marked the truck version, with the rear seat a $300 option, and 'I' would have been the car version with a standard rear seat. A Trooper I never came. Isuzu imported it as a truck to avoid Japan's car import quotas, and paid the 25 percent truck duty instead.

Q: Which engine should I look for?
A: The 1988–91 2.6-liter 4ZE1 is fuel-injected and makes 120 hp; the optional 1989–91 2.8-liter GM V6 makes 122 hp with more torque. The 1984 1.95-liter made 82 hp and the 1985–87 2.3-liter about 96 hp, so early trucks are slow.

Q: Was there a diesel in the US?
A: Yes. 1984 trucks could have a 2.2-liter pushrod diesel with 62 hp, and from 1985 Isuzu offered a 2.2-liter turbo-diesel (80 hp in the 1987 brochure), which wasn't sold in California. They're rare now; Bring a Trailer sold a 1986 turbo-diesel five-speed for $8,200 in November 2025.

Q: How does the four-wheel drive work?
A: It's part-time with a two-speed transfer case on its own lever. From 1985 Isuzu fitted auto-locking front hubs, so once they're engaged you can shift between 2WD and 4WD without stopping. Some trucks had Aisin manual hubs instead. Don't drive in 4WD on dry pavement.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: The 1984 1.95-liter was rated at 21 mpg city and 27 highway, and Car and Driver averaged 21 mpg. Isuzu's 1987 brochure lists 17 city and 20 highway for the 2.3-liter five-speed and claims up to 438 miles per tank of gas.

Q: How much can it carry?
A: Car and Driver's 1984 two-door had a 1,222 lb payload rating. Isuzu's 1987 brochure lists 1,374 lb (two-door) and 1,319 lb (four-door) for gas trucks, and 79 cubic feet of cargo space with the rear seat removed.

Q: How big is the fuel tank?
A: The 1984 truck Car and Driver tested had a 13.2-gallon tank. From 1985 Isuzu quoted 21.9 gallons.

Q: Is a Holden Jackaroo or Isuzu Bighorn the same truck?
A: Yes. The Jackaroo (Australia and New Zealand), Bighorn (Japan), Subaru Bighorn, Chevrolet Trooper and Venezuela's Caribe 442 are all the same UBS truck. SsangYong's Korando Family was built under licence with its own bodywork. Imports of Japanese and Australian versions can bring diesel engines the US never got.

Q: What is one worth?
A: Bring a Trailer sales from late 2024 to mid-2026 ranged from $3,500 (a 2.6-powered 1986) to $14,250 (a 1986 Trooper II LS two-door five-speed), with most clean drivers between $7,000 and $9,500. A 1991 Bighorn Irmscher turbo-diesel sold for $25,000 in August 2025.

Q: Can I still get parts?
A: Service parts such as filters, belts, hubs, CV axles and brake parts are still listed for 1988–91 Troopers at RockAuto. Trim and body parts are harder. Owners on Overland Bound say parts support for Isuzu light trucks has gone downhill, and point to Planet Isuzoo for help.

## Isuzu Trooper (second generation) (1991–2002)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/trooper/trooper-2/
Codes: UBS25, UBS26, Acura SLX, Monterey

Verdict: The Trooper grew up, got an aluminium V6 and a cabin big enough to hold a dance in, and then got caught in the most famous rollover fight in SUV history. It's a properly capable box with a solid rear axle. Just keep a quart of oil and the dipstick handy.

In December 1991 Isuzu replaced the Trooper with a completely new one, and Japan liked it enough to give the Bighorn a Special Award in the 1992/93 Japan Car of the Year. It was bigger, softer and far more powerful than the tall, narrow original, with a new aluminium V6 that Isuzu said it had built specifically for the truck. Underneath it was still a ladder frame with a live rear axle and a two-speed transfer case. It also stayed a box, just a wider one with rounded edges, and it went on to wear more badges than almost anything else on the road.

### THE V6S: 6VD1 AND 6VE1
Isuzu's 1992 US brochure introduced the 3.2-liter V6 with an aluminium block and heads, four valves per cylinder, a variable intake system and distributorless ignition. The Trooper S got a single-cam version with 175 hp and 188 lb-ft, and the LS a twin-cam with 190 hp and 195 lb-ft. Both are 75-degree V6s with belt-driven cams. For 1996 a revised single-cam engine made 190 hp, and that's what the new Acura SLX used.
For 1998 the 6VE1 arrived: a longer-stroke 3.5-liter twin-cam rated at 215 hp and 230 lb-ft at 3,000 rpm, with cast-iron cylinder liners in an aluminium block. MotorTrend thought it smoother and much torquier than the old 3.2. Owners later found the catch. NHTSA's complaint files for 1998–2000 Troopers are full of 3.5s burning a quart every few hundred miles, and several ran dry and seized with no warning light. One long-time owner on Bob Is The Oil Guy blames too few oil-return drains in the piston skirts, which clog and let the rings stick.

### AUTO HUBS, SHIFT-ON-THE-FLY, THEN TORQUE ON DEMAND
The chassis was a big step up. Front suspension is independent, with double wishbones and torsion bars, and the rear is a coil-sprung live axle on a multi-link location, with Acura quoting 7.5 inches of wheel travel at each end. Disc brakes were fitted at all four wheels. Buyers could have a five-speed manual or a GM 4L30-E four-speed automatic with 'power' and 'winter' modes, and in 1992 a limited-slip rear differential was standard on the LS. The trucks were rated to tow 5,000 lb, and Isuzu's brochure claimed they could climb a 39-degree slope.
Four-wheel drive stayed part-time at first, with automatic front hubs. Some 1996 trucks gained shift-on-the-fly, and the 1998 facelift added a Borg-Warner Torque On Demand system on S Performance and S Luxury trucks. In '4WD Auto' it uses sensors in the transfer case to send torque to the front axle when the rear slips, which suited snowy commutes. The 1998 update also brought a new grille, bumper, headlamps and front fenders and a body-coloured hard spare-tire cover. The grille changed again for 2000, and 2000–02 automatics got Grade Logic, which downshifts on steep descents.

### 'NOT ACCEPTABLE'
On August 20, 1996, Consumers Union, the publisher of Consumer Reports, labelled the Trooper and its Acura SLX twin 'Not Acceptable'. It said both had tipped up high on two wheels in emergency maneuvers during its road tests. The October 1996 issue described the 1995–96 Trooper as dangerously prone to tipping during sudden lane changes, while three other SUVs in the test were not. Consumers Union also petitioned NHTSA to open a defect investigation. The damage was immediate: Trooper sales fell by more than half in the first six months of 1997, to 4,313 from 9,290, and SLX sales fell 63.2 percent to 448.
NHTSA ran its own tests and in July 1997 denied the petition, saying it found no evidence that an investigation would lead to a defect finding or recall. Isuzu then sued Consumers Union for $242 million, arguing that the testers had steered harder than any real driver would. Judge Richard Paez ruled that Isuzu's public campaign made it a public figure, which raised the bar for proving defamation. In April 2000 a federal jury in Los Angeles found that seven of 15 disputed statements were false, and one was made with reckless disregard for the truth. It still awarded Isuzu nothing, and both sides claimed victory.
Isuzu later put the cost of the affair at $244 million, and the bad press is often blamed for the SLX's early death. For owners today the lesson is practical rather than legal. A tall, narrow-tracked truck on soft springs leans, and NHTSA's 1995–96 complaint files include owners worried about rollover; one 1996 complaint records the front ride height being lowered at the torsion bars to cure a top-heavy, tippy feel. Keep lifts modest, keep weight off the roof and keep the shocks fresh.

### ONE BOX, MANY BADGES
General Motors, Isuzu and Honda turned the UBS into a badge-engineering showcase. Honda sold it in Japan as the Horizon from 1994 to 1999 and in America as the Acura SLX (see the sidebar). In Europe it was the Opel Monterey from 1992 to 1999, and in Britain the Vauxhall Monterey from spring 1994. Hagerty UK says that one was well reviewed, beating a Range Rover and a Mitsubishi Shogun in one 1994 group test, but found little more than 4,000 buyers. Australians bought it as the Holden Jackaroo and the more luxurious Holden Monterey, and Holden Special Vehicles built 79 HSV Jackaroos and 234 Jackaroo SEs. Subaru sold a Lotus-tuned Bighorn until 1994.
Outside North America the engine list was longer. A 2.6-liter four was offered in some markets, and diesels started with the 3.1-liter 4JG2 turbo-diesel (114 PS in export form). From 1998 they moved to the direct-injection 3.0-liter 4JX1 with about 159 PS. What Car? rated the 3.0 turbo-diesel the better buy for towing and off-road work in the UK, and called the Trooper one of the very best in the sticky stuff, though less good on the road.

### HOW IT ENDED
Isuzu dropped the Trooper in the US after 2002, replacing it with the smaller Axiom and the GMC Envoy-based Ascender. The last Japanese Bighorn was built in September 2002, when Isuzu stopped making its own passenger vehicles, though the Philippines kept selling a 3.0 diesel Trooper until 2005. The UBS left a good competition record: a Marathon-class win and 12th overall in the 1994 Paris–Dakar, and Australian Safari wins for Bruce Garland's Holden Jackaroos in 1996 and every year from 1999 to 2002.
Today it's a cheap way into a solid-rear-axle, low-range four-door with a huge cargo bay. On Bring a Trailer, second-generation Troopers have sold for $6,000 to $14,250 since late 2024, and an Acura SLX for $11,250. An Overland Bound owner with 203,000 miles on his 1998 summed it up: it averages 16–17 mpg, gets a quart of oil every 700–800 miles, and has needed little else.

### Engineering
The UBS is a body-on-frame wagon with independent front suspension on torsion bars and a coil-sprung, multi-link live rear axle. It has four-wheel ventilated disc brakes and an Isuzu 75-degree aluminium V6 in the US. Four-wheel drive was part-time with automatic hubs, then shift-on-the-fly, and from 1998 Borg-Warner's Torque On Demand on some trims. Wheels bolt on with six studs on a 139.7 mm circle.
- Chassis: Galvanized steel body on a ladder frame (Wheelbase 108.7 in (2,760 mm) for the five-door; 2,330 mm for the three-door.)
- Front Suspension: Independent double wishbone, torsion bars (7.5 in of wheel travel and a 26 mm anti-roll bar (Acura SLX spec). Ride height is set at the torsion-bar adjusters.)
- Rear Suspension: Multi-link live axle on coil springs (7.5 in of travel and a 19 mm anti-roll bar. A limited-slip differential was optional, and standard on the 1992 LS.)
- 4Wd System: Part-time with auto hubs; shift-on-the-fly from 1996; TOD from 1998 (Borg-Warner Torque On Demand on S Performance and S Luxury trucks in 1998. Two-speed transfer case throughout.)
- Engines (Us): 3.2 L 6VD1 SOHC / DOHC V6; 3.5 L 6VE1 DOHC V6 (1998–2002) (175–190 hp from the 3.2; 215 hp and 230 lb-ft from the 3.5. Belt-driven cams; aluminium block with iron liners.)
- Transmissions: 5-speed manual or GM 4L30-E four-speed automatic (Power and winter (third-gear start) modes; Grade Logic on 2000–02 automatics.)

- 1996–1997 (US) · UBS25 Trooper / Acura SLX · 6VD1 3.2 L SOHC V6 (revised) · 190 hp @ 5,600 / 188 lb-ft @ 4,000 · Shift-on-the-fly on some trucks. The 1995–96 Trooper and SLX were rated 'Not Acceptable' by Consumer Reports in 1996.
- 1998–2002 (US) · UBS26 Trooper / Acura SLX (to 1999) · 6VE1 3.5 L DOHC V6 · 215 hp @ 5,400 / 230 lb-ft @ 3,000 · Facelift, Torque On Demand on some trims, body-color hard spare cover. Watch the oil consumption.
