### Buying checks
- Check the oil on any 3.5 (1998–2002): Pull the dipstick before anything else and ask how much oil it uses. NHTSA's complaint files describe 6VE1s using a quart every 450–1,000 miles and several that ran dry and seized without an oil-light warning. A truck with a documented engine rebuild or replacement can be the better buy.
- Inspect the 4L30-E automatic: One long-time owner on Bob Is The Oil Guy says most failures of these gearboxes come from running low on fluid, and that they're very sensitive to fill level. Look for leaks at the accumulator cover and drain bolt, check the fluid, and make sure every gear engages cleanly hot and cold.
- Test the Torque On Demand system (1998+): A flashing TOD light and shudder usually point to the transfer-case or driveshaft speed sensors, according to Edmunds forum owners. One was quoted about $700 for the pair. Test 4WD Auto, 4H and 4L on loose ground.
- Listen for stalling at stops: Many 1998–2000 owners told NHTSA about stalling when slowing or turning, and about upper and lower intake manifold gaskets replaced more than once. Edmunds owners call the 3.5's intake gasket a common fault.
- Ask for the timing-belt and water-pump receipt: Both V6s have belt-driven cams. Owners on Edmunds plan the belt, water pump and spark plugs around 75,000 miles, and one on Bob Is The Oil Guy says the belt is good for about 100,000 miles. With no records, do it now and confirm the interval in the manual.
- Make sure the 4WD actually engages: Bob Is The Oil Guy owners say the front-axle 4WD actuator is known to seize in rust-prone areas. Lock it in, drive on gravel and listen for the front axle pulling.
- Check that the recalls were done: Accelerator cables that can stick on 1992–95 trucks (04V199), cam seal end plugs that can blow out and leak oil on 1992–94 trucks (94V132), loose transfer-case flange nuts on 1998s (98V180) and fuel-line separation in frontal crashes on 2000–01 TOD trucks (00V253, 00V376).
- Look underneath for rust: Bob Is The Oil Guy owners rate Trooper rust as similar to other Japanese trucks of the era, but rust-belt trucks do die of it. One 1996 owner's NHTSA complaint describes chassis corrosion. Check the frame rails, rear suspension mounts and the rear doors.

### Common repairs
#### Manage 3.5 V6 oil consumption
Difficulty 2 / 5 (rebuild 5 / 5) · time Minutes a week; a rebuild takes days · cost A quart at a time, up to an engine rebuild
Symptoms: Oil level dropping between changes, blue smoke, fouled plugs and, in the worst NHTSA reports, an engine that runs dry and seizes without the oil light coming on.
Fix: Check the dipstick at every fuel fill until you know the consumption rate, and top up with the correct grade. A Bob Is The Oil Guy owner recommends the specified 10W-30 and says regular changes help. Replace the PCV valve: Edmunds owners say it sits under the plastic intake cover and is cheap. If consumption keeps rising, a compression and leak-down test will show stuck rings. The permanent cure is a rebuild that addresses the pistons' oil control, and Planet Isuzoo has threads on doing it during a rebuild.
Tools: Funnel · spare quart of oil · socket set for the intake cover · compression and leak-down tester.

#### Replace the intake plenum and manifold gaskets
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Stalling when slowing or at a stop, a rough idle, a check-engine light and, in one NHTSA report, fuel-fouled spark plugs.
Fix: Disconnect the battery and remove the intake cover and air intake. Label and disconnect the vacuum lines, wiring and throttle linkage, unbolt the upper plenum, then the lower intake manifold if it's leaking too. Clean every sealing surface without gouging the aluminium, fit new gaskets, and torque the bolts in the factory sequence. Replace the plugs if they're fouled and clear any stored codes.
Tools: Socket set with extensions · torque wrench · plastic scraper · masking tape for labels · factory torque sequence [CONFIRM IN MANUAL].

#### Timing belt and water pump
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A long day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: None. It's a service item, and owners schedule it around 75,000–100,000 miles. A truck with no record is due.
Fix: Drain the coolant and remove the fan and shroud, the accessory belts and the crank pulley, then the timing covers. Set the engine to top dead center and confirm the timing marks on all the cam pulleys and the crank before removing the old belt. Replace the belt, tensioner, idlers and water pump, plus the cam and crank seals if they're leaking. Turn the engine twice by hand and recheck the marks before reassembly. Refill and bleed the cooling system. A BITOG owner adds: use a genuine Isuzu thermostat.
Tools: Crank-pulley holder · socket set · torque wrench · coolant · factory service manual.

#### Service the 4L30-E automatic
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time A couple of hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Slipping, harsh or delayed shifts, or a fluid leak. Low fluid is the usual cause of failures, according to Bob Is The Oil Guy owners.
Fix: Find and fix any leaks first: the accumulator cover and the drain bolt are known spots. Drop the pan, replace the filter and gasket, and refill to the exact level the manual specifies. The gearbox is very sensitive to fill volume. If the history is unknown, do a few partial fluid changes rather than a pressure flush.
Tools: Drain pan · socket set · torque wrench · fluid pump · Dexron-III-type ATF (Liqui Moly lookup).

#### Fix a flashing TOD light
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An hour or two · cost One owner was quoted about $700 for front and rear sensors
Symptoms: The TOD light flashes, the truck shudders or 4WD Auto stops working.
Fix: Start simple. Edmunds owners suggest cycling into 4L and back, pulling and refitting the TOD fuse, or disconnecting the battery to reset the computer. Then wash the underside, because packed snow and ice can upset the sensors. If the light comes back, check the wiring and connectors at the front and rear driveshaft speed sensors on the transfer case, and replace a faulty sensor.
Tools: Multimeter · socket set · contact cleaner · a pressure washer for the underside.

#### Set ride height at the torsion bars, or fit a mild lift
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An hour, plus an alignment · cost Free to adjust; a Pedders kit costs more
Symptoms: Sagging front end, uneven side-to-side height, or room needed for bigger tires.
Fix: Measure both sides from hub center to fender lip. Turn the torsion-bar adjuster bolts evenly, a little at a time, and settle the suspension between measurements. Edmunds owners note that adjusting one side changes the other, and that the bars may need re-indexing if you run out of adjustment. Don't crank the bars for lift: a higher, stiffer front end makes this tall truck tippier. For real height, Pedders sells a kit of about 50 mm with new torsion bars, coils and shocks; the Gen 2 has two bar lengths, so check yours. Get an alignment afterwards.
Tools: Tape measure · socket and long extension · anti-seize · alignment afterwards.

#### Free a seized front-axle actuator or hub
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time A couple of hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: 4WD light on but no drive to the front, or the front won't disengage.
Fix: Bob Is The Oil Guy owners say the front 4WD actuator is known to seize in rust-prone areas and that it's usually a DIY fix. Unbolt the actuator, clean and lubricate the shift fork and sleeve, check the vacuum or electrical supply, and refit. On trucks with locking hubs, service the hubs at the same time. Some owners convert to manual locking hubs.
Tools: Socket set · penetrating oil · grease · multimeter or vacuum gauge.

#### Front CV axles and boots
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Half a day per side · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Torn boots, grease on the inside of the wheel, or clicking on full lock.
Fix: Support the truck, pull the wheel and hub, separate the knuckle as the manual describes, and pull the axle from the differential. A complete replacement axle is usually quicker than a reboot. Unload the torsion bars first if the job needs it, and recheck ride height and alignment afterwards.
Tools: Socket set · ball-joint separator · new axle nut · torque wrench.

### Baseline service
Baseline everything, and on a 3.5 start by measuring the oil consumption. Acura's factory specifications give the engine-oil and coolant capacities below for the SLX twin. Isuzu's own fluid grades aren't widely published online; the gearbox, transfer-case, axle and steering fluids below come from Liqui Moly's lookup, so confirm viscosities in the owner's manual. Book the timing belt if there's no receipt.
- Engine oil & filter: 3.5: 5.6 US qt (5.3 L) with filter; 3.2: 6.3 US qt (6.0 L) with filter (Acura SLX spec) · 10W-30 recommended by owners for the 3.5 · Then check the level at every fill-up until you know the consumption (Several 3.5s ran dry without the oil light coming on, so don't rely on the warning lamp.)
- PCV valve: Replace · Now (Edmunds owners say it sits under the plastic intake cover. A blocked one makes oil consumption worse.)
- Air & fuel filters: Replace both · Then inspect at every oil change
- Spark plugs & coil boots: Six plugs; inspect the boots · With the timing belt, or now if there's no record (Oil-fouled plugs are a sign of the 3.5's consumption problem.)
- Timing belt, tensioner, idlers & water pump: Full kit · Now if there's no record; owners plan around 75,000–100,000 mi [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Both V6s have belt-driven cams.)
- Coolant & thermostat: 3.5: 11.0 US qt (10.4 L); 3.2: 9.3 US qt (8.8 L) (Acura SLX spec) · Flush now (A Bob Is The Oil Guy owner warns that these aluminium engines can fail head gaskets when the cooling system is neglected or a non-Isuzu thermostat is fitted.)
- Automatic transmission (4L30-E): Dexron-III-type ATF (Liqui Moly lists its ATF III) · Liqui Moly gives 8.6 L (9.1 US qt) for the US SLX and 5.5 L (5.8 US qt) for European Troopers, so measure what you drain · Pan drop and filter now, then partial changes (Very sensitive to fill level; fix leaks first. No pressure flush on an unknown-history gearbox.)
- Transfer case (TOD or part-time): Part-time and shift-on-the-fly cases: 5W-30 engine oil, ≈1.45 L (1.5 US qt) · Torque On Demand case on the 1998–99 SLX 3.5: 75W-90-type gear oil, ≈1.9 L (2.0 US qt) (Liqui Moly lookup; its European Trooper 3.5 entry lists engine oil and 1.45 L, so check what's in yours) · Drain and refill now (Metal in the fluid is a warning sign; one 1999 owner's transfer case was replaced for filings at 25,000 miles.)
- Front & rear differentials: GL-5 hypoid gear oil (Liqui Moly lists 75W-90 to 85W-90 grades) · ≈1.4–1.5 L (1.5–1.6 US qt) front, ≈1.8 L (1.9 US qt) rear · a limited-slip rear takes LSD-rated (LS) oil, which already contains the friction modifier (Liqui Moly lookup) · Drain and refill now (Bob Is The Oil Guy owners describe the rear axle as robust and close to a Dana 44 in design.)
- Power steering fluid: Dexron-III-type ATF (Liqui Moly lookup) · Flush now (Recirculating-ball steering box; check for play.)
- Brake fluid: Flush; four-wheel discs with ABS · Every two years
- U-joints & driveshafts: Grease and check for play · At every oil change
- Front-end wear parts: Ball joints, tie-rod ends, idler arm, sway-bar bushings · Inspect now (Worn sway-bar bushings make a tall truck feel even tippier; owners often fit polyurethane ones.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: Owners put it at about 33 inches. An Overland Bound owner says you can fit 33s before you need a lift, citing a chart on Planet Isuzoo, and an Expedition Portal member says 285/75R16 fits with no lift. Stock was P245/70R16 on 16 x 7 wheels (Acura SLX spec). The bolt pattern is 6 x 139.7 mm with a 100 mm center bore; one owner runs wheels from a 2014 Toyota 4Runner.

Q: Which engine should I buy, the 3.2 or the 3.5?
A: The 1998–2002 3.5 (215 hp, 230 lb-ft) is much stronger, but its oil consumption is notorious, and owners describe engines running dry and seizing. One long-time owner calls the 3.2 adequate but not exciting, with poor mileage and no real vices. If you buy a 3.5, budget for monitoring it, or for a rebuild that fixes the oil control.

Q: Why does the 3.5 burn oil?
A: A Bob Is The Oil Guy owner blames too few oil-return drains in the piston skirts, which clog and let the rings stick. Isuzu told some owners that a quart per 1,000 miles was normal; NHTSA complaints describe far more. Check the level at every fill-up and replace the PCV valve. Planet Isuzoo has threads on rebuild fixes.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: There's no clear sweet spot. The 1992–97 3.2 avoids the 3.5's oil appetite: one Overland Bound owner says the 3.2 'never had an oil consumption issue' and the 1998–2002 3.5s 'did have a bit'. NHTSA's complaint files peak with the 1999 model, and CarComplaints rates 2000 as the worst year, mainly for transmission failures. The 3.5 is the stronger engine, so if you want one, buy on oil-use history and receipts rather than the year.

Q: What was the Consumer Reports rollover controversy?
A: In August 1996 Consumers Union rated the 1995–96 Trooper and Acura SLX 'Not Acceptable', saying they tipped up on two wheels in its avoidance test. NHTSA ran its own tests and refused to open a defect investigation in July 1997. Isuzu sued for $242 million; in April 2000 a jury found some of the magazine's statements false but awarded no damages.

Q: How does the 4WD work?
A: Early trucks are part-time with automatic front hubs: stop briefly, select 4WD, and the hubs lock as you drive off. Some 1996 and later trucks shift on the fly. From 1998 Torque On Demand trucks have a 4WD Auto mode that sends torque to the front axle when the rear slips, plus 4H and 4L.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: 5,000 lb with a braked trailer. That figure appears in Isuzu's 1992 brochure and Acura's 1998 SLX specifications.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: Acura's factory estimates were 15 mpg city and 18 highway for the 1996 3.2, and 15 city and 19 highway for the 1998 3.5. An Overland Bound owner averages 16–17 mpg in his 1998 3.5.

Q: Is the Acura SLX the same truck?
A: Yes: an Isuzu-built Trooper with Acura trim, sold for the 1996–99 model years. It came only with the automatic and the V6s (the 3.2, then the 3.5 from 1998). Acura sold 6,590 of them, so they're rarer than Troopers but mechanically the same.

Q: What about the Holden Jackaroo, Opel Monterey and Bighorn?
A: All UBS Troopers. They're worth knowing about for parts and for diesels: export trucks offered the 3.1-liter 4JG2 and later the 3.0-liter 4JX1 turbo-diesels, which were never sold in the US.

Q: Can I lift it?
A: Yes, modestly. The torsion bars adjust ride height, and Pedders sells a kit of about 50 mm with new torsion bars, coils and shocks for the long-wheelbase Gen 2 (there are two torsion-bar lengths). Given the truck's rollover history, keep it modest and refresh the shocks and sway-bar bushings.

Q: What is one worth?
A: Bring a Trailer sales since late 2024 run from $6,000 (a 2000 Limited) to $14,250 (a 50,000-mile 2001 LS). Low-mileage trucks top the results, and a 1996 Acura SLX sold for $11,250.

# Jeep (1955–present)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/

The civilian Jeep began with the CJ-2A of 1945, and the CJ (Civilian Jeep) line reached the CJ-5 for the 1955 model year, after Kaiser had bought Willys. It was based on the Korean War-era M38A1, and 603,303 were built before it ended in 1983. American Motors bought Kaiser Jeep in 1970 and gave the CJ its own straight-six and V8 engines from 1972. In 1976 AMC stretched the wheelbase to make the CJ-7, which became the definitive square-door CJ. The CJ-7 and the long-wheelbase CJ-8 Scrambler gave way in 1986 to the Wrangler YJ, which AMC had designed to be more comfortable on the road. The Wrangler then moved to coil springs with the TJ and its long-wheelbase Unlimited (LJ), to four doors with the JK Unlimited, and on to today's JL and JL Unlimited, which is also offered as the 4xe plug-in hybrid and the V8 392. The boxy Jeeps weren't all open-topped. The full-size Wagoneer of 1963 became the Grand Wagoneer, a wood-sided V8 wagon built until 1991. In 1984 the unibody Cherokee XJ arrived, and from 1987 it carried the 4.0-liter version of AMC's straight six. Both have their own pages here, as does every Wrangler. Their old rivals are here too: the FJ40 and the Series Land Rover.

Verdict: The Jeep is the boxy 4x4 everyone else gets compared to, even the ones that got there first. It leaks, rattles and rusts, and it keeps selling, mostly to people who have already owned three.

## Jeep CJ-5 (1955–1983)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/cj-5/
Codes: CJ-5, Renegade, Golden Eagle

Verdict: The CJ-5 outlived three corporate owners, four engine families and a television hit piece, and it still feels like the original idea of a Jeep with the corners filed off. Short, loud and happiest on a trail, it is the purest classic Jeep you can still use most weekends.

The CJ-5 went on sale in October 1954 as a 1955 model. It was the civilian version of the Korean War M38A1, built by Willys Motors under Kaiser ownership, and Hagerty says it took that truck's chassis, axles, brakes, suspension and gearbox, then added a rounder body, a bigger windscreen and a lidded glovebox. It was supposed to replace the flat-fendered CJ-3B. Instead the two were built side by side, and the CJ-5 kept going for 29 model years and 603,303 units. The wartime MB, the 1945 CJ-2A (the first production civilian Jeep) and the CJ-3A and 3B came before it. The CJ-5 is where the round-fendered civilian Jeep really starts.

### KAISER'S UNIVERSAL
Early trucks used the Willys F134 Hurricane, an F-head four with intake valves over exhaust, rated at 75 hp and 114 lb-ft (gross), behind a three-speed manual and a two-speed transfer case. Hagerty says it is happy at about 50 mph, which tells you most of what you need to know. From 1961 to 1965 a British Perkins diesel with 62 hp was optional, and from 1961 the Tuxedo Park trim tried to sell the CJ as a sports car with chrome bumpers and bucket seats. It didn't sell well.
The engine that changed things came from Buick. In 1965 Kaiser licensed the 225-cubic-inch V6, branded it the Dauntless and rated it at 155 hp, roughly double the Hurricane. Kaiser fitted a much heavier flywheel to smooth out the odd-fire engine's lumpy firing pattern, and power steering became an $81 option. Buyers loved it: by 1968 about three quarters of CJ-5s left the factory with the V6. The 1969 '462' package and the 1970 Renegade I added a roll bar, skid plate, locking differential and loud paint.

### AMC STRETCHES THE NOSE
American Motors bought Kaiser Jeep in 1970 and dropped the Buick V6 after the 1971 model year. For 1972 the CJ-5 got AMC's 232 straight-six as standard, the 258 as an option (standard in California) and the 304 V8, which Wikipedia says gave the little Jeep a muscle-car power-to-weight ratio. Fitting them meant stretching the wheelbase from 81 to 83.5 inches and the hood and fenders by 5 inches. A new open-knuckle Dana 30 front axle shaved 25 lb and 6 feet off the turning circle, and the fuel tank moved from under the driver's seat to the rear.
The changes kept coming. The 1976 trucks got a reworked tub, a wider and more fully boxed frame, and an AMC 20 rear axle with two-piece shafts in place of the Dana 44. In 1977 the frame was fully boxed, and power front disc brakes and air conditioning joined the options list. In 1979 the 258 with a two-barrel Carter BBD became standard. From 1980 to 1983 the base engine was GM's 151 'Iron Duke' four, branded Hurricane, with an SR-4 four-speed, while the 258 got a Tremec T-176 four-speed.

### THE RIVALS: FJ40 AND SERIES
Two of the CJ-5's great rivals exist because of the Jeep. Rover's Maurice Wilks used an army-surplus Jeep on his farm in Anglesey, and the first Land Rover prototype was built on a Jeep chassis. The production Series Land Rover used no Jeep parts and ended up slightly shorter but wider, heavier and faster than its inspiration. In Japan, Toyota's postwar 'Jeep BJ' was renamed Land Cruiser in June 1954 after Willys complained about the trademark, a few months before the CJ-5 launched. Its successor, the FJ40, arrived in 1960.
On the road, Hagerty reckons the CJ-5 corners better than a contemporary Land Rover, with accurate, if not sporty, steering. Off-road it calls the CJ-5 superb. The Jeep also spread worldwide under licence: Brazil assembled CJ-5s from 1957, and Ford do Brasil kept making them until 1983, with a Pinto-derived 2.3-litre four and, from 1980, an ethanol-fuelled version. Mitsubishi built Japanese Jeeps from the CJ-3B line, competing directly with the Land Cruiser and Nissan Patrol at home.

### 60 MINUTES AND THE LONG GOODBYE
The end is usually blamed on a December 1980 episode of 60 Minutes, in which the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety staged tests suggesting the CJ-5 could roll over at low speed in routine driving. Years later it came out that the testers had managed only eight rollovers in 435 runs, and only after hanging weights in the corners of the body, out of camera shot. The damage was done. By then the 10-inch-longer CJ-7 had been on sale since 1976, and the CJ-5 bowed out after 1983.
The CJ line ended in 1986, and the Wrangler YJ took over as a 1987 model. Today CJ-5s are bought for fun as much as for work. Hagerty's UK guide put clean, usable US cars from about $12,000 and Renegade or Laredo models at about $20,000. It recommends the straight-six for smooth power and lower running costs than the V8. Mechanical, service and body parts are easy to find from US specialists, but special-edition trim and upholstery are not.

- Model Years: 1955–1983 (production from October 1954)
- Built: 603,303
- Owners: Willys / Kaiser (to 1970) · AMC (1970 on)
- Engines: F134 I4 · Perkins diesel · 225 V6 · 232 / 258 I6 · 304 V8 · 151 I4
- Output: 75 hp (F134) to 155 hp (V6)
- Transmissions: T-90, T-14, T-150 3-spd · T-18, SR-4, T-176 4-spd
- Drive: Part-time 4WD, two-speed gear-driven transfer case
- Wheelbase: 81 in (1955–71) · 83.5 in (1972–83)
- Length × Width: 138.2 × 68.5 in
- Height: 67.7 in
- Curb Weight: 2,665 lb (Wikipedia)
- Rear Axle: Dana 44 to 1975 · AMC 20 from 1976

### Engineering
The CJ-5 is a ladder frame, two live axles on leaf springs, a part-time gear-driven transfer case and a removable top. Everything else changed with the owner. Willys and Kaiser trucks have the short 81-inch wheelbase, a closed-knuckle front axle and four-cylinder or V6 power. AMC trucks from 1972 have the longer nose, the 83.5-inch wheelbase, an open-knuckle Dana 30 and inline sixes or a V8. The 1976 and 1977 frame and tub changes split the AMC years again.
- Chassis: Ladder frame · 81 in (1955–71), 83.5 in (1972–83) (Open-channel frame with riveted crossmembers to 1975. From 1976 it was mostly boxed with welded crossmembers and widened toward the rear. Fully boxed from 1977.)
- Suspension: Live axles, leaf springs front and rear (Check spring hangers and shackle mounts for rust, especially at the rear.)
- 4Wd System: Part-time, two-speed, gear-driven (Dana 18 on early trucks, then Dana 20, then Dana 300 from 1980. All gear-driven, with manual locking hubs.)
- Engines: F134 I4 · Perkins diesel · Dauntless V6 · AMC I6 / V8 · Iron Duke I4 (Hurricane 75 hp; Dauntless 155 hp; Hagerty quotes 150 bhp for the 304 V8.)
- Axles: Dana 30 open-knuckle front from 1972 · Dana 44 rear to 1975, AMC 20 from 1976 (The AMC 20's two-piece shafts are the CJ-5's best-known weak link.)
- Brakes & Steering: Drums; power front discs optional from 1977 (Power steering became an $81 option with the V6 in 1965. Hagerty recommends it with the bigger engines.)

### Versions
- 1955–1971 · Willys / Kaiser CJ-5 · F134 Hurricane 2.2 L F-head I4 · 75 hp / 114 lb-ft · T-90 three-speed at launch, 81-inch wheelbase. The four stayed available alongside the V6.
- 1961–1965 · CJ-5 diesel · Perkins 4.192 3.1 L I4 diesel · 62 hp / 143 lb-ft · Rare and slow, according to Hagerty.
- 1965–1971 · Kaiser Jeep CJ-5 V6 · Buick-designed Dauntless 225 3.7 L V6 · 155 hp · Fitted to about 75% of CJ-5s by 1968. Odd-fire, with a heavy flywheel.
- 1972–1978 · AMC CJ-5 (long nose) · AMC 232 I6 · 258 I6 · 304 V8 · 304: 150 bhp (Hagerty) · Wheelbase 83.5 in; new Dana 30 front; 258 standard in California.
- 1979–1983 · AMC CJ-5 (late) · AMC 258 I6 with Carter BBD 2-bbl · 110 hp / 195 lb-ft (1979–81, Offroaders.com) · 115 hp / 210 lb-ft from 1982 · 258 standard from 1979. Jeep-CJ.com dates the 304 option to 1981.
- 1980–1983 · AMC CJ-5 (base four) · GM 151 Iron Duke 2.5 L I4 ('Hurricane') · — · SR-4 four-speed. Jeep-CJ.com's buyer's guide says to avoid it.

### Year-by-year
- 1955: Willys CJ-5 arrives on an 81 in wheelbase, derived from the Korean War M38A1, with the 134 cu in Hurricane four
- 1961–1965: Optional Perkins 192 cu in diesel four (62 hp); Tuxedo Park trim lines run 1961–64
- 1965: Buick-designed 225 cu in Dauntless V6 (155 hp) becomes optional; by 1968 about 75% of CJ-5s have it. Jeep-CJ.com calls the 1966–71 Dauntless desirable, strong and reliable. 'Jeep CJ-5' replaces 'Willys' after 1964 [buy]
- 1971: AMC era begins (bought Kaiser Jeep in 1970); last Buick V6 year; Trac-Lok replaces Powr-Lok; PTOs dropped
- 1972: AMC 232/258 sixes and optional 304 V8; wheelbase stretched 2.5 in to 83.5 in, nose 5 in longer, open-knuckle Dana 30 front, fuel tank behind the rear axle. Hagerty's pick is an AMC-era 232 or 258 six from 1972 on [buy]
- 1976: Revised frame and more rounded tub; new windshield angle, so 1955–75 tops don't fit; AMC 20 two-piece-shaft rear replaces the Dana 44
- 1977: Fully boxed frame; power disc brakes, air conditioning and the Golden Eagle package become options
- 1979: 258 six with two-barrel Carter BBD becomes standard; 1,000-unit Silver Anniversary edition
- 1980–1983: GM 151 Iron Duke four becomes standard with an SR4 four-speed (Jeep-CJ.com calls the Iron Duke a particularly weak engine to avoid); the 258 option gets the T-176 four-speed; locking hubs change to a five-bolt pattern (1980 per Wikipedia, 1981 per Offroaders.com). 1983 is the last year

### Capability
- Wheelbase: 81 in (2,057 mm) 1955–71 · 83.5 in (2,121 mm) 1972–83
- Curb weight: 2,665 lb (1,209 kg) (Wikipedia figure)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 225/75R15 (1980, P-metric equivalent)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x139.7 (5x5.5")
- Center Bore: 108 mm
- Lug Thread: 1/2"-20
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 31x10.50R15 (Owners call 31 in the practical ceiling and 30x9.50s a known-good fit; one long-time owner ran 32x11.50s on stock springs with minor rubbing. Test-fit, since actual diameters vary)
- Biggest tire, 2.5 in lift: 32–33 in (A 2.5 in spring lift plus 3/4 in shackles runs 32s without trouble; 33s fit until the suspension stuffs. Narrow-track CJs need the steering stops reset or the tires hit the leaf springs)
- Biggest tire, 4 in lift: 33x12.50R15 (Usually with flares and trimmed rear wheel openings; 33–35s generally mean cutting the rear openings and revisiting the bump stops)

### Buying checks
- Frame first: Check the whole frame for rust and cracks, especially at the suspension and steering mounts. Jeep-CJ.com flags the front and rear shackle mounts, the area behind the rear wheels and the six body mounts. Mud blocks the drain holes in boxed frames. Hagerty adds the outriggers, which usually rot first.
- Steering box mount: Boxed frames (1976 on) often crack around the steering box, especially with a lift and big tires. Look for cracks, fresh welds and a box that moves when someone turns the wheel.
- The tub: Check the rockers, rear corners, wheel wells, under the roll bar and the floor. Hagerty adds the tops of the inner and outer wheel tubs, the tailgate and the windscreen-to-scuttle joint. Jeep-CJ.com's warning: patches welded over rust become rust. Knock on panels to find filler.
- Windshield frame: Fold the windshield forward and check the bottom of the frame, the hinges and the screw holes. Failed cowl and tailgate gaskets trap water and rot the metal around them.
- Which engine: Hagerty recommends the 232 or 258 six for smooth power and lower running costs than the V8. Jeep-CJ.com says to avoid the 1980–83 Iron Duke. On any engine, look for start-up smoke, rattles and oil or coolant leaks.
- Gearbox and transfer case: Hagerty calls the T-14 three-speed strong and longer-lasting than the later four-speeds, and Jeep-CJ.com rates the T-18 four-speed as the best transmission ever put in a CJ. Check gear-driven transfer cases for leaks and low oil. Test 4WD in high and low range on gravel.
- Wiring and ignition: Hagerty calls ignition the weak point, especially on AMC engines. Be wary of duct-tape splices, wire nuts, Scotch-locks and foil-wrapped fuses. Jeep-CJ.com puts it bluntly: grounding failure is directly proportional to rust.
- Buy a stock one: Jeep-CJ.com says project Jeeps and heavily built trail rigs are generally poor buys and recommends mostly stock trucks. Keep the emissions parts if you can. In some states removing them is illegal.

### Common repairs
#### Steering box mount and frame cracks
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day if the frame is sound; longer with welding · cost Rust Buster RB1008 mount about $125 (Quadratec)
Symptoms: Wandering steering, a box that shifts on the frame when the wheel is turned, or cracks around the box mounting holes. RockCrawler.com reports a CJ-5 that tore its steering box off the frame on a trail.
Fix: RockCrawler's install of a plate-steel bracket: remove the drag link, hoses and steering shaft, pull the box, fit the bracket's studs and spacers with thread-locker, trial-fit and file the bolt holes if needed. Bolt the mount to the box at 65 ft-lb, then to the frame with Grade 8 hardware at 55 ft-lb, adding the through-frame bolt for clamping force. Weld any frame cracks before fitting it. Route the hoses so they can't rub, and reconnect the shaft and tie rod.
Tools: Pitman arm puller · sockets and torque wrench · thread-locker · file · welder for frame cracks · Rust Buster RB1008 (1976–86 CJ-5/7/8)

#### AMC 20 one-piece axle conversion (1976–83)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day to a day · cost Crown RT23007 kit about $410 at Quadratec (October 2026)
Symptoms: Clunks on take-off, a rear hub working loose on its shaft, or worn and spun splines. Quadratec's listing explains the cause: the factory hardened hubs cut splines into softer axle shafts, leaving weak spots in the driveline.
Fix: Replace the two-piece shafts and hubs with one-piece shafts that have the hub flange fixed to the shaft, which stops the splines spinning and handles torsional loads better. Remove the wheels, drums and pressed-on hubs (a hub puller is the usual tool), unbolt the bearing retainers and pull the shafts. Fit the new shafts with their bearings and seals, following the kit instructions. Fit new inner seals while the axle is apart, and refill with gear oil (plus friction modifier for a Trac-Lok).
Tools: Hub puller · slide hammer · seal driver · torque wrench · Crown RT23007 kit (1976–83 CJ-5; not for Quadra-Trac)

#### Clutch bellcrank (Z-bar) rebuild
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost V6 bellcrank about $20 (Crown, Quadratec)
Symptoms: A sloppy or heavy clutch, trouble finding first, or linkage that falls apart. On Jeep-CJ.com, members say the plastic bushings wear out, and that the pivots can break once the motor mounts go.
Fix: Check the motor mounts first, because a sagging engine stresses the bellcrank pivots. Unhook the linkage, remove the bellcrank and replace worn bushings and ball studs, or the whole bellcrank. One forum fix replaces the worn bushing with a ground-to-fit solid rod, with bolts welded into drilled ends as pivots. Grease everything and readjust free play. Some owners switch to a hydraulic clutch when engine torque keeps pushing the linkage out of the throwout lever.
Tools: Wrenches · grease · new bushings or bellcrank · motor mounts if worn

#### Carter BBD rough idle (1979–83 258)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost A can of carb cleaner; rebuild kits are inexpensive
Symptoms: Stumbling, sputtering or stalling at idle and poor fuel economy, but running fine at higher rpm. Offroaders.com says the cause is almost always clogged idle tubes, which let fuel drip from the venturis.
Fix: With the engine running and choke open, look down the throat. Fuel dripping from the idle nozzles confirms it. Remove the air cleaner (tag every hose), the choke plate and rod, then the two screws and the venturi cluster. Check the idle pickup tubes are seated, clear the tubes and nozzles with fine wire and carb cleaner without dislodging the check ball, and reassemble. Tighten the carb body screws, which tend to loosen. For a longer-lasting fix, the article suggests drilling the idle tubes to 0.032 inch. Pre-1979 sixes use a one-barrel Carter YF.
Tools: 3/16 in socket · small screwdrivers · carb cleaner · fine wire · 0.032 in drill bit · Crown 83300057 kit for 1973–78 YF carbs

#### Ignition refresh or HEI swap (AMC sixes)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost The BustedJeep author paid $15 for a junkyard HEI
Symptoms: Hard starting, rough idle, hesitation and poor economy. Hagerty calls ignition the weak point of AMC-engined CJs, and Jeep-CJ.com's write-up blames the factory Duraspark.
Fix: Start with a cap, rotor, plugs and wires. For a bigger upgrade, the Jeep-CJ.com HEI swap uses a 1976–82 GM inline-six HEI distributor with an AMC V8 drive gear. Mark the No. 1 position, remove the old distributor, install the HEI and run it from the constant-12 V firewall wire, not the resistor coil feed. Gap the plugs to .045 in. The firing order is 1-5-3-6-2-4. Set the timing with a light; the write-up says many owners use about 8° BTDC. CJs with a feedback ECM need it bypassed first.
Tools: Timing light · volt meter · soldering iron · plug gapper · HEI distributor and AMC V8 drive gear · 8 mm plug wires

#### Rear main seal (232 / 258 / 304)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day to a day · cost Seal and pan gaskets plus labor
Symptoms: Oil dripping from the joint between the engine and bellhousing.
Fix: Following Jeep's 1973 service-manual procedure (via IFSJA): drain the oil and remove the pan. Remove the rear main cap and discard the lower seal half, loosen the other caps and tap out the upper half with a brass drift. Oil the crank, fit the new upper half with the lip facing the front of the engine, put sealant only on the lower half's end tabs, and seat it in the cap. Seal the cap's chamfered edges, torque the caps to spec and refit the pan with new gaskets. Always replace both halves together.
Tools: Brass drift · torque wrench · Permatex No. 2 or equivalent · two-piece rear main seal · oil pan gasket set

#### Floor pan and tub rust repair
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend per side; a new tub is a full strip-down · cost Key Parts half floor pan about $242; Omix 1955–69 front pan assembly about $1,350
Symptoms: Soft or holed floors, rot along the rockers, rear corners and under the roll bar, and rusty body mounts. Hagerty says floors usually go around the chassis mounts.
Fix: Cut back to clean metal, then fit, clamp and weld in the replacement pan. Jeep-CJ.com warns that patches welded over rust just become rust, so remove all of it. Replace the body-mount bushings while the floor is open, then seam-seal and paint underneath. If the tub is too far gone, Omix and others sell complete steel tubs for 1976–83 CJ-5s.
Tools: Cut-off wheel · MIG welder · clamps · seam sealer · weld-through primer

### Baseline service
A CJ-5 is at least 40 years old and has probably had several owners, each with their own idea of maintenance. Change every fluid, grease every fitting and sort the ignition before you judge how it runs. Specs vary by era and engine; the capacities below are from ExtremeTerrain's CJ chart, which mostly covers AMC-era drivetrains. Check anything for a Willys or Kaiser truck against its manual.
- Engine oil & filter: 5W-30 or 10W-30 · 4.2 L six: 6 qt · 5.0 L 304: 5 qt · 2.5 L four: 4 qt · F134 / V6 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now; then per your owner's manual (These are flat-tappet engines. New drain-plug washer every time.)
- Air filter: Paper element in the factory air cleaner · Baseline now (Fit a new one before tuning the carburetor.)
- Ignition tune-up: Plugs, cap, rotor, wires; points and condenser on pre-electronic trucks · gaps and timing [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now (Hagerty calls ignition the CJ's weak point. The AMC six fires 1-5-3-6-2-4.)
- Coolant & thermostat: 50/50 coolant · 4.2 L: 10.5 qt · 304 V8: 14.5 qt · Iron Duke: 7.8 qt (ExtremeTerrain) · Baseline flush now (ExtremeTerrain lists a three-year IAT formula. Flush until the water runs clear and fit a new thermostat.)
- Belts & hoses: V-belts and molded hoses by engine · Baseline now if cracked, glazed or soft (Old hoses fail from the inside. Squeeze them, and replace any that feel crunchy or spongy.)
- Manual transmission: 80W-90 · T-18: 3.25 qt · T-150: 1.4 qt · SR-4: 1.5 qt · T-176: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · T-90 / T-14: GL-4 (1955 manual) [CONFIRM CAPACITY] · Baseline now (ExtremeTerrain's T-176 figure (3.5 qt / 1.7 L) contradicts itself, so check the manual. On T-14/Dana 18 trucks, oil can migrate from the gearbox into the transfer case, so check both levels.)
- Transfer case: 80W-90 · Dana 300: 2 qt · Dana 20: 1.6 qt · Dana 18: GL-4 [CONFIRM CAPACITY] · Baseline now (All CJ-5 transfer cases are gear-driven. Leaks at the output seals are common and cheap to fix.)
- Front differential: 80W-90 · Dana 30: 1.25 qt · pre-1972 front axle [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now (ExtremeTerrain suggests 75W-140 for towing or extreme use.)
- Rear differential: 80W-90 · AMC 20: 2.4 qt · Dana 44: 2 qt · Trac-Lok: add 4 oz limited-slip additive · Baseline now (Renegades and many V8 trucks have Trac-Lok. Look for a tag on the cover and add friction modifier if it's there.)
- Front wheel bearings & hubs: Repack and adjust · preload [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now; then after deep water crossings (Inspect the manual locking hubs while they're apart. Later trucks use five-bolt hubs, earlier ones six-bolt; Offroaders.com dates the change to 1981, Wikipedia to 1980, so count the bolts.)
- Brake & clutch fluid: DOT 3 · Flush now (Old drum-brake trucks also need the shoes adjusted. Check the wheel cylinders for weeping.)
- Power steering: Power Steering +4, or ATF+4 if unavailable · Check and top up now (Leaks at the box are common. Seal kits are cheap.)
- Grease points: Driveshaft U-joints and slip yokes · shackles · steering joints · Every oil change, and after water (Replace any dry or notchy U-joint now. Greaseable shackles are an easy upgrade.)
- Fuel filter: Inline filter by engine · Baseline now (Old tanks shed rust and varnish. If the filter comes out dirty, inspect the tank and sender.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: In a Jeep-CJ.com thread on stock CJs, members (one running a '79 CJ-5) put 31-inch tires as the safe maximum: one says '31's without rubbing,' and another says 32s rub the rear wheel wells. A little trimming can make 32s fit, but there isn't much to trim ahead of the rear wheels, and most doubt 33s will fit. Old springs sag, so 31s may be the practical limit. Wide tires may need wheels with less backspacing to clear the springs and fenders at full lock.

Q: Which engine should I look for?
A: Hagerty recommends the 1972-on 232 or 258 straight-six for smooth power, relaxed cruising and lower running costs than the V8. Jeep-CJ.com praises the 258 for torque and reliability, and says to avoid the GM Iron Duke four used from 1980 to 1983. The early Hurricane four is authentic but limited by its three-speed. The Dauntless V6 is the period hot-rod choice.

Q: What's the difference between early and late CJ-5s?
A: For 1972, AMC lengthened the wheelbase from 81 to 83.5 inches and the hood and fenders by 5 inches to fit its sixes and V8. AMC trucks also got the open-knuckle Dana 30 front axle. The tub and windshield changed again for 1976, so tops for 1955–75 trucks don't fit 1976–83 trucks.

Q: Is the CJ-5 really a rollover risk?
A: It's short and tall, so drive it with respect. The famous December 1980 60 Minutes segment overstated the case: the IIHS testers got only eight rollovers in 435 runs, and only after hanging hidden weights in the body's corners. A roll bar and seat belts are worthwhile upgrades, and Hagerty advises care on damp roads.

Q: What's wrong with the AMC 20 rear axle?
A: From 1976 the CJ-5 used an AMC 20 with two-piece axle shafts. The hardened hubs cut into the softer shaft splines over time. One-piece axle kits, such as Crown's RT23007 for 1976–83 CJ-5s, fix the hub to the shaft. They don't fit Quadra-Trac axles.

Q: What is the Dauntless V6?
A: It's Buick's 225-cubic-inch V6, which Kaiser licensed in 1965; GM sold Kaiser-Jeep the design and tooling in 1967. It made 155 hp, about double the Hurricane four, and by 1968 about 75% of CJ-5s had it. It's an odd-fire engine, so Jeep fitted a much heavier flywheel to smooth it out. The V6 was dropped after 1971.

Q: Did the CJ-5 get disc brakes?
A: Power front disc brakes became an option in 1977. Earlier trucks have drums all round. Power steering became optional with the V6 in 1965, and Hagerty recommends it with the bigger engines.

Q: What fluids does it take?
A: ExtremeTerrain's CJ chart lists 5W-30 or 10W-30 oil (6 qt for the 4.2, 5 qt for the 304, 4 qt for the 2.5), 80W-90 gear oil in the Dana 30 (1.25 qt), AMC 20 (2.4 qt) and Dana 300 (2 qt), with limited-slip additive for Trac-Lok axles. Brakes take DOT 3. For pre-AMC trucks, a BITOG thread starter summarizes the original 1955 recommendation as GL-4 in the transmission and transfer case [CONFIRM IN MANUAL].

Q: What's a Renegade worth compared with a base CJ-5?
A: Hagerty's UK guide put clean, usable US CJ-5s from about $12,000, with Renegade and Laredo models at about $20,000. Rare special editions command more. Original special-edition trim and upholstery are hard to find, so check that a Renegade is complete before paying a Renegade price.

Q: Can I still get parts?
A: Yes. Hagerty says most mechanical, service and body parts are available from US specialists. Quadratec alone lists Omix and Crown replacement parts back to the 1955 CJ-5, including complete steel tubs, floor pans and F-head gasket sets.

Q: Which transmission is best?
A: Jeep-CJ.com calls the T-18 four-speed (often with a granny-low first) the best transmission ever put in a CJ, and recommends the T-176 among the 1980s gearboxes. Hagerty rates the T-14 three-speed as durable. On 1980–83 trucks, the Iron Duke came with the SR-4 and the 258 with the T-176.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: Condition beats year on a truck this old, but there are two sensible targets. Hagerty would aim for an AMC-era 232 or 258 six from 1972 on, for smooth power and cheaper running than the V8. Jeep-CJ.com and The Drive both rate the Buick Dauntless V6 (optional 1965–71) as strong. The one to skip is a 1980–83 truck with the GM Iron Duke four, which Jeep-CJ.com calls particularly weak; the optional 258 those years is fine. The Drive adds that pre-1976 open frames tend to crack and later boxed frames tend to rust, so check either kind.

## Jeep CJ-7 (1976–1986)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/cj-7/
Codes: CJ-7, Renegade, Golden Eagle, Laredo

Verdict: The CJ-7 is the classic Jeep that still makes sense: a longer wheelbase, real doors, AMC's unkillable 258 six and a gear-driven transfer case. It's also a 40-year-old steel tub on a frame that cracks by the steering box, so bring a magnet and a hammer when you go to look at one.

American Motors bought Kaiser Jeep in 1970 (for $70 million by Wikipedia's account; Jeep's own history says about $75 million), and in 1976 it gave the little CJ-5 a bigger brother. The CJ-7 sat on a 93.5-inch wheelbase, ten inches longer than the CJ-5's, and Jeep says the extra length was there to make room for an automatic transmission. The side openings were squared off to take doors, and for the first time a Jeep CJ could be ordered with a molded plastic hardtop and steel doors. It ran for eleven model years, and Wikipedia counts 379,299 built.

### THE AMC RECIPE
Under the tub, the CJ-7 has two parallel C-section frame rails, stepped outward at the rear so the springs and shocks sit closer to the body, with leaf springs at both ends. The front axle is an open-knuckle Dana 30. At the back is AMC's own Model 20, which has a big 8⅞-inch ring gear but thin 29-spline shafts, each made of two pieces: a hub keyed and nutted onto the shaft. Wheels use the old CJ bolt pattern of 5 on 5.5 inches.
The engines came from AMC. Early trucks had the 232 straight six as standard, with the 258 optional until it became the base six for 1979. The 258 is the one owners talk about: cast iron, seven main bearings, hydraulic lifters and enough low-end torque to idle up a hill. Offroaders.com lists it at 110 hp and 195 lb-ft in 1979–81, then 115 hp and 210 lb-ft from 1982 with a computer-controlled Carter BBD two-barrel. The 304 V8 was offered until 1981, choked by smog equipment to 125 hp by the end. From 1980 a GM 151 'Iron Duke' four was standard, rated at 82 hp. JeepCJ.com's buyer's guide tells you to skip it.

### GEARBOXES, TRANSFER CASES AND QUADRA-TRAC
Early trucks (1976–79) got a three-speed T-150 or the Borg-Warner T-18. From 1977 the T-18A had a 6.32:1 granny first, and Offroaders.com calls it the best transmission the factory ever put in a CJ. Behind it was a Dana 20 with a feeble 2.03:1 low range. The alternative was Quadra-Trac, a Borg-Warner 13-39 chain-drive full-time system bolted to a TH400 automatic. It had a vacuum-operated 'Emergency Drive' lock and an optional bolt-on low-range unit (2.57:1). Jeep had introduced Quadra-Trac on its full-size trucks in the early 1970s (the 1973 model year, by Wikipedia's dating), years before the Grand Wagoneer name existed.
For 1980 everything changed. The Dana 300 arrived with a 2.62:1 low range, and Novak Conversions calls it the 'gold standard' of transfer cases. It came with lighter Borg-Warner gearboxes: the SR-4 in 1980–81, then the T-4 and five-speed T-5 from 1982. Novak's verdict on those is 'essentially a small car transmission in a truck'. The tougher choice was the Tremec T-176 four-speed (1980–86), and a Chrysler TF999 three-speed automatic replaced the TH400.

### WIDE TRACK, GOLDEN EAGLES AND LAREDOS
In 1982 the axles grew. The narrow-track AMC 20 measured 50.5 inches wheel to wheel, and the wide-track version 54.5 inches, which made the CJ-7 noticeably more stable. AMC also understood showroom bait. The Renegade ran the whole production life. The Golden Eagle (on the CJ-7 from 1977 to 1980, tied to the 304 V8 per Wikipedia) added a tachometer, a clock and the big Golden Eagle decals; a white 1980 CJ-7 Golden Eagle named 'Dixie' became famous as Daisy Duke's Jeep on The Dukes of Hazzard. The Laredo (1980–86) brought high-back leather seats, a tilt wheel and a chrome package.
The collectible ones are the Limited, built in 1982–83 (2,500 of them), and the 1982 Jamboree. That was 630 numbered CJ-7s, each with the 4.2-liter six, built for the 30th anniversary of the Rubicon Trail.

### LAST OF A GREAT BREED
The CJ's reputation took a hit in December 1980, when 60 Minutes aired an IIHS rollover demonstration of a CJ-5. AMC green-lit a replacement in 1982, and the Wrangler YJ was designed to be more comfortable on the road and harder to flip, with track bars and anti-roll bars. It was unveiled in February 1986 and went on sale on 13 May 1986. The last CJ-7s carried a dash plaque that read 'Last of a Great Breed', and by then AMC 20 supplies had run so low that some 1986 trucks left the factory with wide-track Dana 44 rear axles.
The CJ-7 has outlived its replacement's reputation. AMC was working with Renault by the end, and Chrysler took over Jeep in 1987. The CJ-8 Scrambler, the YJ and the TJ all owe it something. Against its 1970s rivals, the FJ40 and the Series Land Rover, the CJ-7's case in the US was cheap parts, easy modification and a huge aftermarket, and that case still holds: almost every part is still reproduced.

### Data plate
- Model: Jeep CJ-7
- Model Years: 1976–1986
- Built: 379,299 (Wikipedia)
- Maker: American Motors (AMC)
- Wheelbase: 93.5 in
- Engines: 258 4.2 L I6 · 304 5.0 L V8 (to '81) · 151 / 150 2.5 L I4
- Output (258): 110 hp ('79–'81) → 115 hp / 210 lb-ft ('82–'86)
- Transmissions: T-150, T-18/T-18A, SR-4, T-4, T-5, T-176; TH400, TF999, TF904
- Transfer Case: Dana 20 ('76–'79) · Dana 300 ('80–'86) · Quadra-Trac BW 13-39 ('76–'79)
- Low Range: 2.03:1 (Dana 20) · 2.62:1 (Dana 300)
- Axles: Dana 30 front · AMC 20 rear (Dana 44 late '86)
- Track: Narrow '76–'81 · wide '82–'86
- Wheel Bolt Pattern: 5 x 5.5 in

### Engineering
The CJ-7 is old-school body-on-frame: a steel tub on six body mounts, leaf springs at all four corners, a part-time gear-driven transfer case (or the full-time, chain-drive Quadra-Trac option until 1979), a Dana 30 front axle with locking hubs, and AMC's Model 20 rear axle. Everything bolts together with hand tools, and almost every part is still made.
- Chassis: Twin C-section rails, 93.5 in wheelbase (The rear section is stepped out to bring springs and shocks closer to the body. Check for cracks around the steering box.)
- Front Axle: Dana 30, open knuckle, 5 x 5.5 in (Discs were optional in 1976 and standard from 1977. Six-bolt hubs to 1980, a weaker five-bolt Warn hub from 1981 to 1986.)
- Rear Axle: AMC 20, 8⅞ in ring gear, 29-spline (Keyed two-piece hub-and-shaft design. Narrow track until 1981, wide track from 1982; some 1986 trucks got a Dana 44.)
- Transfer Case: Dana 20 → Dana 300 (1980) (Low range is 2.03:1 in the Dana 20 and 2.62:1 in the Dana 300. Quadra-Trac (BW 13-39, full-time, chain) was optional from 1976 to 1979.)
- Engines: AMC 232 / 258 I6 · 304 V8 · GM 151 / AMC 150 I4 (232: standard six 1976–78. 258: optional, then the base six from 1979; 110–115 hp from 1979, carbureted throughout. 304: until 1981. The four was standard from 1980.)
- Transmissions: T-150, T-18, SR-4, T-4, T-5, T-176, TH400, TF999 (The T-18A granny four-speed (1977–79) and the T-176 (1980–86) are the strong ones.)

### Versions
- 1976–1979 · CJ-7 (narrow track) · 232 I6 (std to '78) / 258 I6 / 304 V8 · 232: 100 hp / 185 lb-ft · 258: 110 hp / 195 lb-ft ('79) · 304: 150 hp ('76–'78), 130 hp ('79) · T-150 or T-18/T-18A with Dana 20 (2.03:1 low), or TH400 with Quadra-Trac BW 13-39. The 258 became the base six for 1979.
- 1980–1981 · CJ-7 (narrow track) · GM 151 I4 (std) / 258 I6 / 304 V8 · 151: 82 hp / 125 lb-ft · 258: 110 hp / 195 lb-ft · 304: 125 hp / 220 lb-ft · Dana 300 arrives. SR-4, T-176 or TF999 auto. Last year of the 304 is 1981.
- 1982–1986 · CJ-7 (wide track) · 151 I4 ('82–'83) / AMC 150 I4 ('84–'86), 258 I6 · 258: 115 hp / 210 lb-ft (computer-controlled BBD) · Axles 4 inches wider. T-4, T-5, T-176, TF999 or TF904 auto. The 258 is the only six.
- 1982–1983 · CJ-7 Limited · 258 I6 · As above · 2,500 built. In 1982 there was also the Jamboree, 630 numbered trucks marking the Rubicon Trail's 30th anniversary.
- 1980–1982 · Export diesel · Isuzu C240 2.4 I4 diesel · — · Built in Ohio for export only. T-176, Dana 300, 4.10 gears.
- 1986 (late) · CJ-7, last builds · 258 I6 · As above · AMC 20 supply ran out and some trucks got a wide-track, 30-spline Dana 44 rear with flanged one-piece shafts (Offroaders.com puts the change between serials ending 049379 and 054173).

### Year-by-year
- 1976: CJ-7 launches on a 93.5 in wheelbase with doors, optional molded hardtop and steel doors, and optional full-time Quadra-Trac (with the TH-400 automatic). Dana 20 transfer case, narrow-track Dana 30 / AMC 20 axles
- 1976–1981: AMC 304 V8 available (3.55 axles); it goes away after 1981, leaving the 258 six as the top engine
- 1977: Golden Eagle package (304 V8) arrives, running through 1980
- 1979: The 258 six replaces the 232 as the standard engine; last year of the Dana 20, Quadra-Trac, the T-150 and the T-18
- 1980: Dana 300 transfer case replaces the Dana 20 on every CJ-7; Laredo trim debuts; Golden Hawk sticker package for one year. Export-only Isuzu C240 diesel runs 1980–82
- 1982: Wide-track Dana 30 front and AMC 20 rear replace the narrow-track axles; 630 numbered Jamboree Editions and the 1982–83 Limited (2,500 built)
- 1985: Canadian Army takes 195 militarised CJ-7s as a stop-gap between the M38A1 and the Iltis
- 1986: Final year; some late trucks get a wide-track Dana 44 rear in place of the two-piece AMC 20 as supplies run out, and the last run wears the 'Last of a Great Breed' dash plaque

### Capability
- Wheelbase: 93.5 in (2,375 mm)
- Curb weight: 2,707 lb (1,228 kg) (Wikipedia figure; varies with engine and top)
- Axle ratios: 3.55 (304 V8) · 3.73 (258 six and 150 four) · 4.10 (diesel) (Wikipedia's figures; Offroaders.com gives 3.54 (1976–79) and 2.73 (1980–86) as the common ratios, so read the axle code)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 205/75R15, 235/75R15
- Bolt Pattern: 5x139.7 (5x5.5")
- Center Bore: 108 mm
- Lug Thread: 1/2"-20
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 31x10.50R15 (Jeep-CJ.com consensus on a 15x8 wheel; one owner reports 32x11.50s with 'very little rubbing', but 32s generally need tired springs. Stock gearing and brakes feel it)
- Biggest tire, 2.5 in lift: 33x12.50R15 (Fits for mild use; reset the steering stops or the tires hit the leaf springs at full lock, and expect contact when the suspension is stuffed)
- Biggest tire, 4 in lift: 33x12.50R15 (The comfortable trail setup for 33s (one 4 in owner still wanted more stuff room); regear from the stock 3.55 or 3.73 ratios)

### Buying checks
- Frame first, everything else second: JeepCJ.com's buyer's guide starts with the frame. Probe the front and rear spring-shackle mounts, where mud blocks the drain holes in the boxed rails, the area behind the rear wheels, and all six body mounts. The guide says to check them with a hammer and screwdriver.
- Look for cracks around the steering box: The guide says the area around the steering box is one of the most common places for a CJ frame to crack, especially on lifted trucks or trucks on big tires. Look for fresh paint, weld beads or splice plates and ask what was done.
- Tub, floors and windshield frame: Check the rockers, rear corners, wheel wells, the area under the roll bar and the floor; lift any carpet. The bottom of the windshield frame and its hinges rust, often from a leaking defroster. On 1982–86 wide-track trucks, check the front-fender shock towers, which trap water.
- Know which gearbox you're buying: A T-18A (1977–79) or T-176 (1980–86) is what you want. The SR-4, T-4 and T-5 are light-duty Borg-Warner boxes that Novak says suffer from sheared splines and stretched cases behind the 258. Check the casting number on the driver's side: 13-32 or 13-40 for an SR-4, 13-51 for a T-4, 13-52 for a T-5.
- Inspect the AMC 20's two-piece shafts: On a stock CJ rear axle the hub is keyed onto the shaft and held with a big nut. If the nut loosens, the key shears and that wheel stops driving. Look for one-piece axle shafts in the receipts, or budget for them. Read the gear-code stamp on the housing to the left of the cover.
- Quadra-Trac trucks need a test: On gravel, try high and (if fitted) low range and listen for chain noise. The JeepCJ.com guide says the chain stretches, possibly to the point of jumping teeth, if the oil level wasn't kept up. Quadra-Trac trucks have drive plates instead of locking hubs, and the vacuum 'Emergency Drive' control locks the center differential; check that it engages.
- Listen to the carburetor: Stumbling and stalling at idle usually means a Carter BBD with clogged idle tubes, and its tangle of emissions vacuum hoses is the other usual suspect. Not a deal-breaker, but price in a clean-up or a Weber or EFI swap.
- Electrics and emissions bits: Duct-tape splices, wire nuts, Scotch-locks and foil-wrapped fuses are warning signs, and most CJ electrical faults come down to rusty grounds. If your state inspects 1980s trucks, check that the TAC air cleaner, EGR, PCV and air-pump hardware are still there; the guide notes air-pump pulleys and brackets are hard to find.

### Common repairs
#### Convert the AMC 20 to one-piece axle shafts
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day, plus tube welding if you do it · cost Offroaders.com puts one-piece shafts at $350+
Symptoms: A clunk under load, a rear wheel that suddenly stops driving, or a hub that wobbles on its shaft. The key between the shaft and the pressed-on hub shears once the big hub nut loosens. Or you've simply bought a CJ with original two-piece shafts and bigger tires.
Fix: Pull the drums, the hub nut and the hub (this needs a proper hub puller), then the backing-plate bolts, and pull the old shafts. Buy the kit for your axle: narrow track for 1976–81, wide track for 1982–86. Install the new one-piece shafts with the bearings and seals supplied (some kits need a special bearing), set the end play, and refit the brakes. While the axle is apart, JeepCJ.com members suggest stitch-welding the tubes to the center section, using three 1 to 1.5-inch welds rather than a continuous bead, to stop the thin tubes from twisting.
Tools: Hub puller · slide hammer · 1/2 in breaker bar · dial indicator for end play · welder (optional) · 80W-90 gear oil.

#### Repair a cracked frame at the steering box
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend, or a day at a weld shop · cost Steel and welding wire; several members recommend paying a weld shop
Symptoms: Steering that wanders or clunks, a steering box that moves when someone turns the wheel with the engine running, or a visible crack in the driver's frame rail near the box. Lifted trucks and trucks on big tires crack more often.
Fix: Find the end of the crack and drill a small hole there to stop it spreading. Remove the box, clean the rail to bare metal and weld the crack. Then add splice plates: one owner cut 1/8-inch plate long enough to extend a few inches past the crack on each side. One member's advice is to weld the top and bottom in intermittent beads (about 1 inch of weld, 2 inches of gap) and leave the plate ends unwelded, because welds concentrate stress. Several owners say their DIY MIG repairs failed next to the welds and a weld shop's held. Add a steering-box brace to tie the box to the opposite rail, and replace any rotted frame sections with weld-in repair pieces.
Tools: Drill and bits · angle grinder · welder (or a shop) · 1/8 in steel plate · clamps · torch for normalizing (optional).

#### Clean the Carter BBD idle tubes
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost A can of carb cleaner and a pair of venturi gaskets
Symptoms: Stumbling and sputtering at idle, stalling at stop signs, poor fuel economy, or an idle that someone has turned up to hide the problem. Offroaders.com says the most common cause is clogged idle tubes letting fuel drip from the venturis, so it runs rich.
Fix: With the engine idling and the choke open, look down the carb: fuel dripping from the venturi nozzles at idle means the idle tubes are clogged. Engine off. Remove the air cleaner (tag the hoses), the choke-plate screws, the choke-rod clip and screw, then the two screws holding the venturi cluster, and lift it out with its two gaskets. Spray everything with carb cleaner without dislodging the center check ball, clear the idle tubes and nozzles with fine wire, and reassemble with every body screw tight. The article says Jeep once recommended drilling the idle tubes to 0.032 in to stop them clogging again. If it still idles badly, look for split vacuum hoses and intake leaks before blaming the carb.
Tools: Screwdrivers · snap-ring pliers · carb cleaner · fine wire · masking tape for labeling hoses.

#### Replace rotten floor pans and body mounts
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend or more per side · cost Panels are cheap; the labor is in the cutting and welding
Symptoms: Daylight through the floor, wet carpet, a tub that shifts on the frame, or body mounts you can push a screwdriver through. The buyer's guide points to the floor, rockers, rear corners and the area under the roll bar.
Fix: Strip the interior and lift the carpet. Cut back to solid metal, then trim the replacement pan to overlap or butt-fit, and plug-weld it along the factory seams. Seam-seal and paint the inside and out. Replace the rubber body-mount bushings at the same time: loosen all six mount bolts, jack the tub a little at each mount, and swap the upper and lower bushings. If a frame-side mount bracket has rotted, weld in a new one before refitting the tub.
Tools: Cut-off wheel · spot-weld drill · MIG welder · panel clamps · seam sealer · weld-through primer · floor jack and wood block.

#### Rebuild rusted rear shackle mounts and replace shackles and bushings
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A day per end · cost Repair sections and shackles are under a few hundred dollars
Symptoms: A rear end that sits crooked or crashes over bumps, squeaking leaf springs, or a shackle hanger with rust holes. The buyer's guide calls the shackle mounts a common rot spot, because mud blocks the boxed frame's drain holes.
Fix: Support the frame on stands and take the weight off the springs. Unbolt the shackle and spring eye, and cut out the rotted hanger section. Weld in a slip-fit repair section, then paint and wax-oil the inside of the rail. Fit new shackles (greaseable ones let you lube the pivots) and new bushings in the spring eyes and frame mounts. Torque the bolts with the truck at ride height so the bushings aren't preloaded twisted.
Tools: Jack stands · cut-off wheel · welder · grease gun · bushing press or vise.

#### Service the front wheel bearings and locking hubs
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours for both sides · cost Bearings, races and seals [price not sourced]
Symptoms: Play at the top and bottom of the tire, growling that changes when you turn, grease flung inside the rim, or hubs that won't engage. The stock five-bolt Warn hubs on 1981–86 CJs are weak, and Quadra-Trac trucks have drive plates rather than hubs.
Fix: Remove the hub, the outer nut, lock washer and inner nut, then pull the rotor and catch the outer bearing. Clean everything, replace bearings and races as pairs, and press the new races in square. Seals come in two sizes (2 1/8 in and 2 5/16 in), so measure the old one first. Pack the bearings fully and tighten the inner nut to 50 ft-lb while turning the rotor to seat them, as the manuals quoted in the Off-Road.com thread say. Then back it off (one owner backs off about 1/6 turn), fit the lock washer and torque the outer locknut to 50 ft-lb and bend the lock-washer lip over it (1981 Jeep factory service manual; the inner nut is set the same way there, 50 ft-lb then back off 1/6 turn), and check end play: the manuals quoted there specify 0.001–0.005 in with a dial indicator. If the six spindle bolts come out, replace the needle bearing inside the spindle too.
Tools: Hub/spindle-nut socket · torque wrench · bearing packer (optional) · race driver or long bolt · brake cleaner · high-quality wheel-bearing grease.

#### Reseal a leaking Dana 300
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–4 hours in the truck · cost A seal kit and 2 quarts of 80W-90
Symptoms: Gear oil on the skid plate, wet yokes or a drip from the rear output. The Dana 300 holds only 2 quarts, so a slow leak can starve it.
Fix: Drain the case and unbolt the driveshafts. Hold the yoke and remove the output nut, then pull the yoke. Pry the old seal out with a big screwdriver or small pry bar, and drive the new one in squarely with a seal driver or a large socket (one owner used a 1 1/2-inch socket), tapping gently so it doesn't distort. Inspect the yoke's seal surface and replace it if it's grooved. Many owners take the chance to switch from strap-style to U-bolt yokes. Refill with 80W-90 to the fill plug.
Tools: Yoke holder or pipe wrench · large socket for the output nut · pry bar · seal driver or 1 1/2 in socket · 80W-90 gear oil.

### Baseline service
Assume a 40-year-old CJ-7 has had nothing done unless there are receipts, and remember that three owners ago someone probably swapped the gearbox, carb or axle. Identify what you actually have first (Dana 20, Dana 300 or Quadra-Trac; which transmission; narrow or wide track), because the fluids differ. Then change every fluid, repack the front bearings and grease every zerk.
- Engine oil & filter (258 I6): About 6 qt including the filter, per a 1984 CJ-7 owner's manual quoted on JeepCJ.com · ExtremeTerrain lists 5W-30 or 10W-30 for CJ engines · Then every 7,500 mi or 7.5 months after a first change at 5,000 (1981 Jeep factory schedule). Many owners use 3,000–5,000 mi on an old carbureted six (Owners report 5 to 5.5 qt reaching FULL depending on the pan and filter, so fill to 5, run it, then top up on the dipstick. The 304 V8 takes 5 qt and the 2.5 four takes 4 qt (ExtremeTerrain). The MFK16 and MFK18 kits below are for 304 and 2.5L trucks, not the 258.)
- Air filter & thermostatic air cleaner (TAC): Paper element in the factory TAC housing · Inspect at every oil change (Check the TAC flapper and its vacuum hose while the lid is off: the BBD and its emissions plumbing run poorly with a stuck flapper or split hoses.)
- Fuel filter: In-line filter, 4.2L · Replace now; the 1981 factory schedule replaces it at 12,500 mi, then every 15,000 mi (Rust from an old tank clogs the filter and the BBD's idle circuits, which is often the real cause of a 'carb problem'.)
- Spark plugs, cap, rotor & wires: Plug part numbers change by year: Crown 4318137 for 1978–80 4.2L, 4318138 for 1981–90 · Replace now, then every 30,000 mi (1981 Jeep factory schedule) (Fresh ignition parts are the cheap first step before blaming the carb.)
- Coolant, hoses & thermostat: 50/50 conventional (IAT) green coolant · 258 (4.2): 10.5 qt · 304 V8: 14.5 qt · 151 Iron Duke: 7.8 qt · AMC 150: 11 qt (ExtremeTerrain) · Flush now. The 1981 factory schedule changes coolant at 12,500 mi or 12.5 months, then at the start of each winter season, keeping a 50/50 mix (Old CJs run warm with partly blocked radiators. Flush the block, replace both radiator hoses and the thermostat, and pressure-test the cap.)
- Drive belts: Belt type depends on year and accessories [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Replace now if cracked or glazed (Inspect the air-pump and power-steering belts too; air-pump brackets are hard to find, so don't lose them.)
- Manual transmission: T-176: 80W-90, about 1.7 L · T-18: 80W-90, 3.25 qt · SR-4: 80W-90, 1.5 qt · T-150: 80W-90, 1.4 qt · T-4/T-5: ATF+4, 2 qt (ExtremeTerrain) · Drain and refill now (ExtremeTerrain lists the T-176 as '3.5 quarts / 1.7 liters'; the liter figure matches 3.5 pints, so fill to the plug rather than by volume. Some owners run synchromesh fluid in T-4s. Check the casting number on the driver's side before you buy fluid.)
- Automatic transmission (if fitted): ExtremeTerrain lists ATF+4; the 1981 Jeep factory manual specifies Dexron or Dexron II for the 999 and 904 · TF999/TF904: 3 qt service fill · TH400 (Quadra-Trac trucks): 6 qt service fill · TH400 is a GM unit: confirm fluid type [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Pan drop, filter and refill now, then every 25,000 mi (10,000 mi in heavy-duty use) per the 1981 factory schedule (A service fill replaces only part of the fluid, so do a second drain-and-fill if the old fluid is dark or burnt.)
- Transfer case: Dana 300: 80W-90, 2 qt · Dana 20: 80W-90, 1.6 qt · Quadra-Trac: Quadra-Trac formula fluid, 2.25 qt (ExtremeTerrain). The 1981 factory manual specifies SAE 85W-90 GL-5 for the Dana 300 · Drain and refill now (Quadra-Trac's chain stretches when the oil is low or old, so don't skip this one. Check the Dana 300's output seals while you're under there.)
- Front axle (Dana 30): 80W-90 gear oil (ExtremeTerrain; the 1981 factory manual specifies SAE 85W-90 GL-5) · 1.25 qt (ExtremeTerrain) · Drain and refill now (Check the axle U-joints for play while you're at the knuckles.)
- Rear axle (AMC 20): 80W-90 gear oil (ExtremeTerrain; the 1981 factory manual specifies SAE 85W-90 GL-5) · 2.4 qt · add 4 oz of limited-slip additive for Trac-Lok (ExtremeTerrain). Late-1986 Dana 44: 2 qt · Drain and refill now (Read the gear-ratio and Trac-Lok code stamped left of the cover while it's clean, and check that the hub nuts on two-piece shafts are tight.)
- Front wheel bearings & hubs: Repack with high-quality wheel-bearing grease · inner nut to 50 ft-lb to seat, back off, then set 0.001–0.005 in end play (manual figures quoted in an Off-Road.com thread) · outer locknut 50 ft-lb with the lock-washer lip bent over (1981 Jeep factory service manual) · Repack now, then every 30,000 mi (15,000 mi in heavy-duty or off-road use) per the 1981 factory schedule, and after any water crossing deep enough to cover the hubs (Hubs are the weak five-bolt Warn type on 1981–86 trucks. Quadra-Trac trucks have drive plates instead, and hubs shouldn't be fitted unless the case has been converted to part-time.)
- Brake & clutch fluid: DOT 3 for the brake master cylinder and, where fitted, the clutch master cylinder (ExtremeTerrain) · Flush now, then per the manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Rubber hoses on a CJ are probably original. 1982–86 trucks use crimped hose-to-steel-line assemblies, so check them for cracks.)
- Power steering fluid: Power steering fluid +4, or ATF+4 if unavailable (ExtremeTerrain) · Check now; replace if dark (Watch the steering box as someone turns the wheel. If the box moves, inspect the frame for cracks before you blame the box.)
- Grease points: Chassis grease at every zerk · At every oil change (Driveshaft U-joints and slip yokes, steering joints, and greaseable shackles if fitted. CJ leaf-spring pivots that have been neglected squeak first and then wear out their bushings.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: A 31x10.50R15 on the right wheel, on a healthy stock CJ-7. Performance Plus Tire's guide says it needs healthy springs and shallow backspacing (about 3.5 in on a 15x8 for narrow-track trucks), and JeepCJ.com owners agree 31s are the practical limit. One member reported 32x11.50s on a stock CJ with very little rubbing. 33x12.50R15s need a lift; most CJs running 33s have about 4 inches of spring lift, though 2.5 inches can work with the right backspacing and some fender trimming. Every CJ-7 used 15-inch wheels on a 5 x 5.5 in bolt pattern, with factory sizes from H78-15 bias-plies to metric radials up to 235/75R15 (Performance Plus).

Q: Should I keep the AMC 20 or swap it?
A: The AMC 20 has a bigger ring gear (8⅞ in) than a Dana 44, but thinner 29-spline shafts, smaller tubes and, on CJs, keyed two-piece hub-and-shaft axles that shear. On a mild truck, one-piece shafts and stitch-welded tubes fix most of it. If you're running big tires and a locker, the usual swap is a Dana 44, and some late-1986 CJ-7s came with a wide-track Dana 44 from the factory.

Q: Which transmission should I look for?
A: The T-18A (1977–79) with its 6.32:1 granny first is the toughest factory CJ gearbox. From 1980, the Tremec T-176 four-speed (3.52:1 first) is the strong option. The SR-4 (1980–81) and the T-4 and T-5 (1982–86) are light-duty Borg-Warner boxes that Novak calls 'essentially a small car transmission in a truck'.

Q: Dana 20 or Dana 300?
A: The Dana 300 (1980–86) has a 2.62:1 low range against the Dana 20's 2.03:1, and helical low-range gears that make it quieter. Novak says there's probably no real strength advantage, and the Dana 20 is shorter, which helps driveshaft angles. For more crawl, TeraFlex's TeraLow gearset gives a Dana 300 a 4:1 low range; one owner's crawl ratio went from 32.3:1 to 49.8:1.

Q: What is Quadra-Trac, and should I keep it?
A: Quadra-Trac was the optional full-time 4WD in 1976–79 CJ-7s: a chain-driven Borg-Warner 13-39 case paired only with a TH400 automatic. It has a vacuum-locked center differential (the 'Emergency Drive' switch) and an optional bolt-on low range (2.57:1). The chain is known for a short life. Mile Marker sold an overdrive gear-and-chain set that also converts it to part-time, and Offroaders.com names the Dana 18 as a good gear-driven replacement because its outputs line up (it needs a transmission swap too).

Q: How do I find my axle ratio?
A: Look for the code stamped on the AMC 20 housing boss to the left of the cover, near the tube. Narrow-track codes differ from wide-track ones: on a wide-track axle, A is 3.54 open, AA is 3.54 Trac-Lok, H is 3.73 open, and C is 4.10 open. Offroaders.com advises confirming with a tape measure or the front axle's Dana tag, because codes conflict between versions. Offroaders.com gives the common Dana 30 ratios as 3.54 for 1976–79 and 2.73 for 1980–86, while Wikipedia pairs the 258 and four with 3.73 and the 304 with 3.55, so check yours rather than assume.

Q: What's the difference between narrow track and wide track?
A: 1976–81 CJ-7s use narrow-track axles, 50.5 in wheel to wheel on the AMC 20. From 1982 the wide-track axles measure 54.5 in, which helps stability. Both use 5 x 5.5 in wheels. The 1982–86 Dana 30 also switched to pin-bolted calipers and crimped brake hoses.

Q: Which engine is the one to have?
A: The 258 straight six (1976–78 trucks may have the smaller 232 six, which was standard until 1979). JeepCJ.com's buyer's guide calls it 'a strong, torquey, reliable motor' and says to avoid the GM Iron Duke four (1980–83). The 304 V8 (to 1981) is quicker but was choked by smog controls by the end: 125 hp in 1980–81 against the 258's 110.

Q: What fluids does it take?
A: ExtremeTerrain's CJ guide lists 80W-90 gear oil for the Dana 30 (1.25 qt), AMC 20 (2.4 qt; add 4 oz of limited-slip additive for Trac-Lok), Dana 300 (2 qt) and Dana 20 (1.6 qt). Quadra-Trac needs its own transfer case fluid (2.25 qt). The T-176, SR-4, T-150 and T-18 take 80W-90; ExtremeTerrain lists ATF+4 for the T-4 and T-5 and for the automatics, while the 1981 Jeep factory manual calls for Dexron or Dexron II in the 999 and 904 automatics and SAE 85W-90 GL-5 in the axles, the manual gearboxes and the Dana 300. The T-4/T-5 and the TH400 (a GM unit) aren't covered there, so check your manual before filling them [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]. Brakes take DOT 3. The 258 takes about 6 quarts of oil including the filter, per ExtremeTerrain and a 1984 owner's manual quoted on JeepCJ.com, and about 10.5 qt of coolant (ExtremeTerrain).

Q: Will Wrangler wheels and parts fit?
A: Not the wheels. CJ axles use 5 x 5.5 in, and later Jeep Dana 30s use 5 x 4.5 in. Lots of other parts carry over, though: the 258 lived on in the YJ until 1990, and outer Dana 30 parts (knuckle outward) swap between CJ versions, so a drum-brake CJ can be converted to discs.

Q: Was there a diesel CJ-7?
A: Only for export. From 1980 to 1982 AMC built CJ-7s in Ohio with Isuzu's 2.4-liter C240 diesel four, a T-176, a Dana 300 and 4.10 axles. None were sold new in the US.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: There's no single answer, so we don't flag one. Owners on Off-Road.com split between 1976–79 trucks, for the T-18 four-speed and the 304 V8 option, and 1982-on trucks with the wider-track axles; a 1986 with the factory Dana 44 rear is a good find. Jeep-CJ.com calls the T-18 the best CJ manual and says to avoid the GM Iron Duke four used from 1980 to 1983. The Drive says to watch out for Quadra-Trac. Buy the best frame you can find, then pick the drivetrain.
