## Jeep CJ-8 Scrambler (1981–1986)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/cj-8/
Codes: CJ-8, Scrambler

Verdict: The Scrambler is a CJ-7 that kept going after the roll bar and grew a little pickup bed. Jeep sold barely 28,000 of them, one went to a president, and now everyone wants one.

Jeep launched the CJ-8 in March 1981, according to 4WDrive, and called it the Scrambler. It was a long-wheelbase CJ-7: 103.5 inches between the axles, 10 more than the CJ-7, with a removable half cab and a small pickup-style box built into the body tub instead of a separate bed. 4WDrive magazine calls it North America's first factory convertible 4x4 pickup. It kept the CJ formula of a ladder frame, leaf springs, live axles, a gear-driven two-speed transfer case and manual locking hubs. It also kept the CJ's open top, the part a pickup normally gives up.

### A PICKUP THAT ISN'T QUITE
4WDrive says the stretch added two feet to the bed and quotes a 636 kg (about 1,400 lb) payload. SlashGear says a hard half cab was standard, with full soft and hard tops available; 4WDrive describes a removable soft or hard cab. Jeep sold the truck on fun as much as utility. eBay Motors notes that the Scrambler name came from an appearance package, and many trucks wore loud decal kits. The SR Sport and SL Sport packages added bigger tires, under-hood insulation and lighting, a three-spoke wheel, chrome trim, carpet and decals. A denim edition topped the range at $8,392.
Under the skin it's a CJ-7 with a longer middle. Like the CJ-7, it moved to wider-track Dana 30 and AMC 20 axles for 1982. The Dana 300 transfer case is a strong, gear-driven unit, according to Jeep-CJ.com. Prices fell quickly. 4WDrive lists a base price of $7,288 at launch and a low of $6,765 in 1982. By 1985 Jeep was throwing in a free soft top to keep the trucks moving.

### WHAT'S UNDER THE HOOD
Engines followed the CJ-7. Early trucks came with GM's 151 Iron Duke four as standard, which SlashGear calls 'relatively wimpy' and Jeep-CJ.com's buyer's guide says to avoid. AMC's own 2.5-litre four replaced it later in the run, rated at 105 hp. Offroaders.com and Wikipedia date the GM 151 in CJs to 1980–83, and the AMC 150 arrived for 1984. The engine to have is the 258 straight-six, rated at 115 hp. No Scrambler had a factory V8.
Manual Scramblers used the BorgWarner SR-4 behind the four and the Tremec T-176 behind the six. Automatics were Chrysler TorqueFlites: the 904 with the four and the 999 with the six. The BorgWarner T-4 four-speed and T-5 five-speed were in the CJ line from 1982, per Offroaders.com (SlashGear dates the Scrambler's T-5 to 1985–86). The T-5 has a 4.03:1 first gear and an overdrive fifth that SlashGear gives as 0.76:1 and Offroaders.com as 0.8. On Jeep-CJ.com, members call it weak and suggest the T-176 as the easiest swap. Most Scramblers have the AMC 20 rear axle, but some 1986 trucks got a Dana 44.

### SLOW SALES, LONG AFTERLIFE
Sales started at 8,355 in 1981 and slid every year to 128 in 1986, and there's debate over whether those last ones were leftovers. That adds up to about 27,800 Scramblers, against more than 379,000 CJ-7s built from 1976 to 1986. The Cherokee-based Comanche effectively replaced it. The rarest variants went abroad or north. Alaska's postal service ordered 230 right-hand-drive automatics with full steel 'World Cab' tops and barn doors. Venezuela and Australia got a similar truck called the CJ8 Overlander, with full-length rear windows.
The low production numbers are why prices have climbed. SlashGear says a well-preserved Scrambler now costs at least $30,000, and eBay Motors featured one showing just under 2,100 miles on its five-digit odometer, with a $39,900 asking price. Long-wheelbase Jeeps came back with the 2004 Wrangler Unlimited (LJ) and the four-door JK Unlimited. Neither has a bed, though, and that is why Scrambler owners keep theirs.

### Data plate
- Model Years: 1981–1986 (launched March 1981)
- Built: ≈ 27,800 (8,355 in 1981 to 128 in 1986)
- Wheelbase: 103.5 in (10 in longer than CJ-7)
- Engines: GM 151 I4 · AMC 150 I4 · AMC 258 I6
- Output: AMC 150: 105 hp · 258: 115 hp
- Manuals: SR-4, T-4, T-176 4-spd · T-5 5-spd
- Automatics: TorqueFlite 904 (I4) · 999 (I6)
- Transfer Case: Dana 300, two-speed, gear-driven
- Axles: Dana 30 front · AMC 20 rear (some 1986 Dana 44)
- Payload: 636 kg (≈1,400 lb), per 4WDrive
- Price New: $7,288 base (1981); $6,765 low (1982)
- Replaced By: Jeep Comanche (pickup) · Wrangler YJ (open Jeep)

### Engineering
The CJ-8 is a CJ-7 with the frame and tub stretched to 103.5 inches. It keeps a boxed ladder frame, leaf springs on live axles, a gear-driven Dana 300 and manual locking hubs. The back of the tub becomes a short bed behind a removable half cab. Everything mechanical is shared with the 1981–86 CJ-7, which makes parts easy. Body panels behind the front seats are Scrambler-specific.
- Chassis: Boxed ladder frame · 103.5 in wheelbase (10 inches longer than the CJ-7. Boxed CJ frames often crack around the steering box.)
- Body: Tub with integral bed · removable half cab (SlashGear says a hard half cab was standard and full tops were available. RHD 'World Cab' full steel top for the Alaska postal trucks.)
- Suspension & Axles: Leaf springs · Dana 30 front · AMC 20 rear (some 1986 Dana 44) (Wide-track axles from 1982. Jeep-CJ.com warns wide-track shock towers can trap water.)
- 4Wd System: Part-time Dana 300, two-speed, gear-driven (Manual locking hubs; every Scrambler has the five-bolt hub pattern.)
- Engines: GM 151 I4 (1981–83) · AMC 150 I4 (1984–86) · AMC 258 I6 (AMC four 105 hp; 258 115 hp. No V8.)
- Gearboxes: SR-4 · T-176 · T-4 / T-5 (from 1982) · TF904 / TF999 auto (T-5: 4.03 first, overdrive fifth. Owners rate the T-176 higher.)

### Versions
- 1981 · CJ-8 (launch) · GM 151 Iron Duke 2.5 L I4 · AMC 258 4.2 L I6 · 258: 115 hp · Narrow-track axles. 8,355 built.
- 1982–1983 · CJ-8 · GM 151 I4 · AMC 258 I6 · 258: 115 hp · Wide-track Dana 30 / AMC 20 axles. SR Sport and SL Sport packages.
- 1984–1986 · CJ-8 (late) · AMC 150 2.5 L I4 · AMC 258 I6 · 105 hp · 115 hp · AMC's own four replaces the Iron Duke. 1985 free soft-top promotion.
- 1982–1986 · CJ-8 with T-4 / T-5 · AMC 258 I6 or 150 I4 · — · BorgWarner T-4 four-speed and T-5 five-speed from 1982 per Offroaders.com (SlashGear says 1985–86 for the T-5). Some 1986 trucks got a Dana 44 rear. Only 128 sold in 1986.
- 1981–1986 · World Cab / CJ8 Overlander · Per market · — · RHD steel full-cab with barn doors: 230 for the Alaskan postal service; Overlander for Venezuela and Australia.

### Year-by-year
- 1981: Scrambler launches: CJ-7 front end on a 103.5 in wheelbase with a removable half cab and integrated pickup box. Best year at 8,355 built
- 1982: 7,759 built
- 1983: 5,405 built
- 1984: 4,130 built; 230 trucks recalled for a left tie-rod end that could crack
- 1985: 2,015 built
- 1986: Final 128 built (whether these were 1985 leftovers is debated); the Comanche replaces it

### Capability
- Wheelbase: 103.5 in (2,629 mm)
- Transfer case: Part-time two-speed with manual locking front hubs (most with four- or five-speed manuals; three-speed automatic optional)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 205/75R15, 235/75R15
- Bolt Pattern: 5x139.7 (5x5.5")
- Center Bore: 108 mm
- Lug Thread: 1/2"-20
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 31x10.50R15 (The CJ owners' consensus for an unlifted CJ-7-bodied Jeep on 15x8 wheels; 32s only on tired springs)
- Biggest tire, 2.5 in lift: 33x12.50R15 (Fits for mild use with the steering stops reset; expect contact when stuffed)
- Biggest tire, 4 in lift: 33x12.50R15 (Comfortable trail setup for 33s; plan on regearing)

### Buying checks
- Rust in the long tub: Check the rockers, the rear corners of the bed, the wheel wells, under the roll bar and the floor. Jeep-CJ.com warns that patches welded over rust become rust. Knock on panels to find filler. Replacement Scrambler tubs exist, but they are a full strip-down job.
- Frame and shock towers: Inspect the whole frame, especially the shackle mounts, the area behind the rear wheels and the body mounts. On 1982–86 wide-track trucks, Jeep-CJ.com says the shock towers can trap water. Mud blocks the drain holes in the boxed rails.
- Steering box mount: Boxed frames often crack around the steering box, especially on lifted trucks with big tires. Look for cracks, fresh welds and movement when someone turns the wheel.
- Engine choice: SlashGear calls the 258 six the most desirable engine. Jeep-CJ.com says to avoid the Iron Duke four. Look for start-up smoke, rattles, and oil weeping from the rear main seal.
- Five-speed health: On 1985–86 trucks, check that the T-5 doesn't jump out of gear or grind. Jeep-CJ.com members call it weak. A T-176 swap is the common fix, and the driveshafts must be modified for length.
- Tailgate, tops and seals: Check the tailgate hardware and weatherstripping and the cowl seals, since failed seals trap water. Tops and half cabs are Scrambler-specific, so price in a replacement if they're missing.
- Originality and paperwork: Jeep-CJ.com recommends mostly stock trucks over projects or heavy trail builds. 4WDrive's featured truck came with a binder documenting its restoration, and paperwork like that matters on a truck this valuable.
- Test drive: Start it cold. Test every gear, 4WD high and low on gravel, the brakes (gently at first), the gauges and the heater. Check for leaks at the transfer case and both axles.

### Common repairs
#### AMC 20 one-piece axle conversion
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day to a day · cost Crown J8133885-1 driver-side kit about $215 at Quadratec (October 2026); the passenger side is a separate kit
Symptoms: Clunks on take-off, a rear hub loosening on its shaft, or spun splines. Quadratec explains that the factory hardened hubs cut into softer axle-shaft splines, leaving weak spots in the driveline.
Fix: One-piece shafts fix the hub flange to the shaft, which stops the splines spinning. Remove the wheels and drums, pull the pressed-on hubs (a hub puller is the usual tool), remove the bearing retainers and pull the shafts. Fit the new shafts with bearings and seals per the kit instructions, replace the inner seals while you're there, and refill with gear oil. Add friction modifier if the axle has a Trac-Lok. Trucks with the 1986 Dana 44 don't need this.
Tools: Hub puller · slide hammer · seal driver · torque wrench · Crown 1982–86 CJ-7/CJ-8 one-piece kits (sold per side)

#### Steering box mount and frame cracks
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day if the frame is sound · cost Rust Buster RB1008 about $125; Fishbone FB26318 also fits CJ-7/CJ-8
Symptoms: Wandering steering, a box that shifts on the frame, or cracks around the box mounting holes. RockCrawler.com blames cheap stamped brackets, age, mileage and big tires.
Fix: RockCrawler's plate-steel bracket install: disconnect the drag link, hoses and steering shaft, remove the box, fit the bracket's studs and spacers with thread-locker and trial-fit, filing the holes if needed. Bolt the mount to the box at 65 ft-lb and to the frame with Grade 8 hardware at 55 ft-lb, adding the through-frame bolt. Weld any existing cracks first. Route the hoses so they can't rub.
Tools: Pitman arm puller · torque wrench · thread-locker · welder for frame repairs

#### T-5 jumping out of gear: rebuild or swap
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend · cost Parts plus labor; a swap adds adapters and driveshaft work
Symptoms: On a 1985 CJ-7 thread, a T-5 behind the 258 popped out of first and third, grinding on downshifts.
Fix: Jeep-CJ.com members' options: rebuild the T-5 with new bearings and synchros, or replace it. They call the T-176 the easiest swap, though the driveshafts must be modified for length. One owner fitted a Ford T-18 using an Advance Adapters kit, a replacement output shaft and four drilled-and-tapped bellhousing holes, and kept his driveshafts. Replace the clutch while the gearbox is out. The T-4 and T-5 take ATF+4 (2 qt), per ExtremeTerrain.
Tools: Transmission jack · snap-ring pliers · bearing puller · adapter kit if swapping

#### Carter BBD rough idle (258)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost A can of carb cleaner
Symptoms: Stumbling or stalling at idle and poor economy, but fine at higher rpm. Offroaders.com says the cause is almost always clogged idle tubes. It also says post-1981 feedback carbs with a stepper motor are 'a bit more troublesome.'
Fix: With the engine running and choke open, look for fuel dripping from the idle nozzles. Tag the hoses, then remove the air cleaner, choke plate and rod, and the venturi cluster (two screws, two small gaskets). Check that the idle pickup tubes are seated, clear the tubes and nozzles with fine wire and carb cleaner without losing the check ball, and reassemble. Tighten the carb body screws. Drilling the idle tubes to 0.032 in reduces clogging. If it still idles badly, check for vacuum and manifold leaks.
Tools: 3/16 in socket · small screwdrivers · carb cleaner · fine wire · 0.032 in drill bit

#### Ignition refresh or HEI swap (258)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost The BustedJeep author paid $15 for a junkyard HEI
Symptoms: Hard starting, rough idle, hesitation and poor fuel economy, which Jeep-CJ.com's write-up blames on the factory Duraspark.
Fix: Start with a cap, rotor, plugs and wires. For the HEI swap, use a 1976–82 GM inline-six HEI with an AMC V8 drive gear. Mark No. 1, swap the distributors and feed the HEI from the constant-12 V firewall wire, not the resistor coil feed. Gap the plugs to .045 in (firing order 1-5-3-6-2-4) and set the timing with a light; many owners run about 8° BTDC. Trucks with the feedback ECM need it bypassed first.
Tools: Timing light · volt meter · soldering iron · plug gapper

#### Clutch bellcrank (Z-bar) rebuild
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost Bushings and a bellcrank are inexpensive
Symptoms: A sloppy clutch, trouble selecting first, or linkage that pops apart. Jeep-CJ.com members say the plastic bushings wear out, and that worn motor mounts can break the pivots.
Fix: Check the motor mounts first. Remove the bellcrank, replace the bushings and ball studs (or the bellcrank), grease it and reset the clutch free play. A forum fix replaces the worn bushing with a ground-to-fit solid rod with welded-in bolt pivots. Some owners convert to a hydraulic clutch when engine torque keeps pushing the linkage out of the throwout lever.
Tools: Wrenches · grease · bushings or bellcrank · motor mounts if worn

#### Rear main seal (258)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day to a day · cost Seal and pan gaskets plus labor
Symptoms: Oil dripping from the joint between the engine and bellhousing.
Fix: Following Jeep's 1973 service-manual procedure (via IFSJA): drain the oil and drop the pan, then remove the rear main cap and lower seal half. Loosen the other caps and tap out the upper half with a brass drift. Oil the crank and fit the new upper half lip-forward. Put sealant only on the lower half's end tabs, seat it in the cap, seal the cap's chamfers and torque to spec. Refit the pan with new gaskets. Always replace both halves together.
Tools: Brass drift · torque wrench · Permatex No. 2 or equivalent

#### Floor, bed and tailgate rust repair
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend per side; a full tub swap is a strip-down · cost Key Parts half floor pan for CJ-7/CJ-8 at Quadratec; complete Omix Scrambler tub also available
Symptoms: Soft floors, rot in the rear bed corners, wheel wells and rockers, and a tailgate rusting around its seal and hardware.
Fix: Cut back to clean metal and weld in replacement panels. Jeep-CJ.com warns that patching over rust only creates more rust. Replace the body-mount bushings and tailgate seal while the truck is apart, then seam-seal and paint. If the tub is too far gone, Omix makes a complete steel tub kit for 1981–86 Scramblers.
Tools: Cut-off wheel · MIG welder · clamps · seam sealer

### Baseline service
Scramblers are rare enough that most have been half-restored at least once, so trust nothing. Change every fluid, grease every fitting, check the ignition and carburetor, and look at the AMC 20 hubs. Capacities below are from ExtremeTerrain's CJ chart, which covers the 1981–86 drivetrains.
- Engine oil & filter: 5W-30 or 10W-30 · 4.2 L six: 6 qt · 2.5 L four: 4 qt · Baseline now; then per your owner's manual (Look for rear-main and valve-cover leaks while you're under there.)
- Air filter: Paper element in the factory air cleaner · Baseline now (Fit a fresh one before you judge the carburetor.)
- Ignition tune-up: Plugs, cap, rotor, wires · gap and timing [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now (The 258 fires 1-5-3-6-2-4. Duraspark pickups and modules are common culprits for poor running.)
- Coolant & thermostat: 50/50 coolant · 4.2 L: 10.5 qt · Iron Duke: 7.8 qt · AMC 2.5: 11 qt · Baseline flush now (Flush until clean, fit a new thermostat and check the overflow bottle for cracks.)
- Belts & hoses: V-belts or serpentine (1984–86 with factory A/C) · molded hoses · Baseline now if cracked or soft (Squeeze every hose and replace any that feel crunchy or spongy.)
- Manual transmission: SR-4: 80W-90, 1.5 qt · T-4 / T-5: ATF+4, 2 qt · T-176: 80W-90 [CONFIRM CAPACITY] · Baseline now (ExtremeTerrain's T-176 figure (3.5 qt / 1.7 L) contradicts itself, so check the manual. Don't put gear oil in a T-5.)
- Automatic transmission: TF904 / TF999: ATF+4 · 3 qt service fill (8.5 qt overhaul) · Drain, change the filter and refill now (A pan drop changes only part of the fluid. Do it twice if the old fluid is dark.)
- Transfer case: Dana 300 · 80W-90 · 2 qt · Baseline now (Output seals weep with age, and kits are cheap.)
- Front differential: Dana 30 · 80W-90 · 1.25 qt · Baseline now (ExtremeTerrain suggests 75W-140 for towing or extreme use.)
- Rear differential: AMC 20: 80W-90, 2.4 qt · Dana 44 (some 1986): 2 qt · Trac-Lok: add 4 oz limited-slip additive · Baseline now (While the cover is off, check the hubs for play. It's the AMC 20's weak point.)
- Front wheel bearings & hubs: Repack and adjust · preload [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now; then after deep water (Every Scrambler uses five-bolt manual locking hubs. Check them for slipping while they're apart.)
- Brake & clutch fluid: DOT 3 · Flush now (Check the rear wheel cylinders and front calipers for weeping.)
- Power steering: Power Steering +4, or ATF+4 if unavailable · Check and top up now (Box seal kits are cheap. Inspect the box mount while you're there.)
- Grease points & fuel filter: U-joints and slip yokes (the long rear shaft especially) · shackles · steering joints · inline fuel filter · Grease every oil change; filter now (Replace dry or notchy U-joints now.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: Jeep-CJ.com members put 31-inch tires as the safe maximum on a stock CJ. They say 32s rub the rear wheel wells without trimming, and doubt 33s will fit. The thread covers CJs generally rather than the Scrambler specifically, but the CJ-8 shares the CJ-7's front end and springs. Saggy old springs and wheel backspacing can make even 31s tight.

Q: How many Scramblers were built?
A: Wikipedia lists 8,355 in 1981, 7,759 in 1982, 5,405 in 1983, 4,130 in 1984, 2,015 in 1985 and 128 in 1986, about 27,800 in total. Some argue the 1986 trucks were leftovers. SlashGear compares that with more than 379,000 CJ-7s.

Q: Which engine should I buy?
A: The 258 straight-six, rated at 115 hp. SlashGear calls it the most desirable option, and Jeep-CJ.com praises it for torque and reliability. The Iron Duke four in early trucks is the one Jeep-CJ.com says to avoid. The later AMC four, at 105 hp, is better. No Scrambler came with a V8.

Q: Which transmission is best?
A: Jeep-CJ.com recommends the T-176 four-speed among 1980s CJ gearboxes, and members call the T-5 five-speed weak. The automatics were Chrysler TorqueFlites: the 904 behind the four and the 999 behind the six.

Q: Is it really a pickup?
A: Sort of. The bed is part of the body tub behind a removable half cab, not a separate box. 4WDrive quotes a 636 kg (about 1,400 lb) payload and a bed two feet longer than the CJ-7's rear tub. SlashGear says full soft and hard tops were available, and with the top off it's a long open CJ.

Q: Did Ronald Reagan really own one?
A: Yes. A blue Scrambler was bought for Rancho del Cielo, and a White House photograph in the National Archives shows Reagan with it there on 2 April 1983. RealTruck identifies it as a 1983 CJ-8 Renegade with about 18,000 miles. It's displayed at the Reagan Ranch Center in Santa Barbara with a 'GIPPER' plate.

Q: What's wrong with the AMC 20 rear axle?
A: Its two-piece shafts let the hardened hub cut into the softer shaft splines over time. One-piece kits for 1982–86 CJ-7s and CJ-8s, such as Crown's, fix the hub to the shaft. Some 1986 Scramblers have a Dana 44 instead, which doesn't have this issue.

Q: What fluids does it take?
A: ExtremeTerrain's CJ chart lists 5W-30 or 10W-30 oil (6 qt for the 4.2, 4 qt for the 2.5), 80W-90 in the Dana 300 (2 qt), Dana 30 (1.25 qt), AMC 20 (2.4 qt) and Dana 44 (2 qt), ATF+4 in the T-4/T-5 (2 qt) and TorqueFlites (3 qt service fill), and DOT 3 brake fluid. Trac-Lok axles need limited-slip additive.

Q: What are the World Cab and Overlander?
A: Right-hand-drive Scramblers with a full-length steel top and rear barn doors in place of the tailgate. The Alaskan postal service bought 230, with automatic transmissions. Venezuela and Australia got a similar CJ8 Overlander with full-length rear windows.

Q: What's one worth?
A: A lot more than it cost new. 4WDrive lists a $7,288 base price at launch. SlashGear says a well-preserved Scrambler now costs at least $30,000, and eBay Motors featured one showing about 2,100 miles on a five-digit odometer, asking $39,900. Rust and originality drive the price.

Q: What replaced it?
A: Wikipedia says the Cherokee-based Comanche pickup effectively replaced the Scrambler in 1986. The open-top CJ itself gave way to the Wrangler YJ in 1987.

## Jeep Wagoneer & Cherokee (SJ) (1963–1983)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/sj-wagoneer/
Codes: SJ, Wagoneer, Cherokee, Cherokee Chief

Verdict: The original Wagoneer invented the luxury 4x4 before anyone had a word for it, and the two-door Cherokee is the same truck with the family sent home and a 401 under the hood. Both are carbureted, leaf-sprung, rust-hungry and far more capable than a woodgrain wagon has any right to be.

Jeep introduced the Wagoneer in November 1962 for the 1963 model year. It replaced the Willys station wagon that had been built since 1946, and it was the first Jeep line that owed nothing to the CJ. Brooks Stevens shaped it, it shared its SJ chassis with the Gladiator pickup, and it offered features unheard of on other mainstream 4x4s: independent front suspension, power steering, an automatic gearbox and optional air conditioning, all behind an overhead-cam six. For 1974 AMC cut two doors off it and called the result the Cherokee. This page covers both, from 1963 to 1983, before the big wagon carried on alone as the Grand Wagoneer.

### THE KAISER WAGONEER (1963–1969)
The first Wagoneers came as two- and four-door wagons and a two-door panel delivery with barn doors. Power came from the 230 cu in 'Tornado' overhead-cam six, rated at 140 hp. Independent front suspension was standard on two-wheel-drive trucks and optional on 4x4s. It was not popular and was dropped from 4WD models in 1965, the same year AMC's 327 V8 (250 hp) and 232 six arrived. Development had taken three years and about $20 million, and Wikipedia notes that the Wagoneer had no direct competitor when it launched; the two-door Range Rover was still eight years away.
The 1966 Super Wagoneer pushed the idea further: a 270 hp four-barrel 327, a tilt wheel, a console-shifted TH400 automatic, air conditioning and a power tailgate window. About 3,989 were built before it ended in 1969, and it is widely regarded as the precursor of today's luxury SUVs. From 1968 to 1971 a Buick 350 'Dauntless' V8 replaced the 327. By the end of 1968 the slow-selling two-door had gone, and every Wagoneer had solid axles and leaf springs at both ends.

### AMC, QUADRA-TRAC AND A TWO-DOOR CALLED CHEROKEE
AMC bought Kaiser Jeep in 1970 and replaced the outsourced Buick engine with its own 360 and, later, the 401 V8. In 1973 it added Quadra-Trac, a Borg-Warner full-time 4WD system that saved owners from locking hubs and a stiff transfer-case lever. In 1974 AMC took the dead two-door Wagoneer, gave it wide D-pillars and long single rear side windows, and sold it as the Cherokee. The 1974 Cherokee brochure is where the term 'Sport Utility Vehicle' first appears, and that February the Cherokee became the first winner of Four Wheeler magazine's Achievement Award.
The Cherokee came as a base model or the sportier S. The Chief package arrived in 1976 with wider axles and bigger fender flares so it could run larger tires, and a four-door Cherokee followed in 1977 (never with the wide-track axles). The Golden Eagle and Golden Hawk were graphics packages, the Laredo from 1980 was mostly an upholstery upgrade, and a Pioneer package arrived for 1983. With the 401's forged crank and rods and 3.07:1 gearing, Wikipedia says a Cherokee could top 100 mph; early ones had 120 mph speedometers.

### THE WAGONEER GOES UPMARKET (1978–1983)
With the Cherokee taking the sporty buyers, AMC moved the Wagoneer upmarket. The Limited arrived mid-1978 with leather, power seats, cruise control, a CB radio and forged aluminum wheels. At $10,500 it was priced against Cadillacs and Lincolns, and Jeep still built 28,871 Wagoneers that year and 27,437 in 1979. The 1979 restyle brought square headlights, aluminum bumpers and the 'pig nose' grille. The 401 had gone after 1978, and after 1979 Chrysler's TorqueFlite 727 replaced GM's TH400.
The 1979 fuel crisis hit hard. Wagoneer output fell to 10,481 in 1980, the 258 six came back as an option, and from 1981 the range ran Custom, Brougham and Limited. The original Borg-Warner Quadra-Trac was gone after 1979, and an NP219 carried the name to early 1982. For 1983 the Selec-Trac system, with a dash switch for 2WD and 4WD, became standard on the Wagoneer. Wikipedia reports EPA figures of 18 mpg city and 25 highway for the six with the automatic and Selec-Trac, remarkable for a full-size SUV.

### 1984: THE SPLIT
For 1984 the unibody Cherokee XJ replaced the SJ Cherokee outright, and AMC meant the compact XJ Wagoneer to replace the big one too. Demand kept the old wagon alive. The Brougham was dropped, the Limited became the Grand Wagoneer, and that truck ran until June 1991. Australia's tariff rules treated separate-frame 4x4s more kindly than unibody vehicles, so SJ Cherokees were assembled in Brisbane until about 1985.
Today the 1963–1983 trucks sit in the shadow of the woodgrain Grand Wagoneer, which makes them the better buy for someone who wants to use one. The two-door Cherokee is the rarer and more off-road-minded of the pair, the era rival to the Scout II and the early Bronco with a much bigger cabin. Restomod builders know it too: Bring a Trailer has sold Hemi-, Vortec- and Viper-swapped examples, one of them for $315,000.

- Production: Wagoneer 1963–1983 (then Grand Wagoneer) · Cherokee 1974–1983
- Plant: Toledo, Ohio · also Brampton (Canada), Rocklea (Australia), Córdoba (Argentina), Mexico City
- Designer: Brooks Stevens
- Engines: 230 OHC I6 · 232/258 I6 · 327 V8 · Buick 350 V8 · AMC 304/360/401 V8
- Transmissions: T-18 4-speed · TH400 (to 1979) · TorqueFlite 727 (1980–)
- Transfer Cases: Dana 20 · Quadra-Trac BW 13-39 · NP208 · NP219 · NP229
- Axles: Dana 44 front · Dana 44 or AMC 20 rear
- Wheelbase: 108.7 in
- Length: 186.4 in
- Width: 74.8 in · up to 78.7 in (wide-track Chief)
- Wagoneer Built: 28,871 (1978) · 27,437 (1979) · 10,481 (1980) · 18,478 (1983)

### Engineering
The SJ is a separate ladder frame with semi-elliptic leaf springs and solid axles at both ends from 1969. The frame got boxed side rails and stronger crossmembers from 1976. Both bodies share a 108.7 in wheelbase and 186.4 in length; the wide-track Chief is up to 78.7 in wide against 74.8 in for the standard track. Engines are AMC sixes and V8s fed by carburetors, and the drivetrain changed with the year. Read the VIN and look under the truck before you buy parts.
- Chassis: SJ ladder frame, 108.7 in wheelbase (Shared with the Gladiator/J-Series pickups. Boxed side rails and stronger crossmembers from 1976.)
- Engines (1974–83): AMC 258 I6 · 360 V8 (2- or 4-bbl) · 401 V8 (Wikipedia gives 110 hp (258), 175 hp (360 2-bbl), 195 hp (360 4-bbl) and 215 hp net (401). The 401 had a forged crank and rods and ended after 1978.)
- Transmissions: T-18 4-speed · TH400 (to 1979) · TorqueFlite 727 (1980–) (The T-18 had a 6.3:1 first gear. The TH400 was a heavy-duty GM box usually found in 3/4- and 1-ton trucks.)
- 4Wd Systems: Dana 20 · Quadra-Trac BW 13-39 · NP208 / NP219 / NP229 (Dana 20 (2.03:1 low) with manuals to 1979. Borg-Warner Quadra-Trac 1973–79 with automatics, vacuum center-diff lock, optional 2.57:1 low range. NP208 part-time, NP219 and NP229 Selec-Trac from 1980.)
- Axles: Dana 44 front · Dana 44 or AMC 20 rear (Dana 44s front and rear through at least 1979; Offroaders.com lists an AMC 20 rear on 1980–86 SJs. Chiefs used wider axles. Check the tag.)
- Brakes & Wheels: Front disc / rear drum · 6x5.5 in from 1974 (Front discs standard on the Wagoneer from 1974, optional on early Cherokees. Brake hardware was mostly GM half-ton parts. Pre-1974 trucks use a five-lug 5x5.5 in pattern.)

### Versions
- 1963–1965 · Wagoneer (Kaiser) · Tornado 230 OHC I6 · 140 hp · Two- and four-door wagons and a panel delivery. IFS optional on 4x4s until 1965.
- 1965–1968 · Wagoneer · Super Wagoneer (1966–69) · AMC 327 V8 · AMC 232 I6 · 250 hp (270 hp Super) · About 3,989 Super Wagoneers built.
- 1968–1971 · Wagoneer · Buick 350 'Dauntless' V8 · 230 hp / 350 lb-ft · Two-doors gone after 1968; solid axles only from 1969.
- 1972–1973 · Wagoneer (AMC) · AMC 258 I6 · 304 / 360 V8 · Varies by year · Quadra-Trac full-time 4WD arrives for 1973.
- 1974–1978 · Wagoneer · Cherokee (2-door, 4-door from 1977) · 258 I6 · 360 V8 · 401 V8 · 110–215 hp (net) · Cherokee launched 1974; Chief wide-track from 1976; Limited Wagoneer from mid-1978.
- 1979–1980 · Wagoneer · Cherokee · 360 V8 (258 I6 returns as an option) · Varies by year · Square-headlight 'pig nose' restyle; 727 auto replaces TH400 after 1979; NP219/NP208 replace the Borg-Warner case for 1980.
- 1981–1983 · Wagoneer Custom/Brougham/Limited · Cherokee · 258 I6 · 360 V8 · Varies by year · Selec-Trac standard on the 1983 Wagoneer; Laredo and Pioneer Cherokees. The SJ Cherokee ends after 1983.

### Year-by-year
- 1963: Wagoneer launched (November 1962) with the 230 OHC Tornado six; two- and four-door wagons and a panel delivery; IFS optional on 4x4s
- 1965: AMC 327 V8 and 232 six arrive; IFS dropped from 4WD models; standard safety package with dual brakes
- 1966: Super Wagoneer: 270 hp 327, TH400, tilt wheel, A/C; about 3,989 built by 1969
- 1968: Buick 350 Dauntless V8 (to 1971); two-door Wagoneer dropped at year-end; solid axles and leaf springs only from 1969
- 1973: Quadra-Trac full-time 4WD introduced, three years after AMC bought Kaiser Jeep
- 1974: Two-door Cherokee launched (base and S); 401 V8 offered; front discs standard on the Wagoneer
- 1976: Boxed frame rails and stronger crossmembers; wide-track Cherokee Chief arrives
- 1977: Four-door Cherokee added
- 1978: Wagoneer Limited arrives mid-year; last year of the 401
- 1979: 'Pig nose' grille, square headlights, aluminum bumpers; last year of the TH400 and the Borg-Warner Quadra-Trac
- 1980: TorqueFlite 727 automatic; NP219 'Quadra-Trac' and part-time NP208; Wagoneer output falls to 10,481 after the fuel crisis
- 1983: Selec-Trac standard on the Wagoneer; Pioneer package; last year of the SJ Cherokee. For 1984 the Wagoneer Limited becomes the Grand Wagoneer

### Capability
- Wheelbase: 108.7 in (2,761 mm)
- Length: 186.4 in (4,735 mm)
- Width: 74.8–78.7 in (1,900–1,999 mm) (wide-track Chief at the top of the range)
- Curb weight: 4,514 lb (2,048 kg) (Wikipedia infobox figure)
- Low range: 2.03:1 (Dana 20) · 2.57:1 (optional Quadra-Trac low-range unit)
- Fuel economy: EPA 18 city / 25 hwy (1983 Wagoneer, 258 six, automatic and Selec-Trac, per Wikipedia; V8s are far thirstier)
- Top speed: Over 100 mph (161 km/h) (401-powered Cherokee with 3.07:1 gearing, per Wikipedia)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 225/75R15 (1976–83 Wagoneer, per TireSize.com), 235/70R15 (alternative listed for the 1976 Wagoneer)
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5") from 1974 · 5x139.7 (5x5.5") on 1962–73 trucks
- Center Bore: 108 mm
- Lug Thread: 7/16" (Quadratec, 1974–91 full-size)
- Lug Torque: 55–65 lb-ft is Quadratec's typical range for 7/16" lugs [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]

### Buying checks
- Rust first: It's the same body as the Grand Wagoneer, and Hagerty's buyer's guide for that truck calls rust the biggest concern: floor pans under the front carpet, the area where the fuel tank meets the body, the frame and underbody, and the front fenders. Original front fenders are no longer made. Floor, rocker and lower-quarter repair panels are still sold.
- Find out which 4WD system it has: This matters for parts, fluids and how it drives. A one-lever floor shifter on a 1974–79 automatic is the Borg-Warner Quadra-Trac; a manual from those years has a Dana 20. The 1980–82 'Quadra-Trac' is really an NP219, and 1980–83 trucks may have a part-time NP208 or, from mid-1982, Selec-Trac with a dash switch.
- Listen in tight turns: The factory manual describes Quadra-Trac 'stick-slip': a low grunting or rasping noise when turning slowly or parking. It's usually the wrong fluid, mismatched tires or uneven pressures. A much louder noise when driving straight points to a stretched chain. Team Grand Wagoneer's chain kit is aimed at trucks with more than about 120,000 miles or skipped fluid changes.
- Check the Chief is a Chief: The real Chief from 1976 has wider axles and flared fenders and was only built as a two-door. On 1981–83 VINs, characters 6–7 read 16 or 17 for a two-door Cherokee and 18 for a four-door; 15 is a Wagoneer. Golden Eagles are Chiefs with a big hood decal, gold-painted steel wheels and denim seats, so look for more than a sticker.
- Drive it cold and hot: Hagerty's Grand Wagoneer specialist blames the Motorcraft carburetor for about 40% of owner headaches. Expect stumbling, hard hot starts and ignition faults on an untouched truck. NHTSA recalled 1975–76 trucks for ignition wiring connectors that could not carry enough current (78V-065).
- Work the tailgate window: The power rear glass has to come down before the tailgate opens. Recall 87V-178 covers 1970–83 Wagoneers and Cherokees whose key-operated window kept closing if the spring-loaded key failed to return. Test the dash switch, the key switch and the glass travel.
- Look at the brakes: Early Cherokees had four-wheel drums as standard, with front discs optional; Wagoneers got front discs as standard from 1974. Check what's fitted and how old the steel lines are. Pre-bent stainless kits exist for 1977-on trucks.
- Budget for scarce parts: Specialists such as Team Grand Wagoneer and BJ's Off Road stock most mechanical and body parts. But on the later Grand Wagoneer, Hagerty's specialist estimates about 20% of restoration parts still come from salvage yards. Two-door-specific trim and glass are harder to find than Wagoneer parts.

### Common repairs
#### Cure Quadra-Trac stick-slip and chain slap (1974–79)
Difficulty 2 / 5 (fluid) · 4 / 5 (chain) · time ≈ 1 hour (fluid) · a weekend (chain) · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: A pulsing grunt or rasp when turning slowly or parking, worst after the truck has sat for a week; or a slapping noise against the case, even at idle, which means a loose chain.
Fix: Set all four tires to the same pressure and make sure they match in size and type. Drain the Quadra-Trac and the low-range unit if fitted, and refill only with Quadra-Trac lubricant, never multigrade detergent oil. The factory manual then says to drive in circles both ways for about 15 minutes without hitting the steering stops. If it still slaps, split the case and fit a new chain and seals; Team Grand Wagoneer says to use about 3 quarts of its Quadra-Trac fluid after a rebuild.
Tools: Drain pan · fluid pump · sockets · for the chain: seal pullers, gasket scraper, case-half gasket and RTV per kit

#### Rebuild the carburetor or convert to throttle-body injection
Difficulty 2 / 5 (rebuild) · 3 / 5 (TBI) · time ≈ An afternoon (rebuild) · a weekend (TBI) · cost TBI conversion about $2,000 in parts plus up to $1,000 labor (Hagerty, Grand Wagoneer)
Symptoms: Stumbling or stalling cold or hot, hard hot starts, rich running, fuel smell.
Fix: Rule out vacuum leaks and ignition faults first. Rebuild with the kit for your year and engine: the V8 two-barrel kit is listed for 1981–91 and the 4.2 kit for 1982–86. Fit a new base gasket and insulator, set the float and choke pull-off to the kit spec, and check timing with a light. Throttle-body injection replaces the carburetor and needs its own pump, return line and wiring; it's the most common long-term fix.
Tools: Carb kit with specs · carb cleaner · vacuum gauge · timing light · for TBI: fuel-line and wiring tools

#### Fix the power tailgate window
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–4 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: The rear glass won't drop, so the tailgate can't be opened, or the glass binds and stalls. On 1970–83 trucks the key switch could stick on (recall 87V-178).
Fix: Test the dash switch and the key switch in the tailgate first. If the motor hums but nothing moves, lower the glass by hand, open the inner panel and inspect the lifter cushions, lifter bar and glass channels. Replace worn cushions and channels, lube the tracks, and fit a new switch kit if the old one is intermittent. Ask a dealer whether the recall work was ever done.
Tools: Trim tools · test light or multimeter · sockets · silicone or lithium lube

#### Patch floors, rockers and lower quarters
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ Several weekends · cost Parts plus bodywork labor
Symptoms: Wet or crunchy carpet, holes under the mats, soft rockers, bubbling paint low on the quarters and around the fuel tank.
Fix: Pull the seats and carpet and wire-brush everything to see how far it goes. Cut back to clean metal and weld in floor sections, rockers and lower-quarter patches, then seam-seal, prime and undercoat. Panels sold for the four-door Wagoneer won't all fit a two-door Cherokee, so test-fit before cutting.
Tools: MIG welder · cut-off wheel · spot-weld drill · clamps · weld-through primer · seam sealer

#### Selec-Trac or NP208 won't engage 4WD (1980–83)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: The 2WD/4WD switch does nothing, the 4WD light stays on or off, or the truck stays in one mode.
Fix: Selec-Trac shifts between 2WD and 4WD with engine vacuum. Trace the hoses from the engine to the reservoir, dash switch and transfer case, and test each with a hand vacuum pump. Replace cracked hoses, the reservoir if it leaks, and the transfer-case switch if the indicator is wrong. Fix leaking yoke seals and refill with fresh fluid: Team Grand Wagoneer says 3 quarts for an NP208, 228 or 229.
Tools: Hand vacuum pump · vacuum hose · multimeter · sockets · fluid pump

#### Tighten up sloppy steering
Difficulty 2 / 5 (rag joint) · 3 / 5 (box seals) · time ≈ 1–2 hours (rag joint) · a day (box reseal) · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Free play at the wheel, a clunk when you turn, power-steering fluid weeping from the box.
Fix: Have a helper rock the wheel while you watch the rag joint, the steering-box input and the linkage. A torn rag joint shows movement between the column and the box; replace it, or fit a complete coupler. If the box leaks, reseal it with the seal kits or replace it. Check tie-rod ends and the drag link while you're there.
Tools: Sockets and wrenches · pitman-arm puller · seal picks · power-steering fluid

#### Service the front hubs, bearings and ball joints (Dana 44)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Wheel play when you rock the tire top to bottom, a growl that changes with speed, uneven tire wear, grease flung on the inside of the wheel.
Fix: Jack the axle, rock each wheel at 12 and 6 o'clock and at 3 and 9. Pull the hub, clean and inspect the bearings and races, repack or replace them with new seals, and set the preload to the manual. If the play is in the knuckle, press out the upper and lower ball joints and fit a new set. Grease the axle U-joints before you reassemble.
Tools: Floor jack and stands · spindle-nut socket · bearing packer · ball-joint press · torque wrench

#### Replace the rear main seal (258 or V8)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A long day · cost $500–1,000 at a shop (Hagerty, 360 V8)
Symptoms: Oil dripping where the engine meets the transmission, with nothing wet above it.
Fix: Rule out the valve covers, intake and oil-pressure sender first, because oil runs back to the bellhousing. Drain the oil and drop the pan; on a full-size Jeep the front axle and crossmember make this the hard part. Remove the rear main cap, roll out both seal halves, fit the new seal, refit the cap to factory torque, and refit the pan with a new gasket.
Tools: Floor jack and stands · engine support · torque wrench · seal pick · RTV per seal instructions · factory manual for torque specs [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]

### Baseline service
Every SJ in this range is over 40 years old, so treat every fluid, hose and ignition part as original unless there are receipts. The drivetrain changed so often that the first job is identifying it: Quadra-Trac, Dana 20, NP208, NP219 and NP229 each need different fluid. We couldn't find a sourced factory capacity table for these years, so engine and axle capacities are marked for confirmation.
- Engine oil & filter: AMC 258 I6 or 360/401 V8 · grade and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now; then per your owner's manual (Filters are listed by engine and year: 4.2 L 1974–80 and 1981–86, V8 1974–83.)
- Air & fuel filters: Air-cleaner element · inline fuel filter · Baseline now; inspect every oil change (A clogged element makes the carburetor run rich. Replace the air-cleaner-to-carb gasket at the same time.)
- Spark plugs, wires, cap & rotor: Gap per underhood label [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now (A full tune-up is the cheapest drivability fix before you blame the carburetor.)
- Coolant, thermostat & hoses: Coolant type and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush and refill now (Replace the thermostat, gasket and radiator hoses together on a truck with no records.)
- Automatic transmission (TH400 or 727): ATF · pan drop with new filter [CONFIRM CAPACITY IN MANUAL] · Baseline now (1974–79 automatics are GM TH400s; from 1980 it's the TorqueFlite 727. The filter kit listed fits the 727.)
- Quadra-Trac transfer case (1974–79): Quadra-Trac lubricant only · no multigrade detergent oil · Baseline now (The factory manual blames the wrong fluid for most stick-slip noise. Drain the low-range unit too if fitted, then drive slow circles both ways for 15 minutes.)
- Transfer case (NP208 / NP219 / NP229, 1980–83): ATF-type fluid (Team Grand Wagoneer) · 3 qt NP208/228/229, 2 qt NP219 · Team Grand Wagoneer: every 50,000 mi in severe use, 100,000 mi normal (Check the yoke seals and, on Selec-Trac, the vacuum hoses while you're there.)
- Front & rear differentials: 75W-90 gear oil · add limited-slip additive for a Trac-Lok · capacities [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now (Dana 44 front; Dana 44 or AMC 20 rear depending on year. Team Grand Wagoneer's Dana 44 kit is 2 quarts of 75W-90 plus additive.)
- Front wheel bearings: Clean, inspect and repack; new seals · Baseline now (Bearing preload is set by hand on these hubs, so follow the manual.)
- U-joints & driveshafts: Grease every zerk; check for play · Every oil change (Check the front axle U-joints at full lock and the slip yokes for clunks.)
- Power steering: Power-steering fluid; flush the old fluid · Baseline now (Look at the rag joint and the box seals while the system is open.)
- Brake fluid, pads & lines: Fluid type per the master-cylinder cap [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush now; then every 2 years (Confirm whether an early Cherokee has front discs or drums before ordering pads.)
- Accessory belts: V-belts on the V8; serpentine on the 1981–86 4.2 · Baseline now (Replace the V8's alternator/AC belts as a matched pair.)
- Leaf springs, bushings & shocks: Stock-height packs front and rear · Inspect now (Sagging springs and dead shocks make the truck wallow; replace bushings while the springs are out.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: We couldn't find a forum consensus we trust for unlifted SJs, so we won't guess. Tire databases list 225/75R15 for 1976–83 Wagoneers (235/70R15 is also listed for 1976). The Cherokee Chief's wider axles and bigger fender flares were added so it could run larger tires. For anything bigger, test-fit at full lock and with the suspension compressed, or add a modest leaf-spring lift. Running bigger tires on yours? Tell us through Show Us Your Rig.

Q: What's the difference between a Wagoneer, a Cherokee and a Grand Wagoneer?
A: They're all SJs on the same 108.7 in wheelbase. The Wagoneer is the four-door wagon from 1963. The Cherokee is the 1974–83 version with two wide-pillar doors (a four-door Cherokee was added in 1977). From 1984 the Wagoneer Limited became the Grand Wagoneer, while 'Cherokee' moved to the compact XJ.

Q: What makes a Cherokee Chief special?
A: The Chief package arrived in 1976 with wider axles and larger fenders so the truck could run bigger tires. It was only offered on two-doors. The 1978–79 Golden Eagle was a Chief with denim upholstery, gold-painted steel wheels and a large gold eagle on the hood.

Q: Which 4WD system do I have?
A: It depends on the year and gearbox. 1974–79 manuals have a gear-driven Dana 20 (2.03:1 low). 1973–79 automatics have the Borg-Warner Quadra-Trac, a chain-drive full-time case with a vacuum-locked center differential. For 1980–82 the 'Quadra-Trac' name went on an NP219. Part-time NP208s appear from 1980, and Selec-Trac (NP229) arrived in mid-1982 and became standard on the 1983 Wagoneer.

Q: Why does my Quadra-Trac groan in parking lots?
A: The factory manual calls it stick-slip: the cone brakes in the center differential stick and release when you turn slowly. It's usually the wrong lubricant, mismatched tires or uneven tire pressures. Drain and refill with Quadra-Trac lubricant and drive in slow circles for about 15 minutes. A loud noise in a straight line is a different problem, usually a stretched chain.

Q: Which engine should I look for?
A: The 360 V8 is the common one and parts are easy. The 401 was offered from 1974 to 1978, made 215 net hp and had a forged crank and rods, and Wikipedia says the SJs still hold the record for the largest engine Jeep ever offered. The 258 six is the economy choice and returned for 1981–83 after the fuel crisis.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: Not much from a V8. Wikipedia cites a combined 11 mpg for the later 5.9 Grand Wagoneer. The best case is the 1983 Wagoneer with the six, an automatic and Selec-Trac, which Wikipedia says was rated at 18 mpg city and 25 highway by the EPA.

Q: Is it really the first SUV?
A: It's the first vehicle sold under that name. Wikipedia, citing Jim Allen, says 'Sport Utility Vehicle' appears for the first time in the 1974 Cherokee brochure. The 1966 Super Wagoneer is widely called the first luxury SUV.

Q: Can I still get parts?
A: Mostly. Many Grand Wagoneer parts listed for 1974–91 fit these trucks, and specialists such as Team Grand Wagoneer and BJ's Off Road stock Quadra-Trac chains and seals, floor pans, tailgate parts and steering parts. Original front fenders and some two-door trim are hard to find.

Q: What are they worth?
A: Bring a Trailer sold 31 SJ Wagoneers and Cherokees between October 2025 and October 2026, with a median of about $19,000. Projects went for a few thousand dollars. A 29,000-mile 1983 Wagoneer Limited made $51,000, an original 1975 Cherokee S $80,000, and a Viper-powered 1979 Cherokee Chief restomod $315,000. Hagerty puts a good-condition 1976 Cherokee Chief at about $14,100.

Q: Are there open recalls I should know about?
A: The big one is NHTSA 87V-178: on 1970–83 Wagoneers and Cherokees the key-operated tailgate window could keep closing if the key didn't spring back to off. NHTSA also lists ignition-connector (1975–76) and rear-wheel-bearing (1979–80) campaigns. Ask a Jeep dealer to check the VIN.

## Jeep Grand Wagoneer (SJ) (1984–1991)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/grand-wagoneer/
Codes: SJ, Grand Wagoneer

Verdict: A 1962 design in a vinyl-wood cardigan, still drinking carbureted 360 V8 fuel when Chrysler finally switched off the Toledo line in 1991. It is slow, thirsty and gloriously out of date, and it invented the idea that a truck could be the nicest car in the driveway. Buy the rust you can see, budget for the rust you can't.

Jeep introduced the Wagoneer in November 1962 for the 1963 model year, and the same SJ body was still in production 29 model years later. By 1991 it was the longest-running domestically produced vehicle on one platform. For its final eight years it was called Grand Wagoneer: a body-on-frame, solid-axle, carbureted-V8 station wagon with simulated woodgrain on its flanks and leather inside. It was sold as the gold standard of the SUV market at a time when nobody had yet called it an SUV.

### THE KAISER ORIGINAL (1963–1969)
Industrial designer Brooks Stevens shaped the Wagoneer for Kaiser-owned Willys, which renamed itself Kaiser Jeep Corporation shortly after launch. It shared its chassis with the Gladiator pickup and was more car-like than any other 4x4 on sale. It offered an overhead-cam 'Tornado' six of 140 hp, independent front suspension, power steering, an automatic gearbox and optional air conditioning. Development took three years and cost about $20 million. When it arrived it had no direct rival: the two-door Range Rover was still eight years away.
The independent front end did not catch on and was dropped from four-wheel-drive models in 1965. An AMC 327 V8 arrived the same year. The 1966 Super Wagoneer added a 270 hp four-barrel V8, a tilt wheel, a console-shifted TH400 and a power tailgate window. Only about 3,989 were built, and Wikipedia calls it the precursor of today's luxury SUVs. From 1968 to 1971 a Buick 350 'Dauntless' V8 did the work.

### AMC TURNS IT INTO A LIMOUSINE
AMC bought Kaiser Jeep in 1970 and refined the truck rather than replacing it. The AMC 360 and 401 V8s arrived after 1971. In 1973 came Quadra-Trac, a full-time 4WD system that saved buyers from locking hubs and a stiff transfer-case lever, and woodgrain side trim appeared from 1971. The 1978 Wagoneer Limited added leather, power seats, cruise control and forged aluminum wheels. At $10,500 it was priced against Cadillacs and Lincolns, and AMC built 28,871 Wagoneers that year.
When the unibody Cherokee XJ arrived for 1984, AMC planned for the compact XJ Wagoneer to replace the big wagon. Demand kept the old truck alive. The Limited became the Grand Wagoneer, which freed the 'Wagoneer Limited' name for the XJ. A cheaper, wood-free Wagoneer Custom lasted only through 1984, and from 1985 there was a single fully loaded version. The 1986 update brought a new grille and hood ornament, a redesigned dash with square gauges, new seats and a Trac-Lok limited-slip for the Selec-Trac driveline.

### CHRYSLER LEAVES IT ALONE
Chrysler agreed to buy AMC on March 9, 1987, and largely left the Grand Wagoneer alone. It still made $5,000 to $6,000 per truck, and Chrysler kept building it with the carbureted AMC 360. The 360 became one of the last carbureted engines in an American-built vehicle. The 1989–91 trucks are considered the best: they got a better A/C compressor to replace the earlier leak-prone unit, a rear wiper, an overhead console with compass and thermometer, keyless entry, electrocoat primer and base-clear paint.
Then fuel prices rose with the 1990 oil shock. Sales fell from more than 10,000 in 1989 to 6,449 in 1990, and only 4,253 were built for 1991. The platform would also have needed major re-engineering for upcoming federal light-truck safety rules. Chrysler announced the end on February 27, 1991, offered a gold 'Final Edition' dash badge, and built the last Grand Wagoneer in Toledo on June 21, 1991. The name came back for one year on the 1993 ZJ Grand Cherokee and then returned in 2021 on the WS-platform Wagoneer and Grand Wagoneer.

### THE AFTERLIFE: RESTOMODS AND RISING PRICES
Specialist shops were refurbishing Grand Wagoneers before Chrysler built the last one. Wagonmaster, founded by Leon Miller in Kerrville, Texas, keeps the original look but replaces the carburetor with throttle-body fuel injection. Classic Gentleman, G.K. Kerr's shop in Bemus Point, New York, looks for low-mileage trucks and offers full rebuilds and color changes. In 2019 DrivingLine reported $40,000 to $80,000 for trucks from either shop. Kerr told Hagerty he won't buy trucks from road-salt states.
Hagerty said its Grand Wagoneer values rose an average of 2–6% with each bi-monthly update, with a 1991 in #2 condition at $36,900 and a #1 at $62,200 when that piece ran. By 2021, Wikipedia notes, Hagerty listed the 1984–91 trucks among the most sought-after vintage cars of the COVID-19 pandemic. The 1984–91 Grand Wagoneer belongs to the same era as the FJ60 Land Cruiser and the four-door Range Rover Classic. Of the three, it is the one most likely to be restored with an EFI V8 and sold as a lifestyle object.

### Data plate
- Platform: SJ (shared with J-Series pickups)
- Production: 1984–June 21, 1991 as Grand Wagoneer (SJ since 1963)
- Plant: Toledo, Ohio
- Engine: AMC 360 (5.9 L) V8, 2-bbl Motorcraft · 4.2 L I6 offered 1984–86
- Transmission: Chrysler A727 three-speed automatic
- Transfer Case: Selec-Trac NP228 / NP229 (2.6:1 low), NP208 on some
- Axles: Dana 44 front (full-floating) · AMC or Dana 44 rear
- Wheelbase: 108.7 in
- Length: 186.4 in
- Fuel Tank: 20.3 US gal with skid plate
- Towing: 5,000 lb (Class III Package B, 1989)
- Built: 101,637 Grand Wagoneers (Hagerty) · 4,253 in 1991

### Engineering
The Grand Wagoneer is a 1963 design updated over the years. It has a separate ladder frame (boxed and strengthened from 1976), leaf springs and solid axles at both ends, a carbureted AMC 360 V8, a Chrysler TorqueFlite 727 three-speed automatic and a chain-drive New Process transfer case. Jeep's 1989 spec sheet lists a 108.7 in wheelbase, 186.4 in length, 10.1 in minimum running clearance, a 20.3-gallon tank behind a skid plate, and P235/75R15 tires on 15x7 six-lug wheels.
- Chassis: SJ body-on-frame, 108.7 in wheelbase (Shared with the J-Series pickups. Boxed side rails and stronger crossmembers from 1976.)
- Engine: AMC 360 (5.9 L) V8, 2-bbl Motorcraft 2150 (8.25:1 compression. Ratings vary by source: Hagerty quotes 140 hp / 280 lb-ft; Offroaders.com and Wikipedia's AMC V8 table give 144 hp / 280 lb-ft for the 1991 two-barrel. Hagerty says a 4.2 L six was the standard engine for 1984–86.)
- Transmission: Chrysler TorqueFlite A727 three-speed auto (Column shift. Hagerty's specialist puts the worst-case rebuild at about $2,000.)
- 4Wd System: Selec-Trac NP228 / NP229 (Vacuum-shifted 2WD/4WD on the fly, 2.6:1 low range (1989 spec). NP229 adds a viscous coupling; some 1984–88 trucks used the part-time NP208.)
- Axles: Dana 44 front · AMC or Dana 44 rear (1989 spec: full-floating Dana 44 front, AMC semi-floating rear, both 2.73:1. Trac-Lok limited slip from 1986. Check the axle tag before ordering parts.)
- Brakes & Steering: Front disc / rear drum · variable-ratio power steering (Recirculating ball, 16:1 to 13:1, 37.7 ft turning circle.)

### Versions
- 1963–1965 · Wagoneer (Kaiser) · Tornado 230 OHC I6 · 140 hp · IFS optional on 4WD (dropped 1965). Two- and four-door wagons and a panel delivery.
- 1965–1968 · Wagoneer / Super Wagoneer · AMC 327 V8 · AMC 232 I6 · 250 hp (270 hp Super) · Super Wagoneer 1966–69, about 3,989 built.
- 1968–1971 · Wagoneer · Buick 350 Dauntless V8 · 230 hp / 350 lb-ft · Last non-AMC engine. Solid axles and leaf springs only from 1969.
- 1972–1983 · Wagoneer (AMC) · AMC 360 / 401 V8 · 258 I6 · Varies by year · Quadra-Trac from 1973, Limited trim from 1978, Selec-Trac standard for 1983.
- 1984–1986 · Grand Wagoneer · AMC 360 V8 (4.2 I6 offered) · 140–144 hp (see engineering) · Renamed from Limited. 1986 refresh: grille, dash, Trac-Lok.
- 1987–1991 · Grand Wagoneer (Chrysler) · AMC 360 V8, 2-bbl · Hagerty: 140 hp / 280 lb-ft · Marine-teak woodgrain from 1987. 1989–91 best of the breed; 1991 Final Edition badge.
- 1993 · Grand Wagoneer (ZJ) · 5.2 L Magnum V8 · 220 hp · A one-year woodgrain Grand Cherokee, 6,378 built. A different truck entirely.

### Year-by-year
- 1984: The SJ Wagoneer Limited becomes the Grand Wagoneer as the compact XJ takes the Wagoneer name; Brougham dropped; a no-woodgrain Wagoneer Custom lasts only this year. 258 six standard and 360 V8 optional, per Hagerty
- 1985: Handling package: revised front anti-roll bar, gas shocks and lower-friction rear springs
- 1986: New four-part grille and stand-up hood ornament; fully revamped interior with square gauges and improved climate control; Selec-Trac gains a Trac-Lok limited-slip; factory power sunroof option
- 1987: 25th anniversary: the 360 V8 becomes the only engine; 'marine teak' woodgrain, Michelin self-sealing P235/75R15s. Chrysler agrees to buy AMC in March
- 1988: First full Chrysler year; carbureted 360 retained; 14,117 built
- 1989: Start of the 'best of the breed' run: more reliable A/C compressor, rear wiper/washer, minivan-sourced overhead console with compass and thermometer, keyless entry, electrocoat primer and base/clear paint, gunmetal wheel inlays [buy]
- 1991: Final year of the 1989–91 'best of the breed' run; buyers after the February 27 discontinuation announcement could add a gold 'Final Edition' dash badge, and Hagerty says low-mileage examples are desirable and expensive. Last truck built June 21, 1991 [buy]

### Capability
- Towing: 5,000 lb (2,270 kg) (Trailer Package B (Class III), 750 lb tongue; Package A is rated 3,500 lb (1989 spec))
- GVWR: 6,200 lb (2,812 kg)
- Fuel tank: 20.3 US gal (77 L) (with skid plate)
- Ground clearance: 10.1 in (257 mm) (minimum running clearance)
- Curb weight: 4,514 lb (2,048 kg)
- Fuel economy: About 11 mpg combined (5.9 L V8)
- Drivetrain: 360 V8, 727 three-speed automatic, Selec-Trac NP229 with 2.6:1 low range, Dana 44 front, 2.73:1 axles (1989 spec)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: P235/75R15 (Michelin Tru Seal self-sealing radial standard from 1987)
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Center Bore: 108 mm

### Buying checks
- Rust first, everything else second: Hagerty's buyer's guide calls rust the biggest concern. Lift the front carpet to see the floor pans, then check where the fuel tank meets the body, the underbody and frame, and the front fenders near the parking lamps. New fenders are no longer available. YourMechanic adds the frame near the fuel-tank skid plate and the rockers, and says the driver's floor is the most common hole.
- Bubbles under the woodgrain: The wood is vinyl. Bubbles under it usually mean rust working from the inside. Replacement Cherry Oak and Marine Teak (1987–91) vinyl kits exist, but the metal underneath has to be fixed first.
- Drive it cold and hot: Kerr estimates the Motorcraft carburetor causes about 40% of owner headaches. Stumbling or stalling cold or hot is common. Also listen for ignition faults and watch the oil-pressure gauge. A rear main seal leak costs $500–1,000 to fix.
- Test 4WD on the move: Selec-Trac should engage on the fly. Check that 4WD engages and disengages properly and shift through every range; low range can grind. Look for leaking transfer-case seals.
- Work every switch: Window flex tracks snap, and window and power-lock switches fail often. The rear-window switch frequently dies, and because the glass must come down to reach the inside tailgate handle, a dead switch can lock you out of the tailgate.
- Check the A/C and the cabin: A/C repairs are expensive. The 1989–91 trucks got a better compressor than the earlier leak-prone one. Sagging headliners and water-damaged door panels are common.
- Know the year: Wikipedia points to 1989–91 for better rustproofing, paint and equipment, and a 1991 Final Edition commands a premium. Hagerty says tan or sand interiors and blue, green or white paint sell best.
- Ask where it lived: Kerr won't buy trucks from road-salt states and estimates about 20% of needed parts have to come from salvage yards. A dry-state truck with a known history is worth paying for.

### Common repairs
#### Rebuild the Motorcraft 2150 or convert to throttle-body injection
Difficulty 2 / 5 (rebuild) · 3 / 5 (TBI) · time ≈ An afternoon (rebuild) · A weekend (TBI) · cost TBI conversion about $2,000 in parts plus up to $1,000 labor (Hagerty)
Symptoms: Hesitation, stumbling or stalling cold or hot, hard hot starts, fuel smell, poor idle. Hagerty's specialist blames the carburetor for about 40% of owner headaches.
Fix: Rule out vacuum leaks and ignition faults first: check every vacuum line and the distributor pickup and module. To rebuild, remove the carb, strip it on a clean bench, replace the base gasket, power valve and internal gaskets from a 2150 kit, set the float and choke pull-off to the kit's specs, and refit on a new base gasket and insulator. Converting to TBI means a throttle body with its own fuel pump, return line, sensors and harness. Most owners who keep the truck do it eventually, and it's the core of the Wagonmaster recipe.
Tools: Carb rebuild kit with specs · gasket scraper · carb cleaner · vacuum gauge · timing light · for TBI: fuel-line tools, wiring tools, laptop or handheld tuner per kit

#### Replace the rear main seal (AMC 360)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A long day · cost $500–1,000 at a shop (Hagerty)
Symptoms: Oil dripping from where the engine meets the transmission, with no obvious leak above it. Hagerty lists rear main leaks as a common 360 fault.
Fix: Rule out the valve covers, intake and oil-pressure sender first, because oil runs downhill to the bellhousing. Then drain the oil, support the engine, and drop the oil pan; on a full-size Jeep, front axle and crossmember clearance make this the hard part. Remove the rear main cap, pull both seal halves, clean the grooves, install the new seal, refit the cap to the factory torque spec, and refit the pan with a new gasket. Fill and check for leaks after a heat cycle.
Tools: Floor jack and stands · engine support · torque wrench · seal pick · RTV per seal instructions · factory service manual for torque specs [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]

#### Fix a dead power window (flex rack and motor)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours per door · cost Under $20 for a flex rack
Symptoms: You can hear the motor run, but the glass doesn't move or moves in jerks. Hagerty says window flex tracks snap often on these trucks.
Fix: Remove the door panel carefully, since water-damaged panels are common and the clips break. Peel back the vapor barrier and support the glass. Unbolt the motor and regulator assembly and inspect the plastic flex rack, which is the usual failure. Fit a new rack, lube the channel, fit new mounting grommets and screws, and check the motor's pigtail connector for corrosion before refitting the panel.
Tools: Door-panel clip tool · glass holder · screwdrivers and sockets · white lithium grease

#### Revive the tailgate window
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–4 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: The rear glass won't go down, so the interior tailgate handle can't be reached. YourMechanic says the tailgate window is 'notorious for failing'.
Fix: Test the dash switch and the key switch in the tailgate first; Hagerty says the rear switch often dies. If the motor hums but the glass doesn't move, open the tailgate inner panel (lower the glass by hand with the manual crank if you need to) and check the lifter cushions and glass channels for binding. Replace worn cushions and channels, lube the tracks, and fit a new switch if needed.
Tools: Trim tools · test light or multimeter · sockets · silicone or lithium lube

#### Patch floors, rockers and lower quarters
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ Several weekends · cost Parts plus bodywork labor
Symptoms: Wet or crunchy carpet, holes under the driver's floor mat, bubbling under the woodgrain, rotten rockers that can let exhaust into the cabin.
Fix: Pull the seats and carpet and wire-brush everything so you can see the full extent. Cut out rot back to clean metal, then trial-fit and weld in repair sections: front driver's and passenger's floor, rear sections, rockers, dog legs and lower quarters. Seam-seal and undercoat. On the outside, remove the woodgrain before welding and put down fresh vinyl afterward.
Tools: MIG welder · cut-off wheel · spot-weld drill · clamps · weld-through primer · seam sealer

#### Drop the fuel tank and replace the skid plate and straps
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Rust where the tank meets the body, a sagging or perforated skid plate, fuel smell, a sending unit that reads wrong. Both Hagerty and YourMechanic name this area.
Fix: Run the tank nearly empty and disconnect the battery. Support the skid plate and tank with a jack, remove the skid-plate bolts and straps, disconnect the filler and vent hoses and the sender wiring, and lower the assembly. Inspect the frame and body above it. Treat the rust, then refit with a new skid plate (or the master kit), insulator mat, straps and fresh hardware.
Tools: Transmission jack or floor jack with board · penetrating oil · fuel-line clamps · sockets

#### Selec-Trac won't engage: vacuum system and transfer-case service
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: The dash 2WD/4WD control does nothing, the truck stays in one mode, or 4WD drops out. Hagerty says to check that 4WD engages on the fly; seals leak with age.
Fix: Selec-Trac uses vacuum to shift between 2WD and 4WD. Check the vacuum lines from the engine to the reservoir, the dash switch and the transfer-case actuator for cracks or disconnected hoses, and test with a hand vacuum pump. On 1984–86 trucks, the transfer-case vacuum switch is a known replacement part. Fix any seal leaks at the yokes, then drain and refill the transfer case (Team Grand Wagoneer recommends a synthetic ATF-type fluid).
Tools: Hand vacuum pump · vacuum hose · sockets · drain pan · fluid pump

### Baseline service
A Grand Wagoneer is at least 35 years old. Treat every fluid, rubber part and ignition part as original unless there are receipts. Capacities below are marked for confirmation because we couldn't find a sourced factory fill table. The parts catalogs split by year: 1984–86 versus 1987–91 (filters, ignition modules), and York versus Sanden A/C compressors (1978–88 versus 1989–91).
- Engine oil & filter: AMC 360 V8 · AMSOIL's 1989 lookup lists 5 qt with filter and 10W-30 or 10W-40 for most climates [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now; then per your owner's manual (The filter changes by year: one for 1984–86, another for 1987–90, and a third for 1991. Order by model year.)
- Air filter & fuel filter: Stock air-cleaner element · inline fuel filter · Baseline now; inspect every oil change (A dirty filter makes the 2150 carb run rich. Replace the air-cleaner-to-carb gasket at the same time.)
- Spark plugs, wires, cap & rotor: 8 plugs · gap per underhood label [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now (Hagerty flags Motorcraft ignition problems. A fresh tune-up is the cheapest drivability fix before you blame the carburetor.)
- Ignition module (carry a spare): Early 1978–1987 / late 1988–1991 · Carry one (Electronic ignition modules are split by year; a spare in the glovebox is cheap insurance on a 30-plus-year-old system.)
- Coolant, thermostat, hoses & cap: AMSOIL's 1989 lookup lists 13.7 qt · coolant type [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush and refill now (Replace the thermostat, gasket, radiator hoses and cap together, and check the thermal fan clutch while the system is open.)
- Automatic transmission (A727) fluid & filter: ATF · drain pan, new filter and gasket · AMSOIL's 1989 lookup lists about 4 qt for a pan drop and 8.6 qt total [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Every 30,000 mi or 3 years with conventional fluid (Team Grand Wagoneer's filter-kit listing) (This is a pan drop, not a flush. Team Grand Wagoneer recommends fully synthetic ATF.)
- Transfer case (NP228 / NP229 / NP208): ATF-type fluid (per Team Grand Wagoneer) · AMSOIL's 1989 lookup lists 5.9 pints for the NP208/NP229 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now; Team Grand Wagoneer suggests every 50,000 mi in severe use, 100,000 mi in normal use (with its synthetic fluid) (While you're under there, check the yoke seals and the Selec-Trac vacuum lines.)
- Front & rear differentials: 75W-90 gear oil · limited-slip additive or LSD-rated oil for Trac-Lok axles · AMSOIL's 1989 lookup lists 2.7 pints front and 3 pints rear [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now (The front is a Dana 44; the rear is an AMC or Dana 44 depending on year. Read the tag and use LSD-compatible oil if the truck has Trac-Lok (standard with Selec-Trac from 1986).)
- U-joints & driveshafts: Grease every zerk; inspect for play · Every oil change (Check the front axle U-joints at full lock and the driveshaft joints and slip yoke for clunks.)
- Front ball joints (Dana 44): Check for vertical and horizontal play · Inspect now (Worn joints show up as wander and uneven tire wear. Replace upper and lower together.)
- Power steering fluid: Power-steering fluid · flush the old fluid · Baseline now (Team Grand Wagoneer notes most owners never flush it. While you're there, check the steering box rag joint.)
- Brake fluid, pads & lines: Brake fluid per the master-cylinder cap [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush now; then every 2 years (Old steel lines on a salt-state truck deserve a hard look. A complete pre-bent stainless kit is available.)
- Accessory belts: Alternator/AC pair and power-steering belt (V8-360) · Baseline now (The 360 uses V-belts. Replace both alternator/AC belts as a matched pair.)
- Leaf springs & shocks: Stock-height leaf springs front and rear · Inspect now (Sagging springs and dead shocks make the truck wallow. Stock-height sets and full nitrogen shock sets are available.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: We couldn't find a forum consensus we trust for the SJ, so we won't guess. The factory size is P235/75R15 on 15x7 six-lug alloys (1989 spec). Anything larger should be test-fitted at full lock and with the suspension compressed. Team Grand Wagoneer sells a 3-inch lift kit with springs and shocks for owners who want more. Running bigger tires on yours? Tell us through Show Us Your Rig.

Q: How much power does the 360 V8 make?
A: It depends on the source. Hagerty quotes 140 hp and 280 lb-ft, and Offroaders.com and Wikipedia's AMC V8 table both give 144 hp (280 lb-ft) for the 1991 two-barrel 360. Either way, the torque is what moves it. The 360 is a tall-deck AMC engine. Chrysler kept building it until 1991, changing only the casting from '360' to '5.9L'.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: Not much. Wikipedia cites a combined 11 mpg, and Hagerty says single digits in town and about a dozen on the highway with the V8. Fuel prices after the 1990 oil shock helped kill the truck. TBI conversions are said to help, but don't expect miracles from a carbureted-era V8 in a 4,000-plus-pound wagon.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: Jeep's 1989 spec lists 5,000 lb maximum trailer weight (750 lb tongue) with the Class III Package B, and 3,500 lb (350 lb tongue) with the Class I and II Package A.

Q: Is it full-time 4WD?
A: Most are Selec-Trac: an NP228 or NP229 (the 229 adds a viscous coupling) with a dash control that shifts between 2WD and 4WD on the move using vacuum. Offroaders.com says some 1984–88 Grand Wagoneers used the part-time NP208 instead. Going between 4-High and 4-Low takes neutral and a crawl of under 5 mph.

Q: Which years should I buy?
A: 1989–91, if you can. Those years got better rust-proofing (electrocoat primer), base-clear paint, an improved A/C compressor, an overhead console, keyless entry and a rear wiper. The 1991 Final Edition carries a premium. Hagerty's specialist adds that low mileage, under about 100,000, is the safest buy.

Q: Carburetor or fuel injection?
A: Every Grand Wagoneer left the factory with a carburetor, a two-barrel Motorcraft on the 360. Throttle-body injection kits are the most common upgrade. Hagerty puts the conversion at about $2,000 in parts and up to $1,000 in labor, and Wagonmaster builds its trucks around a Howell TBI system.

Q: What are they worth?
A: Values rose for years. In one report, Hagerty listed a 1991 at $36,900 in #2 condition and $62,200 in #1, and said a nice #3 driver shouldn't cost much more than $20,000. Restomods from Wagonmaster or Classic Gentleman were $40,000–80,000 in 2019. These figures are dated, so check current Hagerty valuations and recent BaT results.

Q: Is this the same as the Wagoneer Limited (XJ)?
A: No. From 1984 to 1990 Jeep also sold a compact, unibody Wagoneer based on the Cherokee XJ, with woodgrain decals. The Grand Wagoneer is the full-size, body-on-frame SJ.

Q: Can I still get parts?
A: Mostly. Specialists such as Team Grand Wagoneer and BJ's Off Road stock everything from floor pans to woodgrain vinyl. But Hagerty's specialist estimates about 20% of the parts a restoration needs come from salvage yards, and front fenders are no longer available.

Q: Can I replace the woodgrain?
A: Yes. It's vinyl, not wood. The 1987–91 trucks use 'marine teak' and earlier trucks the cherry-oak style, and replacement kits are sold for both. Fix any rust under the old vinyl first, because bubbles usually mean the metal is rotting.
