## Jeep Cherokee XJ (1984–2001)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/cherokee-xj/
Codes: XJ

Verdict: A small box designed by AMC with help from Renault, given one of the best straight-sixes ever bolted into a 4x4 and two solid axles, then sold to suburbia for 18 years. Now it's the budget wheeler everyone recommends. Check the rockers, the floors, the head casting on 2000–01 trucks, and every drop of coolant.

The 1984 Cherokee XJ was Jeep's first all-new design since the 1963 Wagoneer, and the first American off-roader with a unibody, which AMC called 'Uniframe'. It was 1,200 lb lighter, 31 in shorter, 6 in narrower and 4 in lower than the full-size SJ Cherokee it replaced, yet kept 90% of the interior space. It also had better articulation, ground clearance and approach, departure and breakover angles. AMC sold it as a 'Sportwagon'. About 3 million were built through 2001, and it is still the default answer to 'what's a cheap, capable 4x4?'

### AMC, RENAULT AND A $250 MILLION BET
Work began in the late 1970s, when AMC needed something smaller than the SJ and Renault had just bought a 22% stake. Renault pushed for less size and weight and better economy. Styling came from AMC's team under design vice-president Dick Teague. Engineering VP Roy Lunn designed the 'Quadra-Link' coil-sprung front suspension, which locates a solid axle with four control arms and a track bar. Renault's François Castaing planned a light drivetrain around a much smaller engine than 4x4s usually carried. AMC spent $250 million and offered four doors as well as two, which GM's new S-10 Blazer didn't.
Early engines were weak: AMC's 2.5-liter four, a GM 2.8 V6 and a Renault 2.1 turbodiesel. Everything changed for 1987, when AMC introduced its 4.0-liter straight-six with Renix multipoint injection, rated at 173 hp and 220 lb-ft. Wikipedia calls it one of the best 4x4 and off-road engines. It brought the Aisin AW4 four-speed automatic and the NP231 Command-Trac and NP242 Selec-Trac transfer cases. The 1991 'High Output' version made 190 hp with Chrysler's fuel injection and became the engine every XJ shopper looks for.

### CHRYSLER KEEPS THE BOX
Chrysler inherited the XJ when it bought AMC in 1987. The plan was to replace it with the bigger ZJ Grand Cherokee, but the XJ sold too well to kill, so both were built from 1993. The 1997 facelift brought a steel liftgate, a new dash with dual airbags, and a stiffer unibody for less noise and vibration. The 2000–01 trucks got coil-on-plug ignition and 193 hp, and also a cylinder head casting, '0331', that is known to crack between cylinders 3 and 4.
Underneath, XJs differ by year and option. The front axle is always a Dana 30: high-pinion until 1999, low-pinion for 2000–01. At the rear you'll find a Dana 35, a Chrysler 8.25 or, on some 1987–91 tow-package trucks, a Dana 44. The Up Country package added an inch of lift and, per Wikipedia, deleted the rear anti-roll bar. The XJ also spawned the Comanche MJ pickup (1986–92) and a woodgrain Wagoneer Limited that shared its name with the full-size Grand Wagoneer.

### WHY THE CULT EXISTS
Production in Toledo ended in June 2001, and the Liberty took over. Its reputation has grown since. Automobile's Robert Cumberford named it one of the 20 greatest cars of all time and called it 'possibly the best SUV shape of all time'. Kiplinger listed it among 'cars that refuse to die', and NAXJA members routinely report 250,000–300,000 miles on factory drivetrains.
The appeal on the trail is simple. You get a solid axle at both ends, a torquey six, a body roughly the size of a Wrangler YJ, and an aftermarket that sells everything from a 1.5-inch Budget Boost to 6.5-inch long-arm kits. It's the budget alternative to a CJ-7 or an FJ60 for people who want doors, a heater and room for a dog. Just remember that the unibody is the frame: a rusted rail is not a bodywork problem.

### Data plate
- Platform: XJ unibody ('Uniframe')
- Production (Us): 1983 (MY1984) – June 2001, Toledo, Ohio
- Total Built: ≈ 3 million (1983–2001)
- Wheelbase: 101.4 in (2- and 4-door)
- Length: 165.3–168.8 in depending on year
- Engine: 4.0 L AMC I6 · 173–193 hp
- Other Engines: 2.5 I4 · 2.8 V6 · 2.1 and 2.5 turbodiesels
- Transmissions: AW4 auto · BA-10/5, AX-15, NV3550 manuals (4.0)
- Transfer Case: NP231 Command-Trac / NP242 Selec-Trac, 2.72:1
- Front Axle: Dana 30 (high-pinion to 1999, low-pinion 2000–01)
- Rear Axle: Dana 35 · Chrysler 8.25 · Dana 44 (some 1987–91)
- Suspension: Quadra-Link coils front · leaf springs rear

### Engineering
The XJ's body and frame are one welded structure with box-section rails built in. A finished body has about 3,200 welds. Both axles are solid: coil springs and four control arms with a track bar at the front, four-leaf springs and compression shackles at the rear. The wheelbase is 101.4 in on both two- and four-door bodies. All 4WD transfer cases are chain-driven two-speeds in aluminum housings.
- Structure: Unibody 'Uniframe', 101.4 in wheelbase (About 3,200 welds. Stiffened for 1997. Rails rot from inside, so inspect them like a frame.)
- Front Suspension: Quadra-Link: coils, 4 control arms, track bar (Designed by Roy Lunn. Worn track-bar parts are the usual cause of 'death wobble'.)
- Rear Suspension: Four-leaf packs, compression shackles (The Up Country package dropped the rear sway bar and added an inch of lift.)
- Engine: AMC 4.0 L (242 cu in) I6 (173–177 hp Renix (1987–90), 190 hp HO (1991–99), 193 hp / 231 lb-ft coil-on-plug (2000–01).)
- Axles: Dana 30 front · Dana 35, Chrysler 8.25 or Dana 44 rear (Dana 30 low-pinion for 2000–01. The 8.25 went from 27 to 29 splines in late 1996. Dana 44 rear on some 1987–91 tow-package trucks.)
- 4Wd: NP231 Command-Trac / NP242 Selec-Trac (Both 2.72:1 low range (1987–2001). The NP242 adds a full-time 4WD mode. Early trucks used the NP207 or NP228/229.)

### Versions
- 1984–1986 · XJ (AMC) · 2.5 I4 · 2.8 GM V6 · 2.1 Renault TD · 105–117 hp / 110–115 hp / 85 hp · No 4.0. NP207 or NP228/229. T4, T5, AX4, AX5 or A904 gearboxes.
- 1987–1990 · XJ (Renix) · 4.0 I6, Renix MPI · 173 hp (1987) · 177 hp / 224 lb-ft · AW4 auto or Peugeot BA-10/5 then AX-15 manual. NP231/NP242 arrive. No stored codes.
- 1991–1996 · XJ (HO) · 4.0 I6 HO, Chrysler MPI · 190 hp / 225 lb-ft · Chrysler 8.25 rear from 1991. OBD-II and JTEC engine computer for 1996.
- 1997–1999 · XJ facelift · 4.0 I6 HO · 190 hp / 225 lb-ft · Steel liftgate, new dash, stiffer body. NAXJA's favorite: non-ABS 1998–99.
- 2000–2001 · XJ final · 4.0 I6 HO, coil-on-plug · 193 hp / 231 lb-ft · 0331 head (crack-prone), NV3550 manual, low-pinion Dana 30. Six-cylinder only for 2001.
- 1984–1990 · Wagoneer (XJ) · As Cherokee · — · Compact luxury trim with woodgrain decals. Not the full-size Grand Wagoneer.

### Year-by-year
- 1984: Launch: unibody 'Uniframe', Quadra-Link coil front and leaf rear on live axles; 2.5 L AMC four or 2.8 L GM V6; NP207 Command-Trac or NP228/229 Selec-Trac. 1,200 lb lighter and 31 in shorter than the SJ Cherokee. No 4.0 until 1987: Off Road Xtreme recommends staying away from 1984–86 trucks [avoid]
- 1985: Two-wheel-drive model added mid-year; 2.1 L Renault turbodiesel offered in North America 1985–87
- 1987: 4.0 L six (173 hp, Renix injection) replaces the V6; AW4 automatic and NP231/NP242 transfer cases arrive; Chrysler buys AMC. Dana 44 rear with the tow package through 1991
- 1989: Late in the year the Aisin AX15 five-speed replaces the Peugeot BA-10/5 behind the 4.0; ABS-equipped trucks appear
- 1991: 4.0 L 'High Output' with Chrysler multi-point injection, 190 hp; Chrysler 8.25 in rear axle available on non-ABS trucks. The HO is the XJ Off Road Xtreme recommends: easier to diagnose than the Renix 4.0, and more power [buy]
- 1996: OBD-II and Chrysler's JTEC engine computer
- 1997: Facelift: steel liftgate replaces fibreglass, new interior and dash with dual airbags, stiffer unibody and quieter door seals
- 1999: Revised intake manifold mid-year on the 4.0 to offset smaller exhaust ports on the new head casting
- 2000: Coil-on-plug ignition on the 4.0 (193 hp); NV3550 replaces the AX15; front Dana 30 goes low pinion. New '0331' cylinder head: early castings can crack between cylinders 3 and 4 and put coolant in the oil (Wikipedia). A revised 'TUPY' casting arrived late in 2001, so check the head on any 2000–01 [avoid]
- 2001: Final year, 4.0 only; 60th Anniversary edition. Toledo production ends June 2001

### Capability
- Towing: 5,000 lb (2,270 kg) (2001 Sport 4.0 L)
- Payload: 1,150 lb (522 kg) (2001 Sport)
- Fuel tank: 20 US gal (76 L)
- Ground clearance: 10.6 in (269 mm) (2001 Sport)
- Fuel economy: EPA 14 city / 18 hwy (2001 4.0 L 4WD, current EPA method)
- Curb weight: 3,297 lb two-door / 3,355 lb four-door (1,496 / 1,522 kg) (2001 Sport)
- Turning circle: 35.7 ft (10.9 m)
- Wheelbase: 101.4 in (2,576 mm) (same for two- and four-door)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 215/75R15, 225/70R15, 225/75R15
- Bolt Pattern: 5x114.3 (5x4.5")
- Offset: +10 to +25 mm (stock 15x7)
- Center Bore: 71.5 mm
- Lug Thread: 1/2"-20
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 235/75R15 (NAXJA thread: 235/75R15 fits fine on the stock 15x7 (5.25 in backspacing). 30x9.50s rubbed the front control arms at full lock on an '88, and a 255/70R16 rubbed the rear fenders on a loaded 2000; one member says 1997-and-later trucks have less room than earlier ones)
- Biggest tire, 3 in lift: 31x10.50R15 (Expect minor rubbing at full lock; trim the front bumper ends and fender corners and roll the rear quarter seam)
- Biggest tire, 4.5 in lift: 33x12.50R15 (Per ExtremeTerrain's fitment table, on 15x8–17x9 wheels with −12 to +6 mm offset; trimming still likely)

### Buying checks
- The unibody rails come first: Avoid trucks with rust on the unibody frame rails, especially near suspension mounts. If rust reaches the suspension bolts, you may have to cut and repair the rails before a lift. Check the steering-box and track-bar mounts for cracks as well.
- Rockers, floors and lower quarters: Rocker panels under the doors and the lower rear quarters are the usual rust spots. Floors are relatively easy to replace; patch panels are cheap. Rust is much less common on Southwest trucks.
- 2000–01? Check the head: All 2000–01 XJs have the 0331 head. With the oil cap off, shine a light between the cylinder 3 and 4 exhaust rockers: a 'TUPY' mark means a revised head. Unexplained coolant loss, brown coolant or milky oil means a likely crack.
- Idle it until the fan comes on: XJs are known for running hot. Idle for 5–10 minutes, make sure the electric fan kicks in, and watch the gauge on a hill. Bent pulleys suggest an overtightened belt and tired bearings.
- Find the leak before you blame the rear main: Common leaks are the rear main seal, oil pan gasket, valve cover gasket and oil-filter-adapter O-rings. Oil runs down to the bellhousing, so check the top of the engine first.
- Test drive for wobble and wander: Death wobble is usually the track bar. Wandering at speed means worn suspension or steering parts. A transfer case that pops out of 4WD may be worn.
- Know the electronics era: 1987–90 Renix trucks store no fault codes and are diagnosed with a multimeter, so buy one only if you're comfortable chasing sensors. The 1991 HO trucks and later are easier. Avoid 1984–86 unless you plan an engine swap.
- Read the axle tags: ABS trucks have the Dana 35 rear, which is fine stock but weak with big tires. The Chrysler 8.25 is the common, decent rear axle, and a tow-package Dana 44 is worth extra.

### Common repairs
#### Replace a cracked 0331 cylinder head (2000–01)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Unexplained coolant loss, brown or dirty coolant, milky residue under the oil cap, and often a recent overheat. Wikipedia says the crack sits between cylinders 3 and 4 and often shows as a tan line with the valve cover off.
Fix: Confirm with a cooling-system pressure test and by looking through the oil filler (no 'TUPY' mark means an original 0331). Drain the coolant and remove the intake and exhaust manifolds, the coil rail, the valve cover and the rocker assemblies, keeping pushrods in order. Remove the head bolts and lift the head off. Change the oil and filter, then flush the oil again after the first short run to get coolant out. Fit a revised or aftermarket head; never another 0331, and confirm the casting with the seller before you buy (Wikipedia notes even 'TUPY' heads occasionally crack). Use a new gasket and head bolts, torque in sequence to the service-manual spec, then refill and bleed the cooling system. Fix the cooling problem that probably caused the crack.
Tools: Torque wrench · head bolt sequence and spec from FSM [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · gasket scraper · pushrod organizer · coolant pressure tester

#### Replace the rear main seal (4.0 two-piece)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Oil dripping from the joint between engine and transmission. Rule out the valve cover gasket, oil-pressure sender, oil-filter-adapter O-rings and (on distributor engines) the distributor gasket first.
Fix: The 4.0 uses a two-piece seal, so it can be done with the engine in the truck and the transmission in place. Raise the Jeep high and support it, drain the oil and drop the pan. Remove the rear main bearing cap, pull the lower seal half, then work the upper half out by pushing one end around the crank. Clean everything, oil the new seal lips, install the upper half and then the lower half in the cap, fit the cap and torque it to spec. One NAXJA member quotes 80 ft-lb for a 1999 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]. Refit the pan with a new gasket, which is where most comebacks happen.
Tools: Jack and stands · torque wrench · seal pick · RTV per seal instructions · new pan gasket

#### Reseal the oil filter adapter
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost Under $20 in O-rings
Symptoms: Oil on the driver's side of the block and dripping onto the exhaust or crossmember, which is often mistaken for a rear main leak.
Fix: Drain the oil and remove the filter. Unbolt the adapter (on 1991 and later engines it sits next to the starter), clean both faces, fit new O-rings and refit the adapter. Use the correct O-ring set for your year: the adapter changed for 1991.
Tools: Sockets and extensions · filter wrench · drain pan · clean rags

#### Fix the overheating: radiator, fan clutch, pump and mounts
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: The gauge climbs on hills or in traffic, the electric fan doesn't come on, or the radiator's plastic tanks seep. OffroadXtreme found factory radiators cracking from frame twist on the trail.
Fix: Start with the cheap checks: the electric fan and its relay and sensor, the fan clutch (it should resist turning when hot), the thermostat and the cap. Check the engine mounts; a worn mount let one author's fan clutch push into the radiator and close up its fins. Then replace the radiator (a thicker all-aluminum core is the usual upgrade; on 1990–95 trucks the core-support tabs may need grinding), the water pump and the hoses. Refill and bleed thoroughly.
Tools: Coolant drain pan · fan-clutch wrench · sockets · infrared thermometer · funnel kit for bleeding

#### Replace the crankshaft position sensor (hot stalls)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost Sensor plus your time
Symptoms: The engine dies when hot and restarts after cooling. No spark, and fuel pressure checks out but fuel doesn't reach the injectors. Sometimes the gauges go dead or 'no bus' shows on the odometer. NAXJA members call thermal failure 'pretty common'.
Fix: Test it hot, right after it fails, because a bad sensor often tests fine cold. On 1991–2001 4.0 HO engines, unplug the sensor pigtail near the rear of the intake manifold and measure across terminals B and C on the 1K–10K ohm scale. It should read open (infinite). Low resistance means replace it. Fit the sensor for your exact year: the part changed several times.
Tools: Multimeter · long extensions and swivel · flashlight

#### Cure death wobble: track bar, steering linkage and box mount
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Parts plus alignment
Symptoms: Violent front-end shake after a bump at speed, wandering, clunks. OffroadXtreme says the track bar is the usual cause.
Fix: With the engine running and a helper turning the wheel back and forth, watch the track bar ends, the frame-side bracket, the tie-rod and drag-link ends and the steering box for movement. Replace worn bushings or the whole track bar (an adjustable one recenters a lifted axle), tighten the bracket bolts, and replace worn linkage. Inspect the unibody around the steering box and track-bar mount for cracks, which NAXJA members warn about. A steering stabilizer hides wobble; it doesn't cure it.
Tools: Helper · pry bar · tie-rod puller · torque wrench · alignment afterward

#### Replace rusted floor pans and rockers
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend per side · cost Parts plus welding
Symptoms: Wet carpet, holes under the mats, rockers that crumble under a screwdriver, rusted lower rear quarters.
Fix: Strip the interior, cut out the rot back to solid metal, and treat rust you can't cut out. Trial-fit the patch panels, then weld them in with plug or stitch welds. NAXJA members point out that on a unibody almost every panel is structural, so don't rely on screwed-in tin. Seam-seal and coat inside and out, and spray cavity wax into the rockers. If the main rails are rotten, that's a much bigger job; walk away or budget accordingly.
Tools: MIG welder · cut-off wheel · spot-weld drill · clamps · weld-through primer · seam sealer · cavity wax

### Baseline service
XJs are cheap, so most have been run on a budget. Assume nothing has been done. The figures below come from a NAXJA member's fluid-capacity summary (posted in a thread titled '2001 owner's manual fluids', though the post doesn't say which year each figure applies to), with ExtremeTerrain's XJ service guide where noted. The two disagree on AW4 fluid, coolant capacity, transfer-case fill and manual-gearbox oil grade, so check the label on your truck or the manual for your year.
- Engine oil & filter: 4.0: 6.0 qt (5.7 L) with filter · 5W-30 (ExtremeTerrain) · 2.5: 4.0 qt · Baseline now; then per your owner's manual (Check the oil-filter-adapter O-rings while you're under there. They're a common leak that gets blamed on the rear main.)
- Air filter: Panel element, 1987–2001 · Baseline now; inspect every oil change (Crown's master filter kits (MFK8 / MFK9) bundle the oil, air and fuel filters.)
- Spark plugs & ignition: Copper plugs, 0.035 in gap (4.0) · cap, rotor and wires through 1999 · coil rail on 2000–01 · Baseline now (On 2000–01 coil-on-plug trucks, a NAXJA member notes the coil rail is expensive to replace and gets blamed for misfire codes. Rule out plugs and wiring first.)
- Coolant & thermostat: 4.0: 10.5 qt (9.9 L) per the 2001 manual quote; ExtremeTerrain lists 12 qt · IAT through 2000, HOAT for 2001 (ExtremeTerrain) · Flush and refill now (Flush completely when changing coolant types. On 2000–01 trucks, a healthy cooling system is your best protection against a cracked 0331 head.)
- Automatic transmission (AW4): Dexron III/Mercon per the NAXJA summary (ExtremeTerrain lists ATF+4; a NAXJA reply says Chrysler approved ATF+4 for the AW4 from late 2007) · 4 qt drain-and-fill, 8 qt with filter [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now (Do a pan drop and filter change, not a pressure flush. Check the throttle-valve cable adjustment if shifts are harsh or late.)
- Manual transmission: AX-15: 3.32 qt 75W-90 GL-3/GL-4 (not GL-5) · AX-5: 3.3 qt same · NV3550: 2.1 qt Mopar 04874464AA or equivalent · ExtremeTerrain lists GL-5 for the AX-15 and AX-5 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now (NAXJA notes some owner's manuals wrongly list GL-5 for the Aisin boxes.)
- Transfer case (NP231 / NP242): NP231: 2.2 pt (1.0 L) · NP242: 2.85 pt (1.3 L) · Dexron III/Mercon or ATF+3/ATF+4 · ExtremeTerrain lists 1.6 qt ATF+4 for the NP231 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now (If it pops out of 4WD or is hard to shift back to 2WD, the case may be worn.)
- Front axle (Dana 30): 2.5 pt (1.2 L) SAE 75W-90 · Baseline now (Low-pinion on 2000–01 trucks, high-pinion before that. Check the inner axle seals if the knuckles are wet with gear oil.)
- Rear axle (Dana 35 / Chrysler 8.25): Dana 35: 3.5 pt (1.66 L) · 8.25: 4.4 pt (2.0 L) · SAE 75W-90 (75W-140 synthetic suggested for towing) · add 4 oz friction modifier with Trac-Lok · Baseline now (Read the tag. ABS trucks have the Dana 35.)
- Front axle U-joints: 297x/760 series (1996 and later; check earlier ABS/non-ABS sizes) · Inspect now; replace if notchy (Turn each front wheel to full lock and check the axle-shaft U-joints for play or rust bleeding from the caps.)
- Serpentine belt & pulleys: Belt by year and accessory layout · Baseline now (OffroadXtreme says to check pulley alignment: bent pulleys suggest an overtightened belt and tired bearings.)
- Electric cooling fan: Confirm it switches on at idle · Check now (Idle for 5–10 minutes and confirm the fan runs. The assemblies differ for 1987–96 and 1997–2001.)
- Brake fluid & rear brakes: Brake fluid per the master-cylinder cap [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush now; then every 2 years (Larger tires may need more brake-pedal effort. Rear drums on most XJs need adjusting and fresh hardware.)
- Steering box & power steering: Power-steering fluid [CONFIRM TYPE IN MANUAL] · Inspect now (Check the box for seepage, and check the unibody around the box mount for cracks.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: In a NAXJA thread, members agree a 235/75R15 (about 29 in) on the stock 15x7 wheels with 5.25 in backspacing fits fine, and treat a 30x9.50R15 as the practical limit. One owner's '88 on 30x9.50s rubbed only the front control arms at full lock, which a steering-stop adjustment fixes at the cost of turning circle. A 255/70R16 (about 30 in) rubbed the rear fenders on a loaded 2000. Less backspacing pushes the tire out toward the flares.

Q: Which years and engines should I buy?
A: Buy a 4.0. OffroadXtreme recommends the 1991-and-later HO, says 1987–90 Renix trucks suit owners who like diagnosing sensors, and says to avoid 1984–86 (no 4.0). NAXJA members single out non-ABS 1998–99 trucks with the 4.0, AW4, NP231 and 29-spline 8.25 as about the most solid combination. The 2000–01 trucks are good if the head has been checked or replaced.

Q: What's the 0331 head problem?
A: The 2000–01 4.0 got a head with casting number 0331 that can crack between cylinders 3 and 4, letting coolant into the oil. Look through the oil filler between the cylinder 3 and 4 exhaust rockers: a 'TUPY' mark means a revised head, though Wikipedia says even those occasionally crack. Most failures follow an overheat, so keep the cooling system healthy, and never replace a cracked one with another 0331.

Q: Which rear axle do I have, and is it any good?
A: There are three possibilities. The Dana 35 was used on early trucks and on ABS-equipped trucks throughout; it's fine stock but weak with bigger tires. The Chrysler 8.25 is common on non-ABS 1991–2001 trucks and went from 27 to 29 splines in late 1996. The Dana 44 came on some 1987–91 tow-package trucks. The axle tag or the cover shape will tell you.

Q: Command-Trac or Selec-Trac?
A: From 1987 both have 2.72:1 low range. The NP231 Command-Trac is part-time (2H, 4H, N, 4L) and NAXJA calls it better for heavy off-road use. The NP242 Selec-Trac adds a full-time 4WD mode for slippery pavement.

Q: What fluids and capacities does it take?
A: Per a NAXJA member's capacity summary (year not stated): 4.0 oil 6 qt with filter, coolant 10.5 qt, AW4 4 qt drain-and-fill (Dexron III/Mercon), NP231 2.2 pt, Dana 30 2.5 pt 75W-90, Dana 35 3.5 pt, 8.25 4.4 pt, plus friction modifier for Trac-Lok. ExtremeTerrain lists ATF+4 for the AW4, 12 qt of coolant, 1.6 qt for the NP231 and GL-5 oil for the AX-15, so the sources conflict: check your manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]. See 'After you buy it' for the full list.

Q: Why does my XJ overheat?
A: The usual suspects are a clogged or cracked radiator (the factory plastic tanks can split under frame twist), a weak fan clutch, a dead electric fan or relay, an old water pump, and worn motor mounts that let the fan get too close to the radiator. On Renix trucks, check whether someone has converted the cooling system.

Q: What causes death wobble, and how do I fix it?
A: Usually the track bar: worn bushings, a loose bracket or a bent bar. Worn tie-rod ends, the drag link or ball joints can also cause it. Find the loose part with a helper turning the wheel, replace it, and check the unibody around the track-bar and steering-box mounts for cracks. A new steering stabilizer only hides the problem.

Q: How long do they last?
A: NAXJA members report XJs commonly running 250,000–300,000 miles or more on factory drivetrains if they're maintained. The original poster in NAXJA's beginner thread called anything under 100,000 miles hard to find and probably overpriced.

Q: Why is my Renix XJ so hard to diagnose?
A: The 1987–90 Renix computer doesn't store fault codes, so you diagnose sensors with a multimeter. It's well documented, but it's more work than the 1991-and-later Chrysler system, which became OBD-II with the JTEC computer in 1996.

Q: How much lift do I need?
A: It depends on the tires and the trail. The factory Up Country package added an inch. Kits run from TeraFlex's 1.5-inch Budget Boost, through 3-inch leaf-and-coil systems from Zone and Rough Country, to 4.5–6.5-inch long-arm kits. Bigger lifts usually need an adjustable track bar and driveline work.

## Jeep Comanche MJ (1986–1992)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/comanche-mj/
Codes: MJ, Metric Ton, Eliminator

Verdict: A Cherokee XJ from the B-pillar forward and a fully boxed truck frame behind it. Give it the 4.0 six and a Dana 44 and it will carry a ton. About 190,000 were built, Chrysler had little reason to keep it once Dodge had the Dakota, and now the bed, tailgate and taillights are harder to find than the truck. Pull up the carpet before you pull out your wallet.

AMC unveiled the Comanche in August 1985 to more than 1,500 dealers in the ballroom of the MGM Grand in Las Vegas. It was a compact pickup built from the Cherokee XJ: the same unibody, Quadra-Link coil front end and engines from the cab forward, and behind the cab a fully boxed frame and a removable bed. At $7,049 for a two-wheel-drive model it was the cheapest Jeep of 1986. It lasted seven model years and 190,446 trucks, and it was Jeep's last pickup until the Gladiator 27 years later.

### A CHEROKEE WITH A TRUCK BOLTED ON
AMC needed money and needed a truck. Its finances were weak, a new Canadian plant was being built for the Eagle Premier, and compact pickups were selling. The answer was cheap to engineer: keep the XJ's front half and its 'Uniframe' unibody, and graft on a frame for the bed. Wikipedia describes that rear structure as fully boxed rather than the usual open C-channel, with rails more than eight inches deep and a large X-member over the rear axle. AMC had first tried the idea on its 1971 'Cowboy' pickup prototype.
The long-bed, seven-foot truck came first, for 1986. A six-foot short bed followed for 1987, on a 113-inch wheelbase against 119.9 inches for the long bed. Up front was the XJ's coil-sprung Dana 30 (or a beam axle on 2WD trucks). At the back were rear leaf springs much longer than the Cherokee's and, as standard, a Dana 35. The Metric Ton package for long beds added heavier springs, wheels and tires and a Dana 44, raising payload from 1,400 to 2,205 lb. Wikipedia notes that this was more than many full-size pickups could carry.

### FROM A WEAK V6 TO THE 4.0
1986 Comanches had AMC's 2.5-liter four, a carbureted GM 2.8 V6 that made slightly less power than the four, or a Renault 2.1 turbodiesel. For 1987 the 4.0-liter straight-six arrived with 173 hp and 220 lb-ft, about 50% more power than the V6, together with the Aisin AW4 automatic and the NP231 Command-Trac and NP242 Selec-Trac transfer cases. Chrysler bought AMC in March 1987 and mostly left the truck alone. It gained an eight-slot grille for 1988, the sporty Eliminator trim, and the Aisin AX-15 five-speed in place of the Peugeot BA-10/5 during 1989.
For 1991 Chrysler replaced the Renix engine management with its own, and the 4.0 became the 190 hp 'High Output'. Quadratec's fitment listings also show Chrysler 8.25-inch rear axles in 1991–92 trucks. By then, though, the truck had stopped selling. Calendar-year output fell from 43,718 in 1988 to 5,188 in 1991. Jeep-Eagle dealers asked Chrysler to drop it and give them a Dakota-based pickup instead, and Chrysler wanted Jeep to sell SUVs and Dodge to sell trucks. The last Comanche left Toledo on June 12, 1992.

### WHY THEY'RE WORTH SAVING
Today the Comanche is the XJ's rarer, more useful sibling. Comanche Club members got vehicle-in-operation figures from Key Parts showing about 18,600 MJs registered in the US and Canada in late 2021, roughly a tenth of production. Mechanically it is the XJ: the same 4.0, AX-15 and AW4, Dana 30 and NP231, so the drivetrain parts aren't hard to find. The cab interior and everything behind the doors are a different story. Bed sides, tailgates, taillights and bench-seat sliders are MJ-only and getting scarce.
On the trail it behaves like a long Cherokee with a bigger rear overhang. The XJ front suspension, the 4.0 and the easy 4WD conversions owners talk about make it a natural budget builder, and a Metric Ton or 8.25-axle truck has the rear end to carry a camper shell full of gear. Like the CJ-8 Scrambler, it suits owners who want a Jeep with a bed. The modern equivalent is the JL Unlimited-based Gladiator.

### Data plate
- Platform: MJ (XJ-based unibody with boxed rear frame)
- Production: 1985 (MY1986) – June 12, 1992, Toledo, Ohio
- Total Built: 190,446
- Wheelbase: 113 in (6 ft bed) · 119.9 in (7 ft bed)
- Length: 179.2 in (SWB) · 194.0 in (LWB)
- Engine: 4.0 L AMC I6 · 173–190 hp (1987–92)
- Other Engines: 2.5 I4 · 2.8 GM V6 (1986) · 2.1 Renault TD (1986–87)
- Transmissions: A904 · AW4 auto · AX-4, AX-5, BA-10/5, AX-15 manual
- Transfer Case: NP231 Command-Trac / NP242 Selec-Trac, 2.72:1
- Front Axle: Dana 30 (4WD)
- Rear Axle: Dana 35 · Dana 44 (Metric Ton) · Chrysler 8.25 (1991–92)
- Payload: 1,400 lb · 2,205 lb (Metric Ton)

### Engineering
The MJ is an XJ Cherokee from the B-pillar forward: welded unibody, Quadra-Link coil front suspension with four control arms and a track bar, and the same engines and transfer cases. Behind the cab, a fully boxed rear frame with a large X-member over the axle carries a removable bed on long leaf springs. Two wheelbases, 113 in (six-foot bed, from 1987) and 119.9 in (seven-foot bed), share the cab.
- Structure: XJ unibody front, boxed rear frame with X-member (Rails over 8 in deep. NAXJA members say the rear rails are part of the unibody, not bolted on.)
- Front Suspension: Quadra-Link: coils, 4 control arms, track bar (Same as the XJ. 4WD trucks have a Dana 30; 2WD trucks a beam axle.)
- Rear Suspension: Long leaf springs, solid axle (Longer than the Cherokee's. XJ axles aren't drop-in: the spring widths differ.)
- Engine: AMC 4.0 L (242 cu in) I6, 1987–92 (173 hp (1987), 177 hp (1988–90 Renix), 190 hp HO (1991–92). 2.5 I4 throughout.)
- Rear Axles: Dana 35 · Dana 44 · Chrysler 8.25 (1991–92) (The Metric Ton package brings the Dana 44. Offroaders lists an AMC 20 as a 1986 heavy-duty option.)
- 4Wd: NP207 / NP228 (1986) · NP231 / NP242 (1987–92) (2.61:1 low range in 1986, 2.72:1 after. NP231 is part-time; NP242 adds full-time 4WD.)

### Versions
- 1986 · MJ (AMC), LWB only · 2.5 I4 · 2.8 GM V6 · 2.1 Renault TD · V6 slightly weaker than the I4 · Custom, X, XLS trims. NP207/NP228. A904 3-speed auto or AX-4/AX-5/BA-10/5.
- 1987 · MJ, SWB added · 2.5 I4 · 4.0 I6 Renix · 121 hp · 173 hp / 220 lb-ft · AW4 auto. NP231/NP242. Chief, Laredo, Pioneer, SporTruck. Diesel dropped mid-year.
- 1988–1990 · MJ (Chrysler), Renix · 2.5 I4 · 4.0 I6 · 177 hp / 224 lb-ft (4.0) · Eight-slot grille, Eliminator and Olympic Edition (1988). AX-15 replaces BA-10/5 mid-1989.
- 1991–1992 · MJ HO · 2.5 I4 · 4.0 I6 HO · 130 hp · 190 hp / 225 lb-ft · Chrysler engine management. No automatic with the 2.5. Chrysler 8.25 rear available.
- 1986–1992 · Metric Ton (LWB) · As above · — · Heavy-duty springs, wheels and tires and a Dana 44 rear; 2,205 lb payload.

### Year-by-year
- 1985: Unveiled in August at the MGM Grand, Las Vegas, for MY1986: XJ-based, long bed only, 2.5 I4, 2.8 GM V6 or 2.1 Renault turbodiesel; $7,049 base 2WD
- 1987: Short bed (113 in wheelbase) added; 4.0 I6 (173 hp) replaces the V6; AW4 auto; NP231/NP242; Chrysler buys AMC in March; diesel dropped
- 1988: Eight-slot grille; 4.0 rated 177 hp; Eliminator trim and Olympic Edition
- 1989: Aisin AX-15 five-speed replaces the Peugeot BA-10/5 mid-year
- 1991: Chrysler engine management replaces Renix; 4.0 'High Output' 190 hp; Chrysler 8.25 rear appears; no automatic with the 2.5. The 1991–92 HO is the one to buy: easier to diagnose than the Renix 4.0, which is why Off Road Xtreme recommends the HO in the XJ that shares the engine [buy]
- 1992: Final year; production ends June 12, 1992 after 952 trucks built that calendar year

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 205/75R15 (base, Pioneer), 215/75R15 (base, Pioneer), 225/75R15 (Pioneer), 225/70R15 (Eliminator)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x114.3 (5x4.5")
- Center Bore: 71.5 mm

- Biggest tire, Stock, trimmed lift: 31x10.50R15 (NAXJA XJ owners say it needs bump stops or trimming and rubs the lower control arms)
- Biggest tire, 3 in lift: 31x10.50R15 (XJ consensus for a 3 in kit; Rough Country sells 3, 4.5 and 6.5 in kits specific to the MJ's rear springs)

### Buying checks
- Pull up the carpet: NAXJA and Comanche Club members agree: rust is the number-one issue, and unless the truck lived in the Southwest or Southern California, expect it in the floors. Rusty seat brackets or bolts usually mean rusty floor pans below.
- Check where the cab meets the bed, and the rails: Look hard where the bed meets the cab and where the unibody joins the rear frame. NAXJA members warn that bulging rail bottoms mean rust inside. Water also enters through the rear cab bulkhead and window; one member says more than one MJ has gone to the crusher because of it.
- Look for cracks and old welds on the frame: Comanche Club members say to inspect the frame closely for cracks or signs of weld repair, especially on trucks that hauled or towed.
- Bed, tailgate and taillights: These are MJ-only parts and hard to replace. A crushed bed side or a missing tailgate costs more and takes longer to fix than a tired engine.
- Identify the rear axle: An oval cover usually means a Dana 35, and an angular, roughly hexagonal cover means a Dana 44, per NAXJA. A 1991–92 truck may have the Chrysler 8.25. Ask whether it's a Metric Ton truck; sellers often don't know.
- Renix or HO?: 1987–90 4.0s run Renix management, which stores no codes and is diagnosed with a multimeter. 1991–92 HO trucks have Chrysler's system and 190 hp. Both are good engines, but Renix trucks reward owners who like electrical troubleshooting.
- Hydraulic clutch and fuse box: On manual trucks, check the clutch master cylinder. Comanche Club members warn a leak can drip brake fluid into the fuse box, which damages it.
- 2.5 or 4.0?: The 4.0 is the one to have. If you buy a 2.5, Comanche Club members suggest looking for a 4.10 or 4.56 axle ratio. The AX-4 and AX-5 gearboxes behind the 2.5 won't bolt up to a 4.0.

### Common repairs
#### Replace rusted floor pans and rockers
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend per side · cost Parts plus welding
Symptoms: Wet carpet, rusty seat-bracket bolts, holes under the mats, crumbling rockers, and rust at the rear cab bulkhead where the bed meets the cab.
Fix: Strip the cab, cut out the rot to clean metal, and treat what you can't cut. Trial-fit the panels, then plug- or stitch-weld them in. On a unibody, the floor and rockers are structural, so don't rely on screwed-in tin. Seam-seal, paint and wax the cavities. Fix the leak that caused it, usually the rear window and bulkhead seals. If the rails under the cab are swollen with rust, the job is much bigger.
Tools: MIG welder · cut-off wheel · spot-weld drill · clamps · weld-through primer · seam sealer · cavity wax

#### Replace a leaking clutch master cylinder
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours plus bleeding · cost A master cylinder or master kit
Symptoms: A soft or sinking clutch pedal, fluid on the firewall, or electrical faults from fluid dripping into the fuse box below. Comanche Club members also recommend checking the clutch-pedal welds, which some owners found incomplete and cracked.
Fix: Clean any brake fluid off the fuse box and connectors right away. Disconnect the pushrod at the pedal, unbolt the master cylinder from the firewall and remove it with the line. Bleed the hydraulics after fitting, following the part's instructions. Check the pedal pivot and welds while you're under the dash.
Tools: Sockets and extensions · flare-nut wrench · flashlight · brake cleaner · DOT 3 fluid

#### Hot stalls and no-starts: CPS, ballast resistor, grounds
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost A sensor or resistor plus your time
Symptoms: The engine dies when hot and won't restart until it cools, cranks without spark, or the fuel pump won't run. Comanche Club owners name the crankshaft position sensor (CPS) and the Renix fuel-pump ballast resistor as the usual culprits, and say to check the body grounds first for strange electrical faults.
Fix: Test before you buy. Clean and tighten the engine, body and taillight grounds, and the ground at the fuel tank. Then test the CPS hot, right after a failure, with a multimeter against the resistance values for your year. On Renix trucks, check the ballast resistor; a jumper wire from the battery to the pump circuit will prove it at the roadside. Replace the failed part with one for your exact year, because the parts changed for the 1991 HO system.
Tools: Self-ranging multimeter · wire brush · dielectric grease · long extensions

#### Reseal the oil filter adapter
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost Under $20 in O-rings
Symptoms: Oil on the driver's side of the block and dripping off the crossmember. Comanche Club members warn that a bad adapter O-ring is often misdiagnosed as a rear main seal.
Fix: Clean the engine so you can see where the leak starts. Drain the oil, remove the filter, unbolt the adapter, clean both faces, fit new O-rings and refit. Use the 1987–92 O-rings for the MJ's 4.0. Note that Renix-era engines use a metric filter thread; a Comanche Club write-up covers converting to an SAE filter.
Tools: Sockets · filter wrench · drain pan · degreaser · rags

#### Sort out the cooling system (and the Renix closed system)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Parts plus coolant
Symptoms: Overheating on hills or in traffic, coolant loss, or a cracked pressurized plastic coolant bottle. Comanche Club members suggest replacing the plastic bottle with an aluminum one, or converting the 1987–90 Renix closed system to the later open layout.
Fix: Start cheap: test the cap, thermostat, fan clutch and electric fan, and clean the temperature-sender contacts. Pressure-test for leaks. Replace a cracked bottle and tired hoses, and the water pump if it weeps. If you convert a Renix truck to the open system, follow a documented write-up, such as Cruiser54's on Comanche Club, and bleed the system fully afterward.
Tools: Cooling-system pressure tester · fan-clutch wrench · drain pan · funnel kit

#### Rebush the rear leaf springs and shackles
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Bushings, shackles and shocks
Symptoms: Clunks over bumps, a rear end that steers itself, rusted or seized shackles, or bent lower shock-mount bolts. Comanche Club owners recommend upgrading the rear lower shock mounts.
Fix: Support the frame and take the weight off the springs. Soak every bolt in penetrant for a few days first. Unbolt the shackles and front hangers, drop each spring, press out the old bushings and fit new ones (polyurethane needs grease). Fit new shackles, torque everything at ride height, and replace the shocks while you're there.
Tools: Jack stands · penetrating oil · bushing press or vise · torque wrench

#### Fix or bypass the front axle disconnect (CAD)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2–4 hours · cost A manual-disconnect or 'shift-on-the-fly' kit
Symptoms: 4WD that engages at the transfer case but doesn't drive the front wheels, or grinding from the front axle. Comanche Club members say to check the vacuum-operated central axle disconnect before your first trail, and to lock it in or bypass it if necessary.
Fix: Check the vacuum lines and the switch on the transfer case first. If the shift motor or fork is the problem, a manual disconnect kit replaces the vacuum actuator with a cable or lever, or the axle can be made permanently engaged with the right parts. Drain the gear oil, unbolt the shift-motor housing, fit the kit and refill with 75W-90.
Tools: Vacuum gauge or hand pump · sockets · gasket scraper · RTV · gear oil

#### Cure death wobble: track bar and steering
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Parts plus an alignment
Symptoms: Violent front shake after a bump at speed, wandering and clunks. The MJ front end is the XJ's, with the same weak points: the track bar, tie-rod ends, drag link and steering box.
Fix: With the engine running, have a helper turn the wheel back and forth while you watch the track-bar ends and bracket, the tie-rod and drag-link ends and the steering box for movement. Replace worn parts (an adjustable track bar re-centers a lifted axle), tighten everything at ride height, and check the unibody around the steering box for cracks. A steering stabilizer hides wobble; it doesn't cure it.
Tools: Helper · pry bar · tie-rod puller · torque wrench · alignment afterward

### Baseline service
A Comanche is at least 34 years old, and most have spent years as cheap work trucks, so assume nothing has been done. The drivetrain is the XJ's, so the capacities below come from the 2001 Cherokee owner's manual as quoted on NAXJA, for the parts the two share. Check your own truck's manual and the axle tags, especially for Dana 44 and Metric Ton rear axles.
- Engine oil & filter: 4.0: 6.0 qt (5.7 L) with filter · 2.5: 4.0 qt (XJ figures) · Baseline now (Renix-era engines use a metric filter thread. Comanche Club members advise against Fram filters.)
- Ignition: plugs, wires, cap and rotor: Copper plugs, 0.035 in gap (4.0, XJ figure) · Baseline now (Clean the throttle body and IAC and set the TPS to spec while you're there; Comanche Club calls this routine on an old MJ.)
- Coolant & thermostat: 4.0: about 10.5 qt (XJ figure) [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush and refill now (Check the plastic bottle for cracks. Renix trucks have the pressurized closed system.)
- Clutch hydraulics: DOT 3 brake fluid · Inspect and flush now (Look for leaks above the fuse box.)
- Automatic transmission (AW4): 4 qt drain-and-fill, 8 qt with filter (XJ figure) · Dexron III/Mercon per the 2001 manual quote [CONFIRM FOR YOUR YEAR] · Baseline now (Do a pan drop and filter change, not a pressure flush.)
- Manual transmission: AX-15 and AX-5: about 3.3 qt 75W-90 GL-3/GL-4, not GL-5 (NAXJA) · BA-10/5: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now (NAXJA notes some manuals wrongly list GL-5 for the Aisin boxes.)
- Transfer case (NP231 / NP242): NP231: 2.2 pt · NP242: 2.85 pt · ATF (XJ figures) · Baseline now (1986 trucks have the NP207 or NP228; check the tag.)
- Front axle (Dana 30) & CAD: 2.5 pt (1.2 L) SAE 75W-90 (XJ figure) · Baseline now (Check that the vacuum axle disconnect actually engages before the first trail.)
- Rear axle (Dana 35 / Dana 44 / 8.25): Dana 35: 3.5 pt · 8.25: 4.4 pt (XJ figures) · Dana 44: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · SAE 75W-90 · friction modifier with Trac-Lok · Baseline now (Read the axle tag first. Comanche Club members note that some Dana 35s have a metal fill plug, not the rubber one most people expect.)
- U-joints: Front axle shafts and both driveshafts · Inspect now (Turn the front wheels to full lock and check the axle U-joints for play.)
- Brakes: DOT 3 fluid · front discs, rear drums · Flush now; then every 2 years (Rear drums usually need adjusting and fresh hardware. Comanche Club has a brake-upgrade write-up.)
- Grounds & headlights: Engine, body, taillight and fuel-tank grounds · Clean now (Comanche Club members recommend a headlight relay harness for brighter lights and less load on the switch. If you remove the bed, re-ground the harness or it won't start.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: The MJ's front end and fenders are the XJ's, so XJ consensus is a fair guide: a 235/75R15 (about 29 in) on the stock 15 in wheels fits, and a 30x9.50R15 is the practical limit, possibly rubbing the front lower control arms at full lock. NAXJA posters say a 31x10.50 needs bump stops or trimming. We found no separate MJ-only consensus. Load the bed before judging rear clearance.

Q: Which years and engines should I buy?
A: Buy a 4.0, ideally a 1991–92 HO: 190 hp and Chrysler's easier-to-diagnose engine management, the same reason Off Road Xtreme recommends the HO in the XJ. 1987–90 Renix trucks are good too, but they're diagnosed with a multimeter. 1986 trucks have no 4.0. If you do buy a 2.5, Comanche Club members say look for 4.10 or 4.56 gears.

Q: What is a Metric Ton Comanche?
A: A long-bed heavy-duty package with heavier leaf springs, wheels and tires and a Dana 44 rear axle. It raised payload from 1,400 to 2,205 lb. Sellers often don't know they have one, so check the axle and springs.

Q: Which rear axle do I have?
A: The Dana 35 was standard. The Dana 44 came with the Metric Ton package (and on some other trucks; Comanche Club members' trucks include a 1992 short bed with a limited-slip Dana 44). Offroaders lists an AMC 20 as a 1986 heavy-duty option, and Quadratec's locker fitment shows the 27-spline Chrysler 8.25 on 1991–92 trucks. NAXJA: oval cover means Dana 35; angular, roughly hexagonal cover means Dana 44.

Q: Short bed or long bed?
A: The six-foot short bed rides on a 113 in wheelbase and arrived for 1987. The seven-foot long bed is on 119.9 in and was the only length in 1986. The short bed is better on tight trails; Metric Ton trucks are long beds. The Eliminator was short-bed only, per Comanche Club.

Q: Where do they rust?
A: Under the carpet, at the rear cab bulkhead and window seals, where the bed meets the cab, and where the unibody meets the rear frame. NAXJA members say bulging rail bottoms mean rust inside.

Q: Are parts hard to find?
A: Drivetrain and front-end parts are shared with the XJ and easy to find. Comanche Club members say everything behind the doors is different, and the bed, tailgate, taillights and bench-seat sliders are MJ-specific and scarce. An XJ fuel pump and sender don't fit without fabrication.

Q: How much can it tow and carry?
A: Kelley Blue Book lists a 1992 Comanche at 5,000 lb maximum towing and 1,475 lb payload. Wikipedia gives 1,400 lb for a standard truck and 2,205 lb for the Metric Ton package.

Q: Command-Trac or Selec-Trac?
A: From 1987 the NP231 Command-Trac is part-time and the NP242 Selec-Trac adds a full-time 4WD mode. Both have 2.72:1 low range. 1986 trucks used the NP207 and NP228, both with 2.61:1 low range.

Q: Why does my MJ stall when hot?
A: Usually the crankshaft position sensor, which can fail when hot and test fine cold, or, on Renix trucks, the fuel-pump ballast resistor. Comanche Club members say to check the body grounds first for any strange electrical fault.

Q: How many are left?
A: AMC and Chrysler built 190,446. Comanche Club members got 2021 vehicle-in-operation figures from Key Parts showing about 18,600 registered in the US and Canada.

## Jeep Wrangler YJ (1987–1995)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/yj/
Codes: YJ

Verdict: The Wrangler that dared to have square headlights, and spent thirty years being forgiven for it. Under the controversial face it's a wider, calmer CJ-7 on leaf springs, and from 1991 it has the 4.0 straight-six. Buy that one, check the frame, and enjoy the cheapest ticket to a proper old-school Jeep.

In February 1986 American Motors unveiled the 1987 Jeep Wrangler, and on May 13 of that year the first CJ replacement in four decades went on sale. It was called the YJ, and in Canada simply the Jeep YJ, because General Motors of Canada owned the Wrangler name there. Underneath, it was very much an updated CJ-7, with the same 93.4-inch wheelbase, leaf springs at both ends and a body that was largely interchangeable with the old tub. The rectangular headlights were new, and the fight over them has never really stopped.

### A CJ-7 WITH MANNERS
Development of a CJ-7 replacement was approved in 1982. Chuck Mashigan's design was frozen by the fall of 1983, CJ-7-based mules ran late that year, and the first production-body prototypes followed in spring 1984. The brief was to keep the CJ's character while making it calmer on the road. The YJ kept leaf springs similar to the CJ's but made them wider, added track bars and anti-roll bars, and widened the track. Ground clearance dropped slightly as a result.
Wikipedia notes that the anti-roll bars made the Wrangler less easy to flip for untrained or unwary drivers. That mattered for a vehicle being sold to a much wider public than the CJ's farmers and diehards. The YJ also got a bigger windshield, with wipers that parked on the glass because their wider sweep needed the room. Both details disappeared when the TJ arrived. Hagerty calls the square lamps 'a point of contention for many Jeep lovers yet a point of pride for YJ owners', which is a polite way of describing a feud that has lasted since 1986.

### FOURS, SIXES AND A FRENCH GEARBOX
Early YJs offered two engines. The 2.5-liter AMC four had throttle-body injection and 117 hp, which was actually more than the carry-over 4.2-liter six. That carbureted 258 made 112 hp but far more torque, and it fed its Carter BBD through a computer-controlled feedback system with a lot of vacuum hose. The six was originally paired with a Peugeot BA-10/5 five-speed, which ExtremeTerrain calls historically unreliable, and the 1987-only NP207 transfer case. The NP231 replaced the NP207 for 1988, and the Aisin AX-15 replaced the Peugeot from 1989.
The big change came in 1991, when the fuel-injected 4.0-liter six replaced the 258. Hagerty quotes 180 hp, and says it is often the most desirable YJ engine, worth a larger premium over the four. Through the run, the front axle was a Dana 30 with a vacuum-operated disconnect, and the rear was a Dana 35 with a Dana 44 available in some years. Later changes added an extended roll cage for rear shoulder belts (1992), optional anti-lock brakes (1993), an automatic for the four-cylinder (1994), and larger front U-joints (1995).

### ISLANDERS, RENEGADES AND A THEME PARK
The YJ was sold as a fashion item as much as a tool, and the trim list shows it. The Laredo got chrome and a hardtop, the 1988 Sahara got body-color flares and green trail-cloth seats, and the 1988–1993 Islander wore sunset graphics. The Renegade Decor Group, fitted by Autostyle in Detroit from October 1990, added the 4.0, 8-inch alloy wheels and a widebody look for $4,266 over a base Wrangler in 1991. The 1995 Rio Grande closed the run with a Pueblo-themed interior. Sahara YJs also starred in Jurassic Park in 1993. Hagerty's price data says Renegades bring the most today, followed fairly closely by Saharas and Islanders. The Islander runs about 11 percent above a base model.

### HOW IT ENDED
YJs were built in Brampton, Ontario, until that plant closed on April 23, 1992, and then in Toledo, Ohio, the factory that had built Willys Jeeps in the war. Production of the 1995 model year ended in December 1995, with 632,231 YJs built. There was no 1996 Wrangler, although leftover YJs were still being sold into mid-1996. The TJ that followed brought back round headlights and replaced the leaf springs with coils, which made the YJ the last Jeep with a leaf-sprung front axle.
For years that made the YJ the unwanted Wrangler: too new to be a classic CJ and too crude to compete with coil-sprung trucks. Hagerty now puts a median #3-condition YJ at about $8,100, against $9,900 for an earlier CJ-7, and notes that interest is rising, particularly among Gen Xers who grew up with the square-eyed Jeep.

### Data plate
- Chassis: YJ (Jeep YJ in Canada)
- Production: March 1986 – December 1995
- Model Years: 1987–1995 (no 1996)
- Built: Brampton, Ontario (to April 1992) · Toledo, Ohio
- Units: 632,231 through MY1995
- Engines: 2.5 L I4 · 4.2 L I6 (1987–90) · 4.0 L I6 (1991–95)
- Manuals: AX-5 · Peugeot BA-10/5 (1987–89) · AX-15
- Transfer Case: NP207 (1987) · NP231 (1988–95)
- Axles: Dana 30 front · Dana 35 rear (Dana 44 optional)
- Suspension: Leaf springs, track bars, anti-roll bars
- Wheelbase: 93.4 in (2,372 mm)
- Curb Weight: 2,855–3,241 lb

### Engineering
The YJ is a ladder-frame, leaf-sprung Jeep built on the CJ-7's 93.4-inch wheelbase, with wider springs, track bars and anti-roll bars at both ends. The front axle is a Dana 30 with a vacuum disconnect, and the rear is a Dana 35, with a Dana 44 available in some years. Part-time four-wheel drive came through the NP207 for 1987 only and the NP231 from 1988.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, 93.4 in (2,372 mm) wheelbase (The same wheelbase as the CJ-7. The body is largely interchangeable with the CJ tub.)
- Suspension: Leaf springs front and rear (Wider springs than the CJ's, plus track bars and anti-roll bars. This is the last Jeep with a leaf-sprung front axle.)
- Front Axle: Dana 30, vacuum disconnect (The vacuum motor locks the split right-side shaft for 4WD. Larger front U-joints arrived for 1995.)
- Rear Axle: Dana 35 (Dana 44 optional some years) (Trac-Lok limited slip was an option.)
- Transfer Case: NP207 (1987), NP231 (1988–95) (ExtremeTerrain calls the NP207 a poor unit that was dropped after one year.)
- Engines: 2.5 I4 · 4.2 I6 (to 1990) · 4.0 I6 (1991–95) (The 4.2 is carbureted. The 4.0 brought multi-point injection and about 180 hp.)

### Versions
- 1987–1990 · YJ · 4.2 L AMC 258 I6, Carter BBD carb · 112 hp / 210 lb-ft · Peugeot BA-10/5 five-speed for 1987–89, AX-15 from 1989. Three-speed 999 automatic optional.
- 1987–1995 · YJ · 2.5 L AMC 150 I4, throttle-body injection (multi-point from 1991) · 117 hp at launch · AX-5 five-speed. A three-speed 30RH automatic was available from 1994. NHTSA decodes 1991–95 four-cylinder VINs as multi-point injection.
- 1991–1995 · YJ · 4.0 L AMC 242 I6, multi-point injection · ≈180 hp · AX-15 five-speed; the automatic was the A999 for 1991, then the 32RH (Wikipedia). Hagerty calls the 4.0 often the most desirable YJ engine.
- 1991–1994 · YJ Renegade · 4.0 L I6 · ≈180 hp · Renegade Decor Group fitted by Autostyle, Detroit, from October 1990.
- 1995 · YJ Rio Grande · 2.5 L I4 (base S) · — · Final-year trim package that Wikipedia says was added to the base four-cylinder S, with a Pueblo-themed interior. Larger front U-joints this year.

### Year-by-year
- 1987: YJ launches (unveiled February 1986, on sale May 1986) with the 2.5 L four or carbureted 4.2 L six and the NP207 transfer case, used only this year
- 1988: NP231 transfer case replaces the NP207; Sahara trim debuts; Islander package runs 1988–93
- 1989: Aisin AX-15 five-speed replaces the Peugeot BA-10 behind the 4.2 L six
- 1991: Fuel-injected 4.0 L six replaces the carbureted 4.2; Hagerty says the 4.0 sixes are often the most desirable YJs. Renegade Decor Group arrives (built from October 1990) [buy]
- 1992: Brampton plant closes in April and production moves to Toledo; roll cage extended for rear shoulder belts; electronic speedometer
- 1993: Anti-lock brakes become optional
- 1994: Automatic offered with the four; center high-mounted stop lamp. Manual trucks get an external clutch slave cylinder (Wikipedia; 4WD Mechanix says 1993), which is why SlashGear calls 1994–95 the best YJ years: no pulling the gearbox to replace the slave [buy]
- 1995: Larger Dana 30 U-joints (297x) and 1330 rear pinion joint; Rio Grande package; last YJs (there is no 1996 Wrangler)

### Capability
- Towing: 2,000 lb (907 kg) six · 1,000 lb (454 kg) four (Quadratec's 1990 and 1995 spec sheets)
- Payload: 800 lb (363 kg)
- Fuel tank: 15 US gal (57 L) standard; 20 US gal (76 L) optional (Quadratec lists 20 gal for 1995)
- Ground clearance: 8.2 in (208 mm)
- Wheelbase: 93.4 in (2,372 mm)
- Curb weight: 2,855–3,241 lb (1,295–1,470 kg) (varies with engine and equipment)
- Fuel economy: EPA 15 city / 20 hwy (1991 4.0, manual) · 14 / 17 (1995 4.0, manual) (fueleconomy.gov's revised figures)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 205/75R15 or 215/75R15 (base models), 225/75R15 (some trims), 30x9.50R15 LT on 15x8 alloys (Renegade)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x114.3 (5x4.5")
- Center Bore: 71.5 mm
- Lug Thread: 1/2"-20
- Note: Factory torque not confirmed from a YJ owner's manual. Quadratec's generic chart gives 75–85 lb-ft for 1/2 in studs and says to check the owner's manual.
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 30x9.50R15 (Jeep's own Renegade size, so it fits an unmodified YJ; bigger tires on stock springs depend on wheel backspacing and flares.)
- Biggest tire, 2.5 in lift: 31x10.50R15 (Rough Country's 2.5 in YJ kit lists clearance for 31s on 15x8 wheels; test-fit the wheel and tire before you commit.)
- Biggest tire, 4 in lift: 33x12.50R17 (Rough Country's 4 in YJ kit lists 33x12.50 on 17-, 18- and 20-inch wheels; the 20-inch combos need minor trimming. Plan a re-gear from the factory ratio.)

### Buying checks
- Frame, spring hangers and floors first: Quadratec's inspection checklist names the rear leaf-spring mounts, frame rails, skid-plate mounts, rear crossmember, driver-side floor and roll-bar mounts. Lift the carpet: it warns that moisture trapped under old padding rots YJ floor pans from the top down.
- Does 4WD actually engage?: The front axle is engaged by a vacuum motor. If the 4WD light stays off, or 4WD feels inconsistent, suspect dry-rotted, cracked or disconnected vacuum lines. Many owners convert to a cable-operated disconnect.
- Clutch slave cylinder (early YJs): Early manual YJs use an internal slave cylinder built into the release bearing. 4WD Mechanix dates it to 1987–92 with an external slave from 1993; Wikipedia says the slave moved outside the bellhousing for 1994, and Advance Adapters sells its internal-bearing hose kit for 1987–93. When the internal slave leaks, fluid can ruin the clutch disc, and replacing it means pulling the transmission. Look for fluid weeping from the bellhousing and a sinking pedal, and check whether the slave is visible on the outside of the bellhousing.
- Know the gearbox and transfer case: Six-cylinder trucks from 1987–89 may have the Peugeot BA-10/5, which ExtremeTerrain calls historically unreliable. A 1987 may also have the NP207 transfer case. An AX-15 and NP231 combination is what most buyers want.
- Carbureted 4.2 or injected 4.0?: The 1987–90 4.2 uses a computer-controlled Carter BBD with a maze of vacuum lines that are prone to leaks. It can be made reliable, but the 1991–95 4.0 is the engine Hagerty says commands the premium.
- Leaf springs, shackles and bushings: Check for sagging or broken leaves, cracked bushings, rusted shackles and uneven ride height. Most YJs are more than 30 years old, so tired springs are normal and fresh ones change the ride.
- Electrical grounds: Flickering lights, jumping gauges and intermittent starting often come from bad grounds. Quadratec suggests cleaning the firewall ground straps and battery connections before chasing anything bigger.
- The rear axle: Most YJs have the Dana 35 rear. Drivingline calls the same axle in the TJ 'junk' because of its C-clip design, so if you plan bigger tires, price in a Dana 44 swap or upgraded shafts. A factory Dana 44 is worth looking for.

### Common repairs
#### Fix the vacuum front-axle disconnect (or convert to cable)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ An afternoon to diagnose; longer if the axle shift parts are worn · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: 4WD light stays off, the front axle won't drive in 4H, or it engages and drops out with a clunk under load at speed.
Fix: The 4WD Mechanix forum's diagnosis runs in order. First, bleed-down test the shift motor and lines with a hand vacuum pump and gauge, and confirm the motor holds vacuum. Check that the engage and disengage ports at the transfer case switch and motor get steady vacuum (about 17 in. Hg in that thread). Then test the supply side: reserve tank, check valve, hoses and manifold fittings. Tee a gauge into the engage line and road test, watching for drops under load. If vacuum holds, pull the shift motor and inspect the shift fork, clutch hub and axle shafts. The common permanent fix is a cable-operated disconnect, such as the JKS Posi-Lok.
Tools: Hand vacuum pump with gauge · vacuum hose and connectors · check valve · gasket for the disconnect cover.

#### Replace the clutch and internal slave cylinder (early YJs)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A full weekend · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Sinking or spongy clutch pedal, fluid loss from the clutch reservoir, a slipping clutch after fluid has soaked the disc, and fluid at the bottom of the bellhousing.
Fix: On early YJs (1987–92 per 4WD Mechanix; through 1993 per Wikipedia and Advance Adapters) the slave is part of the release bearing inside the bellhousing, so this is a clutch job. 4WD Mechanix's YJ/TJ procedure: remove the transfer case, loosen the hydraulic line with flare-nut wrenches, then drain and cap the line. Loosen the crankshaft position sensor so it isn't damaged, and unclip wiring. Support the transmission on a jack and the engine under the oil pan, and lower no more than about 3 inches. Slide the transmission and bellhousing straight back. Mark the flywheel and pressure plate, loosen the cover bolts in a crisscross pattern, and inspect the flywheel and pilot bearing. Fit a new disc and slave/release bearing, then bleed with clean DOT 3 or DOT 4 fluid.
Tools: Transmission jack · flare-nut wrenches · clutch alignment tool · torque wrench · brake washer (treat old linings as if they contain asbestos) · DOT 3/4 fluid.

#### Rebuild the 4.2's Carter BBD feedback carburetor (1987–90)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day, including diagnosis · cost Rebuild kit plus your time
Symptoms: Stalling, flooding, hunting idle, loss of power or running hot. Many of these are vacuum leaks or ignition faults rather than the carburetor itself.
Fix: Moses Ludel's 4WD Mechanix guide says to diagnose before rebuilding. Check plugs, wires, cap and rotor, the vacuum and centrifugal advance, the PCV and every emissions vacuum hose. Mist penetrant near the throttle shaft ends at idle to find leaks. If the carb is the problem, record the idle mixture screw turns, strip it, and clean metal parts in carb cleaner. Clean rubber, plastic and electrical parts with alcohol. Clear the idle fuel pickup tubes, since a clogged one caused stalling in his example. Free the stepper motor's sticky rack. Set float height with a T-gauge, then the vacuum piston gap, metering rods, pump and choke to the kit specs. Refit with a new base gasket.
Tools: T-gauge · hand vacuum pump · timing light · carb cleaner · alcohol · thread locker · Mopar or Echlin/NAPA premium rebuild kit (Ludel's preference).

#### Replace leaf springs, shackles and bushings
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour per pair of bushings (ExtremeTerrain); longer for full springs · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Sagging or uneven ride height, clunks over bumps, cracked or squeezed-out bushings, broken leaves and rusted shackles.
Fix: Following Skyjacker's YJ instructions: support the frame on stands, remove the wheels, shocks and U-bolts, and hold the axle on a floor jack. Unbolt the old springs. Grease the new urethane bushings and sleeves and press them into the spring eyes. Factory rear springs put the small eye at the rear. Install the springs with the eye and shackle bolts loose, set the axle back on the spring center pins, and fit new U-bolts (the kit specifies 90 ft-lb at the front). Tighten the eye and shackle bolts only with the vehicle on the ground and loaded, then re-torque the U-bolts after 50 and 100 miles. For bushings alone, ExtremeTerrain says to clean the spring eyes and shackle brackets back to bare metal and grease every contact surface.
Tools: Jack stands · floor jack · press or vise for bushings · wire brush · grease · torque wrench · new U-bolts.

#### Replace the rear main seal (4.0 / 4.2 six)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day · cost Seal kit and oil pan gasket; shops charge mostly for labor
Symptoms: Oil dripping from where the engine meets the bellhousing, and an oily transmission and crossmember. Rule out the valve cover and oil pan gaskets first, because oil runs downhill.
Fix: The AMC six uses a two-piece rear main seal that is replaced from underneath without removing the transmission. Drain the oil, remove the starter and the oil pan, and mark the rear main bearing cap so it goes back the same way. Remove both seal halves, using a pick and a thin punch to work the upper half around the crank. Install the new halves with only a dab of RTV where they meet the cap, being careful not to nick the lip (one owner had to buy a second set). Torque the cap bolts to 80 ft-lb, the rear main bearing cap figure for the 4.0 and 4.2 in ExtremeTerrain's YJ engine torque table, refit the pan with a new gasket and refill. While the pan is off, check crank end play.
Tools: Pick · thin punch · torque wrench · RTV · oil pan gasket · new oil and filter.

#### Cut out and replace rusted floor pans
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend per side · cost Panels plus welding consumables, or body-shop labor
Symptoms: Soft, flaking or holed metal under the driver's carpet, water in the footwell, and rust around the seat and roll-bar mounts.
Fix: Pull the carpet and padding: Quadratec notes trapped moisture under old padding is what rots YJ floors. Wire-brush the area to find good metal, mark a cut line inside the sound metal, and cut out the rot without cutting into the frame or body mounts. Trim the replacement pan to overlap or butt the opening, clamp it, tack it, then stitch-weld to avoid warping. Seam-seal and paint both sides, and don't put the old soggy padding back. Repair any body-mount or roll-bar mount areas properly, because those carry loads.
Tools: Cut-off wheel · grinder · MIG welder · clamps · seam sealer · primer and paint.

#### Chase down front-end shimmy and worn steering
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ An afternoon to inspect; parts swaps vary · cost Parts plus alignment
Symptoms: A violent side-to-side shake after a bump at around 45 mph, wandering, or a clunk when you turn the wheel with the engine off.
Fix: Quadratec's death-wobble guide applies to any solid front axle. Disconnect the steering stabilizer so it can't hide anything. Have a helper rock the wheel a quarter turn each way while you watch the track bar for movement at both ends. Jack up the front and check tie-rod ends for play, ball joints by prying the tire, and wheel bearings by rocking the wheel at 12 and 6 o'clock. Inspect control points and bushings. Tighten everything to spec, replace what moves, check tire balance and pressure, then get an alignment from a 4x4-savvy shop. A stronger stabilizer only masks the problem.
Tools: Pry bar · floor jack and stands · torque wrench · helper.

### Baseline service
Assume a 30-year-old YJ has had whatever was cheapest. Change every fluid, chase the vacuum system and grounds, and know which drivetrain you have: the carbureted 4.2 (1987–90) and the injected 4.0 (1991–95) need different tune-up parts, and the 1987–89 six may still have the Peugeot gearbox.
- Engine oil & filter: SAE 10W-30 (Quadratec); ExtremeTerrain lists 10W-30 or 5W-30 · ≈4 qt (2.5) / 6 qt (4.0, 4.2) with filter (Quadratec) · Haynes lists every 7,500 mi or 12 months (3,000 mi in severe use) (Drain-plug torque: ExtremeTerrain's TJ-era table gives 25 ft-lb for the 2.5 and 4.0 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL for your YJ]. ExtremeTerrain lists separate filters for 87–93 and 91–06 engines, so check which one yours takes.)
- Air filter & PCV: Engine air filter and PCV filter/valve · Every 30,000 mi or 24 months (Haynes); sooner on dusty trails. Haynes also lists the fuel filter for 1987–95 models. (On the 4.2, Ludel lists the PCV valve and air cleaner among the first checks before blaming the carburetor.)
- Spark plugs, cap & rotor: Plug torque 27 ft-lb for all YJ engines (ExtremeTerrain's YJ engine torque table, matching its 1997–2006 TJ table) · Every 30,000 mi (Haynes) (Both the 4.2 and 4.0 in the YJ use a distributor. Haynes lists inspecting the plug wires, cap and rotor on 2003-and-earlier models, so do them with the plugs.)
- 4.2 carburetor, fuel filter & vacuum lines (1987–90): Carter BBD feedback carburetor · mechanical fuel pump · Now, then inspect at every service (Ludel says a clogged filter, a weak mechanical pump or a vacuum leak can mimic carburetor faults. Replace brittle vacuum hose before rebuilding anything.)
- Coolant: 50/50 antifreeze and water (ExtremeTerrain) · ≈9 qt (2.5), 10.5 qt (4.0 and 4.2) (Quadratec chart) · antifreeze type [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Every 30,000 mi or 24 months (Haynes) (Inspect the radiator, hoses and fan clutch while you're there. ExtremeTerrain lists a fan clutch that fits all YJs.)
- Manual transmission (AX-5 / AX-15 / BA-10): 75W-90 GL-3 or GL-4 for the AX-5 and AX-15 (ExtremeTerrain) · ≈3.3 qt AX-5/AX-15, 5.2 pints BA-10/5 (Quadratec chart) [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Change now, then every 30,000 mi (Retailer charts disagree slightly on AX-15 capacity (3.25–3.32 qt), so fill to the bottom of the fill hole. Haynes lists a 30,000-mile change.)
- Automatic transmission (999 / 32RH / 30RH): Mopar ATF of the type on the dipstick or in the manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · total capacity 8.3 qt TF999, 17.1 pints 32RH, 7 qt 30RH (Quadratec chart); a pan drop takes much less · Every 30,000 mi, or 12,000 mi in severe use (Haynes) (Change the pan filter at the same time. ExtremeTerrain's YJ torque table gives 35 in-lb for the 30RH/32RH filter screws and 14 ft-lb for the pan bolts.)
- Transfer case (NP207 / NP231): ATF (ExtremeTerrain lists ATF+3 or ATF+4 for the NP231) · NP231 2.2 pints, NP207 4.4 pints (Quadratec chart) · fill until it runs out of the fill hole · Every 30,000 mi (Haynes) (ExtremeTerrain's YJ torque table gives 15–25 ft-lb for the NP231 drain and fill plugs. Inspect the output seals: Quadratec lists them among common leaks.)
- Front & rear differentials: GL-5 80W-90 or 75W-140 synthetic · +4 oz limited-slip additive for Trac-Lok (Quadratec chart) · Dana 30 2.5 pt, Dana 35 3.5 pt, Dana 44 4.0 pt (Quadratec chart) [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Every 30,000 mi (Haynes), and after deep water crossings (ExtremeTerrain) (Cover bolts take 30 ft-lb in ExtremeTerrain's TJ-era table for the same Dana axles [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]. Check the Dana 30 disconnect housing and pinion seals for leaks.)
- Vacuum disconnect system: Shift motor, check valve, reserve tank and hoses · Now, and whenever 4WD is slow to engage (Quadratec lists dry-rotted or cracked vacuum lines as the usual cause of a YJ that won't engage 4WD.)
- Brake & clutch hydraulic fluid: DOT 3 (ExtremeTerrain); Ludel uses DOT 4 in the clutch for heat resistance · About every two years (The clutch shares brake fluid type. On 1987–92 trucks a falling clutch reservoir points to the internal slave.)
- Chassis grease, U-joints & spring bushings: Lubricate chassis components (Haynes) · Every 7,500 mi or 12 months (Haynes) (Grease the steering joints and driveshaft U-joints, and check the shackles and spring bushings for cracks.)
- Electrical grounds & battery: Firewall ground straps and battery terminals · Now (Quadratec suggests cleaning the grounds first when you see flickering lights, jumping gauges or intermittent starting.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: A stock YJ usually takes 30-inch tires on stock rims without trouble. Four Wheel Trends says 31x10.50s can be squeezed on, but they may need wheels with different backspacing and can still rub, so don't wheel that setup hard without a lift.

Q: Which YJ should I buy?
A: Most buyers want a 1991–1995 truck with the fuel-injected 4.0 six. Hagerty calls it often the most desirable engine and says it commands a larger premium over the four. SlashGear narrows it to 1994–95, because earlier manual trucks have the internal clutch slave cylinder that means pulling the gearbox to replace it. For 1987–90, Hagerty says the four- and six-cylinder versions differ by only a few hundred dollars in #3 condition.

Q: Why does the YJ have square headlights?
A: Neither Wikipedia nor Hagerty gives an official reason. Wikipedia says only that the rectangular lamps set it apart from the round-eyed CJs. The TJ brought round headlights back for 1997. Owners who can't live with them fit round-headlight conversion kits.

Q: My 4WD light won't come on. Is the transfer case broken?
A: Probably not. The YJ front axle is engaged by a vacuum motor, and Quadratec says dry-rotted, cracked or disconnected vacuum lines are the usual culprit. Test the system with a hand vacuum pump before buying parts, or convert to a cable-operated disconnect.

Q: Should I avoid the Peugeot gearbox?
A: Six-cylinder YJs from 1987–89 could have the Peugeot BA-10/5 five-speed, which ExtremeTerrain describes as historically unreliable. Wikipedia lists the Aisin AX-15 behind the 4.2 from 1989, and the AX-15 stayed with the 4.0 through 1995. Four-cylinder trucks use the AX-5.

Q: NP207 or NP231 transfer case?
A: The NP207 was used on 1987 YJs only, and ExtremeTerrain calls it a poor unit. The NP231, used from 1988 onward, is the stronger and far better-supported case. A 1988–95 YJ will have the NP231.

Q: Which years have the internal clutch slave cylinder?
A: Sources disagree. 4WD Mechanix says 1987–92 YJs used a slave cylinder built into the release bearing and that 1993 brought the external slave and pivot arm used in the TJ. Wikipedia dates the move outside the bellhousing to 1994, and Advance Adapters lists its internal-bearing hose kit for 1987–93. Treat 1993 as either, and look for an external slave on the bellhousing. The internal type means pulling the transmission to replace it.

Q: What fluids do the axles and transfer case take?
A: Quadratec's factory-based chart lists GL-5 80W-90 or 75W-140 synthetic for the Dana 30, Dana 35 and Dana 44, with 4 oz of limited-slip additive for a Trac-Lok. ExtremeTerrain recommends 75W-140 in the rear for warm-weather towing. The NP231 takes automatic transmission fluid (ExtremeTerrain lists ATF+3 or ATF+4); Quadratec's chart gives 2.2 pints for the NP231 and 4.4 pints for the NP207. Haynes' maintenance schedule changes the transfer case and differential lubricant every 30,000 miles or 24 months. Capacities in retailer charts disagree, so fill to the bottom of the fill hole [CONFIRM IN MANUAL].

Q: Can the 4.2's carburetor be made reliable?
A: Yes. Moses Ludel's 4WD Mechanix guide says the Carter BBD can be reliable when rebuilt to factory specs, and that a clogged fuel filter, a weak mechanical pump or a vacuum leak can mimic carburetor faults. He calls Mopar's multi-point injection conversion the bigger upgrade.

Q: Is a YJ a good investment?
A: Hagerty puts a median #3-condition YJ at about $8,100, against $9,900 for an earlier CJ-7. Its Hagerty Vehicle Rating is 86 and climbing while the CJ's has fallen, although Hagerty says the rating is not a predictor of future collectability. Renegades bring the most, followed by Saharas and Islanders.

Q: What's the difference between the Sahara, Islander and Renegade?
A: The Sahara (from 1988) included most options, with body-color flares, green trail-cloth seats and fog lamps. The Islander (1988–93) had sunset graphics and body-color flares and steps. The Renegade Decor Group (October 1990–94) added the 4.0, 8-inch alloy wheels and a widebody look.
