## Jeep Grand Cherokee ZJ (1993–1998)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/grand-cherokee-zj/
Codes: ZJ, ZG, 5.9 Limited

Verdict: AMC drew it, Chrysler launched it through a plate-glass window, and for a few years it was the SUV every suburb wanted. Now it's one of the cheapest ways into coil springs, solid axles and a 4.0 or Magnum V8. Just budget for the leaks and check the steering.

The ZJ Grand Cherokee went on sale in April 1992 as a 1993 model. It was a bigger, plusher Cherokee XJ that AMC had started developing in the 1980s to replace both the XJ and the full-size Grand Wagoneer. It kept solid axles front and rear on coil springs, offered the 4.0 straight six or a Magnum V8, and introduced a fully automatic full-time 4WD system called Quadra-Trac. Thirty years on, it's the forgotten middle child of the Jeep lineup, and that is exactly why it makes such a good budget wheeler.

### AN AMC IDEA, A CHRYSLER LAUNCH
AMC hired outside designers to sketch a larger follow-up to the XJ, and Larry Shinoda styled a prototype in 1985. Shinoda had to sue to be paid and credited, and after Chrysler bought AMC in 1987 it settled with his estate for more than $200,000. A running pre-production version appeared in 1989 as the 'Jeep Concept 1'. Dodge also built a ZJ-based Ramcharger replacement with its own grille, but cancelled it before launch.
Chrysler built the truck at the new Jefferson North Assembly Plant in Detroit and introduced it at the January 1992 Detroit auto show in style. Chrysler's Bob Lutz drove a red Laredo from the factory to Cobo Hall, then he and Mayor Coleman Young drove it up the front steps and through a plate-glass window into the lobby. Export trucks built by Magna Steyr in Graz, Austria, carry the code ZG.

### WHAT MADE IT DIFFERENT
At launch every ZJ had the 190 hp 4.0 six. Early in 1993 the 5.2 Magnum V8 arrived, making it the only SUV in its class with a V8 option, and with it a woodgrain Grand Wagoneer version that lasted one year and 6,378 trucks. There were three 4WD systems: part-time Command-Trac (NP231), Selec-Trac (NP242) with a full-time mode, and the new Quadra-Trac (NV249). Quadra-Trac was a permanent system with a viscous coupling that sent drive forward when the rear slipped, with no driver input needed. A driver's airbag and four-wheel ABS were standard.
Underneath, both axles sit on coil springs with four control arms and a track bar each, which Jeep called Quadra-Link. It's a close cousin of the setup the Wrangler TJ got for 1997, and much of the TJ and XJ aftermarket bolts on. The ZJ was Motor Trend's 1993 Truck of the Year, the V8 made Car and Driver's Ten Best list, and Petersen's named it 4x4 of the Year in 1993, 1996 and 1998.

### 1996 FACELIFT AND THE 5.9 LIMITED
The 1996 update brought new bumpers and cladding, a bigger grille, a new interior with a passenger airbag, and an OBD-II port. The manual gearbox had already gone after 1994, and Command-Trac and the base SE were dropped. The 4.0 was rerated at 185 hp. The NV249 was revised: from 1996 low range gave a true 50/50 lock instead of still running through the viscous coupling.
For 1998 Jeep fitted the 5.9 Magnum V8 from the Ram pickup to create the 5.9 Limited. It made 245 hp and 345 lb-ft, came with louvered hood, mesh grille, 16 in wheels, 3.73 gears and a rear Trac-Lok, and needed premium fuel. Motor Trend timed it at 6.8 seconds to 60 mph, and Jeep advertised it as the world's fastest SUV. Kevin's Offroad puts 1998 production at 14,286 out of 247,372 Grand Cherokees. Then the WJ arrived and the ZJ was gone.

### THE BUDGET WHEELER
Today the ZJ is cheap. Bring a Trailer's ZJ sales over the past year ran from $4,250 to $18,500, and ordinary trucks change hands for less. OffroadXtreme calls the 4.0 one of Jeep's most reliable engines, if a little underpowered for the ZJ's weight, and the 5.2 'extremely reliable'. The catches are rust, leaks, worn steering and the age of the Quadra-Trac and Selec-Trac cases.
Its contemporaries were the third-generation 4Runner, the Discovery and, further up the price list, the 80 Series and P38 Range Rover. Of that group, the ZJ is usually the cheapest way in. Its successor, the WJ, moved to gerotor-based Quadra-Trac II and Quadra-Drive, so the ZJ remains the last Grand Cherokee with the simpler chain-and-viscous Quadra-Trac.

### Engineering
The ZJ is a unibody SUV with solid axles at both ends, each located by four control arms and a track bar and sprung on coils. The wheelbase is 105.9 in, and Wikipedia gives curb weights of 3,574 lb with the six and 3,901 lb with the V8. Choose your drivetrain carefully: three transfer cases, five automatic gearboxes and several rear axles were fitted over six years.
- Structure: Unibody, 105.9 in wheelbase (Length 178.7 in (1993–95), 181.2 in (1996–98). The Up Country package added taller springs and heavier shocks for about an inch more height.)
- Engines: 4.0 I6 · 5.2 Magnum V8 · 5.9 Magnum V8 (1998) (4.0: 190 hp / 225 lb-ft (1993–95), 185 hp / 220 lb-ft (1996–98). 5.2: 220 hp at launch, later 225 hp / 300 lb-ft. 5.9: 245 hp / 345 lb-ft. A 2.5 VM diesel was export-only.)
- Transmissions: AW4 · 42RE · AX15 manual · 46RH · 44RE · 46RE (AW4 on early 1993 sixes, then 42RE. AX15 five-speed 1993–94 (North America). 46RH on 1993–95 V8s, 44RE on 1996–98 5.2s, 46RE on the 5.9.)
- 4Wd Systems: Command-Trac NP231 · Selec-Trac NP242 · Quadra-Trac NV249 (Command-Trac dropped for 1996. NV249 is full-time with a viscous coupling; from 1996 its low range locks 50/50.)
- Axles: Dana 30 front · Dana 35, Dana 44 or Chrysler 8.25 rear (Rear axle varies by year, engine and package; read the tag. The 5.9 Limited has 3.73 gears and a rear Trac-Lok.)
- Wheels & Brakes: 5x4.5 in bolt pattern · 1/2-20 studs · 71.5 mm bore (Four-wheel ABS standard at launch. Factory tires from 215/75R15 to 245/70R15 and 225/70R16.)

### Versions
- 1993 · Base, Laredo, Limited · Grand Wagoneer · 4.0 I6 · 5.2 V8 (from early 1993) · 190 hp · 220 hp · Launch year. AW4 then 42RE, AX15 manual, 46RH with the V8. Grand Wagoneer: 6,378 built.
- 1994–1995 · SE, Laredo, Limited · Orvis (1995) · 4.0 I6 · 5.2 V8 · 190 hp · 220–225 hp · Manual dropped after 1994. Orvis Edition: 10,020 built in 1995.
- 1996–1997 · Laredo, Limited · Orvis · TSi (1997) · 4.0 I6 · 5.2 V8 · 185 hp · 225 hp · Facelift, passenger airbag, OBD-II. Command-Trac dropped; revised NV249.
- 1998 · Laredo, Limited, TSi · 4.0 I6 · 5.2 V8 · 185 hp · 225 hp · Final year; production ended mid-1998.
- 1998 · 5.9 Limited · 5.9 Magnum V8 · 46RE · 245 hp / 345 lb-ft · One year only: 14,286 built. Louvered hood, mesh grille, 3.73 gears, rear Trac-Lok.
- 1995–1998 · ZG export · 2.5 VM Motori turbodiesel I4 · 114 hp / 221 lb-ft · Built in Graz, Austria, with a five-speed manual. Not sold in the US.

### Year-by-year
- 1992: Revealed at the January Detroit show; 1993-model trucks on sale in April with the 4.0 six only
- 1993: 5.2 Magnum V8, Quadra-Trac (NV249) and the one-year woodgrain Grand Wagoneer arrive early in the year; AW4 replaced by the 42RE mid-year
- 1994: Base model renamed SE; Infinity Gold audio; Grand Wagoneer dropped; last year of the AX15 manual in North America
- 1995: Orvis Edition (10,020 built); SE gains standard power windows, ABS and A/C
- 1996: Facelift and new interior with dual airbags, OBD-II, revised NV249 with a true 50/50 low range; Command-Trac and SE dropped; 4.0 rerated to 185 hp
- 1997: TSi and Laredo Special Edition; 5.2 V8 available with 2WD; last Orvis year
- 1998: One-year 5.9 Limited (245 hp, 14,286 built); production ends mid-1998 as the WJ takes over

### Capability
- Towing: 5,000 lb (2,270 kg) (5.2 V8 at launch and 4.0 by 1995, per Wikipedia)
- Fuel tank: 23 US gal (87 L) (87 octane; the 5.9 needs premium)
- Fuel economy: EPA 14/19 mpg (4.0) · 12/17 (5.2) · 11/16 (5.9) (city/highway, 4WD automatic, current EPA method)
- Curb weight: 3,574 lb (1,621 kg) I6 · 3,901 lb (1,769 kg) V8
- Wheelbase: 105.9 in (2,690 mm)
- Length: 178.7 in (1993–95) · 181.2 in (1996–98)
- 0–60 mph: 8.3 s (5.2, Motor Trend 1995) · 6.8 s (5.9 Limited, Motor Trend 1998)
- Crash rating: IIHS Marginal (moderate overlap, 1996–98) (NHTSA frontal driver 4 stars (1993–95), 3 stars (1996–98))

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 215/75R15 (base/SE, Laredo, TSi), 225/75R15 (most Laredos and early Limiteds), 235/75R15 (1993 Laredo and Limited option), 245/70R15 (1996–98 Laredo option), 225/70R16 (1996–98 Limited, Orvis, 5.9 Limited)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x114.3 (5x4.5")
- Center Bore: 71.5 mm
- Lug Thread: 1/2"-20
- Lug Torque: 75–85 lb-ft is Quadratec's typical range for 1/2" lugs [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 30x9.50R15 (One owner ran 30x9.50 BFGoodrich all-terrains on a stock '93 and said they came close to rubbing but didn't (Off-Road.com forum))
- Biggest tire, 1.5–2 in lift: 30x9.50R15 (31x10.50R15 with trimming) (Rough Country and Zone rate their spacer lifts for 30x9.50s; one Quadratec reviewer fit 31x10.50R15s on the Zone 2 in kit after trimming the front bumper)
- Biggest tire, 3.5 in lift: 31x10.50R15 (Rough Country's 3.5 in kit, with transfer-case drop and fixed lower arms, is rated for 31x10.50s)

### Buying checks
- Rust is the deal-breaker: OffroadXtreme says nearly every ZJ outside the desert has some rust, usually on the lower doors, the rockers and the bottom of the hatch, which can stop it opening. Heavy rust in the unibody frame rails is a reason to walk away.
- Test for death wobble at 35–50 mph: Hit a bump in that speed range and feel for violent shaking from the front axle. OffroadXtreme says the lower track bar bolt is usually the cause, though worn tie-rod ends, ball joints and bushings also contribute. NHTSA recalled some 1993 trucks for front lower control arm cam bolts (93V-051).
- Work the transfer case through every mode: Find out whether it has Command-Trac, Selec-Trac or Quadra-Trac, then shift through every position on a loose surface. OffroadXtreme says Selec-Trac linkages often stick, and many owners swap to the simpler part-time NP231. Quadra-Trac needs four matching tires; NHTSA recalled 1996 trucks because the front axle could overheat on the temporary spare.
- Find the leaks: On the 4.0, OffroadXtreme lists the rear main seal, oil pan gasket, valve cover gasket and oil filter adapter gasket. On the V8s it's the rear main, the valve covers and the oil pressure sending unit. Most are easy fixes, but a rear main can be a multi-day job.
- Watch the temperature gauge: OffroadXtreme lists an insufficient cooling system among the common ZJ faults. Let the truck idle hot, then drive it up a hill, with the A/C on if it has it. A tired radiator or fan clutch is cheaper to fix before you tow or wheel it.
- Test the small stuff: OffroadXtreme's list: rear hatch stuck shut, failed alarm systems, broken auto-dimming mirrors and dead rear wiper motors. On a Limited, check the overhead trip computer and the EVIC warning display too.
- Check the recalls were done: Two big ones: 13V-252, where Chrysler inspected the rear structure and fitted a tow hitch to protect the fuel tank in rear impacts, and 02V-053, a secondary detent for a shifter that could appear to be in Park when it wasn't. A Jeep dealer can check the VIN.
- Know what you're buying: 1993–95 trucks have the driver's airbag only and pre-OBD-II diagnostics; 1996–98 trucks have dual airbags and OBD-II. A real 5.9 Limited has a louvered hood, a mesh grille, 16 in five-spoke wheels and came only in Deep Slate, Stone White or Bright Platinum. OffroadXtreme warns that the factory axles can struggle behind the 5.9.

### Common repairs
#### Kill the death wobble: track bar, tie rods and ball joints
Difficulty 2 / 5 (bolts) · 3 / 5 (ball joints) · time ≈ 1 hour (inspection and bolts) · a day (ball joints) · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Violent front-end shaking after a bump at 35–50 mph that only stops when you slow right down; vague steering and wander.
Fix: With the truck on the ground, have a helper rock the steering wheel while you watch every joint. Start with the track bar: OffroadXtreme says the lower track bar bolt is the usual cause. Clean and torque the bolts to the manual and replace a worn track bar or bushing. Then check the tie-rod ends, drag link, steering-box mounts and ball joints, and replace anything with play. Finish with an alignment.
Tools: Torque wrench · tie-rod end puller · ball-joint press · pry bar · factory manual for torque specs [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]

#### Stop the 4.0's oil leaks
Difficulty 2 / 5 (adapter, valve cover) · 4 / 5 (rear main) · time ≈ 1–2 hours (adapter) · a weekend (rear main) · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Oil on the driver's side of the block, drips from the pan or bellhousing, burning smell from the exhaust manifold.
Fix: Clean the engine and drive it to find the source. The oil filter adapter has two O-rings: remove the filter and adapter, fit new O-rings and refit. Replace the valve cover gasket if oil is seeping from the cover. For the oil pan or rear main seal you'll need to drop the pan, which takes room under the front of the truck, and OffroadXtreme warns the rear main can be a multi-day job.
Tools: Sockets and extensions · torque wrench · gasket scraper · RTV · seal pick · floor jack and stands

#### Fix the Magnum V8's oil leaks
Difficulty 2 / 5 (sender) · 3 / 5 (valve covers) · time ≈ 1 hour (sender) · half a day (valve covers) · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Oil running down the back of the block, a flickering oil-pressure gauge, oil on the exhaust manifolds.
Fix: OffroadXtreme names the rear main seal, valve cover gaskets and oil pressure sending unit as the V8's usual leaks. Check the sender first: it's cheap, and a leaking one also makes the gauge unreliable. Replace it, then reseal the valve covers with new gaskets, torquing the bolts evenly to the manual spec. A rear main leak on the V8 is a pan-off job like the six's.
Tools: Oil-pressure sender socket · sockets and extensions · torque wrench · gasket scraper

#### Sort out a sticky or binding transfer case
Difficulty 2 / 5 (linkage, fluid) · 4 / 5 (rebuild) · time ≈ 1–2 hours · a weekend for a rebuild · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: The lever won't go into a mode or won't come out, 4WD won't engage, or a Quadra-Trac truck binds and scrubs in tight turns.
Fix: Check the shift linkage first: OffroadXtreme says Selec-Trac linkages often stick, so clean, lube and adjust the linkage and bushings. Then drain and refill the case; ExtremeTerrain lists 1.1–1.5 quarts of ATF+4 for the NP231, NV242 and NV249. On a Quadra-Trac, make sure all four tires match in size and wear. If an NV249 still binds after that, the viscous coupling is the likely suspect. Many owners swap a worn-out NP242 for a simpler NP231.
Tools: Sockets · fluid pump · linkage bushings · for a rebuild: snap-ring pliers, seal pullers, press

#### Free a stuck rear hatch
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–3 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: The liftgate won't open from the handle or the remote, or won't latch shut.
Fix: OffroadXtreme lists a stuck rear hatch as a common ZJ fault, and rust at the bottom of the hatch can stop it opening. Get it open from inside: remove the interior trim panel and work the latch by hand. Clean and lube the latch and linkage, replace broken rods or clips, and check the latch bumpers. NHTSA recalled 1993 trucks because grease made the latch bumpers swell and jam the latch pawl (93V-055).
Tools: Trim-panel tool · screwdrivers · penetrating oil · white lithium grease

#### Refresh the cooling system
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Temperature climbing on hills, when towing or at idle with the A/C on; coolant smell; a low-coolant warning on the EVIC.
Fix: OffroadXtreme lists an insufficient cooling system among the ZJ's common problems. Pressure-test the system and check the radiator for blocked fins and leaking tanks. Replace the thermostat, check the fan clutch (or the electric fan on a 5.9) and replace old hoses. Then fill with the correct coolant and bleed out the air. ExtremeTerrain lists 12 quarts for the 4.0 and 14.9 for the V8s.
Tools: Cooling-system pressure tester · drain pan · hose-clamp pliers · funnel

#### Stalling at speed: check the crankshaft position sensor
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time About an hour, once diagnosed · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: The engine cuts out without warning, often warm and sometimes at highway speed. It may restart after sitting, or crank but not start. NHTSA's complaint file holds dozens of ZJ stalling reports in which the crankshaft position sensor was replaced, sometimes more than once (e.g. ODI 878399, 10460757).
Fix: Read any stored codes first (1996–98 trucks are OBD-II). Then inspect the sensor's harness for chafing and heat damage. One 1995 owner traced his stalling to a broken front motor mount that let the engine tug on the crank-sensor leads until they chafed through and shorted (NHTSA ODI 784679), so check the mounts too. If the wiring and mounts are good, replace the sensor. Stalling has other causes, including a failing fuel pump (see below), so confirm the diagnosis before you buy parts.
Tools: OBD-II scanner (1996–98) · multimeter · sockets and extensions · flashlight

#### Fuel pump failure and a flaking tank
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Half a day (tank drop) · cost Parts plus labor; one 1995 owner reported $600 for the pump plus $300 to flush the tank (NHTSA ODI 761423)
Symptoms: Hesitation, low fuel pressure, stalling or a crank-no-start, and replacement pumps that keep failing. Fuel-pump complaints to NHTSA cluster on 1995–96 trucks. Several owners were told debris from inside the plastic tank had clogged the pump (ODI 756730, 8001105, 758045).
Fix: Confirm low pressure with a gauge before you condemn the pump. Run the tank low, support it, disconnect the lines and straps, lower it and pull the pump module. Look inside the tank: if the lining is flaking or there's sediment, clean or replace the tank, or the new pump will clog too. Several owners went through multiple pumps before the tank was dealt with. Fit a new strainer with the pump and replace rusty straps. While the tank is down, check that recall 13V-252 (rear-impact fuel tank protection) was done.
Tools: Fuel-pressure gauge · floor jack and tank support · fuel-line disconnect tools · sockets · drain can

### Baseline service
Most ZJs have done 150,000 miles or more and been through several owners, so assume nothing has been done. ExtremeTerrain's ZJ capacity guide gives the factory fluids and capacities below. For engine oil, ExtremeTerrain and AMSOIL's application guide disagree on every engine's capacity, so fill to the dipstick and check your owner's manual. Service the transfer case and both axles even if the seller says they were done.
- Engine oil & filter: 5W-30 or 10W-30 (AMSOIL: 10W-30 above −18 °C, 5W-30 below 16 °C) · capacity with filter, sources disagree: ExtremeTerrain 4.0 5 qt · 5.2 4 qt · 5.9 6 qt; AMSOIL (1998) 4.0 6 qt · 5.2 5 qt · 5.9 5 qt [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now; then every 3,000–5,000 mi (While the filter is off a 4.0, look for oil around the filter adapter O-rings.)
- Air filter: Drop-in panel element · Baseline now; inspect every oil change (Check the airbox and intake tube for cracks.)
- Spark plugs & ignition: Copper plugs · 4.0 gap 0.035 in (0.89 mm) · V8 gap 0.040 in (1.0 mm) · Baseline now (ExtremeTerrain lists NGK or Champion copper plugs. Replace the cap, rotor and wires on a truck with no records.)
- Coolant, thermostat & hoses: 50/50 IAT coolant · 4.0: 12 qt · V8: 14.9 qt (ExtremeTerrain) · Flush and refill now (ExtremeTerrain says flush the system completely if you change coolant types.)
- Automatic transmission: ATF+4 · service fill 3.5 qt (AW4, 42RE, 44RE) or 3 qt (46RH, 46RE) · Baseline now: pan drop and filter (A pan drop and new filter, not a flush. ATF+4 supersedes the older ATF+3 (ExtremeTerrain).)
- Manual transmission (AX15): 75W-90 GL-5 · 3.27 qt (ExtremeTerrain) · Baseline now (Only 1993–94 sixes in North America had the five-speed.)
- Transfer case (NP231 / NV242 / NV249): ATF+4 · 1.1–1.5 qt (ExtremeTerrain) · Baseline now (On Quadra-Trac, keep all four tires matched; the system works the viscous coupling constantly.)
- Front & rear differentials: 80W-90 · Dana 30 front 1.3 qt · Dana 35/44 rear 1.8–2 qt · add 4 oz friction modifier for Trac-Lok (ExtremeTerrain) · Baseline now (Read the rear axle tag first: Dana 35, Dana 44 and Chrysler 8.25 were all fitted.)
- U-joints & driveshafts: Inspect for play; grease where fitted · Every oil change (Check the front axle shaft U-joints at full lock.)
- Power steering: Power Steering Fluid +4 (ATF+4 if unavailable) (ExtremeTerrain) · Baseline now (Look for leaks at the steering box seals while you're under there.)
- Brake fluid, pads & rotors: DOT 3 (DOT 4 acceptable) (ExtremeTerrain) · Flush now; then every 2 years (Four-wheel ABS was standard; old fluid is hard on the ABS unit.)
- Belts & hoses: Serpentine belt and tensioner · Baseline now (Replace cracked heater and radiator hoses at the same time as the belt.)
- Steering & suspension joints: Track bars, tie rods, ball joints, control-arm bushings · Inspect now (Worn joints and bushings set up death wobble. Check the lower track bar bolt first.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: About 30 in. Factory sizes ran from 215/75R15 to 245/70R15 and 225/70R16, all roughly 28 in tall. A 30x9.50R15 is the practical limit on stock springs: one owner ran 30x9.50 BFGoodrich all-terrains on a stock '93 and said they came close to rubbing but didn't. Rough Country and Zone rate their 1.5–2 in spacer lifts for 30x9.50s, and Rough Country's 3.5 in kit for 31x10.50s.

Q: Six or V8?
A: OffroadXtreme calls the 4.0 one of the most reliable engines Jeep ever built, but a little underpowered for a heavier truck. The 5.2 has more power and torque, is very reliable, and is in most ZJs. The 1998-only 5.9 is rare, and the factory axles can struggle behind it. EPA figures are 16 mpg combined for the 4.0, 14 for the 5.2 and 13 for the 5.9.

Q: Which 4WD system is best?
A: It depends what you want. Command-Trac (NP231, 1993–95) is part-time and the simplest. Selec-Trac (NP242) adds a full-time mode, but OffroadXtreme says its linkage often sticks and many owners swap in an NP231. Quadra-Trac (NV249) is full-time with a viscous coupling and needs no driver input. Before 1996 its low range still ran through the coupling; from 1996 low range locks 50/50.

Q: What causes death wobble on a ZJ?
A: It's violent front-axle oscillation after a bump, usually between 35 and 50 mph. OffroadXtreme says the lower track bar bolt is the usual culprit, but worn tie rods, ball joints and bushings all add to it. Fix every loose joint, not just the one you find first.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: Wikipedia says the 5.2 V8 was rated for up to 5,000 lb at launch, and the 4.0 was rated for 5,000 lb by 1995. Check the trailer-tow package and your owner's manual. The fuel-tank recall (13V-252) remedy was a Chrysler-designed hitch, so many trucks already have one.

Q: What fluids and capacities does it take?
A: ExtremeTerrain's ZJ guide: 5W-30 or 10W-30 oil, 50/50 IAT coolant (12 qt six, 14.9 qt V8), ATF+4 in the automatics and transfer cases (1.1–1.5 qt), 80W-90 in the axles with 4 oz of friction modifier for a Trac-Lok, and a 23-gallon tank of 87 octane. The 5.9 needs premium. Oil capacity is disputed: ExtremeTerrain gives 5 qt for the 4.0, while AMSOIL's 1998 lookup gives 6 qt (and 5 qt for both V8s), so fill to the dipstick.

Q: Which rear axle do I have?
A: Check the tag or count the cover bolts; don't guess. Offroaders.com lists the Dana 35 and Chrysler 8.25 in ZJs. Dana 44 rear-axle parts are catalogued for 1996–98 ZJs, and ExtremeTerrain's capacity guide covers both the Dana 35 and 44. The front is a Dana 30.

Q: Is the 5.9 Limited worth the premium?
A: As a collectible it's the one to have: one year only, 14,286 built, 245 hp, 6.8 seconds to 60, and Petersen's 4-Wheel & Off-Road named it 4x4 of the Year. On Bring a Trailer, though, 5.9s have sold for about $6,500–25,500 since 2019, roughly the same as nice 5.2 Limiteds. Remember the premium fuel and the axles.

Q: Are there recalls I should check?
A: Yes. 13V-252 covers 1993–98 trucks, whose fuel tanks could leak in some rear impacts; the remedy was a rear-structure inspection and a free tow hitch. 02V-053 added a secondary detent so the shifter can't sit just out of Park. There are smaller campaigns too, such as the 1996 Quadra-Trac temporary-spare recall (98V-006).

Q: What are the differences between 1993–95 and 1996–98?
A: The 1996 facelift brought new bumpers, cladding and a bigger grille, an all-new interior with a passenger airbag, OBD-II diagnostics and a revised NV249. Command-Trac and the manual gearbox were gone, and the 4.0 was rerated from 190 to 185 hp. In IIHS testing, 1996–98 trucks scored Marginal in the moderate-overlap frontal test.

Q: What are they worth?
A: Not much. Nineteen ZJs sold on Bring a Trailer between October 2025 and October 2026 for between $4,250 and $18,500, with a median of about $9,700. The top result was an 11,000-mile 1998 Limited. In 2017 OffroadXtreme put rough ones at about $1,000 and nice ones at $3,000 and up.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: There's no real consensus, so we don't flag one. SlashGear picks 1993, 1994 and 1998 and says to avoid 1995–96 for transmission complaints, but NHTSA's complaint database holds a similar 1,200 to 1,560 complaints for every ZJ model year, with 1998 logging the most powertrain reports, and CarComplaints.com shows no ZJ year standing out. Buy on condition instead: frame rust, leaks, a transfer case that works in every mode and the 13V-252 hitch recall done. If you want the collectible, it's the 1998 5.9 Limited.

## Jeep Wrangler TJ (1997–2006)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/tj/
Codes: TJ

Verdict: Round headlights back, leaf springs gone, the 4.0 straight-six carried over, and from 2003 a Rubicon with lockers from the factory. For many people the TJ is the sweet spot of the whole Wrangler line. Just check the frame before you fall in love.

On January 2, 1996, Chrysler showed the new Wrangler at the Detroit auto show, and the square headlights were gone. The TJ brought back round lamps and, more importantly, threw out the leaf springs that Jeeps had used since the war. It used coil springs at all four corners on solid axles, with control arms largely borrowed from the Grand Cherokee. It kept the YJ's 93.4-inch wheelbase and its 4.0 straight-six, reached showrooms in April 1996 as a 1997 model, and became the Wrangler many owners still consider the best of the lot.

### A $260 MILLION REINVENTION
Work on a YJ successor began in 1990 in Chrysler's Jeep-Truck Engineering pre-program group under Bob Sheaves and program director Craig Winn. YJ-based mules ran from 1990 to 1993. Michael Santoro's design was chosen in late 1992 and frozen in May 1993, and the program was formally approved in 1993 with a $260 million budget. Drivingline calls that a 'somewhat shoestring budget' and notes that the TJ was the first Wrangler developed with Chrysler's full resources rather than AMC's.
The frame was stiffened, and Drivingline says the new body panels doubled torsional rigidity, making the TJ roughly a third stiffer overall than the YJ. The coil springs and four-link control arms gave much better articulation and a far better ride. The body looked familiar on purpose, but small changes cut drag and noise.

### SIXES, FOURS AND A LOT OF GEARBOXES
The 4.0-liter six was the engine to have. Drivingline lists 181 hp and 222 lb-ft for 1997–99 and 190 hp and 235 lb-ft from 2000. Entry trucks used the 2.5-liter AMC four until 2002, then the 2.4-liter PowerTech four with 147 hp. Automatics were the three-speed 30RH and 32RH until 2002, then the four-speed 42RLE. Wikipedia lists the AX-5 manual with the four, the AX-15 with the six through 1999, the NV3550 for 2000–04, the NV1500 with the 2.4 for 2003–04 and the six-speed NSG370 for 2005–06.
The front axle was a low-pinion Dana 30. The rear was a Dana 35 on most trucks, with a Dana 44 optional on the Sport and Sahara. Drivingline calls the Dana 35 'junk' because of its C-clip design. The NP231 Command-Trac transfer case handled part-time four-wheel drive on everything but the Rubicon.

### THE RUBICON
In summer 2002 Jeep launched the 2003 Wrangler Rubicon, and it changed what buyers expected from a showroom Jeep. It had Dana 44 axles front and rear with 4.10 gears and air-actuated lockers built by Tochigi Fuji Sangyo. Jeep's launch release said the driver could lock them from a dash switch in low range below 10 mph, with the pneumatic pump running at just 5 psi. It also had the NV241OR Rock-Trac transfer case with a 4.0:1 low range, 31-inch Goodyear MT/R tires and diamond-plate sill guards. RockCrawler reported a crawl ratio of 65.92. Jeep's Craig Love said it combined 'what would typically be aftermarket hardware'. Drivingline calls it the most capable factory TJ you can buy. The long-wheelbase Unlimited (LJ) arrived for 2004, and a Rubicon version followed for 2005.

### HOW IT ENDED
Production ran from January 1996 to July 2006, and 2006 was the final model year for both the TJ and the Unlimited. Special editions along the way included the 60th Anniversary (2001, 4,067 built), the Tomb Raider Rubicon (2003), the moss-green Willys (2004–05), the Columbia (2004), and the Golden Eagle and 65th Anniversary in 2006. The JK was unveiled at the Detroit show in January 2006 and went on sale as a 2007 model. It was bigger, wider and available with four doors as the JK Unlimited.
That growth is a big part of the TJ's appeal today. It is still small enough for tight trails, its 4.0 is nearly unkillable when maintained, and the aftermarket for it is enormous. Its enemies are rust, a handful of well-known leaks and, on 2005–06 trucks, an oil pump drive that owners learn to fear.

### Data plate
- Chassis: TJ
- Production: January 1996 – July 2006
- Model Years: 1997–2006
- Engines: 2.5 L I4 (to 2002) · 2.4 L I4 (2003–06) · 4.0 L I6
- Output (4.0): 181 hp / 222 lb-ft → 190 hp / 235 lb-ft (2000–06)
- Manuals: AX-5 · AX-15 · NV3550 · NV1500 · NSG370
- Automatics: 30RH / 32RH (to 2002) · 42RLE (2003–06)
- Transfer Case: NP231 Command-Trac · NV241OR Rock-Trac 4.0:1 (Rubicon)
- Axles: Dana 30 / Dana 35 or 44 · Rubicon Dana 44 / 44, 4.10 (4.11), lockers
- Wheelbase: 93.4 in (2,372 mm)
- Length: 151.2–155.4 in
- Curb Weight: 3,092–3,857 lb (short wheelbase)
- Towing: 2,000 lb (1,000 lb with the 2.4 or some 3.73 automatics)

### Engineering
The TJ is a ladder-frame Jeep with solid axles at both ends, located by coil springs, control arms, track bars and anti-roll bars. The standard wheelbase stayed at 93.4 inches. Most trucks pair a Dana 30 front axle with a Dana 35 or optional Dana 44 rear and the NP231 part-time transfer case. The 2003–06 Rubicon gets Dana 44s at both ends with lockers and the 4:1 NV241OR.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, 93.4 in (2,372 mm) wheelbase (Stiffer than the YJ. The Unlimited (LJ) stretches the wheelbase to 103.4 in.)
- Suspension: Coil springs and control arms, front and rear (The first coil-sprung Wrangler. Track bars and anti-roll bars at both ends.)
- Axles: Dana 30 front · Dana 35 or 44 rear (The Dana 44 rear was optional on the Sport and Sahara, sometimes with Trac-Lok.)
- Transfer Case: NP231 Command-Trac · NV241OR Rock-Trac (Rubicon) (Rock-Trac has a 4.0:1 low range.)
- Rubicon: Dana 44s, 4.10 gears, front and rear lockers (Air-actuated lockers by Tochigi Fuji Sangyo, engaged from a dash switch.)
- Engines: 2.5 I4 (to 2002) · 2.4 I4 (2003–06) · 4.0 I6 (The 4.0 made 181 hp until 1999, then 190 hp and 235 lb-ft.)

### Versions
- 1997–1999 · TJ · 4.0 L AMC I6 · 181 hp / 222 lb-ft · AX-15 five-speed or 32RH three-speed automatic. Drivingline says exhaust manifold cracks are most common on 1997–2000.
- 1997–2002 · TJ SE · 2.5 L AMC I4 · 120 hp / 140 lb-ft · AX-5 five-speed or 30RH three-speed automatic.
- 2000–2006 · TJ · 4.0 L AMC I6 · 190 hp / 235 lb-ft · NV3550 five-speed (2000–04), NSG370 six-speed (2005–06). 32RH auto to 2002, then 42RLE four-speed.
- 2003–2006 · TJ SE · 2.4 L PowerTech I4 · 147 hp / 165 lb-ft · NV1500 five-speed (2003–04) or 42RLE automatic; NSG370 six-speed for 2005–06. fueleconomy.gov lists the 2.4 through 2006.
- 2003–2006 · TJ Rubicon · 4.0 L AMC I6 · 190 hp / 235 lb-ft · Dana 44s with 4.10 gears (Jeep spec sheets also say 4.11) and air lockers, NV241OR 4:1 transfer case, 31-in LT245/75R16 MT/Rs.
- 2005–2006 · TJ · 4.0 L AMC I6 · 190 hp / 235 lb-ft · Quadratec flags these years for OPDA (oil pump drive) failure.

### Year-by-year
- 1997: TJ launches (shown January 1996, in showrooms April 1996) with coil springs at all four corners and round headlights; 2.5 L four or 4.0 L six with the AX-5/AX-15 manuals or 3-speed automatics
- 1997–99: Early-TJ teething: SlashGear notes seven recalls for 1997 and early engine-computer, fuel-system and brake bugs; Driving Line says cracked 4.0 exhaust manifolds are most common on 1997–2000 trucks; Off Road Xtreme says the early cowl vent leaks water onto the floors, a design Jeep revised on later TJs [avoid]
- 1999: 19-gallon fuel tank becomes standard
- 2000: NV3550 five-speed replaces the AX-15 behind the 4.0
- 2001: Thicker, more durable factory soft-top fabric; 60th Anniversary Edition
- 2003: Mid-cycle update: 42RLE four-speed automatic replaces the 3-speed, 2.4 L replaces the 2.5 L four, revised interior. Rubicon arrives with Dana 44s front and rear, air lockers and the 4:1 NV241OR
- 2004: Long-wheelbase Wrangler Unlimited (LJ) joins the range
- 2005: NSG370 six-speed manual replaces the five-speeds
- 2006: Final year: 65th Anniversary and Golden Eagle editions; production ends July 2006

### Capability
- Towing: 2,000 lb (907 kg) 4.0 L · 1,000 lb (454 kg) 2.4 L and 4.0 automatic with base 3.73 axle (2005–06)
- Payload: 800 lb (363 kg)
- Fuel tank: 19 US gal (72 L) (standard from 1999)
- Ground clearance: 8.6–9.1 in (218–231 mm) at the rear axle (2005–06, varies with tires)
- Approach / departure: 42.2° / 31.5° (2005–06)
- Turning circle: 36.7 ft (11.2 m) (curb to curb, 30x9.5 tires)
- Curb weight: 3,200 lb (SE) – 3,857 lb (Rubicon automatic) (2005–06)
- Wheelbase: 93.4 in (2,372 mm)
- Fuel economy: EPA 15 city / 18 hwy (1997 4.0, manual) · 13 / 17 (2005–06 4.0, six-speed) (fueleconomy.gov's revised figures)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 205/75R15, 215/75R15 or 225/75R15 (SE, X, Sport, depending on year), 30x9.50R15 LT (optional on some trims), LT245/75R16 (≈31 in) on 16x8 alloys (Rubicon)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x114.3 (5x4.5")
- Center Bore: 71.5 mm
- Lug Thread: 1/2"-20 (60° cone seat)
- Lug Torque: 85–115 lb-ft (115–156 N·m)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 31 in (Jeep put 31-inch LT245/75R16s on the Rubicon from the factory, and Four Wheel Trends puts the stock-suspension limit at 31x10.50-15 (may rub at full flex). Check wheel backspacing so the tires stay inside the flares.)
- Biggest tire, 2 in lift: ≈31 in (Quadratec's buyer's guide: a 2 in spacer lift typically accommodates up to 31 in tires.)
- Biggest tire, 3 in lift: 33 in (Quadratec's buyer's guide: up to 33 in on its stage-2 suspension lift, 35 in on a long-arm setup. Plan a regear from the stock ratio (3.07 on many 4.0 manuals, per Jeep's 2005–06 specs).)

### Buying checks
- Frame rust, especially the rear control-arm mounts: Quadratec says plainly that TJ frames still rust. Check the rails inside and out, the skid-plate areas and the rear lower control-arm brackets, where it warns rust can become severe enough to cause structural failure. Rick Rotondo adds the transfer-case crossmember and central body mounts to the list.
- Floors and the early cowl leak: Look under the carpet, especially in the front footwells. Off Road Xtreme notes that the cowl vent on early TJs leaks water into the cab, rusting the floor and growing mold in the carpet. Jeep revised the design later.
- Ask about the OPDA on 2005–06 4.0s: Listen for the 'laughing monkey' noise at idle. With no record of a replacement, Quadratec recommends replacing the oil pump drive assembly proactively, because a failure can damage the engine.
- Drive it at 30–50 mph: Off Road Xtreme says that's the speed range to check for death wobble, usually caused by a loose lower track-bar bolt. Check the track bar, ball joints, tie-rod ends, stabilizer and control-arm bushings for wear, and look for bent steering linkage.
- Oil leaks are normal; puddles aren't: The 4.0 commonly leaks from the rear main seal, oil pan gasket, valve cover gasket and oil-filter adapter. Drivingline adds pinion and transfer-case output seals. Price in the rear main seal if the bellhousing is wet.
- Radiator end tanks: The factory radiator has plastic end tanks crimped to an aluminum core, and Quadratec says many start leaking at the upper seams around 100,000 miles. Look for green crust, coolant smell and small leaks. Off Road Xtreme recommends an all-aluminum radiator, partly because the 4.0 runs warm.
- Which rear axle and which gearbox?: Find the axle tag: a Dana 44 rear beats the Dana 35 if you plan bigger tires. Drivingline says the AX-15 has known synchro issues, the NV3550 is stronger, and the 32RH automatic is durable but revs high on the highway.
- Transfer case won't go into 4-Low?: Quadratec says to check the shift linkage first, because it pops out of worn plastic bushings. It's a cheap fix, but it's a good haggling point.

### Common repairs
#### Cure death wobble: track bar, ball joints and tie rods
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ An afternoon to diagnose; a day to replace parts · cost A track bar costs a little over $50 (Drivingline); full steering kits cost more
Symptoms: Uncontrollable side-to-side shaking of the front end, usually triggered by a bump at around 45 mph and stopped only by slowing right down.
Fix: Quadratec's sequence: disconnect the steering stabilizer so it can't mask anything. With the key on and engine off, have a helper turn the wheel a quarter turn each way while you watch both ends of the track bar for movement. Then jack up the front and check tie-rod ends for play, ball joints by prying the tire, and wheel bearings by rocking at 12 and 6 o'clock. Inspect control arms and bushings. Tighten every steering and suspension bolt to spec, replace anything that moves, check tire balance and pressure, and finish with an alignment. Off Road Xtreme says a loose lower track-bar bolt is the most common cause. Drivingline warns a worn, oval frame-side hole may need drilling or an aftermarket bracket.
Tools: Helper · pry bar · floor jack and stands · torque wrench · factory service manual torque specs.

#### Replace the oil pump drive assembly (OPDA)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours, if you're careful with the timing · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: A chirping 'laughing monkey' noise from the top of the engine, most often on 2005–06 4.0s. Left alone, Dorman says the center shaft can seize and destroy the cam bearing, and Quadratec warns failure can damage the engine.
Fix: The OPDA sits where a distributor would be and carries the camshaft position sensor, so its position matters. Following the factory service manual, bring cylinder 1 to top dead center on the compression stroke, mark the sensor's orientation, disconnect it, remove the hold-down clamp and lift the old drive out. Install the replacement in the same orientation so it engages the oil pump, then refit the sensor and complete the manual's synchronization check. Inspect the old unit's upper bushing and gear for wear, and change the oil and filter afterwards in case debris reached it. Dorman's version uses a self-lubricating upper bushing; Crown's moves the seal above the upper bushing.
Tools: Socket set · factory service manual (TDC and sync procedure) · paint marker · scan tool if available.

#### Replace the 4.0's rear main seal
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day for a first-timer · cost Seal kit plus pan gasket; shops charge mostly for labor
Symptoms: Oil weeping from the joint between the engine and bellhousing, and an oily crossmember and transmission. Rule out the valve cover, oil-filter adapter and pan gasket first.
Fix: The 4.0 uses a two-piece rear main seal that can be replaced without removing the transmission. On a TJ, drain the oil, remove the starter and drop the oil pan. Off Road Xtreme warns this may mean removing the front axle for clearance, and Jeepz.com owners loosened the exhaust for room. Mark the rear main cap, remove both seal halves, and install the new halves without nicking the lip (dish soap helps the upper half slide in). Use only a dab of RTV where the halves meet the cap. Make sure you have the right seal for your engine, because 1987–99 and 2000–06 engines take different kits. Check crank end play while you're in there.
Tools: Pick · thin punch · O2-sensor wrench · torque wrench · RTV · jack and stands.

#### Replace a leaking plastic-tank radiator
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours including bleeding · cost Around $150 for a replacement radiator (Drivingline)
Symptoms: Coolant smell, green crust at the top tank seam, and eventually a split tank spraying coolant over the engine.
Fix: From Jeepfan's TJ write-up: let the engine cool and drain the radiator. Disconnect the upper and lower hoses and the transmission cooler lines if fitted, and pop the overflow bottle out of its holder. Loosen the fan shroud and push it back over the fan, since it doesn't need to come out. Remove the radiator bolts and lift it out. Thread the cooler fittings into the new radiator with sealant and drop it in, using the slotted lower bolt holes as a guide. Refit everything, fill with the correct coolant mixed 50/50 with distilled water, run it up to temperature while topping off, and recheck the level after a few drives as air works out.
Tools: Drain pan · hand tools · thread sealant · distilled water · correct coolant.

#### Replace a cracked exhaust manifold
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A long day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: A ticking exhaust leak that's loudest from cold and may fade as the engine warms. Drivingline says it's more common on 1997–2000 trucks and is something you hear more than see.
Fix: Modern Jeeper's TJ/LJ guide: photograph and disconnect everything, then remove the O2 sensors, which can seize. The intake and exhaust manifolds share one gasket, so both come off. The hardest bolts are under the intake beside the exhaust tubes, so use extensions and wobble sockets. Clean the head face with a detail pad, not a grinding wheel. Fit the new gasket and manifold, put the intake back on top, then tighten the remaining fasteners. Reinstall the O2 sensors with anti-seize and check the new manifold's clearance to the front driveshaft.
Tools: Extensions · wobble sockets · flex-head ratcheting wrenches · O2-sensor socket · anti-seize · Loctite.

#### Repair rusted rear lower control-arm mounts
Difficulty 5 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend per side · cost Repair section plus welding, or shop labor
Symptoms: Flaking, swollen or holed frame around the rear lower control-arm brackets, clunks from the rear, or a bracket that moves. Quadratec warns it can lead to structural failure.
Fix: Rick Rotondo's Quadratec guide on a 1998 TJ: support the frame on stands, remove the rear wheels, hold the axle on a jack, and unbolt the upper and lower arms, sway-bar link and shock on one side. Mark at least 1 inch of overlap past the rot, then cut out the bad frame, the sway-bar mount and the factory arm mount. Avoid the brake hose and fuel lines, and do not cut the body mount. Mock up the replacement section, trace and grind to bare metal, tack weld, recheck measurements, then fully weld. Prime and paint or coat it, refit the arms with Loctite, torque everything to spec, and recheck after a day. Rotondo says it's only for people experienced in cutting, grinding and welding.
Tools: Floor jack and stands · grinder · cutting wheel · welder · primer, paint or POR-15 · torque wrench.

#### Fix a transfer case that won't shift (linkage bushings)
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost A few dollars in bushings
Symptoms: The shifter moves but the transfer case won't go into 4-Low, or the lever flops around. The rod has usually popped out of a worn plastic bushing.
Fix: Quadratec says to check this first when a TJ won't engage 4-Low. Under the Jeep, find the rod between the shifter and the NP231 or NV241OR range lever. Pop the rod out, pry out the old bushing, and press in a new one. Reconnect the rod and check that the shifter reaches every detent and the transfer case fully engages 2H, 4H, N and 4L. If the linkage has worn badly, or a body or motor-mount lift has changed its geometry, an adjustable or upgraded linkage is the permanent fix.
Tools: Pliers · small pry bar · grease.

### Baseline service
Baseline everything, then deal with the TJ-specific items: crawl under it with a hammer and light to check the frame, listen for the OPDA on a 2005–06 4.0, and confirm which gearbox, transfer case and rear axle you have. Coolant and automatic-fluid specs changed during the run, so check the owner's manual or the labels on your truck before you buy fluids.
- Engine oil & filter: 4.0: 6 qt with filter · 2.4: 4 qt · 10W-30 or 5W-30 (ExtremeTerrain) · Haynes lists every 7,500 mi or 12 months (Drain-plug torque is 25 ft-lb for the 4.0 and 2.5 and 20 ft-lb for the 2.4 (ExtremeTerrain's factory-spec table). Look for leaks at the oil-filter adapter gasket while you're under there, because it's a known 4.0 leak.)
- OPDA check (2005–06 4.0): Oil pump drive / camshaft synchronizer · Now, unless there's a receipt (Quadratec recommends replacing it proactively on 2005–06 trucks with no records. Listen for the 'laughing monkey' chirp at idle.)
- Air filter & PCV: Engine air filter and PCV · Every 30,000 mi or 24 months (Haynes); sooner in dust (Quadratec lists aging throttle-position, crank and O2 sensors as causes of stalling and rough idle, so a fresh filter rules out the easy stuff first.)
- Spark plugs: ExtremeTerrain's engine tables give 27 ft-lb for the 4.0 and 2.5 and 250 in-lb for the 2.4, but its ignition table says 30 ft-lb for all engines [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Every 30,000 mi (Haynes) (Haynes lists inspecting the plug wires, cap and rotor on 2003-and-earlier models (the 1997–99 4.0 and the 2.5 have a distributor).)
- Coolant & radiator: ≈9 qt (2.4, 2.5), 10.5 qt (4.0), 50/50 (Quadratec chart) · coolant type: conventional vs Mopar HOAT changed around 2001 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Every 30,000 mi or 24 months (Haynes) (Inspect the plastic radiator end tanks for seam leaks. Quadratec says they often start around 100,000 miles.)
- Manual transmission: AX-5/AX-15: 75W-90 GL-3 or GL-4 (ExtremeTerrain), ≈3.3 qt · NV3550: Mopar manual transmission fluid, about 2 bottles (4x4xplor) · NV1500: 4.8 pints · NSG370: 3.17 pints (Quadratec chart) [CONFIRM TYPE IN MANUAL] · Change now, then every 30,000 mi (The NV3550 fill and drain plugs take a 17 mm Allen bit, and the oil-pan skid may need to come off (4x4xplor). Fine filings on the magnet are normal, but chunks are not.)
- Automatic transmission (30RH / 32RH / 42RLE): 42RLE: ATF+4, ≈4 qt pan drop, 8.8 qt dry (ExtremeTerrain) · 30RH/32RH: ATF type per the dipstick/manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Every 30,000 mi, or 12,000 mi in severe use (Haynes) (Change the filter with the fluid. Filter screws take 35 in-lb (30RH/32RH) or 45 in-lb (42RLE) (ExtremeTerrain's factory-spec table). Drivingline calls the 2003–06 four-speed heat-sensitive, so consider a cooler if you tow or crawl.)
- Transfer case (NP231 / NV241OR): NV231: ATF+3 or ATF+4, 2.2 pints · NV241OR: ATF+4, 4.2 pints (ExtremeTerrain, Quadratec charts) · fill until it runs out of the fill hole · Every 30,000 mi (Haynes) (On a TJ the skid plate has to be lowered for a proper drain (4x4xplor). Drain and fill plugs take 15–25 ft-lb (ExtremeTerrain's factory-spec table). Check the output seals and the shift-linkage bushings while you're there.)
- Front & rear differentials: GL-5 80W-90 or 75W-140 synthetic · Rubicon Dana 44s: 75W-140 synthetic · +4 oz limited-slip additive for Trac-Lok (Quadratec, ExtremeTerrain) · Every 30,000 mi, and after deep water (ExtremeTerrain) (Cover bolts take 30 ft-lb (ExtremeTerrain's factory-spec table). Drivingline says to check the Dana 30's pinion seal and U-joints.)
- Steering & front end inspection: Track bar and bolts, ball joints, tie-rod ends, drag link, stabilizer · Now, and after any lift or hard trail day (Torque the track-bar bolts to spec first. Off Road Xtreme says a loose lower bolt is the most common cause of death wobble.)
- Brake & clutch fluid: DOT 3 (ExtremeTerrain) · About every two years (The TJ's external clutch slave shares brake fluid. Flush both.)
- Chassis grease & U-joints: Lubricate chassis components (Haynes) · Every 7,500 mi or 12 months (Haynes) (Grease the steering joints and driveshaft U-joints, and look over the control-arm bushings.)
- Frame & floor rust inspection: Rails, rear lower control-arm brackets, transfer-case crossmember, body mounts, footwells · Now, then every winter (Quadratec warns rust at the rear lower arm brackets can cause structural failure. Clean and coat the frame inside and out before it gets there.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: Four Wheel Trends says the biggest tire you can generally run on a stock TJ and keep full function is a 31x10.50-15, and that even that size may rub at full flex, which a washer or two on the steering stops usually cures. The Rubicon came from the factory on 31-inch LT245/75R16 Goodyear MT/Rs.

Q: Four-cylinder or 4.0?
A: Get the 4.0 if you can. Drivingline strongly recommends the six, which makes 190 hp and 235 lb-ft from 2000 against 120 hp for the 2.5 and 147 hp for the 2.4. The fours are reliable but run out of power once you add bigger tires, and swapping in a 4.0 later costs about as much as a V8 swap.

Q: What is the 'laughing monkey' noise?
A: It's the sound of a failing oil pump drive assembly (OPDA), which Quadratec flags on 2005–06 4.0 TJs. Dorman says the factory upper bushing is starved of oil, and if the shaft seizes it can destroy the cam bearing. Replace it if there's no record it has been done.

Q: What causes death wobble, and will a new stabilizer fix it?
A: Worn or loose steering and suspension parts cause it, most often the track bar and its bolts, and Off Road Xtreme singles out a loose lower track-bar bolt. Quadratec says a bigger steering stabilizer only masks the problem. Find and replace the part that moves, then align.

Q: Is the Dana 35 rear axle really that bad?
A: Drivingline calls it 'junk' and says its C-clip design is unreliable in stock form, while the low-pinion Dana 30 front is fine up to about 35-inch tires. A factory Dana 44 rear was optional on the Sport and Sahara and standard on the Rubicon. Otherwise, budget 'a couple grand' for a bolt-in upgrade.

Q: What does the Rubicon add?
A: Dana 44 axles front and rear with 4.10 gears (Jeep spec sheets also list 4.11), air-actuated front and rear lockers that engage in low range below 10 mph, the NV241OR Rock-Trac transfer case with a 4.0:1 low range, 31-inch MT/R tires, 16-inch wheels and diamond-plate sill guards. RockCrawler reported a 65.92:1 crawl ratio. It was sold for 2003–06.

Q: Which manual transmission is best?
A: Drivingline says the AX-15 has notable synchro issues and the NV3550 that replaced it is stronger. Wikipedia lists the AX-15 for 1997–99, the NV3550 for 2000–04 and the six-speed NSG370 for 2005–06, though some sources say the six-speed arrived earlier. Fours used the AX-5 and, for 2003–04, the NV1500.

Q: How much can a TJ tow?
A: Jeep's 2005–06 spec sheet rates the 4.0 at 2,000 lb, but the 2.4 and the 4.0 automatic with the base 3.73 axle at 1,000 lb, so check your build. Wikipedia gives 2,000 lb for the TJ and 3,500 lb for the long-wheelbase Unlimited.

Q: What coolant does it take?
A: Quadratec's factory-based chart gives about 9 qt for the four-cylinders and 10.5 qt for the 4.0, mixed 50/50. Owners commonly report a change from conventional green coolant to Mopar's HOAT type around 2001, but we couldn't confirm the exact changeover from a primary source, so check the label on the overflow bottle and the owner's manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]. Don't mix types.

Q: What gear oil goes in the axles?
A: Quadratec's factory-based chart lists GL-5 80W-90 or 75W-140 synthetic, 75W-140 synthetic for the Rubicon's Dana 44s, and 4 oz of limited-slip additive for a Trac-Lok. ExtremeTerrain recommends 75W-140 in the rear for warm-weather towing. Haynes' schedule changes the differential lubricant every 30,000 miles or 24 months.

Q: Why does my TJ leak oil?
A: The usual spots on the 4.0 are the rear main seal, oil pan gasket, valve cover gasket and oil-filter adapter gasket. Off Road Xtreme notes the valve cover has many bolts and takes longer than expected. Drivingline says the two-piece rear main can be replaced without pulling the transmission.

Q: TJ or LJ (Unlimited)?
A: The Unlimited, sold for 2004–06, stretches the TJ by 15 inches, 10 of them in the wheelbase (103.4 in versus 93.4 in). Drivingline says that adds cargo room and stability on steep trails, but the LJ costs more because it was built for only three model years.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: There's no consensus year, which is why we only flag the early trucks. SlashGear rates mid-to-late TJs among the most desirable Wranglers and points manual buyers to 2005–06 for the NSG370 six-speed. RealTruck, on the other hand, lists 2005 and 2006 among its worst Wrangler years, and Quadratec says 2005–06 4.0s need the oil pump drive assembly checked or replaced. Driving Line doesn't pick a year at all: it says get the six-cylinder. Every TJ frame can rust, so the frame matters more than the model year. Check the rear lower control-arm mounts first.

## Jeep Wrangler Unlimited (LJ) (2004–2006)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/tj-unlimited/
Codes: LJ, TJ Unlimited

Verdict: The LJ is a TJ that went to the gym and grew ten inches of wheelbase, which turned out to be exactly the right number. Jeep sold it for barely two and a half model years and buyers mostly shrugged. Now everyone wants one, and the sellers know it.

In April 2004, eighteen years after the CJ-8 Scrambler went away, Jeep brought back a long-wheelbase Wrangler. It stretched the TJ by 10 inches between the axles and about 15 inches overall, and called it the Wrangler Unlimited. Owners call it the LJ. That gave a two-door Wrangler 2 more inches of rear legroom, 13 more inches of cargo space and a tow rating of 3,500 lb instead of 2,000. It sold for $24,995 at launch and lasted barely two and a half model years. Then it became one of the most chased Wranglers ever built.

### THE SCRAMBLER'S WHEELBASE, RETURNED
The LJ's 103.4-inch wheelbase is almost exactly the 103.5 inches of the CJ-8 Scrambler it was reviving. The longer frame gets one extra crossmember, and the body grows behind the rear wheels. That stretch is why the rear overhang is the LJ's one real off-road compromise: Jalopnik's David Tracy lists a 27.7-degree departure angle, and the low transfer-case skid makes the belly the next thing to touch.
Mechanically it is a late TJ. The engine is the 4.0-liter AMC-derived straight six, rated at 190 hp and 235 lb-ft. Standard LJs got a Dana 44 rear axle with a 3.73 limited-slip and the Command-Trac NV231 transfer case with a 2.72:1 low range. The standard short-wheelbase TJ made do with a Dana 35 unless you ticked the right option boxes. Automatics used the 42RLE four-speed, and Jeep's 2004½ spec sheet lists only that automatic for the first LJs. For 2005, manual Wranglers moved from the NV3550 five-speed to the six-speed NSG370.

### THE RUBICON UNLIMITED
For 2005, Jeep gave the long-wheelbase body the Rubicon drivetrain. The Rubicon Unlimited had Dana 44 axles at both ends with air-actuated lockers, the Rock-Trac NV241 transfer case with a 4:1 low range, 4.10 gears (Jeep's spec sheet says 4.11), diamond-plate rocker guards and LT245/75R16 Goodyear MT/R tires. You could have it with the six-speed manual or the four-speed automatic.
Jeep also built 1,000 numbered 'Sahara Edition' Unlimited Rubicons in 2005 to cash in on the film Sahara. All were Light Khaki, with a chrome grille, khaki tops, graphite Moab wheels, two-tone seats and a numbered dash badge. In Jalopnik's breakdown, the Rubicon LJ is the one that puts the whole formula together: TJ coil springs, a fully boxed frame and a wheelbase in the trail 'sweet spot', plus a factory locker on each axle.

### WHY COLLECTORS CHASE THEM
Jalopnik, citing forum and sales data, puts LJ production at about 47,000 over the run, roughly 20 percent of Wrangler sales in those years. That isn't rare by Jeep standards. What made them collectible is that the LJ has no direct replacement. In 2007 the JK Unlimited grew four doors, a 116-inch wheelbase and about 350 more pounds. The LJ is still the only factory Wrangler that combines two doors, a long wheelbase, a coil-sprung solid-axle chassis and the 4.0 straight six.
Hagerty's valuation team says later TJs, 'and especially the Unlimited Rubicon, have been the priciest TJ on the market.' Jalopnik called the LJ the 'holy grail' of Jeeps. Unrusted, unmodified examples now command a clear premium over short-wheelbase TJs, while a clapped-out one is still just a TJ with more frame to rot.

### HOW IT ENDED
The TJ family finished with the 2006 model year. Its replacements debuted at the January 2006 Detroit show. The JK two-door kept a short wheelbase, and the JK Unlimited replaced the LJ with four doors and a wheelbase about 13 inches longer again. The long two-door Wrangler was never offered again, and the TJ and LJ were the last Wranglers with the AMC-derived 4.0 straight six.

### Data plate
- Code: LJ (TJ long wheelbase)
- Model Years: 2004.5–2006
- Assembly: Toledo, Ohio
- Engine: 4.0 L OHV I6, 190 hp / 235 lb-ft
- Transmissions: 42RLE 4-spd auto · NSG370 6-spd manual (2005–06)
- Transfer Case: NV231 (2.72:1) · NV241 Rock-Trac (4:1, Rubicon)
- Axles: Dana 30 / Dana 44 LSD · Rubicon: Dana 44 / Dana 44, air lockers
- Wheelbase: 103.4 in
- Length: 167 in (171 in with spare)
- Departure / Breakover: 27.7° / 21.4°
- Towing: 3,500 lb
- Fuel Tank: 19 gal

### Engineering
Underneath, the LJ is a TJ with a longer ladder frame (fully boxed, according to the Jeep engineer Jalopnik interviewed) and one extra crossmember. It has coil springs and live axles at both ends, located by four links and a track bar at each end, and recirculating-ball steering. Every LJ got the stronger Dana 44 rear axle. Rubicon Unlimiteds add a Dana 44 front axle, air lockers and a 4:1 transfer case.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, 103.4 in wheelbase (10 in longer than the 93.4 in TJ, with one extra crossmember. About 167 in long, or 171 in with the spare.)
- Suspension: Coil springs on live axles (Leading arms and a track bar in front, trailing arms and a track bar at the rear, with stabilizer bars and gas-charged shocks at both ends (Jeep's 2004½ spec sheet).)
- Engine: 4.0 L 'Power Tech' OHV I6 (190 hp at 4,600 rpm and 235 lb-ft at 3,200 rpm. Cast-iron block and head, 6 qt of oil.)
- Transmissions: 42RLE 4-spd auto; NSG370 6-spd manual (2005–06) (The 42RLE has an overdrive lockout switch on the dash. Manual TJs used the NV3550 five-speed through 2004.)
- Transfer Case: NV231 Command-Trac (2.72:1) or NV241 Rock-Trac (4:1) (Both part-time with no center differential. Rock-Trac only on the 2005–06 Rubicon Unlimited.)
- Axles: Dana 30 / Dana 44 (std.); Dana 44 / Dana 44 (Rubicon) (Standard LJs: limited-slip 3.73 rear. Rubicon: air lockers front and rear with 4.10 gears.)

### Versions
- 2004.5 · LJ (Unlimited) · 4.0 L I6 · 190 hp / 235 lb-ft · Launched April 2004 at $24,995. Dana 44 limited-slip rear (3.73), NV231 transfer case; Jeep's 2004½ spec sheet lists the 42RLE automatic.
- 2005–2006 · LJ (Unlimited) · 4.0 L I6 · 190 hp / 235 lb-ft · NSG370 six-speed replaces the five-speed manual. Watch for OPDA wear on 2005–06 engines.
- 2005–2006 · LJ Rubicon (Rubicon Unlimited) · 4.0 L I6 · 190 hp / 235 lb-ft · Dana 44 front and rear with air lockers, 4:1 Rock-Trac, 4.10 gears, LT245/75R16 MT/Rs, diamond-plate rockers.
- 2005 · Sahara Edition Unlimited Rubicon · 4.0 L I6 · 190 hp / 235 lb-ft · 1,000 numbered, all Light Khaki, tied to the film Sahara. Manual and automatic versions.
- 1997–2006 · TJ (short wheelbase), for reference · 2.5 / 2.4 I4, 4.0 I6 · Up to 190 hp · 93.4 in wheelbase, 2,000 lb tow rating, Dana 35 rear on many trims. See the TJ page.

### Year-by-year
- 2004: Wrangler Unlimited launches in April 2004 (the 2004½ model): 103.4-inch wheelbase (10 in longer than a TJ), one extra frame crossmember, standard Dana 44 rear with 3.73 gears, NV231 transfer case and 3,500 lb towing
- 2005: Unlimited Rubicon arrives with front and rear locking Dana 44s, the Rock-Trac NV241OR and 245/75R16 MT/Rs; NSG370 six-speed replaces the five-speed manual
- 2005: Sahara Edition Unlimited Rubicon: 1,000 numbered trucks, all Light Khaki
- 2006: Final year; production ends in July 2006 and the four-door JK Unlimited takes over for 2007

### Capability
- Towing: 3,500 lb (1,588 kg) (against 2,000 lb for a short-wheelbase 4.0 TJ)
- Payload: 800 lb (363 kg)
- Fuel tank: 19 US gal (72 L)
- Ground clearance: 8.3 in (212 mm) rear axle · 9.2 in (235 mm) running (2004½ Unlimited)
- Approach / departure / breakover: 43.1° / 27.7° / 21.4° (2004½ Unlimited)
- Turning circle: 36 ft (11.2 m) (curb to curb)
