- Cargo volume: 28.5 cu ft (0.807 m³)
- Fuel economy: EPA 13 city / 16 hwy (auto) · 13 / 17 (six-speed) (2005–06 Wrangler 4.0 ratings; EPA has no separate Unlimited listing)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 30x9.5R15 LT on 15x8 cast-aluminum wheels (Unlimited), 245/75R16 Goodyear MT/R (Unlimited Rubicon)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x114.3 (5x4.5")
- Center Bore: 71.5 mm
- Lug Thread: 1/2"-20 (60° cone seat)
- Lug Torque: 85–115 lb-ft (115–156 N·m)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 31 in (The Unlimited Rubicon came with ≈31-inch LT245/75R16s from the factory; Four Wheel Trends puts the stock-suspension limit at about 31x10.50. Check wheel backspacing so the tires stay inside the flares.)
- Biggest tire, 2 in lift: ≈31 in (Quadratec's buyer's guide (TJ): a 2 in spacer lift typically accommodates up to 31 in tires.)
- Biggest tire, 3 in lift: 33 in (Quadratec's buyer's guide (TJ): up to 33 in on its stage-2 suspension lift, 35 in on a long-arm setup. The low-hanging fuel tank is worth a skid plate (Driving Line).)

### Buying checks
- Get under it with a flashlight and a hammer: Quadratec calls frame rot near the rear lower control-arm brackets 'the TJ issue'. The other early-rot zones are the transfer-case crossmember area and the central body mounts. A clean outside means nothing. Probe the inside of the rails and the arm brackets, and walk away from anything that's flaking through.
- 2005–06: ask about the OPDA: Late 4.0 engines can wear out the oil pump drive assembly. Owners describe the warning noise as a 'laughing monkey' squeal. Quadratec says that if there's no record of it being replaced or updated, deal with it proactively.
- Is it a real Rubicon Unlimited?: Rubicons have a Dana 44 front axle, an NV241 Rock-Trac transfer case, air lockers and 4.10 gears. Check that both lockers engage, that 4-Low is the 4:1 Rock-Trac, and that a Sahara Edition has its numbered dash badge. Rubicon decals are cheap; Dana 44 fronts are not.
- Drive it at 30–50 mph over bumps: OffroadXtreme suggests testing for death wobble in that speed range. A loose lower track-bar bolt, bent steering linkage, worn ball joints or tie-rod ends can all start it. On lifted examples, also check the rear track-bar bracket on the axle for cracks.
- Look for leaks, and price them: The 4.0 commonly seeps from the rear main seal, oil pan, valve cover and oil-filter adapter gasket. Pinion and transfer-case output seals weep too. Mostly this is money rather than doom, but the rear main seal is a big job.
- Check the radiator tanks: Factory TJ radiators have plastic end tanks crimped to an aluminum core. Quadratec says many start leaking at the upper seams around 100,000 miles. Look for green crust and a coolant smell.
- Shift into 4-Low, twice: The factory 'Z-bar' transfer-case linkage pops out of worn plastic bushings, and the symptom is a Jeep that won't go into 4-Low. The bushings are cheap; a missed diagnosis is not.
- Judge the modifications: A lifted LJ needs a longer or adjustable track bar, alignment correction and often a slip-yoke eliminator above 2 inches of lift. Ask who did the work, and inspect welds on frame repairs and brackets.

### Common repairs
#### Replace the oil pump drive assembly (2005–06 4.0)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Parts plus labor; ExtremeTerrain rates the install 'difficult' and suggests a professional
Symptoms: A squeak or 'laughing monkey' chirp from the back of the engine, sometimes with a check-engine light. Left alone, Quadratec warns, OPDA failure can damage the engine.
Fix: The OPDA sits in the block where a distributor would be. It drives the oil pump and carries the camshaft position sensor, so it must go in with the engine at top dead centre on cylinder 1 and be indexed so the cam sensor stays in sync with the crank. Follow the factory service manual's alignment procedure. Remove the cam sensor, unbolt the hold-down and lift the old drive out. Fit the replacement with a new gasket at the same orientation, then check cam/crank sync with a scan tool. ExtremeTerrain says the factory unit's two bronze bushings sit either side of a seal that starves the upper bushing of oil, and the redesigned part moves the seal above the top bushing.
Tools: Socket set · factory service manual for TDC and indexing · scan tool to verify cam/crank sync · new camshaft position sensor (5149034AA for 2005–06 4.0) if the old one is suspect.

#### Repair rotted rear control-arm frame mounts
Difficulty 5 / 5 · time A weekend per side · cost Frame sections plus welding; Quadratec calls shop cost 'prohibitive' for an old Jeep
Symptoms: Flaking, swollen or holed frame around the rear lower control-arm brackets, the transfer-case crossmember or the central body mounts. Quadratec's correspondent found all three on a 1998 TJ with 190,000 miles.
Fix: Only for someone who can cut and weld. Support the frame on stands, jack the axle, then unbolt the upper and lower control arms on one side, the sway-bar link and, if needed, the shock. Mark at least 1 inch of overlap and cut out the rotten section and the old arm mounts, without cutting the body mount and keeping clear of brake and fuel lines. Mock up the new section, grind to bare metal, measure, tack, measure again, then weld it fully. Prime and coat it, and refit the arms with thread locker and correct torque. Re-check after a day, or a mile, and then monthly. One side at a time.
Tools: Welder · cutoff wheel and grinder · jack stands · floor jack · torque wrench · thread locker · rust-proof coating. Rust Buster sections are side- and year-specific (2003–06 differ from 1997–02).

#### Hunt down death wobble and set toe in the driveway
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon to diagnose; minutes to set toe · cost Usually a track-bar bushing, tie-rod end or ball joints, plus an alignment
Symptoms: Violent front-end shake after a bump, usually at 45–65 mph, that stops only when you slow right down.
Fix: Start at the front track bar. With the Jeep on the ground, have a helper rock the steering wheel a quarter turn each way while you watch both track-bar ends and the bracket holes; any side-to-side movement is a fault. Then check the tie-rod ends, drag link, ball joints, control-arm bushings, wheel bearings and tire balance. Quadratec says a steering stabilizer rarely fixes the cause. Replace the worn part and re-torque the front-end hardware. Set toe-in by loosening the tie-rod sleeves and turning the tie rod until the front of the tires is about 1/16 inch (no more than 1/8 inch) closer than the rear. Center the wheel with the drag-link turnbuckle, then get a proper alignment.
Tools: 13 mm and 15 mm sockets · tape measure · pipe wrench or locking pliers · a helper · torque wrench.

#### Replace the radiator before the plastic tank lets go
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost Radiator plus coolant
Symptoms: Coolant smell, green crust or seepage at the upper tank seam, often around 100,000 miles, and creeping temperatures on the trail. OffroadXtreme notes that the 4.0 runs hot and recommends an all-aluminum radiator.
Fix: With the engine cold, drain the coolant and remove the upper and lower hoses. On automatics, disconnect the transmission cooler lines and cap them. Unbolt the fan shroud and lift it back over the fan, then remove the radiator mounts and lift the radiator out. Transfer any brackets, fit the new radiator and shroud, reconnect everything, refill and bleed the air out with the heater on high. Buy the right radiator for your transmission: Griffin's ExactFit listed here is for manual-transmission Jeeps, and CSF's 3426 is specific to 2005–06.
Tools: Drain pan · pliers for the hose clamps · line wrench for the cooler lines · funnel · coolant to the spec on the cap and in the owner's manual.

#### Replace a throttle position or crank sensor
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time Under an hour (Quadratec's TPS how-to) · cost One sensor
Symptoms: Stalling, rough idle or random check-engine lights. Quadratec's example was a TJ throwing P0122 that stalled while driving; automatics rely on the TPS to run properly. Aging crankshaft-position, throttle-position and oxygen sensors are all common failures.
Fix: For the TPS: disconnect the negative battery terminal, then unplug the TPS, IAC motor and MAP sensor connectors. Remove the intake tube and unclip the throttle cable (plus the kickdown and cruise cables where fitted). Remove the four throttle-body bolts, take the TPS off with a T25 Torx, fit the new sensor with the supplied hardware, and refit the throttle body, replacing the gasket if it's tired. For a crank sensor, Mopar's 4727451AA is listed for 2003–06 4.0 TJs.
Tools: 13 mm (or 1/2 in) socket for the battery · 5/16 in driver · 10 mm socket · T25 Torx · code reader.

#### Fix a transfer case that won't go into 4-Low
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time Under an hour · cost A few dollars in bushings, or an adjustable linkage
Symptoms: The lever moves but the transfer case won't fully engage 4-Low, or pops out of it. Quadratec says the factory 'Z-bar' linkage pops out of worn plastic bushings.
Fix: Put the lever in neutral, chock the wheels and crawl under. Pry the linkage rod ends off the shifter and transfer-case arms, replace the worn plastic bushings, and snap the linkage back on. If the Z-bar is bent or the geometry has changed after a lift, fit an adjustable linkage and set it so the lever fully reaches every detent. Then test 4-Hi, N and 4-Lo with the engine running.
Tools: Flat screwdriver or trim tool · pliers · wheel chocks.

#### Replace a front axle U-joint and unit bearing
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Half a day per side · cost U-joint plus hub
Symptoms: A squeak that fades as speed rises, a vibration or bind on slow turns as if you were in 4WD, and visible play in the axle-shaft U-joint. Quadratec's correspondent found the hub was worn too once it was apart.
Fix: Jack up the axle and remove the wheel. Remove the two caliper bolts and hang the caliper so it isn't supported by the brake hose, then pull the rotor. Stop the hub from turning and break the 36 mm axle nut loose with a long breaker bar. Remove the three bolts behind the knuckle and tap the hub out. Slide the axle shaft out, remove the U-joint clips and press out the old joint. Press in the new joint, being careful not to disturb the needle bearings, then refit the clips, shaft, hub and brakes. Anti-seize the hub, torque everything to spec, and expect the other side to need the same soon.
Tools: 36 mm socket · big breaker bar · 13 mm sockets · press (strongly preferred) · snap-ring pliers · anti-seize · torque wrench.

#### Stop the rear main seal leak
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A long day or more · cost Seal kit plus oil-pan gasket; labor-heavy if paid for
Symptoms: Oil dripping from the joint between engine and transmission and a wet bottom of the bellhousing. Rule out the valve cover and oil-filter adapter gasket first, because oil runs downhill.
Fix: Clean the area and confirm the source. The seal is reached from below, which means dropping the oil pan. OffroadXtreme notes that on a TJ this can mean lowering the front axle to get the pan out. With the pan off, replace the seal following the kit's instructions and the factory manual's torque specs, then refit the pan with a new gasket and refill the oil. Do the oil-filter adapter O-rings while you're under there.
Tools: Jack stands and floor jack (to lower the front axle if needed) · torque wrench · RTV per the factory manual · drain pan · factory service manual.

### Baseline service
Assume nothing has been done. Even a low-mile LJ is now 20 years old, so rubber, coolant and gear oil have aged regardless of mileage. On 2005–06 trucks, put the OPDA at the top of the list. On every LJ, put the frame inspection there too, before you spend a cent on mods.
- Engine oil & filter: SAE 10W-30 · 6 qt with filter (4.0 L) · Then per the owner's manual schedule [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Look at the oil-filter adapter gasket and the rear main seal while you're under there: both are common 4.0 leak points.)
- Oil pump drive assembly (2005–06): Updated OPDA with relocated seal · Once, unless there are receipts (Listen for the 'laughing monkey' squeal; the replacement must be indexed to keep the cam sensor in sync.)
- Engine air filter: Factory airbox element · Inspect at every oil change; more often on dusty trails ([CONFIRM part fitment for your intake])
- Spark plugs: 6 plugs (Crown 56041402AB listed for 1999–06 TJ & Unlimited) · Replace now if there's no record [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Check the plug wires and coil while you're there.)
- Coolant, thermostat & hoses: 10.5 qt (4.0 L); coolant type per the cap/manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush now; replace the thermostat and hoses if they're original (Inspect the radiator's plastic end tanks for seepage at the upper seams, a known 100k-mile failure.)
- Serpentine belt: Crown 4060882 listed for 2000–06 TJ & Unlimited 6-cyl · Replace if it's cracked, glazed or of unknown age (Spin the tensioner and idler pulleys while the belt is off.)
- Automatic transmission (42RLE): ATF+4 · 4 qt service fill · Drain and refill now, with a new filter (A service fill only replaces part of the fluid. Do two drain-and-fills rather than a high-pressure flush.)
- Manual transmission (NSG370): 3.17 pints; Mopar Manual Transmission Lubricant (as specified for the NSG370) [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Change now if there's no record (The NSG370 uses a hydraulic clutch with a dual-mass flywheel. Check the clutch fluid (DOT 3) too.)
- Transfer case: NV231: 2.2 pints · NV241 Rock-Trac: 4.2 pints · ATF+4 · Change now (Check the output seals and the shifter-linkage bushings at the same time.)
- Front & rear differentials: Dana 30: 2.5 pints · Dana 44: 4.0 pints · GL-5 80W-90 or 75W-140 synthetic; Rubicon 75W-140; Trac-Lok rear needs 4 oz of limited-slip additive · Change both now, and after any deep water crossing (Standard LJs have a limited-slip Dana 44 rear, so don't forget the friction modifier.)
- Driveshaft & front axle U-joints: Greasable 1310 driveshaft joints · axle-shaft U-joints · Grease now and at every oil change if greasable (Check for play by hand. A front axle U-joint that binds on slow turns is due.)
- Brake & clutch fluid: DOT 3 · Flush now, then every 2–3 years [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Manual LJs share the brake fluid type in the clutch hydraulics.)
- Front-end inspection & toe: Track bar, tie rods, drag link, ball joints, bushings · Now, and after any lift or hard trail day (Re-torque the front-end hardware. Set toe to about 1/16 in in, then get a proper alignment.)
- Frame & body-mount inspection: Rear lower control-arm mounts, transfer-case crossmember, center body mounts · Now, then every spring in salt country (Clean, treat and oil the frame inside and out. Catching surface rust now saves a welder later.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: The LJ uses the TJ's axles, flares and suspension, so the TJ answer applies: Four Wheel Trends puts the stock-suspension limit at about a 31x10.50, which may still rub at full flex until you add a washer or two to the steering stops. Jeep itself sent the Rubicon Unlimited out on LT245/75R16 (about 31-inch) tires at stock height. For 33s, plan on a lift; Quadratec's buyer's guide pairs 33s with a 3-inch-class suspension lift.

Q: What's the difference between an LJ and a TJ?
A: The LJ has 10 more inches of wheelbase (103.4 in against 93.4 in), is about 15 inches longer overall, and has 2 more inches of rear legroom and 13 more inches of cargo length. It tows 3,500 lb instead of 2,000. Every LJ also got a Dana 44 rear axle (limited-slip on standard models, locking on the Rubicon), which many short TJs lacked.

Q: How many LJs were built?
A: Jalopnik's tally from forum and sales data puts it at about 47,000 across 2004–2006, roughly 20 percent of Wrangler sales in that period. Driving Line says a little over 46,000, fewer than 13,000 of them Rubicons. The 2005 Sahara Edition Unlimited Rubicon was a numbered run of 1,000.

Q: Why are LJs so expensive now?
A: There's never been a replacement. It's the only factory Wrangler with two doors, a long wheelbase, coil springs and the 4.0 straight six, and the Rubicon version adds lockers at both ends. Hagerty says late TJs, 'especially the Unlimited Rubicon,' have been the priciest TJs on the market.

Q: Which years and drivetrains should I look for?
A: 2005–06 brought the NSG370 six-speed manual. Those years also need the OPDA checked. The 2005–06 Rubicon Unlimited is the one with front and rear Dana 44s, air lockers and the 4:1 Rock-Trac. A 2004 or non-Rubicon LJ still has the Dana 44 rear and is a better starting point for a build than a Dana 35 TJ.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: Jeep rated the LJ at 3,500 lb, against 2,000 lb for the short-wheelbase TJ.

Q: What fluids does it take?
A: Quadratec's factory-based chart gives the 4.0 6 qt of 10W-30 with a filter and 10.5 qt of coolant. The 42RLE takes ATF+4, 4 qt at a service fill. The NSG370 takes 3.17 pints. The NV231 takes 2.2 pints and the NV241 Rock-Trac 4.2 pints of ATF+4. The Dana 30 takes 2.5 pints and a Dana 44 4.0 pints of GL-5 80W-90 or 75W-140 synthetic. Rubicons specify 75W-140 synthetic, and a Trac-Lok rear needs 4 oz of limited-slip additive.

Q: What's the OPDA problem?
A: The oil pump drive assembly on 2005–06 4.0 engines can wear. The warning sign owners describe is a 'laughing monkey' noise, and if it's ignored the engine can be damaged. Replacements with a relocated seal are cheap; the indexing to keep the cam sensor in sync is the fiddly part.

Q: What fuel economy and range should I expect?
A: Jeep's 2005–06 TJ spec sheet originally listed 16/20 mpg (city/highway) for the 4.0 with either transmission, on the short-wheelbase truck. EPA's revised figures on fueleconomy.gov are lower: 13/16 for the automatic and 13/17 for the six-speed. The LJ carries a 19-gallon tank (Jeep's 2004½ spec sheet). Bigger tires, a lift and a roof load cost several mpg.

Q: What about the low belly and the rear overhang?
A: Jalopnik flags both. The departure angle is 27.7 degrees, and the transfer-case skid hangs low, so a high-clearance or 'tummy tuck' skid is a common first mod. Rough Country's 1126 is listed for 2003–06 TJ and Unlimited.

Q: Do I need a slip-yoke eliminator if I lift it?
A: Quadratec says lift-kit makers strongly recommend an SYE and a CV driveshaft above 2 inches of lift, and treat it as required at 4 inches or more, to cure vibration and stop the slip yoke pulling out of the transfer case.

## Jeep Wrangler JK (2-door) (2007–2018)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/jk/
Codes: JK

Verdict: The JK took the Wrangler from a summer toy to a computer-controlled, power-windowed mainstream hit, and the two-door is the version that kept the old-school wheelbase. Buy a 2012-on Pentastar unless you enjoy merging slowly. Then check the ball joints, because JK ones wear quickly.

In January 2006, Chrysler group CEO Tom LaSorda drove a new Wrangler up a flight of steps and through a plate-glass window at the Detroit auto show. The JK was a clean-sheet redesign from the DaimlerChrysler years. It was wider than the TJ by 3.4 inches of track and had 2 inches more wheelbase, yet it was 2.5 inches shorter overall. It also ran almost everything except the steering through computers, a first for a Wrangler. Purists grumbled. Then it went on to set new Wrangler sales records anyway.

### BIGGER, WIDER, WIRED
Mark Moushegian's design won an internal competition by 2003 and was frozen in January 2004. The JK kept the things that make a Wrangler a Wrangler: a separate body and frame, live axles front and rear on coils, a fold-flat windshield, removable doors and part-time four-wheel drive. Around them came stability control, off-road-tuned ABS and traction control acting as an electronic limited slip. It also got power windows and locks, available navigation and, on the Rubicon, an electronic front sway-bar disconnect. With the factory 32-inch tires, the two-door Rubicon is quoted at a 44.3-degree approach and a 40.4-degree departure.
The four-door JK Unlimited arrived at the same time and stole the show. By mid-2017, Autotrader counted three-quarters of new Wranglers for sale as four-doors. The two-door kept the 95.4-inch wheelbase that Quadratec calls 'still nimble, just slightly longer' than a TJ, which is why trail regulars still seek it out.

### THE MINIVAN ENGINE, THEN THE PENTASTAR
From 2007 to 2011 the JK used the 3.8-liter EGH V6, the same pushrod engine as Chrysler's minivans and the Pacifica. It made 202 hp and 237 lb-ft by Jeep's 2008 figures, and it came with the six-speed NSG370 manual or the 42RLE four-speed automatic. It was adequate in the way a tent is adequate housing. The 2011 model year brought a fully redesigned interior, with a new dash, steering-wheel controls, available heated leather and Bluetooth.
For 2012 the 3.6-liter Pentastar replaced it, with 285 hp and 260 lb-ft, and Mercedes' five-speed W5A580 automatic replaced the 42RLE. Quadratec says the change meant the Wrangler 'is no longer the rolling brick it was'. The early Pentastar had a teething problem: Chrysler replaced faulty left cylinder heads (excessive cylinder leakage, showing up as misfires) on some 2012–13 engines and extended their warranty to 10 years or 150,000 miles. Diesel JKs, using VM Motori's 2.8, were sold outside the US only.

### RUBICONS, MOABS AND WILLYS WHEELERS
Every Rubicon has Dana 44 axles at both ends with electric lockers, the Rock-Trac NV241 transfer case with a 4:1 low range, 4.10 gears, rock rails and the sway-bar disconnect. Sport and Sahara models used a Dana 30 front, a Dana 44 rear (Quadratec says fewer than a thousand early 2007s got a Dana 35) and the 2.72:1 Command-Trac. A rear locker on a non-Rubicon was a rare option.
The special editions came thick and fast. The 2012 Call of Duty: MW3 edition wore AEV bumpers and a sculpted hood. The 2013 Moab brought AEV-style steel bumpers and sliders but kept the 2.72:1 transfer case. The 2013 10th Anniversary Rubicon was the edition chosen for the one-millionth JK, built on May 17, 2013. The 2014 Rubicon X added steel bumpers and a Power Dome hood. For 2015 the lineup included the Willys Wheeler and the Rubicon Hard Rock.

### HOW IT ENDED
For 2018 the JK was built alongside the new JL at Toledo, with a 'Wrangler JK' fender decal to tell them apart, and a final Golden Eagle edition. The last one rolled off the line on April 27, 2018, and its plant was retooled to build the Gladiator pickup. The JK is the Wrangler that made the aftermarket explode: Mopar alone offered more than 250 accessories for the 2012 model. That's why a used JK today is rarely stock, and why you should inspect what the last owner bolted on as carefully as what Jeep did.

### Data plate
- Code: JK (2-door)
- Production: Aug 2006 – Apr 27, 2018 (Toledo, Ohio)
- Model Years: 2007–2018
- Engines (Us): 3.8 L EGH V6 (2007–11) · 3.6 L Pentastar V6 (2012–18)
- Output: 202 hp / 237 lb-ft → 285 hp / 260 lb-ft
- Transmissions: NSG370 6-spd · 42RLE 4-spd · W5A580 5-spd
- Transfer Case: NV241 Command-Trac 2.72:1 · Rock-Trac 4:1
- Wheelbase: 95.4 in
- Width: 73.7 in
- Approach / Departure (Rubicon): 44.3° / 40.4°
- Towing: 2,000 lb
- Fuel Tank: 18.6 gal
- Wheel Bolt Pattern: 5 x 5 in

### Engineering
The JK has a ladder frame with coil-sprung live axles at both ends, each located by four links and a track bar, and recirculating-ball steering with a damper. The drivetrain is a part-time two-speed transfer case with no center differential. Standard models get a Dana 30 front and Dana 44 rear. Rubicons get Dana 44s at both ends with electric lockers, a 4:1 Rock-Trac and an electronic front sway-bar disconnect. Nearly every system is electronically controlled.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, 95.4 in wheelbase (2 in longer than the TJ, with 3.4 in more track. 61.9 in track front and rear on 2007–11 trucks.)
- Engine 2007–11: 3.8 L EGH OHV V6 (202 hp / 237 lb-ft (Jeep, 2008). Shared with Chrysler minivans. 6 qt of 5W-20.)
- Engine 2012–18: 3.6 L Pentastar DOHC V6 (285 hp / 260 lb-ft. Coil-on-plug ignition. The plastic oil filter housing sits in the engine valley.)
- Transmissions: NSG370 6-spd manual · 42RLE 4-spd (2007–11) · W5A580 5-spd (2012–18) (The W5A580 is Mercedes' NAG1 family. Both automatics use ATF+4.)
- Transfer Case: NV241 Command-Trac 2.72:1 · Rock-Trac 4:1 (Rubicon) (Part-time, no center differential.)
- Axles: Dana 30 / Dana 44 · Rubicon Dana 44 / Dana 44 with Tru-Lok e-lockers (Rubicons use 4.10 gears. Fewer than a thousand 2007s had a Dana 35 rear.)

### Versions
- 2007–2010 · JK 2-door (X/Sport, Sahara, Rubicon) · 3.8 L EGH V6 · 202 hp / 237 lb-ft · NSG370 six-speed or 42RLE four-speed. Hill Start Assist from 2009; easier-folding soft top in 2010.
- 2011 · JK 2-door · 3.8 L EGH V6 · 202 hp / 237 lb-ft · New interior: dash, steering-wheel controls, available heated leather. Last year of the 3.8 and 42RLE.
- 2012–2018 · JK 2-door · 3.6 L Pentastar V6 · 285 hp / 260 lb-ft · W5A580 five-speed auto or NSG370. EPA 17/21 mpg (2012 2-door). Revised oil filter housing from 2014.
- 2012–2013 · Pentastar early engines · 3.6 L Pentastar V6 · — · Some left cylinder heads failed (misfire codes); warranty extended to 10 years/150,000 miles.
- 2007–2018 · Rubicon (incl. 10th Anniversary, Rubicon X, Hard Rock) · 3.8 then 3.6 · As above · Dana 44s front and rear, e-lockers, 4:1 Rock-Trac, 4.10 gears, sway-bar disconnect, LT255/75R17 BFG KM.
- 2007–2018 (ex-US) · JK 2.8 CRD · VM Motori 2.8 L turbo-diesel I4 · 177 hp / 302 lb-ft, later 197 hp · Never sold in the US.

### Year-by-year
- 2007: JK launch (production from August 2006): 3.8 EGH V6 (202 hp) with a 6-speed manual or 4-speed 42RLE auto; Rubicon has Dana 44s with lockers, 4:1 Rock-Trac and a sway-bar disconnect; the four-door Unlimited is new. First-year trucks drew several recalls (SlashGear), 2007–08 log the most complaints on CarComplaints.com (CarGurus), and Driving Line warns the 3.8 burns oil, leaks intake gaskets and cracks exhaust manifolds [avoid]
- 2009: Hill Start Assist standard; Trailer Sway Control available
- 2010: Easier-folding soft top; Uconnect on MyGig-equipped trucks
- 2011: Fully redesigned interior with steering-wheel controls, Bluetooth, and available heated seats and leather. Mopar's JK-8 pickup kit for the Unlimited also arrives.
- 2012: 3.6 Pentastar V6 (285 hp, 260 lb-ft) and 5-speed W5A580 automatic replace the 3.8 and the 4-speed. The Pentastar is the engine to have (Quadratec, Driving Line); Driving Line's daily-driver pick is a 2013 or newer [buy]
- 2012–13: Some Pentastars have faulty left cylinder heads (misfire codes); covered by the X56 extension to 10 years/150,000 miles
- 2013: Second windshield-washer nozzle returns; one-handed rear-seat fold; Moab edition with AEV bumpers. The millionth JK is built in May 2013.
- 2014: Clear park and turn lamps; optional 6.5 in Uconnect; Rubicon X edition
- 2015: Willys Wheeler and Rubicon Hard Rock join the range; Torx tool kit for doors and windshield standard; Alpine audio option
- 2018: Final year, sold alongside the new JL with 'Wrangler JK' fender decals; Golden Eagle edition. Production ends April 27, 2018.

### Capability
- Towing: 2,000 lb (907 kg)
- Payload: 1,000 lb (454 kg) (2007 spec)
- Fuel tank: 18.6 gal (70 L)
- Ground clearance: 8.8–10.2 in (224–259 mm) (X to Rubicon, 2007 spec)
- Approach / departure / breakover: 44.3° / 40.4° / 25.4° (Rubicon on 32 in tires)
- Fuel economy: EPA 17 city / 21 hwy (2012 two-door, 3.6 Pentastar)
- Curb weight: 3,760–4,104 lb (1,706–1,862 kg) (2007 X to Rubicon)
- Wheelbase: 95.4 in (2,423 mm)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 225/75R16 or 245/75R16 (X/Sport), 255/75R17 (Sport S, Sahara and most special editions), 255/70R18 (Sahara option, 70th Anniversary), LT255/75R17 BFGoodrich Mud-Terrain (Rubicon)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x127 (5x5")
- Center Bore: 71.5 mm
- Lug Thread: 1/2"-20 (60° cone seat)
- Lug Torque: 100 lb-ft (Northridge4x4); ExtremeTerrain gives an 85–125 lb-ft range [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 33 in (e.g. 285/70R17) (JEGS puts the stock-height limit at about 33 in. Driving Line fitted 35x12.50R17s to a stock-height 2017 JK Unlimited Sport on 4.75 in-backspacing wheels after removing the front splash guard, and concluded that real off-road use needs aftermarket or heavily trimmed flares.)
- Biggest tire, 2.5 in lift: 35x12.50 or 285/75R17 (285/75R17 works on factory 17s; 35x12.50 wants 18x9 or 20x9 wheels at about 0 to +1 mm offset.)
- Biggest tire, 3.5 in lift: 37 in (JEGS says 37s need about 3.5 in of lift and advises axle, driveshaft and gearing upgrades; 40s need about 4.5 in.)

### Buying checks
- Which engine? Check the VIN year: 2007–11 trucks have the 3.8 and the four-speed automatic; 2012-on trucks have the Pentastar and the five-speed. The Pentastar is the one most buyers want. On a 2012–13, ask whether the left cylinder head was ever replaced: Chrysler extended coverage on affected heads to 10 years or 150,000 miles, which has run out on most of them by now.
- Look into the engine valley (2012–18): Quadratec says the Pentastar's plastic oil filter housing 'has a bad habit of cracking'. Look for oil pooled under the intake plenum, a burning-oil smell or slow oil loss. Because the housing contains the oil cooler, coolant can leak there too. Many owners fit an aluminum housing.
- Jack up the front axle: JK ball joints often wear surprisingly quickly, especially with 35s, bumpers and winches. Check for vertical wheel play, steering looseness, uneven tire wear and highway wander. Then drive it at 45–65 mph over bumps to rule out death wobble.
- Listen at cold start: A tick-tick-tick that fades as the engine warms is usually snapped rear exhaust manifold bolts, which Quadratec calls notorious on both the 3.8 and the 3.6. It isn't urgent, but it's a negotiating point.
- Electrical gremlins and water: JK electrical faults often trace to the TIPM (Totally Integrated Power Module) or a failing clockspring. Symptoms include airbag lights, dead steering-wheel controls, fuel-pump problems and wipers with a mind of their own. Water in the cabin makes them worse, so lift the carpets and look for damp.
- Inspect the front axle C's on modified trucks: On 35-inch tires or bigger, hard use can bend the Dana 30's C-shaped knuckle ends where the ball joints sit. Look for odd camber, strange tire wear and whether gusset plates or a truss are already fitted.
- Prove the Rubicon hardware works: Engage both lockers and the sway-bar disconnect, and confirm 4-Low is the 4:1 Rock-Trac. A Moab or Willys Wheeler looks the part but has the 2.72:1 transfer case, and lockers were optional at best.
- Read the lift like a résumé: Most JKs are modified. A quality lift should include a correct track bar, geometry correction and an alignment. Cheap spacer lifts with 35s are where worn joints and death wobble come from.

### Common repairs
#### Replace the Pentastar oil filter housing (2012–18)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time About 6 hours in one owner's write-up, including prep · cost Housing plus gaskets; under $30 in special tools for the Curbside Classic author
Symptoms: Oil (and sometimes coolant) pooling in the valley between the cylinder banks, a burning smell, slow oil loss. You often won't see drips on the ground until the leak is bad.
Fix: Remove the engine cover and intake duct. Unplug the intake connectors (the MAP sensor's red tab first), the vacuum hoses and the throttle-body brackets, then remove the seven captive 8 mm bolts and lift off the upper intake. Unplug the injectors and right-bank coils, vacuum away debris, plug the ports, and remove the eight lower-intake bolts, supporting the manifold out of the way. Unplug the oil and coolant sensors and the coolant hose, then remove the five E8 Torx bolts and lift out the housing. On the bench, move the cooler and sensors (with thread sealant) to the new housing. Fit new gaskets and O-rings and bolt it down in the specified sequence. The filter cap is 18 lb-ft. Reassemble, change the oil (6 qt of 5W-20) and check for leaks. 2014-on housings differ from 2012–13, so buy for your year.
Tools: 27 mm and 19 mm deep sockets · E8 external Torx · 24 mm cap socket · inch-pound torque wrench · 8, 10 and 13 mm sockets · magnet and pick · shop vac.

#### Cure death wobble: track bar, tie rods and steering
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon to diagnose · cost Often a track-bar bushing or end, tie-rod ends or a drag link, plus an alignment
Symptoms: Violent side-to-side shaking of the front end after a bump at 45–65 mph that won't stop until you slow right down.
Fix: Start with the front track bar. With the Jeep on the ground, have a helper turn the wheel about a quarter turn each way while you watch the track-bar ends and bracket holes; any movement is a fault. Then check the tie-rod ends, drag link, ball joints, control-arm bushings, wheel bearings, and tire balance and pressure. Quadratec says a stabilizer 'rarely fixes the root cause'. Replace the worn parts, torque all front-end hardware to spec (Northridge4x4's chart gives 125 ft-lb for both front track-bar bolts and 63 ft-lb for the tie-rod end nuts; confirm against the factory manual), and finish with a proper alignment. On lifted trucks, a correctly sized adjustable track bar re-centers the axle.
Tools: Helper · pry bar · torque wrench · sockets · tape measure.

#### Press in new ball joints
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A day for both sides · cost Ball joint set plus a rented ball-joint press
Symptoms: Vertical play at the top and bottom of the tire, wandering, uneven tire wear, and wobble after bumps. Quadratec says factory JK ball joints 'often wear surprisingly quickly', especially on heavy, lifted trucks.
Fix: Support the truck on stands and remove the wheel, caliper, rotor and unit bearing to free the axle shaft. Separate the tie rod and drag link, remove the knuckle, then press the old upper and lower joints out of the axle C. Inspect the C for bends and cracks at the same time. Press in the new joints with the correct adapters, refit the knuckle and torque the castle nuts to spec (Northridge4x4 lists 75 ft-lb for the upper and lower ball-joint nuts). Finish with an alignment. Adjustable or heavy-duty kits are worth it on 35s.
Tools: Ball-joint press and JK adapter set · pickle fork or tie-rod puller · large sockets · torque wrench · new cotter pins.

#### Replace a front unit bearing
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time A couple of hours per side · cost One hub and bearing assembly
Symptoms: Play when you rock the tire with the truck in the air, a growl that changes with steering, and, as part of the death-wobble checklist, looseness in the front end.
Fix: Support the axle and remove the wheel, then the caliper (hang it, don't let it hang from the hose) and rotor. Remove the axle-shaft nut, then the bolts holding the unit bearing to the knuckle from behind, and tap the hub free. Clean the knuckle bore, anti-seize it, fit the new hub, and torque the bolts and axle nut to the factory spec (Northridge4x4 lists 75 ft-lb for the hub bolts and 100 ft-lb for the 35 mm axle nut). Mopar lists different hubs for 2007–10 and 2011–18 trucks, so buy by year.
Tools: Large axle-nut socket · breaker bar · torque wrench · anti-seize · hammer.

#### Fix a ticking exhaust manifold (broken bolts)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Half a day to a day, depending on how the bolts come out · cost Gaskets and hardware; more if a broken bolt has to be drilled out
Symptoms: A tick-tick-tick on cold start that quiets as the engine warms, from a leak at the rear of a manifold. Quadratec says the rear manifold bolts on both the 3.8 and 3.6 are 'notorious for snapping'.
Fix: Find the leak with the engine cold (a manifold that's black at the flange or a snapped bolt head is the giveaway). Penetrating oil the studs for a day or two. Unbolt the downpipe and remove the manifold. Extract broken bolts by drilling and using an extractor, or by welding a nut onto the stub. Chase the threads, fit new hardware and gaskets, torque to spec and reconnect the exhaust.
Tools: Penetrating oil · sockets and extensions · left-hand drill bits and extractors (or a welder) · thread chaser · torque wrench.

#### Replace the clockspring
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An hour or two · cost One clockspring
Symptoms: Airbag warning light, horn or steering-wheel buttons that don't work, and cruise or audio controls dropping out. Quadratec lists it with the TIPM as the usual JK electrical culprits. On 2007–10 trucks, check recall 16V-290 first: Chrysler recalled the clockspring because dust contamination could stop the driver's airbag from deploying.
Fix: Point the wheels straight ahead. Disconnect the battery and wait for the airbag system to discharge, as the factory manual specifies. Remove the airbag module and steering wheel, then the column shrouds. Unplug and remove the old clockspring and fit the new one centered, following its instructions (don't spin it). Reassemble, reconnect the battery and clear any codes. Quadratec Academy has a step-by-step JK video.
Tools: Torx and metric sockets · steering-wheel puller if it's stuck · trim tools · factory manual for the airbag procedure.

#### Change the spark plugs (and don't over-torque the Pentastar)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An hour or two · cost Six plugs
Symptoms: Misfires, rough idle and lost economy, or simply a truck past the interval. ExtremeTerrain quotes Chrysler's interval as 102,000 miles [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]. ExtremeTerrain suggests pulling one plug for inspection at 60,000 on modified, trail-used trucks.
Fix: On the 3.8, pull the wires by the boots. On the 3.6, unclip each coil-on-plug connector and remove the coil (typically one 10 mm bolt). Gap the new plugs at 0.050 in for the 3.8 (Champion RE14PLP5) or 0.043 in for the 3.6 (Champion RER8ZWYCB4). Torque them to 13 lb-ft (±2) on the 3.6. ExtremeTerrain gives 12 lb-ft for the 3.8 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]. The Pentastar's 12 mm plugs in aluminum heads don't tolerate over-torquing. Add dielectric grease to the boots.
Tools: 5/8 in spark plug socket · extensions · 3/8 in torque wrench · gap gauge · dielectric grease.

#### Gusset or truss a bent front axle
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A day (welding required) · cost Gusset/truss kit plus welding
Symptoms: Camber you can't align out, odd tire wear or changed steering on a JK running 35s or bigger. Quadratec warns that heavy tires and hard use can bend the axle C's where the ball joints sit.
Fix: Have the axle checked first: a bent C needs straightening or a replacement housing before any gusset goes on. On a straight axle, strip the paint and coatings where the gussets and truss go and tack them in place. Weld in short alternating beads to limit heat distortion, then let it cool and coat it. Many owners do it with the axle out of the Jeep, along with the ball joints.
Tools: Welder · grinder · clamps · axle stands · rust-proof coating.

### Baseline service
Most JKs have been lifted, re-tired or wheeled, so baseline the drivetrain fluids and the front end first. On a 2012–18 Pentastar, look into the engine valley for oil-filter-housing leaks before you do anything else. Buy by engine and year: the filter, plugs, thermostat housing and coolant type all changed during the run.
- Engine oil & filter: 5W-20 meeting MS-6395 · 6 qt (3.8 and 3.6) · Jeep: 8,000 mi or 6 months on the Pentastar, never over 10,000; sooner for severe use (The Pentastar's cartridge filter lives in the top-mounted housing (24 mm cap; don't yank the filter or you can break the pressure-relief valve). The filter changed for 2014.)
- Oil filter housing inspection (2012–18): Plastic housing/cooler in the engine valley · Now, and with a flashlight at every oil change (Oil or coolant pooled under the plenum means it's time for the aluminum upgrade.)
- Engine air & cabin filters: Factory airbox element and cabin filter · Inspect at every oil change; replace when dirty (Dusty trail use clogs the air filter fast.)
- Spark plugs: 3.8: Champion RE14PLP5, 0.050 in, 12 lb-ft per ExtremeTerrain [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · 3.6: Champion RER8ZWYCB4, 0.043 in, 13 lb-ft · ExtremeTerrain quotes Chrysler's 102,000 mi [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]; inspect at 60,000 on modified or trail trucks (The 3.8 uses plug wires; the 3.6 is coil-on-plug.)
- Coolant & thermostat: 3.8 and 2012 3.6: HOAT, ≈13 qt · 2013-on 3.6: OAT 10-yr/150k, 10.5 qt · Flush now if there's no record, then per the coolant's life (Don't mix HOAT and OAT; check which one is in the tank before topping up.)
- Automatic transmission: ATF+4 · 42RLE: 4 qt service fill · W5A580 (NAG1): 5.3 qt service fill · Drain and refill (with a filter) now if there's no record (A service fill only changes part of the fluid; do it twice rather than flushing.)
- Manual transmission (NSG370): Mopar Manual Transmission Lubricant · 1.6 qt · Change now if there's no record (The clutch hydraulics use DOT 3 brake fluid; check the clutch master level.)
- Transfer case (NV241): ATF+4 · 2.1 qt · Change now (Same fluid for Command-Trac and Rock-Trac.)
- Front & rear differentials: 80W-90 (75W-140 for towing) · Dana 30: 2.1 pt · Dana 44 front: 2.7 pt · Dana 44 rear: 4.75 pt · Trac-Lok: add 4 oz limited-slip additive · Now, and every 15,000 mi with heavy use or after deep water (ExtremeTerrain) (You can check JK diff levels without pulling the cover.)
- Driveshaft U-joints: 1350-series joints · Inspect now; grease if greasable (Lifted JKs chew through rear driveshaft joints. Check for play by hand.)
- Front-end inspection: Track bar, tie rods, drag link, ball joints, unit bearings · Now, and after every lift install or hard trail day (Re-torque the hardware and align. This is your death-wobble insurance.)
- Power steering fluid: Power Steering Fluid +4 (ATF+4 acceptable) · Check level and condition now (Big tires work the steering box and pump hard.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 · Flush now, then every 2–3 years [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (The same reservoir type also feeds the clutch on manual trucks.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: 33 inches is the usual answer, with caveats. ExtremeTerrain says many JK owners fit 33s on a stock suspension, but fender rubbing will probably show up off-road at full flex, and width matters as much as height. On JK-Forum, owners of stock two-door Rubicons report 285/75R17s clearing on pavement, with rubbing on the control arms at full lock that adjusting the steering stops can cure. Not every wheel works: one owner couldn't fit 285/75R17s on AEV Pintlers without a lift. 255-width 33s are the safe bet; 35s need a lift.

Q: 3.8 or 3.6, which should I buy?
A: The 3.6 Pentastar (2012–18) makes 285 hp against the 3.8's 202, and comes with a five-speed automatic instead of a four-speed. Quadratec says the 2012 switch ended the JK's 'rolling brick' era. The 3.8 is simpler and cheaper to buy. On a Pentastar, budget for the oil filter housing.

Q: What's the Pentastar cylinder head problem?
A: Some early 2012–13 Wrangler Pentastars had faulty left cylinder heads. Chrysler's bulletin describes excessive cylinder leakage showing up as misfire codes (P0300, P0302, P0304 or P0306); owners also reported a tick from the left bank. Chrysler replaced heads under warranty, fitted redesigned heads to new engines from 2012 (AutoGuide), and in 2014 extended coverage on affected heads to 10 years or 150,000 miles (Warranty Bulletin D-14-12, code X56).

Q: What causes death wobble and how do I fix it?
A: Looseness or wear in the front end, most often the track bar, tie-rod ends, ball joints, control-arm bushings or wheel bearings, usually set off by a tire imbalance or a bump at 45–65 mph. A stabilizer only masks it. Find and replace the worn part, torque the hardware and align the truck.

Q: Is the Rubicon worth it over a Sport?
A: If you'll wheel it, yes. You get Dana 44s at both ends instead of a Dana 30 front, front and rear electric lockers, a 4:1 Rock-Trac instead of 2.72:1, 4.10 gears and the electronic sway-bar disconnect. Retrofitting all of that to a Sport is a big, expensive job. A Moab or Willys Wheeler looks the part but keeps the 2.72:1 transfer case.

Q: How much can a 2-door JK tow?
A: 2,000 lb, against 3,500 lb for the four-door Unlimited, per Quadratec's 2012 spec summary. Maximum payload is about 1,000 lb.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: The EPA rated a 2012 Pentastar two-door at 17 mpg city and 21 highway. The tank holds 18.6 gallons. Lifts, 33–35 inch tires and steel bumpers cost several mpg.

Q: What fluids does it take?
A: Per ExtremeTerrain's JK chart: 3.8 and 3.6 engines take 6 qt of 5W-20. Coolant is HOAT for the 3.8 and 2012 3.6 (about 13 qt), and OAT for 2013-on 3.6s (10.5 qt). The 42RLE takes ATF+4 (4 qt service fill), the W5A580/NAG1 ATF+4 (5.3 qt service fill), and the NSG370 1.6 qt of Mopar Manual Transmission Lubricant. The NV241 takes 2.1 qt of ATF+4. The Dana 30 front takes 2.1 pints, the Dana 44 front 2.7 pints and the Dana 44 rear 4.75 pints of 80W-90, with 75W-140 recommended for towing. Trac-Lok rears need 4 oz of limited-slip additive.

Q: How often should I change the oil?
A: Quadratec cites Jeep's 8,000 miles or six months for the Pentastar, and never more than 10,000. Severe use (towing, dust, off-road) shortens it. Mopar specifies oil meeting MS-6395. Note that the oil filter changed in 2014, so buy the right one.

Q: Why does it tick at cold start?
A: Usually broken rear exhaust manifold bolts letting the manifold leak until it heats up and seals. It's very common on both the 3.8 and the 3.6.

Q: What are the TIPM and clockspring problems?
A: The TIPM is the JK's central power-distribution module. With a failing clockspring, it's the usual source of airbag lights, dead steering-wheel controls, fuel-pump problems and wipers with a mind of their own. Water in the cabin makes it worse.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: A 2012-on Pentastar. Quadratec calls it a generally strong engine, while Driving Line says the 2007–11 3.8 burns oil, leaks intake gaskets and cracks exhaust manifolds, and has seen some spin bearings by 100,000 miles. Driving Line's daily-driver pick is 2013 or newer; SlashGear rates 2012–13 as the standout years. The year to be wary of is 2007: several first-year recalls, and CarComplaints.com logs more complaints for 2007 and 2008 than for any other Wrangler year. Not everyone agrees on the Pentastar's first years, either: RealTruck lists 2012–14 among its worst, citing engine complaints. So on a 2012–13 ask about the left cylinder head, and on any Pentastar check the oil filter housing.

## Jeep Wrangler JK Unlimited (2007–2018)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/jk-unlimited/
Codes: JK Unlimited, JKU

Verdict: The Jeep that let Wrangler people have children, friends and luggage at the same time. The four-door JK turned a toy into a family car and an overland platform, and by 2017 three in four new Wranglers for sale were four-doors. Get the Pentastar, check the front end, and pack lighter than you think.

On April 12, 2006, at the New York Auto Show, Jeep did something it had resisted for 65 years: it put four doors on a Wrangler. The JK Unlimited kept everything that made a Wrangler a Wrangler (a separate frame, solid axles at both ends, a windshield that folds and doors that come off) and added 20.6 inches of wheelbase so adults could sit in the back. It was priced from $21,000. Purists predicted disaster. By mid-2017, three-quarters of the new Wranglers listed for sale were four-doors.

### LONGER THAN EVERYTHING BEFORE IT
Jeep had stretched its short-wheelbase rig before, with the CJ-8 Scrambler and the TJ-based Wrangler Unlimited (LJ), but both added about 10 inches and kept two doors. The JK Unlimited added 20, for a 116-inch wheelbase against the two-door JK's 95.4, and yet it was only 14 inches longer overall than the 2006 LJ. It went on the line in August 2006 alongside the two-door at Toledo, Ohio, and it was the only four-door convertible on sale in America from the death of the Hummer H1 until the Ford Bronco arrived in July 2021.
Mechanically it is the same truck as the two-door. Driving Line's buyer's guide calls the two nearly identical and admits a soft spot for the Unlimited. X (later Sport), Sahara and Rubicon trims were offered from day one. Base trucks got a Dana 30 front axle, a Dana 44 rear and the Command-Trac transfer case with a 2.72:1 low range. The Rubicon added Dana 44s at both ends with electric Tru-Lok lockers, the 4:1 Rock-Trac transfer case and an electronically disconnecting front sway bar. Two-wheel-drive Unlimiteds were sold until 2010; from 2011, every one was a 4x4.

### 3.8 VERSUS 3.6
The JK's original engine was the minivan-derived 3.8-liter EGH V6, rated at 202 hp and 237 lb-ft, with a six-speed NSG370 manual or a four-speed 42RLE automatic. In a heavy four-door it was hard work, and Driving Line lists its habits: burning oil, intake-gasket failures, cracked exhaust manifolds, and a heat-stressed automatic once owners fitted bigger tires. The 2011 update gave the cabin a proper redesign, but the engine had to wait.
For 2012 the Pentastar 3.6 arrived with 285 hp and 260 lb-ft, plus a five-speed W5A580 automatic. Quadratec's spec history says it stopped being a 'rolling brick'. The Pentastar isn't flawless: some 2012–2013 Wrangler engines (2011–2013 across Chrysler's range) got a 10-year/150,000-mile warranty on the left cylinder head, and the plastic oil filter housing in the valley is a known leaker. It's still the JK engine to buy, and Driving Line recommends a 2013 or later truck for daily use.

### THE OVERLAND JEEP
The long wheelbase changed what a Wrangler was for. The four-door rode better, had a usable cargo area behind the rear seat and was rated to tow 3,500 lb against the two-door's 2,000. An industry grew up around it: roof racks, drawer systems, bumpers, and full conversions such as AEV's Brute, a 139-inch-wheelbase double-cab pickup inspired by the Defender 130. Mopar's own JK-8 Independence kit turned an Unlimited into a two-seat pickup in 2011.
The catch is weight. Payload is roughly 900 to 1,300 lb depending on year, trim and source, and a JKU with steel bumpers, a winch, a rooftop tent and two adults goes through that quickly. Expedition Portal's long-running payload thread is full of owners over their door-sticker rating. Their advice: spend on springs and shocks, and cut weight before you add more armor.

### HOW IT ENDED
Toledo built its millionth JK on May 17, 2013. The JK's last model year, 2018, overlapped the new JL Unlimited, and fender decals told the two apart. Production ended on April 27, 2018, and the plant was retooled to build the JL-based Gladiator pickup. The JL kept the formula and fixed much of what JK owners complained about, but it didn't make the JKU obsolete. A well-sorted 2012–2018 Unlimited is still one of the cheapest ways into a solid-axle overland rig that will happily take 35s, and it is far easier to find parts for than a Land Cruiser 80.

### Engineering
The JK Unlimited is a body-on-frame four-door convertible with coil springs and solid axles front and rear, part-time four-wheel drive with a two-speed transfer case, and a 116-inch wheelbase. Unlike the TJ it replaced, it runs nearly everything except the steering through computer control, and it brought stability control to the Wrangler for the first time.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, 116 in wheelbase (20.6 in longer than the two-door JK's 95.4 in; about 185 in overall.)
- Front Axle: Dana 30 (Sport/Sahara) · Dana 44 (Rubicon) (Driving Line rates the Dana 30 at about 35-in tires; on both axles the tubes and C-ends can bend.)
- Rear Axle: Dana 44 (Rubicon gets an electric Tru-Lok locker; Trac-Lok limited slip was optional on other trims. Quadratec says a few very early trucks had a Dana 35.)
- 4Wd System: Command-Trac 2.72:1 · Rock-Trac 4:1 (Both are versions of the NV241 part-time case; the 4:1 low range was Rubicon-only.)
- Engine: 3.8 EGH V6 (2007–11) · 3.6 Pentastar V6 (2012–18) (202 hp / 237 lb-ft, then 285 hp / 260 lb-ft. A 2.8 VM diesel was sold outside the US.)
- Rubicon Extras: Front & rear lockers, sway-bar disconnect (Plus 4.10 gears, 32-in BFGoodrich mud-terrains and rock rails.)

### Versions
- 2007–2011 · JK Unlimited 3.8 · 3.8 L EGH V6 · 202 hp / 237 lb-ft · NSG370 6-speed manual or 42RLE 4-speed auto. 4x2 Unlimited offered until 2010; interior redesign for 2011.
- 2012–2018 · JK Unlimited 3.6 · 3.6 L Pentastar V6 · 285 hp / 260 lb-ft · NSG370 manual or W5A580 5-speed auto. Quadratec says the oil filter changed for 2014.
- 2007–2018 · Rubicon Unlimited · As above · — · Dana 44 axles front and rear with Tru-Lok lockers, Rock-Trac 4:1, electronic sway-bar disconnect, 4.10 gears.
- 2011–2018 (export) · Unlimited CRD · 2.8 L VM turbodiesel I4 · 200 PS · Upgraded 2.8 from 2011 with the five-speed W5A580. Not sold in the US.
- From c. 2012 · AEV Brute · Various · — · Aftermarket 139-in-wheelbase double-cab pickup conversion of the Unlimited, retired after four years.
- 2018 · JK Unlimited (final year) · 3.6 L Pentastar V6 · 285 hp / 260 lb-ft · Sold alongside the new JL, with 'Wrangler JK' fender decals; production ended April 27, 2018.

### Year-by-year
- 2007: JK launch (production from August 2006): 3.8 EGH V6 (202 hp) with a 6-speed manual or 4-speed 42RLE auto; Rubicon has Dana 44s with lockers, 4:1 Rock-Trac and a sway-bar disconnect; the four-door Unlimited is new. First-year trucks drew several recalls (SlashGear), 2007–08 log the most complaints on CarComplaints.com (CarGurus), and Driving Line warns the 3.8 burns oil, leaks intake gaskets and cracks exhaust manifolds [avoid]
- 2009: Hill Start Assist standard; Trailer Sway Control available
- 2010: Easier-folding soft top; Uconnect on MyGig-equipped trucks
- 2011: Fully redesigned interior with steering-wheel controls, Bluetooth, and available heated seats and leather. Mopar's JK-8 pickup kit for the Unlimited also arrives.
- 2012: 3.6 Pentastar V6 (285 hp, 260 lb-ft) and 5-speed W5A580 automatic replace the 3.8 and the 4-speed. The Pentastar is the engine to have (Quadratec, Driving Line); Driving Line's daily-driver pick is a 2013 or newer [buy]
- 2012–13: Some Pentastars have faulty left cylinder heads (misfire codes); covered by the X56 extension to 10 years/150,000 miles
- 2013: Second windshield-washer nozzle returns; one-handed rear-seat fold; Moab edition with AEV bumpers. The millionth JK is built in May 2013.
- 2014: Clear park and turn lamps; optional 6.5 in Uconnect; Rubicon X edition
- 2015: Willys Wheeler and Rubicon Hard Rock join the range; Torx tool kit for doors and windshield standard; Alpine audio option
- 2018: Final year, sold alongside the new JL with 'Wrangler JK' fender decals; Golden Eagle edition. Production ends April 27, 2018.

### Capability
- Towing: 3,500 lb (1,588 kg)
- Payload: 1,000–1,150 lb (454–522 kg) (2007–11; Quadratec's two spec sheets disagree)
- Fuel tank: 21.6 gal (82 L) (2007 spec)
- Ground clearance (axle): 10.5 in front / 10.1 in rear (267 / 257 mm) (Rubicon on LT255/75R17)
- Approach / departure / breakover: 44.4° / 40.5° / 20.8° (Rubicon on LT255/75R17)
- Fuel economy: EPA 16 city / 20 hwy (2017, 3.6 automatic (16/21 manual))
- Curb weight: 4,075–4,340 lb (1,848–1,969 kg) (2007–2011 X manual to Rubicon auto)
- Turning circle: 41.2 ft (12.56 m) (curb to curb, 225/75R16 tires)
- Wheelbase: 116.0 in (2,946 mm)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: P225/75R16 (X/Sport), P245/75R16 (option), P255/75R17 (Sahara), P255/70R18 (Sahara option), LT255/75R17 BFGoodrich Mud-Terrain (Rubicon)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x127 (5x5")
- Center Bore: 71.5 mm
- Lug Thread: 1/2"-20 (60° cone seat)
- Lug Torque: 100 lb-ft (Northridge4x4); ExtremeTerrain gives an 85–125 lb-ft range [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 33 in (e.g. 285/70R17) (JEGS puts the stock-height limit at about 33 in. Driving Line fitted 35x12.50R17s to a stock-height 2017 JK Unlimited Sport on 4.75 in-backspacing wheels after removing the front splash guard, and concluded that real off-road use needs aftermarket or heavily trimmed flares.)
- Biggest tire, 2.5 in lift: 35x12.50 or 285/75R17 (285/75R17 works on factory 17s; 35x12.50 wants 18x9 or 20x9 wheels at about 0 to +1 mm offset.)
- Biggest tire, 3.5 in lift: 37 in (JEGS says 37s need about 3.5 in of lift and advises axle, driveshaft and gearing upgrades; 40s need about 4.5 in.)

### Buying checks
- Pick your engine first: 2007–2011 trucks have the 3.8 and four-speed automatic; 2012–2018 have the Pentastar and five-speed. Driving Line suggests 2013 or later for a daily driver and says any year is fine for a weekend trail rig.
- Drive it over a pothole at 50 mph: Death wobble usually shows up at 45–65 mph after a bump. Have someone turn the wheel a quarter turn each way with the engine running while you watch both ends of the front track bar. Any movement at the bushing or bracket is a red flag.
- Look at the oil filter housing: On a 3.6, pull the engine cover and look for oil in the valley at the back of the engine, and for oil on the bellhousing. The plastic housing is a known leaker. Curbside Classic's 2015 JK started leaking at about 55,000 miles.
- On a 3.8, check for oil burning and manifold ticks: Ask how much oil it uses between changes, and listen for a cold-start exhaust tick, which can mean a cracked manifold. Driving Line also lists intake-gasket failures and, on hard-used engines, ring and main-bearing failures from about 100,000 miles.
- 2012–2013: ask about the left cylinder head: Chrysler extended the warranty on the left cylinder head of affected 2012–2013 Wrangler Pentastars (2011–2013 across its range) to 10 years or 150,000 miles; its bulletin covers excessive cylinder leakage showing up as misfire codes. Ask whether the head has been replaced and get the dealer record.
- Sight down the front axle: On lifted trucks with big tires, look for bent axle tubes or C-ends and uneven tire wear. Check for a truss. A bent Dana 30 housing usually means replacing it, often with a Dynatrac or Currie unit.
- Weigh the build against the door sticker: Bumpers, a winch, a rack and a tent can put a JKU over its payload before anyone gets in. Check the sticker, and look at the rear coils and the bump-stop gap for sag.
- Modified Jeeps: price the parts, then get a shop inspection: Driving Line's advice is to research every listed aftermarket part, have a 4x4 shop inspect the truck, and assume a heavily built Jeep has had a hard life.

### Common repairs
#### Chase down death wobble (track bar first)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–3 hours to diagnose; longer if parts need replacing · cost From free (re-torquing) to about $250–$400 for a JK track bar, per ExtremeTerrain's price guide
Symptoms: Violent side-to-side shaking of the steering wheel and front axle, usually at 45–65 mph after a bump or bridge seam, which stops only when you slow right down.
Fix: Check the front track bar first: with the engine running, have a helper turn the wheel a quarter turn each way while you watch both ends. If the bar moves without the bolt, or one end moves and the other doesn't, the bushing or bracket is worn. ExtremeTerrain lists the frame-side bolt at 125 ft-lb. Then work through the ball joints, tie-rod and drag-link ends, control-arm bushings and wheel bearings, and check tire balance and pressure. Replace whatever is loose, re-torque everything with the Jeep on the ground, and get an alignment. Quadratec and ExtremeTerrain both warn that a new steering stabilizer only hides the cause.
Tools: Helper · torque wrench · large sockets · pry bar · floor jack and stands · paint pen to mark bolts.

#### Replace the Pentastar oil filter housing / cooler (2012–2018)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 6 hours the first time (one owner's log) · cost Housing plus gaskets and an oil change; tools under $30 for one owner
Symptoms: Oil pooling in the valley under the intake, running over the back of the engine and dripping from the bellhousing. Sometimes coolant leaks too.
Fix: Remove the engine cover and intake duct, then disconnect the injectors, coils, vacuum lines and brackets. Take off the upper intake (seven 8 mm bolts) and the lower manifold (eight bolts). Unplug the two sensors on the cooler and remove its five E8 external-Torx bolts. Mop the oil out of the valley, move the sensors and fittings to the new aluminum housing, fit new gaskets and O-rings, and torque in sequence. Reassemble, then refill the oil and coolant. Plug the intake ports with towels while you work. Don't overtighten the filter cap, which is specified at 18 lb-ft. Curbside Classic suspects overtightening contributes to the cracking.
Tools: E8 external-Torx socket · 27 mm and 19 mm deep sockets · inch-pound torque wrench · hose clamp pliers · trim tool · shop vac · Dorman 926-876 aluminum housing (as used by Curbside Classic).

#### Replace a cracked 3.8 exhaust manifold (2007–2011)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day per side, more if studs break · cost Manifold plus gaskets and studs; studs that snap add drilling time
Symptoms: A ticking or puffing noise at cold start that quietens as the engine warms, a smell of exhaust in the engine bay, and soot marks at the manifold-to-head joint.
Fix: Driving Line names cracked exhaust manifolds as a 3.8 weak point. Soak the studs in penetrating oil the night before. Unbolt the heat shield and the downpipe flange, then remove the manifold nuts. Inspect the studs and replace any that are stretched or corroded. Clean the head flange, fit new gaskets and a new manifold, and torque the nuts evenly from the center out. Check the oxygen sensor connectors and the downpipe gasket while you're in there.
Tools: Penetrating oil · long extensions and swivels · stud extractor · torque wrench · new manifold studs and nuts.

#### Press in new front ball joints
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A day for both sides · cost About $40–$60 a pair for stock joints, $200–$250 for a heavy-duty set of four (ExtremeTerrain)
Symptoms: Clunks over bumps, wandering, uneven tire wear, or play when you rock a lifted wheel top to bottom. Worn joints can contribute to death wobble.
Fix: Lift and support the axle, then remove the wheel, caliper, rotor, ABS sensor and the hub/bearing. Pull the axle shaft, then separate and remove the knuckle. Press out the upper and lower joints with a ball-joint press and the correct adapters, and press in the new ones square. Refit everything, torque to the factory figures (Northridge4x4 lists 75 ft-lb for the ball-joint nuts, 75 ft-lb for the hub bolts and 100 ft-lb for the axle nut), and get an alignment. Many owners replace the hub bearings and axle-shaft U-joints at the same time.
Tools: Ball-joint press and JK adapter set · axle-nut socket · breaker bar · torque wrench · pickle fork or hammer for the tapers.

#### Replace a front hub and bearing
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours per side · cost A hub assembly per side
Symptoms: A growl that changes with speed or while turning, play when you rock the wheel at 12 and 6 o'clock, or an ABS light from a damaged sensor.
Fix: Lift the corner and remove the wheel, caliper bracket and rotor. Unplug the ABS sensor, remove the axle nut and the three hub bolts from the back of the knuckle, and pull the hub (it may need persuading). Clean the knuckle face, fit the new hub, and torque the bolts and axle nut (Northridge4x4: 75 ft-lb hub bolts, 100 ft-lb axle nut). Mopar lists different hubs for 2007–2010 and 2011–2018 JKs, so order by year.
Tools: Large axle-nut socket · breaker bar · torque wrench · wire brush · anti-seize for the hub-to-knuckle face.

#### Truss a front axle before it bends (or after)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend with welding · cost Truss kit plus welding; a bent housing needs replacing, not trussing
Symptoms: Toe that won't stay in alignment, inside-edge tire wear, or a visibly bent tube after a hard hit. It's common on lifted trucks running 35s and up on the factory axle.
Fix: Driving Line says the small tubes and C-ends on both the Dana 30 and the Rubicon's Dana 44 can bend with oversized tires, and points to EVO Manufacturing trusses as a preventive fix. Check the housing is straight first, because a truss locks in whatever shape it has. Strip the axle (or at least remove the brackets that are in the way), grind the tubes clean, tack the truss in place, then weld in short alternating stitches to limit heat distortion. Paint it and re-check the alignment. If the housing is already bent, Dynatrac and Currie sell replacement housings.
Tools: MIG or stick welder · grinder · straightedge or axle-alignment check · paint.

#### Re-spring the rear for an overland load
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost A pair of rear coils plus shocks; more if you go to a full lift
Symptoms: A rear end that sags below the front, bottoms out on washboard, or sits on the bump stops with a full load of water, fuel and gear.
Fix: Weigh the loaded truck first. Expedition Portal owners say the rear axle and suspension are the weak points under long-term heavy loads, and recommend springs and shocks rather than frame or axle changes. Support the frame, lower the axle on a jack after disconnecting the rear shocks, sway-bar links and track bar if needed, then swap the coils and fit the matching jounce bumpers. Refit at ride height and torque the suspension bolts with the Jeep on its wheels.
Tools: Floor jack and frame stands · sockets · torque wrench · spring compressor not usually needed on JK rear coils.

### Baseline service
With no receipts, assume nothing has been done. Change every fluid, and know which engine you have: the 3.8 (2007–2011) and the Pentastar (2012–2018) use different filters, plugs and automatic transmissions. Check the Pentastar's oil filter housing for leaks at the first oil change. Then do the gear oil, which is the service owners skip most. Rubicons and trucks with Trac-Lok need the right axle oil, and a limited-slip axle needs friction modifier.
- Engine oil & filter: 3.6: 6 qt SAE 5W-20 meeting MS-6395 (5W-30 permitted) · 3.8: 6.0 qt with filter, 5W-20 or 5W-30 per the filler cap · Then per the oil-life monitor or owner's manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (The Pentastar uses a cartridge filter under a 24 mm cap on top of the engine. Quadratec notes the filter changed for 2014, so buy for your year, and says to pull the old element gently because the pressure-relief valve is in the cap. Don't overtighten the cap; Curbside Classic gives 18 lb-ft.)
- Engine air filter: Panel filter in the airbox · Inspect at every oil change; more often on dusty trails (If a snorkel or aftermarket intake is fitted, check the clamps and seals as well as the element.)
- Cabin air filter: Quadratec lists JK cabin filters from the 2011 model year on · Replace when dirty [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Quadratec lists separate cabin filters for 2011–2013 and later JKs.)
- Spark plugs: 3.6 Pentastar: 0.043 in (1.10 mm) gap · KBB's schedule lists spark plugs at 100,000 mi (Pentastar plugs are under the intake plenum on the rear bank, so it's a good time to look for oil filter housing seepage. 3.8 plugs: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL].)
- Coolant, thermostat & hoses: 3.8 and 2012 3.6: HOAT 5-year/100,000-mile, about 13 qt · 2013–18 3.6: Mopar 10-year/150,000-mile OAT (MS.90032), 10.5 qt (ExtremeTerrain) · KBB's schedule lists coolant at 100,000 mi; inspect hoses at every service (Don't mix HOAT and OAT; check what's in the tank before topping up. On a 3.6, a coolant leak in the valley can come from the oil cooler, not the water pump.)
- Automatic transmission: W5A580 (2012–18): Mopar ATF+4, 5.3 qt service fill / 8.1 qt overhaul · 42RLE (2007–11): ATF+4, about 4.0 qt drain-and-fill / 8.8 qt total · KBB lists transmission fluid at 100,000 mi; sooner if you tow or run big tires (Driving Line says heat kills both automatics, especially with oversized tires, towing or hard off-road use, and recommends an auxiliary cooler and proper gearing. A drain-and-fill with a new filter is the usual DIY.)
- Manual transmission (NSG370): Mopar manual transmission lubricant meeting MS-9224 · 1.6 qt · Change on a truck with unknown history [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Driving Line says the NSG370 can grind, pop out of gear and get noisy, and recommends regular fresh fluid. A 2007 lube chart gives 22 ft-lb for the fill and drain plugs.)
- Transfer case (NV241 Command-Trac / Rock-Trac): Mopar ATF+4 · 2.1 qt · Change on purchase, then per the severe-service schedule [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Remove the fill plug before the drain plug. Both are chain-driven cases with aluminum housings (Driving Line), so don't overtighten the plugs.)
- Front axle: GL-5 80W-90 · Dana 30 (186 FBI): 2.1 pt · Dana 44 (216 FBI, Rubicon): 2.7 pt · Change on purchase and after deep water crossings (If the oil looks milky, water has got in through the axle vent or seals.)
- Rear axle (Dana 44): GL-5 80W-90 · 226 RBI: 4.75 pt · synthetic 75W-140 for trailer towing · add 4 oz Mopar limited-slip additive to Trac-Lok axles · Change on purchase; more often if you tow (A tag on the cover marks a limited-slip axle. Rubicon lockers don't need friction modifier.)
- Power steering fluid: Mopar Power Steering Fluid +4 or Mopar ATF+4 · Refresh the reservoir if the fluid is dark (Big tires work the steering box hard. Look for leaks at the box and the pressure lines.)
- Brake & clutch fluid: Mopar DOT 3 (DOT 4 acceptable if DOT 3 isn't available) · Flush on purchase, then every 2–3 years [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Manual trucks share the fluid type in the clutch master cylinder.)
- U-joints & driveshafts: Front axle-shaft U-joints, plus driveshaft joints where greaseable · Inspect at every oil change; grease any zerks (Rubicon Dana 44 front U-joints take a beating with lockers and big tires, so carry a spare.)
- PCV valve: Engine-specific · Inspect with the plugs (A sticking PCV valve adds to oil consumption, which matters on a 3.8.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: 33s. JK-Forum owners agree that most 285/70R17s (about 33 inches) fit on stock wheels, at stock height, with the stock bump stops. Expect light rubbing at full lock and at full flex, where they touch the flares, liners and sometimes the front sway bar. A steering-stop washer and the right backspacing help. ExtremeTerrain says 35s need at least a 2–3-inch lift, the right wheel offset and possibly new gears.

Q: 3.8 or 3.6?
A: The 3.6 Pentastar (2012–2018) by a mile: 285 hp against 202, plus a five-speed automatic instead of the four-speed. The 3.8 is known for burning oil, intake-gasket leaks and cracked exhaust manifolds. Driving Line suggests a 2013 or later truck for daily use. A cheap 3.8 can still make a good trail rig if you accept its limits.

Q: How much can a JK Unlimited tow?
A: 3,500 lb, with a 350-lb tongue weight for the 2017 Rubicon. That's against 2,000 lb for the two-door. For heavy towing the factory manual calls for synthetic 75W-140 in the rear axle.

Q: What's the payload?
A: Less than you think. Quadratec lists 1,067–1,301 lb for 2012 four-doors depending on trim. For 2017, KBB lists 880–1,000 lb and Cars.com gives the Rubicon 1,178 lb against a 5,700-lb GVWR. Your door-jamb sticker is the number that counts, and a fully built overland JKU often exceeds it.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: The EPA rated the 2017 Unlimited 3.6 at 16 mpg city and 20 highway with the automatic (16/21 manual), and KBB lists a 22.5-gallon tank. Bigger tires, a lift and a rack all bring that down.

Q: What oil does it take?
A: 3.6 Pentastar: six quarts of 5W-20 meeting Chrysler MS-6395, or 5W-30 in hot climates. The filter is a cartridge under a cap on top of the engine, and Quadratec notes the filter changed for 2014, so buy for your year. The 3.8 also takes about six quarts with the filter, in 5W-20 or 5W-30; check the oil filler cap.

Q: Which Unlimiteds have lockers?
A: Every Rubicon has electric Tru-Lok lockers front and rear. Per Wikipedia, a rear locker was optional on X and Sahara for 2007, then only on select X models for 2008–2009; later the only non-Rubicon options were the 2015 Wrangler X and the 2016 75th Anniversary Edition. A Trac-Lok limited slip was the usual non-Rubicon option.

Q: Will the Dana 30 front axle handle 35s?
A: Driving Line rates the non-Rubicon Dana 30 at about 35-inch tires. The tubes and C-ends can bend with big tires or hard use, and that's true of the Rubicon's Dana 44 too. Trusses help prevent it; replacement housings from Dynatrac or Currie are the cure.

Q: What do I do if it gets death wobble?
A: Grip the wheel, don't brake hard, and slow down smoothly until it stops. Then fix the cause: start with the track bar, then the tie-rod ends, drag link, ball joints, control-arm bushings and wheel bearings, and check tire balance. A new steering stabilizer only masks it, and an alignment comes last.

Q: What's the Pentastar cylinder-head issue?
A: In June 2014 Chrysler extended the warranty on the left cylinder head of some 2011–2013 3.6 V6s (2012–2013 on the Wrangler) to 10 years or 150,000 miles after cylinder-leakage misfires. Dealers replaced the head where testing showed excessive leakage, and AutoGuide reported that redesigned heads went into production in 2012. The extension has now run out, so a 2012–2013 truck with a misfire on that bank deserves a careful look.

Q: Is the four-door worse off-road than the two-door?
A: On tight, technical trails the 116-inch wheelbase gives up breakover angle and turning circle compared with the 95.4-inch two-door. Everywhere else it rides better and carries more. Driving Line says the two are mechanically nearly identical and recommends driving both before you choose.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: A 2012-on Pentastar. Quadratec calls it a generally strong engine, while Driving Line says the 2007–11 3.8 burns oil, leaks intake gaskets and cracks exhaust manifolds, and has seen some spin bearings by 100,000 miles. Driving Line's daily-driver pick is 2013 or newer; SlashGear rates 2012–13 as the standout years. The year to be wary of is 2007: several first-year recalls, and CarComplaints.com logs more complaints for 2007 and 2008 than for any other Wrangler year. Not everyone agrees on the Pentastar's first years, either: RealTruck lists 2012–14 among its worst, citing engine complaints. So on a 2012–13 ask about the left cylinder head, and on any Pentastar check the oil filter housing.
