## Jeep Wagoneer & Grand Wagoneer (WS) (2022–present)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/jeep/wagoneer-ws/
Codes: WS, Wagoneer, Grand Wagoneer, Wagoneer L, Grand Wagoneer L

Verdict: Jeep spent a decade promising to bring back the Grand Wagoneer, then built a 6,000-pound, three-row, air-sprung luxury barge that took four years to remember it was a Jeep. It tows 10,000 pounds and will happily do a fire road, but it isn't the woody you're thinking of, and nobody at Jeep claims it's a rock crawler.

The WS is Jeep's full-size, body-on-frame, three-row SUV, revealed on March 11, 2021 as the 2022 Wagoneer and Grand Wagoneer and built at Warren Truck Assembly in Michigan. It borrows two of the most loved names in the family, from the SJ Wagoneer of 1963 and the original Grand Wagoneer, and aims them at the Chevrolet Tahoe, the Cadillac Escalade and the Range Rover. It launched with Hemi V8s, switched to a twin-turbo straight six, and spent its first five years arguing with itself about whether it was even a Jeep.

### TEN YEARS OF 'SOON' (2011–2021)
Sergio Marchionne promised a new Grand Wagoneer at the Detroit show in January 2011, then planned on a Grand Cherokee and Durango platform. The project slipped repeatedly: a 2013 delay, a dealer preview promised for August 2015, teaser photos in October 2016 pointing at a 2019 model, and another delay in March 2017. In 2017 FCA committed $1 billion to retool Warren Truck for it, a figure that later rose to $1.5 billion. Spy photographers caught a Ram 1500-based test mule in December 2019, and COVID pushed production back again.
Jeep showed the Grand Wagoneer Concept on September 3, 2020, with no Jeep badge anywhere on it, and revealed the production trucks on March 11, 2021. Stellantis described them as a 'premium extension of the Jeep brand', with Wagoneer-certified dealers, a client-service concierge and ten written promises to every owner. Wagoneer and Grand Wagoneer shared one body on a new frame that MotorTrend says is loosely based on the Ram 1500 (DT), but different enough that almost nothing is shared, and 2 inches wider than the Ram. They are built on the same Warren line as the Ram 1500 Classic.

### TWO NAMES, ONE TRUCK, NO BADGE
Here is the part that confused everyone. The Wagoneer and the Grand Wagoneer are the same size. The Wagoneer (Series I, II, III and Carbide) was the mainstream model aimed at the Tahoe. The Grand Wagoneer (Series I, II, III and Obsidian) was the luxury version aimed at the Escalade and Navigator, with a two-tone black roof, fender flares, power side steps, bigger screens and, at launch, a CNBC-reported top price above $111,000. For 2023 Jeep added the Wagoneer L and Grand Wagoneer L, a foot longer on a 130-inch wheelbase. MotorTrend says buyers thought the Grand Wagoneer was a stretched Wagoneer. It wasn't: 'Grand' meant pricier, not bigger.
The branding didn't help. Wikipedia describes the launch branding as 'Wagoneer by Jeep', and the trucks wore Wagoneer badges with no Jeep logo. On February 29, 2024, Jalopnik reported that Jeep CEO Antonio Filosa had said Wagoneer would stop being a sub-brand once the electric Wagoneer S launched, and that future Wagoneers would wear Jeep badges. On October 14, 2025, Jeep revealed the facelifted 2026 Grand Wagoneer: the standalone Wagoneer nameplate was dropped, every truck became a Grand Wagoneer, Jeep badges went on front and rear, the Series trim names were replaced, and pricing started at $64,740. MotorTrend's headline that day was blunt: 'The Jeep Wagoneer Is Dead'.

### FROM HEMI TO HURRICANE
The 2022 Wagoneer used the 5.7-liter Hemi V8 with Stellantis's 48-volt eTorque mild-hybrid system, rated at 392 hp and 404 lb-ft on a 3.21 axle ratio. The 2022 Grand Wagoneer got the 6.4-liter Hemi with 471 hp and 455 lb-ft on a 3.92 axle. Both drove through an eight-speed ZF-designed 8HP75 automatic. For 2023 the 3.0-liter Hurricane twin-turbo straight six arrived in the L models: 420 hp and 468 lb-ft in standard-output form, or 510 hp and 500 lb-ft as the high-output engine in the Grand Wagoneer. It was also offered as an option above the 5.7 in the regular Wagoneer.
For 2024 the V8s were dropped and every WS got a Hurricane. Jeep kept the 10,000-pound tow rating and said the six was up to 15 percent more efficient than the V8 it replaced. The high-output engine went up to 540 hp and 521 lb-ft for 2025. For 2026 only the 420-hp standard-output engine is offered, and the high-output version is on hold while Jeep readies a range-extended plug-in hybrid with a 92-kWh battery. Asked about a Hemi comeback, Jeep chief Bob Broderdorf told MotorTrend 'no announcements at this time'.

### HOW BOXY, HOW OFF-ROAD, HONESTLY
Boxy, yes, in the way a filing cabinet is boxy: slab sides, an upright tailgate and a seven-slot grille stretched across 214.7 inches of body, or 226.7 inches for an L. Car and Driver says the 2026 facelift made the design squarer still, with the headlights set higher. But this is a fully independent family hauler, not a solid-axle truck. It has short- and long-arm front suspension with aluminum lower arms and a five-link independent rear on coil springs or Quadra-Lift air springs. The SJ's leaf springs and Dana 44 front axle are a world away.
Jeep never gave it a Trail Rated badge. The best setup is the Advanced All-Terrain Group, which adds a two-speed transfer case (2.64:1 low), a 3.92 axle, a rear electronic limited-slip differential, 18-inch all-terrain tires, skid plates, tow hooks and a 48:1 crawl ratio. With the air suspension in Off-Road 2 it has 10 inches of clearance, 25/24/22-degree approach, departure and breakover angles, and 24 inches of wading depth. MotorTrend ran an Advanced All-Terrain Wagoneer for 20,672 miles. Its verdict: keep it to dirt and fire roads, because the belly is too low and the flanks too exposed for anything harder, even at full height. The Grand Wagoneer is better at reaching a trailhead with a 10,000-pound camper than at driving the trail itself.

### Data plate
- Platform: WS (body-on-frame)
- Revealed: March 11, 2021 (2022 model year)
- Plant: Warren Truck Assembly, Warren, Michigan
- Engines: 5.7 Hemi eTorque V8 · 6.4 Hemi V8 (2022–23) · 3.0 Hurricane twin-turbo I6 (2023–)
- Output: 392–540 hp depending on engine and year
- Transmission: 8-speed 8HP75 automatic
- 4Wd: Quadra-Trac I / II, Quadra-Drive II (2.64:1 low)
- Suspension: Independent front and rear; coils or Quadra-Lift air
- Wheelbase: 123.0 in · 130.0 in (L)
- Length: 214.7 in · 226.7 in (L)
- Curb Weight: 5,960–6,420 lb · 6,068–6,704 lb (L)
- Ground Clearance: 8.0 in normal · 10.0 in Off-Road 2 (air)
- Towing: Up to 10,000 lb

### Engineering
The WS has a separate, fully boxed high-strength-steel ladder frame with crossmembers welded inside and out, aluminum hood and doors, a composite liftgate and about 6,500 welds in the body. MotorTrend says it is loosely related to the Ram 1500 (DT) but shares almost nothing with it, and MotorTrend's 2026 coverage calls the platform STLA Frame. Suspension is independent at all four corners, on coils or four-corner air springs with semi-active damping. Power goes through a ZF-designed 8HP75 eight-speed automatic to one of three Quadra-Trac or Quadra-Drive systems. Rear-wheel drive was offered on the Wagoneer, while four-wheel drive was standard on the Grand Wagoneer.
- Chassis: Body-on-frame, fully boxed rails, 123.0 in / 130.0 in (L) wheelbase (Loosely Ram 1500 (DT)-based but 2 in wider, with almost nothing shared, per MotorTrend. Frame-mounted steel blockers behind the front tires help in small-overlap crashes.)
- Suspension: Independent: SLA front, five-link rear (Aluminum front lower arms and knuckles, cast-aluminum rear links. Steel coils with monotube shocks as standard, Quadra-Lift air springs with semi-active damping optional on Wagoneer and standard on Grand Wagoneer.)
- Quadra-Lift Air: Five heights, 3.6 in total span (Park −1.6 in, Aero −0.6 in, normal 8.0 in, Off-Road 1 9.0 in, Off-Road 2 10.0 in of ground clearance. Closed-loop system with an external valve block and a secondary reservoir.)
- 4X4 Systems: Quadra-Trac I · Quadra-Trac II · Quadra-Drive II (QT I is full-time and single-speed, with no low range. QT II and QD II have a two-speed transfer case with 2.64:1 low. QD II adds a rear electronic limited-slip diff. Selec-Terrain has Auto, Sport, Rock, Snow and Sand/Mud modes.)
- Engines: 5.7 Hemi eTorque V8 · 6.4 Hemi V8 · 3.0 Hurricane twin-turbo I6 (392 / 471 hp for the V8s (2022–23). The Hurricane makes 420 hp in standard-output form and 510 hp (2023–24) or 540 hp (2025) in high-output form. 2026 is standard-output only.)
- Capability: 25° / 24° / 22° · 24 in wading · 10,000 lb tow (Approach, departure and breakover angles are at maximum air height. The Advanced All-Terrain Group gives a 48:1 crawl ratio.)

### Versions
- 2022–2023 · Wagoneer (WS) · 5.7 Hemi V8 with 48 V eTorque · 392 hp · 404 lb-ft · 3.21 axle. Coils standard, air optional. RWD or 4x4. Hurricane optional for 2023.
- 2022–2023 · Grand Wagoneer (WS) · 6.4 Hemi V8 · 471 hp · 455 lb-ft · 3.92 axle, Quadra-Drive II and air suspension standard. Series I–III and Obsidian.
- 2023–2025 · Wagoneer · Wagoneer L · 3.0 Hurricane twin-turbo I6 (standard output) · 420 hp · 468 lb-ft · L is 12 in longer on a 130 in wheelbase. Hurricane-only from 2024.
- 2023–2024 · Grand Wagoneer · Grand Wagoneer L · 3.0 Hurricane twin-turbo I6 (high output) · 510 hp · 500 lb-ft · The V8 was dropped for 2024. Series I–III and Obsidian trims.
- 2025 · Grand Wagoneer · Grand Wagoneer L · 3.0 Hurricane HO · 540 hp · 521 lb-ft · The last year of the separate Wagoneer nameplate.
- 2026– · Grand Wagoneer · Grand Wagoneer L (facelift) · 3.0 Hurricane (standard output) · 420 hp · 468 lb-ft · One name, Jeep badges, no chrome. New Upland off-road trim (short wheelbase only). Range-extended PHEV announced.

### Year-by-year
- 2011: Sergio Marchionne announces the Grand Wagoneer name will return (Detroit auto show, January)
- 2020: Grand Wagoneer Concept shown September 3 with no Jeep badging
- 2022: Launch model year (revealed March 11, 2021): Wagoneer 5.7 eTorque (392 hp) and Grand Wagoneer 6.4 (471 hp). Early builds hit by air-suspension TSB 02-001-22 and several software recalls
- 2023: Wagoneer L and Grand Wagoneer L (130 in wheelbase) debut with the 3.0 Hurricane twin-turbo six: 420 hp, or 510 hp high-output in Grand Wagoneers
- 2024: Hemi V8s dropped, all trucks Hurricane-powered. February: Jeep says Wagoneer will stop being a sub-brand. IIHS 2024 Top Safety Pick (Wagoneer)
- 2025: High-output Hurricane rises to 540 hp and 521 lb-ft. Last year of the standalone Wagoneer nameplate
- 2026: Facelift revealed October 14, 2025: every truck is a Grand Wagoneer, Jeep badges, no chrome, new trims including the short-wheelbase Upland. Standard-output 420-hp Hurricane only. Starts at $64,740

### Capability
- Towing: Up to 10,000 lb (4,536 kg) (Properly equipped Wagoneer. Motor1 reported 9,860 lb for the 2023 Grand Wagoneer.)
- Ground clearance: 8.0 in (203 mm) normal · 10.0 in (254 mm) Off-Road 2 (Quadra-Lift air suspension)
- Approach / departure / breakover: 25° / 24° / 22° (At maximum air-suspension height)
- Wading depth: 24 in (610 mm)
- Crawl ratio: 48:1 (Advanced All-Terrain Group, 2.64:1 low range, 3.92 axle)
- Fuel economy: EPA 16 city / 26 hwy / 19 combined (2023 Wagoneer 4x4, 420-hp Hurricane, per MotorTrend. MotorTrend averaged 16.4 mpg over 20,672 miles.)
- Curb weight: 5,960–6,420 lb (2,703–2,912 kg) · L: 6,068–6,704 lb (2,752–3,041 kg)
- Wheelbase / length: 123.0 / 214.7 in · L: 130.0 / 226.7 in

### Buying checks
- Run the VIN for recalls first: NHTSA lists more than a dozen WS campaigns. Many are rear-camera software fixes (23V-577, 24V-436, 24V-944, 26V-326, 26V-531). There's also an airbag-control software fix (21V-873), a B-pillar trim that can foul the curtain airbag (23V-545), third-row belt buckles (23V-716), door and window trim that can fall off (25V-593, 25V-642), roof-rack crossbar pivot bolts (26V-584) and TPMS software (26V-559). Make sure each one is closed.
- Cycle the air suspension through every height: On an air-sprung truck, run it from Park to Off-Road 2 and back with the engine idling, and look for a 'Service Air Suspension' message. Early 2022 trucks built on or before February 15, 2022 are covered by TSB 02-001-22: unseated air lines, an unplugged control module, disconnected height sensors and even red shipping caps left on the compressor vent hose.
- Ask whether the software is current: This truck runs on software. Bulletins cover blank or frozen 10.1- and 12-inch center screens (radio update TSB 08-039-22), power-steering module flashes (08-202-22) and telematics resets (08-173-21). MotorTrend's long-term Wagoneer was updated at every dealer service. Check the screens, cameras, remote start and app connection before you sign.
- 2022 5.7 eTorque: test low-speed stop-start: In 2024 NHTSA opened a probe into reports of 2022 Ram 1500s and Wagoneers losing power, with the engine shutting off at low speed. On a test drive, do several stops and restarts in traffic and note any warning lights. Ask whether any dealer work was done on the eTorque system or the 48 V battery, which sits under the cabin floor.
- Know which 4x4 system it has: Quadra-Trac I is single-speed, with no low range. For trails, look for Quadra-Trac II or Quadra-Drive II with the 2.64:1 low range. Best of all is the Advanced All-Terrain Group, with a 3.92 axle, rear electronic LSD, 18-inch all-terrain tires, skid plates and tow hooks. A rear-drive Wagoneer is a different vehicle altogether.
- Check the oil in the service records: The standard-output Hurricane specifies 0W-20, while the high-output Hurricane in Grand Wagoneers specifies 0W-40 (MS-A0921). A Grand Wagoneer serviced with the wrong oil by a quick-lube shop is a reason to ask more questions. The 6.4 also uses 0W-40, and the 5.7 uses 0W-20.
- If you'll tow, look for the right package: The 10,000-lb rating applies to properly equipped Wagoneers. The Heavy-Duty Trailer Tow package adds the trailer brake controller, hitch zoom and heavy-duty cooling. MotorTrend found the hitch sat oddly high, so they needed a big drop hitch, and the air suspension kept adjusting ride height with a trailer attached.
- Price it against a new one: A new 2026 Grand Wagoneer starts at $64,740, so check new-truck pricing and incentives before paying close to that for a used one. Bring a Trailer has sold only one WS so far: a 2025 Grand Wagoneer L Series III for $78,500 in January 2026.

### Common repairs
#### Diagnose a 'Service Air Suspension' warning
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours to inspect · cost Covered by TSB 02-001-22 on affected 2022 trucks; parts plus labor otherwise
Symptoms: 'Service Air Suspension' in the cluster, the truck stuck at one height, or air ride not working front and rear. On early 2022 trucks the code C15AE-00 (compressor pressure line leak) is common.
Fix: Start with what FCA's TSB checks. Put the truck in Tire Jack mode from the radio's Suspension menu before you lift it. Remove the front inner wheel liners. Check that the air suspension control module connector is fully seated and the compressor vent hose is connected with no red shipping caps left on it. Confirm that each air line goes into its spring up to the tape mark, within 1 mm. Check that the front and rear ride-height sensors are plugged in and their linkage rods are attached. Deflating the springs and clearing codes needs a scan tool with air-suspension functions (the dealer uses wiTECH). Leaks after that call for soapy water on the lines and the valve block.
Tools: Scan tool with ASCM functions · lift or jack stands · trim-clip tools for the wheel liners · soapy water spray

#### Change the oil and filter (Hemi or Hurricane)
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 45 minutes · cost MotorTrend paid $156.79 and $173.90 for dealer 10k and 20k services, including a tire rotation
Symptoms: The oil-life monitor is due, or the history is unknown.
Fix: Warm the engine, lift the truck safely and drain the oil. AMSOIL lists drain-plug torque at 20 ft-lb on the 3.0 Hurricane and 25 ft-lb on the 6.4. Fit the correct filter: AMSOIL lists WIX WL10255 for the standard-output 3.0, WIX 57045 for the high-output 3.0 and WIX 57060 for the 5.7 and 6.4. Refill with the correct grade: 0W-20 (MS-6395) for the 5.7 and the standard-output 3.0, or 0W-40 (MS-A0921) for the 6.4 and the high-output 3.0. Capacity is 7 qt for the V8s and 7.5 qt for the Hurricane. Check the level, then reset the oil-life monitor.
Tools: Socket for the drain plug · filter wrench · torque wrench · drain pan · jack stands or ramps

#### Service the front and rear differentials
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–1.5 hours · cost Parts only: about 5–6 pints of synthetic 75W-85
Symptoms: Unknown history, a deep water crossing, or towing. You may hear whine or chatter in tight turns from the electronic LSD.
Fix: Both axles take synthetic 75W-85 GL-5. AMSOIL lists the 215FD front at 2.3 pints and the 260RDU rear at 3 pints on Hurricane and 6.4 trucks (its 2022 5.7 entry shows 2.3 pints without ELSD and 2.7 with). Remove the fill plug first so you know you can refill, then drain, refit the drain plug and fill to the bottom of the fill hole. The owner's manual calls for friction-modified 75W-85 in the rear, whether it has the electronic LSD or a mechanical LSD. AMSOIL's lookups cite Mopar 75W-85 with modifier (P/N 68083381AA), but its entries disagree on which rear axle needs it, so check the part number with the dealer.
Tools: Fluid pump · sockets or hex bits for the plugs · drain pan · torque wrench

#### 8HP75 automatic: fluid and pan service
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2 hours · cost Parts plus a scan tool, or a shop job
Symptoms: High mileage, heavy towing or an unknown history. Harsh or slurred shifts are the warning sign.
Fix: The 8HP75 takes SL076-spec ATF, and AMSOIL lists 9 to 9.5 qt total fill. A pan drop changes only part of that. Drain, replace the pan and gasket as RockAuto lists them for these trucks, then fill and check the level by the service manual's procedure. That procedure depends on fluid temperature, so you need a scan tool to read it. Overfilling or underfilling a ZF eight-speed causes more problems than it fixes. If the truck is under warranty, have the dealer do it.
Tools: Scan tool that reads transmission temperature · fluid pump · torque wrench · drain pan · lift

#### Front and rear brake pads and rotors
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours for both axles · cost Parts plus a brake-fluid flush
Symptoms: Pulsing under braking, squeal, or a pad-wear warning. A 6,000-plus-lb SUV that tows is hard on brakes.
Fix: These trucks have a switch-operated electric parking brake. Before you work on the rear calipers, put it in service mode with a scan tool or by the owner's-manual method so the motors retract. Pull the calipers, replace the pads and rotors, clean and grease the slide pins, torque everything to spec and bed the pads in. Flush the DOT 3 fluid at the same time if the history is unknown.
Tools: Scan tool for the electric park brake · caliper piston tool · torque wrench · brake cleaner

#### Blank screens and glitches: updates and the battery
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 30 minutes to an hour · cost Free under warranty; a battery if it's weak
Symptoms: A blank or unresponsive 10.1- or 12-inch center screen, a rear camera that doesn't show, Wi-Fi or remote functions dead, or warning messages after a short drive.
Fix: Check the battery first, because low voltage causes all kinds of module faults. Test it, then clean and tighten the terminals. Next, look for over-the-air radio updates in Uconnect settings. FCA also has a bulletin on how to install them. Bulletins for dealer flashes include TSB 08-039-22 for blank center screens, which FCA says must be done before the display is replaced, plus 08-202-22 for the power-steering module and 08-173-21 for the telematics box. Several camera faults are recalls rather than TSBs, so run the VIN.
Tools: Battery tester · terminal brush · a USB drive if an update calls for one

#### Engine air filter and Hurricane spark plugs
Difficulty 1 / 5 (filter) · 3 / 5 (plugs) · time ≈ 10 minutes (filter) · 1–2 hours (plugs) · cost Parts only
Symptoms: Dusty-road use, a misfire code or an unknown history.
Fix: The air filter is a tool-free job: unclip the airbox, swap the element and wipe out the housing. On the Hurricane, take off the engine cover and the coils to reach the plugs, blow debris out of the wells before removing each plug, and torque the new plugs to the service-manual figure. The owner's-manual maintenance plan replaces the Hurricane's plugs every 60,000 miles, on mileage alone.
Tools: Plug socket with extension · torque wrench · compressed air · dielectric grease

### Baseline service
A WS is new enough that most are still under factory or extended warranty, so get every recall and software flash done at the dealer first. Then baseline the fluids most owners skip: both axles, the transfer case, the transmission and brake fluid. Specs differ by engine. The standard-output Hurricane, the high-output Hurricane and the two Hemis use different oils and filters. Fluid types, schedules and the oil and coolant capacities below are from the 2022 and 2025 Wagoneer owner's manuals on Mopar's site; axle and transmission capacities are from AMSOIL's application lookups.
- Engine oil & filter: 5.7: 0W-20 (MS-6395), 7 qt · 6.4: 0W-40 (MS-12633), 7 qt · 3.0 SO: 0W-20 (MS-6395), 7.5 qt · 3.0 HO: 0W-40 (MS-A0921), 7.5 qt · Baseline now; then per the oil-life monitor (Filters per AMSOIL: WIX 57060 (5.7 and 6.4), WL10255 (3.0 SO), 57045 (3.0 HO). Drain-plug torque 20 ft-lb (3.0) or 25 ft-lb (6.4).)
- Engine air filter: Panel element in the airbox · Baseline now; check after dusty trips (Tool-free.)
- Cabin air filter: Behind the glove box, in the fresh-air inlet · replace every 12,000 mi (19,000 km) (2022 and 2025 owner's manuals) · Baseline now (Unclip the glove box from its hinges to reach the access door; the filter's arrow shows the airflow direction. Part number not confirmed.)
- Spark plugs: Hurricane I6: 6 plugs · Hemi V8: 16 plugs · 3.0 Hurricane every 60,000 mi · 5.7 every 100,000 mi · 6.4 every 90,000 mi (owner's-manual maintenance plan; mileage only, no time limit) (Hemis use two plugs per cylinder.)
- Coolant: Mopar 10-year/150,000-mile OAT coolant meeting MS.90032 · 5.7: 17 qt (2022 manual; AMSOIL lists 16.9 qt) · 6.4: 18.8 qt · 3.0: 16.6 qt engine plus intercooler circuit, 3.2 qt in the 2025 manual (2.9 qt in the 2022 manual) · Inspect now; the schedule says flush and replace at 10 years or 150,000 mi (The Hurricane has a separate intercooler coolant circuit that takes the same OAT coolant, so check it too.)
- Automatic transmission (8HP75): SL076-spec ATF · 9–9.5 qt total fill · Baseline if towing or unknown history; dealer or a shop with a scan tool (The level check depends on temperature. A pan drop replaces only part of the fluid.)
- Transfer case: "Mopar Mobile LT" (as printed in the 2022 and 2025 owner's manuals) · capacity not listed · Baseline now if it has low range and has been used off-road or for towing (The maintenance plan says inspect it every 30,000 mi and change it at 150,000 mi. AMSOIL lists no fluid for it. Quadra-Trac I (single-speed), Quadra-Trac II and Quadra-Drive II use different cases.)
- Front differential (215FD): 75W-85 GL-5 synthetic · 2.3 pt · Baseline now; again after deep water (Synthetic is required.)
- Rear differential (260RDU): 75W-85 GL-5 synthetic · 3 pt (AMSOIL lists 2.3–2.7 pt for the 2022 5.7) · Baseline now; more often when towing (The 2022 and 2025 owner's manuals list friction-modified GL-5 75W-85 synthetic for the rear whether it has the electronic LSD (Mopar ELSD axle lubricant) or a mechanical LSD (Mopar Mechanical Limited Slip axle lubricant). AMSOIL cites Mopar P/N 68083381AA, but we couldn't match that number to either variant.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 (Mopar, SAE J1703) · DOT 4 acceptable · Flush now if the history is unknown. The 2022 and 2025 maintenance plans list brake inspections but no fluid-replacement interval. (Electric park brake: use service mode before you touch the rear calipers.)
- Quadra-Lift air suspension: Cycle Park → Off-Road 2; listen for the compressor; scan for codes · Inspect now (On early 2022 trucks, check TSB 02-001-22 items: air lines seated to the tape mark, control-module plug, vent hose and height-sensor links.)
- Batteries (12 V and 5.7 eTorque 48 V): Load-test the 12 V battery; check the eTorque system on 5.7 trucks · Now (Low voltage causes many WS electronic faults. The 5.7's 48 V pack mounts to the cabin floor.)
- Driveshafts, CV axles and boots: Inspect the boots and joints; check for play · Now and after every rough-road trip (The fully independent front and rear use CV axles, so a torn boot fills with grit fast.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: We couldn't find an owner consensus we trust yet, so we won't guess. Factory sizes are 275/65R18 all-terrains with the Advanced All-Terrain Group, 275/55R20 and 285/45R22, on a 6x139.7 bolt pattern. Limitless Tire's fitment guide lists 275–305 mm widths on 18- to 26-inch wheels. Test-fit anything taller at full lock in Off-Road 2 and at Park height, because the air suspension drops the body 1.6 inches. Running bigger tires on yours? Tell us.

Q: What's the difference between a Wagoneer and a Grand Wagoneer?
A: Price and equipment, not size. Both share the same body and wheelbase. Through 2025 the Grand Wagoneer added standard air suspension, Quadra-Drive II, a two-tone roof, fender flares, power side steps, bigger screens and the bigger engine (6.4 Hemi, then the high-output Hurricane). The long 'L' versions of each are 12 inches longer. From 2026 every truck is called Grand Wagoneer.

Q: Is it actually any good off-road?
A: Good for its size, but it isn't a Wrangler. It isn't Trail Rated. With the Advanced All-Terrain Group it has low range, a rear electronic LSD, skid plates, 10 inches of clearance and a 48:1 crawl ratio. MotorTrend's 20,000-mile test truck was happiest on dirt and fire roads. Its belly sat too low and its flanks were too exposed for harder trails, even at maximum height.

Q: Does it have lockers or low range?
A: There are no lockers. Quadra-Trac II and Quadra-Drive II have a two-speed transfer case with 2.64:1 low range. Quadra-Drive II adds a rear electronic limited-slip differential. Quadra-Trac I is single-speed with no low range, and rear-drive Wagoneers have no 4x4 at all.

Q: Which engine should I buy: Hemi or Hurricane?
A: The 5.7 eTorque (2022–23 Wagoneer) and the 6.4 (2022–23 Grand Wagoneer) are familiar Hemis. The 3.0 Hurricane twin-turbo six makes more power and torque. Jeep said the 420-hp version is up to 15 percent more efficient than the V8, and MotorTrend loved its smoothness. The 2022 5.7 eTorque was part of a 2024 NHTSA probe into engines shutting off at low speed, so check its history.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: Up to 10,000 lb for a properly equipped Wagoneer, which Jeep calls best in class. Motor1 reported a 9,860-lb rating for the 2023 Grand Wagoneer. Get the Heavy-Duty Trailer Tow package for the brake controller and extra cooling, and a deep drop hitch: MotorTrend found the receiver mounted high.

Q: What fuel economy does it get?
A: MotorTrend's 2023 4x4 Wagoneer with the 420-hp Hurricane was rated 16 mpg city, 26 highway and 19 combined. Over 20,672 miles it averaged 16.4 mpg, and its best tank was 20.3 mpg.

Q: What oil does it take?
A: It depends on the engine. The 5.7 and the standard-output 3.0 take 0W-20 meeting MS-6395. The 6.4 and the high-output 3.0 in Grand Wagoneers take 0W-40, with the 6.4 calling for MS-12633 and the HO Hurricane for MS-A0921. The owner's manual and AMSOIL both list 7 qt with the filter for the V8s and 7.5 qt for the Hurricane.

Q: Why doesn't it have a Jeep badge?
A: At launch in 2021, Wagoneer was sold as a premium extension of Jeep with its own badges, dealer program and concierge. In February 2024 Jeep said it would stop being a sub-brand and future Wagoneers would wear Jeep badges. The facelifted 2026 Grand Wagoneer, revealed October 14, 2025, has Jeep logos front and rear.

Q: Can I lift it?
A: Coil-spring trucks can take Rough Country's 3-inch bolt-on kit (60800) for 2022–2025 4WD Wagoneers. It does not fit trucks with Quadra-Lift air suspension. Air-sprung trucks already lift themselves to 10 inches of clearance in Off-Road 2.

Q: Is it reliable?
A: Too new for a long record. NHTSA lists more than a dozen recalls, mostly software, camera and trim fixes. Early 2022 trucks had an air-suspension assembly TSB. MotorTrend's long-termer needed only two routine services totalling $330.69 in 20,672 miles. Buy one with the recalls done and the warranty still running.

# Toyota Land Cruiser (1951–present)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/

It started as a 1951 prototype called the BJ, went into regular production in 1953, and picked up the name Land Cruiser in June 1954 — coined by Toyota's Hanji Umehara. What followed is one of the longest-running nameplates in the business and a lineage that splits, roughly, into two tribes: the utilitarian short- and long-wheelbase workhorses, and the station wagons that slowly learned to carry families in comfort without forgetting how to cross a riverbed. The utility line runs from the FJ40 — built from 1960 into the mid-1980s and the truck that made the name in America — through the long-wheelbase FJ45 to the 70 Series, introduced in 1984 and still in production for Africa, Australia, Latin America and the Middle East. The wagon line begins with the FJ55 'Iron Pig' (1967–1980), Toyota's first purpose-built Land Cruiser wagon, then the 60 Series, the coil-sprung 80 Series, the V8 100 and 200, and today's 300 Series. America's relationship with the name has been complicated lately. Toyota confirmed in December 2020 that the big wagon would leave North America after 2021, and the 300 Series has never been sold here. The name came back for 2024 on the smaller, Prado-derived 250 Series — a hybrid with center and rear lockers standard. For hands-on owners, though, the heart of the family is still the older iron: solid axles, straight-sixes and a parts network that never really closed.

Verdict: The truck the rest of the world actually depends on — the one that turns up, fully loaded, in places where a breakdown isn't an inconvenience but a plot twist. Seven decades in, Toyota still hasn't figured out how to make it fragile.

## Toyota Land Cruiser J20 / J25 (FJ25) (1955–1960)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj25/
Codes: FJ25, FJ28, F 3.9 I6

Verdict: The FJ25 is the Land Cruiser before anyone knew what a Land Cruiser was: one gear in the transfer case, drums at every corner and a 3.9-litre six that Toyota sold against the Jeep on horsepower alone. Only about 220 Land Cruisers reached America from 1958 to 1960, and the survivors are worth more as history than as trail rigs.

The 20 Series is where the Land Cruiser stopped being a police jeep and became a product. Toyota had renamed its BJ 'Jeep' the Land Cruiser in June 1954, after Willys objected to the use of its trademark, and the second-generation truck that followed in 1955 was redesigned for civilian buyers. Toyota's own lineage pages date the launch to November 1955 (its UK history says August). It got rounder bodywork, a roomier cabin and, within months, the 3.9-litre F straight-six. The short-wheelbase FJ25 is the one everyone remembers, but the family also included the longer FJ28, early B-engined BJ trucks and a run of vans and fire engines.

### FROM POLICE JEEP TO EXPORT HERO
The name came first. Wikipedia quotes technical director Hanji Umehara explaining that Toyota's real rival in export markets was Land Rover, so the new name had to sound no less dignified than 'Land Rover.' Toyota's UK history says the first export shipment went to Pakistan in 1954 and Saudi Arabia followed in 1955. That makes the J20 the first Land Cruiser built with export in mind: Toyota says the 20 Series was the generation that began shipping to North America and other overseas markets in large volume. It came with export suspension uprated over the Japanese spec, because, as Toyota UK puts it, Japan had no highways at the time.
Toyota's 75-year history tracks the numbers. Land Cruiser exports went from 98 in 1955 to 518 in 1956, then jumped to 2,502 in 1957, when Toyota tried to make up for weak domestic sales overseas. Venezuela took 52 in autumn 1956 and 795 in 1957 for oilfields and cattle ranches. Burma got 22 in July 1956 as war reparations, and Australia got a dozen in August 1957. Toyota UK adds that after US military trials in 1957, Land Cruisers made up 38.2 percent of all vehicles exported from Japan that year, across every brand. The cheap little Toyota had become Japan's most important export.

### THE F ENGINE AND A VERY SIMPLE DRIVELINE
At launch the J20 offered two petrol sixes: the 3.4-litre B from the BJ and the 3.9-litre F, which had previously been used only in the fire-engine chassis. Toyota says the range was cut to the F alone in mid-1956. Toyota's lineage page rates the FJ25's F at 105 PS (net) at 3,200 rpm. A period US dealer checklist posted on IH8MUD pitched the FJ25 against the CJ-5 as having 'almost twice the horsepower at no extra cost.' Wikipedia says the engine was also moved 120 mm forward to free up cabin space, and that the ride improved with longer leaf springs adapted from Toyota's light truck.
The rest is crude by modern standards. Toyota describes the four-wheel-drive J20 as having a one-speed transfer case: no low range, which didn't arrive until the FJ40 in 1960. A four-speed floor-shift manual (as listed by Bring a Trailer, RM Sotheby's and Barrett-Jackson for surviving trucks) did the work instead. Toyota also built a rear-drive version for police patrol work. Wheelbases were 2,285 mm (FJ25) and 2,430 mm (the longer FJ28), with a 2,650 mm chassis added near the end in 1959. Brakes were drums all round.

### AMERICA, AUSTRALIA AND BRAZIL
America came late and slowly. Autoblog's visit to the Land Cruiser Heritage Museum describes the first Land Cruiser sold in the US: a 1958 FJ25 ordered by Rose Toyota and delivered at the port, because the dealership wasn't finished yet, to a Long Beach schoolteacher. It was the only Land Cruiser Toyota sold in America that year, alongside 287 Toyopet Crowns. The import figures compiled in IH8MUD's FJ2X registry show 61 Land Cruisers in 1959 and 162 in 1960.
Australia was a bigger deal. Wikipedia credits B&D Motors with importing FJ25/28 cab-chassis trucks from 1959 and says the Land Cruiser was the first Japanese vehicle regularly exported to Australia. A handful went to work for Thiess on the Snowy Mountains Scheme. In Brazil, Toyota began building the FJ25L in São Bernardo in May 1959. Its 75-year history calls this its first full-fledged overseas knockdown production. Brazil switched to Mercedes-Benz diesels and the Bandeirante name in 1962 and kept building the 25-based truck until 1968. Japan replaced the J20 with the 40 Series in 1960.

### THE COLLECTOR'S TRUCK
Today the FJ25 is a collector's piece first and an off-roader a distant second. IH8MUD's FJ25 Owners Group runs a worldwide count of surviving 20 Series trucks and a VIN registry, and warns about 'Frankencruisers': FJ40 tubs wearing an FJ25 frame number. Most of the FJ25s sold on Bring a Trailer since 2019 were restored in Colombia or Costa Rica and imported later. On Bring a Trailer, FJ25s sold for $14,001 to $39,000 between 2019 and 2026, and RM Sotheby's got $70,000 for a restored 1960 soft-top in 2019.

### Data plate
- Chassis: J20 (FJ25 / FJ28; early B-engined trucks)
- Production: 1955–1960 (Japan) · 1959–1968 (Brazil)
- Launch: November 1955 (Toyota global) · August 1955 (Toyota UK)
- Engine: F 3,878 cc OHV I6 (B 3.4 L to mid-1956)
- Output: 105 PS net @ 3,200 rpm (FJ25)
- Transmission: 4-speed manual
- Transfer Case: Single-speed, part-time 4WD
- Wheelbase: 2,285 mm (FJ25) · 2,430 mm (FJ28)
- Length × Width × Height: 3,838 × 1,665 × 1,855 mm (FJ25)
- Curb Weight: 1,425 kg (FJ25)
- Brakes: Drums all round
- Us Imports: 1 (1958) · 61 (1959) · 162 (1960), per IH8MUD registry

### Engineering
The J20 is a 1950s utility truck in its purest form: a ladder frame, leaf springs on solid axles, a big slow-revving six and a transfer case that only connects the front axle. Many engine parts are shared with early FJ40s, but the chassis, body and much of the trim are unique, which is why surviving FJ25 owners trade parts among themselves rather than at the parts counter.
- Chassis: Ladder frame · 2,285 mm (FJ25) / 2,430 mm (FJ28) (A 2,650 mm chassis was added in 1959, the basis for the rare four-door FJ35V van.)
- Suspension: Solid axles, leaf springs front and rear (Longer springs than the BJ; IH8MUD members say the FJ25's rear springs and spring hangers are unique, while the fronts match the 40.)
- 4Wd System: Part-time, single-speed transfer case (No low range. A two-wheel-drive police version was also built.)
- Engine: F 3.9 L (3,878 cc) OHV I6 (105 PS net at 3,200 rpm (Toyota). Early trucks could have the 3.4 L B six until mid-1956.)
- Gearbox: 4-speed manual, floor shift (Low first gear does the work that a low-range transfer case would do on later trucks.)
- Brakes: Four-wheel drums, cast-iron master cylinder (IH8MUD: both shoes are identical (no leading/trailing), set with cam adjusters; 1-inch wheel-cylinder cups.)

### Versions
- 1955–1956 · B-engined J20 · B 3.4 L OHV I6 (petrol) · 85 PS (BJ figure) · Carried over from the BJ; Toyota dropped it from the J20 range in mid-1956.
- 1955–1960 · FJ25 (short wheelbase) · F 3.9 L OHV I6 (petrol) · 105 PS net @ 3,200 rpm · 2,285 mm wheelbase; soft-top, hardtop and pickup bodies. The truck most collectors mean by 'FJ25.'
- 1955–1960 · FJ28 (longer wheelbase) · F 3.9 L OHV I6 · 105 PS · 2,430 mm wheelbase; pickups, vans and the very rare FJ28L survivors.
- 1960 · FJ35V (J30) · F 3.9 L OHV I6 · — · Four-door Gifu-bodied van on the 2,650 mm J20 chassis, built for nine months; Wikipedia says about 60 were made.
- 1959–1961 · FJ25L (Brazil) · F 3.9 L OHV I6 · — · Toyota do Brasil's first local build, from May 1959.
- 1962–1968 · TB25L / OJ31L / OJ32L (Bandeirante) · Mercedes-Benz OM324 3.4 L diesel · — · Brazilian 25-based trucks with Mercedes diesels, built until August 1968.

### Year-by-year
- 1951: Toyota 'Jeep' BJ prototype with the 3.4 L B six; civilian series production from 1953
- 1954: Renamed Land Cruiser in June because 'Jeep' was a Willys-Overland trademark; Toyota UK says the first export shipment went to Pakistan
- 1955: 20 Series launched (November per Toyota global, August per Toyota UK) on 2,285 and 2,430 mm wheelbases with B and F sixes
- 1956: Range cut to the 3.9 L F engine alone in mid-year; exports reach Venezuela and Burma
- 1957: Land Cruiser exports jump to 2,502 (Toyota); first dozen shipped to Australia in August
- 1958: First Land Cruiser sold in the US, a single FJ25 through Rose Toyota
- 1959: 2,650 mm chassis added; Toyota do Brasil begins FJ25L production in May; owners report the 'Thunderbird' emblem on 1959s
- 1960: Last J20s; the four-door FJ35V van is built for nine months; the 40 Series takes over in August
- 1962: Brazil's 25-based Bandeirante switches to a Mercedes-Benz OM324 diesel; built until August 1968

### Capability
- Curb weight: 1,425 kg (3,142 lb) (FJ25, Toyota figure)
- Wheelbase: 2,285 mm (90.0 in) (FJ25; FJ28 2,430 mm)
- Length × width × height: 3,838 × 1,665 × 1,855 mm (FJ25, Toyota figure)
- Engine output: 105 PS net @ 3,200 rpm (F 3,878 cc, Toyota figure)
- Low range: None (Single-speed transfer case (Toyota))

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 16-in six-lug steel wheels, 6.00-16 military-style tires (restored 1960 FJ25L on BaT)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: No forum consensus (Restored trucks run period 6.00-16s; one 1959 on Bring a Trailer wore 265/75R16 all-terrains on its 16-in steel wheels. IH8MUD members warn that 15-in disc-brake wheels hit the FJ25's tie-rod ends, 15-in drum wheels won't clear the drum rivets, and most other 16-in wheels have too small a center bore.)

### Buying checks
- Prove it's really a 25: IH8MUD's FJ25 group has seen FJ40 tubs on rebuilt frames wearing FJ25 VIN plates. Real FJ25 tells include the fuel tank under the seat, round rear wheel cut-outs, a flat floor with no hump for an offset transfer case, a centered rear differential and an FJ25-specific steering center link. Photograph the frame from underneath, especially the crossmembers and spring hangers, before you pay a 25 price.
- Match the numbers: The data plate lists frame and engine numbers, and FJ25 VINs read like 9FJ25-12645L (year digit, model, serial, L for left-hand drive). Registry members note engines weren't installed in strict numerical order, but the block number should sit in the right range for the frame. Check the block stamping against the plate; Bring a Trailer listings photograph both.
- Know where it was restored: Most FJ25s sold in the US recently were refurbished in Colombia, Costa Rica or elsewhere in Latin America and then imported. That's fine, but restoration quality varies. Look for cracked paint at panel joints, swapped seats and later running gear. Get the title and import paperwork in order before you pay.
- Original engine or a 2F?: Swaps are common, and the market notices. In June 2025 a 2F-powered 1959 FJ25 sold on Bring a Trailer for $14,250. In July 2026 a refurbished F-powered 1959 sold there for $37,500. A later 2F head on an F block is a 'Frankencruiser' sign that IH8MUD members flag.
- Wheels and FJ25-only parts: FJ25 wheels are scarce. IH8MUD members report that 15-inch disc-brake wheels hit the tie-rod ends, 15-inch drum wheels won't clear the FJ25's drum rivets, and most other 16-inch wheels have too small a center bore. Rear spring hangers and bolts, top bows and the pre-1960 toolbox lid (diagonal ribs, five catches) are FJ25-specific, so missing pieces are expensive to find.
- Brakes and hydraulics: Specter Off-Road lists its FJ25 brake and clutch master-cylinder kits (1-inch bore, cast iron) as discontinued, so check that the hydraulics work before you buy. Some restored trucks have front disc conversions, which make them safer but less original.
- Year details matter to purists: Owners report that 1958-and-earlier trucks (and some 1959s) use a three-bolt front-fender-to-frame pattern, that the 1959 wears the 'Thunderbird' emblem rather than the oval, and that the cradle-style front engine mount and the old toolbox lid both changed around 1960. If you're paying for originality, get the details checked by someone from the owners' group.

### Common repairs
#### Drum brake reline and adjustment
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day for all four wheels · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Pulling, a long pedal or brakes that need pumping, on a truck with four drums and no booster.
Fix: Following an IH8MUD FJ25 Owners Group walkthrough: strip each backing plate and set all adjusters to minimum before fitting new shoes. The upper adjuster turns 270 degrees from its flat side and the lower one 180 degrees, with a notch visible from the back. Both shoes are identical, with no leading or trailing shoe. Lube the shoe contact points and the felt washer under the retainer, then fit the horseshoe clip. Hone the wheel cylinders and fit 1-inch cups. Refit the drums and pump the pedal. Then bring each adjuster out until the shoe just drags and back it off slightly: lower adjusters first, then upper.
Tools: Drum and hub tools · channel-lock pliers (horseshoe clips) · wheel-cylinder hone · 1-inch cups (NAPA 1499 per the IH8MUD FJ25 part list) · DOT 3 fluid

#### Master cylinder rebuild (brake and clutch)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 3–4 hours including bleeding · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: A sinking pedal, fluid at the firewall, or a clutch that won't fully release.
Fix: The FJ25's brake and clutch master cylinders are 1-inch-bore cast-iron units. Specter Off-Road lists its FJ25 kits (014-02-FJ25 brake, 018-02-FJ25 clutch) as discontinued, so look for cups of the same bore or have the bores sleeved by a specialist. Strip, hone and inspect the bore, fit new cups and seals, and check the cap. IH8MUD members found vented caps arrived on early-1960s trucks, and earlier caps may not be vented. Bleed both systems with fresh DOT 3.
Tools: Hone · brake fluid · flare-nut wrenches · bleeder kit

#### Water pump rebuild
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost About $125 for a professional rebuild (IH8MUD member report)
Symptoms: Weeping from the pump weep hole, a growling bearing or wobble at the fan.
Fix: New early pumps are hard to find, so owners rebuild the original. One IH8MUD member found that the early pump bearing (Toyota 90369-30008, cross-referenced as Koyo 885141 / FAG W2503) is the same bearing used in the Willys Jeep pump, and that Jeep rebuild kits (BB707) supply the bearing and seal. Others send pumps to a water-pump rebuilder; one member reported about $125. Fit a new bypass hose while it's apart.
Tools: Puller · press · gasket scraper · Willys-type rebuild kit or professional rebuild

#### Ignition tune-up (points, condenser, short-reach plugs)
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost About $24 for a points and condenser combo (Cruiser Corps)
Symptoms: Hard starting, misfire or a rough idle on a truck that hasn't been tuned in years.
Fix: Fit new points and condenser and set the gap. Cruiser Corps gives 0.018 in for its 1958–75 F-engine set. The FJ25 takes short-reach plugs: the IH8MUD FJ25 part list gives Champion J8C, NGK B6S or Nippondenso W14-U. Early distributors use a vacuum advance in which the whole distributor body moves. IH8MUD members found aftermarket Delco units on some trucks and advise against them. Replace the cap and rotor if they're cracked or tracked.
Tools: Feeler gauges · dwell meter or timing light · short-reach plugs

#### Valve adjustment and valve cover reseal
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost Valve cover gasket about $17 (Cruiser Corps)
Symptoms: Ticking from the top end, oil weeping down the block, or poor running from tight valves.
Fix: The F engine has adjustable rockers, and the procedure is the same as on an early FJ40. Warm the engine, find tight and loose valves with go/no-go feeler gauges, then shut it off and adjust cylinder by cylinder with the intake just closed. Use the clearances in your manual. Fit a new cork gasket: the IH8MUD FJ25 part list gives Toyota 11253-60010 for the original cover gasket.
Tools: Feeler gauges · 17 mm wrench · screwdriver · new gasket

#### Radiator re-core or replacement
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours to remove and refit · cost One owner was quoted $950 to re-core; members say later OEM radiators cost under $400
Symptoms: Creeping temperature, a weeping core or a radiator a shop refuses to repair.
Fix: Early radiators have horizontal fins and are heavy. One IH8MUD seller found the same radiator part number in Toyota books from 1958 to 1962, so FJ25 and early FJ40 radiators match. Owners report using Cool Cruisers of Texas radiators without problems, and one says new late-model OEM radiators 'fit right in' if originality isn't the goal. The original tanks can also be re-cored. Flush the block, fit a new cap and hoses, and check the fan shroud.
Tools: Drain pan · hose clamps · new radiator cap

#### Carburetor and fuel-system refresh
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost SOR carb kits about $82
Symptoms: Stumbling, rich running or a truck that won't start after sitting.
Fix: One IH8MUD owner got a truck that had sat for 15 years running again by cleaning the carburetor, blowing out the fuel lines and adding fresh fuel. For a full rebuild, the FJ25 part list says an F-engine Keyster kit works, but its main metering rod and jet are wrong for the FJ25. Keep the original jet and rod, or source FJ25-correct ones. Specter Off-Road's 1961–62 kit is discontinued and its 1963–68 kits remain listed. Replace the metal-bowl fuel filter element and check the mechanical pump.
Tools: Carb cleaner · screwdrivers · float gauge · fuel line

### Baseline service
Any FJ25 is now more than 65 years old, so assume nothing has been done and service everything. Toyota's capacities below are for the F engine as fitted to the 40 and 55 Series (compiled on IH8MUD from Toyota publications). The FJ25's own gearbox and transfer case aren't in that table, so check its figures in an FJ25 manual.
- Engine oil & filter: F engine: 7 L, API SD in Toyota's table · canister (cartridge) filter element, Toyota 04152-60060 · Baseline now; then per the owner's manual (Early F engines use a canister filter, not a spin-on. An IH8MUD member says the dealer element comes with its gasket and washer. Use a modern oil suited to a flat-tappet engine.)
- Ignition: plugs, points, condenser: Short-reach plugs (Champion J8C / NGK B6S / ND W14-U per the IH8MUD FJ25 list) · points gap 0.018 in (Cruiser Corps, 1958–75 F) · Baseline now (Set timing with the octane adjuster after replacing points. Check that the moving-body vacuum advance works.)
- Valve lash: Adjustable rockers · clearances [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Check now (Same procedure as an early FJ40 F engine. New cork cover gasket.)
- Coolant, thermostat & hoses: F engine: 15.2 L (Toyota's early table lists plain water; use ethylene-glycol coolant) · Flush now (FJ25 hose part numbers on IH8MUD: upper 90916-01019, lower hoses 90916-01021, thermostat 90916-03014.)
- Fuel filter & pump: Metal-bowl filter with element (Toyota 04234-30010 per the IH8MUD FJ25 list) · mechanical pump · Replace element now (Old fuel varnishes carburetors. Clean the bowl and blow out the lines before rebuilding the carb.)
- Gearbox & transfer case: Gear oil per FJ25 manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Toyota's 40-series table specifies API GL-4 SAE 90 for its gearboxes and transfer case) · Baseline now (The FJ25 has a single-speed transfer case and a different four-speed from the 40-series J30/H41, so don't borrow the 40-series capacities.)
- Front & rear differentials: Hypoid gear oil [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Toyota's 40-series table: API GL-5 80W-90, 2.5 L) · Baseline now (The FJ25 has a centered rear differential. IH8MUD says its rear axle isn't the same as an FJ40's centered axle, so don't assume parts swap.)
- Brake & clutch fluid: DOT 3 / SAE J1703 · Flush now (Two cast-iron master cylinders (brake and clutch). Look for weeping wheel cylinders on all four drums.)
- Chassis grease, U-joints & wheel bearings: Chassis: moly lithium NLGI-2 · wheel bearings: lithium multipurpose NLGI-2 (Toyota 40-series table) · Grease now; repack wheel bearings now (The IH8MUD FJ25 list cross-references front inner bearings (Federal-Mogul 26820/26882), outer (BR2720/BR2788) and rear (Koyo R139B).)
- Belts: Fan belt, Toyota 90916-02008 (IH8MUD FJ25 list) · gear-driven camshaft, so no timing belt · Inspect now (The F engine drives its camshaft by gears. Toyota's 13523-60030 is listed as the steel replacement for the original fiber cam gear.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: There's no forum consensus for the FJ25, and the bigger problem is wheels. Restored trucks on Bring a Trailer have worn 6.00-16 military-style tires, and one 1959 ran 265/75R16 all-terrains on its 16-inch steel wheels. IH8MUD members warn that 15-inch disc-brake wheels hit the FJ25's tie-rod ends and 15-inch drum wheels won't clear the drum rivets. Stay with 16-inch wheels and a period-sized tire unless you want to start modifying the truck.

Q: Does it have low range?
A: No. Toyota describes the four-wheel-drive J20 as having a one-speed transfer case. The four-speed manual's low first gear has to do the crawling. Toyota's two-speed transfer case arrived with the 40 Series in 1960.

Q: What engine does it have?
A: Usually the 3.9-litre F inline-six, which Toyota rates at 105 PS (net) in the FJ25. Early J20s could also have the 3.4-litre B six carried over from the BJ, but Toyota says the range was cut to the F alone in mid-1956.

Q: What's the difference between FJ25, FJ28 and FJ35?
A: The FJ25 is the 2,285 mm short wheelbase. The FJ28 is the longer 2,430 mm version, used for pickups and vans. The FJ35V was a four-door van on the 2,650 mm chassis added in 1959. Wikipedia says the FJ35V was built for only nine months in 1960 and that about 60 were made.

Q: How many came to the US?
A: Very few. The first US Land Cruiser was a single 1958 FJ25 sold through Rose Toyota. It's now at the Land Cruiser Heritage Museum. IH8MUD's FJ2X registry lists import figures of 61 Land Cruisers in 1959 and 162 in 1960.

Q: Is it really a FJ25 or a rebodied FJ40?
A: Check the frame, not the plate. IH8MUD members point to the under-seat fuel tank, round rear wheel cut-outs, a flat floor without an offset transfer-case hump, a centered rear differential and FJ25-specific spring hangers and steering center link. A VIN plate on a later tub, or a 2F head on an F block, is a warning sign.

Q: Can I still get parts?
A: Engine and many service parts are shared with early F-engined FJ40s and still sold by specialists such as Cruiser Corps and Specter Off-Road. FJ25-specific chassis, body and hydraulic parts are another matter: Specter lists its FJ25 master-cylinder, clutch and distributor-cap items as discontinued, so owners trade among themselves through the IH8MUD FJ25 Owners Group.

Q: How do the brakes work, and are they safe?
A: They're four-wheel drums with no booster. Each drum has two identical shoes, set with upper and lower cam adjusters. Kept adjusted, they stop like a 1950s truck should, which isn't well by modern standards. Some restored FJ25s sold on Bring a Trailer have front disc conversions.

Q: What's one worth?
A: Bring a Trailer FJ25 sales ran from $14,001 (2024) to $39,000 (2021), with a 2F-swapped 1959 at $14,250 in 2025 and a refurbished F-powered 1959 at $37,500 in 2026. CLASSIC.com shows 1957 FJ25s selling at Mecum and Barrett-Jackson for $33,000 in 2026. RM Sotheby's sold a restored 1960 soft-top for $70,000 in 2019.

Q: Can I import one into the US?
A: Yes. Every J20 is far older than the 25-year threshold for NHTSA's import exemption, and most FJ25s sold in the US recently came from Latin America. Allow for state titling and emissions rules (California is the hard one) and make sure the paperwork matches the frame number.

## Toyota Land Cruiser FJ40 (1960–1984)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj40/
Codes: FJ40, BJ40

Verdict: The FJ40 is a farm implement that accidentally became a fashion icon: leaf springs, a straight-six with the manners of a tractor and steering vague enough to count as a suggestion. It is also the reason anybody outside Japan cares what a Land Cruiser is.

Toyota launched the 40 Series in 1960 as a ground-up replacement for the 20 Series, and then barely changed it for nearly a quarter of a century. Toyota's own UK history notes the 1979 facelift was the first visual change in 19 years. Underneath sat solid axles on leaf springs at both ends and, for the first time in a Land Cruiser, a two-speed transfer case. The short-wheelbase FJ40 is the one on posters, but the J40 family also included the medium-wheelbase FJ43 and the long-wheelbase FJ45 pickups and wagons.

### A JEEP RIVAL THAT OUTSOLD EVERYTHING
In America the FJ40 was pitched against the Jeep and it worked. Toyota's pressroom says the Land Cruiser was the company's best-selling vehicle in the US until 1965, when the Corona passenger car took over; Wikipedia records global output passing 50,000 that year. Toyota's US pressroom says the FJ40 came to America in 1960, two years after the first Land Cruiser was sold here; Hagerty dates FJ40 imports from 1963, so the exact start depends on whom you ask. Either way, a little Japanese 4x4 was carrying the brand in its biggest export market before most Americans had heard of Toyota.
The engine did a lot of the persuading. The 3.9-liter F straight-six made 125 hp in Toyota's US history, and Hagerty calls it 'virtually indestructible' and essentially a reverse-engineered Chevrolet 235 'Stovebolt' six (Wikipedia says the bottom end is closer to GMC's 236 six, so treat the family tree as folklore). It drove a three-speed column-shift manual at launch. Diesels came later for other markets, the H six in the long-wheelbase HJ45 from 1972 or 1973 (sources differ) and the four-cylinder B in 1974, but Wikipedia notes diesel 40s were never sold to the general US public; a few arrived as mine trucks.

### QUIET EVOLUTION
Changes came mechanically rather than visually. US trucks got the 4.2-liter 2F and a four-speed in 1975, along with rear barn doors and, a year earlier, a standard roll bar. Front disc brakes arrived in 1976. In 1979 came the square headlight bezels, optional power steering and air conditioning on petrol trucks, and a switch from 4.11 to 3.70 axle gears. IH8MUD members still steer first-time buyers to post-1976 trucks for the discs and the 2F, and warn that 1980-and-later bodies seem to rust more readily.
The truck stayed crude to the end. Retro Rides sums up the driving experience as vague steering, wayward handling, a harsh ride on heavy leaf springs and a cabin that gets very hot in summer. That's part of the appeal: almost everything on it can be reached with a 17 mm wrench and a bit of patience. Free-wheeling front hubs became standard in Australia from 1982, and a five-speed arrived later in the run, but US buyers never saw much luxury.

### THE END, AND THE AFTERLIFE
The 1983 model year was the last for US FJ40s; Wikipedia estimates only about 300 were imported that final year. Production ended in most markets in 1984, when the 70 Series took over the utility role, though Canada got a run of BJ42 diesels with a five-speed overdrive. Brazil kept going much longer: the Toyota Bandeirante used the 40's body with Mercedes-Benz and later Toyota diesels until 2001, giving the basic shape more than four decades of production.
Values climbed sharply in the 2010s, then settled. In 2019 Hagerty put the average #2-condition FJ40 at $47,375, down 7.6 percent since 2016, while Retro Rides tracks an Australian example rising from $4,400 in 1995 to $33,000 in 2024. Toyota noticed too: in 2021 it announced GR Heritage Parts reproductions for the 40 Series, starting with engine, driveline and exhaust components. The FJ40's legacy even includes the 2007 FJ Cruiser, which borrowed its white roof and round headlights.

### Data plate
- Chassis: J40 (FJ40 / BJ40 / HJ40 family)
- Production: 1960–1984 (Brazil to 2001)
- Last Us Model Year: 1983 (about 300 imported)
- Engine (Us): F 3.9 L I6 to 1975 · 2F 4.2 L I6 from 1975
- Output: F 125 hp · 2F 135 hp / 200–210 lb-ft
- Transmission (Us): 3-spd manual · 4-spd from 1975
- Drive: Part-time 4WD, two-speed transfer
- Wheelbase: 2,285 mm (90.0 in)
- Length: 3,840 mm (151 in)
- Weight: 1,480 kg soft top · 1,554 kg hard top
- Brakes: Drums; front discs from 1976 (US)
- Axle Ratio (Us): 4.11, then 3.70 from 1979

### Engineering
The FJ40 is about as simple as a 4x4 gets: a ladder frame, live axles on leaf springs, drum brakes until 1976 and a big, slow-revving straight-six. The front axle uses closed knuckles with Birfield CV joints and tapered knuckle bearings set up with shims, the same basic design Toyota carried into the FJ60 and FJ62.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, 2,285 mm (90.0 in) wheelbase (FJ43 used 2,430 mm; long-wheelbase FJ45s 2,650 or 2,950 mm.)
- Suspension: Solid axles, leaf springs front and rear (Lifted trucks are prone to shackle inversion, hence anti-inversion shackles and plates.)
- 4Wd System: Part-time, two-speed transfer case (The first Land Cruiser with a two-speed transfer case. A split case arrived around 1980.)
- Engine: F 3.9 L (to 1975) / 2F 4.2 L OHV I6 (F rated 125 hp in Toyota's US history; 2F 135 hp. Pushrod valvetrain needs periodic adjustment.)
- Gearbox: 3-speed, then 4-speed (US 1975) (Column-shift three-speed at launch; H55F five-speed swaps are a popular upgrade.)
- Brakes & Steering: Drums to 1975; front discs from 1976 (US) (Power steering optional on petrol trucks from 1979; manual recirculating-ball box before that.)

### Versions
- 1960–1974 · FJ40 (early) · F 3.9 L OHV I6 (petrol) · 125 hp (Toyota US) · Three-speed manual, four-wheel drums, 4.11 gears in the US.
- 1975–1978 · FJ40 (mid) · 2F 4.2 L OHV I6 (petrol) · 135 hp / 200–210 lb-ft · Four-speed manual in the US; barn doors from 1975; front discs from 1976.
- 1979–1984 · FJ40 (late) · 2F 4.2 L OHV I6 (petrol) · 135 hp / 200–210 lb-ft · Square headlight bezels, optional power steering and A/C, 3.70 gears in the US. Last US model year 1983.
- 1974–1984 · BJ40 / BJ42 · B 3.0 L, later 3B 3.4 L I4 diesel · 80–90 hp · Not sold to the US public; Canada got the BJ42 with a five-speed in 1984.
- 1972–1984 · HJ45 / HJ47 · H 3.6 L, later 2H 4.0 L I6 diesel · 94–105 hp · Long-wheelbase diesels for export markets.
- 1968–2001 · Bandeirante (Brazil) · Mercedes-Benz, then Toyota 14B diesel · 77–95 hp · Brazilian-built 40 body; production ended in 2001.

### Year-by-year
- 1960: J40 series launched in Japan with the 3.9 L F six, a three-speed and a two-speed transfer case
- 1963: Hagerty's date for the start of US FJ40 imports (Toyota's US pressroom says 1960); by 1965 the Land Cruiser is Toyota's best-selling vehicle in America
- 1974: Factory roll bar becomes standard on US FJ40s
- 1975: 4.2 L 2F replaces the F with a four-speed; rear barn doors on US trucks
- 1976: Front disc brakes, on top of the 2F and four-speed from 1975. IH8MUD members say most buyers prefer 1976-on trucks for those reasons, with 1978 the coveted year [buy]
- 1977: Front door vent windows deleted; rear vent windows added to US hardtops
- 1979: Optional power steering and A/C, square grille bezels, US axle ratio raised from 4.11 to 3.70 for highway cruising
- 1984: End of J40 production in most markets, replaced by the 70 Series; Brazil's Bandeirante continues to 2001

### Capability
- Curb weight: 1,480 kg (3,263 lb) (FJ40, Japanese-market figure)
- Wheelbase: 2,285 mm (90.0 in)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: H78-15 (≈205/75R15) on 15x5.5 steel wheels
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Offset: 3.25 in backspacing (OEM 15x5.5 steel)
- Note: Cruiser Corps lists the same 15x5.5 OEM steel wheel for 1958–1990 FJ40, FJ45, FJ55, FJ60, FJ62 and BJ trucks, and advises against tires wider than 10.5 in on it.
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 31x10.50R15 (IH8MUD's 'tried and true' answer. 33x9.50R15 fits on stock rims but rubs at the rear over bumps or at full flex; owners fix it with 1-inch bump-stop spacers and by adjusting the front steering stops.)

### Buying checks
- Rust beats everything: IH8MUD veterans rank rust above every mechanical issue combined. Check door bottoms, the rear sill, the body behind the under-seat fuel tank, wheel wells, the outer front fender brace, inside sills and windscreen pillars. Get underneath and look at all of the metal.
- Body mounts and floors: On 1979-and-later trucks, look hard at the body mounts. If they're heavily rusted, expect the floor pans and door pillars to be rotten too. Reproduction floor pans exist, but a badly rusted frame may not be worth saving.
- Frame ends: Check the rear frame horns and the body around them, a spot IH8MUD members flag as the biggest worry on many listings.
- Signs of hard wheeling: Heavily dented skid plates, gouged differential drain plugs and leaf springs with a slight S-shape all suggest a hard life. None is fatal, but they mean work ahead.
- Driveline slop and leaks: Check both driveshafts for play ('any slop is too much'), look for cracks or welds on the transfer case, and watch for leaks at the transmission, transfer case, axles and wheels. Oil between engine and gearbox often means a rear main seal.
- Compression, not the odometer: Mileage tells you little on a truck whose engine may have been rebuilt. A compression test does. Members put a full 2F rebuild at $2,000–3,000 in the mid-2000s, and expect $1,000–2,000 of catch-up work after purchase.
- Brakes and fluids: Four-wheel drums need constant adjustment. Black brake or clutch fluid suggests the previous owner skipped bleeding, and probably other maintenance too.
- Smog and wiring: In smog-check states, make sure the emissions equipment is all present and the truck passes. Messy wiring is a sign of future electrical gremlins.

### Common repairs
#### Front knuckle and Birfield rebuild
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Two days the first time; half a day once experienced · cost Knuckle kit about $160 (Cruiser Corps) plus seals and grease
Symptoms: Grease and gear oil oozing from the knuckle wiper seals, a mix of grease and 90-weight inside the knuckle, or play when you lift a front wheel and shove it.
Fix: Pull the hub and spindle, slide out the Birfield, then remove the steering-arm cones (they stick, so use penetrating oil and tap the arm from below) and the top and bottom knuckle caps. Clean everything, replace the inner axle seal, knuckle bearings and wiper seals, repack the Birfield and knuckle, and reassemble. Bottom shims center the knuckle and top shims set preload: if preload is low, remove shims from the top. One IH8MUD write-up set preload at 4–5 lb with shims; check your factory service manual for the exact figure and where to hook the spring scale.
Tools: Hub socket · brass drift · spring scale · seal driver · torque wrench · Cruiser Corps knuckle kit 514-108 (1958–9/1975) or 514-109 (9/1975–1/1990) · OEM knuckle wiper kit · moly grease

#### Valve adjustment on the F / 2F
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost Valve cover gasket about $17–22 (Cruiser Corps) plus washers
Symptoms: Loud ticking from the top end (loose valves), or poor running and burned valves (tight valves, which are the ones to worry about).
Fix: Warm the engine. With it idling, use go/no-go feeler gauges to find the tight and loose valves. Shut down and adjust only those: turn the engine until a cylinder's intake valve has just closed, rotate a few degrees more, then set both valves for that cylinder. Valve layout front to back is E-I-I-E-E-I-I-E-E-I-I-E. Pulling the spark plugs makes turning the engine by hand easier, and a long screwdriver in the plug hole finds top dead center. Use the clearances in your service manual.
Tools: Feeler gauges (fresh ones; soft gauges bend) · 17 mm wrench (a 17/19 mm socket-ended flex wrench helps) · new valve cover gasket and acorn-nut washers

#### Carburetor rebuild
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Keyster kit about $35
Symptoms: Hesitation, stumbling, rough idle or stalling at low rpm on a truck with an original carburetor.
Fix: Read the carburetor number stamped on the body first: Cruiser Corps lists more than a dozen Keyster kits for FJ40, FJ45 and FJ55 carburetors from 1966 to 1984, matched by carb number and date range. Strip, clean and rebuild with the correct kit, set the float level, and check vacuum lines and choke operation while it's off.
Tools: Screwdrivers · carb cleaner · correct Keyster rebuild kit (by carb number, e.g. 21100-60280 for 9/1973–9/1975)

#### Front disc brake conversion (pre-1976 trucks)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 4 hours with a bolt-on kit · cost Kits about $550–700; a mini-truck parts swap about $800
Symptoms: Drum brakes that pull, fade or need constant adjustment on a 1960–1975 truck.
Fix: Bolt-on kits replace the front drums with bracketed calipers and rotors: remove the hub cover, snap ring, drum and hub, fit the bracket, test-fit the rotor (Off-Road.com's install had to grind the hub slightly, only to the casting mark), refit the hub, mount the caliper, fit new lines and bleed. The DIY route on IH8MUD swaps 1979–85 Hilux/4Runner knuckles with later Land Cruiser calipers and vented rotors, but means rebuilding the knuckles and sorting tie-rod geometry.
Tools: Hub tools · grinder · flare-nut wrenches · brake bleeder · Cruiser Corps kit A151 (front, 8/1970–9/1975) or similar

#### Lift and anti-inversion shackles
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day · cost Old Man Emu 2" kits about $2,350 (Cruiser Corps)
Symptoms: Sagging springs, cracked leaves, or a rear shackle that flips over center on a lifted truck.
Fix: Old Man Emu's 2-inch FJ40 kits come with springs, Nitrocharger shocks, greaseable shackles and pins, bushings, U-bolts and a steering damper. Swap one axle at a time with the frame supported. If you reuse factory shackles with lifted springs, OME's FK08 anti-inversion plates weld to the frame to stop them binding over center. Note the spring-bushing size change around 7/1980: Cruiser Corps says two-bolt spring pins mean the early small bushings.
Tools: Jacks and stands · breaker bar · welder (anti-inversion plates) · ARB/OME kit (e.g. ARB-103 for 1975–8/1980) · urethane bushing kit A216

#### Floor pan replacement
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend per side · cost OEM-reproduction pan about $195 each
Symptoms: Soft or holed floors, often found with rotten body mounts on 1979–84 trucks.
Fix: Pull the seats and floor mats, cut back to clean metal, fit and clamp the reproduction pan, and weld it in. IH8MUD's old-school advice: cut out the rust, weld in steel, and use filler only to smooth the surface. Seam-seal and paint underneath before refitting.
Tools: Cut-off wheel · MIG welder · clamps · seam sealer · Cruiser Corps 605-111L (left front, 1979–1984 FJ40/FJ45)

#### Tighten sloppy steering
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day for a seal job · cost Power-steering seal kit about $91; Saginaw conversion about $900
Symptoms: Excessive play or backlash at the wheel after tie rods and the center arm have been checked, or fluid weeping from a factory power-steering box.
Fix: On 1979–84 trucks with factory power steering, rebuild the box with fresh seals and O-rings, replacing any worn internals. Manual-steering trucks often get a GM Saginaw power-steering conversion. Cruiser Corps recommends reading the full procedure first and having a qualified technician install it.
Tools: Pitman arm puller · seal kit 520-139 (1979–10/1984 FJ40/45) or conversion kit 524-117

#### Five-speed swap
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A long weekend · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Screaming highway rpm on 33s with a 1:1 top gear.
Fix: The H55F five-speed has a 0.845:1 fifth and a much deeper first. On 1975–80 FJ40s with a four-speed, the IH8MUD guide lists floor and transmission-cover changes, a custom crossmember, transfer-case shift linkage and boot, driveshaft length changes, speedometer cable and parking-brake work. Early three-speed trucks also need a bellhousing and frame-crossmember changes. Fit an oiler for fifth gear: Cruiser Corps says the H55F needs a split transfer case built 10/1982 or later, which has the oiler provision.
Tools: Transmission jack · H55F (input shaft to suit the engine) · oiler pipe · shifter · linkage kit · gaskets

### Baseline service
Every FJ40 is now 40 to 60 years old, so start from zero: change every fluid, grease every fitting and set the valves. Fluid types and capacities below are from Toyota publications as compiled on IH8MUD for the 40 and 55 series.
- Engine oil & filter: 2F: 7.8 L (≈8.2 qt) with filter · F: 7 L · factory spec API SC/SD (use a modern oil suited to a flat-tappet engine) · Baseline now; then per your owner's-manual schedule (One IH8MUD owner warns the owner's manual figure led him to overfill; another always uses 8 qt in a 2F with a filter change. Fill to the dipstick, not the book. New drain-plug washer every time.)
- Air filter: Paper element in the factory air cleaner · Baseline now (Replace it before you judge how the carburetor runs.)
- Ignition tune-up: Plugs, points (where fitted), cap & rotor · gap and dwell [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now (Check fuel and ignition basics before blaming the carburetor.)
- Valve lash: Adjustable rockers · clearances [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Check now; then periodically (The F and 2F have adjustable rockers that need periodic checks; tight valves are the ones that burn. Valve layout front to back is E-I-I-E-E-I-I-E-E-I-I-E.)
- Coolant & thermostat: Ethylene-glycol coolant · 2F: 16.5 L (the original F table lists 15.2 L) · Baseline flush now (The early F-engine table even lists plain water; use proper ethylene-glycol coolant now, flush until it runs clear, fit a fresh thermostat and check the bypass hose.)
- Manual transmission: API GL-4, SAE 90 · J30 3-speed 1.7 L · H41 4-speed 3.1 L · Baseline now (A swapped-in H55F five-speed takes 4.9 L (60/70-series table) and needs its fifth-gear oiler.)
- Transfer case: API GL-4, SAE 90 · 1.7 L (2.1 L with PTO) · Baseline now (A PTO winch also has its own gearbox: front winch GL-4 SAE 90, 600 cc.)
- Front & rear differentials: API GL-5 hypoid 80W-90 · 2.5 L each · LSD oil for limited-slip · Baseline now (Gear oil mixed into the knuckle grease points to failed inner axle seals.)
- Front knuckles & Birfields: Molybdenum-disulfide lithium-base grease, NLGI-2 · Check now; repack with any seal job (Weeping at the wiper seals or a mix of grease and 90-weight inside means a knuckle rebuild.)
- Steering box & power steering: Manual box: API GL-4 SAE 90, 600 cc · power steering (1979–84): ATF Dexron, 0.8 L total · Check level now (Top up the manual box through its fill plug; most play is in the box, center arm and tie-rod ends.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 (SAE J1703) · Baseline flush now (Bleed every corner and look for weeping wheel cylinders on drum-brake axles.)
- Chassis grease, U-joints & wheel bearings: Chassis: moly lithium NLGI-2 · driveshafts & wheel bearings: lithium multipurpose NLGI-2 · Grease now and at every oil change; repack wheel bearings now (Grease the spring pins/shackles (greaseable pins if fitted), driveshaft U-joints and slip yokes.)
- Fuel filter: Inline filter · Replace now (Do it before or with any carburetor rebuild.)
- Belts & hoses: V-belts and radiator hoses · gear-driven camshaft, so no timing belt · Inspect now; replace anything cracked or original (The F-series engine drives its camshaft by gears, so there's no timing belt or chain to schedule.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: The 'old tried and true' answer on IH8MUD is 31x10.50R15 on stock wheels and suspension. 33x9.50R15 is a popular size on stock 15-inch rims too, but owners report rubbing at the rear over bumps or at full flex. One fixed it with 1-inch spacers under the bump stops, and another had to adjust the front steering stops. One member said 33x10.50s looked 'pretty stuffed.'

Q: Which years should I look for?
A: Most buyers prefer 1976-and-later trucks for front disc brakes and the 4.2 L 2F. 1979 added optional power steering and A/C and taller 3.70 gears in the US. IH8MUD veterans like the '78 and would consider 1979–83 at the right price, but note that 1980-and-later bodies seem to rust more readily.

Q: Three-speed or four-speed?
A: The four-speed arrived with the 2F in 1975 in the US. Most owners prefer it, especially on 33-inch tires. If you want overdrive, the H55F five-speed swap is well documented, though it takes floor, crossmember, linkage and driveshaft work.

Q: Did the US get diesel FJ40s?
A: Not for the general public. Diesel 40s were never sold to US retail buyers, though some arrived as mine trucks. Canada was the exception in 1984, when it got the BJ42 diesel with an overdrive five-speed for about CA$14,000.

Q: Does it have power steering?
A: Only as an option on petrol FJ40s from 1979. Earlier trucks have manual steering, and many owners fit a GM Saginaw power-steering conversion. It isn't a casual bolt-on, and Cruiser Corps recommends professional installation.

Q: Are the drum brakes OK?
A: They work, but they need constant adjustment. Front discs came on US trucks in 1976. Bolt-on conversion kits exist for 1970–75 trucks, and IH8MUD has a write-up using mini-truck knuckles with later Land Cruiser calipers and rotors.

Q: What are the lift options?
A: The common choice is an Old Man Emu 2-inch kit with greaseable anti-inversion shackles. For bigger lifts, some owners go spring-over-axle, which IH8MUD members say gives roughly 6 inches and is usually paired with power steering.

Q: Should I swap in a V8?
A: Plenty of owners have. Hagerty notes many FJ40s got small-block Chevy V8s on the secondary market. The stock six is durable, though, and a healthy 2F with good compression will run a long time.

Q: Can I still get parts?
A: Yes. Toyota announced GR Heritage Parts reproductions for the 40 Series in 2021, starting with engine, driveline and exhaust parts. Specialists such as Cruiser Corps, CruiserTeq, Cool Cruisers of Texas and JT Outfitters stock everything from knuckle kits to floor pans.

Q: What's one worth?
A: It depends heavily on condition and originality. In 2019 Hagerty put the average #2-condition FJ40 at $47,375, after a 7.6 percent drop since 2016, with a 1968 at $49,100 and a 1975 at $44,800. Retro Rides says tidy Australian examples run roughly AU$30,000–50,000 and that US prices are far higher.
