## Toyota Land Cruiser FJ45 / FJ55 (1960–1984 (FJ45) · 1967–1980 (FJ55))
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj45-fj55/
Codes: FJ45, FJ55

Verdict: The FJ45 is the 40 Series stretched until it could carry a squad or a pallet; the FJ55 is what happened when Toyota decided American families wanted one too. The Iron Pig is ungainly, rust-prone and impossible to find panels for, and people who own one would not swap it for anything.

Every Land Cruiser wagon you've ever seen traces back to two awkward long-wheelbase trucks. The FJ45 stretched the FJ40 into pickups, cab-chassis, hardtops and a short-lived four-door wagon. The FJ55, launched in August 1967, was something new: Hagerty calls it Toyota's first Land Cruiser designed from the start as a wagon, and Wikipedia calls it the first 'real' station wagon in the line. Americans nicknamed it the Iron Pig: Hagerty says the two-tone paint made the front end look like a pig's snout. Wikipedia records 'Moose' as another nickname.

### THE LONG-WHEELBASE WORKHORSE
The FJ45 grew out of the 40 Series from the beginning. Wikipedia lists a four-door FJ45V wagon on a 2,650 mm wheelbase and, from 1963, a 2,950 mm long-wheelbase pickup and cab-chassis. Those long trucks became export staples. Truck Encyclopedia describes the super-long version as a major military troop carrier, often with the windshield folded flat, and notes the Irish Army took 77 FJ45s in 1977. They were praised for speed and reliability, and they rusted badly in the Irish wet.
The four-door FJ45V was the shortest-lived variant. Wikipedia says it was replaced by the FJ55 in 1967, and Truck Encyclopedia says only about 60 of the J30-style FJ45-V/LV wagon bodies were built. The pickups carried on through the 1970s, picking up the H diesel in the HJ45 from 1972 or 1973 (sources differ) and the 2H six in the HJ47 from 1980, before the 70 Series replaced the lot in 1984.

### THE IRON PIG
The FJ55 was aimed squarely at North America and Australia. It used the FJ40's drivetrain under a four-door body on a 2,700 mm wheelbase, about 16 inches longer than the FJ40's according to Toyota. Under it was the first Land Cruiser frame with fully boxed members. In the US, Hagerty says, it was sold against the Chevrolet Suburban and Kaiser/Jeep Wagoneer, and it brought a rare luxury: a bottom-hinged tailgate with a power window, worked from a dash switch or the key.
Mechanical changes tracked the FJ40. From 1967 to 1974 it used the 3.9-liter F six at 125 hp with a three-speed manual whose first gear lacked synchromesh. In 1975 the 4.2-liter 2F (135 hp), a four-speed and front disc brakes arrived, along with a domed hood to clear the new induction system. Toyota UK says the design brief was a wagon that could cruise comfortably at 80 mph without losing the 40's off-road ability, and that it made up about 11 percent of Land Cruiser sales by the time production ended in July 1980.

### HOW IT ENDED, AND WHY THEY'RE SO RARE
The FJ60 replaced the FJ55 in 1980, taking the wagon idea upmarket with air conditioning and a proper interior. That left the Iron Pig as a working truck that was driven until it dissolved. Hagerty says rust is the top concern and complete replacement panels generally don't exist (specialists sell only repair sections such as rockers and lower-fender patches), and trim and weatherstripping are hard to find. Low production and high attrition, it notes elsewhere, are why good ones are rare.
Rarity has started to show up in prices. In Hagerty's FJ55 buyer's guide (first published in 2021 and updated in 2023), the median FJ55 value for all conditions was $34,500 and for #2 condition $46,300, with the median quoted value up 65.8 percent since 2020. Gen X buyers accounted for 58.5 percent of the quotes. The FJ45 is rarer still in the US and turns up mostly as imported pickups and troop carriers. Bring a Trailer lists both as separate model pages.

### Data plate
- Chassis: J45 (FJ45/HJ45/BJ45) · J55 (FJ55)
- Fj55 Production: August 1967 – July 1980
- Fj45 Production: 1960–1984
- Fj55 Wheelbase: 2,700 mm (106.3 in)
- Fj45 Wheelbase: 2,650 mm wagon · 2,950 mm pickup
- Engine: F 3.9 L I6 (to 1974) · 2F 4.2 L I6 (1975–)
- Output: 125 hp (F) · 135 hp (2F)
- Transmission: 3-spd (non-synchro 1st) · 4-spd from 1975
- Drive: Part-time 4WD, two-speed transfer
- Frame: Ladder; fully boxed on FJ55
- Brakes: Drums; front discs from 1975 (FJ55)
- Nicknames: Iron Pig · Moose

### Engineering
Both trucks share the 40 Series mechanicals: leaf-sprung live axles, closed-knuckle front axle with Birfield joints, a two-speed part-time transfer case and Toyota's long-stroke F or 2F straight-six. The FJ55 adds a longer, fully boxed frame and a wagon body, and the long FJ45 runs single rear wheels, which Truck Encyclopedia notes limited payloads in military service.
- Chassis: Ladder frame; FJ55 fully boxed (FJ55 2,700 mm wheelbase. FJ45: 2,650 mm (wagon) or 2,950 mm (pickup and cab-chassis).)
- Suspension: Solid axles, leaf springs front and rear (Shared design with the FJ40.)
- 4Wd System: Part-time, two-speed transfer case (Same basic transfer case as the FJ40.)
- Engine: F 3.9 L to 1974 · 2F 4.2 L from 1975 (OHV straight-sixes, 125 hp and 135 hp. Diesel HJ45/HJ47 versions for export.)
- Gearbox: 3-speed (non-synchro first), then 4-speed (Four-speed arrived with the 2F in 1975.)
- Brakes: Drums; front discs from 1975 (FJ55) (Disc conversions are common on earlier trucks.)

### Versions
- 1960–1967 · FJ45V · F 3.9 L I6 · 125 hp · Four-door wagon on a 2,650 mm wheelbase; replaced by the FJ55.
- 1963–1984 · FJ45 pickup / cab-chassis · F, then 2F I6 · 125–135 hp · 2,950 mm long wheelbase. Military troop carriers in many markets.
- 1972–1980 · HJ45 · H 3.6 L I6 diesel · 94 hp · Long-wheelbase diesel for export.
- 1980–1984 · HJ47 / BJ45 · 2H 4.0 L I6 / 3B 3.4 L I4 diesel · 90–105 hp · Last long-wheelbase 40s before the 70 Series.
- 1967–1974 · FJ55 · F 3.9 L I6 · 125 hp · Three-speed with non-synchro first; drum brakes.
- 1975–1980 · FJ55 (FJ56 in Japan) · 2F 4.2 L I6 · 135 hp · Four-speed, front discs and domed hood. Production ended July 1980.

### Year-by-year
- 1960: FJ45V four-door wagon (2,650 mm) launched alongside the short-wheelbase 40
- 1963: 2,950 mm long-wheelbase FJ45 pickup and cab-chassis added
- 1967: FJ55 wagon launched in August with Toyota's first fully boxed frame, replacing the FJ45 wagon
- 1972: HJ45 launched with the 3.6 L H diesel six; FJ55 gets revised side markers
- 1975: 4.2 L 2F and a four-speed replace the 3.9 L F and three-speed; FJ55 gets a domed hood (sold as the FJ56 in Japan)
- 1978: FJ55 rear lamps move lower with integrated turn signals and reverse lights
- 1980: FJ55 production ends in July; HJ47 and BJ45 arrive
- 1984: End of J40-family production in Japan; Venezuela built long-chassis trucks until 8/1985

### Capability
- Wheelbase: 2,700 mm (106.3 in) FJ55 · 2,650 mm wagon / 2,950 mm pickup FJ45
- Length (FJ55): 4,675 mm (184 in)
- Curb weight (FJ45V): 1,850 kg (4,079 lb) (Japanese-market figure)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: H78-15 (≈205/75R15) on 15x5.5 steel wheels
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Offset: 3.25 in backspacing (OEM 15x5.5 steel)
- Note: Cruiser Corps lists the same 15x5.5 OEM steel wheel for 1958–1990 FJ40, FJ45, FJ55, FJ60, FJ62 and BJ trucks, and advises against tires wider than 10.5 in on it.

### Buying checks
- Rust is the deal: On an FJ55, Hagerty's checklist starts at the roof near the drip rails, then the cowl, fenders, doors, rocker panels and wheel arches. Under it, check the frame rails, body mounts and anywhere mud collects.
- Judge the old repairs: Replacement panels generally don't exist for the FJ55, so past rust repairs were fabricated. Look closely at how well they were done, since redoing them is expensive.
- Trim and seals: Weatherstripping and trim are hard to find. A truck with complete trim is worth more than its paint suggests.
- Interior condition: Vinyl seats tear and original dash tops and rubber mats go brittle. Original, undamaged interiors are the most desirable.
- Test the tailgate window: The FJ55's power tailgate window works from a dash switch or the key. Make sure it does, with the tailgate both up and down. A dead window is often a stuck safety switch or a corroded power strip, but it can also be a stripped regulator (see the repair below).
- Brakes: Stock drums are adequate if they work well and the powertrain is stock. Disc upgrades are common and parts are easy to find; check what's been fitted and how.
- Engine health: The F and 2F are durable with basic maintenance and periodic valve adjustments. Compression matters more than mileage, and mechanical repairs are cheap next to rust repair.
- Know which truck it is: Check the wheelbase and engine code against the chassis plate: FJ45 wagons, pickups and diesel HJ/BJ versions differ, and export-spec trucks are sometimes misidentified.

### Common repairs
#### Front knuckle and Birfield rebuild
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Two days the first time · cost Knuckle kit about $160 (Cruiser Corps)
Symptoms: Grease and gear oil weeping past the knuckle wiper seals, sludge inside the knuckle, or play in the front wheel.
Fix: Same job as an FJ40: pull the hub, spindle and Birfield, remove the steering-arm cones and knuckle caps, then replace the inner axle seal, knuckle bearings and wiper seals. Repack and reassemble, using top shims to set knuckle-bearing preload and bottom shims to center the knuckle. Use the spec from the factory service manual.
Tools: Spring scale · brass drift · seal driver · Cruiser Corps kit 514-108 (FJ40/45/55, 1958–9/1975) or 514-109 (9/1975–1/1990) · knuckle wiper kit · moly grease

#### Carburetor rebuild
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Keyster kit about $35
Symptoms: Stumbling, hesitation, rough idle or stalling at low rpm.
Fix: Identify the carburetor by the number on its body, since Cruiser Corps sells more than a dozen different Keyster kits for FJ40, FJ45 and FJ55 carburetors built between 1966 and 1984. Strip, clean and rebuild, set the float, and check vacuum lines and the choke while it's apart.
Tools: Screwdrivers · carb cleaner · Keyster kit matched to the carb number

#### Valve adjustment
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost Valve cover gasket about $17–22 (Cruiser Corps) plus washers
Symptoms: Ticking from the top end, or a rough-running engine with tight valves.
Fix: Hagerty notes the F and 2F want periodic valve adjustments. With the engine warm, find tight and loose valves with go/no-go feeler gauges at idle, then shut down and adjust only those, setting each cylinder's pair once its intake valve has just closed. Tight valves are the dangerous ones because they can burn.
Tools: Feeler gauges · 17 mm wrench · valve cover gasket

#### Front disc conversion
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 4 hours with a bolt-on kit · cost Front kit about $700 (Cruiser Corps, 8/1970–9/1975)
Symptoms: Fading or pulling drum brakes on an early truck.
Fix: Bolt-on kits replace the front drums with brackets, calipers and rotors; the job is hub off, bracket on, rotor and hub back on, caliper mounted, new lines and a full bleed. IH8MUD's mini-truck knuckle conversion, written up on a 1972 FJ40, is also reported to work on an FJ55.
Tools: Hub tools · flare-nut wrenches · brake bleeder · Cruiser Corps kit A151 (front) or A150 (front and rear, 8/1970–8/1980)

#### Fabricate rust repairs
Difficulty 5 / 5 · time Days to weeks · cost Parts plus a lot of labor
Symptoms: Bubbling at the drip rails, cowl, rockers and wheel arches, or soft frame rails and body mounts.
Fix: Because complete FJ55 panels generally don't exist, repairs mean cutting out rot and either fitting the few repair sections sold (rockers, lower-fender patches) or forming patches by hand, then welding, seam-sealing and protecting the area. Fix structural metal (frame rails and body mounts) before cosmetic panels, and get a professional opinion on the frame first.
Tools: MIG welder · cut-off wheel · sheet-metal brake or hammer-and-dolly set · seam sealer

#### Fresh springs, shackles and bushings
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day · cost OME FJ45 2" kits about $2,300–2,700 (Cruiser Corps)
Symptoms: Sagging, cracked or S-shaped leaf springs and worn bushings.
Fix: Old Man Emu's FJ45 kits (1963–80 and 1980–84) include springs, shocks, greaseable shackles and pins, bushings, U-bolts and a steering damper. Cruiser Corps notes the OEM round washer must be used at the spring-to-frame pin instead of OME's teardrop washer. Confirm fitment before ordering parts for an FJ55, which isn't listed for these kits.
Tools: Jacks and stands · breaker bar · ARB-120 (FJ45 1963–1980) or equivalent kit · bushing kit

#### Clutch master and slave cylinders
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day including bleeding · cost Aisin master about $115 and slave about $35 (Cruiser Corps); OEM master rebuild kit about $51
Symptoms: A clutch that slowly loses pressure, has to be double-pumped to shift without grinding, or a pedal that sinks. Look for fluid under the dash or around the slave on the bellhousing.
Fix: Off-Road.com's FJ40 project, which shares the early clutch hydraulics with the FJ45, replaced the master, the slave and the hose. Pump the old fluid out. Unbolt the slave (two bolts), fit the new one with thread-locker and set the fork pushrod with its locknut. Free the old line with penetrating oil and flare-nut wrenches. Under the dash, pull the cotter pin and spring at the pedal, then remove the three 12 mm master bolts. Fit the new master with a new cotter pin, connect the line and don't overtighten the banjo bolt. Fill with DOT 3, bleed at the slave with a helper, then adjust the pedal rod and slave pushrod. Bench-bleed the new master, and keep the pedal down until the bleeder is closed. Check fitment by build date: Cruiser Corps lists this master for 1970–75 trucks and the slave for 1974–80.
Tools: 12 mm socket and wrench · 12 mm and 16 mm flare-nut wrenches · needle-nose pliers · bleeder hose and bottle · thread-locker · DOT 3 fluid

#### FJ55 power tailgate window won't move
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time An afternoon to a weekend · cost Often only cleaning, wiring and a power strip; a used motor or regulator if the gear is stripped
Symptoms: The rear glass won't go up or down from the dash switch or the key. It may work only with the tailgate down. Or you hear the motor clunk while the glass stays put.
Fix: IH8MUD members work from the simple stuff inwards. The tailgate has a safety switch: the motor won't run unless its plunger is pushed in. Slop in the gate or a broken plastic actuator can leave the switch open. Next, check the power strip and the harness where it flexes at the hinge; one owner found his strip 'rotten' and replaced it. A meter will tell you whether power reaches the motor when you press the dash switch. If the motor runs on direct battery power but the glass doesn't move, suspect a stripped regulator gear. Members say the glass tray has to be separated from the regulator by driving out two clips, and that the mechanism is often packed with old grime. Be gentle with the glass: one owner broke a donor truck's window getting it down.
Tools: Screwdrivers · multimeter · jumper leads and a 12 V battery · drift and hammer for the tray clips · grease

### Baseline service
Every FJ45 or FJ55 is now 40 to 60 years old, so start from zero: change every fluid, grease every fitting and set the valves. Fluid types and capacities below are from Toyota publications as compiled on IH8MUD for the 40 and 55 series; the FJ55 shares the FJ40's F/2F engine and driveline lubricants.
- Engine oil & filter: 2F: 7.8 L (≈8.2 qt) with filter · F: 7 L · factory spec API SC/SD (use a modern oil suited to a flat-tappet engine) · Baseline now; then per your owner's-manual schedule (One IH8MUD owner warns the owner's manual figure led him to overfill; another always uses 8 qt in a 2F with a filter change. Fill to the dipstick, not the book. New drain-plug washer every time.)
- Air filter: Paper element in the factory air cleaner · Baseline now (Replace it before you judge how the carburetor runs.)
- Ignition tune-up: Plugs, points (where fitted), cap & rotor · gap and dwell [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now (Check fuel and ignition basics before blaming the carburetor.)
- Valve lash: Adjustable rockers · clearances [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Check now; then periodically (Hagerty notes the F and 2F want periodic valve adjustments; tight valves are the ones that burn. Valve layout front to back is E-I-I-E-E-I-I-E-E-I-I-E.)
- Coolant & thermostat: Ethylene-glycol coolant · 2F: 16.5 L (the original F table lists 15.2 L) · Baseline flush now (The early F-engine table even lists plain water; use proper ethylene-glycol coolant now, flush until it runs clear, fit a fresh thermostat and check the bypass hose.)
- Manual transmission: API GL-4, SAE 90 · J30 3-speed 1.7 L · H41 4-speed 3.1 L · Baseline now (A swapped-in H55F five-speed takes 4.9 L (60/70-series table) and needs its fifth-gear oiler.)
- Transfer case: API GL-4, SAE 90 · 1.7 L (2.1 L with PTO) · Baseline now (A PTO winch also has its own gearbox: front winch GL-4 SAE 90, 600 cc.)
- Front & rear differentials: API GL-5 hypoid 80W-90 · 2.5 L each · LSD oil for limited-slip · Baseline now (Gear oil mixed into the knuckle grease points to failed inner axle seals.)
- Front knuckles & Birfields: Molybdenum-disulfide lithium-base grease, NLGI-2 · Check now; repack with any seal job (Weeping at the wiper seals or a mix of grease and 90-weight inside means a knuckle rebuild.)
- Steering box & power steering: Manual box: API GL-4 SAE 90, 600 cc · power steering (where fitted): ATF Dexron, 0.8 L total · Check level now (Top up the manual box through its fill plug; most play is in the box, center arm and tie-rod ends.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 (SAE J1703) · Baseline flush now (Bleed every corner and look for weeping wheel cylinders on drum-brake axles.)
- Chassis grease, U-joints & wheel bearings: Chassis: moly lithium NLGI-2 · driveshafts & wheel bearings: lithium multipurpose NLGI-2 · Grease now and at every oil change; repack wheel bearings now (Grease the spring pins/shackles (greaseable pins if fitted), driveshaft U-joints and slip yokes.)
- Fuel filter: Inline filter · Replace now (Do it before or with any carburetor rebuild.)
- Belts & hoses: V-belts and radiator hoses · gear-driven camshaft, so no timing belt · Inspect now; replace anything cracked or original (The F-series engine drives its camshaft by gears, so there's no timing belt or chain to schedule.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: We couldn't find a solid FJ55- or FJ45-specific consensus. They use 40 Series axles, and for the stock FJ40, IH8MUD's 'tried and true' size is 31x10.50R15, with 33x9.50R15 fitting but rubbing at full flex. Try any size on your own truck before committing.

Q: What's the difference between an FJ45 and an FJ55?
A: The FJ45 is the long-wheelbase version of the 40 Series: pickups and cab-chassis on 2,950 mm and an early four-door wagon on 2,650 mm. The FJ55 (1967–80) is a purpose-built four-door wagon on a 2,700 mm wheelbase with its own fully boxed frame.

Q: Why is it called the Iron Pig?
A: Hagerty traces the name to the FJ55's front end, where the two-tone paint made it resemble a pig's snout. Wikipedia also records 'Moose.'

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: There's no settled answer. Later trucks have the 4.2 L 2F, a four-speed and front disc brakes (the domed hood is the easy tell), and factory power steering came at the very end. Even IH8MUD members disagree on exactly when those arrived, with some 1974–75 trucks carrying odd mixes of parts. Earlier trucks use the 3.9 L F and a three-speed whose first gear has no synchro, which some collectors prefer for originality. Owners agree on one thing: rust is your biggest enemy, so buy the straightest body you can find.

Q: Can I get body panels?
A: Not complete ones. Hagerty says replacement panels generally don't exist and missing metal usually has to be fabricated, and trim and weatherstripping are hard to find. Cruiser Corps does sell FJ55 repair sections, including outer rockers and lower-fender patch panels with the inner brace. Buy the most solid truck you can afford.

Q: Are the drum brakes good enough?
A: Hagerty says stock drums are adequate if they're in good order and the powertrain is stock. Disc conversions are common and parts are easy to find.

Q: What are the lift options?
A: Old Man Emu makes 2-inch kits for the FJ45 (1963–80 and 1980–84), sold through specialists such as Cruiser Corps, with greaseable shackles and a steering damper. Confirm fitment for an FJ55 before ordering.

Q: Is the engine reliable?
A: Yes, with basic care. Hagerty calls the F and 2F durable with basic maintenance and periodic valve adjustments, and says mechanical repairs are easy and cheap compared with rust repair.

Q: What's an FJ55 worth?
A: In Hagerty's FJ55 buyer's guide (first published in 2021 and updated in 2023), the median value for all conditions was $34,500 and for #2 condition $46,300, with quoted values up 65.8 percent since 2020. Its earlier wagon-values piece mentioned private sales approaching six figures.

Q: Were FJ45s really used by armies?
A: Yes. Truck Encyclopedia describes the super-long-wheelbase FJ45 as a major military export used as a troop carrier, and the Irish Army took 77 FJ45s in 1977.

## Toyota Land Cruiser FJ60 (1980–1987)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj60/
Codes: FJ60, 2F 4.2 I6

Verdict: The FJ60 is the Land Cruiser that learned to carry a family and a cooler without forgetting it was a truck. A carbureted 2F, a four-speed, leaf springs and round headlights make it slow, thirsty and wonderful, provided you can find one whose rear frame rails are still there.

Toyota introduced the 60 Series in 1980, in the middle of the second oil crisis, to compete in a market that was just starting to call itself 'SUV.' It replaced the FJ55 Iron Pig and kept the old recipe underneath: ladder frame, leaf springs and solid axles. What changed was the cabin. Wikipedia lists air conditioning, a rear heater and an upgraded interior. Toyota UK adds that it was the first Land Cruiser with sound insulation and wall-to-wall upholstery, plus a front anti-roll bar and softer springs.

### A WAGON FOR THE EIGHTIES
The new body was rounder, with front wings integrated into the bodywork for the first time and a wide-set grille. An optional high-roof version arrived in 1981, the same year Land Cruiser sales passed one million. Toyota offered five-, six-, eight-, nine- and ten-seat layouts in different markets, and Flexmotor says the 60 was the first Land Cruiser offered in named trim levels (STD, GX and, later, VX). Silodrome compares the step up in comfort to a Range Rover of the period, which is generous, but not by as much as you'd think.
American FJ60s kept the 4.2-liter 2F straight-six from the FJ40, carbureted and rated at 135 hp and 210 lb-ft, with a four-speed manual and a two-speed, part-time transfer case. Other markets moved faster. Wikipedia dates the five-speed to 1982 (Toyota UK says 1983), and says the 4.0-liter carbureted 3F replaced the 2F outside North America in 1984 (as the FJ61), and the 12H-T turbo-diesel appeared in 1985. US buyers got none of that and stuck with the 2F until the FJ62 arrived for 1988.

### LIVING WITH ONE
On the road the FJ60 is slow; Corsetti Cruisers says it tops out around 65 mph. In the dirt it is the same tough truck as the 40, with closed-knuckle Birfield front axles and plenty of clearance. The weak points are age and the smog system. Corsetti lists carburetor rebuilds, tangled vacuum lines, knuckle sludge, steering wobble on lifted trucks, worn engines past 200,000 miles and, above all, rust. Its rust list starts with the windshield corners and ends with the rear wheel wells, which it calls the place every 60 starts to rot.
1981–87 trucks also carry a High Altitude Compensation system that, Corsetti says, advances ignition timing above about 3,930 feet. Many owners have replaced the factory carburetor with a Weber, but Corsetti recommends sticking with the factory carb because the Weber bypasses HAC and brings emissions and jetting headaches. The other common upgrade is a five-speed. In April 1985 Toyota lengthened the H42 four-speed with a spacer where the H55F's fifth gear sits, so on later trucks the five-speed is close to a direct swap.

### THE COLLECTOR'S 60
The FJ60 gave way to the fuel-injected, automatic FJ62 for the 1988 US model year, and Toyota UK says the 60 Series ended Japanese production in December 1989 after 406,700 were built (Wikipedia says 1990), and Venezuela kept assembling them until 1992. For years they were cheap old wagons. Hagerty now calls the round-headlight, manual FJ60 the more collectible of the two, and its wagon-values piece (around 2020) put the median quote for FJ60s and FJ62s at $18,500, with demand apparently overtaking that for Jeep Grand Wagoneers.
That interest has spawned a restomod industry. Shops such as Corsetti Cruisers build FJ60s with modern engines and interiors, while IH8MUD's 60 Series Wagons forum remains the place to learn how to keep a stock one running. The 80 Series replaced the whole line in 1990, swapping leaf springs for coils, but the FJ60 has its own following of owners who like its simplicity.

### Data plate
- Chassis: J60 (FJ60)
- Us Model Years: 1981–1987
- Engine (Us): 2F 4.2 L OHV I6, carbureted
- Output: 135 hp @ 3,600 · 210 lb-ft @ 1,800
- Transmission (Us): H41F/H42F 4-spd manual
- Drive: Part-time 4WD, two-speed transfer
- Length: 184 in
- Width: 70.9 in
- Height: 69.5 in
- Curb Weight: 4,246 lb
- Fuel Tank: 23.8 gal
- Towing: 3,500 lb

### Engineering
The FJ60 is a 40 Series drivetrain wearing a family wagon's clothes. It keeps the ladder frame, live axles on leaf springs and closed-knuckle front axle with Birfield joints, and adds a front anti-roll bar, softer springs and power steering. US trucks use the carbureted 2F and an H42 four-speed manual feeding a two-speed, part-time transfer case.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, four-door wagon body (Low-roof (1,750 mm) or high-roof (1,950 mm) versions.)
- Suspension: Solid axles, leaf springs; front anti-roll bar (Softer springs than earlier Land Cruisers. Lifted trucks are prone to steering wobble.)
- 4Wd System: Part-time, two-speed transfer case (Split transfer case shared in design with late 40s.)
- Engine (Us): 2F 4.2 L OHV I6, carbureted (135 hp @ 3,600 rpm, 210 lb-ft @ 1,800 rpm (Corsetti). High Altitude Compensation on 1981–87 trucks.)
- Gearbox (Us): H41F/H42F four-speed manual (US-only gearbox; pre-4/1985 'short' and post-4/1985 'long' (spacer) versions. The H55F five-speed was used elsewhere.)
- Brakes: Front discs, rear drums (Front discs and rear drums on US trucks.)

### Versions
- 1980–1987 · FJ60 (US) · 2F 4.2 L I6 (carb) · 135 hp / 210 lb-ft · Four-speed manual only in the US. US model years 1981–87.
- 1984–1988 · FJ61 (export) · 3F 4.0 L I6 (carb) · — · 3F replaced the 2F outside North America.
- 1980–1986 · BJ60 · 3B 3.4 L I4 diesel · ≈ 90 hp · Not sold in the US.
- 1980–1990 · HJ60 · 2H 4.0 L I6 diesel · ≈ 105 hp · Naturally aspirated diesel (Wikipedia's infobox dates it from 1982). Not sold in the US.
- 1985–1990 · HJ61 · 12H-T 4.0 L I6 turbo-diesel · 134 bhp / ≈ 315 lb-ft · Direct injection; considered the most desirable 60 outside the US.
- 1988–1990 · FJ62 (US) · 3F-E 4.0 L I6 (EFI) · 155 hp / 220 lb-ft · The FJ60's US successor, automatic only.

### Year-by-year
- 1980: 60 Series introduced with A/C, a rear heater and a nicer cabin; the US gets the 2F carbureted six and a four-speed for 1981
- 1981: Tie-rod recall on 1981 trucks; a high-roof version is introduced
- 1982: Five-speed H55F arrives in other markets (Wikipedia; Toyota UK says 1983); US trucks keep the four-speed
- 1984: Most markets get the 4.0 L 3F; North America keeps the 2F
- 1985: April 1985 running change: the H42 gets a spacer that makes later trucks H55F-ready, and suspension parts split (OME kits fit 4/1985–1/1990); HJ61 12H-T turbodiesel launched abroad
- 1987: Last US FJ60 model year; the FJ62 replaces it for 1988

### Capability
- Towing: 3,500 lb (1,590 kg) (Corsetti)
- Fuel tank: 23.8 US gal (90 L)
- Fuel economy: 11 city / 18 hwy mpg (Corsetti)
- Curb weight: 4,246 lb (1,926 kg)
- Dimensions: 184 x 70.9 x 69.5 in (L x W x H)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 15-inch factory wheels, 6 or 7 in wide
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Offset: 3.25 in backspacing (OEM 15x5.5 steel)
- Note: Cruiser Corps lists the same 15x5.5 OEM steel wheel for 1958–1990 FJ40, FJ45, FJ55, FJ60, FJ62 and BJ trucks, and advises against tires wider than 10.5 in on it.
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 31x10.50R15 or 33x9.50R15 (Corsetti runs 31x10.50s on stock springs. IH8MUD owners run 33x9.50s unlifted, but 33x12.50s won't fit without a lift.)
- Biggest tire, 2.5 in (OME) lift: 33x10.50R15 (Corsetti's setup. One IH8MUD owner fits 34x10.5 KO2s on a heavy-duty OME kit. Corsetti says don't go wider than 10.5 in or taller than 33 in on a factory rim, and fit a steering damper.)
- Biggest tire, 2.5 in + 2 in body lift lift: 35 in (35s rub on a 2.5-inch OME kit alone. IH8MUD owners add a body lift, shackle or spring changes, or about 4 inches of lift.)

### Buying checks
- Rear frame rails first: Corsetti calls it the most important check: drop the spare if you have to and look at the rear frame rails. If the frame is rusted through, walk away. IH8MUD members agree the rear channel near the spare is usually the worst frame spot.
- The other rust spots: Check the windshield gasket corners (peel the rubber back a little), roof drip rails, tailgate hinge areas, inner wheel wells behind the rear seat, front fenders, rockers and rear wheel wells. A missing or uneven mud flap can hide a patched fender, and a magnet finds filler.
- Floor under the rear seat: IH8MUD buyers' threads add the floor pan under the back seat to the list, along with behind the mud flaps.
- Compression test high-mileage trucks: On trucks past 200,000 miles, or that have sat or had several owners, do a compression test. Corsetti's numbers for the 2F: around 160–165 psi is excellent, under 120 means caution, under 100 means don't buy, with no more than 10 percent spread between cylinders.
- Smog equipment and vacuum lines: IH8MUD members call emissions equipment the biggest headache. Check that it's all there, look for cracked or disconnected vacuum hoses, and expect to rebuild the carburetor.
- Knuckles, steering and power-steering leaks: Sludge at the front knuckles means seals are due. Drive it and feel for wobble, especially on a lifted truck. A shiny, wet driver's-side axle and spring usually means the power-steering box or pump is leaking.
- Budget for rubber: Hoses, seals, bushings and diaphragms go hard with age, and most will need replacing. One IH8MUD member put catch-up maintenance at several thousand dollars.
- Which four-speed?: Look for a spacer between the transmission and transfer case. If it's there, it's a post-4/1985 'long' H42, and a five-speed swap is straightforward.

### Common repairs
#### Carburetor rebuild and vacuum check
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day · cost About $300 for a rebuild (Corsetti)
Symptoms: Stumbling, hesitation, sputtering, rough running or stalling at low rpm. If it only runs with the choke off, suspect the EGR valve.
Fix: Corsetti says the most frequent problem is simply a loose or broken vacuum hose or wiring connection, so check fuel and ignition basics, then every vacuum line, before blaming the carb. Rebuild the factory carburetor and check the EGR valve while you're there. Above 3,930 feet, check the High Altitude Compensation system, which a Weber carb bypasses. Trucks over 200,000 miles will likely need a full set of vacuum hoses.
Tools: Carb rebuild kit · vacuum hose · vacuum diagram · vacuum gauge · carb cleaner

#### Compression test before you buy or rebuild
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost Cost of a gauge
Symptoms: Low power, blow-by or an unknown engine history on a truck past 200,000 miles.
Fix: With the engine warm, pull all six plugs, disable the ignition, hold the throttle open and crank each cylinder for the same number of strokes. Corsetti's guide for a healthy 2F is 160–165 psi, with caution under 120 and walk away under 100. Readings should be within 10 percent of each other. Significant wear usually means valves, seats and rings, so a full rebuild.
Tools: Compression gauge · spark-plug socket · remote starter switch

#### Front knuckle rebuild
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Two days the first time · cost $200–600 (Corsetti), mostly labor; kits about $120–160
Symptoms: Grease sludge leaking from the steering knuckles where axle grease has got past the seals.
Fix: Pull the hub, spindle and Birfield, remove the knuckle caps and bearings, replace the inner axle seal, knuckle bearings and wiper seals, then repack and reassemble. Top shims set knuckle-bearing preload. On 1981 trucks, check whether the factory steering recall parts were fitted.
Tools: Spring scale · seal driver · Cruiser Corps kit 595-102 or 514-109 · knuckle shim and gasket kit 595-101 · moly grease

#### Cure the death wobble
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost Steering damper up to about $112
Symptoms: Violent front-end shake after a bump, especially on lifted trucks; or a shake you feel in the truck but not the steering wheel.
Fix: Inspect tie-rod ends, the drag link, knuckle preload and the steering box mounts first. Corsetti fits an Old Man Emu steering damper to every FJ60, lifted or not. Expect the factory stabilizer to be hard to remove without an air tool. If the wheel is calm but the truck still shakes, the driveshaft probably needs balancing, which is common past 200,000 miles.
Tools: Impact wrench · Old Man Emu steering damper (OMESD24 in OME's 60 Series kits)

#### H55F five-speed swap
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend; the pilot bearing took Off-Road.com's author a full day · cost Parts plus labor; flywheel resurfacing about $30
Symptoms: About 3,250 rpm at 75 mph in fourth gear.
Fix: On post-4/1985 trucks the H55F is direct-fit. Drain and remove the driveshafts, starter, clutch slave and transfer-case shift lever, support the engine and drop the four-speed. Replace the clutch, pilot bearing and rear main seal, resurface the flywheel, then fit the H55F with its fifth-gear oiler, plug the crossbar hole in the transfer case and use new gaskets and staked nuts. Pre-4/1985 trucks also need shift-linkage and driveshaft changes. The 0.84 fifth drops highway rpm to about 2,750 at 75 mph.
Tools: Transmission jack · 32 mm and 36 mm sockets · clutch alignment tool · clutch kit · gaskets · fifth-gear oiler

#### Replace the front heater core
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Core about $230 (Cruiser Corps)
Symptoms: Coolant smell in the cabin, a damp passenger carpet, poor heat or unexplained coolant loss.
Fix: Drain the coolant, disconnect the heater hoses at the firewall, remove the dash panels and heater box, and swap the core. Refill and bleed. Cruiser Corps warns that a leaking core can corrode the floorboards under wet carpet, so dry and check the floor while it's apart.
Tools: Basic hand tools · coolant · Cruiser Corps 520-127 front heater core (8/1980–8/1987)

#### Two-inch lift with fresh springs
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day · cost Old Man Emu kits about $2,400 (Cruiser Corps)
Symptoms: Sagging leaf springs, worn shocks or a nose-down stance.
Fix: Old Man Emu sells 2-inch kits for FJ60s in light, medium and heavy load ratings, split at April 1985. They include springs, Nitrocharger shocks, greaseable anti-inversion shackles and pins, bushings, U-bolts and a steering damper. Change one axle at a time with the frame supported, and grease the new shackles and pins.
Tools: Jacks and stands · breaker bar · ARB/OME kit (pre- or post-4/1985) · grease gun

### Baseline service
An FJ60 is now 40-plus years old and most have passed 200,000 miles, so treat every fluid and grease point as unknown. Fluid types and capacities below are from Toyota publications as compiled on IH8MUD for the 60 and 70 series (US FJ60: 2F engine and H41F/H42F four-speed; the H55F five-speed was never fitted to US trucks at the factory).
- Engine oil & filter: 2F: 8 L (≈8.5 qt) with filter · factory spec API SF (use a modern oil suited to a flat-tappet engine) · Baseline now; then per your owner's-manual schedule (Fill to the dipstick rather than the book figure; one IH8MUD 2F owner uses 8 qt with a filter change.)
- Air filter: Paper element · Baseline now (Check the air cleaner's vacuum hoses while the lid is off.)
- Ignition tune-up: Plugs, cap, rotor & wires · gap [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now (Corsetti's first check for a stumbling FJ60 is a loose or broken vacuum hose or wiring connection, so do ignition and vacuum before the carb.)
- Valve lash: Adjustable rockers · clearances [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Check now; then periodically (Like every F-series engine, the 2F wants periodic valve adjustments (Hagerty's FJ55 guide says the same of the F and 2F).)
- Coolant & thermostat: Ethylene-glycol coolant · 16.5 L · Baseline flush now (Coolant smell or a damp passenger carpet points to the front heater core.)
- Manual transmission: API GL-4/GL-5, SAE 90 · H41 4-speed 3.5 L (H42 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]) · H55F 5-speed (swapped) 4.9 L · Baseline now (H55F swap guides call for the fifth-gear oiler to be fitted; confirm it's there.)
- Transfer case: API GL-4/GL-5, SAE 90 · 2.2 L (with H41/H55F) · Baseline now (Check the front output seal for weeping.)
- Front differential: API GL-5 hypoid 80W-90 · 3.0 L · Baseline now (Fill to the bottom of the fill hole.)
- Rear differential: API GL-5 hypoid 80W-90 · 2.5 L · LSD oil for limited-slip · Baseline now
- Front knuckles & Birfields: Molybdenum-disulfide lithium-base grease, NLGI-2 · Check now; repack with any seal job (Corsetti's tell: grease sludge leaking from the knuckles where axle oil has got past the seals.)
- Power steering: ATF Dexron / Dexron II · 0.81 L total (0.39 L reservoir only) · Baseline flush now
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 (SAE J1703) · Baseline flush now (Bleed all four corners; inspect the rear hoses and hard lines.)
- Chassis grease, U-joints & wheel bearings: Steering link ends: moly lithium NLGI-2 · driveshafts & wheel bearings: lithium multipurpose NLGI-2 · Grease now and at every oil change; repack wheel bearings now (A shake you feel in the truck but not the wheel is usually driveshaft balance or U-joints (Corsetti).)
- Fuel filter, belts & hoses: Inline fuel filter · V-belts · gear-driven camshaft, so no timing belt · Replace filter now; inspect belts and hoses (Corsetti says trucks past 200,000 miles will likely need a full set of vacuum hoses too.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: 33x9.50 fits on stock suspension; one IH8MUD member runs them on a stock FJ62 with 240,000 miles. 33x10.50 might fit, but 33x12.50s won't without a lift: one '87 FJ60 on a 2.5-inch BDS lift still rubbed its inner wheel wells at full stuff. Corsetti runs 31x10.50R15s on stock springs and says not to go wider than 10.5 in or taller than 33 in on a factory rim; Cruiser Corps also advises against tires wider than 10.5 in on the 15x5.5 OEM steel wheel.

Q: FJ60 or FJ62?
A: The FJ60 (US 1981–87) has round headlights, the carbureted 4.2 L 2F and a four-speed manual. The FJ62 (1988–90) has fuel injection, an automatic, square headlights and a plusher cabin. Hagerty calls the FJ60 the more collectible. The FJ62 is easier to live with in traffic.

Q: Did US FJ60s get a five-speed?
A: No. US trucks used the H41F/H42F four-speed. The H55F five-speed went into other markets from 1982–83, and swapping one in is close to direct on post-April-1985 US trucks.

Q: What's the High Altitude Compensation system?
A: It's emissions equipment on 1981–87 trucks that Corsetti says advances ignition timing above about 3,930 feet. A Weber carburetor bypasses it and costs performance, so Corsetti recommends keeping the factory carb.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: Corsetti lists 3,500 lb.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: Corsetti lists 11 mpg city and 18 highway with a 23.8-gallon tank. In practice, bigger tires and a roof rack make it worse.

Q: How do I tell if the engine is tired?
A: Do a compression test. Corsetti's benchmarks for a 2F are about 160–165 psi when excellent, caution under 120 and walk away under 100, with no more than 10 percent spread. The 2F reportedly reaches 300,000 miles with care.

Q: What lift should I run?
A: The classic setup is an Old Man Emu 2-inch kit with greaseable shackles and a steering damper. Kits are split by build date (before or after April 1985) and load rating. Corsetti fits an OME steering damper even on unlifted trucks.

Q: Can I import a diesel HJ61?
A: None were sold new in the US, but the 25-year rule now covers every 60 Series. Silodrome calls the 12H-T-powered GX the most desirable 60. Check EPA and state registration rules before buying.

Q: What's an FJ60 worth?
A: Hagerty's wagon-values piece (around 2020) put the median quote for FJ60s and FJ62s at $18,500, called the FJ60 the pick for collectibility and said demand appeared to be overtaking Jeep Grand Wagoneers. Rust-free restored and restomod trucks sell for much more.

## Toyota Land Cruiser FJ62 (1988–1990)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj62/
Codes: FJ62, 3F-E 4.0 I6

Verdict: The FJ62 is where the Land Cruiser put on a collared shirt: fuel injection, an automatic, square headlights and power everything, all on the same leaf-sprung frame that crossed the Outback. It is the easiest old Cruiser to drive every day, and one of the hardest to find without rust.

The FJ62 is the last and most civilized of the 60 Series, and in America it marked the point where the Land Cruiser started to become a luxury vehicle. Hagerty says it brought two Land Cruiser firsts to the US: electronic fuel injection, on the 4.0-liter 3F-E six, and an automatic transmission. Toyota's own history picks out the new dash, the upgraded interior and the rectangular headlamps that make a 1988 easy to spot. Underneath, it's still a ladder-frame, leaf-sprung, solid-axle truck, much like the FJ60 it replaced.

### BUILT FOR JAPAN, SOLD TO AMERICA
The FJ62 started at home. Wikipedia dates the 3F-E injected engine to 1987, when the FJ62G VX allowed the Land Cruiser to be registered in Japan as a passenger vehicle rather than a commercial one. That meant comfort features: Flexmotor lists power windows and locks among the new options. The US got the FJ62 for the 1988 model year, and for American buyers it was a noticeably more comfortable, easier-driving truck than the FJ60.
The 3F-E made 155 hp at 4,000 rpm and 220 lb-ft at 3,000 rpm, against the FJ60's carbureted 135 hp and 210 lb-ft. It drove through Toyota's A440F four-speed automatic, the only US transmission, an automatic Toyota UK says first went into the 60 Series in 1984 as the first of its kind in a Japanese 4x4. Corsetti Cruisers lists the curb weight at 4,480 lb, 234 lb more than an FJ60, and fuel economy of 12 mpg city and 19 highway, one better than the carbureted truck.

### STILL A TRUCK UNDERNEATH
For all the velour and power windows, the FJ62 kept the 60 Series hardware: leaf springs, a closed-knuckle Birfield front axle and a two-speed, part-time transfer case. That makes it as capable in the dirt as an FJ60 and as simple to work on, with many parts shared across the 40, 55 and 60 Series. Toyota UK says push-button electro-pneumatic four-wheel-drive engagement replaced manual levers on 60s from August 1986; which markets and models got it isn't clear from that history, so whatever your truck has, check that four-wheel drive and low range engage cleanly.
The 3F-E has its own following. IH8MUD members note that in US trucks it was used only in the FJ62 and the 1991–92 FJ80, and consider a well-kept example with 159,000 miles to have plenty of life left. The common gripes are the ones you'd expect on a 35-year-old truck: oil leaks, vacuum leaks that cause a rough idle, tired A/C and, above all, rust. As one member put it, 'any '88 Cruiser is going to leak some oil, from somewhere.'

### THE END OF THE LEAF-SPRING WAGON
Japanese production of the 60 Series ended around the turn of 1990; Toyota UK puts the total at 406,700. Venezuela kept building 60s for its own market until 1992, and Wikipedia says the last carbureted 3F FJ62 rolled out of the Cumaná plant that year. In the US the FJ62 handed over to the 80 Series for 1991, which kept the 3F-E and automatic for two years but switched to coil springs and full-time four-wheel drive.
That makes the FJ62 the last leaf-sprung Land Cruiser wagon sold in America, and the most comfortable vintage Cruiser you can drive every day. Hagerty calls the round-headlight FJ60 the bigger collector's prize and its wagon-values piece (around 2020) put the median quote for FJ60s and FJ62s at $18,500, but the FJ62's fuel injection and automatic make it the easier truck to live with. Restomod shops such as Corsetti Cruisers build both.

### Data plate

- Us Model Years: 1988–1990
- Engine: 3F-E 4.0 L OHV I6, EFI
- Output: 155 hp @ 4,000 · 220 lb-ft @ 3,000
- Transmission: A440F 4-spd automatic
- Drive: Part-time 4WD, two-speed transfer
- Length: 184 in
- Width: 70.9 in
- Height: 68.9 in
- Curb Weight: 4,480 lb
- Fuel Tank: 23.8 gal
- Towing: 3,500 lb

### Engineering
The FJ62 is a 60 Series chassis with a modernized powertrain: the fuel-injected 3F-E four-liter six and an A440F four-speed automatic feeding a two-speed, part-time transfer case. Suspension is still leaf springs on solid axles, with the closed-knuckle Birfield front axle shared with the FJ60 and late FJ40.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, four-door wagon body (Same body structure as the FJ60, with a new nose and square headlights.)
- Suspension: Solid axles, leaf springs front and rear (Old Man Emu kits for 4/1985–1/1990 trucks fit the FJ62.)
- 4Wd System: Part-time, two-speed transfer case (Toyota UK says push-button electro-pneumatic engagement replaced levers on 60s from August 1986; confirm what your truck has.)
- Engine: 3F-E 4.0 L OHV I6, fuel-injected (155 hp @ 4,000 rpm, 220 lb-ft @ 3,000 rpm. Also used in the 1991–92 FJ80.)
- Gearbox: A440F four-speed automatic (The only US transmission; H55F manual swaps are possible but involved.)
- Brakes: Power-assisted ventilated front discs, rear drums (Corsetti lists 'power ventilated disc/drum.')

### Versions
- 1987–1990 · FJ62G VX (Japan) · 3F-E 4.0 L I6 (EFI) · — · Allowed passenger-vehicle registration in Japan.
- 1988–1990 · FJ62 (US) · 3F-E 4.0 L I6 (EFI) · 155 hp / 220 lb-ft · A440F automatic only, square headlights, new dash.
- to 1992 · FJ62 (Venezuela) · 3F 4.0 L I6 (carb) · — · Built at Cumaná for the local market after Japanese production ended.
- 1985–1990 · HJ61 · 12H-T 4.0 L I6 turbo-diesel · 134 bhp · The diesel 60 the US never got.
- 1981–1987 · FJ60 (US) · 2F 4.2 L I6 (carb) · 135 hp / 210 lb-ft · The FJ62's predecessor, four-speed manual.
- 1991–1992 · FJ80 (US) · 3F-E 4.0 L I6 (EFI) · 155 hp · The successor carried the 3F-E over for two years.

### Year-by-year
- 1987: 3F-E fuel-injected 4.0 L introduced; the FJ62G VX lets Toyota sell the Land Cruiser in Japan as a passenger vehicle
- 1988: US FJ62 replaces the FJ60: 155 hp 3F-E, A440F four-speed automatic, square headlights, plusher cabin
- 1990: Japanese production ends; the 80 Series replaces it for the 1991 US model year, keeping the 3F-E and A440F
- 1992: Last FJ62s built in Venezuela, with a carbureted 3F

### Capability
- Towing: 3,500 lb (1,590 kg) (Corsetti)
- Fuel tank: 23.8 US gal (90 L)
- Fuel economy: 12 city / 19 hwy mpg (Corsetti)
- Curb weight: 4,480 lb (2,032 kg)
- Dimensions: 184 x 70.9 x 68.9 in (L x W x H)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 15-inch factory wheels, 6 or 7 in wide
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Offset: 3.25 in backspacing (OEM 15x5.5 steel)
- Note: Cruiser Corps lists the same 15x5.5 OEM steel wheel for 1958–1990 FJ40, FJ45, FJ55, FJ60, FJ62 and BJ trucks, and advises against tires wider than 10.5 in on it.
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 33x9.50R15 (An IH8MUD owner runs them with no problems. 31x10.50R15 is the common choice and looks right at stock height; 33x12.50s won't fit without a lift.)
- Biggest tire, 2.5 in (OME) lift: 33x10.50R15 (Corsetti's FJ62 setup with an OME steering damper. Corsetti says don't go wider than 10.5 in or taller than 33 in on a factory rim.)
- Biggest tire, 2.5 in + 2 in body lift lift: 35 in (35s rub on a 2.5-inch OME kit alone. Owners say the A440F auto and stock gears struggle with 35s.)

### Buying checks
- Rear frame rails: Corsetti says this is the most important check on any 60: drop the spare if necessary and inspect the rear frame rails. Rusted through means walk away.
- The usual 60 rust spots: Windshield gasket corners, roof drip rails, tailgate hinge areas, inner and outer rear wheel wells, front fenders and rockers. Trucks from salted-road states rust fast; a magnet finds filler around the wheel wells and tailgate.
- Find the oil leak: Most will have one. Before blaming the rear main seal, IH8MUD members suggest checking that the oil pan bolts are torqued to spec and that the valve cover gasket isn't the real culprit.
- Rough idle: Usually a tune-up item or a vacuum leak rather than anything serious, but it's a useful bargaining point.
- Test the A/C and the 4WD: Check that the A/C compressor engages; it may just need a recharge. Engage four-wheel drive and low range on a loose surface and make sure the push-button system works.
- Knuckles and steering: Look for sludge at the front knuckles, and drive it to check for wobble or wander, especially on a lifted truck.
- Power-steering leaks: A wet, shiny driver's-side axle and spring usually means the power-steering box or pump is leaking.
- Ask about the transfer case: IH8MUD members treated a transfer-case rebuild at 74,000 miles as a red flag on one truck. Ask why any major driveline work was done.

### Common repairs
#### Chase down a rough idle
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–3 hours · cost Hoses and tune-up parts
Symptoms: Rough or hunting idle, hesitation, or a hiss under the hood.
Fix: Start with a tune-up: plugs, cap, rotor and wires. Then check every vacuum hose, since IH8MUD members point to vacuum leaks as the most likely cause on the 3F-E. Replace hard or cracked hoses rather than patching them, and recheck the idle once warm. Trucks over 200,000 miles will probably need a full set of vacuum hoses.
Tools: Vacuum gauge · smoke tester or carb cleaner spray · vacuum diagram · hose and clamps

#### Diagnose oil leaks before pulling the transmission
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours to diagnose · cost Gaskets; a rear main seal job is far more
Symptoms: Oil drips at the bellhousing or under the engine.
Fix: Clean the engine, then drive and look again. IH8MUD members point out that a leak near the rear main is often just oil pan bolts not tightened to spec, or a valve cover gasket running down the back of the block. Torque the pan bolts and replace the valve cover gasket before committing to a rear main seal, which means removing the transmission.
Tools: Degreaser · torque wrench · valve cover gasket · UV dye (optional)

#### Front knuckle rebuild
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Two days the first time · cost $200–600 (Corsetti); kits about $120–160
Symptoms: Grease sludge leaking from the steering knuckles.
Fix: Pull the hub, spindle and Birfield, remove the knuckle caps and bearings, replace the inner axle seal, knuckle bearings and wiper seals, then repack and reassemble. Top shims set knuckle-bearing preload; follow the factory service manual for the spec.
Tools: Spring scale · seal driver · Cruiser Corps kit 595-102 or 514-109 (to 1/1990) · knuckle shim and gasket kit 595-101 · moly grease

#### Two-inch lift with steering damper
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day · cost Old Man Emu kits about $2,400 (Cruiser Corps)
Symptoms: Sagging springs, worn shocks, or front-end shake after bumps.
Fix: Old Man Emu's FJ60/FJ62 kits for 4/1985–1/1990 trucks include springs, Nitrocharger shocks, greaseable shackles and pins, spring bushings, U-bolts and an OMESD24 steering damper. Choose light, medium or heavy load springs for how the truck is equipped. Corsetti fits an OME damper to every 60 it builds, lifted or not.
Tools: Jacks and stands · breaker bar · ARB-111 (medium load) or equivalent kit · grease gun

#### Fix power-steering leaks
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Seals or a rebuilt box/pump
Symptoms: Fluid on the driver's-side axle and spring, low fluid, or a groaning pump.
Fix: Clean everything and find the source: the steering box, the pump or a hose. Replace hoses first, since they're cheapest. A leaking box needs resealing or a rebuilt unit, after which you refill and bleed by turning lock to lock with the engine running.
Tools: Line wrenches · Pitman arm puller (box removal) · power-steering fluid · drain pan

#### Rust repair at the rear wheel wells
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend per side · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Bubbling at the rear wheel arches, a patched-feeling inner well, or a mud flap that sits unevenly.
Fix: Fold the rear seat and peel back the inner wheel-well cover to see the inside. Cut out rust to clean metal, weld in patch panels, seam-seal and protect the area. Corsetti calls inner wheel-well rust common and relatively easy to repair; frame-rail rust is a different matter and needs professional assessment.
Tools: Cut-off wheel · MIG welder · seam sealer · rust converter and cavity wax

#### Push-button 4WD stuck on: vacuum solenoid and lines
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost Vacuum hose, or a replacement solenoid valve; IH8MUD owners report paying anywhere from a $17.77 donor part to about $400 for a new Toyota one
Symptoms: The green 4WD light stays on after you switch 4WD off, the front driveshaft won't turn by hand with the switch off, or the truck won't shift in or out of 4WD.
Fix: On the FJ62's push-button system, vacuum solenoid valves (VSVs) on the passenger-side firewall send vacuum to the transfer-case actuator. With the switch off and the truck in neutral on the parking brake, check for vacuum at each side of the solenoid. IH8MUD owners trace most cases to a burnt-out solenoid, but others found a clogged vacuum line or one corroded at a bracket, so check the lines and the actuator diaphragm before buying parts. One owner's interim fix is to pull a vacuum line and apply vacuum to the correct port by hand to get it out of 4WD. Don't swap the two lines: one engages 4WD and the other releases it. Replace the solenoid, or follow the IH8MUD write-ups that adapt a junkyard Toyota VSV or a MAC valve.
Tools: 12 mm wrench or socket · screwdriver · hand vacuum pump or gauge · vacuum hose · labels for the lines

#### Fuel tank leak and the 91V-110 recall
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day to drop and replace the tank · cost Free if the recall is still open and parts are available; otherwise a tank, filler hose and lines
Symptoms: Fuel smell, or fuel dripping near the rear axle, especially when filling. NHTSA owner complaints describe a tank split at a spot weld and a corroded fuel line in the left rear wheel well.
Fix: NHTSA campaign 91V-110 covers 1980–1990 Land Cruisers, including every FJ62 year: heat and load can pressurize the tank and crack the welds that hold its internal separator, and Toyota's remedy was a new, improved tank. Run the VIN through NHTSA's recall lookup and ask a Toyota dealer whether the work was ever done; several owners told NHTSA the parts weren't available when they tried. If you're replacing it yourself, drain the tank, support it on a jack, disconnect the filler hose, lines and sending unit, and drop it. While it's down, replace the rubber filler hose and grommets and inspect the steel fuel lines, which can corrode through.
Tools: Fuel-safe drain container · floor jack · sockets and extensions · line wrenches · new hose clamps

### Baseline service
An FJ62 is now 35+ years old, so treat every fluid and rubber part as suspect. The good news is that it's simple: a pushrod six with no timing belt, one automatic, a gear-driven part-time transfer case and two greased-knuckle solid axles. The specs below come from Toyota publications compiled on IH8MUD.
- Engine oil & filter: 3F-E: 7.8 L (8.2 US qt) with filter change, 7.0 L without, 8.0 L dry (Toyota 3F-E repair manual supplement) · API SC–SF or better; Toyota's temperature chart runs from 5W-30 for cold climates to 20W-50 for hot ones, with 10W-30 and 15W-40 between · Then every 3,000–5,000 mi [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Fill to the dipstick, not a number: the oil cooler holds some oil, and IH8MUD owners report 7–8.5 qt depending on how fully it drained. Pre-filling the filter helps.)
- Air filter & intake hose: Paper element for 3F-E · Inspect at every oil change (Check the rubber intake hose for cracks while the lid is off; an air leak after the meter can upset the EFI.)
- Ignition tune-up & PCV: Plugs, wires, cap, rotor and PCV valve · plugs ND W16EXR-U or NGK BPR5EY, gapped 0.8 mm (0.031 in) (Toyota 3F-E repair manual supplement) · Now, then per the owner's manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (The F-series is an OHV engine (Wikipedia), so there is no timing belt to budget for. IH8MUD members start rough-idle hunts with a tune-up and a full set of vacuum hoses.)
- Coolant & hoses: Ethylene-glycol coolant · 17.5 L with the front heater only, 19.5 L with front and rear heaters (Toyota 3F-E repair manual supplement); an IH8MUD compilation of Toyota data lists 16.5 L · Flush now, then every 2 years [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Replace any hose that is hard or swollen, and check the upper thermostat housing and radiator for old repairs; overheating history matters on a big iron six.)
- A440F automatic transmission: Dexron II ATF · 5 L drain-and-refill, 15 L dry fill (Toyota publications via IH8MUD) · Then per the owner's manual schedule [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (A drain-and-refill only changes about a third of the fluid, so do two or three a few hundred miles apart on unknown fluid rather than a pressure flush. Drop the pan and change the strainer once.)
- Transfer case: API GL-4 or GL-5, SAE 90 · 2.1 L with the A440F (Toyota publications via IH8MUD) · Then per the owner's manual schedule [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Fill until it runs out of the fill hole, and remove the fill plug before the drain plug.)
- Front differential: API GL-5 hypoid gear oil, SAE 80W-90 · 3.0 L (Toyota publications via IH8MUD) · Then per the owner's manual schedule [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Milky oil means water got in through the breather or seals, common after deep crossings.)
- Rear differential: API GL-5 hypoid gear oil, SAE 80W-90 · 2.5 L; LSD oil if fitted with a limited-slip (Toyota publications via IH8MUD) · Then per the owner's manual schedule [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Check the pinion seal and axle-end seals for weeps while you're under there.)
- Steering knuckles (closed Birfield): Molybdenum-disulfide lithium-base grease, NLGI-2 (Toyota publications via IH8MUD) · Inspect now; rebuild if leaking (Grease weeping from the knuckle wipers is the classic 60-series leak (Corsetti). If the knuckle grease is runny, gear oil is getting past the inner axle seal.)
- Power steering fluid: Dexron or Dexron II ATF · 0.81 L total, 0.39 L reservoir only (Toyota publications via IH8MUD) · Refresh now if dark (Check the box, pump and hoses for weeps at the same time; leaks often show on the driver's-side axle and spring.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 / SAE J1703 (Toyota publications via IH8MUD) · Flush now, then every 2 years [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Old fluid in a 30-year-old system means sticky calipers and corroded lines; inspect the hard lines while bleeding.)
- Chassis grease points: Driveshafts: lithium-base NLGI-2 · steering link ends: moly lithium NLGI-2 (Toyota publications via IH8MUD) · At every oil change (Grease the U-joints and slip yokes. Greaseable shackles and pins, like those in OME kits, need regular grease too.)
- Fuel filter: EFI in-line filter for FJ62 · Replace now if there's no record (An old filter starves the EFI and can mimic a rough-idle or vacuum problem.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: On a stock FJ62, one IH8MUD member runs 33x9.50s with no problems. 33x10.50 might fit, but 33x12.50s won't without a lift. Many owners choose 31x10.50R15, which looks right at stock height or on an OME lift. Corsetti says not to go wider than 10.5 in or taller than 33 in on a factory rim, and Cruiser Corps advises against tires wider than 10.5 in on the 15x5.5 OEM steel wheel.

Q: FJ62 or FJ60?
A: The FJ62 has fuel injection, 155 hp, an automatic and a plusher cabin, so it's easier to drive every day. The FJ60 has the carbureted 2F, a four-speed manual and round headlights. Hagerty calls the FJ60 the more collectible of the two.

Q: Is the 3F-E the same engine as an early 80 Series?
A: Yes. IH8MUD members note that in US trucks the 3F-E was used only in the FJ62 and the 1991–92 FJ80, so parts and knowledge carry across.

Q: Can I convert it to a manual?
A: Yes, with an H55F five-speed, but it's a big job. You'll need a manual bellhousing, flywheel, clutch, pedal and hydraulics, crossmember and floor modifications, shift linkage, driveshaft changes and some wiring.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: Corsetti lists 3,500 lb, the same as the FJ60.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: Corsetti lists 12 mpg city and 19 highway with a 23.8-gallon tank. Real-world numbers on bigger tires are lower.

Q: Is a little oil leak normal?
A: On a truck this age, mostly yes. As one IH8MUD member put it, 'any '88 Cruiser is going to leak some oil, from somewhere.' Check the pan bolts and valve cover gasket before assuming it's the rear main seal.

Q: What lift should I run?
A: The common setup is an Old Man Emu 2-inch kit for 4/1985–1/1990 trucks, in light, medium or heavy load ratings, with greaseable shackles and a steering damper.

Q: What was the FJ62G VX?
A: The Japanese-market version introduced in 1987 with the 3F-E. Wikipedia says it let the Land Cruiser be sold in Japan as a passenger vehicle rather than a commercial one.

Q: What's one worth?
A: Hagerty's wagon-values piece (around 2020) put the median quote for FJ60s and FJ62s at $18,500, and called the FJ60 the pick for collectibility. Restomod FJ62s from specialist shops sell for far more.

Q: What oil and fluids does it take?
A: Toyota's 3F-E repair manual supplement lists 7.8 liters (8.2 quarts) of oil with a filter change, API SC–SF or better, with the viscosity chosen from a temperature chart that runs from 5W-30 to 20W-50. Coolant capacity is 17.5 liters, or 19.5 with the rear heater. An IH8MUD compilation of Toyota data lists Dexron II for the A440F (5 liters on a drain-and-refill), GL-4 or GL-5 SAE 90 for the transfer case, GL-5 80W-90 for both differentials, Dexron or Dexron II for the power steering and DOT 3 brake fluid. Fill the engine to the dipstick, though, because the oil cooler holds some oil.
