## Toyota Land Cruiser 70 Series (1984–present)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/70-series/
Codes: J70, 76, 78, 79

Verdict: The 70 is the Land Cruiser Toyota forgot to stop building, and nobody who needs one has ever complained. Leaf springs, a part-time transfer case, manual hubs and a cabin with all the sound deadening of a grain silo: it is a farm tool that happens to cross continents.

The 70 Series arrived in 1984 to replace the 25-year-old 40 Series as the Land Cruiser that does the hard work, while the 60 Series wagon line drifted toward comfort and, eventually, the 80 Series. More than four decades later it is still in production. It has been built in Japan, Portugal, Venezuela and Colombia, and it has served as a troop carrier, a mine truck and a military patrol vehicle. What it has never been is a new car you can buy at an American Toyota dealer.

### A 40 SERIES IN A SQUARER SUIT
The styling kept a family resemblance to the 40 but went more angular, and the range came in every length a farmer could want. Wikipedia's breakdown is the one owners use: 70 and 71 were the short wheelbase, 73 and 74 the medium, 75 and later 78 and 79 the long-wheelbase pickups and troop carriers, and 76 and 77 the semi-long four-door wagons. The letters in front give the engine away, so an FJ70 has the 3F petrol six, an HJ75 the 2H diesel, and an HZJ75 the 1HZ.
There were lighter-duty 70s as well, sold as the Bundera, the Land Cruiser II and eventually the Prado. That branch grew softer with each update, and by 1997 the Prado had become the 90 Series with no real connection to the workhorse. Some markets got odd variants, too: Portugal, Spain and Italy received a BJ73 with a VM Motori five-cylinder turbo-diesel, built by Salvador Caetano in Portugal.

### LEAVES, COILS AND A V8
The big mechanical change came with the August 1999 facelift. The front axle moved from leaf springs to coils with leading arms, the rear leaves got longer for more articulation and a better ride, wheels went from six studs to five, and the long-wheelbase models were renamed 78 (troop carrier) and 79 (pickup). The short-wheelbase truck disappeared from most markets, and Japanese sales ended in June 2004 because the truck couldn't meet Japan's NOx and particulate rules.
In 2007 Toyota fitted the 4.5-liter 1VD-FTV turbo-diesel V8. It needed a wider chassis, a wider front axle and a new nose that finally did away with the flat fenders every commercial Land Cruiser had worn since the 40. The four-door 76 wagon was added to the range, and a dressed-up GXL trim arrived. Petrol 70s swapped the 1FZ six for the 1GR-FE V6 in 2009, and a double-cab 79 with a 130-liter tank followed in 2012.

### THE TRUCK THAT WON'T RETIRE
In Australia, where the 70 is part of the furniture, the V8 picked up a diesel particulate filter and piezo injectors in late 2016 to meet Euro 5. The same update gave the single-cab ute curtain and driver's-knee airbags and a thicker, stronger chassis, which earned it five ANCAP stars. In 2023 came a 2.8-liter four-cylinder turbo-diesel with a six-speed automatic, LED headlights and a 40 Series-style gauge cluster. Japan, which had already given the 70 a one-year 30th-anniversary run in 2014–15, put it back on sale in November 2023.
The V8 didn't survive. Toyota Australia ended production of the V8 wagon and troop carrier in September 2024, citing 'changing regulations and community expectations,' and kept only the GXL pickups going into 2025. The four-cylinder makes 201 hp and 369 lb-ft (500 Nm) with the automatic, and from October 2024 it was also offered with a five-speed manual, detuned to 332 lb-ft. Unsealed 4X4's verdict is that plenty of enthusiasts still prefer the pre-DPF 2007–2016 V8s, mainly because they're mechanically simpler.

### HOW AN AMERICAN GETS ONE
Toyota never offered the 70 in the United States. Canada got a few BJ70s for the 1985–87 model years with the 3B and 13B-T diesels, and as of 2022 Canadian mines could still buy them through Toyota Industrial Sales Canada. For everyone else in North America, the route is the gray market. Since 1989 NHTSA has exempted vehicles more than 25 years old from the rules it administers, so each year a new batch of older 70s becomes legal to import.
That's why the IH8MUD 70-Series Tech forum is full of American owners with BJ74s, HJ75s and 1HZ troopies, and why the 80 Series and the 70 often share a driveway. If you want the 80's toughness without the 80's comfort, the 70 is the purer version. It also makes the 100 Series and 200 Series look positively soft.

### Data plate
- Chassis: J70 (70/71/73/74/75/76/77/78/79)
- Production: 1984–present
- Assembly: Japan · Portugal · Venezuela · Colombia (1993–2008)
- Bodies: Wagon, troop carrier, single- and dual-cab pickup
- Wheelbases: 2,310 · 2,600 · 2,730 · 2,980 · 3,180 mm
- Front Axle: Live, leaf (to 1999) / coil (1999 on)
- Rear Axle: Live, leaf springs
- Drive: Part-time 4WD, manual locking hubs
- V8 (Aus): 1VD-FTV 4.5 L turbo-diesel, 2007–2025
- Fuel Tank: 130 L (79 cab-chassis & dual cab); 180 L total (2024 76 wagon)
- Us Sales: Never sold new; Canada BJ70 MY 1985–87

### Engineering
Under the boxy body is a heavy-duty ladder frame, in more wheelbases than any other Land Cruiser line, with live axles at both ends. Every heavy-duty 70 has a leaf-sprung rear axle. The front ran on leaf springs until 1999 and on coils with leading arms after that. Drive goes through a part-time transfer case with high and low range and manual locking hubs, and Toyota offered selectable front and rear lockers in some markets.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, five wheelbases (2,310 mm short-wheelbase up to the 3,180 mm 79 pickup. The 2007 frame got wider to fit the V8.)
- Front Suspension: Live axle: leaf springs, then coils from 1999 (The 1999 facelift brought coil springs with leading arms and a slightly lighter front axle.)
- Rear Suspension: Live axle on leaf springs (On every heavy-duty 70. Rear leaves were lengthened in 1999 for more articulation and a softer ride.)
- 4Wd System: Part-time, high and low range (Manual locking hubs on a full-floating front axle. Rear axles came in semi- and full-floating versions.)
- Lockers: Selectable front and rear (market-dependent) (Factory options in some markets. ARB and Harrop are the usual aftermarket routes.)
- Engine (Aus 2007–2025): 1VD-FTV 4.5 L turbo-diesel V8 (DPF added from late 2016. The last V8s were GXL utes delivered in late 2025. Elsewhere: the 1HZ diesel six, the 1GR-FE V6 and, from 2023, the 2.8 L 1GD-FTV four.)

### Versions
- 1984–1990 · BJ70/73/75 · FJ70/73/75 · HJ75 · 3B / 13B-T diesel I4 · 3F petrol I6 · 2H diesel I6 · — · Original leaf-sprung trucks. Canada got a few BJ70s (MY 1985–87).
- 1990–1999 · HZJ7x · PZJ7x · FZJ7x · 1HZ 4.2 diesel I6 · 1PZ 3.4 diesel I5 · 1FZ 4.5 petrol I6 (from 1992) · — · The 1HZ became the default workhorse engine and is still offered in some markets.
- 1999–2007 · HZJ76/78/79 · HDJ78/79 · 1HZ · 1HD-FTE 4.2 turbo-diesel I6 (1998–2007) · — · Second facelift: coil-sprung front axle, five-stud wheels, 78 troopy and 79 pickup names.
- 2007–2025 · VDJ76/78/79 · 1VD-FTV 4.5 L turbo-diesel V8 · — · Wider front track and frame, 76 wagon added, DPF from late 2016. V8 wagon and troopy production ended September 2024; GXL utes ran into late 2025.
- 2009–present · GRJ76/79 · 1GR-FE 4.0 L petrol V6 · — · Replaced the 1FZ in petrol markets such as the Middle East, Bolivia and Colombia.
- 2023–present · GDJ76/79 · 1GD-FTV 2.8 L turbo-diesel I4 · 201 hp / 369 lb-ft (auto) · 332 lb-ft (manual) · First six-speed automatic in a 70, plus a five-speed manual in Australia from October 2024. Back on sale in Japan from late 2023.

### Year-by-year
- 1984: 70 Series replaces the 40 as the heavy-duty Land Cruiser: short, medium and long wheelbases, leaf springs front and rear
- 1985–1987: BJ70 sold in small numbers in Canada (3B, later 13B-T); diesels switch from 12 V to 24 V for the 1986 model year
- 1990: 4.2 L 1HZ diesel straight-six arrives (HZJ7x) and stays in production for decades in less-regulated markets
- 1992: 4.5 L 1FZ petrol straight-six replaces the 3F (FZJ7x)
- 1999: Second facelift: coil-sprung live front axle, longer rear leaf springs, 5-stud wheels; pickup becomes the 79, Troop Carrier the 78; short wheelbase dropped in most markets
- 2004: Japanese sales end in June because the 70 can't meet Japan's NOx and particulate law
- 2007: Big facelift for the 4.5 L 1VD-FTV turbo-diesel V8: wider front track and chassis, flat front fenders gone, 76 four-door wagon and GXL grade added. Unsealed 4X4 says many enthusiasts favour the 2007–16 V8s, which are simpler because they have no DPF [buy]
- 2009: 4.0 L 1GR-FE V6 replaces the 1FZ in petrol markets
- 2012: Double-cab HZJ79 pickup added on the long 3,180 mm wheelbase
- 2014: Limited '30th Anniversary' GRJ76 wagon and GRJ79 double cab return to Japan for one year (V6, 5-speed manual)
- 2016: From late 2016 (Euro 5), the V8 gets a diesel particulate filter and piezo injectors; the single-cab ute gains curtain and knee airbags and a stronger chassis for a five-star ANCAP rating. The DPF is the most-discussed fault on later V8s
- 2023: 2.8 L 1GD-FTV four-cylinder with 6-speed automatic added alongside the manuals; LED headlights, 40-Series-style gauges. The 70 returns to Japanese showrooms in November
- 2024: Australian V8 wagon, Troop Carrier and GX utes end production in September; GXL V8 utes continue to late 2025. A 5-speed manual 2.8 arrives in October

### Capability
- Towing: 3,500 kg (7,716 lb) braked / 750 kg (1,653 lb) unbraked (2024 Australian-market 2.8 L 79 and 76)
- Payload: 1,280–1,380 kg (79 GXL cab-chassis); 1,115–1,215 kg (76 GXL wagon) (2024 Australian spec)
- Fuel tank: 130 L (34.3 US gal) on the 79 cab-chassis; 180 L total on the 76 wagon (2024 Australian spec)
- Ground clearance: 302–330 mm (79); 290–317 mm (76) (unladen, 2024 Australian spec)
- Approach / departure: 33–35° / 27–29° (79); 33–35° / 23–25° (76) (2024 Australian spec)
- Fuel economy: 9.6 L/100 km combined (about 24.5 US mpg) (Toyota claim, 2024 2.8 L automatic)
- Curb weight: 2,395 kg (5,280 lb) (2024 76 GXL wagon)
- Turning circle: 14.4 m (79); 13.6 m (76) (kerb to kerb)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 265/70R16 on 16x7 alloy (2024 79 GXL cab-chassis, Australia), 225/95R16 on 16x6 steel (2024 76 GXL wagon, Australia)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x150 (1999 facelift on); earlier trucks use 6-stud wheels
- Offset: about +5 mm (factory 16x7 on the 79)
- Center Bore: 110.3 mm
- Lug Thread: M14x1.5
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 235/85R16 (IH8MUD consensus for a stock long-wheelbase 70. 285/75R16 goes on but rubs inside at full lock on factory steel wheels unless the wheel offset changes; sagging old springs make everything rub sooner.)

### Buying checks
- Check the A-pillars for rust: Unsealed 4X4 says rust usually starts from the inside, so look for bubbling and flaking paint and run a magnet over suspect areas. Coastal trucks rot in the A-pillars and let water in. The magazine knows of one owner who paid nearly A$15,000 to replace both pillars, so its advice is to walk away.
- Look at the rear spring hangers: Trucks that regularly ran over GVM on rough roads can crack at the weld where the rear spring hanger meets the frame. Look for cracks, fresh welds or reinforcement plates, and listen for a clunk under load.
- Open the airbox: On the V8, a weak airbox seal lets dust past the filter. Unclip the lid and check the clean side of the filter: if there's dust there, Unsealed says the engine is on borrowed time.
- Shift through every gear: Crunching between second and third points to worn synchros. Unsealed 4X4 blames GL-5 oil, whose extreme-pressure additives attack the yellow-metal synchro rings, and says to use GL-4 75W-90. Other spec sheets list GL-4 or GL-5, so check what your manual calls for.
- Test the clutch on tuned trucks: The stock clutch is built for stock power. If the revs rise without the truck accelerating, or it bites at the very top of the pedal, budget for a heavy-duty clutch.
- Jack up the front wheels: Grab each front tire at 12 and 6 o'clock and rock it. Play or a hum that rises to a howl with speed points to front wheel bearings, which work hard on heavy, big-tired 70s.
- Ask about the DPF (late-2016-on V8s): Look for DPF warning lights, smoke or a history of limp mode, especially on trucks that mostly did short trips.
- Importing? Check the build date: For a US import, NHTSA's exemption is based on age: the truck must be more than 25 years old. Check the build plate before you pay, and remember that a lot of imports have spent their lives working on farms or mine sites.

### Common repairs
#### Adjust or replace the front wheel bearings
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day for both sides · cost About A$500 a side at a mechanic, per Unsealed 4X4
Symptoms: A hum from the front that becomes a growl, then a howl, and gets louder with speed. With the wheel off the ground, there's play when you rock it at 12 and 6 o'clock.
Fix: The 70 uses the same tapered-roller hub design Toyota has used since the 40 Series. Remove the locking hub, take off the lock nut with a 54 mm socket and tighten the bearing back up. Sometimes that and fresh grease are all it needs. If the bearings are worn, replace them. Many owners service the swivel hubs at the same time, since they need doing periodically anyway.
Tools: 54 mm hub socket · torque wrench · bearing grease · new tapered roller bearings and seals if replacing.

#### Stop dust getting past the airbox (1VD V8)
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 15 minutes to check · cost Free to check; an aftermarket airbox costs more
Symptoms: Red dust on the clean side of the filter, MAF sensor faults, limp mode in the middle of a dusty trip, or a noisy turbo.
Fix: Unclip the airbox lid and inspect the downstream side of the filter. Some mechanics grease the factory seal and some owners make their own seals from silicone and D-rubber, but Unsealed's preferred fix is an aftermarket airbox that seals the intake properly. If you find dust, clean the MAF sensor and check the turbo for shaft play.
Tools: Screwdriver · torch · MAF cleaner · replacement seal or aftermarket airbox.

#### Fit proper bulb-type door seals
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost A couple of hundred dollars for a four-door 76, per Unsealed
Symptoms: Wind noise that gets worse with age, whistling at town speeds, diesel fumes in traffic, and a dusty dash after a day on dirt roads.
Fix: The factory flat pinch-weld seals never fully close the gap. Pull them and fit bulb-type seals that compress when the door shuts. Unsealed notes the door openings have stayed the same since 1985, so the same seals fit every 70.
Tools: Trim tool · bulb-type door seal kit · adhesive if the kit calls for it.

#### Refill the manual gearbox with the right oil
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost The price of the oil
Symptoms: Crunching shifts, especially between second and third.
Fix: Drain the gearbox and refill with GL-4 75W-90, which is what Unsealed specifies for the V8 trucks (confirm the grade in your manual, since some spec sheets allow GL-4 or GL-5). Unsealed warns that the extreme-pressure additives in GL-5 attack the yellow metal in the synchros. Pause briefly mid-shift and avoid forcing shifts when the box is cold. If it still crunches, plan a rebuild before the gear teeth get damaged, and do the clutch at the same time.
Tools: Drain and fill plug wrenches · fluid pump · GL-4 75W-90 gear oil.

#### Repair a cracked rear spring hanger
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A day, with welding · cost Parts plus fabrication labor
Symptoms: A clunk from the rear under heavy load, such as towing up a hill, and a wandering feel in corners if the crack has grown.
Fix: Unsealed's order: have the crack professionally welded, add chassis bracing straight away from someone who's very good with a MIG, then fit the GVM upgrade the truck should have had in the first place. After that, check the area at every service.
Tools: Welder and grinder (or a fab shop) · bracing plates · GVM-rated springs.

#### Upgrade the clutch on a tuned V8
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A day · cost Parts plus labor; tuning shops often bundle a tune with a clutch
Symptoms: Revs climb while acceleration stays the same or drops off, the clutch bites only near the top of the pedal, and shifts start grinding.
Fix: Replace the clutch with a heavy-duty unit rated for the torque you're making. If the gearbox is already crunchy, rebuild it while it's out.
Tools: Transmission jack · clutch alignment tool · heavy-duty clutch kit.

#### Revive or upgrade the alternator
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Hard starting, slow charging of auxiliary batteries and charging warnings on the dash.
Fix: The stock 130–150 A alternator sits low and catches mud and dust. Rinse it with a low-pressure hose after every trip. If you've added big lithium systems, Unsealed says to fit a bigger alternator, such as a 240 A Jaylec unit or a sealed one, and to use a proper DC-DC charger.
Tools: Basic hand tools · low-pressure hose · uprated alternator if needed.

#### Make the air conditioning work
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost A few hundred dollars
Symptoms: The cabin never gets cool on a hot day, and the back seat of a 79 dual-cab is miserable.
Fix: Clean the condenser of dust, grass and bugs first. Then consider an AC amplifier such as Freezebrain, which plugs into the factory controller to lower the evaporator temperature and can add idle-up control.
Tools: Soft brush and hose · plug-in AC controller.

### Baseline service
Most 70s in the US are 25-year-old grey imports (1HZ, 1PZ, 1HD-FTE or petrol 3F/1FZ), while newer markets got the 1VD-FTV V8, so first confirm the exact model code and engine on the VIN plate. Specs below are given for the 4.5 V8 (VDJ79, Roughtrax) and the 1HZ (Toyota publications via IH8MUD); anything else, check the manual. Unsealed's rule applies to all of them: service history beats odometer.
- Engine oil & filter: 1VD-FTV: ≈9.5 L with filter, SAE 5W-30 ACEA C2 (Roughtrax; its table mislabels the engine, so confirm) · 1HZ: 9.5 L with filter, API CD (Toyota publications via IH8MUD) · Then per the owner's manual schedule [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (On post-2016 DPF trucks a low-ash C-spec oil matters; don't fill one with old-school high-ash diesel oil.)
- Air filter & airbox seal: Inspect the clean side of the filter · Every service, and after every dusty trip (Unsealed: the 1VD airbox seal lets dust past the filter, causing MAF faults and turbo wear. Dust on the clean side means fit a sealed aftermarket airbox now.)
- Fuel filter & water separator: Diesel filter element; drain the separator · Replace now if there's no record, then per the manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Imported or outback-fuelled trucks may have seen dirty diesel; cheap insurance for injectors.)
- Coolant: VDJ79: 14.8 L Toyota pink Super Long Life (Roughtrax) · 1HZ: 11.6 L ethylene-glycol with front/rear heaters (Toyota publications via IH8MUD) · Flush now if the color or history is unknown (Don't mix coolant types; check the radiator for packed dust and grass, since a blocked core also kills the AC.)
- Manual gearbox: V8: GL-4 75W-90 per Unsealed and 70 Series Store, which both warn against GL-5 (Roughtrax lists GL-4 or GL-5) · V8 capacity: Roughtrax says 2.7 L, 70 Series Store about 4.5 L [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · 1HZ: 4.9 L, GL-4 or GL-5 SAE 90 (Toyota 1991 owner's manual) · Change now on an unknown truck (Unsealed: GL-5's extreme-pressure additives attack the brass synchros, so crunchy 2nd–3rd shifts can be the wrong oil.)
- Transfer case: VDJ79: 1.5 L, SAE 75W-90 GL-4/GL-5 (Roughtrax) · 1HZ: 2.2 L, SAE 90 GL-4/GL-5 (Toyota publications via IH8MUD) · Then per the owner's manual schedule [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Part-time two-speed case; check for weeps at the output seals.)
- Front differential: VDJ79 with diff lock: 2.8 L, 75W-85 GL-5 (Roughtrax) · 1HZ: 2.6 L, GL-5 (Toyota publications via IH8MUD) · Then per the owner's manual schedule [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Check the breathers after any water crossing; milky oil means water got in.)
- Rear differential: VDJ79: 2.4 L, 75W-85 GL-5; LSD axles take Toyota-specific LSD oil (Roughtrax) · 1HZ: 2.5 L, GL-5 (Toyota publications via IH8MUD) · Then per the owner's manual schedule [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (If the truck has a factory rear locker, test it on a low-traction surface.)
- Swivel hubs & front wheel bearings: Steering knuckles: moly-disulfide lithium grease NLGI-2 · wheel bearings: lithium multi-purpose NLGI-2 (Toyota publications via IH8MUD) · Inspect and re-preload now; service periodically (Unsealed: the tapered-roller hubs often just need the 54 mm locknut nipped up and fresh grease, and owners do the swivels at the same time.)
- Power steering fluid: Dexron-II ATF on older 70s (Toyota 1991 owner's manual) · V8: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Refresh if dark (Check the box and hoses for weeps, and the drag link and tie-rod ends for play while you're there.)
- Brake & clutch fluid: DOT 3 or 4, SAE J1703 (Roughtrax) · Flush now, then every 2 years [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (A soft or high-biting clutch on a tuned V8 is the clutch itself (Unsealed), not the fluid; test it under load.)
- Chassis grease & spring hangers: Propshaft U-joints: lithium-base NLGI-2 (Roughtrax) · At every service (Unsealed says to check the rear spring hangers for cracks at every service, especially on utes that have been run over GVM.)
- Timing belt (1HZ and other belt-driven diesels): The 1HZ drives its camshaft with a timing belt (Wikipedia) · Toyota's 1991 owner's manual says a timing-belt warning light comes on every 100,000 km on the diesels and the belt should be replaced when it does · Replace now if there's no receipt, then every 100,000 km (Confirm whether your engine uses a belt before budgeting; kits with the water pump are available for the 1HZ.)
- DPF, alternator & charging (late V8): Late-2016-on V8s have a DPF (Unsealed) · A spirited highway run every 1,000–2,000 km (Unsealed: short-trip DPF trucks clog. Rinse the low-mounted alternator with a low-pressure hose after muddy trips, and fit a DC-DC charger for big auxiliary batteries.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: The IH8MUD consensus for a stock-height long-wheelbase 70 is 235/85R16, about 31.7 inches. 285/75R16 (33 inches) will go on, but on factory steel wheels owners report it rubs on the inside at full lock unless you change wheel offset. Short-wheelbase owners in the same thread treat 255/85R16 (about 33 inches) as the sensible upper limit, and the one running them has a lift. Sagging old springs make everything rub sooner.

Q: Can I buy one in the US?
A: Not new. Toyota never sold the 70 in the United States. Canada got a few BJ70s for the 1985–87 model years and, as of 2022, Canadian mining companies could still buy them. Americans import older trucks under the rule NHTSA set in 1989 exempting vehicles more than 25 years old.

Q: What do 76, 78 and 79 mean?
A: Body and wheelbase. Since 1999, 78 is the long-wheelbase troop carrier and 79 the long-wheelbase pickup (single and, from 2012, dual cab); the 76 is the four-door wagon. Earlier, 70/71 were short wheelbase, 73/74 medium, 75 long, and 77 a semi-long wagon.

Q: Which years and engines are best?
A: Unsealed 4X4 says many enthusiasts prefer the 2007–2016 V8s, which don't have a DPF, but that service history matters more than the year. For US imports, the age rule means older trucks, typically with the 1HZ, 2H, 3B or 13B-T diesels or the 3F and 1FZ petrol sixes.

Q: Did it come with lockers?
A: Selectable front and rear lockers were factory options in some markets. Otherwise ARB Air Lockers and Harrop electric lockers are the common add-ons; one IH8MUD owner runs Harrop E-lockers in a BJ74.

Q: Is there an automatic?
A: Rarely. Most 70s are manual, but a four-speed auto was offered on a few versions: FJ73 (1985–1992), BJ74, HZJ73/77 (1990–1999) and HZJ74/76K (1999–2004). The 2.8 L four that arrived in 2023 came with a six-speed automatic.

Q: Does it have a DPF?
A: Australian V8s got a diesel particulate filter from September 2016 to meet Euro 5. Earlier V8s don't have one. Unsealed recommends a good highway run every 1,000–2,000 km to let it regenerate.

Q: Why are the rear wheels inboard of the fronts on V8 trucks?
A: To make room for the 1VD-FTV, Toyota fitted a wider front axle and frame in 2007, which left the front and rear tracks different. Superior Engineering's coil conversion is one of the aftermarket fixes Unsealed mentions for equalizing them.

Q: Is the V8 really gone?
A: In Australia, yes. V8 wagon and troop carrier production ended in September 2024, and the GXL pickups were the last V8s, shipping until late 2025. The 2.8 L four replaced it: 201 hp and 369 lb-ft with the six-speed automatic, or 332 lb-ft with the five-speed manual added in October 2024.

Q: Is it reliable?
A: Overall, yes, says Unsealed: a strong engine and a tough driveline, with many trucks running very high mileage. The known weak points are mostly about use and comfort: DPFs on late V8s, clutches on tuned trucks, gearbox synchros, front wheel bearings, dust past the airbox, leaky door seals, weak AC and frame cracks on overloaded pickups.

Q: Leaf springs or coils up front?
A: Leaf springs up to the 1999 facelift, then coils with leading arms. The rear stayed on leaf springs.

## Toyota Land Cruiser 80 Series (1990–1997)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/80-series/
Codes: FJ80, FZJ80, HZJ80, HDJ80

Verdict: The 80 is what happens when an engineering team is told to build a family wagon and quietly builds an expedition vehicle instead. Coil springs, solid axles, full-time four-wheel drive and, if you found the right one, three lockers — it is the last Land Cruiser that feels like it was designed by people who own winches.

Toyota unveiled the 80 Series in October 1989 and put it on sale in early 1990, and it remains the Land Cruiser people argue about at campfires. It was the first Land Cruiser wagon on coil springs at all four corners, the first with full-time four-wheel drive, and the last US-market Land Cruiser with both a straight-six and a solid front axle (Hagerty goes further and calls it the last Land Cruiser with either, which overlooks the solid-axle 105 Series and the 70 Series sold elsewhere). Toyota's own GR Heritage Parts team still calls its off-road performance the best any Land Cruiser has ever had, which is a strong claim from a company that also builds the 70.

### BORN TO REPLACE A LEGEND
The 80 replaced the 60 Series, and Slee Off-Road describes it as the first major wagon redesign since the 60 arrived in 1980. The 60 rode on leaf springs; the 80 threw them out for coils front and rear, stretched the wheelbase to 112.2 inches — a figure Hagerty notes the big wagons have kept ever since — and switched from part-time to full-time four-wheel drive with a lockable center differential for North America and Europe.
It didn't start with a clean-sheet engine, though. The first US trucks, sold as 1991 and 1992 models under the FJ80 code, carried over the 4.0-liter 3F-E straight-six and A440F automatic from the FJ62. They also had a semi-floating, C-clip rear axle with drum brakes, no ABS, no airbags and no factory lockers — honest, slightly underpowered trucks that today are the cheapest way into an 80.

### THE FZJ80 GROWS UP
For 1993 the truck got the engine it deserved: the 4.5-liter, 24-valve, twin-cam 1FZ-FE, rated at 212 hp and 275 lb-ft against the old 3F-E's 155 hp. The code changed to FZJ80, 16-inch wheels arrived, ABS-equipped trucks got a full-floating rear axle with disc brakes and a viscous coupling in the center diff (HF2AV transfer case), and US buyers could tick the option box for electric front and rear lockers. Combined with the center lock, that made it one of very few showroom SUVs you could buy with all three differentials locked.
The 1995 update brought the redesigned dash with airbags, the Toyota emblem in place of the TOYOTA lettering across the grille, the A343F automatic (some '95s kept the A442F), a mass-airflow meter, and voluntary OBD-II compatibility that became full OBD-II for 1996. Owners on IH8MUD say none of it compares with the 1993 engine change, which is why the whole 1993–97 FZJ80 run is the one to shop. In 1996 Lexus launched the LX 450 on the same body, and 1997 closed the US run with the 40th Anniversary Limited Edition (4,744 sold) and the Collector's Edition.

### WHAT MADE IT SPECIAL
Outside the US, the 80 was a different animal again. Depending on the market it came with the 1HZ 4.2-liter diesel, the 1HD-T turbo-diesel or the later 1HD-FT, and Japan, Africa and Australia kept part-time four-wheel drive as an option. That global spread is why parts and know-how flow so freely between American, Australian and Middle Eastern owners, and why an American owner's fix often comes from an Australian forum thread, or the other way around.
What hands-on owners love is that it is still a truck they can fix. The front axle is a closed-knuckle design with Birfield CV joints that you can strip, repack and reseal in a driveway; the drivetrain is overbuilt; and the aftermarket — from Old Man Emu and ARB to Slee Off-Road and Metal Tech 4x4 — has spent three decades refining it. One owner quoted in Slee's guide weighed his fully built FZJ80 at 6,640 pounds, split 3,200 front and 3,480 rear. That's a lot of truck, and a pretty even balance.

### HOW IT ENDED — AND WHY IT'S WORTH SO MUCH NOW
Japanese production ended in 1997, and in January 1998 the 100 Series took over with V8 power and, in the US, independent front suspension — more comfortable, less beloved in the dirt. The 100 also became the basis for the Lexus LX 470, the LX 450's successor. The 80 didn't vanish all at once, though: Wikipedia records the last ones being assembled in Venezuela as late as 2007, a decade after Japan moved on, and the solid-axle, straight-six formula lived on in the 70 Series.
For two decades the 80 was simply a cheap, thirsty old wagon. Then prices took off. In the Hagerty story that marked the turn, a 1,005-mile 1994 FZJ80 sold on Bring a Trailer for $141,000, nearly triple Hagerty's top-condition value at the time; the author called it 'the 993 of Land Cruisers.' Ordinary trucks haven't gone that far, but tired FZJ80s near 300,000 miles still change hands for more than $20,000, which says a lot about how few people want to let them go.

### Data plate

- Production: 1990–1997 (Japan); Venezuela to 2007
- Us Model Years: 1991–1997
- Engine (Us '93–'97): 1FZ-FE 4,477 cc DOHC 24v I6
- Output: 212 hp @ 4,600 · 275 lb-ft @ 3,200
- Transmission (Us): 4-spd auto (A440F / A442F / A343F)
- Drive: Full-time 4WD, lockable center diff
- Wheelbase: 112.2 in

### Engineering
Under the 1990s wagon body is a proper truck: a ladder frame, live axles on coil springs at both ends, and a full-time transfer case with a center differential you can lock. US trucks got the 4.5-liter 1FZ-FE from 1993, and the front axle uses Birfield CV joints inside sealed knuckles, a design owners have been rebuilding in their driveways for thirty years.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, 112.2 in wheelbase (The 100, 200 and 300 Series wagons kept the same wheelbase figure.)
- Suspension: Solid axles, coil springs front and rear (First Land Cruiser wagon on coils; radius arms up front, Panhard rods locate the axles.)
- 4Wd System: Full-time with center diff (Open center diff (HF2A) on early and drum-brake trucks, lockable in 4HI and auto-locked in 4LO; ABS trucks (US from 1993) use the HF2AV case with a viscous coupling.)
- Lockers: Optional electric front and rear (Factory option on US trucks from 1993–1997; with the center lock, three lockers total.)
- Engine: 1FZ-FE 4.5 L DOHC 24-valve I6 (212 hp @ 4,600 rpm, 275 lb-ft @ 3,200 rpm (US). 1991–92 US trucks: 4.0 L 3F-E, 155 hp.)
- Axles & Brakes: Full-float rear, four-wheel discs (ABS trucks '93+) (1991–92 US trucks, and non-ABS trucks after that: C-clip semi-float rear with drums. Front: closed knuckles with Birfield joints.)

### Versions
- 1990–1992 · FJ80 · 3F-E 4.0 L I6 (petrol) · 155 hp · US 1991–92: A440F auto, C-clip semi-float rear with drums, no lockers, no ABS or airbags. 155 hp is the US rating; Toyota quotes 112 kW (150 hp) elsewhere.
- 1993–1997 · FZJ80 · 1FZ-FE 4.5 L DOHC 24v I6 (petrol) · 212 hp / 275 lb-ft · US mainstream. Full-float rear with discs (ABS trucks), optional front and rear lockers.
- 1990s (non-US) · FZJ80 · 1FZ-F 4.5 L I6 (carbureted) · 188 hp / 268 lb-ft · Carbureted version for some export markets.
- 1990–1997 · HZJ80 · 1HZ 4.2 L I6 diesel · 96 kW (129 hp) / 271 N·m · Naturally aspirated diesel; not sold in the US.
- 1990–1997 · HDJ80 · 1HD-T / 1HD-FT 4.2 L I6 turbo-diesel · 115 kW (154 hp) / 357 N·m (1HD-T) · Direct-injection turbo-diesels; 1HD-FT is the later, improved version. Not sold in the US.
- 1996–1997 · Lexus LX 450 · 1FZ-FE 4.5 L I6 · 215 hp / 275 lb-ft (Lexus rating) · Rebadged FZJ80 with softer suspension and a plusher cabin.

### Year-by-year
- 1990: 80 Series launched (shown at the October 1989 Tokyo Motor Show); all-coil suspension, with full-time 4WD on North American and European trucks
- 1991: First US model year (FJ80): 3F-E 4.0 L carried over from the FJ62, A440F auto, front disc / rear drum brakes, semi-float rear axle, no ABS, airbags or factory lockers; center-diff lock switch standard
- 1993: FZJ80 arrives: 4.5 L 24-valve 1FZ-FE, A442F auto, 16-inch wheels, larger brakes (from October 1992 production); ABS trucks get a full-floating rear axle with discs and the viscous-coupling HF2AV transfer case; factory front and rear lockers (option K294) become optional; center-diff switch dropped (wiring stays); A/C switches from R12 to R134a in May 1993. This 1993–97 FZJ80 run is the one owners recommend over the 3F-E trucks; the 1995–97 changes are minor by comparison [buy]
- 1994: Thicker front drive flanges from April 1994 build (43421-60040 replaces 43421-60022); last year of the TOYOTA-lettered grille
- 1995: Redesigned dash with dual airbags, new Toyota oval logo, mass-air-flow meter and voluntary OBD-II compatibility, A343F automatic (some '95s kept the A442F), washer-type lug nuts, in-line catalytic converters, 2-row aluminum radiator replaces the 3-row brass core
- 1996: Fully OBD-II; ABS and airbags standard; Lexus LX 450 twin launched
- 1997: Final US year: 40th Anniversary Limited Edition (4,744 sold) and Collector's Edition; last year of the electric front locker; rear sway-bar frame brackets changed to a bottom-mount style

### Capability
- Towing: 5,000 lb (2,270 kg) (KBB maximum for 1997; don't tow from the four holes in the rear crossmember, which aren't rated for towing in the US)
- Payload: 1,719 lb (780 kg) (1997)
- Fuel tank: 25.1 US gal (95 L)
- Ground clearance: 10.8 in (274 mm) (1997)
- Fuel economy: 12 city / 14 hwy mpg (KBB, 1997)
- Curb weight: 4,751 lb (2,155 kg) (1997 US; GVWR 6,470 lb)
- Turning circle: 40.4 ft (12.3 m) (turning diameter, 1997)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 275/70R16 on 16-inch wheels (1993–97), 15x7 alloys (1991–92, unique to those years)
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Center Bore: 106.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M12x1.5
- Lug Torque: ≈76 lb-ft (103 N·m) alloy · ≈109–116 lb-ft (148–157 N·m) steel [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
- Note: Lug nuts changed from conical to washer type in 1995, so match nuts to the wheel. IH8MUD's birf-repack guide gives 76 ft-lb for alloys and 109 ft-lb for steel wheels; Rough Trax's Australian data gives 103 N·m and 157 N·m and says to confirm with Toyota. US owners quote about 75 lb-ft for alloys from the 1995-on owner's manual.
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 285/75R16 (≈33 in) (IH8MUD's safe answer. Owners also report 305/70R16 and 295/75R16 fitting, depending on wheel width and offset; 35s rub badly on a stock truck.)
- Biggest tire, 2 in (OME) lift: 35 in, e.g. 315/75R16 (Christo Slee: 35s work on a 2-inch Old Man Emu lift but will probably rub at full flex unless you lower the bump stops. Re-gear (4.56/4.88/5.29) is advised over the stock 4.11s.)

### Buying checks
- Pull the knuckle fill plug: Slee's inspection list says to look for oil and caked grease on the outside of the front knuckles, a sign the inner axle seals failed a long time ago. Remove the square fill plug and sample the grease: if it's runny, diff oil is getting into the knuckle.
- Look for coolant at the head: Check the head-to-block joint for antifreeze weeping, ask whether the radiator has been replaced (a possible sign of past overheating), and look for deposits in the overflow bottle. Head gaskets are on every 80 buyer's list of common problems.
- Rust in the footwells and rear windows: Get under it and check the front footwells on both sides and the body around the rear windows, which buyers' guides single out (owners report the same), especially on trucks from salted-road states. Also check under the battery tray for corrosion, which Slee's list calls out.
- Cracks around the steering box: The frame around the steering box is a known weak point, more so on trucks that have run 33s or bigger. Look for cracks and ask whether a reinforcement plate has been fitted.
- Test the lockers properly: If it has factory lockers, engage them in low range on a loose surface and make sure they actually lock. Actuators that won't engage are a common fault, and an actuator rebuild usually fixes them.
- Know which year you're looking at: 1991–92 FJ80s have the 4.0 L 3F-E, a C-clip semi-float rear with drums and no factory lockers. From 1993 you get the 4.5 L 1FZ-FE, optional lockers and a full-float rear with discs on ABS trucks. The automatic type is printed on the driver's-door label: A442F on 1993–94 trucks, A343F on most 1995–97 trucks (some '95s kept the A442F).
- Check for accident repairs: Late 80s had VIN stickers on almost every body panel, so check they're on the doors, hood and tailgate. Look for overspray, weld marks on the inner fenders and core support, filler (use a magnet) and pulling marks on the frame.
- Look behind the dash: Built trucks often have a mess of accessory wiring. Pop the panel under the steering column, look for extra leads on the battery positive and check they're fused, and test every light and switch.

### Common repairs
#### Front knuckle / Birfield rebuild
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A full weekend for both sides · cost Kit about $125 (Cruiser Outfitters FA9097) plus bearings, grease and labor
Symptoms: Gear oil and grease caked on the outside of the knuckles, runny grease at the knuckle fill plug, wheel-bearing play or noise, or a seal that started weeping after the last service.
Fix: Remove the wheel, hang the caliper on wire, then pull the dust cap, snap ring, flange nuts and cone washers (a brass drift loosens the cone washers). Remove the lock nuts with a 54 mm hub socket and pull the hub and rotor. Unbolt the spindle, unplug the ABS sensor gently, then with the wheel straight ahead and the Birfield flats vertical, slide the axle out. Replace the inner axle seal, knuckle bearings and wiper seals, clean the Birfield and repack it and the knuckle with moly grease, then reassemble with new gaskets. IH8MUD's guide sets bearing preload by torquing the inner nut to 43 ft-lb, backing off, then 48 in-lb, with the lock nut at 47 ft-lb, and suggests checking the result with a spring scale. IH8MUD's guide torques the flange nuts to 26 ft-lb and the caliper bolts to 90 ft-lb on reassembly.
Tools: 54 mm (2-1/8") hub socket · torque wrench to 100 ft-lb · brass drift · seal puller and driver · snap-ring pliers · 6–12 lb spring scale · Cruiser Outfitters FA9097 kit (Koyo knuckle bearings, NOK inner axle and hub seals, gaskets, wiper seals) · moly and high-temp grease. Note: drive flanges got thicker after April 1994 (43421-60040 vs. early 43421-60022), so check before you mix parts.

#### Replace the 'PHH' (pesky heater hose)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost About $20 in generic hose and clamps; bypass kits about $45
Symptoms: A coolant leak low on the driver's side of the engine, or an original-looking hose clamp on a high-mileage truck. Members warn a failure on the trail can leave you completely stranded, which is why many replace it before it fails.
Fix: The PHH is a short hose, roughly 3 inches long, low on the block. It joins the hard pipe that runs from the heater valve, behind the EGR, to the block near cylinders 5 and 6, and is easiest to see from the driver's front wheel well. Drain some coolant, work the old hose off, fit the new one with good clamps, refill and bleed. Replace the nearby bypass hose, just above and forward of it, at the same time.
Tools: Basic hand tools · hose pick · coolant · new hose (owners report using Gates heater hose) and clamps; aftermarket bypass kits are also available.

#### Starter contacts and plunger
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Intermittent no-crank: you turn the key and get a click, or nothing, until the third or fourth try.
Fix: Disconnect the battery. Remove the starter-side front wheel and the rubber splash guard. Unbolt the automatic-transmission dipstick tube (one bolt on the intake manifold, one below the starter), move it aside without disconnecting its hoses, and plug the lower tube so nothing falls into the transmission. Disconnect the two starter leads, remove the two bell-housing bolts and slide the starter out through the wheel arch. Remove the three screws on the contact cover, fit new contacts in the same orientation, and replace the plunger as well since it wears too. Reassemble in reverse.
Tools: 10 mm (battery), 12 mm (dipstick tube), 14 mm (terminal nuts), and 17 mm plus 19 mm spanners for the bell-housing bolts, per the IH8MUD write-up · small socket or screwdriver for the three contact-cover screws · starter contact set and plunger. The intake manifold stays on.

#### Power-steering leak? Check the reservoir first
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost Seals from a parts store
Symptoms: Power-steering fluid weeping around the top of the system. It's often blamed on hoses or the pump, but Unsealed 4X4 says the usual culprit is the rubber seals inside the reservoir.
Fix: Remove the reservoir, carefully pry open the crimped lip, replace the internal rubber seals and re-crimp the top. Refill with Toyota-spec fluid and bleed by turning lock to lock with the engine running. Only replace hoses or rebuild the pump if the leak comes back.
Tools: Basic hand tools · small pry tool and crimping pliers · replacement reservoir seals · power-steering fluid.

#### Rear axle seals and bearings (1991–92 semi-float)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day per side · cost One owner was quoted about $1,300 at a shop (seals, shoes, drums, fluid)
Symptoms: Gear oil soaking the rear drum brake, cracked or contaminated shoes, and grabby rear brakes at low speed.
Fix: Remove the diff cover, take out the pinion-shaft spacer (center shaft) and the C-clips, and slide the axle shafts out. Pull the old bearing and seal with a slide hammer or puller, seat the new ones with the correct driver, check the shaft for grooving, then refit. Because the shoes are oil-soaked, replace them along with the drum hardware and the wheel cylinder if it's weeping. Do both sides. The bearings on this axle run in gear oil, so there is nothing to repack.
Tools: Slide hammer or bearing puller · seal and bearing drivers · bearing 90365-47013 and seal 90311-47001 (as listed in the IH8MUD thread) · rear shoes and hardware · gear oil. Later full-float trucks use a different hub-and-seal procedure.

#### Diagnose coolant in the oil before tearing down
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time Testing ≈ 2–3 hours; a head job is far longer · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Milky oil, a dropping coolant level, coolant weeping where the head meets the block, or a radiator that's already been replaced.
Fix: Test before you take anything apart. Do a compression test, a leak-down test and a cooling-system pressure test, and use a block tester to check the coolant for exhaust gas. On the 1FZ-FE the oil cooler can also leak coolant into the oil, so pressure-test or replace it before blaming the head gasket. If the head has to come off, have the head and block deck checked for flatness and cracks, and use new head bolts or studs torqued to spec.
Tools: Compression and leak-down testers · cooling-system pressure tester · combustion-leak (block) tester · if needed, an OEM head gasket set and the service manual.

#### Reinforce the frame at the steering box
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A day, with welding · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Cracks in the frame around the steering-box mounts, a loose-feeling steering box, or wandering steering on a truck with big tires.
Fix: Clean the frame around the steering box and inspect it closely. Have any cracks stopped and repaired, then weld on a fabricated reinforcement plate, which several 4x4 fabricators sell for the 80. While you're there, check the box mounting bolts and the upper Panhard-rod frame mount.
Tools: Welder and grinder (or a fab shop) · reinforcement plate · torque wrench.

#### Re-set the rear brake proportioning valve after a lift
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost No parts needed
Symptoms: Weak rear braking or a changed pedal feel after lifting the truck, because the load-sensing proportioning valve (LSPV) now reads the truck as lightly loaded.
Fix: An owner's measurement in Slee's guide: the LSPV contact point sits 38 mm from the pivot on a rod about 600 mm long, so movement at the rod end is about 1/15.75 of the movement at the valve body. For a 75 mm lift, lower the LSPV body by about 4.8 mm, then fine-tune with the rod-end adjuster (about ±6 mm). Mark the original position before you move anything.
Tools: Wrenches · ruler or calipers · paint pen to mark the start point.

### Baseline service
Assume nothing was done: an 80 is now 30-plus years old, and IH8MUD's factory-sourced lubricant table plus Slee's buyer checklist make the knuckles, the 'PHH' and the diff/transfer oils the priorities. Specs below are from Toyota service publications as compiled on IH8MUD; US trucks are the 1991–92 FJ80 (3F-E) and 1993–97 FZJ80 (1FZ-FE).
- Engine oil & filter: 1FZ-FE: API SH grade, 7.4 L (≈7.8 qt) with filter · 3F-E: 7.8 L (≈8.2 qt) with filter · Baseline now; then per your owner's-manual schedule (Timmy the Toolman's FZJ80 service uses Toyota filter 90915-YZZD3 and drain-plug washer 90430-12031, with the drain plug at 20 ft-lb.)
- Air filter: Paper panel element · Baseline now; check at every oil change on dusty trails (Cheap insurance on a truck with unknown history — a dirty element is one of the 'owner neglect' signs Slee tells buyers to look for.)
- Spark plugs, cap, rotor & wires: FZJ80: Denso/OEM plugs · FJ80: NGK · gap [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now if no records (Both engines are distributor-fired, so do cap, rotor and plug wires at the same time.)
- Coolant & thermostat: Ethylene-glycol Toyota coolant · FZJ80 13.4 L / FJ80 19.5 L (with front & rear heaters) · Baseline flush now (Timmy the Toolman refills with Toyota Red and lists thermostat 90916-03117 and gasket 16346-66020 for the FZJ80. Slee says to check the overflow bottle for deposits and look for a replaced radiator as overheating clues. Inspect the PHH while it's drained.)
- Automatic transmission fluid: ATF Dexron II spec (Dexron III / Valvoline MaxLife used as backward-compatible substitutes) · FJ80 (A440F): 6 L drain-and-refill, 15.4 L dry · FZJ80 (A343F): Toyota table on IH8MUD says 1.9 L drain-and-refill, Rough Trax says 6.0 L [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now with 2–3 drain-and-fills or a cooler-line exchange (A pan drain only replaces a fraction of the fluid. FZJ80 drain-and-refill quantity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]; Timmy the Toolman buys three gallons for a full cooler-line flush and torques the drain plug (gasket 12157-10010) to 20 ft-lb. Avoid a pressure-machine flush on a high-mileage unit with unknown history.)
- Transfer case (center diff): API GL-4/GL-5 SAE 75W-90 · 1.7 L (HF2AV) / 1.3 L (HF2A) · Baseline now (The fill plug is the 24 mm plug at about 8 o'clock looking from the rear (IH8MUD). Drain/fill plugs 27 ft-lb, gasket 90430-18008 (Timmy the Toolman).)
- Front differential: API GL-5 hypoid 80W-90 · 2.8 L listed — fill to the bottom of the fill hole · Baseline now; with ARB Air Lockers Slee's guide suggests about every 20,000 km (Owners on IH8MUD report a locking front diff drains close to 4 qt and takes about 3.75 qt, more than the book figure, so buy extra. Drain/fill plugs 36 ft-lb (Timmy the Toolman). Milky or very high oil can mean water or knuckle-seal trouble.)
- Rear differential: API GL-5 hypoid 80W-90 · 3.25 L (FZJ80); FJ80 table lists 2.8 L · LSD oil if limited-slip · Baseline now (Factory-locker trucks: if the locker won't engage, Slee's guide points to an actuator rebuild rather than the diff itself. Semi-float 1991–92 axles leak gear oil onto the brakes when the outer seals go.)
- Front knuckles / Birfields: Molybdenum-disulfide lithium-base grease, NLGI-2 · Check now; repack whenever the inner axle seals are replaced (Slee's check: pull the square knuckle fill plug and sample the grease. Runny grease means diff oil is getting past the inner axle seal, and caked grease outside the knuckle means the seals failed long ago — plan a full knuckle rebuild.)
- Power steering: ATF Dexron II · 0.75 L total (FJ80 table) · Baseline flush now (If it's weeping at the top, Unsealed 4X4 says the reservoir's internal seals are the usual culprit before hoses or the pump.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 (SAE J1703 / FMVSS 116) · Baseline flush now (Re-check the rear LSPV setting if the truck has been lifted (see the repair above).)
- Driveshafts & U-joints: Lithium-base multipurpose grease, NLGI-2 · Grease now and at every oil change (Grease the U-joints and slip yokes and check them for play.)
- Fuel filter: Toyota canister filter · Replace now if there's no record of it (Different filters for 1991–92 FJ80 and 1993–97 FZJ80.)
- Belts, hoses & the PHH: Accessory belts and coolant hoses · the 1FZ-FE uses a timing chain, not a belt · Inspect now; replace anything original (Replace the PHH and the bypass hose just above and forward of it while you're there. IH8MUD members report using Gates heater hose and good clamps instead of a $45 bypass kit.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: The safe answer from IH8MUD is 285/75R16, about 33 inches, which fits a stock 80 without drama. Owners also report 305/70R16 and 295/75R16 fitting, though wheel width and offset matter as much as the tire size. 35s 'fit, but rub like mad' on a stock truck. Christo Slee's advice is that 35s work with a 2-inch Old Man Emu lift, but you'll probably rub at full flex unless you lower the bump stops. Stock size is 275/70R16.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: For most people, a 1993–97 FZJ80. On IH8MUD the advice is consistent: the 4.5 L 1FZ-FE makes 212 hp against the 3F-E's 155 (one member calls the 3F-E 'a relic'), it could be ordered with front and rear lockers, and ABS trucks got a full-float rear with disc brakes. Owners there say the 1995–97 changes (airbags, new dash, OBD-II, the A343F) are small next to the 1993 engine switch, so condition and lockers matter more than which FZJ80 year it is. The trade-off is the 1FZ-FE's head gasket, which owners treat as part of owning one. The 1991–92 FJ80 is simpler and cheaper but slower, with a semi-float rear and drum brakes.

Q: Did it come with lockers?
A: Factory electric front and rear lockers were an option on US trucks from 1993 to 1997; 1991–92 trucks didn't offer them. Every 80 has a center differential that can be locked. Retrofitting factory lockers means welding, the locker ECU, harnesses and new axle shafts, so Slee says ARB Air Lockers are usually the cheaper route.

Q: Can I lock the center diff in high range on a 1993–97?
A: Slee's guide says the center-diff lock switch was standard on 1991–92 US trucks and omitted from 1993 on the full-floater, disc-brake trucks, though the wiring stayed in the harness. Adding the switch lets you lock the center diff in high range; Slee also says unplugging a connector on the transfer case gives control of the lock in low range.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: Kelley Blue Book lists a 5,000 lb maximum for the 1997 model. IH8MUD members quoting the owner's manual cite 3,000 lb normally and 5,000 lb with the tow package. Don't tow from the four bolt holes in the rear crossmember: Slee notes they aren't rated for towing in the US, so use a frame-mounted receiver.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: Not much. KBB lists the 1997 at 12 mpg city and 14 highway (13 combined) on a 25.1-gallon tank. Bigger tires, armor and a roof rack only make it worse.

Q: Should I re-gear for bigger tires?
A: 1FZ-FE trucks came with 4.11 gears on stock 275/70R16 tires. Slee says to drop to 4.56, 4.88 or 5.29 if you go up in tire size, and suggests driving a truck with the setup you're considering first. Slee's own 4-inch, 35-inch-tire build uses 4.88s with ARB lockers.

Q: What are the lift options?
A: The classic choice is an Old Man Emu kit of about 2 inches. Slee's own 4-inch kit, with coils, machined radius arms and an adjustable Panhard bar, is designed for up to 35-inch tires. Bigger lifts usually need extended brake lines (Metal Tech sells them for 3–6 inch lifts), adjustable rear links, and a proportioning-valve reset.

Q: What fluids and capacities does it take?
A: Rough Trax 4x4's FZJ80 data lists 7.4 L of engine oil with the filter, 13 L of coolant, 1.4 L in the transfer case, 2.7–2.8 L in the front diff, 3.0–3.25 L in the rear diff, and 6.0 L for an automatic sump drain. A Toyota-sourced table compiled on IH8MUD gives 1.7 L for the HF2AV transfer case and only 1.9 L for an A343F drain-and-refill, so the transmission figure in particular is [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]. Figures vary by market and equipment.

Q: Is it reliable? What actually breaks?
A: It's a tough truck, but now it's a 30-year-old one. The usual list: head gaskets on the 1FZ-FE, leaking knuckle seals, wheel bearings, frame cracks around the steering box, worn starter contacts, the 'pesky heater hose,' power-steering leaks, power windows, fraying seat belts and cracked dashes. Toyota fitted larger brakes from October 1992, so the 1991–92 trucks stop noticeably worse.

Q: Is a Lexus LX 450 the same truck?
A: Mechanically, yes. The LX 450 (1996–97 US) is an FZJ80 with softer suspension, a plusher cabin, body cladding and its own grille and wheels, with the same 1FZ-FE engine.

## Toyota Mega Cruiser (1995–2001)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/mega-cruiser/
Codes: BXD10, BXD20V, 15B-FT 4.1 I4 TD

Verdict: Toyota's answer to the Humvee: 2.17 metres wide, portal hubs, four-wheel steering and three locking diffs, driven by a 4.1-litre four-cylinder diesel from a truck. Only 133 were registered as civilian cars in Japan, so the hardest part of owning one is finding one.

The Mega Cruiser is the largest 4WD Toyota has ever built, and it exists because the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force wanted its own Humvee. The military version is the Kōkidōsha, or High Mobility Vehicle, model code BXD10. In January 1996 Toyota put a civilian version on sale in Japan, the BXD20V, aimed at disaster rescue rather than the school run. It shares nothing with any 80 Series or 70 Series except the badge and the attitude, and it looks enough like an H1 that Japan nicknamed it the 'Japanese Hummer'.

### THE KŌKIDŌSHA
Toyota developed and supplied the High Mobility Vehicle, which Japanese sources say Hino builds. From 1993 the JGSDF put test batches with its trials unit, the Infantry School Regiment and the 1st Airborne Brigade, then trial-deployed it to 2nd Division units in 1994. Regular deliveries began with the 1st Infantry Regiment in spring 1995. It carries a ten-soldier squad, tows mortars and trailers, and became the base for missile launchers and other specialist versions. Troops call it the 'Kōki'.
The early trucks used the 15B-FT, a 4.1-litre direct-injection turbo-diesel four from Toyota's Dyna light trucks. Vehicles procured from fiscal 1999 to 2003 got the electronically injected 15B-FTE. From fiscal 2004 the HMV switched to Hino's N04C engine, which changed the model code to XCD10. Only the 15B-engined trucks are BXD10s. By the count in Japanese Wikipedia, more than 3,000 HMVs and derivatives have been built, and the JGSDF is still buying them.

### A RESCUE TRUCK FOR CIVILIANS
A prototype appeared at the 30th Tokyo Motor Show in October 1993. Toyota's launch release on 9 January 1996 pitched the Mega Cruiser at rescue and reconstruction work after natural disasters, and at research and exploration in harsh conditions. Final assembly was at Gifu Auto Body in Kakamigahara. It cost ¥9.62 million (¥9.8 million after the 1999 engine change), about the same as a Toyota Century or Honda NSX of the day, and there was no tachometer.
The buyers were mostly institutions: the Japan Automobile Federation (JAF), fire and rescue services and local governments. Gifu Prefectural Police run one as a disaster vehicle, the only Mega Cruiser police car in Japan. The Maritime Self-Defense Force chose the civilian Mega Cruiser rather than the HMV, and the Air Self-Defense Force uses it as an off-base rescue vehicle. Production ended in August 2001 and sales that December. According to Japanese sources, new registrations totalled 133, including some high-roof trucks that never appeared in the catalogue.

### HOW IT WORKS
Hub-reduction gears at each wheel let Toyota mount the drive shafts high and run 37-inch tires. Toyota quotes a practical ground clearance of 420 mm. To keep the space under the frame clear, the transmission, transfer case, prop shafts and differentials are all mounted as high as possible, which leaves a huge tunnel between the front seats. The brakes are inboard ventilated discs next to the differentials, because there's no room for them inside the hubs. Suspension is double wishbones on longitudinal torsion bars at all four corners.
Drive is full-time 4WD through a four-speed lockup automatic and a two-speed transfer case with a centre diff lock. Front and rear axles have Torsen limited-slip diffs, and each can be locked. Reverse-phase four-wheel steering turns the rear wheels up to 12 degrees, which gives a 5.6-metre turning radius on a 3,395 mm wheelbase. An optional system could deflate the rear tires on the move for mud and snow. One Japanese line sums it up: if you get this stuck, the only thing left is something with tracks.

### COMING OF AGE ABROAD
Mega Cruisers leaked out of Japan as gray imports to places like Australia and Russia. The first ones turned 25 in 2020–21, which made them legal to import into the US under NHTSA's 25-year rule. Jalopnik reported that the Land Cruiser Heritage Museum in Utah already had one. Since then Bring a Trailer has listed both civilian trucks and ex-military BXD10s. In 2026 Japan donated 30 HMVs to Ukraine.
In Japan the civilian truck has become hard to keep on the road. Ibaraki Prefecture sold the Mega Cruiser a local bank had donated to it for disaster duty, citing difficulty getting parts, and the 3,780 kg gross vehicle weight means a holder of a standard licence issued after March 2017 can't legally drive one there. Rare, enormous and short of spares, it's a truck for collectors with a plan.

### Data plate
- Model Codes: BXD10 (military HMV) · KC-BXD20V (civilian)
- Civilian Sales: January 1996 – December 2001 (production to August 2001)
- Assembly: Gifu Auto Body, Kakamigahara (civilian)
- Engine: 15B-FT / 15B-FTE 4,104 cc I4 turbo-diesel
- Output: 155 PS / 39.0 kgm → 170 PS / 43.0 kgm
- Transmission: 4-speed lockup automatic, 2-speed transfer
- Lockers: Centre, front, rear (Torsen front and rear)
- Dimensions: 5,090 × 2,170 × 2,075 mm
- Wheelbase: 3,395 mm
- Curb Weight: 2,850 kg (1996) · 2,900 kg (1999)
- Clearance: 420 mm
- Turning Radius: 5.6 m
- Payload / Seats: 600 kg · 6
- Civilian Registrations: 133

### Engineering
The Mega Cruiser rides on a straight ladder frame with four-wheel independent suspension (double wishbones and longitudinal torsion bars) and hub-reduction gearing at each wheel. That gearing raises the half-shafts for 420 mm of clearance under 37-inch tires and adds a final reduction, so the truck can creep up steep grades on torque-converter creep alone. Full-time 4WD, a locking centre diff, Torsen front and rear diffs with their own locks, and hydraulic reverse-phase rear steer complete the package.
- Frame: Ladder frame, 3,395 mm (133.7 in) wheelbase (The HMV chassis was also used for longer-wheelbase Super Dyna and Coaster 4WD variants.)
- Engine: 15B-FT 4.1 L I4 turbo-diesel (Direct injection, intercooled. 155 PS at 3,200 rpm and 39.0 kgm (282 lb-ft) at 1,800 rpm. Became the 15B-FTE (170 PS, 43.0 kgm) from May 1999.)
- Driveline: 4-speed lockup auto, 2-speed transfer (Full-time 4WD with a centre diff lock. Torsen LSDs front and rear, each with a lock.)
- Suspension: Independent, torsion bars (Double wishbones at all four corners. The long torsion bars and the weight give a good ride.)
- Hubs & Brakes: Hub reduction · inboard vented discs (Brakes sit next to the diffs to cut unsprung weight. Backlash in the reduction gears makes the truck pitch under hard braking.)
- Steering: Reverse-phase 4WS, 12° rear (5.6 m turning radius. The rear steer centres itself on a spring when the hydraulics are off.)

### Versions
- 1993– · BXD10 (JGSDF HMV) · 15B-FT 4.1 L I4 TD · 155 PS · Military Kōkidōsha. Trials from 1993, regular deliveries from spring 1995.
- FY1999–2003 · BXD10 (JGSDF HMV) · 15B-FTE 4.1 L I4 TD · 170 PS · Electronic injection to meet stricter emissions rules.
- FY2004– · XCD10 (JGSDF HMV) · Hino N04C 4.0 L I4 TD · — · Not a BXD10. Hino engine, still in production.
- Jan 1996 – Apr 1999 · BXD20V (civilian) · 15B-FT 4.1 L I4 TD · 155 PS / 39.0 kgm (282 lb-ft) · ¥9.62 million. 2,850 kg curb weight.
- May 1999 – Dec 2001 · BXD20V (civilian) · 15B-FTE 4.1 L I4 TD · 170 PS / 43.0 kgm · ¥9.8 million. 2,900 kg. Production ended August 2001.

### Year-by-year
- 1993: JGSDF begins trials of the High Mobility Vehicle. A civilian prototype is shown at the 30th Tokyo Motor Show in October
- 1995: Regular HMV deliveries begin with the 1st Infantry Regiment in spring. Civilian production starts late in the year
- 1996: 9 January: civilian Mega Cruiser (BXD20V) goes on sale at Toyota Store dealers. 15B-FT, 155 PS, ¥9.62 million
- 1999: May: civilian truck switches to the electronically injected 15B-FTE (170 PS, 43.0 kgm); price ¥9.8 million. The HMV gets the same engine from FY1999
- 2001: Civilian production ends in August and sales in December, after 133 registrations
- 2004: HMV moves to Hino's N04C engine as the XCD10. Later military trucks are not BXD10s
- 2020–21: The earliest trucks pass 25 years old and become legal to import into the US
- 2026: Japan delivers 30 HMVs to Ukraine as part of a vehicle donation

### Capability
- Payload: 600 kg (1,323 lb) (Toyota, 1996)
- Ground clearance: 420 mm (16.5 in) (Toyota)
- Turning radius: 5.6 m (18.4 ft) (Reverse-phase 4WS, Toyota)
- Curb weight: 2,850 kg (6,283 lb) (1996. 2,900 kg for 1999 trucks)
- Gross vehicle weight: 3,780 kg (8,333 lb) (Cargo-registered six-seater, Japanese sources)
- Fuel tank: 28.5 US gal (108 L) (The Drive. The JGSDF lists 108 L for the HMV)
- Fuel economy: ≈22 mpg at a constant 37 mph (Toyota claim reported by The Drive)
- Dimensions: 5,090 × 2,170 × 2,075 mm (200.4 × 85.4 × 81.7 in)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 37x12.50R17.5 LT 8PR (Japanese sources)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 37x12.50 (factory) (It leaves the factory on 37s with 420 mm of clearance. We found no owner reports of fitting bigger tires.)

### Buying checks
- Civilian or military?: A BXD20V civilian wagon and an ex-JGSDF BXD10 soft-top are different trucks with different values. Ex-military trucks have arrived via third countries (one BaT truck was repainted in Dubai and titled as a 1990), so check the import paperwork and the chassis plate.
- Do the 4WS and tire deflation work?: Several BaT trucks were sold with inoperative four-wheel steering or central tire inflation, or with parts such as the deflator hose missing. Check them, because these systems are part of what you're paying for.
- Underbody rust: BaT sellers have noted rust on the underside, painted-over underbodies and rust repair before a repaint. Get under it with a light and a probe, especially around the hub-reduction housings and frame.
- 24-volt electrics: The truck runs a 24-volt electrical system. Budget for batteries in pairs, and make sure any added accessories are wired for 24 V.
- Parts supply: Ibaraki Prefecture sold its Mega Cruiser partly because parts were hard to get. The 15B engine family was also used in Dyna light trucks, which helps with engine service items, but body and driveline parts are specialist. Find your source before you buy.
- Size and access: It's 2,170 mm wide, 5,090 mm long and 2,075 mm tall, so measure your garage, check parking and trail widths, and remember the high sills that need the grab handles.
- Service records and import papers: Recent BaT trucks with records listed axle-shaft, wheel-bearing, motor-mount, gasket and differential-fluid work. Receipts like these, plus clean import documents and a title, add real value.

### Common repairs
#### Hub-reduction and differential gear oil
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Half a day · cost Gear oil plus your time
Symptoms: No records, weeping seals at the hub housings or diffs, or noise from the driveline.
Fix: Drain and refill both differentials, the transfer case and all four hub-reduction housings with the oils specified in the factory manual. One BaT seller had the differentials serviced with fresh fluid before sale. Look for metal on the drain plugs and leaking seals while you're there.
Tools: Factory manual for fill levels [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · drain pans · fluid pump

#### Rear axle shaft and wheel bearings
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Most of a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Clunks, play or noise at a corner. BaT trucks have had a left-rear axle shaft replaced and the wheel bearings serviced.
Fix: Support the truck safely (it weighs about 2.9 tonnes), remove the wheel and hub-reduction assembly following the factory manual, and replace the worn shaft or bearings. Refill the hub housing with fresh oil.
Tools: Heavy-duty jack and stands rated for 3+ tonnes · factory manual · bearing tools

#### Engine and transmission mounts
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Half a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Vibration or clunking on take-off. One BaT truck had both its motor mounts and front mounts replaced.
Fix: Support the engine, unbolt and replace the mounts, then check the exhaust and driveshaft clearances.
Tools: Engine support · metric sockets

#### Engine gaskets and leaks (15B-FT)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Oil seeping from the sump, valve cover or exhaust manifold. One BaT truck had the oil pan, valve cover and exhaust manifold gaskets replaced, plus a coolant reservoir hose.
Fix: Clean the engine, find each leak and replace the gaskets. Because the 15B is a light-truck diesel, a Toyota truck dealer may be able to source engine gaskets more easily than body parts.
Tools: Metric sockets · gasket scraper · torque wrench

#### Fuel filter and batteries
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time 1–2 hours · cost Parts only
Symptoms: Hard starting, or a truck that has been sitting. BaT trucks had fuel filters and batteries replaced after import.
Fix: Replace the fuel filter and bleed the system. Fit matched batteries for the 24 V system and check the charging voltage.
Tools: Basic hand tools · fuel filter wrench · multimeter

#### Inboard disc brake service
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day for all four · cost Genuine pad kits about $80–84 and discs about $87 each at Nengun (October 2026), plus labor
Symptoms: Grinding, a pull under braking, a soft pedal, or simply no records. All four brakes are ventilated discs mounted inboard, so they sit under the truck rather than behind the wheels, and they're easy to neglect. One BaT seller listed brake service among recent work.
Fix: Support the truck securely on stands rated for its weight and work from underneath. At each brake, check pad thickness, disc condition, hoses and caliper seals. Replace pads and discs as a set per axle, clean the pad contact points, then bleed the system with fresh fluid. Front and rear parts carry different Toyota part numbers, so order by axle, and use the factory manual for torque values.
Tools: Jack and heavy-duty stands · socket set · torque wrench · brake bleeder · brake cleaner · factory service manual.

#### Underbody rust treatment
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend · cost Materials plus labor
Symptoms: Scale on the frame, suspension arms and hub-reduction housings. BaT sellers keep finding it: rust on the underside of several civilian trucks, visible rust on the underside components of a BXD10 soft-top, an underbody painted black over earlier rust, and one truck that needed rust repair before its repaint.
Fix: Wash the underside and let it dry. Probe the frame, suspension mounts and hub-reduction housings for scale and pitting, and get anything structural looked at before you coat it. Wire-brush loose rust back to firm metal, apply a rust converter, then prime. Spray cavity wax inside the frame rails and an underbody wax over the visible underside, keeping it off brake parts and exhaust. Recheck every year.
Tools: Pressure washer · wire brushes and a wire wheel · heavy-duty jack stands · cavity-wax wand · protective gear.

### Baseline service
No factory owner's manual or service data for the Mega Cruiser is available online in English, so this list gives the systems to baseline and leaves the fluid specs for you to confirm in the Japanese factory manual. Assume nothing has been done since import unless there are receipts.
- Engine oil & filter: Diesel engine oil for the 15B-FT/FTE · [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (The 15B family was also used in Toyota's Dyna light trucks, which may help with filter sourcing.)
- Fuel filter: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (BaT trucks had theirs replaced after import.)
- Air filter: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase
- Coolant & hoses: Toyota long-life coolant type · [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (One BaT truck needed a new coolant reservoir hose.)
- Automatic transmission: ATF to the factory spec · [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Drain and fill at purchase (Four-speed lockup automatic.)
- Transfer case: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (Test the centre diff lock and low range.)
- Front & rear differentials: Gear oil suitable for Torsen LSDs · [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (Test both diff locks.)
- Hub-reduction housings (×4): [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (Check for seal leaks and play, and listen for gear noise.)
- Brakes: Brake fluid to the reservoir marking · At purchase (The inboard discs sit next to the differentials. Check them for oil contamination from diff seals.)
- 4WS hydraulics: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Inspect at purchase (The rear steer centres on a spring if the hydraulics fail, so a truck can drive normally with the 4WS dead.)
- Tires & pressures: 37x12.50R17.5 LT · 140 kPa front / 240 kPa rear (Japanese sources) · At purchase (Check the date codes on imported tires and test the rear tire-inflation option if fitted.)
- Batteries (24 V): Matched batteries for the 24-volt system · At purchase (Test the charging voltage.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: It already wears 37s. Japanese sources give the factory tire as 37x12.50R17.5 LT, and BaT trucks run 37x12.50 tires on 17-inch steel or aftermarket wheels. We found no owner reports of going bigger. With hub reduction and 420 mm of clearance, it doesn't need more.

Q: Is it a Land Cruiser?
A: No. It shares the Cruiser name and Toyota's off-road ethos, but it's a separate design built from the JGSDF High Mobility Vehicle, with hub reduction, independent suspension at all four corners and four-wheel steering.

Q: How many were made?
A: Japanese sources put civilian new-car registrations at 133. The Drive cites the same figure from Toyota. The military HMV is a different story: more than 3,000 have been built including derivatives, and it's still in production with Hino engines.

Q: Can I import one to the US?
A: Yes. The first trucks became eligible under NHTSA's 25-year rule from 2020–21, and several are now titled in the US. Check your state's emissions and titling rules, and get the import paperwork with the truck.

Q: What engine does it have?
A: The 15B-FT, a 4,104 cc direct-injection turbo-diesel four with an intercooler: 155 PS at 3,200 rpm and 39.0 kgm (282 lb-ft) at 1,800 rpm. From May 1999 it became the electronically injected 15B-FTE, with 170 PS and 43.0 kgm.

Q: Does it have lockers?
A: Three. The centre diff locks through the two-speed transfer case, and the front and rear Torsen limited-slip diffs each have a lock as standard.

Q: How tight does it turn?
A: Reverse-phase rear steering turns the rear wheels up to 12 degrees, for a 5.6-metre turning radius despite a 3,395 mm wheelbase.

Q: What tire pressures does it run?
A: Japanese sources give unequal pressures: 140 kPa front and 240 kPa rear, chosen for rough-terrain performance. The optional system could lower the rear pressures on the move.

Q: How much does one cost?
A: On Bring a Trailer, civilian trucks have sold for $167,500 (January 2024) and $84,000 (June 2025), and other civilian trucks were bid to $82,000–144,000 without selling. Ex-military BXD10s were bid to $32,025–43,999 in 2024 without selling.

Q: What fuel economy and range does it get?
A: The Drive reports that Toyota quoted about 22 mpg at a constant 37 mph, with a 28.5-gallon tank. Real-world highway economy isn't documented.
