## Toyota Land Cruiser Prado 90 (1996–2002)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/prado-90/
Codes: J90, KZJ95, VZJ95, KDJ95

Verdict: The Land Cruiser America wasn't allowed to have: a 3rd-gen 4Runner's bones under a full-time-4WD Land Cruiser badge, with a diesel the US never got. Now that the calendar has done its work, it's the most affordable way to park a real JDM Land Cruiser in your driveway. Just keep that diesel cool.

On 8 May 1996 Toyota launched a Land Cruiser that most Americans have never seen in the metal. The second-generation Prado, the J90, was the mid-size Land Cruiser: a ladder-frame wagon with full-time four-wheel drive, coil springs at both ends, and the independent front suspension it shared with the Hilux Surf, the truck North America bought as the 3rd-gen 4Runner. It went on sale in Japan, Australia, Britain and Latin America, but never in the United States. That held for a quarter of a century, until the 25-year import rule started letting them in.

### A LAND CRUISER FOR PEOPLE
The first Prado had been a lighter-duty offshoot of the 70 Series. Toyota made the J90 a series of its own and, in its own words, pointed it toward a more passenger-oriented four-wheel drive. There were two bodies: a three-door, five-seat short wheelbase on 2,370 mm and a five-door, eight-seat long wheelbase on 2,675 mm. Toyota gave the short one a sportier face and the long one a more rugged one. The drivetrain switched from part-time to full-time 4WD, and the suspension (double wishbones at the front, a four-link coil-sprung axle with a lateral rod at the back) was the same as the Hilux Surf's. 'Prado', Toyota notes, is Portuguese for a meadow or field.

### FOUR ENGINES AND NO V8
At launch you had a choice of two engines. The new one was the 3.4-liter 5VZ-FE V6 with 185 PS, the same family of V6 Americans got in the 4Runner. The carry-over was the 3.0-liter 1KZ-TE four-cylinder turbo-diesel, which gained an intercooler and 140 PS. A 2.7-liter 3RZ-FE four with 150 PS followed in April 1997. In July 2000 Toyota replaced the 1KZ-TE in Japan with the 1KD-FTV, its new common-rail D-4D: 170 PS and 352 Nm, and the first vehicle that engine ever went into.
Market by market, the line-up varied. Australia launched the Prado in July 1996 with petrol engines only and didn't get a diesel until March 2000, when the 96 kW 1KZ-TE arrived with a five-speed manual; an automatic followed that October. 4X4 Australia's buyer's guide, written with hindsight, advises steering clear of the 2.7 four. Britain called the truck the Land Cruiser Colorado, to tell it apart from the bigger 'Amazon', and Venezuela sold the three-door as the Toyota Merú.

### THE 1999 FACELIFT
Toyota gave the J90 its minor change on 9 June 1999. Both bodies got big multi-reflector headlights and clear-lens lamps front and rear, plus a new grille, bumper, door trim and instruments, including a newly offered Optitron cluster and a Field Monitor display that switched to color. Underneath, Toyota added 'Active TRC' traction control for loose and muddy surfaces, and from August 1999 vehicle stability control on the main automatic grades. A TX Limited special edition arrived at the same time with roof rails, wood-grain trim and the Optitron gauges. Five-door trucks grew slightly, to 4,690 mm long.

### WHY AMERICANS ARE BUYING THEM NOW
The J90 was replaced in October 2002 by the Prado 120, although Sofasa kept assembling it in Colombia until 2009. In the US it stayed off-limits until each truck turned 25, counted from its month of manufacture, so the first J90s became legal imports in 2021. In January 2022 IH8MUD started a 90 Series FAQ because 'Prado 90's [were] finally available for US import'. By 2026 Bring a Trailer had a model page for them, and most of the trucks sold there went for $10,000 to $16,000.
Living with one in America is easier than you'd think. The front suspension and plenty of hardware are shared with the 3rd-gen 4Runner. IH8MUD members have fitted 4Runner front rotors (Toyota 43512-35210), the rear rotors match the 80 Series, and US Land Cruiser specialists now stock 9x Prado ball joints, brakes and axle kits. The rest is a job for a Japanese parts catalogue and a VIN or frame number. Just remember the Prado has rear discs where many 4Runners have drums, and that its rear axle shafts have a different bolt pattern.

### Data plate
- Chassis: J90 (VZJ/RZJ/KZJ/KDJ 90 three-door, 95 five-door)
- Production: May 1996 – 2002 (Japan); Colombia 1999–2009
- Engines: 5VZ-FE 3.4 V6 · 3RZ-FE 2.7 I4 · 1KZ-TE 3.0 TD · 1KD-FTV 3.0 TD
- Output (Japan): 185 PS V6 · 150 PS 2.7 · 140 PS 1KZ-TE · 170 PS 1KD-FTV
- Drive: Full-time 4WD, lockable center diff
- Wheelbase: 2,675 mm (105.3 in) 5-door · 2,370 mm (93.3 in) 3-door
- Length: 4,675 mm, 4,690 mm from mid-1999 (5-door) · 4,240 mm (3-door)
- Width / Height: 1,820 mm / 1,880 mm
- Curb Weight: 1,740 kg (3-door V6) – 1,960 kg (5-door 1KZ-TE)
- Fuel: 90 L (UK KZJ95) · 159 L total in Australian trucks with a sub tank
- Wheels: 6 x 139.7 mm, M12 x 1.5, 106.1 mm bore
- Us Status: Never sold new; 25-year import

### Engineering
The J90 is a body-on-frame wagon with double-wishbone independent front suspension and a four-link, coil-sprung live rear axle with a lateral rod, the same layout as the Hilux Surf and 3rd-gen 4Runner. Unlike those trucks, every Prado has full-time four-wheel drive with a lockable center differential. Wheels are 6 on 139.7 mm with M12 x 1.5 nuts.
- Chassis: Ladder frame; 2,675 mm (105.3 in) 5-door, 2,370 mm (93.3 in) 3-door (Five-door seats eight, three-door five.)
- Front Suspension: Double wishbones, coil springs (Shared with the Hilux Surf/4Runner, so 4Runner shocks and lift parts bolt on.)
- Rear Axle: Live axle, four links, lateral rod, coils (Semi-floating, with disc brakes. Shaft bolt pattern differs from the 4Runner's.)
- 4Wd System: Full-time with lockable center diff (Some manual trucks lock the center diff automatically when you select low range.)
- Lockers: No factory axle lockers in Australia (Center lock only; owners add ARB Air Lockers.)
- Engines: 5VZ-FE 3.4 V6 · 3RZ-FE 2.7 I4 · 1KZ-TE / 1KD-FTV 3.0 TD (The 1KD-FTV common-rail diesel replaced the 1KZ-TE in Japan in July 2000.)

### Versions
- 1996–2002 · VZJ90 / VZJ95 · 5VZ-FE 3.4 L V6 · 185 PS (136 kW) · Launch petrol engine. Belt-driven cams, non-interference.
- 1997–2002 · RZJ90 / RZJ95 · 3RZ-FE 2.7 L I4 · 150 PS (110 kW) · Added in April 1997. Timing chain. 4X4 Australia says to skip it.
- 1996–2000 (Japan) · KZJ90 / KZJ95 · 1KZ-TE 3.0 L turbo-diesel I4 · 140 PS · Intercooled, indirect injection. Australia got it only from March 2000 (96 kW).
- 2000–2002 (Japan) · KDJ90 / KDJ95 · 1KD-FTV 3.0 L common-rail turbo-diesel I4 · 170 PS (125 kW) / 352 Nm · From July 2000; the first application of the 1KD.
- 1999–2009 · J90 (Sofasa, Colombia) · 3RZ-FE 2.7 I4 / 5VZ-FE 3.4 V6 · — · Built in Colombia largely unchanged: three-door 2.7 and five-door V6.

### Year-by-year
- May 1996: J90 launched in Japan (8 May): three-door and five-door, 5VZ-FE V6 and 1KZ-TE diesel, full-time 4WD
- July 1996: Australian launch, petrol engines only; Britain gets it as the Land Cruiser Colorado
- April 1997: 2.7 L 3RZ-FE four added (150 PS). 4X4 Australia tells buyers to steer clear of the 2.7 unless they want to punish themselves [avoid]
- June 1999: Facelift: multi-reflector headlights, clear lenses, new grille and dash, Active TRC; VSC on main auto grades from August; TX Limited edition
- 1999: Sofasa begins assembling the J90 in Colombia
- Oct 1999: Factory 'Crawler' tracked snow version announced (TECS)
- March 2000: Australia finally gets a diesel: 96 kW 1KZ-TE with a five-speed manual (automatic from October)
- July 2000: 1KD-FTV common-rail D-4D (170 PS, 352 Nm) replaces the 1KZ-TE in Japan, its first application
- Oct 2002: Replaced by the Prado 120 (Colombian production continues to 2009)
- 2021: The first J90s turn 25 and become legal US imports
- 2027: The last 2002-built J90s reach 25 years

### Capability
- Fuel tank: 90 L (23.8 US gal) UK KZJ95 · 159 L (42 US gal) total in Australian trucks (Roughtrax; 4X4 Australia)
- Curb weight: 1,740 kg (3,836 lb) 3-door V6 · 1,890 kg 5-door V6 · 1,960 kg (4,321 lb) 5-door 1KZ-TE (Toyota, Japanese launch spec)
- Gross vehicle mass: 2,540 kg (3-door) / 2,680 kg (5-door) (Roughtrax, KZJ90/95)
- Ground clearance: 230 mm (9.1 in) (5VZ-FE TZ donor for the Crawler, per Toyota's brochure)
- Turning circle: 11.6 m (4X4 Australia)
- Dimensions: 4,675–4,690 × 1,820 × 1,880 mm (5-door) (Toyota)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 265/70R16 on 7Jx16 ET15 (GXL/VX-type and 1KD-FTV trucks), 215/80R16 on 6Jx16 ET30 (base trims)
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Offset: +15 mm (7Jx16) / +30 mm (6Jx16)
- Center Bore: 106.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M12x1.5
- Lug Torque: 110 N·m (81 lb-ft) per Roughtrax; confirm with Toyota
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 265/75R16 (Doesn't rub unless the springs have sagged (IH8MUD). Needs the 7-inch rims: ExplorOz owners say it's too wide for the 6-inch base rims.)
- Biggest tire, Any lift: 285/75R16 (Rubs with or without a lift, on the upper control arm and a rear pinch weld that can be ground down (IH8MUD).)
- Biggest tire, 2–3 in lift: 255/85R16 (33 in) (Taller and lighter than a 285/75 and easier on the front end, but it needs a lift. Above 2–3 in, plan on a diff drop to protect the CVs.)

### Buying checks
- Ask when the lower ball joints were done: Australia recalled a range of five-door Prados in May 2005 (PRA 2005/7749) because a scratched joint could wear and separate from the knuckle. AustralianCar.Reviews says joints still fail after the recall, and IH8MUD owners replace them preventively with genuine Toyota parts, because a joint can feel tight and still let go.
- Diesel: hunt for signs of overheating: On the 1KZ-TE, overheating is how heads crack. Look for coolant bubbling into the overflow bottle, coolant loss or discoloration, and a gauge that climbs on hills or in traffic. Known causes include a tired viscous fan hub, a blocked radiator and a seized wastegate actuator. On a 260,000 km truck, one IH8MUD member's verdict was that 'the head on the 1kz has already been done', so ask for the receipt.
- Check the ATF for coolant: The automatic's oil cooler sits inside the engine radiator, so a crack lets coolant into the transmission. Pink, milky fluid on the dipstick is a deal-breaker, or at least a new radiator and a transmission rebuild.
- Rear axle flange recall (early trucks): Prados built from 17 April 1996 to 6 January 1999 were recalled in Australia (PRA 2006/8499) because the rear axle-shaft flange could crack after repeated hard driving on winding roads, and in the worst case let the wheel come off. A Japanese import won't have the paperwork, so inspect the flanges.
- Know which engine you're buying: The model code tells you: VZJ = 3.4 V6, RZJ = 2.7 four, KZJ = 1KZ-TE diesel, KDJ = 1KD-FTV diesel (July 2000 on, Japan). '90' is the three-door, '95' the five-door. The V6 has a timing belt, and the 2.7 a chain.
- Timing belt history: HD Automotive gives the 1KZ-TE belt interval as 100,000 km or 5–6 years, and the 5VZ-FE V6 is a 90,000-mile belt. With no receipt, budget for the belt and water pump on day one.
- Import paperwork: A US truck should come with proof that it was at least 25 years old on entry (the date runs from manufacture), the customs entry and the NHTSA HS-7 and EPA 3520-1 declarations. Check that your state will title and register it before you buy, especially California.
- Test the sub tank and CV boots: On trucks with a sub tank, check that the switch-over works: AustralianCar.Reviews warns the mechanism can seize and the fuel go stale if it was never used. While you're underneath, look for split CV boots and grease on the inside of the front wheels.

### Common repairs
#### Replace the front lower ball joints
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day for both sides · cost Parts only; buy genuine Toyota, as IH8MUD owners report early failures with cheap aftermarket joints
Symptoms: Heavy steering, poor self-centring, vibration or shudder in turns, a torn boot, or simply no record that they've ever been changed. A worn joint can let go without warning.
Fix: Support the truck on stands, remove the wheel and take the load off the lower arm. Remove the castle nut and split the taper from the lower control arm, then unbolt the four bolts that hold the ball joint to the back of the knuckle and fit the new joint. Toyota superseded the original 43340-39325 / 43330-39415 joints to 43340-39465 (left) and 43330-39585 (right). One IH8MUD owner's ball-joint bolts worked loose, and he blamed the anti-seize he'd put on the threads, so torque them per the factory manual and use thread-locker, not anti-seize. Finish with an alignment.
Tools: Floor jack and stands · 14/19/24 mm sockets · ball-joint separator · torque wrench · thread-locker · new cotter pins · eight knuckle bolts 90105-10406 (per ToyoDIY, quoted on IH8MUD)

#### 1KZ-TE timing belt and water pump
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time HD Automotive says labor is often quoted at around an hour for the belt · cost HD Automotive's 1KZ belt kit lists at AUD $246; its 'major front service kit' adds the water pump and fan belts
Symptoms: No warning; it's on a schedule. HD Automotive quotes 100,000 km or 5–6 years, Roughtrax's UK sheet 60,000 miles or 60 months.
Fix: Drain the coolant and remove the fan and shroud, drive belts, crank pulley and timing covers. Line up the timing marks, then replace the belt, tensioner pulley and hydraulic tensioner, plus the cam, crank and injection-pump seals. If you do the water pump at the same time, as HD Automotive recommends, fit a new gasket and refill with Toyota long-life coolant. Rotate the engine by hand twice and recheck the marks before you button it up.
Tools: Metric sockets · crank-pulley holder and puller · seal puller · torque wrench · factory manual or Gregory's 1KZ-TE manual for torques and timing marks

#### Cooling-system overhaul on a 1KZ-TE (save the head)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ A day if you do the hoses and fan hub too · cost A Koyorad KZJ95 automatic radiator lists at AUD $379 at HD Automotive; one IH8MUD owner paid AUD $200 for a Koyo locally
Symptoms: The temperature gauge climbs on hills, while towing or in hot traffic; coolant smells, or the level keeps dropping. AustralianCar.Reviews says overheating on this engine 'requires urgent attention' because it cracks heads.
Fix: Replace the radiator with an OEM-spec unit, not a cheap aluminum one. IH8MUD members tried one that didn't fit the mounts or take the factory cap. On automatics, keep the trans cooler in the new radiator. Replace the radiator and heater hoses and, as one owner learned, the small coolant hoses to the turbo. Check the viscous fan hub (a weak hub shows up as heat in traffic) and that the wastegate actuator moves freely. Refill and bleed with Toyota long-life coolant.
Tools: Drain pan · hose-clamp pliers · 10/12 mm sockets · coolant funnel · Toyota red or blue long-life coolant

#### Replace a cracked 1KZ-TE cylinder head
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend for a capable home mechanic · cost Parts plus a head; AustralianCar.Reviews recommends a genuine Toyota head because some non-genuine heads have had casting faults
Symptoms: Bubbles or coolant pushing into the overflow bottle, coolant loss, rapid overheating, rough running and lost power. A pressure test may not show the crack.
Fix: Fix whatever made it overheat first (radiator, fan hub, wastegate, hoses), or the new head will crack too. Remove the timing belt, intake and exhaust, injector lines and turbo oil and coolant lines, then the head. Have the block deck checked, fit a genuine head gasket, and reassemble with a fresh timing belt. An IH8MUD member's 'lessons learned' thread is a reminder to put the washers back under the head bolts.
Tools: Full metric socket set · torque wrench and angle gauge · straight-edge and feeler gauges · factory or Gregory's manual for the head-bolt sequence

#### 5VZ-FE timing belt and water pump (V6 trucks)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ 8–14 hours the first time (AdventureTaco, on the same engine in a Tacoma) · cost Parts plus a long day
Symptoms: None until it snaps. The 5VZ-FE is non-interference, so a broken belt strands you but shouldn't bend valves. Plan on about 90,000 miles.
Fix: It's the same job as on a 3rd-gen 4Runner. Drain the coolant, remove the fan, shroud and drive belts, then the upper timing covers. Hold the crank pulley, break the bolt, pull the pulley and lower cover, and set cylinder 1 to TDC. Replace the belt, idlers, hydraulic tensioner, cam and crank seals, water pump and thermostat. Rotate the engine twice to confirm the marks, then torque the new crank bolt. The 4Runner part numbers below are the common ones, but check them against your Prado's frame number in an EPC.
Tools: Harmonic-balancer holder · puller · cam-pulley holder · seal puller · torque wrench · new crank bolt

#### Rebuild the rear axle seals and bearings
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day for both sides · cost Seals, bearings and retainers; Cruiser Outfitters sells a complete kit
Symptoms: Gear oil on the inside of the rear wheel or brakes, a low diff level, or a clunk in reverse after the diff has run low.
Fix: Drain the diff, remove the wheel and rear brake, unbolt the axle-shaft retainer and pull the shaft. Replace the inner seal in the housing. Once a seal has leaked, the bearing's grease has usually washed out, so IH8MUD members replace the bearing too, which means pressing it and its retainer collar off and on. If the seal is the same superseded part as on a 3rd-gen 4Runner, look up the 'retainer flip' method: the new seal sits further inboard. Refit with new gaskets and O-rings and refill the diff.
Tools: Slide hammer or axle puller · 20-ton press · seal driver · torque wrench · gear oil

#### Front pads and rotors, using 4Runner interchange
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2 hours · cost Pads and rotors; IH8MUD members source them in the US
Symptoms: Pulsing pedal, grooved or thin rotors, squealing pads.
Fix: IH8MUD's 90 Series FAQ confirms the front rotor is Toyota 43512-35210, as used on 1995–2002 V6 4Runners and Tacomas. Make sure you get the larger V6 rotor, because four-cylinder 4Runners used a smaller one that won't fit. Members list the rear rotors as 42431-60200/-60201, the same as the 80 Series. Remove the caliper, hang it, swap the rotor and pads, clean and grease the slides, and bed in the pads.
Tools: Metric sockets · C-clamp or piston tool · brake cleaner · high-temperature grease · torque wrench

#### Diagnose a sub tank that won't switch
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours to diagnose · cost Usually one valve
Symptoms: You flick the sub-tank switch, the sub-tank light comes on, but the main-tank gauge keeps falling.
Fix: On the 1KZ-TE, the lift pump is part of the injection pump, so the lines between tank and pump are under vacuum. An IH8MUD member suggests starting at the fuel-tank switch-over valve (he found it listed as Toyota 77710-60040): check that it gets power when you flick the switch, and that it actually changes over. AustralianCar.Reviews warns that a sub tank that was never used can seize its switching mechanism and leave stale fuel behind, so drain old fuel before you trust it.
Tools: Multimeter · wiring diagram for your engine (petrol and diesel circuits differ) · fuel-safe catch can

### Baseline service
Assume a 25-year-old import has had nothing done, whatever the auction sheet says. On a diesel the priorities are the timing belt and the cooling system, because heat is what kills a 1KZ-TE head. Specs below are from Roughtrax's KZJ90/95 data sheet unless noted. Petrol oil capacities are from Penrite's lookup for Australian Prados. V6 and 2.7 petrols differ in other ways too, so confirm in the manual for your engine.
- Engine oil & filter: 1KZ-TE: 7.7 L with filter, SAE 5W-40, API SL/CF · 5VZ-FE V6: 5.2 L with filter · 3RZ-FE 2.7: 5.4 L with filter (Penrite lookup) · petrol oil grade [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Every 6,000 mi or 12 months (6 months in severe use) (Roughtrax's UK schedule. Replace the sump-plug washer every time.)
- Engine air filter: Panel element · Inspect at every oil change; more often on dusty trails (A diesel that breathes dust wears fast. Check the airbox seals too.)
- Fuel filter (diesel): Diesel filter with water separator [CONFIRM PART BY FRAME NUMBER] · Every 12,000 mi or 12 months (Drain the water trap whenever the warning light comes on, and after filling from a questionable source.)
- Timing belt, tensioner & water pump: 1KZ-TE: belt, tensioner pulley, hydraulic tensioner, seals · 5VZ-FE: belt 13568-69095 (4Runner part) · 3RZ-FE: chain · 1KZ-TE: 100,000 km or 5–6 years (HD Automotive); Roughtrax says 60,000 mi or 60 months · 5VZ-FE: about 90,000 mi (If there's no receipt, do it now and replace the water pump at the same time.)
- Coolant, radiator & hoses: 9.5 L (11 L with rear heater) · Toyota red or blue Long Life Coolant · Every 36,000 mi or 36 months (On a 1KZ-TE, also replace the small turbo coolant hoses and check the viscous fan hub. The automatic's cooler is inside the radiator, so a leak here can contaminate the ATF.)
- Automatic transmission fluid: 3.0 L per drain-and-fill, 10.1 L dry · Dexron II/III or Toyota T-IV (Roughtrax lists these as guidance only) · Then per the owner's manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Look for pink, milky fluid (coolant from the radiator cooler) before you do anything else. Do repeated drain-and-fills rather than one flush.)
- Manual gearbox: 2.2 L, SAE 75W-90, API GL-4 or GL-5 · Every 24,000 mi or 24 months (An IH8MUD member cautions that if a GL-5 oil isn't labeled safe for yellow metals, you should use GL-4 in the gearbox.)
- Transfer case: 1.2 L, SAE 75W-90, API GL-4 or GL-5 · Every 24,000 mi or 24 months (Full-time case with a center lock. Check that the lock engages and that its dash light comes on.)
- Front & rear differentials: 75W-90 GL-4/5 · front 1.1 L · rear 2.9 L (open or locker), or 2.6 L of LSD-rated hypoid oil if you have an LSD · Front every 36,000 mi · rear every 18,000 mi (If the rear has run low it can clunk in reverse. Check the inner axle seals while you're there.)
- Power steering fluid: 0.8 L, Dexron II/III ATF · Refresh if dark (An IH8MUD member notes Toyota sells a pump seal kit (04446-60091) for the diesel's power-steering pump.)
- Brake & clutch fluid: 1.2 L, DOT 3 or DOT 4 (SAE J1703/4) · Brakes every 18,000 mi · clutch every 24,000 mi (Rear discs on every Prado. Front rotors are the 4Runner V6 part 43512-35210.)
- Propshaft grease points: Lithium-base NLGI No. 2 · Every 6,000 mi or 6 months (3,000 mi or 3 months in severe use) (Grease the U-joints and slip yokes.)
- Lower ball joints & CV boots: Inspect; genuine Toyota 43340-39465 / 43330-39585 if replacing · Inspect at every service (AustralianCar.Reviews) (Replace any joint with play or a torn boot, and replace them anyway if there's no record. Toyota's split CV-boot kit can be fitted without removing the driveshaft.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: 265/75R16 (about 31.6 in). An IH8MUD member who has owned both a 90 and a 95 says it won't rub on stock suspension unless the springs have sagged, and ExplorOz members add that it needs the 7-inch rims of a GXL-type truck, because it's too wide for the 6-inch rims on base models. 285/75R16 rubs with or without a lift, on the upper control arm and a rear pinch weld. For 33s, the same IH8MUD member suggests a lift and 255/85R16s.

Q: Can I legally import and register one in the US?
A: Yes, once it's 25 years old. NHTSA lets a vehicle at least 25 years old in without meeting US safety standards, counting from its date of manufacture, and EPA exempts vehicles at least 21 years old in original configuration. J90 production began in 1996, so the first trucks qualified in 2021, and the last 2002 builds qualify during 2027. Titling and emissions are up to your state, and California is the hardest.

Q: Is it just a 3rd-gen 4Runner?
A: Under the skin, nearly. Toyota says the Prado and Hilux Surf (the 4Runner) shared their suspension: double wishbones at the front and a four-link coil rear axle. 4Runner shocks, front rotors and lift kits bolt on. The differences that matter: every Prado has full-time 4WD, it has rear disc brakes, it has a different body, and it offers diesels the 4Runner never got in the US.

Q: Which engine should I buy?
A: The 1KZ-TE diesel is simple but cracks heads if it overheats. The 1KD-FTV (Japan, July 2000 on) has 170 PS and a 16-valve head that an IH8MUD member says is far less crack-prone, but its common-rail injectors cost much more to replace. The 3.4 V6 is the 4Runner's proven 5VZ-FE. 4X4 Australia's advice is to avoid the 2.7 four.

Q: Does it have lockers?
A: Every J90 has full-time 4WD with a center-diff lock. ExplorOz members say Australian J90s had no factory front or rear axle lockers. On some manual trucks the center diff locks mechanically whenever you select low range, while others have a dash switch. ARB Air Lockers are the usual retrofit.

Q: When is the timing belt due?
A: HD Automotive gives the 1KZ-TE belt as 100,000 km or 5–6 years (Roughtrax's UK schedule says 60,000 miles or 60 months). The 5VZ-FE V6 belt is about 90,000 miles, and that engine is non-interference. The 2.7 3RZ-FE has a timing chain.

Q: What fluids and capacities does a KZJ95 take?
A: Per Roughtrax's KZJ90/95 sheet: engine oil 7.7 L with filter (5W-40, API CF); coolant 9.5 L, or 11 L with a rear heater; manual gearbox 2.2 L and transfer case 1.2 L of 75W-90 GL-4/5; front diff 1.1 L and rear 2.9 L (2.6 L of LSD oil if you have an LSD); automatic 3.0 L per drain-and-fill; power steering 0.8 L of Dexron II/III. Confirm against your manual.

Q: What are the lift options?
A: Prado-specific kits exist: Dobinsons sells an IMS kit for the Prado 90/95, and an IH8MUD member notes Ironman made one too. Because the front end is the same as a 3rd-gen 4Runner's, 4Runner kits fit. One owner found a 2.5 in OME 4Runner kit gave about 3.5 in on his 90, and he needed a diff drop and stronger front axles. Above 2–3 in, members warn, the CV joints suffer.

Q: Where do I get parts in the US?
A: Many wear parts cross over from 3rd-gen 4Runners and Tacomas. For the rest, IH8MUD members look up genuine part numbers by frame number in an online EPC such as Partsouq, Amayama or ToyoDIY. Cruiser Outfitters (CruiserTeq) in Utah stocks 9x Prado ball joints, brakes and axle kits.

Q: What's one worth?
A: On Bring a Trailer, 19 J90s sold between December 2024 and October 2026, mostly for $10,000–$16,000. The extremes were $9,500 for a 1996 KZJ90 and $34,500 for a 1997 KZJ90. Diesels dominate the listings.

## Toyota Land Cruiser 100 Series (1998–2007)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/100-series/
Codes: UZJ100, FZJ105, HZJ105, HDJ100

Verdict: The 100 is the Land Cruiser that went to finishing school: a V8, independent front suspension and a cabin you could take to the opera. The purists sulked, and it turned out to be one of the most durable big wagons on the trail. Budget for the timing belt, though.

In January 1998 Toyota replaced the eight-year-old 80 Series with a wagon that broke two Land Cruiser traditions at once. The 100 was the first Land Cruiser with a V8, which Toyota added specifically to sell more trucks in North America, where it was the only engine offered. It was also the first with independent front suspension, chosen along with rack-and-pinion steering to improve on-road handling. Off-roaders grumbled, and they had a point. They also kept buying them.

### FROM 404T TO 'GRAND CRUISER'
Development started in 1991 under the code name 404T, and the design was frozen in mid-1994. Toyota previewed the truck as the 'Grand Cruiser' at the 32nd Tokyo Motor Show in October 1997. Takeo Kondo is credited as designer, Araco built it in Toyota City, and from 2003 to 2008 it was also assembled in China.
Under one body there were really two trucks. The 100 had a slightly wider chassis, IFS and the new engines. The 105 carried over most of the 80's chassis and drivetrain: coil-sprung solid axles at both ends and straight-six petrol and diesel engines, sold only in Africa, Australia, Russia and South America. You can tell them apart at a glance. The IFS 100 often sits lower at the front, and its wheels are almost flat where the 105's are dished, which lets both keep similar track widths.

### THE AMERICAN 100
US trucks were all UZJ100s with the 4.7-liter 2UZ-FE V8, rated at 230 hp and 320 lb-ft, driving through an A343F four-speed automatic and an HF2A full-time transfer case. Slee Off-Road notes that, unlike the 80, it has no viscous coupling, just a center differential you can lock. The rear axle is a semi-floating, 32-spline unit with a 9.5-inch ring gear. A rear electric locker was optional only for 1998 and 1999. For 2000 Toyota dropped it, added VSC and A-TRAC traction control, and swapped the weak two-pinion front differential for a four-pinion unit.
The 2003 update was the big one: an A750F five-speed automatic, drive-by-wire throttle, 235 hp, stronger U-joints and fatter driveshafts, 4.10 gears and 17-inch wheels as standard. Late trucks gained VVT-i, and Kelley Blue Book lists 275 hp and 332 lb-ft from 2005. Active Height Control was standard on the LX 470 from launch; owners report it also turns up as an option on some Land Cruisers, so check which suspension a given truck has.

### THE LUXURY TWINS
The 100 was also the basis for the Lexus LX 470, sold in Japan as the Toyota Land Cruiser Cygnus. Slee's guide says the Lexus shares the drivetrain but adds body cladding, projector headlights, backlit gauges and standard AHC with adaptive damping from 1998. In 2002 the Cygnus and LX 470 got Night View, which projected an infrared camera image onto the windshield, and they were the first Toyota vehicles with a rollover sensor. In Britain and Ireland the 100 was called the Land Cruiser Amazon. When Toyota marked the Land Cruiser's 50th anniversary in 2000 with commemorative models, global production had reached 3.72 million.

### HOW IT ENDED
The 100 got a series of small facelifts (lights, grille, spoiler and equipment) and stayed in production until August 2007. The 200 Series then kept the formula of V8 power, independent front suspension and a luxury twin in the LX 570. Wikipedia rates the 100 as durable and reliable, with two known weak spots on hard-worked trucks: cracked IFS lower wishbones on trucks that often hit the bump stops, and broken front differentials, mostly on 1998–99 two-pinion units.
Meanwhile, the solid-axle 70 Series kept going for buyers who wanted nothing to do with IFS. Today the 100 is a well-documented truck: IH8MUD's 100-series FAQ links to write-ups on everything from the 90,000-mile timing belt to lower ball joints, heater-hose tees and AHC fluid flushes.

### Data plate
- Chassis: J100 (UZJ100 / HDJ100 / FZJ105 / HZJ105)
- Production: January 1998 – August 2007
- Us Model Years: 1998–2007
- Engine (Us): 2UZ-FE 4.7 L DOHC 32v V8
- Output: 230 hp → 235 hp ('03) → 275 hp (late, VVT-i)
- Transmission (Us): 4-spd A343F; 5-spd A750F from 2003
- Drive: Full-time 4WD, lockable center diff (HF2A)
- Wheelbase: 112.2 in (2,850 mm)
- Length: 192.5 in ('05)
- Curb Weight: 5,115–5,425 lb
- Ground Clearance: 9.8 in
- Towing: 6,500 lb (2002–06)
- Wheel Bolt Pattern: 5 x 150 mm

### Engineering
The 100 has a ladder frame, slightly wider than the 80's, with independent front suspension on torsion bars and rack-and-pinion steering, plus a coil-sprung live rear axle. US trucks use the 4.7-liter 2UZ-FE V8 and a full-time transfer case with a lockable center differential. The wheel pattern changed to 5 on 150 mm with M14 x 1.5 studs.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, 2,850 mm (112.2 in) wheelbase (Slightly wider than the 80's to make room for IFS.)
- Front Suspension: Independent, torsion bars (A Land Cruiser first. Ride height is set at the torsion-bar adjusters; rack-and-pinion steering (variable-ratio from 2003).)
- Rear Axle: Live axle on coils, 9.5 in ring gear (Semi-floating, 32-spline shafts, four-pinion diff. 4.30 gears early, 4.10 from 2003.)
- 4Wd System: HF2A full-time with center diff lock (No viscous coupling. VSC and A-TRAC traction control from 2000.)
- Lockers: Rear e-locker optional 1998–1999 only (The front diff had two pinions until the 2000 model year, then four.)
- Engine (Us): 2UZ-FE 4.7 L DOHC V8 (230 hp at launch, 235 hp from 2003, and 275 hp / 332 lb-ft with VVT-i on late trucks.)

### Versions
- 1998–2002 (US) · UZJ100 · 2UZ-FE 4.7 L V8 · 230 hp / 320 lb-ft · A343F four-speed auto. Rear locker option for 1998–99; 4-pinion front diff, VSC and A-TRAC from 2000.
- 2003–2004 (US) · UZJ100 · 2UZ-FE 4.7 L V8 · 235 hp / 320 lb-ft · A750F five-speed auto, drive-by-wire, stronger driveshafts, 4.10 gears, 17-inch wheels.
- 2005–2007 (US) · UZJ100 · 2UZ-FE 4.7 L V8 with VVT-i · 275 hp / 332 lb-ft · VVT-i engine; KBB lists 275 hp and 332 lb-ft from the 2005 model year.
- 1998–2007 · HDJ100 · 1HD-FTE 4.2 L turbo-diesel I6 · 150 kW / 430 Nm · IFS only. Europe, the UK and Japan from launch; Australia from October 2000. Not sold in the US.
- 1998–2007 · FZJ105 / HZJ105 · 1FZ-FE 4.5 L I6 / 1HZ 4.2 L diesel I6 · — / 96 kW · Solid axles front and rear, carried over from the 80. Africa, Australia, Russia, South America.
- 1998–2007 (US) · Lexus LX 470 · 2UZ-FE 4.7 L V8 · Same as UZJ100 · AHC and adaptive damping standard from 1998; body cladding and a plusher cabin.

### Year-by-year
- 1998: UZJ100 launches in the US with the 4.7 L 2UZ-FE V8, the only US engine. It's the first Land Cruiser with independent front suspension and the first with a V8
- 1998–1999: Selectable rear diff locker offered as an option, and only in these two model years. Off-roaders still hunt for them, but they come with the weaker front diff below
- 1998–1999: Two-pinion front differential. It's the most common source of front-diff failures when the truck is driven hard [avoid]
- 2000: Four-pinion front diff fitted from late 1999 production (model year 2000) with fewer reported failures; 50th Anniversary commemorative models in several countries
- 2003–2007: Five-speed A750F automatic replaces the four-speed, with a no-contact throttle sensor; the late (2006–07) trucks add the VVT-i 2UZ-FE. These are the years owners most often point buyers to, and some say the five-speed matters more than the extra VVT-i power [buy]
- 2003–2006: Model years covered by the side curtain airbag recall (16V065000)
- 2007: Last model year; production ends in August 2007

### Capability
- Towing: 6,500 lb (2,948 kg) (2002–2006 per KBB; 5,500 lb for a 1999)
- Payload: 1,470 lb (667 kg) (2005, KBB)
- Fuel tank: 25.4 US gal (96 L) (2005, KBB)
- Ground clearance: 9.8 in (249 mm) (2005, KBB)
- Fuel economy: 12 city / 16 hwy / 14 combined mpg (2005, KBB)
- Curb weight: 5,390 lb (2,445 kg) (2005, KBB)
- Turning circle: 39.7 ft (12.1 m) diameter (2005, KBB)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 275/70R16 (e.g. 2000), 275/65R17 (e.g. 2006)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x150
- Center Bore: 110 mm
- Lug Thread: M14x1.5
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 285/75R16 or 285/65R18 (about 33 in) (IH8MUD FAQ answer. 295/75R16 fits with 1/2 to 1 inch of clearance at full lock, which is tight; one owner measured 3/4 inch to the rear plastic liner on 285/75s.)
- Biggest tire, 2 in lift: 295/70R18 or 285/75R18 (Tundra 18s) (Needs a little trimming and the pinch-weld fold. You may have to remove the washer-bottle cover or move the bottle, and owners add extended front bump stops.)
- Biggest tire, 2–3 in lift: 315/75R16 / 35x12.50R16 (Fits, but rubs the plastic liner up front and the rear sheet metal at full compression. Owners adjust turn stops and bump stops, and some add a mild body lift to keep full travel.)

### Buying checks
- Ask for the timing-belt receipt: The 2UZ-FE uses a belt, and owners treat the 90,000-mile service (belt, water pump, thermostat, often idlers and seals) as essential. With no paperwork, assume it's due and price it in.
- Know which front diff you're buying: Model-year 1998 and 1999 trucks have the two-pinion front differential that Wikipedia says fails most often under shock loads. The 2000 model year switched to a stronger four-pinion unit, but 1998–99 are also the only years with the optional rear locker.
- Have the heater-hose tees been done?: The plastic tees in the heater hoses get brittle and can crack, dumping coolant. IH8MUD calls them part of the 90k service that most shops, Toyota dealers included, skip.
- Listen at cold start: A tick or pop that sounds like an exhaust leak can be a spark plug working loose. IH8MUD's warning thread says to check the plugs before anything else, because a plug that blows out can take the cylinder-head threads with it.
- Inspect the IFS: Look for cracks in the lower wishbones on trucks that have been driven hard enough to hit the bump stops, and check the lower ball joints and CV boots for play or splits.
- Try a cold start more than once: Slee lists worn starter contacts as a known issue. The symptom is a click with no crank on the first try or two.
- AHC trucks: check the ride height: On an LX 470, or one of the late Land Cruisers with AHC, make sure it levels itself and holds height. Ask when the AHC fluid was last flushed; owners on IH8MUD cite a 60,000-mile interval.
- Do the body and wiring checks: Slee's inspection list applies here too: overspray, filler, frame-straightening marks, a rat's nest of accessory wiring under the dash, and fluids that look neglected. Cracked leather seats are common and costly to re-skin.

### Common repairs
#### Timing belt, water pump and thermostat (the 90k service)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A long weekend (one owner logged about 15 relaxed hours) · cost About $600 in parts for one IH8MUD owner's full kit
Symptoms: No symptoms until it breaks. It's on the service schedule at 90,000 miles, so a truck without receipts is due.
Fix: Drain the coolant, cover the radiator with cardboard, then remove the fan, belts and crank pulley. You'll need a big wrench, a cheater bar and something to hold the crank. Replace the timing belt, tensioner and idlers, the water pump with its gasket and O-ring, the thermostat and gasket, and ideally the cam and crank seals while you're in there. One IH8MUD write-up recommends taking photos and bagging bolts as you go, and finds the factory manual a general guide rather than a step-by-step.
Tools: 3/4-in drive breaker bar and cheater · crank-holding tool · pulley puller · seal puller · thread locker · FIPG gasket maker. IH8MUD parts list (check fitment for your year): water pump 16100-59275-83, timing belt 13568-09070, serpentine belt 90916-02586, thermostat 90916-03100 + gasket 16346-50010, idlers 13503-0F010 / 13505-0F010, crank seal 90311-A0001, cam seals 90311-38065 (x2).

#### Replace the heater-hose pipe tees
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost Under $15 in parts; a dealer charges $100–200+
Symptoms: None until a brittle tee cracks and you lose coolant, possibly a long way from home.
Fix: With the engine cold, remove the engine cover and lean in from the side. The tees sit deep in the engine bay, so expect a long reach. Unclip the ground wire attached to the heater hose, work the clamps off with pliers, pull the hoses (soapy water helps), fit new tees and refill the coolant. Replace both, because the hot side fails first.
Tools: Step stool · pliers · flat screwdriver · soapy water · Toyota pipe tee 87248-60460 (x2).

#### Press in new lower ball joints
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A day · cost Ball joints plus a 20-ton press if you don't own one
Symptoms: Clunks over bumps, play at the bottom of the knuckle, or simply a high-mileage truck with original joints.
Fix: Support the truck on frame stands, pull the wheels and skid plates, and back the torsion-bar adjusters all the way off. Mark and slide back the torque arms, then remove the lower shock bolt, sway-bar link, cotter pin and ball-joint nut. Break the taper, pull the lower arm, remove the C-clip and press out the old joint (a 2-inch conduit coupler makes a good receiver). Press in the new joint with a 2-inch pipe nipple, refit the clip and reassemble in reverse order, following the factory manual for bolt torques. Reset the torsion bars and get an alignment.
Tools: 20-ton shop press · 22, 19, 14 and 24 mm sockets · snap-ring pliers · sledge or pickle fork · lower ball joint (e.g. Cruiser Outfitters SUS43340) · factory manual section SA-73.

#### Replace the starter contacts
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 3 hours with experience (one owner's first try took 6.5) · cost About $25 in contacts
Symptoms: The solenoid clicks but the starter doesn't turn, usually on a cold start, then it fires after two or three tries.
Fix: Disconnect the battery. The starter sits under the intake manifold, so remove the V-bank cover, the intake tube and airbox lid, the accelerator cable and the throttle body, then every hose and the ground strap on the manifold, and lift the manifold off. Photograph everything first. Pull the starter, open the solenoid cover and fit new contacts and a plunger. Moving the wiring-harness bracket out of the way makes the manifold easier to refit. Some owners, like the author of IH8MUD's '90K and starter replacement job' thread, do it during the timing-belt service.
Tools: 10, 12 and 14 mm wrenches and sockets · camera for reference photos · starter contact and plunger kit · new intake gaskets.

#### Flush the AHC fluid
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost Toyota AHC fluid; one member priced it at about $30–35 a gallon
Symptoms: Old, dark fluid, a truck that's slow to level, or a lift via the height-sensor links that has left the reservoir low.
Fix: Park on level ground with the suspension in N, engine off. Suck the reservoir empty and refill with fresh AHC fluid. Bleed one corner at a time (front driver, front passenger, rear driver, rear passenger): open the bleeder until that corner bottoms out, close it, start the engine and let the truck re-level, then switch off. Repeat until clean fluid comes out of each bleeder, and never let the reservoir run low.
Tools: 10 mm wrench · clear tube and catch bottle · fluid extractor or turkey baster · Toyota AHC fluid.

#### Check spark plugs for walking out
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2 hours · cost Eight plugs (90080-91180 per the IH8MUD 90k list)
Symptoms: A tick-tick or pop-pop at cold start that sounds like an exhaust leak and, as the plug loosens, doesn't go away when warm. Premature coil-boot and coil failures.
Fix: Pull the coils and check every plug's torque. If one is loose, replace the set and torque them correctly; the thread quotes the factory spec as 13 ft-lb. If the tick is still there afterward, then look for an exhaust leak. A plug that has blown out usually needs a thread insert in the head.
Tools: Spark-plug socket and extension · torque wrench (inch-pound range) · dielectric grease for the coil boots.

#### Set the front ride height at the torsion bars
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour plus an alignment · cost Free to adjust; new torsion bars cost more
Symptoms: A front end that has settled or sits lower than the rear, or new tires that need more clearance.
Fix: Each torsion bar has an adjuster bolt under the truck, one per side. Turn them evenly and measure both sides, keeping some rake, since IH8MUD members point out the 100 handles best with the rear a little higher. Clean and anti-seize the adjuster threads. If you need real lift or more load capacity, fit uprated torsion bars and matching rear coils, then align.
Tools: Socket and long extension · tape measure · anti-seize · Old Man Emu torsion bars (303001) and rear coils (2865) if upgrading.

### Baseline service
Assume nothing was done unless there are receipts: on a 100 the big-ticket items are the 90,000-mile timing belt, the drivetrain gear oils that owners skip, and (on LX 470s and any AHC-equipped Land Cruiser) the AHC fluid. Note which transmission you have: 1998–2002 trucks use the A343F four-speed, 2003–07 the A750F five-speed, and Slee says the 2004 update moved to ATF WS and Super Long Life Coolant.
- Engine oil & filter: SAE 5W-30 · ≈6.8 L with filter (Roughtrax); Amsoil lists 7.2 qt for 2005–07 VVT-i trucks · Then per the owner's manual schedule [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (The IH8MUD 90k list gives the dealer filter as 90915-YZZD3 and says a larger JDM filter (90915-20004) is available and preferred by some owners.)
- Engine air filter & cabin filter: Air filter 17801-50040 (IH8MUD 90k list) · Inspect at every oil change; replace when dirty (The cabin filter is easy to forget; IH8MUD's 100-series FAQ links an LX 470/Land Cruiser cabin-filter DIY.)
- Spark plugs: Iridium 90080-91180 ×8 · factory torque 13 ft-lb (IH8MUD) · Iridiums are due at 120,000 mi, but IH8MUD members do them with the 90k timing belt (While the coils are out, check every plug for tightness: a tick or pop at cold start can be a plug walking out of the head.)
- Timing belt, tensioner, idlers & water pump: Belt 13568-09070 · tensioner 13540-50030 · idlers 13503-0F010 / 13505-0F010 · pump 16100-59275-83 (IH8MUD 90k list) · Every 90,000 mi; a truck with no receipt is due now (Do the thermostat (90916-03100), cam seals and crank seal while you're in there. IH8MUD members say the cam seals are more work on the 2005–07 VVT-i engine.)
- Coolant, hoses & heater tees: ≈15 L (Roughtrax). 1998–2003: Toyota red Long Life Coolant · 2004–07: pink Super Long Life Coolant, premixed (Slee) · Red LLC every 30,000 mi or 2 years; pink SLLC at 100,000 mi, then every 50,000 mi (Slee) (Replace the plastic heater-hose tees (87248-60460) preventively; IH8MUD says they go brittle and can dump the coolant. Radiator hoses 16571-50150 / 16572-50150 and the bypass hose are worth doing with the timing belt.)
- Drive belt & tensioner: Serpentine belt 90916-02586 · belt tensioner 16620-0W101 (IH8MUD 90k list) · Replace with the timing belt, or sooner if cracked or chirping (The serpentine belt comes off for the timing belt anyway, so replace it and spin-check the idler and tensioner.)
- Automatic transmission fluid: A343F (1998–2002): Toyota T-IV, ≈2.0 L per drain-and-fill · A750F (2003–07): ≈3.0 L per drain-and-fill, ≈10.6 L dry; ATF WS on trucks without a dipstick (Roughtrax) · Then per the owner's manual schedule [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Slee: from 2004 the dipstick was deleted (level is set at the overflow plug) and ATF WS is not interchangeable with T-IV or Dexron. A drain-and-fill only swaps the sump portion, so repeat it rather than doing one big flush on unknown fluid.)
- Transfer case: GL-5 75W-90 · 1.4 qt (IH8MUD DIY); Roughtrax lists 1.5 L · Then per the owner's manual schedule [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (HF2A full-time case, no viscous coupler (Slee). Crack the 24 mm fill plug before the drain, torque the drain plug to 27 ft-lb and don't overtighten: the case can crack. Synthetic can quiet cold-morning whine.)
- Front differential: GL-5 80W-90 hypoid · 1.8 qt (IH8MUD write-up); Roughtrax lists 1.6 L · Then per the owner's manual schedule [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (The IFS front diff has Allen-head plugs and too little clearance for squeeze bottles, so bring a pump. Two-pinion on 1998–99, four-pinion from 2000 (Slee).)
- Rear differential: GL-5 80W-90 hypoid (LSD-rated per the write-up) · 3.5 qt (IH8MUD); Roughtrax lists 3.2 L, 3.3 L for LSD · Then per the owner's manual schedule [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (9.5-inch ring gear. 1998–99 trucks could have the optional electric rear locker, so test that it engages (Slee).)
- Power steering fluid: Dexron-III ATF (Amsoil lookup) · capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Refresh by suction-and-refill of the reservoir if dark (Rack-and-pinion IFS; Slee notes variable-gear steering arrived later in the run.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 (Amsoil lookup; Roughtrax allows DOT 3 or 4) · Then every 2–3 years [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (The 100 has a hydraulic brake booster with an electric pump: bleed with the key ON so the pump runs, and expect the ABS and brake lights to come on during the job. IH8MUD members bleed front left, front right, then the rears, and the factory manual describes extra steps for bleeding the actuator.)
- AHC fluid (LX 470; AHC-equipped Land Cruisers): Toyota AHC fluid 08886-01805 (2.5 L can) · ≈4.5 L system, forum estimate (Roughtrax) · An IH8MUD member's 2000 owner's manual lists replacement at 60,000 mi (Never top up with brake fluid; one IH8MUD owner's truck went soft after a dealer did. Bleed each corner with the engine off and the suspension in N.)
- Driveshaft grease points: Lithium-base NLGI No. 2 for the U-joints (Roughtrax) · At every oil change (IH8MUD's FAQ links a driveshaft lubing schematic; any hand grease gun fits the zerks.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: The 100-series FAQ answer on IH8MUD is 285/75R16 on 16-inch wheels or 285/65R18 on 18s, both about 33 inches. 295/75R16s do fit, with half an inch to an inch of clearance at full turn, but owners call it tight. Even 285/75s can be snug at the rear: one owner measured 3/4 inch to the plastic wheel-well liner.

Q: Does it have lockers?
A: Every 100 has a center differential you can lock. A rear electric locker was a factory option only for 1998 and 1999. From 2000 Toyota relied on A-TRAC traction control instead, so ARB Air Lockers are the usual retrofit.

Q: What's the deal with the 1998–99 front differential?
A: Those years have a two-pinion front diff, and Wikipedia says the pinion could flex away from the ring gear under shock loads. Most reported failures are on 1998–99 trucks. Toyota fitted a four-pinion diff from the 2000 model year, and failures dropped.

Q: When is the timing belt due?
A: At the 90,000-mile service. Owners replace the belt, water pump, thermostat and often the idlers, tensioner and cam and crank seals at the same time. IH8MUD has a full parts list and several step-by-step write-ups.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: If you want the best road truck, 2003–07. IH8MUD's new-owner thread lists the five-speed A750F as the reason, and several owners there reckon the gearbox is a bigger step than the 2006–07 VVT-i engine's extra power, which costs a lot more. On Expedition Portal, one owner calls 2003–05 'THE years' and warns that the VVT-i trucks' air-injection system is expensive to fix. 1998–99 trucks are the only ones with the optional rear locker, but they also have the two-pinion front diff and, Slee notes, throttle-sensor faults. Condition and the timing-belt history matter more than any year.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: Kelley Blue Book lists 6,500 lb for 2002–2006 models (5,500 lb for a 1999). From 2003 a bolt-on factory hitch was offered, and the rear crossmember was changed to take it.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: KBB lists 12 mpg city and 15–16 highway, with a 25.4-gallon tank on a 2005. Lifts, 33s and a roof rack make that worse.

Q: Should I worry about AHC?
A: The LX 470 had Active Height Control and adaptive damping as standard from 1998, and owners report it was also optional on some Land Cruisers. It works well when maintained. Keep up with fluid flushes (owners cite 60,000 miles), and to lift an AHC truck you can adjust the height-sensor links, as IH8MUD's FAQ covers.

Q: Was there a solid-axle 100?
A: Yes, the 105 (FZJ105 and HZJ105), with coil-sprung solid axles at both ends and straight sixes carried over from the 80. It was never sold in the US; it went to Africa, Australia, Russia and South America.

Q: Is the Lexus LX 470 the same truck?
A: Mechanically, yes: same chassis and drivetrain. The LX 470 adds body cladding, a plusher cabin and standard AHC with adaptive damping. Slee notes that it often got features before the Land Cruiser did.

Q: What are the lift options?
A: The common setup is Old Man Emu: uprated torsion bars up front, matching coils at the rear and new shocks, sold as a kit of about 1.5 inches. The torsion-bar adjusters handle front height. IH8MUD's FAQ also links a thread on Slee's front diff drop, and any height change needs an alignment.

## Toyota Land Cruiser Prado 120 (2002–2009)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/prado-120/
Codes: J120, GRJ120, KDJ120

Verdict: America knows this truck as the GX 470. Everywhere else it was the Prado: the same frame and Torsen center diff with a sensible V6 or a frugal diesel in place of the Lexus V8. It's a brilliant tourer as long as you ask, early and loudly, who last looked at the diesel's injector seats.

The 120 is the Prado that America did get, just not under that name. Toyota launched the third-generation Land Cruiser Prado in Japan on 7 October 2002 on a new, stiffer frame, and the next month Lexus started selling the same truck in the US as the GX 470, with a V8. Everyone else got fours, V6s and diesels, a Torsen center differential they could lock, and up to 180 liters of fuel in Australian five-doors. It's softer, heavier and cleverer than the Prado 90, and the diesel has a flaw you need to know about before you buy.

### DESIGNED IN FRANCE, BUILT IN JAPAN
Development started in 1997. The design came from Lance Scott at Toyota's ED² studio in France, whose proposal was picked in late 1999. Toyota built the 120 from September 2002 to August 2009 at its Honsha and Tahara plants, adding Toyota Auto Body from May 2006, and FAW Toyota assembled it in Chengdu, China. Toyota says the new high-rigidity frame improved handling, stability and quietness. The front suspension was revised for reliability, and the 120 shares suspension parts with the 4th-gen 4Runner and the FJ Cruiser.
The clever bits were in the drivetrain and electronics. A newly developed Torsen limited-slip center differential, lockable for the rough stuff, replaced the J90's center diff. Active traction control could manage climbs and descents, and top grades added Toyota's H∞-TEMS adaptive dampers and electronically controlled rear air suspension. Australians got Hill-start and Downhill Assist Control, and a 4-star ANCAP rating in 2003. A short three-door version (J125) had only an 87-liter tank, with no sub tank.

### 1GR, 1KD AND THE REST
At launch in Japan, the engines were the 3.4-liter 5VZ-FE V6 and 2.7-liter 3RZ-FE four from the J90, plus a 3.0-liter intercooled turbo-diesel. In July 2004 the new 4.0-liter 1GR-FE V6 replaced the 5VZ-FE there, and in August the 2.7-liter 2TR-FE replaced the 3RZ-FE. Australia had the 1GR-FE from its 2003 launch, at 179 kW and 376 Nm. It's a timing-chain engine, and CarsGuide owners reported 18 L/100 km against Toyota's 13.6 claim. A five-speed automatic arrived for the V6 in late 2005, and 4X4 Australia suggests buying that or the six-speed manual rather than the early four-speed.
Diesels varied by market. Toyota's model list includes KDJ120s from 2002, so Japan had the 1KD-FTV common-rail engine from the start. Australia kept the older 1KZ-TE at 96 kW until late 2006, when the Euro IV version of the 1KD-FTV arrived with 127 kW, 410 Nm, a five-speed automatic and a six-speed manual. In 2006, diesels passed half of Australian Prado sales. Some markets also had the naturally aspirated 5L-E.

### THE INJECTOR-SEAT PROBLEM
The 1KD-FTV's Achilles heel is the copper seat under each injector. When a seat leaks, blow-by gas gets into the rocker cover, mixes with the oil and cooks into carbon. The carbon blocks the oil pickup in the sump, starves the engine and can wipe out the bottom-end bearings. Symptoms are white smoke and a rattle on a cold start. AustralianCar.Reviews says aluminum seats replaced the copper ones from August 2007, and that the injectors themselves often fail at 120,000–140,000 km, sometimes as early as 75,000 km.
CarsGuide's 2012 used-car review warned that a seized engine could mean 'a total write-off', with a replacement engine costing about A$15,000, and reported that New Zealand owners were having the seals replaced every 45,000 km. Unsealed 4X4 now suggests seals every 40,000 km. The cheap pre-purchase check is a flashlight through the sump drain-plug hole: if the pickup screen is coated in anything but oil, walk away or budget for a sump-off clean.

### WHERE IT LEFT THE PRADO
Toyota replaced the 120 with the J150 in September 2009. That truck kept the suspension layout and the 2.7 four and 4.0 V6, finally merged the Prado and Hilux Surf into one line, and added crawl control and Multi-Terrain Select. The Prado line finally reached American showrooms as the 250 Series, badged simply Land Cruiser. In the US, the 120 is still off-limits: the first trucks turn 25 from September 2027. Until then, the closest thing on an American title is its Lexus twin, which is why GX 470 forum threads read like Prado 120 forum threads.

### Data plate
- Chassis: J120 (five-door 120/121, three-door 125)
- Production: September 2002 – August 2009
- Japan Launch: 7 October 2002
- Engines: 1GR-FE 4.0 V6 · 1KD-FTV / 1KZ-TE 3.0 TD · 5VZ-FE 3.4 V6 · 3RZ-FE / 2TR-FE 2.7 I4
- Drive: Full-time 4WD, Torsen LSD center diff with lock
- Wheelbase: 2,790 mm (109.8 in) 5-door · 2,455 mm (96.7 in) 3-door
- Length: 4,715 mm (5-door) · 4,340 mm (3-door)
- Curb Weight: 1,830 kg (3-door V6) – 1,970 kg (5-door V6), Japanese spec
- Fuel: 87 L main + 93 L sub (Australian 5-door) · 87 L (3-door)
- Towing: 2,500 kg braked (Australia, 2006–08)
- Wheels: 6 x 139.7 mm, M12 x 1.5; stock 265/65R17
- Us Status: Never sold; sold as the Lexus GX 470. Import-eligible from late 2027

### Engineering
The 120 rides on a new high-rigidity ladder frame with double-wishbone independent front suspension and a coil-sprung, four-link live rear axle with a lateral rod. Top grades swap the rear coils for electronically controlled air springs. Every 120 has full-time four-wheel drive through a Torsen limited-slip center differential that can be locked, plus brake-based Active TRC. Wheels are 6 on 139.7 mm.
- Chassis: High-rigidity ladder frame; 2,790 mm (109.8 in) 5-door, 2,455 mm (96.7 in) 3-door (Shares suspension parts with the 4th-gen 4Runner and FJ Cruiser.)
- Front Suspension: Double wishbones, coil-overs (Revised over the J90 for reliability, per Wikipedia. Same lower ball joints and hubs as the GX 470.)
- Rear Suspension: Four-link live axle, lateral rod; coils or air (Electronically controlled rear air on top grades (Australian Grande; Japanese TZ G Selection).)
- 4Wd System: Full-time, Torsen LSD center diff with lock (Two-speed transfer case; Active TRC, VSC, HAC and DAC.)
- Rear Diff: LSD on Australian GX/GXL; open on VX/Grande (Per ExplorOz owners. Roughtrax's UK spec sheet lists rear diff-lock variants.)
- Engines: 1GR-FE 4.0 V6 · 1KD-FTV / 1KZ-TE 3.0 TD · 5VZ-FE 3.4 V6 · 3RZ/2TR 2.7 I4 (Chains on the 1GR and 3RZ; belts on the 5VZ, 1KZ and 1KD.)

### Versions
- 2002–2004 (Japan) · VZJ120 / 121 / 125 · 5VZ-FE 3.4 L V6 · 136 kW (185 PS) · Replaced by the 1GR-FE in Japan in July 2004.
- 2002–2004 · RZJ120 / 125 · 3RZ-FE 2.7 L I4 · 110 kW (150 PS) · Replaced by the 2.7 L 2TR-FE (TRJ120/125) in August 2004.
- 2003–2009 · GRJ120 / 121 · 1GR-FE 4.0 L V6 · 179 kW / 376 Nm (Australia) · Timing chain. Four-speed auto at first, five-speed from late 2005.
- 2002–2009 · KDJ120 / 121 / 125 · 1KD-FTV 3.0 L common-rail turbo-diesel I4 · 127 kW / 410 Nm (Euro IV, from late 2006) · Japan from launch; Australia from 2006 with a 5AT/6MT. Copper injector seats until August 2007.
- 2003–2006 · KZJ120 · 1KZ-TE 3.0 L turbo-diesel I4 · 96 kW / 343 Nm · Australia's diesel until the 1KD arrived; five-door only.
- 2002–2009 (US) · Lexus GX 470 (UZJ120) · 2UZ-FE 4.7 L V8 · — · The US-market twin, with a V8 and rear air suspension.

### Year-by-year
- 1997: Development begins; design work follows in 1998, and Lance Scott's ED² (France) proposal is picked in late 1999
- Oct 2002: Launched in Japan on 7 October; production began in September. Lexus starts US sales of the GX 470 twin in November
- 2003: Australian launch with the new 4.0 L 1GR-FE V6 (179 kW), the 1KZ-TE diesel and the 2.7; 4-star ANCAP. 14,639 sold in Australia that year
- April 2003: Australian recall PRA 2003/6123 for the fuel pulsation damper on early GRJ120s
- July/Aug 2004: Japan: 1GR-FE replaces the 5VZ-FE, and the 2TR-FE replaces the 3RZ-FE
- Late 2005: Five-speed automatic arrives for the V6. 4X4 Australia says to skip the earlier four-speed V6 autos and buy a five-speed (or the rare six-speed manual) [buy]
- May 2006: Toyota Auto Body joins production
- Late 2006: Euro IV 1KD-FTV (127 kW, 410 Nm) with 5AT and 6MT; Australia's diesel switches from the 1KZ-TE. Until August 2007 the 1KD has copper injector seats, which can fail and let blow-by gases carbon up the oil pick-up, so ask whether they have been replaced [avoid]
- Aug 2007: Aluminium injector seats replace the failure-prone copper ones on the 1KD-FTV; equipment and safety upgrades. 4X4 Australia rates the 2006–08 trucks as the high point of the 120 [buy]
- Aug 2009: Production ends; the J150 Prado replaces it in September
- Aug 2024: Every J120 is now at least 15 years old, the threshold for Canadian import
- Sept 2027: The first J120s turn 25 and become eligible for US import

### Capability
- Towing: 2,500 kg (5,512 lb) braked (Australian 2006–08 trucks, per 4X4 Australia)
- Fuel tank: 87 L + 93 L sub tank = 180 L (47.6 US gal) (Australian five-door; three-door 87 L only; UK five-door 95 L (Roughtrax))
- Fuel economy: 9.3 L/100 km diesel · 13.6 L/100 km V6 (official); owners report up to 18 L/100 km for the V6 (CarsGuide)
- Curb weight: 1,830 kg (4,034 lb) 3-door V6 – 1,970 kg (4,343 lb) 5-door V6 (Toyota, Japanese spec)
- Gross vehicle mass: 2,800 kg (Roughtrax, KDJ120)
- Dimensions: 4,715 × 1,875 × 1,855–1,870 mm (5-door) (Toyota, Japanese spec)
- Safety: 4-star ANCAP (2003) (GXL and VX/Grande variants)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 265/65R17 on 7.5Jx17 ET30
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Offset: +30 mm (stock 7.5Jx17)
- Center Bore: 106.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M12x1.5
- Lug Torque: 113 N·m (83 lb-ft) per Koleso; Roughtrax lists 112 N·m
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 265/70R17 (ExplorOz owners report 'no rubbing issues', matching the GX 470 consensus on the same chassis.)
- Biggest tire, Stock (16-in wheels) lift: 265/70R16 (A common upsize 'without bother' (ExplorOz), but one owner says 16-inch rims may need caliper grinding to clear on a 120.)
- Biggest tire, 2 in (50 mm) lift: 285/70R17 (≈33 in) (Needs at least 50 mm of lift and +50 offset wheels (stock is +30), or trimming of the body mount behind the mud flap.)
- Biggest tire, Lifted lift: 285/75R16 (Fitted to lifted Prados 'with a little rubbing' (ExplorOz).)

### Buying checks
- 1KD-FTV: injector seats and oil pickup: Ask for injector-seat (washer) receipts. Listen for a rattle and look for white smoke on a cold start, then shine a light through the sump drain-plug hole. CarsGuide and Unsealed 4X4 both say carbon on the pickup screen means a suspect engine. Trucks built from August 2007 got aluminum seats.
- 1KD-FTV: injector age: AustralianCar.Reviews says the injectors typically fail at 120,000–140,000 km. Signs are a loud knock when cold, rough idle, poor running under load and worse fuel economy. Both it and 4X4 Australia suggest testing them at every service and replacing them at about 100,000 km, so ask whether they've been done.
- Timing belt or chain?: The 1GR-FE V6 and the 2.7 fours use chains. The 1KD-FTV, 1KZ-TE and 5VZ-FE use belts, and HD Automotive quotes Toyota's 1KD interval as 150,000 km or five years. No receipt means budget for the belt and water pump.
- Cracked dash and split rear door: CarsGuide reports dashboards cracking near the passenger airbag on early 120s, and rear-door skins splitting along the hinge side under the weight of the spare. Check both, and look closely at the door if a heavier spare tire has been fitted.
- Rear air suspension (Grande and top grades): If it has air springs, check that it levels and holds height overnight. 4X4 Australia warns that self-leveling rear air makes aftermarket suspension 'a much bigger (and more expensive) task' than on coil-sprung trucks.
- V6 transmission: 4X4 Australia suggests skipping the early four-speed automatic V6 in favor of the five-speed auto (late 2005 on) or the rarer six-speed manual.
- Test the center diff lock: Engage the center lock off pavement and make sure the light comes on and goes off. IH8MUD's GX 470 pre-buy advice applies to the Prado's shared system: a seized actuator is an expensive surprise on a truck that's never left the road.
- Import eligibility: A J120 can't be imported into the US until it's 25 years old by date of manufacture. The first ones qualify from September 2027. A '2003 Prado' advertised as US-legal today should set off alarms.

### Common repairs
#### 1KD-FTV injector seats (washers) and oil-pickup check
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time Workshop-dependent; often done alongside an injector service · cost HD Automotive lists a genuine 1KD injector fitting kit at AUD $169; dropping and cleaning the sump adds labor
Symptoms: White smoke and a rattle after a cold start, oily carbon in the rocker cover, and in the worst case low oil pressure from a blocked pickup.
Fix: Unsealed 4X4's advice: if the seats are leaking, have them replaced, and have the mechanic check the oil pickup for contamination. Pull the injectors, clean the bores and fit new seats and O-rings from a genuine fitting kit. Then shine a light through the drain-plug hole at the pickup screen. If there's anything on it but oil, drop the sump and clean the pickup before the engine starves. Unsealed suggests replacing the seals every 40,000 km. Stop the engine at once if the oil-pressure light comes on.
Tools: Injector puller · torque wrench · new seats/washers and O-rings · flashlight · sump gasket maker or gasket · fresh oil and filter

#### Replace worn 1KD-FTV injectors
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A diesel-specialist job for most owners · cost HD Automotive lists genuine Denso 1KD injectors for the Prado at AUD $2,200, or AUD $2,790 as a kit with lines
Symptoms: A loud knock when cold, poor fuel economy, rough or erratic idle, and rough running under load. AustralianCar.Reviews puts typical failure at 120,000–140,000 km, but has seen them go at 75,000.
Fix: Have a diesel specialist test the injectors first. Unsealed 4X4 says to repair or replace any that fail. Replace them as a set with new seats and O-rings, and new high-pressure lines if you buy the kit, then clear the codes and road-test. AustralianCar.Reviews links worn injectors on the 2006–09 Euro IV engine to cracked pistons, which is why it suggests servicing them every 100,000 km.
Tools: Diesel diagnostic scan/test equipment (specialist) · injector puller · torque wrench

#### 1KD-FTV timing belt and water pump
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 1.5–2 hours of workshop time with the water pump (HD Automotive) · cost HD Automotive's genuine 1KD belt kit lists at AUD $446
Symptoms: None until it fails, and HD Automotive notes the 1KD is an interference engine, so a broken belt means serious internal damage. Interval: 150,000 km or five years per HD Automotive; Roughtrax's UK sheet gives 100,000 miles or 120 months.
Fix: Remove the fan and shroud, drive belt and crank pulley, then the timing covers. Set the timing marks and replace the belt, hydraulic tensioner, idler pulley and front cam and crank seals (all in the genuine kit). Unsealed 4X4 says to replace the water pump with the belt, or before 150,000 km anyway, and to check the drive-belt idler bearings while you're there. Turn the engine over by hand to confirm the marks before you start it.
Tools: Crank-pulley holder and puller · seal puller · torque wrench · factory manual for torques and marks

#### Clean a carboned-up 1KD intake and EGR, then fit a catch can
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Unsealed 4X4 calls the cleaning 'extremely laborious' · cost HD Automotive's 1KD intake-clean gasket kit lists at AUD $230
Symptoms: Reduced performance and a choked, flat feel on a high-kilometer common-rail diesel.
Fix: Oily exhaust gas fed back through the EGR coats the intake in carbon on any common-rail diesel with EGR, the 1KD included. Remove the intake plumbing and EGR parts, scrape and clean them (or use a chemical clean), and refit with new gaskets. Then fit an oil separator (catch can) so oil mist is trapped before it gets back into the intake. Unsealed points out that blanking the EGR is illegal for road use.
Tools: Metric sockets · scrapers and solvent · new intake gaskets · catch-can kit

#### Front lower ball joints
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day for both sides · cost Parts plus alignment
Symptoms: Torn boots weeping grease, clunks over bumps, vague steering.
Fix: It's the same front end as the GX 470. Support the truck, remove the wheel and separate the lower ball joint from the knuckle and arm. Then either press in a new joint (owners cite MOOG and Sankei 555 replacements) or fit a complete lower arm with joint and bushings. Make sure the grease fitting faces somewhere you can reach, grease the new joint if it came dry, and get an alignment. On KDSS-equipped GX 470s, buy KDSS-specific parts.
Tools: Ball-joint press · joint separator · torque wrench · grease gun

#### Replace a front wheel bearing hub
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2 hours per side · cost A complete hub assembly bolts in, so no press is needed
Symptoms: A growl or vibration from one front corner that changes with speed or load.
Fix: This is the same hub as the GX 470, FJ Cruiser and 4Runner. Pull the dust cap and break the axle nut with a 35 mm socket. Remove the caliper and rotor, then the four 17 mm bolts holding the hub to the knuckle. Once they're cracked loose, switch to an open-end wrench, because the bolts can't come fully out with the hub in place. Knock the hub free, keep or replace the O-ring behind it, and bolt in the new assembly with a new axle nut.
Tools: 35 mm socket · breaker bar · 17 mm open-end wrench · hammer · torque wrench · new axle nut

#### Rear air springs: repair or convert to coils
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2 hours for a simple coil swap · cost Usually cheaper to convert than to buy new air parts, according to GX 470 owners
Symptoms: The rear sags overnight or sits on the bump stops, the compressor runs constantly, and the height-control light blinks.
Fix: Confirm the leak with soapy water where each bag folds over its perch. To stay on air, replace both springs, plus the compressor if it has worn out chasing leaks. To convert, support the axle, remove the shocks, cut the air lines, pop the upper clip on each bag and fit a coil-conversion kit with springs, retainers and isolators. Most kits are sold for the GX 470's identical rear layout, so confirm Prado fitment with the vendor. Recheck bolt torque after 100 miles.
Tools: Floor jack · jack stands · flat screwdriver · line cutters · torque wrench · coil-conversion kit

#### Front CV axle or boots
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours per side · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Grease flung around the inside of the wheel, split boots, clicking on tight turns.
Fix: Loosen the axle nut with the wheel on the ground, then lift the truck. Separate the lower ball joint or tie rod so the knuckle can swing, pull the axle out of the hub and pop the inner joint out of the differential. Fit the new axle (or rebooted original), torque the axle nut, then stake or pin it. Expedition Portal's GX 470 project used factory Toyota axles.
Tools: Axle-nut socket · breaker bar · pry bar · joint separator · torque wrench · new axle nut

### Baseline service
On a 1KD-FTV, 'baseline' starts with the injectors: get the seats and injectors tested or replaced and the oil pickup inspected before you worry about anything else. Specs below are from Roughtrax's KDJ120 (1KD-FTV) data sheet unless noted. 1GR-FE and 2.7 petrol oil capacities are from Penrite's lookup for Australian Prados. 1GR-FE, 1KZ-TE and petrol-four trucks differ, so confirm in the manual for your engine.
- Injector seats, injectors & oil pickup (1KD-FTV): Genuine fitting kit (seats/washers, O-rings) · injectors tested by a diesel specialist · Seals every 40,000 km (Unsealed 4X4) · injectors tested every service and replaced about every 100,000 km (4X4 Australia; AustralianCar.Reviews) (Inspect the pickup screen through the drain-plug hole at the first oil change. Aluminum seats replaced copper from August 2007.)
- Engine oil & filter: 1KD-FTV: 7.4 L with filter, SAE 5W-30, API CF / ACEA B1/B5 · 1GR-FE: 5.2 L with filter · 3RZ-FE 2.7: 5.1 L with filter (Penrite lookup) · petrol grades and other engines [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Every 6,000 mi or 12 months (6 months in severe use) (Unsealed 4X4 suggests 5,000 km changes and quality oil on a 1KD, which helps against cold-start rattle.)
- Timing belt & water pump (1KD-FTV, 1KZ-TE, 5VZ-FE): 1KD: genuine kit (belt, hydraulic tensioner, idler, seals) + Aisin pump · 1GR-FE and 2.7 fours: timing chain · 1KD: 150,000 km or 5 years (HD Automotive, quoting Toyota); Roughtrax's UK sheet gives 100,000 mi or 120 months (The 1KD is an interference engine. Unsealed 4X4 says to do the water pump with the belt, and before 150,000 km either way.)
- Fuel filter (diesel): Diesel filter with water trap [CONFIRM PART BY FRAME NUMBER] · Every 12,000 mi or 12 months (Common-rail injectors hate water and dirt, so this is cheap insurance on a 1KD.)
- Coolant & thermostat: ≈11.0 L (auto) / 11.3 L (manual), less with a viscous heater · Toyota pink Super Long Life or blue Long Life Coolant · Every 20,000 mi or 24 months (Roughtrax) (Watch for a falling level without hose leaks, which on a 1KD usually means the water pump (Unsealed 4X4).)
- Automatic transmission fluid: 3.0 L per drain-and-fill, 10.6 L dry · Toyota T-IV (trucks with a dipstick) or ATF WS (no dipstick) · Then per the owner's manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Check which fluid your gearbox takes before you top up, because WS and T-IV aren't interchangeable.)
- Manual gearbox: 2.2 L, SAE 75W-90, API GL-4 or GL-5 · Every 24,000 mi or 24 months
- Transfer case: 1.4 L, SAE 75W-90, API GL-4 or GL-5 · Every 24,000 mi or 24 months (Torsen center with a lock. Cycle the lock and check that its light comes on and goes off.)
- Front & rear differentials: 75W-90 GL-4/5 · front 1.4 L · rear 3.05 L (5-door), 2.95 L with diff lock, 2.5 L (3-door) · LSD: 3.05 L of LSD-rated hypoid oil · Front every 36,000 mi · rear every 18,000 mi (Australian GX/GXL trucks have a rear LSD (ExplorOz), so use LSD-rated oil.)
- Power steering fluid: 1.0 L, Dexron II/III ATF · Refresh if dark (Check the steering-rack boots for splits while you're under the front.)
- Brake & clutch fluid: 1.2 L, DOT 3 or DOT 4 (SAE J1703/4) · Brakes every 18,000 mi · clutch every 24,000 mi
- Propshaft grease points: Lithium-base NLGI No. 2 · Every 6,000 mi or 6 months (3,000 mi or 3 months in severe use)
- Front end: ball joints, CV boots, hubs: Inspect for play, torn boots and bearing noise · At every service (Shared with the GX 470. The sway-bar D-bushings are a cheap refresh while you're there.)
- Rear air suspension (if fitted): Air springs, compressor, height sensor · Check that it levels and holds height overnight (Fitted to the Australian Grande and top Japanese grades. If the bags leak, a GX 470-type coil conversion is the common fix.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: The stock size is 265/65R17 on a 7.5Jx17 +30 wheel. ExplorOz owners run 265/70R17 'with no rubbing issues', which matches the GX 470 consensus on the same chassis. 285/70R17 (about 33 in) needs at least a 50 mm (2 in) lift and +50 offset wheels, or some trimming of the body mount behind the mud flap. On 16-inch wheels, a 265/70R16 is a common upsize, but one owner says 16s may need caliper grinding on a 120.

Q: Can I import one into the US?
A: Not yet. NHTSA's 25-year exemption runs from the date of manufacture, and 120 production started in September 2002, so the first trucks qualify from September 2027 and the last (August 2009) in 2034. Canada's 15-year rule already covers every J120, but a Canadian-registered Prado still has to be 25 to come south.

Q: Is a Prado 120 just a Lexus GX 470?
A: Same platform, different truck. The GX 470 got the 4.7 V8, plusher trim and US-market equipment; the Prado got fours, V6s and diesels, and Australian versions got a 93-liter sub tank. Suspension, hubs, ball joints, CV axles and much of the armor are shared, which is why IH8MUD runs them in one forum.

Q: What's the 1KD-FTV injector problem?
A: The original injector seats were copper and leak with age. Blow-by then mixes with the oil, forms carbon and can block the sump pickup, starving the engine. Aluminum seats replaced copper from August 2007. Separately, injectors often fail at 120,000–140,000 km. Check the seat history, look for white smoke or a rattle on a cold start, and inspect the pickup through the drain-plug hole.

Q: Which engine should I buy?
A: The 1GR-FE 4.0 V6 (179 kW) is the durable, chain-driven choice. 4X4 Australia says V6s have passed 300,000 km, but it's thirsty: 13.6 L/100 km officially and up to 18 in owners' hands. The 1KD-FTV diesel (127 kW and 410 Nm from 2006) is the tow rig, but only with injector-seat records. The 1KZ-TE has 96 kW and indirect injection, so it's simpler but slower.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: For a V6, anything from late 2005: 4X4 Australia says to skip the earlier four-speed autos and buy a five-speed. For the 1KD-FTV diesel, AustralianCar.Reviews says aluminium injector seats replaced the failure-prone copper ones from August 2007, so a later truck, or an earlier one with receipts for new seats, is the safer buy. 4X4 Australia calls the 2006–08 trucks the high point of the model's reputation. Either way, service records beat the build date.

Q: Does it have lockers?
A: Every 120 has a Torsen limited-slip center differential with a lock, plus Active TRC. According to ExplorOz owners, Australian GX and GXL grades had a rear LSD, while VX and Grande had an open rear diff and relied on traction control. A rear diff lock shows up in some markets' specs, but ARB Air Lockers are the usual retrofit.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: 4X4 Australia calls the 2006–2008 trucks' 2,500 kg (5,512 lb) braked rating 'low'. If you tow, the diesel's torque is the reason to buy one.

Q: What fluids and capacities does a KDJ120 take?
A: Per Roughtrax's 1KD 120 sheet: engine oil 7.4 L with filter (5W-30); coolant about 11 L of Toyota pink Super Long Life or blue Long Life; automatic 3.0 L per drain-and-fill (10.6 L dry), T-IV if it has a dipstick and WS if not; manual 2.2 L and transfer case 1.4 L of 75W-90; front diff 1.4 L; rear 3.05 L on a five-door (2.95 L with a diff lock), with LSD oil in an LSD; power steering 1.0 L of Dexron II/III. Confirm against your manual.

Q: How big are the fuel tanks?
A: Australian five-doors carry 180 L in total: an 87-liter main tank plus a 93-liter sub tank. Three-doors have only the 87-liter tank, and Roughtrax lists a 95-liter tank for UK five-doors.

Q: Should I keep the rear air suspension?
A: It rides well while it's healthy, but the bags and compressor are wear items, and 4X4 Australia warns that air makes aftermarket suspension much harder and more expensive. Most owners who lift convert to coils with kits built for the GX 470's identical rear end.
