## Toyota Land Cruiser 200 Series (2007–2021)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/200-series/
Codes: UZJ200, VDJ200

Verdict: The 200 is a nearly three-ton bank vault with a 5.7-liter V8 and a crawl-control button, and it is far better in the dirt than anything with a heated steering wheel has any right to be. It was also the last of its kind in America: when it left after 2021, the big V8 Land Cruiser went with it.

Toyota launched the 200 Series in late 2007 with a new frame and platform, bigger brakes, a strengthened front suspension, skid plates and roof pillars redesigned for rollover protection. In the US it came with one engine, the 5.7-liter 3UR-FE V8 at 381 hp, in a single trim level. Sadayoshi Koyari, the lead engineer known as 'Mr Land Cruiser', famously called it (as Unsealed 4X4 recounts) 'the strongest Land Cruiser ever produced by Toyota.' Fourteen years later Toyota pulled the Land Cruiser from North America, and the 200 became the last full-size Land Cruiser wagon sold there.

### A FIVE-YEAR PLAN
Work on a successor to the 100 Series began in 2002 under Koyari and Tetsuya Tada. A production design was settled in 2004, ten years after the 100's, and prototypes were tested for more than two years, from 2004 to early 2007. Production started in September 2007 at Toyota's Yoshiwara and Tahara plants. In Venezuela it went on sale that November under the nickname 'Roraima', after Mount Roraima.
Underneath, it shared its platform with the Lexus LX 570 and was related to the Tundra and Sequoia of the same era. The global range was huge: a 4.0 V6, three petrol V8s and the 4.5-liter 1VD-FTV twin-turbo diesel V8, a twin-turbo version of the engine in the 70 Series. Unsealed 4X4 says the diesel made up about 90 percent of 200 sales in Australia.

### ELECTRONICS THAT EARN THEIR KEEP
The 200 brought a set of off-road aids no previous Land Cruiser had. CRAWL works like off-road cruise control, holding a slow, steady speed with throttle and brakes. There was also Downhill Assist Control, a multi-terrain ABS calibration, and KDSS, the Kinetic Dynamic Suspension System, which frees up wheel articulation off-road while keeping body roll in check on the highway. US trucks used an AB60F six-speed automatic, a JF2A full-time transfer case and 3.90 gears.
There was no 2012 model year in the US. Slee notes that 2011 production ran late and the 2013s started early. The 2013 facelift added Multi-Terrain Select with five modes, Turn Assist for tight trails, and front, side and rear cameras. For 2016 came the biggest change: an AE80F eight-speed automatic, taller 3.30 gears, larger front brakes, Toyota Safety Sense and new styling front and rear.

### HOW IT ENDED
To mark 60 years since the FJ40, Toyota built the Heritage Edition for 2020 and 2021. It was a two-row truck in black or white with bronze BBS forged wheels, a Yakima MegaWarrior basket, no running boards and a vintage Land Cruiser badge on the rear pillars. Wikipedia puts the 2020 run at 1,200 trucks. In December 2020 Toyota told Road & Track the Land Cruiser would leave North America after 2021, and production ended in March 2021.
Elsewhere the 300 Series took over. Americans waited until 2024, when the name came back on the smaller, Prado-based 250 Series. The LX 570 also ended in 2021, and Lexus replaced it with the LX 600. For American buyers who want a big V8 Land Cruiser wagon with a frame under it, the 200 is the last one.

### Data plate
- Chassis: J200 (URJ200 US · VDJ200 · UZJ200 · GRJ200)
- Production: September 2007 – March 2021
- Us Model Years: 2008–2011, 2013–2021 (no 2012)
- Engine (Us): 3UR-FE 5,663 cc DOHC 32v V8
- Output: 381 hp @ 5,600 · 401 lb-ft @ 3,600
- Transmission (Us): 6-spd AB60F; 8-spd AE80F from 2016
- Drive: Full-time 4WD, lockable center diff (JF2A)
- Wheelbase: 112.2 in (2,850 mm)
- Length: 194.9 in ('21)
- Curb Weight: 5,690–5,815 lb
- Ground Clearance: 8.9–9.1 in
- Fuel Tank: 24.6 gal
- Towing: 8,100–8,500 lb

### Engineering
The 200 is built on a new, stronger frame with independent front suspension and a coil-sprung live rear axle. The clever part is KDSS, a system that frees up articulation off-road and stiffens the truck on the road. US trucks use the 5.7-liter 3UR-FE, a 32-valve DOHC, chain-driven V8 with dual VVT-i, and full-time four-wheel drive with a lockable center differential.
- Chassis: New ladder frame, 112.2 in wheelbase (Stronger front suspension, skid plates and reinforced roof pillars. Shares its platform with the LX 570.)
- Suspension: IFS front, coil-sprung live rear axle, KDSS (KDSS has two lock valves (5 mm hex). They are opened during suspension work and must be closed again afterward.)
- 4Wd System: Full-time, JF2A transfer case (Lockable center differential. Slee's US spec list includes no factory axle lockers.)
- Off-Road Aids: CRAWL, Downhill Assist, multi-terrain ABS (2013 added five-mode Multi-Terrain Select, Turn Assist and multi-terrain cameras.)
- Engine (Us): 3UR-FE 5.7 L DOHC 32v V8 (381 hp @ 5,600 rpm, 401 lb-ft @ 3,600 rpm. Chain-driven cams, dual VVT-i.)
- Transmission: AB60F 6-speed (2008–15) / AE80F 8-speed (2016–21) (Axle ratio went from 3.90 to 3.30 with the eight-speed.)

### Versions
- 2008–2015 (US) · URJ200 · 3UR-FE 5.7 L V8 · 381 hp / 401 lb-ft · AB60F six-speed, 3.90 gears. No 2012 model year in the US; 2013 facelift added MTS and cameras.
- 2016–2021 (US) · URJ200 · 3UR-FE 5.7 L V8 · 381 hp / 401 lb-ft · AE80F eight-speed, 3.30 gears, bigger front brakes. Heritage Edition 2020–21.
- 2007–2012 · UZJ200 · 2UZ-FE 4.7 L V8 · 271 hp / 410 Nm · Early petrol V8 in Australia and Hong Kong; also the Middle East and Japan at launch.
- 2009–2021 · URJ202 · 1UR-FE 4.6 L V8 · 313–318 hp / 460 Nm · Replaced the 2UZ in Japan in 2009 and in several other markets later.
- 2007–2021 · VDJ200 · 1VD-FTV 4.5 L twin-turbo diesel V8 · Up to 268 hp / 650 Nm · The global favorite. Piezo injectors and a DPF arrived with the 2015 update. Never sold in the US.
- 2007–2021 · GRJ200 · 1GR-FE 4.0 L V6 · — · Entry engine in the Middle East and elsewhere. The only 200 offered with a five-speed manual.
- 2008–2021 (US) · Lexus LX 570 · 3UR-FE 5.7 L V8 · 383 hp / 403 lb-ft (Lexus rating) · AHC and adaptive damping standard; spindle grille from 2013.

### Year-by-year
- 2008: 200 Series launches in the US (production from September 2007) with the 5.7 L 3UR-FE V8 and 6-speed automatic, KDSS, CRAWL control and a new, stronger frame
- 2008–2011: Model years covered by the floor-mat pedal and TPMS recalls
- 2013: First facelift (released December 2011): previously optional kit made standard; Multi-Terrain Select, Multi-Terrain Monitor, Off-Road Turn Assist and Trailer Sway Control added. Unsealed 4X4 calls 2012–15 the sweet spot for many buyers, and IH8MUD owners point US shoppers to 2013–15 trucks [buy]
- 2015–16: Diesel markets only: the late-2015 facelift adds a DPF to the 1VD-FTV V8. Unsealed 4X4 reports DPF trouble and a Toyota recall on 2015–16 diesels. US petrol trucks never had a DPF [avoid]
- 2016: Second facelift: 8-speed automatic, larger front brakes, 3.30:1 axle ratio in place of 3.90:1, new nose and tail lights, bigger screens
- 2018–2019: Model years covered by the Denso fuel-pump recall
- 2020: Heritage Edition for the FJ40's 60th anniversary: 1,200 built for the 2020 model year, five seats, US only
- 2021: Final US model year; the 300 Series is not sold in North America, and the nameplate returns on the smaller 250 for 2024

### Capability
- Towing: 8,100 lb (3,674 kg) (2016–2021 per KBB; 8,500 lb for 2008, 8,200 lb for 2015)
- Payload: 1,320 lb (599 kg) (2021, KBB)
- Fuel tank: 24.6 US gal (93 L) (KBB)
- Ground clearance: 8.9 in (226 mm) (2021, KBB)
- Fuel economy: EPA 13 city / 17 hwy / 14 combined (2021) (KBB; most earlier years 13/18/15)
- Curb weight: 5,815 lb (2,638 kg); 5,715 lb Heritage Edition (2021, KBB)
- Turning circle: 38.7 ft (11.8 m) diameter (2021, KBB)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 285/60R18 (US)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x150
- Center Bore: 110 mm
- Lug Thread: M14x1.5
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 285/65R18 (IH8MUD: fits with zero rubbing. 285/70R18 rubs a bit but is manageable; 275/70s are the 'tried and true' size.)
- Biggest tire, 2.5–3 in lift: 285/75R17 or LT285/70R18 (about 34 in) (A common size on lifted trucks in the forum's 35-inch roll call, usually with aftermarket upper control arms and wheels.)
- Biggest tire, 3 in lift: 35x12.50R17 (Owners report front mud flaps removed, a Slee KDSS relocation, light fender-liner trimming and aftermarket wheels. Without those, 35s rub on the stock upper control arms and KDSS arms. One set measured just over 34 inches mounted.)

### Buying checks
- Look for pink crust at the water pump: Dried pink coolant running down the front of the engine from the water-pump weep hole is the classic 3UR sign. One owner's build thread notes the engine is known for water-pump weeps around 100,000 miles, and that the pump usually gives plenty of warning.
- Scan for air-injection codes: A check-engine light with VSC and traction-control lights on together often turns out to be the secondary air-injection system, such as code P2438 for the pressure sensor. It's emissions-related and the truck drives normally, but a seller who has cleared codes is hiding a repair.
- If the suspension has been touched, check the KDSS valves: After a lift or shock swap, the two KDSS valves must be closed again. One IH8MUD owner found a shop had left them fully open and the truck rolled alarmingly on uneven roads. Check them with a 5 mm hex key, and test-drive on a winding road.
- Listen for a driveline clunk: A thunk when stopping and pulling away usually isn't the transmission. Unsealed 4X4 traces it to dry universal joints, especially on trucks that cross water. Ask when the driveshafts were last greased.
- Check the oil filter cap: The 3UR has a plastic oil filter housing cap that wrenches round off and that can warp or crack with age. Look for leaks and chewed edges.
- Know which phase you're buying: 2008–2011: six-speed, 3.90 gears. 2013–2015: facelift with Multi-Terrain Select, Turn Assist and cameras. 2016–2021: eight-speed, 3.30 gears, bigger brakes, Toyota Safety Sense. There's no 2012 in the US.
- Ask about towing: KBB lists 8,500 lb for 2008 and 8,100 lb for 2016–2021. A truck that pulled a heavy trailer for years deserves a closer look at the transmission fluid, the brakes and the rear springs.
- Diesel (non-US) 200s: injectors, DPF and airbox: On the 1VD-FTV, Unsealed's big three are injector problems (rough idle, smoke, poor economy), DPF and EGR trouble on 2015-on trucks, and dust getting past the airbox seal.

### Common repairs
#### Replace a weeping water pump
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A few hours · cost Pump and gasket plus coolant; one owner paid for 'a few hours of shop time'
Symptoms: Dried pink coolant trailing down the front of the engine from the water-pump weep hole, and a slowly dropping coolant level.
Fix: Following the factory manual, drain the coolant, remove the fan, drive belt and anything else in front of the pump, then fit the new pump with a new gasket. Refill and bleed the cooling system. The build-thread owner also replaced the fan bracket, because its bearing had been sitting in leaking coolant.
Tools: Basic metric sockets · belt tool · coolant catch tub · Aisin water pump and gasket · Toyota long-life coolant · fan bracket if contaminated.

#### Diagnose secondary air-injection faults
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 1–3 hours to diagnose · cost Parts plus labor; sensor first, pumps and valves cost more
Symptoms: A check-engine light, often with the slip light flashing and 'Check VSC' on, that may come and go, especially in cold or damp weather. Codes such as P2438 (pressure sensor circuit high, bank 2). Owners on Tundra sites also report P2440–P2443.
Fix: Read the code before you buy parts. IH8MUD members point to the factory description for P2438: pressure in the air-injection system is above its threshold, so suspects are the pressure sensor, its wiring or the ECM. If the light clears on its own, start with the sensor and wiring. Because the 3UR also powers the Tundra and Sequoia, their forums are a good source of fixes. Toyota extended warranty coverage on this system for 2007–2010 Tundras and 2008–2010 Sequoias; the Land Cruiser wasn't named.
Tools: OBD-II scanner with Toyota enhanced codes · multimeter · factory wiring diagram.

#### Close the KDSS valves after suspension work
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 15 minutes · cost Free
Symptoms: Alarming body roll on uneven roads, or a truck that feels wrong right after a lift or shock install.
Fix: Chock the wheels and get under the truck. The two KDSS valves are opened during suspension work and must be closed again afterward. Find both valves and confirm they're closed with a 5 mm hex key. If anyone has worked on the suspension, check them before your next drive.
Tools: 5 mm hex key · wheel chocks · torch.

#### Grease the driveshaft U-joints
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 30 minutes · cost A tube of grease
Symptoms: A clunk when you come to a stop, as if you'd nudged the car ahead, and another clunk when you pull away.
Fix: Unsealed 4X4 says the clunk is usually dry universal joints, not the transmission or the differentials. Grease washes out in water crossings and breaks down under heavy crawling. Grease every U-joint and slip joint on both driveshafts about every six months, and again after deep water. If the clunk is still there, then start looking at the drivetrain.
Tools: Grease gun with a needle or angled coupler · quality chassis grease · creeper.

#### Swap to an aluminum oil filter cap
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 20 minutes at an oil change · cost About half the $60+ retail price of the plastic cap, per IH8MUD
Symptoms: A plastic cap that rounds off, lets the wrench slip, warps or cracks after many heat cycles.
Fix: An IH8MUD member found the aluminum cap from the Venza 3.5 V6 fits once you move over the internal parts. Bend up the two small tabs on the Land Cruiser cap's perforated support tube, push down, turn it about 45 degrees and lift it out. Watch for the spring and the drain-valve disc underneath. Fit the tube into the aluminum cap the same way and bend the tabs flat. Refill the oil, start the engine and check for weeps.
Tools: Flat screwdriver · cap-type filter wrench · aluminum cap 15620-31060 (as listed in the IH8MUD thread).

#### Add rear air helper springs for towing
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2 hours on a lift · cost $200–250 for one IH8MUD owner
Symptoms: Almost 4 inches of sag at the hitch with a 5,000 lb trailer and about 600 lb of tongue weight, even with weight distribution set up.
Fix: Raise and support the rear, then disconnect the rear shocks so the axle can drop. Fit the air bags inside the rear coil springs, route the air lines away from heat, and add an onboard compressor with a union tee if you want to adjust them from the cab. Reconnect the shocks; the owner needed a long steel bar to compress the suspension enough to line them up. Run about 35 psi when towing.
Tools: Jack stands · long pry bar · Firestone 4164 air-bag kit · Air Lift 25804 compressor · Air Lift 21838 union tee · RTV · zip ties · marine grease.

#### Seal the airbox (1VD diesel)
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 15 minutes to check · cost Free to check; an aftermarket airbox costs more
Symptoms: Red dust on the clean side of the filter, MAF faults, limp mode and, in bad cases, a failed right-hand turbo.
Fix: Pop the airbox lid and check under the filter. Some mechanics grease the filter's sealing surface, but Unsealed would fit an aftermarket airbox that seals properly. If dust has got in, clean the MAF and check the turbo for shaft play.
Tools: Screwdriver · torch · MAF cleaner · grease or an aftermarket airbox.

#### Replace leaking injectors (1VD diesel)
Difficulty 5 / 5 · time ≈ A long day or more · cost About A$4,000 in parts for a DIY job, plus a few thousand more for labor, per Unsealed
Symptoms: Rough idle, smoke, poor fuel economy, sludge in the intake and DPF trouble, often caused by leaking injector seat washers.
Fix: Unsealed's advice is to replace all eight injectors with updated seat washers rather than one at a time, because single replacements often failed again within months. Do it under warranty where possible. Out of warranty, many specialists will do it for less than a dealer.
Tools: Workshop manual · injector puller · new injectors and updated washers (all eight) · a diagnostic tool to code the injectors.

### Baseline service
Assume nothing was done. The 200 is easy to keep alive, but 'lifetime' fluids, dry U-joints and a weeping water pump are common on high-mileage trucks. Specs below are for the US 3UR-FE V8. Intervals come from Toyota's 2021 Warranty & Maintenance Guide; capacities come from AMSOIL's lookup for a 2020 truck (8-speed). Trucks from 2008–2015 have the 6-speed AB60F, and the 1VD diesel is different again, so check capacities against your manual.
- Engine oil & filter: SAE 0W-20 · ≈7.9 qt with filter · drain plug 30 ft-lb · Then every 10,000 mi / 12 months (Toyota); 5,000 mi in dusty or towing use (Cartridge filter under a plastic cap that's easy to round off. See the aluminum-cap swap above. Replace the cap O-ring with every change.)
- Engine air filter: OE-type panel filter · Every 30,000 mi (Toyota); inspect every 5,000 mi on dirt roads (Check that the airbox lid seals and look for dust on the clean side.)
- Cabin air filter: OE-type · Clean at 15,000 mi, replace every 30,000 mi (Toyota)
- Spark plugs: 8 × OE-type iridium (3UR-FE) · Every 120,000 mi (Toyota); replace at purchase if the history is unknown and the truck is near that mileage (Check the spark-plug tube seals for oil while the coils are out.)
- Coolant: Toyota Super Long Life Coolant (pink, pre-mixed) or equivalent · ≈17.1 qt system · First at 100,000 mi / 120 months, then every 50,000 mi / 60 months (Toyota) (Look for dried pink crust at the water-pump weep hole and fan bracket. See the water pump repair above.)
- Automatic transmission: Toyota Genuine ATF WS · 8-speed AE80F ≈10.7 qt total fill · Toyota specifies replacement at 60,000 mi only for towing or heavy loads, otherwise inspection only. Most owners drain-and-fill at purchase. (There's no dipstick. The level is set at a specified fluid temperature through the overflow (check) plug. A drain-and-fill replaces only part of the fluid, so repeat it rather than pressure-flushing. 2008–2015 trucks use the 6-speed AB60F: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] for capacity.)
- Transfer case: Toyota Genuine Transfer Gear Oil LF, SAE 75W (owner-reported; AMSOIL's lookup lists no transfer-case spec) · [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] for spec and capacity · Replace under Toyota's special operating conditions (dirt roads, towing); otherwise inspect. Change at purchase if there's no record. (Use the transfer-case oil your manual names; it is a light 75W oil, not ordinary 75W-90 gear oil. Toyota's guide lists replacement for dirt-road and towing use.)
- Front & rear differentials: Toyota Genuine Differential Gear Oil LT 75W-85 GL-5 · front ≈4 pt, rear ≈8.9 pt · Front every 15,000 mi and both at 30,000 mi when towing or heavily loaded (Toyota); otherwise inspect (Always crack the fill plug before draining. Fit new plug gaskets.)
- Driveshaft grease points: Lithium chassis grease at every U-joint and slip yoke · Every 15,000 mi, with a propeller-shaft bolt re-torque (Toyota). Also after deep water. (Dry U-joints cause a clunk on stop and take-off. See the U-joint repair above.)
- KDSS: Sealed hydraulic system: no fluid service · At purchase and after any suspension work (Make sure both KDSS valves are closed (5 mm hex) and check the cylinders and lines for weeping. See the KDSS repair above.)
- Power steering fluid: Dexron III-type ATF · Inspect the level and condition (Toyota); [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] for the exact fluid (Look for wet hoses at the pump.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 (FMVSS 116) · Toyota lists inspection only. Flush at purchase if there's no record.
- Drive belt & tensioner: Serpentine belt with automatic tensioner · Inspect at 60,000 mi, then every 15,000 mi (Toyota) (Replace the belt if you're doing the water pump and the fan is already off.)
- 12 V battery: OE-size battery · Load-test at purchase (Weak batteries cause odd electronic faults on these trucks.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: On IH8MUD, one owner says 285/65R18 'will fit fine with zero rubbing' on a stock truck and 285/70R18 'will rub a bit but should be manageable'; others in the same thread report the 285/70 needs heat-gunning and trimming of the plastic, so treat 285/65R18 as the no-work size. One owner running 285/70R17s on aftermarket wheels reported light rubbing on the plastic liner, fixed with a heat gun. The tire-database thread calls 275/70s 'tried and true'. For anything bigger, check the forum's 200 Series Tire and Wheel Size Database.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: KBB lists 8,500 lb for 2008, 8,200 lb for 2015 and 8,100 lb for 2016–2021. An IH8MUD owner with a 2013 quotes 8,500 lb with an 850 lb maximum tongue weight. Weight distribution helps the short 112-inch wheelbase, and rear air helpers fix sag.

Q: Six-speed or eight-speed?
A: 2008–2015 trucks have the AB60F six-speed with 3.90 gears. 2016–2021 trucks have the AE80F eight-speed with 3.30 gears and bigger front brakes. If you plan big tires on an eight-speed truck, re-gearing (Nitro's 4.88s are a common choice) restores the lost low-end response.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: Unsealed 4X4 says many buyers see 2012–15 as the sweet spot: updated over the early trucks, but before the DPF that arrived on diesels in late 2015. On IH8MUD, owners point US shoppers to 2013–15 trucks, which have taken most of the depreciation, while 2016–21 add the eight-speed and more safety kit (one owner adds that the eight-speed didn't improve fuel economy much). Unsealed's last word applies everywhere: service history matters more than the model year.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: KBB lists 13 mpg city and 18 highway (15 combined) for most years, and 13/17 (14 combined) for 2021, on a 24.6-gallon tank. Toyota's 2013 press release specifies regular 87 AKI gasoline, not premium.

Q: Does it have lockers?
A: US trucks have full-time four-wheel drive with a lockable center differential, plus A-TRAC, CRAWL and (from 2013) Multi-Terrain Select. Front and rear lockers are aftermarket; ARB Air Lockers and Harrop E-lockers are both common in IH8MUD build signatures.

Q: What is KDSS, and does it complicate a lift?
A: The Kinetic Dynamic Suspension System lets the wheels articulate more off-road while controlling body roll on the road. It complicates lifts a little: the KDSS valves are opened during suspension work and must be closed afterward. IH8MUD has a warning thread from an owner whose shop left them open.

Q: Was there a diesel in the US?
A: No. North America only ever got the 5.7-liter 3UR-FE petrol V8. The 4.5-liter twin-turbo 1VD-FTV diesel was sold in Australia, Europe, the Middle East and elsewhere.

Q: What breaks?
A: On US 3UR trucks: water pumps around 100,000 miles, secondary air-injection faults, plastic oil filter caps and dry U-joints. On diesels: injectors, the DPF and EGR on 2015-on trucks, and dust past the airbox. Unsealed also notes some 200s have a vibration that owners argue about.

Q: What's special about the Heritage Edition?
A: Built for 2020 and 2021 to mark 60 years since the FJ40: two rows of seats, black or white paint, bronze BBS forged wheels, a Yakima MegaWarrior basket, no running boards or side moldings, and a vintage Land Cruiser badge. Wikipedia says 1,200 were built for the 2020 model year.

Q: Why did Toyota stop selling it in the US?
A: In December 2020 Toyota told Road & Track that the Land Cruiser would end in North America after 2021. The name came back in 2024 on the smaller 250 Series, and the 300 Series flagship isn't sold in the US.

Q: Is the Lexus LX 570 the same truck?
A: It shares the platform and the 3UR-FE (Lexus rates it at 383 hp and 403 lb-ft), but the LX 570 adds standard AHC height control and adaptive damping, 20-inch wheels and a lot more leather.

## Toyota FJ Cruiser (2007–2014 (US) · to 2022 elsewhere)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/fj-cruiser/
Codes: XJ10, GSJ15, 1GR-FE 4.0 V6

Verdict: Toyota took the FJ40's face, bolted it to a Prado-family frame and gave it a rear locker. The blind spots are enormous and the back seat is for close friends only, but few new trucks of the 2000s went further off the pavement without a single aftermarket part.

The FJ Cruiser began as a show car. Toyota unveiled the concept, painted Voodoo Blue, at the Detroit auto show in January 2003, showed the production version at Chicago in February 2005, and had its subsidiary Hino Motors start building it at Hamura, Japan, in January 2006. Underneath was a ladder frame closely related to the Land Cruiser Prado's; on top sat a cartoon of the FJ40, white roof and all. America got it for model years 2007 through 2014. Other markets kept it until a 1,000-unit Final Edition for the Middle East closed out production in December 2022.

### A FORTY FOR A NEW CENTURY
By the time FJ40 production ended in 1984, the Land Cruiser had grown bigger and plusher. According to Larry Edsall's book on the truck, the idea of a new FJ with the old one's toughness came from product planner Dave Danzer and sales vice-president Yoshi Inaba in the mid-1990s. Danzer and Akio Toyoda quietly set up a shop at the NUMMI plant to test it, putting the bodies of Brazilian Toyota Bandeirantes, which descended from the FJ40, on Tacoma underpinnings. Toyota's Calty design studio in California then took over.
Inside Toyota the project was called the Rugged Youth Utility, aimed at young male buyers the company felt it was losing. Several concepts were tried before a retro design by Jin Won Kim, a 24-year-old Calty designer, won, with William Chergosky drawing the interior. The FJ40 cues are everywhere: a near-vertical windshield with three wipers, TOYOTA spelled out across the grille instead of the corporate badge, round headlights and a white roof. Rear-hinged access doors replaced the B-pillars, and high-strength steel took over their side-impact job.

### DEVELOPED ON THE RUBICON
From mid-2004 Toyota ran development mules over the hardest trails it could find, including Moab, the Angeles National Forest, the Mojave Desert and the Rubicon, and retuned the A-TRAC traction control and the suspension as a result. Underneath, the FJ shares hardware with the 120-series Prado, the 4th-gen 4Runner and the GX 470: double-wishbone front suspension, a four-link coil-sprung rear axle with a lateral rod, and the 4.0-liter 1GR-FE V6. A 4x4 FJ has 9.6 inches of ground clearance and, Toyota says, can wade 28 inches of water.
The drivetrain choice is the interesting part. The six-speed manual came only with full-time 4WD: a Torsen center differential splits torque 40:60, locks at 50:50, and 3.909 axle gears give a 41.84:1 crawl ratio. The five-speed automatic got part-time 4WD, 3.727 gears and a 33.76:1 crawl ratio, and was also sold as a 4x2. Toyota's 2014 specifications list the rear electric locker as standard with the manual and optional with the automatic, and A-TRAC as part of an option package on 4x4s.

### THE PRICE OF STYLE
The styling that sold the truck also held it back. Reviewers praised its off-road ability and criticized its huge blind spots, small cargo area and cramped, awkward rear seat. Toyota added an optional backup camera for 2009 and new front-seat hinges for easier rear access in 2011. US sales fell from 56,225 in 2006 to 11,941 in 2009, and critics blamed rising fuel prices, more competition in the segment and the Jeep Wrangler.
Toyota's answer for 2010 was a dual VVT-i version of the 1GR-FE, with 259 hp on 87-octane fuel instead of 239 hp on 91, and slightly better economy. Early trucks also had a structural problem. The inner fender aprons in the engine bay of 2007 and some early 2008 trucks could bulge and crack, and Toyota changed the design. Owners still report cracked aprons on early trucks, so that's the first thing to look for when you open the hood.

### HOW IT ENDED
From 2008, Toyota built short runs of Trail Teams Special Editions, each in one color with blacked-out trim, TRD wheels and Bilstein shocks. On 5 November 2013 it announced that 2014 would be the last US model year, and the final Trail Teams truck became the Ultimate Edition: 2,500 built in Heritage Blue with a white grille surround, remote-reservoir rear Bilsteins, an aluminum front skid plate and, on automatics, CRAWL control. By the end of 2013, US sales alone had passed 200,000.
Production continued for other markets. Exports to Australia ended in August 2016, Japan got a Final Edition in September 2017 and stopped sales in January 2018, and the Middle East Final Edition closed production in December 2022. Toyota reused the name, though not the formula, for the 2026 Land Cruiser FJ, a smaller Hilux-based truck with a 2.7-liter four that isn't planned for North America. The original is now a collectible: on Bring a Trailer in late 2026, prices ran from $12,500 to more than $56,000.

### Data plate
- Chassis: XJ10 (GSJ15 4x4 · GSJ10 4x2)
- Production: January 2006 – December 2022, Hino, Hamura
- Us Model Years: 2007–2014
- Engine: 1GR-FE 4.0 L DOHC V6
- Output: 239 hp (2007–09) · 259–260 hp (2010–14)
- Transmission: 6-spd manual RA61F · 5-spd auto A750F/A750E
- Drive: Full-time 4WD (manual) · part-time 4WD or 4x2 (auto)
- Axle Ratio: 3.909 (manual) · 3.727 (auto 4x4)
- Wheelbase: 105.9 in (2,690 mm)
- Ground Clearance: 9.6 in (4x4)
- Fuel Tank: 19 gal
- Towing: 5,000 lb; 4,700 lb (2014, SAE J2807)

### Engineering
The FJ Cruiser is a body-on-frame truck built from Toyota's mid-size Prado family of parts: independent double-wishbone front suspension, a four-link coil-sprung live rear axle and the 4.0-liter 1GR-FE V6. What's underneath depends on the gearbox. Manual trucks have full-time 4WD with a lockable Torsen center differential. Automatics have part-time 4WD, with an electric actuator that connects the front axle when you shift into four-wheel drive.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, 105.9 in wheelbase (Similar, but not identical, to the two-door Prado's. Rear-hinged access doors and no B-pillar.)
- Suspension: Double wishbone front, 4-link coil rear (7.87 in front and 9.1 in rear wheel travel (2014 spec). Parts shared with the Prado 120, 4Runner, Tacoma and Hilux.)
- 4Wd · Manual: Full-time, Torsen center diff (VF4B) (40:60 split, 50:50 locked. 3.909 gears for a 41.84:1 crawl ratio.)
- 4Wd · Automatic: Part-time (VF2A), front axle disconnect (3.727 gears, 33.76:1 crawl ratio. Both transfer cases have a 2.566 low range.)
- Engine: 1GR-FE 4.0 L DOHC V6 (239 hp / 278 lb-ft on 91 octane (2007–09). Dual VVT-i from 2010: 259–260 hp on 87.)
- Traction: Rear e-locker, A-TRAC (Locker standard with the manual, optional with the automatic (2014 spec). 8-inch ring gears front and rear.)

- 2010–2014 (US) · GSJ15 4x4 / GSJ10 4x2 · 1GR-FE 4.0 V6, dual VVT-i · 259 hp / 270 lb-ft (2010); 260 hp / 271 lb-ft (2011–14) · Runs on regular. Trail Teams editions every year; CRAWL control on 2013–14 Trail Teams automatics.

### Year-by-year
- 2003: FJ Cruiser concept shown in Voodoo Blue at the Detroit auto show
- 2005: Production version shown at the Chicago auto show in February; Hino starts building it at Hamura in January 2006
- 2007: Launch: 239-hp 1GR-FE on premium, six-speed manual (full-time 4WD) or five-speed automatic; 3,200 TRD Special Editions. CarGurus says owners report far more problems with 2007s than any other year, and inner fender aprons on early trucks can bulge and crack. IH8MUD owners add that some builds before February 2007 had a brittle rear ring and pinion [avoid]
- 2008: Side curtain and torso airbags standard; first Trail Teams Special Edition (Iceberg, 3,200 built)
- 2009: Optional backup camera; no Trail Teams edition, a TRD package instead. US sales fall to 11,941
- 2010: Dual VVT-i 1GR-FE: 259 hp on regular fuel, slightly better economy, and a slightly larger rear diff. CarGurus ties the fender-apron bulge mainly to 2007–09 trucks, so 2010–14 are the years owners usually steer buyers toward [buy]
- 2011: 260 hp; new front-seat hinges for easier rear-seat access; RHD sales begin in Australia and New Zealand
- 2013: CRAWL control on Trail Teams automatics; access-door panel recall covers 2007–2013 trucks
- 2014: Final US model year; 2,500 Trail Teams Ultimate Editions in Heritage Blue
- 2016–2018: Australian exports end in August 2016; Japan Final Edition in September 2017, Japanese sales end January 2018
- 2022: Middle East Final Edition (1,000 units); production ends in December

- Payload: 1,272 lb (577 kg) (2014, KBB)

- Fuel economy: EPA 17 city / 20 hwy (2014 auto 4x4); 15 / 18 (2014 manual) (2007–09 4x4s 14–16 city / 18–20 hwy on premium)
- Curb weight: 4,295 lb (1,948 kg) (2014 base spec, KBB)
- Turning circle: 40.7 ft (12.4 m) (2014, KBB)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: P265/70R17 on 17-inch steel or alloy wheels (standard, per Toyota's 2014 specs), 265/75R16 / LT265/75R16 BFGoodrich on 16-inch TRD wheels (TRD and Trail Teams trucks)
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Center Bore: 106.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M12x1.5
- Lug Torque: 83 lb-ft (113 N·m)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 285/70R17 (about 33 x 11 in) (One owner's only rubbed the driver's-side mud flap under compression, cured by heating and flattening it. A stricter IH8MUD view: only 31–32 in clears in every situation without a body mount chop.)
- Biggest tire, 3 in (OME) lift: 285/70R17 (Slee told one owner this is the limit without body trimming; owners run it on factory wheels with no rub. ARB told another owner 285/75R17.)
- Biggest tire, 3 in + body mount chop lift: 305/70R17 to 35 in (Owners run 305/70R17s and 34s with chopped mounts and plastic trim removed; one still rubs at full compression. A club pair on 35s touches only at extreme flex and full lock. Watch wheel backspacing: wide tires on factory wheels hit the upper control arm.)

### Buying checks
- Get under it with a hammer and a light: Frame rust is the FJ's big weakness in salt-belt states. An IH8MUD member who shopped the Northeast said every truck he looked at had rot around the rear control-arm brackets or had already been patched. Another warned about rust hidden under thick fresh undercoating. Rust Buster's list of FJ repair sections (rail ends, center rails, crossmembers, coil buckets, body mounts) shows where to probe.
- Open the hood and look at the inner fenders: The engine-bay inner fender aprons on 2007 and some early 2008 trucks could bulge and crack, and Toyota changed the design. Owners on IH8MUD report cracks that never grew and others that went all the way through. Look on both sides behind the headlights and price in a repair if they're split.
- Check the rear access doors: The front seat-belt retractors are mounted in the rear-hinged access doors, and the door panels can crack after years of being slammed. Toyota recalled 2007–2013 trucks for it (NHTSA 13V098000). Run the VIN for open recalls and look at the inner door panels.
- Feel for a clunk when it downshifts: A harsh jolt into first after sitting in Drive, as if you'd been rear-ended, is covered by Toyota bulletin T-SB-0046-12 for 2007–2013 FJ Cruisers and Tacomas. Greasing a dry rear driveshaft slip yoke often fixes it. Ask whether the driveshafts have been greased; Toyota calls for it every 5,000 miles on dirt, salt or when towing.
- Manual trucks: listen at the clutch: A squeak or rattle from the gearbox that stops when you press the clutch is T-SB-0365-10 on 2007–2011 six-speed FJs: updated release bearing, fork support and release cylinder, with the transmission out. Manuals are much rarer than automatics, so expect to search harder.
- Test every 4WD mode: Shift into 4H and 4L, try the rear locker and A-TRAC, and watch for warning lights that stay on. On automatic trucks the front axle is engaged by an electric disconnect actuator on the front differential; IH8MUD owners say they fail mostly from unsoldered internal contacts or water getting in.
- Know which engine you're buying: 2007–2009 trucks make 239 hp and are rated on premium fuel; the dual VVT-i engine from 2010 makes 259–260 hp on regular. 4x2 automatics exist, so check the transfer-case lever. Trail Teams editions are monotone with blacked-out trim; confirm a claimed edition with the window sticker or a dealer build record.
- Clear the smaller recalls too: 2014 trucks built 7–20 August 2013 need a new intermediate steering shaft (15V081000). Ultimate Editions had front lower ball-joint and lower-arm bolts checked for torque (14V539000). Trucks with the TRD brake kit or Toyota auxiliary driving lamps have their own campaigns.

### Common repairs
#### Repair rotted rear frame sections
Difficulty 5 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend or more, with welding · cost Rust Buster lists its rear rail kit at about $180 per side; welding labor extra
Symptoms: Flaking, swollen or holed frame rails, rear control-arm brackets and crossmembers, often hidden under fresh undercoating on salt-belt trucks.
Fix: Probe the rear frame, the lower-link brackets, the crossmembers and the coil-spring buckets with a hammer and pick. Wire-brush and treat surface rust; anything rotted through has to be cut out and replaced. Rust Buster makes FJ-specific caps for the last 28.75 inches of the rails and for the center rail section, plus crossmembers, coil buckets and body mounts shared with the 4Runner. All of them need welding. One IH8MUD owner replaced his rear lower-link frame brackets with Rust Buster pieces and added weld-on reinforcement.
Tools: MIG welder · grinder and cutoff wheels · jack stands · rust converter · Rust Buster RB8432 (rear rail), RB8433 (center rail) and RB8427 (rear control-arm crossmember) as needed.

#### Cure the downshift clunk at the rear driveshaft
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 30 minutes · cost A tube of grease; a replacement rear driveshaft under T-SB-0046-12 was quoted at roughly $350–550
Symptoms: A harsh jolt, as if you'd been rear-ended, when the transmission drops into first after the truck has been sitting in Drive. Toyota's bulletin covers 2007–2013 FJ Cruisers and Tacomas.
Fix: Start with grease. A dry slip yoke binds and then lets go. Toyota's schedule says to lubricate the propeller-shaft spiders and slide yokes with lithium chassis grease, use molybdenum lithium grease on the double-cardan joint, and re-torque the shaft bolts. Do it every 5,000 miles if you drive on dirt or salted roads or tow. If the clunk survives a proper greasing and the driveshaft is confirmed as the cause, T-SB-0046-12 calls for a new rear driveshaft.
Tools: Grease gun with a needle or angled coupler · lithium chassis grease · moly grease for the double-cardan · torque wrench.

#### Fix a failed front-axle disconnect actuator (automatic 4x4s)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost Free if you can solder; a replacement actuator costs more
Symptoms: The transfer case goes into 4WD but the front wheels don't drive. The actuator may have water inside.
Fix: On part-time trucks an electric actuator on the front differential slides a collar to connect the passenger-side axle when you shift into 4WD. IH8MUD member BMThiker says most failures come from internal contacts that only rest on their terminals; he opened the housing and soldered the motor and switch contacts. Water can also get in through a failed seal, a cracked housing or a damaged breather tube. On the trail, remove the actuator (a few 12 mm bolts), move the shift fork and slide the collar over by hand, then refit it to get 4WD back.
Tools: 12 mm socket · soldering iron and solder · dielectric grease · tools to drop the skid plate if fitted.

#### Replace a front wheel bearing hub
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2 hours per side · cost One IH8MUD owner paid about $85 for a Beck/Arnley assembly
Symptoms: A growl or vibration from one front corner. One owner's bearing failed at 64,000 miles.
Fix: Pull the dust cap and break the axle nut with a 35 mm socket and a long bar. Remove the caliper and rotor, then the four 17 mm bolts that hold the hub to the knuckle. Once they're cracked loose, switch to an open-end wrench, because the bolts can't back fully out with the hub in place. Knock the hub free and keep or replace the large O-ring behind it. A complete hub-and-bearing assembly bolts straight in, which saves you pressing a bearing without a 20-ton press.
Tools: 35 mm socket · breaker bar · 17 mm open-end wrench · big hammer · torque wrench · new axle nut.

#### Silence a squeaking clutch release bearing (six-speed)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ 3.2 hours (Toyota flat rate) · cost Was covered by the 5-year/60,000-mile powertrain warranty; now parts plus transmission labor
Symptoms: A squeak or rattle from the transmission with the clutch pedal up that goes away when you press the pedal (2007–2011 FJ six-speeds).
Fix: T-SB-0365-10: remove the release cylinder and the transmission, then fit the updated release cylinder, fork support and release bearing, inspect the clutch cover and reinstall. Order the bearing that matches the maker stamped on the edge of the clutch cover: Aisin 31230-60241 or LuK 31230-60231. The bulletin lists FJ release cylinder 31470-60361 and fork support 31236-35050. With the gearbox out, it's the time to fit a new clutch if it's worn.
Tools: Transmission jack · 10 mm union-nut (flare) wrench · multi-purpose grease · Toyota repair manual.

#### Chop the front body mounts for bigger tires
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day, with welding · cost $34.95 for Metal Tech's plates, plus welding
Symptoms: Oversize or wide tires rubbing at full lock or under compression, usually the inside of the tire hitting the front body mount.
Fix: IH8MUD owners say rubbing on FJs is as much about tire width and wheel backspacing as diameter, and that the front body mount is the usual contact point at full lock. The fix is to cut the mount back and weld a cap over the opening. Metal Tech's laser-cut 3/16-inch plates show what to cut and come with instructions a welding shop can follow. Also remove or heat and reshape the plastic mud flap, which one owner found was the only thing his 285/70R17s touched on stock suspension.
Tools: Cutoff wheel or plasma · welder · heat gun for the mud flap · primer and paint.

#### Check, and live with or fix, cracked inner fender walls
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ 15 minutes to inspect · body-shop work to repair · cost Free to inspect. A proper repair is body-shop labor, and Toyota's own fix meant pulling the dash and front end.
Symptoms: A bulge, then a crack or tear, in the engine-bay inner fender aprons at the crumple zones, usually on both sides. 2007 and early-2008 trucks are the usual victims. Owners have filed dozens of NHTSA complaints. In the worst ones, the fenders dropped and bound on the doors or changed the door gaps.
Fix: Open the hood and look along both aprons behind the headlights. If you see a bulge, scrape back the undercoating: one IH8MUD member's 'small bulge' turned out to be a crack once a Toyota factory rep cleaned it off. Plenty of cracks stop growing. One 2007 owner cracked his at 58,000 miles and traded the truck at 107,000 with little change, and another's grew slowly after a hard landing in a ditch. Toyota's warranty fix used redesigned aprons with support brackets welded inside, which meant removing the dash and front end. An IH8MUD member warned that welding sparks under the dash started a fire that destroyed one FJ, so any welder needs to strip or shield the dash first. For a truck with open cracks, have a body shop weld and reinforce the apron, then seal and paint it. With a heavy steel bumper and winch, avoid dropping the nose hard.
Tools: Flashlight · plastic scraper · camera and tape measure to log crack length over time · for the repair: welder, weld-through primer, seam sealer, paint

#### Repair a chip before the windshield cracks
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 30 minutes for a chip · replacement is a glass-shop job · cost One IH8MUD member paid $50 for a chip repair. Early replacement quotes on IH8MUD ran about $1,600–1,800 with dealer glass.
Symptoms: Chips from road debris that grow into long cracks, often from the bottom center of the glass. More than 60 NHTSA complaints across the 2007–2014 model years describe cracked FJ windshields, some after a pothole or cold weather and some from owners on their third or fourth windshield.
Fix: The nearly upright glass takes the full force of every rock, so fix chips while they're small. A resin repair kept one IH8MUD member's small crack from spreading. If it has to be replaced, have the shop order a new top molding too. An IH8MUD member said it often gets ruined coming off; his dealer molding was about $278. Another member listed PPG FW02652 as the replacement glass. After a replacement, check for leaks at the top molding and A-pillars in the first rain or car wash.
Tools: Windshield chip repair kit · glass cleaner · razor blade · UV light or sunshine to cure the resin

### Baseline service
Assume nothing has been done, and assume the driveshafts have never seen grease. Intervals below come from Toyota's 2011 FJ Cruiser Warranty & Maintenance Guide; capacities come from AMSOIL's lookups for 2011 and 2007 trucks. Specs changed in 2010 (0W-20 oil, larger oil capacity, 75W-85 diff oil), so check your owner's manual for 2007–2009 trucks.
- Engine oil & filter: SAE 0W-20 (2010–14) · ≈6.4 qt with filter; 2007–09 ≈5.5 qt (AMSOIL lists 5W-30) · drain plug 30 ft-lb · Every 10,000 mi / 12 months on 0W-20; every 5,000 mi / 6 months on dirt roads, when towing or carrying heavy loads (Toyota) (If the last change wasn't 0W-20, Toyota says to change it again at 5,000 miles.)
- Engine air filter: OE-type panel filter · Replace every 30,000 mi; inspect every 5,000 mi on dirt or dusty roads (Toyota) (Check the airbox seal while you're there.)
- Cabin air filter: OE-type · Replace every 30,000 mi (Toyota); sooner in dust or heavy traffic
- Spark plugs: 6 × OE-type plugs (1GR-FE) · Every 120,000 mi (Toyota); replace at purchase if the history is unknown near that mileage
- Coolant: Toyota Super Long Life (pink) or equivalent non-silicate, non-amine, non-borate HOAT · ≈10.4 qt (auto) / 9.9 qt (manual) · First at 100,000 mi / 120 months, then every 50,000 mi / 60 months (Toyota) (Inspect hoses and connections for corrosion and leaks at the same time.)
- Automatic transmission (A750F / A750E): Toyota ATF WS · ≈11 qt total fill, ≈3.2 qt per drain-and-fill · Toyota lists replacement at 60,000 mi only for towing or heavy loads, otherwise inspection. Drain and fill at purchase if there's no record. (A drain-and-fill replaces only part of the fluid; repeat it rather than pressure-flushing.)
- Manual transmission (RA61F): 75W-90 GL-4 or GL-5 · ≈3.8 pt · drain and fill plugs 27 ft-lb · Replace every 30,000 mi when towing or heavily loaded (Toyota); otherwise inspect (Change it at purchase on a manual truck with no records.)
- Transfer case: Toyota transfer gear oil, grade [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · ≈2.1 pt part-time (auto), ≈3 pt full-time (manual), per AMSOIL's 2007 listing · Replace every 30,000 mi on dirt roads or when towing (Toyota); otherwise inspect
- Front & rear differentials: 75W-85 GL-5 (2011 listing) · front ≈3.4 pt (auto) / 3.0 pt (manual), rear ≈5.3 pt (5.2 pt with locker) · Replace front and rear every 15,000 mi when towing or heavily loaded (Toyota); otherwise inspect (AMSOIL's 2007 listing gives 75W-90 or 90 grade, so check the manual for early trucks. Crack the fill plug before you drain, and check the breathers after water crossings.)
- Driveshaft grease points: Lithium chassis grease at the spiders and slide yokes; molybdenum lithium grease at the double-cardan joint · Every 5,000 mi on dirt roads, salted roads or when towing, with a propeller-shaft bolt re-torque (Toyota) (Dry slip yokes cause the downshift clunk. See the driveshaft repair above.)
- Brake fluid (and clutch fluid on manuals): DOT 3 · Toyota lists clutch-fluid replacement every 30,000 mi for trucks used daily off-road at high rpm and low speed; otherwise inspect. Flush both at purchase if there's no record.
- Power steering fluid: Dexron III-type ATF (AMSOIL listing) · Inspect level and condition (Look for wet hoses at the pump and rack.)
- Drive belt: Serpentine belt with automatic tensioner · First inspection at 60,000 mi / 72 months, then every 15,000 mi / 18 months (Toyota)
- Ball joints, boots & chassis bolts: Visual inspection and torque check · Inspect ball joints, dust covers and drive shaft (CV) boots at 15,000 mi intervals; tighten chassis and body nuts and bolts regularly if you drive on dirt roads or tow (Toyota) (Check the CV boots after every trail trip; a split boot lets grit into the joint.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: About a 285/70R17 (roughly 33 x 11 inches). One owner on stock suspension found his only rubbed the driver's-side mud flap under compression and fixed it by heating and flattening the flap. A long-time IH8MUD member's stricter view is that only a 31–32 inch tire clears in every situation; above that you need a body mount chop. Width and wheel backspacing matter as much as diameter, because the inside of the tire hits the front body mount at full lock.

Q: What fits with a 3-inch lift?
A: With a 3-inch Old Man Emu lift, Slee Off-Road told one owner the limit is 285/70R17 unless you trim the body, and ARB told another 285/75R17. Several owners run 285/70R17s on factory wheels that way without rubbing. With the front body mounts chopped, owners run 305/70R17s, though one still rubs at full compression. One club's two FJs on 35s have trimmed body mounts and touch only at extreme flex and full lock.

Q: Manual or automatic?
A: They're different trucks underneath. The six-speed manual has full-time 4WD with a lockable Torsen center differential, 3.909 gears and a 41.84:1 crawl ratio. The five-speed automatic has part-time 4WD, 3.727 gears and a 33.76:1 crawl ratio. Toyota's 2014 specifications list the rear locker as standard on the manual and optional on the automatic. Manuals are much less common.

Q: Does it have lockers?
A: A rear electric locker, plus A-TRAC brake-based traction control in an option package on 4x4s. There's no factory front locker; one IH8MUD member fitted a Harrop E-Locker to his front diff. On very early trucks the rear locker could override A-TRAC. Toyota synchronized the two on the 2007 TRD Special Edition and in all production from November 2006.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: Toyota originally rated the FJ at 5,000 lb for both 4x4 and 4x2. Under the SAE J2807 standard, the 2014 rating with the Class IV hitch was 4,700 lb.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect, and does it need premium?
A: EPA ratings for 4x4s range from 14 city / 19 highway (2009 manual) to 17/21 (2010 automatic); a 2014 automatic is 17/20 and a manual 15/18. 2007–2009 trucks were rated on premium. The dual VVT-i engine from 2010 is rated on regular, although Toyota recommends premium for towing, off-roading and high altitude.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: 2010–14 if you can. Those trucks have the dual VVT-i engine on regular fuel, and CarGurus says the inner-fender bulge mostly shows up on 2007–09 trucks, while 2007 draws far more owner complaints than any other year. IH8MUD owners add that some pre-February 2007 builds had a brittle rear ring and pinion, so check the door-jamb build date. They also point out that an early truck you plan to re-gear anyway isn't much of a loss. Rust history and how the truck was used matter more than the year.

Q: What is the inner fender problem?
A: The engine-bay inner fender aprons on 2007 and some early 2008 trucks could bulge and crack, and Toyota changed the design. Owners report everything from cracks that never grew to splits that went right through. Check both sides before you buy.

Q: How long do they last?
A: On IH8MUD's high-mileage thread, one Ontario owner passed 450,000 km (about 280,000 miles) on the original engine and transmission, and a Toronto owner reported 300k on a 2007 with one clutch replacement. Another member reports 250,000 miles of hard use without burning or leaking oil between oil changes.

Q: What were the Trail Teams editions?
A: Monotone, black-trimmed, TRD-equipped FJs built in one color per year: Iceberg 2008 (3,200), Sandstorm 2010 (1,500), Army Green 2011, Radiant Red 2012 and Cement Gray 2013 (2,500 each), and the 2014 Heritage Blue Ultimate Edition (2,500). There wasn't one for 2009; a white TRD package filled the gap.

Q: Is the 2026 Land Cruiser FJ the same truck?
A: No. The Land Cruiser FJ (J240) is a smaller Hilux-based truck with a 2.7-liter four-cylinder and a six-speed automatic, built in Thailand from 2026. Toyota hasn't planned it for North America or Europe.

## Toyota Land Cruiser Prado 150 (2009–2023)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/prado-150/
Codes: J150, KDJ150, GDJ150, TRJ150, GRJ150

Verdict: Fourteen years, three diesels' worth of arguments and one very long DPF lawsuit, and the 150 still ended up as the default way to cross Australia with the kids in the back. It's a Lexus GX 460 that kept its overalls on.

The fourth-generation Prado went on sale in Japan on 14 September 2009 and stayed in production until October 2023, which is long enough to outlast most of the cars it was meant to compete with. Underneath is Toyota's F2 ladder-frame platform, shared with the 5th-gen 4Runner and the FJ Cruiser. America never got a Toyota-badged one. It got the GX 460 instead, which is the same truck with a V8, softer leather and a Lexus price.

### MORE ELECTRONICS, SAME FRAME
Toyota's launch release talked about two things: a stiffer version of the traditional full frame, and a lot of new off-road electronics. The 150 introduced KDSS with a new electric accumulator to free up the anti-roll bars, Crawl Control with five speed settings, Multi-Terrain Select, and what Toyota called the world's first Multi-Terrain Monitor, a set of cameras that show the ground around the wheels. A display in the gauges even tells you which way the front wheels are pointing when you've lost track on a rock step.
There were five-door and three-door bodies (the short one is the J155), and the engine list depended on where you lived: the 2.7-litre 2TR-FE four and 4.0-litre 1GR-FE V6 petrols, and the 3.0-litre 1KD-FTV turbo-diesel. Japan dropped the three-door at launch. Australia kept it as the SX and ZR until the 2013 facelift, when slow sales killed it. Some markets put the spare under the floor and others hung it on the tailgate, freeing space for a 63-litre auxiliary tank alongside the 87-litre main one.

### THREE FACELIFTS AND A NEW DIESEL
The first facelift arrived in Japan on 10 September 2013 and in Australia that October: a bigger grille, new bumpers and lamps, LED low beams on upper grades, retuned suspension and a fifth Multi-Terrain Select mode. In June 2015 the 1KD-FTV was replaced by the 2.8-litre 1GD-FTV (130 kW and 450 Nm in Australian trim), the V6 gained dual VVT-i, and both moved to the six-speed Aisin AC60F automatic. The 1GD also brought a diesel particulate filter, which became the defining problem of this generation.
The second facelift landed on 12 September 2017 in Japan, Europe and Australia, with a new face and, in Japan, LED headlights and Toyota Safety Sense as standard. Australia kept the V6 until that point. The last big update came in August 2020: a ball-bearing turbo and revised internals took the 1GD-FTV to 150 kW and 500 Nm, braked towing went to 3,000 kg, the manual gearbox was dropped, and a 9-inch screen finally brought Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

### THE DPF YEARS
On paper the 1GD was the better engine. In practice, Prados, HiLuxes and Fortuners with the new diesels built in the DPF era gained a reputation for filters that failed to regenerate, clouds of white smoke and a foul smell. Toyota made a manual regeneration switch standard from June 2018 and developed a hardware and software repair in May 2020, but owners went to court anyway. The case ran for seven years (see the sidebar) and ended in a $750 million settlement agreed in October 2026.
The older engine has its own story. Unsealed 4X4 says the 1KD-FTV's injector seat washers could fail and, combined with weaker piston crowns than earlier engines, crack a piston. Toyota's advice became: don't tune it, service the injectors around every 100,000 km and don't work it hard for long periods. Both stories are known, though, and both have fixes, which is why a well-documented 150 still sells quickly.

### HOW IT ENDED
By the time the 150 bowed out, Toyota Australia said it had sold more than 320,000 Prados there since 1996, and the Prado had been the country's best-selling large SUV in ten of the previous twelve years. It was replaced by the boxy J250 Prado, sold in the US as the 250 Series Land Cruiser, which moved to the TNGA-F platform.
That leaves the 150 as the last Prado on the old F2 frame, and the most common one on the touring trails of Australia, Africa and the Middle East. In America it's still a gray-market curiosity. The earliest trucks don't turn 25 until late 2034, so for now the closest you can legally get is a GX 460.

### Data plate
- Chassis: J150 (J155 three-door)
- Production: October 2009 – October 2023
- Platform: Toyota F2 ladder frame
- Assembly: Tahara and Hamura (Hino), Japan; Chengdu, China (2013–2020); Vladivostok, Russia (2013–2015)
- Wheelbase: 2,790 mm five-door / 2,450 mm three-door
- Diesels: 1KD-FTV 3.0 (to 2015) · 1GD-FTV 2.8 (2015-on)
- Petrols: 2TR-FE 2.7 I4 · 1GR-FE 4.0 V6 · 7GR-FKS 3.5 V6 (China)
- Transmission: 5/6-speed manual, 4/5/6-speed automatic
- 4Wd: Full-time, two-speed transfer, Torsen locking centre diff
- Fuel: 150 L (87 + 63) where fitted
- Towing: 2,500 kg braked, 3,000 kg from the 2020 update (Australia)
- Us Twin: Lexus GX 460 (URJ150)

### Engineering
The 150 uses a ladder frame (Toyota's F2 platform) with independent front suspension and a coil-sprung solid rear axle, the same layout as the GX 460 and 5th-gen 4Runner. Full-time 4WD runs through a two-speed transfer case and a Torsen centre differential that can be locked. Higher grades add KDSS, adaptive dampers and rear air springs with self-levelling. The headline electronics were Crawl Control, Multi-Terrain Select and the Multi-Terrain Monitor camera system.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, Toyota F2 (Shared with the Lexus GX 460, 5th-gen 4Runner and FJ Cruiser. 2,790 mm wheelbase for the five-door, 2,450 mm for the three-door.)
- Diesels: 1KD-FTV 3.0 → 1GD-FTV 2.8 (The 1KD (2009–2015) has a timing belt. The 1GD (2015–2023) has a chain and a DPF, at 130 kW / 450 Nm, then 150 kW / 500 Nm from 2020 (Australia).)
- Petrols: 2TR-FE 2.7 I4 · 1GR-FE 4.0 V6 (The V6 left Japan in 2015 and Australia in 2017. China got a 3.5 7GR-FKS V6 from 2015.)
- Driveline: Full-time 4WD, Torsen centre with lock (Two-speed transfer case. Aisin AC60F six-speed automatic from 2015.)
- Suspension: IFS front, coil-sprung solid rear (KDSS (introduced on the 150) on upper grades. The Kakadu adds adaptive dampers and rear air suspension with auto-levelling.)
- Fuel: 87 L main + 63 L sub-tank (150 L in total where the spare hangs on the tailgate. Under-floor spare versions lose the sub-tank.)

### Versions
- 2009–2015 · KDJ150 / KDJ155 · 1KD-FTV 3.0 L I4 turbo-diesel · 127 kW · The original diesel, with a timing belt. Injector seat-washer failures can crack pistons; service the injectors.
- 2009–2017 · GRJ150 · 1GR-FE 4.0 L V6 · 207 kW / 381 Nm (from June 2015) · Japan to 2015, Australia to 2017. Dual VVT-i and a six-speed auto from 2015.
- 2009–2023 · TRJ150 / TRJ155 · 2TR-FE 2.7 L I4 · 120 kW / 246 Nm (Japan) · The entry petrol. Still paired with a four-speed automatic in Toyota Japan's 2013 price list.
- 2015–2020 · GDJ150 · 1GD-FTV 2.8 L I4 turbo-diesel · 130 kW / 450 Nm · Timing chain, DPF. Covered by the Australian DPF class action for vehicles sold October 2015 to April 2020.
- 2020–2023 · GDJ150 · 1GD-FTV 2.8 L I4 turbo-diesel · 150 kW / 500 Nm · Ball-bearing turbo, auto only in Australia, 3,000 kg braked towing, CarPlay and Android Auto.
- 2010–2023 (US) · URJ150 · 1UR-FE 4.6 L V8 · 301 hp / 329 lb-ft · Sold in the US as the Lexus GX 460.

### Year-by-year
- 2009: J150 launches in Japan on 14 September and in Australia on 16 November. Debut of KDSS with an electric accumulator, Crawl Control, Multi-Terrain Select and the Multi-Terrain Monitor
- 2009: Unsealed 4X4 flags launch-year trucks for airbag recalls and electrical gremlins [avoid]
- 2010: April: left-hand-drive Prados included in Toyota's VSC software recall after the Lexus GX 460 'Don't Buy' episode
- 2012: Australian Altitude grade added between GXL and VX
- 2013: First facelift (Japan 10 Sept, Australia October): new grille, bumpers and lamps, LED low beams, retuned suspension, five-mode MTS. Three-door dropped in Australia. Unsealed 4X4 calls 2013–15 a sweet spot for many buyers: past the early faults and before the DPF [buy]
- 2015: June: 1GD-FTV 2.8 diesel (130 kW / 450 Nm) replaces the 1KD-FTV 3.0. AC60F six-speed auto. DPF arrives. V6 dropped in Japan
- 2015–2020: Diesels sold October 2015 to April 2020 covered by the Australian DPF class action [avoid]
- 2017: Second facelift on 12 September. V6 dropped in Australia. Unsealed 4X4 flags 2017 trucks for head-unit, ESC-light and shift glitches and says not to buy one without paperwork showing they've been fixed [avoid]
- 2018: June: manual DPF regeneration switch standard
- 2020: August update: 150 kW / 500 Nm, 3,000 kg braked towing, auto only, 9-inch screen with CarPlay and Android Auto. Unsealed 4X4 calls 2020–on trucks the most desirable, and 4X4 Australia says this update finally resolved the DPF problem [buy]
- 2023: Production ends in October; replaced by the J250

### Capability
- Towing: 3,000 kg (6,614 lb) braked (August 2020 update, Toyota Australia. Earlier trucks are rated at 2,500 kg (5,512 lb))
- Fuel tank: 150 L (39.6 US gal): 87 L main + 63 L sub (Toyota Australia, 2020)
- Fuel economy: 7.9 L/100 km (ADR combined) (2020 2.8 auto. Carsales measured 13.4 L/100 km towing a 2,300 kg caravan)
- Wheelbase: 2,790 mm (109.8 in) five-door / 2,450 mm (96.5 in) three-door
- Curb weight: 2,230–2,455 kg (4,916–5,412 lb) (Range across versions, Wikipedia)

### Wheels and tires
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: ≈32 in (e.g. 255/70R18; 275/65R17 with a slight liner rub) (Consensus from owners of the twin Lexus GX 460, which shares the body and suspension. Test-fit on a Prado, whose bumpers differ by grade.)
- Biggest tire, 2–2.5 in lift: 35 in (GX 460 owners report it needs upper control arms, the right offset, a body-mount chop, liner removal and pinch-weld work.)

### Buying checks
- Which diesel, and what's been done: A 1KD-FTV (2009–2015) needs its timing belt at 150,000 km, and Unsealed 4X4 recommends servicing the injectors every 100,000 km. Listen for a cold-start knock or rattle and look for black smoke, which can mean the injectors are going. A 1GD-FTV (2015-on) has a chain but a DPF. Paperwork matters more than the odometer.
- DPF history on 2015–2020 diesels: Ask whether the truck has the manual DPF regeneration switch (standard from June 2018) and the free 2020 exhaust hardware and software fix. Heavy white smoke, a foul smell, limp mode or rising fuel use point to a filter that isn't regenerating. A truck used only for short city trips is the riskiest.
- Dust in the 2.8's intake: Unsealed 4X4 says the 1GD's airbox seal can let fine dust past the filter and coat the MAF sensor, which puts the truck in limp mode. Pull the filter and look for dust on the clean side.
- Early brakes: Unsealed 4X4 reports that pre-2012 trucks could get a spongy or very hard pedal with a hiss from the booster. Toyota revised the booster and master cylinder, and the common fix is to fit the later parts.
- Suspension bushes and rear air: Lower shock bushes and lower control-arm bushes wear, especially if aftermarket suspension was tightened with the truck hanging on a hoist. Kakadu rear air springs leak with age. Auto Buyers Guide says factory shocks are often tired by 100,000 km.
- Tailgate and dash: The tailgate-mounted spare can make the door sag, so open and close it. Auto Buyers Guide also reports cracked dash tops on early trucks that lived in the sun.
- 2009 and 2017 electronics: Unsealed 4X4 flags the launch year and the 2017 facelift year for electrical gremlins, including airbag recalls on 2009 trucks and head-unit, ESC-light and shift complaints on 2017s. Look for evidence that they've been sorted.
- Underbody and towing life: Check sills, bash plates and chassis rails for off-road damage and coastal rust, and ask what it has towed. Many 150s have pulled caravans at or near their 2,500–3,000 kg limit for years.

### Common repairs
#### Timing belt (1KD-FTV 3.0 diesel)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Most of a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: None until it fails. Unsealed 4X4 and Auto Buyers Guide both put the change at 150,000 km, so a 1KD truck without a receipt is due.
Fix: Replace the belt with its tensioner and idlers to the factory procedure. Unsealed 4X4's warning: a fragile coolant return fitting on the radiator sits right in the way and can't be replaced on its own. Break it and you're buying a radiator, so protect it before you start. The 2.8 1GD-FTV uses a chain and has no belt interval.
Tools: Factory repair manual (Toyota TIS) · crank pulley holder · timing belt kit for 1KD-FTV

#### 1KD injector service and seat washers
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A day · cost Parts plus labor. Much less than a cracked piston.
Symptoms: Knocking, a noisy idle, black smoke, poor economy and crankcase pressure, according to Unsealed 4X4.
Fix: Have the injectors tested (back-leak or flow) and replace them and their sealing washers if they're out of spec. Toyota's guidance, as reported by Unsealed 4X4, was to service the injectors around every 100,000 km and to avoid tuning the 1KD. Don't keep driving a truck that knocks, because a failed seat washer can lead to a cracked piston.
Tools: Diesel specialist for testing · injector puller · new injector washers and seals · torque wrench

#### DPF regeneration problems (1GD-FTV)
Difficulty 2 / 5 (diagnosis) – 4 / 5 (replacement) · time From a highway drive to a dealer visit · cost Toyota's 2020 remedy is free of charge. Unsealed 4X4 puts a replacement system at 'at least a couple grand'.
Symptoms: Heavy white smoke, a foul smell, DPF warnings, limp mode and higher fuel use, mostly on trucks that only do short trips.
Fix: First confirm the free Toyota repair (revised exhaust hardware and software, available since May 2020) has been done. Use the manual regeneration switch, standard from June 2018, and drive at sustained highway speed regularly. Unsealed 4X4 also suggests asking for a manual regen at each service on short-trip trucks. Deleting the DPF is illegal.
Tools: Toyota dealer check by VIN · scan tool that can command a regeneration

#### EGR and intake clean
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Half a day to a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Sluggish response, smoke and DPF trouble. Unsealed 4X4 has seen diesel intake runners choked down to a hole the size of a 5-cent coin, and says the 2.8's EGR cooler likes to leak.
Fix: Remove and clean the intake and EGR valve every 50,000–100,000 km or so, as Unsealed 4X4 suggests, and check the EGR cooler for coolant leaks while it's apart. Replace gaskets rather than reusing them.
Tools: Basic metric tools · carbon cleaner and scrapers · new intake and EGR gaskets

#### Dusted MAF on the 2.8
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time 30 minutes · cost Air filter, MAF cleaner
Symptoms: Sudden power loss and limp mode with a 'see your dealer' message after fine dust, per Unsealed 4X4.
Fix: Fit a fresh filter and check that it seals all round the airbox. Clean the MAF sensor with spray cleaner (Unsealed 4X4 mentions blowing past it with compressed air). In bulldust country, change the filter well before the book interval.
Tools: Screwdriver · MAF sensor cleaner · new air filter

#### Early brake booster and master cylinder (pre-2012)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Half a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: A spongy or very hard pedal with a hissing booster.
Fix: Unsealed 4X4 says the common fix is to swap both the booster and master cylinder for the revised parts from a later Prado, then bleed the brakes.
Tools: Flare-nut wrenches · brake bleeding kit · DOT fluid

#### Suspension bushes, shocks and rear air springs
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Half a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Clunks, a jiggly ride, uneven rebound, or a harsh rear end on air-sprung Kakadus.
Fix: Replace worn shock and lower control-arm bushes. Tighten suspension bolts with the truck at ride height on its wheels, not hanging on a two-post hoist, which Unsealed 4X4 says is a common cause of early bush failure. Replace leaking rear air springs or convert the rear to coils.
Tools: Floor jack and stands · metric sockets · torque wrench

### Baseline service
Toyota Australia's owner's-manual site was offline while we researched this, so the fluid specs below come from Toyota Japan's own owner's manuals for the Japanese-market 150 (the 2011 petrol edition and the 2020 1GD-FTV edition), plus Penrite's lookup for Australian trucks. Japan never got the 1KD-FTV, and other markets can specify different grades, so check your own manual. The jobs that matter on a 150 depend on the engine: the 1KD-FTV needs its timing belt and injectors looked after, and the 1GD-FTV needs its DPF and intake kept healthy.
- Engine oil & filter: 1GD-FTV (Japanese manual, 2020): ACEA C5 0W-20 recommended, JASO DL-1 0W-30 or 5W-30 acceptable · 7.2 L oil only, 7.7 L with filter (Penrite lists 7.5 L with filter for Australian DPF trucks) · 1KD-FTV: 7.0 L with filter (Penrite) · petrols (Japanese manuals): 1GR-FE 5.7 L / 6.1 L with filter; 2TR-FE 5.5 L / 5.9 L with filter in 2020, 5.0 L / 5.7 L in 2011 · Australian-market grades [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase. Auto Buyers Guide's advice is fresh oil every 10,000 km. (The Japanese manual specifies low-ash ACEA C5 oil for the 1GD-FTV, warns that other grades shorten the life of the emissions system, and sets oil and filter changes at about 20,000 km or 12 months. Check the logbook for intervals that were stretched.)
- Air filter: Panel element · check the seal all round the airbox · At purchase, then much more often in dust (1GD trucks can dust the MAF if the seal leaks (Unsealed 4X4). Look at the clean side of the box.)
- Fuel filter / water separator: Diesel fuel filter · [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase, then per the manual, sooner on bush fuel (Clean fuel matters to the injectors on both diesels.)
- Timing belt (1KD-FTV only): Belt, tensioner and idlers · Every 150,000 km (Protect the fragile radiator return fitting during the job. The 2.8 1GD-FTV has a chain.)
- Injectors (1KD-FTV): Test, and replace the seat washers · Around every 100,000 km (Toyota guidance reported by Unsealed 4X4) (Knocking or black smoke means stop and test before a piston cracks.)
- DPF, EGR and intake (1GD-FTV): Confirm the 2020 Toyota remedy and the manual regen switch · Intake and EGR clean every 50,000–100,000 km (Unsealed 4X4) (Check the EGR cooler for coolant leaks while it's apart.)
- Coolant: Toyota Genuine Super Long Life Coolant (Japanese manuals) · 1GD-FTV: 10.2 L engine plus 2.6 L intercooler circuit · 1GR-FE: 11.0 L · 2TR-FE: 8.1 L · At purchase if there's no record (Check the radiator, and the return fitting if the 1KD belt has been done.)
- Automatic transmission: Toyota ATF WS for every engine in the Japanese manuals: 1GD-FTV 9.6 L, 1GR-FE 10.9 L, 2TR-FE 9.9 L (2011) or 8.5 L (2020) · Australian 1KD-FTV automatic [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Drain and fill at purchase on a tow vehicle (Auto Buyers Guide: hunting or shudder under load points to old fluid or a tired torque converter.)
- Transfer case: Toyota Genuine Transfer Gear Oil LF, SAE 75W · 1.4 L (Japanese manuals; Penrite also lists 1.4 L) · At purchase (Engage 4H, 4L and the centre lock on soft ground to test the actuator.)
- Front & rear differentials: Toyota Genuine Differential Gear Oil LT, API GL-5 SAE 75W-85 · front 1.4 L · rear 2.7 L, or 2.65 L with the diff lock · Torsen rear LSD: Toyota Differential Gear Oil LX, GL-5 75W-85, 2.55 L (Japanese manual, 2020) · At purchase, and after any deep water crossing (Front diff service is easier with the bash plate off. Use the LX oil if your truck has the Torsen rear LSD.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 or as marked on the reservoir · At purchase (On a pre-2012 truck, check the pedal for the booster fault.)
- Suspension & KDSS: Inspect bushes, shocks, KDSS cylinders and rear air springs · At purchase (Check that the truck sits level after standing overnight (Kakadu rear air).)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: Owner consensus on the Lexus GX 460, the US twin with the same body and suspension, is about 32 inches. 255/70R18 fits with no rubbing, 265/70R18 touches the plastics at full lock, and on 17s a 275/65R17 shows only a slight liner rub at full turn. Prado bumpers and grades differ, so test-fit before you buy. 33s need a lift, and 35s need a 2–2.5 in lift plus upper control arms, a body-mount chop and trimming.

Q: Is it the same as a Lexus GX 460?
A: Underneath, yes. Wikipedia lists the Lexus GX 400/460 as the 150's twin. The US-market GX 460 uses the 1UR-FE 4.6 V8, which no Toyota-badged Prado got. The Prado's engines are the 2.7 and 4.0 petrols, the 1KD-FTV 3.0 and 1GD-FTV 2.8 diesels, and a 3.5 V6 in China.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: Early trucks are rated at 2,500 kg braked. After the August 2020 update, Toyota Australia quotes a maximum of 3,000 kg braked. Carsales' tow test recommends staying under about 2,500 kg in practice.

Q: Timing belt or chain?
A: The 1KD-FTV 3.0 diesel (2009–2015) has a belt, due at 150,000 km. The 1GD-FTV 2.8 diesel (2015-on) has a chain.

Q: Does my 2.8 have the DPF problem?
A: Diesels sold in Australia between October 2015 and April 2020 were covered by the class action. Toyota made a manual regeneration switch standard from June 2018 and has offered a free hardware and software fix since May 2020. Ask a dealer to check the VIN.

Q: Which years are best?
A: Unsealed 4X4's summary: 2009–2012 are cheaper but have the early issues, 2013–2015 are a sweet spot for many buyers, 2015–2019 get the 2.8 but in the early DPF era, and 2020-on are the most desirable, with 150 kW and CarPlay. It also flags 2009 and 2017 for electrical gremlins.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: The 2020 2.8 diesel is rated at 7.9 L/100 km (ADR combined). Carsales saw 7.2 L/100 km on easy freeway running and 13.4 L/100 km towing a 2,300 kg caravan.

Q: How much fuel does it carry?
A: 150 litres: an 87-litre main tank and a 63-litre sub-tank. On trucks with the spare under the floor instead of on the tailgate, the spare takes the sub-tank's place.

Q: What is KDSS and which grades have it?
A: The Kinetic Dynamic Suspension System hydraulically links the front and rear anti-roll bars. It firms them up on the road and frees them off-road for more articulation. The 150 introduced it with an electric accumulator. In Australia it's on the VX and Kakadu.

Q: Can I import one to the US?
A: Not yet. Toyota never sold the Prado 150 in the US, and NHTSA's 25-year exemption means the first trucks (built from October 2009) don't become eligible until late 2034. Check your state's emissions rules even then.

Q: Is the 1KD engine reliable?
A: Mostly, if it's been serviced. Its known weakness is failing injector seat washers, which can crack a piston, so injector servicing is part of normal maintenance. Unsealed 4X4 notes that only a small percentage of Australian Prados were affected.
