## Toyota Land Cruiser 250 Series (2024–present (US))
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/250-series/
Codes: J250

Verdict: Toyota took the Land Cruiser away from America, thought about it for a few years, and brought back a Prado in a 1980s costume, which turns out to be exactly what most of us wanted. It's smaller, cheaper and boxier than the truck it replaced, and it comes with lockers as standard. The one thing it doesn't come with is a big fuel tank.

In December 2020 Toyota confirmed that the Land Cruiser would leave North America after the 2021 model year, ending the run of the V8 200 Series. The gap lasted two model years. On 2 August 2023 Toyota unveiled the J250. Most of the world knows it as the fifth-generation Land Cruiser Prado, but in the US it is sold simply as the Land Cruiser. It is a two-row midsize SUV rather than a three-row full-size one, it is boxier, and it starts at a much lower price than the 200 did. In North America it comes only as a hybrid. The full-size flagship, the 300 Series, still isn't sold here.

### A PRADO BY ANY OTHER NAME
Americans have owned Prados for years without being told. The previous J150 Prado was sold in the US as the Lexus GX 460, and the J250 has a Lexus twin of its own in the GX 550, which uses a 349-hp twin-turbo V6. This time the Toyota-badged truck came too. It sits on the GA-F body-on-frame platform shared with the 300 Series. Toyota claims frame rigidity is up 50 percent and overall rigidity 30 percent, and the 250 is the first 'light-duty' Land Cruiser with electric power steering, which is what makes lane-tracing assist possible.
Outside the US the engine list is long. Depending on the market, the 250 is offered with a 2.4-liter turbo petrol, a 2.7-liter petrol four, the familiar 2.8-liter 1GD-FTV turbo-diesel, or that diesel with a 48-volt mild-hybrid system, which is what Australia and Western Europe get. Europe mostly calls it plain 'Land Cruiser' and keeps the Prado name only where the 300 is also sold. The US and China get the gasoline hybrid only. Every version is a four-cylinder.

### BACK TO THE BOX
Wikipedia credits project chief designer Yoshito Watanabe's team with returning to practicality, durability and dependability, following a basic direction set by former Toyota CEO Akio Toyoda. They also made it look like a 1980s Land Cruiser again. The square body draws on the 60 Series. The base '1958' grade and the launch First Edition get round LED headlamps behind a TOYOTA heritage grille, and the mid-grade 'Land Cruiser' uses rectangular lamps that Toyota says were modeled on the FJ62. Toyota also says it optimized the A-pillar position so you can see more of the trail.
The US launched with three grades: the 1958 at $55,950 plus $1,395 destination, the Land Cruiser, and a First Edition limited to 5,000 trucks for North America. The First Edition came with a roof rack, rock rails and a front skid plate. Car and Driver's First Edition test car reached 60 mph in 7.7 seconds. The magazine's staff liked the slimmer size and the 40- and 80-series design cues. They complained about the thin sheet metal and doors you have to slam.

### THE HYBRID IN THE ROOM
The US powertrain is the i-FORCE MAX: a 2.4-liter turbocharged four with a 48-hp electric motor in the bell housing of an eight-speed automatic, for 326 hp and 465 lb-ft. The hybrid battery is a 1.87 kWh nickel-metal-hydride pack. The EPA rates it at 22 city, 25 highway and 23 combined, compared with 14 combined for the last V8 200, and Car and Driver averaged 20 mpg over its test. Full-time four-wheel drive with a two-speed transfer case is standard, and so are locking center and rear differentials on every US grade.
The catch is the fuel tank. It holds 17.9 gallons, and with the mileage above, overlanders start looking at the fuel gauge sooner than they would like. Slee Off-Road's Arctic Trucks build swaps in a 29-gallon tank, which is more than 50 percent more. Owners also note that the battery's location gives the cargo area a sloped floor. On long, steep descents, several owners on LandCruiserForum.com report brake fade from relying on Downhill Assist alone. At the Pikes Peak brake check, a ranger measured one owner's rotors at 575°F.

### SO FAR, SO TOYOTA
Americans bought it. Wikipedia counts 29,113 US sales in 2024 and 43,946 in 2025. With the First Edition gone, Toyota's 2027 line-up is two grades: the 1958 at $58,180 and the Land Cruiser at $64,255 (base MSRP, per Toyota). New options are an 'Inked' paint color and a $980 raised air intake, which Motor1 is careful to point out is not a watertight snorkel.
The recall list so far is mostly software and paperwork: an instrument-cluster update for displays that can go blank at start-up, a corrected load-capacity label on some distributor-accessorized 2024 trucks, a rear-camera fix, and an interim notice in 2026 for a fuel-pipe connector that can come loose. None of it is the kind of mechanical horror story that gets a truck a reputation, though it also isn't the 'never needs anything' legend some buyers expect. Notably, the US 250 doesn't use the V35A twin-turbo V6 whose bearing recalls have affected the Lexus LX, Tundra and some 2024 GX 550s.

### Data plate
- Chassis: J250 (US hybrid: TJH250)
- Platform: GA-F body-on-frame
- Unveiled: 2 August 2023
- Us Model Years: 2024–present
- Engine (Us): T24A-FTS 2.4 L turbo I4 + motor
- Output: 326 hp · 465 lb-ft (combined)
- Transmission: 8-spd auto
- Drive: Full-time 4WD, Torsen center w/ lock, 2-speed
- Wheelbase: 112.2 in
- Length: 193.8 in ('24)
- Curb Weight: 5,037 lb ('24)
- Ground Clearance: 8.7 in (221 mm)
- Angles: 31° approach · 25° breakover · 22° departure
- Fuel Tank: 17.9 gal
- Towing: 6,000 lb

### Engineering
Under the retro bodywork is a modern Toyota truck: a ladder frame on the GA-F platform it shares with the 300 Series and the Lexus GX 550, an independent front end with a coil-sprung solid rear axle, and a full-time four-wheel-drive system. In US trucks that's paired with a 2.4-liter turbo-hybrid and lockers as standard. The wheelbase is 112.2 inches, the same figure the 80 Series introduced.
- Chassis: GA-F (TNGA-F) ladder frame, 112.2 in wheelbase (Toyota claims frame rigidity up 50% and overall rigidity up 30% over the previous Prado.)
- 4Wd System: Full-time, Torsen center diff with lock, 2-speed transfer (Electronically shifted high and low range; normal torque split is 40/60 front to rear.)
- Lockers: Center and electronic rear, standard (US) (The rear locker can split power 50/50 across the axle. No factory front locker.)
- Engine (Us): T24A-FTS 2.4 L turbo I4 + 48-hp motor (326 hp and 465 lb-ft combined; 1.87 kWh, 288 V NiMH hybrid battery.)
- Suspension: Independent front, coil-sprung live rear axle (A Stabilizer Disconnect Mechanism (SDM) for more articulation is available on the Land Cruiser grade and was fitted to the First Edition.)
- Steering & Aids: Electric power steering; CRAWL, Multi-Terrain Select (First light-duty Land Cruiser with EPS. CRAWL Control has five speeds; Multi-Terrain Select works in 4HI and 4LO.)

### Versions
- 2024–present · TJH250 (US, China) · T24A-FTS 2.4 L turbo I4 hybrid · 326 hp / 465 lb-ft · i-FORCE MAX, 8-speed auto. The only US powertrain.
- 2024–present · J250 (Middle East and others) · T24A-FTS 2.4 L turbo I4 (petrol) · 278 hp / 430 Nm · Non-hybrid turbo four with an 8-speed auto.
- 2024–present · J250 (Japan, Eastern Europe, others) · 2TR-FE 2.7 L I4 (petrol) · 161 hp / 246 Nm · 6-speed auto. Japan's 7-seat VX uses it.
- 2024–present · J250 (Europe, Japan, Middle East) · 1GD-FTV 2.8 L turbo-diesel I4 · 201 hp / 500 Nm · 6- or 8-speed auto depending on market.
- 2024–present · J250 (Australia, Western Europe) · 1GD-FTV 2.8 L diesel, 48 V mild hybrid · 201 hp / 500 Nm · 8-speed auto. The only engine in Australian 250s.
- 2024–present · Lexus GX 550 (twin) · V35A-FTS 3.4 L twin-turbo V6 · 349 hp / 479 lb-ft · Same GA-F platform; the US-market V6 alternative.

### Year-by-year
- 2023: J250 revealed on 2 August 2023: GA-F frame shared with the 300, electric power steering, full-time 4WD with lockable Torsen centre diff
- 2024: US launch with the i-Force Max 2.4 L turbo hybrid only, in 1958, Land Cruiser and First Edition grades (First Edition limited to 5,000 for North America)
- 2024–2025: Model years covered by the combination-meter and camera recalls
- 2027: New Inked paint, optional raised air intake (not a sealed snorkel), heated and ventilated second-row seats in the Premium Package. Toyota.com lists base MSRPs of $58,180 (1958) and $64,255 (Land Cruiser)
- 2024–2027: All model years included in the fuel-tube leak recall (26V673000) announced October 2026, so check that it's been done

### Capability
- Towing: 6,000 lb (2,720 kg) braked / 1,650 lb (750 kg) unbraked (Owner's manual)
- Payload: 1,100–1,300 lb (500–590 kg) (Owner's manual vehicle capacity weight, varies with seating, moonroof and stabilizer disconnect)
- Fuel tank: 17.9 US gal (68 L) (Owner's manual; 91 octane or higher)
- Ground clearance: 221 mm (8.7 in) (Wikipedia; KBB lists 8 in minimum for the US 2024)
- Approach / departure / breakover: 31° / 22° / 25° (maximum figures, Wikipedia)
- Fuel economy: EPA 22 city / 25 hwy / 23 combined (Car and Driver averaged 20 mpg in testing)
- Curb weight: 5,037 lb (2,285 kg) (2024, KBB)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 245/70R18 on 18x7 (1958), 265/70R18 on 18x7.5 (Land Cruiser, First Edition), 265/60R20 on 20x7.5 (Premium Package)
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Offset: +60 mm (Land Cruiser / First Edition 18x7.5)
- Center Bore: 95.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M14x1.5
- Lug Torque: 97 lb-ft (131 N·m)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 285/70R18 (about 33.7 in) (Owners report no rubbing on gentle trails on 18x9 +40 wheels. 275/70R18 (about 33 in) fits the stock 1958 wheels, and an LT275/70R18 KO3 just fits the spare well.)
- Biggest tire, 1.5 in level lift: 285/70R17 (Fits with no rubbing on a First Edition with a 1.5-inch leveling kit and 17x9.5 −12 wheels (Threepiece).)
- Biggest tire, Stock + trimming lift: 35x12.50R17 (Shown on a 1958 with 17x8 +25 wheels. Needs the mud flaps, crush brackets and front canards removed (they unbolt) and the fender liners reshaped with a heat gun.)

### Buying checks
- Know which grade you're looking at: The 1958 has round lamps, cloth seats, 245/70R18 tires on 18x7 wheels and no stabilizer disconnect. The Land Cruiser grade has rectangular lamps, 265/70R18 tires, and SDM availability. The 2024 First Edition (5,000 built for North America) keeps the round lamps and adds rock rails, a front skid and a roof rack. Premium Package trucks ride on 20-inch wheels with 265/60R20 tires.
- Run the VIN for recalls: Campaigns so far include an instrument-cluster software update for displays that can go blank (about 82,000 Toyota and Lexus vehicles, announced May 2026), a corrected load-capacity label on certain 2024 trucks accessorized by Gulf States Toyota, a rear-camera software fix, and a 2024–2027 recall (Toyota 26TA23, interim notice 26TB23; NHTSA 26V673000) for a fuel-tube connector that can disconnect and leak. Check NHTSA or the Toyota app.
- Listen for squeal in reverse: Front-brake squeal when backing up is covered by TSB T-SB-0006-26, which supersedes T-SB-0046-25 and replaces pads and shims after a technician confirms the problem. Owners say you can tell it's been done from the newer anti-rattle springs on the caliper.
- Check the hybrid-battery vents: The cooling intakes look like speaker grilles in the lower side trim at the rear door opening. Make sure nothing is blocking them. Owners have found cargo and even a plastic bag over them, and some owners got battery cooling-fan maintenance warnings at low mileage; in one case the dealer found nothing and cleared a reminder it thought had been set at the wrong interval.
- Test the 12 V battery: Owners on LandCruiserForum.com report no-starts after leaving doors or the hatch open for a few minutes at camp. Have the 12 V battery load-tested and ask whether it has been replaced.
- Look underneath: On used trucks, pull the front skid plate. Owners report stripped skid-plate bolt threads from repeated oil changes. Look for trail damage, and check whether any lift kit came with an alignment.
- Ask for diff and transfer-case service records: The owner's manual calls for 75W-85 GL-5 in the differentials, and owners report the dealer parts counter doesn't always stock it. Ask what was used.
- Do the range math: A 17.9-gallon tank at the EPA's 23 mpg combined is about 410 miles in theory, and less with bigger tires, a roof rack or a trailer. If you travel remote, budget for jerry cans or an aftermarket long-range tank.

### Common repairs
#### Engine oil and filter change
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost Oil and filter only
Symptoms: Scheduled service. Many owners also change the factory oil early, at around 1,000–1,500 miles.
Fix: Warm the engine, then remove the front skid plate. Owners call it easy, but check the bolts, since some threads have been damaged. Drain the oil, replace the filter, refit the drain plug with a new gasket, and fill with 0W-20. Owners on LandCruiserForum.com report a capacity of about 5.9 quarts. Confirm it against your owner's manual and check the dipstick before refitting the skid. A Fumoto-style drain valve with a hose makes later changes cleaner, though the pan won't drain completely either way.
Tools: Socket set · drain pan · filter wrench · 0W-20 oil · OEM filter 90915-10009 (as reported by an owner) · new drain-plug gasket · optional Fumoto valve.

#### Differential and transfer-case fluid
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost Fluid only
Symptoms: Scheduled service, or after deep water crossings or heavy towing.
Fix: Remove the skid plate if needed. On each unit, loosen the fill plug first so you know you can refill, then drain, refit the drain plug and fill until fluid reaches the bottom of the fill hole. The manual calls for 75W-85 GL-5 gear oil in the differentials and Toyota 75W 'LF' in the transfer case. Toyota dealers don't always stock either, so owners have used Amsoil 75W-85 in the diffs and Red Line MT-LV in the transfer case. Keep your receipts in case of a warranty claim.
Tools: Socket set · fluid pump · drain pan · 75W-85 GL-5 gear oil · 75W transfer-case fluid · new plug gaskets.

#### Fix front-brake squeal in reverse
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost Covered by TSB under warranty
Symptoms: Squealing from the front brakes when backing up, especially at low speed.
Fix: Under warranty, ask the dealer for T-SB-0006-26 (pads and shims; it replaced T-SB-0046-25). Owners report rotors aren't part of the fix. One owner fixed it himself by fitting the revised anti-rattle springs from the TSB on both the lower and upper pins and greasing the pad contact points. He didn't replace pads or rotors, and he says the squeak is completely gone.
Tools: Basic hand tools · brake grease · TSB anti-rattle springs (and pads/shims if following the full TSB).

#### Clear the hybrid-battery cooling intakes
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 15 minutes · cost Free; filters if replaced
Symptoms: A 'battery cooling fan maintenance' message, or a fan running louder than usual.
Fix: Open the rear door and find the grille-like intakes low in the side trim on each side. Remove anything blocking them, such as bags, gear or dust, and keep cargo clear of them. If the warning keeps coming back on a low-mileage truck with clean vents, have the dealer scan it. One dealer cleared a reminder it believed had been set at 5,000 miles instead of 50,000 at the factory.
Tools: Vacuum · trim tool if removing covers.

#### Keep the 12 V battery alive at camp
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 30 minutes · cost Battery monitor and jump pack
Symptoms: The truck won't go into Ready after the doors or hatch have been open for a while with the engine off.
Fix: Load-test the 12 V battery and replace it if it's weak. Owners recommend carrying a lithium jump pack, fitting a Bluetooth battery monitor (the Ancel BM300 and BM200 Pro have been mentioned) to watch state of charge, or starting the hybrid system before a long unloading stop. One owner warns that a big aftermarket AGM may sit at a partial charge, because the hybrid system doesn't fully top it off.
Tools: Battery tester · jump pack · battery monitor · 10 mm wrench.

#### Make room for 35s
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day plus alignment · cost Wheels and tires plus labor
Symptoms: Rubbing at full lock or compression after fitting tires over about 33 inches.
Fix: Threepiece's fitment guide: remove the mud flaps, crush brackets and canards (they bolt or clip on and can go back later). Invert and heat-form the plastic fender liners. If you still need room, radius the back of the front fenders or trim a few inches from the front bumper. Offset matters: the guide's 35-inch example on a stock-height 1958 used 17x8 +25 wheels, and it warns that near-zero offsets add a lot of poke. Get an alignment afterwards.
Tools: Socket set · trim tools · heat gun · cutting tool · 17-inch or 18-inch wheels with the right offset (6x139.7, 95.1 mm bore, M14x1.5 lugs).

#### Sunroof leak and a damp headliner
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour to clean the drains; a dealer visit if the seal is at fault · cost Free to clean; seal work under warranty
Symptoms: Water dripping through the overhead console with the roof shut, a damp headliner or passenger footwell, or a musty smell after rain. NHTSA complaints include a rear section of the sunroof that doesn't seal and a cabin that smells of mildew every time it rains.
Fix: Open the roof and clean out the housing, especially the corners where the drains are. One LandCruiserForum owner found his corner drains plugged with leaves and plant matter, so water overflowed into the headliner. He cleared it with rags, a shop vac and compressed air. Keep the seals clean and the drains clear. If water still gets in once the drains are clear, it's a warranty job: UK owners report dealers removing the glass and fitting a new seal under Toyota's instructions, and one says his dealer found a TSB involving new sealant (no number was given). Some trucks needed more than one visit.
Tools: Shop vac · compressed air · rags · flashlight

#### Quiet a vibrating driver's mirror
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 30 minutes · cost A few dollars in thin plastic and felt
Symptoms: At highway speed the driver's mirror glass shakes enough to blur the view. Owners say the passenger side is solid. One NHTSA complainant says the dealer confirmed it and called it common to all Land Cruisers.
Fix: Report it to the dealer first, while it's under warranty. On LandCruiserForum, dealers have tightened the mirror or replaced the whole assembly, sometimes twice, without curing it. Owners think the driver-side assembly simply has too much play, and their fix is a shim. One member cut a C-shaped piece of thin plastic lid with peel-and-stick felt on both faces and reported about a 90% reduction, with a little shake left on rough roads. Another used a roughly 1.6 mm Rubbermaid lid and says pivoting the mirror forward makes it easier to fit. A bare plastic shim rubbed the paint when the mirror folded, so use the felt.
Tools: Scissors or a craft knife · thin plastic lid · adhesive felt

### Baseline service
Even a low-mileage 250 is worth baselining. Many owners change the factory oil early, and the diff and transfer fluids are rarely touched under the 'inspect only' schedule. Specs below are from Toyota's US 2024 Land Cruiser Owner's Manual (OM60U35U) and its Warranty & Maintenance Guide for the i-FORCE MAX hybrid (T24A-FTS).
- Engine oil & filter: ILSAC GF-6A SAE 0W-20 (5W-20 only as a stopgap) · 5.9 qt with filter · Then every 10,000 mi / 12 months; 5,000 mi for dusty or towing use (Toyota) (Remove the front skid plate. Check the level with the hybrid system off after about 5 minutes. Many owners do the first change early, at 1,000–1,500 mi.)
- Engine air filter: OE-type panel filter · Replace every 30,000 mi; inspect more often on dirt roads (Toyota)
- Cabin air filter: OE-type · Replace every 30,000 mi (Toyota)
- Hybrid battery cooling intake filter: Vacuum-clean the filter behind the cargo-area side vents · Inspect every 5,000 mi, clean every 20,000 mi (Toyota) (The Owner's Manual walks through the cleaning. If the filter is damaged, have the dealer replace it. Keep cargo off the vents.)
- Spark plugs: NGK DILZKAR8E7H iridium · 0.028 in (0.7 mm) gap, do not adjust · Every 40,000 mi (Toyota) (That interval is short because the engine is turbocharged. Don't assume a V8-style 120k plug life.)
- Coolant (engine, power control unit, intercooler): Toyota Super Long Life Coolant or equivalent · engine 12.2 qt (14.3 qt with rear A/C), power control unit 2.5 qt · Intercooler coolant first at 150,000 mi, then every 50,000 mi; engine/inverter coolant is inspected (Toyota) (There are three separate cooling loops. Check each reservoir level.)
- Automatic transmission (8-speed): Toyota Genuine ATF WS · 13.2 qt reference capacity · Replace at 60,000 mi when towing or heavily loaded, or with lots of idling (Toyota); otherwise inspect (The manual warns that non-WS fluid can cause noise or damage. The level is checked by temperature (no dipstick), so most owners leave this to a dealer.)
- Transfer case: Toyota Genuine Transfer Gear Oil LF, SAE 75W · 1.48 qt · Every 30,000 mi when driving on dirt or towing (Toyota); otherwise inspect (Dealers don't always stock LF. Owners have used Red Line MT-LV. Keep receipts for warranty.)
- Front & rear differentials: Toyota Genuine Differential Gear Oil LT 75W-85 GL-5 · front 1.29 qt, rear 5.94 qt · Front every 15,000 mi and both at 30,000 mi when towing or heavily loaded (Toyota); otherwise inspect (The rear locker is standard in the US. Loosen the fill plug before you drain.)
- Driveshaft grease points: Lithium chassis grease NLGI 2 on the spiders; moly-lithium or lithium NLGI 2 on the front slide yoke · Lubricate and re-torque the propeller-shaft bolts every 15,000 mi (Toyota)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 (SAE J1703) or DOT 4 (SAE J1704) · Inspect (Toyota); flush if the history is unknown
- 12 V battery: 12.0 V or higher open voltage (Toyota test: power off, high beams on for 30 s first) · Test at purchase (A weak 12 V battery stops the hybrid system going to Ready. See the repair above.)
- Drive belt: Automatic tension · Inspect at 60,000 mi, then every 15,000 mi (Toyota)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: Factory tires are about 31.5 inches on the 1958 and 32.6 inches on the other grades. Threepiece's fitment guide shows 275/70R18s (about 33 inches) on stock wheels and suspension with plenty of clearance and no trimming. Owners go a bit bigger: 285/70R18s (about 33.7 inches) on stock suspension, including one reported on 18x9 +40 wheels with no rubbing on gentle trails. An LT275/70R18 KO3 (33.2 inches) just fits in the spare well. 35s are possible on stock suspension, but only after removing the mud flaps, crush brackets and canards, heat-forming the fender liners and choosing the right wheel offset.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: 6,000 lb, according to Toyota, and the 1958 grade comes with a trailer brake controller. Owners note that a small engine doesn't give much engine braking, so on long grades use the transmission and low range rather than the service brakes alone.

Q: What fuel economy and range should I expect?
A: The EPA rates it at 22 city, 25 highway and 23 combined. Car and Driver averaged 20 mpg, and Flexmotor saw about 21 off-road and 24 on the highway. The tank holds 17.9 gallons, which is why long-range tanks and jerry cans are popular.

Q: Does it have lockers?
A: Every US grade has a locking center differential and an electronic locking rear differential. There's no factory front locker. Slee's AT37 build added an ARB Air Locker up front.

Q: Why only a four-cylinder hybrid? Can I get the diesel?
A: North America and China only get the 2.4-liter i-FORCE MAX hybrid. The 2.8-liter diesel, the 2.7 petrol and the non-hybrid 2.4 turbo are sold elsewhere. If you want a V6 on this platform in the US, the Lexus GX 550 has a 349-hp 3.4-liter twin-turbo.

Q: Is it a 'real' Land Cruiser or just a Prado?
A: It's a Prado, and the Prado has always been a real Land Cruiser: ladder frame, live rear axle, full-time 4WD with low range. It shares the GA-F platform with the 300 Series, and its 112.2-inch wheelbase is the same figure the 80 Series introduced. It's smaller than the 200 Series it replaced in the US and seats two rows, not three.

Q: Which grade should I buy for off-road use?
A: The 1958 is the cheapest way into center and rear lockers, but it doesn't offer the Stabilizer Disconnect Mechanism, which gives the front axle more articulation. The Land Cruiser grade (and the 2024 First Edition) can have SDM and comes on wider 265/70R18 tires. For 2027 the 1958 starts at $58,180 and the Land Cruiser at $64,255 (base MSRP).

Q: What oil and fluids does it take?
A: 0W-20 engine oil (owners report about 5.9 quarts with the filter), 75W-85 GL-5 in the differentials according to the manual, and Toyota 75W 'LF' in the transfer case. Check the owner's manual for your truck's exact figures.

Q: What are the lift options?
A: ICON sells 1.25–3 inch systems for the 250, Dobinsons offers a 2-inch kit, and Slee's dealer build used an ADS 2.5-inch system. Threepiece tested a 1.5-inch Tuff Country leveling kit with 285/70R17s and reported no rubbing.

Q: Is the new raised air intake a snorkel?
A: No. The $980 factory raised intake offered for 2027 isn't watertight, so Motor1 notes it doesn't improve wading the way a sealed snorkel would. It helps with dust.

Q: Is it reliable? Any recalls?
A: It's early days. Recalls so far are an instrument-cluster software update, a corrected load-capacity label, a rear-camera fix, and a 2024–2027 fuel-tube connector recall. Common owner complaints are front-brake squeal in reverse (fixed by a TSB), 12 V battery drain, and hybrid-battery fan warnings. The US 250 doesn't use the V35A V6 involved in the LX and Tundra bearing recalls.

## Toyota Land Cruiser 300 Series (2021–present)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-cruiser/300-series/
Codes: VJA300, FJA300, GRJ300

Verdict: This is the Land Cruiser the rest of the world gets and America has to admire from a distance. It's lighter, stiffer and quicker than the 200, and its engineers used a 30-year-old 80 Series as the benchmark. The only way to buy one in the US is with a Lexus badge on the front.

Toyota unveiled the J300 on 9 June 2021 to replace the 200 Series, which had been on sale since 2007. The V8s are gone. In their place is a pair of twin-turbo V6s: a 409-hp 3.4-liter petrol and a 304-hp 3.3-liter diesel. The truck rides on a new body-on-frame platform and weighs about 200 kg less than the 200. It went on sale in the UAE and Kuwait within weeks, then Japan, Australia, South Africa and much of Asia. It has never been sold in the US or Canada. Wikipedia cites slow sales of the 200 and limited production capacity. North America gets the truck as the LX 600 instead.

### BENCHMARKING THE 80
Chief engineer Takami Yokoo made an unusual choice for a flagship launch: he compared the new truck to a 30-year-old one. 'We actually used the Land Cruiser 80 as a guidepost,' he told reporters, adding that 'even 30 years after it first appeared, it has the best rough road performance of any Land Cruiser.' The team kept the wheelbase that started with the 80 Series, and Yokoo summed up the brief as being 'the partner that will get you home safely, no matter where you go.'
To find what needed fixing, Toyota drove the outgoing 200 around Australia. The trip showed that drivers got tired, so the engineers changed the suspension geometry to make it smoother on pavement. Laser welding that joins two types of metal increased torsional rigidity and helped take out about 200 kg (440 lb). The engine sits lower and further back, and a V6 replaces the V8, so the nose is lighter. Dakar Rally driver Akira Miura did test driving and reported much better control and balance.

### WHAT'S UNDER IT
The platform is GA-F, which the 250 Series and the Lexus GX later shared. Most markets get the V35A-FTS 3.4-liter twin-turbo petrol V6 (VJA300) or the F33A-FTV 3.3-liter twin-turbo diesel (FJA300), both with a 10-speed automatic. Some markets also keep the old 4.0-liter 1GR-FE V6 with a six-speed (GRJ300). The chassis gets an upgraded Electronic Kinetic Dynamic Suspension System (E-KDSS), adaptive variable suspension, Multi-Terrain Select with new Deep Snow and Auto modes, and an underbody camera.
For the first time there's a GR Sport. Auto Bild described it as inspired by the Dakar Rally, and it is the version to have off-road: it has front and rear locking differentials, while the standard truck has only a center lock. Ground clearance is 230 mm and the approach angle is 32 degrees, and overall length, width and wheelbase are largely the same as the 200's. ANCAP's 2022 rating scored it 89 percent for adult occupants and 88 percent for children.

### THE WAITING GAME
Demand overwhelmed supply. In January 2022 Auto Bild reported that Toyota's Japanese website was telling buyers to expect waits of up to four years, a backlog it compared to the Mercedes G-Class's. Germany wasn't expected to get the 300 at all, and kept the older J150 Prado instead. A hybrid, the VJH300, arrived in 2025, launching first in the UAE with a new front end. Japan got an updated range with the hybrid on 1 October 2026, according to Wikipedia.

### THE AMERICAN WORKAROUND
For Americans, importing a 300 isn't a realistic option, because of the 25-year rule; one IH8MUD member worked out that 2047 is the first year a 2022 truck becomes legal. The practical answer is the LX 600, unveiled on 13 October 2021 on the same platform with the 409-hp V35A and a 10-speed. The 457-hp LX 700h hybrid followed, and the LX 700h Overtrail, announced in October 2024, has front, center and rear lockers like a GR Sport.
Being the US version has a downside: the US recalls. NHTSA campaigns 24V381 and 25V767 cover V35A engines in the Lexus LX, Tundra and some GX 550s in which machining debris can damage the main bearings, causing knocking, rough running or a stall. 25V767 alone lists 9,895 LX models built between February 2022 and April 2024. Separately, Lexus is updating transmission software on about 4,400 2025–26 LX 600s. The sources here don't say whether overseas 300s with the same engine are covered, so owners outside the US should check with their local Toyota distributor.

### Data plate
- Chassis: J300 (VJA300 / FJA300 / GRJ300 / VJH300)
- Platform: GA-F body-on-frame
- Unveiled: 9 June 2021
- Chief Engineer: Takami Yokoo
- Engine (Petrol): V35A-FTS 3.4 L twin-turbo V6
- Output: 409 hp · 650 Nm
- Engine (Diesel): F33A-FTV 3.3 L twin-turbo V6 · 304 hp · 700 Nm
- Transmission: 10-spd auto (6-spd on GRJ300)
- Weight Vs. 200: ≈ −200 kg
- Ground Clearance: 230 mm
- Angles: 32° approach · up to 26.5° departure
- Us Availability: Not sold; see Lexus LX 600

### Engineering
The 300 keeps the formula that made the name: a separate ladder frame, full-time four-wheel drive with low range, and stabilizer bars that are hydraulically linked by E-KDSS. Toyota rebuilt everything around that formula. The frame is lighter and stiffer, the twin-turbo V6 sits lower and further back, and there's a 10-speed automatic, adaptive dampers and a camera that shows what's under the truck.
- Chassis: GA-F (TNGA-F) ladder frame (Redesigned to be lighter and more rigid; length, width and wheelbase are largely the same as the 200's.)
- Weight: About 200 kg (440 lb) lighter than the 200 (Laser welding of mixed metals; Toyota also claims a lower center of gravity and better weight distribution.)
- Engines: 3.4 L twin-turbo petrol V6 · 3.3 L twin-turbo diesel V6 (V35A-FTS: 409 hp / 650 Nm. F33A-FTV: 304 hp / 700 Nm. Some markets keep the 4.0 L 1GR-FE.)
- Transmission: 10-speed automatic (AWR10L65) (GRJ300 (1GR-FE) keeps the 6-speed AC60F.)
- Suspension: E-KDSS + adaptive variable suspension (Upgraded hydraulic stabilizer-disconnect system for articulation; Multi-Terrain Select with Deep Snow and Auto modes.)
- Lockers & Geometry: Center lock standard; front + rear on GR Sport (230 mm ground clearance, 32° approach, up to 26.5° departure.)

### Versions
- 2021–present · VJA300 · V35A-FTS 3.4 L twin-turbo V6 (petrol) · 409 hp / 650 Nm · 10-speed auto. Replaces the V8s.
- 2021–present · FJA300 · F33A-FTV 3.3 L twin-turbo V6 diesel · 304 hp / 700 Nm · 10-speed auto. Wikipedia lists the figures from 2022.
- 2021–present · GRJ300 · 1GR-FE 4.0 L V6 (petrol) · ≈ 271 hp / 385 Nm · Carried-over naturally aspirated V6 with a 6-speed auto, for some markets.
- 2025–present · VJH300 · V35A-FTS 3.4 L twin-turbo V6 hybrid · 457 hp / 790 Nm · Debuted in the UAE with a redesigned front end; on sale in Japan from 1 October 2026.
- 2021–present · GR Sport · Petrol or diesel V6 (by market) · — · First GR Sport Land Cruiser: front and rear lockers, extra body adhesive, about 5 mm shorter.
- 2022–present · Lexus LX 600 / 700h (J310) · V35A-FTS 3.4 L twin-turbo V6 (+ hybrid on 700h) · 409 hp (600) · 457 hp (700h) · The North American 300. LX 700h Overtrail has three lockers.

### Year-by-year
- 2021: Unveiled 9 June 2021 on the GA-F frame, about 200 kg lighter than the 200. V8s are dropped for the 3.4 V35A-FTS twin-turbo petrol V6 and 3.3 F33A-FTV twin-turbo diesel V6 with a 10-speed automatic
- 2021: Japan sales from 2 August; GR Sport added, the first Land Cruiser grade with front and rear diff locks on top of the centre lock
- 2021: Australian launch on 5 October in GX, GXL, VX, Sahara, GR Sport and Sahara ZX grades
- 2021–24: Early Australian trucks are covered by recalls XGG22 (stability control may not default to on; built 16 July 2021 to 1 April 2022) and ZGG04 (10-speed can creep in neutral; built 16 July 2021 to 12 January 2024). Both are software fixes, so check they have been done
- 2024: February: Toyota pauses shipments of the F33A-FTV diesel and the 300s and LXs that use it after Toyota Industries finds irregularities in engine certification testing
- 2024: The smaller J250 takes over the Land Cruiser name in North America; the 300 is never offered in the US or Canada
- 2025: Hybrid powertrain introduced, debuting in the UAE with a redesigned front fascia
- 2026: Updated Japanese range from 1 October: hybrid in ZX and GR Sport; diesel in ZX, GR Sport and GX
- 2026: Performance Hybrid reaches Australia in GR Sport and Sahara ZX grades: 3.4 twin-turbo V6 plus a 36 kW motor, 341 kW/790 Nm combined, 3,500 kg towing

### Capability
- Towing: 3,500 kg (7,716 lb) braked (same as the 200)
- Ground clearance: 230 mm (9.1 in) (Wikipedia; Toyota NZ's preliminary figure was 235 mm)
- Approach / departure: 32° / 25° (Australian-market spec; Wikipedia gives up to 26.5° departure depending on version)
- Wading depth: 700 mm (27.6 in) (Toyota NZ preliminary figure, as reported by CarMag)
- Curb weight: 2,310–2,645 kg (5,093–5,831 lb) (Wikipedia, varies by market and grade)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 18-inch wheels on base grades; 20-inch on top grades (market-dependent)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x150
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 275/70R18 or 285/70R18 (about 33.3–33.7 in) (IH8MUD owners report no rubbing on stock suspension. One LX owner on 275/70R18s had no rub at any AHC height or at full lock.)
- Biggest tire, Stock + wheels lift: 295/70R18 to 35 in (295/70R18s on stock wheels have been reported on an LX 700h Overtrail. Dissent Off-Road told a member that 35s on a +40 mm offset wheel fit with minimal to zero trimming.)

### Buying checks
- Accept that it's an LX in the US: The 300 isn't sold in the US or Canada and can't be legally imported under the 25-year rule for a long time. For North American buyers, the LX 600 or LX 700h is the 300 Series you can actually buy.
- Run the VIN against the V35A recalls: NHTSA campaigns 24V381 and 25V767 cover V35A engines in which machining debris can damage the main bearings, causing knocking, rough running, a no-start or a stall. 25V767 lists 9,895 2022–2024 LX models built from 26 February 2022 to 2 April 2024; 24V381 covered earlier engines. Ask whether the engine has already been replaced, which several IH8MUD members' trucks have had.
- Check the transmission software recall: NHTSA 26V094000 (Lexus 26LA01) covers about 4,400 2025–26 LX 600s: if a transmission solenoid fails, the transmission and engine ECUs can lose communication and the transmission can damage itself. Dealers update the transmission ECU software for free. In Australia, Toyota recalled 11,020 300s built from February to December 2025 for the same kind of fault. A failed solenoid can let the transmission over-rev, damaging it or leaking fluid onto the hot exhaust; dealers reprogram the transmission ECU (CarExpert, February 2026).
- Test-drive in traffic, not just on the highway: Owners of 2022–24 LX 600s describe a clunk into first gear and hesitation when accelerating from a rolling stop. Some blame the pre-collision system intervening. Drive one through a few stop-and-go junctions before you buy. Owners say the LX 700h hybrid doesn't do it.
- Work the rear hatch: One IH8MUD owner's power hatch beeped and refused to close. The cause was a sticking left-side pinch sensor, which was replaced. Open and close it several times.
- AHC or not, and which locker count?: Many LX trims have height-adjustable AHC suspension, and armor is specific to it: Slee sells separate non-AHC LX 600 sliders, for example. Overtrail and GR Sport trucks have front and rear lockers; standard trucks have only the center lock. Know which one you're buying.
- Ask about fluid changes: Owners on IH8MUD do early differential and transfer-case changes (around 20,000–30,000 miles) after reports of debris in Tundra differential oil. Records of early oil and gear-oil changes, or oil-analysis reports, are a good sign.
- Diesel: how was it driven?: Ask whether a diesel 300 lived in town or towed heavy. Short trips are hard on the DPF and EGR, and heat soak from heavy towing or sand work is linked to bearing wear (Unsealed 4X4). Check the oil level, ask how much it uses between services, and confirm software updates and recall work are done. Look at the fuel-filter area for damage or a guard.

### Common repairs
#### Transfer case and front diff fluid service
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1.5 hours · cost Fluid and washers
Symptoms: Scheduled service. One IH8MUD owner also reported less low-speed 'rocking' in traffic after changing the transfer-case fluid at 19,500 miles.
Fix: Remove the skid plate (two bolts to loosen, per one owner). Always remove the fill plug first, then drain and refill. Figures an owner posted from the service data: transfer case 1.89 qt, plugs 37 N·m (27 ft-lb); front diff 1.23 qt, plugs 39.2 N·m (29 ft-lb); rear diff (with limited-slip) plugs 49 N·m (36 ft-lb). The factory transfer-case fluid is Toyota LF 75W. While the skid is off, grease the driveshaft zerks.
Tools: Socket set · torque wrench · fluid pump · Toyota LF 75W (transfer) and the specified gear oil · new washers: copper for the front drain, flat for the transfer case, collapsible for the front fill and rear drain/fill (as identified by an owner) · grease gun.

#### Early oil change and oil analysis
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour plus lab turnaround · cost Oil, filter and a lab kit
Symptoms: A new or new-to-you V35A truck, especially one built before the recall fixes.
Fix: Many owners change the factory fill early, around 1,000 miles, and send a sample to a lab such as Blackstone. One owner found heavy machining debris in a 2024 GX's oil at 800 miles and much less in a December 2024-build LX at 1,000 miles. Others report high iron and copper at the first change that settled to normal by the third. Repeat the analysis every few changes and keep the reports.
Tools: Socket set · filter wrench · 0W-20 oil (owners report running 0W-20; check your manual) · oil-analysis kit.

#### ATF drain-and-fill
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost Fluid (one owner estimated about 12 qt for a full exchange)
Symptoms: Rough or erratic shifts on a truck with 'lifetime' fluid, or towing and hard off-road use.
Fix: The 10-speed uses thin Toyota WS fluid and has a strainer, not a serviceable filter. An IH8MUD member argues that the lifetime-fill recommendation lets wear metals build up in the valve body. Owners do a drain-and-fill or a staged exchange with WS or a WS-compatible fluid, then set the level with the factory temperature-based check procedure. If you don't have the procedure and a scan tool to read fluid temperature, have a shop do it.
Tools: Socket set · fluid pump · scan tool (Techstream or similar) to read ATF temperature · Toyota WS or a WS-compatible fluid · service manual.

#### Rear hatch won't close
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost Pinch sensor plus labor
Symptoms: You press the hatch button, it beeps once as if it's going to close, then beeps twice and doesn't move.
Fix: First, clean the rubber pinch strips along both sides of the hatch opening and check nothing is caught in them. On the IH8MUD owner's truck the left-side pinch sensor was sticking, and replacing it fixed the problem. Under warranty, let the dealer do it.
Tools: Trim tools · replacement pinch sensor (left or right as diagnosed).

#### Driver's-side windshield rattle
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 30 minutes · cost Free; a little foam
Symptoms: A rattle at the bottom corner of the windshield.
Fix: Two owners traced it to leaves trapped under the hood near the hinge and in the well where the wiper linkage connects. Open the hood, vacuum out the debris, and fit a strip of foam to keep leaves from getting back in.
Tools: Shop vacuum · closed-cell foam strip.

#### Tame rolling-stop hesitation
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 15 minutes · cost Free (or an OBD tool)
Symptoms: Delayed or missing throttle response, or a clunk into first, when accelerating from a rolling stop. Owners say it's worse in Sport and Sport+ modes.
Fix: As an interim fix until Lexus updates the software, owners set the pre-collision system (PCS) to its minimum distance using the screen in front of the driver; turning PCS off also works but loses a safety system. Some use Carista to keep the PCS setting across restarts (and to quiet the ventilated-seat fans). Make sure any software recall is done first.
Tools: None, or an OBD-II dongle with Carista.

#### Diesel: keep the DPF and EGR healthy
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time A weekly highway run; an intake clean is a workshop job · cost Workshop labor for the intake clean
Symptoms: Loss of power, a check-engine light or limp mode on an F33A diesel, sometimes with extra smoke and fuel use.
Fix: Unsealed 4X4 puts most of it down to town driving: repeated stop-start trips can stop the DPF from finishing a regeneration, and the EGR slowly chokes the intake manifold. Its advice is a highway run at least weekly and an intake clean, chemical or manual, at least once a year. The same article reports failures of the 'seventh injector', which sprays diesel into the exhaust to help regeneration. They bring limp mode, smoke and a fault code the dealer has to clear. A Toyota technician told Unsealed it happens to most trucks at around 20,000 km, which the author says he can't verify. Toyota can reportedly tune the problem out, though some owners say it comes back. Make sure all software updates are done.
Tools: OBD-II scanner to read codes · workshop for the intake clean

#### Diesel: guard the exposed fuel filter
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 5 minutes for a bolt-on guard (maker's claim) · cost GMF4x4 FG-2014 guard A$160 (Frankies Auto Electrics, 2026)
Symptoms: The engine cuts out off-road and there's a pool of diesel near the right rear wheel.
Fix: Unsealed 4X4 says the diesel's plastic fuel filter sits by the rear wheel arch, where rocks and sticks can hit it, and recommends an aftermarket protection plate. GMF4x4's FG-2014 is 3 mm powder-coated steel. It bolts on with the supplied hardware and needs no drilling or cutting. If the filter or housing is already cracked, replace it and follow the workshop manual's fuel-priming procedure before you try to restart.
Tools: Basic socket set

### Baseline service
Toyota never sold the 300 in the US, so the specs below are for its US twin, the Lexus LX 600 (same V35A-FTS twin-turbo V6 and 10-speed). They come from AMSOIL's LX 600 lookup and service-data figures posted by IH8MUD owners. Diesel (F33A-FTV) and hybrid trucks differ, and service intervals vary by market, so check your owner's manual. Baselining matters more than usual here because of the V35A machining-debris recall.
- Engine oil & filter: SAE 0W-20 · ≈7.7 qt with filter · drain plug 30 ft-lb, new plug and gasket · At purchase. Toyota Australia's schedule is every 6 months or 10,000 km (CarExpert, 2026); for a US LX and other markets [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]. Many owners shorten it and send samples for oil analysis. (On a US LX 600, check that engine recall 25LA07/25LB07 has been done. Repeat oil analysis every few changes and keep the reports.)
- Engine air filter: OE-type panel filter · interval [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase; more often in dust
- Cabin air filter: OE-type · At purchase
- Spark plugs (petrol) / glow plugs (diesel): OE-type iridium plugs (V35A) · interval [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Per the maintenance schedule (It's a twin-turbo engine, so don't assume a 120k plug interval.)
- Coolant: Toyota Super Long Life Coolant or equivalent · ≈11.7 qt · Inspect at purchase; replacement [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
- Automatic transmission (10-speed): Toyota Genuine ATF WS · ≈12.2 qt total fill · Toyota calls it lifetime fill. Owners drain-and-fill or do a staged exchange at 20,000–30,000 mi. (There's a strainer, not a serviceable filter, and no dipstick. The level is set at a specified ATF temperature, read with a scan tool, through the check plug. One LX 700h owner got about 5 qt out of the pan. On a 2025–26 LX 600, check that the transmission recall has been done.)
- Transfer case: Toyota Genuine Transfer Gear Oil LF 75W · 1.89 qt · plugs 37 N·m (27 ft-lb) · Owners suggest 30,000–40,000 mi at most (Remove the fill plug first. The plug washers are flat, not crush washers. Removing the skid plate means loosening two bolts.)
- Front & rear differentials: 75W-85 GL-5 (Toyota LT) · front 1.23 qt, plugs 39.2 N·m (29 ft-lb) · rear with LSD 5.55 qt, plugs 49 N·m (36 ft-lb) · At purchase; change the front about twice as often as the rear (The front holds just over 1 qt and comes out dirtier. Trucks with a limited-slip rear need LSD-rated oil (one F Sport carries an 'LSD only' tag). Washers: copper on the front drain, crush-type on the front fill and on the rear drain and fill.)
- Driveshaft grease points: Chassis grease at every zerk (about four) · Whenever the skid plate is off (An owner found the front zerks hard to reach (frame and exhaust in the way). One took three pumps before grease showed at the seals.)
- E-KDSS / AHC suspension: Sealed hydraulic systems · fluid [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Inspect at purchase (Check the cylinders, lines and accumulators for weeping. Lexus trucks with AHC: make sure every height mode works.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 or DOT 4 (FMVSS 116) · Flush at purchase if the history is unknown
- 12 V battery: OE-size battery · Test at purchase
- Drive belt: Automatic tension · Inspect at purchase

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: IH8MUD owners report 275/70R18 (about 33.3 inches) and 285/70R18 KO3s (about 33.7 inches) with no rubbing on stock suspension. One LX owner with 275/70R18s had no rub at any AHC height, at full lock, in drive or reverse. 295/70R18s on stock wheels have been reported on an LX 700h Overtrail, and Dissent Off-Road told a member that 35s on a +40 mm offset wheel fit with minimal to zero trimming.

Q: Can I buy a 300 Series in the US?
A: Not new. It isn't sold in the US or Canada, and the 25-year import rule rules out bringing one in for decades. The Lexus LX 600 and LX 700h are the same truck under the skin and are sold in North America.

Q: Why didn't Toyota sell it in America?
A: Wikipedia cites slow sales of the 200 Series and limited production capacity. The smaller 250 took over the Land Cruiser name in the US for 2024.

Q: Which engines are there?
A: It depends on the market: a 3.4-liter twin-turbo petrol V6 (409 hp), a 3.3-liter twin-turbo diesel V6 (304 hp), a carried-over 4.0-liter V6 in some places, and since 2025 a 457-hp V6 hybrid. All but the 4.0 use a 10-speed automatic.

Q: Does it have lockers?
A: Every 300 has a lockable center differential. The GR Sport adds front and rear lockers. On the Lexus side, the LX 700h Overtrail has all three, and Wikipedia also lists a Japan-only LX 'Offroad' trim with three.

Q: How much lighter is it than the 200?
A: About 200 kg (440 lb), thanks to the redesigned GA-F frame and laser-welded mixed-metal construction. The V6s are also lighter than the V8s they replaced and sit further back.

Q: Is the twin-turbo V6 reliable?
A: The US LX 600 shares the V35A with the Tundra, and both are covered by recalls 24V381 and 25V767 for machining debris that can ruin the main bearings. Later engines were built with improved processes or an improved main bearing, and some are still under investigation. Owners routinely do early oil changes and oil analysis.

Q: What did Toyota use as the benchmark?
A: The 80 Series. Chief engineer Takami Yokoo said the 80 still had 'the best rough road performance of any Land Cruiser,' and the 300 keeps the wheelbase the 80 introduced.

Q: How long was the waiting list?
A: In January 2022 Auto Bild reported Toyota Japan quoting waits of up to four years for new orders.

Q: How safe is it?
A: ANCAP's 2022 rating, aligned with Euro NCAP, scored 89% for adult occupants, 88% for child occupants, 81% for vulnerable road users and 77% for safety assist.

Q: What fluids and capacities does it take?
A: From service data posted by an IH8MUD owner: transfer case 1.89 qt of Toyota LF 75W, front diff 1.23 qt. Owners also report using 0W-20 engine oil. Check your own service manual, since markets and drivetrains differ.

Q: Is the V6 diesel reliable?
A: Mostly, but it has known issues. Unsealed 4X4's 2026 round-up of owner reports lists DPF and EGR trouble in town driving, oil consumption of up to 1.7 L between services, seventh-injector faults, and a torque dip at about 2,200–2,500 rpm when towing over 3 t, which a Toyota ECU update fixes or at least minimises. It also reports bearing failures linked to heat soak in the hot-vee layout under hard work such as sand driving and heavy towing, though it calls their incidence 'statistically low'. In February 2024 Toyota paused F33A-FTV engine shipments after Toyota Industries found irregularities in certification testing.

# Land Rover Series & Defender (1948–present)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/

Land Rover started in 1948 as a stopgap: Rover's chief designer Maurice Wilks proposed a light agricultural and utility vehicle, and the first prototype was skinned in Birmabright aluminium alloy because steel was rationed and aluminium wasn't. It was launched at the Amsterdam Motor Show in April that year, and the Series I, II, IIA and III that followed ran until 1985. In 1983 the One Ten arrived with coil springs and permanent four-wheel drive borrowed from the Range Rover Classic, followed by the Ninety in 1984. In 1990 they became the Defender 90, 110 and 130, and the line kept going until 29 January 2016, a 67-year run counted back to the 1948 original. The Discovery (1989) took the same Range Rover chassis in a family-friendly direction. Americans mostly know the classic Defender through a short official window: 525 NAS Defender 110s for 1993 (500 US, 25 Canada), then the NAS Defender 90 through 1997, before the 25-year import rule opened the gray-market floodgates. The badge returned in 2020 as the unibody L663 Defender, while the Ineos Grenadier picked up the ladder-frame torch.

Verdict: The original farm-gate-to-Sahara tool: slow, leaky, drafty, and still the shape every other boxy 4x4 gets measured against.

## Land Rover Series I–III (1948–1985)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/series/
Codes: Series I, Series II, Series IIA, Series III, 88, 109

Verdict: A tractor that learned to do 55 mph, built from aluminium because steel was rationed, and still the vehicle that taught most of the world what a 4x4 is. Slow, loud, honest, and fixable with the tools in a farm shed.

The Series Land Rover is the original: a boxed steel ladder frame, two beam axles on leaf springs, a four-speed gearbox and flat aluminium panels you can unbolt with hand tools. It was meant to be a stopgap for a car company with an empty factory, and it outlived nearly everything else that company built. Today a good one is a collector's car with a Hagerty valuation, but underneath it is still a farm implement, and the owners who get the most out of them treat it exactly like one.

### A JEEP, A FARM AND A STEEL SHORTAGE
After the war Rover had a bombed Coventry factory, a shortage of steel and no affordable car to build. Chief designer Maurice Wilks, who used an army-surplus Jeep on his farm on Anglesey, proposed a light agricultural and utility vehicle with a power take-off. The first prototype used a Jeep chassis, a Rover P3 engine and gearbox, Birmabright alloy bodywork and a steering wheel in the middle, which earned it the nickname 'centre steer'. Early trucks were painted light green because surplus aircraft cockpit paint was available.
The production truck dropped the centre steering and every Jeep part, gained its own transfer box, and was launched at the Amsterdam Motor Show in 1948 on an 80-inch wheelbase with a 1.6-litre four of about 50 bhp. The freewheel four-wheel-drive system was replaced during 1950–51 by a simpler dog-clutch arrangement. A Tickford-bodied, wood-framed Station Wagon arrived in 1949 and flopped, with fewer than 700 sold. Land Rover learned the lesson fast: wheelbases grew to 86 and 107 inches in 1954, then 88 and 109 in 1956, and a 2.0-litre diesel followed in 1957.

### SERIES II AND IIA: THE SHAPE EVERYONE DRAWS
The 1958 Series II brought David Bache's wider 'barrel side' body and the 2.25-litre petrol four, though the first 1,500 or so short-wheelbase trucks kept the 2.0. The 109 Station Wagon could be had as a 12-seater, which in Britain counted as a bus and dodged purchase tax. The IIA of 1961 added a 2.25 diesel, and from 1967 long-wheelbase models could have a 2.6-litre six with servo brakes. Just 811 of those were NADA (North American Dollar Area) trucks, the only long-wheelbase models built for the US and Canada.
By February 1968 total production was just under 600,000, with more than 70% exported, and sales peaked in 1969–70 at over 60,000 a year. From February 1969 home-market trucks moved their headlamps out of the grille panel and into the wings, which is the quickest way to tell a late IIA from an early one. Hagerty notes that because so few were sold in the US, a IIA feels more exotic here than a comparable Jeep or Land Cruiser, and the market has priced that in.

### SERIES III AND THE LONG GOODBYE
The 1971 Series III was a modernisation by Land Rover standards: synchromesh on all four forward gears, a plastic grille, a moulded plastic dashboard with the instruments moved in front of the driver, and the 2.25's compression raised from 7:1 to 8:1. Long-wheelbase trucks got the one-piece Salisbury rear axle as standard. The millionth Land Rover rolled off the line in 1976, but North American factory sales had already ended in 1974, so most Series IIIs in the US arrived later through private import.
Land Rover kept fixing the known weak spots. In 1980 the 2.25 petrol and diesel engines got five-main-bearing crankshafts and the axles and hubs were strengthened, and in 1982 the driveshaft spline count went from 10 to 24 to deal with rear half-shafts that snapped under overloaded commercial use. A County station wagon trim arrived in April 1982, and a Stage 1 V8 (the Rover 3.5 detuned to 91 hp, with permanent four-wheel drive) ran from 1979 to 1985. Roughly 440,000 Series IIIs were built before the coil-sprung One Ten and Ninety took over.

### WHY THEY STILL MATTER
A Series truck is about as mechanically transparent as a motor vehicle gets. There is no ECU, the body panels unbolt, the rear half-shafts slide out of fully floating hubs without even jacking the truck up, and the parts catalogue from Vermont to Solihull is still enormous. The same simplicity explains its faults: leaf springs ride hard, the gearbox wears out first and second, the steel chassis and bulkhead rot where mud sits, and a 2.25 petrol is happiest at 50–55 mph.
None of that has hurt values. In 2019 Hagerty reported a median 'Excellent' value of $39,000 for Series II/IIA trucks, with petrol engines worth more than diesels and soft-tops slightly ahead of wagons. Every boxy 4x4 on this site, from the Range Rover Classic to the Ineos Grenadier, is in some way an argument with this vehicle about how much comfort a working truck is allowed to have.

### Data plate
- Production: 1948–1985
- Launch: Amsterdam Motor Show, 1948
- Designer: Maurice Wilks
- Wheelbases: 80 · 86/88 · 107/109 in
- Chassis: Boxed steel ladder frame
- Body: Aluminium alloy panels, steel bulkhead
- Suspension: Leaf springs, beam axles
- 4Wd: Selectable (permanent on Stage 1 V8)
- Engines: 1.6 · 2.0 · 2.25 petrol/diesel · 2.6 I6 · 3.5 V8
- Us Factory Sales: Ended 1974
- 1,000,000Th Land Rover: 1976
- Series Iii Built: ≈ 440,000

### Engineering
Every Series truck uses the same basic recipe: a fully boxed, welded steel ladder frame, beam axles on semi-elliptic leaf springs, a four-speed gearbox with a two-speed transfer box, and selectable four-wheel drive. The body is aluminium alloy panels bolted to the frame and a steel bulkhead, a choice made in 1948 because steel was rationed and kept even after aluminium became more expensive. The result is light, rust-resistant on top and rust-prone underneath, and almost entirely serviceable with hand tools.
- Chassis: Boxed steel ladder frame (Rear crossmember and outriggers are the usual rot spots.)
- Body: Aluminium alloy panels (Birmabright on the first trucks; corrodes where it touches steel.)
- Suspension: Leaf springs, beam axles (Parabolic springs are the common comfort upgrade.)
- 4Wd: Selectable, dog clutch (Freewheel system replaced around 1950; Stage 1 V8 got permanent 4WD.)
- Rear Axle: Rover type, Salisbury on LWB (Salisbury standard on Series III 109; some late IIAs had it too.)
- Gearbox: 4-speed manual + 2-speed transfer (Full synchromesh only from the Series III.)

### Versions
- 1948–1951 · Series I 80-inch · 1.6 petrol I4 · ≈ 50 bhp · Launch model; freewheel 4WD until around 1950.
- 1952–1958 · Series I 80 / 86 / 88 / 107 / 109 · 2.0 petrol I4; 2.0 diesel (1957–58) · 52 hp (diesel) · Wheelbases grow in 1954 and again in 1956.
- 1958–1961 · Series II 88 / 109 · 2.25 petrol I4 (early SWB kept 2.0) · 72 hp · Bache's barrel-side body and wider track.
- 1961–1971 · Series IIA 88 / 109 · 2.25 petrol & diesel; 2.6 petrol I6 (LWB, from 1967) · 77 hp (2.25 petrol), 94 hp (2.6) per Hagerty · Headlamps in wings from Feb 1969 (home market).
- 1971–1985 · Series III 88 / 109 · 2.25 petrol & diesel; 2.6 six · — · All-synchro gearbox; 24-spline shafts from 1982.
- 1979–1985 · Stage 1 V8 (mostly 109) · 3.5 Rover V8 · 91 hp · Permanent 4WD; only 24 built as 88s.

### Year-by-year
- 1948: Launched at the Amsterdam Motor Show: 80-inch wheelbase, 1.6 petrol
- c. 1950: Freewheel 4WD replaced by selectable four-wheel drive via a dog clutch (1950–51)
- 1952: Larger 2.0 petrol replaces the 1.6 (1950–52, sources differ)
- 1954–56: Wheelbases grow to 86/107, then 88/109 in 1956; 2.0 diesel follows in 1957
- 1958: Series II: wider 'barrel side' body and 2.25 petrol
- 1961: Series IIA: 2.25 diesel; 2.6 six in the 109 from 1967. Classic Car Hub calls an 88 or 109 IIA the sweet spot of the Series range [buy]
- 1969: Headlamps move into the wings on home-market IIAs (February)
- 1971: Series III: all-synchro gearbox, plastic grille and new dash. Octane calls it by far the easiest Series to live with and suggests a short-wheelbase 2.25 petrol [buy]
- 1974: Factory sales to North America end
- 1979: Stage 1 V8 (3.5 Rover V8, permanent 4WD), mostly 109s
- 1980–82: Axles and hubs strengthened (1980); half-shaft splines go from 10 to 24 (1982)
- 1985: Series production ends; the coil-sprung One Ten (1983) and Ninety (1984) replace it

### Capability
- Fuel economy: 14–17 mpg (imperial), 2.25 petrol (AULRO owners; best about 21 mpg at a steady 50 mph in a SWB)
- Comfortable cruise: 55–60 mph (2.25 petrol) (60–65 mph on the flat with a Fairey overdrive, per Rovers North forum members)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 7.50x16 (factory option, tube-type rims)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x165.1 (5x6.5"), shared with Defender steel wheels
- Offset: Defender/NAS 110 steels fit but sit about 3 in wider overall
- Center Bore: Defender alloys won't clear Series hubs
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 235/85R16 (Fits a stock 88 or 109 once the steering stops are adjusted so the tyre clears the chassis at full lock. 215/85R16 is also close to the 7.50x16 size; 265/75R16 on 5.5 in rims rubbed the frame for one owner. Original rims are tube-type; fit tubeless tyres only on rims with safety humps.)

### Buying checks
- Chassis rear crossmember and outriggers: These are repaired or replaced more than anything else on a Series frame. Feel along the top of the box sections and above the bump stops, where off-road loads concentrate. Heavy rot can mean a replacement chassis, which series123's guide puts at £1,000-plus in the UK, so make sure the price reflects it.
- Bulkhead and door hinges: Check the lower bulkhead, the footwell corners and around the door hinges, plus anywhere the aluminium body touches steel: body-to-chassis mounts and where the wings bolt to the bulkhead. Serious bulkhead rot usually means the body has to come off.
- Gearbox jumping out: First and second wear and can jump out of gear. Press and release the throttle in each gear on the test drive, try every ratio including low range, and listen for noises. The series123 guide rates the Series III gearbox as weaker than the Series II's.
- Mismatched differentials: Owners sometimes fit a taller rear differential for economy. If front and rear ratios don't match, the truck will fight itself in four-wheel drive. Drive a short distance on soft ground to confirm 4WD engages and behaves.
- Half-shafts and drive flanges: A clunk from the rear when you come to a stop (the 'Salisbury clunk' on later trucks) usually means worn splines in the drive flange. Rovers North forum members report flanges strip out occasionally and recommend carrying a spare. Check for play in the propshaft UJs too.
- Springs and mounts: Leaves should be uniform and the truck should sit level. Look for cracked or welded spring hangers; rust at the spring mounts is an MOT failure in the UK.
- Engine health: Low knocking points to worn crank bearings; a lighter, rapid tapping may just be tappets needing adjustment. Occasional blue smoke can be valve-stem seals, continuous blue smoke means rings and bores, and black smoke points at the carburettor.
- Wheels and tyres: Original Series rims are tube-type. Tubeless radials need wheels with safety humps (later Defender-style wheels), and you shouldn't run tubes in tubeless wheels. Check what's fitted before you assume the tyres are a simple swap.

### Common repairs
#### Swivel housing rebuild (Series IIA/III)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Several hours per side · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Oil weeping past the swivel seal, pitted chrome on the swivel ball, wandering or heavy steering.
Fix: Strip the hub and swivel housing, fit the new top pin, Railko bush with bottom wafer, bottom bearing and race, gaskets and swivel seal. Rovers North says to soak the Railko bush and wafer in 75-90 gear oil overnight and to lubricate the assembly with 75-90 oil rather than grease packs. Set preload with top-pin shims (removing shims tightens it), measuring turning effort with a spring scale with the big seal removed and the bolts fully tightened. Take the preload range from the workshop manual for your model.
Tools: Spring/fish scale, torque wrench, hub nut spanner · Rovers North RNA3181P swivel rebuild kit (IIA 1962–71 and Series III non-V8, one side, no ball) · 75-90 gear oil

#### Rear half-shaft and drive flange swap
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time About an hour per side · cost Parts only
Symptoms: Clunk when stopping or taking up drive, a wheel that won't drive, or a snapped shaft (usually at the diff end).
Fix: The rear hubs are fully floating, so the shaft can come out without jacking the truck. Remove the six drive-flange bolts and the hub cap, pull the flange and shaft, and inspect the splines on both. Fit a new flange (and shaft if needed), clean both mating faces, add a thin film of RTV, and refit the six bolts to the specified torque. Upgraded 24-spline shafts are common; check flange bolt patterns (Series flanges have six bolts, Defender flanges five) before ordering.
Tools: Sockets, torque wrench, RTV sealant · drive flange, half-shaft, gasket

#### Leaf spring and chassis bush replacement
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A weekend for all four springs · cost Parts plus your patience
Symptoms: Clonks over bumps, the truck leaning or sitting low, cracked or perished bushes, or you're fitting parabolics.
Fix: Take the springs and shackles off first, then deal with the chassis bushes. Rovers North members drive the old bush out with an air chisel and a worn socket the size of the outer shell, or burn the rubber out with a MAPP torch once the bolt is free, then cut the remaining shell lengthwise with a reciprocating saw from the inside out without cutting the frame. Fit new bushes and springs following the workshop manual.
Tools: Air chisel or MAPP torch, reciprocating saw, drifts, jack and stands · spring and chassis bushes, shackle pins, springs (or parabolics)

#### Clutch cross-shaft pins
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A day with the floor out · cost Pins and bushes are cheap; a seized pin can mean gearbox removal
Symptoms: Clutch pedal suddenly stops a quarter to a third of the way down and the clutch won't disengage, while the hydraulics still work through their full stroke when disconnected.
Fix: Disconnect the slave push rod and work the pedal to confirm the master and slave are fine. Lift the floor panels to reach the cross-shaft, check the pins, coupling tube and spherical bushes, then replace sheared pins (one Rovers North contributor recommends hardened pins), a coupling with elongated holes, and worn bushes. In one reported case a sheared pin was seized in the shaft and the transmission had to come out.
Tools: Basic hand tools, drifts · clutch cross-shaft pins, coupling, cross-shaft bushes

#### Rear crossmember and outrigger repair
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A weekend or more · cost Panels are cheap; welding is the bill
Symptoms: Flaking or perforated steel at the rear crossmember, soft outriggers, fresh underseal hiding something.
Fix: Clean back to bare metal and assess. Outriggers and rear crossmembers are bolt-on or weld-in replacement sections; cut out the rotten section, fit the new one square to the frame and seam-weld it, then protect the inside of the box sections. If the main rails are thin as well, a galvanised replacement chassis is the permanent answer.
Tools: Welder, grinder, cutting discs, rust protection · replacement crossmember and outriggers or a galvanised chassis

#### Fit 235/85R16s and set the steering stops
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time An hour plus tyre fitting · cost Tyres plus fitting
Symptoms: Tyres touching the frame at full lock after fitting larger or wider tyres.
Fix: 235/85R16 is the most-recommended size on the Rovers North forum, close to (but a little wider than) the factory 7.50x16 option. If the tyres touch the chassis at full lock, wind out the steering stop bolts on the swivel housings until there's clearance. Expect a slightly bigger turning circle.
Tools: Spanners · 235/85R16 tyres on suitable rims (tube-type Series rims need tubes; tubeless tyres want rims with safety humps)

#### Steering relay: free it, reseal it, refill it
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A day; the radiator has to come out · cost One owner's rebuild cost about $8; a replacement relay was about $100 plus shipping (Rovers North forum)
Symptoms: Steering that is very heavy or tight, especially on a truck that has stood outside for years, or oil weeping from the bottom of the relay.
Fix: The relay is the box-shaped unit in the chassis crossmember ahead of the radiator. It isn't the steering box at the foot of the column. Rule out dry ball joints and the steering damper first. Rovers North forum members say the radiator has to come out to reach the relay bracket bolts. A stubborn relay can be rebuilt without pulling it from the chassis, and one owner freed a seized unit with a 3 ft pipe over the arm. Inside, the bushes need lubrication. One owner found his 'bone dry' and could turn the shaft by hand with pliers after the rebuild. For a leak, members say you can remove the retaining ring and bottom plate and fit a new seal without stripping the whole relay. Refill with 90-weight gear oil.
Tools: Spanners and sockets · ball-joint splitter · 3 ft pipe for leverage · relay seals · 90-weight gear oil

#### Gearbox jumping out of gear: find the cause
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time An hour for the external checks; a weekend or more if the gearbox comes out · cost Detent springs and adjustments are cheap; internal repairs are parts plus a lot of labor
Symptoms: The lever pops out of gear, often second or fourth, on the overrun or over bumps. Some owners resort to holding it in, or to a bungee cord on long trips.
Fix: Start with the cheap checks that Rovers North forum members suggest. Look for play in the gear lever and its mounting: one owner tightened it and it 'totally' stopped jumping out of second. The same owner also found a dragging, bent clutch disc. Next, take off the top PTO cover and check the mainshaft nut for free play; an overdrive has to come off to reach it. With the cover off, inspect the selector forks and detent springs. Worn forks, a loose circlip on the gear cluster or worn synchros mean the box comes out. If the speedo also wanders and transfer-box oil leaks between the handbrake drum and its backing plate, one member says the rear output shaft nut has backed off. It gets 90 ft-lb.
Tools: Spanners and sockets · torque wrench · top cover gasket · transmission jack if the box has to come out

### Baseline service
A Series truck has no service computer and no idea when it was last looked after, so assume nothing: change every oil, grease every nipple and adjust every brake before you trust it. The Series Land Rover owner's 'green bible' (workshop manual) lists the full service schedule; the items below are what owners on LandyZone and Rovers North treat as the catch-up.
- Engine oil & filter: 20W-50 mineral oil (the period handbook specified a 20W grade) · 2.25: about 1.9 US gal (≈7.2 L) including the filter (Series123); one owner's shop manual gives 13 pints plus 1.8 pints for the filter, which he works out as 7.4 US qt (≈7 L) · Then per manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Owners stick with mineral oil; one warns that semi-synthetics can loosen old deposits in a worn engine. Petrol and diesel 2.25s use element-type or spin-on filters depending on year.)
- Air cleaner: Oil-bath canister on most trucks · refill grade [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Clean and refill at every oil change; more often in dust (If a previous owner swapped to an SU carburettor, check the SU dashpot has oil too.)
- Ignition (petrol): Points gap and timing per manual · plugs N12Y (8:1 CR) or N8 (7:1 CR) · Check points and timing at every service (Owners list checking the points gap as a routine job; match the plug to your engine's compression ratio.)
- Heater plugs (diesel): 2.25 diesel heater plugs · Test at purchase; replace failed plugs (Hard cold starts on a 2.25 diesel usually mean heater plugs before anything more expensive.)
- Coolant: Antifreeze mix [CONFIRM IN MANUAL for type and capacity] · Flush and refill now; then per manual (Check the block drain plug and core plugs for weeps while it's drained.)
- Gearbox & transfer box: EP90 gear oil · Series II/IIA: gearbox 2.5 imp pt (3 US pt, ≈1.4 L), transfer box 4.5 imp pt (≈5.5 US pt, ≈2.6 L), per Series123 and the workshop manual quoted on the Rovers North forum · Series III [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Drain and refill now; then per manual (Check the transfer box output seal: oil leaking past it soaks the transmission handbrake shoes. Owners buy EP90 in 20 L drums because a Series uses a lot of it.)
- Front & rear differentials: EP90 gear oil · capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Drain and refill now; then per manual (Don't put one-shot swivel grease in the diffs; owners say drain it if someone has.)
- Swivel housings: 75-90 gear oil on IIA/III with the Railko bush (Rovers North) · Check level every service; refill now (Rovers North advises oil, not grease packs, for the Railko bush, and warns that running free-wheeling hubs unlocked starves the swivels of lubrication.)
- Grease points: Grease all nipples: propshaft UJs and sliding joints, steering and spring shackles · Every service ('Do all the grease nipples' is the first line of most owners' service lists.)
- Wheel bearings & front hubs: Check play and adjust; check the front hubs are full · Now, then annually (Wider tyres are harder on wheel bearings, according to Rovers North forum members.)
- Brakes & brake fluid: Brake fluid [CONFIRM IN MANUAL for DOT grade] · adjust drum brakes · Fluid every 2 years; adjust shoes at every service (Series drum brakes need regular manual adjustment; owners note they will need adjusting on any truck you buy.)
- Clutch hydraulics: Same fluid as the brakes · Bleed or flush with the brakes ('Don't forget the clutch' — the slave cylinder is easy to overlook.)
- Fuel filter: Cartridge filter (diesel) or in-line element (petrol) · Replace now (Old tanks shed rust and sediment; a new filter is cheap insurance.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: 235/85R16 is the size most owners recommend: a Rovers North forum member calls it close to, but a little wider than, the factory-optional 7.50x16, and it should fit a stock 88 or 109 once the steering stops are adjusted so the tyre clears the frame at full lock (expect a slightly bigger turning circle). 215/85R16 is also close to 7.50x16. 265/75R16 on stock 5.5-inch rims rubbed the frame by about half to three-quarters of an inch for one owner, and another found 265s too wide on a 109. Original rims are tube-type, so check the wheels before fitting tubeless radials.

Q: What's the difference between a Series I, II, IIA and III?
A: Series I (1948–58) has flat sides and 80, 86/88 or 107/109-inch wheelbases. Series II (1958–61) brought the wider 'barrel side' body and the 2.25 petrol. Series IIA (1961–71) looks almost identical but added the 2.25 diesel and the 2.6 six, and late home-market IIAs have headlamps in the wings. Series III (1971–85) has a plastic grille, a plastic dash with instruments in front of the driver and an all-synchro gearbox.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: Depends what you want. Series Is are the collectors' trucks. Classic Car Hub calls an 88- or 109-inch Series IIA the sweet spot, with good parts supply and a well-documented spec. Octane says the Series III is by far the easiest to live with and recommends a short-wheelbase 2.25 petrol for most buyers, or a Stage 1 V8 if you want something special; Series123 notes the III's gearbox isn't as strong as the II's. Heritage Parts Centre also rates the 2.25 petrol the preferable engine.

Q: Were Series Land Rovers sold new in the US?
A: Yes, but not many. Factory sales to North America ended in 1974. Only 811 of the long-wheelbase IIAs with the 2.6 six were NADA (North American Dollar Area) trucks, the only long-wheelbase models built for the US and Canada.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: Owners on AULRO report roughly 14–17 mpg (imperial) for a 2.25 petrol in normal use, with a best of about 21 mpg at a steady 50 mph in a short-wheelbase truck. Loaded, hilly driving pulls it back toward 14. In US gallons, knock about a sixth off those figures.

Q: How fast will it cruise?
A: Owners on the Rovers North forum put the comfortable cruise for a 2.25 petrol at 55–60 mph. With a Fairey overdrive, 60–65 on the flat is realistic. One owner advises 3,000–3,400 rpm for the four-cylinder petrol and warns that sitting at 4,000-plus wears engines out faster.

Q: Why do Series rear half-shafts break?
A: Partly the design of the shafts and partly overloading in commercial use. Land Rover strengthened the axles and hubs in 1980 and increased the driveshaft spline count from 10 to 24 in 1982. Forum members say shafts usually break at the differential end, and worn drive flanges announce themselves with a clunk well before they strip.

Q: Should I fit free-wheeling front hubs?
A: Rovers North advises against it on Series IIA/III swivels with the Railko bush: running the hubs unlocked stops the front driveline turning, which it says starves the swivel ball, Railko bush and front propshaft of lubrication. If you fit them anyway, lock them in regularly.

Q: Petrol or diesel? Soft top or wagon?
A: On value, Hagerty found in 2019 that Series II/IIA petrol trucks were worth about 6% more than diesels and soft-tops about 2% more than wagons. In use, the 2.25 petrol is the more pleasant road engine; the early 2.0 and 2.25 diesels are slow even by Series standards.

Q: What are the rust spots?
A: The aluminium body doesn't rust but corrodes where it touches steel. The steel parts do rust: rear crossmember, outriggers, chassis box sections above the bump stops, the lower bulkhead and footwells, door hinge areas and door bottoms.

Q: Can I put tubeless tyres on the original wheels?
A: Not properly. Original Series rims are tube-type. Tubeless radials need wheels with safety humps, which later Defender wheels have. Don't fit inner tubes in tubeless wheels.

Q: How many were built?
A: Just under 600,000 by February 1968, more than 70% of them exported. The 1,000,000th Land Rover was built in 1976, and about 440,000 Series IIIs were made between 1971 and 1985.
