## Land Rover 90 / 110 / Defender (1983–2016)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/defender-90-110/
Codes: One Ten, Ninety, 127 / 130, NAS 110, NAS 90

Verdict: A Series Land Rover that finally got coil springs, then refused to change anything else for 33 years. Americans got a few thousand officially; everyone else got a legend.

The classic Defender is what happens when a company finds the right answer in 1948 and spends the next six decades only fixing the bits that hurt. Under the slab-sided aluminium skin sits a steel ladder frame, two beam axles and bolted-on panels. It is not quick, quiet or watertight. It is, however, the vehicle that taught several generations of overlanders that you can rebuild anything in a campsite if the thing was designed by people who expected you to.

### FROM SERIES TO ONE TEN
By the early 1980s the leaf-sprung Series III was feeling its age. Land Rover's fix was to raid its own luxury shelf: the One Ten of 1983 got coil springs front and rear and permanent four-wheel drive with a centre differential, both lifted from the Range Rover Classic. The short-wheelbase Ninety followed in 1984 and the long One Two Seven in 1985.
Engines were a grab bag at first: 2.25-litre petrol and diesel carry-overs, a 2.5 diesel making a heroic 68 hp from 1984, and the Rover 3.5 V8 that turned the 90 into something approaching brisk. A Diesel Turbo arrived in 1986, and in 1990 the 200Tdi finally gave the truck a diesel worth having, with 107 hp and 195 lb-ft. It is still the engine many gray-market shoppers go looking for, because there is very little on it that a laptop needs to diagnose.

### THE DEFENDER NAME, AND AMERICA
When the Discovery arrived in 1989, the plain-named Land Rover needed a name of its own. It became the Defender 90, 110 and 130, with badges changing for the 1991 model year. The 300Tdi replaced the 200Tdi in 1994, the five-cylinder Td5 came in 1998, and the Ford-sourced 2.4 'Puma' diesel with a six-speed arrived in 2007. Through all of it, the basic shape barely moved.
North America's official ration started with the 1993 NAS (North American Specification) Defender 110: 525 trucks, 500 for the US and 25 for Canada, all Alpine White, all 3.9-litre V8 with a five-speed manual, full external roll cage and a numbered badge. The NAS Defender 90 followed from 1994, first as a soft-top and later with a removable fibreglass roof panel or a full hard-top, and the last 1997 trucks got a 4.0 V8 and a ZF four-speed automatic. ECD puts total NAS production at about 7,059.

### WHAT MADE IT SPECIAL
The genius is that almost nothing is precious. Body panels are aluminium bolted to a steel frame, the axles are solid, the transfer box is a two-speed LT230 with a centre diff you lock by hand when the going gets slippery, and the parts catalogue is still enormous decades later. Owners fix their own swivels, timing belts and outriggers because the job is genuinely within reach, and an aftermarket from Solihull to Vermont exists to help.
It also leaks, rattles, rusts at the steel bits and steers like a boat with opinions. That's the deal. In return you get short overhangs, a body you can see the corners of, a cabin you can hose out, and a silhouette so recognizable that Ineos built a whole company, and the Grenadier, around missing it. Love it or hate it, nobody has ever mistaken one for a crossover.

### HOW IT ENDED, AND THE 25-YEAR AFTERLIFE
US sales stopped after the 1997 model year; regulations arriving for 1998, including airbag and side-impact door requirements, made the old body uneconomic to certify. Production for everyone else ended on 29 January 2016, after a 67-year run counting the Series, and the name came back in 2020 on the unibody, independently sprung L663 Defender. Whatever you think of the new one, it ended the era of the separate chassis and beam axles at Land Rover.
Meanwhile federal law did the rest. NHTSA lets a vehicle at least 25 years old, counted from its date of manufacture, be imported without meeting FMVSS, so every year another batch of Euro-market 90s and 110s becomes legal. That market has teeth: in 2014 Homeland Security agents seized more than two dozen Defenders imported by one North Carolina enthusiast over suspected VIN swaps; after a legal fight they were found correctly imported and ordered returned in 2015. Not every owner was so lucky: Hagerty reported one whose undocumented truck was seized and apparently lost. Buy the paperwork before you buy the truck.

### Data plate
- Production: 1983–29 Jan 2016
- Names: One Ten (1983), Ninety (1984), Defender from 1990
- Wheelbases: 90 · 110 · 127/130
- Chassis: Steel ladder frame
- Body: Aluminium panels, steel bulkhead
- Suspension: Coil springs, beam axles
- 4Wd: Permanent, lockable centre diff
- Transfer: LT230 (LT95 on early V8)
- Engines: 3.5/3.9/4.0 V8 · 2.5 D/TD · 200Tdi · 300Tdi · Td5 · 2.4/2.2 Puma
- Nas 110 (1993): 525 built (500 US, 25 CA)
- Nas Total: ≈ 7,059 (ECD)
- Us Import: 25 years from date of manufacture

### Engineering
The 90/110 is a Series Land Rover rebuilt on Range Rover hardware: a boxed steel ladder frame carrying beam axles on coil springs, permanent four-wheel drive through a two-speed transfer box with a lockable centre differential, and aluminium body panels bolted to a steel bulkhead. That layout makes it tough and endlessly repairable, and also explains its two big weaknesses: steel parts rust where mud and water sit, and the drivetrain was built for a 1980s power level.
- Chassis: Steel ladder frame (Mild steel; rear crossmember and outriggers rot first.)
- Body: Aluminium panels on steel bulkhead (Panels oxidise and lift paint rather than rusting; the steel bulkhead and footwells do rust.)
- Suspension: Coil springs, beam axles (Front and rear coils, lifted from the 1970 Range Rover.)
- 4Wd: Permanent, lockable centre diff (Lock it before prolonged wheelspin; the stock diff's small gears can fail.)
- Transfer: LT230 two-speed (Used through the Defender run (early V8 One Tens had the LT95), plus Discovery 1 and Range Rover Classic.)
- Steering: Swivel-ball front axle (Chrome balls and seals need periodic attention; preload set with shims.)

### Versions
- 1983–1990 · One Ten / Ninety / One Two Seven · 2.25 petrol & diesel, 2.5 D, 2.5 petrol, 3.5 V8, 2.5 Diesel Turbo · 68 hp (2.5 D) to 134 hp (V8, 1986) · Coil springs and permanent 4WD arrive; Ninety from 1984.
- 1990–1994 · Defender 90 / 110 / 130 · 2.5 200Tdi; 3.5 V8 · 107 hp / 195 lb-ft (200Tdi) · Defender name adopted; badges change for 1991 model year.
- 1993 · NAS Defender 110 · 3.9 Rover V8, 5-speed manual · — · 525 built (500 US, 25 Canada), Alpine White, external cage.
- 1994–1997 · NAS Defender 90 · 3.9 V8 manual; 4.0 V8 + ZF 4-speed auto (1997) · — · Soft-top and hard-top; final 300 in Willow Green.
- 1994–1998 · Defender 90 / 110 / 130 · 2.5 300Tdi · 111 bhp / 195 lb-ft · Watch the timing-belt alignment issue.
- 1998–2007 · Defender Td5 · 2.5 Td5 five-cylinder · 122 hp · Electronically managed; injector-loom oil wicking is the known gremlin.
- 2007–2016 · Defender 'Puma' · Ford 2.4 then 2.2 (2012) diesel, 6-speed · 122 hp / 265 lb-ft · Production ended 29 January 2016.

### Year-by-year
- 1983: One Ten launches with coil springs and permanent 4WD; Series III engines carried over
- 1984: Ninety arrives; 2.5 diesel and wind-up windows
- 1985: V8 offered in the Ninety with the LT85 five-speed; 2.5 petrol; One Two Seven launched
- 1986: 2.5 Diesel Turbo arrives (85 hp); V8 up to 134 hp
- 1990: 200Tdi direct-injection diesel (107 hp); 127 becomes the Defender 130. ECD calls the 200Tdi one of the most dependable engines ever fitted to a Defender [buy]
- 1991 MY: Ninety and One Ten renamed Defender 90 and 110
- 1993: NAS Defender 110 for the US and Canada: 525 built, 3.9 V8, five-speed, external cage
- 1994: 300Tdi and R380 gearbox; NAS Defender 90 (3.9 V8, manual) goes on sale. Specialists rate the 300Tdi the most reliable Defender engine; check the revised timing-belt kit [buy]
- 1997: Final NAS D90s get the 4.0 V8 and ZF four-speed auto; last 300 in Willow Green; US sales end
- 1998: Td5 five-cylinder replaces the Tdi; electronically managed
- 1998–2002: Early '10P' Td5s: oil-pump-drive and head-stud failures (fixed within two years) and cylinder heads that crack around the injectors. 15P engines and '52-plate-on trucks are fine [avoid]
- 2007: Ford-sourced 2.4 'Puma' diesel, six-speed, new dash and forward-facing rear seats
- 2011: PistonHeads' sweet spot among the Puma Defenders: a 2011 truck, 2.4 or the 2.2 that followed, for the best mix of 'sortedness' [buy]
- 2016: Production ends 29 January at Solihull

### Capability
- Towing: 7,716 lb (3,500 kg) braked (750 kg unbraked; 2004 90/110/130 per CarsGuide, same figures for a 2009 90 per GoAuto)
- Fuel tank: 79.5 L (21 gal) (1993 Defender 110 V8; a 2009 Defender 90 is listed at 60 L)
- Approach / departure: 47° / 47° (2009 Defender 90 (Puma), per GoAuto)
- Wading depth: 500 mm (19.7 in) (2009 Defender 90, per GoAuto)
- Fuel economy: 12–16 mpg (V8), 23–27 mpg (300Tdi), 22–26 mpg (Td5), 20–25 mpg (Puma) (ECD's estimates (method not stated); V8 12–14 in real-world use)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 235/85R16 (110, classic factory size), 265/75R16 (NAS Defender 90), 235/80R16 / 265/75R16 (1998 data, per Limitless Tire)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x165.1 (5x6.5")
- Offset: ET20–35 range by body (no single factory figure)
- Center Bore: 114.3 mm
- Lug Thread: M16x1.5
- Lug Torque: 130 N·m (96 lb-ft) for alloy wheels and 108 N·m (80 lb-ft) for steel wheels (Haynes); a 1993 NAS 110 V8 data set also gives 130 N·m, and one other data set gives 170 N·m
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 255/85R16 (≈33 in) (The popular upgrade. Owners report rub on the front radius arms at full lock (wind out the steering stops), against the 45 L auxiliary tank on 110s, and close to the spring brackets at full compression.)
- Biggest tire, 2 in lift: 285/75R16 (≈33 x 11.4 in) (A 110 owner on 2 in, no spacers, reports light rub on the radius arms at full lock. 295/85R16 is a taller, narrower option with little tread choice.)
- Biggest tire, 3 in lift: 315/75R16 (35x12.50R16) (AULRO owners needed 2–3 in of lift plus extended flares or trimming, offset wheels (8–10 in wide), extended bump stops, castor correction, stronger halfshafts/CVs and lower gearing. A Tdi will feel gutless.)

### Buying checks
- Paperwork and VIN first: Match the VIN plate on the brake servo with the number stamped on the front chassis rail. For gray-market imports, make sure the build date really is 25+ years old; federal agents have seized Defenders over alleged VIN swaps, and owners without paperwork lost them.
- Rear crossmember: It takes towing and winching loads and rots from the inside out. Fibreglass, fresh underseal or chunky checker plate can hide it, so get under with a light and ask for the underside to be cleaned.
- Bulkhead, footwells and outriggers: Check the bulkhead sides, bottom corners and the top under the vent flaps, plus the footwells and the outrigger behind the front wheel. Repair is real money; a new bulkhead runs about £1,600 in the UK.
- Swivel balls and steering play: Pitted chrome balls chew their seals and wear the swivel pins. Vague or wobbly steering with excess play points here; budget for rebuild kits if the balls are rusty or weeping.
- Transfer box noise and leaks: Listen for whine and clunks in low range. Oil leaking from the LT230 can coat the transmission handbrake shoes; check the rear output seal and intermediate shaft area.
- 300Tdi timing belt history: Ask whether the revised timing kit (Land Rover STC4096L-type, with flanged crank pulley and spaced idler) has been fitted. Early setups could let the belt track off and wear.
- Td5 oil in the loom: Pull the barrel connector between the engine and injector harnesses. Oil there means it's wicking toward the ECU under the seat.
- NAS authenticity: A real 1993 NAS 110 or 1994–97 NAS 90 carries a numbered NAS badge and a US-market VIN. Plenty of Euro trucks have been dressed up as NAS; check against the registry discussions on Defender Source.

### Common repairs
#### Swivel housing rebuild and preload
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour both sides for a shim/preload adjustment; longer for a full rebuild · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Grease or oil weeping from the swivel seal, pitted chrome ball, wobbly or vague steering.
Fix: Support the chassis on stands, pull the wheels and disconnect the track rod. Rebuild with new bearings, seals and gaskets, fit the swivel pins with shims, torque lower then upper bolts, and check turning effort with a spring balance at the track-rod bore before fitting the seal. Workshop-manual text quoted on Defender2: 1.16–1.46 kg once initial inertia is overcome, with the swivel bearing housing-to-axle bolts at 73 Nm, lower swivel pin bolts at 25 Nm and top pin bolts at 65 Nm (thread sealant STC50552 on the pin bolts). The manuals disagree, though: a RAVE table quoted on AULRO matches those bolt torques (65 Nm upper, 25 Nm lower, 73 Nm housing-to-axle), but a 05/99 workshop-manual table quoted in the same thread gives 78 Nm for both upper and lower pins, and a Defender2 owner reports the older manual's 22–28 Nm lower figure against 78 Nm in a newer one. The 1983–1995 workshop manual and Haynes give a turning effort of 3.6–4.5 kg rather than 1.16–1.46 kg. Use the manual for your exact axle [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]. Add or remove top-pin shims to adjust, then refill with one-shot grease.
Tools: Axle stands, spring balance, vernier, torque wrench · Rovers North RNA3178 swivel rebuild kit with ball (1994–98 Defender, one side) · one-shot grease

#### Top up a leaking swivel with one-shot grease
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time Short job · cost Price of a grease pack
Symptoms: Grease smeared on the inside of the wheel and around the swivel seal retainer.
Fix: Remove the seal retaining ring (six 8 mm nuts on the Defender), clean the seal area, then turn the wheel to full lock away from the side you're filling so the housing doesn't overlap the ball, and fill through the filler plug. One pack per side is roughly right; the grease is runny.
Tools: 8 mm socket, rags · one-shot swivel grease (Britpart and Land Rover packs)

#### 300Tdi timing belt with revised kit
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Several hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Due on the service interval, belt edge wear, or debris inside the timing cover; early-type kits can let the belt track off.
Fix: Lock the cam and crank with the timing tool, remove the front cover, fit the revised kit (flanged crank pulley, idler with integral spacer, tensioner, gasket). On early-type engines, remove the separate spacer washer because the new idler includes it. Land Rover later reduced the torque used to tension the belt (applied to the tensioner before its bolt is tightened) to 11 Nm, according to both Glencoyne and an AULRO member, and earlier manuals may not include the change: Glencoyne gives the old figure as 15 Nm, the AULRO member as 14 Nm. This is the belt-tension setting, not the bolt's clamping torque.
Tools: Timing tool DA3140, torque wrench · STC4096L modified timing belt kit

#### Td5 injector harness oil leak
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Short for the injector harness; much bigger if the main loom is contaminated · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Oil and dust on the ECU plug under the driver's seat, misfires or running issues.
Fix: The injector harness lives inside the rocker cover; oil wicks out through the plug seal and along the main loom to the ECU. Remove the acoustic cover, unplug the barrel connector and check for oil. Replace the injector harness; if oil has reached the main engine loom, replace that too. Light contamination can be flushed with contact cleaner, but replacement is the real fix.
Tools: Basic hand tools, contact cleaner · genuine injector harness

#### LT230 rear output seal and flange
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time A few hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Oil running down the back of the transfer box, contaminated transmission handbrake.
Fix: Confirm the source first: on an LT230 the intermediate shaft is a common leak. Drop the propshaft, remove the rear flange nut and flange (can be done in situ), tap off the dust cap, replace the rear seal and felt washer, then refit with a new M20 nyloc nut and fresh flange bolts torqued to spec.
Tools: Large socket for M20 nut, flange holding tool, seal driver · rear output seal, felt washer, nyloc nut

#### Chassis outrigger and rear crossmember repair
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A weekend or more · cost Outriggers about £30 each; a galvanised replacement chassis supplied and fitted for under £5,000 (UK), per PistonHeads
Symptoms: Perforated outriggers, flaking rear crossmember, failed inspection.
Fix: Cut out rotten outriggers or crossmember sections and weld in new ones, then treat the inside of the frame. If the rot is widespread, a galvanised chassis swap is often the better answer.
Tools: Welder, grinder, cavity wax · replacement outriggers and crossmember

#### Bulkhead footwell repair
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time Weekend · cost Repair panels cheap; used bulkhead from about £650, new about £1,600 (UK)
Symptoms: Damp carpets, holes in the footwells or the bottom corners of the bulkhead.
Fix: Strip interior trim, cut back to clean steel, weld in repair panels, then seal and wax. Fix the leak source too (windscreen and vent seals) or it will happen again.
Tools: Welder, grinder, seam sealer · footwell repair panels

### Baseline service
Assume nothing has been done. Most of these trucks are 25 to 40 years old and have usually had several owners. Change every fluid, re-grease the swivels and propshafts, and confirm the timing-belt history on a Tdi. Specs differ between the US V8 (NAS) trucks and the 200/300Tdi, Td5 and Puma diesels, so identify the engine and gearbox first. Fill the axles, transfer box and swivels to their level plugs on level ground rather than trusting a book capacity.
- Engine oil & filter: NAS 3.9 V8: API SG/SH, SAE 5W-30 or 5W-40 · ≈6.7 L with filter. 300Tdi: ≈6.65 L with filter (Comma lists 10W-40). Td5: 7.8 L with filter, 5W-40 or 5W-50 (Haynes). 2.4 Puma (2007–12 MY) and 2.2 (2012 MY on): 6.85 L service fill with filter, 5W-30 to WSS-M2C913-B or C, or WSS-M2C934-B for the 2.2 with DPF (Land Rover oil chart) · At purchase, then every 5,000–6,000 mi (Comma: 10,000 km / 6 months for the 300Tdi) (The V8 and Tdi engines use the short spin-on filter. The Td5 also has a centrifugal oil-filter rotor that needs servicing.)
- Air filter: OE-type element for your engine · At purchase; more often in dust (Check that the dump valve at the bottom of the airbox isn't split, because it lets unfiltered air in.)
- Fuel filter: Diesel: OE-type element (Tdi: AEU2147L). V8: threaded inline EFI filter ESR4065 (Rovers North lists it for the NAS 90 and 110; Lucky8 for Defender '94–'97) · At purchase (Diesel trucks that sat for a long time collect water and sludge, so drain the sedimenter as well.)
- Glow plugs / spark plugs: Tdi: ETC8847 glow plugs ×4. V8: Rovers North lists ERR3799 for the 3.5/3.9/4.0/4.2 EFI V8; gap [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase if there's no record, or if cold starts are slow (A cold start that smokes and stumbles on a Tdi usually means one or more glow plugs have failed.)
- Timing belt (300Tdi / 200Tdi): Revised kit (flanged crank pulley, idler, tensioner). V8 and Td5 use timing chains, not belts · Every 60,000 mi or 5 years per Lucky8. Glencoyne says 60k or 72k depending on model. Do it at purchase if there's no record (Land Rover revised the 300Tdi tensioner, idler and bottom pulley because belts were wearing early. A yellow paint square on the timing cover was meant to show the fix had been done, but it isn't reliable.)
- Coolant: 50/50 ethylene glycol antifreeze and water · NAS V8 ≈12.8 L. 300Tdi ≈11.1 L · At purchase, then every 2 years (Comma: 40,000 km / 24 months) (The aluminium V8 can't take overheating. Check the radiator for blocked fins and the viscous fan for drag while the system is drained.)
- Manual gearbox (R380 / LT77): Handbook: ATF M2C33-F or G (as quoted on AULRO) · ≈2.4 L (Comma lists its 75W-80 MTF for the 300Tdi R380) · Drain and refill at purchase (Check the level at the side filler with the truck level. A notchy second gear or third-gear synchro problem on an R380 isn't fixed by changing the oil. A 1993 NAS 110 (LT77) data set lists 2.67 L.)
- Automatic (1997 NAS D90 ZF 4HP22): Dexron IID ATF · 9.1 L listed total fill · Drain and refill at purchase (Draining the pan only replaces part of the 9.1 L. Do two drain-and-fills rather than a pressure flush on an old box, and change the pan filter.)
- Transfer box (LT230): EP90 / 80W-90 gear oil, API GL-4 or GL-5 · ≈2.3 L · At purchase (Comma: change every 40,000 km / 24 months) (The filler at the back of the case is tapered, so it feels tight before it is fully seated. Don't overtighten it. Use a new copper washer on the drain plug. The intermediate shaft and rear output seals are the usual leaks.)
- Front & rear axles: EP80W-90 GL-4/GL-5 · front ≈1.7 L. Rear ≈1.7 L on the Rover axle (one data set lists 2.3 L for the NAS D90). 110/130 (Salisbury) rear 2.26 L, 90 rear 1.7 L (Haynes) · At purchase, then every 2 years (Comma: 40,000 km / 24 months) (Fill each axle to the level plug on level ground. The Tdi manual figure is 1.7 L, but one Defender2 owner got nearly 2 L into a rear axle on level ground, so trust the level plug rather than the book. Use a new drain-plug washer.)
- Swivel housings: Early trucks: EP90 · 0.35 L per side (handbook). From about 1994: one-shot swivel grease STC3435, one sachet per side · Check at purchase and every service. Comma says change every 40,000 km / 24 months (Lucky8 lists the STC3435 sachet for the NAS Defender 90 ('94–'97) and the Defender 110 ('93), but a 1997 NAS D90 data set still lists 0.35 L of EP oil, and JC's British 4x4's 52,500 km service checklist for the NAS 90 and 110 also calls for EP gear oil in the swivels, so check what is actually in yours before topping up [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]. An AULRO owner's 1994 swivel took about 450 ml to reach the level plug, so fill until it just dribbles out. Weeping seals mean the chrome ball is pitted. See the repairs above.)
- Power steering & steering box: Dexron IID ATF (Haynes) · 2.8 L system. The 1993 US service checklist says ATF Type F instead, so check what's in yours before topping up. Steering box: EP80W-90 · Check at purchase (Leaks from the box's input seal or sector shaft are common. Top up and watch the level.)
- Brake & clutch fluid: DOT 4 · At purchase, then every 18 months (Comma: change every 30,000 km / 18 months) (The hydraulic clutch shares the fluid type. A soft clutch pedal usually means the slave cylinder is failing.)
- Propshaft grease points: Multipurpose lithium grease on the UJs and sliding joints · At purchase. Comma says check UJs every 12 months and sliding joints every 24 months (A clunk on take-up usually means a dry UJ or a worn sliding spline. Grease them before chasing the gearbox.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: 235/85R16 is the classic factory size on 110s and the 'sweet spot' most owners recommend; NAS D90s came on 265/75R16. 255/85R16 (about 33") is the popular upgrade and generally fits at stock height, but owners report rubbing on the front radius arms at full lock (fix by winding out the steering stops), against the 45 L auxiliary tank on 110s, and close to the spring brackets at full compression on 90s.

Q: Can I import a Defender into the US?
A: Yes, if it's at least 25 years old counted from its date of manufacture: NHTSA lets those vehicles in without meeting FMVSS (declared under Box 1 on the HS-7). Newer trucks must comply, which a classic Defender can't. Check EPA and your state's emissions rules too, and make sure the VIN, chassis number and build date line up.

Q: Which Defenders are 25-year-eligible right now?
A: Everything built at least 25 years before the import date, so in late 2026 that's trucks built up to late 2001. That covers 200Tdi, 300Tdi, V8 and early Td5 Defenders (the Td5 arrived in 1998). The Ford 'Puma' Defenders from 2007 won't start qualifying until 2032.

Q: What is a NAS Defender?
A: North American Specification Defenders were the ones Land Rover sold new in the US and Canada: 525 1993 Defender 110s (500 US, 25 Canada) and Defender 90s from 1994 to 1997, all V8. About 7,059 were built in total.

Q: Why did Land Rover stop selling the Defender in the US after 1997?
A: Regulations taking effect for 1998, including airbag and side-impact door requirements, made it too expensive to keep the old body compliant. The Defender name returned to US showrooms in 2020 on the all-new L663.

Q: Which engine should I buy?
A: For a gray-market truck, the 300Tdi is the simple, mechanical favourite; check the revised timing kit has been fitted. The 200Tdi is cruder but similar. The Td5 is more powerful (122 hp) but electronically managed, so check for oil in the injector loom. In the US, NAS trucks are all 3.9/4.0 V8, which is thirsty but easy to service.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: For a 25-year-legal import, the Tdi years. ECD rates the 300Tdi (1994–98) the top choice for longevity and the 200Tdi (1990–94) a close second, and Classic Car Hub says if you remember one engine number, make it 300Tdi. Early '10P' Td5s have known head and oil-pump-drive problems, so look for a 15P engine or proof of repair. Among the Puma trucks, PistonHeads points to a 2011. Whatever the engine, the chassis, bulkhead and rear crossmember decide what it's worth.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: ECD estimates 12–16 mpg for the factory V8 (12–14 in real-world use), 23–27 mpg for the 300Tdi, 22–26 mpg for the Td5 and 20–25 mpg for the Puma diesels; it doesn't say how they were measured. Roof racks, big tyres and a heavy right foot will take you well under those.

Q: How much can a classic Defender tow?
A: CarsGuide lists 3,500 kg (7,716 lb) braked for 2004 Defender 90, 110 and 130 variants, and GoAuto gives the same 3,500 kg braked / 750 kg unbraked for the 2009 Defender 90. Unbraked trailers are limited to 750 kg. Check your own truck's plate and handbook; the rear crossmember condition matters more than the brochure number.

Q: When do I lock the centre diff?
A: Whenever you expect prolonged wheelspin: mud, snow, ice, sand, steep loose climbs. The LT230's stock centre diff has small gears that can fail if a front wheel spins for long, and the diff lock removes that risk. Unlock it on grippy surfaces to avoid driveline wind-up.

Q: Does it rust?
A: The aluminium panels don't rust, but they oxidise, lifting paint and eventually perforating. The steel parts rust: chassis rear crossmember, outriggers, bulkhead footwells and corners, door frames and hinge mounts. Budget for welding unless the truck already has a galvanised chassis.

## Land Rover Defender (L663) (2020–present)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/defender-l663/
Codes: L663, 90, 110, 130

Verdict: The Defender that shares nothing with the Defender: an aluminium monocoque on independent air springs that will out-climb its ancestor and then massage your back on the way home. Brilliant off-road, a little too clever for its own good in the workshop.

The L663 is the argument that ended an argument. For years, purists insisted a Defender needed a ladder frame and beam axles. Land Rover built one with neither, gave it permanent four-wheel drive, a two-speed transfer box, locking differentials and 900 mm of wading depth, and sold it in America again. It is quicker, safer, quieter and more capable than the truck it replaced. It is also a modern JLR, which means the things that go wrong are sensors, software and converters rather than swivel seals.

### BREAKING THE LINEAGE
Land Rover showed its hand early with the DC100 concept at the 2011 Frankfurt Motor Show, a 100-inch-wheelbase sketch of a modern Defender. The production truck, styled under Gerry McGovern, was unveiled at Frankfurt on 10 September 2019. It was the first all-new Defender since 1983 and, by Land Rover's account, shares no components or technology with its predecessor: the body is an aluminium monocoque on JLR's D7x platform, and the live axles are gone in favour of all-round independent suspension.
Production moved too. The L663 is built at JLR's plant in Nitra, Slovakia, which opened on 25 October 2018. Deliveries of the five-door 110 began in early 2020, the three-door 90 followed late that year, and the 130 later kept the 110's wheelbase but added a longer rear overhang for eight seats. For the classic Defender faithful in the US, the more important news was simpler: after the NAS trucks left in 1997, Land Rover was selling a Defender here again.

### WHAT IT CAN ACTUALLY DO
The hardware list reads like a checklist written by someone who'd been told it would be soft. Permanent four-wheel drive through a ZF eight-speed automatic and a two-speed transfer case, a bevel-gear centre differential splitting torque 50/50 that you can lock, and a locking rear differential. Every 110 rides on air suspension, which lifts it to 291 mm of ground clearance; the 90 can have coils (about 225 mm) or air. Land Rover quotes 900 mm (35.4 in) of wading depth on air (850 mm on a coil-sprung 90), and Wade Sensing uses the cameras to show you how deep you are.
It is a working truck in the numbers that matter to overlanders, too. Land Rover quotes up to 3,500 kg of towing in the UK and up to 8,200 lb in the US, a 300 kg (661 lb) static roof load for a rooftop tent, and up to 370 lb of dynamic roof load on the 110 and 130 with off-road tyres and the Expedition Roof Rack. Unusually for a unibody, a 4,536 kg load-rated front winch is officially supported. Off-road it simply walks up things the Series trucks would have had to winch.

### ENGINES, V8S AND THE OCTA
Engines are JLR's Ingenium family: a 2.0 turbo petrol P300, a 3.0 mild-hybrid straight-six P400, a P400e plug-in hybrid for the 110, and in Europe and Australia a run of diesels, first 2.0 four-cylinders and then 3.0 mild-hybrid sixes badged D200, D250, D300 and later D350. From 2021 the supercharged 5.0 V8 P525 added 518 bhp, and 300 all-black V8 Bond Editions marked the truck's role in No Time to Die.
Then Land Rover went further. The OCTA, announced in July 2024, uses BMW's 4.4-litre twin-turbo mild-hybrid V8 with 635 PS (626 hp in US trim) and claims 0–60 mph in 3.8 seconds. It gets hydraulically interlinked 6D Dynamics suspension, sits wider and higher than a standard Defender, and fits 33-inch tyres from the factory. Land Rover has since taken an OCTA-based rally-raid Defender, the D7X-R, to the Dakar, where it won the Stock category on its 2026 debut. The G-Class now has a genuine rival on every surface.

### LIVING WITH IT
The motoring press loved the new truck; owners have been more mixed. A TFL review collected reader accounts of faults within the first few hundred miles, and Defender2.net's L663 Faults & Fixes board is busy with DC-DC converter failures on mild hybrids, DPF and EGR sensor codes on the diesels, steering knocks and recall campaigns. None of it is the stuff you fix with a 13 mm spanner in a field, and an independent diagnostic tool has become as common an accessory as a roof rack.
The 26MY facelift, unveiled on 28 May 2025, brought flush lights and a 13.1-inch screen but left the structure alone. In September 2026 the Defender Wolf Series II, built on the same D7x platform, was launched to bid for the UK Ministry of Defence's Light Mobility Vehicle tender, putting the name back where the Series started. If you want the old recipe of separate chassis and beam axles, the Ineos Grenadier exists precisely because this truck abandoned it.

### Data plate
- Production: 2019–present (2020 model year on)
- Unveiled: Frankfurt, 10 Sep 2019
- Plant: Nitra, Slovakia
- Design: Gerry McGovern
- Platform: D7x aluminium monocoque
- Bodies: 90 (3-door) · 110 · 130 (5-door)
- Wheelbase: 2,587 mm (90) · 3,022 mm (110/130)
- Suspension: Independent; air (110), coil or air (90)
- Drivetrain: ZF 8-speed auto, 2-speed transfer, locking centre
- Ground Clearance: Up to 291 mm (air)
- Wading: 900 mm (35.4 in)
- Towing: Up to 3,500 kg / 8,200 lb

### Engineering
The L663 throws out the ladder frame entirely. Its aluminium monocoque (JLR's D7x platform) carries independent suspension at all four corners, air-sprung on every 110 and optional on the 90, which gets coils as standard. Drive is permanent through a ZF eight-speed automatic and a two-speed transfer case with a lockable 50/50 centre differential and a locking rear differential. Off-road capability comes as much from software (Terrain Response 2, All-Terrain Progress Control, Wade Sensing) as from hardware, which is both why it is so good and why owners carry diagnostic tools.
- Body: Aluminium monocoque (D7x) (No separate chassis; integrated body and frame.)
- Suspension: Independent, air or coil (Air standard on the 110; the 90 offers coils or air.)
- 4Wd: Permanent, lockable centre diff (Bevel-gear centre diff, 50/50 split.)
- Transfer: Two-speed (high/low) (Behind a ZF eight-speed automatic.)
- Rear Diff: Locking / Electronic Active (Listed alongside torque vectoring by braking.)
- Wading: 900 mm (35.4 in) (Air suspension; 850 mm on coil-sprung 90s. OCTA is quoted at one metre.)

### Versions
- 2020–2021 · 90 / 110 (Europe) · 2.0 Ingenium diesel I4 (D200, D240) · 200 / 240 PS, 430 Nm · Replaced by six-cylinder diesels for the 2021 model year.
- 2020– · 90 / 110 / 130 · 2.0 turbo petrol I4 (P300) · 300 PS, 400 Nm · Entry petrol; basis of the US 30th Anniversary Edition.
- 2020– · 90 / 110 / 130 · 3.0 turbo MHEV I6 (P400) · 400 PS, 550 Nm · Up to 395 hp in US-market quotes.
- 2020– · 110 · 2.0 PHEV I4 (P400e) · 404 PS system · Plug-in hybrid, 110 only; not sold in the US.
- 2021MY– · 90 / 110 / 130 · 3.0 MHEV diesel I6 (D200, D250, D300; D350 added later) · 200–350 PS, 500–700 Nm · Not listed by Land Rover USA.
- 2021– · 90 / 110 / 130 · 5.0 supercharged V8 (P525) · 525 PS (518 bhp), 625 Nm · Basis of the 300-unit Bond Edition.
- 2024– · 110 OCTA · 4.4 twin-turbo MHEV V8 (BMW S68) · 635 PS, 750 Nm · 6D Dynamics, 33-inch tyres, 323 mm clearance.

### Year-by-year
- 2019: Revealed at Frankfurt on 10 September; built at Nitra, Slovakia
- 2020: 110 deliveries begin; the 90 follows, offered in the US as a 3.0 six First Edition
- 2021 MY: 3.0 six-cylinder MHEV diesels replace the 2.0 diesels (outside the US); P525 V8 joins
- 2023 MY: Three-row 130 on sale in the US; 500-unit 30th Anniversary Edition for North America
- 2024: BMW-engined OCTA (P635, 6D Dynamics, 33-in tyres) revealed; D350 diesel added to the range around this time (timing varies by market)
- 2020–2024: Mild-hybrid trucks covered by DC-DC converter recalls; check the remedy is done
- 2026 MY: First major update, unveiled 28 May 2025: flush lights, revised front and rear aprons

### Capability
- Towing: 8,200 lb (3,500 kg) braked (750 kg unbraked)
- Roof load: 370 lb dynamic (110/130), 260 lb (90); 661 lb (300 kg) static (with off-road tyres and Expedition Roof Rack; V8s have no dynamic rating)
- Fuel tank: 89–90 L usable (23.5–23.8 gal) (Defender 90, by engine)
- Ground clearance: Air 216 mm std / 291 mm off-road (11.5 in); coil 225 mm (226 mm at off-road setting) (Defender 90)
- Approach / departure / breakover: Air (off-road height) 37.5° / 40° / 31°; coil 31° / 37.9° / 25° (Defender 90)
- Wading depth: 900 mm (35.4 in) air, 850 mm coil (OCTA quoted at 1 m)
- Fuel economy: EPA 18 city / 22–23 hwy (3.0 MHEV six); 14–15 / 18–19 (5.0 V8) (2026 model year)
- Curb weight: 2,065–2,228 kg (4,553–4,912 lb) DIN (Defender 90 five-seat, by engine)
- Turning circle: 11.3 m (37.1 ft) kerb to kerb (Defender 90)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 255/70R18, 255/65R19, 255/60R20, 275/45R22
- Bolt Pattern: 5x120
- Offset: ET20–45 range by trim
- Center Bore: 72.6 mm
- Lug Thread: M14x1.5
- Lug Torque: 103 lb-ft (140 N·m)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 275/60R20 (≈33 in) (A Defender2.net owner runs it on a coil-sprung truck on stock 8.5 in 20s with no spacers and no rubbing; others warn it can touch on some setups. 275/55R20 clears on air at full articulation, and Australian owners run 275/65R18 LT on 18s. The OCTA fits 33s from the factory.)
- Biggest tire, 2.5 in (lift rods, air) lift: 35x12.50R18 (Lucky8's 110 build: Proud Rhino lift rods keeping air suspension, 18 in wheels, some lower bumper trimming, custom fender brackets, smaller rear calipers to clear the 18s and relocated intercoolers.)

### Buying checks
- Recall and campaign status: Have a dealer or diagnostic tool confirm every open campaign is closed. Owners on Defender2.net report an airbag recall and the E005 campaign for 3.0 Ingenium diesels built between 1 March 2024 and 18 April 2026, where the auxiliary belt idler pulley can damage the oil pressure and temperature sensor, causing an oil leak and possible stalling.
- Oil-change history: The headline service interval is long, and some trucks reach their first service on the original oil. Defender2.net members note the oil-change interval is driven by a separate condition-based counter and many owners change oil every 7,000–10,000 miles. A truck with only dealer visits at 21,000-mile intervals deserves a closer look.
- DC-DC converter (mild hybrids): MHEV trucks have suffered DC-DC converter failures, with owners reporting waits of two weeks to two months for parts. Ask whether it has been replaced and whether the relevant software updates are done.
- Diesel DPF and sensor codes: Frequent regenerations (every 35–100 miles) and codes such as P24C6/P24C7 (PM sensor temperature) or P0401 (EGR flow) are documented on the diesels. Scan for stored codes and ask about regeneration frequency before buying a high-mileage D250/D300.
- Steering knock on rough roads: Several owners report knocking through the steering on corrugations, traced variously to the lower steering-column UJ, track rod ends, front lower control arms or a replacement steering rack under warranty. Wiggle the wheel at a standstill and listen.
- Coolant loss (P400): Petrol six-cylinder owners report coolant loss from turbo coolant line O-rings, leaky expansion tanks and stone-damaged auxiliary radiators behind the front intakes. Check the level cold and look for crusty residue.
- Coil or air, and which body: Land Rover fits air to every 110; a 90 can be either. Coil 90s ride and tow fine but lose the air trucks' height adjustment, sit at about 225 mm instead of up to 291 mm, and are rated to wade 850 mm rather than 900 mm.

### Common repairs
#### Engine oil and filter (3.0 Ingenium diesel)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2 hours including undertray removal · cost Oil and filter
Symptoms: Due on the oil-life counter, or you want shorter intervals than the factory schedule.
Fix: Drain through the sump plug: remove the two underbody shields (and any aftermarket front guard) to reach it. Defender2.net owners report refills of about 8.5–8.8 litres for the 3.0 diesel; one used 0W-30 to JLR spec 03-5007 with a new filter. Extraction through the dipstick tube works but the tube catches on ledges in the block, so mark the depth on your probe. Reset the oil service counter afterwards with a diagnostic tool, or the truck won't know it has fresh oil.
Tools: Sockets for the undertray, sump plug socket, filter tool, extractor (optional), diagnostic tool such as a GAP IIDTool · 0W-30 to JLR 03-5007 · oil filter LR133455 (3.0 six, per LR Direct fitment)

#### Lower steering shaft joint and gaiter
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time 1–2 hours · cost Gaiter £10–50 aftermarket; joint around £200
Symptoms: Split rubber boot on the lower steering shaft, often spotted on weekly checks or flagged at MOT, sometimes with a knock through the wheel.
Fix: The joint is held by two bolts; the upper section slides up to release it. A member quotes the workshop manual as calling for new bolts torqued to 30 Nm. You can fit just the boot if the joint is good, but it's awkward; replacing the joint assembly is easier.
Tools: Sockets, torque wrench · joint LR033648 (RHD) or LR033647 (LHD), bolts QYG500090 and LR116214 per Defender2.net

#### PM sensor for P24C6 / P24C7
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost Price of the sensor
Symptoms: Engine light after cold starts, codes P24C6/P24C7 (particulate matter sensor temperature circuit), and regenerations every 100 miles or so.
Fix: One owner of a 2022 D250 replaced the PM temperature sensor, the last sensor in the exhaust after the DPF. After a week of cold starts and about 150 miles the light hadn't returned and short-trip regenerations stopped. Clear the codes afterwards.
Tools: Sensor socket, penetrating oil, diagnostic tool · Bosch 0281008520 per Defender2.net (another member cross-references LR146856)

#### Chase a P0401 EGR flow fault
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Diagnosis can take several drives · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Judder and hesitation at low-speed acceleration, especially on 1–2 and 2–3 shifts, then P0401 (EGR flow insufficient) and sometimes P006B.
Fix: Log demanded versus actual EGR valve position with a diagnostic tool. In one documented 3.0 diesel case, the dealer replaced the inlet manifold pressure sensor but the fault returned. A member pointed to the exhaust pressure sensor in the 90-degree bend just after the turbo, whose narrow pipe can block with soot and confuse the EGR logic. If the valve itself is sticking, clean or replace it; short-trip use makes this worse.
Tools: Diagnostic tool with live data, sockets · exhaust pressure sensor pipe, EGR valve (as diagnosed)

#### Coolant loss on the P400
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2 hours plus diagnosis · cost One Australian owner paid AU$580 (about $320 parts, $260 labour)
Symptoms: Coolant dropping from max to min within 100–150 km with no obvious puddle.
Fix: Pressure-test the system, then check the turbo coolant feed and return lines (their O-rings are a known leak), the expansion tank and its level sensor, and the auxiliary radiators behind the front intakes for stone damage. Replace the leaking lines with new seals and refill and bleed.
Tools: Cooling-system pressure tester, sockets · turbo coolant lines and O-rings, coolant to spec

#### Track rod end for a random clunk
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours per side, plus alignment · cost Parts plus alignment
Symptoms: Metallic clunk when steering or when the suspension articulates, at no particular angle.
Fix: Check bushes and the track rod ends before assuming a wheel bearing. One owner traced the noise to a track rod end: count the threads to keep the toe close, split the taper with a ball-joint splitter (the hardest part of the job), fit the new end and get the alignment checked.
Tools: Ball-joint splitter, spanners, torque wrench · track rod end

#### Re-bond lifting wheel-arch extensions
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time An hour per arch · cost Price of tape and adhesion promoter
Symptoms: The outer edge of a dealer-fitted arch extension peeling away from the body.
Fix: The extensions' outer edge is held by double-sided tape, so most failures are preparation. Remove the extension, clean both surfaces thoroughly, use adhesion promoter and refit with fresh tape; a member suggests 3M VHB-type foam mounting tape.
Tools: Trim tools, cleaner, adhesion promoter · 3M 5925 VHB tape (25 mm)

### Baseline service
The L663 tells you when it wants a service, but its oil-life counter and the 21,000-mile/two-year headline interval are optimistic for how most owners use their trucks, and many used examples have only ever had dealer visits. Baseline the fluids, check every recall campaign is closed, and reset the service counters with a diagnostic tool afterwards.
- Engine oil & filter: Diesel: 0W-30 to JLR 03.5007 · ≈8.5–8.8 L (3.0 diesel, owner-measured). Petrol: 0W-20 (per Defender2.net members) [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Then every 7,000–10,000 mi (owner practice); oil analysis on one D300 suggested 6,000 (The oil-change interval runs on its own condition-based counter, separate from the 21,000-mile service counter. Draining via the sump plug means removing the undertrays; dipstick-tube extraction works if the probe reaches the bottom.)
- Air filter: Genuine or equivalent element · Every 20,000 mi (owner schedule) (One owner swapped air and fuel filters early at 22,000 miles; off-road dust shortens this.)
- Cabin filter: Genuine or equivalent element · Every 20,000 mi (owner schedule)
- Fuel filter (diesel): Genuine or equivalent element · Every 20,000 mi (owner schedule) (Diesel trucks only.)
- Spark plugs (petrol): [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Per manual (P300, P400, V8 and OCTA only.)
- ZF 8-speed automatic: ZF 8HP fluid and filter-pan kit [CONFIRM fitment and capacity] · Owners: every 50,000–60,000 mi; the 6-year dealer service includes it (A D300 owner paid £599 for a ZF-specialist gearbox service at 85,000 miles and logged improved clutch pressures afterwards.)
- Transfer case & differentials: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL for fluid types] · Owners: every 30,000–50,000 mi; dealer schedule includes transfer box and rear diff at the 63,000-mile service (Do them sooner if you wade or spend long periods in low range, where water contamination is a risk.)
- Auxiliary drive belt & tensioner: Genuine belt and tensioner · Inspect now; owners replace with the 50,000-mile fluids (Defender2.net members call the aux belt a known issue (one car has had two). Also confirm recall E005 (idler pulley clash, 3.0 diesels built 1 Mar 2024–18 Apr 2026) is done.)
- Coolant: JLR-approved coolant [CONFIRM IN MANUAL for type and capacity] · Check level cold now; per manual thereafter (P400 owners report losses from turbo coolant line O-rings, expansion tanks and stone-damaged auxiliary radiators behind the front intakes.)
- Brake fluid & flexi hoses: Land Rover brake fluid [CONFIRM IN MANUAL for grade] · Per manual; the 6-year dealer service includes new fluid and brake flexi hoses
- Brake pads & discs: Inspect thickness and disc condition · Now, then at each service (One owner reported a warped disc on a 2024 110; check for judder on the test drive.)
- Recalls, software & 12 V system: Dealer campaign check; current software · Now, then annually (Confirm the airbag recall and E005 campaigns, and on MHEVs ask about DC-DC converter history and software updates. Owners avoid loading the 12 V system with screen heaters right after a cold start.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: 275/60R20 (about 33 inches) is the popular step up from the factory 255/60R20. A Defender2.net owner fitted it to a coil-sprung truck on stock 8.5-inch 20s with no spacers and reports no rubbing, even off-road; others warn it can touch on some setups. 275/55R20 runs without rubbing on air suspension at full articulation, and Australian owners run 275/65R18 LT on 18s. The OCTA fits 33s from the factory because its axles move forward slightly.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: Land Rover quotes up to 3,500 kg (UK) and up to 8,200 lb (US). Owners describe the air-sprung 110 as a very stable tow vehicle because it self-levels.

Q: How deep can it wade?
A: 900 mm (35.4 in) on air suspension, with Wade Sensing using the cameras to show water depth. Land Rover's 21MY Defender 90 data sheet rates coil-sprung 90s at 850 mm, and the OCTA is quoted at one metre.

Q: Can I put a rooftop tent on it?
A: Yes. Land Rover quotes a static roof load of up to 661 lb (300 kg) and a dynamic load of up to 370 lb on the 110 and 130 (260 lb on the 90) with off-road tyres and the Expedition Roof Rack. V8 models have no dynamic roof rating, and the OCTA's is zero in OCTA mode.

Q: Coil or air suspension?
A: Land Rover fits air to every 110. The 90 can have coils or air. Coil 90s give about 225 mm of ground clearance against up to 291 mm at off-road height on air, wade 850 mm instead of 900 mm, and lose the height-adjustable modes.

Q: Does it have locking diffs?
A: It has a lockable centre differential and a locking rear differential (Land Rover's Electronic Active Differential), plus brake-based torque vectoring and a two-speed transfer case.

Q: Can it take a winch?
A: Yes. A front-mounted 4,536 kg (10,000 lb) load-rated winch is officially supported, which is unusual for a unibody.

Q: How often should I change the oil?
A: The headline service interval is up to 21,000 miles or two years, but Defender2.net members point out that oil changes are flagged by a separate condition-based counter, often around 15,000 miles for diesels in mixed use. Many enthusiasts change oil every 7,000–10,000 miles regardless.

Q: Which engine should I buy?
A: US trucks launched with 2.0 four-cylinder and 3.0 six-cylinder engines, and Land Rover USA's current 110 spec page lists only the 3.0 six, with the OCTA sold as its own model (EPA still lists 2026 2.0 and 5.0 V8 trucks). In Europe and Australia the D250/D300 diesels are the long-distance favourites, though the mild hybrids have had DC-DC converter failures and the diesels have DPF and EGR sensor faults.

Q: Is it reliable?
A: It's better than its reputation off-road and worse than a Toyota in the workshop. A TFL review collected early-ownership faults, and common owner reports include DC-DC converters on MHEVs, PM/EGR sensor codes on diesels, steering knocks and several recall campaigns. Keep it on warranty or budget for a diagnostic tool and a good specialist.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: EPA rates the 2026 3.0 mild-hybrid six at 18 mpg city and 22–23 mpg highway, the 5.0 V8 at 14–15 city and 18–19 highway, and the OCTA at 15/19. Land Rover's 21MY Defender 90 data sheet quotes 7.6 L/100 km (NEDC equivalent) for the diesel. One D300 owner reported 40 mpg (imperial) cruising at 110 km/h across France.

## Land Rover Discovery Series I (1989–1998)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/discovery-1/
Codes: Discovery 1, 200Tdi, 300Tdi, 3.9 / 4.0 V8

Verdict: A Range Rover Classic in a cheaper suit, with Maestro switchgear, Marina door handles and two sunroofs that leak on schedule. Underneath it's the same coil-sprung, LT230-driven toolkit as a Defender, which makes it the bargain boxy truck nobody has quite noticed yet.

The first Discovery was Land Rover's answer to a simple problem: the Range Rover had drifted upmarket, the Japanese were selling family 4x4s by the boatload, and the company had a superb chassis it could reuse. So it took the Range Rover's frame, coil springs and permanent four-wheel drive, wrapped them in a cheaper, taller, more practical body, and created the first Land Rover sold as a family car. It is tough, simple and endlessly fixable. It also rusts, leaks and was assembled from whatever the Rover Group parts bin had in it that week.

### PROJECT JAY
Developed under the code name 'Project Jay', the Discovery was unveiled at the 1989 Frankfurt Motor Show and went on sale in Britain that October. At launch it was a three-door only; the five-door followed in 1990. The 64 original press cars, registered 'G-something WAC', are now known to enthusiasts as 'G-WACs' and are increasingly collectable. The body kept much of the Range Rover's structure, including door shells and window frames under its own aluminium skins, but stretched the rear, raised the roof for optional third-row jump seats and moved the spare wheel onto a side-hinged rear door.
Land Rover handed the interior to Conran Design Group with instructions to ignore conventional car design, and the result won a British Design Award in 1989. Early trucks were trimmed in light 'Sonar Blue', with magazine nets over the windscreen and a removable holdall in the console. The hardware was pure parts bin: switchgear and instruments from the Austin Maestro and Montego, vents from the Rover 800, Freight Rover van headlamps, Maestro van tail lights and Morris Marina door handles.

### ENGINES AND THE 1994 REFRESH
At launch you could have the new 2.5-litre 200Tdi or the 3.5 Rover V8, first on twin SU carburettors and from 1990 on Lucas 14CUX fuel injection. A 2.0-litre Mpi petrol four was briefly offered for British and Italian tax reasons and disappeared because it simply wasn't enough engine. In 1992 the Tdi became available with an automatic, beige trim joined the blue, and an SE pack added alloys, driving lights and roof bars.
The 1994 update was the big one: the 300Tdi replaced the 200Tdi, the 3.9 V8 replaced the 3.5, manual trucks got the stronger R380 gearbox, and a new 'soft-feel' dashboard made room for airbags. The LT230 transfer box with its lockable centre differential and the Tdi engines are shared with the Defender of the same era, so drivetrain parts are still easy to find.

### AMERICA AND THE CAMEL TROPHY
The Discovery arrived in the US for the 1994 model year, with airbags to meet federal rules and the 3.9 V8 from the Range Rover as the only engine. The 1996–98 US trucks are badged 4.0 but have the same displacement; the changes were a stiffer block, new pistons and the switch from 14CUX to the GEMS engine management that made them OBD-II compliant. Land Rover Special Vehicles built 250 AA Yellow 'XD' trucks for North America in 1997, with Safety Devices roof racks and brush guards.
The Discovery's best publicity came from the Camel Trophy. From the 1990 event in Siberia, when the main vehicle was a three-door 200Tdi, to Mongolia in 1997, the Discovery was the event's principal car, switching to 300Tdis from 1995, all in Sandglow yellow and heavily modified by Land Rover Special Vehicles. In Japan, Honda sold it as the Honda Crossroad thanks to Rover's tie-up with Honda, which ended after BMW bought Rover in 1994.

### WHY IT'S A BARGAIN BOXY TRUCK
Underneath, a Discovery 1 is a Range Rover Classic on coils with Defender-grade drivetrain parts, and that makes it a cheap way into proper Land Rover off-roading. The LT230 and the Tdi engines are shared with trucks that have huge aftermarkets, and the coil springs give a far better ride and more articulation than a leaf-sprung Series truck.
The catch is the body. LandyZone's members sum up buying advice as rust: sills, rear floor, boot floor, inner wings and body mounts, plus sunroofs whose drains were badly designed from the start. Every Disco 1 is now more than 25 years old, so European 300Tdi trucks can be imported to the US under the 25-year rule, and the model was replaced in 1998 by the Discovery Series II. Find a dry one, or budget for a welder.

### Data plate
- Production: 1989–1998
- Code Name: Project Jay
- Launch: Frankfurt Motor Show, 1989
- Plant: Solihull, UK
- Bodies: 3-door, 5-door, 3-door Commercial
- Wheelbase: 100 in (2,540 mm)
- Chassis: Steel ladder frame (Range Rover Classic)
- Suspension: Coil springs, beam axles
- 4Wd: Permanent, lockable centre diff, LT230
- Engines: 200Tdi · 300Tdi · 2.0 Mpi · 3.5/3.9 V8
- Us Model Years: 1994–1998, V8 only
- Also Sold As: Honda Crossroad (Japan)

### Engineering
The Discovery 1 is a Range Rover Classic underneath: a steel ladder frame on a 100-inch wheelbase, beam axles on coil springs (the rear axle located by an A-frame), and permanent four-wheel drive through a two-speed transfer box with a lockable centre differential. The handbrake is a drum on the back of the transfer box, so with the centre diff locked it holds both propshafts. Body panels mix Range Rover structure with the Discovery's own aluminium skins.
- Chassis: Steel ladder frame, 100-in wheelbase (Shared with the Range Rover Classic.)
- Suspension: Coil springs, beam axles (Rear A-frame ball joint is a regular wear item.)
- 4Wd: Permanent, lockable centre diff (Two-speed LT230 transfer box.)
- Handbrake: Drum on transfer box output (Locks both props when the centre diff is locked.)
- Gearbox: 5-speed manual or ZF 4HP22 auto (Stronger R380 manual from 1994.)
- Body: Range Rover structure, own aluminium skins (Steel inner structure, sills and floors are what rot.)

### Versions
- 1989–1990 · 3-door · 2.5 200Tdi; 3.5 V8 (twin SU carbs) · — · Launch model; 64 'G-WAC' press cars.
- 1990–1994 · 3- and 5-door · 2.5 200Tdi; 3.5 V8i (Lucas 14CUX) · 83 kW / 265 Nm (Tdi); 115 kW / 260 Nm (V8i), Australian spec · Five-door from 1990; Tdi automatic from 1992.
- Pre-1994 · UK & Italy · 2.0 Mpi petrol I4 · — · Tax-break special; dropped for lack of power.
- 1994–1998 · 3- and 5-door · 2.5 300Tdi; 3.9 V8 · — · Facelift, new dash with airbags, R380 manual.
- 1994–1995 · US (NAS) · 3.9 V8, Lucas 14CUX · — · First US Discoveries; V8 only.
- 1996–1998 · US (NAS) · '4.0' V8 (same 3,946 cc), GEMS · — · OBD-II compliant; 250 AA Yellow XDs in 1997.

### Year-by-year
- 1989: Unveiled at Frankfurt; UK sales from October, three-door only; 200Tdi and 3.5 V8
- 1990: Five-door added; V8i with Lucas 14CUX injection
- 1992: Automatic offered with the 200Tdi; SE pack introduced
- 1994: Facelift: 300Tdi, 3.9 V8, stronger R380 manual, new dash with airbags. Guides call the 300Tdi the sensible choice, and it commands a premium over the V8 [buy]
- 1994 MY: US sales begin, V8 only (3.9 with 14CUX)
- 1996 MY: US trucks switch to the GEMS-managed '4.0' V8 (same 3,946 cc) for OBD-II
- 1997: US XD special: 250 built in AA Yellow
- 1998: Series I ends in the autumn as the Discovery Series II arrives

### Capability
- Towing: 7,716 lb (3,500 kg) braked (750 kg unbraked; 1996 Tdi auto, NZ spec)
- Fuel tank: 89 L (23.5 gal)
- Ground clearance: 206 mm (8.1 in) (unladen)
- Curb weight: 2,080 kg (4,586 lb) (1996 Tdi auto five-door; GVM 2,720 kg)
- Turning circle: 11.9 m (39 ft) (kerb to kerb)
- Fuel economy: About 10.5 mpg (imperial) at 100–120 km/h (one 3.9 V8 owner on LandyZone; Tdis do far better)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 205/80R16 (6Jx16), 235/70R16 (7Jx16)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x165.1 (5x6.5")
- Offset: ET33 (stock)
- Center Bore: 114.3 mm
- Lug Thread: M16x1.5
- Lug Torque: 96 lb-ft (130 N·m) commonly listed for Land Rovers of this era [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 245/75R16 (≈30.5 in) (LandyZone owners recommend going no bigger on a stock-height, stock-geared truck. The factory 205/80 and 235/70 are almost the same height.)
- Biggest tire, 2 in lift: 33 in (Owners run 33s on lifted trucks. Fit longer springs and extended shocks and lower the bump stops so the body isn't hit at full compression; one owner going from 31 to 33 in still planned a 4.1 ring-and-pinion to restore gearing.)
- Biggest tire, 3 in+ lift: 35 in (Needs offset wheels to keep a usable turning circle, caster-corrected arms and wide-angle props on bigger lifts, and at least a 4.1 (ideally 4.37) ring-and-pinion.)

### Buying checks
- Sills, floors and inner wings: On LandyZone the standard buying advice is a list of rust: sills, rear floor, boot floor, inner wings, then everything else. Three-doors are reported to be worse. Lift the carpets, check the boot floor and its support strap, and push on the sills where the body mounts sit.
- Rear chassis and body mounts: Look at the mounts where the large rear crossmember meets the chassis rails, the rearmost body mounts and the box sections around the fuel tank. Galvanised replacement chassis exist, which tells you how often the originals give up.
- Sunroofs and headlining: Most Disco 1s have two sunroofs, and they leak around the plastic surround and through split drain tubes. A sagging or stained headlining and wet carpets are the clues. A LandyZone member points to the 1998 Anniversary model as a way to dodge the sunroofs, and the US XD was built without them.
- Swivels and front end: Pitted swivel balls weep oil and chew seals; look for oil on the inside of the front wheels. Check the swivel ball part number too: owners report the superseded FTC5366 ball doesn't machine-match the earlier FRC7065.
- Driveline backlash (manual Tdi): A jerky take-off on a manual 300Tdi is often the rear propshaft's rubber coupler or worn splines. With the centre diff locked, turn the front and rear props by hand in opposite directions; there should be only a little movement.
- V8 cooling and idle: Overheating V8s and Tdis can be an airlock, a failed cap or a head gasket. Bleed and test before condemning the engine. On 14CUX trucks, a hunting or high idle points at the idle air control valve or a vacuum leak.
- 300Tdi timing belt: Like the Defender, the 300Tdi should have the revised timing-belt kit (Land Rover STC4096L-type) fitted. Ask for proof.
- Japanese imports: Japanese-market re-imports are popular because they rot less, but LandyZone members note they're generally automatics and usually have sunroofs.

### Common repairs
#### Reseal leaking sunroofs and replace drains
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time A day with the headlining out · cost Sealant, seals and drain tube
Symptoms: Water dripping from the roof lining or rear vents, wet carpets, sagging or stained headlining.
Fix: The outer plastic surround often leaks where it meets the metal roof; LandyZone's long-running guide says a bead of silicone around that joint can cure it. If not, drop the visors and headlining (crosshead and Torx T20 fixings), remove the sunroof frame, clean off old sealant, reseal the frame-to-roof seal and replace split drain tubes and cups. Check the roof-rail foam pads while the lining is out.
Tools: Torx T20, screwdrivers, trim tools, silicone sealant · sunroof drain tube EEH100720 (per LandyZone) · roof-rail foam pads

#### Rear propshaft rubber coupler
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost Parts only
Symptoms: Clonk or jerk on take-off and gear changes, visible cracks or splits in the rear propshaft's rubber 'doughnut' coupler.
Fix: Support the prop, unbolt it from the coupler and the coupler from the output flange, fit a new coupler (owners recommend original-equipment quality) with new nuts and bolts, and torque up. Some owners instead convert to a Defender-style prop and flange with a conventional UJ to remove the backlash.
Tools: Spanners and sockets, torque wrench · rubber propshaft coupler, nuts and bolts

#### Idle air control valve (14CUX V8)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour plus diagnosis · cost Price of the valve
Symptoms: High idle on start-up (1,100–2,000 rpm), hunting idle, or idle that won't drop despite the ECU asking for about 700 rpm.
Fix: Rule out vacuum leaks, then watch the valve with RoverGauge, which can read the 14CUX and command the stepper open and closed. Clamping the bypass hose is a quick test. One owner replaced the IACV, temperature sensor and plenum gaskets before finding the new aftermarket IACV itself was faulty; a second replacement fixed it.
Tools: RoverGauge and cable, hose clamp, multimeter · idle air control valve, plenum gaskets as needed

#### Swivel housing rebuild
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time A day for both sides · cost A UK owner was quoted £300 labour for both swivels, wheel bearings, prop UJs and the A-frame joint
Symptoms: Oil on the inside of the front wheels, pitted chrome balls, vague steering.
Fix: Strip the hub, stub axle and CV, unbolt the swivel housing and fit a new ball, bearings and seals, setting preload with shims as in the workshop manual. Check the new ball against the old: one owner found the superseded FTC5366 sat the CV sleeve 2 mm further out than the original FRC7065 and locked the assembly. Also note ABS and non-ABS swivel parts differ.
Tools: Hub nut socket, torque wrench, spring balance · swivel ball (FRC7065 still stocked by Paddock Spares per LandyZone), seal and bearing kit

#### Sill and boot-floor repair
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time Several weekends · cost Panels are cheap; welding hours aren't
Symptoms: MOT advisories, soft metal at the sills or body mounts, daylight through the boot floor.
Fix: Work in small sections. Replace the boot floor and its support, fabricate or buy the lips it sits on, and replace sills with box section (owners make their own and buy mounts separately) or pressed repair panels. Treat and protect everything you can reach while the floor is out. If the chassis itself is thin, galvanised replacements are available.
Tools: MIG welder, grinder, joddler, bead roller (optional) · sill panels, boot floor panel, body mounts

#### Overheating: bleed and cap before head gasket
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost A cap and coolant
Symptoms: Coolant pushed out of the expansion tank, rising temperature after recent leaks or top-ups.
Fix: LandyZone members advise ruling out an airlock (a thermostat sitting in air won't open) and a weak pressure cap, which lowers the boiling point, before pulling the head. Bleed the system properly, fit a new cap, and only then do a combustion-gas test if the symptoms continue.
Tools: Coolant, bleed procedure from the workshop manual, block tester · expansion tank cap

#### 300Tdi timing belt with revised kit
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Several hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Due on interval, or belt debris inside the timing cover.
Fix: Same job as on a 300Tdi Defender: lock the cam and crank, fit the revised kit with its flanged crank pulley and spaced idler, and remove the separate spacer washer on early engines because the new idler includes it.
Tools: Timing tool, torque wrench · STC4096L modified timing belt kit

### Baseline service
Every Discovery 1 is now 25-plus years old and many have had years of cheap ownership, so baseline everything, starting with the timing belt on a 300Tdi and the fluids in a transfer box and axles that may never have been changed. Do it with the truck on stands so you can inspect the rust and bushes at the same time.
- Engine oil & filter: Grade per handbook [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · spin-on filter (Tdi and V8 share ERR3340) · Then per manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Check for a leaking oil-filter housing gasket on the 300Tdi while you're there.)
- Air filter: Paper element · Replace now (200Tdi and 300Tdi/V8 use different elements.)
- Fuel filter (Tdi): Canister or cartridge diesel filter · Replace now (Prime the system afterwards per the workshop manual.)
- Timing belt (300Tdi): Revised kit (STC4096L type) with flanged crank pulley and spaced idler · Now unless documented; then per manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Early kits could let the belt track off; make sure the revised parts are fitted.)
- Auxiliary belt & tensioner: Poly-V belt and tensioner · Inspect now; replace if cracked or noisy
- Glow plugs (Tdi) / spark plugs (V8): Tdi heater plugs · V8 plugs per engine · Test glow plugs now; replace V8 plugs and leads (On 14CUX V8s, new plugs and HT leads are part of curing poor running before chasing sensors.)
- Coolant & hoses: Antifreeze [CONFIRM IN MANUAL for type] · 15 psi cap on Tdi · Flush now; then per manual (300Tdi fill method from LandyZone: fill the tank to just under the mark, fit the cap, top up through the thermostat-housing plug, run it hot, then recheck when cold. The Y-piece is meant to make it self-bleeding.)
- Automatic gearbox (ZF 4HP22): ATF Dexron II · about 4–5 L from a pan drain · Drain, new filter and refill now (Only part of the fluid comes out of the pan, so some owners do a second change a few hundred miles later. Check the level with the engine running after cycling through the gears, not engine-off.)
- Manual gearbox (R380): [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Drain and refill now (A jerky take-off is more often the rear prop coupler than the gearbox.)
- Transfer box (LT230) & axles: 90-grade GL-4 gear oil per the owner's handbook (75W-90 or 80W-90 multigrade accepted by owners) · one owner bought 7 L for axles and transfer box · Drain and refill now (Check the LT230 rear output seal so oil doesn't reach the transmission handbrake.)
- Swivel housings: Lubricant varies by build [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Check now; rebuild if weeping (Grease on the inside of the brake disc points to failed hub or swivel seals.)
- Power steering: Land Rover PAS fluid · Change fluid and inspect hoses now (Foaming and a whining pump usually mean air getting in through a perished feed hose or cap seal; bleed at the nipple on top of the steering box.)
- Brake fluid: Land Rover brake fluid [CONFIRM IN MANUAL for grade] · Flush now; then per manual
- Grease points & suspension bushes: Grease propshaft UJs; inspect A-frame ball joint and all bushes with the axle hanging · Every service (LandyZone members find worn rear trailing-arm and A-frame bushes only with the chassis lifted and a long pry bar.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: Factory sizes were 205R16 and 235/70R16, which are almost the same height. On a stock-height, stock-geared truck, a LandyZone owner recommends going no bigger than 245/75R16 (about 30.5 inches), which several members run. Owners do run 33s and bigger with lifts; one member says 35s want at least a 4.1 and ideally a 4.37 ring and pinion.

Q: When was it sold in the US?
A: From the 1994 to 1998 model years, always with the V8: 3.9 litres with Lucas 14CUX injection at first, then the GEMS-managed '4.0' (same 3,946 cc) from 1996 for OBD-II.

Q: How is it related to the Range Rover Classic and Defender?
A: It uses the Range Rover Classic's chassis, suspension and four-wheel-drive system, much of its body structure, and the same LT230 transfer box and Tdi engines as the Defender of the same era.

Q: Can I import a diesel Disco 1 into the US?
A: Every Discovery Series I was built by 1998, so all of them are now more than 25 years old. NHTSA allows vehicles at least 25 years old (from date of manufacture) to be imported without meeting FMVSS; check EPA and your state's rules and make sure the VIN and build date line up.

Q: Which engine should I buy?
A: The 300Tdi is the enthusiast favourite: mechanical, economical and shared with the Defender, though it needs the revised timing kit. The 200Tdi is cruder but similar. The V8 is smoother and easy to source in the US but thirsty and sensitive to cooling problems.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: Condition first: Disco 1s rot in the sills, floors and rear chassis, so a solid truck of any year beats a shiny rotten one. After that, the 1994-on facelift with the 300Tdi is the one guides point to; Classic Car Hub calls it the more sensible choice and says it commands a premium over the V8. One LandyZone member's tip is a late ES (1997–98 model year), or a 1998 Anniversary for most of the kit without the leaky sunroofs. US trucks were all V8s.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect from the V8?
A: Not much. One owner of a 3.9 V8 reported about 10.5 mpg (imperial) at 100–120 km/h and was trying to get closer to 14. Tired V8s lose economy as the camshaft wears, according to experienced members.

Q: How do I lift it?
A: Two inches is the common, sensible lift using longer springs and extended shocks; owners advise lowering the bump stops so the body isn't damaged at full compression. Owners running bigger lifts fit caster-corrected (6-degree) arms and wide-angle propshafts, and regear for big tyres.

Q: Does it rust?
A: Yes, badly. The usual places are the sills, rear floor and boot floor, inner wings, body mounts and the rear chassis around the crossmember. Three-doors are reported to be worse.

Q: Why do the sunroofs leak?
A: The plastic surround leaks where it meets the metal roof, the frame seal is flimsy, and the drain tubes and cups split with age. LandyZone owners call the drain installation 'appalling'. Resealing and new drains usually cure it.

Q: Which Discoveries did the Camel Trophy use?
A: The Discovery was the main Camel Trophy vehicle from 1990 to 1997: 200Tdis from Siberia (1990, three-door) to South America (1994), then 300Tdis from 1995 to Mongolia in 1997. Japan and Germany also got Sandglow Camel Trophy special editions.

Q: What is a Honda Crossroad?
A: A badge-engineered Discovery 1 sold in Japan by Honda, a product of Rover's cross-holding with Honda that ended when BMW bought Rover in 1994.
