## Land Rover Discovery Series II (1998–2004)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/discovery-2/
Codes: L318, Td5, 4.0 / 4.6 V8, ACE, SLS

Verdict: The last Discovery with a proper ladder frame and two live axles, smothered in BMW-era electronics that range from clever (ACE) to cursed (an injector loom that pipes engine oil into the ECU). Buy the chassis, not the options list, and keep a Nanocom in the glovebox.

Land Rover said the Series II had 720 differences from the Discovery 1, and every one of them seems to have a wire attached. Underneath it is still the old recipe: a steel ladder frame on a 100-inch wheelbase, a beam axle at each end, permanent four-wheel drive and a two-speed LT230 transfer box. On top sits a longer body, seven forward-facing seats, a new five-cylinder diesel and a stack of systems with acronyms. It was the last Land Rover SUV built on the bones of the 1970 Range Rover, and it is now one of the cheapest ways into a properly capable coil-and-axle Land Rover.

### 720 DIFFERENCES
The Series II arrived in autumn 1998, four years after BMW bought Rover Group. Every body panel changed except the outer skin of the rear door. The tail grew to make room for adults in all seven seats on the SE7, at the cost of a longer rear overhang and a slightly worse departure angle. The rear lights moved up above the window line, the paddle door handles went, and the wheel pattern changed from the Discovery 1's 5x6.5 in to 5x120 mm, the same as the Range Rover P38.
Under the skin the front axle swapped the old chrome swivel balls for upper and lower ball joints, again shared with the P38, and the rear axle was located by a Watts linkage. Some trucks got self-levelling rear air springs (SLS), and European type approval for the seven-seat version was only granted to air-sprung examples. Production ran at Solihull, with assembly also in Jordan and Malaysia.

### TD5, THOR AND A LOT OF SENSORS
Diesel buyers got the Td5, a 2.5-litre five-cylinder with electronic unit injectors, a chain-driven camshaft and two oil filters, one of them centrifugal. It came from the Rover 'Storm' project, not from BMW, and made 136 hp in Discovery tune. Wikipedia records two early mechanical faults, a failing oil-pump drive and 'head shuffle' from weak studs, both fixed within two years. Owners will tell you about the third: oil wicking down the injector harness and into the ECU.
Petrol trucks got the 4.0-litre 'Thor' V8 from the P38, the same 3,946 cc as before but with a different crank, cross-bolted mains, new rods and pistons and Bosch management. American buyers only ever got V8 automatics, and from the 2003 model year the US truck switched to the 4.6. Then there was ACE, Active Cornering Enhancement: hydraulic rams on the anti-roll bars that can counter up to 1 g of lateral force. It made a tall truck corner flat, and it gave owners a whole new set of pipes to corrode.

### THE MISSING LEVER AND THE 2003 FACELIFT
Early Series IIs still had a lockable centre differential in the transfer box, but Land Rover left out the linkage to work it, believing traction control and the new Hill Descent Control made it redundant. Owners disagreed. Fitting a Discovery 1 lever, or a kit such as Ashcroft's, became one of the classic Disco 2 upgrades, and the facelift brought the lever back as an option, standard on high-spec trucks.
The facelift (owners call it the D2a) arrived for 2003 with pocketed headlamps like the new Range Rover's, revised rear lamps with the indicators moved up out of the bumper, and the 4.6 V8 for North America. The Td5 had gone to Euro 3 spec in 2002, with an EGR system and smoother low-speed throttle. In 2003, Land Rover prepared 62 Discovery 2s for the first G4 Challenge, where competitors drove them through Las Vegas and Moab. The final trucks left Solihull in late May 2004 to make way for the Discovery 3.

### WHY BUY ONE NOW
Because the hard parts are simple. Live axles, coil springs (or air springs that convert to coils in an afternoon), an LT230 that is shared with the Defender, and a chassis that takes 285/75R16s with about three inches of lift. The Td5 is slow in stock form but responds well to tuning, though Famous Four warns it is 'not quite a DIY Land Rover'; you need a diagnostic tool for some jobs. The V8 sounds lovely and drinks accordingly.
The catch is rust. The rear of the frame, around the fuel tank and the rear crossmember, rots from the inside out, and LandyZone members price a replacement chassis and the work at close to £10,000. Fresh under-seal can hide it, so get underneath with a hammer. A rust-free Disco 2 with documented head gaskets or injector loom work is a better buy than a shiny one with every option still fitted.

### Data plate
- Production: 1998–2004
- Model Code: L318
- Plant: Solihull, UK (kits in Jordan and Malaysia)
- Body: 5-door, 5 or 7 seats
- Wheelbase: 100 in (2,540 mm)
- Length: 185.2 in (4,705 mm)
- Chassis: Steel ladder frame
- Suspension: Coils, beam axles; optional SLS and ACE
- 4Wd: Permanent, LT230, lockable centre diff
- Engines: Td5 2.5 I5 · 4.0 V8 · 4.6 V8 (US 2003–04)
- Wheels: 5x120, M14x1.5 nuts
- Us Model Years: 1999–2004, V8 automatic only

### Engineering
The Discovery Series II keeps the Range Rover Classic formula of a steel ladder frame on a 100-inch wheelbase, beam axles on coil springs and permanent four-wheel drive through an LT230 transfer box, but changes almost everything bolted to it. The front axle uses ball joints instead of swivel housings, the rear axle is located by a Watts linkage and can carry self-levelling air springs, and optional ACE fights body roll hydraulically. Engines, ABS, traction control, Hill Descent Control and suspension are all managed electronically, so a diagnostic tool such as a Nanocom or Hawkeye is part of the toolkit.
- Chassis: Steel ladder frame, 100-in wheelbase (Rear section and crossmember rot from the inside.)
- Front Axle: Beam axle, coil springs, ball joints (No chrome swivels; ball joints shared with the P38.)
- Rear Axle: Beam axle, Watts linkage (Coils, or optional self-levelling air springs (SLS).)
- 4Wd: Permanent, LT230 two-speed (Centre diff lock fitted, but no lever until the facelift.)
- Ace: Hydraulic active anti-roll bars (Counters up to 1 g of lateral force; pipes corrode.)
- Engines: Td5 2.5 I5 diesel; 4.0/4.6 V8 (US trucks: V8 automatic only.)

### Versions
- 1998–2002 · L318, pre-facelift · Td5 2.5 I5 (10P) · 136 hp; 221 lb-ft manual, 232 lb-ft auto · Early oil-pump bolt and head-stud fixes; no CDL lever.
- 1998–2002 · L318, pre-facelift · 4.0 Thor V8 · 188 hp / 250 lb-ft (final 4.0 spec) · From the P38; 1999–2002 MY in the US.
- 2002–2004 · Td5 Euro 3 · Td5 2.5 I5 (15P) · 136 hp · EGR and revised low-speed throttle response.
- 2002–2004 · L318 facelift (D2a) · 4.0 V8 (UK and others) · 188 hp / 250 lb-ft · Pocketed headlamps; CDL lever back as an option.
- 2003–2004 MY · US facelift · 4.6 V8, 4-speed auto · 218 hp / 300 lb-ft (final 4.6 spec) · S, SE and HSE, plus seven-seat S7, SE7 and HSE7.
- 2003–2004 · UK run-out · Td5 or 4.0 V8 · — · Pursuit, Landmark and ES Premium 'Definitive Editions'.

### Year-by-year
- 1998: Series II launched in the autumn: Td5 diesel and 4.0 'Thor' V8, optional SLS and ACE; centre diff lock fitted but no lever
- 1999 MY: US sales begin, 4.0 V8 automatic only
- 1998–2000: Early Td5 oil-pump drive and head-stud ('head shuffle') problems, fixed within two years; ACE pipe and idler-pulley recalls [avoid]
- 2002: Td5 moves to Euro 3 (15P) with EGR and better low-speed throttle response
- 2003 MY: Facelift (D2a): pocketed headlamps, new rear lamps, CDL lever back as an option; US trucks get the 4.6 V8
- 2003: 62 Discovery 2s prepared for the first G4 Challenge (Las Vegas and Moab stage)
- 2003–04: US owners report slipped and cracked liners on late 4.0 and especially 4.6 blocks [avoid]
- 2003–04: UK run-out 'Definitive Editions': Pursuit, Landmark and ES Premium
- 2004: Final trucks leave Solihull in late May; Discovery 3 (LR3) takes over

### Capability
- Towing: 7,716 lb (3,500 kg) braked (750 kg unbraked; 2001 Td5 manual, Australian spec)
- Payload: 1,510 lb (685 kg) (2001 Td5 manual, Australian spec; GVM 2,750 kg)
- Fuel tank: 95 L (25.1 US gal)
- Curb weight: 4,543–4,895 lb (2,061–2,220 kg) (range across versions)
- Fuel economy: EPA 12 city / 16 hwy / 13 combined (2002 4.0 V8 auto; 2003 4.6: 11 / 14 / 12)
- Dimensions: 185.2 in long, 74.4 in wide, 76.4 in tall (100-in wheelbase)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 215/75R16 (7Jx16), 235/70R16 (7Jx16), 255/65R16 (8Jx16), 255/60R17 (8Jx17), 255/55R18 (8Jx18)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x120
- Offset: ET57 (listed OE fitments)
- Center Bore: 70.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M14x1.5
- Lug Torque: 96 lb-ft (130 N·m) per wheel-data listings; confirm in your handbook
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 245/75R16 (Discoweb owners recommend 245s for a stock truck. 265/75R16 fits at stock height but rubs the plastic behind the fog lamps at full lock or needs the front bumper trimmed.)
- Biggest tire, 2 in lift: 265/75R16 (The common choice with a mild OME-type lift; one owner with a 2-inch lift reports no rubbing.)
- Biggest tire, 3 in lift: 285/75R16 (Needs a little more than the standard OME lift (owners use OME 751 springs and reset the SLS height to get nearly 3 inches); expect gearing and halfshaft-strength concerns.)

### Buying checks
- Rear chassis and crossmember: The back of the frame, around the fuel tank and the rear crossmember, rots from the inside out where mud and water collect. Look closely at the rear chassis legs, the crossmember and the suspension hangers, because owners report hangers collapsing. Replacement rear quarter and half chassis sections exist, and so do whole galvanised frames, which tells you how common this is.
- Sills, arches, boot floor and body mounts: One LandyZone member's under-seal inspection turned up rotten footwells, inner and outer sills, all four arches, the boot floor and both rear body mounts, with a £5,040 repair quote. Expect to find at least twice the rust you can see once you start cutting.
- Td5 head, fuel in the oil: Famous Four says Td5 cylinder-head failure is now quite common and expensive. Check the dipstick: a level that is too high suggests diesel in the oil. Failed injector sealing washers cause the same symptom and are much cheaper to fix, so diagnose before you condemn the head.
- Oil in the ECU plug: Lift the ECU out of its tray by the battery and look at the connectors. Oil there means the injector harness seals under the rocker cover have failed, and in time that causes misfires and poor starting. The fix is a cheap harness, but neglected trucks may also have oil in the main engine loom.
- Diesel leak at the back of the Td5: Diesel weeping from the rear of the cylinder head on the driver's side is usually the fuel pressure regulator. Fix it quickly: Famous Four warns that leaking fuel can drip onto the starter motor and kill it.
- V8 cooling and head gaskets: Ask for head-gasket and cooling records. An Expedition Portal buyer's guide says gaskets often go between 50,000 and 70,000 miles and advises avoiding trucks with a compromised cooling system. Owners also report slipped or cracked cylinder liners, especially on 2003–04 4.6s, which mean an engine rebuild with top-hat liners or a replacement block.
- SLS, ACE and the 'three amigos': A tail that sags overnight means leaking SLS air springs. Oil on the chassis rails or around the anti-roll bars means ACE leaks, which Famous Four calls 'very expensive to rectify'. ABS, TC and HDC lights together (the 'three amigos') are often a dirty or failed wheel sensor, but can be a failing ABS modulator costing thousands.
- Centre diff lock and propshafts: Pre-facelift trucks have the lock in the transfer box but often no lever, unless someone has fitted one. On the test drive, a severe shimmy points to worn propshaft joints; the front shaft's double-cardan joint has non-greasable UJs from the factory, and the rear rubber coupling cracks.

### Common repairs
#### Td5 injector harness replacement
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2 hours · cost Harness about £30 (discovery2.co.uk); ECU-plug cleaning included
Symptoms: Oil inside the red ECU plug, poor starting, misfires or rough running, injector fault codes.
Fix: Disconnect the battery and lift the ECU out to check the plugs; clean oil out of the connector with a fast-drying solvent. Remove the acoustic cover and rocker cover, unclip the five injector plugs and the plug where the main loom meets the injector harness, and lift the harness out. Clean the bore where the harness connector seals into the head, fit the later modified harness with new O-rings, clip everything home and refit the rocker cover with a new gasket. Some owners also flush oil out of the main loom with solvent.
Tools: 1/4-in ratchet and 8, 10 and 13 mm sockets, torque wrench, solvent cleaner, RTV · AMR6103 harness, NYX100080 O-rings, rocker cover gasket

#### Td5 oil pump bolt (preventive)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Half a day · cost A bolt, a sump gasket and RTV
Symptoms: None until it fails: the bolt holding the oil-pump sprocket can loosen and fall out, and the engine is destroyed. Early engines are most at risk, but owners have found loose bolts on 2003–04 trucks too.
Fix: Support the truck high on the chassis so the front axle drops, and remove the front crossmember (eight bolts) to get the sump out. Drain the oil, unclip the gearbox cooler pipe, remove the four bellhousing bolts, the rotor-filter drain pipe and the sump bolts (note the three lengths near the bellhousing). Swap the sprocket bolt for the superseded pre-thread-locked bolt at 25 Nm (18 lb-ft), fit a new sump gasket dry with RTV at the marked joints, and refit within 20 minutes. Check the power-steering pipe that chafes against the sump while you're there.
Tools: Axle stands, 3/8-in torque wrench, RTV sealant · M6 oil-pump bolt, sump gasket; power-steering pipe ANR6974 if chafed (per discovery2.co.uk)

#### Td5 fuel pressure regulator
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost Regulator about £80 (discovery2.co.uk, 2008)
Symptoms: Diesel leaking from the back of the engine on the driver's side; fuel smell.
Fix: Remove the acoustic cover and the engine lifting bracket for room. Loosen the top two bolts, unplug the sensor, remove the hidden bottom bolt with a long extension, then release the two quick-release fuel pipes and the last bolt. Don't lose the small gauze filter and O-ring behind the regulator. Fit a new gasket and O-ring, torque the three bolts to 25 Nm (18 lb-ft), reconnect and prime the system. Order the regulator by chassis number: the 2003-on version has an extra return pipe.
Tools: 1/4-in ratchet and extensions, 10 and 13 mm ratcheting spanners, torque wrench · regulator, gasket and O-ring

#### SLS air springs, or convert to coils
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost A pair of air springs, or a coil conversion kit
Symptoms: The rear sags overnight or when parked, then pumps back up; the compressor runs for long periods. Ignored leaks burn out the compressor.
Fix: Chock the front wheels, support the chassis by the rear radius-arm mounts and the axle on jacks, and remove the wheels. Open the compressor box on the chassis rail and slowly crack the two outer air unions (not the middle one) to deflate. Pop the retaining clips, collapse the spring, undo its air union, rotate it 90 degrees and lift it out. Replace both sides. To convert instead, fit Discovery 2 (not Discovery 1) spring seats, coils and shocks, and have the SLS switched off with a diagnostic tool.
Tools: Trolley jack, axle stands, 10 mm spanner, spring compressor for coils · air springs and clips, or a conversion kit

#### ACE leaks: pipes, filter or delete
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Half a day to a weekend · cost Pipes are cheap; one owner's previous owner spent about $4,000 on the system
Symptoms: Hydraulic fluid on the chassis or around the anti-roll bars, ACE warning, body roll returning. Pipes rust through and the aluminium valve block pits until its seals fail.
Fix: Trace the leak: pump banjo, steel lines along the chassis, actuator seals or the valve block. Replace corroded pipes with new Dowty washers (an NHTSA recall had dealers re-torque or replace the pump banjo bolt). Change the high-pressure filter in the bottom of the valve block at 72,000 miles: heat the steel cap, use a 10 mm hex, pull the filter straight out with an M6 bolt, refit at 35 Nm. Refill with Land Rover PAS fluid STC50519, which ACE shares with the steering. Owners who give up fit standard anti-roll bars and a non-ACE belt.
Tools: 10 mm hex socket, breaker bar, heat, flare spanners · pipes, Dowty washers, filter, fluid

#### Three amigos: ABS sensors and hubs
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–3 hours · cost A sensor, or a front hub assembly (about £160–260, per discovery2.co.uk)
Symptoms: ABS, TC and HDC warning lights on together, sometimes intermittently.
Fix: Read the codes with a Nanocom, Hawkeye or similar to find the wheel. Clean the sensor and its tone ring, check the wiring and connector, and replace the sensor if needed. Play in a front wheel bearing can also trigger the lights; the front bearing is part of the hub assembly, and the hub nut is torqued to 490 Nm (360 lb-ft). If the codes point to the modulator, check for the 2004 NHTSA modulator-cover recall and change the brake fluid before replacing the unit.
Tools: Diagnostic tool, multimeter, big torque wrench for hubs · wheel-speed sensors, hub assembly

#### V8 head gaskets and cooling refresh
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A weekend, plus machine-shop time · cost One US owner paid about $1,250 at an independent shop, including $640 labour and head skimming
Symptoms: Coolant loss, overheating at idle, coolant weeping at the head-to-block joint, mayonnaise under the filler cap.
Fix: Strip the intake, rocker gear and heads; check the heads for warp and have them skimmed (one owner's warped heads needed 0.003–0.004 in taken off after 130,000 miles). Check the bores for a liner standing proud or cracks behind it before you spend money on gaskets. Refit with new composite gaskets and new head bolts. While it's apart, renew the thermostat, radiator, hoses and viscous fan; some owners fit the cooler Td5 thermostat and an OBD gauge, because they don't trust the dash gauge.
Tools: Full socket set, torque wrench with angle gauge, straightedge and feeler gauges · head gasket set, head bolts, cooling parts

#### Rear chassis and crossmember repair
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time Several weekends, or a week on a ramp · cost LandyZone members put a new chassis plus the work at close to £10,000; patch repairs much less
Symptoms: Flaking or holed metal at the rear crossmember, rear chassis legs and around the fuel tank; collapsed suspension hangers; MOT failures.
Fix: Drop the fuel tank to see the real extent. Small holes can be plated, but most owners cut out the rear quarter or rear half and weld in a replacement section, or swap the whole frame for a galvanised one. Treat the inside of the rails with cavity wax afterwards, because that's where the rot starts.
Tools: MIG welder, grinder, axle stands, tank support · rear quarter or half chassis, crossmember, body mounts

### Baseline service
Most Discovery 2s have had years of cheap ownership, so assume nothing has been done. Change every fluid, and on a Td5 pull the ECU plugs to look for oil and decide whether to drop the sump for the oil-pump bolt. On a V8, refresh the cooling system before anything else. Do it on axle stands so you can inspect the rear chassis at the same time.
- Engine oil & filters (Td5): 5W-30 fully synthetic (as used by the dealer, per discovery2.co.uk) · 7.2 L · spin-on filter plus centrifugal rotor filter · Now; then per service schedule [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Change both filters. The rotor filter sits next to the turbo under a lid held by two 10 mm bolts (10 Nm); sump plug 17 mm, 23 Nm with a new washer.)
- Engine oil & filter (V8): [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now (A service kit covers oil, air and fuel filters in one order.)
- Fuel filter (Td5): Spin-on filter with water sensor, under the right rear wheel arch · Now (Transfer the water sensor hand-tight (it's plastic), make sure only one seal sits on the housing, pre-fill with diesel, then follow the purge procedure: ignition on for 3 minutes, then crank with the throttle floored.)
- Air filter: Paper element · Replace now
- Glow plugs (Td5) / spark plugs (V8): Td5 glow plugs · V8 double-platinum plugs · Test glow plugs now; replace V8 plugs and leads
- Timing (Td5): Duplex timing chain, no belt · No routine replacement (Wikipedia notes the camshaft is driven by a duplex chain, so there's no belt interval. The serious Td5 timing-gear risk is the oil-pump sprocket bolt below.)
- Oil-pump bolt (Td5): Superseded pre-thread-locked M6 bolt, 25 Nm · Once, if there's no record (Sump off with the front crossmember removed; fit a new sump gasket. Check the power-steering pipe that chafes on the sump.)
- Auxiliary belt: Poly-V belt; part depends on A/C and ACE · Inspect now; replace if cracked or noisy (Listen for squealing idlers and the A/C clutch bearing. Early ACE trucks had an idler-pulley recall (NHTSA 00V142).)
- Coolant, hoses & thermostat: Antifreeze type [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush now (On a V8, replace the thermostat, hoses and viscous coupling as a set unless there are receipts; owners treat cooling as the V8's life insurance.)
- Automatic gearbox: ATF [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · about 4–5 L drains from the pan · Drain, new filter and gasket now; second drain a few hundred miles later (Pan drain plug 15 Nm, pan bolts 8 Nm, fill plug 30 Nm. Fill through the side plug with the engine running until a 2 mm bead runs out. A 2000 NHTSA recall (00V377) covered water getting into the ATF through the breather.)
- Transfer box (LT230): 75W-90 gear oil (Texaco Multi-Gear 75W/90R per the manual) · 2.0 L refill, 2.3 L dry · Drain and refill now (Undo the fill plug first. Drain plug 30 Nm, fill plug 25 Nm; you'll need a pump. Check the output seals while you're there.)
- Front & rear axles: Same 75W-90 as the transfer box · about 3.5 L for both axles · Drain and refill now; sooner after deep wading (The fill plugs are plastic (21 mm) and break: crack them before draining. Drain plug 64 Nm, fill plug 10 Nm.)
- Power steering & ACE fluid: Land Rover PAS fluid STC50519 (shared reservoir, separate halves) · Change now (Steering: bleed through the nipple into a container while topping up. ACE: drain at the valve block and change the high-pressure filter (72,000-mile item), cap 35 Nm.)
- Brake fluid: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL for grade] · Flush now (Old fluid is one cause of the ABS 'three amigos'.)
- Propshafts & suspension bushes: Grease the UJs that have nipples; inspect the front double-cardan joint, the rear rubber coupling, Watts linkage and ball joints · Every service (The front shaft's double-cardan joint has non-greasable UJs from the factory and can damage the transfer box when it fails.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: Discoweb owners recommend 245/75R16 for a stock-height truck. Several run 265/75R16 at stock height, but they rub at full lock on the plastic behind the fog lamps or need the front bumper trimmed. With a 2-inch lift such as the OME kit, 265/75R16 is the common choice; 285/75R16 wants nearer 3 inches and raises gearing and halfshaft-strength concerns.

Q: Td5 or V8?
A: The Td5 makes its torque low down and responds well to tuning, but it needs a diagnostic tool for some jobs and has known weak spots: the injector harness, the fuel pressure regulator, the early oil-pump bolt and, increasingly, cylinder heads. The V8 is smoother and quicker than a stock Td5 but thirsty, and head gaskets and liners are its big risks. In the US every Disco 2 is a V8.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: There isn't an agreed best year. Wikipedia notes early Td5s (1998–2000) suffered oil-pump-drive and head-stud failures that were fixed within two years. In the US, an Expedition Portal buying guide says 2003–04 trucks were the worst for cracked oil pumps and more prone to loose liners, and a LandRoverForums thread gives the 2003–04 4.6 the worst reputation, though other owners there still vote for the 2004 for its facelift and diff-lock lever. Whatever the year, buy the one with head-gasket, cooling and chassis receipts.

Q: What changed with the 2003 facelift?
A: Pocketed headlamps, revised rear lamps with the indicators moved up out of the bumper, the centre diff lock lever back as an option (standard on high-spec trucks) and, in North America, the 4.6 V8 instead of the 4.0. Td5s had already gained Euro 3 tune and EGR in 2002.

Q: Does my truck have a centre diff lock?
A: Every Series II has a lockable centre differential in the LT230, but early trucks were built without the lever. Owners fit a Discovery 1 linkage from a truck with the same transmission (manual and auto parts differ) or a kit such as Ashcroft's. On early trucks, don't cut the CDL input wire to the ABS ECU: the ECU uses it to stop traction control fighting the locked diff.

Q: Should I keep ACE?
A: Opinion is split. ACE fans say the truck corners far better and has more articulation off-road; others fit standard anti-roll bars once the pipes or valve block start leaking. Repairs to a tired system can run to thousands, so price it before you buy.

Q: Can I convert the SLS to coils?
A: Yes, and it's a common job. Fit Discovery 2 rear spring seats (Discovery 1 seats are shallower), coils and matching shocks, or a ready kit from Terrafirma, Rovers North or Atlantic British. The SLS then needs switching off with dealer software or an aftermarket tool.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: The EPA rated a 2002 4.0 V8 automatic at 12 mpg city, 16 highway and 13 combined, and a 2003 4.6 at 11 city, 14 highway and 12 combined. Td5s do much better, though no US figure exists because they were never sold there.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: Australian specs for a 2001 Td5 manual list 3,500 kg (7,716 lb) braked and 750 kg unbraked, with a 2,750 kg gross vehicle mass.

Q: Can I import a Td5 Discovery 2 into the US?
A: Once it is 25 years old by date of manufacture, yes: NHTSA exempts it from FMVSS. Series IIs were built from 1998 to May 2004, so as of October 2026 trucks built before October 2001 qualify, and later Td5s follow month by month. Check EPA and state rules as well.

Q: What fluids does the Td5 take?
A: discovery2.co.uk's owner uses 5W-30 fully synthetic, the same oil his dealer used, with 7.2 litres including both filters. The transfer box and both axles take 75W-90 gear oil: about 2.0 litres to refill the LT230 (2.3 from dry) and about 3.5 litres for the two axles together.

Q: How is it related to the Discovery 1 and the P38?
A: It keeps the Discovery 1's 100-inch ladder frame and LT230, but borrows a lot from the P38: the 4.0 'Thor' V8, the 5x120 wheel pattern and the front ball joints. The rear propshaft coupling fits Discovery 1, Discovery 2 and P38.

## Land Rover LR3 / Discovery 3 (2004–2009 (US: 2005–2009))
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/lr3/
Codes: L319, LR3, Discovery 3, 4.4 V8 · 4.0 V6 · 2.7 TDV6

Verdict: The Discovery that swapped beam axles for air springs and software, and somehow got better off-road for it. It's also heavy, complicated and cheap for a reason, so buy the best-documented one you can find and keep a diagnostic tool in the glovebox.

On 2 April 2004 Land Rover replaced the last Discovery that still rode on 1970 Range Rover bones with something completely new. The Discovery 3, sold in North America as the LR3, kept the family's stepped roof and upright glass but threw away the beam axles, coil springs and ladder-frame simplicity of the Discovery Series I and its successor. In their place came height-adjustable air suspension at all four corners, a body welded to its own chassis, and a rotary knob that told the truck what kind of ground it was on. Purists sneered. Then the reviews arrived.

### A CLEAN SHEET FROM THE FORD YEARS
The Discovery 3 was the first Land Rover designed after the company and BMW parted ways in 2000, and it arrived almost four years after Ford bought the brand. It was revealed in April 2004 and made its international debut at the British International Motor Show that May. In North America and the Middle East it was badged LR3, partly because of negative quality associations with the Discovery name and, Land Rover said, an American preference for alphanumeric model names; the second Freelander became the LR2 there too.
Everything under the skin came from the Ford family. American trucks got a 300 hp 4.4-litre Jaguar-derived V8 or, in early years, a 216 hp 4.0-litre Ford V6. In Europe the big seller was meant to be the 2.7-litre TDV6, a Ford/PSA-developed V6 diesel with 195 hp and 440 Nm. The diesel came with a six-speed manual as standard; a ZF six-speed automatic was optional on the diesel and standard on the V8, and every version had a two-speed transfer box and permanent four-wheel drive.

### INTEGRATED BODY FRAME AND CROSS-LINKED AIR
Land Rover called the new structure Integrated Body Frame. The engine bay and passenger cell are built as a monocoque, then joined to a basic ladder frame that carries the gearbox and suspension. Land Rover claimed the best of both worlds; critics pointed at a curb weight of 5,426 lb. It is heavier than a pure monocoque but adds strength and toughness, and Land Rover tucked the vital parts up into the body-frame to protect ground clearance.
The suspension is independent double wishbones on air springs, like the Range Rover L322. It can lower for loading, run low at speed and rise for clearance, from 7.3 in at standard height to 9.4 in at off-road height. Off-road, the air springs are cross-linked so that when one wheel drops the other rises, mimicking a beam axle. If the chassis touches the ground at off-road height, the system senses the lost load and lifts another inch. Britain and Europe also got a five-seat, coil-sprung base TDV6 without Terrain Response.

### A KNOB THAT DOES THE THINKING
Terrain Response was the headline. Instead of asking the driver to choose gears, ride height, locking strategy and throttle response, the Discovery 3 offered a dial with settings that included Grass-Gravel-Snow, Sand, Mud and Ruts, and Rock Crawl. Land Rover said engineers studied more than 50 off-road surfaces to calibrate it. In Rock Crawl the suspension goes to full height with maximum articulation, the differentials lock and the driver is prompted to select low range; in Sand the traction control is primed for wheelspin and the throttle is sharpened.
Underneath, a computer-controlled, progressively locking centre differential kept torque flowing, and a similar locking differential was available for the rear axle. The press loved it. Richard Hammond called it the 'best 4x4 of all time', Australia's 4WD press named it 4WD of the Year, and Jeremy Clarkson drove one to the summit of Cnoc an Fhreiceadain near Tongue in northern Scotland, a 307 m hill no vehicle had reached before.

### LIVING WITH ONE NOW
The bargain is obvious: Bring a Trailer LR3s have recently sold for between about $3,000 and $23,000, with a median near $9,000, for a seven-seat truck that will follow a 100 Series almost anywhere. The catch is everything that makes it clever. Air springs, compressors and height sensors age, the electronic parking brake jams, heavy weight eats front lower-arm bushes, and PistonHeads notes that in 2012 Warranty Direct logged more claims on the Discovery 3 than on any other used car from a European maker.
Diesel buyers outside the US also have to accept the TDV6's crankshaft and bearing failures, which Land Rover's own bulletin blames mainly on bearing shells located incorrectly at assembly. American trucks dodge that bullet with the V8, which drinks fuel at an EPA-rated 12–13 mpg in town but is the engine the US aftermarket knows best. Either way, an IIDTool or similar Land Rover diagnostic tool turns most of the scary warnings into Saturday jobs.

### LEGACY
The Discovery 3 platform underpinned the Range Rover Sport, and in 2009 it became the Discovery 4 (LR4 in North America), which kept the Integrated Body Frame and added restyled lights, a new grille and smoother bumpers. Late Discovery 3s from 2008–09 had already gained body-colour bumpers, clear side indicators and a Harman/Kardon stereo upgrade. Today the LR3 is the cheapest way into air-sprung, Terrain Response Land Rover off-roading, with a busy aftermarket of lift rods, sliders and coil conversions behind it.

- Production: 2004–2009
- Code: L319
- Launch: Revealed 2 April 2004; British International Motor Show, May 2004

- Engines: 4.4 V8 · 4.0 V6 · 2.7 TDV6

### Engineering
The Discovery 3 is built around Land Rover's Integrated Body Frame: a monocoque engine bay and cabin joined to a ladder frame that carries the gearbox and suspension. All four wheels hang on independent double wishbones with air springs, cross-linked off-road to behave like a beam axle. Drive goes through a two-speed transfer box (2.93:1 low) with a progressively locking centre differential, and an electronically locking rear differential was available. Terrain Response, Hill Descent Control, four-wheel electronic traction control and an electronic parking brake round out a truck that is as much a network of control modules as a 4x4.
- Body: Integrated Body Frame (Monocoque cabin and engine bay on a ladder frame.)
- Suspension: Independent, four-corner air (Cross-linked off-road; 9.4 in clearance at off-road height.)
- 4Wd: Permanent, two-speed, 2.93:1 low (Computer-controlled, progressively locking centre diff.)
- Rear Diff: Optional electronic locker (Land Rover calls it the electronic torque managed (ETM) unit.)
- Terrain Response: Driver-selected terrain modes (Sets ride height, gearbox, throttle, traction and diff locking.)
- Parking Brake: Electronic, 210 mm duo-servo shoes (Actuator and cables are a known weak spot.)

### Versions
- 2004–2009 · Discovery 3 (UK/Europe/RoW) · 2.7 TDV6 diesel · 195 hp (145 kW) / 440 Nm · Six-speed manual standard, ZF six-speed auto optional.
- 2004–2007 · Discovery 3 (UK) · 4.4 V8 petrol · 300 hp / 425 Nm · Automatic only; petrol dropped in the UK in 2007.
- 2004–2009 · Discovery 3 base (UK/Europe) · 2.7 TDV6 · 195 hp / 440 Nm · Five seats, coil springs, no Terrain Response.
- 2005–2007 MY · LR3 (US) · 4.0 Ford SOHC V6 · 216 hp · Base, then SE V6 for 2007; dropped for 2008.
- 2005–2009 MY · LR3 (US) · 4.4 V8 (Jaguar AJ-V8 family) · 300 hp / 315 lb-ft (427 Nm) · ZF 6HP26 six-speed auto; V8-only from 2008.
- 2008–2009 · Facelift · As above · — · Body-colour bumpers, clear side indicators, Harman/Kardon upgrade.

### Year-by-year
- 2004: Discovery 3 revealed 2 April; British International Motor Show debut in May; UK sales from August with 2.7 TDV6 or 4.4 V8
- 2005 MY: LR3 launches in North America with the 4.4 V8 or the 216 hp 4.0 V6. First-year trucks carry the most NHTSA complaints (96, against 8 for 2008) and five recalls; ReRev names 2005 the year to avoid [avoid]
- 2005–06 MY: Clockspring, fuel-breather and ignition-key recalls; check they were done
- 2006: UK XS and GS trims replace the S (September); Discovery 3 runs the G4 Challenge
- 2007: UK drops the 4.4 V8; US drops the base model and offers the V6 only in the SE
- 2008 MY: US V8 only; seven seats standard; facelift with body-colour bumpers, clear side indicators and Harman/Kardon upgrade. ReRev rates 2008–09 the most reliable LR3s, and they log the fewest NHTSA complaints [buy]
- 2009: Final year; Discovery 4 / LR4 replaces it in September 2009 [buy]

### Capability
- Towing: 7,716 lb (3,500 kg) braked (1,654 lb (750 kg) unbraked; US V8 launch spec)
- Payload: GVWR 7,121 lb (3,230 kg) (Curb weight 5,426 lb, so roughly 1,700 lb payload)
- Fuel tank: 22.8 US gal (86.3 L)
- Ground clearance: 7.3 in (185 mm) standard · 9.4 in (240 mm) off-road height
- Approach / departure / breakover: 37.2° / 29.6° / 27.9°
- Wading depth: 700 mm (27.6 in)
- Wheel articulation: 255 mm front · 330 mm rear
- Fuel economy: EPA 12–13 city / 17 hwy (4.4 V8) (4.0 V6: 13/18 (2005). UK TDV6 auto: 27.2 mpg (imperial) per PistonHeads)
- Curb weight: 5,426 lb (2,461 kg) (US V8 launch spec)
- Turning circle: 37.6 ft (11.45 m) (Curb to curb)
- Low range: 2.93:1 (Two-speed transfer box)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 255/60R18 on 8Jx18 (US SE), 255/55R19 on 8Jx19 (US HSE), 255/50R20 on 8.5Jx20 (option)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x120
- Offset: ET53 (stock 18 and 19 in)
- Center Bore: 72.6 mm
- Lug Thread: M14x1.5
- Lug Torque: 103 lb-ft (140 N·m)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 265/65R18 or 285/60R18 (≈31 in) (Fit at factory height on 18-inch wheels. 275/65R18 (≈32 in) is about the limit: owners zip-tie the front-left height-sensor wire to the frame rail and reshape the right-rear liner near the third-row heater hoses.)
- Biggest tire, 2–2.5 in (lift rods) lift: 275/65R18 (≈32 in) (The common choice with Proud Rhino, Johnson or Terrafirma rods; may rub slightly at full lock, cured by heat-reshaping the liner. One owner advises staying under 32 in overall.)
- Biggest tire, +2 in coil conversion lift: 32–33 in (Lucky8 says Terrafirma's HD coil conversion clears 32–33 in tyres with minor trimming, depending on wheels and offset.)

### Buying checks
- TDV6 bottom end: Land Rover bulletin SSM71816 covers crankshaft and main-bearing failures on the TDV6, caused mainly by bearing shells located incorrectly at assembly and by shells rotating in use. Listen for a rumble or knock that worsens under load, and an oil-pressure light at low revs. Failures are rare but very expensive, and the UK has a whole industry selling reconditioned TDV6 engines.
- Air suspension: Run it through every height with the engine on, check it sits level, and leave it overnight to see whether a corner sags. Leaks, height-sensor faults and tired compressors are the usual causes. A compressor that runs for a long time, overheats or slows before cutting out is on its way out.
- Electronic parking brake: Check that it applies and releases cleanly, more than once. PistonHeads says the EPB often clogs with dirt and a replacement unit can cost over £1,000; owners of the closely related LR4 on LandRoverWorld describe $900–2,200 shop quotes for actuator and cable work.
- Front lower arms and bushes: A 5,400 lb truck wears out its bushes, ball joints, wheel bearings and brakes. Look for split boots and oil weeping from the hydraulic rear bushes of the front lower arms, and budget for seized bolts if they need doing.
- ZF six-speed automatic: Feel for judder and harsh shifts and ask when the fluid was last changed. Land Rover's long fluid interval was optimistic; PistonHeads suggests changing it about five times as often. Coolant can also reach the gearbox through the heat exchanger in the radiator, so look for milky fluid.
- TDV6 belts, flywheel and EGR: Ask for proof of the timing belt, tensioner, pulleys and water pump; PistonHeads advises doing them within six years or 60,000 miles. Manual trucks can eat dual-mass flywheels and clutches at low mileage, and EGR valves often fail.
- 4.4 V8 cooling: The plastic thermostat housing and its coolant tube can crack and drip. Check around the front of the engine for dried coolant, and make sure the temperature gauge stays steady on a long run.
- Electrics, A/C and recalls: Expect warning lights and test everything: central locking, windows, rear wiper, sat-nav, A/C (compressors and pipes corrode), battery and alternator. In the US, run the VIN for open recalls, including the 2005–06 steering-wheel clockspring campaign.

### Common repairs
#### Rebuild or replace the air suspension compressor
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Half a day · cost Rebuild kit vs. complete compressor kit
Symptoms: Slow height changes, suspension faults, a compressor that gets very hot and slows before cutting out with an error. One DISCO3.CO.UK owner's unit reached 90°C in about 90 seconds.
Fix: Owners rebuild the original Hitachi with a piston glide ring, fresh desiccant and filters and an aluminium dryer cap, or fit a complete new unit. Don't wait: a failing compressor lets the dryer's silica turn to dust, which can reach and damage the valve blocks. Expect seized unions at the dryer (penetrating oil and time), use silicone grease on the O-rings, check the bracket bushes, and fit a new relay. Converting to the later AMK compressor is a factory-approved upgrade but needs a software update.
Tools: Sockets, penetrating oil, silicone grease, push-fit couplings if pipes must be cut · compressor overhaul kit JPO500010 · dryer VUB504700 · relay YWB500220

#### Front air spring or strut
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time An evening per side · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: One corner leans or drops, the fault keeps coming back, or you hear air hiss over bumps. A soapy-water test shows the leak.
Fix: Pull the suspension fuse, support the body on stands and remove the wheel. Support the lower strut bolt with a jack, remove the two top nuts in the wheel well and the third in the engine bay (lift the heat shield first), and crack the air line slowly, letting any pressure bleed off before it comes apart. Either fit a complete strut or swap the bag onto the old damper with new O-rings and spacers, then refit and let the system fill. Some owners recalibrate the height afterwards.
Tools: 15 mm sockets, swivel, breaker bar, 12/13 mm spanner for the air line, jack and stands · front strut RNB501580 or air spring LR016403 · seal LR016412

#### Ride height sensor replacement
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour plus calibration · cost Price of the sensor
Symptoms: Uneven ride height, suspension warning lights, or a truck that won't hold the height it's asked for. Height-sensor faults are one of the electrical causes of air-suspension trouble.
Fix: Each corner has its own sensor linked to a suspension arm. Unplug it, unbolt the sensor and its link, fit the new one and check the arm moves freely. Repair a corroded plug with the harness repair kit rather than living with it. The suspension usually needs calibrating after a sensor is replaced; Gap's IIDTool offers an individual sensor calibration that doesn't need a level floor.
Tools: Basic sockets, dielectric grease, diagnostic tool for calibration · LR020155 (FL) / LR020157 (FR) / LR020159 (RL) / LR020161 (RR)

#### Electronic parking brake actuator
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time Many hours the first time (one LR4 owner took 11) · cost LR4 owners report $900–2,200 shop quotes; a gear kit is cheap
Symptoms: The parking brake won't apply or release, or the motor grinds or whines without effect. A seized EPB can leave the truck stuck.
Fix: In an emergency, PistonHeads notes the EPB can be released manually with the jack handle through a metal loop behind a plastic panel. For the repair, the actuator sits ahead of the rear frame rail with very little clearance; owners remove the module and cables, then fit a gear repair kit or a complete actuator. One LandRoverWorld LR4 owner traced his fault to the cable adjusting bolt being threaded in too far and reset it to five turns into the tube. Check the rear shoes and their hardware while you're there.
Tools: Torx bits, sockets, patience · gear repair kit DA9223 · actuator LR019223 · parking brake shoes LR031947

#### Front lower control arms and bushes
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time 45 min per side on a lift; a full day if bolts are seized · cost One owner was quoted $1,400 for both arms plus alignment
Symptoms: Clunks, vague steering, tyre wear, split boots and oil leaking from the hydraulic rear bush.
Fix: Soak the fixings for days beforehand. Many bolts come out with heat or a drift; seized ones are cut with a reciprocating saw and carbide blades, which is why Lucky8 sells arm kits with new hardware. You may need a puller to push the drive shaft back through the hub. Fit the new arms or bushes and get an alignment straight away; one owner warns a badly misaligned truck can drop to its bump stops on the way to the shop, and a restart pumps it back up.
Tools: Torque wrench to about 300 Nm, 18/21/22 mm sockets, reciprocating saw with carbide blades, heat, 3-jaw puller · arm kit with hardware · bush LR073366

#### ZF 6HP26 fluid, pan and filter
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost About the price of a service kit
Symptoms: Judder, flare or harsh shifts, an unknown service history, or a weeping valve body sleeve.
Fix: The filter is built into the plastic pan, so you replace the pan. Drain, drop the pan, and replace the valve body sleeve (a common leak point) while it's open. Refill with ZF-spec fluid and follow the factory fill-and-level procedure with the fluid at the specified temperature. Workshop data quotes 9.5 litres for a dry fill; a pan change takes far less, so some owners repeat it to refresh more of the fluid.
Tools: Sockets, fluid pump, scan tool or thermometer for the level check · pan LR007474 · sleeve TZV500010 · ATF TYK500050

#### TDV6 timing belt and water pump
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A full day · cost Parts plus significant labor
Symptoms: Due on age or mileage, no paperwork, or a weeping water pump. PistonHeads also notes the oil-pump casing that the timing-belt tensioner bolts to can snap off.
Fix: PistonHeads advises replacing the belt, tensioner, small pulleys and water pump within six years or 60,000 miles. Lock the engine with the correct timing tools before removing the old belt, fit the full kit and pump, and turn the engine by hand before starting. Note there are separate Euro 3 and Euro 4 belt kits for the 2.7, so match the kit to your engine.
Tools: TDV6 timing tool set, torque wrench, coolant · Euro 4 kit LR019115 or Euro 3 kit 1324390 · water pump LR009324

#### 4.4 V8 thermostat housing and coolant tube
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours plus an hour to bleed · cost A housing and coolant
Symptoms: A slow coolant drip from a crack in the plastic thermostat housing, low coolant, rising temperature.
Fix: Drain the coolant, remove the engine cover, air box and intake, the throttle body and the hoses to the housing, then the eight T30 Torx bolts; the assembly is sealed by three O-rings, not sealant. Fit the new LR005631 assembly as one piece (one owner split it, damaged an O-ring and made a new leak) and tighten the bolts evenly. Refill with OAT coolant and bleed patiently through the expansion tank and bleed screw, ideally with a vacuum filler.
Tools: 6/8/10/13 mm sockets, T30 Torx, wobble extensions, pick, vacuum coolant filler · LR005631 · LRN2279 coolant

### Baseline service
Most LR3s have had cheap ownership for years, and on this truck deferred maintenance shows up as warning lights. Baseline the fluids in the ZF gearbox, transfer box and diffs that many owners never touch, do the TDV6 timing belt unless there's proof, and check the air suspension and parking brake with a diagnostic tool while the truck is on stands.
- Engine oil & filter (4.4 V8): SAE 5W-30 to WSS-M2C205-A per the workshop manual · 7.7 L (8.1 US qt) with filter · Then per manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (4.0 V6 and 2.7 TDV6 use different filters; check grade and capacity for those engines in the manual.)
- Air filter: Paper element · Replace now
- Cabin filter: Pollen or activated-carbon element · Replace now
- Spark plugs (V8) / glow plugs (TDV6): LR005253 plugs (V8) · 1354289 glow plugs (TDV6) · Replace V8 plugs if undocumented; test glow plugs
- Coolant: OAT ethylene-glycol coolant without methanol (Havoline XLC type) · 9.3 L, or 10 L with rear heater · Flush now; Lucky8 lists 5 years / 105,000 mi for LRN2279 (On the 4.4 V8, inspect the plastic thermostat housing and coolant tube while you're there.)
- Automatic gearbox (ZF 6HP26): ZF-spec ATF (workshop manual lists Shell M1375.4) · 9.5 L dry fill · Pan, filter and fluid now (PistonHeads: Land Rover's interval was long; change it far more often. Replace the valve body sleeve while the pan is off.)
- Transfer box: Land Rover transfer fluid (workshop manual lists Shell TF 0753) · about 1.4–1.5 L · Drain and refill now (Lucky8 lists IYK500010 as the LR3 transfer fluid.)
- Front & rear differentials: Open diffs: Castrol SAF-XO 75W-90 · front 0.61 L, rear 1.1 L · ETM locking rear: Castrol SAF Carbon Mod Plus, 1.5 L · Drain and refill now (A rear locker needs its own fluid; don't fill it with ordinary gear oil.)
- Power steering: Land Rover PAS fluid STC50519 · 0.85 L · Inspect hoses; refresh if dark
- Brake fluid: DOT 4 ESL (workshop data lists Shell Donax YB) · Flush now
- Timing belt (2.7 TDV6): Belt, tensioner, pulleys and water pump · Now unless documented; PistonHeads advises within 6 years / 60,000 mi (Separate Euro 3 and Euro 4 kits exist; match the kit to your engine.)
- Accessory belts (4.4 V8): Primary and secondary poly-V belts, tensioner · Inspect now; replace if cracked or noisy
- Air suspension: Leak test, compressor run and temperature, height sensors · Check now; service the dryer if the compressor is tired (Read the suspension codes with a diagnostic tool; a dryer full of powdered desiccant can damage the valve blocks.)
- Parking brake & suspension bushes: EPB apply and release, rear shoes, front lower-arm bushes and ball joints · Inspect now (PistonHeads: dirt clogs the EPB, and the truck's weight wears bushes, ball joints and bearings.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: On 18-inch wheels, 265/65R18 or 285/60R18 (about 31 in) fit at factory height without modification. 275/65R18 (about 32 in) is about the biggest that works at stock height, and owners report it needs the front-left height-sensor wire zip-tied to the frame rail and a little liner reshaping; one owner's 285/65R18s rubbed slightly at full lock. With lift rods, 275/65R18 is the common choice. One owner advises staying under 32 in overall.

Q: Is it body-on-frame?
A: Sort of. Land Rover's Integrated Body Frame builds the engine bay and cabin as a monocoque, then joins them to a basic ladder frame that carries the gearbox and suspension. It is heavier than a pure monocoque but stronger and tougher.

Q: Which engine should I buy?
A: In the US the choice is the 300 hp 4.4 V8 (all years) or the 216 hp 4.0 V6 (2005–07). The V8 is the common one, shared with the 2006–09 Range Rover Sport and L322 Range Rover. Elsewhere most trucks have the 195 hp, 440 Nm 2.7 TDV6, which is far more economical but carries crank-bearing and timing-belt risks.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: Later is better, within reason. The 2005 LR3 has the most NHTSA complaints (96, against 8 for 2008 and 3 for 2009) and five recalls, and ReRev names 2005 the one to avoid and 2008–09 the most reliable. Raw complaint counts aren't adjusted for how many were sold, though, and PistonHeads still calls any phase-one Discovery 3 a high-risk purchase, so a thick service file beats a late build date.

Q: Is the TDV6 crank failure real?
A: Yes, though it's uncommon. Land Rover bulletin SSM71816 covers crankshaft and main-bearing failures, mainly caused by incorrectly located bearing shells at assembly. Symptoms are a knock or rumble that worsens under load, sometimes with the oil-pressure light. Carbuyer calls it rare, unpredictable and very costly.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: 7,716 lb (3,500 kg) braked and 1,654 lb (750 kg) unbraked, according to Land Rover's launch specifications.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: EPA ratings for the V8 are 12–13 mpg city and 17 highway, depending on year; the V6 is rated 13/18 for 2005. In the UK, PistonHeads quotes 27.2 mpg (imperial) for the automatic TDV6 and 18.8 mpg for the V8.

Q: How do I lift it?
A: The cheap route is lift rods, which replace the links on the factory height sensors so the air suspension sits about 2–2.5 in higher (Proud Rhino, Terrafirma and Lucky8 make them). A diagnostic tool such as Gap's IIDTool can change the programmed heights instead. If you've had enough of air, Terrafirma sells +2 in coil conversions and Old Man Emu coil springs for the LR3 are sold too.

Q: Does it have locking differentials?
A: Every truck has a computer-controlled, progressively locking centre differential. A locking rear differential (Land Rover's electronic torque managed unit) was optional. Terrain Response controls how hard both lock in each mode.

Q: What goes wrong with the air suspension?
A: Leaking air springs, height sensors, compressors and the electrics. A failing compressor overheats and slows; if ignored, the dryer desiccant can break down and damage the valve blocks. Many owners rebuild the Hitachi compressor; the later AMK unit needs a software update to fit.

Q: My parking brake is stuck. How do I release it?
A: PistonHeads says a seized EPB can be released manually using the jack handle through a metal loop behind a plastic panel. The underlying fault is usually the actuator or its cable adjustment, and dirt build-up is a known cause.

Q: What's the difference between an LR3 and a Discovery 3?
A: Nothing structural: LR3 is the North American and Middle Eastern name. The engines differ by market, with the V8 and V6 petrols in North America and the TDV6 diesel as the main engine elsewhere.

Q: How deep can it wade?
A: Land Rover's launch specification quotes a 700 mm (27.6 in) wading depth. Raise the suspension to off-road height before you go in.

## Land Rover LR4 / Discovery 4 (2009–2016 (US: 2010–2016))
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/land-rover/lr4/
Codes: L319, LR4, Discovery 4, 5.0 V8, 3.0 SC V6, SDV6

Verdict: The last Discovery with a ladder frame under it, air springs that cross-link like beam axles, and Terrain Response at the twist of a dial. It's a brilliant expedition wagon wrapped round a cooling system made of plastic that's slowly giving up, so budget for that before you budget for the roof tent.

The Discovery 4, sold as the LR4 in North America and the Middle East, is a thorough rework of the Discovery 3 rather than a new truck. It keeps the stepped roof, the 113.6-inch wheelbase and the Integrated Body Frame, a monocoque body bolted to a ladder chassis, and adds a new face, a nicer cabin and much better engines. It is the last Discovery built that way. That makes it a seven-seat expedition truck with independent air suspension, a two-speed transfer box and Terrain Response, all for less than a used Land Cruiser. The catch is that it is still a Land Rover, and the bills arrive in plastic.

### A FACELIFT THAT WENT DEEP
Land Rover unveiled the Discovery 4 in the summer of 2009 and put it on sale in Britain on 1 September that year; in the US it arrived as the 2010 LR4. The nose, lamps and grille were smoothed to match the 2010 Range Rover and Range Rover Sport, and the dash was redone with a TFT driver's display and simpler switchgear. Most of the money went underneath, though: Range Rover Sport brakes, thicker anti-roll bars, a better ZF six-speed automatic, and Terrain Response retuned with a Sand launch mode and a Rock Crawl mode that brakes gently at walking pace.
The cross-linked air suspension and the electronically locking centre differential carried over from the LR3 (Discovery 3), and a locking rear differential stayed on the options list. Under the body is the same 'Integrated Body Frame' Land Rover introduced in 2004: build the passenger cell and engine bay as a monocoque, then mate it to a ladder frame that carries the gearbox and suspension. It's heavy, at about 5,600 lb for a US V8, but it's strong.

### V8, THEN A SUPERCHARGED SIX
In America the LR4 launched with Jaguar Land Rover's new direct-injection 5.0-litre V8, rated at 375 hp and 375 lb-ft, from the same AJ133 family that went into the 2010 Range Rover. Europe mostly got diesels: a 3.0-litre twin-turbo V6 with 600 Nm, sold from the 2011 model year as the SDV6 alongside a single-turbo TDV6, plus a basic 2.7 TDV6 that was dropped for 2011. Diesel Discoveries in Europe also got the ZF eight-speed automatic for 2012, two years before America did.
The 2014 model year changed the US truck more than any facelift did. The V8 gave way to a supercharged 3.0-litre V6 with 340 hp and 332 lb-ft, the six-speed became a ZF eight-speed with stop-start, and a lighter single-speed transfer case became standard. If you wanted low range and the active locking rear differential, you now had to tick the $1,350 Heavy Duty package, which also added a full-size spare. EPA combined economy went from 14 mpg for the V8 to 16 mpg for the V6.

### WHAT IT'S LIKE TO OWN ONE
Owners on LandRoverWorld and Expedition Portal tend to tell the same story. The truck is superb off-road and on a long drive, and it will tow 7,716 lb. It also eats brakes, and its cooling system is full of plastic crossover pipes and coolant manifolds that crack between roughly 50,000 and 100,000 miles. Early 5.0 V8s added a timing-chain tensioner problem, covered by Land Rover bulletin LTB00474 for 2010–2012 trucks in a published VIN range. The air suspension, meanwhile, will eventually want a compressor, a strut or a valve block.
None of that makes it a bad buy. It makes it a truck to buy with records, a scan tool and a plan. An Expedition Portal owner put it bluntly: a $14,000 LR4 can need $5,000–8,000 of deferred maintenance in the first year, and the purchase price is only the price of admission. Sort the cooling system and the chains, though, and the LR4 is far more capable on a trail than most luxury SUVs. When Car and Driver lined it up against the Lexus GX 460 and three road-biased rivals in 2011, it finished fourth of five, which says more about the test than the truck.

### THE END OF THE LADDER
In March 2012 the one millionth Discovery came off the Solihull line, a Discovery 4, and Land Rover drove it and two sister trucks from Solihull to the Beijing Motor Show, recreating a 1950s overland expedition. That car is now on permanent display at the British Motor Museum in Gaydon. Discovery 4 production ran until 2016; owners report that the US line-up ended with Landmark and HSE Silver trims in the 2016.5 model year. Its successor, the 2017 Discovery, switched to a lighter unitary body and dropped the numeric suffix. That leaves the LR4 as the last Discovery with a separate frame under it, closing a line that began with the 1989 original.

### Data plate
- Model Code: L319
- Names: Discovery 4 · LR4 (N. America, Middle East)
- Production: 2009–2016
- Us Model Years: 2010–2016
- Plant: Solihull, UK
- Construction: Integrated Body Frame
- Wheelbase: 113.6 in (2,885 mm)
- Length: 190.5 in (4,838 mm)
