- Us Engines: 5.0 V8 · 3.0 supercharged V6
- Curb Weight: From 5,617 lb (V8)
- Max Towing: 7,716 lb (3,500 kg)

### Engineering
Underneath the LR4 is the Discovery 3's Integrated Body Frame: a monocoque passenger cell and engine bay mounted to a separate ladder frame that carries the drivetrain and suspension. All four wheels are independently sprung on air struts that the computer can cross-link, so when one wheel drops, its partner on the same axle rises, as on a beam axle. Ride height runs from access height to an off-road setting with 9.4 in (240 mm) of ground clearance. Terrain Response sets throttle, gearbox, differentials, traction control and ride height for the selected surface.
- Construction: Integrated Body Frame (Monocoque body bolted to a ladder chassis.)
- Suspension: Independent, cross-linked air (Off-road height gives 9.4 in of clearance; the Euro handbook also lists a coil-sprung 2.7 diesel.)
- 4Wd: Permanent, two-speed with locking centre diff (2014–16 US base trucks: single-speed with a Torsen centre diff.)
- Rear Diff: Optional electronic locker (Part of the 2014–16 Heavy Duty package in the US.)
- Traction: Terrain Response, HDC (Sand launch and Rock Crawl brake functions new on D4.)
- Us Engines: 5.0 V8, then 3.0 supercharged V6 (375 hp V8 (2010–13); 340 hp SC V6 (2014–16).)

### Versions
- 2010–2013 MY · LR4 (US) · 5.0 V8 (AJ133) · 375 hp / 375 lb-ft · ZF six-speed auto; two-speed transfer box.
- 2014–2016 MY · LR4 (US) · 3.0 supercharged V6 (AJ126) · 340 hp / 332 lb-ft · ZF 8HP70 eight-speed; single-speed transfer standard, two-speed in HD package.
- 2009–2010 · Discovery 4 (Europe) · 2.7 TDV6 · 190 PS / 440 Nm · Base GS and Commercial; six-speed manual or auto.
- 2009–2016 · Discovery 4 (Europe) · 3.0 TDV6 / SDV6 twin-turbo diesel · 211–258 PS / 520–600 Nm · Eight-speed auto for diesels from 2012.
- 2009–2013 · Discovery 4 (some markets) · 4.0 V6 petrol; 5.0 V8 petrol · 219 PS (V6); 375 PS (V8) · V8 sold outside the UK; the 4.0 V6 in some Asian markets.
- 2014–2016 · Discovery 4 (some markets) · 3.0 supercharged V6 · 340 PS / 460 Nm · Replaced the petrol V6 and V8.

### Year-by-year
- 2009: Discovery 4 unveiled in the summer; UK sales from 1 September. Diesels: 2.7 TDV6 and new 3.0 twin-turbo V6; petrol 5.0 V8 in non-UK markets
- 2010 MY: LR4 launches in the US with the 375-hp 5.0 V8, ZF six-speed and two-speed transfer box
- 2010–13 MY: 5.0 V8 timing-chain tensioners and levers wear: bulletin LTB00474 covers 2010–12 trucks in VIN range AA513326–CA652214, revised parts start at VIN DA696315 (mid-2013), and a US class action covered 2012–14 5.0 trucks. Buy only with the invoice [avoid]
- 2011 MY: Europe: 2.7 TDV6 dropped; 3.0 diesel offered as TDV6 and SDV6
- 2012: Europe: diesels get the ZF eight-speed; HSE Luxury edition; one millionth Discovery built in March
- 2013 MY: Last US V8 year, with minor styling and option updates. The revised chain tensioners, levers and guides arrive partway through the year (from VIN DA696315), so check the VIN or the invoice
- 2014 MY: 3.0 supercharged V6 (340 hp), ZF 8HP70 and stop-start; single-speed transfer standard in the US, low range and active rear locker only in the $1,350 HD package
- 2014: XXV special edition marks 25 years of the Discovery
- 2015 MY: ABS-software recall 15V214000 for early builds; smartphone app integration and side steps standard (US)
- 2016 MY: Final US year; owners report HSE Silver and Landmark trims replacing HSE and HSE Lux for 2016.5
- 2016: Production ends; the 2017 Discovery (L462) replaces it with a unitary body

### Capability
- Towing: 7,716 lb (3,500 kg) braked (gross train weight 14,859 lb (6,740 kg))
- Gross vehicle weight: 7,143 lb (3,240 kg)
- Roof load: 165 lb (75 kg) (including the rack)
- Fuel tank: 23 US gal (86 L) usable (petrol; diesels 82 L)
- Ground clearance: 9.4 in (240 mm) at off-road height (7.3 in (185 mm) at standard height)
- Approach / departure: 36.2° / 28.1° (off-road height; Land Rover quotes the ramp angle as 125.4°)
- Wading depth: 28 in (700 mm) (off-road height; 24 in (600 mm) at standard height)
- Fuel economy: EPA 12–13 city / 17 hwy (V8); 15 / 19 (SC V6) (14 and 16 mpg combined; premium fuel)
- Curb weight: 5,617 lb (2,548 kg) V8; 5,655 lb SC V6 (handbook (V8); 2014 HSE fact sheet (V6))
- Turning circle: 37.5 ft (11.45 m) (curb to curb)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 255/50R19 (8J and 9J x 19), 255/50R20 (8.5J x 20)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x120
- Offset: +53 mm (stock 19x8)
- Center Bore: 72.6 mm
- Lug Thread: M14x1.5
- Lug Torque: 98 lb-ft (133 N·m), from the 2016 owner's handbook as quoted by an owner
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 265/50R20 · 265/65R18 on aftermarket 18s (LandRoverWorld owners run 265/50R20 with no rubbing; it's also the largest size that fits the spare well inflated. 285/50R20 rubs slightly at full lock and the spare must be deflated to fit. On 18-inch wheels, 265/65R18 doesn't rub at standard height and 285/60R18 brings only mild liner rub at full compression or lock.)
- Biggest tire, 2.5 in (lift rods) lift: 275/65R18 – 265/70R18 (≈33 in) (One owner ran 275/65R18 and moved to 265/70R18 with lift rods and strut spacers; he reports the 275s sit very close to the upper control arms, and that 12.5-inch-wide 33s are unlikely to fit without rubbing the arms or popping the arch trims.)

### Buying checks
- Coolant smell, coolant top-ups, crossover history: The plastic coolant crossover pipes and manifolds are the LR4's best-known weak point on both the 5.0 V8 and the 3.0 SC V6. Owners report failures from about 50,000 miles and treat 60,000–90,000 miles as replacement time. A sweet coolant smell after a drive, a falling expansion tank or a 'low coolant' message means it's already started. Ask for invoices showing genuine crossover pipes, the water pump and the thermostat.
- 5.0 V8: cold-start rattle: Land Rover bulletin LTB00474 covers a rattle or click from the front of the engine on 2010–2012 MY LR4s in VIN range AA513326–CA652214, caused by worn timing-chain tensioner levers. The fix is two tensioners (LR051008) and two levers (LR051013); the revised levers have a steel insert, and old and new parts must not be mixed. Listen to a stone-cold start, and get proof of the work if the VIN is in range. A ticking roughly once a second is more likely the fan clutch.
- Air suspension: the overnight test: Raise the truck to off-road height, then check that it stays level overnight and that the compressor doesn't run constantly. A truck that sags after a few days has a leak at a strut, valve block or Voss fitting. Owners trace leaks with soapy water. If the compressor has been replaced, Arnott notes that the LR3/LR4 unit needs a software update and a new relay.
- Which drivetrain do you have?: Every 2010–2013 US LR4 has a two-speed transfer box. From 2014 the base truck is single-speed with a Torsen centre differential, and low range plus the active rear locker came only with the $1,350 Heavy Duty package, which also brought a full-size spare. Owners check the 4x4 information screen (a single centre-lock icon means no HD package) and the spare, and look under the rear axle for the locker's actuator motor.
- 3.0 SC V6: supercharger rattle: A rattle like gravel in a can from the top of the engine at idle is usually the supercharger's spring-type coupler isolator wearing out. A supercharger rebuilder quoted on LandRoverWorld says it starts going at around 50,000 miles. It isn't urgent, but the supercharger has to be partly dismantled or removed, so it pairs naturally with the rear coolant manifold job.
- Front lower control arms and brakes: At 5,600-plus lb, the LR4 is hard on lower control-arm bushings, ball joints and brakes. Clunks over bumps, steering wander and uneven tyre wear point at the arms. Owners say brakes wear quickly and cost a lot to replace, and early trucks had a TSB for rear brake squeal when reversing.
- Recalls: Run the VIN through NHTSA. Every 2010–2016 LR4 is in campaign 21V635000 for a fuel-pump flange that can crack and leak. Some 2012–2013 trucks built in August–September 2012 are in 15V386000 for panoramic-roof adhesive, and some 2015s are in 15V214000 for ABS software that can disable stability control and Hill Descent Control.
- Oil changes and records: The factory oil interval was 15,000 miles. Owners on LandRoverWorld and Expedition Portal recommend 5,000–7,500 miles, and some link the 5.0 chain-guide wear to long intervals. A truck with dealer stamps at 15,000 miles and no chain or cooling work is a project priced as a driver.

### Common repairs
#### Coolant crossover pipe, water pump & thermostat (5.0 V8)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 1 day DIY (pump and both pipes) · cost One owner's dealer bill for pump, front and rear manifolds, hoses and belts on a 2015: $5,500
Symptoms: Coolant smell after driving, slowly falling coolant level or 'low coolant' warning, crusty coolant around the front of the engine or the back of the block, rising temperature under load.
Fix: Drain the coolant. Remove the engine covers and air intake to reach the front crossover (water pump outlet to block, LR018275) and the rear heater manifold. Pull the pipes and make sure no broken pipe ends or O-rings stay behind in the block. Clean the ports, fit new O-rings lubricated with coolant (not grease), and seat the new pipes squarely. Owners warn against cheap copies and fit genuine or aluminium parts. Replace the water pump and thermostat while you're in there, then refill with the correct 50/50 coolant and bleed the system.
Tools: Metric sockets, hose-clamp pliers, pick for old O-rings, drain pan · genuine LR018275 crossover, rear heater manifold LR122709, water pump LR097165 (per Lucky8 listings), O-rings LR010800

#### Supercharger-off cooling refresh & isolator (3.0 SC V6, 2014–16)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A weekend DIY · cost Parts plus several hours' labour; the supercharger must come off
Symptoms: Coolant odour with no visible leak, slow coolant loss, a gravelly rattle from the supercharger at idle.
Fix: On the SC V6 the front 'Y' crossover sits under the supercharger. Drain the coolant, remove the charge-air cooler and supercharger (it sits on two dowel pins; rock it from the snout and pry gently, minding the knock sensors underneath), then replace the front crossover (redesigned LR090630 and LR092992), the rear heater manifold, the water pump and the thermostat. One owner found his front pipe eaten away above the O-rings at 50,100 miles. Replace the supercharger coupler isolator while the blower is off. Refill and bleed the system.
Tools: Metric sockets and Torx, pry bar, new gaskets and O-rings · LR090630, LR092992 front crossover, LR109401 rear manifold, LR097165 pump, LR095895 thermostat kit (one owner's DIY list)

#### Timing chain tensioners & guides (5.0 V8)
Difficulty 5 / 5 · time Land Rover allows 8.1 h for tensioners and levers; one shop quoted 18.75 h for a full chain kit · cost Dealer quotes around $4,500 on LandRoverWorld; one full kit job was $2,346 in parts plus about $2,500 labour
Symptoms: Rattle or click from the front of the engine, more pronounced at idle and most obvious on a cold start.
Fix: LTB00474 calls for two new tensioners (LR051008) and two tensioner levers (LR051013). The revised levers have a steel insert, and Land Rover's follow-up note SSM71893 warns that old and new parts must never be mixed. Many independents fit the full chain kit with guides while the engine is open. The engine must be locked at the correct position with the 5.0 V8 timing tools, and the tensioners reset on reassembly. Do the water pump and crossover pipes at the same time.
Tools: 5.0 V8 timing tool set, crank pulley remover/installer, torque wrench · tensioners LR051008 ×2, levers LR051013 ×2 (per LTB00474), cam cover gaskets

#### Air suspension compressor
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost About C$1,000 quoted on LandRoverWorld; compressors run $559–889 at Lucky8
Symptoms: Slow to rise, 'suspension fault' message, compressor running constantly or overheating, truck stuck at a low height.
Fix: Find the leak first, or a new compressor will burn out too: raise the truck, pull the EAS fuse overnight and measure each corner, and soap-test struts, valve blocks and Voss fittings. Fit the new compressor with a new relay, and don't overtighten the Voss fittings. LR4s left the factory with Hitachi or, later, AMK units, and the EAS software must match the pump fitted, so recalibrate with a dealer tool or a GAP IIDTool. The compressor sits low beside the sill, which is why some rock sliders are designed to shield it.
Tools: Jack and stands, sockets, soapy water, GAP IIDTool or dealer diagnostics · compressor (Hitachi LR023964 or AMK LR072537), relay

#### Air strut / air spring replacement
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours per axle · cost Parts from about $258 for a front air spring to $509 for a complete rear strut
Symptoms: One corner sags overnight, the truck leans when parked, hissing from a wheel well, bouncy ride from a leaking damper.
Fix: Confirm the corner with an overnight drop test and soapy water. Support the truck on stands at the chassis, deflate the system with a diagnostic tool, disconnect the air line and height-sensor link, and unbolt the strut. Arnott advises supporting the vehicle while a new spring first inflates so the bag can't fold under, replacing springs in pairs, and checking the damper, since oil from a leaking shock can ruin a new air spring.
Tools: Jack and stands, sockets, spring tools for the front strut, diagnostic tool to deflate and recalibrate · air spring or complete strut

#### Front lower control arms (bushings & ball joints)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 3–4 hours for both sides · cost Kits $329–739 at Lucky8; one owner was quoted about C$1,200 for rear arms
Symptoms: Clunk over bumps, wandering on the highway, uneven front tyre wear, torn ball-joint boots.
Fix: Most owners replace the whole arm, with its bushings and ball joint, rather than pressing in new bushings. Support the truck, separate the ball joint, remove the inner mounting bolts and swap the arm. Lucky8 warns that the original bolts often rust into the arm and frame and have to be cut out, so buy the hardware kit. Finish with an alignment.
Tools: Sockets, breaker bar, ball-joint separator, reciprocating saw for seized bolts · arm kit with hardware

#### Automatic transmission fluid & pan/filter service
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2–4 hours · cost About C$1,000 at a shop per LandRoverWorld; kits $279 (six-speed) and $578 (eight-speed) at Lucky8
Symptoms: Harsh or flared shifts, judder, a weeping pan or valve-body sleeve. The handbook calls the fluid 'filled for life', but owners and specialists change it.
Fix: 2010–2013 trucks use a ZF six-speed with a plastic pan and integral filter; 2014–2016 trucks use the ZF 8HP70, whose LR065238 pan also carries the filter. Drain, drop the pan, replace the valve-body sleeve on six-speeds, fit the new pan, then follow the factory fill-and-level procedure, which is done at a specified fluid temperature. Several six-speed owners have switched to a steel pan with a separate filter to make future services easier.
Tools: Torx and sockets, fluid pump, scan tool to read fluid temperature · pan with filter, sleeve, ZF-spec fluid

#### Brake pads, discs & parking-brake shoes
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours per axle · cost Pads from about $55 (rear) and $72 (front, 2010–13); full Terrafirma kits from $328
Symptoms: Wear warnings, vibration under braking, squeal when reversing (early trucks had a TSB for rear squeal), a weak electronic parking brake.
Fix: Pads and discs are conventional: retract the piston, swap pads with new wear sensors, and replace discs if they're under minimum thickness or lipped. Owners note the rear-squeal fix works best with new rotors as well as pads. The parking brake uses shoes inside the rear disc. Inspect them whenever the discs are off, and follow the workshop-manual procedure for the electronic parking brake before you work on them.
Tools: Sockets, caliper piston tool, torque wrench, diagnostic tool for EPB service mode · pads, discs, sensors, EPB shoes

### Baseline service
Most LR4s are now past 100,000 miles on a 15,000-mile factory oil interval, and the handbook calls the gearbox 'filled for life'. Baseline everything, and treat the cooling-system plastics and the air suspension as part of the service, not as optional extras. Fluid specs below are from Land Rover's Discovery 4 owner guides; check your own handbook for 2014–16 SC V6 figures.
- Engine oil & filter: 5.0 V8: SAE 5W-20 to WSS-M2C925-A, 8.0 L (17 US pt) with filter · 3.0 SC V6: 5W-20 to WSS-M2C925-A (2014 TSB); owners report 0W-20 to STJLR.51.5122 for 2015–16, ≈8 L [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Then every 5,000–7,500 mi (owner practice; factory interval was 15,000 mi) (Cartridge filter (LR011279) sits on top of the engine; the housing is marked with its torque (25 N·m). Most owners extract the oil from the top.)
- Engine air filter: LR011593 element (5.0 V8 and 3.0 SC) · Replace now; check often on dusty trails (Direct-injection engines don't forgive dust, and one owner found sand packed around the injectors after desert trips.)
- Cabin filter: JKR500010 · Replace now
- Spark plugs: 5.0 V8: NGK LR032080 ×8 · 3.0 SC V6: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Replace now unless documented (While the coils are out, look for oil in the plug wells (the 5.0 timing kit includes new plug-tube seals).)
- Coolant & cooling plastics: 50% Castrol SF antifreeze and water · 5.0 V8: 17 L (36 US pt) refill · 3.0 SC V6: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Pressure-test now; crossover pipes, manifolds, pump and thermostat at 60,000–90,000 mi if undocumented (owner practice) (This is the LR4's weakest system. Replace the expansion-tank cap too, and use genuine or aluminium pipes rather than cheap copies.)
- Automatic transmission: 2010–13 ZF six-speed: Shell ATF M1375.4 · 2014–16 ZF 8HP70: ZF-spec fluid [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Handbook says 'filled for life'; Lucky8 recommends 50,000–75,000 mi for the eight-speed (The filter is built into the pan on both gearboxes, so a proper service means a new pan. Fill and level at the specified temperature.)
- Transfer box: Shell TF 0753 · 1.5 L (3.2 US pt) · 2014–16 single-speed unit: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Change now if undocumented
- Front differential: SAF XO · 0.56 L (1.1 US pt) wet fill · Change now if undocumented
- Rear differential: Open: SAF XO · 1.18 L (2.49 US pt) · Electronic locking: Castrol SAF Carbon Mod Plus · 1.72 L (3.64 US pt) · Change now if undocumented (The locking diff needs its own friction-modified fluid; don't use the open-diff oil.)
- Brake fluid: Shell DOT4 ESL, or a low-viscosity DOT4 meeting ISO 4925 class 6 and LRES22BF03 · Flush now; then [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Check pads, discs and parking-brake shoes while the wheels are off.)
- Power steering fluid: Texaco Cold Climate PAS fluid · Check level and hoses now
- Drive belts: 5.0 V8: primary LR011345, secondary LR012663 · Inspect now; replace if cracked or coolant-soaked (A coolant leak can soak the belts and make them slip, as one owner found.)
- Air suspension health check: Overnight drop test at off-road height; compressor run time; soap-test fittings · Now, and before any long trip (Leaks kill compressors. If the compressor has been changed, make sure the EAS software matches the Hitachi or AMK unit fitted.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: US trucks came on 255/50R19 or 255/50R20. On the 20s, LandRoverWorld owners say 265/50R20 fits at standard height without rubbing and is the largest size that still fits the spare well when fully inflated. A 285/50R20 rubs slightly at full lock and needs the spare deflated to fit underneath. Owners who switch to aftermarket 18-inch wheels run 265/65R18 with no rubbing at standard height; 285/60R18 brings only mild liner rub at full compression or lock.

Q: 5.0 V8 or 3.0 supercharged V6?
A: The 2010–2013 V8 makes 375 hp and 375 lb-ft and has a two-speed transfer box as standard, but 2010–2012 engines in the bulletin's VIN range can need timing-chain tensioners. The 2014–2016 V6 makes 340 hp and 332 lb-ft, gets the eight-speed and a better EPA rating (16 vs 14 mpg combined), but has its own supercharger-isolator and cooling-pipe issues, and needs the HD package for low range.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: There's no clean answer. The 2010–13 V8s are the ones with standard low range, but treat every one as a timing-chain risk until you see the tensioner and lever invoice; the class-action settlement covered 2012–2014 5.0 trucks. The 2014–16 supercharged V6 avoids that problem and ReRev rates those years best, but low range and the rear locker came only with the Heavy Duty package, and the plastic cooling parts fail on both engines. Buy the records, then the year.

Q: Does my LR4 have low range and a rear locker?
A: All 2010–2013 US LR4s have the two-speed transfer box. Owners disagree on whether every 2010–2013 truck also got the rear locker, so check physically or with a VIN decode. For 2014–2016, low range and the active rear locker came only with the Heavy Duty package ($1,350), which also included a full-size spare.

Q: Is the 5.0 timing-chain problem a deal-breaker?
A: No, if it's been done or priced in. Bulletin LTB00474 covers 2010–2012 LR4s in VIN range AA513326–CA652214, and the fix is new tensioners and steel-insert levers (8.1 hours of labour by Land Rover's own timing). Don't assume a 2013 is immune: a parts-catalogue lookup posted on LandRoverWorld shows the revised tensioners, levers and guides only from VIN DA696315, partway through 2013, and a US class action settled in 2021 covered 2012–2014 LR4s and Range Rover Sports with the 5.0. Many owners stress shorter oil-change intervals.

Q: How often should I replace the coolant crossover pipes?
A: There's no factory interval, but owners treat them as a maintenance item: failures are reported from about 50,000 miles, replacement every 60,000 is considered cautious, and past 100,000 miles original pipes are 'borrowed time'. The SC V6 can overheat quickly once coolant is lost, so don't ignore a coolant smell.

Q: What oil does it take, and how much?
A: The 5.0 V8 takes SAE 5W-20 meeting WSS-M2C925-A, about 8.0 litres (17 US pints) with the filter. Land Rover's 2014 service bulletin also specifies 5W-20 to WSS-M2C925-A for the SC V6, and owners say 2015–16 handbooks call for 0W-20 to STJLR.51.5122. The oil level is shown electronically rather than on a conventional dipstick, and most owners extract the old oil from the top and change the cartridge filter on top of the engine.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: The advertised maximum is 7,716 lb (3,500 kg) braked, and the gross train weight is 14,859 lb. One LandRoverWorld owner tows a 6,600-lb boat and trailer and came away impressed. The Discovery 4 also added Trailer Stability Assist.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: EPA ratings: 12/17 mpg city/highway (14 combined) for the 2010 V8, 13/17 for 2013, and 15/19 (16 combined) for the 2014–2016 SC V6, all on premium. An Expedition Portal V8 owner averages about 14 mpg. The petrol tank holds 86 litres (23 US gal).

Q: Can I lift it and keep the air suspension?
A: Yes. Lift rods that replace the height-sensor links, such as Proud Rhino's PR25, raise it about 2.5 in with no reprogramming. One LandRoverWorld owner found that strut spacers with 18-inch wheels drove far better than lift rods with wheel spacers. If you're done with air altogether, Terrafirma sells a +2 in air-to-coil conversion.

Q: Which scan tool do owners use?
A: The GAP IIDTool is the common choice. Owners use it to reset ride height and to match the EAS software to a replacement Hitachi or AMK compressor. A generic OBD-II reader can't do those jobs.

Q: How deep can it wade?
A: Land Rover quotes 700 mm (28 in) at off-road height and 600 mm (24 in) at standard height.

Q: Was the diesel sold in the US?
A: No. US LR4s were petrol-only: the 5.0 V8 for 2010–2013 and the 3.0 SC V6 for 2014–2016. The TDV6 and SDV6 diesels were sold elsewhere.

# Lexus LX & GX (1996–present)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/

Lexus got into the off-road business the way a rich kid gets into punk rock: by borrowing a band that was already good. The first LX 450, which reached US buyers as a 1996 model, was almost entirely the J80 Land Cruiser with leather, wood and a new grille. Every LX since has been built on the Land Cruiser of its day, from the 100 Series-based LX 470 through the 200 Series-based LX 570 to today's 300 Series-based LX 600. The GX arrived for 2003 as the smaller sibling, built on the J120 Land Cruiser Prado that the rest of the world got and North America didn't. It was followed by the Prado 150-based GX 460 for 2010 and, for 2024, the GX 550, which shares the GA-F platform with the J250 Land Cruiser 250 / Prado. For the hands-on crowd the appeal is simple: Toyota's ladder frames, low-range transfer cases and famously long-lived engines, sold new to people who mostly never left the pavement. That means plenty of well-maintained, lightly abused trucks on the used market, along with the expensive suspension gadgets that luxury brought with them.

Verdict: Land Cruisers that went to finishing school and somehow kept their boots on. The badge says country club; the frame rails say Gobi Desert.

## Lexus LX 450 (1996–1997)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/lx450/
Codes: J80, FZJ80, 1FZ-FE

Verdict: An 80 Series Land Cruiser that went to the tailor and came back with cladding, softer springs and a $7,000 premium. Under the leather it still has solid axles at both ends, which is exactly why people want one.

The LX 450 was Lexus's first SUV, and it was barely disguised. Take a late 80 Series Land Cruiser, give it a new grille, body cladding, different wheels, softer suspension and extra sound insulation, and you have it. Underneath sit a ladder frame, coil-sprung solid axles front and rear, full-time four-wheel drive with a lockable center differential and Toyota's 4.5-liter 1FZ-FE straight-six. Electric front and rear lockers were optional. It was sold in the US for just two model years, 1996 and 1997, and it remains the only LX with a solid front axle.

### A TRUCK BORN OF A TRADE WAR
The LX 450 exists because of a tariff threat. In the mid-1990s trade fight between the US and Japan, Washington threatened 100 percent tariffs on Japanese luxury cars, but SUVs weren't on the list. A rebadged Land Cruiser gave Lexus a flagship that was exempt, and it needed very little development money. Production began in November 1995, the first truck came off the line that December, and US sales started in January 1996. The tariffs never happened, because the two governments reached a gentlemen's agreement.
Lexus aimed it squarely at the Land Rover crowd, meaning the Range Rover and the Discovery. The ad line was "It's everything a Lexus is, and everything a Lexus isn't." Canada got it from 1997. Toyota had pulled the Land Cruiser from Canada in 1996, so for a while the LX was the only way Canadians could buy an 80 Series new.

### WHAT $7,000 BOUGHT YOU
At launch the LX 450 listed at $47,995, about $7,000 more than a base Land Cruiser at $40,678. A Land Cruiser optioned to match cost $46,968, so the real premium was closer to a thousand dollars. Slee Off-Road's 80 Series guide lists the differences. The LX got a revised stereo with a subwoofer in the center console, an optional factory cell phone, softer suspension, cladding on the doors, fenders and tailgate, bigger rear bumper corners, a plastic cover over the rear crossmember, two-tone mud flaps, automatic climate control, softer leather and more sound deadening.
Mechanically it was the 1995–1997 FZJ80 drivetrain. That means the 24-valve 1FZ-FE (212 hp and 275 lb-ft by most period spec sheets, although Wikipedia gives 215 hp), the A343F four-speed automatic, 4.11 axle gears and 275/70R16 tires. The only factory options were a console CD changer, a moonroof and the electric lockers. Those lockers are the option to look for today. On an Expedition Portal thread, forum regulars valued them at about $2,500 on a used truck.

### THE SLOW-SELLER THAT WASN'T
Lexus expected to sell around 4,000 in 1996. It sold more than 5,000, sold out its first allocation and had a two-month waiting list. Sales passed 9,000 in 1997, and the truck topped J.D. Power's Initial Quality Survey among full-size SUVs. The weak spot was the engine. Critics thought 212 hp wasn't enough for a 5,000-lb truck, so the model cycle was cut short. For 1998 the 100 Series-based LX 470 took over, with a V8, independent front suspension and hydraulic height control.
That changeover is the reason the LX 450 has a cult following now. It was the last LX with a live front axle, and the LX 470 that replaced it dropped the factory lockers in the US. Every 80 Series part, lift and armor kit fits, and Metal Tech 4x4 sells sliders and rear links labeled for both the 80 Series and the LX 450. You pay a little more for the badge, and in return you usually get a truck that spent its first decade on a country-club driveway.

### LIVING WITH ONE NOW
The newest LX 450 is now nearly 30 years old, so condition matters far more than spec. The forums agree on the big three. The 1FZ-FE head gasket becomes a concern past about 150,000 miles. The front knuckles and birfields need a rebuild when their seals start weeping. And there's the PHH, short for "pesky heater hose": a 3-inch coolant hose under the intake that can strand you when it pops. None of these is exotic. Each one is documented on IH8MUD and Slee's site, and each is the kind of weekend job the owners' community has turned into a rite of passage.

### Data plate
- Chassis: J80 (FZJ80)
- Years: 1996–1997 MY (built Nov 1995–Dec 1997)
- Engine: 1FZ-FE 4.5 L I6, 24-valve DOHC
- Output: 212 hp / 275 lb-ft (Wikipedia: 215 hp)
- Transmission: A343F 4-speed automatic
- 4Wd: Full-time, 2-speed, locking center diff
- Axles: Solid front & rear, coil springs, 4.11 gears
- Lockers: Front & rear electric (optional)
- Wheelbase: 112.2 in
- Weight: ≈ 2,255 kg (4,970 lb)
- Towing: 2,268 kg (5,000 lb)
- Stock Tire: 275/70R16

### Engineering
The LX 450 is an FZJ80 underneath. It has a ladder frame, coil springs on solid axles at both ends and full-time four-wheel drive through a two-speed transfer case with a viscous-coupled center differential. US trucks lock the center diff automatically in low range, which also switches off the ABS. The 1995–1997 trucks got the A343F four-speed automatic, airbags, OBD-II diagnostics (fully compliant from 1996) and in-line catalytic converters. Electric front and rear lockers were a factory option.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, J80 (Same frame and body as the FZJ80 Land Cruiser. The LX adds cladding and a covered rear crossmember.)
- Engine: 1FZ-FE 4.5 I6 (24-valve twin-cam straight-six with a timing chain. Head gaskets are the known weak point at high mileage.)
- Transmission: A343F 4-speed auto (Replaced the A442F during 1995. The transmission type is printed on the driver's door label.)
- 4Wd: Full-time, 2-speed (Viscous-coupled center diff that locks automatically in low range. A high-range switch can be added to the existing wiring.)
- Axles: Solid front & rear (Birfield CV joints in the front knuckles. Since 1993, ABS-equipped 80s have a full-floating rear axle with disc brakes. Gears are 4.11:1.)
- Lockers: Front & rear optional (Electric. The switch part number is 84725-60020.)

### Versions
- 1991–1992 · FJ80 (Land Cruiser) · 3F-E 4.0 I6 · 150 hp / 214 lb-ft · The 80 Series arrives in the US with full-time 4WD and coil springs. No lockers, ABS or airbags.
- 1993–1994 · FZJ80 (Land Cruiser) · 1FZ-FE 4.5 I6 · 212 hp / 275 lb-ft · New 4.5-liter engine. Optional factory lockers. Full-floating rear axle with disc brakes on ABS trucks.
- 1995 · FZJ80 (Land Cruiser) · 1FZ-FE 4.5 I6 · 212 hp / 275 lb-ft · New dash with airbags, a new grille badge, and the A343F transmission replacing the A442F.
- 1996 · FZJ80 · LX 450 · 1FZ-FE 4.5 I6 · 212 hp / 275 lb-ft · LX 450 launch (US sales from January 1996). Fully OBD-II compliant. More than 5,000 sold.
- 1997 · FZJ80 · LX 450 · 1FZ-FE 4.5 I6 · 212 hp / 275 lb-ft · Final year. More than 9,000 sold, and Canada gets the LX. Toyota sells 40th Anniversary Land Cruisers alongside it.

### Year-by-year
- Nov 1995: Production starts in Toyota City. The LX 450 is essentially an FZJ80 Land Cruiser with a new grille, side cladding, wheels, a plusher interior and softer suspension.
- 1996: US sales start in January 1996 at a $47,995 base price, about $7,000 over the Land Cruiser. Over 5,000 sold in the first year. Fully OBD-II compliant.
- 1997: Final year. Over 9,000 sold, and Canada gets the LX in place of the Land Cruiser.
- Dec 1997: Production ends. The V8 LX 470 debuts at the Los Angeles show the same month.

### Capability
- Towing: 5,000 lb (2,268 kg) (use a frame-mounted receiver)
- Fuel tank: 25.1 US gal (95 L)
- Fuel economy: EPA 12 city / 14 hwy / 13 combined (regular fuel)
- Curb weight: 4,970 lb (2,255 kg)
- Wheelbase: 112.2 in (2,850 mm)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: P275/70R16
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 285/75R16 (≈33 in) (The usual answer on healthy stock-height springs. Some rubbing is possible at full flex or full lock, and anything bigger starts rubbing.)
- Biggest tire, 2 in (Old Man Emu) lift: 35 in (Possible, but expect to rub when crawling unless you lower the bump stops. Plan to regear from the stock 4.11s to 4.56, 4.88 or 5.29.)

### Buying checks
- Head gasket history: Look for coolant at the head-to-block joint and ask whether the gasket has been replaced. One Expedition Portal regular calls 1FZ-FEs past 150k miles prone to failure and those past 200k very prone. Others think the worry is overblown. Either way, receipts for a properly done head gasket job add real value.
- Knuckle seals: Caked grease and oil on the outside of the steering knuckles means the inner axle seals failed a while ago. Slee suggests pulling the square fill plug on the knuckle. If the grease inside is runny, diff oil is getting into the knuckle.
- Lockers that work: If the truck has the factory lockers, turn them on in low range on a loose surface and make sure they engage. A dead locker is often a seized actuator, which can be rebuilt.
- Cooling system and PHH: A replaced radiator or deposits in the overflow bottle can point to past overheating, which is bad news for the head gasket. Ask whether the PHH and the bypass hoses under the intake have been replaced. Use Toyota red coolant.
- Accident and rust history: Slee's checklist covers overspray, filler (check with a magnet), uneven panel gaps and missing VIN stickers. Late 80s had a sticker on every body panel. Get underneath and check the frame for pull marks and rust.
- Records over miles: Forum regulars put service records ahead of mileage. If the driveline, diffs, birfields and bearings haven't been serviced within 150k miles, one Expedition Portal member says to budget about $2,000.
- Hidden wiring: Look under the dash below the steering wheel and at extra wires on the battery terminal. A rat's nest of accessory wiring usually means the rest of the work wasn't done properly either.
- Drive it: Check that the transmission shifts smoothly, the brakes don't pull or pulse, the steering is free of noises from lock to lock, and there's no vibration at highway speed. Blue or white smoke on acceleration means walk away.

### Common repairs
#### Front knuckle rebuild and birfield repack
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Varies. Allow a weekend for a first rebuild. · cost Rebuild kit about $126–$130 (Cruiser Corps, Low Range Off-Road). Wheel bearings are extra.
Symptoms: Grease and oil caked on the outside of the knuckle balls, runny grease at the knuckle fill plug, and diff oil migrating into the knuckles.
Fix: Following Jim Phillips's IH8MUD write-up: pull the wheel and caliper (hang it, don't let it dangle), then the dust cap, snap ring, flange nuts, cone washers and locknuts, and slide off the hub and rotor. Unbolt the spindle, unplug the plastic ABS sensor gently, set the steering straight ahead and pull the axle and birfield. Pull the spring out of the inner seal lip before prying the old seal out, so it can't drop into the axle tube. Clean, repack and reassemble with new gaskets and seals. Set wheel bearing preload to 43 ft-lb, rotate, back off, then 3 ft-lb, lock nut to 47 ft-lb, and check for 6–12 lb on a spring scale. Flange nuts take 26 ft-lb and caliper bolts 90 ft-lb. Trunnion bearings are worth doing at the same time.
Tools: Torque wrench · brass drift · 54 mm hub socket · seal puller · snap-ring pliers · spring scale · moly and MP grease · knuckle rebuild kit (Cruiser Corps SKU 595-106; bearings 595-184)

#### PHH (heater hose) replacement
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon. It's easier if the starter is already out. · cost About $20 in Gates hose and clamps, or a bypass kit for about $45 (owner reports)
Symptoms: A coolant leak low on the driver's side of the engine, or a sudden loss of coolant that leaves you stranded. Old original clamps are a warning sign on their own.
Fix: Follow the hard metal heater pipe from the heater valve down the driver's side of the engine. The PHH is the short rubber hose (about 3 in) joining that pipe to the block, below the intake manifold. The best view is from the driver's front wheel well. Replace it with quality hose and clamps. While you're there, do the bypass hose just above and forward of it and the formed hose under the intake. Slee's site has a photo write-up. Refill with Toyota red coolant and bleed the system.
Tools: Hose pliers · long extensions · drain pan · coolant · replacement hose and constant-tension clamps, or a PHH bypass kit

#### Head gasket replacement
Difficulty 5 / 5 · time Multi-day. The head has to go to a machine shop. · cost Head machining $185–$650 depending on the work. Gaskets and seals about $260 (2013). One Expedition Portal member put a full shop job at $2,000+.
Symptoms: Coolant loss, overheating, combustion gases in the coolant (confirm with a block test kit) and coolant weeping at the head-to-block joint.
Fix: Confirm with a combustion leak test first. Pull the head and have it checked for flatness, decked and pressure-tested. Shops also commonly do a valve job and new valve seals. Use a valve-grind gasket set, an EGR gasket, a water-return pipe gasket, a distributor O-ring and FIPG. OEM gaskets are the forum default. Cometic MLS gaskets need very flat, finely finished surfaces. Inspect the timing chain tensioner and the plastic guides while it's apart, because they can break, especially on 1993–early 1994 engines. Some owners wish they'd replaced the head studs too.
Tools: Full metric socket set · torque wrench · engine hoist (optional) · combustion leak tester · FSM · gasket set and FIPG

#### Center diff lock (CDL) switch install
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time Under 1 hour · cost $79 for the 1995–1997 Slee kit (TOY1002), per Off-Road.com
Symptoms: You want to lock the center differential in high range on snow, sand or washboard, but US trucks only lock it automatically in low range.
Fix: Take off the center dash face, mount the switch in a blank and plug it into the factory harness, which is already wired for it. Then put the dash back together. Lock the center diff only on loose surfaces.
Tools: Trim tools · screwdriver · CDL switch kit

#### Power-steering reservoir seal leak
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost A few dollars in seals
Symptoms: A steady power-steering fluid leak that has been blamed on the hoses or the steering box.
Fix: Unsealed 4X4 says the usual culprit is the reservoir itself. There is one seal under the cap and another under the top plate. Remove the reservoir, carefully pry open the crimps on the lip, replace both seals, re-crimp the top and refit it. Top up with DEXRON-type ATF.
Tools: Flat screwdriver · pliers · replacement seals · ATF

#### Rear axle stud and cone-washer repair
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ half a day · cost Parts plus machining
Symptoms: Snapped rear axle-flange studs.
Fix: The usual cause is a warped axle flange face from hammering on the shaft to free the cone washers. That loads one stud at a time until they break. Free the cone washers by tapping the stud ends with a brass drift, or use a small screwdriver in the washer slot. Have a warped flange refaced on a lathe so it sits square. Upgrading from 8 mm to 10 mm studs at the same time is a common choice.
Tools: Brass drift · small screwdriver · new studs and cone washers · machine shop for refacing

#### Parking brake that won't hold
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ An hour to adjust; half a day for shoes and hardware · cost Free to adjust; shoes, struts and hardware if worn
Symptoms: The handbrake won't hold the truck on a slope, or the lever comes up a long way before it bites.
Fix: Unsealed 4X4 blames four things: poor adjustment, poor maintenance, worn 'dog bones' (the shoe struts) and the lever design. Check the lining on the small shoes inside the rear disc hats before you adjust anything. Adjust the shoes at the drum first, then the cable at the lever. Upgrades include longer dog bones for more shoe contact, and lever kits that move the pivot point to pull more cable. Unsealed admits no fix lasts forever, so chock the wheels on steep camp sites anyway.
Tools: Jack and stands · wheel-off sockets · brake adjusting tool · flashlight

#### Driveline clunk: grease the slip yokes
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours to pull and grease both shafts · cost A tube of grease
Symptoms: A clunk or a 'grabbing' feel when you take up drive, shift into gear or get on and off the throttle.
Fix: IH8MUD's long-running clunk thread usually blames dry driveshaft splines. Members pulled the shafts, marked both halves so the phasing goes back the same, and hand-greased the splines. For some, doing just the front shaft cured it. To prevent it, give the slip-yoke zerks a couple of shots at the first sign of clunking, then look for fresh grease on the shaft after a few miles. Don't keep pumping until you're sure the shaft passes grease: over-greasing can hydrolock it, though that's rare. An Australian owner was told by a Toyota mechanic that too much grease can stop the slider moving and to stop at two squirts. Members used Mobil 1 red and Schaeffer's #229 Ultra Red Moly. If it still clunks, check front diff backlash, which contributed for one member.
Tools: Grease gun · paint pen to mark phasing · sockets and wrenches for the flange bolts

### Baseline service
Assume nothing was done. A 1996–1997 LX 450 is at least 28 years old, and IH8MUD and Expedition Portal regulars rate service records above mileage. Change every fluid, repack the knuckles and inspect the cooling system in your first weekend. That gives you a known baseline and the best early warning of head-gasket or knuckle trouble.
- Engine oil & filter: 10W-30 (above −18°C) or 5W-30 (below 10°C) · 7.8 qt with filter · Then every 3,000–5,000 mi [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Drain plug torque is 18 ft-lb. An oil analysis on the first drain gives a useful head-gasket baseline. Look for coolant in the oil.)
- Air filter: 1FZ-FE panel element · Inspect every oil change, more often on dirt roads (Check the intake hose and boot for cracks. IH8MUD regulars list a worn intake hose as a common 80 Series fault.)
- Spark plugs, wires & distributor: Denso OEM plugs [CONFIRM GAP IN MANUAL] · At purchase if no record (The 1FZ-FE uses a distributor and plug wires, so replace the wires with the plugs on an unknown truck. Spark plug tube seals stop oil pooling in the plug wells.)
- Coolant, thermostat & radiator cap: Toyota red coolant · 14.8 qt (front heater) / 15.9 qt (front + rear heaters) · Flush at purchase [CONFIRM INTERVAL IN MANUAL] (Overheating is what kills 1FZ head gaskets. Expedition Portal regulars say to use Toyota red only and to check the water pump, fan clutch and thermostat. A replaced radiator or crud in the overflow bottle are clues to past overheating (Slee).)
- Heater and bypass hoses (PHH): Rubber hoses under the intake, driver's side · Replace at purchase if original (The PHH and the bypass hoses above it can strand you when they fail. Original clamps mean original hoses.)
- Automatic transmission fluid (A343F): Dexron III-type ATF (AMSOIL lists AF3 for the A343F) · 11.6 qt total fill · Drain-and-fill at purchase (A pan drain only replaces part of the 11.6 qt, so repeat the drain-and-fill a couple of times rather than pressure-flushing an old transmission.)
- Transfer case: GL-4 or GL-5 gear oil · 3.6 pt · At purchase (The center diff is viscous-coupled on these trucks. Note any binding or clunks in tight turns on pavement.)
- Front & rear differentials: GL-5 90 (80W-90 below −18°C) · front 5.5 pt with locker / 5.9 pt without · rear 7 pt · At purchase, and after any deep water crossing (If the truck has factory lockers, test them in low range on a loose surface (Slee). Water in the gear oil means bad breathers or seals.)
- Front knuckles / birfields: Moly grease in the birfields, MP grease in the wheel bearings · Repack at purchase if there's no record (Pull the square knuckle fill plug. Runny grease means diff oil is getting past the inner axle seals (Slee). See the knuckle rebuild above for preload specs.)
- Power steering fluid: DEXRON-III ATF · At purchase (Persistent leaks are often the reservoir seals, not the box or the hoses (Unsealed 4X4).)
- Brake fluid & pads: DOT 3 hydraulic brake fluid (AMSOIL application guide) · Flush at purchase (Slee reports front pads lasting about 10–15k miles (1997 pads last longer). If the truck has been lifted, the load-sensing proportioning valve needs readjusting.)
- Drive belts: 1FZ accessory belts · Replace at purchase if they're cracked or there's no record
- Driveshafts & U-joints: MP grease at every zerk, including the slip yokes · At purchase and every oil change (Overland Tailor's IH8MUD write-up blames most 80 Series driveline vibrations and clunks on driveshafts that were never serviced.)
- Fuel filter & PCV valve: OEM fuel filter · PCV valve · At purchase if there's no record [CONFIRM INTERVAL IN MANUAL]

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: The stock size is 275/70R16. On a stock-height 80 Series or LX 450 with healthy springs, the usual answer is 285/75R16, about 33 in. Owners report it works, with some rubbing possible at full flex or full lock. Anything bigger starts rubbing. Slee's guide notes that 35s are possible with a 2-in Old Man Emu lift, but expect to rub when crawling unless you lower the bump stops.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: A 1997 spec sheet lists a 2,268 kg (5,000 lb) maximum trailer weight. Slee warns that the four bolt holes in the black rear crossmember (covered by trim on the LX) aren't rated for towing in the US, so use a frame-mounted receiver hitch.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: The EPA rates both years at 12 mpg city, 14 highway and 13 combined on regular fuel. Bigger tires and a roof rack push that lower.

Q: What fluids and capacities does it take?
A: According to AMSOIL's 1997 LX 450 lookup: engine oil 7.8 qt with filter (10W-30 above -18°C, 5W-30 below 10°C). Coolant 14.8 qt with the front heater only, or 15.9 qt with front and rear heaters. The A343F transmission takes 11.6 qt total. The transfer case takes 3.6 pt of GL-4 or GL-5 gear oil. The front diff takes 5.5 pt (with locker) or 5.9 pt (without) and the rear diff 7 pt, both GL-5 90-weight. Power steering uses DEXRON-III ATF.

Q: Does it have lockers?
A: Every LX 450 has a center differential that locks automatically in low range. Electric front and rear axle lockers were a factory option, and BaT listings describe triple-locked trucks. If yours has them there are locker controls on the dash. Test them in low range on a loose surface before you buy. For unlocked trucks Slee recommends ARB Air Lockers, which cost less than retrofitting the factory units.

Q: Can I lock the center diff in high range?
A: Not from the factory. US trucks from 1993 on had the switch deleted but kept the wiring. A plug-in CDL switch (Slee TOY1002 for 1995–1997) adds high-range locking in under an hour.

Q: How worried should I be about the head gasket?
A: Worried enough to budget for it, but not enough to panic. Expedition Portal regulars say 1995–1997 1FZ-FEs are the ones to watch, and that risk climbs past 150k and especially 200k miles, with overheating in hot climates as a trigger. A properly done gasket job with receipts adds about $1,500–$2,000 in value. Others note plenty of unreplaced gaskets go past 200k without trouble.

Q: Should I regear for bigger tires?
A: The 1FZ-FE trucks come with 4.11 gears. Slee suggests regearing to 4.56, 4.88 or 5.29 when you go up in tire size. Opinions vary on the right ratio, so its advice is to drive a truck with the setup you're considering first.

Q: What's the difference between an LX 450 and a 1996–1997 Land Cruiser?
A: Mechanically, very little. The LX has softer suspension, extra sound deadening, softer leather, auto climate control, a console subwoofer, body cladding, larger rear bumper corners and two-tone mud flaps. The LX mud flaps don't swap onto a Toyota. Parts and aftermarket kits for the FZJ80 fit both.

Q: What lift options are there?
A: Old Man Emu coil-and-shock kits are the classic answer. Slee's guide mentions OME 2-in lifts with 35s, and owners run OME 850/864-series coils. Metal Tech 4x4 sells 1.5-in and 2-in front spacer plates, adjustable rear upper and offset lower links, sway-bar drop brackets and caster plates for the 80 Series and LX 450. If you lift the truck, readjust the load-sensing brake proportioning valve.

Q: Which year should I buy?
A: There are only two, and they're nearly the same. The 1996 and 1997 trucks both have the A343F, airbags and OBD-II. Buy the one with the best records, the healthiest knuckles and working lockers. Factory lockers add about $2,500 in value according to forum regulars, so a locked truck is worth the wait.

## Lexus LX 470 (1998–2007)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/lx470/
Codes: J100, UZJ100, 2UZ-FE

Verdict: A 100 Series Land Cruiser with a hydraulic party trick: it rises on its toes to clear a rock, then kneels so you can load the groceries. Keep up with the AHC fluid and the timing belt and it may well outlast the people who sold it new.

The LX 470 is a 100 Series Land Cruiser, sharing its floor pan and most of its body panels, with Lexus fitting the expensive suspension from day one. Underneath are a ladder frame, a solid rear axle, torsion-bar independent front suspension, full-time four-wheel drive with a lockable center differential, and Toyota's 4.7-liter 2UZ-FE V8. On top of that sits Adjustable Height Control (AHC), a hydraulic system that raises the truck for trails and lowers it for loading, plus Adaptive Variable Suspension (AVS) for the dampers. The Land Cruiser didn't get AHC even as an option until 2006. Every LX 470 had it from launch.

### A V8 AND A NEW FRONT END
Critics had called the LX 450 underpowered, so its replacement got a V8. The LX 470 debuted at the Los Angeles Auto Show in December 1997, and sales began in the second quarter of 1998. The 2UZ-FE made 230 hp from launch. It is a quad-cam, 32-valve engine with a timing belt, which shapes the ownership experience. The bigger change was up front. The live axle gave way to independent suspension with torsion bars, a first for the Land Cruiser line, and Wikipedia's Land Cruiser article says that change limited off-road capability and durability.
The lockers went too. The LX 450's optional electric front and rear lockers disappeared from the US LX. A rear locker stayed available in Canada for 1998 and 1999. In their place came the transfer case's locking center differential and, from 2000, A-TRAC brake-based traction control with VSC. Also in 2000, the front differential went from two pinion gears to four. One IH8MUD veteran warns that pre-2000 front diffs "can grenade with little stress."

### THE HYDRAULIC TRICK
AHC replaces most of the conventional springing with hydraulics. There are actuators at each corner, gas-charged accumulators (owners call them globes or spheres), a pump and a reservoir. On IH8MUD, owners compare the settings like this: Normal sits at roughly Land Cruiser height, Low is a little over an inch lower, and High is 2–3 inches above a Land Cruiser. AVS picks from 64 damper settings in under 2.5 milliseconds at each wheel, with normal, comfort and sport modes. Both High and Low drop back to Normal above about 20 mph, one owner notes.
It works brilliantly while the fluid is fresh and the globes are charged. Lexus recommends an AHC fluid flush every 60,000 miles, according to the IH8MUD how-to thread, and owners who do it report a dramatically softer ride. When the globes go the ride turns harsh, and the usual test is to watch the reservoir level change between High and Low. Owners also take the cheap way out. They adjust the AHC height sensors for about 2 in of lift, or remove the system entirely and fit conventional springs and shocks, as at least one BaT truck has.

### YEAR BY YEAR
The LX got the clever features early. The 2001 trucks got DVD navigation and a Mark Levinson option, and in 2002 Night View infrared became an option, a head-up display that projected a thermal image onto the windshield. The 2003 refresh was the big one. It brought a new front end, the A750F five-speed automatic, Variable Gear Ratio Steering, 275/60R18 tires, side curtain airbags, 235 hp and stronger driveshafts with bigger U-joints. For 2006, VVT-i raised output to 275 hp and LED taillights arrived. The last hurrah was a 2007 Limited Edition of 400 trucks in Black Onyx with stone leather.
Not everything aged gracefully. Lexus recalled about 39,000 2003–2007 trucks in 2010 because a hard pothole hit could unseat a snap ring on the steering shaft. The 2UZ also has a habit of loosening its spark plugs, which IH8MUD members have documented in detail. The early tick is often mistaken for a cracked exhaust manifold, which on these engines is also common.

### HOW IT ENDED
US sales were 14,732 in calendar 2000 and slid steadily to 2,468 in 2007, when the 200 Series-based LX 570 arrived with a 383-hp 5.7-liter V8. The LX 470 had collected J.D. Power initial-quality awards (2000, 2002 and 2004) and was named the most reliable luxury SUV over three years in 2005. Its little brother, the GX 470, had arrived for 2003 with the same 2UZ-FE V8.
Two decades on, the LX 470 is a bargain for anyone who can wrench. High-mileage trucks with full records are common. IH8MUD signatures list LX 470s past 290,000 miles, and parts, armor and how-tos for the 100 Series fit the LX almost without exception. The AHC is the one thing that scares buyers off. Kept up, it's a genuine off-road advantage. If you'd rather not keep it up, the conversion is well documented.

### Data plate
- Chassis: J100 (UZJ100)
- Years: 1998–2007 MY
- Engine: 2UZ-FE 4.7 L V8, timing belt
- Output: 230 hp → 235 hp (2003) → 275 hp VVT-i (2006)
- Transmission: A343F 4-spd (to 2002) / A750F 5-spd (2003+)
- 4Wd: Full-time HF2A, low range, locking center diff
- Front Suspension: Torsion-bar IFS with AHC hydraulics
- Rear Axle: Solid, 9.5-in ring gear, AHC
- Wheelbase: 112.2 in
- Towing: 6,500 lb (with tow package)
- Stock Tire: 16-in wheels → 275/60R18 (2003+)
- Us Sales: 68,940 (calendar 2000–2007)

### Engineering
The LX 470 is built on the UZJ100 ladder frame. It has torsion-bar independent front suspension, a solid rear axle, and full-time 4WD through an HF2A two-speed transfer case with a lockable center differential and no viscous coupler. Lexus added hydraulic Adjustable Height Control and Adaptive Variable Suspension from launch. IH8MUD members note the brakes use a high-pressure pump instead of a vacuum booster, so a brake fault is something to diagnose with a scan tool, not ignore.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, UZJ100 (Shares the floor pan and most body panels with the 100 Series Land Cruiser.)
- Engine: 2UZ-FE 4.7 V8 (32-valve quad-cam with a timing belt. VVT-i from 2006. The starter sits under the intake manifold.)
- Transmission: A343F 4-spd → A750F 5-spd (Five-speed from 2003. Slee's 100 Series guide says the transmission went sealed (no dipstick) with WS fluid in 2004.)
- 4Wd: Full-time HF2A, low range (Lockable center diff with no viscous coupler. VSC and A-TRAC from 2000.)
- Suspension: Torsion-bar IFS + AHC/AVS (Hydraulic height control raises the truck about 2–3 in over Land Cruiser height in High, per owners.)
- Axles: 9.5-in rear, 4-pinion (Semi-floating 32-spline rear. Front diff upgraded from 2 to 4 pinions in 2000. Ratio 4.30, then 4.10 from 2003 (Slee, 100 Series).)

### Versions
- 1998–1999 · UZJ100 · 2UZ-FE 4.7 V8 · 230 hp · Launch. A343F four-speed, 16-in wheels, AHC and AVS standard. Rear locker in Canada only. 2-pinion front diff.
- 2000–2002 · UZJ100 · 2UZ-FE 4.7 V8 · 230 hp · VSC, A-TRAC and brake assist added, plus the stronger 4-pinion front diff. Nav and Mark Levinson from 2001, Night View from 2002.
- 2003–2005 · UZJ100 · 2UZ-FE 4.7 V8 · 235 hp · Facelift. A750F five-speed, VGRS steering, 275/60R18 tires, curtain airbags and stronger driveshafts. Sealed transmission from 2004.
- 2006–2007 · UZJ100 · 2UZ-FE 4.7 V8 (VVT-i) · 275 hp · VVT-i and LED taillights. The 2007 Limited Edition was 400 trucks in Black Onyx.

### Year-by-year
- 1998: Debuts at the December 1997 LA show and goes on sale in Q2 1998. 2UZ-FE 4.7 V8 (230 hp), A343F four-speed, torsion-bar IFS, with AHC and AVS standard. Front and rear lockers dropped, except for a rear locker on Canadian 1998–1999 trucks.
- 2000: VSC, brake assist and A-TRAC become standard, and the stronger 4-pinion front differential arrives.
- 2001: DVD navigation and a standard Mark Levinson audio system.
- 2003: Facelift. A750F five-speed automatic, 18-in wheels (275/60R18), VGRS steering, curtain airbags and ULEV-II certification at 235 hp. Forum regulars call 2003–05 the years to get, mostly for the five-speed. [buy]
- 2006: VVT-i raises output to 275 hp. LED taillights. One Expedition Portal regular warns the 2006–07 air-injection system can be costly to repair.
- 2007: Final year. 400 Limited Editions in Black Onyx. Production ends in October 2007.

### Capability
- Towing: 6,500 lb (2,948 kg) (with tow package)
- GVWR: 6,856 lb (3,110 kg) (2002 Canadian spec)
- Fuel tank: 25.4 US gal (96 L)
- Ground clearance: 8.66 in (220 mm) (at the rear differential)
- Approach / departure: 30° / 23° (normal) · 32° / 27° (AHC high)
- Fuel economy: EPA 12 city / 16 hwy / 13 combined (2003) (12 / 15 / 13 for 2007)
- Curb weight: 5,401 lb (2,450 kg) (2002)
- Turning circle: 39.7 ft (12.1 m)
- Wheelbase: 112.2 in (2,850 mm)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: P275/70R16 on 16x8 alloys (1998–2002), 275/60R18 (2003–2007)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x150
- Lug Thread: M14x1.5 (22 mm nuts)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 285/75R16 or 285/65R18 (≈33 in) (The IH8MUD 100 Series FAQ answer. One owner found 295/75R16 a tight fit on a stock '99 that might not clear at full bump and full lock.)

### Buying checks
- AHC health: Cycle the truck through Low, Normal and High and watch it level. Look for fluid at the actuators and lines. Check the reservoir level in High and in Low. One IH8MUD member says that if pressures and heights are in spec, a 7-graduation difference means the globes are shot. A harsh, jiggly ride points the same way. Find out when the fluid was last flushed.
- Timing belt records: The 2UZ-FE uses a timing belt with a 90k-mile service. Forum regulars say to confirm the 90k or 180k service has been done if the truck is near those mileages, and to have the water pump, idlers and tensioner done at the same time.
- Ticks at cold start: A tick that fades as the engine warms is often a cracked driver's-side exhaust manifold, which CarSpec calls common on the 2UZ. IH8MUD members warn that the same sound can be a spark plug working loose, so check the plugs before blaming the manifold.
- Brake warning lights: The 100 Series uses a high-pressure brake booster pump and accumulator instead of a vacuum booster. ABS and BRAKE lights plus a warning tone, or a pedal that sinks, mean a scan-tool diagnosis, not a guess. IH8MUD ran a poll on total brake failures, so treat it seriously.
- Steering and front end: Check for power-steering leaks at the rack, play in the steering and torn CV boots. Lexus issued a ball-joint inspection TSB in 2002. Confirm that the 2010 steering-shaft recall (2003–2007 trucks) was done.
- 1998–1999 throttle gremlins: Slee lists accelerator and throttle position sensor faults on 1998–1999 trucks that can leave the truck not responding to the throttle. Make sure the throttle response is clean on the test drive.
- Rust and use: Forum members report plenty of rusty trucks from the northern US. Get underneath with a light. Like any Land Cruiser, a high-mileage truck with full records beats a low-mileage truck with none.
- Starter health: A slow or intermittent crank usually means worn starter contacts. The starter sits under the intake manifold, so it's a big job, and owners usually do it with the timing belt.

### Common repairs
#### AHC fluid flush and bleed
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour (owner report) · cost About 2 cans of Toyota AHC fluid (part 08886-01805, $22/can in 2005) plus about $20 in supplies
Symptoms: A harsh or bouncy ride, dark or metallic-gray fluid in the reservoir, sluggish leveling, or a flush that's overdue (owners say Lexus recommends one every 60k miles).
Fix: Following the IH8MUD how-to: park on level ground, select Low and switch off. Remove the old fluid from the reservoir with a turkey baster or fluid evacuator and refill with new AHC fluid. Fit clear tubing to the bleeder on the driver's front actuator, open it until that corner settles, close it, then start the truck and let it re-level. Repeat for the passenger front, driver rear and passenger rear, topping up as you go. Keep cycling until clean fluid comes out of every corner. Soak the rear bleeders in penetrating oil the day before, because they rust and round off.
Tools: 10 mm wrench · clear tubing · catch bottle · fluid evacuator or turkey baster · penetrating oil · Toyota AHC fluid 08886-01805

#### AHC height-sensor lift
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon plus an alignment · cost A can of AHC fluid, scrap aluminum flat stock and an alignment
Symptoms: You want more ground clearance in Normal without giving up AHC.
Fix: Measure the ride height at each corner first. With the ignition off, shorten the front height-sensor links to raise the front about 2 in. Going to 2.5 in means trimming the heim joint, and one side is reverse-threaded. The single rear sensor gives about 1.75 in with its mount slid to the top. More than that needs a 2-in extension bracket. Top up the AHC fluid, do a diff drop if you don't have one, and get an alignment. ATS4X4's advice, quoted in the thread, is to keep at least 70 mm of front droop so the CV boots survive. Lift too far and High mode will refuse to stay up.
Tools: 10 mm socket · cut-off wheel · aluminum flat stock · drill · AHC fluid · tape measure

#### Timing belt, water pump and 90k service
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A weekend (about 15 leisurely hours in one write-up) · cost About $600 in parts for a full refresh in one owner's write-up. One owner's 180k service invoice ran about $1,900 in labor, including a snorkel install.
Symptoms: The mileage says 90k, 180k or 270k with no proof the belt was done, or there's a weeping water pump or a rough idler bearing.
Fix: Drain the coolant, protect the radiator with cardboard and remove the fan, shroud and belts. Hold the crank and break the crank-pulley bolt loose with a long breaker bar, then pull the pulley. Remove the timing covers, set the timing marks and replace the belt, both idlers, the tensioner, the water pump and the thermostat. Cam and crank seals and radiator hoses are cheap to add. Reassemble, refill and bleed the cooling system. IH8MUD's 90k parts list gives the timing belt as 13568-09070 (check for supersessions).
Tools: ¾-in breaker bar · crank-pulley holder and puller · seal puller · thread locker · FIPG · drain pan · FSM

#### Starter (or starter contacts) replacement
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time Big job: the intake manifold has to come off · cost Parts plus labor (contacts kit or reman starter)
Symptoms: Clicking or no-crank conditions that come and go and get worse until it won't start.
Fix: The 2UZ's starter lives in the engine's V, under the intake manifold. Disconnect the battery, then remove the intake plumbing and intake manifold, with rags stuffed in the ports so nothing drops into the engine. Unbolt the starter and either rebuild the contacts and plunger or fit a new or reman unit. Owners often do this at the timing-belt halfway point, when the water pump and thermostat housing are out, because access is better.
Tools: Long extensions · magnetic pickup · 22 mm wrench (fuel line) · new intake gaskets · rags

#### Spark plug check and replacement
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time An afternoon · cost A set of 8 plugs (Denso or NGK) plus coil boots
Symptoms: A tick-tick-pop at cold start that can sound like an exhaust leak, a misfire or coil failure. In the worst case a plug blows out of the head and takes the threads with it.
Fix: Blow out the plug wells before loosening anything. Remove the coils, check every plug for tightness and replace them using genuine parts. Don't use anti-seize. Toyota's 2UZ-FE spec is 13 ft-lb (17.5 N·m) in the engine section of the factory repair manual, which lists 15 ft-lb (20 N·m) in its ignition section. One veteran IH8MUD poster uses 18 ft-lb. Fit new coil boots and seals and torque the coil bolts to 66 in-lb. He recommends checking the plugs whenever the tick appears and at every timing-belt service.
Tools: Spark plug socket · extensions · torque wrench (in-lb and ft-lb) · compressed air · plugs · coil boots

#### Exhaust manifold replacement
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time Same-day job at a specialist shop · cost Parts plus labor (high, because the engine mounts must come out)
Symptoms: A tick from the engine bay that's loudest cold and fades as the manifold heats and expands.
Fix: CarSpec found the crack where the flange is welded to the first pipe of the manifold. The fix is a new manifold assembly. The engine mounts have to be released and the engine raised to reach the lower studs, and rusted fasteners are the main fight. Rule out loose spark plugs first.
Tools: Penetrating oil · stud extractor · engine support or jack · new gaskets and studs

#### Steering rack replacement
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time A full day, with a friend · cost About $530 for a new OEM rack bought through a friend in 2013 (retail $700+), plus coolant, oil, power-steering fluid and an alignment
Symptoms: Power-steering fluid leaking from the rack boots, play in the steering or a heavy feel.
Fix: In the IH8MUD write-up, the oil filter housing comes off first to make room. It has coolant lines, so be ready to catch about half a quart of oil and half a gallon of coolant. Then unbolt the column coupler, both hard lines and the rack mounts, spin the rack off the tie-rod ends and work it out through the frame. Install the new rack centered, reconnect everything, refill and bleed, and get an alignment.
Tools: Long extensions · universal joints · 17 mm line wrench · metric sockets · new oil-filter-housing gasket · rack bushings

### Baseline service
Most LX 470s on the market are past at least one 90k service interval, so verify or do the timing belt first. Then flush the AHC fluid, which most owners have never done, and baseline every gear oil. Slee notes the major specs changed in 2003–2004 (five-speed, WS fluid, long-life coolant), so check which side of the line your truck falls on.
- Timing belt, water pump, idlers & tensioner: Timing belt 13568-09070 per IH8MUD's 90k list (check for supersessions) · Every 90k mi. Do it at purchase if there's no proof. (Owners add the thermostat, cam and crank seals, and often the starter, which is easier to reach at this point in the job.)
- Engine oil & filter: ≈ 8 qt with filter (IH8MUD 90k list) · grade [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · filter 90915-YZZD3 · Then every 5,000 mi [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (IH8MUD notes a larger JDM-spec filter is available as an alternative to YZZD3.)
- Air filter: 17801-50040 per IH8MUD 90k list · Every oil change on dirt roads
- Cabin filter: UZJ100/LX470 element · At purchase (IH8MUD has an LX470 cabin filter DIY.)
- Spark plugs & plug check: Iridium plugs, 8 (Denso SK20R11 or NGK IFR6A11, gap 1.0–1.1 mm, per the 2UZ-FE repair manual) · torque 13–15 ft-lb (17.5–20 N·m) · Replacement due at 120k. Check tightness at every timing belt service or whenever you hear a tick. (2UZ plugs can walk out and blow out of the head. Don't use anti-seize.)
- AHC fluid: Toyota AHC fluid 08886-01805 · about 2 cans for a full flush · Every 60k mi (per owners citing Lexus) (Empty the reservoir in Low, then bleed each corner until clean fluid comes out (see the repair above). Compare reservoir levels in High and Low to judge the globes.)
- Coolant: Pink Super Long Life Coolant, premixed (2004+). Earlier trucks were originally on a 30k / 2-yr coolant. · SLLC: first change at 100k, then every 50k (Slee) (Replace the brittle plastic heater-hose tees with metal ones before they crack (IH8MUD FAQ).)
- Automatic transmission fluid: A343F (1998–2002): ATF T-IV [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]. A750F 2004+: ATF WS only, which isn't interchangeable. · Drain-and-fill at purchase (From 2004 there's no dipstick. Level is checked at the overflow plug (Slee). One owner reports about 6 qt per drain-and-fill. Repeat rather than flush.)
- Transfer case: GL-5 75W-90 · ≈ 1.3–1.4 qt · At purchase, then every 30k (Full is level with the bottom of the fill hole. Plug gaskets are 90430-18008 (IH8MUD).)
- Front & rear differentials: SAE 90 in warm climates or 80W-90 in cooler ones (FSM, quoted on IH8MUD) · front under 2 qt · At purchase, every 30k, and soon after any water crossing (Pull the fill plug first. The front uses a 10 mm Allen, the rear a 24 mm plug. Rear plugs are 35 ft-lb on 2002 FSM spec. A forum veteran says US 1998–99 LXs have a limited-slip rear [CONFIRM LSD ADDITIVE NEED IN MANUAL]. Clogged diff breathers are common.)
- Driveshafts & U-joints: MP grease at every zerk · At purchase and every oil change (Owners say shops often skip the front shaft zerk hidden above the skid plate. Drop the skid and grease it.)
- Serpentine belt & idlers: OEM belt 90916-02586 per IH8MUD 90k list · With the timing belt
- Brake fluid: Fluid type per reservoir cap [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush at purchase (The brake system uses a high-pressure pump and accumulator, not a vacuum booster. Follow the IH8MUD brake-flush procedure and take any ABS/BRAKE warning seriously.)
- Fuel filter & PCV valve: UZJ100/LX470 fuel filter · PCV valve (1998–07/2002 part shown) · At purchase if there's no record [CONFIRM INTERVAL IN MANUAL]

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: The IH8MUD 100 Series FAQ answer is 285/75R16 or 285/65R18, both about 33 in, with no lift. An owner with a stock '99 found 295/75R16 a tight fit that might not clear at full bump and full lock. Stock sizes were 16-in wheels to 2002 and 275/60R18 from 2003.

Q: How much can an LX 470 tow?
A: 6,500 lb with the towing package.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: The EPA rates a 2002 truck (four-speed) at 12 city, 15 highway and 13 combined. Five-speed trucks are rated 12 city, 15–16 highway and 13 combined. All run on regular fuel.

Q: Is it a timing belt or a chain?
A: A belt. The 2UZ-FE is due every 90k miles. Owners replace the water pump, idlers, tensioner and thermostat at the same time, and often the starter or its contacts too, since the intake is already half apart.

Q: Should I keep the AHC?
A: If it's healthy, yes. It gives you adjustable ground clearance a spring truck can't match, and a fluid flush is a one-hour job. Owners whose AHC failed have switched to conventional suspension instead. One IH8MUD member went to Old Man Emu 2.5-in heavy springs and called it much cheaper than replacing AHC sensors and actuators, which another member described as very expensive.

Q: How do I lift an LX 470?
A: The cheapest way is to adjust the AHC height-sensor links. That gives about 2 in up front (2.5 in with a trimmed heim joint) and about 1.75 in at the rear, or more with an extended bracket. Keep at least 70 mm of front droop for CV boot life, add a diff drop and get an alignment. The other route is removing the AHC and fitting conventional torsion bars, springs and shocks.

Q: Does it have lockers?
A: US trucks have a lockable center differential, plus brake-based A-TRAC from 2000. A factory rear locker was only offered on Canadian LX 470s in 1998–1999. Aftermarket air lockers are the usual upgrade.

Q: Which years should I buy?
A: 2003–2005 is the closest thing to a consensus. An Expedition Portal regular calls 2003–05 'THE years to get', and IH8MUD members single out the 2003-on five-speed automatic and redesigned dash. 2000 added VSC, A-TRAC and an improved front differential, so 2000–02 trucks are a cheaper runner-up. 2006–07 trucks get VVT-i and more power but also an air-injection system one member warns can be costly to fix. 2003–2007 trucks should have had the steering-shaft recall done.

Q: What's different from a 100 Series Land Cruiser?
A: The LX has the same drivetrain but different styling and equipment. It had AHC and AVS standard from 1998 (the Land Cruiser only got AHC as an option in 2006), front and rear automatic climate control, a power tilt and telescoping column, projector lows and fogs, body cladding and its own gauges and wheels.

Q: Are there recalls I should check?
A: Yes. The big one is the July 2010 recall of about 39,000 2003–2007 LX 470s, which replaced the steering-shaft snap ring and added a retainer. There was also a 2004 US recall that added a resistor to dim daytime running lights that were too bright. In Australia, front rotor bolts and a dash wiring harness were recalled too.

Q: What's that tick from the engine?
A: It could be either of two common 2UZ problems. A cracked driver's-side exhaust manifold ticks when cold and fades as it warms. A spark plug working loose makes a similar sound and is far more dangerous, because it can blow out of the head. IH8MUD members recommend checking the plugs first.
