### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: P265/60R18 109H on 18x7.5 alloys
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Offset: +25 mm (stock 18x7.5)
- Lug Torque: 83 lb-ft (112 N·m)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 255/70R18 (≈32 in) (Reported to fit with no rubbing. 265/70R18 tends to touch plastics at full lock. On 17s, 275/65R17 shows only a slight liner rub at full turn.)
- Biggest tire, 2–2.5 in lift: 35 in (Needs new upper control arms, the right wheel offset, a body mount chop, fender liners removed, pinch welds hammered down and an aftermarket front bumper for extra caster.)

### Buying checks
- Service history first: GXOR's buying guide puts maintenance records ahead of mileage. A high-mileage truck with records beats a low-mileage one without. Pull the Lexus dealer history on the Lexus Drivers site before you go and look.
- Coolant on the bell housing: Crawl behind a front wheel and look up at the transmission bell housing. Pink crust there points to the coolant valley leak, which shows up around 100k miles. Also check the water pump weep hole at the front of the engine.
- Oil around the filter: Oil residue near the oil filter and lower engine can be the driver-side timing cover, not the filter. Dealers have quoted $2,600–3,500 because the engine has to come down. Price it in or walk.
- Cold-start shifting: Drive it from a cold start for 15 minutes. If it won't shift 3–4 and throws P2714/P0761 with VSC and 4LO lights, you've found the solenoid problem that has led some owners to $7–8k transmission replacements.
- Secondary air pump (2010–2013): Failures of the pump and its air injection valves were common on early trucks and can put the truck in limp mode. Lexus extended coverage. Check whether the updated parts are already in.
- Center diff lock and driveshaft: Lock and unlock the center diff. A seized actuator can cost $1k+. Listen for driveshaft clunks. Grease is a temporary fix, and a Lexus TSB covers updated parts.
- Rear air springs: Premium ('10–'13) and Luxury ('14-on) trucks ride on rear air. Look for sag after sitting overnight and a busy compressor. ClubLexus regulars say failures are rarer than on the GX 470 and fixes are cheap, but check anyway.
- Frame rust and radiator: Frame rust is the dealbreaker on salt-belt trucks. GXOR also notes radiators often start leaking between 100k and 150k miles. It's an easy job, but factor it in.

### Common repairs
#### Coolant valley leak
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ 6–8 hours shop labor, a long weekend DIY · cost About $1,500 at a dealer (≈ $200 parts + 6–8 h labor). About $110 minimum DIY.
Symptoms: The coolant level keeps dropping, with pink or red coolant running down the back of the engine and the transmission bell housing. It typically appears around 100k miles on 1UR-FE engines.
Fix: Disconnect the battery and remove the engine cover and intake. Unbolt the intake manifold (ten 10 mm fasteners), then the EGR cooler, bypass lines and PCV housing. Lift the front of the PCV housing before sliding it forward. Scrape and clean the valley plate flange, apply fresh FIPG, then reassemble to torque spec with new gaskets and O-rings. Refill with Toyota Super Long Life coolant and bleed. Many owners do the water pump and thermostat while they're in there.
Tools: E8 female Torx · 10–14 mm sockets and extensions · torque wrench (7–35 ft-lb) · plastic scrapers · brake cleaner · shop vac · FIPG 00295-00103 · coolant pipe O-rings 96761-35035 (×2) · intake gaskets 17171-0S030 (×2) · EGR gaskets 25685-38010 and 25629-38010 · PCV valve 12204-38010 (optional)

#### Water pump
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Half a day DIY · cost One owner paid $688 labor at a dealer, plus about $125 for the pump
Symptoms: Seepage or crust at the water pump weep hole, often found at a routine service, and a coolant level that slowly drops. Owners have reported leaks from about 28k to 100k+ miles.
Fix: Drain the coolant from the radiator petcock (driver's side, underneath). Remove the fan and shroud, then the drive belt. Unbolt the pump, clean the mating surface and fit the new pump with its gasket. Replace the belt while it's off. Refill with pink Toyota Super Long Life coolant, not red, and bleed the system.
Tools: Basic metric sockets · slim 10 mm wrench for the fan nuts · water pump 16100-09525 · drive belt 90916-A2033 · about 2 gal Toyota SLLC (pink)

#### Secondary air pump and valves (2010–2013)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ half a day · cost Check dealer coverage first. Lexus extended warranty coverage on the '10–'13 pump and valves (program ZLH); confirm the terms and your truck's eligibility with a dealer.
Symptoms: Check engine light with P2440, P2442, P2445 and/or P0418, sometimes with limp mode.
Fix: The pump's foam filter breaks down, and the pump shreds it and blows debris into the air injection valves. Replace the pump and both valves with Lexus's redesigned parts. The pump sits behind the front right headlight. GXOR describes a temporary way out of limp mode: unplug the pump and clear codes. The check engine light comes back, but limp mode stays off.
Tools: Basic hand tools · scan tool to clear codes · updated OEM pump and both air injection valves

#### P2714 / P0761 cold-start shift problem
Difficulty 2 / 5 (fluid side) – 5 / 5 (transmission) · time 1–2 hours for fluid and sensors · cost Owners cite $7–8k for a replacement transmission. Fluid and sensors cost far less.
Symptoms: On cold starts, especially below about 50°F, the truck won't shift 3–4 within the first 5–15 minutes. It sets P2714 and P0761 and turns on the check engine, VSC and 4LO lights.
Fix: IH8MUD's summary thread lists the usual escalation. Start with an ATF drain and fill, clean the MAF and throttle body, and clean and reseat the related connectors. Then replace both transmission speed sensors, then the solenoids. Some owners manually shift the first 15 minutes (upshifting around 2,200–2,600 rpm) as a workaround. Recent posts report success with a seal-conditioning ATF additive. Once reverse or 3–4 won't engage at all, the transmission is likely done.
Tools: Scan tool · ATF and fill tools · MAF and throttle-body cleaner · speed sensors 89413-0C011

#### Timing cover oil leak
Difficulty 5 / 5 · time ≈ 10 hours dealer labor · cost $2,600–3,500 quoted by dealers (owner reports)
Symptoms: Oil residue around the oil filter area and bottom of the engine, traced to the driver-side timing cover.
Fix: Dealers drop the engine to reseal or replace the cover. One IH8MUD owner documented doing the valve covers, cam towers, coolant valley and timing cover together at home on a 177k-mile truck, working from the factory service manual and labeling every fastener. It's a big job. Some owners just monitor slow seeps and check levels at each oil change.
Tools: Factory service manual · full metric socket set · FIPG · timing cover seal · head gasket set if doing cam towers · painter's tape and cups for fastener labeling

#### Rear air spring replacement or coil conversion
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost "A couple hundred" dollars for aftermarket air springs (owner report). Coil kits cost more.
Symptoms: Rear sags after sitting, the compressor runs a lot, or the height-control warning appears. This applies only to trucks with rear air ('10–'13 Premium and '14-on Luxury).
Fix: Support the axle on stands, remove the wheels and release the air springs. Either fit new air springs or convert to coils with a bolt-on kit. Lifting a truck with rear air means converting first. Southern Style Offroad's kit adds adjustable spacers to correct KDSS lean. If you convert and plan to add Crawl Control later, you'll need the non-AVS crawl switch (84970-60090).
Tools: Floor jack · stands · basic metric sockets · coil conversion kit (e.g. Metal Tech 4x4 Stage 3 stock height, or Southern Style Offroad) or replacement air springs

#### Add Crawl Control and Multi-Terrain Select
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2 hours · cost Parts only (factory switches)
Symptoms: Not a fault. Most 2010–2019 US trucks left the factory without Crawl Control or MTS.
Fix: Lift the center console trim and swap in the factory switch panels. Then run a yaw-rate sensor zero-point calibration (the OBD-wire method is covered in linked videos). Don't search parts by VIN, because you may be sent the wrong part.
Tools: Trim tools · MTS 859A1-60020 ('10–'13) or 859A1-60040 ('14–'19) · Crawl 84970-60070 (with AVS/RAHC) or 84970-60090 (without, or converted)

### Baseline service
The 1UR-FE has a timing chain, so a GX 460 baseline is all fluids plus the known leak points. Check the coolant valley, the water pump weep hole and the timing cover before you buy. Specs come from the Lexus GX 460 owner's manual (OM60G24U), and intervals from the 2016 Lexus maintenance schedule.
- Engine oil & filter: SAE 0W-20 ILSAC (5W-20 only as a stopgap) · 8.2 US qt (7.8 L) with filter · At purchase, then every 10,000 mi / 12 months. Every 5,000 mi / 6 months for off-road, towing or dusty use. (Cartridge filter under a plastic cap. GXOR's maintenance page links a ClubLexus thread on swapping the cap for a metal one.)
- Air filter: 1UR-FE panel element · Every 30,000 mi. Inspect more often off-road.
- Cabin filter: Cabin air filter element · Every 30,000 mi
- Spark plugs: Denso SK20HR11 iridium · gap 1.1 mm. Do not adjust the gap. · Every 120,000 mi
- Coolant: Toyota Super Long Life (pink) · 16.3 US qt with rear heater, 14.5 US qt without · First at 100,000 mi / 120 months, then every 50,000 mi / 60 months (Use pink Super Long Life, not the older red Long Life. While you're there, look for pink crust at the rear of the valley and at the water pump weep hole.)
- Automatic transmission (6-speed): Toyota Genuine ATF WS only · 11.6–11.8 US qt total (reference) · Drain-and-fill at purchase. The schedule calls for a change every 60,000 mi when towing. (A drain-and-fill is also the first step in the P2714/P0761 cold-shift fix. Repeat it rather than power-flushing.)
- Transfer case: Toyota Genuine Transfer Gear Oil LF, SAE 75W · 1.5 US qt (1.4 L) · At purchase, then every 30,000 mi off-road or towing
- Front & rear differentials: Toyota Genuine Differential Gear Oil LT 75W-85 GL-5 · front 1.48 US qt (1.40 L), rear 2.85 US qt (2.70 L) · At purchase, then every 15,000 mi if you tow (Front diff service is easier with the skid plate off.)
- Power steering fluid: ATF Dexron II or III · Check level and leaks at purchase
- Brake fluid: SAE J1703 or FMVSS No. 116 DOT 3 · Every 30,000 mi (GXOR links a ClubLexus thread on bleeding the brakes with Techstream.)
- Propeller shaft grease: Spiders: lithium chassis grease NLGI No. 2 · slide yoke: moly lithium or lithium multipurpose NLGI No. 2 · At purchase, then within 24 hours of any water crossing
- Fuel filter: North American trucks use the strainer sock on the in-tank pump (GXOR) · No scheduled change (Replace it only if you have the pump out.)
- Rear air suspension & KDSS: Air springs, compressor/dryer and height sensors · KDSS cylinders and lines · Inspect at purchase (Check that the truck holds height overnight, and look for weeping at the KDSS cylinders and lines.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: Stock is P265/60R18, about 30.5 in. One owner reports 255/70R18 (about 32.1 in) fitting a stock 460 with no rubbing. 265/70R18 tends to touch plastics at full lock. On 17s, GXOR's database has 275/65R17 on stock suspension with only a slight liner rub at full turn. Treat about 32 in as the no-lift limit. 33s want a lift, and 35s need a 2–2.5 in lift plus UCAs, a body mount chop, liner removal and pinch-weld work.

Q: Is it a timing belt or chain?
A: Chain. Unlike the GX 470's 2UZ-FE, the 1UR-FE has no belt interval. You still need to watch the water pump, because it often leaks well before the engine is worn.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: Up to 6,500 lb.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: The EPA rates the 2010 GX 460 at 15 mpg city, 20 highway and 17 combined, and the 2023 at 15/19/16, on premium fuel. It's a 5,100-plus-lb truck with a V8, so bigger tires and roof racks pull that down.

Q: Which trims have rear air suspension?
A: The 2010–2013 Premium, and the 2014-on Luxury, which is the equivalent trim after the reshuffle. Those trucks also get AVS adaptive dampers. Lifting one means converting the rear to coils first.

Q: Can I add Crawl Control or Multi-Terrain Select?
A: Yes, on 2010–2019 trucks of any trim, using factory switch panels and a zero-point calibration. Part numbers differ by year and by whether the truck still has AVS/RAHC. Retrofit details for 2020-on trucks are unknown.

Q: Does KDSS matter for mods?
A: Yes. KDSS is standard, so buy KDSS-specific front skids (ARB and ASFIR both make versions). Expect some lean after a rear coil conversion. Southern Style Offroad's kit includes spacers to correct it.

Q: Which years should I buy or avoid?
A: 2014 and later. ClubLexus moderators call air-pump failure common on 2010–2013 trucks and say it should be far less of an issue on 2014-on, though the valves can still fail. 2014-on also gets the spindle-grille facelift; 2020-on Off-Road package trucks add Crawl Control, MTS and a transmission cooler, and 2022–2023 add CarPlay. If you buy a 2010–2013, confirm the updated air-pump parts are in. Lexus changed little mechanically, so condition and records still matter more than year.

Q: What was the Consumer Reports 'Don't Buy' about?
A: In April 2010, the stability control was slow to catch a lift-off oversteer slide. Toyota recalled the trucks for a VSC software update, and Consumer Reports lifted the label on May 7, 2010.

Q: Is it reliable?
A: The core drivetrain has a good reputation. The well-documented failures are leaks and accessories: water pumps, the coolant valley, the timing cover, early air pumps and, on some trucks, the cold-start P2714/P0761 shift fault. Budget for those, and a 200k-mile GX 460 is not unusual.

Q: Can I use 5th-gen 4Runner parts?
A: Often, yes. IH8MUD's build guide notes that 5th-gen 4Runner KDSS-compatible front skids and gas-tank skids usually swap over, and some 4th-gen V8 4Runner transmission and transfer-case skids have been used. Bumpers and body parts are GX-specific.

## Lexus GX 550 (2024–present)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/lexus/gx550/
Codes: J250, GA-F, V35A-FTS

Verdict: Lexus finally drew a GX with a ruler and gave the Overtrail a rear locker to match. The V8 is gone, though, and the first-year engines have an asterisk.

The third-generation GX looks like what people wanted the GX 460 to look like: square, upright and visibly built for a trail. Underneath is the GA-F ladder-frame platform it shares with the new Prado, sold in the US as the 250 Series Land Cruiser, and with the LX 600. It also has a 349-hp twin-turbo V6, a 10-speed automatic, full-time four-wheel drive through a locking Torsen center differential and, on the Overtrail grades, the first factory rear locker ever fitted to a GX.

### REVEALED BEFORE ITS OWN TWIN
Lexus showed the GX on June 8, 2023, ahead of the Land Cruiser Prado it's based on, which tells you how important the GX had become in America. The GX 460 was outselling itself in old age, with US sales above 30,000 in both 2021 and 2023. Production of the new truck started in November 2023 at Toyota's Tahara plant in Japan, the only place the GX is built.
The Overtrail grades grew out of Lexus's 'Overtrail Project,' first shown at the Tokyo Outdoor Show. They get 33-inch all-terrain tires on 18-inch wheels, a body 4.52 in wider than the old GX, E-KDSS and an electronically locking rear differential. Expedition Portal's first look called it the best overland Lexus yet 'by a wide margin.' It also noted the front fascia was designed with aftermarket bumpers and hidden winch mounts in mind.

### WHAT CHANGED UNDERNEATH
The 4.6-liter V8 is gone. In its place is the V35A-FTS 3.4-liter twin-turbo V6 from the LX 600 and Tundra, tuned here to 349 hp and 479 lb-ft. That's 48 more hp and 150 more lb-ft than the 460. The wheelbase grows to 112 in, which Expedition Portal points out is the same as the 80, 100 and 200 Series Land Cruiser wagons. KDSS goes electronic: E-KDSS can decouple the front and rear anti-roll bars at the push of a button instead of relying on purely hydraulic balancing.
Lexus also fitted a redesigned transfer case with faster high-low shifts and a center diff that splits torque 50:50. Multi-Terrain Select gets Auto, Sand, Mud and Rock modes in low range, plus Auto, Dirt, Sand, Mud and Deep Snow in high. Five-speed Crawl Control returns. The official angles are 26° approach, 24° breakover and 21° departure. The EPA rates it at 15 mpg city, 21 highway and 17 combined, which is only a modest improvement over the V8.

### THE ASTERISK
The V35A arrived with baggage. In November 2025, Toyota filed recall 25V-767 covering about 127,000 Tundras and Lexus LXs and GXs whose engines may contain machining debris that can damage the main bearings. Possible symptoms include knocking, rough running, a no-start or a loss of power while driving. The GX population is 3,717 US-market 2024 trucks built between May 31, 2023 and April 10, 2024. At filing, Lexus said the remedy was still being developed. It has since been set: dealers inspect the No. 1 main bearing using inspection software and drive data and replace the engine if needed, and owner letters went out on August 28, 2026.
Toyota's report says some later engines were made with improved manufacturing processes and some with an improved main bearing. For a used buyer, that makes the VIN check the most important step in any GX 550 inspection. Buyers clearly didn't flinch. US sales reached 30,914 in 2024 and 37,180 in 2025, the best year the GX has ever had in the US. The square GX turned out to be the one Lexus should have built years ago, and the platform it shares with the 6th-gen 4Runner and the 250 means the aftermarket arrived early.

### Data plate
- Chassis: GA-F ladder frame (J250 family)
- Years: 2024 MY–present
- Engine: V35A-FTS 3.4 L twin-turbo V6
- Output: 349 hp / 479 lb-ft
- Transmission: 10-speed automatic
- 4Wd: Full-time, low range, Torsen locking center
- Lockers: Rear e-locker (Overtrail)
- Wheelbase: 112.2 in
- Angles: 26° / 24° / 21° (approach / breakover / departure)
- Towing: 7,601–9,096 lb by grade (2027)
- Epa: 15 city / 21 hwy / 17 combined
- Built: Tahara, Japan

### Engineering
The GX 550 rides on the GA-F platform, a ladder frame shared with the LX 600, the Land Cruiser 250/Prado and, according to Expedition Portal, the 300 Series and the Tundra. Front suspension is a new double wishbone design, the rear is multi-link, and AVS adaptive damping is available. Full-time 4WD runs through a redesigned two-speed transfer case and a Torsen limited-slip center differential that locks. Overtrail grades add an electronic rear locker and E-KDSS.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, GA-F (Shared with the LX 600 and the Land Cruiser 250/Prado. 112-in wheelbase.)
- Engine: V35A-FTS 3.4 TT V6 (349 hp and 479 lb-ft. 2024 engines are covered by recall 25V-767.)
- Transmission: 10-speed automatic (Direct Shift-10AT.)
- Driveline: Full-time 4WD (Torsen LSD center diff with a lock, 50:50 split. Faster high/low range shifts.)
- Lockers: Rear e-locker (Overtrail) (Electronically controlled and switched from the console. There's no front locker.)
- Suspension: Double wishbone / multi-link (AVS available. E-KDSS, which disconnects the anti-roll bars, is standard on the Overtrail grades.)

### Versions
- 2024–present · GA-F (J250) · V35A-FTS 3.4 TT V6 · 349 hp / 479 lb-ft · Premium and Premium+. Seven seats. 2027 towing ratings are 9,063 lb and 9,041 lb.
- 2024–present · GA-F (J250) · V35A-FTS 3.4 TT V6 · 349 hp / 479 lb-ft · Luxury and Luxury+. Seven seats and AVS. 2027 towing ratings are 7,844 lb and 7,601 lb.
- 2024–present · GA-F (J250) · V35A-FTS 3.4 TT V6 · 349 hp / 479 lb-ft · Overtrail and Overtrail+. Rear e-locker, E-KDSS, 33-in A/T tires on 18s and a 4.52 in wider body. 2027 towing rating is 9,096 lb.
- 2024 (built May 2023 – Apr 2024) · GA-F (J250) · V35A-FTS 3.4 TT V6 · 349 hp / 479 lb-ft · 3,717 US trucks are in engine recall 25V-767. Launch towing rating was 8,000 lb.

### Year-by-year
- 2024: Revealed June 8, 2023 on the GA-F platform with a 349 hp 3.4 twin-turbo V6 and a 10-speed. Six grades, including the new Overtrail and Overtrail+ with a rear e-locker and 33-in A/Ts. Production started in November 2023.
- 2024: 3,717 early US trucks (built May 2023 – April 2024) are in engine recall 25V-767. Check the VIN.
- 2025: Driver memory settings and a power steering column on every grade. The Overtrail and Overtrail+ gain a 1-in suspension lift. NHTSA lists the 25V-767 engine recall for 2024 GXs only.
- 2027: Minor updates: ventilated rear outboard seats on Luxury, Luxury+ and Overtrail+, plus extended keyless entry. Powertrain unchanged.

### Capability
- Towing: 7,601–9,096 lb by grade (2027 Lexus figures. Launch spec was 8,000 lb for Premium, Premium+ and Overtrail)
- Approach / breakover / departure: 26° / 24° / 21° (Lexus's best-case figures)
- Fuel economy: EPA 15 city / 21 hwy / 17 combined (premium fuel)
- Curb weight: ≈5,470–5,710 lb (2,480–2,590 kg) (2024, per NHTSA VIN data)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 33-in all-terrains on 18-in wheels (Overtrail)
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 275/70R18 (≈33.2 in) (Many LC250/GX 550 owners run it without mods, and 265/70R18 fits with no problems. 285/70R18 is where rubbing starts.)
- Biggest tire, Level / small lift lift: 35 in (35s generally need a leveling kit or a small lift.)

### Buying checks
- Run the VIN for 25V-767: 2024 GX 550s built May 31, 2023 to April 10, 2024 may be in the engine debris recall (Lexus campaign 25LA07). Check lexus.com/recall or nhtsa.gov/recalls, and get the dealer paperwork showing what was done.
- Listen to a cold start: The recall's listed symptoms are knocking, rough running, a no-start and a loss of power. Any knock from a V35A is a stop-and-ask-questions noise, not a negotiating point.
- Overtrail or not?: If you want the rear locker, E-KDSS and 33s from the factory, it has to be an Overtrail or Overtrail+. Other grades have the locking center diff but no axle locker.
- Seats vs. capability: Seven seats are listed only on the Premium and Luxury grades. Families that need a third row are buying a different GX from the overlanders.
- Tire upgrades: Trucks already on bigger tires may have a top-shock spacer or adjusted control arms. Ask what was done to clear them, and check for rub marks on the liners at full lock.
- Aftermarket wiring: Lights, compressors and dual batteries are popular early mods. Look for tidy fusing and switch panels, not taps into factory harnesses.

### Common repairs
#### Engine recall 25LA07 (25V-767) check
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 10 minutes to check. Dealer time varies. · cost Free under recall
Symptoms: Possible engine knocking, rough running, a no-start or a loss of motive power. Many affected trucks show no symptoms.
Fix: Enter the VIN at lexus.com/recall or nhtsa.gov/recalls. NHTSA's recall record now gives the remedy: dealers inspect the No. 1 main bearing using inspection software and drive data and replace the engine if necessary, free of charge. Owner letters were mailed August 28, 2026. If your truck is affected, get the inspection result, and any engine replacement, in writing and keep the records. Future buyers will ask.
Tools: VIN · Lexus dealer

#### Fitting 33–35 in tires
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–4 hours · cost Tires and parts
Symptoms: Not a fault. You want more sidewall and clearance than the factory tires provide.
Fix: Owners report 265/70R18 on factory suspension and many running 275/70R18 (about 33.2 in) without modification. One GX 550 owner runs 275/70R18 KO3s on stock wheels with an 8 mm top shock spacer and billet rear lower control arms and has no rub at full articulation. 285/70 is where rubbing starts. 35s generally need a small level or lift, and one owner of the twin LC250 runs 35x11.50R18 with a 1.5-in front lift and a 15 mm rear spacer.
Tools: Floor jack · stands · spring compressor if using spacers · torque wrench · alignment afterward

#### Oil and filter change on the V35A-FTS
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost Oil, a filter and a drain-plug gasket
Symptoms: The oil maintenance reminder is on, or it's been 10,000 miles or 12 months since the last change. Lexus's schedule cuts that to 5,000 miles or 6 months if you mostly drive dirt or dusty roads, make short trips below freezing, or idle a lot.
Fix: Lexus's GX 550 owner's manual calls for ILSAC GF-6A SAE 0W-20. You can use 5W-20 in a pinch, but the manual says to go back to 0W-20 at the next change. It lists 7.7 qt with the filter and 7.4 qt without. The filter and drain plug are underneath. On the LC250, which shares the GA-F body but not the engine, owners on IH8MUD's oil-change thread say only the front skid plate has to come off. Several found the factory filter fitted very tightly, so have a cap-style wrench ready. AMSOIL's GX 550 lookup gives 30 ft-lb for the drain plug with a new gasket. Refill, warm the engine, shut it off, wait about five minutes and read the dipstick, as the manual describes. Then reset the oil maintenance reminder, which the manual lists among the items to initialize.
Tools: Cap-style filter wrench · drain pan · torque wrench · tools for the front skid plate · a funnel that reaches into the filler neck (an LC250 owner found a standard funnel won't stay upright) · new drain-plug gasket. An LX 600 owner on the same thread, whose truck has the same V35A, uses Toyota filter 90915-10010. Confirm the filter for your VIN with a Lexus parts counter.

#### Cabin filter, engine air filters and wiper blades
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 30 minutes · cost Filters and blades
Symptoms: Weak airflow from the vents, a musty smell, a dusty filter after trail miles, or wipers that streak. The 2024 Lexus schedule replaces both the engine air filter and the cabin air filter every 30,000 miles and inspects the wiper blades at every service.
Fix: Cabin filter, from the owner's manual: turn the engine switch off, open the glove box and lift out its removable tray, then remove the panel behind it. Unlock the filter cover, ease it out of its claws without forcing them, and pull out the filter case. Fit the new filter so the 'UP' marks on the filter and the case both point up. Lexus warns against running the A/C with no filter in place. Engine air: the manual doesn't give a procedure, but it does warn that driving with the air cleaner filter removed can cause excessive engine wear. K&N's fitment listing for the 3.4 V6 says two filters are required, so plan on buying a pair. On a dusty trip, check them more often than the 30,000-mile interval.
Tools: Hands, plus a trim tool for the glove-box panel · shop vac for the airboxes

#### Front brake squeal and pad checks
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 15 minutes to inspect · 1–2 hours for front pads · cost Covered under warranty if the bulletin applies; otherwise pads, hardware and fluid
Symptoms: A squeal from the front brakes when driving forward or in reverse. Lexus bulletin L-SB-0036-24 covers it on some 2024 GX 550s. Owners of the twin LC250 on LandCruiserForum mostly hear it first thing in the morning, or when it's cold and humid.
Fix: If the truck is under warranty, start at the dealer and ask about L-SB-0036-24. A LandCruiserForum member said the bulletin repair is almost a carbon copy of a Tundra fix. On the LC250, where a Toyota representative said there was no Toyota-side bulletin, one dealer replaced the front pads, rotors and pad shims under warranty. Some owners found the squeal faded after a series of moderate-to-hard stops, but for others it came back. For your own checks, the Lexus schedule inspects pads and discs every 5,000 miles. The owner's manual gives a pad wear limit of 0.04 in (1 mm) and accepts DOT 3 or DOT 4 brake fluid. It also says the reservoir level drops slightly as the pads wear. Torque the wheel nuts to 97 ft-lb and recheck them after 1,000 miles.
Tools: Torque wrench to 100 ft-lb · caliper piston tool or large C-clamp · brake cleaner · pad-slide grease · fluid baster for the reservoir

#### Tire rotation, wheel swaps and TPMS registration
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour, plus a 10–30 minute drive · cost Free if you do it; new sensors for a second wheel set
Symptoms: It's 5,000 miles since the last rotation. Or the tire positions are wrong on the display after a rotation, or you're fitting a second set of wheels. If the sensor IDs aren't registered, the manual says the TPMS light blinks for a minute after about 20 minutes of driving and then stays on.
Fix: The Lexus schedule rotates the tires every 5,000 miles. Torque the wheel nuts to 97 ft-lb and recheck them after 1,000 miles. After a rotation, register the wheel positions. Park for 15 minutes or more with the engine off, then start it and choose Vehicle customize > Tire pressure > Tire rotation > Continue on the center display. Drive at about 25 mph or faster, with occasional left and right turns, for 10–30 minutes. Reversing clears the data. New sensors use 'New tire registration' on the same menu, and the GX stores two sets of IDs ('Set 1' and 'Set 2'), so a winter or trail wheel set can be swapped in about two minutes once registered. If you change tire size or run different pressures, set the tires cold and then use 'Set current air pressure.' Lexus warns the system may not work properly on non-genuine wheels. Every wheel needs a sensor. The spare hangs under the rear on a chain, and the holding bracket is tightened to 34.7 ft-lb.
Tools: Floor jack and stands · torque wrench · tire gauge · a quiet road for the registration drive

#### 12V battery: test, jump-start or replace
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 45 minutes to replace · cost A battery, or nothing for a test
Symptoms: Slow cranking or a no-start, the smart access system not unlocking the doors, or a red or clear eye in the battery indicator (on trucks that have one). Blue means good, clear means it needs charging, and red means replace.
Fix: The battery sits under the engine compartment cover: push the tab in, pull the lock release, lift the cover, then pull it forward. To jump-start, open the positive terminal cover, remove the engine cover, and connect to the positive terminal and the metal ground point the manual shows (not the negative terminal). Run the donor vehicle for about five minutes before you try to start. To replace, turn the engine switch off, disconnect the negative terminal first, and fit a battery with the same LN4 case size, at least 80 Ah (20-hour rate) and at least 689 CCA. The manual warns that a battery of a different size can't be secured properly, and an unsuitable one may not restart the engine. Afterwards, re-initialize the power back door, and the moonroof and power running boards if fitted, plus the power windows if they act up. The engine may not start on the first try after reconnection. If you're planning a dual-battery setup, a GX 550 owner on IH8MUD says there's practically no room under the hood with the twin turbos, intakes and intercooler, so he put a lithium battery and a DC-DC charger behind the second row.
Tools: Socket set · battery tester or multimeter (12.3 V or higher with the headlights test in the manual) · jumper cables · terminal brush. The smart key uses a CR2032, which the schedule replaces at 30,000 miles. Lexus recommends a dealer do it.

#### Clear the camera, cluster and label recalls
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 10 minutes to check. Dealer or over-the-air update. · cost Free under recall
Symptoms: The rearview camera freezes or goes blank in reverse on trucks with Panoramic View Monitor (25V-744, 2024–2025). The instrument cluster may not show some warnings or indicators (26V-341, 2024). The load-carrying-capacity modification label may show the wrong values (26V-179, 2024–2025).
Fix: Run the VIN at nhtsa.gov/recalls or lexus.com/recall. NHTSA's records give the remedies. For 25V-744, dealers update the parking-assist software (Lexus 25LB06). For 26V-341, the combination-meter software is updated over the air (Lexus 26LA06/26LB06). For 26V-179, dealers replace the label (Lexus 26LA04/26LB04). Note that NHTSA's database lists the truck as model 'GX', so a search for 'GX 550' can come back empty. The Lexus schedule also checks for available over-the-air software updates at every service.
Tools: VIN · Lexus dealer · cellular or Wi-Fi connection for the OTA update

### Baseline service
The GX 550 is new, so a baseline mostly confirms the engine recall status and the service history, then starts the off-road fluid intervals. Intervals below come from the 2024 Lexus schedule; fluid types and capacities come from the current GX 550 owner's manual (OM6A563U). The manual calls its capacities reference quantities, so fill to the level marks.
- Engine oil & filter: ILSAC GF-6A SAE 0W-20 (5W-20 only as a stopgap) · 7.7 qt (7.3 L) with filter, 7.4 qt without · drain plug 30 ft-lb (AMSOIL) · At purchase, then every 10,000 mi / 12 months. Every 5,000 mi / 6 months for off-road, towing or dusty use. (The filter and drain plug are underneath, behind the front skid plate. Reset the oil maintenance reminder afterwards.)
- Air filter: V35A-FTS element · Every 30,000 mi. Inspect more often off-road. (K&N's fitment listing says the 3.4 V6 takes two filters.)
- Cabin filter: Cabin air filter element · Every 30,000 mi
- Spark plugs: DENSO EC22HPR-D7 iridium · gap 0.028 in (0.7 mm); don't adjust the gap · Every 40,000 mi (40k, 80k and 120k in the 2024 schedule)
- Engine & intercooler coolant: Toyota Super Long Life or equivalent non-silicate, non-amine, non-nitrite, non-borate HOAT coolant · engine 13.8 qt (16.1 qt with rear A/C), intercooler 3.9 qt · First at 100,000 mi / 120 months, then every 50,000 mi / 60 months (The schedule lists the engine and intercooler coolant together. Lexus says to have a dealer do the replacement.)
- Automatic transmission (10-speed): Toyota Genuine ATF WS · 11.73 qt total (reference); AMSOIL lists 5.4 qt as the initial fill · Every 60,000 mi if you tow, carry heavy loads or idle a lot (Lexus warns that any other fluid can cause noise, vibration or damage, and says to see a dealer for replacement.)
- Transfer case: Toyota Genuine Transfer Gear Oil LF, SAE 75W · 1.88 qt · Every 30,000 mi off-road or towing
- Front & rear differentials: Toyota Genuine Differential Gear Oil LT 75W-85 GL-5 · front 1.23 qt · rear 7.22 qt, or 6.87 qt with the rear locker · Every 15,000 mi if you tow (Overtrail trucks with the rear locker take slightly less oil in the rear.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 (SAE J1703) or DOT 4 (SAE J1704) · Every 30,000 mi (2024 schedule) (The manual's pad wear limit is 0.04 in (1 mm).)
- Vacuum pump vane & caps: Vacuum pump vane and vane caps · Replace at 120,000 mi (2024 schedule) (This is a GX 550-specific schedule item. The guide says never to reuse the old caps.)
- Propeller shaft grease: Lithium chassis grease NLGI No. 2 · At purchase, then within 24 hours of any water crossing (The schedule also calls for tightening the propeller shaft bolts if you tow.)
- 12V battery: LN4 case · at least 80 Ah (20-hour rate) and 689 CCA · Test at purchase (After a battery swap, re-initialize the power back door (and the moonroof and running boards if fitted).)
- Tires & rotation: Overtrail 265/70R18 at 35 psi; 20s and 22s at 33 psi · wheel nuts 97 ft-lb · Rotate every 5,000 mi (2024 schedule), then register wheel positions (Check the spare too. It hangs under the rear on a chain.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: The Overtrail comes on 33-inch all-terrains and 18-inch wheels. On IH8MUD's LC250/GX550 tire thread, 265/70R18 fits with no problems and many owners run 275/70R18 (about 33.2 in) without mods. 285/70R18 is where rubbing starts. 35s generally need a level or small lift.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: At launch, Lexus quoted up to 8,000 lb. Current Lexus specs list it by grade: 9,063 lb (Premium), 9,041 lb (Premium+), 7,844 lb (Luxury), 7,601 lb (Luxury+) and 9,096 lb (Overtrail).

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: The EPA rates it at 15 mpg city, 21 highway and 17 combined. Expedition Portal called the combined figure a surprise, even though it beats the GX 460.

Q: Is my GX 550 part of the engine recall?
A: Possibly, if it's a 2024. Recall 25V-767 (Lexus 25LA07) covers 3,717 US-market 2024 GXs built between May 31, 2023 and April 10, 2024, for machining debris that can damage the engine. Check your VIN at lexus.com/recall or nhtsa.gov. The remedy is a No. 1 main-bearing inspection, with engine replacement if needed.

Q: What does the Overtrail get that other grades don't?
A: An electronically locking rear differential, E-KDSS that disconnects the anti-roll bars, standard 33-inch A/T tires on 18s, and a wider body. Seven seats are listed only for the non-Overtrail grades.

Q: How does the 4WD work?
A: It's full-time 4WD on every GX 550, with a Torsen limited-slip center differential that locks and splits torque 50:50. A two-speed transfer case gives you low range. Multi-Terrain Select offers Auto, Sand, Mud and Rock in low range, and Auto, Dirt, Sand, Mud and Deep Snow in high. Crawl Control works in low range at five speeds.

Q: Is it a Land Cruiser underneath?
A: Yes. It shares the GA-F platform with the Land Cruiser Prado, sold in the US as the Land Cruiser 250, and with the LX 600. The GX was revealed first, on June 8, 2023.

Q: What are the off-road angles?
A: Lexus quotes up to 26° approach, 24° breakover and 21° departure.

Q: Is there a hybrid?
A: At launch, Lexus said a hybrid powertrain would come to the US later. US GX 550s use the 3.4-liter twin-turbo V6.

Q: V6 or the old V8: which is stronger?
A: On paper, the V6. It makes 349 hp and 479 lb-ft, compared with 301 hp and 329 lb-ft from the GX 460's 4.6 V8. The V8's advantage is its long track record, while the V35A is still early in its story and has had recalls.

Q: What oil does it take, and how much?
A: Lexus's owner's manual calls for ILSAC GF-6A 0W-20 and lists 7.7 qt with a new filter (7.4 qt without). 5W-20 is allowed only as a stopgap until the next change. The standard interval is 10,000 miles or 12 months, or 6 months / 5,000 miles if you mostly drive dirt or dusty roads, make short trips below freezing, or idle a lot.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: It's too new for a consensus. The one documented problem year is 2024: recall 25V-767 covers early 2024 trucks for V35A machining debris, so check the VIN and get the dealer paperwork. NHTSA lists that recall for 2024 GXs only; 2025 trucks share the camera-software and load-label recalls but not the engine one.

# Mitsubishi Pajero / Montero (1982–2021 · new generation 2026)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/pajero/

Mitsubishi had assembled Jeeps under licence since 1953, but the licence wouldn't let it export them. So in 1978 a small design team started, almost unofficially, on a 4x4 of Mitsubishi's own: independent front suspension, car-like comfort and a dash with an inclinometer. The Pajero went on sale in Japan in May 1982. North America, Spain and most of Latin America got it as the Montero, because 'pajero' is a crude insult in Spanish. Britain called it the Shogun, and from 1987 to 1989 Dodge sold the three-door in the US as the Raider. This guide covers the two body-on-frame generations. The first Pajero (1982–1991) won its class on its Paris–Dakar debut in January 1983 and won the whole rally in 1985. The second (1991–1999) brought Super Select 4WD, 3.0 and 3.5 V6s, the 2.8 4M40 turbo-diesel and the Evolution homologation special, and it outsold the original: Mitsubishi's designers put it at 1.15 million in eight years and seven months. In 1999 the third generation went monocoque, with a built-in ladder frame and independent rear suspension, and the fourth generation carried the same layout from 2006 until production ended in 2021. The Montero left the US after the 2006 model year. Over 40 years Mitsubishi sold more than 3.3 million Pajeros. In 2026 the name returned on a new body-on-frame SUV based on the Triton pickup.

Verdict: The Japanese 4x4 that went to the Sahara to prove it wasn't soft, then won the Dakar more times than any other car. It wore three names on three continents, and plenty of Land Cruiser owners learned to dislike all of them.

## Mitsubishi Pajero / Montero (First Generation) (1982–1991)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/pajero/pajero-gen1/
Codes: L040, L140, Montero, Shogun, Dodge Raider

Verdict: Planned as a long shot, it won Paris–Dakar at its third attempt and kicked off Japan's RV boom. In America it was a Montero or a Dodge Raider. Either way you get a simple torsion-bar 4x4 with an inclinometer on the dash and a lot of Dakar legend for not much money.

Mitsubishi had built licensed Jeeps since 1953, but the licence wouldn't let it export them, and in Japan the Land Cruiser was taking its customers. In the summer of 1978 a tiny team led by Shinji Yokoyama began a 'preliminary project', because nobody would yet fund a real one. Designer Kiyoshi Honda had a Mercedes G and a Ford Bronco at the technical centre for reference. The open-top Pajero II concept was a hit at the 1979 Tokyo Motor Show, and the production Pajero went on sale in May 1982. Management planned on just 1,000 a month in Japan and 1,600 overseas.

### A JEEP WITH A HEATED SEAT
The recipe was new for a Japanese 4x4: a ladder frame with double-wishbone independent front suspension on torsion bars, power steering, suspension seats and a turbo-diesel option. Interior designer Hiroshi Mizutani borrowed from aircraft cockpits and put an inclinometer in the middle of the dash, which he believes was the first three-dimensional inclinometer in any car. The short three-door came with a metal or canvas top. A five-door long wheelbase arrived in February 1983 on a 106.1-inch wheelbase, against 92.5 inches for the short one.
Engines included a 2.0 petrol (turbocharged in some markets), the 2.6 4G54 four, the 2.3 4D55 diesel and turbo-diesel, and from 1986 the 2.5 4D56 turbo-diesel. A four-speed automatic came in 1985. The 1987 Exceed added two-tone paint and heated seats. In 1988 the 3.0 6G72 V6 and an intercooled 2.5 diesel joined the range, and long-wheelbase trucks swapped leaf springs for three-link coil rear suspension. Every truck had part-time 4WD.

### PARIS–DAKAR, 1983–1985
Mitsubishi worried buyers would see a comfortable 4x4 as a soft one, so it went to the Dakar. In January 1983 it entered four nearly standard canvas-top Pajeros with the 2.6 four. Andrew Cowan won the unmodified production class and finished 11th overall in a field of 385 entrants, and Georges Debussy was second in class and 14th overall. The overall winner was Jacky Ickx in a Mercedes 280 GE. In 1984 Cowan moved up to the modified class with a metal-top Pajero running the Starion's 2.6 turbo, up from 110 to 170 PS. He finished third overall behind a Porsche and Patrick Zaniroli's Range Rover.
Mitsubishi then signed Zaniroli, and for 1985 built a prototype with a carbon-Kevlar body, a longer wheelbase, three-link rear suspension and 225 PS from the turbo 2.6. Zaniroli and Jean Da Silva won the 22-day, 10,284 km rally from Versailles, with Cowan second, the first overall Dakar win for a Japanese manufacturer. A Toyota 60 Series was third. A privately entered Pajero won the unmodified production and marathon classes as well. Be clear what won, though: the 1985 winner was a works prototype, not a showroom truck.

### MONTERO, SHOGUN AND DODGE RAIDER
The name became a problem abroad. 'Pajero' comes from the Pampas cat, but in Spanish it's a crude insult, so North America, Spain and most of Latin America got the Montero. In Britain it became the Shogun. US Monteros had a 2.6 G54B four rated at 109 hp and 142 lb-ft, and later the 3.0 6G72 V6 at 143 hp and 168 lb-ft. They came with automatic locking front hubs, an inclinometer pod and a suspension driver's seat.
Chrysler sold the short three-door as the Dodge Raider from 1987 to 1989, alongside the Ram 50 and the new Dakota, and never offered the five-door. The 2.6 was standard and the V6, with a 'V6' grille badge, followed a year later. A base Raider listed at $12,830 in 1989, cheaper than a Pathfinder or a 4Runner. CarSalesBase counts 19,539 US sales in 1987 and fewer than 10,000 in each of the next two years, and Dodge didn't sell another compact SUV until the 2007 Nitro.

### LEGACY
The second generation took over in January 1991. Mitsubishi had underestimated the first: domestic sales started at 670 a month and reached 3,000 a month by the end, and Mitsubishi's designers credit it with starting Japan's RV boom. Hyundai built a licensed version as the Galloper from 1991 to 2003. Mitsubishi also built about 150 yellow short-wheelbase Camel Trophy Editions with the 4D56. The Japan Automotive Hall of Fame named the 1982 Pajero a Historic Car in November 2023, and designer Kiyoshi Honda says the Middle East called it the 'Mercedes-Benz of the Desert'.

### Data plate
- Chassis: L040 / L140 (L041G–L149G)
- On Sale: May 1982 – January 1991 (Japan)
- Us Names: Mitsubishi Montero · Dodge Raider (1987–1989)
- Uk Name: Mitsubishi Shogun
- Assembly: Pajero Manufacturing Co., Sakahogi, Gifu
- Engines (Us): 2.6 G54B I4 · 3.0 6G72 V6
- Output (Us): 109 hp / 142 lb-ft (2.6) · 143 hp / 168 lb-ft (V6)
- Drive: Part-time 4WD, two-speed transfer case
- Front Suspension: Double wishbones, torsion bars
- Wheelbase: 92.5 in SWB / 106.1 in LWB
- Length: 157.3 in SWB / 183.1 in LWB
- Dakar: Class win 1983 · 3rd overall 1984 · overall win 1985 (prototype)

### Engineering
The first Pajero is a ladder-frame truck with double-wishbone independent front suspension on torsion bars, unusual in a 4x4 of its day, and a live rear axle. That axle sat on leaf springs at first; long-wheelbase trucks got three-link coil springs from 1988. The 4WD is part-time with freewheeling front hubs (automatic on US trucks). Engines ranged from Astron fours and turbo-diesels to the 3.0 V6 from 1988.
- Chassis: Ladder frame · SWB 2,350 mm (92.5 in), LWB 2,695 mm (106.1 in) (Three-door SWB from 1982; five-door LWB from February 1983.)
- Front Suspension: Double wishbones on torsion bars (A first for Mitsubishi's 4x4s, chosen for on-road stability. Steering is integral ball-nut.)
- Rear Axle: Live axle: leaf springs, then three-link coils (LWB trucks switched to three-link coils in 1988; BaT's 1988 Montero Sport (SWB) still has leaves.)
- 4Wd System: Part-time, two-speed transfer case (US trucks have automatic locking front hubs. Don't use 4WD on dry pavement.)
- Engines: 4G54 2.6 I4 · 6G72 3.0 V6 · 4D55/4D56 turbo-diesels (US: 2.6 at 109 hp; the V6 joined in 1988 (Raider) at 143 hp. The US trucks we found on BaT are all petrol.)
- Instruments: Inclinometer, voltmeter, oil-pressure pod (Mizutani's cockpit-inspired centre gauge pod carried over to later Pajeros.)

### Versions
- 1982–1991 · L040 (4G54 / G54B) · 2.6 L SOHC I4 · US: 109 hp / 142 lb-ft · The US engine; 103 PS in European trim. Starion-derived turbo versions powered the 1984–85 Dakar cars.
- From 1982 · L040 (4G63) · 2.0 L I4 (turbo in some markets) · — · Japanese and other markets. 'Turbo' badging on some LWB trucks.
- 1982–1986 · L040/L140 (4D55) · 2.3 L diesel / turbo-diesel I4 · 75 PS JIS (NA) · 80 hp SAE (turbo) · Early turbo-diesel option, unusual for a 4x4 at launch.
- 1986–1991 · L040/L140 (4D56) · 2.5 L turbo-diesel I4 · 62 kW (84 PS); 70 kW (95 PS) intercooled · Intercooler added in 1988. Timing belt.
- 1988–1991 · L040/L140 (6G72) · 3.0 L SOHC V6 · US: 143 hp / 168 lb-ft · Raider V6 from 1988. Australia's NF Superwagon V6 got rear disc brakes.
- 1987–1989 (US) · Dodge Raider · 2.6 I4 · 3.0 V6 · As Montero · Three-door only, sold by Dodge dealers. Base MSRP $12,830 in 1989.

### Year-by-year
- 1982: On sale in Japan in May: short-wheelbase three-door with a metal or canvas top. Petrol and diesel fours, part-time 4WD, torsion-bar IFS
- 1983: Five-door long wheelbase arrives (February) and the high roof follows (July). Paris–Dakar debut in January: class win and 11th overall for Andrew Cowan
- 1984: Uprated turbo-diesels. Cowan third overall on the Dakar in a modified-class Pajero
- 1985: Four-speed automatic added (April). Zaniroli and Da Silva win the Paris–Dakar overall in a works prototype. LWB models get four-wheel discs and adjustable shocks
- 1986: 4D56 2.5 turbo-diesel replaces the 2.3
- 1987: Exceed flagship (September). Dodge Raider (three-door) goes on sale in the US
- 1988: 3.0 6G72 V6 and an intercooled 2.5 turbo-diesel. LWB trucks switch to three-link coil rear suspension. Raider V6 (US)
- 1989: Last Dodge Raider model year
- 1991: Replaced by the second generation in January. Final US model year for the first-generation Montero (RS and LS)

### Capability
- Wheelbase: 2,350 mm (92.5 in) SWB · 2,695 mm (106.1 in) LWB
- Length: 3,995 mm (157.3 in) SWB · 4,650 mm (183.1 in) LWB
- Height: 1,849 mm (72.8 in) SWB · 1,890 mm (74.4 in) LWB
- Seats: Up to 7 in the LWB with the folding third row

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 15-inch steel or optional alloy wheels on US Monteros and Raiders (BaT listings)

### Buying checks
- Rust: windshield frame, roof and floors: Bring a Trailer's 1989 Raider showed corrosion on the bonnet, the windshield surround and the roof, and its 1988 Montero Sport had corrosion and failing clearcoat. Check the windshield frame, the roof gutters, the floors, the rear wheel arches and the chassis rails.
- Steering linkage: Every first-generation chassis code is on Mitsubishi's pitman-arm notice. Check for play and inspect every ball-joint boot. A cracked boot means the joint needs replacing.
- Listen for chain rattle on the 2.6: The 4G54 runs a timing chain and a balance-shaft chain. A rattle at cold start means a chain-and-guide job, so budget for both chains.
- Test the hubs and 4WD: Engage 4H and 4L on gravel. The automatic hubs should lock and release cleanly. A truck that's been driven in 4WD on pavement may have a stressed driveline.
- Check the paperwork and the odometer: Two of the BaT trucks we read about had odometer problems: a Raider with a Carfax mileage inconsistency and a Montero Sport issued 'Not Actual Mileage' titles several times. Pull a history report.
- Know which engine and rear suspension you're getting: A 'V6' grille badge marks the 3.0. Leaf-sprung and coil-sprung rear ends take different parts. Any diesel in the US is a later import, so check its paperwork.
- Run the VIN for recalls: US recalls include front seat-belt buckle buttons (95V103: 1986–91 Montero and 1987–89 Raider), throttle icing on 1989 trucks (89V030 for the Montero, 89V027 for the Raider) and a leaking oil-pressure sender on 1984 Monteros (84V098).
- Budget for the small stuff: BaT sellers regularly list air conditioning that doesn't work, a missing headliner, and replaced fuel pumps, shocks, wheel cylinders and power-steering lines. Most are simple fixes that add up.

### Common repairs
#### Inspect the pitman-arm ball joint and steering boots
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost Free to inspect; a pitman arm or ball joints if worn
Symptoms: Wander, play at the wheel, or split ball-joint boots. Mitsubishi Japan's notice lists every first-generation code (L041G–L149G). It warns that on old, hard-used trucks with integral ball-nut steering, a corroded pitman-arm ball joint can break and cause loss of steering.
Fix: Lift the truck and rock each steering rod and arm by hand. Look for play, loose mounts, bends and missing split pins. Replace any ball joint whose boot is cracked, because water has probably got in. To check the pitman joint, loosen the relay-rod nuts at the pitman and idler arms but leave them on, break the tapers, then remove the nuts and the rod (idler end first). Push the boot up, wipe off the grease and feel the stud where the boot lip runs. A dent or catch means a new pitman arm. If it's smooth, grease the boot lip with molybdenum-disulfide chassis grease, refit, torque the nuts to 44 N·m and grease through the nipple. Mitsubishi recommends new boots every five years on trucks used off-road.
Tools: Jack and stands · ball-joint separator · torque wrench · grease gun · molybdenum-disulfide chassis grease.

#### Timing and balance-shaft chains (2.6 4G54)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend · cost A two-chain kit plus gaskets
Symptoms: A chain rattle from the front of the engine, worst at cold start. The 4G54 has Mitsubishi's 'Silent Shaft' twin balance shafts, and aftermarket timing kits for the Montero's 4G54 include two chains, tensioners and guides.
Fix: Drain the coolant and remove the fan, radiator, accessory belts and crank pulley, then the timing cover. Set the engine at TDC on No. 1 and note how the balance-shaft and camshaft marks line up before you remove anything. Replace both chains, the sprockets if they're worn, the guides and the tensioner as a set. Follow the factory manual's alignment marks for both the balance-shaft chain and the cam chain; misaligned balance shafts will vibrate. Use new gaskets and seals, refill and bleed the cooling system.
Tools: Factory service manual · crank-pulley holder and puller · torque wrench · gasket scraper · RTV and new gaskets.

#### Fuel pump, filter and the 'won't stay running' fix
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–3 hours · cost A pump, a filter and hose
Symptoms: Hard hot starts, stumbling or dying under load. Several Bring a Trailer sellers list a replaced fuel pump and filter in recent work on 2.6 Raiders and Monteros.
Fix: Start by replacing the fuel filter and any perished rubber fuel hose, then check fuel delivery. If the original pump is weak, replace it with the correct part. TimmyTheGreaseMonkey has a video on converting a Dodge Raider or first-generation Montero to an electric fuel pump, and another on his 'must-have upgrades' for these trucks.
Tools: Line wrenches · hose clamps · fuel-rated hose · fire extinguisher · a pressure gauge if you have one.

#### Set the front ride height at the torsion bars
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour plus an alignment · cost Free to adjust
Symptoms: A nose-down stance, or one front corner lower than the other. Like every Pajero up to 1999, the first generation has double-wishbone front suspension on torsion bars.
Fix: With the truck on level ground, measure the front ride height on both sides. Turn the torsion-bar adjusters evenly to raise the low side, settle the suspension and measure again. Clean and anti-seize the adjuster threads. Get an alignment afterwards. If the bars are badly sagged or you carry a heavy bar and winch, replace them rather than winding them up further.
Tools: Jack and stands · tape measure · socket and long extension · anti-seize.

#### Rear drum brakes and wheel cylinders
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost Wheel cylinders, shoes and hardware
Symptoms: A spongy pedal, fluid on the inside of the rear tyre, or pulling under braking. US Raiders and Monteros on Bring a Trailer have front discs and rear drums, and one seller replaced the wheel cylinders along with the shocks and idler arm.
Fix: Pull the drums and photograph the shoe and spring layout before you take anything apart. Replace the wheel cylinders, shoes and hardware on both sides, clean the backing plates, adjust the shoes, and bleed the brakes with DOT 3, the fluid AMSOIL lists for this truck.
Tools: Brake-spring tool · flare-nut wrench · bleeder hose · DOT 3 fluid.

#### Check the automatic locking hubs and part-time 4WD
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours to check; longer to rebuild a hub · cost Free to check
Symptoms: 4WD that won't engage or won't release. US trucks have automatically locking front hubs as standard. Mitsubishi says the first generation's part-time system binds ('tight-corner braking') if you use 4WD on dry pavement.
Fix: On loose ground, shift into 4H and drive forward until the hubs engage, then try 4L. Shift back to 2H and reverse a few metres to release the auto hubs; Mitsubishi describes the old procedure of stopping and backing about a metre. If one side won't engage, pull the hub, clean it, check the internals, and regrease it with the correct hub grease. Never run 4WD on dry pavement in this truck.
Tools: Snap-ring pliers · hub socket · wheel-bearing grease · factory manual.

#### Fix oil leaks: valve covers, intake gasket and oil-pressure sender
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–4 hours for valve covers or a sender; longer for an intake gasket or front seal · cost Gaskets and a sender are cheap; labor is the bill
Symptoms: Oil on the exhaust manifolds, a burning smell after a drive, or wet patches under the engine. Bring a Trailer sellers list new valve cover gaskets and an oil-pressure sender on a 1989 Raider V6, and new valve cover and intake gaskets on a 1990 Montero 3.0. A 1988 Montero Sport 2.6 sold with an oil leak noted. Mitsubishi recalled 1984 Monteros (84V098) because the oil-pressure sender could leak oil.
Fix: Degrease the engine, run it, and find the highest wet spot, because oil runs downhill. For valve covers, remove whatever crosses them (ignition leads, hoses, brackets), clean both sealing faces, fit new gaskets and bolt grommets, and tighten the bolts evenly in stages to the factory figure. A leaking oil-pressure sender is a quick swap: unplug it, unscrew it, and fit the new one with sealant on the threads only. Intake-gasket and front-seal leaks are bigger jobs. On the 1989 Raider the front timing-cover seal and oil-pan seal were done together, along with three belts and the crankshaft pulley.
Tools: Degreaser · socket set · torque wrench · gasket scraper · oil-pressure-sender socket · thread sealant · factory service manual.

#### Rust repair: windshield frame, roof and floors
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend for surface rust; much longer if panels need cutting out · cost From a can of primer to a body-shop bill
Symptoms: Bubbling paint along the windshield surround, roof gutters and hood, and soft spots in the floors and rear arches. Bring a Trailer's 1989 Raider showed corrosion on the hood, windshield surround and roof. Its 1988 Montero Sport had corrosion and failing clearcoat.
Fix: Pull the trim and seals around the problem area and probe with a pick until you reach sound metal. Surface rust can be wire-brushed or blasted back to bright steel, then primed and painted. Anything holed has to be cut out and patched: coat the joint faces with weld-through primer, weld the patch in short stitches to limit heat distortion, then seam-seal and paint. Finish by spraying a cavity coating inside the sills and rails, and refit windshield and gutter seals with fresh sealant so water can't get back in.
Tools: Pick and wire brushes · angle grinder with flap and cutting discs · MIG welder · panel clamps · seam sealer · cavity-spray wand.

### Baseline service
These trucks are now 35–44 years old, so do everything. On the US 2.6 four that means oil, the timing chains if they rattle, a fresh fuel system and every gear oil, including the transfer case and the limited-slip rear if fitted. Capacities are AMSOIL's lookup figures for a US 1989 Montero 2.6; V6 and diesel trucks differ. The automatic-transmission figure and the oil and brake-fluid intervals come from Liqui Moly's lookup, which uses Mitsubishi's European data.
- Engine oil & filter: 5W-30 or 10W-30 grades listed by temperature · ≈5.5 US qt with filter (2.6) · Mitsubishi's European schedule: every 10,000 km (≈6,000 mi) or 6 months, or 5,000 km (≈3,000 mi) in severe use (Liqui Moly lookup) · US schedule [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (AMSOIL lists a WIX 51381 filter for the 2.6.)
- Timing drive: 4G54 2.6: chains (timing and balance shaft) · 4D56 2.5 TD: belt · Inspect for rattle now; belt engines on the receipt or now [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (On a diesel import with no records, assume the belt is due.)
- Ignition: plugs, cap, rotor and wires: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now (One BaT seller listed a new distributor cap and ignition wires in recent work.)
- Fuel filter, pump & hoses: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Now (Old rubber fuel hose is a fire risk; replace it with fuel-rated hose.)
- Coolant: ≈8.5 US qt system capacity (2.6) · Flush now (Replace old hoses and the thermostat at the same time.)
- Manual transmission (V5M21): GL-4 75W-85 or 80W · 5.3 US pints · Change now
- Automatic transmission: Dexron-III-type ATF (Liqui Moly lists its ATF III) · ≈7.2 L (7.6 US qt) for the European 2.6 and 3.0 V6 automatics (Liqui Moly lookup; AMSOIL gives no data for the US 1989 2.6 automatic) · Drain and refill now
- Transfer case: GL-4 · 4.6 US pints · Change now
- Front differential: GL-5 80W-90 · 2.3 US pints · Change now
- Rear differential: GL-5 80W-90 · 3.8 US pints · Change now (A limited-slip rear needs LSD-rated oil; AMSOIL quotes Mitsubishi P/N 8149630EX or equivalent.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 · Flush now, then every 2 years or 30,000 km (Mitsubishi's European schedule, Liqui Moly lookup) (Inspect the rear wheel cylinders and flexible hoses.)
- Power steering fluid: Dexron-II-type ATF · Change now (One BaT Raider seller replaced the power-steering lines and belt.)
- Steering linkage & ball-joint boots: Molybdenum-disulfide chassis grease; relay-rod nuts 44 N·m (Mitsubishi) · Inspect now; Mitsubishi recommends new boots every 5 years (See Mitsubishi's pitman-arm procedure under Repairs.)
- Front hubs & wheel bearings: Wheel-bearing grease; new seals · Now (Service the automatic locking hubs at the same time.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: We couldn't find a clear forum consensus for the first generation. Documented examples include a BaT 1990 Montero LS on 285/70R17 tyres (about 33 inches) on aftermarket 17-inch wheels; the listing doesn't mention a lift. Most first-generation trucks run 15-inch wheels. Measure your clearance at full lock and full stuff before you buy tyres.

Q: Is the Dodge Raider the same as the Montero?
A: Yes. It's the three-door Pajero/Montero, built by Mitsubishi and sold by Dodge from 1987 to 1989, with the 2.6 four and, from 1988, the 3.0 V6. Dodge never sold the five-door.

Q: Did the Pajero really win the Dakar?
A: Yes. Patrick Zaniroli and Jean Da Silva won the 1985 rally overall, with Andrew Cowan second. It was the first overall win for a Japanese manufacturer, but the winning car was a works prototype. A production-based Pajero won its class on the 1983 debut, and Cowan was third overall in 1984.

Q: Can I drive it in 4WD on the road?
A: No. The first generation has part-time 4WD with no centre differential. Mitsubishi itself names tight-corner binding on pavement as the system's weakness, and it's why Super Select was developed for the second generation. Use 4WD on loose or slippery surfaces only.

Q: Which engine should I look for?
A: In the US: the 2.6 four (109 hp) or, from 1988, the 3.0 V6 (143 hp). The V6 is the better highway engine. Japanese and European imports may have the 2.5 4D56 turbo-diesel, which got an intercooler in 1988 and uses a timing belt.

Q: What do they sell for?
A: On Bring a Trailer since 2024, US Monteros and Raiders have sold for $3,850 to $24,000. Clean, original V6 LS trucks are at the top, and Raiders have sold between $5,100 and $11,300. Imported Pajeros (2.5 turbo-diesels and V6s) have sold for about $3,850 to $16,250 on BaT since 2021.

Q: What does 'Pajero' mean?
A: The name comes from the Pampas cat, Leopardus pajeros. Mitsubishi used Montero in North America, Spain and most of Latin America because the word is a crude insult in Spanish, and Shogun in the UK.

Q: Can I import a diesel or JDM first-generation Pajero to the US?
A: Yes. Every first-generation truck is now more than 25 years old, which meets NHTSA's exemption. The EPA rules are separate: the vehicle must be in original configuration (or have an equivalent EPA-certified engine). Then check your state's titling rules.

Q: What's the gauge pod on the dash?
A: An inclinometer, flanked by a voltmeter and an oil-pressure gauge. Interior designer Hiroshi Mizutani modelled it on aircraft and crane controls and believes it was the first three-dimensional inclinometer in a production car.

Q: Leaf springs or coils?
A: Early trucks have leaf-sprung rear axles. Long-wheelbase trucks switched to three-link coil springs in 1988; short-wheelbase US trucks such as BaT's 1988 Montero Sport kept leaves. Check under the truck before you order springs or shocks.

## Mitsubishi Pajero / Montero (Second Generation) (1991–1999)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/pajero/pajero-gen2/
Codes: V20, V40, V55W Evolution, Montero, Shogun

Verdict: The Pajero grew up: Super Select let you leave it in four-wheel drive on the highway, the V6s made it quick, and the Evolution made it faintly ridiculous. Keep the timing belt fresh and the cooling system honest and it's as tough as its Dakar record.

Mitsubishi launched the second Pajero in January 1991, and its designers admit their toughest rival was the first one. Work started in the autumn of 1986, when the original was still selling strongly. Early scale models scored worse in surveys than the truck they were meant to replace. The finished design was longer, wider and 50 mm lower overall, but the driver's eye point dropped only 30 mm, because rally driver Kenjiro Shinozuka insisted that visibility is vital. It worked: Mitsubishi's designers say it sold 1.15 million in eight years and seven months, and at one point it was Japan's best-selling new car of the month.

### SUPER SELECT: FOUR MODES, ONE LEVER
The first Pajero's part-time 4WD bound up on tight paved corners. To engage it you had to stop, lock the freewheeling hubs and roll back about a metre. The second generation fixed that with Super Select 4WD, which Mitsubishi calls a world first and which North America knew as Active-Trac. One gated lever offers 2H, 4H with an open centre differential for full-time use on any surface, 4HLc with the centre locked, and 4LLc in low range. You can shift between 2H and 4H on the move; Wikipedia and JDMBUYSELL give the limit as 100 km/h. Instead of hubs, a dog clutch on the front differential disconnects the right-side front axle in 2H and 4H. Bring a Trailer's listings note a viscous coupling in US Active-Trac transfer cases.
The rest of the spec sheet was just as ambitious. A pneumatic rear locker was a factory option and engages only in 4HLc or 4LLc. Multi-mode ABS works in every Super Select mode. Optional electronic dampers have Soft, Medium and Hard settings. Body styles were metal-top and canvas-top short wheelbases and semi-high and high-roof long-wheelbase wagons. Its rivals were the Land Cruiser 80, the Patrol Y60 and the Isuzu Trooper, and Super Select was the Pajero's trump card.

### THE ENGINES: TWO V6S, TWO DIESELS
At launch you could have the 6G72 3.0-litre SOHC 12-valve V6 or the 4D56 2.5-litre intercooled turbo-diesel. The diesel's top-mounted intercooler is fed through two hidden scoops at the top of the grille and ducts in the bonnet. In July 1993 Mitsubishi added the 6G74 3.5-litre DOHC 24-valve V6, rated at 215 hp and 228 lb-ft in the US Montero SR, and the 4M40 2.8-litre intercooled turbo-diesel, along with a larger transmission and transfer case. Wikipedia lists 92 kW and 294 Nm for the 4M40 in this Pajero. In 1996 the 3.0 got a 24-valve head and coil-pack ignition; BaT lists a 1995 Montero LS at 177 hp and 188 lb-ft.
Two details matter for owners. The V6s and the 4D56 use timing belts, and the 4M40 uses a chain. And the 3.5 changed: Australian owners say the NJ and NK used the DOHC 3.5 and the 1997-on NL switched to a SOHC 3.5 with less peak power but a broader spread of torque. BaT's 18k-mile 1998 Montero is rated at 200 hp. The US Monteros we found on Bring a Trailer are all V6s; the diesel Pajeros in the US today are Japanese-market imports.

### THE EVOLUTION
For 1997 the Dakar banned manufacturers from the prototype class and outlawed petrol turbos, so Mitsubishi built a T2 car from the short-wheelbase second-generation Pajero, kept the production 6G74 V6 and stiffened the chassis. Shinozuka won and became the first Japanese driver to win the Dakar overall, and Pajeros filled the top four places. For 1998, with new FIA rules, Mitsubishi needed a road car to base the next T2 car on. That road car was the Pajero Evolution (V55W): wider tracks, double-wishbone independent rear suspension, overfenders, an aluminium bonnet with a scoop, Recaro seats and a 3.5-litre 6G74 with MIVEC variable valve timing and a dual-plenum variable intake.
Japanese catalogues rate the road car at 280 PS. About 2,693 were built, and Bring a Trailer sellers put the number with a five-speed manual at around 600. Jean-Pierre Fontenay won the 1998 Dakar in the competition version, again with Pajeros in the first four places, and Mitsubishi says its cars won 15 of the 16 special stages. That independent rear end became the basis for the third-generation Pajero.

### HOW IT ENDED
The monocoque third generation arrived in Japan in 1999 and reached the US for the 2001 model year, so the last second-generation Monteros are 2000 models. Production carried on elsewhere: as the Pajero SFX in India until 2012, in the Philippines until 2008, and in China, where Changfeng's Leopaard models were built from 1995 to 2021. In 1998 export and Gulf trucks got the 'blister' wide-fender facelift.
Late trucks have one modern problem. NL Pajeros built from 31 May 1996 to 30 September 2000 with the NADI 5-AT driver's airbag inflator are subject to a buy-back in Australia, because no replacement inflator exists. In the US, the same issue is NHTSA recall 20V035000 for 1998–2000 Monteros. Check the VIN before you buy.

### Data plate
- Chassis: V20 series (V21W–V26W, V43W–V46W) · V55W Evolution
- Production: January 1991 – 1999 (Japan)
- Us Model Years: 1992–2000 (Montero)
- Assembly: Pajero Manufacturing Co., Sakahogi, Gifu
- Engines: 6G72 3.0 V6 · 6G74 3.5 V6 · 4D56 2.5 TD · 4M40 2.8 TD
- Output (Us): 177 hp (3.0 24v) · 215 hp (3.5 DOHC) · 200 hp (3.5 SOHC)
- Drive: Super Select 4WD: 2H / 4H / 4HLc / 4LLc
- Locker: Pneumatic rear (optional)
- Wheelbase: 95.3 in SWB / 107.3 in LWB
- Length: 163.0 in SWB · 185.2–186.6 in LWB
- Wheel Bolt Pattern: 6 x 139.7 mm, M12 x 1.5
- Sales: ≈1.15 million in 8 years 7 months (Mitsubishi design team)

### Engineering
The second Pajero keeps the first one's recipe: a ladder frame, double-wishbone front suspension on torsion bars and a live rear axle on coil springs. The steering is integral ball-nut (recirculating ball); rack and pinion didn't arrive until the third generation. Super Select 4WD replaced part-time 4WD and freewheel hubs, and a pneumatic rear locker was optional. US Monteros were V6s; elsewhere you could have the 4D56 or 4M40 turbo-diesel.
- Chassis: Ladder frame · SWB 2,420 mm (95.3 in), LWB 2,725 mm (107.3 in) (SWB stretched 70 mm and LWB 30 mm over the first generation.)
- Front Suspension: Double wishbones, torsion bars (Ride height is set at the torsion-bar adjusters. Owners report the bars sag on high-mileage trucks.)
- Rear Axle: Live axle on coil springs (Only the Evolution (V55W) got independent double-wishbone rear suspension.)
- 4Wd System: Super Select 4WD (Active-Trac in the US) (2H · 4H (open centre) · 4HLc · 4LLc. The front axle disconnects with a dog clutch, not hubs.)
- Lockers: Pneumatic rear locker optional (Works only with the centre diff locked (4HLc or 4LLc). Listed on the US SR and on BaT's 1998 Montero.)
- Engines: 6G72 3.0 V6 · 6G74 3.5 V6 · 4D56 2.5 TD · 4M40 2.8 TD (The 6G74 and 4M40 arrived in July 1993. The V6s and 4D56 use belts; the 4M40 uses a chain.)

### Versions
- 1991–1996 · V20/V40 (6G72) · 3.0 L SOHC 12v V6 · Up to 109 kW / 235 Nm · Launch petrol engine. US Montero from the 1992 model year.
- 1991–1999 · V20/V40 (4D56) · 2.5 L intercooled turbo-diesel I4 · 73 kW (99 PS) · Top-mounted intercooler fed by hidden grille scoops. Timing belt. Not sold new in the US.
- 1993–1996 (US SR 1994) · V40 (6G74 DOHC) · 3.5 L DOHC 24v V6 · 153 kW (208 PS); US SR 215 hp / 228 lb-ft · Added July 1993 with a larger transmission and transfer case.
- 1993–1999 · V40 (4M40) · 2.8 L intercooled turbo-diesel I4 · 92 kW / 294 Nm · Timing chain. Not sold new in the US.
- 1996–1999 · V20/V40 (6G72 24v) · 3.0 L SOHC 24v V6 · 132–133 kW; US 177 hp / 188 lb-ft · Coil-pack ignition replaced the distributor.
- 1997–2000 (US to MY2000) · V40 (6G74 SOHC) · 3.5 L SOHC 24v V6 · Up to 139 kW / 306 Nm; US 200 hp / 228 lb-ft · Australian NL. Japan's Wide models also offered a 3.5 GDI from May 1997.
- 1997–1999 · V55W Evolution · 3.5 L DOHC MIVEC V6 (6G74) · 280 PS · Homologation special: IRS, wide tracks, aluminium bonnet. About 2,693 built.

### Year-by-year
- 1991: Second generation launched in Japan on 22 January 1991. Super Select 4WD, multi-mode ABS and optional electronic dampers. 6G72 3.0 SOHC 12v V6 and 4D56 2.5 intercooled turbo-diesel. Exports began later in the year
- 1992: First US model year for the second-generation Montero (Active-Trac 4WD)
- 1993: July: 6G74 3.5 DOHC 24v V6 (US SR: 215 hp) and 4M40 2.8 intercooled turbo-diesel arrive, with a larger transmission and transfer case. Slight restyle
- 1996: 3.0 V6 gains a 24-valve head and coil-pack ignition (US: 177 hp / 188 lb-ft). 2.4 four added for some SWB markets
- 1997: May: Japanese 'Wide' models with wheel-arch flares and a 3.5 GDI V6. Australia's NL switches to a SOHC 3.5 (US 1998: 200 hp). Pajero Evolution (V55W) goes on sale in September/October
- 1998: Export and Gulf trucks get the 'blister' wide-fender facelift; airbags standard on 3.5 models in those markets. Beware the NADI driver airbag: 1998–2000 US Monteros are under recall 20V035000 for a new inflator, and in Australia Mitsubishi is buying back NL Pajeros built 31 May 1996 to 30 September 2000 because no replacement exists [avoid]
- 1999: The monocoque third-generation Pajero replaces it in Japan (August)
- 2000: Final US model year for the second-generation Montero; the third generation arrives as a 2001 model
