- Evolution weight: 1,970 kg (4,343 lb) (V55W manual)
- Evolution dimensions: 4,075 × 1,875 × 1,915 mm (160.4 × 73.8 × 75.4 in)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 235/75R15 on 15x6 steel wheels (1996 NL GLX, Australia, per owner), 15-inch alloys on US Montero LS and SR (Bring a Trailer listings)
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Lug Thread: M12x1.5
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 31x10.50R15 (≈265/75R16 on 16s) (An Australian owner calls 31x10.5R15 'a good tyre size' for the NL. BaT's 1994 Montero SR runs 31x10.50R15s on factory 15-inch alloys, and a 1995 Pajero sold on 265/70R16. Expect some contact at full lock and full stuff; bigger tyres need a lift.)

### Buying checks
- Ask for the timing-belt receipt: On the V6s and the 4D56 the belt is a scheduled part, and owners say the 3.5 doesn't survive a snapped belt. Australian owners use about 100,000 km. With no proof, price in a belt, tensioner, idlers and water pump. The 4M40 uses a chain.
- Look hard at the V6 cooling system: Check for milky oil, coolant loss and a temperature gauge that wanders. ExplorOz mechanics describe the V6 Pajeros as prone to head gaskets and say the heads crack. A combustion-leak test before purchase costs very little.
- Blue smoke on the overrun: Worn valve stem seals are a known V6 complaint. One Australian owner says they 'normally need replacing at 200,000 km', and Montana Montero has a video on why Monteros burn oil. Watch the exhaust after a long idle and on the first blip of the throttle.
- Exercise the Super Select lever: On loose ground, go through 2H, 4H, 4HLc and 4LLc. The lights should stop flashing once each mode engages. A light that keeps flashing, or a front axle that won't engage, points to the vacuum system. Owners say the system misbehaves on trucks that rarely use 4WD.
- Check the steering linkage: Mitsubishi's pitman-arm notice covers every second-generation code, the Evolution included. Feel for play at the pitman and idler arms and inspect every boot. A cracked boot means the joint needs replacing.
- Measure the front ride height: Tired torsion bars leave the nose low, and a bull bar makes it worse. Uneven ride height side to side or a nose-down stance means the bars need adjusting or replacing.
- Rust in the sills and chassis: Steven Taylor's Mk2 Pajero video shows sill replacement and chassis welding on a 2.8. BaT's 1998 Montero needed its underside treated. Probe the sills, the rear chassis rails and the spring mounts.
- Run the VIN for recalls: US recalls include the 1998–2000 NADI driver airbag (20V035000), cracking front brake hoses on 1992–94 trucks (96V143), chafing brake lines on 1997–98 trucks (98V220) and a loose crank-pulley bolt on 1992–96 3.0s (00V311001). In Australia, NL airbag trucks are being bought back.

### Common repairs
#### Timing belt, tensioner and water pump (6G72 3.0 / 6G74 3.5)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A long day · cost Australian owners quoted about A$650–1,000 in 2006, the top figure including a water pump
Symptoms: Usually none before it fails. A whirring from the belt area can mean an over-tight belt or a failing idler. Australian owners change it about every 100,000 km and warn that the 3.5 has no valve clearance if the belt breaks, while the 3.0 does. Treat those as owner reports and check your engine.
Fix: Set the engine at TDC and remove the accessory belts, fan and crank pulley. Replace the belt, idler and tensioner pulleys, and the water pump while you're there. Owners describe a spring-loaded tensioner on the 3.0 they worked on and a hydraulic one on the 3.5. On the 3.5, they compress the tensioner ram slowly in a vice and pin it, then preload the offset tensioner pulley before pulling the pin. One owner sets the preload with a torque wrench at 25 in-lb (SOHC) or 50 in-lb (DOHC); confirm the figures in the factory manual. Another rotates the crank two turns, waits a few minutes and checks that the pin still slides freely. Check the hydraulic tensioner for leaks and fit a new genuine crank-pulley (balancer) bolt, because owners report reused bolts breaking. A loose crank-pulley bolt is also the subject of NHTSA recall 00V311001 on 1992–96 3.0 Monteros. Montana Montero has a video walk-through of the job on a Montero.
Tools: Crank-pulley holding tool · torque wrench (inch-pound range) · vice to reset the hydraulic tensioner · pin or drill bit to lock it · gasket scraper · coolant.

#### Cure a flashing 4WD light (front axle engagement)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–3 hours to diagnose and fix · cost Usually a vacuum solenoid or hose; parts plus your time
Symptoms: The Super Select lights keep flashing after you select 4H, or the front axle never engages. Owners say the system 'sometimes plays up if not used very much'.
Fix: In 2H and 4H a dog clutch on the front differential disconnects one front axle shaft, and Super Select uses it to engage the front axle. A light that keeps flashing means the front axle hasn't engaged. Start with the cheap parts: inspect every vacuum hose between the engine, the solenoid valves and the front-diff actuator for cracks or loose ends, then test each solenoid. The Montero Ventures video shows a flashing-light fault cured by replacing a vacuum solenoid valve. Afterwards, cycle through 2H, 4H, 4HLc and 4LLc on loose ground, and use 4WD regularly so the system doesn't seize from disuse.
Tools: Hand vacuum pump with gauge · multimeter · basic hand tools · replacement vacuum hose.

#### Inspect the pitman-arm ball joint (Mitsubishi's procedure)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost Free to inspect; a pitman arm or boots if worn
Symptoms: Steering play, a clunk through the wheel, or a split ball-joint boot. Mitsubishi Japan warns that on old, hard-used trucks with integral ball-nut steering, corrosion and wear can break the pitman-arm ball joint and cause loss of steering. Every second-generation chassis code, the V55W Evolution included, is on its list.
Fix: Following Mitsubishi's notice: lift the truck and rock every steering rod and arm by hand, looking for play, loose mounts, bends or missing split pins. Check every dust boot. A cracked boot may have let in muddy water, so replace that ball joint complete. To check the pitman joint, loosen the relay-rod nuts at the pitman and idler arms but leave them on, break the tapers, then remove the nuts and the relay rod (idler end first). Push the pitman-arm boot up, wipe off the grease and feel the stud where the boot lip runs. If you can feel a dent or a catch, replace the pitman arm. If it's smooth, grease the boot lip with molybdenum-disulfide chassis grease, refit the relay rod, torque the nuts to 44 N·m and pump grease in through the nipple. Mitsubishi recommends new boots every five years on trucks that go off-road often.
Tools: Jack and stands · ball-joint separator or hammer · torque wrench · grease gun · molybdenum-disulfide chassis grease.

#### Reset or upgrade the front torsion bars
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour to adjust; half a day to replace the bars · cost Free to adjust; uprated bars and rear coils as a kit
Symptoms: The nose sits low. One ExplorOz contributor says many high-mileage Pajeros 'almost look like they're sitting on the front bump stops.' A heavy steel bull bar makes it worse.
Fix: If the bars aren't badly sagged, wind the adjusters up evenly to restore ride height. Measure both sides and get an alignment. Be aware that winding them up adds preload and puts more twist on tired bars. If the bars have sagged a lot, or you run a bar and winch, fit uprated torsion bars and match them with stiffer rear coils so the front and rear balance. One Australian owner reported 65 mm of lift and a firm ride from a TJM kit.
Tools: Jack and stands · tape measure · socket set for the adjusters · alignment afterwards.

#### V6 head gasket replacement (and do it properly)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 days · cost Parts plus machine-shop crack test and skim
Symptoms: Coolant loss, milky oil on the dipstick or under the filler cap, overheating. One NJ 3.0 owner on ExplorOz had replaced the head gasket twice in about three years. Mechanics in that thread say the V6s have a weak spot for head gaskets and that the heads 'do crack a fair bit'.
Fix: Follow the factory workshop manual's head-bolt loosening and torque sequence exactly. Have both heads crack-tested and skimmed rather than assuming they're good, and check the block deck for flatness. Use a quality gasket set (the mechanics in the thread name ACL and Fel-Pro). While it's apart, do the timing belt, the crank and cam seals, the water pump and the O-rings on the heater pipe in the engine valley. Flush the cooling system and refill with fresh coolant.
Tools: Factory manual · 1/2-in torque wrench · straight edge and feeler gauges · machine shop for crack test and skim · labelled bags for bolts.

#### Replace the front brake hoses
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost A pair of hoses and a bottle of DOT 3
Symptoms: Cracked, chafed or weeping front hoses. NHTSA recall 96V143 says the wheel-side front hoses on 1992–94 Monteros could crack at full steering lock and full suspension travel. Recall 98V220 covers 1997–98 front brake lines chafing through at the inner-fender pass-through.
Fix: Check whether the recalls were done, then inspect the hoses at full lock with the suspension drooped. Clamp the hose or fit a pedal holder to limit fluid loss, swap the hose with new sealing washers, and check that it doesn't touch anything at either lock or at full droop. Bleed the brakes with DOT 3, the fluid AMSOIL's lookup lists for these trucks.
Tools: Flare-nut wrenches · hose clamp · new copper washers · bleeder hose and bottle · DOT 3 fluid.

#### Replace the V6 valve stem seals (blue smoke)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend with the heads on · cost A seal set is cheap; the labor isn't. Cheapest when the heads are already off
Symptoms: A puff of blue smoke at start-up or after a long idle, smoke on the overrun, and oil use with no external leaks. Worn valve stem seals are a known V6 complaint. One ExplorOz owner says they 'normally need replacing at 200,000 km', and another warns that when they wear out it means 'a lot of smoke or [an] expensive repair'.
Fix: First rule out the rings: a compression and leak-down test tells you whether the cylinders are healthy. With the heads on, the job means removing the intake plenum and valve gear, holding each valve shut with compressed air through the spark-plug hole while you compress its spring, then pulling the old seal and pressing on a new one. If the heads are coming off for gaskets anyway (see the head-gasket job), have the machine shop fit new seals and check the guides at the same time. Follow the factory manual for cam timing and torque values on reassembly.
Tools: Compression and leak-down tester · spark-plug-hole air adapter and compressor · overhead valve-spring compressor · seal pliers and installer · torque wrench · factory service manual.

#### Sill and chassis rust repair
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend to several, depending on what you find · cost From a can of cavity wax to a fabrication bill
Symptoms: Bubbling at the sills and rear wheel arches, flaking chassis rails and soft spring mounts. Steven Taylor's Mk2 Pajero video shows sill replacement and chassis welding on a 2.8, and BaT's 1998 Montero needed its underside treated.
Fix: Get the truck on stands, wash the underside and scrape off loose underseal. Probe the sills, the rear chassis rails and the spring mounts with a pick or screwdriver. Surface rust can be ground or blasted back, treated, primed and painted. Holed sills have to be cut out and replaced with new sections: weld-through primer on the joint faces, short stitch welds, then seam sealer and paint. Rotten chassis or spring-mount metal is structural and is a job for a fabricator. Finish by spraying a cavity coating inside the sills and rails.
Tools: Jack stands · pick or screwdriver · angle grinder · MIG welder · panel clamps · seam sealer · cavity-spray wand.

### Baseline service
Assume nothing has been done without receipts. On a 3.0 or 3.5 V6 the big item is the timing belt with its idlers and water pump. Then do every gear oil, because the transfer case, both diffs and any factory limited-slip are rarely serviced. Capacities below are AMSOIL's lookup figures for US 1993 3.0 and 1997 3.5 Monteros; Liqui Moly's lookup gives matching diff and transfer-case figures for the 3.5, and supplies the oil and brake-fluid intervals. Confirm them for your engine and gearbox, especially on diesel imports.
- Engine oil & filter: SAE 5W-30 preferred (10W-30 above −18 °C) · ≈5.2 US qt with filter (US 3.0 and 3.5) · Every 7,500 mi or 12 months, or every 3,000 mi or 3 months in severe use (US Montero 3.5, Liqui Moly lookup). Mitsubishi's European schedule for the 3.0 and 3.5 is 15,000 km or 12 months. (AMSOIL lists a WIX 51334 filter for both V6s. Diesel 4D56/4M40 capacities differ.)
- Timing belt, tensioner, idlers & water pump: 6G72 and 6G74: belt · 4D56: belt · 4M40: chain · Australian owners use ≈100,000 km on the V6s [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Owners report the 3.5 is an interference engine and the 3.0 is not. With no receipt, do it now.)
- Spark plugs: Platinum plugs on the V6s (owner reports) [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Usually done with the timing belt (One owner couldn't reach the last two plugs on a '96 and paid a mechanic.)
- Air filter & fuel filter: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Fuel filter: owners quote 40,000–60,000 km depending on model (On a truck with no history, change both.)
- Coolant: ≈10 US qt system capacity (US V6) · Flush now, then per manual (V6 head gaskets have a reputation, so a clean, correctly filled cooling system is cheap insurance. Bleed out the air carefully.)
- Automatic transmission: AMSOIL code AF2 (Dexron-II-type ATF) · 5.8 US qt drain-and-fill; 7.6 qt total (V4AW2) or 10.4 qt total (V4AW3, and AW30-40LE on the 3.5) · Drain and refill now; repeat to refresh more of the fluid (A drain-and-fill replaces only about half the fluid, so do two at the oil changes rather than one flush.)
- Manual transmission: GL-4 75W-90 or 75W-85 · 5.3 US pints (3.0) / 6.8 pints (V5MT1, 3.5) · Change now, then per manual
- Transfer case (Super Select): GL-4 gear oil · 4.9–5.3 US pints depending on transmission · Change now (Owners say the Super Select system plays up when it's not used. Fresh oil and regular use help.)
- Front differential: GL-5 80W-90 · 2.3–2.5 US pints · Change now (Check the vacuum actuator and its hoses while you're under there.)
- Rear differential: GL-5 80W-90 · 5.5 US pints (1993 3.0) / 6.8 pints (1997 3.5) · Change now (A limited-slip rear needs LSD-rated oil; AMSOIL quotes Mitsubishi P/N 8149630EX or equivalent. Locker-equipped trucks: check the air lines and actuator for leaks.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 · Flush now, then every 2 years or 30,000 km (Mitsubishi's European schedule, Liqui Moly lookup; its US Montero listing gives only a yearly check) (Inspect the front hoses at full lock (recalls 96V143 and 98V220).)
- Power steering fluid: Dexron-II-type ATF · Change now
- Steering linkage & ball-joint boots: Molybdenum-disulfide chassis grease; relay-rod nuts 44 N·m (Mitsubishi) · Inspect now; Mitsubishi recommends new boots every 5 years on off-road trucks (Follow Mitsubishi's pitman-arm inspection (see Repairs).)
- Front wheel bearings: Repack with wheel-bearing grease; new seals · Now, then with brake jobs (The seller of BaT's 177k-mile 1994 SR repacked the bearings and replaced the seals, upper ball joints and CV axles in one go.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: We found no single forum consensus, but the evidence points to about 31 inches. An Australian owner lists the 1996 NL GLX's stock tyres as 235/75R15 on 15x6 steel wheels and calls 31x10.5R15 'a good tyre size'. BaT's 1994 Montero SR runs 31x10.50R15s on its factory 15-inch alloys, and a 1995 Pajero sold on 265/70R16s. Go bigger and you'll want a lift, and probably some trimming.

Q: Can I drive in 4WD on the highway?
A: Yes, in 4H. That's the point of Super Select: 4H is full-time 4WD with an open centre differential, so it doesn't bind on pavement. 4HLc and 4LLc lock the centre and are for loose surfaces only. You can move between 2H and 4H on the move.

Q: Does it have a locker?
A: A pneumatic rear locker was a factory option. It works only with the centre differential locked, in 4HLc or 4LLc. BaT's 1994 Montero SR and 1998 Montero both have locking rear differentials. Check the dash switch and the air lines before you assume a truck has one.

Q: Which engine should I buy?
A: The 3.0 V6 is the common US engine. Australian owners say it has valve clearance if the belt breaks, but it's down on power. The 3.5 is the strong one: 215 hp in the DOHC US SR, 200 hp in the later SOHC Montero. Outside the US, the 4M40 2.8 turbo-diesel has a timing chain and a good reputation, but some owners report head problems. The 4D56 2.5 is slower and belt-driven.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: There's no buyer consensus on a best year. JDM Buy Sell's guide doesn't name one, and owners argue about engines rather than years. What you can avoid is the NADI driver airbag. NHTSA recall 20V035000 covers 1998–2000 US Monteros, with a free replacement inflator, and Mitsubishi Australia is buying back NL Pajeros built between 31 May 1996 and 30 September 2000 because no replacement inflator exists. Run the VIN before you pay.

Q: Is the 3.5 an interference engine?
A: Australian owners on ExplorOz say the 3.5 has no clearance if the belt breaks and the 3.0 does. Treat that as owner experience and confirm with the factory manual or a specialist. Either way, the belt is a scheduled part, so change it on time.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: Owners report about 13–14 L/100 km around town and about 11 on the highway from a 3.5 petrol, and 14 highway and 16 town from an NL GLS automatic. Towing pushes that to about 20. A 3.0 owner averaged 11.3 L/100 km. One owner towing almost constantly with a DOHC 3.5 saw 25–30 L/100 km. Diesels are 10–20% better, according to an owner who runs one.

Q: Pajero, Montero or Shogun: what's the difference?
A: Just the name. Montero was used in North America, Spain and most of Latin America, because 'pajero' is a crude insult in Spanish. Shogun was the UK name. The name Pajero comes from the Pampas cat, Leopardus pajeros.

Q: Can I import a Japanese-market Pajero or Evolution into the US?
A: Yes, if it's at least 25 years old, counted from its own build date. Every second-generation truck now qualifies. The EPA's exemption is separate: it needs the vehicle in original configuration (or with an equivalent EPA-certified engine) and at least 21 years old. State rules vary, and California is the hard one.

Q: What's a Pajero Evolution worth?
A: On Bring a Trailer, sold Evolutions from late 2024 to October 2026 ran from $19,500 to $49,997, with a median of about $32,000. Low-kilometre trucks and the rare five-speed manuals sit at the top.

Q: What are the lift options?
A: Uprated torsion bars at the front and coils at the rear. Old Man Emu torsion bars for 1991-on Mitsubishis are sold in the US, and Dobinsons sells a 45 mm kit for the NH–NL Pajero. One Australian owner reported 65 mm of lift from a TJM kit. Owners say to match front and rear spring rates, and you'll need an alignment.

Q: Are there safety recalls I should know about?
A: The big one is the NADI driver airbag: NHTSA 20V035000 for 1998–2000 Monteros, and a buy-back program for affected NL Pajeros in Australia, because no replacement inflator exists. Earlier trucks have brake-hose recalls (96V143, 98V220) and a 3.0 crank-pulley bolt recall (00V311001).

# Nissan Patrol (1951–present)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/nissan-patrol/

Nissan has built the Patrol since 1951, which makes it the company's longest-running nameplate. The first 4W60 looked a lot like a Willys Jeep and was sold only in Japan. The 60 Series arrived in October 1960 in short- and long-wheelbase (G60) form, and between 1962 and 1969 it was sold through Datsun dealers in the US and Canada, the only time a Patrol was sold in North America until the Patrol-based Infiniti QX56 arrived for 2011 (and, from the 2017 model year, the Nissan Armada). The 160 Series (sold in Australia as the MQ, then as the MK after its 1983 update) replaced it in 1980 on leaf springs, with straight-six petrol engines and the SD33 diesel. Then came the two trucks this site cares most about. The Y60, or GQ (1987–1997) was the first Patrol with coil springs at both ends, and it went toe-to-toe with the 80 Series Land Cruiser. The Y61, or GU (from late 1997) kept the solid axles, added the TD42 turbo-diesels and the infamous ZD30, and was still being built for the Middle East in 2024. The Y62 of 2010 switched to independent front suspension and V8 petrol power. North America got it first as the Infiniti QX56 for 2011 and then, from the 2017 model year, as the Nissan Armada. A seventh-generation Y63 was unveiled in Abu Dhabi in September 2024. For hands-on owners, though, the Patrol that matters is still the solid-axle iron: big pushrod sixes, a two-speed transfer case, and front axles that Australians beat on for decades.

Verdict: The Land Cruiser's oldest sparring partner, and the one Americans mostly know from imported photos of the Outback. The coil-sprung GQ and GU are the reason Australians still argue about which Japanese wagon is tougher.

## Nissan Patrol 60 Series (1960–1980)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/nissan-patrol/patrol-60/
Codes: 60, G60, K60, KG60, WG60, H60, L60

Verdict: The 60 is the Patrol Americans could actually buy, for seven years, from a Datsun dealer, with a cowboy on the TV ads. It's a 4.0-litre truck-engined six, a three-speed and a twin-stick transfer case in a body that looks like a Jeep that went to finishing school. Most survivors stateside now arrive by ship from Colombia.

In October 1960 Nissan replaced the Jeep-like 4W66 Patrol with the 60 Series, and then built it for twenty years. Wikipedia lists the soft-top 60 on a 2,200 mm wheelbase and the G60 on 2,500 mm, with an extra-long H60 that could seat eight. Hardtops (KG60) followed in 1963. Under every one sat Nissan's P-series straight-six, a three-speed gearbox and a two-speed transfer case with part-time four-wheel drive. It was Nissan's answer to Toyota's FJ40, and from 1962 to 1969 it was also the only Nissan-badged vehicle sold in America.

### THE P-SERIES SIX
The engine is the 60's whole personality. Wikipedia traces the P back to Nissan's pre-war Type A, a licence-built Graham-Paige design, by way of the sidevalve NC six it replaced. The P kept the same 3,956 cc and 85.7 x 114.3 mm bore and stroke but moved the valves overhead. It launched at 125 PS at 3,400 rpm, rose to 135 PS and reached 145 PS with the 1965 changes. It has bathtub-shaped combustion chambers and a fully balanced seven-bearing crank. Later versions were badged P40, and a fire-service PF version got a stronger alternator and a block heater.
It's a long-stroke truck engine, and it sounds like one. Australian 60s were rated at 93 kW, according to GoAuto, and Bring a Trailer's listings quote 145 hp for 1960s US trucks, 130 hp for 1971 Colombian trucks and 128 hp with 217 lb-ft for the last four-speed trucks of 1980–82. The same basic six carried on in the 160/MQ as the P40 and in Spain's 260 until 1993, which is why Patrol people still recognise its rocker cover.

### DATSUN'S COWBOY TRUCK
Canadian and American buyers could get a Patrol from 1962 until 1969, sold through Datsun dealers. Nissan's US heritage page says the Patrol was the only vehicle sold and marketed in the US as a Nissan before 1983. Datsun's first American TV commercial was shot in 1963 for the Patrol. When the company heard that Roy Rogers liked the truck, it offered him a Patrol and two pickups instead of a fee, and Goodwood says the singing cowboy went on to front Datsun's low-budget TV ads.
Restorer SNLC, who cites twenty years with these trucks, wrote on IH8MUD that America got short-wheelbase L60 soft-tops and KL60 hardtops, all with a three-speed, a twin-stick transfer case and a light-duty C216 rear axle. Dealers fitted Warn free-wheeling hubs and a Koenig PTO winch driven from a Nissan PTO box. Then Nissan stopped. Curbside Classic says it's unclear why imports ended after 1969. The next Patrol-based vehicle sold in North America was the Infiniti QX56 of 2010, a cousin of the Y62.

### SIMPSON DESERT, JONGAS AND COLOMBIA
Nissan Australia claims the 60 was the first vehicle to drive across the Simpson Desert, in 1962, and re-enacted the trip in 2012 to promote the Y62. Goodwood notes that a Toyota Land Cruiser support vehicle may have got there first, so treat the claim as marketing history. In India, the Vehicle Factory Jabalpur began assembling the Patrol as the Jonga around 1969. Wikipedia says it served the Indian Army until the late 1990s. In Bangladesh's Chittagong Hill Tracts, Patrol 60s and Jongas still work as Chander Gari, carrying passengers and produce. They're the trucks in this page's photos.
The 60 outlived its own replacement in some places. Bring a Trailer has sold Colombian-market Patrols titled as 1980 and 1982 'LG-61' trucks that keep the 60's body but use a four-speed. Colombia also keeps restorations going: SNLC's 1964 got new floor pans and an OEM steering-box seal from there. By the time the coil-sprung Y60 arrived in 1987, Japanese production of the 60 had been over for seven years, and the Y61 that followed shared nothing with it but the name. Nissan's Heritage Collection in Nashville keeps a 1967 found as a barn find on an Iowa farm.

### Data plate
- Chassis: 60 / G60 / H60 · K60 & KG60 hardtops · WG60 wagon
- Production: October 1960–1980 (Japan)
- Us Sales: 1962–1969, through Datsun dealers
- Engine: P 3,956 cc OHV I6 (later P40)
- Output: 125 PS → 135 PS → 145 PS (1965)
- Bore × Stroke: 85.7 × 114.3 mm
- Gearbox: F3B83L 3-speed, later 4-speed
- Transfer: Two-speed, twin-stick, part-time 4WD
- Wheelbase: 2,200 mm (60) · 2,500 mm (G60)
- Suspension: Leaf springs, live axles front and rear
- Brakes: Drums all round
- Wheels: 16-in steel, 7.00-16 / 7.50x16 tyres

### Engineering
The 60 is a 1950s recipe done carefully: a ladder frame, leaf springs and live axles at both ends, closed-knuckle front swivels, drum brakes all round, and a big, slow overhead-valve six. A transmission-mounted drum handbrake, a PTO take-off and dealer-fitted hubs and winches tell you it was built for work, not commuting.
- Chassis: Ladder frame · 2,200 mm (60) / 2,500 mm (G60) (Extra-long H60 seated eight (Wikipedia).)
- Engine: P 3,956 cc OHV I6 (125 → 135 → 145 PS (1965); 7-bearing crank (Wikipedia).)
- Gearbox: F3B83L 3-speed, later 4-speed (US trucks were always 3-speed, per restorer SNLC.)
- 4Wd System: Part-time, two-speed twin-stick (Low range 2.264:1 (Truck Encyclopedia).)
- Axles: Closed-knuckle front · C216 rear (US) (Tracta joints before about 1968, then Birfields; H260 rear on heavy-duty Latin American trucks (SNLC).)
- Brakes: Drums all round + transmission drum handbrake (Unassisted on early trucks; many now converted to vacuum assist (BaT).)

### Versions
- 1960–1980 · 60 soft-top (SWB) · P 4.0 L OHV I6 · 125–145 PS · 2,200 mm wheelbase. Left-hand-drive L60 for export.
- 1960–1980 · G60 (LWB) · P 4.0 L OHV I6 · 125–145 PS · 2,500 mm wheelbase; GL60 in left-hand drive.
- 1963–1980 · KG60 / KL60 hardtop · P 4.0 L OHV I6 · 125–145 PS · Hardtop added in 1963; the KL60 was the US hardtop.
- 1960s–1970s · H60 / WG60 / VH60 · P 4.0 L OHV I6 · — · Extra-long wheelbase eight-seater, wagon and van bodies.
- 1960s–1970s · Fire Patrol (FG60 and others) · P; PF fire-service variant · — · A2-class pump with PTO; a 2WD version without the front drive also existed.
- 1969 on · Jonga (India) · P engine; later Hino 4.0 L diesel · — · Built by Vehicle Factory Jabalpur; fewer than 200 civilian diesels sold in 1996.
- 1980–1982 · LG-61 (Colombia) · P 4.0 L OHV I6 · 128 hp / 217 lb-ft · 60-series body with a four-speed, per BaT listings.

### Year-by-year
- 1960: 60 Series launched in October: soft-top 60 (2,200 mm) and G60 (2,500 mm) with the P 4.0 L OHV six
- 1962: US and Canadian sales begin through Datsun dealers; Nissan Australia claims the first Simpson Desert crossing
- 1963: KG60 hardtop added; Datsun's first US TV commercial is shot for the Patrol
- 1965: P engine uprated to 145 PS
- c. 1966: Speedometer drive redesigned with a splined pinion behind the 4WD flange (restorer SNLC)
- c. 1968: Birfield front-axle joints replace Tracta joints (SNLC)
- 1969: Last US year; Indian assembly as the Jonga begins
- 1980: Replaced in Japan by the 160 Series; Colombian 'LG-61' trucks with the 60 body and a four-speed are titled into the 1980s

### Capability
- Engine output: 125 PS → 145 PS (1965) (P 3,956 cc OHV I6 (Wikipedia); 93 kW in Australian tune (GoAuto))
- Torque: 285 Nm (210 lb-ft) (Truck Encyclopedia; BaT quotes 217 lb-ft for 1980–82 trucks)
- Wheelbase: 2,200 mm (86.6 in) · 2,500 mm (98.4 in) G60
- Low range: 2.264:1 (Truck Encyclopedia)
- Seating: Up to eight in the extra-long H60

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 7.00-16 or 7.50x16 bias-ply on 16-in steel wheels (US trucks; IH8MUD, BaT), Some later and Colombian trucks on 15-in wheels (BaT)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 30x9.50R15 (on 15-in wheels) (What a 1969 on Bring a Trailer runs. We couldn't find a forum consensus for the 60.)
- Biggest tire, Longer rear shackles lift: 33x12.50R15 (A 1982 Colombian LG-61 on BaT with Mickey Thompson tyres and longer rear shackles.)
- Biggest tire, 2 in (springs) lift: 7.50x16 (A restorer's choice with a 2-in Alcan spring lift (IH8MUD). Narrow and tall, to keep the period look.)

### Buying checks
- Rust in the usual places: SNLC's restoration needed new rear floor steel, fender kick-vent repairs and new metal under the gearbox crossmember. A 1965 on BaT had rust through the driver's footwell. He also found that Nissan didn't seam-seal the body seams on early trucks, so rust starts inside the joints. Check floors, footwells, kick vents, door bottoms and the crossmember under the transmission mounts.
- US-delivered or imported?: US trucks were short-wheelbase L60 and KL60s with 80-mph speedometers. A 1965 on BaT with a US-market chassis number (4-L60-02697) had one, while Colombian trucks show km/h. Many 60s now for sale in the US came from Colombia in the past few years. Check the import papers and title, and that the chassis plate matches.
- Transfer-case seals and the handbrake: SNLC says it's common for old Patrols to blow the front or rear output seals on the transfer case, and a leaking rear seal ruins the transmission-mounted drum handbrake. Look for oil on the handbrake drum and ask whether the parking brake actually holds. One 1967 on BaT had no working parking brake.
- Brakes that work on all four wheels: These are four-wheel drum trucks. One BaT 1967 had its rear brakes disabled. SNLC had none of four master cylinders good enough to use without boring and sleeving. Budget for wheel cylinders, hoses and a master cylinder unless the seller has receipts.
- Front swivels and axle joints: Early trucks used Tracta joints and later ones Birfields, according to SNLC. Pitted knuckle balls are the big problem: without a smooth surface for the seal, he warns, keeping the knuckle dry is very difficult. Look for weeping swivel seals and play at the top and bottom of each wheel.
- Original engine and fuel system: The P six used a single-barrel Hitachi carburettor. Some BaT trucks now run electric fuel pumps that bypass the mechanical pump, and one has an aluminium radiator and a plastic tank. Those changes are reasonable on a driver but worth knowing on a 'correct' restoration.
- Dealer options worth money: A front PTO winch (Koenig, with Nissan's PTO box) and 1960s Warn hubs are period US dealer options. SNLC says a complete PTO assembly can sell for $1,000 among Patrol people, and that only about a quarter of US trucks had a PTO winch.
- Mileage and paperwork: Five-digit odometers have rolled or been replaced on many trucks. Several recent BaT listings were sold with 'true mileage unknown'. Judge on condition and documented work, not the odometer.

### Common repairs
#### Front swivel (closed-knuckle) rebuild
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend per axle · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Grease and oil weeping from the knuckle seals, play in the swivel, or heavy, notchy steering.
Fix: SNLC's rebuild of a 1964's front axle: strip the hub, spindle and axle shaft (Tracta or Birfield joint), then the knuckle cap and kingpin or trunnion bearings. Check the knuckle balls. If they're pitted, find a better housing; he built one good axle from the best parts of three. The aftermarket knuckle seal he used isn't split like the original, so it must go on the knuckle ball before the knuckle. Fit it facing the right way. Set swivel preload by measuring turning force with a spring scale, as for any closed-knuckle axle, and do the same for wheel-bearing preload.
Tools: Hub nut socket · bearing and seal drivers · spring scale · torque wrench · workshop manual for preload figures

#### Rear axle shaft bearing
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day per side · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Gear oil on the rear brake shoes, a rumble from one rear wheel, or axle end-play.
Fix: SNLC says the rear wheel bearing on the 60 isn't shimmed for preload. It's preset by the spacer under the bearing and bearing cage, which is why the nut must be torqued properly: 157 ft-lb in the early manual and over 200 ft-lb in late-1970s manuals. Pull the shaft (it needs the right puller to leave the bearing cage), press the bearing off and the new one on with a drift or pipe, with the wheel studs fitted first. Then shim the shaft for factory end-play. He made his own socket for the bearing nut.
Tools: Slide-hammer axle puller · press · large socket or home-made nut tool · torque wrench · dial indicator

#### Transfer-case output seals
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Oil on the transmission-mounted handbrake drum, a handbrake that won't hold, or drips from the transfer flanges.
Fix: Old Patrols commonly blow their transfer-case front or rear output seals, according to SNLC, and if the rear one goes, it destroys the handbrake. Drop the driveshaft, remove the flange nut and flange, and replace the seal. He found Nissan's OEM seals were double-lipped and much better than the single-lip aftermarket seals in his truck. If the handbrake drum or band lining is oil-soaked, clean or reline it at the same time.
Tools: Flange holding tool · seal puller · seal driver · torque wrench

#### Drum brake overhaul
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Pulling, a low or spongy pedal, seized adjusters or wheel cylinders on a truck that has been parked.
Fix: Strip each drum, clean and inspect the shoes and drums, and replace wheel cylinders and hardware. SNLC found seized rear adjuster pistons and trashed rear backing plates on his 1964, and none of four master cylinders were usable until one was bored and sleeved in stainless. Fit new flexible hoses, bleed the system and adjust the shoes. Many owners have added vacuum assist; check that any conversion was done properly.
Tools: Brake spring tools · flare-nut spanners · bleeder kit · drum gauge

#### Reseal the P-series six
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ A day for valve cover, sump and manifold gaskets · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Oil weeping from the rocker cover, sump or manifold joints, or a tired head gasket on a high-mileage engine.
Fix: RockAuto lists gasket sets for the 1967 Patrol 4.0 (head gasket set, valve-cover, sump, intake/exhaust manifold and full engine sets), so routine resealing is easy. Clean the mating faces, use new gaskets, and torque in the sequence from the workshop manual. When SNLC rebuilt a 1964's P engine, he also rebuilt the single-barrel Hitachi carburettor with a quality kit; do the carb at the same time if it's leaking or flooding.
Tools: Torque wrench · scraper · feeler gauges for valve lash

#### Leaf springs and hangers
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day per axle · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Sagging, a harsh ride, home-made hangers, or cracked leaves.
Fix: SNLC fitted Alcan leaf springs with a 2-inch lift to his 1964 and matched them to the stock eye-to-eye length (48.5 in on the rear of a 1977 Patrol ute). He replaced home-made shackle hangers with NOS Nissan parts from an Australian supplier. Support the chassis, swap one axle at a time, fit new bushes and U-bolts, and keep the hangers in their stock locations if you're restoring.
Tools: Jacks and stands · breaker bar · penetrating oil · welder if hangers are replaced

#### Fix the speedometer drive after fitting free-wheeling hubs
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day with the transfer case out · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: A dead speedometer after fitting free-wheeling hubs, or a stripped speedometer pinion.
Fix: Early trucks (before about 1966) drove the speedometer from the very front of the transfer case with a crush-sleeve pinion, which only worked because there were no free-wheeling hubs. SNLC says Nissan redesigned it around 1966 with a splined pinion behind the 4WD flange in the transfer nose cone, and he upgraded his 1964 to that later design for Warn hubs. Pinion tooth counts also changed with tyre size, so match the gear to your tyres.
Tools: Transfer-case tools · seal driver · correct speedo pinion for your tyre size

### Baseline service
Every 60 is at least 45 years old, and most have had several owners and at least one hard life. Assume every fluid is old, every grease point is dry and every rubber part has hardened. We couldn't find a factory manual for the 60 online. The capacities below come from Penrite's lookup for the Australian G60 (P engine, 1968–1980) and are approximate, so check grades in a Nissan workshop manual and fill to the level plug.
- Engine oil & filter: About 5.3 L service refill (Penrite lookup, G60; it doesn't say whether that includes the filter) · [CONFIRM GRADE AND FILTER TYPE IN MANUAL] · Baseline now (Check for sludge on the first change and look for leaks at the rocker cover and sump gaskets, which are catalogued and cheap.)
- Spark plugs, points & distributor: Six plugs; check the distributor, coil and leads · Replace now (Some trucks have a water-protected distributor, and SNLC calls a NOS one very hard to find. Keep the original if it works.)
- Carburettor & fuel system: Single-barrel Hitachi carburettor; glass sediment bowls · Inspect now; rebuild if leaking (Old fuel and rusty tanks cause most running faults. Several trucks now have electric pumps added; check the wiring and fuse.)
- Coolant & hoses: Fresh coolant; new top and bottom hoses · Flush now (Old radiators clog. SNLC had his radiator rebuilt during the restoration.)
- Gearbox, transfer case & PTO box: Gear oil · gearbox about 2.0–2.3 L, transfer case about 3.4 L (Penrite lookup, G60) · [CONFIRM GRADE AND PTO-BOX CAPACITY IN MANUAL] · Baseline now (Check the transfer output seals while you're there. A leaking rear seal ruins the transmission-mounted handbrake.)
- Front & rear differentials: Hypoid gear oil [CONFIRM GRADE IN MANUAL] · front about 1.2 L, rear about 1.0–2.0 L depending on axle (Penrite lookup, G60) · Baseline now (US trucks have a C216 rear axle; heavy-duty trucks an H260.)
- Front swivels (knuckles) & wheel bearings: Inspect knuckle balls and seals; repack wheel bearings · Inspect now (Pitted knuckle balls won't hold a seal.)
- Brake fluid & drums: Fluid per the master-cylinder cap [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush now (Check every wheel cylinder and the master cylinder bore. Make sure all four drums actually brake.)
- Handbrake band & drum: Transmission-mounted drum with a band; three adjustments · Inspect and adjust now (If it's oily, fix the transfer seal first, then clean or reline.)
- Driveshafts, U-joints & slip joints: Grease every nipple · Grease now and at every oil change (SNLC fitted Spicer joints specified for a Dana 44 and modified them slightly to fit. The slip-joint felt seal is no longer available, so he made one.)
- Generator & battery: Generator charging system · Test now (Check the generator bearings and brushes and clean every earth.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: We couldn't find a forum consensus for the 60, so here's what's documented. Stock was a narrow 16-inch bias-ply, 7.00-16 or 7.50x16 depending on the truck. One 1969 on Bring a Trailer runs 30x9.50 tyres on 15-inch wheels. A 1982 Colombian LG-61 runs 33x12.50 tyres on 15s, with longer rear shackles. Narrow tall tyres such as a 7.50x16 suit the truck's look, gearing and steering best.

Q: How many were sold in the US?
A: Nissan hasn't published a figure we could find. The most specific number is a restorer's on IH8MUD: 2,616 from 1962 to 1969, about 950 of them soft-tops. He's unsure whether that includes Canada. A Curbside Classic reader estimated about 4,000.

Q: What engine does it have?
A: Nissan's P-series 3,956 cc overhead-valve straight-six, rated at 125 PS at first and 145 PS from 1965. It's the same family as the P40 in the 160/MQ. Wikipedia traces it back to the pre-war Graham-Paige-based Type A.

Q: Three-speed or four-speed?
A: Wikipedia says the F3B83L gearbox started with three speeds and later had four. Restorer SNLC says every US truck was a three-speed with a twin-stick transfer case. The Colombian LG-61 trucks sold on BaT have four-speeds.

Q: What's a 60 worth?
A: On Bring a Trailer in 2025–26, ten 60-series trucks sold for $6,000 to $23,000. Most fell between about $10,000 and $18,000. The top sale was a refurbished 1965 from Colombia; the cheapest was a rusty US-market 1965 with a patina repaint.

Q: Are parts available?
A: More than you'd think. RockAuto lists gasket sets, spark plugs, hoses and drum brake hardware for the 1967 Patrol 4.0. SNLC says bearings and seals aren't a problem, that engine rebuild kits and body parts are sold in the US, and that OEM seals and floor pans can still be found in Colombia. Trim rubber and NOS parts are the hard ones.

Q: Can I import one from Colombia or Australia?
A: Yes. Every 60 is well past the 25-year mark, so NHTSA's exemption from federal safety standards applies. Many US trucks on Bring a Trailer are recent Colombian imports titled in Florida. State titling and emissions rules still apply.

Q: Did a Patrol really cross the Simpson Desert first?
A: Nissan Australia says the 60 Series was the first vehicle to cross the Simpson Desert, and re-enacted the 1962 trip in 2012. Goodwood notes that a Toyota Land Cruiser support vehicle may have arrived first, so the claim is disputed.

Q: Is a Jonga a Patrol?
A: Essentially. Wikipedia says India's Vehicle Factory Jabalpur began assembling the quarter-ton Patrol as the Jonga around 1969. Indian Army Jongas served until the late 1990s, and a civilian diesel version sold fewer than 200 in 1996.

Q: Free-wheeling hubs and a winch: original or not?
A: Both can be correct for a US truck. SNLC says 1960s Warn hubs were sold by US dealers, and dealers fitted Koenig winches driven from Nissan's PTO box. He puts the share of US trucks with a PTO winch at about a quarter.

## Nissan Patrol 160 / MQ (1980–1989)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/nissan-patrol/160-mq/
Codes: 160, 161, MQ, MK, Safari

Verdict: The MQ is the Patrol that went soft, though only by 1980 standards: carpets, colours and graphics on top, and leaf springs, a C200 front diff and a slow, tough diesel six underneath. Few people treat it gently now, which is why the survivors are usually rusty, re-sprung and still running.

In 1980 Nissan replaced the long-running 60 Series Patrol with the 160, sold in Australia and New Zealand as the MQ and, after a 1983 update, unofficially called the MK. In Japan it became the Safari. Underneath it was still a 1960s recipe: a separate chassis, live axles and leaf springs at both ends, and a two-speed offset transfer case. GoAuto called it 'a decisive step towards civility': more space, a less truck-like cabin, better ride and braking, and a long list of variants aimed at Toyota's 40 Series and 60 Series Land Cruisers.

### FOUR ENGINES AND A 24-VOLT DIESEL
GoAuto says Australia's MQ launched with the 3.2-litre (3,246 cc) SD33 diesel six, rated at 70 kW and 215 Nm, with the 2.8-litre L28 petrol six (88 kW, 201 Nm) arriving in April 1981 and a short-lived 4.0-litre P40 petrol rated at 90 kW and 280 Nm. Owners describe the P40 as rare and very torquey, and the L28 as the one that will rev all day. A four-speed manual was standard. From late 1981 the seven-seat Deluxe wagon could have a three-speed automatic, which Wikipedia says was limited to long-wheelbase L28 trucks.
The SD33 is the engine with a story. It's a slow overhead-valve diesel six built for trucks and forklifts. Wikipedia notes the same engine powered International Scout II diesels in the late 1970s, and a turbo version went into 6,400 Scouts in 1980. In the MQ it ran 24-volt electrics with twin batteries, one on each side of the engine bay. 4X4 Australia notes the later switch to 12 volts made the truck much easier to fit with accessories.

### THE MK UPDATE
The 1983 facelift turned the 160 into the 161. Wikipedia says the Australian 'MK' label never appeared in Nissan literature or parts catalogues. Rectangular headlights replaced round ones, the front suspension was upgraded and most models got a fifth gear. A high-roof wagon arrived, along with the SD33T turbo-diesel, which 4X4 Australia lists at 81 kW and 255 Nm. Wikipedia says the turbo engines got a larger clutch and oil cooler, and that the naturally aspirated SD33 switched to three-ring pistons, oil squirters and a spin-on oil filter. The Datsun badge disappeared in 1984 in most markets.
By 1985, GoAuto counts 21 Australian variants, from a two-seat rural hardtop to a seven-seat Deluxe wagon. Power steering and a limited-slip rear differential were standard by then. 4X4 Australia remembers the bright colours and 'loud' graphics of the era. GoAuto also lists an updated P40 petrol rated at 84 kW and 270 Nm by 1985. Owners also list the MK's extra inner-guard bracing, stepped rear shackles and bigger front shackle bolts among the differences.

### SPAIN, IRAN AND THE LONG TAIL
Nissan bought into Spain's Motor Ibérica in 1980, and the first Spanish-built Patrol left the Zona Franca plant near Barcelona in early 1983, according to Wikipedia. To meet local-content rules it used a Spanish Perkins MD27 four-cylinder diesel, later replaced by the Nissan-built 2.8-litre A428 and its turbocharged version. Spain's facelifted version became the 260, built into the 2000s. Wikipedia also lists 160 production in Iran by Pars Khodro (1984–2003), South Africa (1983–1991) and the Philippines.
The coil-sprung Y60 'GQ' replaced the 160 from 1987, and forum regulars still tell would-be MQ buyers to 'buy a GQ' instead. Owners on NissanPatrol.com.au report MKs passing 780,000 and even 900,000 km on their original engines, along with rust bad enough that the trucks can't be driven without serious welding. Both stories are typical of the 160. Today it's the cheapest way into an old-school leaf-sprung Patrol, and the parts that matter most (swivel-hub kits, springs and bearings) are still sold for it in Australia.

### Data plate
- Chassis: 160 (1980–83) · 161 (1983-on)
- Market Names: MQ / MK (Australia) · Safari (Japan) · Datsun Patrol to 1984
- Production: 1980–1989 (Wikipedia); Japan to 1987
- Engines: SD33 · SD33T · L28 · P40 (Australia)
- Output: SD33 70 kW · SD33T 81 kW · L28 88 kW · P40 90 kW
- Transmission: 4-spd manual (MQ) · 5-spd (most MK) · 3-spd auto (LWB L28)
- Transfer Case: Two-speed, offset
- Wheelbase: 2,350 mm SWB · 2,970 mm LWB
- Length: 4,105 mm SWB · 4,690 mm LWB
- Width: 1,690 mm
- Axles: C200 front · H233 rear (H260 utes)
- Weight: 1,880 kg (1985 Safari hardtop, KR161)

### Engineering
The 160 is a leaf-sprung, live-axle Patrol of the old school: a ladder frame, semi-elliptic leaf springs at both ends, kingpin swivel hubs, a two-speed transfer case and a choice of engines that all trade speed for torque. Underneath the MQ and MK are much the same truck. The differences are in the front suspension, shackles, electrics and gearbox.
- Chassis: Ladder frame · 2,350 mm SWB / 2,970 mm LWB (Hardtops, soft-tops, wagons, vans, utes, cab-chassis and fire trucks.)
- Suspension: Live axles on leaf springs, front and rear (Owners report MQs used straight shackles and MKs stepped ones, and that diesel and petrol spring packs differ.)
- 4Wd System: Part-time, two-speed offset transfer case (1:1 high and a low range (Wikipedia).)
- Axles: C200 front · H233 rear (H260 on some utes) (Some European trucks used a C200 rear; LSD was standard in Australia by 1985 (GoAuto).)
- Engines: SD33 3.2 L diesel · SD33T · L28 2.8 L · P40 4.0 L (SD33 70 kW / 215 Nm and SD33T 81 kW / 255 Nm in Australian tune.)
- Brakes: Ventilated front discs, rear drums (Per Nissan's heritage data for a 1985 Safari (KR161).)

### Versions
- 1980–1983 · MQ (160) diesel · SD33 3.2 L OHV I6 diesel · 70 kW / 215 Nm · Launch engine in Australia; 24-volt electrics with twin batteries; four-speed manual.
- 1981–1983 · MQ (160) petrol · L28 2.8 L SOHC I6 · 88 kW / 201 Nm · From April 1981; three-speed auto optional on the LWB Deluxe from late 1981.
- 1980s · MQ / MK P40 · P40 4.0 L OHV I6 · 90 kW / 280 Nm · GoAuto calls the first version short-lived; an updated 84 kW / 270 Nm P40 was listed by 1985.
- 1983–1987 · MK (161) turbo-diesel · SD33T 3.2 L turbo-diesel I6 · 81 kW / 255 Nm · 12-volt, larger clutch and oil cooler; five-speed manual on most models.
- 1980–1987 · Safari (Japan) · SD33 / SD33T; PF40 in fire trucks · 95 PS / 120 PS (Japanese ratings) · Hardtop, high-roof hardtop, Extra Van and fire-truck chassis. High-roof van and SD33T from 1983.
- 1983–1988 · Spanish-built (Nissan Motor Ibérica) · Perkins MD27, then A428 / A428T 2.8 L I4 diesel · — · Local-content engines. The facelifted Spanish truck became the 260.

### Year-by-year
- 1980: 160 Series replaces the 60; Australian MQ launches with the SD33 diesel (GoAuto); Japan renames it Safari
- 1981: L28 petrol six arrives in April; three-speed automatic option for the LWB Deluxe wagon late in the year
- 1983: 161 'MK' facelift: rectangular headlights, upgraded front suspension, five-speed on most models, SD33T turbo-diesel, high roof; Spanish production begins in Barcelona
- 1984: Datsun badge dropped in most markets; Iranian production starts at Pars Khodro
- 1985: 21 Australian variants; power steering standard and an updated P40 listed (GoAuto)
- 1987: Coil-sprung Y60 arrives; a Patrol (car 211, Prieto/Termens) finishes ninth overall and wins the Paris–Dakar diesel class
- 1989: End of the 160 run, according to Wikipedia's production dates; Spain's derivative continues as the 260

### Capability
- Curb weight: 1,880 kg (4,145 lb) (1985 Safari hardtop AD (KR161), Nissan)
- Wheelbase: 2,350 mm SWB · 2,970 mm LWB
- Length: 4,105 mm SWB · 4,690 mm LWB (Wikipedia; the 1985 Safari hardtop is 4,230 mm (Nissan))
- Track (front / rear): 1,415 / 1,405 mm (1985 Safari hardtop, Nissan)
- Engine output: SD33 70 kW / 215 Nm · SD33T 81 kW / 255 Nm · L28 88 kW / 201 Nm · P40 90 kW / 280 Nm (Australian ratings (GoAuto, 4X4 Australia))

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 205/80R16 (1985 Safari hardtop, Nissan heritage data), 16-in steel wheels
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 31x10.50 (What an ExplorOz owner ran on stock, sagged springs; 32x11.5 may fit once tired springs are replaced.)
- Biggest tire, 2 in lift: 33 in (2-in lift springs and shocks; guard clearance is tight, but MQs don't have much wheel travel (ExplorOz).)
- Biggest tire, 2 in + 2 in body lift lift: 35 in (One owner's recipe; 38s took a 3-in body lift plus 1.5-in longer shackles. Avoid a spring-over (too much sway, he says).)

### Buying checks
- Rust: where to look: NissanPatrol.com.au members list roof gutters, the plenum under the windscreen (a leak there rots the floor and the low-set body mounts), front floor pans, the radiator support, the inner guard under the battery tray, door bottoms, rear lower quarter panels and the top of the rear wheel arch. Chassis-to-body mount points are where the worst rust lives.
- Turbo or not?: A turbo SD33T has 'Turbo' on the rocker cover and a turbocharger on the exhaust side. Owners warn that some non-turbo engines wear turbo rocker covers, so look for the turbo itself.
- 24 or 12 volts: MQ SD33 diesels ran 24-volt electrics with twin batteries; MKs are 12-volt. The engine number won't tell you. Owners say the starter, injection-pump solenoid and glow plugs are the voltage-sensitive parts, so a half-converted truck can be a headache.
- Which diff is under it: Rear axles were C200, H233 or H260 (utes) depending on market and model. The ratio is stamped on a tin plate at the front of the driver's-side inner guard (for example HG43 means H233, 4.3:1). Members warn that MQ H233 parts and lockers aren't interchangeable with the later H233B in GQs and GUs.
- Can you undo the plugs and grease it?: One member's advice: make sure you can crack the drain and fill plugs on both diffs, the gearbox and the transfer case, and buy a good grease gun. The leaf-sprung Patrol has far more grease nipples than a coil-sprung GQ, including greasable shackles.
- Suspension history: Original springs are 40 years old and usually sagged. Ask what's been replaced. Owners say a rebuild with new leaves, U-bolts, shocks and shackles quickly costs more than an MQ is worth, and shackle extensions can invert.
- Overheating and the head gasket: An SD33T that keeps losing coolant isn't automatically a head-gasket job. Forum diagnosis starts with the radiator, cap, hoses, thermostat and fan clutch. If the head does come off, the SD33T needs its own head gasket; the non-turbo SD33 gasket doesn't fit it correctly.
- Import paperwork (US): Nissan never sold the 160 Patrol new in the US. US examples on Bring a Trailer came from Japan (Safari fire trucks), South Africa and Colombia. Check the title, the import documents and that the chassis number matches.

### Common repairs
#### Swivel hub (kingpin) and front wheel bearing rebuild
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day for both sides · cost Full swivel kit about A$223; wheel-bearing kit about A$54
Symptoms: Grease and oil weeping from the swivel seals, play at the top and bottom of the wheel, or a rumbling front wheel bearing.
Fix: The 160 uses kingpin swivel hubs. A complete rebuild kit for MQ 160s (Basco Wholesale, via Bunnings Marketplace) contains four wheel bearings, four kingpin bearings, two needle-roller bearings, two 65-88-11/16.5 oil seals and a swivel gasket and seal kit. Jack and support the axle, remove the hub cap or free-wheeling hub (if fitted), the wheel bearings and the stub axle, and draw out the axle shaft. Unbolt the kingpin caps, keeping each shim pack with its cap, and drop the swivel housing off the kingpin bearings. Replace the bearings, inner seal and swivel wiper seal, then refit with the original shims. Set kingpin preload and wheel-bearing preload to your workshop manual, then refill or regrease as the manual specifies.
Tools: Hub nut socket · bearing driver and seal driver · spring balance for preload · torque wrench · new shims if preload is out

#### Leaf springs, shackles and bushes
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day per axle · cost A$1,250–1,800 for springs, shocks and shackles in owners' 2003–04 reports
Symptoms: A truck that sits low or leans, harsh ride, cracked leaves, or shackles worn at the pins.
Fix: Support the chassis and replace one axle at a time: unbolt the shock, loosen the U-bolts, remove the shackle and front pin, swap the spring pack and fit new bushes, U-bolts and shackles. Members point out that MQs use straight shackles and MKs stepped ones, that MK front shackle bolts are larger, and that diesel and petrol spring packs differ because of engine weight. Order springs to suit your engine and load. Avoid shackle extensions on road trucks, which can invert. A 2-in lift spring set with matching shocks is the usual upgrade.
Tools: Jacks and stands · breaker bar · penetrating oil · grease gun

#### SD33/SD33T overheating: cooling system before the head
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day for the cooling system; two days for a head job · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Coolant disappearing with no visible leak, pressurised hoses after hard work, or temperature that climbs when a thermostat is fitted.
Fix: Members' advice on an SD33T that kept boiling after a pressure-tested, rebuilt head: start with the radiator. Have it properly cleaned or replaced, then fit a new cap, top and bottom hoses and the correct thermostat, and check the fan clutch hub. Never run it without a thermostat. If temperature rises with one fitted, there's a flow restriction. Use real coolant: owners report water pumps wearing out on engines run on plain water. If the head must come off, buy an SD33T-specific head gasket, as the non-turbo gasket doesn't fit the turbo engine correctly.
Tools: Cooling-system pressure tester · infrared thermometer · torque wrench (head) · workshop manual

#### Extend the axle, gearbox and transfer breathers
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost About the price of a breather kit
Symptoms: Water in the diff or gearbox oil after crossings, or snagged and split breather lines.
Fix: Owners found a clear tube linking the MQ's gearbox and transfer case breathers, with only the front diff breather running up to the inner guard; the front axle also has an equaliser tube between the diff and axle housing. The common fix is to fit new seals and separate breather lines run high into the engine bay, terminated with small filters. One member uses 6 mm Teflon tube with push-in fittings and Ryco fuel filters as caps.
Tools: Spanners · hose · cable ties · push-in fittings

#### Steering: drag link and joints
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2 hours · cost MQ drag link about A$111 (Patrolapart)
Symptoms: Wandering, clunks over bumps or play at the wheel. Owners rebuilding tired MQs report worn ball joints throughout.
Fix: With the wheels straight, check each steering joint for play while a helper rocks the wheel. Split the tapers with a puller or fork, fit the new drag link and set its length to centre the steering box. Torque the castle nuts and fit new split pins, then get the alignment checked.
Tools: Ball-joint separator · torque wrench · split pins

#### SD33 slow cranking or no-start
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–3 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Clicking relays, a starter that barely turns the engine, or a truck that needs several key cycles to start.
Fix: Forum diagnosis: clean and tighten every battery terminal, the starter connections and the body earth. Measure battery voltage while cranking; below 10 V means the battery is finished. Feel the heavy cables after a start attempt, since heat shows the bad connection. Owners say the SD33 needs a strong battery to turn over. On 24-volt MQs, both batteries must be healthy and matched, and the starter, injection-pump solenoid and glow plugs are 24-volt parts.
Tools: Multimeter · wire brush · terminal protectant · heavy-gauge jumper leads

#### Fit a rear locker
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Lifting a rear wheel on cross-axle ruts and losing drive, even with the LSD.
Fix: Identify the diff first. Members say the MQ wagon's bolt-in-centre H233 (plate code HG) isn't the GQ/GU H233B, and that lockers made for the H233B (ARB RD135/RD136) don't fit it. One member gives the ARB Air Locker for the MQ H233 as RD04; confirm it against ARB's current application chart. Utes with the H260 need a different unit. Have the carrier set up by a diff shop if you aren't equipped to set backlash and preload.
Tools: Diff shop or bearing puller, dial indicator, torque wrench · air compressor and lines for an Air Locker

### Baseline service
Every 160 is at least 37 years old and most have worked hard, so assume every oil is old and every grease point is dry. We couldn't find factory capacities published for the 160 online. Treat the specs below as types, and check quantities in the Nissan 160/61-series workshop manual.
- Engine oil & filter: Diesel-rated oil [CONFIRM GRADE & CAPACITY IN MANUAL] · SD33 changed from a paper cartridge to a spin-on filter at the 1983 update (Wikipedia) · Baseline now (Check which filter your engine takes before you go shopping. Turbo SD33Ts have piston oil squirters and a bigger oil cooler, which makes clean oil even more important.)
- Fuel filter & water trap (diesel): Engine-bay fuel filter [CONFIRM PART BY ENGINE] · Replace now (Old diesel and water kill injection pumps. Drain the trap and replace the element before chasing poor running.)
- Air filter: Engine-specific element · Replace now (Check the airbox seals and the intake hose for splits, especially on turbo engines.)
- Coolant, thermostat, hoses & cap: Anti-corrosion coolant, never plain water · correct thermostat fitted · Flush now (Owners trace SD33 overheating to blocked radiators and missing thermostats, and water-pump wear to plain water.)
- Glow plugs & batteries (diesel): 24-volt system on MQ SD33s, 12-volt on MKs · Test now (Test each glow plug and both batteries under load. A weak battery on a 24-volt pair drags the other down.)
- Manual gearbox & transfer case: Gear oil [CONFIRM GRADE & CAPACITY IN MANUAL] · Baseline now (Crack the fill plug before the drain plug. Members warn seized plugs are common. The gearbox and transfer case breathers are linked by a tube on some MQs.)
- Front differential (C200) & rear (H233 / H260): Hypoid gear oil; LSD-rated oil if the rear has a limited-slip diff [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Baseline now (LSD was standard in Australia by 1985. Note the ratio plate on the driver's-side inner guard while you're there.)
- Swivel hubs & front wheel bearings: Kingpin swivels with wiper seals; repack wheel bearings · Inspect now; rebuild if weeping or loose (Full rebuild kits for the MQ 160 include kingpin bearings, needle rollers and swivel seals.)
- Chassis grease: shackles, spring pins, driveshafts: Grease every nipple · Grease now and at every oil change (A leaf-sprung Patrol has many more grease nipples than a GQ, including greasable shackles.)
- Brake fluid & hydraulics: Fluid per the master-cylinder cap [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush now (Front ventilated discs and rear drums. Check the flexible hoses and rear wheel cylinders on a truck that has sat.)
- Steering joints & drag link: Check for play · Inspect now (Tired MQs usually need several joints at once.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: About 31x10.50. In an ExplorOz thread, an owner on stock, saggy springs was running 31x10.5s, and another suggested 32x11.5s might fit once springs were reset. The consensus for 33s is a 2-inch spring lift. For 35s, owners add a 2-inch body lift, and 38s took a 3-inch body lift with longer shackles. MQs don't have much wheel travel, so guard clearance is tight but workable.

Q: MQ or MK: how do I tell them apart?
A: MQs have round headlights, a two-spoke wheel and a flat radio pod. MKs have rectangular headlights, a three-spoke wheel, a tapered pod with a clock, separate rear indicators in the bumper and extra inner-guard bracing. Owners add that MQs use straight shackles and MKs stepped ones, MQ diesels are 24-volt, and MK petrols could have a factory five-speed.

Q: Which engine should I buy?
A: For touring, most owners want the SD33T turbo-diesel. The non-turbo SD33 is slow but long-lived: members report MKs past 780,000 and 900,000 km on original engines. The L28 petrol revs freely but has less torque, and the P40 4.0 is rare and the torque king. On a steep riverbed, one owner says the L28 'has to scream' where the turbo diesel is just above idle.

Q: Is my SD33 24-volt?
A: If it's an MQ diesel with batteries on both sides of the engine bay, almost certainly. MKs are 12-volt. You can't tell from the engine number. Owners say the starter, injection-pump solenoid and glow plugs are the parts that differ by voltage.

Q: Can I bolt a turbo onto a non-turbo SD33?
A: People have, but owners advise against it for a remote-area truck. The SD33T differs in its head gasket, pistons and rings, piston oil squirters, injection-pump delivery valves and injectors. Using an SD33 head gasket on a turbo engine can block water and oil passages.

Q: What diff ratio do I have?
A: Read the tin plate at the front of the driver's-side inner guard (HG43 means H233, 4.3:1) or the tooth count stamped on the crown wheel. Owners list roughly 4.625 for MQ L28/SD33, 4.11 for the P40, 4.33 for MK and 4.88 for H260 utes, and say all except the H260 centres interchange.

Q: Can I fit a locker?
A: Yes, but buy for the right diff. Members say the MQ's H233 isn't the GQ/GU's H233B, so H233B lockers such as ARB's RD135/RD136 won't fit. One member gives ARB's MQ H233 part as RD04. Check ARB's current application chart before ordering.

Q: Should I convert it to coil springs?
A: Forum regulars mostly say no: Nissan already did the conversion, and it's called the GQ. If you love the MQ/MK body, one member suggests putting it on a GQ rolling chassis rather than engineering coils into a leaf-spring frame.

Q: Was it sold in the US, and can I import one?
A: Not new. Every 160 is past the 25-year mark, so NHTSA's safety-standard exemption applies. Bring a Trailer has sold Japanese Safari fire trucks, a South African L28 wagon and a Colombian P40 hardtop in the US. State titling and emissions rules still apply.

Q: What's one worth?
A: Not much, by classic-4x4 standards. Bring a Trailer sales of 160-series trucks from 2021 to 2026 ran from $7,500 (a 1981 Safari fire truck) to $12,750 (a 1982 P40 two-door from Colombia), with a South African L28 wagon at $12,000.
