## Nissan Patrol Y60 (GQ) (1987–1997)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/nissan-patrol/y60/
Codes: Y60, GQ, GR, Safari

Verdict: The coil-sprung Patrol that beat Toyota to the punch by three years and never stopped reminding Land Cruiser owners about it. It's slow, thirsty and always on the lookout for rust, and in TD42 form it's close to unkillable.

The Y60 Patrol, sold in Australia as the GQ, is the truck that made Toyota nervous. When it arrived in the late 1980s it was the first Patrol with coil springs at both ends: a three-link live axle up front, a five-link live axle out back, power steering as standard, and a separate ladder frame underneath. The 60 Series Land Cruiser it fought in showrooms was still on leaf springs. Nissan kept that advantage until Toyota launched the 80 Series in 1990, and Australians have been arguing about which one is tougher ever since.

### COILS, SIXES AND A TWO-SPEED BOX
Production started in Japan in 1987, where the truck was also sold as the Nissan Safari, and Nissan's Barcelona plant in Spain built it from 1988. Underneath, it was refreshingly old-school. Every engine was a straight six: the 4.2-litre TB42 petrol (125 kW and 325 Nm on a carburettor), the 4.2-litre TD42 diesel (85 kW, 264 Nm), and the 3.0-litre RB30 petrol borrowed from Nissan's passenger cars. A 2.8-litre RD28T turbo-diesel joined later. Drive went through a five-speed manual or four-speed automatic to a two-speed transfer case with part-time 4WD.
The wagons came in short- and long-wheelbase form (2,400 and 2,970 mm), plus a high-roof version, and there were utes and cab-chassis models too. Those workhorses kept a leaf-spring rear axle until 1994, when Nissan offered the wagons' coil rear as an option. Most Y60s left the factory with a rear limited-slip differential. Some got a vacuum or electric rear diff lock, a rear sway-bar disconnect, or even a front winch driven from a power take-off, with its lever beside the gearstick.

### THE TD42, AND EVERYTHING ELSE
The engine that built the legend is the TD42. It's a cast-iron, overhead-valve, indirect-injection diesel whose camshaft is driven by gears rather than a belt or chain, which CarsGuide calls a 'set-and-forget system'. It's slow and thirsty, at roughly 12 to 14 L/100 km on the highway, but it is reputed to reach half a million kilometres if serviced. Early engines wear a silver rocker cover. From August 1993 Nissan lightened the TD42 to save fuel and let it rev harder, and Wikipedia notes this weakened it. Those engines, and later ones, wear black covers.
The petrol engines are the other side of the coin. 4X4 Australia's own 1988 TB42 project car, an automatic, hit boiling point on its first High Country climb and boiled over three more times before the top, and its writer admits 'the TB42 loves a drink'. CarsGuide warns that petrol heads can crack, especially on LPG after the coolant has run low, and Wikipedia lists head-gasket trouble on hard-driven TB42s and RD28Ts. The 1992 Series 2 update brought fuel injection for the TB42, bigger brakes and wheels, and standard limited-slip diffs and automatic free-wheeling hubs. A 1994 facelift added a new grille.

### WHAT MADE IT SPECIAL
In the bush, the GQ simply worked. Coil springs gave it axle articulation and a ride the leaf-sprung competition couldn't match, and its axles earned a reputation for strength. That made the GQ the default heavy tourer and club truck across Australia, Africa and the Middle East. Even Ford wanted one. Under Australia's Button car plan Ford sold the Y60 as the Ford Maverick from the late 1980s to 1994, changing little but the badges. And Team Nissan France Dessoude was still racing Y60-based Patrol GRs in the Dakar Rally's T1 class in 1998.
The Patrol also has a tighter connection to America than its absence suggests. Datsun dealers sold the 60 Series here from 1962 to 1969, but the Y60 was never offered in the US. Every Y60 is now more than 25 years old, which puts it inside the federal 25-year exemption from US safety-standard compliance. Bring a Trailer lists a steady flow of imported right-hand-drive Safaris and Patrols, many of them TD42 or RD28T manuals from Japan and Europe.

### HOW IT ENDED, AND WHY IT STILL MATTERS
The Y61, or GU, took over in late 1997. 4X4 Australia describes it as essentially a GQ platform underneath, with a wider body, a better interior and about 230 kg more weight. That continuity is why GQ owners still share parts, forums and bolt-on hardware with GU owners. Much of the GU's running gear, from the swivel hubs and radius-arm bushes to ARB Air Lockers and steering dampers, is sold as fitting both trucks.
Today the GQ occupies the same place in Australian off-roading that the 60 and 80 Series do in American trail culture. It's cheap enough to modify without guilt, simple enough to fix with hand tools, and big enough to carry a family and a fridge to the end of the track. It isn't fast, the petrol engines drink like it's still 1988, and rust is never far away. But with a TD42 and a set of 33s, few trucks this old are still this capable.

### Data plate
- Chassis: Y60 (GQ in Australia; GR in Europe)
- Production: 1987–1997 (Safari, Japan) · Barcelona, Spain 1988–1998
- Also Sold As: Nissan Safari (Japan) · Ford Maverick (Australia, 1988–1994)
- Body: 3- and 5-door wagon, high roof, ute, cab-chassis
- Wheelbase: SWB 2,400 mm (94.5 in) · LWB 2,970 mm (116.9 in)
- Length: SWB 4,340 mm · LWB 4,810 mm
- Suspension: Coil-sprung live axles: 3-link front, 5-link rear
- Transfer Case: Two-speed, part-time 4WD
- Engines: TD42 · TD42T (Japan) · TB42S/E · RD28T · RB30S
- Gearboxes: FS5R50A 5-speed manual · RE4R03A 4-speed auto
- Diffs: Rear LSD on most; H233 rear (H260 leaf cab-chassis)
- Fuel Tank: 100 L main (optional 100 L second tank on utes)

### Engineering
The GQ is a body-on-frame truck with solid axles at both ends. Coil springs replaced the old Patrol's leaves, with radius arms and a panhard rod at the front and a five-link rear. A two-speed transfer case and free-wheeling front hubs give part-time 4WD. The engines are big, slow-revving straight sixes, and the TD42 diesel's camshaft is gear-driven. Most of what goes wrong is heat, rust, and front swivels that have been neglected.
- Chassis: Ladder frame · SWB 2,400 mm / LWB 2,970 mm (Separate body-on-frame construction. Wagons came in standard and high-roof forms; utes and cab-chassis rode on the long frame.)
- Front Suspension: Live axle, three-link, coil springs (Radius arms and a panhard rod locate the axle. Sway bar and power steering standard. Steering swivels on kingpin bearings set with shims.)
- Rear Suspension: Live axle, five-link, coil springs (Utes and cab-chassis kept leaf springs until a coil rear became an option in 1994. Some trucks have a rear sway-bar disconnect.)
- 4Wd System: Part-time, two-speed transfer case (Free-wheeling front hubs: manual on DX and RX, automatic on ST and Ti (Australian trims).)
- Differentials: Rear LSD on most · H233 rear (H260 on leaf cab-chassis) (Some had a vacuum or electric rear diff lock. ARB makes front and rear Air Lockers for the GQ.)
- Signature Engine: TD42 4.2 L OHV diesel I6 (Gear-driven camshaft and indirect injection. 85 kW / 264 Nm. Silver rocker cover until the lightened 1993 engine (black).)

### Versions
- 1987–1997 · Y60 (GQ) · TD42 · 4.2 L OHV diesel I6 · 85 kW / 264 Nm · The legend. Silvertop until August 1993, then the lighter 'Blacktop'. Manual-only in Australia, per CarsGuide.
- 1987–1992 · Y60 (GQ) · TB42S · 4.2 L OHV petrol I6, carburettor · 125 kW / 325 Nm · Torquey and thirsty. Watch for cracked heads, especially on LPG.
- 1992–1997 · Y60 (GQ Series 2) · TB42E · 4.2 L OHV petrol I6, EFI · 135 kW / 320 Nm (Wikipedia; CarsGuide quotes 129 kW for Australia) · Fuel injection arrived with the 1992 Series 2, along with bigger brakes and standard LSD and auto hubs.
- c. 1990–1997 · Y60 (GQ) · RB30S · 3.0 L SOHC petrol I6 · 100 kW / 224 Nm · Five-speed manual only. The budget engine; 4X4 Australia dates its local arrival to 1990.
- 1992 or 1995–1997 (Australia; sources differ) · Y60 (GQ) · RD28T · 2.8 L SOHC turbo-diesel I6 · 92 kW / 255 Nm (Wikipedia; 85 kW / 235 Nm in Australia per 4X4 Australia) · Five-speed manual only. CarsGuide dates it to the 1992 update; 4X4 Australia says 1995. Belt-driven cam, so it needs timing-belt services. Head gaskets suffer if it's thrashed.
- Early 1990s–1997 (Japan) · Safari (Y60) · TD42T · 4.2 L turbo-diesel I6 · — · Japan's Safari replaced the TD42 with the turbocharged TD42T. Wikipedia's Patrol article says 1991, its TD-engine article says 1993. Many have since been imported to the US under the 25-year rule.
- 1988–1994 · Ford Maverick (Australia) · 4.2 L petrol or diesel I6 · As Patrol · A Button-plan rebadge in base, XL and XLT trims. Mechanically a GQ.

### Year-by-year
- 1987: Y60 launches in Japan as the Safari (October/November). It's the first Patrol on coil springs: three-link live front axle, five-link rear on wagons. TD42 diesel and TB42 petrol 4.2 L sixes
- 1988: Australian (GQ) launch. Spanish production begins in Barcelona for Europe, where it's sold as the Patrol GR. Ford sells a rebadged version in Australia as the Maverick until 1994. Four-speed automatic added
- 1991: Japan gets the 7-seat Safari and the TB42E. Wikipedia's Patrol article says the turbo TD42T replaced the TD42 in Japan this year (its engine article says 1993). In Australia the rear lamps move into the bumper to meet ADRs, but not on European trucks
- 1992: Australian GQ Series 2: fuel injection for the TB42, oil cooler and EGR for the RD28T (in markets that had it), bigger brakes and wheels, standard limited-slip diff and auto-free-wheeling hubs, side-intrusion bars
- 1993: From August, the TD42 is lightened to save fuel and rev higher; Wikipedia says this weakened it. Early engines have a silver rocker cover and later ones a black one (Wikipedia's engine article dates the colour change to around 1995). Owners disagree on whether the difference matters in a stock truck
- 1994: Minor facelift with a new grille. Coil-sprung rear axle becomes an option on the utility, which previously had leaf springs
- 1995: 4X4 Australia dates the 2.8 L RD28T's Australian arrival to 1995 (CarsGuide says 1992); Wikipedia lists the RX grade from 1994–95. In Japan, Autech launches the Safari Adieu, a high-roof hearse conversion
- 1996–1997: Europe gets the LW, a lightweight-body version built for off-road championships. Wagons give way to the Y61 from late 1997; Australian UY60 cab-chassis sales run to 1999

### Capability
- Towing: 2,800 kg (6,173 lb) braked / 750 kg (1,653 lb) unbraked (1997 Australian ST, 4.2 L petrol manual)
- Fuel tank: 95 L (25.1 US gal) (1997 ST per CarExpert. Wikipedia gives 100 L for wagons, plus an optional 100 L second tank on the utility.)
- Curb weight: 2,100 kg (4,630 lb) (1997 ST. A 1991 Japanese Granroad is 2,110 kg.)
- Turning circle: 13.4 m (44 ft) (kerb to kerb, 1997 ST)
- Wheelbase: 2,400 mm (94.5 in) SWB / 2,970 mm (116.9 in) LWB

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 265/70R16 on 16x8 alloy (1997 Australian ST), 31x10.50R15 (Japanese Safari Granroad, 1991), 215/80R16 or 6.50R16LT on 16x6 steel (base and work models)
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Offset: about +5 mm on factory 7x15 and 8x16 wheels; about +30 mm on 6x16 steel
- Center Bore: 110.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M12x1.25
- Biggest tire, 2 in lift: 33x12.50R15 or 285/75R16 (NissanPatrol.com.au consensus: 'just about everyone with a 2" lifted GQ runs 33x12.5'. The front mud flaps (or their brackets) usually have to go, and 33x12.50s on -22 mm offset rims stick out past the factory flares. Narrower 33x10.50s avoid that. Expect some rubbing at full flex; some owners add radius-arm spacers.)

### Buying checks
- Rust first, everything else second: Forum veterans check the roof gutters, the sliding rear-window frames, the door sills and jambs, the front guards, the backs of the rear wheel arches and the upper firewall. Lift the rear carpets too, because sand under the mats can eat the floor pans. A freshly painted GQ can be hiding gutter and rear-quarter rust.
- Look for oil on the swivel hubs: Greasy gunk on the front swivels usually means the inner axle seal has failed and diff oil is getting past swivel seals that were never designed to hold oil. That's a front-axle teardown, so price it in. Look for oil on the brake backing plates as well, a sign of worn axle seals. CarsGuide adds that leaks from the rear diff seals are common on GQs, though regular servicing usually cures them.
- Drive it at 70–80 km/h (45–50 mph): Early GQs suffered a front-end shimmy at about 70–80 km/h. Most were fixed under warranty by removing knuckle shims to take out free play, but a worn truck can bring it back. Owners also report shakes around 110 km/h, so test at highway speed and check the tie rods, panhard rod and radius-arm bushes.
- Know which engine, and which rocker cover: The TD42 is the safe bet if it has been kept cool. A silver rocker cover means a pre-August-1993 engine, from before Nissan lightened it. Petrol TB42s and turbo RD28Ts have a history of head problems when worked hard. Ask about the cooling system, look for milky oil and coolant stains, and walk away from a truck that 'just needs a head gasket'.
- Open and close every door: If a door drops when you open it, the hinge pins are worn, a well-known GQ problem. Wikipedia also records cracking rear-door hinges from the weight of the spare. Both are fixable with hinge-pin kits or new genuine hinges, but they tell you how hard the truck has been used.
- Test 4WD in high and low range: Check that the free-wheeling hubs lock and unlock smoothly, then drive in 4H and 4L on dirt. One forum tip is a tight circle in low range, which should scrub the tyres. Listen for gearbox whine or clunks, check that it doesn't jump out of gear on overrun, and inspect the gearbox crossmember for rock damage. Wikipedia also records fifth-gear bearing failures in high-mileage European five-speeds.
- Be wary of automatics: Members of the NissanPatrol.com.au forum report trouble with GQ automatics, with rebuilds around A$3,000. The auto's cooler also sits inside the radiator, so a truck that overheats can cook its transmission too. A manual with a service history is the conservative choice.
- If it's lifted, check the details: On lifted GQs, confirm that the brake lines were extended, the rear load-proportioning valve was adjusted, and caster was corrected with offset radius-arm bushes. Bent rear lower control arms and stone-damaged rods suggest it has been driven hard.

### Common repairs
#### Swivel hub (kingpin) bearing and seal rebuild
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A full day per side for a first-timer · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Greasy gunk on the front swivel balls, steering that wanders, or play when you rock the top of the tyre with the wheel off the ground. On a GQ the swivel and CV bearings run in grease. If diff oil is leaking out of the swivels, the inner axle seal has failed.
Fix: Jack up and support the front, then remove the wheel, free-wheeling hub, CV circlip, brake caliper (hang it up, don't let it dangle), wheel bearings and hub. Unbolt the swivel housing from the axle, pull the CV and axle shaft, and replace the inner axle seal while it's out. Replace the upper and lower kingpin bearings and the swivel cap seals (owners often damage the caps on removal), then reassemble. Set kingpin preload with the factory shims and fit new wiper seals on the swivel ball. Repack with fresh grease and, if any diff oil was lost, top up the front diff.
Tools: Seal driver kit · bearing race drift · 54 mm hub-nut socket · circlip pliers · torque wrench · spring scale for preload · CV and high-temperature bearing grease. Work clean and keep the parts in order: forum members prefer a good pictorial to the Gregory's manual.

#### Front wheel bearing service
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours per side · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Rumble or growl that changes with speed, play at the wheel, or bearing grease slung onto the brake parts. It's also due whenever you rebuild the swivels.
Fix: Following a NissanPatrol.com.au how-to: support the front on stands and remove the wheel. Take off the free-wheeling hub, the CV circlip, the hub internals and the 'egg ring'. Unbolt the caliper and rest it on the swivel. Flatten the locking plate, undo the outer 54 mm bearing nut, remove the plate and the second 54 mm nut, then slide the hub and rotor off. Punch out the pressed-in races, remove the rear seal and bearings, then fit the new races, bearings and seal. Adjust bearing preload to the manual before locking the nuts. Don't rest the axle on the new seal during reassembly.
Tools: 54 mm hub-nut socket (the only special tool) · punch and hammer · seal driver · high-temperature bearing grease · brake cleaner. Some owners fit the later GU-style hub nut system in place of the GQ lock nut.

#### Cure the front-end shimmy
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–4 hours to diagnose and fix · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: The steering wheel shakes at about 70–80 km/h (45–50 mph), sometimes again around 110 km/h, and often after hitting a bump. CarsGuide notes early GQs did this from the factory.
Fix: Start with the cheap things: tyre balance, wheel bearings and tie-rod ends. Then check the panhard-rod bushes and the radius-arm bushes for splits and movement while a helper rocks the steering. CarsGuide says the factory fix on early trucks was to remove shims from the top and bottom of the steering knuckles to take out free play, so check kingpin preload. Replace anything worn, have the front end aligned, and fit a fresh steering damper last, since a damper hides worn parts rather than fixing them.
Tools: Pry bar · ball-joint/tie-rod separator · torque wrench · a helper on the steering wheel. Alignment afterward.

#### TD42 tappet adjustment and rocker cover reseal
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: A louder-than-usual top-end clatter, or an oily rocker cover. One forum member says the TD42's tappets want adjusting about every 20,000 km, and that poor early servicing leads to serious valve-train wear.
Fix: With the engine cold, remove the rocker cover. Turn the crank to TDC on cylinder 1 and adjust valves 1, 2, 4, 5, 8 and 9. Rotate to TDC on cylinder 6 and adjust 3, 6, 7, 10, 11 and 12. One forum member sets 0.35 mm at ambient temperature; confirm the intake and exhaust figures in the workshop manual. Fit a new rocker-cover gasket and breather seals, then refit the cover evenly.
Tools: Feeler gauges · ring spanner and screwdriver for the adjusters · large socket to turn the crank · new gasket kit.

#### Cooling system refresh (overheating prevention)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: The temperature gauge climbs on long climbs or when towing, the truck boils at low speed, or the clutch fan roars without cooling much. GQs have a reputation for heat, and an overheated head is the expensive end of that story. On automatics, the transmission cooler is inside the radiator.
Fix: Pressure-test the system and check the radiator for blocked cores. Replace the top and bottom hoses and the thermostat (TD42 trucks use a 76°C genuine unit). Inspect the water pump for weeping and the fan clutch for slip, and bleed the system properly. CarsGuide says most TD42 overheating is on modified trucks: aftermarket turbos add heat, front-mounted intercoolers and driving lights block airflow, and big tyres make the engine work harder. If the head has already been cooked, have it pressure-tested and checked for warp at a machine shop before refitting.
Tools: Cooling-system pressure tester · drain pan · hose pliers · new clamps · coolant (type per manual).

#### Re-pin dropping front doors
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours per door · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: The door drops when opened and has to be lifted to latch. Forum members call door hinges a common GQ problem; worn pins can be in either or both hinges.
Fix: Support the door on a jack with a block of wood, or with a helper. Drive out the old hinge pin, then press out the worn bushes and fit new pins and bushes, one hinge at a time so the door stays aligned. If the hinge itself is worn or cracked, fit a genuine replacement hinge set and adjust the door gaps before tightening.
Tools: Punch and hammer · vise or press · floor jack and wood block · grease.

#### RD28T timing belt service
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day for a first-timer · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: No warning before it breaks. Unlike the gear-driven TD42 and TB42, the RD28T's camshaft is belt-driven, so a truck with no receipts should be treated as due. Owners on ExplorOz report doing it at about 100,000 km; confirm the interval in the manual.
Fix: Use a kit that includes the tensioner and idler, because one owner found both noisy and loose once the old belt was off. Remove the fan, belts and harmonic balancer; soaking the crank bolt overnight helped one first-timer. Line up the timing marks, then fit the belt, tensioner, idler, and the crank and cam seals while you're in there. Forum members suggest replacing the balancer bolt in case it's torque-to-yield, and checking the Woodruff key. Wikipedia's RD-engine article warns that diesel vibration can loosen the crank/balancer bolt and recommends thread-locker on reassembly.
Tools: Harmonic balancer puller · crank-holding tool · breaker bar · torque wrench · seal puller.

#### Replace radius-arm and panhard bushes (with caster correction)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day to a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Clunks over bumps, vague steering, the shimmy above, or a lifted truck that wanders because the lift has reduced caster. One owner expects to replace the bushes, springs and clutch at around 200,000 km.
Fix: Support the chassis with the axle on a jack, then unbolt one radius arm at a time so the axle stays located. Press out the old bushes and press in new ones. On lifted trucks, fit offset caster-correction bushes at the diff end to restore caster. Do the panhard-rod bushes at the same time, torque everything at ride height, and get an alignment.
Tools: Hydraulic press or bush tool · floor jack and stands · long breaker bar · torque wrench.

### Baseline service
Assume nothing has been done unless there are receipts. On a GQ, the jobs that matter most are the cooling system, TD42 tappets, a timing belt on RD28T and RB30 engines, gear oils (with LSD oil in the rear), and the front swivels, which run in grease and quietly fill with diff oil when the inner seals fail. Capacities below are owner-reported figures from forum threads (grades quoted from Gregory's), so confirm them in a workshop manual for your engine.
- Engine oil & filter(s): 4.2 six: ≈8.2 L (one 1990 GQ DX owner's fill; engine type not stated). Grades quoted range from Gregory's 20W-40 to 15W-40 diesel oil [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Change now, then at short intervals for an old diesel [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (The TD42 uses two spin-on filters. HD Automotive's listing for the Ryco Z115 says two are required. TB42, RD28 and RB30 each take their own filter.)
- Air filter: Engine-specific element: oval for TB42 (and GU TD42 NA), cylindrical for RD28, separate EFI element for TB42E · Inspect every service; replace when dirty, sooner on dusty roads (Check the airbox seals and the snorkel joints too. A dusty diesel intake is how TD42s die young.)
- Fuel filter: Diesel: engine-bay filter on the driver's side (TD42/RD28). EFI petrol: in-line filter under the bonnet · Replace now [CONFIRM INTERVAL IN MANUAL] (Imported trucks may have sat for years. Drain water from the diesel filter and bleed the system afterward.)
- Valve clearances (TD42 tappets): One forum member sets 0.35 mm at ambient temperature [CONFIRM INTAKE/EXHAUST IN MANUAL] · A forum member suggests about every 20,000 km (TDC on cylinder 1: adjust valves 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 9. TDC on cylinder 6: adjust 3, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12. Fit a new rocker-cover gasket.)
- Glow plugs (diesel) / spark plugs (petrol): TD42: genuine single-pole glow plugs. RD28: its own plugs. TB42: genuine plug set · Test glow plugs now; replace spark plugs now on petrol trucks (A slow cold start on a diesel is usually glow plugs or the glow-plug relay before it's anything worse.)
- Timing belt (RD28T and RB30 only): Belt, tensioner and idler kit; TD42 and TB42 have gear-driven cams and no belt · Now if there are no receipts; ExplorOz owners report about 100,000 km [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Replace the crank and cam seals while you're in there, and consider a new balancer bolt.)
- Coolant, thermostat, hoses & belts: TD42 thermostat: genuine 76°C, part 21200-58G04 · coolant type [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush and refill now; hoses if they're original or soft (Overheating is the GQ's signature failure, and on automatics the transmission cooler is inside the radiator. Pressure-test the system and check the fan clutch.)
- Manual gearbox: 75W-90 GL-4 · ≈3.9 L (Gregory's, quoted by owners) · Change now (Owners describe the big gearbox behind the 4.2-litre engines as very strong; listen for whine and check the shifter boot for splits that let in water.)
- Automatic transmission (RE4R03A): ATF per manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Drain-and-fill now if there's no record (Rebuilds reportedly cost around A$3,000. Fix any cooling problems first, because the trans cooler is inside the radiator, and check the cooler lines for leaks.)
- Transfer case: 75W-90 GL-4 · ≈2.0–2.2 L (owner figures) · Change now (The front diff, gearbox and transfer case share one breather in the passenger guard. Make sure it isn't blocked.)
- Front differential: 80W-90 GL-5 (Gregory's) · ≈5–5.4 L (owner figures) · Change now, and after deep water crossings (If the front diff has been losing oil, check the swivels: a failed inner axle seal pushes diff oil into the grease-filled swivel hub.)
- Rear differential (LSD): LSD-rated gear oil; owners use 85W-140 LS · ≈2.5–3.0 L · Change now (Most GQs have a rear LSD. Use limited-slip oil or add a friction modifier if it chatters in corners. The stock rear breather vents near the fuel tank, so extend it.)
- Swivel hubs & front wheel bearings: Grease-lubricated CV and swivel bearings; kingpin preload set with shims · Inspect now; repack and reseal if there's any oil or play (Repack the wheel bearings with high-temperature grease. Greasy gunk on the swivel balls usually means a leaking inner axle seal, not a swivel seal.)
- Brake fluid, pads & hoses: Fluid type per the cap/manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]; twin-piston front calipers on EFI TB42E trucks, single-piston on non-EFI ones (per Patrolapart pad listings) · Flush now (If the truck has been lifted, check that the brake lines were lengthened and the rear proportioning valve was adjusted.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: 4X4 Australia says its 1988 GQ wore 31-inch all-terrains from the factory, and 31x10.50R15 or a similarly sized 16-inch tyre is the safe size on standard suspension. A 33 does fit 'into the GQ wheel arch, but only just', according to the Patrol 4x4 Club SA forum. On NissanPatrol.com.au, owners say 33x12.5s on zero-offset rims scrub the inner guards at full flex. The common recipe is a 2-inch lift with 33x12.5R15s on negative-offset wheels (owners quote -22 to -24 mm), which push the tyres out past the factory flares. Even then, expect some rub at full lock or full flex, often on the front mud-flap bracket.

Q: Which engine should I buy?
A: The TD42 diesel, if you can find a good one. It has a gear-driven cam, it's simple, and it's reputed to last half a million kilometres when serviced and kept cool. Early 'Silvertop' engines predate the August 1993 lightening that Wikipedia says weakened it. The TB42 petrol makes more power but is thirsty, and petrol heads crack, especially on LPG. The RD28T needs timing belts and dislikes being thrashed, and the RB30 is the economy option.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: No particular year. Guides and owners choose a GQ by engine, not by build date. 4X4 Australia says the TD42 was the outback tourers' favourite for its simplicity and 'legendary reliability', and NissanPatrol.com.au members say TD42s fetch a premium over the TB42 petrol and the smaller engines. Wikipedia notes that the RD28T and TB42 suffer head-gasket trouble when driven hard, and Perth dealer Westside Auto calls the RD28T underpowered for towing. Some owners prefer a pre-August-1993 'Silvertop' TD42, because Wikipedia says the lightened engine is weaker, but others say the black-tops are still very strong. Buy the best-kept TD42 manual you can find.

Q: What's a 'Silvertop' versus a 'Blacktop' TD42?
A: It's the colour of the rocker cover. Early naturally aspirated TD42s have silver covers. Wikipedia's Patrol article says Nissan lightened the engine in August 1993 to cut fuel use and raise its rev limit, which weakened it, and that the lightened engine wears a black cover. Its TD-engine article says turbo TD42s and non-turbo engines built after 1995 are black. CarsGuide adds that the later pistons were less tolerant of aftermarket turbo kits, and that owners cracked pistons by running too much boost.

Q: Does it have lockers?
A: Most Y60s have a rear limited-slip differential, and LSDs became standard with the 1992 Series 2 in Australia. Some variants had a factory vacuum or electric rear diff lock. For selectable lockers, ARB makes front and rear Air Lockers for the GQ. The rear version depends on your diff: H233 on most trucks, or H260 (34- or 37-spline) on leaf-sprung cab-chassis models.

Q: Can I legally bring one into the US?
A: The Y60 was never sold new in the US. Datsun dealers sold the older 60 Series only from 1962 to 1969. Every Y60 is now more than 25 years old, which puts it inside NHTSA's exemption from federal safety-standard compliance for vehicles at least 25 years old. Check EPA and state titling rules too. Bring a Trailer's Patrol page shows a steady stream of imported Y60 Safaris and Patrols, most of them right-hand-drive manuals.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: Not much. CarsGuide puts a TD42 at roughly 12–14 L/100 km on the highway (about 17–20 mpg), plus a couple of litres around town and much more when towing. The petrol sixes are thirstier still: 4X4 Australia's carbureted TB42 project truck needed extra fuel on the roof rack because 'the TB42 loves a drink'. All wagons have a 100-litre main tank, and long-range replacements are available.

Q: Why do GQs overheat, and how do I stop it?
A: CarsGuide says most TD42 overheating happens on modified trucks: aftermarket turbos add heat, intercoolers and driving lights in front of the radiator block airflow, and big tyres make the engine work harder. 4X4 Australia's TB42 project truck boiled on a long climb until it got a genuine radiator and a better fan. Keep the radiator clean, use the correct thermostat (76°C on the TD42), replace hoses and fan clutches, and watch the gauge.

Q: What oils and capacities does it take?
A: One owner on NissanPatrol.com.au quotes the Gregory's manual for his 1990 GQ DX 4.2 manual: 20W-40 engine oil, 75W-90 GL-4 in the manual gearbox and transfer case, and 80W-90 GL-5 in both diffs. His own fills were about 8.2 L of engine oil, 3.9 L in the gearbox, 2.2 L in the transfer case, 5.4 L in the front diff and 3.0 L of 85W-140 in the rear. Owners with LSDs use LSD-rated oil (85W-140 LS is common). A TD42 takes two oil filters. These are owner figures, not factory data, so confirm them in your workshop manual for your engine.

Q: Is a Ford Maverick the same truck?
A: Yes. Under Australia's Button car plan, Ford sold the Y60 as the Ford Maverick from the late 1980s to 1994, and Curbside Classic says the visual changes were limited to badging. It came as wagons, a ute and a cab-chassis in base, XL and XLT trims with the 4.2-litre sixes. Patrol parts suppliers list GQ parts as fitting the Maverick.

Q: GQ or GU: which should I buy?
A: 4X4 Australia describes the GU as essentially a GQ platform underneath, with a wider body, better refinement and about 230 kg more weight. It also brings the later TD42T and TB48 engines, but also the troubled ZD30 four-cylinder diesel. The GQ is lighter, simpler and usually cheaper, and much of the suspension and axle hardware is shared. See the Y61 GU page for the other side of the argument.

Q: Automatic or manual?
A: Manual, if you can. CarsGuide says every TD42 sold in Australia was a manual, and the RD28T and RB30 were manual-only. NissanPatrol.com.au members report problems with GQ automatics and rebuilds of around A$3,000. The auto's transmission cooler sits inside the radiator, so cooling problems become transmission problems.

## Nissan Patrol Y61 (GU) (1997–2016 (later in some markets))
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/nissan-patrol/y61/
Codes: Y61, GU, GR

Verdict: The GU is the Patrol that kept the solid axles and coils of the GQ, added a squarer body and spent nineteen years in Australian showrooms. Buy the right engine and it's one of the great touring wagons. Buy an early ZD30 without paperwork and you might be buying a set of pistons.

In December 1997 Nissan replaced the Y60 'GQ' with a Patrol that looked new but thought the same way. The Y61, sold as the GU in Australia and the Safari in Japan, kept a separate chassis, coil springs and a live axle at each end on the wagon, at a time when Toyota was giving the 100 Series independent front suspension. Nissan Australia sold 104,510 GU wagons and 37,112 cab-chassis between 1997 and October 2016, according to figures quoted by JDM Buy Sell, and Middle East production carried on into 2024. Few 4x4s have had a run that long.

### SAME RECIPE, SQUARER BOX
Underneath, the GU is an evolution of the GQ. Wikipedia notes larger CV joints, manual gearboxes with fewer synchros, and wider axle housings to suit the new body, with the same H233 and H260 differential centres. The five-door wagon rides on a 2,970 mm wheelbase, and some markets also got a 2,400 mm three-door. Body styles were the seven-seat wagon, a cab-chassis (the UY61 in Australia), sold with either a leaf-sprung or a coil-sprung rear, and a two-door pickup. Japan also got a two-door hardtop and a four-door van.
The engine list at launch covered every taste. Australian Series I trucks offered the 4.5-litre TB45E petrol six, the 2.8-litre RD28ETi turbo-diesel six, and the 4.2-litre TD42 diesel. The TD42T turbo-diesel joined the ST in 1999. CarsGuide notes that the RD28 had a timing belt, the TD42 timing gears, and the ZD30 and petrol sixes chains. Manuals were five-speeds: the FS5R30A behind the RD28 and the FS5R50B behind everything else.

### THE ZD30 PROBLEM
Series II arrived in 2000 with the engine that defines the GU's reputation: the 3.0-litre ZD30DDTi, a four-cylinder turbo-diesel with a Bosch VP44 pump, rated at 116 kW. It was cheaper than the 4.2 six and could be had with an automatic. CarsGuide says it 'has a history of breaking pistons due to poor engine management and boost spikes'. Too many engines died early, usually through a holed crown or a cracked ring land on the number three or four piston, and the fix was a bottom-end rebuild.
Nobody has published a definitive cause. The suspects are the EGR system upsetting the mixture and creating hot spots, oil from the crankcase vent fouling the mass-airflow sensor, and boost spikes from a slow-reacting turbo control. Nissan also originally specified 6 litres of oil. After reports of oil starvation it raised the capacity to 8.3 litres and told dealers to shorten and recalibrate the dipsticks. In September 2004 a Nissan service bulletin, quoted by owners on ExplorOz, also tightened the oil spec to ACEA B3 or JASO DH-1 with 10W-40 strongly recommended. Owners responded with what forums call 'engine saver' mods: boost and EGT gauges, catch cans, and in many cases a blanked EGR.

### SERIES BY SERIES
Series III, from late 2001, brought the 4.8-litre TB48DE petrol six, a DOHC 24-valve engine rated at 185 kW in Australia, and later the intercooled TD42Ti. The 2003 Japanese facelift is credited to Junichi Sakai. The big visual change came with Series IV in October 2004: boxy wheel-arch flares, new headlights, grille and tail-lights, a new interior, and 17-inch alloys on the ST and Ti. There was no Series V; the next update was GU VI in September 2007.
By 2007 the TD42 was gone (4X4 Australia says 2006; Wikipedia says the TD42Ti couldn't meet Euro IV for 2007), and a common-rail ZD30 became the only diesel, at 118 kW and up to 380 Nm. CarsGuide suggests that the common-rail system may have helped with the boost and mixture problems. Dual front airbags only became standard across the range that year. By the end in Australia, the 3.0 was the only engine left.

### THE LONG GOODBYE
The petrol-only Y62 reached Australia in 2013, so the GU stayed on sale beside it until 2016. It finished with the 300-unit Legend Edition: an ST with the common-rail 3.0, a rear diff lock, and $10,000 of genuine accessories including a steel bull bar with a Warn winch, a snorkel, a roof rack and a tow bar. Because the newer truck had no diesel, late GUs held their value. Wikipedia lists a worldwide phase-out in 2014, but sales continued in South Africa, the Middle East and parts of Africa, Asia and South America. Production reportedly ended in 2024.
Its rivals were Toyota's IFS 100 Series and its solid-axle 105, with the 70 Series as the cab-chassis alternative. The GU's case is simple: coil-sprung solid axles, a huge aftermarket and a truck that UN agencies and armies still drive. Pick the engine carefully and it can last for decades.

### Data plate
- Chassis: Y61 (wagon) · UY61 (AU cab-chassis)
- Built: Oct 1997 – 2024 (Japan; also Spain, South Africa, Morocco, Philippines, Pakistan)
- Australia: 1997–2016 · 104,510 wagons, 37,112 cab-chassis (per JDM Buy Sell)
- Wheelbase: 2,970 mm (5-door) · 2,400 mm (3-door, some markets)
- Suspension: Live axles on coils (wagon); leaf or coil rear (cab-chassis)
- Diffs: H233B / H260
- Petrol: TB45E 4.5 I6 · TB48DE 4.8 I6
- Diesel: RD28ETi 2.8 · ZD30DDTi 3.0 · TD42 / TD42T / TD42Ti 4.2
- Manual: FS5R30A / FS5R50B five-speed
- Auto: RE4R03A 4-sp · RE5R05A 5-sp
- Towing: Up to 3,500 kg braked (4.2 TD / 4.8 wagon)
- Japan Name: Nissan Safari

### Engineering
The GU is a traditional ladder-frame 4x4 with a beam axle and coil springs at each end on the wagon. The front axle is located by radius arms and a panhard rod, which is why lifted GUs need caster correction. Drive is part-time 4WD with low range and auto-locking free-wheel hubs as standard on many trucks. The engine range is the main thing that separates good GUs from expensive ones.
- Chassis: Ladder frame · 2,970 mm (5-door) / 2,400 mm (3-door, some markets) (Wagon, UY61 cab-chassis and two-door pickup. Cab-chassis trucks came with either leaf or coil rear suspension.)
- Suspension: Live axles on coils (wagon) (Radius arms and a panhard rod at the front. Lifts of about 2 in or more usually need caster-correction bushes. Series 2-on wagons use a different front panhard rod and bushes from GQ and early GU trucks (per Patrolapart's listings), so order for your build.)
- Differentials: H233B and H260 centres (Wider housings than the GQ, with the same centres. Some GUs have an H233B rear and some an H260, so check before you buy a locker.)
- 4Wd System: Part-time, dual range (Engaged mechanically (CarsGuide). Auto-locking hubs can unlock when you rock a stuck truck, so many owners fit manual hubs.)
- Engines: TB45E / TB48DE petrol; RD28ETi, ZD30DDTi, TD42 / TD42T / TD42Ti diesel (Output ranged from 91 kW for the non-turbo TD42 to 185 kW for the TB48 (Australian figures).)
- Gearboxes: FS5R30A / FS5R50B manual; RE4R03A 4-sp / RE5R05A 5-sp auto (The four-speed auto was offered with the TB45 and ZD30, and the five-speed auto with the TB48.)

### Versions
- 1997–1999 (Series I) · Y61 / UY61 · TB45E 4.5 petrol · RD28ETi 2.8 TD · TD42 4.2 D · TD42T (from 1999) · 145 kW · 95 kW · 91 kW · 114 kW · Australian launch range. RD28 was manual only.
- 2000–2001 (Series II) · Y61 · ZD30DDTi 3.0 TD (Bosch VP44) · 116 kW · Automatic available. The non-turbo TD42 reportedly left the wagon range. This is the ZD30 era to check most carefully.
- Late 2001–2004 (Series III) · Y61 · TB48DE 4.8 petrol · TD42Ti (2003) · 185 kW (TB48, Australia) · ST-L petrol added in mid-2003; intercooled TD42Ti (114 kW / 360 Nm) from 2003.
- Oct 2004–2007 (Series IV) · Y61 · Carry-over range · — · Facelift with box flares, new headlights, grille and tail-lights, a new interior and 17-in alloys on ST and Ti. Revised 180 kW / 400 Nm TB48 from February 2006 (GoAuto). There was no Series V.
- 2007–2016 (Australia) · Y61 / UY61 · ZD30 3.0 common-rail TD · 118 kW / 380 Nm (manual), 354 Nm (auto; 4X4 Australia quotes 345 Nm) · TD42 dropped because it couldn't meet Euro IV. Dual airbags standard from 2007. Ended with the 300-unit Legend Edition.
- 1997–2024 (Middle East, Africa, etc.) · Y61 Patrol Safari / Super Safari · TB48DE 4.8 · ZD30 3.0 · 280 hp SAE gross (TB48, 2017 brochure) · Built in Japan until 2024. Rear diff lock on the Super Safari.

### Year-by-year
- 1997: Y61 (GU) launches in late 1997. Widened diff housings around the same H233/H260 centres, bigger CVs, better seats and NVH. Engines: TB45 petrol, RD28ETi turbo-diesel and naturally aspirated TD42
- 1999: TD42T turbo-diesel added (to the ST in Australia). It's mechanically injected with no electronic engine control. CarsGuide calls the TD42 turbo-diesel 'the pick of the Patrol engines from this era' [buy]
- 2000: GU II (April): 3.0 L four-cylinder ZD30DDTi diesel arrives with an optional automatic. The naturally aspirated TD42 reportedly left the wagon range around this time. Early ZD30s (2000–2003 in Westside Auto's guide) are known for piston and bottom-end failures [avoid]
- 2001: GU III (October): new nose and the 4.8 L DOHC TB48DE petrol six (185 kW / 420 N·m)
- 2003: Factory-intercooled TD42Ti arrives, with electronic injection timing from February. ST-L grade added. 4X4 Australia rates its reliability and simplicity for remote travel, and Westside Auto names the 2005–07 TD42T ST and ST-L as the GU's sweet spot [buy]
- 2004: GU IV facelift (October): new headlights, box flares and larger tail lights. Wikipedia credits this refresh with fixing the ZD30's variable-geometry-turbo trouble
- 2006: Revised 180 kW / 400 N·m TB48 from February (GoAuto). 4X4 Australia and Marque News date the end of the TD42 family in Australian GUs to 2006; CarsGuide and Wikipedia say 2007
- 2007: GU VI (September; there was no GU V): the common-rail ZD30 is the only diesel, and Wikipedia says the TD42Ti couldn't meet Euro IV. Westside Auto calls the common-rail engine improved, but CarsGuide's Q&A still fields piston-failure questions from owners of 2008–09 ZD30s, so there's no clean cut-off
- 2010–2013: GU VII from early 2010. In Australia the petrol models are replaced by the Y62 in February 2013, and the diesel GU carries on alongside it
- 2016: Australian run ends with the ST-based Legend Edition, limited to 300 units. Production for the Middle East, Africa and fleet buyers continued into 2024

### Capability
- Towing: 3,500 kg (7,716 lb) braked (2003 ST 4.8 L manual); 3,200 kg (7,055 lb) braked / 750 kg unbraked (2012 ST 3.0 L manual) (Australian spec. The 2016 Legend Edition is rated 3,200 kg (manual) or 2,500 kg (automatic).)
- Payload: about 480 kg (1,060 lb) (GVM minus kerb weight: 3,060 − 2,581 kg (2012 ST 3.0) and 3,000 − 2,516 kg (2003 ST 4.8))
- Fuel tank: 95 L main plus 30–36 L sub-tank (25.1 + 7.9–9.5 US gal) (2003 and 2012 Australian ST; the Middle East Super Safari has a 40 L sub-tank)
- Ground clearance: 210 mm (8.3 in) (unladen, Australian ST)
- Approach / departure: 37° / 31° (Australian ST)
- Fuel economy: 10.9 L/100 km combined (about 21.6 US mpg) (ADR 81/02, 2012 ST 3.0 L diesel manual)
- Curb weight: 2,516 kg (5,547 lb) for the 2003 ST 4.8; 2,581 kg (5,690 lb) for the 2012 ST 3.0
- Turning circle: 12.5 m (41 ft) (kerb to kerb, LWB wagon)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 235/80R16 on 6x16 steel (base fitment), 275/70R16 on 16x8 alloy (2003 Australian ST), 275/65R17 on 17x8 alloy (2012 ST; 2016 Legend Edition), 265/75R16 (Australian cab-chassis)
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Offset: about +35 mm (6x16 steel); about +10 mm (8x16 and 8x17 alloy)
- Center Bore: 110.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M12x1.25
- Lug Torque: 118–147 N·m (87–108 lb-ft)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 265/75R16 (popular); 285/75R16 fits (ExplorOz owners call 265/75R16 the best size for a stock GU. Others run 285/75R16 (about 33 in) on stock height without trouble.)
- Biggest tire, 2 in lift: 285/75R16 or 33-inch (Expect to trim or remove the front mud flaps, and the rear-door spare may need a spacer to clear the bar. 315s and 35s scrub without more lift or offset wheels.)
- Biggest tire, 3 in lift: 285/75R16 (Fits fine. 315s will scrub at full lock. At 4 in, owners run 315/75R16 on wheels with about 20 mm more offset.)

### Buying checks
- Identify the engine and series first: Make sure the engine and gearbox match the build date and series. A 'Series III ZD30' and a 'Series IV TB48' are different buys. A ZD30 sold as 'overhauled' should come with an itemised list: head, bores, pistons, bearings and rings, not just new pistons and a turbo.
- ZD30: demand oil history and check the dipstick: Look for regular oil changes and the right grade: a September 2004 Nissan bulletin, quoted by owners, calls for ACEA B3 or JASO DH-1 oil with 10W-40 strongly recommended. Nissan Europe's Y61 service manual schedules ZD30 oil and filter every 15,000 km or 12 months, or every 7,500 km or 6 months in severe use such as towing, dust or short trips. Check your own market's service book; many owners change it more often. Fuel in the oil is bad news. One forum veteran says heavy soot within 5,000 km points to an open EGR, and another warns that factory intercoolers eventually leak, so check for oil staining. Listen for knocks on a cold start.
- Cooling under load: Every GU engine can overheat when towing, and the TD42 has a particular reputation for it. Check the radiator core, the foam seals between condenser and radiator, and the fan clutch (it should drag and turn only about half a revolution when cold). Watch the temperature gauge on a long climb.
- Manual gearbox: Drive through every gear. Owners report fifth-gear spline and hub problems and worn 2nd-to-3rd synchros on the five-speed.
- Rear axle seals, diffs and underbody: Put it on a hoist. Look for wet rear backing plates from leaking axle seals, bash plates pushed up into what they're meant to protect, and damage to sills and bumpers. Find out whether the rear diff is an H233B or an H260 if you plan to fit a locker.
- Cab-chassis: look behind the cab: ExplorOz members report cracks in GU cab-chassis frames just behind the cab and near the rear axle on heavily loaded trays, repaired by plating. Check under any big service body.
- Rear barn door and dash: Owners report cracks in the big rear door that carries the spare, down the side of the window on the left-hand side. Dashboard tops can blister; Nissan Japan extended the warranty to seven years on specified wagons built August 2004 to June 2007.
- Previous lift work: A lifted GU that wanders or steers vaguely probably needs caster correction. Lifts of about 3 in or more also need longer panhard rods, drag-link changes and longer brake lines. Ask what was fitted and whether it was certified.

### Common repairs
#### ZD30 'engine saver' setup (gauges, oil level, breather)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day to a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: None until a piston fails, usually number three or four. Warning signs include high EGTs when towing, boost spikes or drops under load, sooty oil, and oil consumption.
Fix: Make sure the dipstick and service fill reflect Nissan's revised 8.3-litre capacity (a Nissan representative quoted on ExplorOz advised 9 litres at a change), use ACEA B3 or JASO DH-1 10W-40 oil, then check the oil daily on hard trips. Fit a boost gauge and a pyrometer (EGT gauge) and learn what's normal. One owner saw 300–450 °C at highway speed with the EGR working and about 600 °C on a steep climb at full throttle. Back off before EGTs climb. Fit a catch can so crankcase oil doesn't reach the intake and MAF sensor, and keep the MAF clean. Blanking the EGR is common but disputed: one owner saw lower highway boost and higher EGTs after blanking it and refitted the valve. It is also an emissions device, so check your local rules.
Tools: Pyrometer probe drilled into the exhaust manifold (pre-turbo) · boost gauge tee into the intake · catch can kit · MAF cleaner

#### Front wheel bearing service and hub seals
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours per side · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Play in the wheel when rocked top to bottom, grinding, grease on the inside of the rim, or an auto hub that runs hot after a drive.
Fix: Put the axle on stands and remove the wheel. Set the auto-locking hub to LOCK, remove its six 8 mm Allen bolts and pull the hub. Undo the two 22 mm caliper (torque member) bolts and tie the caliper out of the way. Remove the snap ring, washer and thrust ring, the lock-washer screws and lock washer, then the bearing lock nut. Pull the hub, catching the outer bearing, then lever out the seal and remove the inner bearing. Clean and repack both bearings, and fit a new seal. On reassembly, the Gregory's manual quoted on ExplorOz says to torque the lock nut to 167–196 Nm while rotating the hub, back it off, retighten to 3–5 Nm, then check the preload with a spring gauge (0–18.6 N starting force). Nissan's own Y61 service manual (FA section) gives the same figures, with zero axial end play. A Lonard's procedure gives different figures, so follow the Nissan ones.
Tools: 8 mm Allen key · 22 mm socket and breaker bar · GU hub-nut socket · circlip pliers · seal driver (the old seal flipped over works) · wheel-bearing grease · spring gauge

#### Cure overheating under load (TD42 and others)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2 hours to a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Temperature gauge climbs when towing or climbing in fifth gear on hot days, and the A/C cuts out because of the radiator temperature sensor.
Fix: Clean the radiator core thoroughly. Owners note that blocked internal tubes won't clear with a flush, so a recore or new radiator may be needed. Refit or replace the foam seals between the condenser and radiator so air can't bypass the core. Check the viscous fan clutch: when cold it should drag and spin only about half a turn. Check that the underbody air dam and wheel-well rubbers are in place, especially on lifted trucks. Fit a new thermostat and coolant at the correct mix. Fit an EGT gauge and drive by it: drop from fifth to fourth when towing, and back off when temperatures climb past what you've learned is normal. One ZD30 owner sees 300–450 °C at highway speed and about 600 °C on a long, steep climb.
Tools: Radiator brushes and fin comb · coolant pressure tester · EGT gauge

#### Caster correction after a lift
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day (bushes) to a full day (arms) · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Light, wandering steering that won't self-centre after a suspension lift.
Fix: Lifting a radius-arm front axle rotates it and reduces caster. One owner with a nominal 2 in kit (closer to 3 in in practice) fitted 2° caster-correction bushes and reported a clear improvement. Press the old radius-arm bushes out at the chassis end and press in offset bushes, set to add caster. For lifts of about 3 in or more, forum members also recommend an adjustable or longer panhard rod to re-centre the axle, drag-link changes and longer brake lines. Get a wheel alignment afterwards. Series 2-on wagons use a different front panhard rod from GQ and Series 1 trucks, so order for your build.
Tools: Bush press or a shop press · jacks and stands · alignment afterwards

#### Rear axle seal and bearing leak
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day per side · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Wet backing plate or inner rim, oily brake shoes or pads, a falling diff oil level.
Fix: Rear axle oil seals are a known GU leak. Drain or lower the diff oil, remove the wheel and brake, and undo the axle retainer. Pull the axle with a slide hammer, then replace the inner oil seal in the housing. If the bearing is rough, have the bearing and collar pressed off and on at a shop. Clean contaminated brake parts or replace them, refit the axle and refill with LSD-rated gear oil if the diff is a limited-slip. Nissan's Y61 service manual specifies Nissan Hypoid LSD gear oil (KLD31-14002), or API GL-5 SAE 140 with 10% by volume of LSD friction modifier (38469-C6000), which matches what an owner quoted on ExplorOz. A non-LSD diff takes API GL-5, with 80W-90 preferred in cold and warm climates.
Tools: Slide hammer · seal puller and driver · access to a press · brake cleaner

#### Fit a rear locker
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A full day (setup is critical) · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Not a fault. The rear LSD on many GUs isn't enough on rocky climbs and cross-axle ruts.
Fix: First find out which rear diff you have. Harrop's GU ELocker and the Detroit H233 unit suit the H233B only, and the GU used both H233B and H260 rear centres. Remove the axles and carrier, swap the ring gear onto the locker, and fit new carrier bearings. Set preload and backlash and check the tooth pattern before refilling. Air lockers need a compressor and air line, and electric lockers need wiring to a dash switch. Shops usually do this, because a bad setup ruins the ring and pinion.
Tools: Bearing puller and press · dial indicator · inch-pound torque wrench · marking compound

#### Swap auto-locking hubs for manual hubs
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Front drive drops out when you rock a stuck truck back and forth. CarsGuide notes this is a known trait of the auto hubs.
Fix: With the axle on stands, remove the six Allen bolts holding each auto hub (as in the bearing service above), pull the hub assembly and fit the manual hub kit according to its instructions. Check the bearing preload while you're there. Run both hubs in LOCK whenever you're in 4WD.
Tools: 8 mm Allen key · circlip pliers · grease

### Baseline service
Assume nothing has been done without receipts. On a GU, the job that matters most depends on the engine. A ZD30 needs proof of frequent oil changes and the revised oil level. A TD42 needs a cooling system that can cope with towing. Every GU needs the diff, transfer and hub servicing that bush trucks skip. Fluids and capacities below come from Nissan's Y61 service manual unless marked. Its maintenance schedules are the European ones, so check your own market's service book, and fill to the plug rather than by volume.
- Engine oil & filter: ZD30: ACEA B3 or JASO DH-1, 10W-40 strongly recommended (Nissan bulletin, Sept 2004), revised capacity 8.3 L. TB48: owner's manual says 5W-30. Nissan's 2002 service manual: ZD30 outside Europe API CD, CE, CF, CF-4 or JASO DH-1 (in Europe API CF-4 or ACEA B3; never API CG-4), 8.2 L with filter. TD42/TD42T: API CC to CF-4 or JASO DH-1, 10.5 L with filter. TB45: 7.6 L, and TB48DE: 6.8 L with filter (petrol API SE to SL or ILSAC). Nissan Europe's 2004 supplement prefers 5W-30 for diesels there, so the grade depends on market and climate · Nissan Europe schedule: ZD30 and TB48 every 15,000 km or 12 months, RD28 every 10,000 km or 6 months, halved in severe use such as towing, dust or short trips. Other markets: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]. Many owners change ZD30 oil more often when towing (On a ZD30, confirm the dipstick has been recalibrated to the revised capacity. Sludge or grit under a cold oil filler cap is a bad sign.)
- Air filter & MAF sensor: Dry element; engine-specific (check the listing for your engine) · Inspect at every service, more often in dust (On the ZD30, oil on the MAF sensor (from crankcase venting or an over-oiled aftermarket filter) is a suspected cause of bad fuelling. Clean it with MAF cleaner and consider a catch can.)
- Diesel fuel filter: ZD30: spin-on filter with water-drain cock. Screw it on until it seats, then turn a further 2/3 of a turn, and bleed the air afterwards (Nissan service manual) · Replace at purchase. Nissan Europe schedule: ZD30 every 45,000 km or 36 months (every 22,500 km in dusty or extreme conditions); RD28 every 40,000 km. Drain the water trap regularly (Early ZD30s are known for fuel-pump and fuel-system trouble (the Bosch VP44 pump), and clean fuel is cheap insurance.)
- Glow plugs (diesels): [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Test if cold starts are slow (Worn glow plugs are a common cause of hard starting on older diesels.)
- Timing drive: RD28: belt. ZD30 and TB45/TB48: chain. TD42: gears · RD28 belt: Nissan Europe's schedule replaces it at 80,000 km or 48 months (90,000 km for high-mileage use). Replace it if there's no record (Only the 2.8 RD28 has a belt to budget for. Wikipedia warns the RD's crank/balancer bolt can work loose, so use thread-locker on reassembly.)
- Coolant, radiator & fan clutch: Ethylene-glycol Nissan Genuine Engine Coolant or equivalent (L2N in Europe), at a 50% mix (Nissan's L2N comes premixed; 50% protects to −35 °C). Capacity with front heater ≈ 12.7–13.2 L (ZD30), 15.1 L (TD42), 12.0 L (TB45), 13.0–13.8 L (TB48) (Nissan service manual) · Flush and refill at purchase. Nissan Europe: first at 90,000 km or 60 months, then every 60,000 km or 48 months (Clean the core, refit the condenser foam seals and check the fan clutch (about half a turn when cold). This matters most on a TD42 that tows.)
- Manual gearbox oil: API GL-4. Nissan's service manual lists the FS5R30A at 5.1 L (75W-90), and the FS5R50B at 3.8 L in the 1998 edition (also the handbook figure quoted on ExplorOz) but 3.5 L in the 2001–02 supplements, which give 75W-90 and then 75W-85. Check which gearbox you have before filling · Change at purchase (Check the fifth gear and the 2nd-to-3rd shift while you're under there. Both are known weak spots.)
- Automatic transmission fluid: ≈ 3–4 L drains from the pan, about 12 L total (2001 ZD30 owner). Nissan service manual: 4-speed RE4R03A 11.8 L with converter, Genuine Nissan ATF or equivalent (Dexron III/Mercon); TB48 5-speed RE5R05A 10.4–10.7 L, Nissan Matic Fluid J only · One owner cites Nissan at 40,000 km for ATF (A pan drain changes only about a third of the fluid. Do several drain-and-fills, or have a transmission shop exchange it through the cooler line (about 16 L).)
- Transfer case: ≈ 1.9 L (handbook figure, and also quoted by a 2001 ZD30 owner as Dexron III). Nissan's service manual confirms the TX12A transfer at 1.9 L, Genuine Nissan ATF (Dexron III) or API GL-4 (75W-90 preferred) · Change at purchase (Nissan schedules it with the LSD oil: replace every 60,000 km (30,000 km when towing or on rough roads). Don't mix ATF and gear oil; drain fully if you switch.)
- Front & rear differentials: Front ≈ 5.4 L (Nissan service manual; also the handbook figure on ExplorOz). Rear: 2.1 L with LSD (outside Europe); H233B 2.4 L open or 3.0 L with diff lock; H260 4.7 L open or 3.7 L with lock (Nissan service manual; the older ExplorOz handbook figure is also 2.1 L). Open diffs take API GL-5, with 80W-90 preferred in cold and warm climates. An LSD takes Nissan Hypoid LSD gear oil (KLD31-14002) or API GL-5 SAE 140 plus 10% LSD friction modifier (38469-C6000); owners also use 85W-140 LSD oil · Change at purchase and after deep water crossings (CarsGuide says hard-used GUs need regular diff oil changes. Note whether your rear is an H233B or an H260.)
- Front wheel bearings, hubs & swivels: Repack with wheel-bearing grease. Nissan's service manual (and Gregory's, quoted on ExplorOz): lock nut to 167–196 Nm while rotating, back off to zero, retighten to 3–5 Nm twice, preload 0–18.6 N at a hub bolt, zero end play. Repack the axle joint with NLGI No. 2 lithium grease · At purchase, then Nissan Europe replaces the grease every 30,000 km on the ZD30 schedule (40,000 km on the 1998 RD28 schedule), and after water crossings (CarsGuide also recommends lubricating the front swivel joints on hard-used trucks. Auto hubs should be warm, not hot, after a drive.)
- Brakes & brake fluid: DOT 3 (Nissan service manual, outside Europe); DOT 3 or DOT 4 in Europe. Never mix the two · Flush at purchase, then every 2 years (Nissan Europe schedule) (Check for gear oil on the rear brakes from leaking axle seals, and that the calipers clear your wheels. Caliper sizes vary by year.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: 265/75R16 is the popular stock-height size on ExplorOz, and some owners run 285/75R16 (about 33 in) on 16-inch rims. One owner runs 305/70R16 on a 2004 GU with only a 'tiny' scrub at full lock in reverse. Bigger sizes such as 305/70R17 and 35s are generally reported with at least a 2 in lift and the mud flaps removed. Many GUs won't take 15-inch rims over their brakes. In Australia, check your state's current limit on tyre-diameter increases; owners note Nissan sold a replacement tyre placard for 265/75R16.

Q: Which engine should I buy?
A: CarsGuide says it would be 'very leery of any RD28 or ZD30-powered example, especially if it has covered a lot of kilometres', and that the 4.2 diesel and petrol sixes 'seem to offer a better package'. It names injection-pump failures and blown head gaskets as the RD28's problems, and calls the petrols 'guzzlers'. Owners describe the TD42T as very reliable if it's kept cool and full of oil.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: For a touring diesel, the TD42 years. CarsGuide calls the TD42 turbo-diesel 'the pick of the Patrol engines from this era', and Westside Auto names the 2005–07 TD42T ST and ST-L as the GU's sweet spot for reliability. The TD42T arrived in 1999 and the intercooled TD42Ti in 2003, and Australian sources date the end of the TD42 to 2006 or 2007. Be wary of 2000–2003 ZD30s. In the Gulf, where petrol GUs dominate, CarSwitch rates the 2008–10 Safaris as the most refined Y61s.

Q: Is the ZD30 really that bad, and which years were fixed?
A: Nobody agrees on a cut-off and no failure rate has been published. Typical failures are a holed or cracked number three or four piston, and Nissan raised the oil capacity to 8.3 L and recalibrated the dipsticks. Perth dealer Westside Auto says the 2000–2003 engines earned the reputation for 'grenading' and calls the 2007-on common-rail engine improved. One forum veteran says most bugs were ironed out by 2003, but CarsGuide was still answering piston-failure questions about 2008 and 2009 ZD30s in 2022 and 2025. Many high-mileage ZD30s run fine. Buy on service history and condition, not on the year alone.

Q: Should I blank the EGR on a ZD30?
A: It's the most argued-about ZD30 mod. Some owners blank it to keep soot out of the intake and report quicker spool. Others have seen highway boost drop and EGTs rise after blanking it, and refitted it. If you do it, fit boost and EGT gauges so you can see the effect. The EGR is an emissions control device, so check your local roadworthiness rules.

Q: How much can a GU tow?
A: CarsGuide lists braked towing limits of 3,500 kg for the 4.2 turbo-diesel and 4.8 petrol wagons, 3,200 kg for the 3.0 diesel wagon, 3,140 kg for the 4.5 petrol, 2,800 kg for the 2.8 diesel, and up to 2,500 kg for the cab-chassis and ute, all with a suitable heavy-duty towbar. The 2016 Legend Edition is rated at 3,200 kg as a manual and 2,500 kg as an auto.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: Nissan Australia quoted 17.2 L/100 km (ADR combined) for the 4.8-litre petrol, and CarsGuide expects at least 15 L/100 km on a highway cruise from the petrols and 20-plus in town. A 2010 common-rail ZD30 DX cab-chassis is listed at 12.5 L/100 km combined (15.9 urban, 10.5 highway), and the 2012 ST manual wagon at 10.9 L/100 km. A loaded touring truck on big tyres will use more.

Q: Does it have lockers?
A: Japanese Safaris had a rear LSD as standard from September 1999, and later Australian cab-chassis list an LSD as standard. A factory rear diff lock is documented on the 2016 Legend Edition and the Middle East Super Safari. For everything else, ARB Air Lockers, Harrop ELockers and Detroits are the usual upgrades. Check whether your rear diff is an H233B or an H260 before you order.

Q: What oil does a ZD30 take, and how much?
A: Nissan's September 2004 service bulletin, quoted by owners on ExplorOz, requires ACEA B3 or JASO DH-1 oil and strongly recommends 10W-40. The capacity was raised from 6 L to 8.3 L, and dealers recalibrated the dipsticks, so make sure yours has been done and fill to the revised mark. A Nissan representative quoted on ExplorOz advised using 9 L at changes and checking the oil daily when working hard. Confirm the change interval in your handbook.

Q: How do I tell the series apart?
A: Series I–III (1997–2004) have the original smooth arches and smaller tail-lights; GU III (October 2001) got a new nose. The October 2004 Series IV facelift added box-style flares, new headlights, grille and tail-lights, and 17-inch alloys on the ST and Ti. There was no Series V; GU VI arrived in September 2007 and GU VII in 2010. A diesel GU built from 2007 has the common-rail ZD30, because the TD42 had gone by then.

Q: Can I import one to the US or Canada?
A: The US 25-year exemption counts from each vehicle's month of manufacture, so early GUs from 1997 to 2001 are now eligible. EPA rules also require the original engine configuration or a certified replacement. Canada's limit is 15 years. Bring a Trailer has sold several Y61-era Safaris and Patrols.

Q: Why does the front drive drop out when I'm stuck?
A: CarsGuide says the standard auto-locking hubs 'have the potential to disengage when, for instance, rocking back and forth to free a stuck vehicle'. That's why many owners fit manual hubs and lock them whenever they're in 4WD. The GU's transfer case is engaged mechanically, so follow the owner's-manual procedure for shifting into 4WD.

## Nissan Patrol Y62 / Armada (2010–present)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/nissan-patrol/y62/
Codes: Y62, Z62, Armada (2017–2024)

Verdict: The Y62 traded the Patrol's live axles for a 5.6-litre V8, independent suspension and a clever hydraulic anti-roll system, and the Gulf loved it for it. Americans got the same truck as the Armada, minus the locker and the clever bits, which makes it the most capable family hauler nobody takes off-road.

Nissan launched the sixth-generation Patrol, the Y62, in Abu Dhabi on 13 February 2010, which tells you who it was built for. It broke with six decades of Patrol tradition. The Y61 it replaced kept solid axles at both ends, as had every Patrol before it, from the leaf-sprung 160/MQ to the coil-sprung Y60. The Y62 got independent suspension at all four corners, a direct-injection 5.6-litre V8 and an optional hydraulic system whose rams do the work of both dampers and anti-roll bars. In North America the same truck became the Infiniti QX56 in 2010 and the Nissan Armada for 2017–2024.

### A V8 AND FOUR INDEPENDENT CORNERS
The engine is the VK56VD, rated at 298 kW at 5,800 rpm and 560 Nm at 4,000 rpm in the Patrol, according to 4X4 Australia. Wikipedia says entry-level trims first used a 236 kW VK56DE V8 and, from 2017, a 4.0-litre VQ40DE V6 with 205 kW. All models have had a seven-speed automatic since 2017. Early entry trims offered a five-speed automatic or a six-speed manual. There's no diesel, which South Africa's Cars.co.za lists as one of the truck's weaknesses.
Underneath is a separate frame with a two-speed transfer case. Patrolapart describes the Y62's 4WD as an electronic multi-plate clutch unit that needs Nissan's ATX 90A fluid. The driver picks Auto, 4H or 4L, plus Sand, Rock and Snow modes. Non-US trucks have a rear differential lock and hill descent control, and Cars.co.za lists a helical limited-slip rear diff as well. 4X4 Australia's tester praised the wheel travel, low range and traction control, and grumbled that the traction control switches off when the rear locker is engaged.

### HYDRAULIC BODY MOTION CONTROL
HBMC is the Y62's party trick. Nissan's description: the hydraulic cylinders at each wheel are cross-linked by pipes in two circuits, so when the truck leans into a corner, fluid from the outside cylinders flows into an accumulator and raises roll stiffness. Off-road, each wheel is free to rise or drop with the ground. Nissan says it needs no power source, so it costs nothing in fuel. 4X4 Australia puts it more simply: the rams act as both the shock absorbers and the sway bars. Wikipedia says Nissan developed it and tested it on the Patrol in the Middle East.
The catch arrives when you want to lift it. On NissanPatrol.com.au, one owner's research found that HBMC front springs can't be swapped on their own, only as complete shock-and-spring units, and another watched his rear end sink three inches under 280 kg of ball weight. Ontrack's 2-inch lift kits for HBMC trucks are designed to fit without disturbing the system's pressure. When Nissan Australia and Premcar built the 2023 Patrol Warrior, they kept HBMC and re-valved it. Not every Y62 has it: Wikipedia says the Gulf-market Desert Edition used conventional suspension, and the US Armada never offered it.

### BUILT FOR THE GULF
The Y62 went on sale in Dubai on 1 April 2010. By mid-May, dealer Arabian Automobiles had delivered more than 450 and was taking desert-safari operators dune-bashing in them. Nissan claimed more than 13,000 hours of testing in local deserts. It paid off. In The National's 2013 report, Nissan Middle East said Patrol sales had grown 66 per cent in a year, to more than 14,000 across the region, giving it 22 per cent of the Gulf SUV segment.
The love has lasted. Bestselling Cars Blog reports the Patrol was the UAE's best-selling vehicle of 2024, its first win since 2020. Gulf Business's 2024 interview with Nissan's Middle East chief calls it 'a cultural symbol'. Gulf buyers got grades from XE to LE Platinum City, plus a Nismo with 319 kW, Bilstein dampers and 22-inch forged wheels, launched in Dubai. Japan, oddly, never got the Y62 new. Wikipedia says it was export-only, and most Y62s in Japan are reverse-imported US Armadas.

### THE ARMADA YEARS AND WHAT CAME NEXT
Nissan showed the second-generation Armada in Chicago in 2016, and it went on sale that August as a 2017 model, built in Kyushu alongside the Patrol. It had a 390 hp VK56VD and a seven-speed automatic, and a 2021 refresh added 10 hp and 19 lb-ft. AutoGuide reported that US buyers didn't get the Patrol's locking differentials, disconnecting sway bars or HBMC, and that the US truck had its own suspension tuning. What it kept was the frame, low range and 8,500 lb of towing. It was the first Patrol-based Nissan sold in America since the 60 Series left in 1969.
The Y62 had a 2014 facelift, a heavier one in 2019 (the Armada's came for 2021) and limited editions such as the 2021 Middle East 70th Anniversary. Australia got the Warrior in 2023, with a 50 mm lift, 295/70R18 Yokohama all-terrains and 323 mm of ground clearance. Its successor, the Y63, was unveiled in Abu Dhabi on 3 September 2024 with V6 engines, including a 425 hp twin-turbo, and a nine-speed automatic. Its Armada twin went on sale in the US that December. Wikipedia says the Y63 reaches Australia in November 2026, so the Y62 is still on sale in some markets as this is written.

### Data plate
- Chassis: Y62 (Infiniti twin: Z62)
- Launch: 13 February 2010, Abu Dhabi
- Built By: Nissan Shatai, Japan (Armada: Kanda, Kyushu)
- Engine: VK56VD 5.6 L V8 (VK56DE / VQ40DE on entry grades)
- Output: 298 kW / 560 Nm · Armada 390–400 hp
- Gearbox: 7-speed automatic (RE7R01A)
- 4Wd: Auto / 4H / 4L, with Sand, Rock and Snow modes
- Suspension: Independent all round; HBMC optional
- Ground Clearance: 272–273 mm (Patrol) · 323 mm (Warrior)
- Fuel Tank: 140 L (Patrol)
- Towing: 3,500 kg (Patrol) · 8,500 lb (Armada)
- Us Version: Nissan Armada, 2017–2024

### Engineering
The Y62 is still a body-on-frame truck with a real low range, but it's the first Patrol with independent suspension at both ends. The big V8, the seven-speed automatic and a clutch-type transfer case are shared across the Patrol, Armada and Infiniti QX56/QX80. The rear locker and the HBMC hydraulics are what separate a Gulf or Australian Patrol from a US Armada.
- Chassis: Body-on-frame · independent suspension all round (Built by Nissan Shatai in Japan; the Armada in Kanda, Kyushu.)
- Engine: VK56VD 5.6 L V8 · 298 kW / 560 Nm (Armada: 390 hp, then 400 hp from 2021.)
- Gearbox: RE7R01A 7-speed automatic (Nissan Matic-S fluid (Patrolapart).)
- 4Wd System: All-Mode 4x4: Auto / 4H / 4L (Sand, Rock and Snow modes; ATX 90A transfer fluid.)
- Diffs: Electronic rear locker + helical rear LSD (Patrol only; the US Armada has neither locker.)
- Suspension: HBMC hydraulic roll control (Cross-linked rams and accumulators; not on the Armada or Desert Edition.)

### Versions
- 2010– · Patrol Y62 (V8) · VK56VD 5.6 L V8 · 298 kW / 560 Nm · Main Gulf and Australian engine; 7-speed auto.
- 2010–c. 2017 · Patrol Y62 entry grades · VK56DE 5.6 L V8 · 236 kW / 526 Nm · Five-speed auto or six-speed manual on early entry trims (Wikipedia).
- 2017– · Patrol Y62 XE / SE (Middle East) · VQ40DE 4.0 L V6 · 205 kW / 394 Nm · Entry-level V6 grades.
- 2010s– · Patrol Nismo (Gulf) · VK56VD 5.6 L V8 · 319 kW (428 hp) · Bilstein dampers, 22-in forged wheels; facelifted in 2021.
- 2017–2020 · Armada (US) · VK56VD 5.6 L V8 · 390 hp / 394 lb-ft · No lockers or HBMC; 2WD or 4WD; regular fuel per EPA.
- 2021–2024 · Armada (US) refresh · VK56VD 5.6 L V8 · 400 hp / 413 lb-ft · New nose and C-shaped LED lights; EPA lists premium fuel.
- 2023– · Patrol Warrior (Australia) · VK56VD 5.6 L V8 · 298 kW / 560 Nm · Premcar conversion: 50 mm lift, 295/70R18 tyres, re-valved HBMC.

### Year-by-year
- 2010: Y62 launched in Abu Dhabi on 13 February and on sale in the UAE from 1 April; Infiniti QX56 (Z62) brings the platform to North America
- 2010–2012: Early trucks: CarSwitch flags transmission valve-body issues and early fit-and-finish problems [avoid]
- 2013: Patrol Y62 launched in Australia
- 2014: First facelift (June): revised tail lights and LED headlights

- 2016: Second-generation Armada (Y62) on sale in the US in August as a 2017 model; Series 3 Patrols get an electronic thermostat from February
- 2017: VQ40DE V6 for entry Middle East grades; seven-speed automatic standard across the range
- 2019: Second Patrol facelift with a new front end and Nissan Intelligent Mobility driver aids. CarSwitch and Westside Auto rate these 2020-on facelift Patrols as the most desirable used Y62s [buy]
- 2021: Armada refresh (on sale January): new nose, 400 hp, premium fuel per EPA; Middle East 70th Anniversary edition in December
- 2023: Patrol Warrior by Premcar in Australia: 50 mm lift, 295/70R18 tyres, re-valved HBMC
- 2024: Y63 unveiled in Abu Dhabi (3 September); third-generation Armada on sale in the US in December

- Towing: 3,500 kg (7,716 lb) Patrol · 8,500 lb (3,856 kg) Armada (Braked; Cars.co.za, 4X4 Australia, AutoGuide)
