- Ground clearance: 272–273 mm (10.7 in) Patrol · just over 9 in Armada · 323 mm Warrior (Cars.co.za, 4X4 Australia, AutoGuide)
- Approach / breakover / departure: 34.3° / 24.4° / 26.2° (South African Patrol (Cars.co.za))
- Fuel economy: EPA 13 city / 18 hwy / 15 combined (Armada 4WD) · 14.4 L/100 km ADR (Patrol) (4X4 Australia averaged 15.2 L/100 km on test)
- Curb weight: 2,884 kg (6,358 lb) Warrior (72 kg more than the Ti it's based on (4X4 Australia))
- Payload: 736 kg (Warrior) (4X4 Australia)
- GVM: 3,620 kg (Warrior, +120 kg over standard) (4X4 Australia)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 265/70R18 (Australian Ti; 2017 Armada SV), 275/60R20 (2017 Armada SL and Platinum), 275/50R22 (22-in wheel packages), 295/70R18 (2023 Patrol Warrior)
- Bolt Pattern: 6x139.7 (6x5.5")
- Offset: +40 mm (factory)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 275/70R18 (Listed by 6061 Works as a mild upgrade, about 15 mm taller than stock. We couldn't verify an owner consensus for anything bigger.)
- Biggest tire, 29 mm (Warrior) lift: 295/70R18 (Nissan Australia and Premcar's factory-backed combination, with re-valved HBMC.)
- Biggest tire, 2 in lift: 295/70R18 (6061 Works' recommendation after a 2-in lift; offsets of +18 to +25 mm suit wider tyres.)
- Biggest tire, 2 in + regear lift: 35 in (Nissan sells front and rear crown-wheel-and-pinion sets for Y62s on 35s (Patrolapart).)

### Buying checks
- Shift quality: CarSwitch says the RE7R01A seven-speed in early Y62s (2010–2014) has a reputation for valve-body problems, costing AED 5,000–12,000 to fix in the UAE. Test for harsh shifts, delayed engagement and shudder between second and third. One Australian owner reported his Y62 holding gears under hard acceleration while towing, even after a warranty transmission.
- Signs of a hard desert life: CarSwitch's desert checklist: gouged skid plates and crossmembers, compacted sand in the frame rails and behind the inner guard liners, fine sand in the air filter, and ABS, stability or TPMS warnings on a cold start.
- Patrol or Armada?: A US Armada has no rear locker, no disconnecting sway bars and no HBMC (AutoGuide). If you want a locker, you're shopping for a Patrol, and a Y62 Patrol isn't old enough to import into the US under the 25-year rule.
- HBMC and lift kits: If the truck has HBMC, ask what's been done to it. One owner found HBMC front springs only come as complete shock-and-spring assemblies, and HBMC-specific kits such as Ontrack's are designed to fit without disturbing the system. Look for wet hydraulic lines and fittings at each corner and a truck that sits level.
- Modifications and warranty: Cars.co.za advises avoiding heavily modified examples. One NissanPatrol.com.au member was told by his dealer that drivetrain problems wouldn't be covered after a lift.
- Towing history: Owners report the rear of an HBMC truck sagging under heavy ball weights. Many towing rigs have airbag kits designed for HBMC. A transmission cooler or deep pan is a good sign on a truck that has towed.
- Armada recalls: Check the VIN with NHTSA. The 2020–2021 Armada fuel-pump recall (21V373) replaces a pump whose impeller can swell and stall the engine. The 2026 campaign 26V455 corrects the axle-weight label on Armadas with 22-inch wheels.
- Brakes and tyres: It's a heavy truck (a Warrior weighs 2,884 kg). Cars.co.za notes the weight wears brakes and tyres quickly, so check pad and rotor thickness and tyre wear before you price the truck.

### Common repairs
#### Automatic transmission fluid and filter service
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Harsh or late shifts, flare between gears, or fluid that's dark and smells burnt, especially on a truck that tows.
Fix: The RE7 seven-speed uses Nissan Matic-S fluid and has its filter inside the pan. Drain the fluid, drop the pan, replace the filter and pan gasket, clean the pan and refit it. Refill with Matic-S through the fill plug and set the level using the procedure in the workshop manual, which depends on fluid temperature [CONFIRM PROCEDURE IN MANUAL]. Owners who tow often fit a deeper cast pan (Patrolapart's adds 3 L) and an auxiliary cooler.
Tools: Socket set · drain tray · fluid pump · scan tool or thermometer for fluid temperature · torque wrench

#### Fit an auxiliary transmission cooler
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 3–4 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: High transmission temperatures when towing, climbing or crawling in sand.
Fix: Mount the cooler core ahead of the radiator using the kit's brackets, route the supplied hoses into the transmission cooler circuit, and clamp everything clear of the fan and exhaust. Top up the fluid afterwards. The kit's maker suggests adding about 1 L of full-synthetic fluid. Run the engine, check for leaks and recheck the level.
Tools: Socket set · hose cutter · clamps · drip tray

#### Brake pads and rotors
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours per axle · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Squealing or grinding, a brake warning light, pedal pulsation, or stopping that feels weak under load.
Fix: Support the truck, remove the wheels, unbolt the caliper and carrier, and hang the caliper so the hose isn't stretched. Fit new rotors and pads with the supplied shims and hardware. Clean and grease the slide pins, push the pistons back carefully, torque the carrier and caliper bolts to the manual, then bed the pads in. Genuine Nissan front and rear kits each come with four pads.
Tools: Jack and stands · caliper piston tool · torque wrench · brake cleaner

#### No-start: brake light switch
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 30 minutes · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: The push-button start won't crank the engine, often along with brake lights that don't work.
Fix: With push-button start, the truck needs a signal that the brake pedal is pressed before it will start. Patrolapart says that signal comes from the brake light switch on the pedal assembly. Check the brake lights first. If they don't work and the truck won't start, unplug the switch at the pedal, remove it, fit the new one and set its adjustment to the manual before reconnecting.
Tools: Torch · basic hand tools · multimeter

#### Front wheel hub and bearing
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2 hours per side · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: A hum or grinding that rises with road speed, vibration through the wheel, or an ABS light.
Fix: The Y62's front bearing comes as a hub assembly with the bearing pre-greased and the ABS speed sensor attached. Patrolapart's unit fits either side. Remove the wheel, caliper and rotor and the axle nut, unplug the ABS sensor, unbolt the hub from the knuckle and fit the new assembly. Torque the hub bolts and axle nut to the manual.
Tools: Axle nut socket · breaker bar · torque wrench · puller if the hub is seized

#### Serpentine belt and tensioner
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Squeal from the front of the engine, a vibrating belt, or a cracked or glazed belt.
Fix: Note the belt routing before you start. Rotate the automatic tensioner to release the tension and remove the belt. Check the tensioner and idlers for noise and wobble, and replace the tensioner if it's weak. The belt drives the alternator, power steering pump and A/C compressor, so a failure can mean losing power steering and charging. Fit the new belt and release the tensioner slowly.
Tools: Long-handled ratchet or belt tool · torch

#### Thermostat and water pump
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2–4 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Overheating, an engine that runs cold, an erratic temperature gauge, or coolant weeping from the front of the engine.
Fix: Know your series first. Patrolapart lists an 82°C thermostat that needs no gasket for Series 1 and 2 trucks, and an electronically controlled thermostat assembly for Series 3 trucks from February 2016. Drain the coolant, replace the thermostat (and the water pump and its separate gasket, if it's leaking or noisy), refill with Nissan blue long-life coolant and bleed the system.
Tools: Socket set · drain tray · coolant funnel · torque wrench

#### Front inner CV boot
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 3 hours per side · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Grease flung around the inside of the wheel or on the suspension, or a clicking CV joint on full lock.
Fix: Replace a split boot before dirt gets into the joint. Remove the driveshaft from the hub and diff, cut off the old boot, clean out the old grease, pack the joint with the sachet of CV grease supplied, and fit the new boot and clamps. Patrolapart says lifted trucks put extra strain on the boots.
Tools: Axle nut socket · CV clamp pliers · circlip pliers · torque wrench

### Baseline service
A used Y62 has usually done one of three jobs: school runs, desert weekends or towing a caravan across Australia. Baseline everything, and pay special attention to the transmission and transfer-case fluids, which are model-specific. The oil, plug, diff and brake-fluid specs below are from Nissan USA's owner's manuals for the Armada, the US-market Y62. Patrols sold elsewhere may specify different grades, so check your own manual.
- Engine oil & filter: 6.5 L with filter, 6.2 L without (2018 and 2020 US Armada owner's manuals; Penrite's Australian Patrol data also gives 6.5 L) · Armada grade: Nissan Motor Oil 0W-20 SN, or a synthetic 0W-20 GF-5 SN (2020 manual) · Patrol grade outside the US [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Nissan spin-on filter (shared with the Y61 TB45/TB48) · Baseline now (The same genuine filter fits the GU's petrol sixes and the Y62's VK56.)
- Air filter: Genuine VK56 element; Donaldson or Ryco for aftermarket airboxes · Replace now; check after every sandy trip (CarSwitch says fine sand in the filter is a sign of hard desert use.)
- Cabin filter: Pollen filter above the heater fan · Replace now (A clogged filter cuts airflow and strains the fan.)
- Spark plugs: Eight plugs, genuine Nissan or NGK equivalent · Armada manual lists DILKAR7B11, gap 1.1 mm · replace every 105,000 mi (168,000 km), or sooner if the gap exceeds 1.35 mm · Replace if no record (Misfires can damage the catalytic converters.)
- Coolant & thermostat: Nissan blue long-life coolant, 50/50 premix · Flush if no record (Series 1–2 trucks use an 82°C thermostat; Series 3 on (from 02/2016) use an electronic thermostat assembly.)
- Automatic transmission fluid & filter: Nissan Matic-S; filter inside the pan · Service now if no record; more often if towing (Early 2010–2014 trucks have a reputation for valve-body problems (CarSwitch). Fresh fluid is cheap insurance.)
- Transfer case: Nissan ATX 90A · 1.5 L service refill · Change now if no record (The Y62's electronic multi-plate clutch transfer case needs the specified fluid.)
- Front & rear differentials: Armada manual: front Nissan Hypoid Super GL-5 80W-90 (conventional, not synthetic); rear Hypoid Super-S GL-5 75W-90 synthetic (2018) or Hypoid Fluid S1 GL-5 75W-80 (2020) · front 1.6 L, rear 2.3 L (Penrite, Australian Patrol) · rear has a helical LSD and, on Patrols, an electric locker: Patrol rear grade [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Change now if no record, and after deep water. The Armada schedule says to change it every 20,000 mi (32,000 km) or 24 months when towing or driving rough or muddy roads. (Extend the breathers before wading.)
- Brake fluid, pads & rotors: Nissan Super Heavy Duty Brake Fluid or equivalent DOT 3 (Armada manual) · replace every 20,000 mi / 24 months (2018 schedule) or 30,000 mi / 36 months (2020 schedule); every 10,000 mi / 12 months in severe use · Flush now; measure pads and rotors (The weight wears brakes quickly (Cars.co.za).)
- Serpentine belt & tensioner: Single belt drives the alternator, power steering and A/C · Inspect now (Replace the tensioner if the belt squeals or vibrates.)
- HBMC system (if fitted): Inspect the rams, lines and accumulators at each corner · Inspect now (Look for wet fittings and check the truck sits level. Lifted trucks should have an HBMC-specific kit.)
- CV boots & ball joints: Inspect the inner and outer boots and all four ball joints · Inspect now (Split boots let in grit fast, especially on lifted trucks.)
- Battery: Driver's-side main battery, N70 size (Patrolapart) · Load-test now (Load-test it and check the terminals; replace with the correct N70 size.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: We couldn't find a solid owner consensus for a stock Y62. Stock is 265/70R18 on Australian Patrols and the Armada SV, or 275/60R20 on higher grades. 6061 Works lists 275/70R18 as a mild upgrade, about 15 mm taller than stock. For 295/70R18, Nissan's own Warrior needed a 29 mm suspension lift, and 6061 Works recommends that size after a 2-inch lift. Nissan sells re-gear sets for trucks on 35s.

Q: Is the Armada the same truck as the Patrol?
A: The 2017–2024 Armada shares the Y62's frame and powertrain and is built alongside it in Japan. AutoGuide reported that the US version lacked the Patrol's locking differentials, disconnecting sway bars and HBMC, and had its own suspension tuning.

Q: Can I import a Y62 Patrol into the US?
A: Not yet, unless it was built to US standards. NHTSA's 25-year exemption counts from the date of manufacture, so the earliest 2010 Y62 Patrols become eligible around 2035. Until then the Armada is the US-legal Y62.

Q: What is HBMC, and does it stop me lifting the truck?
A: Hydraulic Body Motion Control cross-links hydraulic rams at each wheel through accumulators, so they act as both dampers and anti-roll bars. You can lift an HBMC truck, but you need a kit designed for it. One owner says HBMC front springs only come as complete assemblies, and Ontrack's 2-inch kits are designed to keep the system's pressure intact.

Q: Which years should I buy or avoid?
A: CarSwitch, a UAE used-car marketplace, rates 2015–2017 trucks as the value sweet spot and the 2020–2021 facelifts as the best recent buys. Perth dealer Westside Auto calls the 2020-on facelift Patrols the most desirable on the used market. CarSwitch suggests caution with 2010–2012 trucks because of transmission valve-body problems and early fit-and-finish issues. In the US, run any 2020–2021 Armada's VIN for the fuel-pump recall.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: The EPA rates every 2017–2024 Armada 4WD at 13 mpg city, 18 highway and 15 combined. In Australia the official Patrol figure is 14.4 L/100 km, and 4X4 Australia averaged 15.2 L/100 km on test, or about 12 to 13 on the freeway.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: 3,500 kg braked for the Patrol (Cars.co.za, 4X4 Australia) and 8,500 lb for the 2017 Armada (AutoGuide). Owners of HBMC trucks report rear sag under heavy ball weights, and airbag kits are made specifically for HBMC suspension.

Q: Does it need premium fuel?
A: The EPA lists regular fuel for 2017–2020 Armadas and premium for the 2021–2024 trucks with the 400 hp tune.

Q: Was there a diesel?
A: No. The Y62 was sold with petrol V8s and, in some markets, a 4.0 V6. Cars.co.za lists the lack of a turbo-diesel among its weaknesses.

Q: What transmission fluid does it take?
A: Nissan Matic-S in the seven-speed automatic, and Nissan ATX 90A in the transfer case. Patrolapart gives the transfer-case service refill as 1.5 litres.

Q: What replaced it?
A: The Y63 Patrol, unveiled in Abu Dhabi on 3 September 2024, with a 3.8 V6 or a 3.5 twin-turbo V6 (425 hp, 700 Nm) and a nine-speed automatic. The matching Armada went on sale in the US in December 2024, and Wikipedia says Australia gets the Y63 in November 2026.

# Land Rover Range Rover (1970–present)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/

The Range Rover arrived in June 1970 as "A Car For All Reasons": a 100-inch-wheelbase, coil-sprung, permanently four-wheel-drive wagon with an all-alloy Rover V8 and aluminium panels hung on a steel frame. It was conceived as something a Land Rover owner could also drive to dinner, and it accidentally invented the luxury 4x4 in the process. Five generations later, the name has drifted steadily up-market. The Classic (1970–1996) and the P38A (1994–2002) kept a separate ladder chassis and live axles; the L322 (2002–2012) went monocoque with all-independent air suspension and BMW-shared hardware; the L405 (2012–2021) went all-aluminium; and the L460, revealed in October 2021, added a seven-seat option, plug-in hybrids and a BMW-sourced 4.4 V8. For BoxyTrucks readers, the sweet spot is the old stuff. The Classic is the one you can fix in a driveway with hand tools, a Rovers North catalogue and a forgiving spouse. The later trucks remain astonishingly capable off-road, but they are rolling networks of sensors and air springs — wonderful when right, ruinous when not.

Verdict: The truck that taught a farm tool to wear a suit — and, for its first quarter-century, never forgot where it parked its wellies.

## Land Rover Range Rover Classic (1970–1996)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/classic/
Codes: RRC, LSE / County LWB

Verdict: The original luxury 4x4, with the soul of a farm truck. Buy the rust-free one and you'll forgive it everything — buy the shiny rusty one and it'll teach you to weld.

In June 1970, Rover launched a two-door wagon with a 100-inch wheelbase, long-travel coil springs, permanent four-wheel drive, disc brakes at every corner and an all-alloy 3.5-litre V8 — and called it "A Car For All Reasons." Nobody had built anything quite like it. It would cross a ploughed field at lunchtime and the M1 at teatime, and it would go on doing so for 26 years and 326,070 examples. The Range Rover Classic is the reason "luxury SUV" is a phrase. Happily for us, under the walnut it is still a ladder frame, two beam axles and a V8 you can fix with spanners.

### A WAGON IN DISGUISE
The project began in 1967 as the "100-inch Station Wagon", led by Charles Spencer "Spen" King with Gordon Bashford, with David Bache shaping the body. Prototypes wore "Velar" badges — from the Latin velare, "to veil or cover", according to Land Rover — to keep the press guessing. The recipe was radical for a Land Rover: coil springs rather than leaf springs, a Buick-derived all-alloy V8, and aluminium body panels hung on a steel frame. It was so well resolved visually that in 1971 a quarter-scale model took a leading role in the 'Idea and Form' design exhibition at the Musée des Arts Décoratifs, in the Louvre's Pavillon de Marsan — which Land Rover still bills as the first vehicle displayed at the Louvre.
For its first 11 years the Range Rover was a two-door only, with a rubber-and-vinyl interior. The four-door finally arrived in July 1981, and two-door UK sales ended in 1984, although two-door production carried on until January 1994, mostly for France. Through the 1980s the truck crept upmarket: Lucas electronic fuel injection replaced carburettors in 1986, the ZF four-speed automatic joined the range, and the luxury Vogue badge became the template for everything that followed.

### AMERICA, LONG WHEELBASES AND AIR
A US launch was first pencilled in for mid-1971 at $5,300, but federal regulations and British Leyland's finances killed it. Grey-market importers (including Aston Martin's US arm) filled the gap until the factory US model was officially introduced at the Los Angeles Auto Show in January 1987, with imports beginning on 16 March. Only four-doors came over, through Baltimore and Long Beach, and in 1988 Playboy named it the "Best 4x4" — which tells you exactly which crowd the marketing department was chasing.
The engine grew with the image: 3.9 litres for the 1989 model year, and 4.2 litres in 1992 for the new long-wheelbase model, sold as the LSE in Britain and the County LWB in the US. That truck stretched the wheelbase to 108 inches and introduced electronic air suspension, which reached customers in late 1992 for the 1993 model year. The last big change was the "soft dash" of the 1995 model year, which replaced the original hard-plastic dashboard owners nicknamed the "Airfix dash" and was derived from the facelifted Discovery's dashboard, with Rover 800 switches.

### WHAT MADE IT SPECIAL
The Classic's party trick was articulation with comfort. Long-travel coils on beam axles let it flex like a farm truck yet ride like a saloon, and the permanent 4WD with a dual-range transfer box meant there was no lever-pulling panic when the mud arrived. Early trucks used the LT95 four-speed with an integral transfer box; from 1983 the five-speed LT77 got a separate LT230 transfer case, and from 1989 a chain-driven Borg Warner unit with a viscous coupling replaced the manually locked centre differential. Range Rovers won the first Paris–Dakar in 1979 and won again in 1981, and in 1987 a Turbo D set speed and endurance records, including 24 hours at over 100 mph.
The engineering also trickled down. The coil-sprung, permanent-4WD layout was carried into the One Ten and Ninety — later the Defender 90/110 — which also borrowed the Range Rover's 3.5 V8 and, initially, its LT95 gearbox. And in 1989 Land Rover built the Discovery on the Range Rover's 100-inch chassis with a cheaper interior and a smaller diesel. Every boxy Land Rover of the next three decades owes something to Spen King's wagon.

### THE LONG GOODBYE
The successor, internally P38A, was unveiled in September 1994 as the "New Range Rover" — and the old truck refused to leave. Renamed the "Range Rover Classic", it stayed in production alongside the P38A until 1996, with the 1995 County and County LWB marking the final US model year. Today the Classic sits in the odd spot of being both a collector car and a genuinely useful trail truck. Hagerty UK says values rose almost tenfold over a decade, with Velar prototypes and early two-doors at the top. But the bones that matter — frame, axles, coils, V8 — remain refreshingly agricultural, and that is exactly why it still belongs on a trail.

### Data plate
- Built: 1970–1996 · Solihull, UK
- Production: 326,070
- Body: 2-door (1970–94), 4-door (1981–96)
- Chassis: Steel ladder frame, alloy panels
- Wheelbase: 100 in · 108 in (LSE / County LWB)
- Suspension: Coil springs, live axles · EAS 1993+
- Engines: Rover V8 3.5 / 3.9 / 4.2
- Diesels: VM 2.4/2.5 · 200Tdi · 300Tdi (non-US)
- Gearboxes: LT95 4-spd · LT77 5-spd · TorqueFlite 3-spd · ZF 4-spd auto
- Transfer: LT95 integral · LT230 · Borg Warner w/ viscous (1989+)
- Towing: 3.5 tons
- Us Sales: 1987–1995, four-door only

### Engineering
Underneath the Vogue badges, the Classic is pure Land Rover: a steel ladder frame, live axles front and rear on long-travel coil springs, permanent four-wheel drive through a two-speed transfer box, and an all-alloy V8. The body is unstressed aluminium panels on a steel frame — the panels don't rust, the steel under them does. That simplicity is why so many survive, and why the hard parts (frame, crossmembers, sills) are where your money goes.
- Chassis: Steel ladder frame (100 in (2,540 mm) wheelbase; LSE / County LWB stretched to 108 in (2,743 mm) from 1992.)
- Body: Aluminium panels on a steel frame (Unstressed alloy skins; the steel frame, sills and floors are the rust risk.)
- Suspension: Coil springs, live axles (Long-travel coils from day one; electronic air suspension on 1993-on LWB and some upper trims.)
- Drivetrain: Permanent 4WD, two-speed (LT95 with integral transfer; LT77 + LT230 from 1983; chain-drive Borg Warner with viscous coupling from 1989.)
- Engine: Rover all-alloy V8 (3.5 (carb, then Lucas EFI from 1986), 3.9 from 1989, 4.2 for LWB from 1992. VM and Tdi diesels outside the US.)
- Brakes: Four-wheel discs (Disc brakes at all four corners from launch; ventilated fronts and ABS added around 1990.)

### Versions
- 1970–1985 · 100-in, 2-door (4-door from 1981) · 3.5 V8, carburettors · 135 hp (101 kW) at launch · LT95 4-speed with integral transfer box; power steering added 1973; 5-speed LT77 from 1983.
- 1986–1989 · 100-in, 2/4-door · 3.5 V8, Lucas EFI · 110 kW (Australian spec) · EFI and ZF 4-speed auto; US imports start March 1987 (4-door only).
- 1986–1992 · 100-in, non-US · VM 2.4 then 2.5 turbo-diesel · — · VM Motori diesel; Turbo D set 24-hour records at over 100 mph in 1987.
- 1989–1995 · 100-in, 4-door · 3.9 V8 EFI · 130 kW claimed (Australian spec) · Borg Warner chain transfer with viscous coupling; ABS arrives.
- 1992–1995 · 108-in LSE / County LWB · 4.2 V8 EFI · Nearly 200 hp · Electronic air suspension (1993 MY on); soft dash for 1995.
- 1992–1996 · 100-in, non-US · 200Tdi, then 300Tdi (from late 1994) · — · Land Rover's own direct-injection diesels; keep the timing belt current.

### Year-by-year
- 1970: Launched in June as a two-door: carburettored 3.5 Rover V8 (135 hp), coil springs, four-wheel discs and permanent dual-range 4WD with a manual centre diff lock.
- 1973: Power steering added.
- 1981: Factory four-door arrives in July, following approved conversions such as Monteverdi's.
- 1983: LT77 five-speed and separate LT230 transfer box replace the LT95 combined box.
- 1985: ZF four-speed automatic replaces the three-speed Chrysler TorqueFlite; new instrument pod.
- 1986: Lucas fuel injection replaces carburettors in most markets; VM 2.4 Turbo D diesel launched for Europe; facelift with plastic slatted grille.
- 1987: Factory US imports begin 16 March 1987 — four-door only.
- 1989: 3.9 V8 replaces the 3.5; Borg Warner chain transfer case with a viscous-coupling centre diff replaces the manually locked unit; VM diesel grows to 2.5.
- 1992: 108-in LSE (UK) / County LWB (US) with the 4.2 V8; Land Rover's own 200Tdi replaces the VM diesel.
- 1993: Electronic air suspension arrives on high-end 1993 model-year trucks (mainly LWB). Rides beautifully; pumps, sensors and valve blocks fail, and many have since been coil-converted.
- 1994–95: Renamed 'Classic' alongside the new P38A; Discovery-derived 'soft dash' fitted to run-out trucks; 300Tdi replaces 200Tdi late 1994.
- 1996: Production ends after 26 years.

### Capability
- Towing: 3.5 tons (claimed at the 1970 launch)
- Fuel tank: 81.8 L (21.6 US gal) (1992 3.9 V8)
- Fuel economy: EPA 11 city / 15 hwy / 13 combined (1990 3.9 automatic; 1995 County LWB 4.2 rated 11/15/12)
- Wheelbase: 100 in (2,540 mm); LWB 108 in (2,743 mm)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 205R16 on 6J x 16 (ET33), 235/70R16 on 7J x 16 (ET33)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x165.1 (5x6.5")
- Offset: ET33 (stock steel/alloy, 31–35 mm range)
- Center Bore: 114.3 mm
- Lug Thread: M16x1.5 per wheel-spec databases [CONFIRM ON YOUR STUDS — not verified against a factory source]
- Lug Torque: 96 lb-ft (130 N·m)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 245/75R16 (Fits on stock coils once the steering stops are adjusted to stop rubbing at full lock; some owners squeeze in 265/75R16 with slight chassis rub cured by the stops.)
- Biggest tire, 2 in lift: 235/85R16 or 265/75R16 (Owners on a 2-in OME lift run either size with no trimming. Expect to wind the steering stops out; the 265s cost turning circle and some owners needed longer stop bolts to stop them hitting the radius arms.)

### Buying checks
- Get under it before you look at the paint: The aluminium skins hide a steel frame. Check body mounts, the rear crossmember, frame sides, inner rear wheel arches, inner front wings and both sills. Pre-1983 trucks are mostly bolted together and easier to repair.
- Lift the carpets and open the boot: Owners say to check under the front carpets for floor rot. Boot floors are suspect on post-1989 trucks, and the steel upper tailgate commonly rusts.
- Listen to the V8: Listen for bottom-end knocks and timing-chain rattle. Look for weeping head gaskets — cheap if caught early — and be wary of anything that hints at a slipped liner, which means a rebuild.
- Test the viscous coupling (1989-on): Tyres scrubbing or chirping on tight, slow turns means the centre viscous coupling may have seized, turning the truck into a permanently locked 4x4. With the transfer case in neutral and the handbrake on, a jacked front wheel should turn slowly with resistance — not stay locked solid.
- Interrogate the air suspension: On EAS trucks, pumps, height sensors and valve blocks fail and leak, and few parts are shared with the later P38A system. Many have been converted to coils — fine, as long as it was done with a proper kit.
- Look for oily swivels: Leaking swivel-ball seals are chronic. Check the chrome balls for pitting and wet seals, and confirm the swivel housing has its own lubricant; it is separate from the front diff.
- Check the small electrics: Window switches and seat controls often fail (usually cheap). On cars with electric seats, a leaking battery can kill the seat ECU and stop seats and mirrors moving.
- Ask about LPG and the timing belt: One UK specialist recommends removing LPG conversions because they are often poorly fitted and can harm the engine. On 200Tdi and 300Tdi diesels, get proof the timing belt was changed in the last five years.

### Common repairs
#### Swivel ball seal replacement and regrease
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Varies · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Oil weeping from the swivel housings onto the chrome balls and wheels; the truck rolling while in park can mean a CV joint ran dry and failed.
Fix: Remove the bracket that retains the swivel seal on the back of the hub. Cut out the old seal (Dremel or heavy side cutters). Pull the spring from the new seal and cut the seal so it can be wrapped around the axle housing, then refit it with the cut at the top, rejoin the spring, and seal the cut with silicone. Let it cure for a day, drain the old oil, and refill the swivel with the correct Land Rover swivel grease. For peace of mind, strip and repack the CV joints too (owners estimate 3–4 hours).
Tools: Dremel or heavy side cutters · basic sockets · new swivel seals · silicone · swivel grease

#### Viscous coupling replacement (Borg Warner transfer case)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 3 hours · cost Exchange VC about £340 + VAT, plus a £75 core deposit (Ashcroft)
Symptoms: Tyres scrub or chirp on tight, slow turns; premature tyre wear on the edges; the truck needs a lot of throttle in slow, tight corners; driveline wind-up. A jacked-up wheel won't turn by hand.
Fix: Confirm the diagnosis: transfer case in neutral, handbrake on, jack one front wheel — it should turn slowly with resistance. If it is locked solid, replace the coupling before it damages the diffs or CV joints. One owner swapped it with the transfer box still in the truck in about three hours.
Tools: Jack and stands · basic hand tools · viscous coupling RTC6044 (same part on Classic and P38A)

#### Air suspension to coil conversion (1993–95)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 3.5 hours · cost Kit plus labor (replacing a failed air system can cost around $4,000)
Symptoms: Truck sagging at one corner overnight, the compressor running constantly, height-sensor or valve-block faults, or a truck that won't rise to off-road height.
Fix: Fit a purpose-built conversion kit, which replaces the air springs with coils and comes with the required hardware and instructions, and removes the compressor and valve block from the system. Atlantic British says its kit gives about 2 inches of lift on a short-wheelbase truck; one LWB owner reported 1.5–2 inches.
Tools: Spring compressor · jack and stands · Rovers North RNK5105 or Atlantic British RRC 93–95 coil conversion kit

#### Heater core / blower motor (dash out)
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ 9–10 hours (owners report about 12 book hours) · cost Core about $150 (as reported by owners); labor is the cost
Symptoms: No heat, a sweet smell or fogged windows (core), or a dead or noisy blower — Atlantic British suggests replacing the blower around 150,000 miles.
Fix: Disconnect the battery and note the radio code. Drain the coolant, remove both front doors, the left footwell panels, the dash fascia, the instrument panel, the radio surround and the dash top. Lower the A/C unit without discharging it. Disconnect the heater hoses at the firewall and remove the four heater-box bolts. Split the box, swap the core (owners recommend the all-metal type) and/or the blower, test before reassembly, then refill and bleed the cooling system.
Tools: Phillips and flat screwdrivers · 10 mm deep sockets · trim and radio tools · drill · soldering iron and heat-shrink · new hose clamps · Atlantic British kit #8844 for blower upgrade

#### Front radius arm bushes (chassis end)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Varies · cost Terrafirma poly kit about $66
Symptoms: Vague or wandering steering, clunks over bumps, and cracked or perished rubber where the radius arms meet the chassis.
Fix: Support the chassis on stands, take the weight off the front axle, unbolt the radius arm at the chassis mount and swap in the new bushes.
Tools: Jack and axle stands · large sockets · pry bar · Terrafirma TF1003 (replaces NRC4514; also fits Defender and Discovery 1)

#### Rear crossmember replacement
Difficulty 5 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 full days · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Rust holes in the boxed rear crossmember, a sagging or bulging rear floor, cracked welds, movement under load, or a tailgate that no longer lines up.
Fix: Strip the load floor, carpets and trim. Cut out the rotten section and clean back the mating edges. Trial-fit the new crossmember so it is square and level, then clamp and tack it, recheck it, and weld it out without overheating the frame. Dress the welds, then prime, seam-seal and paint. Refit the floor and check that the tailgate still aligns.
Tools: Angle grinder · spot-weld cutter · MIG welder · clamps · squares and straightedge · rust treatment, primer, seam sealer · replacement crossmember

#### Cooling system refresh
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Varies · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Creeping temperature gauge, coolant weeps, or simply unknown history on an aluminium V8 that hates overheating.
Fix: Replace the radiator, viscous fan coupling, water pump, thermostat and hoses as a set, then refill with a 50/50 coolant mix and bleed the air out. The aluminium block and heads depend on the cooling system.
Tools: Basic sockets · drain pan · radiator, viscous fan, water pump, thermostat, hoses, clamps · antifreeze

### Baseline service
Most Classics are now 30 to 50 years old, and their records rarely cover the transfer box, swivels or ATF. Change every fluid and fix the cooling system before anything else, because the aluminium V8 doesn't tolerate overheating. Identify your transfer box before you buy oil: the chain-drive Borg Warner (with a viscous coupling) and the gear-drive LT230 take different fluids.
- Engine oil & filter: API SG, SAE 10W-40 or 10W-50 · ≈6.7 L (1991 3.9 V8 data). Later 3.9/4.2: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase, then every 3,000–5,000 mi (These engines aren't fussy about oil brand; Hagerty UK's specialist uses about 7 L of 20W-50 every 6,000 miles or 12 months. A fresh filter matters. The ERR3340 filter covers the RRC, P38 and Defender V8s.)
- Air filter: OE-type element · At purchase (Check the airbox dump valve and the intake hoses for splits. Unmetered air upsets the Lucas/GEMS fuelling.)
- Fuel filter: OE-type EFI filter [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (Old fuel lines and rusty tanks are common on trucks that have sat. Inspect the rubber lines while you're under there.)
- Spark plugs & ignition: Plug type and gap per manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase if there's no record (Fit new plugs, leads, a distributor cap and rotor as a set. Tired leads cause a lot of rough running on these V8s.)
- Coolant: 50/50 ethylene glycol antifreeze and water · ≈11.4 L · At purchase, then every 2 years (Replace the hoses and thermostat at the same time. Check the viscous fan and the radiator core. See the cooling refresh in the repairs above.)
- Automatic transmission (ZF 4HP22 / 4HP24): Dexron IID ATF · ≈9.5 L total fill (1991 data) · Drain and refill at purchase (A pan drain only exchanges part of the fluid. Do two drain-and-fills and change the pan filter rather than pressure-flushing an unknown box.)
- Transfer box: Borg Warner chain case: Dexron IID ATF (M2C33G / Texaco 4291 also listed) · ≈1.7 L. Gear-driven LT230 trucks: EP90 GL-4/5 · ≈2.3 L · At purchase (Do the jacked-wheel viscous-coupling test while you're under the truck (see repairs). A seized coupling causes driveline wind-up on tight turns.)
- Front & rear axles: 80W/90 EP gear oil, API GL-4 or GL-5 · ≈1.7 L each · At purchase, then every 2 years (Fill to the level plug on level ground. Pinion seal weeps are common on old trucks.)
- Swivel housings: Gear oil 90 EP/80W EP · ≈0.33 L per side (1991 data), or one-shot swivel grease STC3435 on later trucks · Check at purchase and at every service (Lucky8 lists the STC3435 sachet for the RRC ('87–'95). Owners regrease when they fit new seals (see repairs). Oil on the chrome ball means it's time for a seal.)
- Power steering: Dexron IID ATF · ≈2.8 L system · Check at purchase (Leaks from the steering box are common, so watch the reservoir level for a few weeks.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 4 · At purchase, then every 2 years (ABS trucks (from about 1990) have a pump and accumulator. Bleed per the manual and check that the pump doesn't run constantly.)
- Air suspension (1993–95 LWB / air trucks): No fluid. Leak-check the springs, valve block, compressor and reservoir [CONFIRM IN MANUAL for dryer service] · At purchase (An overnight sag at one corner or a compressor that runs constantly means there's a leak. Many owners convert to coils (see repairs).)
- Propshafts & UJs: Multipurpose lithium grease · At purchase, then at every service (Grease the UJs and sliding joints. A clunk on take-up usually means a dry UJ.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: The usual forum answer is 245/75R16 (about 30.5 inches) on stock coils, with the steering stops adjusted to stop rubbing at full lock. Some owners run 265/75R16 with slight chassis rub fixed by the stops. 235/85R16 generally needs a lift or some trimming on these 100-inch trucks.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: Bad. The EPA rated a 1990 3.9 automatic at 11 mpg city and 15 highway (13 combined), and the 1995 County LWB 4.2 at 11/15 (12 combined). Hagerty says careful driving helps.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: Towing capacity is quoted at 3.5 tons. Note that Hagerty says coil-sprung trucks are more reliable but less suited to towing than the air-suspension trucks.

Q: Air suspension or coils — and should I convert?
A: Electronic air suspension arrived on late-1992 trucks for the 1993 model year, mainly the LWB. It rides beautifully but pumps, height sensors and valve blocks fail. Bolt-in coil conversion kits are widely available for 1993–95 trucks and take about 3.5 hours.

Q: Does it have a centre diff lock?
A: It depends on the year. Earlier trucks have a manually lockable centre differential. From 1989 a chain-driven Borg Warner transfer case with a viscous coupling locks automatically. On those trucks, check that the viscous coupling hasn't seized.

Q: Can I add lockers?
A: Yes. ARB makes Air Lockers for Rover-type banjo differentials in both 10-spline (RD127) and 24-spline (RD128) versions. Check which axle shafts your truck has before ordering.

Q: Which years or versions should I buy?
A: Buy the most rust-free truck you can afford; condition matters more than the year. Values run from Velar prototypes to two-doors to four-doors, and fuel-injected and LSE four-doors are worth more than carburettor trucks. In the US, choose between 1987–92 coil-sprung SWB trucks and the 1993–95 County LWB with the 4.2 and air suspension. The 1995 trucks get the soft dash.

Q: Is it reliable?
A: It can be, if you look after it. Jalopnik's experts say rust is what kills Classics, not the engine. Refresh the whole cooling system, keep up with oil changes, and expect electrical gremlins. Treat it as a third car or a project rather than a daily driver unless it has been sorted.

Q: What oil and how often?
A: Hagerty's specialist recommends good-quality 20W-50, changed every 6,000 miles or 12 months. Some owners change it every 3,000 miles. Separately, check the oil in the swivel housings — it is not shared with the front diff.

Q: Was there a diesel, and did the US get one?
A: Yes, but not in the US. The VM Motori 2.4 turbo-diesel arrived in 1986 and grew to 2.5 in 1989. Land Rover's 200Tdi replaced it in 1992, followed by the 300Tdi at the end of 1994. US trucks were all petrol V8s.

Q: Did the US get the two-door?
A: Not officially. Factory US imports from March 1987 were four-door only. Earlier two-doors in America came through grey-market importers.

## Land Rover Range Rover P38A (1994–2002)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/p38/
Codes: P38A

Verdict: The last Range Rover with a ladder frame and beam axles, wrapped in a 1990s electronics experiment. Cheap to buy, cheap to fix yourself, and ruinously expensive to pay someone else to love.

Following a 24-year-old legend is a thankless job, and the P38A did it in September 1994 with a straight face. Land Rover called it the New Range Rover; everyone else named it after the office block the engineers worked in. Underneath the squarer, plusher body it was still a proper Rover: a separate steel chassis, live axles front and rear, a two-speed transfer box and the faithful aluminium V8. On top it piled self-levelling air suspension, a body computer under the right-hand front seat and enough wiring to cable a small town. Thirty years on, that split personality is exactly why it is both the bargain and the booby trap of the Range Rover family.

### PEGASUS, DISCOVERY AND BLOCK 38A
The project started life as "Pegasus", then wore the cover name "Discovery" to confuse snooping journalists — awkward, since Land Rover had a real Discovery on sale. When the team moved into Block 38A at Solihull, the building's name stuck, and P38A it has been ever since. Inside the company it was the LP. Styling director George Thomson's in-house design was chosen over a Bertone proposal, and production at Solihull began in 1994 with sales running to the 2002 model year in the US.
It could have been very different under the bonnet. During development a pair of prototypes was fitted with BMW's 5.4-litre M73 V12 from the 750i, but the idea was shelved and never reached production. Instead buyers got the Rover V8 in 4.0 and new 4.6-litre forms, plus — outside North America — a 2.5-litre BMW M51 straight-six turbodiesel with 136 hp. The petrol V8s could be had with an R380 five-speed manual or ZF automatics; the 4.6 was automatic-only.

### AIR, ELECTRONS AND A SMARTER TRANSFER BOX
The headline hardware was the Electronic Air Suspension, developed from the late Classic LSE system. It offers five heights — Access, Motorway, Standard, Off-Road and an Off-Road Extended setting the computer selects on its own when it senses the truck is beached. It lowers itself at speed and lifts for obstacles, which is lovely until a perished air spring or tired compressor leaves one corner kneeling in your driveway.
The drivetrain went electronic too. The BorgWarner 4462 transfer box shifts between high and low range with an electric actuator rather than a lever, selected through an H-gate on automatic trucks and a dash switch on manuals, and the truck has to be nearly stopped to change. Traction control started out rear-only on the 4.0 and diesel, with the 4.6 getting four-wheel control; from mid-1999 the V8s switched from Lucas GEMS to Bosch Motronic engine management, and later trucks got four-wheel traction control across the range.

### WHY IT'S STILL WORTH YOUR WEEKENDS
Strip away the reputation and the P38 is a long-travel, beam-axle 4x4 with real low range, 3,500 kg of braked towing capacity and a 100-litre tank — a better overland base than its price suggests. The aftermarket agrees: Terrafirma makes sliders, winch bumpers, a snorkel and lift springs for it, and Lucky8 developed a 4-inch coil kit on its own P38 project truck. Converting to coils is a bolt-in job if you'd rather not carry an air compressor through the backcountry.
The flip side is that P38s are now cheap enough to be neglected. Classic magazines put good runners at a couple of thousand pounds and project cars at a few hundred, and plenty have had years of deferred maintenance. Ignore the cosmetics and buy on cooling-system health, a dry body computer and a working EAS; then budget for blend motors, heater O-rings and bushes. Do it yourself and the P38 is one of the best-value long-travel 4x4s on the road.

### THE END OF THE LADDER
The P38 was the last Range Rover with a separate chassis, live axles, a manual gearbox option and a classic two-speed transfer box. Its replacement, the L322, was developed under BMW with a monocoque body and independent air suspension, and every Range Rover since has followed that path. For buyers who want the ladder frame, the P38 sits between the hand-tool simplicity of the Classic and the computer-dependent L322. It's the last one you can still fix with mostly analogue hardware, plus a diagnostic tool for the electronics.

### Data plate
- Built: 1994–2002 MY · Solihull, UK
- Production: ≈167,000 (uncited Wikipedia figure)
- Body: 5-door wagon
- Chassis: Separate steel frame
- Wheelbase: 2,746 mm (108.1 in)
- Length: 4,712 mm (185.5 in)
- Suspension: Beam axles · EAS, 5 heights
- Engines: Rover V8 4.0 / 4.6 · BMW 2.5 TD6
- Gearboxes: ZF 4HP22 / 4HP24 auto · R380 5-spd
- Transfer: BorgWarner 4462, electric hi/lo
- Towing: 3,500 kg braked
- Fuel: 100 L

### Engineering
The P38 is a transitional truck: Classic-style bones with an electronic nervous system bolted on. A separate steel chassis carries two beam axles on air springs, permanent four-wheel drive runs through an electronically shifted BorgWarner two-speed transfer box, and power comes from the long-serving aluminium Rover V8 or a BMW diesel six. The mechanical parts are tough and well supported by the aftermarket. The weak spots are the systems controlling them: the EAS valve block and compressor, the climate-control blend motors and the body computer.
- Chassis: Separate steel frame (Strengthened over the Classic with new welding methods for better corrosion resistance.)
- Suspension: Beam axles on air springs (EAS has five heights from Access to Off-Road Extended. Terrafirma sells bolt-in coil conversions.)
- Petrol Engines: Rover V8 4.0 / 4.6 (GEMS management to mid-1999, Bosch Motronic after that. 4.0s tend to blow head gaskets; 4.6s tend to slip liners.)
- Diesel: BMW M51 2.5 TD six (136 hp, 270 Nm. EGR and a plastic inlet manifold on post-1998 engines. Not sold in the US.)
- Transfer: BorgWarner 4462, electric shift (High and low range are selected electronically, and the truck has to be nearly stopped to change.)
- Traction: ABS + traction control (Rear-only traction control at first on the 4.0 and diesel. Four-wheel control on the 4.6 from new and on later trucks.)

### Versions
- 1994–1999 · P38A, 108-in WB · 4.0 V8 (GEMS) · ≈188–190 hp · R380 5-speed manual or ZF 4HP22 auto. Rear-only traction control at first.
- 1994–1999 · P38A, 108-in WB · 4.6 V8 (GEMS) · ≈218–230 hp (market-dependent) · ZF 4HP24 auto only. 4-pin rear diff and four-wheel traction control.
- 1994–2002 · P38A, 108-in WB · 2.5 BMW M51 TD6 · 136 hp / 270 Nm · Non-US. EGR, plastic intake and a MAF sensor on post-1998 engines.
- 1999–2002 · P38A, 108-in WB · 4.0 / 4.6 V8 (Bosch) · As above · Bosch Motronic replaces Lucas GEMS mid-1999, with revised mounts and a structural sump. Four-wheel traction control on later trucks.
- 2000–2002 · Facelift · All · — · Clear front and rear indicators, new wheels and more standard kit. Special editions include the Holland & Holland, Westminster and Bordeaux.

### Year-by-year
- 1994: Launched 28 September 1994. Rover V8 4.0 and 4.6 with Lucas GEMS management, BMW 2.5 turbo-diesel outside the US, five-height electronic air suspension and an electrically shifted BorgWarner 4462 transfer box.
- 1995: First US model year. The 4.0 gets rear-only traction control and a 2-pin rear diff; the 4.6 comes only with the ZF 4HP24 auto and has a 4-pin rear diff and four-wheel traction control.
- 1998: Land Rover 50th Anniversary edition shown at the Toronto show in February. Diesels gain EGR, a plastic inlet manifold and a MAF sensor (post-1998 engines).
- 1999: Bosch Motronic (from the BMW E38 7 Series) replaces GEMS mid-year, with revised engine mounts and a structural alloy sump. Later trucks get four-wheel traction control across the range.
- 2001: Production ends; the L322 replaces it.
- 2002: Last US model year.

### Capability
- Towing: 7,716 lb (3,500 kg) braked (750 kg (1,653 lb) unbraked; 4.6 HSE spec)
- Roof load: 165 lb (75 kg) (4.6 HSE spec)
- Fuel tank: 26.4 US gal (100 L)
- Ground clearance: 8.3 in (210 mm) (4.6 HSE spec at standard height)
- Fuel economy: EPA 12 city / 16 hwy / 13 combined (2000 4.0 auto; the 4.6 rated 11/14/12)
- Curb weight: 4,478 lb (2,031 kg) (4.6 HSE)
- Turning circle: 39.0 ft (11.9 m)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 235/70R16 on 7J x 16 (ET57), 255/65R16 on 8J x 16 (ET57)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x120
- Offset: ET57 (stock 16-in; 55–59 mm range)
- Lug Torque: 80 lb-ft (108 N·m) per the owner's handbook as quoted by owners; some data sources list 130 N·m, so check your handbook
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 245/75R16 or 255/70R16 (About 30–30.5 in. 255/70R16 runs without rubbing on standard suspension; 245/75R16 clears full lock at standard and high heights but rubs at the lowest height and can touch the back of the arch at full compression. 265/75R16 rubs on axle crossup.)
- Biggest tire, 4 in lift: Up to 32.5 in (Lucky8's recommendation for its 4-in Terrafirma coil kit, developed on its P38 project truck.)

### Buying checks
- Coolant history comes first: The V8's big failure is coolant loss: 4.0s usually blow head gaskets and 4.6s slip cylinder liners. The system holds roughly 11.4 litres. Check the level and condition, ask about overheating, and look up the hose and thermostat history. A properly rebuilt engine needs top-hat liners or a new block.
- Look for a wet floor and a wet body computer: Damp in the passenger or driver footwell often means leaking heater matrix O-rings. Water in the cargo area or spare-wheel well points to failed tailgate seals. Remove the lower trim at the right-hand front seat (the passenger seat on US trucks) and check the Body Electrical Control Module (BECM) for water damage, because a drowned BECM is the expensive version of this problem.
- Cycle the air suspension: Raise the truck to its highest setting and look at all four air springs. Listen for the compressor running constantly or cycling often, which points to leaks. An EAS warning or a lean on one corner can mean a tired height sensor. Springs are cheap from aftermarket suppliers (under £100 each), so a leak is a negotiating point, not a deal-breaker.
- Read the HVAC display: A 'book' symbol on the climate-control LCD means a stored hard fault, commonly the blend motors, blower relays or A/C. Test full cold on recirculation and cycle every vent. Replacing blend motors properly means taking the dash apart, and a dealer quote can run close to $2,000.
- Shift into low range: With the truck almost stopped, select low and then high again a few times. Hesitation, 'Select Neutral' or gearbox-fault messages can come from the transfer-box motor, its harness, or a misaligned XYZ gear-position switch. Listen for centre-diff clonks on tight turns.
- Check rust where it hides: The panels are mostly aluminium, but rear arches are the worst cosmetic rust spot and the tailgate rusts under its plastic flap. Check the rear brake lines and look for chassis damage from off-road use.
- Plug in a diagnostic tool: Check that all warning lights come on with the ignition and go out (the ABS light should go out once you drive off). A P38-capable tool such as Blackbox Solutions' Nanocom will read the EAS, BECM and HVAC fault logs that a basic OBD reader can't.
- Petrol V8, and buy on condition: UK buyers' guides say choose the petrol V8 and pick on condition rather than 4.0 vs 4.6. Be wary of LPG conversions without documented professional fitting. The diesel is slow and has its own head-gasket and fuel-system issues.

### Common repairs
#### Cooling hose and thermostat refresh (GEMS V8)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Half a day · cost About $260 for a complete hose and thermostat kit, plus coolant
Symptoms: An ageing cooling system on a 4.0 or 4.6. Cracked or soft hoses, a high or overfilling expansion tank, or a heater that blows lukewarm. On these engines, overheating is what leads to slipped liners and blown head gaskets.
Fix: Remove the reservoir cap and drain the system from the radiator's bottom plug with a 12 mm Allen socket. Expect roughly 11–12 litres (about 3 US gallons). The thermostat is an external 'artificial heart' unit held by its hoses next to the radiator. Replace it with the lower hose from underneath, then do the top hose, heater hoses and bypass hoses. While the hoses are off, unbolt and check the metal down-tube for rust blockage. There is no bleed screw. Fill, warm the engine fully, let it cool completely, then top up again. Run the heater to confirm the core isn't air-locked.
Tools: 12 mm Allen socket on a ½-in drive · hose-clamp pliers · 5-gallon drain pan · Atlantic British kit 9369SKA (1995–99 GEMS trucks)

#### EAS valve block reseal and compressor rebuild
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Varies · cost O-ring and piston-seal kits are cheap. Most of the cost is your time
Symptoms: The truck sags overnight, the compressor runs for a long time or keeps cycling, the reservoir is slow to fill, or there's an audible hiss from the valve block or silencer.
Fix: Remove the valve block and compressor (the EAS box is on the left side of the engine bay). Spray soapy water over the solenoids and fittings while the system is under pressure to find the leaks. Replace the solenoid O-rings and the O-rings on the manual-inflation T-pieces and 8 mm lines. Check that each kit's O-ring sizes actually match. On the compressor, check the piston liner and seal, the reed valve and its shim, and the O-ring under the reed. Some owners also replace the thermal overload switch on the compressor board.
Tools: O-ring kit · compressor piston/seal kit · soapy water · basic hand tools · Nanocom or Faultmate to read and clear EAS faults

#### Air spring replacement
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Varies · cost Aftermarket springs under £100 each. About £350 genuine
Symptoms: One corner drops after parking, cracked or bulging bellows when the truck is at full height, or EAS faults that come back after you clear them.
Fix: Raise the truck and support the chassis securely on stands. Never leave it resting on a deflated spring. Depressurise the spring (the system runs at about 10 bar / 150 psi), clean around the fitting, and cap the line. Release the spring's retaining clips and fixings and swap in the new spring. Lower the chassis onto it and refit the clips. Reconnect the line, reinflate, and leak-test with soapy water. Off-roaders often choose uprated springs such as Arnott's Gen III.
Tools: Jack and axle stands · line caps · eye protection · soapy water · diagnostic tool if faults are logged

#### Heater matrix O-rings (wet footwell)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Varies · cost O-rings are pennies. A new matrix runs from about £60 (Bearmach) to about £400 (genuine Valeo)
Symptoms: Wet carpet beside the transmission tunnel that smells or tastes sweet, a misting windscreen, or a coolant level that keeps dropping.
Fix: Start with the O-rings at the matrix pipe connection, which go brittle after 15–20 years. Owners report the pipes come out without removing the dash. The retaining screw is often seized, so put grinding paste on the screwdriver tip, or drill the head off if you have to. Don't overtighten on reassembly, because the joint has to move with heat. If the matrix itself leaks, replacing it means pulling the dash and console. Pressure-test the old and new cores at about 20 psi, and test them hot. Clear the drain under the core while you're in there.
Tools: Screwdrivers · drill · grinding paste · new O-rings · Nissens 70220/70230 or equivalent matrix if replacing

#### Blend motor diagnosis
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Varies · cost Motors come pre-wired in a three-pack. Owners quote dealer repairs close to $2,000
Symptoms: Hot air on one side and cold on the other, a 'book' symbol on the climate display, or temperature that doesn't change.
Fix: Do the cheap checks first: blower and blend-motor relays, clogged pollen filters, and coolant level and bleeding. If a motor runs on direct voltage but won't move its flap, the flap may be jammed by a warped plenum, or the motor's internal potentiometer may be worn. Owners use a Nanocom's 'calibrate flaps' function after fitting new motors. As a winter stopgap, one owner unplugged a dead motor and set its flap open by hand.
Tools: Multimeter · relays · pollen filters · Nanocom/Faultmate · replacement motors

#### XYZ gear-position switch alignment
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Varies · cost About $100 for the alignment tool, plus a switch if yours has failed
Symptoms: 'Select Neutral' or gearbox-fault messages during range changes, wrong gear indication, or the transfer box refusing to change range.
Fix: The transmission ECU reads the transfer-box motor position as a Gray code, so check the motor harness and its earth first. Then check the XYZ (inhibitor/gear-position) switch on the auto gearbox. Set it with the dealer alignment tool LRT-44-011 rather than by eye. Atlantic British has reissued that tool and published a video of the procedure.
Tools: XYZ switch alignment tool LRT-44-011 · multimeter · diagnostic tool

#### Front suspension bushes and ball joints
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time 4–6 hours for all four ball joints · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Vague steering, wander, clonks over bumps, uneven tyre wear. The front usually wears out first.
Fix: Replace the radius arm bushes and the swivel ball joints, which need a special press tool. Polyurethane bush kits such as Polybush are popular. Use poly at both ends of the truck, and don't put poly in the Panhard rod. Check the dampers, drop links and ABS sensors while you're there.
Tools: Ball-joint press · breaker bar · bush kit (e.g. Polybush radius-arm-to-axle kit)

### Baseline service
The P38 rewards a full catch-up service more than almost any other Range Rover. Overheating causes the V8's slipped liners, and neglected EAS and gearbox fluid cause most of the expensive failures. Change every fluid, refresh the cooling system, and leak-test the air suspension before you trust it. Note whether the engine is a GEMS (1995–98) or Bosch (1999–2002) V8, because some parts differ.
- Engine oil & filter: API SG/SH or ACEA A2:96, SAE 5W-40 or 5W-50 · ≈5.8 L drain & refill (6.6 L dry) · At purchase, then every 5,000–6,000 mi (Check the dipstick for mayonnaise and the expansion tank for oil. Either one points to head-gasket or liner trouble.)
- Air & cabin filters: OE-type engine air element, plus the pollen/cabin filter pair · At purchase (Clogged pollen filters affect the climate control and can look like a blend-motor fault (see repairs).)
- Spark plugs & leads: Plug type and gap per manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase if there's no record (Misfires on Bosch trucks often come from the leads and coils. Replace the plugs and leads as a set.)
- Fuel filter: V8: OE-type EFI filter [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]. 2.5 DSE diesel: STC2827 · At purchase (Do the diesel filter at purchase on non-US 2.5 DSE trucks.)
- Coolant, hoses & thermostat: 50/50 ethylene glycol antifreeze and water · ≈11.4 L · At purchase, then every 2 years (Replace the hoses, thermostat and expansion-tank cap as a set (see repairs). There's no bleed screw. Warm the engine, let it cool, then top up.)
- Automatic transmission (ZF 4HP22 on 4.0 / diesel, 4HP24 on 4.6): Dexron III ATF · ≈11 L total fill (4HP24 figure; 4HP22 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]). A drain and refill takes about 5 L · Drain and refill at purchase. Repeat after a few hundred miles (An owner on rangerovers.pub measured about 5 L from a drain and refill. Two drain-and-fills refresh most of the fluid without the risk of a flush.)
- Transfer box (Borg Warner 44-62 Hi/Lo): Dexron III ATF · ≈2.0 L drain & refill (2.4 L dry) · At purchase (Range-change faults ('Select Neutral') are usually electrical or an XYZ switch problem, not low oil. See repairs.)
- Front & rear differentials: Hypoid gear oil, API GL-5 [CONFIRM grade IN MANUAL] · ≈1.6 L each drain & refill (1.7 L dry) · At purchase, then every 2 years (Fill to the level plug on level ground. Check the pinion seals.)
- Front ball joints (no oil-filled swivels): Sealed ball joints. There's no swivel oil or grease to change · Inspect at purchase (Unlike the Classic and Defender, the P38 front axle uses press-fit ball joints. Check them for play while the wheels are off.)
- Power steering: Dexron III ATF (or Texamatic 9226) · ≈1.7 L · Check at purchase (Check the steering box and the PAS cooler pipes for weeps.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 4 · At purchase, then every 2 years (An ABS pump that keeps running, or ABS warnings, need diagnosis with a Nanocom or a similar tool.)
- EAS air suspension: System runs at about 10 bar / 150 psi. No fluid · Leak-test at purchase. Drain any water from the reservoir and check the dryer (Park overnight at normal height and check each corner in the morning. Spray soapy water on the springs and valve block to find leaks (see repairs). Never work under a truck resting on deflated springs.)
- Drive belt: Poly-V serpentine belt · At purchase (Inspect the tensioner and idler pulleys while the belt is off.)
- Propshafts & UJs: Multipurpose lithium grease · At purchase (Grease the UJs and sliding joints. Worn UJs feel like a clunk on take-up.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: Forum reports say 245/75R16 or 255/70R16, roughly 30 to 30.5 inches. One owner runs 255/70R16 on standard suspension with no rubbing. Another found 245/75R16 clears at full lock at standard and high ride heights, but rubs at the lowest height and can touch the back of the arch at full compression. 265/75R16 (about 31.6 in) rubs when the axles cross up unless you lift the truck and fit an adjustable Panhard rod.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: Poor. The EPA rated a 2000 4.0 automatic at 12 mpg city, 16 highway and 13 combined, and the 4.6 at 11/14/12. The tank holds 100 litres (about 26 US gallons).

Q: How much can a P38 tow?
A: 3,500 kg (7,716 lb) braked and 750 kg unbraked, according to published spec sheets for the 4.6 HSE.

Q: 4.0 or 4.6 — which should I buy?
A: Buy the better truck. Buyers' guides say choose on condition rather than displacement. The 4.0 is more likely to blow a head gasket and the 4.6 more likely to slip a liner, so cooling-system history matters more than size. The 4.6 has more power, a 4-pin rear diff and four-wheel traction control from new. It came only with the ZF automatic.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: Hagerty's advice is to buy on condition and specification rather than age, adding that the electrical faults that dogged these trucks are now understood and fixable. ReRev says 1998 drew the most complaints of any Range Rover year on CarComplaints. Mid-1999-on V8s have Bosch Motronic instead of GEMS, but no guide we found says that alone makes them the better buy; cooling-system history matters more.

Q: Do I have a GEMS or a Bosch engine?
A: Open the hood. A rectangular plenum with '4.0' or '4.6' embossed in the middle means GEMS, the earlier Lucas system. A cluster of intake tubes and no label means Bosch Motronic, which arrived mid-1999. The two use different parts, so check before ordering.

Q: Does it have low range and locking diffs?
A: It has full-time four-wheel drive with a two-speed BorgWarner 4462 transfer box, switched electrically. Slow almost to a stop before changing range. There are no factory locking diffs; traction control brakes a spinning wheel instead (rear-only on early 4.0 and diesel trucks, all four wheels on the 4.6 and on later trucks). For bigger tyres, Ashcroft makes heavy-duty 4.10 ring-and-pinion sets for the P38's diffs.

Q: Should I convert to coil springs?
A: It's a common way to simplify the truck. Terrafirma's standard-height kit TF223 is a bolt-in swap. Before you do it, note that air springs are cheap now and leaks are often just perished seals that are easy to fix. UK guides say coil conversions are becoming less popular as EAS parts get cheaper, and a healthy EAS gives you the extra off-road height.

Q: What lift options exist?
A: Lucky8's 4-inch kit (Terrafirma heavy-duty springs, +2-in Pro Sport shocks, mounting plates and an EAS override harness) was developed on its own P38 project truck. Lucky8 recommends tyres up to 32.5 in with it. Owners also report about 2 in of lift from Arnott Gen III air springs with Terrafirma shocks. Bigger lifts usually need double-cardan driveshafts (Tom Wood's) to cure vibration, and adjustable Panhard rods to re-centre the axles.

Q: Is the BMW diesel worth having?
A: It's the economy choice outside the US: a 2.5-litre BMW M51 six with 136 hp and 270 Nm. UK buyers' guides still recommend the petrol V8 and warn about diesel head gaskets (especially on remapped trucks), glow plugs and fuel-system parts. It was never sold in North America.

Q: What maintenance gets skipped that I shouldn't skip?
A: Coolant hoses and thermostat: Land Rover's schedule says every 90,000 miles. Automatic gearbox oil about every 70,000 miles. The V8's mass airflow sensor at about 90,000 miles. Ignition leads, which wear quickly on the V8. The EAS compressor filter.

Q: Why does the driver's or passenger's footwell get wet?
A: Usually the heater matrix O-rings, or a blocked drain under the heater box. Sometimes it's a leaking matrix. Clogged drains and failed seals can also let water reach the body computer under the seat, so fix wet carpets quickly.
