## Land Rover Range Rover L322 (2002–2012)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/l322/
Codes: L322

Verdict: A Munich-engineered, Solihull-built limousine that still walks up a rock garden on its tiptoes. Buy the paperwork, not the paint. The timing chains decide whether it's a bargain or a boat anchor.

The third Range Rover was a clean break. The P38 had wrapped new electronics around old Land Rover hardware. The L322 threw out the ladder frame and the beam axles and started again: a unitary body, independent air suspension at all four corners and, at launch, BMW engines and electronics. Purists called it heresy. Then they drove it off-road and found that its cross-linked air springs let the wheels droop and stuff much like the old live axles did. Twenty years later it's the cheapest way into a properly capable luxury 4x4, and a minefield for anyone who buys one without receipts.

### THE BMW RANGE ROVER FORD LAUNCHED
Under BMW ownership the project was codenamed L30. Joint Rover and BMW teams developed it, first at BMW's FIZ research centre in Munich and then at Solihull for the final stages. The plan was to share electronics and core engines with the E38 7 Series. Then BMW sold Land Rover to Ford about two years before production started, though the contract kept BMW involved until volume production was under way. Ford renamed the project L322, and the truck went on sale in 2002, arriving in North America as a 2003 model.
That handover explains the L322's three engine eras. Early petrol trucks used BMW's 4.4-litre M62 V8 (286 PS), and outside North America there was a BMW 2.9-litre Td6 diesel. For the 2006 model year Ford switched to Jaguar's AJ-V8 in 4.4-litre (305 PS) and 4.2-litre supercharged (400 PS) forms, behind a six-speed ZF. The 2010 facelift brought Jaguar Land Rover's 5.0-litre V8s: 375 PS naturally aspirated, 510 PS supercharged.

### A LIVE AXLE IN DISGUISE
The off-road trick was in the plumbing. MacPherson struts at the front and double wishbones at the rear ride on air springs, and the valves linking each side's springs can make the suspension behave like a live axle when the truck is crossed up. Permanent four-wheel drive runs through a chain-driven two-speed transfer case that can shift between high and low on the move. Early trucks used a Torsen centre differential with a 50:50 split that could send up to 65% of torque to either axle.
From the 2007 model year the L322 got the Terrain Response system from the LR3 and Range Rover Sport, a lockable centre differential and, on Supercharged models (optional elsewhere), an electronically locking rear diff. That year also brought stiffer anti-roll bars and air springs, and the TDV8 twin-turbo diesel replaced the BMW six outside North America. Later updates revised the sand, rock-crawl and hill-descent programs, added hill-start assist, and the 2011 4.4 TDV8 with ZF's eight-speed automatic.

### LIVING WITH ONE NOW
The L322's reputation is mostly about three failures. The BMW M62's nylon timing-chain guides go brittle with age and break, and a broken guide can wreck the engine. The 5.0-litre V8 has its own chain-tensioner and guide wear, and replacing the chains is a big, specialist job. The air suspension, as on every Range Rover since, eventually needs compressors, springs and height sensors. Owners who keep L322s running long-term replace the guides before they fail, service the 'sealed for life' gearboxes anyway, and treat a diagnostic tool as standard equipment.
Get past that and the truck rewards you. Running parts are cheap from aftermarket suppliers, Atlantic British publishes free how-to videos for most routine jobs, and the aftermarket offers sump guards, bush kits and sensor-rod lifts. A well-sorted 2007–2009 or a documented 2011–2012 is one of the most comfortable ways to reach a trailhead. With a sensor-rod lift and all-terrain tyres, it will keep going after the trailhead too.

### LEGACY
Land Rover built 293,494 L322s before the all-aluminium L405 replaced it in 2012. It set the template every Range Rover since has followed: monocoque body, four-corner air suspension, and electronics deciding how the power reaches the ground. Atlantic British's ROVERLOG blog says it ranks second only to the Classic in Range Rover fans' affections. In its day it was the truck that bridged the gap between a Land Cruiser 100 or LX 470 and a W463 G-Class — plusher than the Toyotas, more road-friendly than the Mercedes.

### Data plate
- Built: 2001–2012 · Solihull, UK
- Production: 293,494
- Codename: L30 (BMW era) → L322
- Body: 5-door steel monocoque
- Wheelbase: 2,880 mm (113.4 in)
- Length: 4,950–4,976 mm
- Suspension: Independent air, cross-linked
- Petrol: BMW 4.4 · AJ-V8 4.4/4.2SC · 5.0/5.0SC
- Diesel (Non-Us): Td6 · 3.6 TDV8 · 4.4 TDV8
- Transfer: 2-speed chain, shift-on-the-move
- Towing: 3,500 kg braked
- Fuel: 100 L

### Engineering
The L322 swapped Land Rover's traditional ladder frame for a stiff steel monocoque and replaced live axles with four-corner independent air suspension. Off-road ability comes from software and plumbing instead: cross-linked air springs that imitate axle articulation, a two-speed chain-drive transfer case, a centre diff that was a Torsen until 2006 and lockable from 2007, and traction control on every corner. Engines came from three owners: BMW (2002–05), Jaguar (2006–09) and JLR's own 5.0 V8s (2010–12).
- Body: Steel monocoque (The first unitary-body Range Rover, with a 2,880 mm (113.4 in) wheelbase.)
- Suspension: 4-corner independent air (Struts at the front, wishbones at the rear. Cross-linked valves imitate live-axle articulation off-road.)
- Transfer: 2-speed chain drive (High and low range can be selected on the move. A Torsen T-2 centre diff (50:50, up to 65% either way) until 2006.)
- Lockers: Locking centre diff 2007+ (Terrain Response arrived for 2007. An electronic rear locker was standard on Supercharged and optional on other models.)
- Petrol V8S: BMW M62 4.4 → AJ-V8 4.4 / 4.2 SC → 5.0 (286 PS (BMW), 305/400 PS (Jaguar), and 375/510 PS for the 5.0 NA and supercharged.)
- Gearboxes: ZF 5HP · GM 5L40-E · ZF 6HP · ZF 8HP (The GM five-speed was paired only with the Td6 diesel. The eight-speed came for 2011 with the 4.4 TDV8.)

### Versions
- 2002–2005 · L322 (BMW era) · 4.4 BMW M62 V8 · 286 PS / 440 Nm · ZF 5-speed auto. Plastic timing-chain guides are the known weak spot.
- 2002–2006 · L322 (BMW era) · 2.9/3.0 BMW M57 Td6 · 177 PS / 390 Nm · GM 5L40-E auto. Never EPA-listed (not sold in the US).
- 2006–2009 · L322 facelift · 4.4 AJ-V8 / 4.2 AJ-V8 supercharged · 305 PS / 400 PS · Jaguar engines, ZF 6-speed. Terrain Response and a locking centre diff from MY2007.
- 2007–2010 · L322 · 3.6 TDV8 · 272 PS / 640 Nm · Twin-turbo diesel V8 (non-US).
- 2010–2012 · L322 2010 facelift · 5.0 V8 / 5.0 V8 supercharged · 375 PS / 510 PS · LED lights, TFT instrument panel. Check the timing-chain tensioner and guide history.
- 2011–2012 · L322 · 4.4 TDV8 · 313 PS / 700 Nm · ZF 8HP70 eight-speed (non-US).

### Year-by-year
- 2002: Launched in early 2002 as a 2003 model in North America. First monocoque Range Rover, with four-corner independent air suspension, BMW M62 4.4 V8 (and M57 Td6 diesel elsewhere), and a ZF five-speed auto.
- 2003–05: BMW-engined trucks. The nylon timing-chain guides go brittle, so buy only with receipts or plan to replace them. The 2003–05 front-diff coupling recall also applies. [avoid]
- 2006: Facelift. Jaguar AJ-V8 4.4 (305 PS) and 4.2 supercharged (400 PS) replace the BMW V8, with ZF six-speed autos and a new touchscreen infotainment system.
- 2007: Terrain Response, a locking centre diff, an electronic rear diff (standard on Supercharged), Brembo brakes and an electronic handbrake; TDV8 replaces the Td6 outside the US, and the switchblade key arrives mid-year. Guides and owners rate 2007–09 Jaguar-engined trucks the most dependable L322s [buy]
- 2010: Facelift: 5.0 V8 (375 PS) and 5.0 supercharged (510 PS), LED-accented headlights and a 12-in TFT instrument panel. The 5.0's timing-chain tensioners wear; buy a 2010–12 only with proof of updated parts [avoid]
- 2011: 4.4 TDV8 with ZF 8HP70 eight-speed (non-US); reclining rear seats.
- 2012: Final year. The L405 is unveiled at the Paris show.

### Capability
- Towing: 7,716 lb (3,500 kg) braked (750 kg unbraked; 2011 MY GTW 6,700 kg)
- Payload: 1,345 lb (610 kg) (GVW 3,200 kg minus 2,590 kg vehicle weight with full tank (2011 MY NAS))
- Roof load: 220 lb (100 kg) (110 lb (50 kg) off-road; includes the Land Rover roof rack)
- Fuel tank: 26.7 US gal (101 L) usable
- Ground clearance: 11.1 in (283 mm) (minimum, at off-road height)
- Approach / departure: 29° / 24.2° (standard); 34° / 26.6° (off-road height) (at curb weight, no tow hitch; 2011 MY)
- Wading depth: 27.6 in (700 mm)
- Fuel economy: EPA 12 city / 19 hwy / 15 combined (2011 5.0; 2004 BMW 4.4 rated 11/15/12, 2008 4.4 and 4.2 SC 12/18/14)
- Curb weight: 5,710 lb (2,590 kg) (2011 MY 5.0, including full fuel)
- Turning circle: 39.4 ft (12 m) (curb to curb)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 255/55R19 on 8J x 19 (2011 MY US), 255/50R20 on 8.5J x 20 (2011 MY US), Earlier trucks: 235/65R18, 255/60R18; 21–22 in options
- Bolt Pattern: 5x120
- Center Bore: 72.6 mm
- Lug Thread: M14x1.5
- Lug Torque: 103 lb-ft (140 N·m)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 265/60R18 (on 18s) / 275/55R20 (on 20s) (265/60R18 (about 30.5 in) fits with no problems, including off-road. Owners warn against 265/65R18, which can rub when the air suspension drops. 275/55R20 clears the bump stops but rubs the liners at full lock. Check that a taller spare still fits the well.)

### Buying checks
- Demand timing-chain paperwork: On 2003–2005 BMW-engined trucks, look for receipts for chains and guides, or budget for them. The nylon guides go brittle and break, and owners report failures clustering around 130,000–170,000 miles. On 2010–2012 5.0s, check for tensioner and guide updates. Listen for a rattle on a cold start.
- Cycle the air suspension through every height: The compressor should be barely audible. Grinding means it's on its way out. Watch for slow rises, a lean, or warnings. On 2003–05 trucks, corroded or seized height sensors can stop the truck adjusting without leaving any fault codes.
- Test low range and the range-change motor: Select low and back again with the truck stationary. A range-change motor that has seized from lack of use can cost about £1,000 to fix. Make sure Hill Descent Control works too.
- Treat 'sealed for life' gearboxes as unsealed: Hesitant shifts or warning lights point to gearbox trouble. Ask whether the fluid and filter have ever been changed. Atlantic British recommends a service every 60,000 miles on later ZF six-speeds, including the leak-prone valve-body sleeve. A rebuild costs about £2,000 in the UK.
- Listen at full lock: Knocking at low speed on full lock can mean a front differential problem, and many were recalled. Clonks over bumps from the rear point to perished hub bushes.
- Read the codes before and after the drive: A pre-purchase diagnostic scan is cheap insurance. Read the codes before and after a long test drive, because sellers can clear faults just before you arrive. Check that every warning light comes on with the ignition and then goes out.
- Hunt for water and oil: Check for water in the rear fuse box and under the carpets. Check the M62 for valve-cover and other oil leaks, and look for white coolant streaks around the expansion tank. Expansion tanks fail.
- Check the brakes and wheels: L322s are hard on brakes; expect discs and pads about every 30,000 miles. Avoid 22-inch wheels with low-profile tyres, which ride badly and pinch-puncture easily.

### Common repairs
#### Ride height sensor replacement (2003–2005)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Varies · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: The air suspension won't change height or adjusts erratically, often with no stored fault codes. The sensor pivots seize, and cracked rear sensor bodies let water in, which corrupts the readings.
Fix: Rear: the sensor sits against the rear subframe on the lower control arm. Clean and unplug the connector. Undo the 13 mm-head bolt and nut that hold the link to the arm, then remove the two screws holding the sensor to its bracket (they're often rusted, so use penetrating oil and locking pliers). Fit the new rubber-bushed sensor with its new screws, check that the arm moves freely, refit the nut while holding it with a 10 mm spanner, and pack the connector with dielectric grease. The front sensors are done the same way.
Tools: 10 & 13 mm spanners · penetrating oil · locking pliers · dielectric grease · LR020627 (FR) / LR020626 (FL) / LR032106 (rear, both sides)

#### BMW M62 timing chain guides (2003–2005 4.4)
Difficulty 5 / 5 · time ≈ 2 days (owner estimate, engine in car) · cost About £600 in parts (owner figure). Atlantic British's complete kit TCKL322 lists at $1,849.95
Symptoms: Clatter on a cold start, more chain noise as the engine ages, or in the worst case an oil-pressure light. Nylon guide debris can block the oil pickup.
Fix: With the engine in the car, remove the front of the engine, the valve covers and the sump. Replace the upper and lower chains, the centre and outer guide rails, the tensioners and the tensioner arm, and fit new timing-cover, valve-cover and VANOS seals. Owners say getting the crankshaft nut off is the hardest part (one used a homemade locking bar and a scaffold-pole extension). Drop the sump to check for guide fragments while you're in there.
Tools: M62 engine timing/setting tools · crank-locking bar · breaker bar · 32 mm deep socket (ground down) for solenoids · VANOS seal tool · kit TCKL322 or equivalent

#### Cold-start rattle: VANOS seals and non-return valves
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Varies · cost Valves cost a few pounds each. A VANOS seal kit and tool run about £120
Symptoms: A brief rattle on a cold start that goes away on a quick restart, on a BMW 4.4 whose guides may still be fine.
Fix: Before condemning the chains, change to a good fully synthetic 5W-30 or 5W-40 with a quality (Mann or genuine) filter. Owners report the rattle stopping after the filter change alone. Next, replace the VANOS solenoid seals and the oil non-return valves behind the solenoids. Some say the real culprits are two non-return valves in the block under the head gasket. If it still rattles, move on to the tensioners and then the guides, which means dropping the sump.
Tools: VANOS seal tool · ground-down 32 mm deep socket · quality oil filter

#### Transfer case range-change faults
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Varies · cost About £1,000 if the motor has to be replaced
Symptoms: A chime and a warning message, then the transfer case drops into neutral. Low range engages but high won't, or a 'trans failsafe' message appears.
Fix: Rarely used range-change motors seize, and their contacts wear. Check that the connections under the transfer case are clean and plugged in. Try the reset owners use: fit a spare 5A fuse in position 37 of the main fuse box, cycle the ignition, remove the fuse, then cycle the hi/lo selector. One owner fixed worn contacts by taking off the contact cover under the case and adjusting them. Replace the motor if it has seized.
Tools: 5A fuse · contact cleaner · basic sockets · diagnostic tool

#### Differential and transfer case oil change (2003–2005)
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time Varies · cost About $220 for a kit with oil and new drain/fill plugs
Symptoms: An overdue service. Old oil breaks down and collects condensation, and water in the diffs or transfer case destroys bearings.
Fix: Drain and refill the front differential, rear differential and transfer case from their drain and fill plugs, using new plugs. Atlantic British recommends doing this every 60,000 miles.
Tools: Drain pan · fluid pump · socket/hex set · Atlantic British kit DTCM200A

#### ZF six-speed transmission service (2006–2012)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour (owner estimate; one dealer quoted 7 hours) · cost About $280 for the kit
Symptoms: Slow or harsh shifts, fluid weeping from the valve-body connector sleeve, or a high-mileage 'sealed for life' gearbox that has never been serviced.
Fix: Drop the pan with its integral filter, replace the leak-prone valve-body sleeve, fit a new pan and gasket, and refill with ZF Lifeguard fluid to the correct level. Atlantic British recommends doing it every 60,000 miles. Some owners also fit new valve-body 'bridge' seals as preventive maintenance.
Tools: Atlantic British kit TRANSM300SKA (pan, sleeve, 7 qt ZF Lifeguard) · fluid pump · torque wrench · scan tool for fluid temperature

#### 5.0 V8 timing chains (2010–2012)
Difficulty 5 / 5 · time Varies · cost Genuine kit TCK5030 lists at $1,499.95. The special tool kit lists at $1,249.95
Symptoms: A rattle on cold starts from worn tensioner-to-guide contact. Ignore it and the chain can jump timing or snap.
Fix: Atlantic British says this job is not recommended for DIY. It means stripping the front of the engine, replacing all three chains, the guides, shoes and tensioners, and usually the water pump, thermostat and cam sprockets as well. Fit the updated parts and keep the receipts, because buyers will ask for them.
Tools: TCK5030 kit · TCK5030TOOL timing/crank tool set · crank holding tool · front seal tool

### Baseline service
Assume nothing was done. The L322 spans five petrol and diesel engines and three transfer boxes, so confirm exactly what you have (engine, model year, open or locking rear diff, NV225 or DD295 transfer box) before ordering a single fluid. Land Rover's differentials and DD295 transfer box take an exact measured fill, not 'fill until it drips', and the friction-modified fluids are not interchangeable.
- Engine oil & filter: BMW 4.4 (2002–05): fully synthetic to ACEA A3/B3, ≈8.5 L refill · Jaguar 4.4/4.2 SC (2006–09): 5W-30, ≈7.7 L with filter · 5.0 NA/SC (2010–12): 5W-20 to WSS-M2C925-A, 8.0 L · 3.6 TDV8: 5W-30 to WSS-M2C913-B/-D (STJLR.03.5003), ≈9.5 L service fill · 4.4 TDV8 (2011–12, DPF): 5W-30 to WSS-M2C934-B / STJLR.03.5005, 9.0 L · Land Rover North America's 2006–08 schedule: every 7,500 mi or 6 months. Land Rover's 2012 UK/European plan: 15,000 mi or 12 months (4.4 TDV8: 16,000 mi). Trucks with the OIL SERVICE/INSPECTION indicator follow it, per the owner guide. Owner practice is every 10,000 mi or sooner (The DPF diesels must have low-SAPS oil to the exact spec. Owners warn against overfilling the Jaguar V8: put in 6–6.5 L, run it, then top up to the dipstick.)
- Engine air filter: BMW 4.4: PHE000050 (pair) · Jaguar 4.4/4.2 SC: PHE500021 · Td6: PHE000040 · LRNA 2006–08 schedule: every 60,000 mi or 48 months. Change it far sooner on dusty roads; Land Rover says arduous use needs more frequent service (Cheap insurance on a truck with unknown history. Check the airbox for leaves and mouse nests while it's open.)
- Cabin (pollen) filter: Correct filter by model year [CONFIRM BY VIN] · Then every 15,000 mi or 12 months (LRNA 2006–08 schedule) (A clogged cabin filter makes the climate control work harder and can hide a damp footwell smell.)
- Spark plugs: Jaguar 4.4 (2006–09): Champion LR005253 x8 · 5.0 V8 (2010–12): genuine set of 8 · At 105,000 mi on 2006–08 US trucks (LRNA schedule); other years [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (If the history doesn't show plugs, do them. On the 5.0, inspect the coil packs and plug-well seals at the same time.)
- Coolant: 2002–05: 50% extended-life coolant (Havoline XLC type), ≈13 L refill · 2010–12: 50% Castrol SF antifreeze, 15 L (5.0 NA) / 16 L (5.0 SC) / 14 L (diesel) · Change if the history is unknown; then every 10 years on petrols (LRNA 2006–08 schedule, Land Rover owner guides). The older owner guide gives 4 years for diesels (Don't mix antifreeze types. On the 5.0, look for weeps at the plastic coolant pipes and the water-pump outlet; on the Jaguar V8s, check the heater and oil-cooler hoses.)
- Automatic transmission fluid: ZF 5HP24 (BMW 4.4): Esso LT71141, ≈6.0 L refill · GM 5L40-E (Td6): Texaco ETL-7045E · ZF 6HP26 (2006–09 and 2010–12): Shell ATF M1375.4 / ZF Lifeguard 6 · Then every 60,000 mi (Atlantic British recommendation). Land Rover's 2006–08 US schedule says fluid and filter at 10 years or 150,000 mi (A pan drop only renews part of the fluid: one owner drained about 4 qt from a 10-qt 6HP26. On the 6-speed the filter is built into the plastic pan, so a new filter means a new pan; replace the leak-prone valve-body sleeve while it's off. Fill and level at temperature per the workshop procedure. Drain-and-fill, don't pressure-flush.)
- Transfer case: NV225 (2002–05 petrol, Td6 to 2006): Castrol BOT 26 FMB 1 75W-90, ≈1.0 L · Magna Steyr DD295 (Jaguar/5.0/TDV8 trucks, 2006 onward per Lucky8 fitment — [CONFIRM BY VIN] on 2006 MY): Shell TF 0753, 1.5 L · Then every 60,000 mi (Atlantic British recommendation). Land Rover's 2006–08 US schedule: at 75,000 and 150,000 mi (The DD295 has an electronically controlled multi-plate centre clutch, so only the friction-modified TF 0753 will do. Specialist Glenrands reports 1.1–1.2 L typically goes back in on a service, so buy 2 L. Replace the drain/fill washers (IYF500010 / IYF500030).)
- Front & rear differentials: Front: Castrol SAF-XO 75W-90, 0.75 L refill · Rear non-locking: SAF-XO, 1.14 L · Rear electronic locker: Castrol SAF Carbon Mod Plus 75W-90 (LR019727), 1.55 L · Then every 60,000 mi (Atlantic British recommendation). Land Rover's 2006–08 US schedule: electronic rear diff at 75,000 and 150,000 mi; front and rear axle oil every 10 years (Identify the rear diff first: the electronic locker has a cylindrical motor on top with a cable. Pump in the exact quantity rather than filling to drips, which overfills and aerates the oil. Diff plugs often seize, so crack the fill plug before you drain anything.)
- Power steering fluid: Texaco Cold Climate PSF 14315 · reservoir ≈1.6 L · Check level and hoses at purchase. Land Rover's 2006–08 US schedule only checks and tops up the fluid, with no replacement interval (Look for weeping at the rack and pump hoses while the truck is up on stands.)
- Brake fluid: Shell DOT4 ESL, or a low-viscosity DOT4 meeting ISO 4925 class 6 (2011 handbook) · Change at purchase if undated; then every 3 years regardless of distance (Land Rover owner guides, LRNA 2006–08 schedule) (The low-viscosity spec matters for the ABS and stability system. Standard DOT4 is for topping up only.)
- Drive belts & tensioner: BMW 4.4: primary LR051050 + A/C belt · 5.0: primary LR064185 + secondary belt · Replace at purchase if the age is unknown. LRNA's 2006–08 schedule replaces the drive belts at 150,000 mi and the supercharger belt at 105,000 mi (Addicted Motors' 'must-do' L322 kit puts both belts on the list alongside the transmission service and front control arms.)
- Air suspension health check: Compressor, drier, valve blocks, air springs and height sensors · At purchase, then whenever the truck sits low after standing (Leave it overnight and measure each corner. Time how long the compressor runs. On 2003–05 trucks, height-sensor faults often store no code. Replace the compressor relay with the compressor: it's a known weak point.)
- Fuel filter: BMW 4.4: WFL000021 · 3.6 TDV8: WJI500030 · Td6: WFL000070 · At purchase on diesels [CONFIRM IN MANUAL for the diesel interval]; Land Rover's 2006–08 US petrol schedule replaces it at 150,000 mi (On the 2006–09 Jaguar petrols the filter is part of the in-tank sender assembly, so it isn't a routine item.)
- Battery & charging: Load-test the battery; check charging voltage · At purchase (Low voltage on an L322 throws a cascade of unrelated air-suspension and transmission warnings. Rule out the battery before you chase faults.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: On 18-inch wheels, owners say 265/60R18 (about 30.5 in) fits with no problems, including off-road. 265/65R18 has been warned against because it can rub when the air suspension drops. On 20s, 275/55R20 clears the bump stops but rubs the liners at full steering lock. Check that a taller spare still fits in the well.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: Thirsty. The EPA rated a 2004 BMW 4.4 at 11 mpg city, 15 highway and 12 combined; a 2008 4.4 or 4.2 Supercharged at 12/18/14; a 2011 5.0 at 12/19/15; and a 2011 5.0 Supercharged at 12/18/14. The tank holds 100 litres.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: 3,500 kg (7,716 lb) braked and 750 kg unbraked. A 2002 4.4 HSE weighs about 2,430 kg at the curb.

Q: Which years and engines should I buy or avoid?
A: Owners and buyers' guides generally rate the 2007–2009 Jaguar-engined trucks best: Terrain Response, a locking centre diff and the six-speed ZF. Buy a 2003–2005 BMW 4.4 only with receipts for timing guides (or if you'll do them yourself). Buy a 2010–2012 5.0 only with evidence that the chain tensioners and guides have been updated.

Q: Does it have low range and lockers?
A: Every L322 has full-time four-wheel drive with a two-speed chain-drive transfer case you can shift on the move. 2003–2006 trucks use a Torsen centre diff and open axles with traction control. From 2007 the centre diff can lock under Terrain Response, and an electronic rear locker was standard on Supercharged models and optional on others.

Q: How do I lift an L322?
A: The usual way is longer ride-height sensor links. Atlantic British's RHSRAL322 rods make the air suspension think it's low, so it holds about 2.5 in of extra height all the time, enough for bigger all-terrains. Its listed fitment is 2005–2012 trucks.

Q: Is the air suspension a deal-breaker?
A: No, but budget for it. Springs leak, compressors fail slowly and noisily, and 2003–05 height sensors seize. Genuine parts are expensive (a full air-ride restoration kit for 2003–05 trucks lists at about $2,450), but each part can be replaced on its own. Some long-term owners convert to coils after spring failures.

Q: Are the gearboxes really 'sealed for life'?
A: No. Early petrol trucks use a ZF 5HP24, and Td6 diesels use a GM 5L40-E that Australian testers call so bad owners treat it as a service item. Both left the factory with 'sealed for life' stickers. Atlantic British recommends a fluid and filter service every 60,000 miles on the later ZF six-speed.

Q: How do I tell which engine I'm looking at?
A: For US trucks, go by model year: 2003–2005 is the BMW 4.4, 2006–2009 the Jaguar 4.4 or 4.2 supercharged, and 2010–2012 the 5.0 or 5.0 supercharged. Parts suppliers split their catalogues the same way, so order by engine as well as year.

Q: My BMW 4.4 rattles on cold starts — are the guides gone?
A: Not necessarily. Owners trace many short cold-start rattles to VANOS seals, solenoid non-return valves or a poor oil filter. One owner's rattle stopped after switching to a Mann filter. A rattle that keeps getting worse, or that shows up with low oil pressure, is a different matter. Stop driving and check the guides.

Q: Is it actually good off-road?
A: Yes. Club 4X4 calls it great off-road, and its cross-linked air springs are designed to mimic live-axle articulation. On any truck you're considering, check that low range engages and that Hill Descent Control works. The usual first mods for trail use are a sump guard, a sensor-rod lift and all-terrain tyres.

- FullFatRR forum (L322 tyre-size discussions cited on the BoxyTrucks L322 page): https://fullfatrr.com/forum/

## Land Rover Range Rover L405 (2012–2021)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/l405/
Codes: L405

Verdict: An aluminium-bodied air-sprung limousine that will still claw up a rutted hillside if you ask nicely. Buy one with a service history thicker than its door cards, and a warranty for when it doesn't.

The fourth-generation Range Rover broke cover at the 2012 Paris Motor Show and did something no full-size 4x4 had done before: it threw away the steel. Land Rover calls the L405 the first production SUV with an all-aluminium monocoque, and the diet was dramatic — the body-in-white was 39 percent lighter and the whole truck shed about 420 kg (926 lb) against the steel L322. It still had a two-speed transfer box, cross-linked air springs and a 900 mm wading depth. It was simply built from the same stuff as a beer can.

### LIGHTER, STIFFER, POSHER
Gerry McGovern's design team kept the floating roof, the clamshell bonnet and the upright glasshouse, then smoothed everything else. Underneath, the aluminium shell was built in a new all-aluminium facility at Solihull, using a high-strength alloy with up to 50 percent recycled content. The weight saving went straight into performance and economy: launch engines were a supercharged 5.0 V8, a 3.0 TDV6 and a 4.4 SDV8, all driving through a ZF eight-speed automatic and a Magna Steyr DD295 two-speed transfer case with a 50/50 torque split.
Off-road, the numbers moved the right way. In a UK road test of the launch TDV6, Land Rover quoted 303 mm of ground clearance (up 17 mm), a 900 mm wading depth (up 200 mm), and approach and departure angles of 34.7 and 29.6 degrees. Terrain Response 2 could now read the surface itself and choose between grass/gravel/snow, mud, sand and rock crawl. It would also back off the active anti-roll bars to let the wheels droop when it sensed the truck was off the tarmac.

### STRETCHED, HYBRIDISED, FACELIFTED
The range grew sideways for nine years. A long-wheelbase version, 200 mm longer between the axles at 3,122 mm, arrived at the 2013 Los Angeles show. A supercharged 3.0 V6 joined in 2014, an SDV6 diesel-electric hybrid followed, and Special Vehicle Operations turned the 5.0 V8 up to 550 PS, then 565 PS, for the SVAutobiography Dynamic. America finally got a diesel, the 254 hp Td6, for the 2016 model year. It was rated at 22 mpg city and 28 highway, against 14 and 19 for the supercharged V8.
The 2018 facelift brought a four-bar grille, new LED lights, thicker glass, and a second touchscreen in place of the climate knobs. The P400e plug-in hybrid followed, pairing a 2.0-litre Ingenium four with a 13.1 kWh battery and an 85 kW motor for 404 PS. Late trucks gained Ingenium straight-sixes, including a 3.0 mild-hybrid petrol for the 2020 model year. One planned derivative never made it: the three-door, 999-unit SV Coupé, shown at Geneva in 2018, was cancelled in January 2019 for financial reasons.

### THE CATCH
All that cleverness has a price, and second owners pay it. Specialist guides single out pre-2015 cars for the most electrical and body faults. The 3.0 TDV6 family is known for crankshaft and bearing failures, which a 2014 Land Rover bulletin blamed mainly on bearing shells being located wrongly or rotating. The supercharged 5.0 V8 eats timing-chain guides and cracks its plastic coolant pipes, and the air suspension wants compressors and struts. NHTSA lists keyless door-latch recalls for 2013–2016 trucks and front-knuckle cracking recalls for 2014–2017 trucks. None of that stops a sorted L405 being a superb, genuinely capable expedition limo — exactly why Lucky8 built a lifted, winched, rock-slidered 'Project L405' out of a supercharged one.

### LEGACY
The L405 ran from 2012 to 2021, which Top Gear noted is an age in motoring terms, and the Velar, named after the 1967 prototypes, was spun off during its lifetime. It was replaced by the L460 in late 2021. For off-roaders it is now the newest full-size Range Rover with real aftermarket support: lift rods, rock sliders, hidden winch mounts and 285-section all-terrains. Treat it like the 2.3-tonne computer it is, and it will go most places a Land Cruiser 200 goes — just more quietly, and with more dashboard messages.

### Data plate
- Built: 2012–2021 · Solihull, UK
- Model Years: 2013–2021
- Body: All-aluminium monocoque, 5-door
- Wheelbase: 2,922 mm · LWB 3,122 mm
- Length: 4,999 mm · LWB 5,199 mm
- Kerb Weight: 2,160–2,360 kg
- Suspension: Cross-linked air, adaptive dampers
- Transfer: Magna Steyr DD295, two-speed
- Gearbox: ZF 8HP eight-speed auto
- Engines: 5.0 SC V8 · 3.0 SC V6 · 3.0 TDV6/SDV6 · 4.4 SDV8 · P400e · 3.0 I6 MHEV
- Wading: 900 mm
- Towing: Up to 3,500 kg (V8s)

### Engineering
The L405 is a unibody truck with no separate frame. The structure is a riveted and bonded aluminium monocoque, sprung on cross-linked air springs at all four corners and driven full-time through a two-speed transfer case. It is light for its size, and it was properly engineered for off-road work. It is also completely dependent on its electronics: ride height, roll control, traction and even the transfer-case logic all go through modules that want a diagnostic tool, not a spanner.
- Body: All-aluminium monocoque (Body-shell 39% lighter; whole truck about 420 kg lighter than the steel L322.)
- Suspension: Cross-linked air springs (Access, normal and off-road heights plus automatic levelling; adaptive dampers and hydraulic anti-roll (Dynamic Response).)
- Transfer: Magna Steyr DD295 two-speed (Permanent 4WD, 50/50 torque split, high and low range.)
- Gearbox: ZF 8HP eight-speed auto (Fitted to every engine in the range.)
- Traction: Terrain Response 2 (Auto-detects surface; grass/gravel/snow, mud, sand, rock crawl; hill descent control and hill start assist.)
- Wading: 900 mm (Up 200 mm on the L322; 303 mm max ground clearance quoted at launch (TDV6).)

### Versions
- 2013–2021 · SWB 2,922 mm · LWB 3,122 mm (from 2014) · 5.0 supercharged V8 · 510 PS (2013–16), 525 PS (2017–) · US mainstay; 375 PS naturally aspirated 5.0 in some markets. Timing chain and coolant pipes are the watch items.
- 2014–2021 · SWB / LWB · 3.0 supercharged V6 · 340 or 380 PS · Shares the supercharger-isolator and plastic-coolant-pipe weaknesses of the V8 family.
- 2013–2021 · SWB / LWB · 3.0 TDV6 / SDV6 diesel · 258 PS (US Td6: 254 hp, 2016 MY on) · The economical pick; crank and bearing failures are documented on the TDV6 family.
- 2013–2021 · SWB / LWB (non-US) · 4.4 SDV8 diesel · 340 PS · Rated by specialists as good and reliable; watch EGR and turbo breather leaks.
- 2015– (UK) · SWB / LWB (non-US) · 3.0 SDV6 Hybrid · 340 PS, 700 Nm · 35 kW motor in the gearbox; PistonHeads dates UK availability to 2015. Basis of the Queen's State Review car.
- 2019 MY–2021 · Facelift, SWB / LWB · P400e 2.0 Ingenium PHEV · 404 PS, 640 Nm · 13.1 kWh battery and 85 kW motor; arrived with the four-bar-grille facelift.
- 2015–2021 · SVAutobiography (Dynamic) · 5.0 supercharged V8 · 550 PS, then 565 PS · SVO flagship; 565 PS cars quoted at 0–60 mph in 4.3 s.

### Year-by-year
- 2012: Unveiled at the Paris Motor Show and on sale late in the year as a 2013 model. All-aluminium monocoque about 420 kg lighter than the L322, ZF 8HP on every engine, Terrain Response 2, and a 5.0 V8 (375 or 510 PS supercharged), TDV6 or SDV8.
- 2013–14: Early trucks. Specialist guides single out pre-2015 cars for the most electrical and body faults, and recalls cover door latches, airbags and the brake vacuum hose. [avoid]
- 2014: Long wheelbase (3,122 mm) arrives, including the US-market Autobiography Black. 3.0 supercharged V6 (340 or 380 PS) added.
- 2016: Td6 diesel (254 hp) arrives in the US.
- 2018: Facelift. Four-bar grille, new LED daytime running lights, thicker glass, and a dual-screen infotainment system where a second LCD replaces the climate knobs. Seat controls move to the doors. ReRev rates 2018–21 the most reliable L405s [buy]
- 2019: P400e plug-in hybrid (2.0 Ingenium, 404 PS) offered.
- 2020: 3.0 Ingenium straight-six mild hybrid (P400) arrives. AutoTrader.ca recommends a 2020-or-newer truck with this engine if the budget allows. [buy]
- 2021: Final model year; the L460 is revealed in October 2021.

### Capability
- Towing: 7,716 lb (3,500 kg) braked (V8s; 3.0 V6s rated 3,000 kg (Australian figures))
- Payload: 1,764 lb (800 kg) (5.0 V8 NA: GVW 3,000 kg minus 2,200 kg curb (NAS owner guide))
- Roof load: 220 lb (100 kg) (maximum crossbar load, on top of the rails and crossbars)
- Fuel tank: 27.7 US gal (105 L) usable (V8 petrol; V8 diesel 103 L, V6 diesel 88 L)
- Ground clearance: 8.7 in (220.5 mm) (minimum, at standard road height; 303 mm max quoted at launch (TDV6, off-road height))
- Approach / departure / breakover: 31.4° / 30.7° / 134.8° (Land Rover's measure) (at curb weight and standard road height, no tow bar)
- Wading depth: 35.4 in (900 mm) (at Off-Road 2 height)
- Fuel economy: EPA 14 city / 19 hwy / 16 combined (2016 5.0 supercharged; 3.0 SC V6 17/23/19; Td6 diesel 22/28/24)
- Curb weight: 4,850–5,203 lb (2,200–2,360 kg) (SWB, by engine; V6 diesel from 2,160 kg)
- Turning circle: 41.7 ft (12.7 m) (wall to wall)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 235/65R19 on 7.5J x 19, 255/55R20 on 8.5J x 20, 275/45R21 on 9.5J x 21, 275/40R22 on 9.5J x 22
- Bolt Pattern: 5x120
- Center Bore: 72.6 mm
- Lug Thread: M14x1.5
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 285/50R20 (About 31.2 in. FullFatRR consensus is that it won't rub in any height mode, and the spare still fits the well. 275/55R20 (about 31.9 in) is also common but may catch at full lock. Owners treat 20 in as the smallest wheel that reliably clears the brakes.)

### Buying checks
- Check every recall is closed: NHTSA lists keyless door-latch recalls for 2013–2016 trucks (doors may unlatch) and front-suspension knuckle recalls for 2014–2017 trucks (the upper knuckle joint can crack). AutoTrader.ca counted at least 19 safety recalls on this generation in Canada. Trucks that left the dealer network early are the most likely to have open campaigns. Run the VIN.
- Be extra careful with pre-2015 trucks: PistonHeads' L405 guide says early cars had the most electrical and body problems. It advises a warranty, saying Land Rover's own cover for early cars costs around £1,400 a year after a free inspection. Panel fit on the rear doors, tailgate and bonnet is a known weak spot, and so are door seals.
- Listen to the front end on a rough road: Coast and brake moderately over broken tarmac. Clunks or pops point to worn front track control arms or rear lower arms (around £700 fitted as a pair, per PistonHeads) — or, on 2014–2017 trucks, to the knuckle recall. AutoTrader.ca says not to take delivery of one with unusual front-end noise.
- Watch the ride height overnight: Compressors fail and air springs split, and PistonHeads calls both 'known things.' Look for a corner that sags after standing, a compressor that runs constantly, or suspension faults on the dash. Check that every height mode works: access, normal and off-road.
- Cold-start a 5.0 V8 yourself: A rattle lasting a second or two on a cold start is the classic sign of tired timing-chain guides and tensioners, particularly on 2010–2014 engines. Fault codes P0016–P0019 come later. A metallic rattle at idle can instead be the supercharger coupler or isolator. Look for coolant loss too: the plastic crossover pipes crack.
- Ask how the diesel was serviced: TDV6/SDV6 crank-bearing failures are documented in Land Rover bulletin SSM71816 and in owner threads. Owners suspect oil sludging under long intervals and the wrong oil grade play a part. Ask for regular servicing with the correct oil. On the 4.4 SDV8, check for EGR faults and oily turbo breather pipes (up to £850 to replace).
- Test the screens and switches: Infotainment freezes, dead cameras and Bluetooth faults are common and often fixed by software. If the head unit goes black or won't boot, assume an expensive repair until proved otherwise. Check the start/stop and steering-wheel buttons, the interior door releases, and the rotary gear selector, which can fail to rise.
- Look at the wheels, and the transfer-case history: PistonHeads says the 22-inch wheels are soft and buckle on potholes, so check them for bends. AutoTrader.ca advises that any non-factory wheels come from a reputable brand and be rated for the truck's weight. Transfer-box and differential oil should be changed at around 30,000 miles, so ask for proof.

### Common repairs
#### Front air strut replacement
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours per side (forum labour estimate for full-size Range Rover struts) · cost Front strut about $730–$830 (Lucky8 BWI/OE listings), plus labor
Symptoms: One front corner sitting low after standing, a hiss when the truck lowers to access height, the compressor working overtime, or air-suspension faults that come back after recalibration.
Fix: Relieve the system pressure (it runs up to 10 bar) and disconnect the battery. With the wheels straight, raise the truck, support it safely and remove the wheel. Unplug the strut's electrical connector, release the air line and remove its fitting, then remove the sensor-wire and brake-line bracket and the lower strut bolt. Unhook the anti-roll bar link from the strut clevis and separate the upper control arm ball joint from the knuckle. Remove the top mount nuts, swing the knuckle out and lift the strut out. To fit: leave the air fitting on the new strut, install the strut and lower bolt, reconnect the upper arm, clevis, sway-bar link and brackets, fit the top bolts, then remove the shipping pin and push the air line home until it locks. Plug in the connector, torque everything to factory spec, refit the wheel and recalibrate the ride heights.
Tools: Jack and stands · sockets and ball-joint separator · Arnott ASE-3756 (new electronic) or AS-3067 RH / AS-3068 LH (remanufactured, 2013–2018), or OE LR079515 RH · diagnostic tool with air-suspension calibration (e.g., GAP IID)

#### Air-suspension lift rods (height-sensor links)
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 20–30 minutes · cost About $99 per set (Lucky8)
Symptoms: Not a fault — it's the cheapest lift on the planet. The truck sits too low for bigger tyres or rough tracks, or scrapes its sills in ruts.
Fix: Remove the factory ride-height sensor rods at each corner and fit the longer links in their place: short rods at the front, long rods at the rear. The links fool the sensors into reading the truck as lower than it is, so the air springs raise every height mode by 1, 1.5 or 2 inches depending on the kit. No coding is needed and Terrain Response keeps working. Get a wheel alignment afterwards.
Tools: Basic hand tools · Proud Rhino PR25DEF-1 (1 in), PR25DEF-1.5 (1.5 in) or PR25D5 (2 in) lift rods · alignment afterwards

#### Front lower control arms (clunk fix)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Varies · cost Around £700 fitted for the common arm pair (PistonHeads); arms from about $290 a pair aftermarket, $785 genuine, $489 polybushed
Symptoms: Knocks or clunks from the front over broken surfaces and under moderate braking; vague steering; uneven tyre wear.
Fix: First run the VIN for the 2014–2017 front-knuckle recall, because a cracking upper knuckle joint can also make noises and is fixed free by dealers. If the knuckles are clear, support the truck on stands, remove the wheel, unbolt the lower arm from the knuckle and the subframe, swap in the new arm, and do the final bush torque with the suspension at ride height. Recalibrate the ride height if a height sensor was disturbed, then align.
Tools: Jack and stands · large sockets and breaker bar · ball-joint separator · LR072469 (LH) / LR072471 (RH) arms, or Lucky8 polybushed kit NFLCKPB · alignment afterwards

#### 5.0 supercharged cooling-pipe and water-pump refresh
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time Varies — the rear crossover pipe sits under the supercharger · cost Shop price about CA$1,800–3,200 for the pipes (supercharger removal), plus CA$900–1,500 for a water pump; ARC050 aluminium pipe kit $199
Symptoms: Unexplained coolant loss, sweet smell, weeping at the back of the engine or around the thermostat housing. Plastic pipes typically go around 100,000 km and water pumps around 80,000–140,000 km.
Fix: Drain the coolant and remove the supercharger to reach the valley. Replace the factory plastic rear crossover pipe, front Y-tube, oil-cooler-to-water-pump adapter and front crossover bypass with aluminium parts. Do the water pump and thermostat housing while it's apart. Refit the supercharger with new gaskets, then refill and bleed the system. The supplier recommends professional installation.
Tools: Full socket set and torque wrench · coolant and drain pan · ARC050 kit (LR122709/LR109402 rear crossover, LR092992 Y-tube, LR028136 adapter, LR090630 bypass) or SCV85LAUCK kit with water pump and aluminium thermostat housing

#### 5.0 V8 timing chains, guides and tensioners
Difficulty 5 / 5 · time Varies — a shop job · cost About CA$4,500–7,500 at a specialist; genuine 34-piece kit $1,599
Symptoms: A rattle for a second or two on a cold start, later joined by cam-timing codes P0016, P0017, P0018 or P0019.
Fix: Lock the engine at the correct position with the JLR timing tools before anything comes apart. Replace both cam chains, the tensioners and blades, both guides, the auxiliary drive chain with its tensioner and guide, and the cam lubricating jets, then refit with new rocker-cover gaskets and spark-plug seals. Don't reuse old tensioners or guides: reusing tired parts is the shortcut that brings the truck back on a hook.
Tools: JLR camshaft and crank locking tools · torque wrench · Lucky8 5LTCK genuine kit (chains LR032048, tensioners LR051008, blades LR051013, guides LR051011/LR051012, aux chain LR032087)

#### Supercharger coupler / isolator
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time Varies — the snout must come apart · cost About CA$900–1,500 for the isolator; CA$2,000–2,800 for a full snout rebuild
Symptoms: A metallic rattle or knock from the front of the engine at idle, often mistaken for timing chain; a louder-than-normal whine means dry snout bearings.
Fix: Rule out the timing chain first with a cold-start listen and a scan for cam-timing codes. Then remove the supercharger snout, replace the spring-type isolator or coupler and, if they're noisy, the snout bearings, and reassemble with a new gasket. One supercharger rebuilder says the stock spring-type isolator usually starts failing from around 50,000 miles. Check isolator/coupler fitment for your engine's build year before ordering.
Tools: Sockets and torque wrench · snout gasket · 5.0 supercharger repair kit (Lucky8 lists LR088564)

#### Auxiliary stop/start battery
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Varies · cost About $288 for the AGM auxiliary battery (Lucky8)
Symptoms: Stop/start that works only sometimes or not at all, rough or slow restarts, low-voltage warnings and odd infotainment behaviour.
Fix: Test the main battery first, since it is separate and a weak one also upsets stop/start. If the auxiliary battery is at fault, replace it with an AGM unit and register the new battery with a diagnostic tool so the battery-management system uses the right charging strategy. Check for any outstanding software updates.
Tools: Battery tester · basic sockets · LR047630 / LR176847 auxiliary battery · diagnostic tool for BMS registration

### Baseline service
Baseline everything, and before anything else run the VIN through Land Rover's recall lookup (the 2014–17 knuckle recall alone is worth it). Land Rover calls the ZF eight-speed 'filled for life' and gives the diffs and transfer box exact wet-fill volumes, so treat the official capacities below as the target and measure what goes in.
- Engine oil & filter: Petrol 5.0 V8 / 3.0 V6 SC: 0W-20 to STJLR.51.5122 (the launch handbook listed 5W-20 to WSS-M2C925-A), 8.0 L for the V8 · TDV6/SDV6 (DPF): 5W-30 to STJLR.03.5005 / WSS-M2C934-B, 6.0 L · SDV8 (DPF): same spec, 9.4 L · Then every 10,000 mi or sooner (owner practice); [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] for the factory schedule (The DPF diesels are fussy about oil, so only use oil approved to STJLR.03.5005. Don't overfill the SDV8: put in about 8.5 L, wait, then top up using the electronic level check.)
- Engine air filters: LR011593 (two elements on the V8) · Then every oil service if you run dirt roads; [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Two elements on the V8. Replace both.)
- Cabin (pollen) filter: LR036369 · Then annually
- Spark plugs (petrol): 5.0 V8: set of 8 (LR032080 in Britpart's kit DA6099) · [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Supercharged V8s with no proof of plugs get them now. Check the coil packs and plug-well seals while you're there.)
- Coolant: 1:1 Havoline XLC antifreeze and water · refill 6.83 L (5.0 NA), 8.83 L (5.0 SC), 8.93 L (V6 diesel), 7.13 L (V8 diesel) · Change if the history is unknown; then [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (On the 5.0 SC, unexplained coolant loss usually means the plastic pipes under the supercharger (see the repair above), not the radiator.)
- ZF 8HP70 transmission: Shell ATF L12108 · Land Rover lists it as 'filled for life' · Lucky8 recommends fluid and filter every 50,000–75,000 mi, sooner if you tow (The filter is built into the pan (LR065238), so a service means a new pan. Drain and refill, then level-check at the specified temperature with a scan tool. Don't flush.)
- Transfer box: Shell TF 0753 (TL 7300), 1.5 L · Then every 60,000 mi (owner practice) (Use only TF 0753-spec fluid: the centre clutch depends on its friction modifiers. Put in a measured fill. Replace the M16 drain/fill washers (IYF500030).)
- Front & rear differentials: Front: Castrol SAF-XO, 0.54 L wet fill · Rear non-locking: SAF-XO, 0.85 L · Rear electronic locker: Castrol BOT 720, 1.25 L · Then every 60,000 mi (owner practice) (These are much smaller fills than the L322 figures you'll find on forums. Use the L405 numbers. The electronic locker takes its own fluid.)
- Dynamic Response hydraulic fluid: Texaco Cold Climate PAS fluid 33270 (V8 diesel and V8 SC with Dynamic Response) · Check level and look for leaks at purchase (Trucks with Dynamic Response have hydraulic active anti-roll bars. Leaks at the bar actuators or valve block are expensive, so look for them before you buy.)
- Brake fluid & pads: Shell DOT4 ESL, or low-viscosity DOT4 to ISO 4925 class 6 and LRES22BF03 · Change at purchase if undated; then [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Check pad and rotor thickness at all four corners. Heavy trucks with big wheels eat rear pads.)
- Air suspension health check: Compressor, struts, height sensors · At purchase, then whenever a corner sits low after standing (Measure each corner after the truck has stood overnight and listen for the compressor running too often. Front struts are the common failure (see the repair above).)
- Main & auxiliary batteries: Main battery plus an AGM auxiliary stop/start battery (LR047630 / LR176847) · Load-test both at purchase (Weak batteries cause phantom faults on the L405. Register any new battery with a scan tool so the battery-management system uses the right charge strategy.)
- Supercharger isolator & timing-chain listen (5.0 SC): Cold-start listen and a scan for P0016–P0019 · At purchase (A cold-start rattle or cam-timing codes point to the timing chains. A rattle at idle points to the supercharger isolator. Know which before you buy.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: On 20-inch wheels, the FullFatRR consensus is 285/50R20 (about 31.2 in). Two owners run them, one calls them probably the largest that won't rub in any height mode, and the spare still fits the well. 275/55R20 (about 31.9 in) is also fitted by 'quite a few' owners, though one member predicted it might just catch at full lock. Twenty inches is the smallest rim owners trust to clear the brakes, and 255/60R20 tyres on new-Defender wheels also fit. Want bigger? Lucky8 has a video on trimming the bumper for larger tyres on its lifted Project L405.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: For the 2016 model year, the EPA rated the supercharged 5.0 V8 at 14 mpg city, 19 highway and 16 combined, the 3.0 supercharged V6 at 17/23/19, and the Td6 diesel at 22/28/24. PistonHeads reports about 30 mpg (UK) in real-world driving for the 4.4 SDV8.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: Australian-market figures give 3,500 kg (7,716 lb) braked for the V8s, petrol or diesel, and 3,000 kg for the 3.0 V6s. Check your owner's manual and plate; the figure varies by engine and market.

Q: Which engine should I buy?
A: What Car? calls the 3.0 TDV6 the sensible choice. PistonHeads rates the 4.4 SDV8 as 'a good and reliable engine' without the TDV6's crank issues or timing belt. In the US, the choice is the 5.0 V8 (thirsty, chain and coolant-pipe risks), the 3.0 V6, the Td6 diesel from 2016, or the later hybrids. AutoTrader.ca recommends a 2020-or-newer truck with the straight-six if budget allows.

Q: Is the TDV6 crankshaft failure real?
A: Yes, but it isn't universal. Land Rover service bulletin SSM71816 (May 2014) blamed a 'low incidence' of crank failures mainly on wrongly located or rotating main-bearing shells. In a FullFatRR poll of L405 3.0 owners, 88% reported no issues. The usual advice is the correct oil, shorter oil-change intervals than the maximum, and a warranty that covers the engine.

Q: Does it have low range?
A: Yes. Every L405 has permanent four-wheel drive with a Magna Steyr DD295 two-speed transfer case, a 50/50 split and a low range, managed by Terrain Response 2 with hill descent control. Change the transfer-box and diff oil at around 30,000 miles.

Q: How can I lift it?
A: The easy way is height-sensor lift rods, which raise every air-suspension mode by 1, 1.5 or 2 inches with no electronics. Proud Rhino's rods take about 20–30 minutes to fit, and Lucky8 recommends an alignment afterwards.

Q: Can I work on the air suspension at home?
A: Mostly, with the right scan tool. GAP's IID G4 tool lists air-suspension height adjustment and guided calibration for the L405. 2017–2022 trucks work with the standard tool, but 2013–2016 trucks need the optional adapter version. Struts and the compressor unbolt with hand tools, but the system runs at up to 10 bar, so depressurise it first, and the calibration afterwards needs the tool.

Q: Pre-facelift or facelift?
A: The 2018 facelift added the four-bar grille, new LED lights, thicker glass, Touch Pro Duo screens and the P400e plug-in hybrid. More importantly, PistonHeads says pre-2015 trucks had the most electrical and body faults, ReRev rates 2018–21 the most reliable years (and flags 2017 for windscreen-seal leaks), and AutoTrader.ca suggests a 2020-on straight-six if the budget allows. Later is better.

Q: How deep can it wade?
A: Land Rover quoted 900 mm (35.4 in), 200 mm more than the L322, with up to 303 mm of ground clearance at off-road height.

Q: Was there a long-wheelbase version?
A: Yes. Revealed at the 2013 LA Auto Show with deliveries from early 2014, it has a 3,122 mm (122.9 in) wheelbase and is 5,199 mm long — 200 mm more in each than the standard truck.
