## Land Rover Range Rover L460 (2022–present)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/range-rover/l460/
Codes: L460

Verdict: The most capable limousine ever to ask you to install a software update before breakfast. It will still crawl in low range — just don't expect the aftermarket, or the DC-DC converter, to keep up.

On 26 October 2021, Gerry McGovern pulled the covers off the fifth Range Rover at the Royal Opera House in London — a suitably theatrical venue for a truck that is mostly about refinement. The L460 keeps the family silhouette and the two-speed transfer box, then piles on things no Range Rover has had before: a seven-seat option, four-wheel steering, plug-in hybrids with a real electric range, a BMW-sourced V8 and, from the 2027 model year in America, a fully electric version. It is the most technically ambitious Range Rover yet, and its first few years brought a long list of recalls to match.

### MLA-FLEX AND THE BIG STRETCH
The L460 rides on JLR's MLA-Flex architecture, shared with the third-generation Range Rover Sport. It grew in every direction over the L405: 53 mm longer, 63 mm wider and 35 mm taller, on a wheelbase 75 mm longer at 2,997 mm. The long-wheelbase version adds another 200 mm between the axles, and it is the only body that offers seven seats. JLR claims torsional rigidity is up 50 percent to 50,000 Nm per degree, and a steel closed-section front bulkhead cuts road noise entering the cabin by about 24 percent.
Off-road hardware survived the luxury push. US-spec trucks still list a twin-speed transfer box with high and low range, Terrain Response 2, All Terrain Progress Control and hill descent control. Upper trims get an Electronic Active Differential with torque vectoring, while the SE makes do with an open rear diff and torque vectoring by braking. New tricks include all-wheel steering, the first on a Land Rover, which gives a 10.95 m turning circle. An intelligent AWD system can also disconnect the front axle between 35 and 160 km/h to cut drag losses by 30 percent.

### SIX, EIGHT, PLUG, BATTERY
Engines are all electrified to some degree. The core is JLR's 3.0-litre Ingenium straight-six, as a 400 PS mild-hybrid petrol, as 249–350 PS mild-hybrid diesels outside the US, or as a plug-in hybrid with a 38.2 kWh battery and a 105 kW motor (160 kW on the later P550e). The P440e and P510e launched the PHEVs, and the P550e replaced the P440e for the 2024 model year. The V8 is BMW's twin-turbo 4.4. Early P530s used the N63, and from the 2024 model year JLR switched to the newer S68, which also powers the 615 PS SV. In EPA testing a 2023 P530 managed 16 mpg city and 21 highway, the P400 18 and 26, and the P440e 51 MPGe on electricity.
Then the big one. Range Rover Electric is available to order in the US as a 2027 model, with twin 260 kW motors, 660 lb-ft, an 800-volt battery architecture and an EPA range of 333 miles. Land Rover is careful to say it is still a Range Rover. It quotes a 35-inch wading depth and 5,511 lb of towing, and the battery sits behind a flat, re-engineered underbody meant to cope with sliding over obstacles.

### GROWING PAINS
The launch was rough. Owners on FullFatRR report early cars delivered with downgraded audio and other options because JLR couldn't get the parts. Then came the recalls. NHTSA lists, among others, a blocked cam-carrier oil channel (2022–2023 L460s; the same campaign covers 2020–21 L405s), badly welded second-row seat frames on 2022–2023 seven-seaters, damaged tail-light links, and 2024 trucks with body panels that may not have been bonded properly. UK owners also reported a rear-subframe cracking recall in 2023. The headline problem now is the 48-volt to 12-volt DC-DC converter on mild hybrids: when it fails, the 12-volt battery stops charging. NHTSA recall 26V248000 covers 2020–2024 Range Rovers (including late L405 mild hybrids) with an interim central-software fix, and follow-up campaign 26V599000 adds a further software update, with a final remedy still to come.
None of that changes what it is on a trail: a very wide, very heavy luxury car with low range, clever traction electronics and air suspension that does its job well. What it lacks is an aftermarket. A 2025 FullFatRR thread asking for sliders and underbody protection was told to budget €3,500–4,000 for a fabrication shop. Owners weighing one for African dirt roads were pointed at a Defender or a Land Cruiser 300. Treat the L460 as a superb gravel-and-green-lane machine, and keep it away from rock gardens.

### Data plate
- Revealed: 26 Oct 2021 · Royal Opera House, London
- Built: Solihull, UK (also assembled in Pune, India)
- Platform: JLR MLA-Flex
- Wheelbase: 2,997 mm · LWB 3,197 mm
- Length: 5,052 mm · LWB 5,252 mm
- Width / Height: 2,047 mm / 1,870 mm
- Kerb Weight: 2,454–2,810 kg
- Seats: 4, 5 or 7 (7 in LWB only)
- Steering: All-wheel steer · 10.95 m turning circle
- Transfer: Twin-speed, high/low range
- Engines: 3.0 I6 MHEV/PHEV · 4.4 BMW V8 · 3.0 I6 diesel · Electric
- Towing: Up to 7,716 lb (US)

### Engineering
The L460 is a mixed-material monocoque on JLR's MLA-Flex platform, built for electrification from the start: mild-hybrid, plug-in and battery-electric versions share the same body. It keeps the Range Rover essentials, with air suspension, permanent AWD and a two-speed transfer case on combustion models, then adds rear-wheel steering, a disconnecting front axle and a lot of software. For a hands-on owner, that means fewer bolt-on problems and more electrical ones. A capable scan tool is no longer optional.
- Platform: MLA-Flex monocoque (Claimed 50,000 Nm/deg torsional rigidity (+50%); steel closed-section front bulkhead.)
- Steering: All-wheel steering (First Land Rover with it; 10.95 m turning circle (SWB), 11.54 m (LWB).)
- Suspension: Air, double wishbone / multi-link (Twin-valve monotube dampers managed by Adaptive Dynamics; variable ride height.)
- Drivetrain: iAWD + twin-speed transfer (Front axle can disconnect at 35–160 km/h; high and low range on combustion models.)
- Differentials: Electronic Active Differential (With torque vectoring on upper trims; SE has an open rear diff with torque vectoring by braking (US spec).)
- Powertrains: MHEV · PHEV · BEV (3.0 Ingenium I6, BMW 4.4 V8 (N63 then S68), 38.2 kWh PHEV, 800 V Electric.)

### Versions
- 2022–present · SWB / LWB · P400 3.0 I6 turbo MHEV (P360 also offered) · 400 PS, 550 Nm · EPA 18/26 mpg (2023). US towing up to 7,716 lb.
- 2022–2023 · SWB / LWB · P530 BMW N63 4.4 twin-turbo V8 MHEV · 530 PS, 750 Nm · EPA 16/21 mpg (2023). Engine changed for MY2024.
- 2024–present · SWB / LWB, SV · BMW S68 4.4 twin-turbo V8 MHEV (P530, P615) · 530 PS; 615 PS (SV) · Owners describe it as more refined than the N63.
- 2022–2023 · SWB / LWB (not 7-seat) · P440e / P510e 3.0 I6 PHEV · 440 / 510 PS · 38.2 kWh battery (31.8 usable), 105 kW motor; P440e EPA 51 MPGe.
- 2024–present · SWB / LWB (not 7-seat) · P550e 3.0 I6 PHEV · 550 PS, 800 Nm · Replaced the P440e; 160 kW motor; Land Rover estimates about 50 miles of real-world EV range.
- 2022–present · Non-US markets · D250 / D300 / D350 3.0 I6 twin-turbo diesel MHEV · 249 / 300 / 350 PS · Owners report 24 MY D350s with a shorter 10,500-mile / 12-month service interval.
- 2027 MY (US) · Range Rover Electric · Twin 260 kW motors, 800 V battery · 660 lb-ft · EPA range 333 miles; 35-in wading; 5,511 lb towing.

### Year-by-year
- 2021: Revealed on 26 October 2021 at the Royal Opera House in London. MLA-Flex platform, the first Land Rover with all-wheel steering, and BMW's N63 4.4 V8 in the P530.
- 2022: Production at Solihull from mid-2022. Launch engines: P360/P400 I6 mild hybrids, P530 V8, and P440e/P510e plug-in hybrids (diesels outside the US). A seven-seat LWB followed shortly after launch. Owners say many early trucks were delivered with options deleted during the parts shortage.
- 2022–23: Early trucks carry the most open campaigns: seven-seat frame welds, tail-light links, rear-camera water ingress, the cam-carrier oil channel and the armrest latch. Run the VIN.
- 2024: P550e replaces the P440e and the 615 PS SV arrives. BMW's S68 V8 replaces the N63, and owners rate it more refined. Physical HVAC controls are removed. 2024 trucks have their own recalls (panel bonding, transmission oil pressure, oil filter housing)
- 2024: JLR announces local Range Rover assembly in Pune, India (May 2024).
- 2026: Range Rover Electric unveiled on 2 September 2026 after repeated delays: 800 V, twin 260 kW motors and a 118.5 kWh battery.
- 2027: Range Rover Electric goes on sale in the US as a 2027 model, with 333 miles of EPA range, a 900 mm wading depth and a 5,511 lb towing rating.

### Capability
- Towing: 7,716 lb (3,500 kg) (P400 and V8s; current PHEV 6,614 lb; Range Rover Electric 5,511 lb)
- Wading depth: 35.4 in (900 mm) (combustion models and Range Rover Electric)
- Fuel economy: EPA 18 city / 26 hwy / 21 combined (2023 P400 MHEV; 2023 P530 V8 16/21/18; 2023 P440e 51 MPGe, 21 mpg gas-only)
- Curb weight: 5,410–6,360 lb (2,454–2,885 kg) (by powertrain and body)
- Turning circle: 35.9 ft (10.95 m) SWB; 37.9 ft (11.54 m) LWB (with all-wheel steering)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 255/60R20 on 8J x 20 (ET39.5), 275/55R20 on 8.5J x 20 (ET43.5), 275/50R21 on 8.5J x 21 (ET43.5), 285/45R22 on 9.5J x 22 (ET42.5), 23-in wheels optional
- Bolt Pattern: 5x120
- Offset: ET39.5–43.5 (stock 20–22 in)
- Lug Thread: Wheel bolts (not studs and nuts); earlier Range Rover wheels need the correct flat-seat bolts

### Buying checks
- Run the VIN against every recall: NHTSA lists a stack of campaigns: a cam-carrier oil channel (2022–2023), 7-seat second-row frame welds (2022–2023), tail-light links (2022–2023), rear-camera water ingress (2022–2023) and tailgate camera drain holes (2022–2026), body panels not bonded properly (2024), transmission oil pressure (2024), a cracking oil filter housing (2024), the driver's airbag clockspring connector (2022–2026), and the DC-DC converter (26V248000 and 26V599000, 2022–2024 L460s). Get written confirmation that they're closed.
- Ask about the DC-DC converter: On mild hybrids, a failing 48-volt to 12-volt converter shows 'Stop – electrical fault' with a red battery light and stops charging the 12-volt battery. Owners say it may log no fault and clear itself, only to return. Dealers have had cars waiting weeks for back-ordered modules. NHTSA recalls 26V248000 and 26V599000 are interim software updates, with a final remedy to follow.
- Check that it goes to sleep: Flat 12-volt batteries after a few days parked are a recurring forum topic. Dealers have fixed some with door-module and other software updates, and one owner traced the same symptom to a brake-pedal security lock that kept the car from sleeping. Ask whether it has needed jump-starts, and whether any aftermarket immobiliser or tracker is fitted.
- Check the build spec on early trucks: Owners say many early (2022) trucks were delivered with downgraded audio and other options during the parts shortage. Check the car against its original order or a parts catalogue before paying for options it doesn't have.
- Know which V8 you're getting: P530s built for 2022–2023 use BMW's N63 twin-turbo V8, while 2024-on trucks got the newer S68. Forum owners rate the S68 as significantly more refined. It's also the engine in the SV P615.
- Look at the service history, not just the stamps: Service intervals were up to 21,000 miles or 24 months, and owners report the 2024 model year D350 dropped to 10,500 miles or 12 months. Many owners change the oil more often than the schedule asks. A truck run to the maximum on short urban trips deserves extra scrutiny.
- Check software and connectivity: Updates arrive over the air, but one 2022 owner whose truck was stuck on an old version found reports of a telematics (TCU) problem on some 2022–23 trucks. Check the software version against Land Rover's published releases, and confirm the remote app works.
- Mind the wheel bolts and wheel size: The L460 uses wheel bolts, not the studs and nuts of the L405, so older Range Rover wheels need the correct flat-seat bolts. Owners say 22- and 23-inch wheels ride harshly on broken roads. For trail use, a smaller wheel with more sidewall is the better bet.

### Common repairs
#### Rear brake pads (electric parking brake service mode)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Varies · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: A pad-wear warning (one owner's P440e needed rear pads at 31,000 miles, another owner's at 16,000), or grinding at the rear. NHTSA has several similar complaints from 2023–24 owners, with pads worn out at roughly 10,000–17,000 miles; one 2023 long-wheelbase owner says the dealer blamed the design and fitted a different pad.
Fix: The rear calipers use an electric parking brake, so put the brake into service (maintenance) mode before you push the pistons back. Shops do this with a scan tool. With the truck supported and the wheels off, remove the caliper, swap the pads (one owner fitted genuine pads and found a single wear sensor), refit, then take the brake out of service mode and check it applies properly.
Tools: Jack and stands · sockets · pad spreader · scan tool with EPB service mode (e.g., GAP IID, which lists 2022–2025 L460 support) · new pads

#### 12-volt battery replacement and BMS registration
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Varies · cost Auxiliary stop/start battery about $288 (Lucky8); parts plus labor
Symptoms: 'Low battery, please start engine' messages, a truck that is electrically dead after a few days parked, or alarm and keyless-entry glitches.
Fix: First rule out software (door-module and RFA updates have fixed some drains) and anything keeping the car awake. Then load-test the 12-volt battery. On a 2024 D350, one owner found the lithium-ion starter battery under the driver's seat, only removable with the truck on a ramp. A label under the bonnet says to jump-start at no more than 13.7 V, so don't use a random jump pack. Fit the correct battery type and register it with a diagnostic tool so the battery-management system charges it properly. Some trucks also carry an AGM auxiliary stop/start battery. Check fitment by VIN.
Tools: Battery tester · lift or ramp (lithium battery under driver's seat on some trucks) · LR047630 / LR176847 auxiliary battery where fitted · diagnostic tool for BMS registration

#### 48 V to 12 V DC-DC converter
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time Varies · cost Specialist roughly £700–800 for the part plus about £400 to fit and program; dealers quoted £1,800–2,000 (owner reports)
Symptoms: 'Stop – electrical fault detected' with a red battery light, the 12-volt battery not charging, and possibly loss of drive. Often no stored faults, and it may clear itself before coming back.
Fix: Check first whether NHTSA recalls 26V248000 and 26V599000 (US) have been done. It adds a central software update to stop the converter overloading, and it's free. If the converter has already failed, it has to be replaced and then programmed to the vehicle, so use a dealer or a JLR specialist with the right software. Parts have been back-ordered, so plan on the truck being off the road for a while.
Tools: JLR-capable diagnostic and programming tool · replacement DC-DC converter module

#### Transfer box and driveline oil change
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Varies · cost Genuine fluid about £106 + VAT for 2 litres (owner report), plus labor
Symptoms: Preventive. Owners suggest doing the transfer box at around 60,000 miles, along with the ZF gearbox and both differentials.
Fix: Drain and refill the transfer box with about 2 litres of the fluid Land Rover specifies. Owners argue about cheaper alternatives, and one experienced member insists a generic transfer fluid is the wrong oil for the L460, so check the handbook rather than forum advice. One owner notes the front-axle disconnect clutch uses the same fluid as the active rear differential.
Tools: Sockets and drain plugs/washers · fluid pump · Land Rover-specified transfer fluid (≈ 2 L)

#### Engine oil and filter (shorter interval)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Varies · cost Parts only if DIY
Symptoms: None. Owners just don't trust a 20,000-mile interval, and the 2024 model-year D350 schedule dropped to 10,500 miles or 12 months.
Fix: Drain the sump, replace the cartridge filter and refill with the specified oil, then reset the service counter with a scan tool. Lubricate both sealing rings on the filter's neck, because a dry filter can twist on installation. Many owners on FullFatRR change oil well ahead of the onboard reminder.
Tools: Sockets · filter housing tool · drain pan · new sump plug washer · correct-spec oil · scan tool for service reset (e.g., GAP IID)

#### Factory-style tow hitch and wiring
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Varies · cost About $1,288 (genuine NAS hitch) to $1,628 (Lucky8 receiver + wiring combo)
Symptoms: No receiver, and you have a 7,716 lb-rated truck and a trailer.
Fix: Fit the receiver to the rear structure, run the towing harness, install the towing module (ECU) and fit the bumper trim finisher. The Lucky8 combo fits SWB trucks only, and the supplier needs the VIN because trucks with and without a third row, and different trim colours, take different parts.
Tools: Sockets and torque wrench · trim tools · Lucky8 RRL460TOWKITVINFIRST combo or genuine VPLKT0326 hitch · towing module VPLYT0295

#### Cracked oil filter housing
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time Varies · cost Free under recall 24V-450 (Land Rover N908); otherwise parts plus labor
Symptoms: Oil seeping around the oil filter housing, a hot-oil smell from the engine bay, or the oil level dropping between services. Land Rover recalled certain 2024 Range Rovers, plus some 2023–24 Defenders and 2024 Discoverys, Range Rover Sports and Velars, because the housing can crack and leak oil into the engine compartment, where it can catch fire on hot engine or exhaust parts.
Fix: Run the VIN first. The recall remedy is a new filter housing, oil filter and O-rings, fitted free by a dealer (owner letters went out in June 2024). On a truck outside the recall that's leaking from the same place, the repair is the same: replace the housing with new O-rings and a new filter, following the workshop procedure for your engine, top up the oil and check for leaks at temperature. Clean any oil off the exhaust and undertrays afterwards.
Tools: Sockets and torque wrench · drain pan · new O-rings lubricated with clean oil · brake cleaner and rags

#### Rear camera water damage
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time Varies · cost Free under recalls 24V-947 and 26V-678; otherwise a camera plus labor
Symptoms: A blank, fogged or distorted rear-view image, or a camera fault message when you select reverse. Land Rover has recalled the L460's rear camera twice for water: 2022–23 trucks because water can get inside the camera (24V-947), and 2022–26 trucks because there aren't enough drain holes for water to escape the camera area (26V-678).
Fix: Run the VIN. Under 24V-947 dealers replace the camera; under 26V-678 they drill extra drain holes in the underside of the tailgate trim and replace the camera if it's damaged. Land Rover planned to mail interim owner letters for 26V-678 in December 2026. On a truck you wash often or take through water crossings, keep the area under the tailgate trim clear of mud so water can drain.
Tools: Trim-removal tools · scan tool to calibrate the surround cameras after a camera change (dealer or JLR specialist)

### Baseline service
The L460 is new enough that most trucks will have dealer history. Still, the first job is the recall and software status, because several known faults (DC-DC converter, battery drain) are fixed by updates. Fluid specs differ by powertrain (Ingenium I6 diesel or petrol, BMW V8, PHEV) and the BorgWarner transfer box takes its own fluid, so read the owner's handbook for your VIN rather than reusing L405 figures.
- Recalls & software updates: NHTSA recall lookup by VIN, plus dealer / over-the-air software status · At purchase, then whenever a campaign is announced (Recalls 26V248000 and 26V599000 (US) add central software updates so the 48 V–12 V converter doesn't overload, and door-module and RFA updates have cured some battery drains. All are free and stop expensive failures.)
- Engine oil & filter: D300/D350 Ingenium diesel: 0W-30 to STJLR.03.5007, about 9 L (owner report) · Petrol I6 / PHEV / V8: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · The 2024MY D350 schedule is 10,500 mi or 12 months. Many owners change sooner. (Lubricate both sealing rings on the cartridge filter's neck before fitting, because a dry filter can twist. Reset the service counter with a scan tool afterwards.)
- Engine air filter: [CONFIRM BY VIN] · [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
- Cabin (pollen) filter: [CONFIRM BY VIN] · Then annually
- Spark plugs (petrol / PHEV I6): Genuine iridium plugs, set of 6 (Range Rover I6 3.0, 2021 on) · [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (Applies to the P400 and PHEV Ingenium straight-six. The P530 V8 uses BMW-sourced plugs, so check by VIN.)
- ZF 8-speed transmission: Land Rover-specified ATF [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Owners suggest about 60,000 mi, together with the transfer box and both differentials (Drain and refill, then level-check at temperature with a scan tool. Don't flush.)
- Transfer box: About 2 L of the Land Rover-specified fluid for this BorgWarner unit · [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · About 60,000 mi (owner suggestion) (Forum members argue about it. One experienced owner insists that TF 0753 (the Magna Steyr fluid used in earlier Range Rovers) is the wrong oil for the L460's transfer box. Use the handbook fluid.)
- Front axle disconnect & active rear differential: One owner reports the front-axle disconnect clutch uses the same fluid as the Electronic Active Differential · [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · About 60,000 mi (owner suggestion) (SE trims in the US may have an open rear diff with brake-based torque vectoring, so check which you have before ordering fluid.)
- Brakes: Pads, rotors and brake fluid · fluid [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Inspect at purchase. Owners have needed rear pads at 16,000–31,000 mi (The rear calipers have an electric parking brake, so put them in service mode with a scan tool before you push the pistons back.)
- 12 V batteries: Lithium-ion starter battery on some trucks (under the driver's seat on a 2024 D350), plus an AGM auxiliary battery on stop/start trucks · Load-test at purchase (A bonnet label says to jump-start at no more than 13.7 V. Register any new battery with a scan tool.)
- Underbody & air suspension inspection: Subframes, air springs, all-wheel-steer components · At purchase (There's a FullFatRR thread on cracking L460 subframes, so inspect them on a lift, along with the air springs and their lines.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: There is no forum consensus yet. Owners haven't published L460 all-terrain fitment the way L405 owners have, and the off-the-shelf sensor-link lift kits sold for the L405 don't list the L460. Factory wheels run from 20 to 23 inches, and one owner fitted L460 21s with 275/50R21 tyres to an L405. If you want sidewall, 20-inch wheels are the realistic floor: Lucky8 lists 20×9.5 ET30 wheels for the L460, and L405 20s fit with the correct flat-seat bolts. Test any oversize tyre at full lock and in every height mode before you trust it.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: For 2023, the EPA rated the P400 at 18 mpg city, 26 highway and 21 combined, and the 4.4 V8 at 16/21/18. The P440e plug-in hybrid was rated 51 MPGe on electricity and 21 mpg on petrol alone.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: Land Rover USA quotes up to 7,716 lb for the P400 and the V8s, 6,614 lb for the current plug-in hybrid, and 5,511 lb for Range Rover Electric. Earlier P440e trucks were listed at 5,511 lb. Check the figure for your exact model year and powertrain.

Q: Does it still have low range and a locking diff?
A: Combustion and hybrid models keep a twin-speed transfer box with high and low range. Upper trims get an Electronic Active Differential with torque vectoring, while the base SE has an open rear differential with torque vectoring by braking. Terrain Response 2, All Terrain Progress Control and hill descent control are standard.

Q: N63 or S68 V8?
A: 2022–2023 P530s use BMW's N63 twin-turbo 4.4. From the 2024 model year, JLR fitted BMW's S68, also used in the 615 PS SV. Owners on FullFatRR call the S68 'significantly more refined.' It's too early for long-term reliability data on either in this truck.

Q: How far does the plug-in hybrid go on electricity?
A: PHEVs use a 38.2 kWh battery (31.8 kWh usable) with a 105 kW motor on the P440e/P510e and a 160 kW motor on the P550e. Land Rover estimates about 50 miles of real-world electric range. A 7 kW home charger fills it in about 5 hours, and a 50 kW DC charger gets it to 80% in under an hour.

Q: Is there an electric one?
A: Yes. Range Rover Electric is on order books in the US for the 2027 model year. It has an EPA-estimated range of 333 miles, twin 260 kW motors, 660 lb-ft, 800 V charging (10–80% in about 22 minutes on a 350 kW charger), a 35-inch wading depth and 5,511 lb of towing.

Q: Can I get seven seats?
A: Only in the long-wheelbase body, and Land Rover USA says LWB seven-seaters aren't available as plug-in hybrids or EVs. Four- and five-seat layouts are also offered. Check recall 23V252000 on 2022–2023 seven-seaters for the second-row seat frame welds.

Q: Is it reliable?
A: The early record is mixed. NHTSA lists more than a dozen recalls across the 2023 and 2024 model years, and the DC-DC converter, 12-volt battery drain and software glitches dominate the FullFatRR technical board. Buy one with a warranty, a clean recall record and connected software that actually updates.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: Too early to call. NHTSA lists ten or eleven recalls for each of the 2022, 2023 and 2024 model years, so later trucks aren't clean either: 2022–23 carry the cam-carrier, seat-frame and tail-light campaigns, and 2024 adds panel-bonding, transmission and oil-filter-housing recalls. Owners prefer the 2024-on S68 V8. Buy on a closed recall list, a warranty and software that actually updates, not on the model year.

Q: Can I use a GAP tool on it?
A: Yes. GAP's IID G4 lists 2022–2025 L460s on the standard tool, for fault codes, live data, service resets, calibrations, air-suspension height adjustment and CCF edits. FullFatRR owners use it for proximity-locking and other CCF tweaks.

Q: Can I get sliders or a bash plate?
A: Not easily. A 2025 FullFatRR thread found no off-the-shelf sliders or underbody protection, and members suggested a fabrication shop would charge €3,500–4,000 for tree sliders and plates. It's a gap the aftermarket hasn't filled the way it has for the L405.

# Suzuki Samurai & Jimny (1970–present)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/suzuki/

Suzuki's off-road line began with a purchase. In 1968 it bought the rights to the HopeStar ON360, a tiny 4x4 from the struggling Hope Motor Company, and in April 1970 it launched the result as the Jimny LJ10, the first four-wheel-drive kei car to reach series production. The LJ series grew from a 359 cc two-stroke twin to the 797 cc four-stroke LJ80, and it took the Suzuki name to export markets for the first time. In 1981 the second generation arrived. Export markets knew it as the SJ410 and SJ413, Australians as the Sierra, and Americans, from late 1985, as the Samurai. A 1988 Consumer Reports test, and the libel suit that followed, nearly buried it in the US, but off-roaders adopted it anyway. Spain's Santana and India's Maruti (as the Gypsy) built it for decades. The third-generation Jimny of 1998 swapped the leaf springs for coils and stayed in production for 20 years. The boxy fourth generation followed in 2018. Every generation keeps the same recipe: a separate ladder frame, solid axles front and rear, a part-time transfer case with low range, and very little weight.

Verdict: The smallest proper 4x4 you can buy: ladder frame, two solid axles, low range and almost nothing else. It has been out-climbing trucks three times its size for more than half a century.

## Suzuki Jimny LJ series (1970–1981)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/suzuki/lj-series/
Codes: LJ10, LJ20, LJ50, LJ80

Verdict: A kei-car 4x4 with a 359 cc two-stroke, built as a work tool for Japanese surveyors and foresters, that accidentally made Suzuki a global car company. It's tiny, crude and slow, and it will go almost anywhere a person can walk.

In April 1970 Suzuki launched the Jimny LJ10, the first four-wheel-drive kei car to go into series production. It had a ladder frame, leaf springs on rigid axles, 16-inch wheels and a two-speed transfer case, all powered by a 359 cc air-cooled two-stroke twin making 25 PS. Suzuki pitched it as a 'professional's tool' for surveyors, foresters and anyone hauling goods up mountain roads. Nearly 5,000 sold in Japan in the first year, outselling the Mitsubishi Jeep, and the line that runs through the Samurai to today's Jimny started here.

### A HOPE AND A KEI LOOPHOLE
The design wasn't originally Suzuki's. Hope Motor Company built the HopeStar ON360, a doorless two-seater with a Mitsubishi two-stroke, a Mitsubishi Colt rear axle and Mitsubishi Jeep wheels. It went on sale in April 1968, but Hope sold only a handful, about 15 in Japan and 30 for export by Wikipedia's count, before passing the design to Suzuki that year.
Suzuki fitted its own engine and a new body, and it put the spare wheel inside the truck to keep the length under the 3-metre kei limit, which made the first Jimny a three-seater. As a kei car it got Japan's tax and registration breaks. Early trucks were largely hand-built by a subcontractor, but demand forced Suzuki to set up its own assembly line, and more than 6,000 sold in 1971.

### WATER COOLING, THEN THREE CYLINDERS
The May 1972 LJ20 switched to the water-cooled L50 twin with 28 PS, a vertical-slat grille and a steel-roofed van body. Suzuki says it would climb a 35-degree slope, and that it finished the Mexican 1000 race against 3- to 7-litre foreign rivals after 34 hours without an accident. Left-hand drive signalled export plans. In the US, an importer called International Equipment Co. sold it as the Suzuki Brute.
Kei rules changed in 1976, so the home-market Jimny 55 (SJ10) got the 539 cc LJ50 two-stroke triple. That engine was first used in export trucks from September 1975 with 33 PS, and the export LJ50 went to Australia and, from late 1976, was assembled in New Zealand. Suzuki says the SJ10 could climb 39.7 degrees.

### LJ80: FOUR STROKES AND THE WORLD
The 1977 Jimny 8, the LJ80 abroad, was Suzuki's first car with a four-stroke engine. Its 797 cc F8A four made 41 PS, which allowed taller gearing, and the track was about 100 mm wider. It was also the first Jimny registered in Japan as a small car rather than a kei car, and only 1,799 sold there, because it was really built for export. In Germany it was meant to be called the Eljot until Disney's Pete's Dragon got in the way. Australia called it the Stockman.
Metal doors arrived in 1979, along with the LJ81 pickup on a 2,200 mm wheelbase. The LJ80 was also assembled in New Zealand and Indonesia. Suzuki says it made the Suzuki name known around the world as a four-wheel-drive maker. It was replaced in 1981 by the SJ410, the first of the SJ and Samurai generation.

### Data plate
- Codes: LJ10 · LJ20 · LJ50 (SJ10) · LJ80 (SJ20) · LJ81
- Built: Iwata, Japan · assembled in New Zealand, Indonesia, Kenya
- Years: April 1970 – 1981
- Chassis: Ladder frame, leaf springs front & rear
- Wheelbase: 1,930 mm · 2,200 mm (LJ81 pickup)
- Lj10 Engine: FB 359 cc air-cooled 2-stroke I2 · 25 PS
- Lj20 Engine: L50 359 cc water-cooled 2-stroke I2 · 28 PS
- Lj50 Engine: 539 cc 2-stroke I3 · 33 PS (export)
- Lj80 Engine: F8A 797 cc SOHC I4 · 41 PS · 6.1 kg·m
- Gearbox: 4-speed manual + 2-speed transfer case
- Brakes: Drums all round
- Weight: 600 kg (LJ10) – 715 kg (SJ20)

### Engineering
Every LJ uses the same basic truck. A ladder frame carries the body, and rigid axles hang on semi-elliptic leaf springs at both ends. A four-speed manual feeds a separate two-speed transfer case, and the brakes are drums all round. What changed was the engine: an air-cooled two-stroke twin, then water cooling, then a two-stroke triple, and finally a four-stroke four.
- Chassis: Ladder frame (1,930 mm wheelbase; 2,200 mm on the LJ81 pickup)
- Suspension: Leaf springs, rigid axles (Semi-elliptic leaves front and rear on every LJ)
- Engines: 359 cc twin → 797 cc four (FB air-cooled and L50 water-cooled two-stroke twins, LJ50 triple, F8A four-stroke)
- Gearbox: 4-speed manual (Plus a 2-speed transfer case; ratios varied by year)
- Wheels: 16-in (LJ10) (The LJ20 van had 15-in wheels)
- Weight: 600–715 kg (LJ10 600 kg to SJ20/LJ80 715 kg (Suzuki figures))

### Versions
- 1970–1972 · LJ10 · FB 359 cc air-cooled 2-stroke I2 · 25 PS / 6,000 rpm · First series-production kei 4x4; spare inside, three seats; 600 kg.
- 1972–1976 · LJ20 · L50 359 cc water-cooled 2-stroke I2 · 28 PS / 6,000 rpm · Vertical-slat grille, van body; LJ20F with outside spare for four seats; sold in the US as the Brute.
- 1975–1981 · LJ50 / SJ10 Jimny 55 · LJ50 539 cc water-cooled 2-stroke I3 · 33 PS export · 26 PS Japan · Export from September 1975, Japan from June 1976; LJ51P long-wheelbase pickup for some markets.
- 1977–1981 · LJ80 / SJ20 Jimny 8 · F8A 797 cc 4-stroke SOHC I4 · 41 PS / 5,500 rpm · First four-stroke Suzuki car; wider track, taller gearing; metal doors and LJ81 pickup from 1979.

### Year-by-year
- 1968: Suzuki buys the HopeStar ON360 design from Hope Motor Company
- 1970: April: Jimny LJ10 launches, 359 cc air-cooled two-stroke twin, 25 PS; first series-production kei 4x4
- 1972: May: LJ20 with water-cooled L50 twin (28 PS), vertical grille, steel-roof van
- 1975: September: LJ50 539 cc three-cylinder two-stroke for export (33 PS)
- 1976: June: Jimny 55 (SJ10) in Japan; NZ assembly of the LJ50 begins late in the year
- 1977: Jimny 8 / LJ80: 797 cc F8A four-stroke, 41 PS, wider track, taller gearing
- 1979: Metal doors available; LJ81 pickup on a 2,200 mm wheelbase
- 1981: Replaced by the SJ410

### Capability
- Gradeability: 35° (LJ20) · 39.7° (SJ10) (Suzuki figures)
- Curb weight: 600 kg (LJ10) · 625 kg (LJ20) · 675 kg (SJ10) · 715 kg (SJ20) (Suzuki figures)
- Top speed: 75 km/h (LJ10) · ≈97 km/h (Jimny 55) (Wikipedia)
- Payload: 250 kg (200 kg van), late LJ20 (Wikipedia)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 16-in wheels (LJ10, Suzuki/Wikipedia), 15-in wheels (LJ20 van)
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: Stock size (We couldn't find a sourced owner consensus; stay close to the original size.)

### Buying checks
- Rust in sills, corner posts and floors: These are 45- to 55-year-old steel bodies. LJ80 specialist LJ80.de stocks repair panels for the corner posts, sills, side panels and footwell floors, which hints at where they rot. Probe those areas and the frame before anything else. On one BaT 1972 LJ20, the battery tray had a patch panel and rust.
- Which LJ is it really?: Engines were swapped and bodies updated. The LJ10 has an air-cooled twin and a horizontal-slat grille. The LJ20 has a water-cooled twin and a vertical grille. The LJ50 has a three-cylinder two-stroke, and the LJ80 has a four-stroke four. Count the cylinders and check the cooling system.
- Two-stroke health: On LJ10, LJ20 and LJ50 trucks, a two-stroke that won't idle or smokes heavily may need a full rebuild, and engine parts are scarcer than for the LJ80. Ask what has been done and how the engine is lubricated [CONFIRM IN MANUAL].
- Leaf springs and bushings: Sagging springs and perished bushings are normal at this age. LJ80.de still sells complete front and rear LJ80 spring sets, bushing kits and shackle plates, so it's fixable.
- Brakes are drums all round: Every LJ has four-wheel drum brakes. Check for seized wheel cylinders, a leaking master cylinder and contaminated shoes before driving one anywhere.
- Title and import paperwork: Suzuki didn't sell the LJ in the US itself; LJ20s came in through an independent importer as the Brute. Most US trucks are later imports, like the LJ20 on BaT that was sold new in Australia. Make sure the title and import paperwork match the chassis.
- Originality affects value: Original LJ10 and LJ20 trucks are rare. BaT results show restored LJ20s and early Jimnys selling at about $10,000–11,500, ahead of rougher examples.

### Common repairs
#### Sill, corner-post and floor rust repair
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ Several weekends · cost Parts plus welding
Symptoms: Bubbling paint at the bottom of the corner posts and sills, holed footwells and soft spots around the body mounts.
Fix: Remove the seats and trim, then probe everything. Brace the door openings before cutting, cut back to clean metal and weld in the repair panels. Seam-seal and protect the new metal, and renew the frame-to-body rubbers while the body is loose.
Tools: MIG welder · cut-off wheel · spot-weld drill · clamps · seam sealer

#### Leaf spring bushings and shackles
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Clunks over bumps, the axle shifting under braking, cracked rubber at the spring eyes and shackles, and wandering steering.
Fix: Support the frame and take the weight off one spring. Remove the shackle and spring-eye bolts, press out the old bushings and fit new rubber or polyurethane ones. Replace worn shackle plates and bolts, then torque everything with the truck on its wheels.
Tools: Jack and stands · socket set · bushing press or vise · torque wrench

#### Front wheel bearings and hub seals
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Play at the wheel, a rumble that changes with speed, and grease or gear oil on the brake drum.
Fix: Remove the wheel, hub and drum. Pull the old bearings and seals, clean and inspect the spindle, and pack and fit new bearings with a new hub seal set. Adjust the preload and secure the castle nut with a new split pin.
Tools: Socket set · bearing packer · seal driver · drift

#### Drum brake overhaul
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1 day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Pulling under braking, a low or spongy pedal, fluid behind a drum, or a weak handbrake.
Fix: Remove the drums, replace the shoes, springs and wheel cylinders (or rebuild them), clean and adjust the adjusters and renew the handbrake shoes. Rebuild or replace the master cylinder and bleed the system with fresh fluid.
Tools: Brake spring tool · flare-nut wrenches · brake bleeder

#### Transfer case reseal and mounts
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 1 day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Gear oil weeping from the transfer case, noisy bearings, a clunk from worn mounts, and a split shifter boot letting in water.
Fix: Drain and remove the transfer case. Replace the bearings and gaskets with the rebuild sets, fit new rubber mounts and a new shifter boot, and refill with gear oil to the manual's spec.
Tools: Transmission jack · puller · seal driver · gasket scraper

#### Ignition tune-up (LJ80 points)
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2 hours · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Hard starting, misfires and poor idle on the F8A four-stroke.
Fix: Replace the points and condenser, distributor cap, rotor and plugs, then set the points gap and ignition timing to the manual's figures. Replace the air and fuel filters at the same time.
Tools: Feeler gauges · timing light · dwell meter · plug socket

#### Chassis rust: inspect, treat and wax the frame
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend to clean and treat; welding is extra · cost Materials plus labor; frame welding is a specialist bill
Symptoms: Flaking scale on the frame rails and crossmembers, and rust around the body mounts and spring hangers. Classic Trader's LJ 80 guide calls rust 'a defining drawback', 'especially affecting the steel body panels and chassis', and tells buyers to check the sills, floor panels and frame.
Fix: Wash the underside and scrape off old underseal so you can see the metal. Tap and probe the rails, crossmembers, spring hangers and body-mount points. Anything holed or thin around a mount needs welding by someone who knows frames. On sound metal, wire-brush back to clean steel, then zinc-prime and paint. Finish with an underbody wax, including inside the rails where you can reach. Free seized body-mount bolts with penetrating oil and replace any that are corroded while you're under there.
Tools: Scraper and wire brushes · angle grinder · pick · jack stands · spray gun or aerosol cans · penetrating oil.

### Baseline service
These trucks are 45-plus years old, so rebuild the basics before you trust one. LJ80 capacities below come from Liqui Moly's oil guide (Olyslager data). We couldn't source specs for the two-stroke LJ10, LJ20 and LJ50, so confirm those in a service manual. LJ80.de sells a complete LJ80 inspection kit.
- Inspection kit (LJ80): Filters and service parts for the F8A · At purchase (There's also a kit for the SJ410.)
- Engine oil & filter (LJ80): About 3.0 L (Liqui Moly) · grade [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase, then every 10,000 km / 6 months (Liqui Moly) (Use a new drain-plug washer.)
- Two-stroke lubrication (LJ10/20/50): [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · At purchase (Find out how your engine gets its two-stroke oil before running it.)
- Air filter: LJ80 element · At purchase (Check the rubber boot between the filter and the carburetor.)
- Fuel filter: Inline · At purchase (Old tanks shed rust, so check the filter again after a few tanks.)
- Ignition: Points, condenser, cap, rotor, plugs, leads · At purchase
- Coolant & hoses (LJ20 onward): LJ80: 3.8 L, change every 2 years (Liqui Moly) · LJ20/LJ50: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush at purchase (The LJ10 is air-cooled.)
- Gearbox, transfer case & differentials: LJ80 (Liqui Moly): gearbox 1.0 L · transfer case 0.9 L, GL-4 85W-90 · front and rear diffs 1.3 L each, GL-5 85W-90 hypoid · LJ10–LJ50: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Drain and fill at purchase (Replace the drain-plug seals.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 or DOT 4 (Liqui Moly lists both for the LJ80; LJ80.de sells DOT 4) · Flush at purchase, then every 2 years (Liqui Moly: 40,000 km / 24 months) (Four-wheel drums; check the wheel cylinders.)
- Wheel bearings: Repack with fresh grease · At purchase
- Spring and frame rubbers:  · Inspect at purchase

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: We couldn't find a reliable owner consensus. Suzuki fitted 16-inch wheels to the LJ10 and 15-inch wheels to the LJ20 van. With kei-sized wheel arches and tracks around 1,100–1,200 mm, staying close to the stock size is the safe choice.

Q: What do the LJ codes mean?
A: LJ stands for 'Light Jeep'. In Japan the trucks were also known by chassis codes: SJ10 (Jimny 55) and SJ20 (Jimny 8). Export markets mostly used the LJ names.

Q: Which LJ is easiest to own?
A: The LJ80. It has a four-stroke engine, it was the most widely exported, and specialists such as LJ80.de still stock much of it. Two-stroke LJ10, LJ20 and LJ50 trucks are rarer and more of a collector's project.

Q: How fast is it?
A: Not very. Wikipedia gives the LJ10's top speed as 75 km/h, and about 97 km/h (60 mph) for the 539 cc Jimny 55.

Q: Was the LJ sold in the United States?
A: Not by Suzuki. An importer, International Equipment Co., brought in LJ20s and sold them as the Suzuki Brute. The Samurai of late 1985 was the first four-wheeled vehicle Suzuki itself sold in the US.

Q: How capable is it off road?
A: Suzuki says the LJ20 would climb a 35-degree slope and the SJ10 39.7 degrees, and that an LJ20 finished the Mexican 1000 race after 34 hours. It's light, narrow and has low range, which counts for a lot.

Q: What gear ratios did it have?
A: Wikipedia lists transfer case ratios of 2.57 low / 1.56 high or 3.01 low / 1.71 high depending on the year, and axle ratios of 4.55, 4.87 or 5.66 for the later trucks.

Q: Where do I get parts?
A: For the LJ80, LJ80.de in Germany stocks body repair panels, springs, bearings, brakes and service parts, and publishes a parts catalogue. Some parts are shared with the SJ410. Two-stroke engine parts are harder to find.

Q: What is an LJ worth?
A: Bring a Trailer sales have mostly run from about $4,300 to $11,500, with restored LJ20s and early Jimnys at the top. An LJ80 bid to $18,003 in 2023 without selling.

Q: Is it a kei car?
A: The 359 cc and 539 cc trucks were. The 797 cc Jimny 8 (SJ20/LJ80) was the first Jimny registered as a small car rather than a kei car in Japan.

## Suzuki SJ / Samurai (1981–1998)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/suzuki/samurai/
Codes: SJ410, SJ413, Samurai, JA51, JB31

Verdict: A 2,000-lb ladder-frame 4x4 that Consumer Reports said tipped over and the trail crowd says goes everywhere. Both had a point. Give it some lift, a locker and lower gears and it climbs things that embarrass trucks three times its size.

The second-generation Jimny arrived in 1981 as the export SJ410, a little 1.0-litre box on a ladder frame with leaf springs and solid axles at both ends. In November 1984 Suzuki added the 1.3-litre SJ413, and in late 1985 it brought that truck to the United States as the Samurai, the first four-wheeled vehicle Suzuki sold there. It cost about two-thirds as much as a new Jeep Wrangler and weighed roughly 2,100 lb. Americans bought 47,000 in the first year. Then Consumer Reports rolled one.

### FROM SJ410 TO SAMURAI
The SJ410 replaced the LJ80 in 1981 and was sold as a soft top, a hardtop and a long-wheelbase pickup. Australia called it the Sierra, and Holden sold it as the Drover. The SJ413 that followed in 1984 brought the 1,324 cc G13A four, a five-speed gearbox, front disc brakes, an anti-roll bar and a new dashboard. In Japan it was the Jimny 1300 (JA51), at the time the biggest engine Suzuki sold.
The US Samurai launched in California in November 1985 as a 1986 model, already on the wider track that Suzuki later used for the Samurai worldwide. Suzuki's 1986 brochure lists 1,300 mm front and 1,310 mm rear, against about 1,210 mm on the narrow SJ. It quoted 64 hp, 74 lb-ft, 8.1 inches of ground clearance and 43/38-degree approach and departure angles. MotorTrend timed it at 16.9 seconds to 60 mph. Nobody bought one for the acceleration, and by mid-1988 Americans were buying 8,000 a month.

### THE CONSUMER REPORTS AFFAIR
The July 1988 issue of Consumer Reports rated the Samurai 'Not Acceptable', the first time the magazine had used that rating, saying it tipped up in its short-course accident-avoidance maneuver. According to evidence Suzuki cited in court, the Samurai went through more than three dozen runs on CU's established course with no tip-up. CU then modified the course, and a test driver tipped it onto its outriggers. In June 1988 CU showed reporters video of the tip-ups and asked for a recall. NHTSA denied two 1988 petitions for a defect investigation, saying the evidence didn't show that a vehicle defect, rather than the driver or the environment, caused the rollovers.
The damage was done anyway. Reuters reported that Samurai sales fell about 70 percent. In 1996 Suzuki sued Consumers Union for $60 million over CU's renewed claim that the Samurai 'easily rolls over in turns'. A district judge threw the case out, and in 2003 the Ninth Circuit revived it. In July 2004 the two sides settled with no money paid. CU said it never meant that the Samurai easily rolls over in routine driving, but it stood by its tests, while Suzuki disputed them. NHTSA's Michigan crash data for 1986–90 put the Samurai's single-vehicle rollover rate (29 percent) next to the Wrangler's (28 percent) and below the CJ-7's (46–48 percent). It is still a short, narrow, tall truck, though, and MotorTrend's verdict is that it tips more readily in sudden swerves than most 4x4s.

### THE ROCK-CRAWLING CULT
What sank the Samurai as a commuter made it a legend on the trail. It weighs little, it's narrow, and it has a real transfer case with low range. Lifted on a spring-over, it can be geared down with transfer-case gear sets as low as 6.4:1 and wedged into lines that big trucks can't fit. Trail Tough, a shop started by Samurai enthusiasts in the 1980s, still sells spring-over kits, Sumo gear sets, knuckle-over steering and 1.6- to 2.3-litre Suzuki engine conversions. In 2007 two Chileans drove a modified SJ413 to 6,688 m on Ojos del Salado, a Guinness-certified altitude record for a four-wheeled vehicle at the time.
The other big upgrade is an axle swap. Trail-Gear and Low Range Off-Road sell kits that put 1979–85 Toyota truck axles under a Samurai. On Zukiworld, one builder wrote in 2006 that the Toyota swap had 'become as common as a SPOA lift.' The Toyota axles are about 5 inches wider, take the same brake-line fittings and have a huge aftermarket, but Samurai steering won't fit them. Some builders prefer Dana 44s instead.

### SANTANA, GYPSY AND HOW IT ENDED
Spain's Santana built SJs in Linares from 1985, and because they were more than 60 percent local content they got around Europe's quotas on Japanese imports. Santana built Samurais with Peugeot and later Renault diesels until about 2003–04. In India, Maruti launched the long-wheelbase Gypsy in December 1985. In 1993 it got the 90 mm wider track and became the MG410W, then became the 1.3-litre Gypsy King in 1996. It stayed in production until 2018, a staple of the Indian Army and police.
In the US the Samurai lost its rear seat for 1994 and 1995, because adding the required rear shoulder belts would have meant re-engineering it. It was gone after 1995, replaced in spirit by the Sidekick. Japan got a coil-sprung version (JB32) in 1995, and the line ended there in 1998, when the JB23 Jimny took over.

### Data plate
- Codes: SJ410 · SJ413 · Samurai · JA51 · JB31/JB32
- Built: Iwata, Japan, 1981–98 · Santana (Spain), Maruti (India), Pakistan, Indonesia, Thailand, Colombia
- Us Sales: Late 1985 (1986 MY) – 1995
- Chassis: Ladder frame, leaf springs front & rear

- Track: 1,300 / 1,310 mm (US Samurai)
- Engine: G13A 1,324 cc SOHC I4 · 74 × 77 mm · 8.9:1
- Output: 64 hp @ 5,500 · 74 lb-ft @ 3,500 (1986 US)
- Gearbox: 5-speed manual · 3.652 / 1.947 / 1.423 / 1.000 / 0.795

### Engineering
The SJ is a scaled-down 1950s truck, and that's the point. A separate ladder frame carries a steel body. Both axles are solid and hang on semi-elliptic leaf springs. A gear-driven two-speed transfer case sits behind a five-speed manual, and the front hubs are manual Aisin lockers. There's no center differential, so 4WD is only for loose surfaces. Steering is recirculating ball, and the US truck had power front discs and rear drums.
- Chassis: Ladder frame (2,030 mm (79.9 in) wheelbase; 2,375 mm on long-wheelbase SJ and Gypsy)
- Suspension: Leaf springs, live axles (Front and rear; softened for the US '1988½' update)
- Engine: G13A 1,324 cc SOHC 8V (Carbureted, 64 hp (1986 brochure); throttle-body G13BA from 1990)
- Transfer Case: 2-speed, 2.268 low (Part-time, no center diff; the transfer case mounts on the frame are known to crack)
- Track: 1,300 / 1,310 mm (US Samurai wide track; narrow SJ410/413 about 1,210 / 1,220 mm)
- Weight: 950–965 kg (About 2,094–2,127 lb, convertible and hardtop (1986 US))

### Versions
- 1981–1984 · SJ410 / Jimny 1000 (SJ40) · F10A 970 cc I4 · 45 PS net (export) · Four-speed, drum brakes, narrow track; soft top, hardtop and long-wheelbase pickup.
- 1984–1988 · SJ413 / Jimny 1300 (JA51) · G13A 1,324 cc I4 · 70 PS gross (JA51) · Five-speed, front discs, anti-roll bar, new dash and grille.
- 1986–1989 US · Samurai (carbureted) · G13A 1,324 cc I4 · 64 hp / 74 lb-ft · Wide track from launch; '1988½' softer springs, thicker front anti-roll bar, 0.865 fifth gear.
- 1990–1995 US · Samurai (TBI) · 1.3 I4, throttle-body injection · 66–68 hp (sources differ) · 2WD version 1991–93; rear seat deleted for 1994–95.
- 1985–2004 · Santana SJ / Samurai (Spain) · F10A, G13 petrol; Peugeot XUD9 TD and Renault F8Q diesels · 63–64 PS (diesels) · Softer springs and plusher trim; Samurai chassis from 1990.
- 1985–2018 · Maruti Gypsy (India) · F10A, then G13BA and G13BB · Up to 80 PS (Gypsy King MPFI) · Long wheelbase only; wide-track MG410W from 1993.

### Year-by-year
- 1981: SJ410 (Jimny 1000 in Japan from 1982) replaces the LJ80: F10A 1.0 four, four-speed, drum brakes
- 1984: SJ413 / Jimny 1300 (JA51): G13A 1.3, five-speed, front discs, anti-roll bar, new dash and grille
- 1985: Santana starts building SJs in Spain (March); Maruti Gypsy launches in India (December); US Samurai goes on sale in California in November as a 1986 model
- 1988: '1988½' US update: softer springs, revised shocks, thicker front anti-roll bar, 0.865 fifth gear, new grille, gauges and seats. In July, Consumer Reports rates it 'Not Acceptable'
- 1990: US Samurai gets throttle-body fuel injection (MotorTrend)
- 1991: 2WD Samurai added in the US (to 1993)
- 1994: US rear seat deleted for 1994–95 rather than add rear shoulder belts
- 1995: Last US model year; coil-sprung JB32 launched in Japan in November
- 1998: Japanese production ends; replaced by the JB23 Jimny. Santana and Maruti carry on

- Ground clearance: 205 mm (8.1 in) (1986 US brochure)
- Approach / departure: 43° / 38° (1986 US brochure)
- Turning circle: 5.1 m (16.7 ft) minimum turning radius
- Curb weight: 950 kg (2,094 lb) convertible · 965 kg hardtop

- Fuel tank: 40 L (10.6 US gal)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: P205/70R15 (1986 US brochure)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x139.7 (5x5.5")
- Note: Japan-market Jimny 1000/1300 used 6 bolts on the same 139.7 mm circle
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 215/75R15 (Zukiworld owners: 215/75R15 fits with no modifications; 225s with a little effort.)
- Biggest tire, 1.5–2 in lift: 235/75R15 (≈29 in) (Needs trimming or a 1.5–2 in lift; flatten the inner fender seams. Trail Tough rates its 2 in Old Man Emu kit as right for 29 in tires.)
- Biggest tire, 4.5 in spring-over lift: 31 in (Trail Tough's deluxe SPOA kit is rated for up to 31 in tires, with knuckle-over steering.)

### Buying checks
- Rust and hidden trail damage: MotorTrend's advice is to check the underbody carefully, for rust and also for dents, scrapes and dried mud in hard-to-reach places, which all point to a hard off-road life. If you want a stock truck, an unmodified Samurai is less likely to have been abused.
- Transfer case mounts and frame hangers: Trail Tough calls cracked transfer case mounts and a wallowed-out, bent rear frame hanger common Samurai stress failures, and lower gearing makes them worse. Look at the rubber mounts and the frame brackets on both sides of the case.
- Transfer case that won't shift or sticks in neutral: MotorTrend lists bad transfer-case bushings that can lock the case in neutral. The usual culprit is the plastic 'shift sheet' under the lever. It's a cheap OEM or Delrin part, but check that 4WD and low range both engage.
- Oil leaks and carburetor manners: MotorTrend's known trouble spots include oil leaks at the distributor, leaking brake master cylinders, fiddly carburetors on 1986–89 trucks and failing ECMs on fuel-injected ones. A clean cold start and a steady idle are worth a lot.
- Quality of past modifications: Most Samurais have been modified. A well-built spring-over or engine swap saves you money; a bad one costs you. Check the steering geometry, brake lines at full droop, driveshaft angles and welds. Swapped engines may not pass emissions in some states, and Trail Tough notes that 1996-and-later 1.6 donors are OBD-II and won't be smog-legal in California.
- Is it an automatic? It's a swap: Every US Samurai had a manual gearbox, so an automatic means someone swapped it in. Ask what was done and look for the paperwork.
- Front knuckles weeping gear oil: Oil-soaked knuckles, loose steering and a vague front end point to worn kingpin bearings and inner axle seals. Trail Tough's rebuild kit covers both sides, and it's a common catch-up job.
- Know which Samurai you're buying: For the US, 1986–89 trucks are carbureted (AMSOIL's lookup lists engine code 5) and 1990–95 are injected (code 3). The '1988½' update changed the ride, the gearing and the transfer case drain plugs. Santana and Gypsy trucks use the same basic design, but many parts differ.

### Common repairs
#### Rebuild the front knuckles (kingpins, seals, wheel bearings)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 1 day for both sides · cost Kit $269 (Trail Tough) plus gear oil
Symptoms: Gear oil weeping from the knuckle balls, loose or wandering steering, play when you rock the top of the tire, and grease or oil inside the brake parts.
Fix: Lock out the hubs, lift the front and remove the wheel, caliper, rotor and Aisin hub. Remove the knuckle seal and the upper and lower kingpin caps, separate the knuckle and pull the axle shaft. Replace the inner axle seal, kingpin bearings, wheel bearings, knuckle seal and gaskets, then set kingpin preload as the service manual specifies. Refill the front differential and the knuckles to the levels in the manual.
Tools: Socket set · seal driver · bearing packer · torque wrench · spring scale for kingpin preload · service manual

#### Reinforce cracked transfer case mounts
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day, plus welding · cost Repair kit $45; solid mounts $61.68 a set; Mighty Kong II cradle $335
Symptoms: A clunk when you shift on and off the throttle, a transfer case that sags or rocks, a cracked mounting boss or a frame bracket starting to tear. Lower transfer-case gears make it worse.
Fix: Support the transfer case, unbolt the mounts and inspect the frame hangers. Trail Tough's repair kit restores the wallowed-out hole and bent rear hanger, and you can fit it before or after the frame is damaged. Replace the rubber mounts with OEM or solid ones, or fit a cradle that supports the case on three axes. Trail Tough also points out that gearing down only at the transfer case overloads these mounts, so regear the axles too.
Tools: Jack and stands · welder and grinder · drill · socket set

#### Replace the transfer case shift sheet and seals
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost $14 OEM sheet, $21 Delrin; seal kit $35–40
Symptoms: Sloppy or stiff transfer case lever, trouble finding 4WD or low, a case that pops out of gear, and leaks at the output seals.
Fix: Drain the case. Remove the shifter boot and the top cover, replace the worn plastic shift sheet, check the shift-rail springs and detents, then reseal the cover and output seals with the seal kit. Refill with gear oil (Trail Tough recommends non-synthetic 80W-90 GL-5 in its rebuilt cases) and check that 2H, 4H and 4L all engage.
Tools: Socket set · seal puller and driver · gasket scraper · fluid pump

#### Rear wheel bearing and axle seal
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours per side · cost $56 per side (kit)
Symptoms: Gear oil on the inside of the rear wheel or the brake shoes, a growl that changes with speed, or play in the rear wheel.
Fix: Remove the wheel and drum, disconnect the brake line and remove the backing-plate bolts, then pull the axle. The bearing and retainer are pressed on, so cut the old retainer off carefully and press on the new bearing, retainer and seal. Reinstall, bleed the rear brakes and top up the differential. Trail Tough's SJ410 backing-plate mod lets future axle changes skip opening the brake lines.
Tools: Slide hammer · press or bearing shop · die grinder · brake bleeding kit

#### Timing belt and tensioner (G13A)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 3 hours · cost Belt $24.95; tensioner $55
Symptoms: Unknown belt history, a cracked or glazed belt, or a noisy tensioner. The G13A is a non-interference engine, so a snapped belt strands you but shouldn't bend valves.
Fix: Remove the fan, fan belt, crank pulley and timing cover. Line up the cam and crank timing marks, release the tensioner and change the belt and tensioner. Turn the engine by hand twice and recheck the marks. Replace the cam and crank seals if they're leaking, and check ignition timing afterwards. Use the factory service manual for the interval and torque values.
Tools: Socket set · crank pulley holder · torque wrench · timing light

#### Clutch replacement
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 1 day · cost Deluxe kit $166
Symptoms: Slipping under load in low range, chatter, or a pedal that engages right at the top of its travel.
Fix: Remove the driveshafts, intermediate shaft and transfer case (or drop the transmission with the case attached), then pull the transmission back. Replace the disc, pressure plate, release bearing and pilot bearing, and check the flywheel and rear main seal. Use an alignment tool to install, and adjust the clutch cable.
Tools: Transmission jack · socket set · clutch alignment tool · torque wrench

#### Brake master cylinder and front brake refresh
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 3 hours · cost Master cylinder $120; pads $33; rotors $56 each
Symptoms: A sinking pedal, fluid around the master cylinder or booster, and pulsing or noisy front brakes.
Fix: Bench-bleed the new master cylinder, swap it in and bleed the whole system with DOT 3. While you're there, replace the front pads and rotors, inspect the rear drums and wheel cylinders, and fit extended lines if the truck is lifted.
Tools: Flare-nut wrenches · bench-bleed kit · brake bleeder · C-clamp

### Baseline service
Assume nothing has been done. These trucks are 30-plus years old, and most have been wheeled. US specs below come from AMSOIL's capacity lookups for 1988 and 1992 Samurais, and Liqui Moly's oil guide (Olyslager data) gives matching capacities for the 1988–98 Samurai; confirm them in the factory service manual, especially on Santana, Gypsy or swapped trucks.
- Engine oil & filter: 3.9 qt with filter · 10W-30 or 10W-40 depending on temperature · Every 10,000 km (about 6,000 mi) / 6 months, or 5,000 km / 4 months in severe use (Liqui Moly's Olyslager data for the 1990–98 Samurai) (AMSOIL lists WIX 51348 as the matching filter.)
- Timing belt & tensioner: G13A (1986–89) belt and tensioner · At purchase unless documented, then per manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] (The G13A is a non-interference engine (Wikipedia), so a failure shouldn't bend valves, but it will strand you.)
- Spark plugs, wires, cap & rotor: 1.3 8V plug wire set · At purchase (MotorTrend lists oil leaks at the distributor as a known trouble spot, so check the distributor O-ring while you're there.)
- Air & fuel filters: Carbureted 1986–89; throttle-body injected 1990–95 · At purchase (A carburetor rebuild kit is available if the idle won't settle.)
- Coolant: 5.3 qt · coolant type [CONFIRM IN MANUAL] · Flush at purchase, then every 2 years (Check the radiator, hoses and the 1.3 water inlet pipe.)
- Manual transmission: 2.7 pt · 75W-90 GL-4 · Drain and fill at purchase (Drain and fill plugs differ between 1986–88 and 1988.5–95 trucks.)
- Transfer case: 1.7 pt · GL-4 per AMSOIL; Trail Tough fills its rebuilt cases with non-synthetic 80W-90 GL-5 · Drain and fill at purchase (While it's drained, check the case mounts and the shift sheet.)
- Front differential & knuckles: 3.6 pt (1988) / 4.2 pt (1992) · 75W-90 or 80W-90 GL-5 · Drain and fill at purchase (Weeping knuckles mean seals and kingpin bearings are due.)
- Rear differential: 3.2 pt · GL-5 90 (1988) or 75W-90 (1992) · Drain and fill at purchase (With an automatic locker or spool, use the oil the locker maker specifies.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 · Flush at purchase, then every 2 years (1986–89 trucks use their own master cylinder.)
- Power steering fluid (if fitted): Dexron-III ATF (AMSOIL, 1988) · Check at purchase (Only applies if your truck has power steering.)
- U-joints, steering joint & spring bushings: Multipurpose grease at the grease nipples and propeller-shaft joints; Liqui Moly says check every 20,000 km / 12 months · At purchase, then every oil change (A seized steering joint and crumbling spring or body bushings are normal at this age.)
- Front locking hubs: Aisin manual hubs · Inspect at purchase (Lock and unlock both hubs. They must be locked for 4WD to work.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: About a 215/75R15. On Zukiworld, owners say a 215/75R15 fits a stock Samurai with no modifications and 225s fit with a little effort. A 235/75R15 (about 29 inches) needs trimming and flattened inner fender seams, a 1.5–2 inch lift, or both. Stock tires were P205/70R15 according to the 1986 brochure.

Q: Does the Samurai really roll over easily?
A: It depends who you ask. CU's 1988 'Not Acceptable' rating came from tip-ups in a severe, modified avoidance maneuver, and NHTSA denied petitions to investigate a defect. In the 2004 settlement CU said it never meant the Samurai easily rolls over in routine driving. NHTSA's Michigan data put its rollover rate close to the Wrangler's, but it's still short and narrow, so drive it like one.

Q: Which years should I buy?
A: There's no consensus. MotorTrend says 1986–88 trucks ride more firmly; the '1988½' update brought softer springs, a thicker front anti-roll bar and a 0.865 fifth gear (the 1986 brochure lists 0.795), and 1990–95 trucks have throttle-body injection. On Zukiworld, owners split: some prefer the carbureted 1986–89 trucks because a carb is easy to fix in the field, others the fuel-injected 1990–95 trucks, and one prefers pre-1988½ trucks for their all-metal radiators. Condition and the quality of past modifications matter more than the year.

Q: What engine does it have, and what's the common swap?
A: The 1,324 cc SOHC eight-valve G13A (64 hp), then the injected G13BA. The common upgrade is a 1.6-litre Sidekick or Tracker engine, which bolts to the same mounts. Trail Tough sells kits for 1.6 and 2.0/2.3 Suzuki conversions. Check your state's emissions rules first.

Q: Should I re-gear the transfer case or the axles?
A: Trail Tough's advice is to do both, in that order of importance: choose ring-and-pinion gears to suit the tire size, then pick transfer case gears for crawling. Doing all the reduction in the transfer case overloads the U-joints, the transfer case mounts and the frame brackets.

Q: How much lift do I need for 29s, 31s or bigger?
A: Trail Tough rates the 2-inch Old Man Emu spring kit as 'just right for a 29-inch tire'. Its spring-over kit gives about 4.5 inches of lift for up to 31-inch tires. Bigger than that usually means a body lift, longer shackles, or a Toyota axle swap with custom steering.

Q: Can I put Toyota axles under a Samurai?
A: Yes, and it's a very common swap. 1979–85 Toyota truck axles are about 5 inches wider than the Samurai's and take the same brake fittings. You need a way to deal with the different front spring perch width, flange adapters or redrilled flanges for the driveshafts, and aftermarket steering, because Samurai steering won't fit. Trail-Gear and Low Range Off-Road sell conversion kits.

Q: Why does it grind or vibrate in 4WD high when it's lifted?
A: According to Trail Tough, the transfer case tilts down 7 degrees at the back while the front pinion points up about 9 degrees, so the front driveshaft's U-joint angles work against each other. Lift makes it worse. Tipping the pinion won't fix it, though a CV front driveshaft helps.

Q: What fuel economy and tank range should I expect?
A: Suzuki's 1986 brochure quoted 27 mpg city and 29 highway (1986 EPA estimates) and a 40-litre (10.6 US gallon) tank. Real-world numbers fall with big tires and lift.

Q: What lockers fit?
A: Trail Tough's Spartan automatic locker fits the rear of every Samurai and the front of 1986–89 trucks. ARB Air Lockers and spools are also available. Even an open front diff with a rear locker makes a big difference on the trail.

Q: Are there any recalls?
A: NHTSA lists one US campaign: 95V103008 for 1988–1991 Samurais, which covers front seat belt buckles whose red release buttons can break.
