## Suzuki Jimny JB23 / JB43 (1998–2018)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/suzuki/jimny-jb23/
Codes: JB23, JB33, JB43, JB53

Verdict: A ladder frame, two live axles and a real low range, shrunk until it fits in a Japanese parking space and priced like a hatchback. The Jimny that ran for twenty years is the smallest proper 4x4 you can import, and its only natural predator is road salt.

Suzuki showed the third-generation Jimny at the 1997 Tokyo Motor Show, and it went on sale in Japan in January 1998 as the 1.3-liter Jimny Wide. While rivals were turning small 4x4s into crossovers, Suzuki kept the separate ladder frame, the solid axles and a two-speed transfer case. It then built the thing, mostly unchanged under the skin, for twenty years. It replaced the Samurai in most markets and carried the Jimny name around the world. America was the one big market that never got it new, and Suzuki stopped selling cars in the US altogether in 2012.

### KEI CAR, WIDE CAR
There are really two trucks under one badge. The JB23 is the Japanese kei car: 3,395 mm long and 1,475 mm wide, with no fender flares, small bumpers and a 658 cc turbocharged K6A three-cylinder. It reached showrooms in October 1998, months after the bigger car, because it was designed around new kei rules that hadn't yet taken effect. Everything else is the 'Wide' car, with flares, bigger bumpers and a 1.3-liter four. That's the JB33 with the 80 PS G13BB, then the JB43 with the M13A from January 2000 in Japan. Japan revived the Sierra name for the 1.3 in January 2002, and Australia adopted it in 2007.
The family spread wide. Santana Motor in Spain built the Canvas Top from 1999 to 2009, and its soft tops kept the old G13BB until 2005. Europe got the JB53 diesel, a Santana- and Suzuki-built Jimny with Renault's 1.5 K9K, from 2004 to 2011, though never in Britain or Ireland. GM Colmotores assembled a 'Chevrolet Jimny' in Bogotá from 1999, and Mazda sold the kei car as the AZ-Offroad. Brazil kept building the facelifted 1.3 until 2022, when new rules caught up with the M13A.

### COILS, VACUUM AND A DRY KNUCKLE
The mechanical recipe is old-school 4x4 at three-quarter scale. Both axles are solid beams located by radius arms, and apart from the late SJ 'Coily,' this was the first Jimny on coil springs at all four corners after decades of leaves. Steering is recirculating ball. Drive is part-time with no center differential, so 4WD is for loose surfaces only. Vacuum-locking front hubs let you shift from 2WD to 4WD at up to 100 km/h (62 mph), while low range needs a stop. From about 2005 a push-button, motor-driven transfer case replaced the lever. BigJimny's owners compare the layout to a shrunken Patrol Y61, which is fair, if generous.
The weak point is where the front wheels steer. Each front hub swings on a pair of tapered kingpin bearings inside a knuckle that BigJimny bluntly calls 'poorly sealed by design.' Water and grit get in, the lower bearing wears, the halfshaft seal follows, and the result is the notorious 'death wobble' at around 45–50 mph. Unlike a Land Rover swivel, the Jimny's is meant to run dry with grease, not oil. Fresh Koyo bearings, a new seal and good waterproof grease fix it, and owners who wheel hard do this job often.

### THE M13A YEARS
The engine most export Jimnys carry is the M13A, a 1,328 cc all-aluminum DOHC 16-valve four with a timing chain, so there's no belt to budget for, unlike the G13BB it replaced. The original version made about 82 PS (60 kW). The 2005–06 update added variable valve timing for 85–86 PS (63 kW) and 110 Nm at 4,100 rpm, and from 2007 every petrol Jimny used the VVT engine. BigJimny's verdict is that the G13BB and M13A are 'generally very robust' and mostly suffer sensor and electrical niggles. The gearbox paired with the VVT engine, the R72, is a different story: early boxes, roughly 2005–2008, are known for bearing failures.
Suzuki kept freshening the outside. A deeper front bumper arrived around 2006 and cost some approach angle. In 2012 a squarer grille and a fake hood scoop appeared, and late cars added ESP, TPMS and a traction-control mode that only works in low range. Production ended worldwide in 2018, except in Brazil, as Suzuki retooled for the fourth generation.

### RUST, AND HOW AN AMERICAN GETS ONE
The thing that kills Jimnys isn't the drivetrain. BigJimny's wiki says every generation left the factory with 'particularly poor rust prevention,' and lists the usual spots: body and spring mounts on the chassis, factory welds, the boot floor and the floor under the rear seats, the panels behind the plastic cladding, and the cavity behind each headlamp. Its rust article shows a ten-year-old car with only 60,000 km, mostly on salted alpine roads, and a chassis rail weakened enough to keep a truck off the road. Buy the driest one you can find, then rust-proof it.
For Americans, the clock is the attraction. NHTSA lets anyone import a vehicle that is 25 or more years old, measured from its date of manufacture. That covers every 1998–2001 Jimny today: the first JB33 Wides turned 25 around the start of 2023, the first kei JB23s in late 2023 and the first M13A JB43s in 2025, and each later truck qualifies on its own 25th birthday. That's why US auctions are full of right-hand-drive JB23 turbos, while the 70 Series follows the same path a few sizes up.

### Data plate
- Chassis: JB23 (kei) · JB33 · JB43 · JB53
- Production: 1998–2018 (Brazil to 2022)
- Assembly: Iwata, Japan · Linares, Spain (Santana) · Bogotá, Colombia (GM) · Brazil
- Bodies: 3-door hardtop · 2-door canvas top (Santana, 1999–2009)
- Wheelbase: 2,250 mm (88.6 in)
- Length × Width: Kei 3,395 × 1,475 mm · Wide 3,675 × 1,600 mm
- Suspension: Solid axles, coil springs front and rear
- Drive: Part-time 4WD, low range, vacuum front hubs
- Engines: K6A turbo · G13BB · M13A · M13A VVT · K9K diesel
- Curb Weight: Kei 930–1,000 kg · Wide 960–1,155 kg
- Us Sales: Never sold new; 25-year imports only

### Engineering
A separate ladder frame carries a steel body that isn't structural. Both axles are solid beams on coil springs, located by radius arms and a panhard rod. Power goes to the rear wheels, and a lever (or, from about 2005, push buttons) adds the front axle and a 2:1-ish low range through a separate transfer case. There's no center differential, and the front hubs lock by vacuum.
- Chassis: Ladder frame, 2,250 mm wheelbase (Same wheelbase for the kei JB23 and the Wide/Sierra; the body isn't a load-bearing part.)
- Suspension: Solid axles, coil springs all round (The first full Jimny generation on coils (a late SJ 'Coily' aside). Radius arms and panhard rods locate the axles; the arm mounts are a known rust and wear point.)
- 4Wd System: Part-time, no center diff (Vacuum-locking front hubs allow 2WD to 4WD shifts up to 100 km/h (62 mph). Low range requires stopping.)
- Low Range: 2.145:1 lever box; 2.002:1 push-button manual (BigJimny's ratio tables. Push-button transfer cases arrived around 2005 with the VVT engine.)
- Engine (Export): M13A 1.3 DOHC I4, timing chain (82 PS early, 85–86 PS (63 kW) and 110 Nm with VVT from 2005–06. Early JB33s used the belt-driven G13BB.)
- Steering: Recirculating ball, kingpin knuckles (The knuckles are greased, not oil-filled. Worn kingpin bearings are the main cause of 'death wobble.')

### Versions
- 1998–2018 · JB23 (Japan kei) · K6A 658 cc turbo I3 · 64 PS · Kei-sized with no fender flares. Arrived October 1998; these right-hand-drive turbos dominate US imports.
- 1998–2001 (to 2005 in Spanish soft tops) · JB33 Jimny Wide · G13BB 1.3 SOHC 16v I4 · 80 PS (59 kW) · The first third-gen Jimny on sale, January 1998. Timing belt.
- 2000–2005 · JB43 Wide / Sierra · M13A 1.3 DOHC I4 · 82 PS (60 kW) · Japan from January 2000; other markets 2000–2002. Lever-shift transfer case.
- 2005–2018 · JB43 Sierra / Jimny · M13A VVT 1.3 DOHC I4 · 85–86 PS (63 kW) / 110 Nm · Push-button 4WD, new interior and the R72 gearbox. Facelifts in 2012 and 2014. Brazil built it until 2022.
- 2004–2011 · JB53 DDiS (Europe) · Renault K9K 1.5 turbo-diesel I4 · 65 PS, then 86 PS · Built in Japan and by Santana. The early K9K 700 is the troublesome one. Never sold in the UK or Ireland.
- 1998–2014 · JM23 Mazda AZ-Offroad · K6A 658 cc turbo I3 · 64 PS · Rebadged kei JB23 sold by Mazda in Japan.

### Year-by-year
- 1997: Third-generation Jimny revealed at the Tokyo Motor Show
- 1998: January: 1.3 G13BB Jimny Wide (JB33) on sale in Japan. October: kei JB23 with the K6A turbo and the Mazda AZ-Offroad twin arrive. Europe launch at the Paris show
- 1999: Santana's Canvas Top revealed at the Barcelona show in May; GM Colmotores starts building the 'Chevrolet Jimny' in Colombia
- 2000: January: M13A DOHC engine replaces the G13BB in Japan (JB43); other markets follow by 2002. JB23 gets standard ABS and airbag from October 1999
- 2002: Japan revives the 'Jimny Sierra' name for the 1.3 in January; JB23 grille separates from the hood
- 2004: European JB53 diesel arrives with Renault's 65 PS K9K 700, whose fuel pump failures can ruin the engine [avoid]
- 2005: Push-button electric transfer case, new interior and the R72 manual gearbox. BigJimny says early R72s (about 2005–2008) are prone to bearing failure; listen for noise in third and fourth [avoid]
- 2005–2006: M13A gains VVT (63 kW / 110 Nm); diesel moves to the 86 PS intercooled K9K 266; deeper front bumper hurts approach angle
- 2009: Santana ends its agreement with Suzuki; the Canvas Top is discontinued
- 2012: Facelift: squarer grille, hood scoop, shallower bumper and ISOFIX
- 2014: ESP, low-range traction control and TPMS added where required; new instrument panel and steering wheel
- 2018: Production ends everywhere except Brazil as Suzuki retools for the JB64/JB74; Brazil follows in 2022
- 2023–2026: First JB33s, then JB23s (late 2023) and M13A JB43s (2025) reach 25 years old and become importable to the US

### Capability
- Towing: 1,300 kg (2,866 lb) braked / 500 kg (1,102 lb) unbraked (2017 Jimny Sierra, New Zealand spec)
- Gross vehicle mass: 1,420 kg (3,131 lb) (2017 Sierra)
- Fuel tank: 40 L (10.6 US gal)
- Ground clearance: 190 mm (7.5 in) (unladen)
- Approach / departure: 34° / 46° (2017 Sierra)
- Fuel economy: 7.1 L/100 km combined (about 33 US mpg) (Suzuki claim, 2017 manual)
- Curb weight: 1,062 kg (2,341 lb) (2017 Sierra manual; kei JB23 930–1,000 kg)
- Turning circle: 9.8 m (32.2 ft)
- Engine output: 63 kW (86 PS) / 110 Nm at 4,100 rpm (M13A VVT)

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 205/70R15 on 15x5.5 alloy (JB43 Jimny Sierra, e.g. 2017 New Zealand market)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x139.7 (5x5.5")
- Offset: ET5 (+5 mm) on the factory 15x5.5
- Center Bore: 108.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M12x1.25
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 215/75R15 (BigJimny consensus for an unmodified Wide/Sierra, about 27.7 in. Bigger than this and owners advise regearing to protect the clutch or the automatic's fluid.)
- Biggest tire, 2 in lift: 235/75R15 (About 28.8 in. Forum regulars say a gen 3 still needs some trimming at 2 in, though some owners accept minor rubbing at full flex instead.)
- Biggest tire, 3 in lift: 265/75R15 (≈31 in) (Trimming required, per BigJimny's tire-size notes; plan on lower transfer gearing.)

### Buying checks
- Crawl under it before anything else: BigJimny's buying guide calls rust 'the main issue with most Jimnys.' Look at the body and coil-spring mounts on the chassis, the factory welds and the rear crossmember. A body-on-frame truck can look fine from above while the mounts are rotting. One forum owner's 2000 Jimny failed its UK MOT on two body mounts and the rear crossmember.
- Pull up the boot floor and the rear seat: The rear seat bench lifts out by hand. Check the floor around the rear seat-belt anchors, the tool well above the exhaust and the joint between the rear floor and the inner arches. BigJimny says this is the most common rot-through, and it's worse on soft tops.
- Look behind the headlamps and the cladding: The cavity behind each headlamp is a water drain that rarely drains properly, and the plastic sill and arch cladding hides rust until it's advanced. Pop the inner arch liners if the seller will let you.
- Listen for a clunk pulling away: A clunk from the rear in first gear points to loose or worn radius-arm mounts. The mounting holes can wear oval and the brackets can rust through, which needs welding.
- Drive it at 45–50 mph: Steering shake in that band is the classic Jimny 'death wobble,' usually from worn kingpin bearings. Gear oil weeping onto the swivel balls means the halfshaft seal has gone too. It's fixable, but price it in.
- Engage 4WD on a loose surface: Try 4WD and low range on gravel and listen for the front hubs clicking in. Erratic engagement on lever cars means vacuum leaks. On push-button cars, flashing 4WD lights usually point to the transfer-case actuator or its wiring.
- Abuse the transfer case, briefly: BigJimny's test: a hard launch in first. A loud machine-gun rattle with no movement means a stretched transfer chain. Used transfer cases are cheap, so it's a bargaining point rather than a deal-breaker.
- Importing? Read the build plate: The 25-year exemption runs from the date of manufacture, not the model year, so check the build date before you pay. Get the export certificate and import paperwork, and check how your state titles right-hand-drive kei imports before the truck lands.

### Common repairs
#### Replace the kingpin bearings and halfshaft seal
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day per side · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Steering-wheel shake around 45–50 mph, play when you rock a raised wheel at 12 and 6 o'clock with the brakes held, and diff oil mixed with grease leaking from the swivel ball. A rusted-solid lower bearing can show no play at all.
Fix: Strip the steering knuckle, replace both tapered kingpin bearings (BigJimny recommends Koyo, the OE supplier) and fit the 26 x 38 x 9 mm double-lip Suzuki halfshaft seal rather than a shallower aftermarket one. Pack the bearings with heavy-duty waterproof grease in normal quantities, use only a thin film of sealant on the kingpins, and add Suzuki's preload shims if the wobble persists. Replace the large swivel seal while you're in there.
Tools: Jack and axle stands · torque wrench · bearing drift · gasket sealant · waterproof grease.

#### Chase down a death wobble that isn't the kingpins
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–3 hours per item · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Wobble remains after new kingpin bearings, or a sloppy, wandering feel at speed.
Fix: Work through BigJimny's list in order: worn tie-rod ends (one standard and one reverse thread per rod), worn radius-arm bushes (most often the chassis end of the front arms), wheel balance (beads help with chunky mud tires), and rust on the hub face behind the brake disc that stops the disc and wheel seating square. Warped discs can mimic it too.
Tools: Tie-rod end puller · bush press or drawbolt kit · wire brush for hub faces · alignment afterward.

#### Fix vacuum front hubs that won't engage
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ 1–2 hours to diagnose · cost Often just hose or valve parts
Symptoms: The 4WD light flashes, the front hubs don't click in, or 4WD works one day and not the next. Common on trucks that rarely use 4WD.
Fix: The system only pulls vacuum for a few seconds, so you can't hear a leak. Pull a wheel, disconnect the two hub hoses and apply vacuum with a large syringe to each spigot in turn: the hub should click. If it does, test again at the valve block. The pipe from the intake manifold to the valves is the most common failure, and a leaky 'unlock' valve can stop the 'lock' circuit working. If you're tired of chasing it, BigJimny documents converting to manual or fixed hubs.
Tools: 100 ml syringe · vacuum hose · basic hand tools.

#### Revive the push-button transfer-case actuator
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ 2–3 hours · cost Free if cleaning fixes it
Symptoms: On 2005-on trucks, the green 4WD light flashes (one owner counted 12 flashes) with a click, the 4L light may flash too, and 4WD won't engage even though the hubs lock when tested.
Fix: First rule out the hubs and check the clutch is fully down (or the auto is in neutral). Then check the plugs and wiring on the transfer case. If they're fine, remove the round tin actuator cover at the back of the transfer case. One BigJimny owner found condensation and rust inside, cleaned and dried it, and it worked perfectly afterward. Watch for two springs that fly out when the armature comes out, and set the actuator's position relative to the selector shaft per Suzuki's procedure on reassembly. Change the transfer-case oil while you're there.
Tools: Basic hand tools · contact cleaner · service manual for the actuator alignment procedure.

#### Repair rotten floors, sills and radius-arm brackets
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ Days, with welding · cost Parts plus fabrication labor
Symptoms: Holes in the boot floor or under the rear seats, rust around the seat-belt anchors, MOT or inspection failures on body mounts, or a rear clunk from a corroded arm bracket.
Fix: Cut back to clean metal before judging it: forum regulars warn it always looks worse once cleaned up. Pressed repair floors are available in the UK, and sills and radius-arm brackets come as panels. Weld in new metal, seam-seal and paint, then wax the cavities. If the chassis rail itself or the spring and body mounts are badly rotted, BigJimny warns the truck may be beyond economical repair.
Tools: MIG welder · grinder · seam sealer · cavity wax and underbody coating.

#### Renew radius-arm bushes and check the axle mounts
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: A clunk when letting the clutch up, vague steering, or cracked and split bushes you can open with a screwdriver.
Fix: Unbolt the arms and inspect the mounts on the axle and chassis: BigJimny notes they're thin, wear oval, and on older trucks can corrode and tear off entirely. Press new bushes into the arms (nylon SuperPro-type bushes are easier to fit but ride firmer), check the arms against a straight edge for bends, and torque the bolts with the truck at ride height.
Tools: Bush press or drawbolt set · straight edge · torque wrench.

#### Rebuild a noisy R72 gearbox
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A weekend · cost About £700 at a shop, per BigJimny
Symptoms: Grinding or whining when cruising in 3rd or 4th on 2005-ish to 2008 petrol trucks, and a furry drain plug or metal chunks in the oil.
Fix: Remove the gearbox, split the three-piece case and replace the open deep-groove bearings with metal-shielded ones, as Suzuki's later parts do. BigJimny suspects early oil starvation (some trucks also had leaking prop-shaft center caps). Keep the synchro rings, clips and needle bearings in order. The procedure is in Suzuki supplementary manual 99501-81A10-01E. Do the clutch while the box is out.
Tools: Transmission jack · bearing pullers · impact sockets for pressing bearings · liquid gasket.

#### Change the G13BB timing belt (1998–2001 JB33)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: No visible symptom until it snaps. It's a service item on early 1.3 Jimnys, which are exactly the trucks now eligible for US import.
Fix: Suzuki's interval for the G13BB belt (part 12761-70C00) is 100,000 km. With no receipt, change the belt and tensioner on arrival, and do the water pump at the same time. The M13A that replaced it uses a chain and doesn't need this.
Tools: Timing marks and service manual · tensioner tools · coolant for the pump.

### Baseline service
Specs below are from the Suzuki owner's-manual tables BigJimny reproduces for UK-market M13A VVT trucks, with earlier-engine differences noted. A US import may be a kei JB23 with the K6A turbo, which has its own specs, so confirm your model code first. BigJimny's advice for any secondhand Jimny without history: change every fluid and filter, and the belts, straight away.
- Engine oil & filter: M13A: 4.0 L, API SL/SM or newer, 5W-30 or 10W-30 · G13BB: 3.7–4.2 L depending on type · Suzuki: 15,000 km / 12 months; BigJimny suggests 10,000 km (Factory filter for the VVT engine is Suzuki 16510-61A31 (16510-61A01 and -61A20 also fit). Replace the sump-plug gasket each time.)
- Air filter: Suzuki 13780-81A00 · Suzuki: 45,000 km / 3 years; BigJimny: 25,000–30,000 km, sooner in dust (Check it at every oil change on a truck that sees gravel roads.)
- Cabin filter: Not every Jimny has one fitted · No factory interval; BigJimny suggests about 20,000 km or two years (Purely for the occupants, but worth doing on a dusty import.)
- Spark plugs: M13A VVT: NGK BKR6E-11 / Denso K20PR-U11 (nickel) or NGK IFR6J11 (iridium) · Nickel 45,000 km, iridium 60,000 km (with O2 sensor) (Suzuki prefers iridium plugs, especially in cold climates.)
- Coolant: M13A VVT: 5.2–5.9 L by type · ethylene glycol, silicate-free · 45,000 km / 3 years (non-HOAT) (From 2005 Suzuki's manuals specify silicate-free coolant, and BigJimny applies that to every gen 3. Flush an unknown truck.)
- Manual gearbox: API GL-4 75W-90 · 1.3 L (VVT), 1.1 L (earlier) · BigJimny: 50,000 km / 3 years (On an R72 box, a furry drain plug or metal flakes is the early warning of bearing failure.)
- Automatic gearbox: VVT: Suzuki ATF3317, Mobil ATF3309 or Dexron III · 3.7 L or 5.7 L depending on type · BigJimny: 75,000 km / 4–5 years (BigJimny: the autos 'love fresh ATF'; poor shifts and a top gear that won't select follow neglect.)
- Transfer case: API GL-4 75W-90 · 1.13 L (VVT), 0.7–0.8 L (earlier) · Suzuki: never; BigJimny: 50,000 km / 3–5 years (Check the push-button actuator cover for water ingress while you're under there.)
- Front & rear differentials: API GL-5 80W-90 hypoid · front 1.65 L, rear 1.35 L (VVT); 1.1 L / 1.3 L earlier · Suzuki: never; BigJimny: 50,000 km / 3–5 years (Milky oil after water crossings means the breathers or seals let water in.)
- Kingpins & steering knuckles: Heavy-duty waterproof grease, not oil · Inspect now; rebuild if there's play or leakage (BigJimny: the lower bearing can rust solid on trucks that sat for years and show no play at all, so inspect inside on an unknown truck.)
- Power steering & brake fluid: PS: Dexron IIE or III · brakes: DOT 3 / SAE J1703 · Brakes: 30,000 km / 2 years (Suzuki doesn't define a power-steering interval; refresh it if it's dark.)
- Belts: G13BB timing belt 12761-70C00 · M13A uses a chain · G13BB belt 100,000 km; V-ribbed drive belts 90,000 km / 6 years (Whirring or squealing on an M13A is usually a drive belt, tensioner or alternator bearing (BigJimny's noise guide).)
- 4WD system & vacuum hubs: Exercise 4WD and low range · BigJimny: use it from time to time so parts don't seize (Test hub engagement on a loose surface; dormant vacuum hubs are the usual failure.)
- Underbody rust protection: Clean to bare metal where rusty, then coat and wax cavities · Thoroughly now, then check and touch up yearly (BigJimny: wash the underbody regularly in winter, then drive it dry.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: Stock on the Wide/Sierra is 205/70R15 (about 27.1 inches). BigJimny's consensus is that 215/75R15 (about 27.7 inches) is the largest that fits an unmodified truck. 235/75R15 (about 28.8 inches) wants a 2-inch lift, and forum regulars say gen 3s still need some trimming even then, though a few owners run them with minor rubbing at full flex. Anything bigger than 215 really calls for regearing, or you'll cook the clutch or the automatic's fluid.

Q: Can I legally import one to the US?
A: Yes, if it's at least 25 years old from its date of manufacture, which is the NHTSA exemption in 49 CFR 591.5(i). As of late 2026 that covers trucks built up to about October 2001: JB33 Wides, early JB43s and kei JB23s, plus the Mazda AZ-Offroad. Each later truck becomes eligible on its own 25th birthday. EPA has its own age-based exemption, and your state decides how it's titled.

Q: What's the difference between JB23, JB33, JB43 and JB53?
A: JB23 is the Japanese kei car with the 658 cc turbo three and no fender flares. JB33 is the export 1.3 'Wide' with the G13BB. JB43 is the M13A-engined Wide or Sierra from 2000 to 2018. JB53 is the European diesel with Renault's 1.5 K9K. All four share the 2,250 mm wheelbase.

Q: Which engine should I look for?
A: BigJimny rates both petrol engines as robust. The G13BB uses a timing belt with a 100,000 km interval, while the M13A uses a chain that doesn't need replacing. The M13A VVT (2005–06 on) is the strongest petrol at 85–86 PS, but its R72 gearbox had bearing problems in roughly 2005–2008 trucks. Avoid the early K9K 700 diesel, whose injection pump failures can wreck the engine.

Q: Which years are the best to buy?
A: BigJimny doesn't name a best year, and it rates both petrol engines as robust: the M13A has a timing chain that doesn't need replacing, while the earlier G13B has a cam belt. The ones to be careful with are the early K9K 700 diesels (2003 to about 2006), which it calls statistically very troublesome, and petrols from about 2005–2008 with the early R72 gearbox, whose bearings can fail (about £700 to fix). Late trucks from about 2014 add low-range traction control. Otherwise, rust decides it.

Q: Can I leave it in 4WD on the road?
A: No. There's no center differential, so 4WD on dry tarmac binds the driveline and can break CV joints, and Suzuki only sells the CV joint with the halfshaft. On push-button trucks, check you haven't knocked 4WD on by accident. Use 4WD on snow, mud, gravel, wet grass and sand.

Q: How fast can I shift into 4WD?
A: The vacuum-locking front hubs let you go from 2WD to 4WD-High at up to 100 km/h (62 mph). Low range requires stopping, and on push-button trucks the clutch must be down with the gearbox in neutral.

Q: How much can it tow?
A: A 2017 New Zealand-market Jimny Sierra was rated at 1,300 kg (2,866 lb) braked and 500 kg (1,102 lb) unbraked. Bear in mind that it only has 110 Nm of torque.

Q: What fuel economy should I expect?
A: Suzuki claimed 7.1 L/100 km combined for the 2017 manual Sierra, about 33 US mpg, from a 40-liter (10.6-gallon) tank. Bigger tires, roof racks and the 4-speed automatic all make it worse.

Q: Does it have lockers?
A: Not from the factory: both axles have open differentials, and late trucks add a traction-control mode that only works in low range. BigJimny's owners rate the ARB Air Locker as the best aftermarket option because it's selectable, while Lockright and Kaiser are cheaper automatic lockers that can misbehave on the road.

Q: Should I fill the front swivels with oil like a Land Rover?
A: No. BigJimny warns that Land Rover-trained mechanics sometimes try it. The Jimny's knuckle is a greased, 'dry' joint, and its swivel seal acts more as a dust shield and steering damper than an oil seal. Corroded swivel balls aren't critical either: file them smooth and paint them.

Q: Are wheel spacers OK?
A: Forum regulars advise against them. They shorten the life of the kingpin and wheel bearings dramatically, to as little as six months in hard off-road use according to one experienced owner.

## Suzuki Jimny JB74 / JB64 (2018–present)
URL: https://boxytrucks.com/models/suzuki/jimny-jb74/
Codes: JB64, JB74, JC74

Verdict: Suzuki styled it like a 1970s LJ, kept the ladder frame and two solid axles, and then watched the whole world queue for it. It's slow, it's tiny and it's illegal to import into America until 2043, which only makes people want one more.

Production of the fourth-generation Jimny started at Suzuki's Kosai plant on 29 May 2018, the first time Jimnys had been built there, and the truck went on sale in Japan on 5 July, the first all-new Jimny in twenty years. Its styling looks back to the LJ and SJ/Samurai generations, with flat panels, round lamps and drip rails. Underneath, Suzuki kept the ladder frame, the front-engine rear-drive layout, the part-time 4WD with a low-range transfer gear, and three-link solid axles at both ends. Then demand outran supply in almost every market it entered, and it hasn't fully caught up since.

### KEI JB64 VS SIERRA JB74
As with the JB23 generation, there are two widths. The JB64 is the kei car, sold only in Japan: 3,395 mm long and 1,475 mm wide, with no fender flares, tucked-in bumpers and a turbocharged 658 cc R06A three-cylinder, in XG, XL and XC trims. The JB74 is the one the world knows. Japan calls it the Jimny Sierra (JL and JC trims), and everyone else simply calls it the Jimny. It's 1,645 mm wide with bolt-on flares and has the 1.5-liter K15B.
Both share the 2,250 mm wheelbase, a reworked ladder frame with extra cross members that Wikipedia's development notes credit with about 1.5 times the torsional rigidity, a choice of five-speed manual or four-speed automatic, and standard brake-LSD traction control. That system brakes a spinning wheel so the one opposite can keep pulling, which is useful but no substitute for a locker. Suzuki Australia quotes 210 mm of ground clearance, with approach, breakover and departure angles of 36°, 27° and 47°.

### THE K15B
The K15B replaced the JB43's M13A. It's a 1,462 cc all-aluminum DOHC 16-valve four with variable valve timing, a 74 x 85 mm bore and stroke, a 10:1 compression ratio and a timing chain. In Suzuki Australia's spec it makes 75 kW (102 PS) at 6,000 rpm and 130 Nm (96 lb-ft) at 4,000 rpm. That's a real gain over the old 1.3, but it's still only 1,095 kg of truck being pulled up hills by a naturally aspirated four.
Unsealed 4X4's staff, many of them Suzuki owners, are blunt about it. The engine is 'begging for a few more killer-wasps, or even better, a turbo.' The four-speed automatic is 'way too old to be put into a vehicle in this decade,' and next to it the manual 'feels like it has an extra 30kw available.' Gearing is the other complaint: the transfer case is 'geared way too high for anywhere near sizeable tyres,' so a set of lower gears tends to arrive alongside the first set of bigger tires.

### THE QUEUE
Suzuki UK's entire 2019 allocation of 1,200 cars was sold by December 2018, with waits of up to a year, and some dealers stopped taking deposits. Suzuki blamed a bottleneck at the Japanese factory. In Australia the queue was still up to twelve months in mid-2021, and in Mexico the first 1,000 reserved units sold out in three days. At home, Japanese Jimny sales went from about 11,000–16,000 a year in the old truck's last decade to 30,281 in 2019 and roughly 40,000 a year from 2021. Maruti Suzuki began building Jimnys in India in January 2021 to help supply export markets.
Europe shows the other side of the coin. At 154–178 g/km of CO2, the Jimny dragged Suzuki's fleet average well above the EU target, so the passenger car was withdrawn from the UK in 2020 and returned as a two-seat light commercial vehicle. That too was withdrawn from European sale in 2025.

### FIVE DOORS, AND THE AMERICAN QUESTION
The five-door Jimny (JC74) was revealed in India in January 2023 and launched there on 7 June 2023. Its wheelbase is 340 mm longer at 2,590 mm, and it's built only at Maruti Suzuki's plant in Gurugram for export to almost 100 countries. Australia got it in December 2023 as the Jimny XL. Japan got it on 30 January 2025 as the Jimny Nomade and took about 50,000 orders in four days, against roughly 1,200 cars a month allocated for Japan. Suzuki suspended orders, apologized, raised output to about 3,300 a month and reopened the books on 30 January 2026.
For Americans, none of this is available. Suzuki left the US car market in 2012, and the JB74 was never certified here. In September 2022, CBP seized a 2022 Jimny that a US citizen had bought in Mexico and driven across the border, because DOT ruled it ineligible: it was 'less than 25 years old from the date of manufacture.' The earliest JB74s turn 25 in mid-2043. Until then, the legal way into a small Suzuki in the US is a 25-year-old JB23 or JB43.

### Data plate
- Chassis: JB64W (kei) · JB74W · JC74W (5-door)
- Production: May 2018–present
- Assembly: Kosai, Japan · Gurugram, India (Maruti Suzuki)
- Wheelbase: 2,250 mm (3-door) · 2,590 mm (5-door)
- Length × Width: Kei 3,395 × 1,475 mm · JB74 3,650 × 1,645 mm · XL 3,965 × 1,645 mm
- Engine: K15B 1,462 cc DOHC VVT I4 (kei: R06A 658 cc turbo I3)
- Output: 75 kW (102 PS) / 130 Nm
- Gearboxes: 5-speed manual · 4-speed automatic
- Drive: ALLGRIP PRO part-time 4WD with low range
- Suspension: 3-link rigid axles, coil springs front and rear
- Ground Clearance: 210 mm (8.3 in)
- Us Sales: Never; not importable until 2043

### Engineering
The fourth generation keeps the classic Jimny layout: a separate ladder frame, now with extra cross members, and rigid axles front and rear on coil springs, each located by three links. Drive is rear-wheel by default, with a part-time 4WD system Suzuki calls ALLGRIP PRO adding the front axle and a low range. There's no center differential, and traction control brakes spinning wheels instead of locking diffs.
- Chassis: Ladder frame with added cross members (About 1.5 times the torsional rigidity of the old frame, with redesigned body mounts, per Wikipedia's development notes.)
- Suspension: 3-link rigid axles, coil springs (Same layout front and rear. Unsealed found the stock XL 'ran out of travel quickly' off-road.)
- 4Wd System: ALLGRIP PRO part-time 4WD (2WD-High, 4WD-High and 4WD-Low, no center diff. Manual low range is 2.002:1 per BigJimny's gearing table.)
- Traction: Brake-LSD traction control (Standard on all versions; brakes the slipping wheel of a diagonal pair. Open diffs; no factory lockers.)
- Engine: K15B 1.5 L I4, 75 kW / 130 Nm (Chain-driven DOHC with VVT. Japan's kei JB64 uses the 658 cc R06A turbo three instead.)
- Geometry: 210 mm clearance · 36° / 27° / 47° (Suzuki Australia figures for the 3-door. The 5-door XL keeps the approach and departure angles but drops breakover to 24°.)

### Versions
- 2018–present · JB64 Jimny (Japan kei) · R06A 658 cc turbo I3 · — · No fender flares, 1,475 mm wide. Sold only in Japan, in XG, XL and XC trims.
- 2018–present · JB74 Jimny / Jimny Sierra · K15B 1.5 DOHC VVT I4 · 75 kW (102 PS) / 130 Nm · Global 3-door, 1,645 mm wide. Built in Japan, and in India from January 2021.
- 2020–2025 · JB74 Jimny Commercial (UK/EU) · K15B 1.5 I4 · As JB74 · Two-seat N1 van with up to 863 L of load space, created to cut Suzuki's fleet CO2.
- 2023–present · JC74 5-door (Jimny XL / Nomade) · K15B 1.5 I4 · 75 kW / 130 Nm · 2,590 mm wheelbase, built only in India. India from June 2023, Australia December 2023, Japan January 2025.

### Year-by-year
- 2018: Production starts at Suzuki's Kosai plant on 29 May; Japanese launch of the JB64 Jimny and JB74 Jimny Sierra on 5 July; European debut in Germany in October; South Africa in November
- 2018: Fuel-pump recall covers cars built 9 May to 22 November 2018, with a second campaign to 7 September 2019, and the door-harness airbag recall covers cars built up to 2 December 2020. Have a dealer confirm both were done
- 2018–2019: UK's 1,200-car 2019 allocation sells out by December 2018, with waits of up to a year. Australia launches in January 2019
- 2020: Passenger Jimny withdrawn from the UK in July over CO2; two-seat Jimny Commercial arrives from September. Door-harness airbag recall covers cars built up to 2 December 2020
- 2020: Mexico launch in November; the first 1,000 reserved units sell out in three days
- 2021: Maruti Suzuki starts Indian assembly for export in January. Australia adds the Lite grade in June, with the queue at up to 12 months
- 2023: 5-door JC74 revealed in India in January; Indian launch on 7 June; Australian Jimny XL from 5 December
- 2025: Japan's 5-door Jimny Nomade launches on 30 January and orders are suspended after about 50,000 in four days. Australia pauses 3-door supply for new ADR rules in February. Jimny Commercial withdrawn from European sale
- 2025: Australian Jimny XL stop-delivery from late July; sales resume 27 August after Suzuki confirms no safety or compliance issue
- 2026: Nomade orders reopen in Japan on 30 January. Updated Australian 3-door adds adaptive cruise, lane-keep assist and front and rear parking sensors
- 2043: The earliest JB74s (built from May 2018) turn 25 and become eligible for US import under NHTSA's 25-year exemption

### Capability
- Towing: 1,300 kg (2,866 lb) braked / 350 kg (772 lb) unbraked (Suzuki Australia, 3-door and XL)
- Payload: About 340 kg (750 lb) (3-door, per Unsealed 4X4; Ironman's GVM kit raises it to 690 kg)
- Gross vehicle mass: 1,450 kg (3-door) / 1,545 kg (XL) (Suzuki Australia)
- Fuel tank: 40 L (10.6 US gal)
- Ground clearance: 210 mm (8.3 in) (unladen)
- Approach / breakover / departure: 36° / 27° / 47° (3-door) · 36° / 24° / 47° (XL) (Suzuki Australia)
- Fuel economy: 6.4 L/100 km manual · 6.9 L/100 km auto (Australian ADR 81/02 combined)
- Curb weight: 1,095–1,110 kg (3-door) · 1,185–1,200 kg (XL) (minimum, manual–auto)
- Turning: 4.9 m (3-door) · 5.7 m (XL) (Suzuki Australia lists these as the kerb-to-kerb turning circle)
- Cargo: 85 / 377 L (3-door) · 211 / 332 L (XL), seats up / folded

### Wheels and tires
- Stock tires: 195/80R15 on 15-inch steel or alloy wheels (all Australian grades, 3-door and XL)
- Bolt Pattern: 5x139.7 (5x5.5")
- Offset: ET5 (+5 mm) on 15x5.5
- Center Bore: 108.1 mm
- Lug Thread: M12x1.25
- Biggest tire, Stock lift: 215/75R15 (BigJimny consensus for the largest size suited to the stock rims; it's only slightly taller than stock. Some Australian owners fit 235/75R15s on stock rims, beyond the rims' recommended limits.)
- Biggest tire, 2 in lift: 235/75R15 (Fits a gen 4 with a little trimming of the front bumper, per BigJimny owners; regearing advised.)

### Buying checks
- Check the recall record: EU Safety Gate lists three Jimny recalls: fuel pumps whose resin impellers could swell and stall the engine (cars built 9 May to 22 November 2018, then a second campaign for 12 November 2018 to 7 September 2019), and door wiring harnesses that could break and stop the side and curtain airbags deploying (cars built to 2 December 2020). Ask a dealer to run the VIN.
- Get underneath with a flashlight: BigJimny's wiki says every Jimny generation has 'particularly poor rust prevention' from the factory, and the usual spots are the chassis welds and the body and spring mounts. The JB74 is still young, but a truck from a salted-road region should show evidence of underbody protection.
- Drive it at 45–50 mph: Steering shake in that band was the third generation's signature fault, from kingpin bearings in a poorly sealed knuckle. BigJimny expects the same on the JB74 because the design is so similar, so test-drive at that speed and rock each raised front wheel.
- Inspect any lift kit properly: A good Jimny lift includes caster correction, a crossmember drop, extended brake lines and often a panhard bracket. Pedders notes the factory headlight-leveling bracket can't simply be extended without risk of breaking. Missing pieces mean someone took shortcuts.
- Do the payload math: Unsealed puts the 3-door's factory payload at about 340 kg (750 lb), which a bull bar, winch, roof rack and two adults can use up. In Australia, check for a GVM upgrade plate or engineer's certificate if the truck is heavily accessorized.
- Big tires without gearing?: Anything larger than 215/75R15 really needs lower gearing. Without it, BigJimny owners warn you'll quickly burn the clutch or overheat the automatic's fluid. Ask what ratio changes came with the tires.
- Manual or automatic: Unsealed 4X4 couldn't see 'a viable reason to spend the three extra grand' on the four-speed auto in an XL. The manual is the enthusiast pick, and the autos are slower.
- In the US? Ask how it got here: A 2018-on Jimny can't be legally imported into the US until it's 25 years old. CBP's 2022 Puerto Rico seizure ended with an order to bring the truck into compliance, export it or destroy it. Don't buy one with 'paperwork in progress.'

### Common repairs
#### Diagnose steering wobble (kingpins first)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day per side for kingpins · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: A shaking steering wheel around 45–50 mph, play when a raised front wheel is rocked top to bottom with the brakes held, or oil and grease weeping from the swivel balls.
Fix: Follow BigJimny's death-wobble order. Check tire balance first, then rock each front wheel with an assistant holding the brakes: play that remains points to the kingpin bearings, play that disappears points to the wheel bearings. Check tie-rod ends, radius-arm bushes and the hub face behind the brake disc for rust. If the kingpins are worn, rebuild them with Koyo bearings, a new halfshaft seal and waterproof grease.
Tools: Jack and stands · torque wrench · tie-rod end puller · bearing drift.

#### Fit a 40–50 mm lift properly
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day · cost Roughly A$1,300–3,000 for a kit, per Unsealed's suspension guide
Symptoms: Not a fault. The stock suspension rides choppily, sags under accessories and limits tire size.
Fix: Choose springs rated for your real load: OME offers three front-spring options for stock, bull-bar and bull-bar-plus-winch trucks. Fit caster-correction bushes or adjustable arms, a crossmember drop for driveshaft angle, extended brake lines for droop and a panhard-rod bracket to correct the rear roll center. Sort the headlight leveling, then get a wheel alignment.
Tools: Spring compressor (if needed) · trolley jack and stands · torque wrench · alignment afterward.

#### Upgrade the GVM for touring (Australia)
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ A day plus certification · cost Parts plus fitting and engineering
Symptoms: A bull bar, winch, roof rack, fridge and two adults put the truck over its factory gross vehicle mass of 1,435–1,450 kg.
Fix: Fit a federally approved GVM kit with matched springs and shocks. Ironman's kit raises GVM from 1,435 kg to 1,785 kg (axle limits 800 kg front, 1,100 kg rear) and lifts the truck 45 mm; TJM's XGS GVM+ goes to 1,800 kg. Fitted before registration, the truck gets a new compliance plate. Fitted afterward, a state-approved engineer must inspect it and issue a modification plate.
Tools: As for a lift kit · approved installer for certification.

#### Add a selectable locker
Difficulty 4 / 5 · time ≈ A day per axle at a shop · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: Brake-LSD traction control hesitates or runs out of grip on steep, cross-axled climbs. Unsealed found itself waiting for it to kick in, which cost momentum.
Fix: Unsealed's view is that 'with a pair of lockers it'll go pretty much anywhere.' A selectable air locker behaves like an open diff until you switch it on. Setting up the diff, running air lines, fitting a compressor and wiring switches all need skill, so many owners leave it to a shop.
Tools: Diff setup tools (bearing puller, dial indicator) · compressor and air lines · or a 4x4 shop.

#### Do the first full filter service
Difficulty 1 / 5 · time ≈ 1 hour · cost The price of filters and oil
Symptoms: Unknown service history, a dusty air filter after gravel roads, or a musty cabin.
Fix: Change the engine oil and filter, the air filter and the cabin filter using genuine Gen 4 parts, and check the fluid grades and capacities in your owner's handbook. Inspect the air filter at every oil change if you drive on dirt roads.
Tools: Oil filter wrench · drain pan · basic hand tools.

#### Replace a worn rear wheel bearing
Difficulty 3 / 5 · time ≈ Half a day per side · cost Parts plus labor
Symptoms: A hum or rumble from the rear that changes with speed, or play at the rear wheel when you rock it.
Fix: Pull the axle shaft, press off the old bearing and retainer, press on the new ABS-type bearing and retainer and fit a new axle oil seal. BigJimny's rear wheel bearing guide covers the gen 3 procedure; check your gen 4 manual for differences.
Tools: Slide hammer or puller · hydraulic press · new retainer ring.

#### Rust-proof the chassis and body cavities
Difficulty 2 / 5 · time ≈ A day, plus drying time · cost Materials plus labor
Symptoms: None at first, which is the point. BigJimny's wiki says every Jimny generation has 'particularly poor rust prevention' from the factory. The usual spots are the body and suspension mounting points on the chassis, factory welds on the chassis and axles, the boot floor, under the rear seats, the inner wheel arches and behind the side cladding.
Fix: Wash the underside thoroughly and let it dry. Inspect the body and coil-spring mounts and the chassis welds. BigJimny warns that any existing rust must be removed completely before coating, because rust sealed under a coating keeps spreading out of sight. Treat cleaned spots with a rust converter and primer. Then spray cavity wax inside the chassis rails and body cavities, and an underbody wax over the visible underside. Keep the drain holes clear, and recheck every year, especially after salted roads.
Tools: Pressure washer · wire brushes · jack stands · cavity-wax wand with a long probe · protective gear.

### Baseline service
No US dealer will ever service one, so the owner's handbook is your bible. The grades and intervals below are Suzuki's handbook figures as transcribed by maintenanceschedule.com (2021 JB64/JB74 handbook) and jimny.joker.art.pl (2023 handbook for the five-door JC74, which shares the K15B and gearboxes). Capacities come from Liqui Moly's oil guide (Olyslager data) for the 2018–2024 Jimny 1.5 and match the five-door handbook. On a used truck with gaps in its history, BigJimny's rule for every Jimny applies: change every fluid and filter now.
- Engine oil & filter: SAE 0W-16 preferred; 0W-20 or 5W-30 also approved (API SL or newer, or ACEA A1/B1 or better in Europe) · 3.6 L with filter · Handbook: 20,000 km / 12 months in Europe with ACEA oil (15,000 km otherwise, and in Asia/Australia); 10,000 km / 6 months in severe use (Europe) or 7,500 km (Asia/Australia) (Use a genuine Gen 4 filter.)
- Air filter: Genuine Gen 4 element · Inspect at every oil change if you drive on dirt (BigJimny's gen 3 practice of changing it at around 25,000–30,000 km, or sooner in dust, is a sensible baseline.)
- Cabin filter: Gen 4 pollen filter · About yearly or when musty (Purely for the occupants, but worth doing on a dusty truck.)
- Spark plugs: Iridium: NGK KR6A-10 or Denso ZXU20PR11 · Handbook: 100,000 km / 7 years in Europe; 30,000 km / 24 months in severe use (The K15B is chain-driven, so there's no timing belt to budget for.)
- Coolant: Suzuki Super Long Life Coolant (blue) · 5.0 L manual, 4.9 L automatic · Blue coolant: first change at 160,000 km / 8 years, then every 80,000 km / 4 years (Europe handbook); the green 'Standard' coolant is due twice as often (Suzuki's gen 3 manuals required silicate-free coolant from 2005, according to BigJimny. Don't top up with a generic green, and if you don't know what's in it, change it now.)
- Manual or automatic gearbox: Manual: Suzuki Gear Oil 75W, 1.2 L · Automatic: Suzuki ATF3317 or Mobil ATF3309, 5.7 L total (dry fill) · Shorten if you've fitted bigger tires (Larger tires without regearing make the clutch and automatic work harder, so fresh fluid is cheap insurance.)
- Transfer case: Suzuki Gear Oil 75W · 1.2 L (Liqui Moly; the five-door handbook gives 1.21 L) · Change on an unknown truck (Gen 3 owners change it every 3–5 years despite Suzuki saying 'never.')
- Front & rear differentials: Suzuki Super Gear Oil 75W-85 synthetic (Liqui Moly suggests a GL-5 75W-90 synthetic) · front 1.6 L, rear 1.3 L · Change on an unknown truck and after deep water (Replace the drain gasket each time.)
- Kingpins & front knuckles: Inspect for play and weeping · At every service once the truck sees off-road use (BigJimny expects the gen 3's kingpin wear to carry over because the design is so similar.)
- Brake fluid: DOT 3 / SAE J1703 · Handbook: every 40,000 km / 24 months; flush now on an unknown truck (On manual trucks the clutch shares the brake fluid reservoir (jimny.joker.art.pl). Rear brakes are leading/trailing drums, so check the shoes and wheel cylinders while you're there.)
- Open recalls: Fuel pump (2018–2019 builds) · door harness/airbags (to Dec 2020) · Once, at a Suzuki dealer (Have the dealer run the VIN; recall work is free.)
- Underbody rust protection: Coat the chassis and wax the cavities · As soon as possible, then check yearly (BigJimny: do it while the truck is still clean. Don't wait for rust to start.)

### FAQ
Q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
A: Stock is 195/80R15. The BigJimny consensus is that 215/75R15 is the biggest that suits the stock rims, though it's only slightly taller. Some Australian owners squeeze 235/75R15s on, but those exceed the stock rims' recommended limits. With a 2-inch lift, 235/75R15s fit with a little trimming of the front bumper. Go bigger and you'll want lower gearing.

Q: Can I import a new Jimny into the US?
A: No. It isn't certified for US safety or emissions rules, and NHTSA's exemption only covers vehicles 25 years old from their date of manufacture, which puts the earliest JB74s (built from 29 May 2018) at mid-2043. In 2022 CBP seized a 2022 Jimny bought in Mexico and taken to Puerto Rico, and ordered it brought into compliance, exported or destroyed.

Q: What's the difference between the JB64 and JB74?
A: The JB64 is Japan's kei car, with a 658 cc R06A turbo three, no fender flares and a width of 1,475 mm. The JB74 is the 1.5-liter K15B truck with flares and a width of 1,645 mm, sold as the Jimny Sierra in Japan and as the Jimny everywhere else. They share the 2,250 mm wheelbase and the drivetrain layout.

Q: Should I get the 5-door?
A: Unsealed 4X4 thinks the long-wheelbase versions of Suzuki 4x4s have always been 'far superior,' with more stability, better climbing and more room. The XL's 2,590 mm wheelbase drops breakover from 27° to 24°, but rear cargo space with the seats up goes from 85 to 211 liters.

Q: Manual or automatic?
A: Manual, if you can. The automatic is an old four-speed, and Unsealed says the five-speed manual feels like it has an extra 30 kW by comparison. Suzuki Australia rates the manual at 6.4 L/100 km and the auto at 6.9.

Q: How much can it tow and carry?
A: Suzuki Australia rates it at 1,300 kg (2,866 lb) braked and 350 kg (772 lb) unbraked, with a 1,450 kg GVM for the 3-door. Unsealed puts real payload at about 340 kg, which a bull bar and winch eat quickly. Towing anything bigger than a small trailer is 'not the droid you're looking for.'

Q: Why is it so hard to get one?
A: Demand has run ahead of supply since launch. The UK's 2019 allocation sold out by December 2018, Australia had up to a 12-month queue in 2021, and Japan's 5-door Nomade drew about 50,000 orders in four days in 2025, forcing Suzuki to stop taking orders for a year.

Q: Why was it pulled from Europe?
A: CO2. Even the cleanest manual emitted 154 g/km, far above Suzuki's EU fleet target, so the passenger car was withdrawn from the UK in 2020 and replaced by a two-seat commercial version facing a looser 147 g/km target. Wikipedia records that version leaving European sale in 2025.

Q: Does it have lockers?
A: No. Both diffs are open, and 'brake LSD' traction control brakes a spinning wheel to send torque to the others. ARB lists Air Lockers for the 2019-on Jimny if you want the real thing.

Q: Is it safe?
A: Euro NCAP gave the 2018 3-door Jimny three stars, with 73% for adult occupant protection. Standard equipment varies by market and year. Australian cars now have six airbags, AEB and lane-departure warning, and the 2026 Australian 3-door update added adaptive cruise and front and rear parking sensors.

Q: What's 'little G'?
A: Japanese tuner DAMD sells 'little G.' body kits for the Jimny Sierra that restyle it as a miniature G-Class.
